articles.title: As the CW Turns 20, the Once YA-Focused Network Takes a Look at the Road Ahead
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 30, 2026 8:00am PT As the CW Turns 20, the Once YA-Focused Network Takes a Look at the Road Ahead By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Executive Editor franklinavenue Latest Former CW Bosses Dawn Ostroff and Mark Pedowitz Look Back at the Network’s First 20 Years 3 minutes ago As the CW Turns 20, the Once YA-Focused Network Takes a Look at the Road Ahead 33 minutes ago ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live’ Kicks Off Broadcast’s Fall TV Premiere Week as No. 1 Show in Late Night (EXCLUSIVE) 24 hours ago See All The CW/Getty On a recent Saturday night, the CW found itself in an unusual position: Beating ABC and CBS in total viewers. Credit goes to their coverage of college football, as its Aug. 29 broadcast of a surprisingly competitive matchup between Florida State and New Mexico State averaged 2.1 million viewers, making it the most-watched sports broadcast in network history. Granted, the CW has only been in the sports business for three years. But it was a reminder that, as the network marks its 20th anniversary this month, the broadcast network is admittedly in quite a different place than it was even a few years ago. Related Stories Emmys Live Updates 2026 Emmys In Memoriam Excludes Chuck Norris, 'Buffy' Actor Nicholas Brendon and More And that’s by design: Under new owner Nexstar, which took over the CW in 2022, the network has undergone a rather dramatic transformation. While previous co-owners Warner Bros. and CBS utilized the CW as a place to program young adult dramas from its respective studios, Nexstar has aimed to broaden out the CW to focus on low-cost procedural drama acquisitions, repeatable unscripted fare and live sports that it feels better suits its stations’ needs. Popular on Variety Coincidentally, the final scripted holdover from the previous CW ownership, “All American,” wrapped its run with a series finale on Sept. 28. “I always greatly respected what Warner Bros. and CBS were doing with the CW and the brand they built,” says CW president Brad Schwartz . “But it was very clear when we took over that was probably not the type of business that could survive in the future. Our job was to create a network that the local stations can be successful with. “And that meant, how do we disrupt ourselves and move forward from this young adult scripted brand that was built over years and certainly was defined?” he continues. “Broadcast TV continues to be the greatest platform for bringing the most amount of people together simultaneously. And the product that is the best for doing that is sports. And so, if we were going to evolve the network, get the network to profitability, then moving into sports certainly became a very important strategy.” In building CW Sports, the network started with LIV Golf and then brought in Atlantic Coast Conference college football (joined later by deals with the Mountain West and Pac-12 conferences). The CW also has Professional Bowlers Assn. coverage, AVP beach volleyball and has signed a seven-year deal with NASCAR to air its O’Reilly Auto Parts Series, which consists of 33 races annually. According to NASCAR chief media and revenue officer exec vice president Brian Herbst, the O’Reilly series saw a 6% increase in viewership this year on the CW, on top of a 9% bump the previous year. “Every meeting that we had with the CW/Nexstar folks, it seemed like they were going to be aggressive in building out their content and programming plan,” Herbst says. “And one of the anchor properties that they were betting on was NASCAR. We thought the distribution strategy was great in terms of a free-to-air broadcast network across all 120 million-plus TV homes, as well as a marketing strategy at the Nexstar local station group level … We’re super happy with the results for the first couple of years, and we expect continued growth out of it for the balance of the term.” Meanwhile, the CW reunited with the WWE (which was part of the network’s initial 2006 launch with “Smackdown”) in 2024 with “WWE NXT ,” which airs live on Tuesdays. “Brad and his team are always finding fresh, creative ways to engage our core audience and reach new fans, all while staying true to the NXT brand,” says Shawn Michaels, senior VP of talent development creative at WWE. Schwartz says all of that adds up to 700 hours of live sports this year, up from zero just a few years ago. “The old CW used to just program two hours a night, seven nights a week,” he says. “We’re going to do over 1,250 hours of programming this year. Nearly half of that is now live sports.” Nexstar networks president Sean Compton adds that the company has calibrated the CW’s focus “as a program provider for affiliates. Properties like NASCAR, college football, basketball and WWE [pull] significant numbers of viewers to our stations, and that audience flow strengthens the entire local brand of those stations. That’s the outcome that matters to us the most being a company that owns a lot of local TV stations.” On the unscripted front, the CW has invested in repeatable franchises like the cop docuseries “Police 24/7,” as well as game shows like “Scrabble” (hosted by Craig Ferguson) and “Trivial Pursuit” (hosted by LeVar Burton). All three of those shows have been given large episodic orders so that they can be sold into daytime syndication, including on Nexstar stations. “While the syndication market’s gotten very thin, we’ve built those shows for our primetime audiences while complementing the off-net need for our stations, whether it’s daytime or in fringe time slots,” Compton says. “They debuted this fall in syndication with 94% clearance across the U.S. It’s a theme that we’re less reliant on major studios.” As “All American” ends, the CW continues to focus on acquisitions — particularly from Canada — to fill its scripted needs. That includes “Law & Order Toronto: Criminal Intent,” from Lark Prods., Cameron Pictures, Universal Global TV and Citytv; “Wild Cards,” from Blink49 Studios, Front Street Pictures and Piller/Segan, commissioned for CBC; “Sullivan’s Crossing,” from Reel World Management, CTV and Fremantle; and next up, “Private Eyes West Coast,” from Lionsgate Canada, Piller/ Segan and commissioned for Corus Entertainment in Canada. Lionsgate Television Group chair Kevin Beggs notes that Schwartz did something similar at Pop TV, where he programmed Canadian import “Schitt’s Creek,” which went on to be a critical and awards hit. “They all kind of knew at the CW that they have to reshape the model, and we are happy to be a supplier of that model,” Beggs says. “It’s not for every show, but for a really smart, efficiently produced drama or game show, it makes all the sense in the world — if we can figure out how to budget it correctly and keep the quality at a high level, which is really one of Brad’s skills. That’s how you have a small-budgeted show like ‘Schitt’s Creek’ relative for what he was paying, garner multiple Emmys and become the ‘it’ show of the year. It’s the dream. Everyone says, ‘Well, I want that.’ That’s what he’s doing there, and we’re excited to be part of it.” The CW’s new crop of dramas runs a bit more procedural, and skews broader than the young adult fare that most viewers remember from the network’s first 20 years. But Schwartz notes that the legacy of the CW’s YA fare lives on elsewhere, such as Netflix’s “Wednesday” and Prime Video’s “Sterling Point,” “Off Campus” and “The Summer I Turned Pretty.” “Those all are shows that would be classic CW shows,” he says. “But it was just very clear if you were going to build this business forward and make it profitable, that you had to change it.” ‘Reacher’ Spinoff ‘Neagley’ Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery Richard Madden to Star in Hostage Thriller Series ‘Trauma’ for Prime Video UK, Paramount+ (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Bloodaxe’ Season 2 Adds Five to Cast ‘Rose Hill’ Amazon Series Adds Siobhan McGroarty, Sophia Reid-Gantzert, West Mulholland Marta Kauffman Sets Improvised Sitcom ‘DINKS’ at Amazon Starring June Diane Raphael, Paul Scheer (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Sterling Point’ Renewed for Season 2 at Amazon Loading comments...

articles.title: Bradley Whitford on Reuniting With Aaron Sorkin on Broadway and Getting a Star on the Walk of Fame: ‘Feels Like a Time Machine’
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 30, 2026 8:00am PT Bradley Whitford on Reuniting With Aaron Sorkin on Broadway and Getting a Star on the Walk of Fame: ‘Feels Like a Time Machine’ By Carole Horst Plus Icon Carole Horst Latest ‘Gilmore Girls’ Comes to Life as Winter Holiday Event on Warner Bros. Studio Tour Hollywood in December 1 day ago Netflix’s Animated Drama ‘In Waves’ Opens the American French Film Festival, TV Competition Set 6 days ago ‘Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift’ Ride Opens to Thrill Fans at Universal Studios Hollywood 2 weeks ago See All Todd Wiliamson/Disney For Bradley Whitford , being back on Broadway in “A Few Good Men” and reuniting with writer Aaron Sorkin, feels like “a time machine.” When Whitford was cast in the original 1989 Broadway production of “A Few Good Men,” little did he know a friendship and creative collaboration would be born — one that most notably led to the long-running series “The West Wing.” “It was an extraordinary thing, and it’s where I met Aaron. ‘The West Wing’ never would have happened if that hadn’t happened. It’s where we became friends,” Whitford says on a phone call from his New York base, where he’s in rehearsals for the new production of the iconic play. It opens Oct. 8 at Lincoln Center Theater, just about one week after he receives a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame Sept. 30. “West Wing” co-stars Martin Sheen and Dule Hill are scheduled to speak at the ceremony. In the revival, Whitford tackles Col. Jessup, so memorably played by Jack Nicholson in the 1992 film — and even if you’ve never seen the play or film, you know the line that Nicholson yells at Kaffee (Tom Cruise in the film): “You can’t handle the truth!” Since he landed the role, he’s repeatedly been asked about how he’ll say the iconic line. “I woke up and my lovely wife was kind of gazing at me, and she was just like, ‘How are you going to say it? I heard you running lines last night.’ And I’m like, ‘I’m not gonna do it.’ My own wife. This is ridiculous,” he says with a laugh. “I don’t know how I’m gonna do it. I shouldn’t know how I’m gonna do it. She’s like, ‘Do it,’ and I did it, and she was not impressed.” Sorkin was just 26 and Whitford, 30, when they first met. “We were talking about how strange it is because Aaron is like an institution. I’m doing this play where, frankly, it’s much better to be the understudy who surprises you,” he says in a characteristically self-deprecating way. In the original production, he played both Lt. Ross and the understudy for the role of Lt. Kaffee. “It’s much better to be that than the guy with his name on the poster. I can tell you that.” Whitford jokes about not taking acting seriously — “I love acting, I’m just not sure I respect it,” he says — telling a story about how after an L.A. screening of “Get Out,” “people were blown away.” “All these people, like, blowing smoke up my ass, and I’m kind of believing it,” he says. “My kid turns to me and very casually says, ‘No offense, Dad. I’ve seen dogs be good in movies.’ Which is only devastating because it’s true.” But it’s his way of staying grounded. He allows himself this aphorism: “The best way to take the work seriously is to not take yourself seriously doing the work. There are two atmospheres on a set. One is, ‘I hope you don’t fuck this up,’ and the other is, ‘I can’t wait to see what you’re gonna do.’ And now that I am a white-haired senior citizen about to have the star on the Walk of Fame, I know the best way to get to the good work is for the atmosphere to be more like recess than like school.” The three-time Emmy winner’s resume is packed with memorable characters, from “The West Wing,” “Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip,” “The Handmaid’s Tale” and “Transparent” to “Get Out,” “tick… tick… BOOM!,” “Death by Lightning” and, most recently, “The Diplomat.” But that’s just a fraction of his career. And he hopes to do more comedies moving forward, pointing to a short directed by his wife, Amy Landecker, for Funny or Die called “Bradley Whitford: Emotional Stuntman.” “That may be my favorite part ever,” he says, and you believe him. He also loved the work he did with her — and loved working with her — on her 2025 feature debut, the comedy “For Worse.” As for his honor on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, he feels odd. “I always said, there’s no segues in show business. You feel like you’re starting out, and then suddenly you’re Wilford fucking Brimley,” he says with a wry laugh. He thought about his late parents when he first got the Walk of Fame news. “I wish they could be there because they would really get a kick out of that. They certainly didn’t push me into show business, but I have vivid memories of my father’s joy at a high school play, taking a picture. They would really get a kick out of it that I get to spend all eternity with Allison Janney and Lucille Ball, dodging dog doo.” The kid from Wisconsin got hooked on acting in grade school — “I will probably never be better than I was in seventh grade as Teddy in ‘Arsenic and Old Lace,’” he says. “It sounds really corny, but I was like, Oh, my God! When I play a sport, I have to turn off my brain and my heart. When I read a book, I have to turn off my body. When I play an instrument, I have to stand still. But this is everything,” he remembers. “I really had that moment in seventh grade. Like, holy fuck, I need my brain. I need my heart. I need to prepare. I need to let go. And I guess I still enjoy that.” Back to the present, Whitford is thrilled to be reuniting with Sorkin for “A Few Good Men,” and sees the urgent relevancy to today in this 37-year-old play he says is about obeying — and so much more. “It’s not only about obeying illegal orders, it’s about what I think is a really fundamental question going on in the world: What is the best way to survive? Is it through cooperation, or is it through dominance?” he says. “And I see the play as a kind of an argument about that.” Though it raises questions about how we use the law to solve problems and the men in charge of the military, Sorkin’s writing is still infused with hope. Whitford feels that Sorkin is radical in his own way: “It’s kind of radical not to be cynical.” The actor is outspoken about his progressive politics and works closely with many different organizations. “Something I’ve been saying for a long time is — pulling together what a bunch of people have said — despair is a luxury that my children can’t afford, that their future can’t afford, and action is the antidote,” says Whitford. “What I see as the sort of civic virus of this malignant narcissist who has somehow gotten himself elected again, we have to fight our way out of this. We can’t give in to it.” He continues, “I’m actually amazed because I do a lot of stuff with the Democratic Party in my home state of Wisconsin. My fear is always that young people — justifiably — are going to check out, get cynical about the political process and leave that process and sentence themselves to a gulag dictated by the business interests who do participate in the political process. And I haven’t seen that happen. And I’m actually optimistic about how things are going to change politically, but boy, I didn’t see this coming.” He’s also very aware that some want celebrities to shut up about politics. “There’s nothing less democratic than telling people they should shut up. I try not to censor myself. I always feel like I should be doing more,” he says. “Uninformed celebrities spouting their idiotic political views start with the guy in the Oval Office.” Related Stories Never Mind the IP, Here's How Original Ideas Dominated This Year's Emmy Races 'Widow’s Bay' Wins Most Emmys Ever for a Comedy Series in a Year, Breaking 'The Studio’s' Record ‘Reacher’ Renewed for Season 6 Ahead of Season 5 Premiere ‘House of David’ to End With Season 3 at Amazon, Wonder Project Marta Kauffman Sets Improvised Sitcom ‘DINKS’ at Amazon Starring June Diane Raphael, Paul Scheer (EXCLUSIVE) Penn Badgley to Lead ‘Everyone in My Family Has Killed Someone’ Series at Amazon ‘Sterling Point’ Renewed for Season 2 at Amazon Richard Madden to Star in Hostage Thriller Series ‘Trauma’ for Prime Video UK, Paramount+ (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...

articles.title: Pete Davidson Grows Up: On Leaving ‘SNL,’ Famous Exes, the Joys of Fatherhood and Why He’s Keeping His Hillary Clinton Tattoo
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety Say the name “ Pete Davidson ” aloud, and it will conjure a certain image: a man strutting down the street in baggy pants, swarmed by paparazzi, clenching the hand of a screen beauty with a grin on his face. A man who’s dated everyone from Ariana Grande and Margaret Qualley to Kate Beckinsale and Kim Kardashian , who inspired the term “big dick energy” and the earworm “Thank U, Next.” “There should be a group for us,” Davidson jokes of guys like himself and Jake Gyllenhaal who’ve been the subject of breakup anthems. “It’s something that comes up once in a while. But I think Ariana’s fuckin’ cool and immensely talented and an awesome girl. We’re not texting or whatever, but we’re cool.” Related Stories Zendaya Debuts Pixie Cut and Channels '90s Glamour at the Emmys 'Charlie's Angels' Reunion, Zendaya and 'Buffy' Alums Sarah Michelle Gellar, David Boreanaz Among Confirmed Emmys Presenters Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety It’s easy to see why women are drawn to Davidson. In person, he’s imposingly rangy and muscular and shoots you straight — a working-class fella from Staten Island, unlike those posh theater kids running around Hollywood. He’s also possessed of a wounded, underdog quality that invites warmth. You want him to be OK. Davidson’s lothario image has come to overshadow his obvious talent: In 2014, at the age of 20, he became one of the youngest “Saturday Night Live” cast members ever, regaling audiences with his direct-to-camera monologues about his mental health and the travails of living at home with his mom in Staten Island. By 26, he was starring in his own Judd Apatow-helmed biopic, “The King of Staten Island,” which was supposed to be his “Trainwreck” moment, only to have its release derailed by COVID. In the years since, he’s performed stand-up to sold-out theaters alongside pals Jon Stewart and John Mulaney; popped up in films like “Fast X” and “Dumb Money”; created and starred in “Bupkis,” a critically acclaimed TV series based on his life; dated a Kardashian; hosted his own talk show on Netflix; and fathered a child. Now the 32-year-old is making his big return to the silver screen in November’s “How to Rob a Bank,” playing a wounded war veteran who turns to robbing banks to provide for his family. He took the assignment seriously, packing on 15 pounds of muscle for the role. “I got on all the peptides that everyone’s doing. They work ,” he says. Davidson took Sermorelin and BPC-157 while training around the clock and consuming loads of protein. “I just think it’s really important for people to know that that’s what I did. When someone says, ‘Whoa, you’re in tremendous shape!’ and an actor goes, ‘Yup! Just broccoli, rice and chicken!,’ it’s like, ‘No, dude, you have a fuckin’ vein going from your forehead to your thumb.’” “How to Rob a Bank” is his most dramatic role yet, and he steals every scene he’s in. So are people finally ready to take Davidson seriously? Directed by David Leitch (“Bullet Train”) and hitting theaters Nov. 13, “How to Rob a Bank” is a hyperkinetic action film that follows a group of 20-somethings (led by Nicholas Hoult) who’ve been screwed by the system and turn to bank robbery as payback, livestreaming their heists on social media in the hope of igniting a movement. Davidson plays Vince, Hoult’s second in command and a veteran of the war in Afghanistan whose lungs have been ravaged by exposure to burn pits. “What Pete is doing in this movie isn’t something he’s put on. It’s him ,” says Leitch. “Pete, in real life, is one of the warmest, most engaging people I’ve ever worked with. Disarming. People feel safe around him in about 10 seconds.” Knowing his days are numbered, Vince robs banks to provide for his wife and young child. The film’s most heartbreaking scene sees Davidson’s character singing to his daughter over the phone before a deadly shootout ensues, and the actor nails it. No wonder: Right before filming, Davidson discovered he and his then-partner, Elsie Hewitt, were expecting a daughter. “Once I got in the room [with the young actress], I got really choked up. It really fucked me up.” His voice begins to crack. “What happens to the character is adjacent to what happened to me with my dad” — a firefighter who died in the line of duty on 9/11, when Davidson was 7 — “and the age and all that. … I’m a comic first, so I never understood when actors would be like, ‘It was very painful.’ But it is . It was very tough, and the first time I felt like a real actor because I wasn’t just playing myself.” The first time Davidson played himself was supposed to be his splashy movie-star debut. He’d received plaudits for his turn in the Sundance dramedy “Big Time Adolescence,” but “The King of Staten Island” was an Apatow movie dropping at South by Southwest — or at least that was the plan. It was March 2020, and the festival was canceled due to COVID. With theaters around the country shuttered, the movie was released digitally that June. Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety Davidson’s first thought was “I hope the world is OK.” Then came the intrusive ones. “It definitely helped me believe my self-fulfilling prophecy that I am doomed,” he recalls. The film was a particularly personal one for Davidson. In a story based on his Staten Island upbringing, the comic plays Scott, a 24-year-old high school dropout grappling with the loss of his firefighter father, who died in a blaze when Scott was 7. Scott (named for Davidson’s father) suffers from Crohn’s disease, PTSD and depression — just like Davidson. “I wanted to make ‘The King of Staten Island’ because I was interested in exploring the sacrifice Pete’s father made for others and how it affected Pete and his family,” explains Apatow. “Pete has always been able to find comedy in the most challenging subject matter. He is fearless, never censors his truth and is always willing to show you everything.” Bill Burr, whom he tapped to play his mother’s boyfriend in the film, lauded Davidson’s leadership on set: “He was considerate about everybody else’s time. And as the star, he could’ve requested to be shot out of scenes, and instead, he chose to have his fellow actors wrapped before him. It was a level of maturity and consideration that you don’t see a lot in any business.” It was in the summer of 2023, after the release of “Bupkis,” an autobiographical series on Peacock starring Davidson as himself, that Davidson says he reached rock bottom. He was one year removed from “Saturday Night Live,” which had given him much-needed structure, with no projects on the horizon. “Playing yourself and constantly living in your own crap” had forced him to revisit a number of harrowing moments in his life, so he used drugs to numb the pain. “It was K. I was getting liquid and cooking it,” he says. “And I would do acid and shrooms and whippets and smoke weed all day and eat pills every day. It got scary because I didn’t feel high. I felt high when I wasn’t doing it, so I was like, this is a huge problem.” An emotional FaceTime call with his mother, Amy, convinced him to get clean. “She told me her biggest fear was waking up one day to see on the news that something bad had happened to me,” recalls Davidson. “I reached a point where I couldn’t do that to her anymore.” Davidson checked himself into rehab and, even though Peacock had renewed “Bupkis” for a second season, walked away from the show. He was tired of playing himself, tired of turning his trauma into content. He wanted more for his career. He wanted, more than anything, to be taken seriously. “I was part of the problem of what I hated the most, which was the invasiveness around my personal life. I was just lobbing it up and continuing the narrative,” admits Davidson. He’d gone to rehab plenty of times to placate other people, but never because he really wanted to get clean. “When I turned 30 and I was there, it was a real low point. Nothing much was going on with my career and I was like, ‘This fuckin’ sucks. I can’t do it anymore.’ And it can’t be for anyone or for a job. You really have to want it, and when you’re done, you’re done.” Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety He says he’s sober now, save around “four beers a year.” “I don’t fuck with drugs anymore. It’s been two or three years from doing really hard stuff and about a year or more from weed. Weirdly, the hardest thing to stop was weed,” he says. “And now it’s easy because I have a kid. Anytime there’s ever a thought, I look at my phone background and go, ‘Oh yeah, no.’” On top of kicking drugs, Davidson is in the process of getting most of his nearly 200 tattoos removed. “One, they were fuckin’ horrible,” he cracks. “Two, it was a business decision. I hated coming into the makeup trailer three hours early to spray-paint over horrible fuckin’ tattoos. And third, I was like, ‘I’m not this dude.’ I got these when I was in an immense amount of pain and I was trying to show people my pain.” Davidson has struggled with self-harm. “I used to cut, so some of [the tattoos] covered up the cuts,” he says. He will be keeping a few, though, including the one of Hillary Clinton in a power suit on his right leg: “She stays. That’s my dog. I love Hillary, man. She’s awesome and a good friend.” As I wait for our interview to begin, Davidson is pacing the hotel room. We are moments away from capturing the cover photo — the comedian standing tall and triumphant atop lower Manhattan — and he’s adorned in a striped tracksuit and big dark sunglasses, the latter a remedy for the concussion he suffered days earlier shooting the film “Tommy Karate.” But Davidson seems with it — or is doing a really good job of acting like it. His head isn’t the thing bothering him at the moment. It is Sept. 9, one day before “NYC Still Rising After 25 Years,” a comedy benefit for 9/11 charities at Madison Square Garden organized by Davidson and Stewart and featuring an all-star roster of stand-up comics. Two of Davidson’s pals have bailed at the last minute. He removes his sunglasses and turns to his team. “Why the fuck would they do that?” he says. They shrug their shoulders. Then his phone rings. It isn’t another comedian dropping out of the event, but his ex, Hewitt. He answers and sees their 9-month-old daughter, Scottie, staring back at him. “Hello, sweetie!” he exclaims, beaming from ear to ear. “ Beebeebooboo, ” he coos while taking their FaceTime session to a back room and closing the door behind him. One minute passes. Then two. Then three. A crowd has formed in the room — publicists, assistants, photo editors — waiting on Davidson. We are now running behind schedule. Will he ever emerge? Ten minutes later, the door swings open, and it is as though all his troubles have washed away. Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety “Scottie is my whole life,” Davidson says of his baby girl, who’s named after Davidson’s dad. “I was living or dying on this business and what I thought people thought of me. It was all validation and ‘If I do this, then I’ll do that.’ But as soon as I saw her for the first time, I was like, ‘Oh my God, none of this fuckin’ matters at all . It’s a job. If I get to do cool stuff, great; if not, cool, I get to be home more with my kid.’” This time of year is always tough for Davidson. The loss of his father at such a young age left him with severe PTSD and crippling bouts of depression, which he manages to this day. “It’s tough going to firehouses where a lot of the guys knew my dad. It’s just a lot,” he says. “I got kind of used to it, but this year is different because of my kid. And I’ll be my dad’s age [when he died] in two months. Now I just understand it a little differently.” He pauses. “I understand it more from my mom’s side. That would be like my daughter’s mom not having me around and having to do it alone. My mom did that and never fuckin’ complained once. I look at that like, ‘Holy shit. My mom is the best. How fuckin’ lucky am I?’” There is also “the peanut gallery,” as he calls them — the army of online haters who’ve spent years scolding him for telling the occasional 9/11 joke as a way to cope with his grief. “For a while it bothered me when I would get, ‘Oh, why is he talking about 9/11 and his dad and all this stuff?’ from weird people on the internet, like it was all I talked about. I’ve made maybe five jokes about it in my specials over a span of 16 years, and then every 9/11 I try and do a benefit to help out. So I have my blinders on and do whatever I feel is necessary to do.” I ask Davidson about a recent tale told by President Trump at a 9/11 anniversary event involving a pair of firefighters lifting him from the rubble near ground zero mere moments after the attacks. (Records and eyewitness accounts show he was miles away at Trump Tower.) “Nothing that guy says is surprising anymore,” Davidson laments. “It’s sad that it’s to the point where it’s so ridiculous that you’re like, ‘Yeah, whatever. ’ He’s the drunk uncle, but he has the keys to the nukes. That’s the problem. If he didn’t have those keys, you’d be like, ‘Oh, that’s just the silly drunk uncle. He’s old.’ That’s unfortunate that he said that, though, because that’s definitely not what happened.” As a teenager, Davidson would sit in the back of the bus and write jokes on his way to and from basketball games and try them on his teammates. They eventually goaded a 16-year-old Davidson to enter an open mic night called “Wacky Wednesdays” at The Looney Bin, a Staten Island comedy club tucked inside a bowling alley. “There were four people there, it went good enough, and I really loved it and got addicted to the laughs,” he remembers. “Growing up not having many friends and having a moment where you’re talking and everyone’s listening was very attractive to me.” His first TV performance came on the VH1 reality series “Mob Wives.” Set in Staten Island, the show followed a number of women whose husbands were jailed for mob-related activities. Davidson was 18 and working as a chauffeur in real life, driving a guy around Staten Island. “I had to drive him to a party, and something happened where there was a fight, and he ran back into the car with his suit ripped in half,” Davidson says laughing. “I drove the getaway car. That’s my first TV gig ever.” Then Davidson joined “ SNL .” He got the gig thanks in large part to Bill Hader, who acted with the young comedian in “Trainwreck.” “He was in one scene in the movie, and I thought he was funny, so I texted Lorne [Michaels] and sent him a video of Pete’s stand-up. He obviously loved it,” Hader recalls, adding, “He didn’t need much advice. He was self-possessed and eager to show his stuff.” Davidson says it took him a while to settle into “SNL”: “I wanted to leave after my first year and asked Lorne to leave every year. I was like, ‘I don’t fuckin’ work in this! And I just tell my stand-up on ‘Update’ and then burn it and can’t do it on the road, and I just want to do stand-up,’ and he’d always be like, ‘You’ll figure it out after four years.’ And he was right.” Davidson found his footing with the character Chad, a monosyllabic stoner who navigates intense situations with apathy, and the memorable Please Don’t Destroy sketch “Three Sad Virgins” with Taylor Swift. He decided to walk away from “SNL” in 2022. “After eight years, it was just time. I just happened to be 28 when I left, so it was a little weird, but Lorne was cool with it. I love Lorne. He’s my Yoda. I love him very much, and I’m grateful that we’re still pals.” It was on “SNL” that Davidson met Kim Kardashian. The two shared a kiss as Aladdin and Jasmine in an October 2021 sketch and began dating shortly thereafter. Davidson was thrust into a reality-TV world of prying paparazzi and untold media scrutiny. “I’m one of the survivors — the few and the proud. We’re like the Marines,” he jokes of men who’ve dated Kardashians. “Look, man, that’s a really tough atmosphere if you’re not game. One of the things I love about Kim and that whole family is they’re like, ‘This is what we do.’ I found that very attractive and mature. “And I was never subjected to anything I didn’t want to be a part of. She was super respectful of all of it, but the craze of that lifestyle — being followed everywhere, having security and looking over your shoulder — for a guy with mental stuff, and at the time drug problems, was a little too much for me. But we’re cool, and I have a lot of love for her, and I knew what I was getting into.” Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety The one thing he couldn’t predict was the wrath of her ex, Kanye West . Kardashian was still in the process of divorcing West when she began dating Davidson, and the rapper took it upon himself to make Davidson’s life a living hell, posting threats on Instagram and, in the music video for his song “Eazy,” depicting a Claymation Davidson getting kidnapped and beheaded. “What tripped me out is I was super open about mental stuff — everyone knows this about me — and it’s like he was [saying], ‘Kill yourself.’ And he did push me.” As for whether Davidson, who’s half-Jewish, thinks he’s the reason why West started going on antisemitic rants, he chuckles. “What people don’t understand about that dude — and I’m not one-one-millionth as talented or influential or powerful as that dude, but I have dealt with a fraction of what he’s had to deal with public-wise — is that’ll do it. He’s also lost a parent and has mental stuff, and I don’t know how he deals with it or who he has around him. Probably a lot of people who want to be his friend. I’ve had that. When people are so far up your ass and constantly pushing and provoking you and not showing you love, you want to burn it all. I think it got to a certain point where he was like, ‘Leave me the fuck alone. I’m just going to say crazy shit.’ There’s zero way he really feels like that.” Davidson jokes he did Kardashian a service by absorbing West’s attacks. “I like to think I got that one out of the way for her because whoever that guy was going to be was gonna get it,” he remarks. “I cleared the path for her to get back into the dating pool.” As someone who deals with an immense amount of scrutiny regarding his own appearance, Davidson is pained to see the vitriol another ex, Grande, has been subjected to of late. “I don’t like it at all. It’s not cool. She’s a really strong person — I’ve witnessed it — and I don’t understand it. She knows how to handle this stuff though. She’s been around. So she’ll be OK, but I think it’s fucked up.” The most frustrating thing for Davidson when it comes to his dating life — and the media’s fixation on it — is the amount he feels it’s detracted from his career, reinforcing the idea that he’s unserious, girl-crazy tabloid fodder. “It’s been over a decade. My work and my relevance is super overlooked, and it’s confusing to me,” he declares, suddenly working himself into a lather. We’ve struck a nerve. “I’m still only 32, but I have really crazy credits: nearly a decade at ‘SNL’; I hosted a year after I left; I worked with Gillespie and Gunn and Liman and Leitch and Judd and Edie and Pesci.” (Craig Gillespie, James Gunn and Doug Liman directed Davidson in, respectively, “Dumb Money,” “The Suicide Squad” and the forthcoming “Bitcoin.”) Davidson’s voice is getting louder as he runs through his self-defense. “What the fuck do I have to do? And look, I get it — I’ve dated a lot of people. But so has everyone else! Everyone is fucking everyone in this business! Everyone! And for some reason it’s zeroed in on me, and I can’t feel sorry for myself because I put myself in those situations, but everyone else is doing it. I was in my 20s. Am I not supposed to fuck around and do drugs and have fun and be in Hollywood like everybody else? Sorry, everyone!” If “How to Rob a Bank” is evidence that Davidson can nail a dramatic role, then “Tommy Karate” is the film he believes will really change people’s perception of him as an actor. Directed by Justin Chon from a screenplay Davidson wrote during his rehab stint in 2023, the film centers on Thomas Pitera, aka “Tommy Karate” — a real-life hit man for New York’s Bonanno crime family who is suspected of murdering 60 people. Pitera is tracked down by DEA agent Jim Hunt (Paul Walter Hauser), with Camila Mendes, Simon Rex and Gina Gershon joining in on the fun. When Davidson sent the script around town, it received plenty of positive feedback, except for the idea that Davidson would portray Pitera. “They were like, ‘Pete Davidson? Fuck him, ’” he recalls. “And I was like, ‘OK, I’m pretty used to it.’” He spent years shopping it around and considered letting someone else take on the role until a Zoom chat with Sylvester Stallone convinced him otherwise. Davidson contacted Stallone because he was trying to remake his favorite Stallone movie, the 1981 cop thriller “Nighthawks.” “He said something that really fucked me up,” Davidson recalls. “He goes, ‘I’ve seen some of your work. I think you could be a really good actor, but no one’s ever going to write a part for you that’s good. You have to write it yourself, and you have to take it.’ I was like, ‘Rocky is telling me to make “Rocky.”‘” Pete Davidson in “How to Rob a Bank” Megan Schoenbachler Davidson just wrapped principal photography on “Tommy Karate,” but photos from the Atlanta set depicting him in a clumsy wig and icy blue contacts leaked online, leading to more sniping at his expense. “I wish my fuckin’ wig was set, and I wasn’t eating in my photos. I promise you it doesn’t look like that in the movie,” he says. “If ‘Tommy Karate’ is not my coming-out party, then I have zero pulse on this business at all. I think people are going to be really surprised and be like, ‘What the fuck.’ And I’m not online, but I see what people are saying. It’s all negative. It’s so in the toilet and the bar is so low that it makes me even more excited. I hope more people trash it before it comes out because they really have no fuckin’ idea what we did. We’re really proud of it.” “Tommy Karate” is expected to hit theaters in fall 2027 after making the festival rounds. Davidson also has wrapped “Wizards!,” a stoner comedy from David Michôd, and “Bitcoin,” a thriller about the cryptocurrency and its mysterious founder, Satoshi Nakamoto. He’s happy to be back in New York City, the place he’s called home his whole life. “You can have the absolute worst day of your life in public here, and nobody blinks. Everyone minds their own business because they’ve got somewhere to be,” he says. But he’s mostly excited about spending time with Scottie, pushing her stroller around their Brooklyn neighborhood and trying to make her laugh. “It’s a lot of trial and error and a lot of bombing. If you think I bombed on ‘SNL,’ you should see me with my fuckin’ daughter.” Whenever he talks about Scottie, Davidson lights up. He is adamant that he’s doing a lot better, and Scottie is the reason. “It’s filling a lot of emptiness. If you think the internet’s sick of Pete Davidson, I’m sick of it. I’m exhausted from being me all the time . That it’s all about her first is the best gift ever. It’s an indescribable feeling.” He smiles. “It’s the best, man. articles.title: Billy Joel Gives Health Update After Brain Surgery: ‘I’m OK — It Sounds a Lot Worse Than It Actually Is’
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 30, 2026 8:12am PT Billy Joel Gives Health Update After Brain Surgery: ‘I’m OK — It Sounds a Lot Worse Than It Actually Is’ By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Billy Joel Gives Health Update After Brain Surgery: ‘I’m OK — It Sounds a Lot Worse Than It Actually Is’ 34 minutes ago LCD Soundsystem Announces 2026 NYC Residency — Including 100th Residency Show 1 hour ago Music Industry Moves: Universal Music Names Libby Bush President of Global Brands and Commercial Partnerships; Avex Acquires 85% of Brandon Silverstein’s S10 Entertainment 18 hours ago See All Michael Buckner/Variety/REX/Shutterstock Billy Joel gave a health update during a call-in with fans on his SiriusXM channel this week, noting that he’s doing well after revealing earlier in September that he’d undergone brain surgery to relieve some of the symptoms of normal pressure hydrocephalus, a disorder he was diagnosed with in 2025. “I know people are worried about me because they read that I have a brain disorder, which sounds a lot worse than it actually is,” he told callers. “I’m okay. My balance isn’t that good. Lost a little bit of my hearing, but that may have to do with my age, too, and the rock and roll life and the loud volume probably didn’t help. But I’m fine. I want people to not have to worry about me. I’m okay. And I appreciate your call.” Popular on Variety Related Stories 'The Wire' and 'It' Actor James Ransone Was Excluded From Emmys and Oscars In Memoriam Tributes; His Wife Says 'It's Simply Not Right' How 'The Pitt' Star Isa Briones Achieved Her Greek Goddess Glam at the 2026 Emmys The caller had originally asked about the inspiration for Joel’s 1973 song “Captain Jack,” which is clearly about a drug dealer. “I was living in Oyster Bay, Long Island, across from a public housing area,” Joel recalled. “And I was watching kids from the suburbs scoring drugs from this place. And it seemed odd to me that kids from the suburbs were doing that. It was just kind of a foreign thing to me. I call it a look out the window song. I was just basically in my own apartment looking out the window seeing people coming and going from this drug dealer. It was across the street. And I had his idea for a bassline, it’s a little bit symphonic of a theme and I always wanted to do something with that and the subject of the song seemed to fit with that particular team and that’s how it got written.” The 77-year-old musician revealed in May 2025 that he had been diagnosed with normal pressure hydrocephalus, in which cerebrospinal fluid builds up inside the skull and presses on the brain. He canceled several concerts and said he had been told not to perform until he recovered. Though he returned in January of this year to perform two songs with a tribute band, he said on Sirius that in general his doctors have asked him not to undergo too much stress. articles.title: Former CW Bosses Dawn Ostroff and Mark Pedowitz Look Back at the Network’s First 20 Years
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 30, 2026 8:30am PT Former CW Bosses Dawn Ostroff and Mark Pedowitz Look Back at the Network’s First 20 Years By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Executive Editor franklinavenue Latest As the CW Turns 20, the Once YA-Focused Network Takes a Look at the Road Ahead 30 minutes ago ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live’ Kicks Off Broadcast’s Fall TV Premiere Week as No. 1 Show in Late Night (EXCLUSIVE) 24 hours ago CBS and MTV VMAs Attract a Combined 8.4 Million Viewers, Making it the Most-Watched Since 2015 and Up 51% From Last Year 2 days ago See All Katie Yu / Cate Cameron / Dean Buscher When Warner Bros. and CBS announced the merger of the WB and UPN on the morning of Jan. 24, 2006, the industry was shocked. There had been no rumblings that it might happen, as the two sides behind the deal somehow managed to keep it a secret. “Even then there weren’t many surprises that you could really pull off,” says Dawn Ostroff , who was president of UPN, and after the merger, became the CW ’s entertainment president. “Nobody expected it. Those two networks had been competitors for 10 years, going after the same audience and had really been at each other’s throat. People were astonished!” Related Stories Emmy Producers on Recruiting Taylor Swift, the Ideas She Brought to the Show and How This Year’s Telecast Wound Up Short ‘Charlie’s Angels’ Star Jaclyn Smith on the Emmys Reunion, ‘Snobbism’ Against the Series and Why the Latest Movie Reboot 'Didn't Work' Now, the CW has hit its 20th anniversary — living twice as long as its predecessors. And although the network has evolved under its new Nexstar ownership, for most of those first two decades the CW was known as the home for young adult-oriented series, including “Supernatural,” “Gossip Girl,” “The Vampire Diaries,” “Arrow,” “The Flash,” “One Tree Hill,” “Riverdale,” “Jane the Virgin,” “Crazy Ex-Girlfriend” and “All American” — which just wrapped as the final drama from that two-decade era. Popular on Variety “The CW was always a place where you knew that the people loved the stories they were telling, and loved the shows that they were putting up there,” says Greg Berlanti , who had as many as nine series on the air simultaneously on the network, including massive hits “Arrow” and “The Flash.” “I think we’ll talk about those years at the CW as being a bit of a magical time in this art form.” Ostroff oversaw the birth of the CW, starting with making the difficult decisions of which shows from the WB and UPN to carry over and which ones would have to be canceled. That first year was difficult, Ostroff recalls, as no one understood what “CW” meant (it was the first initials of CBS and Warner Bros., but everyone thought it was “Country/Western,” she recalls). “Here we were, having to formulate a new network that combined those two companies, figuring out a new culture and creating something that everybody would feel a part of. It was a real challenge,” she says. That included audience confusion, as viewers weren’t sure where to find their favorite WB and UPN shows anymore. In some markets, the WB affiliate became the CW, and in other cities, it was the local UPN station that made the transition. “People say, ‘You started at ground zero,’ but I always say, ‘We started about 100 feet below ground zero!’” Ostroff says. “Because between everyone not knowing what CW was and everyone trying to find their favorite shows on different channels, it was just mass chaos.” But then came “Gossip Girl,” which became one of the first homegrown CW success stories. The series made waves starting with its marketing campaign, which promoted the show with the phrase “OMFG” on billboards and in TV spots. “The Vampire Diaries” became a phenom as well — including a Season 4 premiere poster that suggested a ménage à trois between the main characters. “We just made a lot of noise and finally figured out like how we were going to let people know what the CW was,” Ostroff says. Ostroff left in 2011, and Mark Pedowitz took over as the CW president. He familiarized himself with the network’s series by watching every episode, reading every script and then flying across North America to visit producers and talent on sets and over dinners. “We were small enough to do that, and other platforms weren’t really doing that,” he says. “The first show we went up to see was ‘Supernatural.’ And then we just started booking trips wherever they were shooting, whether it be Albuquerque, Toronto, New Orleans, Atlanta. It created a connection.” A year after Pedowitz joined, the CW launched “Arrow” — which would soon turn into a sprawling franchise with “The Flash,” “Supergirl,” “DC’s Legends of Tomorrow,” “Black Lightning” and “Batwoman,” all from Berlanti and Warner Bros. TV. Greg Berlanti with his “Arrowverse” stars Grant Gustin, Melissa Benoist, Caity Lotz and Stephen Amell in 2016. FilmMagic “It allowed us to broaden out from a demographic point of view,” Pedowitz says. “We never lost the roots of who we were, with ‘The Vampire Diaries’ and the rest But [the “Arrowverse”] was huge because it said that our programming, despite whatever limitations we might had had, was as good as anybody else’s.” And although Emmy recognition remained elusive — a sore subject for Pedowitz, who’s still fired up about that snub — shows like “Jane the Virgin” and “Crazy Ex-Girlfriend,” both from CBS Studios, became critical faves and earned big Golden Globes wins. Neither show were ratings hits, but Pedowitz remembers being asked at the time why he kept both shows on the air: “I said, ‘I really like them and I can keep them on the air.’ And we did,” he says. “By the way, ‘Jane the Virgin’ worked extraordinarily well in streaming for us at the CW as well as for Netflix. ‘Crazy Ex-Girlfriend’ was very much a cult following, but it was so different, and no one’s really accomplished what [co-creator and star] Rachel Bloom did since then.” There’s a few that got away: “The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina” wound up at Netflix, and Pedowitz regrets not ordering the pilot “Haunted” to series. Plus, he now believes, “There was much more life left in ‘The Vampire Diaries’ universe.” Yet, the CW was able to survive and thrive thanks to its output deal with Netflix, which started in 2011 and allowed the network to become profitable through licensing. “We created a vibrant business,” Pedowitz says. “And we had the programming to make it vibrant.” That deal ended in 2019, as both CBS and Warner Bros. launched their own streaming services — and by 2022, both companies decided it was time to sell the CW to key affiliate partner Nexstar. Pedowitz looks back at his nearly 12 years running the CW with great memories. “It was the people. As the leader, you try to move it in the direction of the culture that you want to lead in,” he says. “But it’s all depending on the people. They create the culture.” And for 20 years, the CW viewers have agreed. Discovery — in a senior role, according to two industry sources. Earlier in his career, Kreiz co-founded and was chairman and CEO of Fox Kids Europe. articles.title: ‘Final Payment’, ‘Congo Boy’ Win Top Awards At Pingyao International Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz ‘Final Payment’, ‘Congo Boy’ Win Top Awards At Pingyao International Film Festival Iran’s Mohammad Rasoulof & Japanese-Korean Filmmaker Mipo O To Receive Kurosawa Akira Award At Tokyo Film Festival ‘The Assassin(s)’ Tops Korea’s Chuseok Holiday Box Office With 1.5 Million Admissions View All September 29, 2026 8:56pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Closing ceremony of Pingyao International Film Festival 2026 PYIFF Chinese director Niu Niu’s Final Payment scooped the Best Film Award in the Fei Mu Awards of this year’s Pingyao International Film Festival (PYIFF), while Rafiki Fariala’s Congo Boy won Best Film in the festival’s Roberto Rossellini Awards. Final Payment , which also won Best Actor for Niu Jianrong’s performance, revolves around a homeowner clashing with a contractor over the final payment following a set of renovations on his home. PYIFF’s competition jury stated: “Tearing through a very small rip, the film leads us into a reality and emotional landscape so expansive, where we sigh, lament, and reflect. The director’s approach is concise, unpretentious, and masterful, earning the wholehearted recognition of the entire jury.” Related Stories News Pingyao Film Festival Unveils 10th Edition Line-up; 'Spring In A Small Town' Set As Opening Film News Cannes Un Certain Regard Winners: Sandra Wollner's 'Everytime' Takes Top Prize The Best Film award came with a cash prize of $150,000 (RMB1m) with half given to the director for the development of their next film, and half given to the distributor in China. Niu Niu previously directed Mr Junjun , which was awarded with the Jury Award and Youth Jury Award at PYIFF in 2023. Watch on Deadline Also in the Fei Mu Awards, Xu Zao won Best Director for Light Pillar , while Best Actress went to Sun Yi for Wang Xiaozhen’s A Joke . The Jury Award was presented to Dong Jie’s Zoom In, Zoom Out , which had its world premiere in Venice Critics Week, while a special mention went to Cai Chengjie’s Suzhou Quarte t. The Fei Mu awards are focused on the festival’s Hidden Dragons section, which selects first, second and third films from emerging directors making Chinese-language films, while the Roberto Rossellini Awards focus on the Crouching Tigers section for emerging international directors. Congo Boy, which took Best Film in the Roberto Rossellini Awards, also won Best Actor when it premiered in Un Certain Regard at this year’s Cannes film festival. The PYIFF award came with a cash prize of $20,000, with half given to the director for the development of their next film, and half given to the distributor in China. The PYIFF jury stated: “The Jury unanimously has been moved by this autobiographical story, told in a simple style that echoes the great tradition of neorealism. For a film focusing on a character that confronts his world with optimism despite dark times and takes on his shoulders the destiny of his entire family.” Also in this section, the Philippines’ Rafael Manuel won Best Director for Filipiñan a, while the Jury Award went to Ben’imana , directed by Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo, which won the Camera d’Or at this year’s Cannes. The PYIFF jury also awarded Rakan Mayasi’s Yesterday The Eye Didn’t Sleep a Special Mention. Hong Kong filmmaker Ann Hui received the Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon East-West Award, shortly before she receives the Camellia Award at Busan International Film Festival next week. Pingyao’s International Contribution To Chinese Cinema Award went to Marco Müller, who founded the festival with Chinese auteur Jia Zhangke and currently serves as Artistic Director of the Film Art Research Centre at Shanghai University, and veteran producer, director and former chairman of China Film Group Han Sanping. Hello Group chairman Tang Yan was presented with a 10th Anniversary Award. This year’s PYIFF opened on September 24 with a screening of the 4K restoration of Fei Mu’s Spring In A Small Town ; closed with Good Trip , co-directed by Hong Kong filmmakers Norris Wong and Hoi Wong, and also screened Jia’s short film Torino Shadow , which premiered at this year’s Cannes. articles.title: ‘Ted Lasso’ Pays Tribute To Anthony Head – Here’s Why It Happened In Episode 409
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Ted Lasso’ Pays Tribute To Anthony Head – Here’s Why It Happened In Episode 409 Cindy Holland Leaving Paramount Ahead Of WBD Merger ‘Spider-Man’ Sony Universe TV Series Based On Clone Saga Marvel Comics Storyline Nears Amazon Green Light View All September 30, 2026 12:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Anthony Head in "Ted Lasso" Apple TV+. SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Episodes 408 and 409 of Apple TV’s Ted Lasso . A very emotional Ted Lasso episode that included the death of a beloved original character, The Crown & Anchor pub owner Mae Green, played by Annette Badland, also acknowledged the death of the series’ popular recurring cast member Anthony Head , who played the villainous Rupert Mannion in the first three seasons. A card, In Memory of Anthony Head, ran at the end of Season 4’s penultimate episode, “Mae Rides the Bus.” (You can see it below.) Related Stories News Anthony Head Dies: ‘Ted Lasso’ & ‘Buffy The Vampire Slayer’ Actor Was 72 News ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Shocker: Actor Reflects On Death Of OG Character Who “Went In The Very Best Way” “He was a beautiful man, and he will be much missed,” Badland told Deadline during an interview about Mae’s shocking death , reminiscing about famous Season 1 darts scene between Rupert and Jason Sudeikis’ Ted Lasso at Mae’s pub. “He was charming and funny and generous, and we’d have naughty little sort of asides. Ted Lasso was always expected to pay tribute to the veteran British actor who died on June 1 at the age of 72 . When that was not done in the Season 4 premiere, many thought that Head would be honored in an episode he appears in as the season had wrapped production in January, months before his passing. “I assumed he would be in this last [season], and didn’t know, as I think very few people knew, he was ill and just couldn’t do it,” Badland said. Barely referenced in the first seven episodes, Head’s Rupert, ex-owner of AFC Richmond and ex-husband of the club’s current owner Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), came back into the forefront in Episode 8, when Higgins (Jeremy Swift), with the help of Mae and her “Follow the anger” advice, deducted that Rupert had been secretly buying shares to regain control of Richmond. That remained a story thread in Episode 9 until the surprise twist at the end that revealed it was not Rupert but Tracey Ullman’s Zelda Southport who was behind the shady operation and on the verge of becoming a majority owner of the club. The move raised questions whether Ted Lasso had pivoted from Rupert to Zelda as the culprit — and away from a potential Rebecca vs. Rupert battle for control of Richmond — in light of Head’s death (or leading into it). According to sources, no Season 4 storylines were changed following Head’s passing, there had been no formal plans for Head to be in Season 4 and no official approach to him about appearing. It is unclear whether that was related to Head’s health issues which had been kept private. (His cause of death was listed by his daughters as complications due to pneumonia.) Head’s last acting credits were Season 3 of Ted Lasso, which came out in 2023, and the 2024 Prime Video movie Upgraded. It is a longstanding TV tradition for characters to mirror the death of the actors who played them by passing away in the show. Because of the timing of Head’s passing after Season 4 had been completed, that will likely happen in Season 5, which has not been picked up yet but is looking good. ‘Ted Lasso’s Rupert-Zelda Switch The eccentric ultra-wealthy entrepreneur and sports investor Zelda — a polarizing and largely disliked new character introduced in Season 4 — had long been suspected by fans to be the season’s secret villain. Zelda, who had become involved in Richmond’s women’s team with Keeley’s (Juno Temple) enthusiastic support over Rebecca’s serious reservations, was present when Higgins told Rebecca in Season 8 that Rupert was behind the buyouts. In fact, Zelda looked rather nervous for a moment when Higgins announced that he had solved the mystery before he dropped Rupert’s name and she chimed in with “Never underestimate the power of anger as fuel.” (We will likely find out more about her motives in the Season 4 finale.) In Episode 9, Zelda also happened to be there any time Higgins and Rebecca discussed the matter. That included him telling his boss in the office that Rupert’s lawyers were “denying knowing anything about people selling shares but since there has been a pause in buying” and that Rebecca won’t lose control of the club regardless, as long as the Milk sisters, who no one had been able to get ahold of, don’t sell their shares. The three also were together on board the Richmond private jet when Higgins told Rebecca that even without the Milk sisters, the mystery buyer they believed to be Rupert can get 49% of the shares. That may prove a moot point as Zelda was later seen giving her henchman, who had located the sisters, instructions to go as high as needed to secure their shares. With the mystery solved, the producers felt it made sense to run an end card honoring Head in Season 9. Rupert had his Season 4 moment in 408 and 409, so paying tribute to Head following the close of his character’s two-episode arc felt most appropriate. (Running the card at the end of Episode 8 likely also would’ve spoiled the surprise that it wasn’t Rupert who was buying the shares.) Head recurred on the first two seasons of Ted Lasso, becoming a series regular in Season 3. His character Rupert, Rebecca’s vindictive and philandering former husband who lost Richmond to her in the divorce, was the original three-season installment’s main antagonist. He subsequently bought another Premiere League team — West Ham United — and recruited Ted’s kitman turned assistant coach Nathan Shelley (Nick Mohammed) to work with him, before losing it in the Season 3 finale. “We will miss him, I respect him, and it’s a great honor to be in the episode that is dedicated to him,” Badland said. Here is a video of her comments. articles.title: ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Shocker: Actor Reflects On Death Of OG Character Who “Went In The Very Best Way”

The title of the second-to-last episode of Ted Lasso Season 4 hints at a goodbye to a beloved character who has been around since the first season. Episode 9 bids farewell to Richmond’s own Mae Green ( Annette Badland ) who dies doing what she loves: supporting the Lady Greyhounds at their away match against Bristol City in the stands. Related Stories News All The Songs In ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 So Far News ‘Ted Lasso’ Pays Tribute To Anthony Head – Here’s Why It Happened In Episode 409 “That’s what happens. articles.title: Channel 4 Teaming With Stroke Association On Doc Series Spotlighting Young People Recovering From Strokes
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart , Jesse Whittock September 30, 2026 1:26am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Trauma: My Broken Brain' Stream Media Group EXCLUSIVE: Channel 4 is teaming with the Stroke Association on a documentary sereis looking at young people living with the aftermath of a stroke. Trauma: My Broken Brain follows three young survivors through the most frightening days of their lives and the grueling journey back to independence. Every five minutes someone in the UK suffers a stroke – there are 1.4 million stroke survivors living in the UK today – but the aim of the doc is to show that this is only the beginning of recovery. Filmed over a year with access to these young adults at the most terrifying and testing moments of their lives, the series meets Dan (28), a dancer left confined to a wheelchair, barely able to speak following emergency brain surgery; Saskia (22), a self-described social butterfly left bedbound after a brain bleed so severe her family feared she would not survive; and Dec (20), who collapsed just four months into a new relationship and spent weeks in a coma, his family and girlfriend unsure if he would survive. Related Stories Acquisitions Paramount+ Buys British A24 Series 'It Gets Worse', 'Major Players' & 'The Ministry Of Time' News Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra Open To Putting Shows On BBC iPlayer -- Just Don't Mention A Merger Channel 4 has taken the rare step of teaming with a charity on the doc. It is being produced by Stream Media Group , which was also behind the same network’s Anna Richardson: Love, Loss and Dementia , made with the Alzheimer’s Society. Watch on Deadline Channel 4 commissoning exec Simon Lee said: “This is an ambitious and important series that challenges perceptions and gives a voice to young people whose lives have been transformed by stroke, as they embark on the long road that begins after survival.” Stream’s Victoria Noble added: “What struck us throughout filming was how little people understand about stroke. Survival is often seen as the end of the story, when in reality, it is only the beginning. By sharing their journeys with such honesty and courage, Dec, Dan and Saskia revealed the reality of rebuilding a life after stroke, and the truth behind the long and unforgiving journey to reclaim the right to live an independent life. Alongside the extraordinary support of their families, their stories offer a powerful insight into resilience, determination and hope. It’s been a privilege to tell their stories.” Noble is EP with Ben Padfield and producer is Laura Hooper. Series director is Storm Theunissen and production executive is Fiona Ridgers. The show was filmed with access to The Walton Centre NHS Foundation Trust and Clatterbridge Rehabilitation Centre, and Wirral University Teaching Hospital NHS Foundation Trust. articles.title: BBC Studios Scripted Boss Spotlights Strategy Behind Indie & Talent Deals: “We’re Not Going To Spend Millions Buying A Production Company”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max ‘Doctor Who’: Multiple BBC Studios Labels Likely To Apply For Tender Callum Scott Howells & Gabrielle Creevy Leading Adaptation Of Vanessa Savage Thriller ‘The Night They Vanished’ For BBC Studios & Channel 4 BBC Studios Scripted Boss Spotlights Strategy Behind Indie & Talent Deals: “We’re Not Going To Spend Millions Buying A Production Company” View All September 30, 2026 2:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Clockwise Top L-R: Honey, Doctor Who, Alice and Steve, Ann Droid (inst) Jamie Hall BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/James Pardon/Hulu EXCLUSIVE: BBC Studios ’ scripted chief has laid out his strategy for future indie and talent investments that will shy away from “going out and spending £20M ($26.5M) on a production company.” Speaking exclusively with Deadline for his first interview since taking on the Scripted MD role, Jamie Hall said his plan for the Doctor Who , Baby Reindeer and Sherwood maker is instead to strike smaller but more regular deals with top talent and “build creative hubs.” In this vein, Hall said BBC Studios scripted will “move slightly closer” to the strategy of soon-to-be-independent rival ITV Studios. Related Stories Executives BBC Studios Names Mediawan's Sally Habbershaw President Of Global Distribution News 'Doctor Who' Re-Gen Is Go! BBC Calls On Producers To Pitch "Brave" New Vision For Sci-Fi Series Hall came to our interview clutching receipts in the shape of two new labels led by the producers behind Strike and The Detection Club , along with early-stage plans for a label that will focus on digital spin-offs of existing brands. Watch on Deadline BBC Studios runs hefty in-house drama and comedy teams along with majority-owning big beasts of the UK production world like Baby Reindeer maker Clerkenwell Films, Sherwood producer House Productions, Lookout Point and Steve Coogan’s Baby Cow. Hall joined earlier this year , three decades on from his first stint at the BBC (he met his wife working on Our Friends in the North ) from Vice Studios/Pulse Films, where he oversaw the likes of Gangs Of London. At BBC Studios, his remit is to give a shot in the arm to the drama and comedy offering and unearth the next generation of IP at a time when the public service BBC is desperate for funding. His desire echoes that of his boss, BBC Studios Productions chief Zai Bennett, which is to invest in around two to three of these new-look talent labels per year. Other examples include tie-ups with Barbie star Jamie Demetriou, The Ballad of Wallis Island writer Tom Basden, Ted Lasso alum Nick Mohammed and Cunk on Earth creator Diane Morgan. “I inherited a group of great production companies that had been acquired in the way production companies were acquired at the time,” Hall told Deadline from BBC Studios’ Soho outpost. “But I don’t think the market can support that anymore – or, at least, it can only do so very rarely. We’re not going to spend £20 million buying a production company. Instead, we’re building an amazing service at the center of the studio, then creating creative hubs that can tap into our brilliant lawyers, HR, finance and other support functions.” Hall didn’t completely rule out stumping up big bucks to buy an indie outright in the future, but added: “The reality is that I can set up creative pods or labels at a much lower price point, and that feels right.” He said the scripted supremo role at BBC Studios had attracted him because, “I wasn’t simply coming in to mind the wheel. There was a creative renewal that needed to happen – some wiring and plumbing that needed fixing.” Backing up his strategy, Hall unveiled Bristol-based Landed Productions led by Strike and Possession producer Jenny van der Lande, who is leaving her role as Big Talk’s creative director of drama to helm BBC Studios’ first scripted label outside London. Landed Productions will make “premium genre pieces” and van der Lande has multiple writers in mind with whom she wants to develop shows. “Jenny said in our conversations that she doesn’t want to run a production company,” explained Hall. “She wants to work with amazing writers she already has relationships with, then partner up when she gets a greenlight.” Hall’s new-look team, which consists of the likes of CFO Jennifer Dickson, legal chief Anna Beese and production director Alison Loose, has also been busy working on the digital spin-offs label that follows big digital successes for franchises like Dancing with the Stars and EastEnders . This one, which doesn’t yet have a name, will be led by BBC Studios Drama digital chief Katy Karger. “Scripted is probably the hardest area to crack [in digital], so we’re setting up a central digital capability,” said Hall. “When someone pitches a conventional piece of television, we can also pitch to buyers a digital component.” Hall also unveiled CliffEdge Entertainment, led by “real grafter” Deborah Sathe, who is moving across from her role as Senior Creative Director at the in-house BBC Studios Drama Productions. CliffEdge will take some shows off Drama Productions’ hands such as The Detection Club, Silent Witness, Father Brown and Shakespeare and Hathaway , while the Kate Oates-run Drama Productions will continue making soaps and continuing drama. Some staff will move over to CliffEdge. “When I came in, I spent a lot of time getting to know all the creatives in the business and Deb Sathe was one of the people who really impressed me with her energy and what she was building,” added Hall. “She’s a real grafter, but is also incredibly disciplined about making shows at a certain price point. It felt natural for her to have her own entity to run.” CliffEdge comes replete with a greenlight: an adaptation of Vanessa Savage’s gripping thriller The Night They Vanished starring It’s a Sin’s Callum Scott Howells and Gabrielle Creevy ( Black Doves ). That one has been pre-bought by Channel 4 and follows Anna (Creevy), whose world is blown apart when she discovers her childhood house listed on a true crime website as the scene of her family’s future deaths. Intriguing blind date Cai (Scott Howells) runs the true-crime site, but he swears he didn’t post it. “I’ve done the rounds of most of the agencies” The Night They Vanished speaks to what Hall believes BBC Studios can do with big IP. He says he has “done the rounds of most of the agencies to remind them that we’re open” – the day after he chats with Deadline he has a meeting in the diary with Curtis Brown – and is in talks over “a number of pieces of IP that are coming through which are quite interesting.” Driven by the success of Sky and AMC’s Gangs of London, for which he says Pulse was “a bit ahead of the curve,” Hall is chatting to rightsholders about the possibility of revamping in-vogue gaming IP for the small screen. This follows big successes for the likes of HBO’s The Last of Us. Although none of these examples are necessarily franchise-able in the vein of a Gangs of London or Doctor Who, Hall reels off a list of upcoming BBC Studios shows he is buzzing for, including the BBC’s Killing Eve origin story Honey , Netflix surfing drama Breakers and a second season of Disney+ rom-com Alice and Steve. Another hit dominating ratings at the moment is Diane Morgan’s comedy Ann Droid , which poignantly taps into societal paranoia about AI but in an oh-so-gentle way. Having yesterday become the BBC’s biggest new scripted comedy since Ludwig Season 1, Hall reveals there is “real interest” in Ann Droid from American buyers, who are familiar with Morgan from her work as comedy creation Philomena Cunk and could either buy finished tape or commission their own unique version. Hall has plenty experience working for American behemoths and will soon sit down with BBC Studios’ new L.A. chief Ryan O’Dowd to figure out “how we can be better joined up, because inevitably our producers [in the UK] want access to the U.S. market.” This comes at a time when Hall says the co-pro market is “picking up a bit” from the lows of 2025 , although he acknowledges it is “nowhere near what it was in the past and there is still quite a big oversupply in the market of producers and projects.” “If we’re designing a show and the budget is at a [higher] level then we need to start thinking about [co-pros] much earlier in the process,” he added. “What has happened in the past is you develop a show for [BBC drama boss] Lindsay [Salt] and she says she wants it and then you go, ‘Oh crap we can’t finance it with just Lindsay and the tax credit, we need co-pro’. But by then the show has been developed in such a distinct way.” He hopes his experience in the belly of the beast at Vice can help but is so far loving being part of a public service machine, which Hall labels the fourth biggest brand in the world. “Our ultimate owner is the epitome of patient money,” he said. “Whereas when I was at Vice it was owned by three American banks and if we didn’t hit our numbers each quarter we were in trouble.” This unique BBC model helps in the current landscape, Hall reckons, coming as the Banijay-All3Media mega-merger marches on. “I imagine that if you’ve got a super-indie with 130 production companies, the amount of facetime you’re going to have with the boss is quite minimal,” he added. “What I really lean into is the way we’re structured. Zai [Bennett] and I sit opposite each other, across a bank of desks. We don’t have to wait for L.A. to wake up before we make a decision; we can just get on with things.” “Just getting on with things” is a crucial mantra for a BBC Studios scripted operation that is feeling more and more pressure to return funds to the cash-strapped 100-year-old national broadcaster . Is Hall feeling the pressure? “There’s no denying that any headwinds the BBC faces will come and hit us,” he added. “All I can do is manage that and focus on where we can grow our business outside of that [traditional BBC funding] route to help compensate. The BBC gets beat up so much. What we can do inside the studio is really help it and support it.” CA Gov Candidate Steve Hilton On Federal Tax Credits, ParaBros Merger & More ‘Ted Lasso’ Shocker: Actor Reflects On Death Of OG Character BBC Studios Scripted Boss Jamie Hall On Talent Deal Strategy Review & Red Carpet Premiere Photos With Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Callum Scott Howells & Gabrielle Creevy Leading Adaptation Of Vanessa Savage Thriller ‘The Night They Vanished’ For BBC Studios & Channel 4
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max ‘Doctor Who’: Multiple BBC Studios Labels Likely To Apply For Tender Callum Scott Howells & Gabrielle Creevy Leading Adaptation Of Vanessa Savage Thriller ‘The Night They Vanished’ For BBC Studios & Channel 4 BBC Studios Scripted Boss Spotlights Strategy Behind Indie & Talent Deals: “We’re Not Going To Spend Millions Buying A Production Company” View All September 30, 2026 2:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Callum Scott Howells (left) and Gabrielle Creevy Kate Green via Getty EXCLUSIVE: It’s a Sin star Callum Scott Howells and Gabrielle Creevy ( Black Doves ) are leading an adaptation of Vanessa Savage’s romantic thriller The Night They Vanished for BBC Studios and Channel 4 . Cameras have rolled in Wales on the six-part series that tells the story of Anna (Creevy), whose world is blown apart when she discovers her childhood house listed on a true-crime website as the scene of her family’s future deaths. Intriguing blind date Cai (Scott Howells) runs the true-crime site but swears he didn’t post it. The police say it’s a hoax, but Anna’s family have vanished. Related Stories News BBC Studios Scripted Boss Spotlights Strategy Behind Indie & Talent Deals: "We're Not Going To Spend Millions Buying A Production Company" News Channel 4 Teaming With Stroke Association On Doc Series Spotlighting Young People Recovering From Strokes Angharad Elen ( The Light In The Hall ) and Hannah Daniel ( Mudtown ) are adapting Savage’s novel, her third thriller. BBC Studios’ new label CliffEdge Entertainment , which has just been unveiled to Deadline by scripted boss Jamie Hall, is producing and selling worldwide. Channel 4 has pre-bought the drama while we understand a deal with a U.S. buyer is close. Watch on Deadline Additional cast includes Tamzin Outhwaite ( The Wives, Ridley Road, The Tower ) as Anna’s stepmum Jo and Steffan Rhodri ( Gavin & Stacey ) as Idris, Anna’s father, along with Matthew Gravelle ( Mudtown ), Lisa Victoria ( Pobol y Cwm ), Jack Quick ( Pobol y Cwm ), Andrew Lennon ( Death Valley ), Callum Hymers ( The Pact ), and Bella Shewan. Scott Howells is best known for Russell T. Davies’ It’s a Sin and is starring in Deadpoint, another BBC Studios thriller for Channel 4. Creevy plays Eleanor in Netflix hit Black Doves, which will soon launch Season 2. Creevy said: “Anna is a firecracker – sharp, loyal and carrying more hurt than she lets on. The moment her past comes roaring back, she’s forced into a nightmare she thought she’d escaped. It’s a gift of a role and I can’t wait for audiences to unravel the truth with her.” Scott Howells added: “Cai is charming, complicated and never quite what he seems. He could be the love of Anna’s life… or the centre of a terrifying conspiracy. Playing someone who keeps you guessing is exactly the kind of challenge I love.” The Night They Vanished has been pre-bought by Polly Scates, Channel 4 Head of Acquisitions and Felix Jones, Acquisitions Manager. EPs are Sarah Creasey, Sathe, Elen, and Branwen Williams for BBC Studios. Series producer is Sian Elen John and the Director is Geraint Todd.
