articles.title: Sylvester Stallone Thought His Dad Would “Be Proud” To Make ‘Rocky’ Cameo: “It Got Really Nasty”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘Saturday Night Live’: Jalen Brunson’s Knicks Teammates Join Him During Opening Monologue ‘Star Wars’ Is Continuing Skywalker Saga With ‘Spider-Man’ Director Jon Watts Ina Garten Explains Why She’s “Always Said No” To A Biopic: “It’s My Story” View All September 26, 2026 3:10pm Sylvester Stallone and Burgess Meredith in 'Rocky' 1976 Courtesy Everett Collection As Sylvester Stallone made his breakout performance in Rocky , there was one person he couldn’t quite turn into a fan. While discussing his memoir The Steps , releasing Oct. 23, the 3x Oscar nominee recalled things on set getting “really nasty” after giving his real father Frank Stallone Sr. a cameo as the bell ringer in the 1976 boxing drama’s climactic match. “It was like: I just want you to love me for a little bit,” Sly explained to The New York Times . “Like, look what I did! Share it with me. I know you thought I was a fool my whole life, but here we are.” Related Stories Festivals ‘I Play Rocky’s Peter Farrelly Talks Why The Making Of ‘Rocky’ Was The Next Real-Life Story He Wanted To Take A Swing At – Toronto Studio Politics Sylvester Stallone Told Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship Was “Impossible” But Was Appointed Anyway: “It Won’t Work” On the day of filming, Frank Sr. “didn’t ring the bell properly,” as his son “kept fighting and fighting and fighting. Everything’s choreographed. It’s one, two, three, four, bell. Not six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Carl Weathers is like, ‘What’s going on?'” Watch on Deadline Stallone continued, “And of course it ended up in an altercation by the end. It got really nasty. A really bad Italian drama. But for a moment I thought, Jesus, he’d be proud.” Sylvester Stallone in ‘Rocky’ (1976) Everett Collection In the interview, Stallone explained that his father “was very, very cold and tough” until they reconciled upon his death in 2011. “It would be these constant bombastic explosions and then total silence,” recalled Stallone of living alone with his dad. “If he and I were talking and I said, ‘I don’t know if I agree with that,’ he’d start spinning his fork and suck his teeth, and you knew what was coming. The next thing you know, wham! He had very big hands. You learn to duck. I didn’t put a lot of stuff in the book because I didn’t want a pity party, but it was insane.” In the biopic I Play Rocky , premiering Nov. 6 in theaters, Anthony Ippolito plays a young Stallone as he writes the first Rocky movie and fights to star as the titular boxer. articles.title: Robert Eggers Wants To Do ‘Romeo & Juliet’ Because Things Got “So Dark” After ‘Werwulf’, Joking: “So, I’ll Do Something About Two Teenagers Killing Themselves”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘Saturday Night Live’: Jalen Brunson’s Knicks Teammates Join Him During Opening Monologue ‘Star Wars’ Is Continuing Skywalker Saga With ‘Spider-Man’ Director Jon Watts Ina Garten Explains Why She’s “Always Said No” To A Biopic: “It’s My Story” View All September 26, 2026 4:34pm Robert Eggers explains why he wanted to adapt 'Romeo & Juliet' as his next film. 20th Century Fox/courtesy Everett Collection/Gilbert Flores/PMC SPOILER ALERT for anyone who skipped freshman English! Robert Eggers is teasing his take on William Shakespeare’s Romeo & Juliet . During a post-screening Q&A for his latest macabre title Werwulf , premiering Christmas Day, the auteur joked that the famously tragic conclusion of Shakespeare’s 16th century romance would be a welcome “break” from his usual horror work. “I was doing something else,” noted Eggers of plans for his next project in a video from the event. “But what happened was, after Werwulf , I was writing another horror movie, and it got so dark again, and I was like, ‘I need a break. So, I’ll do something about two teenagers killing themselves.'” Related Stories Acquisitions Focus Features Closing In On ‘Romeo And Juliet’ Adaptation From Robert Eggers News ‘Werwulf’ Trailer: Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Willem Dafoe & Lily-Rose Depp Lead The Latest Celluloid Nightmare From Robert Eggers Earlier this week, Deadline reported that Eggers was eyeing a return to Focus Features for his take on Romeo & Juliet , which has sparked some studio competition. Watch on Deadline Details of Eggers’ adaptation are under wraps. His deal is not yet finalized, but we understand he’ll direct and produce this version of the classic play. The deal would reunite him with a studio with whom he’s worked across much of his body of work, including horror titles The Lighthouse (2019), Nosferatu (2024) and Werwulf . Incredible answer from Robert Eggers about why he turned to Romeo & Juliet pic.twitter.com/003vhqRdCN — The King of Burbank @ Beyondfest (@kingofburbank2) September 26, 2026 In Werwulf , a man (Aaron Taylor-Johnson) in 14th century England finds him and his family threatened by a ravenous beast haunting the town. The film also stars Lily-Rose Depp, Willem Dafoe, Ralph Ineson and more. articles.title: Ina Garten Explains Why She’s “Always Said No” To A Biopic: “It’s My Story”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘Saturday Night Live’: Jalen Brunson’s Knicks Teammates Join Him During Opening Monologue ‘Star Wars’ Is Continuing Skywalker Saga With ‘Spider-Man’ Director Jon Watts Ina Garten Explains Why She’s “Always Said No” To A Biopic: “It’s My Story” View All September 26, 2026 6:00pm Chef Ina Garten at her East Hamptons home. Fairchild Archive/PMC After sharing her story in her 2024 memoir Be Ready When The Luck Happens , Ina Garten is reluctant to trust a filmmaker with the adaptation. The Barefoot Contessa celebrity chef recently explained why she’s “never been willing” to make a biopic about her life, despite being “approached” to adapt Be Ready for the big screen. “It’s funny, I don’t make long-term plans. I do what I do as well as I can, and things come along, and I say no to most of them,” she told People . Related Stories News Food Network’s ‘Barefoot Contessa’ Ina Garten Advocates Day Drinking As A Way To Beat Quarantine Blues News Amazon And Oprah Winfrey’s Harpo Entertainment Ink Wide-Reaching Podcast Deal Garten added, “I’ve been approached to do a movie of my memoir, but I know that when a producer or director gets ahold of a story, they want to make it work on film and they’re going to change it. So I’ve never been willing to do that. It’s my story. I get to keep it. And I don’t want people making up things just for dramatic effect. And so I’ve always said no.” Watch on Deadline The 2024 memoir came after Garten ended the nearly 20-year run of her Food Network cooking show Barefoot Contessa , which ran from 2002 to 2021. Since 2022, Garten has hosted her followup Food Network show Be My Guest , inviting friends to her dinner table in her East Hampton, New York home. articles.title: ‘Star Wars’ Is Continuing Skywalker Saga With ‘Spider-Man’ Director Jon Watts
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘Saturday Night Live’: Jalen Brunson’s Knicks Teammates Join Him During Opening Monologue ‘Star Wars’ Is Continuing Skywalker Saga With ‘Spider-Man’ Director Jon Watts Ina Garten Explains Why She’s “Always Said No” To A Biopic: “It’s My Story” View All September 26, 2026 8:07pm Jon Watts is directing the next 'Star Wars' film in the Skywalker Saga. Courtesy Everett Collection/Gilbert Flores/PMC After eight years and countless entries in the expanding onscreen universe, Star Wars is revisiting the Skywalker family with its next project. Deadline can confirm that Lucasfilm has tapped Skeleton Crew co-creator Jon Watts (director of Spider-Man: Homecoming , Spider-Man: Far From Home and Spider-Man: No Way Home ) to helm the first installment in a new trilogy of the Skywalker Saga, which is being penned by Simon Kinberg ( X-Men: Dark Phoenix , Prime’s Mr. & Mrs. Smith ). Kinberg, who previously co-created the DisneyXD animated series Star Wars Rebels (2014-’18), has been working on the new trilogy since 2018, with Daisy Ridley reportedly eyed to reprise her role as Rey, as it will serve in the next chapter of the Skywalker Saga. Related Stories News Damon Lindelof Details His Scrapped ‘Star Wars’ That Would Have Tackled “Nostalgia” & “Revision” News ‘Star Wars: Starfighter’ & ‘Star Wars’ 50th Anniversary Edition To Be Released In Imax 70MM The project reportedly has not yet received a greenlight from parent company Disney. Watch on Deadline Beginning with Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope in 1977 and the sequels Episode V — The Empire Strikes Back (1980) and Episode VI — Return of the Jedi (1983), the Skywalker Saga continued with the prequel trilogy Episode I — The Phantom Menace (1999), Episode II: Attack of the Clones (2002) and Episode III — Revenge of the Sith (2005). Most recently, the franchise left off the Skywalker Saga with the latest trilogy, Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens (2015), Episode VIII — The Last Jedi (2017) and Episode IX — The Rise of Skywalker (2019), which was led by Ridley’s Rey. Since the last chapter in the Skywalker Saga, the Star Wars franchise has expanded with films and streaming series set throughout the onscreen universe, with the next installment Star Wars: Starfighter set for a May 28, 2027 premiere. Lucasfilm had no comment. Knight Edge Media was first to report the news. The 2026 MVP swapped some quips with teammates Karl-Anthony Towns, Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby and Josh Hart during his opening monologue on Saturday’s episode, which comes after they defeated the San Antonio Spurs in June to bring the Knicks their first NBA championship since 1973. articles.title: Film Execs Ponder Federal Film Tax Credit Impact, Timeline & Potential Price Rises — Zurich Summit
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Film Execs Ponder Federal Film Tax Credit Impact, Timeline & Potential Price Rises — Zurich Summit Cinetic Launches Vertical Leap, Investment Vehicle & Producing Pathway For Pro Athletes — Zurich Summit One Year On, Does AI Actress Tilly Norwood Have An Agent? “We Get Loads Of Offers, But No, We Don’t Need It” — Zurich Summit View All September 27, 2026 4:43am Hollywood sign Presley Ann / Getty Images At this weekend’s Zurich Summit a group of film financiers were asked by Deadline for their thoughts on the prospects of a U.S. federal film incentive. Last week, a bipartisan group of lawmakers unveiled the bill for a 20% incentive, which with bonuses could bring the total rebate to 30%. The move has long been called-for by the U.S. industry concerned by the exodus of production overseas. Alex Walton, former Co-Lead & Partner at WME Independent, told the Summit the move was “hugely positive”: “It’s wild to think there hasn’t been an efficient tax credit in America. It has helped many other countries. Spain is booming because of it now; and all over Europe. It’s going to take some time to be realized and for financial institutions to be able to cash flow it. But you’ve got to believe it will happen within the next three-four years, and then that will see all the foreign tax credits compete harder to maintain their positions.” Related Stories News "I Can Promise You, We Had No Idea That 'Obsession' Was Going To Become 'Obsession'", Says Hit Horror Film's Seller -- Zurich Summit Festivals 'Backrooms' Director Kane Parsons Says: "I Don't View It As A Horror Project" - Zurich Summit A start date is not yet set. The proposed text from last week stated that the credit would apply to qualifying film and TV productions beginning in taxable years after December 31, 2026 (effectively targeting projects starting in 2027). But bills can take years to pass. Watch on Deadline Andrea Scarso, Managing Partner at prolific financier IPR.VC, whose credits include Marty Supreme and Materialists , agreed that a U.S. incentive would be “positive” but also cautioned against rising production costs: “It remains to be seen whether the prices and budgets are also going up by the same amount, which is something that happens in some foreign territories when they increase the amount of tax credit or soft money. It’s always a balance. But overall, I think it’s good news.” Sarah Schweitzman, Co-Head CAA Media Finance, noted: “What’s important is that when you look at some of the international markets, you realize that we’re making movies there because of a tax incentive situation and I think if we’re able to federalize a tax incentive program in the U.S. it’s going to create many more jobs and invigorate crews, which is something we absolutely need in the U.S.” A recent Motion Picture Association study claimed that a federal film tax credit could increase U.S. production spending by $125BN and add more than 143,000 jobs by 2035. You can read more about the bill here . articles.title: FilmNation CEO Glen Basner Talks Art Of Film Sales & Financing: “It’s Really Just About Sitting & Listening To The Filmmaking Team” – Zurich Summit
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie ‘Backrooms’ Director Kane Parsons Says: “I Don’t View It As A Horror Project” – Zurich Summit Tales Of Syria’s Disappeared; Lebanese Wartime Adoption & Palestinian Mental Health Set For Cinemed-Aflamuna Project Incubator Netflix-Acquired Animation ‘In Waves’ To Open The American French Film Festival In L.A. View All September 27, 2026 6:59am Glen Basner at 22nd Zurich Film Festival Getty Images for ZFF FilmNation Entertainment Founder and CEO Glen Basner will receive the Game Changer Award this evening at the Zurich Summit , the annual industry event aimed at fostering transatlantic connections taking place within the Zurich Film Festival. As part of the honor, Basner participated in an onstage conversation on Saturday moderated by German Oscar-winning director Edward Berger . Over the course of an hour, the pair dug into Basner’s trajectory from sales rep at his father’s garment business, to heading up one of the world’s top international indie sales, financing and production companies. Related Stories News Film Execs Ponder Federal Film Tax Credit Impact, Timeline & Potential Price Rises -- Zurich Summit News "I Can Promise You, We Had No Idea That 'Obsession' Was Going To Become 'Obsession'", Says Hit Horror Film's Seller -- Zurich Summit Basner and Berger go back a long way, having first met at the beginning of their film careers in the early 1990s at famed New York production company Good Machine. Watch on Deadline Basner arrived there from a five-year stint selling ladies knitted sweaters. He had been bitten by the movie bug while helping childhood friend Edward Burns in his spare time on his first film The Brothers McMullen. Burns then invited Basner onto his second feature She’s The One , which was produced by Good Machine. The rest is history. Berger spent a year and a half at the company from 1994, where his paths crossed with Basner. They have stayed connected ever since, with the pair joining forces professionally again on Berger’s 2024 $100M global box office and streaming hit Conclave . “32 years later, it’s such a full circle moment,” said Berger as they kicked off the conversation. Looking back at his time working with Ted Hope, James Schamus and David Linde at Good Machine, Basner said the lessons he learned there had carried him through his career. “I was taught that you could sell movies around the world and not lie to people… that you can value and appreciate the relationships that you develop around the world and treat people not just as if you’re selling them a product, but that you are really delivering them a work of art, and that you’re there to help support them as they go and release the films country by country,” he said. Berger suggested working there had also taught them resilience, recalling how just prior to their arrival, the company had nearly gone bankrupt after it wrapped Ang Lee’s romantic comedy The Wedding Banquet . “It taught us to go through hard times and get stronger… around the time of The Wedding Banquet, the company was basically bankrupt… they decided let’s cancel the photocopier and scrape every last bit together and go to Berlin,” said the director. The film went on to win the Berlinale’s Golden Bear and then took off at the box office to gross some $23M, against the $1M budget, making it the most profitable U.S. film of 1993. After subsequent stints heading up sales at Focus and then The Weinstein Company, Basner created FilmNation in 2008, initially uniquely as a sales company. He said creating his own company had been a natural move for him given his family background. “My father had his own business, and I wanted to be like my father, so I always had this entrepreneurial bug that I wanted to go out and sort of really test my mettle by being on my own and developing something and seeing if it could succeed,” he said. “So that was something I thought about since the first day that I started working in film.” Eighteen years later, the company has expanded organically into finance, production and TV, with bases in New York and L.A., and string of award-winning features in its filmography including The Big Sick , Promising Young Woman, Anora , Conclave , Maria and upcoming pictures Bunker , Talent for Murder and I Play Rocky to name but a few. “The opportunity was clear in 2008. In those days, there were only two strong and dominant, excellent American international sales companies that were unaffiliated with U.S. distribution,” said Basner. “Pretty much at the same time, they both became U.S. distributors. Summit, which was run by Patrick Wachberger, became a U.S. distributor, and Mandate, Joe Drake’s company, was bought by Lionsgate… so there was this big hole for an American, unaffiliated-with-distribution sales company.” Sales craft Talking about FilmNation’s recent slate, Basner said he had wooed Florian Zeller ahead of getting involved in Bunker . “I told him to his face he was my filmmaker crush of the moment,” he joked. “You said that to me too,” replied Berger in mock disbelief. “I know. It was a different moment,” fired back Basner jovially. He recalled how Zeller had been on the cusp of approaching Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz as FilmNation quietly putting out international sales feelers. “He had said, ‘If they say yes, we’ll move forward. If they don’t do the movie, I don’t think I’m going to do the movie.’ Fortunately, they said yes, and then we just really started the work,” said Basner. The film took a traditional pre-sales route thanks to Zeller’s track-record with Oscar-winner The Father , followed by The Son , it’s A-list cast and a “exquisite” script, with the bulk of the international sales tied up at Cannes in 2025. The U.S. deal to Sony Pictures Classics was sealed in collaboration with CAA Media Finance later on, on the basis of the completed film. “There were distributors that were willing to take the risk. It’s not the easiest thing to say: ‘Here’s the script, here’s the director, here are the actors, and here’s your price’. They don’t really get to sit and have hour-long conversations with the filmmaker to fully understand the movie,” said Basner . “They have to trust us to be able to articulate exactly what the movie is and what the intention is of that filmmaker, so that they can then decide to take the significant risk on a movie like this of pre-buying the film.” Talking about their collaboration on Vatican-set thriller Conclave , revolving around the secretive Vatican process of electing a new Pope, Basner said part of the challenge had been conveying Berger’s vision for the film to buyers. He suggested that on the basis of the screenplay alone – it felt like a story about “a bunch of old men talking in rooms” with a potential $12M to $15M price tag. “But that really wasn’t the movie that you were looking to make… You talked about The Parallax View being a point of reference for you,” said Basner, referring to Alan J. Pakula’s 1974 political thriller. “You talked not just about the architecture of the locations, but the architecture of how you wanted the camera to move and the film to feel… all of a sudden this became a political thriller,” continued Basner. The sales veteran said estimating a value of a film, country by country, came down to a mixture of experience and expertise. “You’re responsible to hit these estimates. And human nature takes over, and sometimes you can get a little bit conservative to make sure that you deliver,’ he said. “What we’ve learned over the years is to trust the business acumen and the marketplace experience that we have, and not be too conservative, but actually just deliver the valuation that we think, and be prepared to stand by it in a real way because it’s our money that we’re investing.” “Part of that is, instead of talking all the time about what the market says and what the market will bear, it’s really about just sitting and listening to the filmmaking team so that you really understand, not what I, Glen Basner, thinks the movie is going to be or should be, but the movie that the filmmaker wants to make.” Basner revealed he was wary of going down the packaging route of attaching known talent when helping get big projects of the ground, suggesting attempts to mitigate risks on films, whether via the cast or other factors, can sometimes lead to less exciting films. “Sometimes we have to take more risk on an unknown actor because they are the best person for that role to make the best version of the movie, and we have to trust that filmmaker to deliver on that, not in a naive way, in a thoughtful way, but really trust that that’s really what’s going to drive the value for that movie,” said Basner. “I really am encouraging everybody to look around, look at what’s working in the marketplace. There are a lot of films that, on paper, did not make sense. The history of our company is predominantly on films that did not make sense to the marketplace at the beginning.” Conclave clash Berger revealed they had not always seen eye-to-eye in the final stages of bringing Conclave to fruition. “After quite a long edit… I was basically done with the film. I’d run out of ideas… I really wanted to go to Venice or at least show them the movie and see if they’d show it,” recalled Berger. “This was in in May. Glenn got on the phone and made me furious. I hated him. He just kind of said, ‘I’m not sure the movie’s ready, don’t rush it…Venice is going to be expensive, and we don’t have American distribution in place’,” he recalled. Lead producer Tessa Ross also felt the movie was “missing something” and after test screenings with friends and family sparked an “ok” response, Berger went back to the edit suite and even reshot one or two scenes. Berger credited Berger and Ross for pushing the extra mile on the film, while his energy levels were low after an arduous months-long edit process. “This is going back to Good Machine, and what I took from Good Machine… which was you can always do better… whether its budget, contract or the cut of the movie,” said Berger. “We just edited and edited and edited and made the music again and revised it, and finally something cracked… little things, just shifted and gave us the confidence that the movie was ready. But it was really half a year later.” Organic expansion Taking stock of FilmNation’s trajectory since 2008, Basner said the expansion into production and TV had been organic. “We never really anticipated becoming the company that we have over time, but things changed. One, as we continued to do our jobs and have success, we gained confidence through experience, and we were ready to do things like fund our own films,” he said. A second development was the convergence of film and TV and other entertainment formats, which has seen the company also embrace TV, podcasts and theater, while retaining its original mission of being a place that enables filmmakers to not just make their film, but to make the very best iteration of their film. “When we’re at our best, that’s exactly what we’re doing. It’s no more complicated than that. And when we are doing it, nothing feels more rewarding than doing that job well,” he said. Looking to near-term goals, Basner said the company was ramping up its productions in the arrival of former 20th Century Fox, DreamWorks and Universal Pictures exec Stacey Snider in the new role of Chief Creative Officer in January. “We are being more ambitious by investing more and making more films. This year we will make four films and a television series, and next year we already have four films in pre-production and hope to make another three,” said Basner. “The arrival of Snider as the Chief Creative Officer was an articulation of our desire to take more risk and to be more productive,” he continued. “Working with her these last nine months, you see this incredible creative talent, you see a skill set and a maturity that we don’t have ourselves, or that I don’t have myself, and it is definitely building confidence to invest further. But it’s really also, as she would say, it’s about making it better. The conversation that you had before: let’s take another look at this. Let’s do it a little bit better. That’s something she reminds me pretty much every day.” Jalen Brunson Brings Knicks To S52 Premiere; Trump & Zohran Mamdani In Cold Open ‘Star Wars’ Continuing Skywalker Saga With ‘Spider-Man’ Director Jon Watts ‘Endgame’ Reissue & Three Other Pics To Top $20M Each In Big Weekend White House Blocks CNN, Networks Suspend Pool Coverage Read More About: Comments

articles.title: What ‘60 Minutes’ Was Missing In Its First Two New Episodes, According to Its Ex-Managing Editor
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All September 25, 2026 4:49pm Norah O'Donnell on the Sept. 13 episode of '60 Minutes.' CBS News “I made a living for 34 years second-guessing everything I see or hear, so you have to take that into consideration.” That’s one of the first things that Guy Campanile, the famously exacting former managing editor of 60 Minutes and a 34-year veteran to CBS News , says to The Hollywood Reporter as he settles into an interview. At CBS News he was known for being ultra-frank even in a workplace that culturally encouraged vigorous debate as part of its story-honing process. (“It’s no secret at CBS News that I do not hold back. Many colleagues appreciated my directness. Some did not,” he wrote in an email to THR .) So he urges THR to take that into account as he offers his thoughts on the 59th season of 60 Minutes so far. His critiques are less stinging than one might assume given his previous assessment of why he and colleagues were fired from the program in May (that they refused to be “accomplices in the destruction of the most prestigious news program on American television”). Overall, Campanile echoes what at least a couple critics have said about the first episode of the 59th season: It didn’t seem much different than recent seasons of the program. “We kept hearing about a notebook full of ideas that the new executive producer had, and the broadcast had been described as a melting ice cube and that changes had to happen,” he says, adding that 60 Minutes also increased its viewership nine percent in the previous season. “And the broadcast I’ve seen the first few weeks, in the broad strokes, in shape and form, not in content, does not look very different. So I’m trying to understand why it was all blown up.” In May, Campanile’s time at CBS came to an abrupt end as he and multiple other staffers — including correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi, Cecilia Vega and senior program leaders Tanya Simon, Draggan Mihailovich and Matthew Polevoy — were ousted from the program. Correspondent Scott Pelley was also fired after a tense confrontation with an incoming leader about changes under CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss . The departures drew intense scrutiny as Weiss, who came up as an opinion journalist without traditional broadcast experience, was early in her tenure and some dismissed staffers alleged that under her leadership execs had attempted to interfere in their coverage for political reasons. Guy Campanile is a 34-year CBS veteran and was managing editor of 60 Minutes . Dave Kotinsky/Getty Images Within this context, Campanile’s biggest critique surrounds the marquee segment of the premiere, an interview with one of the U.S. Air Force officers shot down in Iran and rescued in a daring mission by the U.S. military. The segment struck Campanile as a fitting curtain-raiser to the new season, but the report also raised questions for him. “Where I, as a viewer, got stuck is how do we have the Secretary of Defense and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in that story and not ask about the conduct, the arc and the status of the war?” Campanile notes Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine, both interviewed in the piece, aren’t doing regular briefings on the status of the broadly unpopular war in Iran or many interviews with news outlets. “That made me go, huh, because among some viewers, they may see that as, boy, I guess they didn’t want to ask about the war because they wanted to get this interview with the [officer],” says Campanile. (He says that, during his time at the programs, conditions were never set by subjects for interviews at 60 Minutes ; correspondents could always ask what they wanted.) But CBS did air clips of correspondent Norah O’Donnell asking Hegseth what victory would look like in Iran and querying Caine on Iran’s missile capabilities on CBS Mornings . Her question to Caine about his concern over a munitions shortage also aired on Face the Nation — just not on 60 Minutes . Another Campanile critique: In its second episode of the season, 60 Minutes aired the first TV interview with Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of Lindsay Clancy, a Massachusetts mother who murdered her three children. Clancy’s trial over the summer, which ended in a mistrial, captured global media attention and sparked conversation around postpartum mental illness, making the interview a huge get for 60 Minutes . But watching the segment, Campanile wondered what the larger purpose of the interview was. “I think it’s a high-interest story, just like the fighter pilot’s story was a high-interest story, but you have to bring more than just high interest, at least I believe that to be the case, because otherwise it feels a little tabloid-y,” he says. “And I don’t think that’s what people want from 60 Minutes . I just don’t. I think they want something more thoughtful.” The changes taking place at 60 Minutes and CBS News at large are all the more consequential now that the owner that ushered them in — Paramount Skydance — has settled a lawsuit with 12 state attorneys general to merge with Warner Bros. Discovery. WBD owns CNN, which if the transaction goes through could soon also be owned by Paramount Skydance. Campanile says he has “lots of concerns” about that prospect: “Chief among them is who is running this operation? Is it going to be Mark Thompson or is it going to be Bari Weiss?” He adds that it remains unclear to him how the editorial oversight board required by the settlement would work, given that specifics on the body haven’t been provided. “Much was made of the CBS News ombudsman. That guy’s been missing for a year,” Campanile says. Campanile is continuing to work in journalism, having just launched a media consultancy, FFWD Media Mentor, tailored to early-career and student journalists. The consultancy is geared toward professionals who aren’t receiving much guidance on the job; participants will likely receive some of that no-nonsense feedback Campanile was known for at 60 Minutes . When it comes to his former workplace, the former managing editor says he’s interested to see what the program does in the weeks ahead. “Maybe, maybe there is a secret sauce we didn’t understand, some kind of equation that we never contemplated,” he says of 60 Minutes . “And we’ll all find out together. The viewer has the final vote in all of this. I have said over and over again, you are what the scoreboard says you are… So let’s see where we are in April and March and May, and then the final verdict will come down.” THR

articles.title: ‘SNL’ Promotes Keri Powers to Sole Head of Talent Department, Rebecca Schwartz Upped to Producer
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 25, 2026 5:30pm Keri Powers and Rebecca Schwartz Courtesy of 'SNL' Logo text Saturday Night Live has promoted Keri Powers to serve as the sole head of its talent department, meaning she will lead the team responsible for host, musical guest and guest star bookings for late night show. Rebecca Schwartz has also been upped to producer, increasing her responsibilities supporting the show’s cast and production efforts. The news arrives after SNL ‘s longtime music booker Brian Siedlecki departed from the series; as The Hollywood Reporter previously reported, the program elected not to renew his contract. Siedlecki had worked on SNL for three decades, booking a wide range of musical acts, including everyone from Paul McCartney, Bruce Springsteen, Sabrina Carpenter, Chappell Roan and Olivia Rodrigo. Related Stories Music Warner Music Names Val Blavatnik to Executive Team, Unveils Suite of Leadership Promotions Music Inside the Hollywood Home Studio That's Birthed Several Pop Hits Powers has been with SNL since 2014, while Schwartz has worked on the series since 2015. SNL returns for its 52nd season Saturday at 8:30 p.m. PT/11:30 p.m. ET, live on NBC and Peacock, with NBA star Jalen Brunson as the first host alongside musical guest KATSEYE. New additions to the cast include featured players Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter. There have also been a few departures heading into season 52; Chloe Fineman announced in July that after seven years she was exiting SNL . “Seven years is kind of like the classic way [at SNL ], and then like right as my contract was up, this amazing David E. Kelley opportunity came in like completely out of the blue. I did a little chemistry read and it was off to the races; it just felt like a perfect time,” Fineman told THR of her decision to leave . “I’m really proud of everything, but it’s hard. I’m genuinely really good friends with everybody, and I genuinely couldn’t love that job more. So it’s really bittersweet, but I’m gonna be in New York. I’m down the street. Maybe you’ll see me.” Martin Herlihy, hailing from the comedy group Please Don’t Destroy, has also left the show . Midway into SNL season 51, Bowen Yang announced he’d be leaving the late-night show , just after the cast saw a major exodus. Heidi Gardner, Ego Nwodim, Michael Longfellow, Devon Walker and Emil Wakim were among those who left before season 51. THR

articles.title: ‘To Catch a Predator’ Host Chris Hansen Watches Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ — and He’s Not a Fan
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All September 25, 2026 7:41pm Chris Hansen Jason Mendez/Getty Images Former To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen was interviewed on his podcast Friday to give his unfiltered reaction to A24 ‘s unauthorized, dramatized film about parts of his life, Primetime , which he called overly dramatic, detached from reality, and a “fever dream” — while giving Robert Pattinson ‘s performance a “D” grade. Primetime , which opens Friday in the U.S., is set in 2006 and follows Pattinson’s fictionalized version of Hansen as the popular To Catch a Predator segment on NBC’s Dateline grows into its own primetime block on the network. On the show, Hansen blurred journalistic lines by working with law enforcement and the watchdog group Perverted Justice to intercept adult men as they arrived, unbeknownst to them, at a sting house to meet a minor they’d met online for sex. The men were typically arrested as a result. The series drew mixed reactions, with concerns about potential entrapment-law violations at the forefront of the criticism. Related Stories Movies Chris Hansen Strikes Back at 'Primetime' Movie (Again) With 'I'm Chris Hansen' Documentary Trailer Movies 'Avengers: Endgame' Returns to Box Office With $3.8M Previews as Brad Pitt, Robert Pattinson Join Fray In a brief segment produced for his video podcast, Have a Seat with Chris Hansen , the former NBC News journalist is seen exiting a Times Square AMC after viewing the film for the first time at a Thursday night screening — his first look at the indie drama since its theatrical release. He’s then asked for his first reaction to the Lance Oppenheim-directed film . “It’s hard for me to — obviously, I’m not a judge, because the character is based on me,” he said. “I think because the character is so detached from reality, from anything I’ve ever experienced then or now doing the investigations — I’m not sure what the point of it was.” The rest of the podcast episode has Hansen discussing the film, its director and Pattinson’s portrayal of him with Fox News’ Jesse Watters. Hansen railed against the movie throughout. Oppenheim has said he conceived Primetime after receiving a personalized Cameo video from the To Catch a Predator host. Hansen said on his podcast that he spoke to a mutual friend before seeing the film, and that Oppenheim told the friend it was “something to the effect of, ‘a love letter to Chris Hansen, and it gets a little weird in the storytelling.'” Hansen also flagged inaccuracies in the fictionalized version of his life — including scenes involving Jeff Zucker and Stone Phillips that he insists never happened — and said absolutely nothing in the film was close to reality. He assured viewers he’s not the ratings-obsessed figure the script conjures. His biggest gripe, he said, is that the film portrays him as an aloof parent, which he says is far from how he relates to his kids. As for Pattinson’s take on Hansen circa 2006, Hansen had few kind words. “He’s got work to do. I’m kind of the only guy that counts for this, right?” he said. Days before seeing the movie, Hansen spoke with The Hollywood Reporter ‘s Seth Abramovich about what he knew of the film. A24 hadn’t reached out to him or the production to explain the premise or ask for his input, he said. “Based upon what I’ve seen in the trailer and my understanding of what’s been written about the film, they wanted to create something much darker and way more dramatic,” he said. “I think it’s an insult to the thousands of men and women who work hard every day to protect children from predators. They’ve turned something that is very positive, very challenging and not without risk into what is essentially a horror film.” On Friday, after viewing Primetime , he doubled down with a direct swipe at Oppenheim. “You have to question the motives of not coming forward and talking to me or anybody I’ve worked closely with over the years,” he said. “They didn’t want to hear that Chris Hansen is a good guy. They didn’t want to hear that this work is important. This director had a dark image of what he wanted to do. He wanted to create a horror-like film with interesting photography, and didn’t want to hear anything else.” Hansen continues identifying and capturing potential child predators on Takedown with Chris Hansen . Earlier on Friday, Hansen’s TruBlu streaming network dropped the trailer for I’m Chris Hansen , a documentary centered around the host. THR

articles.title: Ahead of ‘Nobody Wants This’ Season 3, Adam Brody Declares His Support for “A Free Palestine”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 25, 2026 8:33pm Adam Brody attends the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards at Peacock Theater on September 14, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. Amy Sussman/Getty Images Logo text Nobody Wants This star Adam Brody is sharing his thoughts on the ongoing Israel-Gaza war, telling GQ in a new interview that he is in support of “a free Palestine .” The actor, who appears on the Netflix series as a rabbi, discussed his political activism with GQ , and was asked if he thinks Hollywood has gotten more conservative. “I guess outspokenly so, yes. Again, as one side has more power, it makes sense that it draws people to it for all the human reasons that would be attractive: groupthink, your own well-being, your own money and success,” he said. Related Stories News Florence Pugh Says She Was Not "Scared" to Show Support for Palestine: "I Don't Know Why It Took So Long for People to Actually Feel Sympathy" TV 'Nobody Wants This' Takes a Big Step in Season 3 Trailer Brody continued, “Between COVID, a second Trump term, Israel-Gaza, it’s really brought out some different beliefs that I was ignorant to, and then disheartened by.” The interviewer asked the actor how Israel-Gaza has come up in his messaging, to which he responded, “Truthfully, it hasn’t. I have spoken a lot about it privately. I haven’t spoken much about it publicly.” When asked if he’d like to speak about the topic, The O.C. actor said, “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine.” “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago,” he continued. “I’m hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is.” Netflix is gearing up to release the third season of its Jewish rom-com Nobody Wants This on Oct. 22. Brody was nominated for a 2025 Emmy for his role in the series, and won the Critics Choice Award for best comedy actor that same year. In an August 2025 interview with The Hollywood Reporter , series creator Erin Foster said of the show, “It was really important to me and continues to be really important to tell positive Jewish stories. I know that it can be polarizing, but it shouldn’t be. This is not the show to tackle conflict in Israel and Palestine.” “I’m not the person to tell that story,” Foster added. “And after [the attacks on] Oct. 7 happened, there were conversations around if we were going to dive into it, and the truth is, the way that I can get my message across best is by shedding a positive light on Jewish characters and Jewish traditions. I don’t think somebody watching wants to see another voice give you their opinion on what’s happening.” THR

articles.title: Julianne Moore Accepts Zurich’s Golden Icon Award — in German
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 25, 2026 11:44pm Julianne Moore at the 2026 Zurich Film Festival. Courtesy of Getty What can’t Julianne Moore do? The U.S. actress accepted Zurich Film Festival ‘s lifetime achievement honor, the Golden Icon Award, in perfect German on Friday night. She was joined at the ceremony by Jesse Eisenberg , who directs her in his latest feature The Debut , a musical-comedy co-starring Paul Giamatti, which is screening at the 22nd edition in Switzerland this week. Moore called upon her own childhood growing up in Europe while making her acceptance speech. “Thank you for this wonderful honor,” said a translated version of her words. “I know that I am in Switzerland right now, but as a teenager, I lived in Germany. And my teacher there told me that I could become an actress. Had I not moved to Europe with my parents, I would not have had this wonderful life. And I wouldn’t be here with you tonight to speak my bad German to you.” Related Stories Movies 'I Play Rocky,' 'Ray Gunn,' 'Bunker,' 'Wild Horse Nine' and 'Behemoth!' Added to AFI Fest 2026 Movies 'NAZA' Trailer: First Look at 'No Other Land' Directors' Gaza Doc That Sparked Netanyahu Backlash On the carpet ahead of the presentation, the Oscar-winning actress beamed and said she was feeling “pretty good” about the prospect of receiving the prestigious Golden Icon. “And it’s really wonderful to be here with Jesse Eisenberg, who’s such a tremendous talent and has been an unbelievably wonderful creative partner,” she added. “He’s such a genius, so I’m just happy to be sharing this experience with him, and to be here with our movie. Every day was phenomenal. It really was. There’s actually a shot of me that Jesse said was so, so funny because I was making so many dumb faces. But I said, ‘That was just my dumb face!’ I was enjoying it so much.” Eisenberg’s third directorial feature follows Mona Friedman (Moore), who is cast in a bit part at a small community theater and transforms from a shy, unassuming housewife into a zealous method actor willing to do anything to protect the artistic integrity of her marginal role — even if it means waging war against the show’s domineering director (Giamatti). The filmmaker-actor-writer told reporters on the Zurich carpet on Friday: “Mona is me. When I was seven years old in New Jersey in 1990, I was a sad little kid, and then I joined a community theater and I found a home.” On the brilliance of Moore, who starred in Eisenberg’s directorial debut When You Finish Saving the World (2022), he said: “When I started writing it, it was only her, and if she did not want to do it, the movie would have not been made. There’s no one else on the planet, alive or dead or yet to be born, who could play [the role] as good as she [does].” Among Moore’s best-known performances are Still Alice , for which she won the Academy Award, as well as The Hours and The Kids Are All Right . Recent credits include Apple TV’s Echo Valley , Pedro Almodóvar’s The Room Next Door and Netflix limited series Sirens . Next year, she will return to the stage to star in the title role of the Off-Broadway play Faydra . Also on Friday night in Zurich, In Bruges and The Banshees of Inisherin filmmaker Martin McDonagh was given the fest’s A Tribute To… Award. The honor was in celebration of his most recent film, Wild Horse Nine , which is currently making its way around the festival circuit and already generating Oscar buzz, particularly for lead actor John Malkovich . Set shortly before the 1973 military coup in Chile, Wild Horse Nine stars Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as Chris and Lee, longtime CIA partners stationed in Santiago who are dispatched to Easter Island by their bureau chief, MJ (Buscemi) to assist in the U.S.’s covert campaign to undermine the democratically elected Chilean government. Against the surreal backdrop of the island’s monumental Moai statues, the pair begin reckoning with their murky shared past. “I love coming to Zurich, and it’s a tremendous honor,” said the British-Irish creative on the carpet ahead of his ceremony. “I’m excited. I know it’s a great, very cine-literate audience, so I hope they’ll like [ Wild Horse Nine ] as much as the other ones.” He said about travelling to Easter Island: “I visited maybe 15 years ago, and was just struck by the beauty of the place, [and] also the mystery of the Moai heads, and I thought it could be almost a character in a film, and it’s turned out to be that way. I’d worked with Sam Rockwell obviously a bunch of times before, so that’s always a joy. But John Malkovich was new to me, and he’s just perfect for the part. He’s funny and he’s dangerous. And Steve Buscemi and Parker Posey were fantastic too.” These aren’t the only awards Zurich is dishing out. Tom Hiddleston received the Golden Eye on Thursday night as the fest opened with his Everest drama, Tenzing , and John Turturro will also be given the same honor for his starring role in this year’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York . The 22nd Zurich Film Festival runs Sept. 24-Oct. 4. THR

articles.title: Calls From the Dead, a Madrid Dystopia and Kids Swap Among Writers’ Show Pitches as Iberseries
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 26, 2026 1:00am series projects writers and screenwriter Carmen Llano Courtesy of Iberseries & Platino Industria Iberseries & Platino Industria’s sixth edition takes place in Madrid this week, and its jam-packed schedule includes the Thursday, Oct. 1 presentation of six series projects developed by seven screenwriters as part of a collaboration with Fundación SGAE, Spain’s primary collective management organization for intellectual property rights. The series will be in focus during one of the pitching events that will showcase the projects to producers, buyers, investors and other audiovisual industry professionals. The event is designed as “an opportunity to foster the production, financing and international reach of new fiction projects, while reinforcing one of the objectives of Iberseries & Platino Industria: to facilitate connections between creative talent and the different players in the Ibero-American audiovisual industry,” the event organizers highlight. Related Stories Movies Julianne Moore Accepts Zurich's Golden Icon Award -- in German Movies 'NAZA' Trailer: First Look at 'No Other Land' Directors' Gaza Doc That Sparked Netanyahu Backlash Below, THR takes a closer look at the six series projects being pitched in Madrid . La librera by Virginia Burgos (Seville) and Juan Sánchez (Madrid) Synopsis : In the early 1990s, a woman opens the first LGBT bookstore in our country. Over several decades, the business becomes a refuge and a political backroom for an entire community. But the day comes when the neighborhood she helped build turns its back on her, leaving her no choice but to ask herself: “What do you do when nobody needs you anymore?” Takeaways : An LGBT community force and pioneer faces the blues. Do you get the feeling that people will want to find out more about this woman and what is changing for her? Avión by Miguel Cavadas (Vigo) Synopsis : Avión is the village that embodies the utopia of Galician emigration: leaving poor and returning rich. In winter, it is yet another example of rural precarity and aging. In summer, it becomes a festival of money, ranchera music and Mexican flags. Its population quadruples, returning to celebrate, enjoy themselves and show off the transatlantic feat. A microcosm that is neither here nor there, but the coexistence of two worlds that have little or nothing to do with one another: community and individualism, past and present, Galicia’s lowest pensions and Mexico’s greatest fortunes. What happens when those two worlds collide? Takeaways : Don’t expect a theme song like “Sur le Pont d’Avión (Avignon)” for this one – the show sounds much darker and more like a social clash drama that moves you to take a closer look at Galicia. El capricho by Alberto Grondona Synopsis : El capricho is a satirical historical comedy about three women vying for power at the 18th-century Spanish court: Queen María Luisa of Parma, the charismatic Duchess of Alba and the enlightened Duchess of Osuna. Their battles for influence, image and desire, in a Spain on the brink of collapse, are observed and narrated with fierce irony by Francisco de Goya, an uneasy witness who turns palace intrigue into a surprisingly contemporary mirror. Takeaways : A female-led comedic Game of Thrones with Spanish fire and twists will surely turn heads – even if it may remind viewers of the end times. Teléfonos fijos by Ángel Mirou Synopsis : In the modest Recalde neighborhood of Bilbao, landline phones ring in the early hours, waking those who still have them installed in their homes. When they pick up, residents hear the voices of relatives, friends or acquaintances. The callers have only one thing in common: they are dead. Whether the calls are proof that something exists after death or an elaborate fraud based on cutting-edge technology, the lives of those involved will never be the same again. Takeaways : I hear dead people. But in the age of tech scams and AI, can we trust my ears – or your eyes, for that matter!? La edad menor by Roberto Osa Synopsis : In a dystopian Madrid where children become the legal guardians of their parents, María confronts the system when her mother is admitted to La edad menor, an irreversible process of infantilization. While her brother is torn between his sister and power, a devastating secret will reveal that neither resistance nor sacrifice is enough to stop oblivion. Takeaways : Power to the kids! You may look at politicians in your country and think this could actually work. But let’s be honest: there’s something that sounds worrisome, even sinister, about this synopsis. We’ll have to see what’s actually going on here. Trueque by Pedro Pablo Picazo Synopsis : Three families who are very close friends struggle daily with the teenagers at home. Each family has solutions for the others’ children. What if they swap them? What could possibly go wrong? Takeaways : Forget Honey, I Shrunk the Kids! Here comes Honey, I Swapped the Kids . THR

articles.title: Academy CEO Bill Kramer Doubles Down on YouTube Move: “You’ll See a Very Different-Looking Oscars”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 26, 2026 5:42am Zurich Summit 2026 The Hollywood Reporter Does AMPAS CEO Bill Kramer feel as though they’re taking a risk by moving the awards ceremony to YouTube in 2029? “It almost feels risky not to do it,” said Kramer at the Zurich Film Festival Summit event on Saturday afternoon. In a talk titled “The Theatrical Box Office Resurgence! How to Get Audiences’ Attention in the Era of Social Media and Online Platforms?”, Kramer was joined by Backrooms filmmaker Kane Parsons, president and chief content officer at Mattel, Robbie Brenner, and co-president at Sony Pictures Classics, Michael Barker. Related Stories TV Calls From the Dead, a Madrid Dystopia and Kids Swap Among Writers' Show Pitches as Iberseries Movies Julianne Moore Accepts Zurich's Golden Icon Award -- in German Following Kramer’s keynote speech at the Swiss summit, he doubled down on taking the Oscars — which has aired on ABC in the U.S. since 1976 — to YouTube, in a deal that will bring the film industry’s biggest night to millions more people, translated into 30 different languages, for free. He told the room: “As we become more global as an organization, the best way for us to reach a global audience of film lovers, film fans, [and] young artists is YouTube. I think the timing this year — Obsession , Backrooms , you and Curry [Barker],” he said, talking to Parsons. “[It’s] moving in the other direction from YouTube to theatrical for us; we’re an organization that celebrates theatrical filmmaking, but at the same time, the Oscars is a television show, and we want to reach a large audience.” YouTube allows the Academy to directly engage with their audience and film fans in a way that “we just can’t do right now,” continued Kramer. “It gives the Academy more control in engaging with fandom and film lovers and film fans and viewers of the Oscars. Right now more people outside of the U.S. watch the Oscars than in the U.S., and this allows us to capture that audience a lot more,” he said. When probed by Deadline ‘s Andreas Wiseman if he believes the deal to be risky, Kramer said: “Not at all. It almost feels risky to not do it because we’re looking at the future, and the deal starts in [20]29, so that’s our 101st Oscars. And with each month, a larger percentage of the TV-watching audience is on YouTube, and those numbers are increasing. So I don’t think it’s a risk. We have a great partnership with Disney right now. I have to say they’ve been amazing partners and will continue to be for the next two years. But we’re already deep in discussions with [YouTube CEO] Neal Mohan and his team, so I think you’ll see a very different-looking Oscars that allows you to engage with the show in more interactive and deep ways than we can do right now.” He responded when Wiseman asked if the deal was lucrative: “It was a good deal.” As part of the deal, YouTube will broadcast not only the Oscars ceremony itself — which generated $150 million in revenue for the Academy from 2024 to 2025, the vast majority via the TV rights deal with Disney — but also a significant amount of related content. Also coming to YouTube: red carpet pre-show and behind-the-scenes in-show content; the Oscar nominations announcement; the Governors Awards, at which the Academy presents honorary Oscars and occasionally the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award and the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award; the Oscars Nominees Luncheon; the Student Academy Awards ceremony; the Scientific and Technical Awards ceremony; Academy member and filmmaker interviews; film education programs; podcasts and more. The TV audience for the 2026 Oscars declined , drawing 17.86 million viewers on ABC and Hulu, based on Nielsen’s big data plus panel ratings. That’s down about 9 percent from 2025’s Oscars, which drew 19.69 million viewers for a post-pandemic high, and the smallest audience for the awards since 2022, when 16.68 million people watched. The 22nd Zurich Film Festival runs Sept. 24-Oct. 4. THR

articles.title: Kane Parsons Recalls ‘Backrooms’ Trailer “Activated a Desire to See: How Did Hollywood Mess This Up?”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 26, 2026 6:14am Kane Parsons photographed in 2026 Courtesy of Getty Twenty-one-year-old Kane Parsons is reflecting on a whirlwind summer in which the box office was undoubtedly bolstered by the release of his feature debut, Backrooms . Speaking with some of the industry’s top executives at the Zurich Film Festival Summit on Saturday afternoon, the young director spoke about the health of the 2026 box office, which has catapulted YouTube natives Parsons and Obsession ‘s Curry Barker to the top of Hollywood. In a session titled “The Theatrical Box Office Resurgence! How to Get Audiences’ Attention in the Era of Social Media and Online Platforms?”, Backrooms filmmaker Kane Parsons was joined by Academy CEO Bill Kramer , President and chief content officer at Mattel, Robbie Brenner and co-president at Sony Pictures Classics, Michael Barker. Related Stories Movies Academy CEO Bill Kramer Doubles Down on YouTube Move: "You'll See a Very Different-Looking Oscars" TV Calls From the Dead, a Madrid Dystopia and Kids Swap Among Writers' Show Pitches as Iberseries Parsons actually confessed he doesn’t think of A24’s Backrooms , starring Renate Reinsve and Chiwetel Ejiofor, as a traditional horror film. “I didn’t direct it like a horror film. I don’t view it as a horror project. I think that’s just naturally the path of least resistance from a marketing perspective, and it’s what seems comfortable to people as a framing device,” he said. “But I’m going to try to stay as oblivious to those labels as possible, and just focus on [what] think I have greater control now with future projects, so those sort of structures [should] probably be a little less forceful, I think.” He also explained, when asked about how A24 tried to sculpt the marketing and distribution plan for the film, that he believed there wasn’t “a real sense of what it would be prior to the actual release of the film. […] I don’t think there [was] a feeling for what this would really be tapping into with people […], all these people who were familiar with [Parsons’ YouTube series] the Backrooms for years in some vague way. Suddenly, as soon as a trailer [came] out, it just activated a desire to see: ‘How did Hollywood mess this up?'” he remembers. “Or it [was] just a curiosity at the very least. And I like to think we did the core idea that they were familiar with justice.” Justice might be an understatement — the film went on to generate an eye-watering $401 million at the global box office upon its May release. During the panel in Zurich, Backrooms ‘ success was cited as a prime example of a younger generation’s desire to go to the movies. “There’s an appetite,” said Parsons, “[of] Backrooms being a pre-existing but decentralized IP presence online. I think people are just looking for that newness, [a] detachment from more cyclical cultural icons that keep eating themselves,” he said about Hollywood’s tendency to churn out projects rooted in overworked IP. Kramer chimed in to say that he didn’t realise YouTube and movie-going were so well-connected, “in a way that I don’t think we thought was possible. That for me was a big takeaway of this summer,” continued the AMPAS CEO, “and it gives me great hope for the film industry because […] we’re seeing young people come back to the movies, and that’s really key.” He explained: “More than half of our ticket buyers [at the Academy Museum] are under the age of 40, and we sell out every screen. So people love seeing movies in movie theaters. We just needed to attract new fans, and you helped do that, this summer,” Kramer said to Parsons. Parsons concurred. “I think the notion that people around my age gravitate towards short-form material is…,” said Parsons, before Kramer added: “Reductive.” The young director agreed. “Yeah, it’s reductive. I hear that come up a fair bit. [It might be] statistically truthful, but I feel like the sentiment is more that [short-form content] is weaponized, algorithmically incentivized, and it’s not really something I think most people enjoy about their own wiring. They don’t love that their attention spans are being sucked into the spiral of mostly consuming stuff that is that short.” Backrooms follows therapist Dr. Mary Kline (Reinsve), who enters an alternate dimension after her patient disappears inside it. The film adapts Parsons’ viral YouTube series, which he launched as a teenager. However, Parsons was understandably coy about the prospect of a sequel on Saturday, simply telling Zurich: “We’ll see.” The 22nd Zurich Film Festival runs Sept. 24-Oct. 4. THR

articles.title: Scarlett Johansson Takes Break From Filming Overseas for ‘Paper Tiger’ NYFF Premiere After Skipping Cannes: ‘I’m Hallucinating’
articles.full_text: Sep 25, 2026 6:16pm PT Scarlett Johansson Takes Break From Filming Overseas for ‘Paper Tiger’ NYFF Premiere After Skipping Cannes: ‘I’m Hallucinating’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Scarlett Johansson Takes Break From Filming Overseas for ‘Paper Tiger’ NYFF Premiere After Skipping Cannes: ‘I’m Hallucinating’ 12 hours ago New York Film Festival Boss on Scoring ‘Artificial’ and ‘Behemoth’ World Premieres and Why Movies Are ‘Unavoidably Political’ 24 hours ago Paige DeSorbo on Leaving ‘Summer House’ Behind and Speaking Out About a Past Abusive Relationship: ‘Domestic Violence’ Can ‘Truly Happen to Anyone’ 3 days ago See All Getty Images A very jet-lagged Scarlett Johansson reunited with co-stars Adam Driver and Miles Teller for the New York Film Festival premiere of “ Paper Tiger ,” which kicked off the festival’s 64th edition. “I’m hallucinating,” said Johansson, who just got off a long international flight, where she’s filming another movie. “It’s 5 in the morning — which is a great time to be doing an interview on stage.” Related Stories SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture “Paper Tiger” premiered in May at the Cannes Film Festival. However, this marked Johansson’s first time watching the movie (at least in a festival setting); she missed the Cannes premiere because she was shooting yet another movie, “The Exorcist: Martyrs.” Popular on Variety “Don’t rub it in!” Johansson joked about her absence on the French Riviera. Set in 1986, “Paper Tiger” follows two brothers, Irwin and Gary Pearl, whose get-rich-quick scheme to help clean up the Gowanus Canal lands them in the crosshairs of the Russian mafia. Johansson plays Linda, wife of Teller’s character. Johansson, Driver and Teller walked the red carpet with Gray at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall and sat for a post-screening Q&A, during which they spoke about their close camaraderie during production. “No work required. There’s a mutual admiration between the four of us,” Driver said. “A set culture comes from the top down, and James sets a culture where everyone feels free. We immediately felt comfortable with each other.” Added Gray, “We had a nauseatingly lovely set. I love them. I’m not on the Today show. I’m telling you the truth.” Scarlett Johansson, Miles Teller and Adam Driver introduce “Paper Tiger” during the 64th New York Film Festival. Getty Images for FLC Before the screening began, Gray took the stage and consciously kept his intro remarks short and sweet. “When I was in film school many years ago, students would show their films, and the students that talked the most [before] often made the very worst movies,” he said. “So I am going to speak very briefly.” Gray praised the producers and actors who helped bring the film to life and reflected on his early dreams of being a filmmaker. “I can’t help but remember my mother and father when I said I wanted to be a movie director. ‘How are you ever going to do that?’ And here I am,” Gray said. “I’m not sure the lesson in that.” NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim introduced Gray as “one of the great living American filmmakers” and praised the director for championing a “singular” artistic vision. “It’s not easy to make personal films in the current landscape of American cinema,” Lim said. “The fact that there are 24 executive producers credited on this film, like, who speaks to that.” New York Film Festival’s 64th edition, which runs through Oct. 12, will host the world premieres of “Artificial,” Luca Guadagnino’s buzzy movie about OpenAI founder Sam Altman; Ava DuVernay’s documentary “14th”; director Tony Gilroy’s music drama “Behemoth!” with Pedro Pascal, Olivia Wilde and Will Arnett; and Takashi Yamazaki’s kaiju sequel “Godzilla Minus Zero.” “Premiere status is never the be-all and end-all for us,” NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim told Variety ahead of opening night. “Timing is always part of it. But I think we’ve proved in the last few years that we create a pretty interesting context for the launch of a film.” “Paper Tiger” filmmaker James Gray (center) with the film’s stars Roman Engel, Miles Teller, Scarlett Johansson, Adam Driver and Gavin Goudey. articles.title: ‘Hanuman Ansh’ Indian Sleeper Hit’s International Distribution Strategy Unveiled by ‘K.G.F,’ ‘Kantara’ Outfit Hombale Films (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 25, 2026 7:09pm PT ‘Hanuman Ansh’ Indian Sleeper Hit’s International Distribution Strategy Unveiled by ‘K.G.F,’ ‘Kantara’ Outfit Hombale Films (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Hanuman Ansh’ Indian Sleeper Hit’s International Distribution Strategy Unveiled by ‘K.G.F,’ ‘Kantara’ Outfit Hombale Films (EXCLUSIVE) 11 hours ago Tokyo Film Festival Unveils Mizoguchi Retrospective, Anime Award Symposium and Teens Cinema Workshop Milestone 1 day ago Aamir Khan to Receive Screen Icon Award as Singapore Film Festival Opens With Hur Jin-ho’s ‘The Assassin(s)’ 1 day ago See All Hombale Films Indian devotional film “ Hanuman Ansh ” has grossed more than $3.5 million outside its home territory since Hombale Films took it to international audiences, and the company behind the blockbuster “ K.G.F ” and “ Kantara ” franchises has now detailed how it engineered the run. Written and directed by Vishal Chaturvedi and adapted from his book “Divine Detour: That Changed My Life,” the film follows Lakshman Das, a boy who leaves home after his mother dies, searching for the divine. Years of wandering and meditation later, he becomes the saint Neem Karoli Baba, known to devotees as Maharaj-ji. Shobhinaw Satyaa plays the title role opposite Chandan Anand, with Vihaan Shedge as the teenage Maharaj-ji and Anil Rastogi and Purnima Tiwari in supporting roles. Chaturvedi produced with Ragini Sona, Namrata G. Singh and Anupriya A. Nagar under his Swambhu Media Network banner. Related Stories SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture “Our strategy involved taking ownership of all global territories and collaborating with the biggest local partners in each region to ensure the best possible release footprint. By leveraging the data and learnings from our previous releases like ‘Mahavatar Narsimha,’ we were able to tap into the right locations and cinema chains. This targeted approach has yielded spectacular numbers,” says Hombale Films producer Chaluve Gowda. Popular on Variety The Bengaluru banner partnered with Phars in the GCC and Prathyangara in North America, and the film opened internationally on Sept. 11. It marks a first for the company. “‘Hanuman Ansh’ is the first film outside of our own productions that we have full fledgedly distributed internationally. We truly believed in this project, as it perfectly aligns with our vision of taking Indian stories global,” Gowda says. North America leads the overseas tally, with $1.8 million from the U.S. and Canada, according to Hombale’s territory figures. Australia and New Zealand contributed $606,716 and the Gulf Cooperation Council region $577,870, with the U.K. adding $269,837. Singapore brought in $61,334 and Europe $41,171, while the rest of the world accounted for $483,006. Hombale previously backed the animated “Mahavatar Narsimha,” which went on to do more than INR300 crore ($31.3 million) in business. At home, the film has been a sleeper. Made for approximately INR2 crore ($209,000), “Hanuman Ansh” opened in India on Aug. 7 on some 250 screens through Cinépolis India. Word of mouth pushed it past 2,000 screens, and it has since grossed INR340.7 crore ($35.5 million) in seven weeks. Chaturvedi has planned the film as the first part of a trilogy. “We will always support the makers in bringing their ultimate vision to life. These are exactly the kinds of stories we want to champion as a production house, and we will continue to back creators who dare to tell such grand stories with all their heart,” Gowda says.
