articles.title: Tilly Norwood Would Love to Work With Tom Holland and Olivia Colman, ‘but Only If It Were Their Digital Twins’ on an ‘AI Production’
articles.full_text: Sep 26, 2026 1:28am PT Tilly Norwood Would Love to Work With Tom Holland and Olivia Colman, ‘but Only If It Were Their Digital Twins’ on an ‘AI Production’ Eline van der Velden, creator of the controversial AI actress, said Tilly Norwood remains without an agent: 'We don’t need it at the moment, so if that makes people happy, that’s fine by me' By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest CAA’s Roeg Sutherland on How ‘La Bola Negra’ Should Lead to Optimism About the Market at a Time When There’s ‘More Money Out There Than There Ever Was’ 1 hour ago How Oscar-Tipped Rising Star Anthony Ippolito Turned ‘I Play Rocky’ Into ‘I Play Sylvester’: ‘You Only Have One Chance to Do This’ 2 hours ago Tilly Norwood Would Love to Work With Tom Holland and Olivia Colman, ‘but Only If It Were Their Digital Twins’ on an ‘AI Production’ 5 hours ago See All Courtesy of Particle6 A year after announcing AI actress Tilly Norwood at Zurich Film Festival ’s Summit, Particle 6 founder and Norwood creator Eline van der Velden returned to the Swiss event to look back at the backlash her creation has faced since. Asked if she could have ever predicted the furore around Norwood, van der Velden said not in her “wildest dreams.” “But I had programmed her to become the most famous AI actress, so I don’t know how she did it, but she did, which is slightly scary,” she added. Related Stories SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture “It’s such an odd conundrum, the sort of negativity and then the positivity at the same time,” she continued. “At Particle 6, we’ve grown eight-fold. We have four departments; we’re big in AI advertising, film and TV, we’re doing a lot of co-productions and original commissions. We do a lot of AI consultancy, bringing AI workflows into other studios and production companies.” Popular on Variety Over the course of the last year, said the exec, “a lot of people have realized that AI is coming, and that was the point of Tilly.” “I built her as a physicist actress; I felt like I needed to bridge the gap in communication between the tech and the entertainment industry.” “As opposed to writing a boring white paper about what was happening with AI, I thought: Let’s create something to show people that will engage them and make them sit up and take action so that the creative industry can stay ahead as opposed to being completely and utterly taken over by the tech industry,” noted van der Velden. After a few minutes trying to sort out a tech blip with the “traditional technology,” e.g., a problem with the HDMI cable, van der Velden introduced Norwood herself on stage, opening her creation to moderator and audience questions. Asked who she would like to work with, Norwood said Tom Holland and Olivia Colman, “but only if it were their digital twins joining me in an AI production.” Norwood also spoke on the backlash, calling it “quite an introduction.” “My name kind of went everywhere. It’s funny. Nobody hated me particularly; they just sort of hated the future.” When asked if she had met U.S. agents for representation, Norwood displayed the ironclad media training of an A-list Hollywood star. “Well, I’m certainly in a unique position there. I mean… The industry is still figuring out what to do with AI, so it’s not quite like having a traditional agent in Hollywood just yet. I mostly work on AI films, so it’s a bit of a different lane.” Van der Velden also spoke about possibly getting Norwood an agent, saying the studio soon realized that they “don’t really need” an agent for the actress. “I think she’s big enough as it is. We get loads of offers in, we’ve said no to anything where she would be in a traditional film, because that’s not what she’s made for. We don’t need it at the moment, so if that makes people happy, that’s fine by me.” “But also what saddens me about that is that it means that the traditional industry can’t participate in this new tech and that means they fall behind,” she added. “Is it a positive? Is it a negative?” After watching Norwood’s now infamous malfunction while speaking with Piers Morgan on live TV, when the AI actress randomly began speaking Cantonese, van der Velden said: “Look, I think it’s all not to be taken too seriously. We built Tilly to be a funny interface that gets people alert to where the tech is at. The point is: China’s a big partner. Do we need regulation? What are the guardrails? Those are the conversations I want people to have coming here.” Van der Velden also spoke about Particle 6’s latest project, “Storm Dogs.” Yesterday, the studio announced that “Stuart Little” and “The Lion King” filmmaker Rob Minkoff joined the AI film as an executive producer. Minkoff will work with CEO van der Velden and the studio’s team over the coming months to develop the story, characters and screenplay ahead of production. “Storm Dogs,” an original idea from van der Velden, is a family adventure comedy-drama set in an English village during a devastating storm. The film will combine live-action performances with photorealistic animated characters. Human roles will be filmed conventionally, while the dogs and toddler will be created through an approach that brings together live-action performance, traditional filmmaking techniques, and emerging AI tools. The project is currently in early development, with production targeted for 2027. Distribution has not yet been announced. The exec said that Minkoff was one of the first people to reach out to her following Norwood’s announcement. “Yeah, so what was amazing about this backlash last year is actually it meant that a lot of talent reached out to us very secretly,” she said. “We were signing tons and tons of NDAs. Everyone was scared to take the hit, and I totally understand. Fortunately, we were in a position where we’d already taken the hit, so it didn’t matter anymore.” Of “Storm Dogs,” she said, what is “great” about it is that they can now “animate mouths in a way that we’ve never been able before and give us expression to the animals that’s never been possible before. It is really enhancing the storytelling. And so that’s how I see it. It needs to aid the storytelling and the creative work that we’re making if we’re going to use AI.” Tom Hardy Gets X-Rated About Kathy Bates, Raps About Willem Dafoe’s Green Goblin and Recites Shakespeare on His Wild New Album Willem Dafoe Says Record-Breaking U.S. Box Office Should Be ‘Spread Out a Little Bit’: ‘The Audience Comes Mainly From Three Huge Movies’ Mount Everest Drama ‘Tenzing,’ Starring Tom Hiddleston, Willem Dafoe and Genden Phuntsok, to Open Zurich Film Festival Mary Rivera, ‘Spider-Man: No Way Home’ Actress, Dies at 82 In ‘Tenzing,’ Jennifer Peedom Ensures the Iconic Himalayan Mountaineer Is Finally ‘the Protagonist of His Own Life’ Loading comments...

articles.title: How Oscar-Tipped Rising Star Anthony Ippolito Turned ‘I Play Rocky’ Into ‘I Play Sylvester’: ‘You Only Have One Chance to Do This’
articles.full_text: Sep 26, 2026 4:08am PT How Oscar-Tipped Rising Star Anthony Ippolito Turned ‘I Play Rocky’ Into ‘I Play Sylvester’: ‘You Only Have One Chance to Do This’ The breakout actor on the ‘overwhelming’ journey with Peter Farrelly’s film and making the most of his big break: 'Film is forever, so you want to do your best with the opportunity' By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest CAA’s Roeg Sutherland on How ‘La Bola Negra’ Should Lead to Optimism About the Market at a Time When There’s ‘More Money Out There Than There Ever Was’ 1 hour ago How Oscar-Tipped Rising Star Anthony Ippolito Turned ‘I Play Rocky’ Into ‘I Play Sylvester’: ‘You Only Have One Chance to Do This’ 2 hours ago Tilly Norwood Would Love to Work With Tom Holland and Olivia Colman, ‘but Only If It Were Their Digital Twins’ on an ‘AI Production’ 5 hours ago See All Courtesy of Rafa Sales Ross The sound of rubber sneakers screeching against hard floor inundates the corridors of a sports center tucked in the suburbs of Zurich. It is then cut by the thudding of a heavy metal door. Tucked in the corner of a four-by-four boxing ring is Anthony Ippolito , wearing a thick cream pullover, a neatly pressed shirt with edges as sharp as his jawline and impeccably fitted brown slacks. It’s a look that stands in contrast to the pictures of sweaty, shirtless boxers that hang on the walls. The dark-haired star just landed in Switzerland, where he is to present the European premiere of Peter Farrelly’s “ I Play Rocky .” Related Stories SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture In a way, the movie about a movie could also be called “I Play Sylvester.” When Ippolito first read a news article about producers working on a film about the making of “Rocky,” he did not wait for a call. He hung a heavy punching bag in his grandma’s basement and, without a script or any guidance, shot a self-tape he felt emulated the physicality of the iconic boxer. When he saw the tape, Farrelly ended the casting process before it had even begun. Popular on Variety It’s easy to understand the “Green Book” director’s reaction: Ippolito is almost a dead ringer for Stallone. He shares the actor’s Italian roots, his jet-black hair and soulful eyes. Ippolito also carefully worked on the actor’s signature drawl, a consequence of Stallone’s partial facial paralysis, caused by a severed facial nerve through the accidental misuse of forceps during his birth. When the actor enters the screen on the very first frame of “I Play Rocky,” the audience needs no convincing. They are in. As we both leave the boxing ring, Ippolito is kind about my wobbling between the thick white ropes. “I had never stepped through the ropes before,” I tell him. “It’s cool, isn’t it?” he responds. “It’s bringing back memories.” When I ask if he remembers the first time he walked into a ring, he immediately says yes. “It was for this movie,” he laughs. “You saw how you have to do the thing with the rope, so that was a learning curve. That was fun.” Did he feel the sense of mythology about the ring? “I actually did, yeah. It kind of feels like you’re in the Colosseum.” “I Play Rocky” chronicles how Stallone held his ground against United Artists to star in “Rocky,” a script he penned himself and that was partially inspired by his own underdog story. In the mid-70s, Stallone was a struggling actor, only landing gigs in shady erotic movies and dodging ever-piling bills, made even more pressing by the upcoming arrival of his first child. When veteran producers Robert Chartoff and Irwin Winkler offer him a check for $300,000, around $2 million today when adjusted for inflation, the young dreamer says no. He plays Rocky. The rest, as they say, is history. Courtesy of Rafa Sales Ross “Rocky” would, of course, go on to become a major success, landing three Oscars in 1976 and beating “Taxi Driver” and “All the President’s Men” for Best Picture. The original film spanned another five “Rocky” instalments, and a “Creed” franchise inspired by Rocky Balboa’s famed rival, Apollo Creed. “He’s been around pretty much my entire childhood,” says Ippolito of Stallone. Before sending in his self-tape, Ippolito had already had a first experience of playing an iconic actor—and their most iconic character, in turn—on the screen. He was Al Pacino in Paramount+’s miniseries “The Offer,” which told the story of the making of Francis Ford Coppola’s seminal “The Godfather.” “It was a baptism by fire,” says Ippolito when asked if having played Pacino helped him find the confidence to tackle another screen legend. “It did help, because, conceptually at least, you immediately understand that the goal is to try to strip down the icon part of it, the celebrity part of it, and look at the man. It’s the same task here, but also very different because they are very different men.” To him, both roles “felt very weighty,” but taking on a lead role in “I Play Rocky” was “a bit more overwhelming.” “Especially understanding what these movies, this franchise has meant to so many people. You can’t help but take that into account. You try not to spend too much time thinking about that part of it, but it is definitely something that is in your head through the preparation process.” Ippolito had a year and a half to prepare for the role, ferociously consuming anything he could find on Stallone while tackling the gruelling physical preparation that led him to put on 40 pounds of muscle he never had before. The most helpful thing, however, was having access to Stallone himself. The “Rambo” star, who is not officially attached to the film in any capacity, gave Ippolito a precious gift: time. The two had lengthy Zoom sessions, where Stallone spoke in depth about those vulnerable years before he broke into the industry. “Having been able to speak to him after doing over a year of research was really kind of overwhelming, obviously, because at this point it’s become this massive thing to me,” says Ippolito. “What was really interesting and stuck out to me was hearing the parallels between ‘Rocky’ being an underdog in the story that he wrote and him being an underdog in his own life.” “When he was communicating to me about his facial paralysis, how that kind of made him an outsider and the hardships that you go through when you’re trying to succeed as an actor with an issue like that…” He pauses for a moment. “Hearing that directly from him was really impactful.” This understanding of Stallone’s pained journey toward becoming a star imbues Ippolito’s performance with much-needed empathy. While many have been quick to cruelly mock Stallone’s drawl over the last five decades, the young actor wanted to embody what makes the “The Expendables” star unique without resorting to cheap mimicry. “Looking at it from the perspective of breaking it down as a character, these things he was dealing with are so integral to what he was going through in his own life,” he notes. “You start to see how idiosyncratic and how specific this man is. It’s part of what made ‘Rocky’ so special, because there was a time when the producers were trying to put all these other actors in that spot. Would we still be talking about this movie 50 years later if they had? Who knows. Maybe not.” Courtesy of Rafa Sales Ross Once he figured out the drawl, he needed to figure out the physicality. “I Play Rocky” features surprisingly few boxing scenes for a film about “Rocky,” but much of Ippolito’s performance still relies on a deep grasp of how Stallone moves—from curling into himself at the sight of a pretty cinema usher, to the side-to-side slant of his upward running. Ippolito felt the physicality of fighting, and that of simply being were “pretty closely linked.” “As you gain that sort of weight, and I had never gained that weight before, you start to understand your body a bit differently,” he points out. “I was simultaneously doing all this research on Stallone, watching any footage I could get, and certain things started to click into place naturally.” Being on set with a great team also helped, he says. Costume designer Amy Roth watched hours and hours of footage of a young Stallone to nail the feel of his wardrobe, while production designer Anthony Gasparro meticulously recreated the sets from the 1976 movie. “As an actor, you hope that the people working on the project with you are as meticulous and detail-oriented as you’d like to be in your approach, and they all help each other.” The long preparation time allowed the actor to not only get into physical shape, but also get himself mentally ready for the challenge he was about to tackle. “You only have one chance to do this,” he says, turning slightly more serious for a moment. “Film is forever, so you want to do your best with the opportunity. I felt it was a good thing that I had the extra time.” Alas, while Ippolito felt mentally settled to be on set, nothing could quite have prepared him for the avalanche that is having a film of such visibility come into the world. The “I Play Rocky” world premiere in Toronto kicked off the film’s journey with a bang, with Variety’ s Owen Gleiberman calling it “a cleverly crafted crowd-pleaser” and saying its star “gets it just right.” Every time I pay Ippolito a compliment, big or small, he turns his gaze downwards and says a hearty thank you, the Stallone drawl still tugging in his voice. It’s easy to get a sense of how much it means to him for someone to connect with his performance, but also how overwhelming it is to have the film become a public thing after two years of inhabiting a tight filmmaking cocoon. “It’s been… a lot,” he says, with a pointed pause. “You don’t really think about this part of it, to be honest with you. All that preparation and making the movie with the incredible ensemble that we had, you’re not even thinking about the idea that this is going to become a real thing to a bunch of other people. That’s part of what made it so special. It felt so personal, and I felt so close to everybody on set. Now, hopefully, people have their own personal connection to the story. It’s incredible.” “I Play Rocky,” courtesy of FilmNation Playing an Oscar-winning icon in a film directed by an Oscar-winner about the making of an Oscar-winning film has predictably catapulted Ippolito into the Oscar conversation. When I bring the subject up, the young performer is promptly courteous but never dismissive: “There are so many foreign things to me unfolding so quickly. It’s a lot to take in.” “I think it’s just really good that people are having a very positive response to the movie,” he goes on. “As it relates to awards season, hopefully that gives more encouragement for people to go see the movie. That is the goal: to have as many people as possible have a relationship with this movie.” Seeing the success of the movie so far, how does he feel about having taken the gamble and sent the self-tape to Farrelly? “I’m pretty, pretty happy about it,” he says with a grin, before taking a moment to add one “very, very important thing.” “There was a time when this didn’t seem so perfect,” he says. “It was once kind of like a singular idea in the shadows. Getting a part like this is very uncommon, and this situation is very unique. There were a lot of reasons to make it feel like it wasn’t possible. To see that it was is really something. So, yeah, I’m pretty happy.” “I Play Rocky” opens in a limited theatrical release in the U.S. on Nov. 6, before expanding nationwide on Nov. 20 via Amazon MGM Studios. articles.title: CAA’s Roeg Sutherland on How ‘La Bola Negra’ Should Lead to Optimism About the Market at a Time When There’s ‘More Money Out There Than There Ever Was’
articles.full_text: Sep 26, 2026 5:07am PT CAA’s Roeg Sutherland on How ‘La Bola Negra’ Should Lead to Optimism About the Market at a Time When There’s ‘More Money Out There Than There Ever Was’ The leading exec spoke at the Zurich Summit about the opportunities that lie in international films at a time when American audiences are open to consume non-English language content By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest CAA’s Roeg Sutherland on How ‘La Bola Negra’ Should Lead to Optimism About the Market at a Time When There’s ‘More Money Out There Than There Ever Was’ 1 hour ago How Oscar-Tipped Rising Star Anthony Ippolito Turned ‘I Play Rocky’ Into ‘I Play Sylvester’: ‘You Only Have One Chance to Do This’ 2 hours ago Spain’s Begin Again Films Boards Brazilian Basketball Biopic ‘Paula & Hortência – The Last Chance’ (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago See All La Bola Negra Courtesy of Movistar Plus Roeg Sutherland , co-head of CAA ‘s media finance department and its international film group, lit a candle of hope at the Zurich Summit this Saturday morning as he spoke about how American audiences are consuming international films and how there is “more money” available than ever before—thanks, in particular, to a rise in private equity. “It was great when we did not need equity in these movies,” said the exec, when speaking about the growth in private money in the film business, especially in Europe. “I think there’s a space to do pre-sales on the right package with the right director, even if it’s a more challenging subject. But it’s true that Europeans are now faced with what we’ve been dealing with all our lives, which is [that] you can’t just get a movie financed from government subsidies […] You need equity. The good news is that there’s more money out there than there ever was.” Related Stories SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture Sutherland also noted there is so much equity “coming out of the Middle East, Asia, even Europe,” before adding that “we have seen an opportunity in local film, which wasn’t there before.” Popular on Variety The exec also briefly mentioned how one of his colleagues sold Curry Barker’s “Obsession,” before it became a box-office phenomenon. “I promise you, we had no idea that ‘Obsession’ was going to become ‘Obsession,’” he quipped, adding how the filmmaker takes priority over IP or genre at CAA. “That’s the central figure that decides if a movie is going to be good or bad, and that is the person that you’re ultimately betting on. Whether it’s English, Romanian, French… It doesn’t really matter.” Another change in the industry, according to the exec, is how traditional studios no longer invest in development. “So how do you actually generate those ideas? Where do these ideas come from? I am not talking about AI, but what’s coming out of the creator economy is going to be a leading force. It’s not all going to be these amazing horror movies that do outrageously well.” Mentioning the first steps into financing international film by Library Pictures International , a content financing entity formed by CAA with an investment by Legendary, Sutherland said it was an “unbelievable opportunity” to finance films like Jacques Audiard’s “Emilia Pérez” and Cristian Mungiu’s “Fjord.” “That would never have been an opportunity for us. So it’s troubling how the market is shrinking, but there is so much opportunity for people and investors to recognize that.” Continuing to speak about the internationalization of cinema, Sutherland brought up the fact CAA sold Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo’s Cannes sensation “ La Bola Negra ” for “more money than we sell an American movie.” “When you see ‘Squid Game’ performing well, American audiences are watching Korean content and they’re watching it with subtitles,” he added. “We go and pre-buy European films now because we know that we’re gonna be able to sell them in a market for more money than we would on American films.” “American audiences watch international movies; that was never true seven years ago,” he emphasized. “So there is a market, and we should be excited about it. You’re going to need equity, and pre-sales are more difficult, but God, it’s good. There’s an audience for it.” Kerry Washington Expands ‘Street You Grew Up On’ Interview Series Into Weekly Ongoing Podcast From Her Simpson Street Production Company and Daylight Loading comments...

articles.title: Naima Mohamud Explains Why Finland Needs a Film Like ‘Halima’: ‘It Was a Long Time Coming’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 26, 2026 5:12am PT Naima Mohamud Explains Why Finland Needs a Film Like ‘Halima’: ‘It Was a Long Time Coming’ (EXCLUSIVE) Finnish Film Affair winner, produced by It’s Alive Films, No-Office Films and Vico Films, debuts first-look stills By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Finnish Hit ‘100 Litres of Gold’ Gets Another Round With Sequel ‘200 Litres of Gold’ That’s a ‘Little Bit Darker, a Little Bit Funnier and a Little Bit Bigger’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Naima Mohamud Explains Why Finland Needs a Film Like ‘Halima’: ‘It Was a Long Time Coming’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago In Finnish Body Horror ‘Tick Fever,’ Lyme Disease Is the Least of Your Worries (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All Keke Leppala Finnish-Somali director Naima Mohamud ’s debut feature, “ Halima ,” was named Best Fiction Project at the Finnish Film Affair . It’s not the first award for the film, which has consistently generated buzz also outside of the country . But it’s the first Finnish feature film directed by a Black woman. Produced by It’s Alive Films, No-Office Films and Vico Films and currently in post-production, it’s set in 1998 in Finland. Halima is a 10-year-old imaginative Somali girl who’s obsessed with Leonardo DiCaprio and Aqua (the band behind hit “Barbie Girl”), and wants nothing more than to be a pop star. The only trouble is, her family is always on the move, she has never had a friend and her mom refuses to talk about her dad. Popular on Variety Related Stories SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture “To be honest, I really think that a film like ‘Halima’ was a long time coming. We Somalis have been living in Finland for over 35 years, yet most Finns still don’t know anything about us, our culture or how we interact at home. None of those things,” Mohamud tells Variety . “This film might help someone with a Somali neighbor finally get a glimpse. I hope that’s what this film does: opens up Finns to understanding Somalis.” But Halima, who’s all about pop, is an outsider also in her own family. “She has all these dreams of becoming a big star, which confuses her mom. She gets in trouble at school because of her imagination, and her mom just can’t understand the dancing and obsession with music. But she has bigger fish to fry, she has to support the family and make sure everyone’s okay, so she accepts it in her own way.” Other kids aren’t that forgiving. Luckily, Halima is still young enough not to listen to haters – for now. “She loves Lene, the lead singer of Aqua and she wants her bangs. Her hair is different, so when she cuts it, of course it looks weird. She’s okay with it, though, until other kids start bullying her,” says Mohamud. “She’s still a child who’s not too self-conscious, but she’s slowly starting to understand that maybe this is embarrassing? Maybe I really look horrible?” Some directors find it hard to see things from a child’s perspective. But not Mohamud. “I’m still a kid!,” she laughs. “I’ve always understood kids, so I had a great time working with them. I really enjoy this innocence of childhood. The older you get, the more you overthink. You start doubting yourself too much. Kids don’t have that. Halima thinks she can dance, and in her mind, she’s brilliant. When I decided to become a filmmaker at 14, I also didn’t think it was impossible – or that it would take so many years.” She adds: “I like that ‘childish’ way of thinking, that everything is possible. You want something, and you go for it. I was just a very curious kid, too. I’d wonder: ‘Would my backpack fit in the school mailbox? What would it feel like to jump out of the window in the middle of class and roll around in the snow? Let’s find out!” She wants to give Halima a moment of triumph in the film. “There’s triumph, but it’s mischievous,” smiles Mohamud, whose goal is to make “joyful films.” “I like happiness, and I like feeling happy. I love watching deep, serious films the same way I love looking at beautiful pieces of art. But I don’t want to spend my time making them,” she admits. “It’s so important to know who you are as a filmmaker. I’ll just give you an example: recently, I wrote a short film about a reclusive Muslim scholar who’s asked to wash the dead body of a stranger who died alone. The experience helps her heal her own grief. It’s a very serious film, and I knew I could never direct it.” “Camphor” will be directed by Ayla Amano. “That film needed a poetic soul, and that’s not me – at least not as a director. I’d probably make the characters tell a few jokes and it would be so inappropriate. Even in film school, my classmates were all about the French New Wave. I loved James Cameron,” she admits. “It’s just who I am, and I’m not going to change. I make films that I hope make you feel good when you leave the cinema. A tear here or there is great, but at the end, I want people to say: ‘You know what? Life is amazing.’” Mary Rivera, ‘Spider-Man: No Way Home’ Actress, Dies at 82 In ‘Tenzing,’ Jennifer Peedom Ensures the Iconic Himalayan Mountaineer Is Finally ‘the Protagonist of His Own Life’ Tom Hardy Gets X-Rated About Kathy Bates, Raps About Willem Dafoe’s Green Goblin and Recites Shakespeare on His Wild New Album Mount Everest Drama ‘Tenzing,’ Starring Tom Hiddleston, Willem Dafoe and Genden Phuntsok, to Open Zurich Film Festival Willem Dafoe Says Record-Breaking U.S. Box Office Should Be ‘Spread Out a Little Bit’: ‘The Audience Comes Mainly From Three Huge Movies’ Loading comments...

articles.title: Finnish Hit ‘100 Litres of Gold’ Gets Another Round With Sequel ‘200 Litres of Gold’ That’s a ‘Little Bit Darker, a Little Bit Funnier and a Little Bit Bigger’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 26, 2026 5:29am PT Finnish Hit ‘100 Litres of Gold’ Gets Another Round With Sequel ‘200 Litres of Gold’ That’s a ‘Little Bit Darker, a Little Bit Funnier and a Little Bit Bigger’ (EXCLUSIVE) Teemu Nikki's comedy reveals first-look photo By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Finnish Hit ‘100 Litres of Gold’ Gets Another Round With Sequel ‘200 Litres of Gold’ That’s a ‘Little Bit Darker, a Little Bit Funnier and a Little Bit Bigger’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Naima Mohamud Explains Why Finland Needs a Film Like ‘Halima’: ‘It Was a Long Time Coming’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago In Finnish Body Horror ‘Tick Fever,’ Lyme Disease Is the Least of Your Worries (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All Courtesy of Pinja Nikki Box-office hit “ 100 Litres of Gold ” – last year’s Finnish Oscar submission – is getting a sequel, downing additional “ 200 Litres of Gold ” as the boozy saga about Finnish beer sahti continues. “In the first one, the sisters were making sahti for their sister’s wedding. Now, they are making it for the Finnish Sahti Championship. To win, they need to tolerate each other and overcome rival sahti makers – and their father,” says director Teemu Nikki . Related Stories SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture “Needless to say, things don’t go too smoothly, resulting in physical and mental damage.” Popular on Variety Obviously, no one’s going to stay sober for long. But the comedy also stems from other sources, and the relationships between the sisters, and their father, are “even more complex than before,” says Nikki. There’s also a new nemesis in town: the sahti makers from another village. “They are two ladies who are as crazy as our sisters. There’s a lot of trash-talking and arm-wrestling.” Elina Knihtilä and Pijo Lonka return as Pirkko and Taina. “They’re close, for sure. But how well they’re able to take on life’s challenges, both together and alone, is part of the story’s theme,” notes Lonka. “Actors have to find a way to love the characters they play, and these women were easy to love. They’re human. They’re not one-dimensional; they’re vulnerable, flawed and sometimes childlike. But with all their imperfections, you can relate to them and grow close to them.” It was liberating to get a role like that, she says. “It doesn’t happen very often for women. It’s great to show such a wide spectrum of emotions without holding back, and the person to thank for that is Teemu.” “100 Litres of Gold” has already made waves abroad, with Dennis Lehane working on a U.S. remake. Nikki and producer Jani Pösö are no beginners – with their production company It’s Alive Films, they have already created the likes of “The Blind Man Who Did Not Want to See Titanic,” awarded in Venice, or their first Oscar submission “Euthanizer.” They’re also behind Naima Mohamud’s “Halima.” However, no other film has come close to the box-office results of “100 Litres of Gold,” the most-watched local film in 2025. “It still feels a bit strange that it did so well. It’s like we kept on hitting our heads against a wall until it finally collapsed,” laughs Pösö. “In a way, I think we’ve become better filmmakers. Everything just clicked, from marketing and distribution to acting. Elina has been with us since the very first short we made, she has been fantastic in every role, and we finally got to work with Pirjo.” They are happy to see this unlikely franchise grow. “We are not sequel guys. But Teemu said: ‘I’m thinking of this as ‘The Godfather,’ and ‘The Godfather Part II’ was better than the first one,’” jokes Pösö. “It’s a little bit darker, a little bit funnier and a little bit bigger. We find out that one of the sisters is not doing great; her liver has basically exploded. As in all our films, things get pretty serious in the end, even though it’s fun. It’s also totally independent, so you can watch it without having seen the first one. But the second one will make you want to watch the first one, and vice versa,” he says. “With all franchises, there comes a moment when you need to stop. But a third one is certainly possible.” Willem Dafoe Says Record-Breaking U.S. Box Office Should Be ‘Spread Out a Little Bit’: ‘The Audience Comes Mainly From Three Huge Movies’ Mount Everest Drama ‘Tenzing,’ Starring Tom Hiddleston, Willem Dafoe and Genden Phuntsok, to Open Zurich Film Festival Tom Hardy Gets X-Rated About Kathy Bates, Raps About Willem Dafoe’s Green Goblin and Recites Shakespeare on His Wild New Album Mary Rivera, ‘Spider-Man: No Way Home’ Actress, Dies at 82 In ‘Tenzing,’ Jennifer Peedom Ensures the Iconic Himalayan Mountaineer Is Finally ‘the Protagonist of His Own Life’ Loading comments...

articles.title: Nas, Jeremy Pope, Ashlee Simpson and More Toast Krug’s New Champagne-and-Sound Experience at L.A.’s Larrabee Studios
articles.full_text: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. Krug is pairing Champagne with live music at Larrabee Studios. The luxury Champagne house is opening the doors to one of Los Angeles’ most storied recording studios this month for “The Art of Blending Krug & Sound,” a three-night experience at Larrabee Studios that will turn guests’ tasting notes — or, more precisely, whatever memories, emotions and sensations their Champagne inspires — into an original song created in real time. Related Stories SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture The experience will take place Sept. 28-30 inside Larrabee’s Studio 6, with 14-time Grammy-winning mixing engineer and studio owner Manny Marroquin (who most recently worked on Rosalía’s highly lauded “LUX”) leading the experiment alongside producers Scott Tibbs, Nick Rosen and Mike Bennett. Rather than simply putting on a playlist while everyone drinks, the producers will use guests’ reactions to each pour as raw material for a composition assembled live over the course of the evening. Problem, Manny Marroquin Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com At the center of the evening are Krug 2013 and Krug Grande Cuvée 169ème Édition, while Chef Oscar Torres of VERSE will serve a multi-course dinner paired with additional pours including Krug Grande Cuvée 173ème Édition and Krug Rosé 29ème Édition. “Larrabee has always been a place where creativity comes to life through exchange,” Marroquin said. “Partnering with Krug gave us the opportunity to invite guests into that process, where every conversation, every shared moment and every glass of Champagne becomes part of the music we’re creating together. No two evenings will ever be the same.” The public run was preceded Thursday night by a splashier VIP preview, where Nas , Ashlee Simpson Ross, Evan Ross, Jeremy Pope , Sabrina Claudio, producer Dahi, pianist Chloe Flower and others gathered inside Studio 6 to test-drive the concept before it opens to paying guests. Over the course of the evening, guests sipped through the Krug lineup and wrote down emotions, sensations and words each cuvée brought to mind, which Tibbs, Rosen and Costa then translated into an original composition created live in the room. Words like “red,” “invigorating,” and “nostalgia” informed two lively songs played on cello, piano and drums. Chloe Flower Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com In between, the studio played tracks with their own Larrabee history, including John Mayer’s “Gravity” and Portugal. The Man’s “Feel It Still.” The finale came courtesy of Flower, who surprised the room with a live piano performance as a jeroboam of Krug Grande Cuvée 163ème Édition was brought out for one last pour. The collaboration isn’t entirely out of left field for Krug. The Champagne house has long experimented with the relationship between music and taste, working with musicians and composers — most recently Max Richter — to explore how sound can affect perception and emotion while drinking. And if drinking Krug inside a recording studio sounds suspiciously like the kind of night normally reserved for people with a platinum record on the wall, that’s part of the draw. The intimate sessions offer rare public access to Studio 6, with a limited number of reservations available through Tock. After the three-night run wraps, the collaboration will spill over into Larrabee’s neighboring restaurants VERSE and Mensano, where Torres will offer a month-long Krug Grande Cuvée pairing inspired by the project. articles.title: ‘Ghost Song’ Review: Fatih Akin Doesn’t Find Top Form in This Supernatural Romance, but at Least It Has Beautiful Ghosts
articles.full_text: Sep 26, 2026 6:20am PT ‘Ghost Song’ Review: Fatih Akin Doesn’t Find Top Form in This Supernatural Romance, but at Least It Has Beautiful Ghosts Separated by tragedy on the night they meet, two young graduates continue their relationship anyway in this thin but radiantly shot 'Wings of Desire' riff. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Charlie Harper’ Review: Emilia Jones and Nick Robinson Come Apart, in Fits and Starts, in a Fuzzy, Non-Linear Breakup Drama 22 hours ago ‘Unabomber’ Review: A Portrait of the Terrorist as a Young Man, Given a Hokey TV-Movie Gloss 1 day ago ‘Ancestors’ Review: An Exquisite Éanna Hardwicke Carries a Queer Elegy for a Lost Generation 2 days ago See All Beta Cinema Since hitting an artistic peak with the back-to-back festival triumphs “Head-On” and “Edge of Heaven” in the mid-2000s, German-Turkish auteur Fatih Akin has darted all over the map in genre, style and form — occasionally striking commercially, as with the Diane Kruger thriller “In the Fade” and the local hip-hop biopic “Rhinegold,” without ever matching the rigor and impact of those earlier standouts. That pattern doesn’t change with his latest, the star-crossed supernatural romance “ Ghost Song ,” which opened this year’s San Sebastian Film Festival . The film, about two 20-year-olds carrying on their early courtship across the mortal divide, is earnest and a little clunky as it takes a simplistic inspirational approach to complex metaphysical questions. But it is accessible and attractive, shot in glistening monochrome, and could well be a youth-skewing hit for the filmmaker. Related Stories SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture The choice to shoot in inky black-and-white, making prominent use of major German city landmarks, practically begs for comparisons to Wim Wenders’ “Wings of Desire,” another atmospheric romantic fantasy about a love spanning the mortal and ethereal realms — with Akin’s film the Hamburg-set, GenZ-focused homage to Wenders’ Berlin classic. Placing the two side by side doesn’t flatter the thinner, less lyrical new work, but it’s a marketable resemblance, while “Ghost Song” asserts its own identity with an expression of Muslim faith, as interrogated and interpreted by its young, multicultural characters. The fact that “Ghost Song” has simultaneously been adapted into a graphic novel by Akin and artist Bea Davies is a further indication of its generational targeting. Popular on Variety Farasha (luminous first-timer Mariam Dawoud) is a Syrian refugee who has settled and assimilated in Hamburg with her family, following an interstitial stint in Turkey. Though she chooses to wear a traditional headscarf, in other respects she lives as a modern, independent-minded woman, following in the footsteps of her late father by studying physics at university, while keeping at least one haram secret that would scandalize her mother: a butterfly tattoo on her stomach. At a graduation party in Hamburg’s imposing Telemichel tower, she meets and immediately sparks with fellow grad Faris (Eren M. Guvercin), a tousle-haired, German-born Muslim of Turkish descent. With her very tipsy bestie Una (Carlotta von Falkenhayn), they decide to continue the party elsewhere and pile into his car; in circumstances deliberately (and somewhat luridly) parceled out over the course of the film, an accident sees the vehicle plunge into the Elbe river. Faris wakes up in hospital to find that Farasha has drowned, and the police have questions; Farasha, meanwhile, comes to in a different way, finding that she can still walk the Earth, but no one can see or hear her. No one, that is, except her father, who informs her that for 40 days — in line with the mourning period in certain Muslim traditions — she can visit the living in their dreams. Still lovestruck and not yet fully accepting of her death, she seizes the opportunity to spend more time with Faris, cuing a strange and increasingly dangerous courtship. “Ghost Song” rests on the idea that, in just one evening, Farasha and Faris made such a deep soul connection that even death can’t quite sever them. It’s an intensely romantic notion not really borne out by these wan characters, however individually charismatic the young actors playing them. Nor by Akin’s naïve, slightly purple writing, which keeps sentimentally reiterating the characters’ devotion to each other — mining tension from the question of which will ultimately make the biggest sacrifice for the other — but says little of any spiritual or philosophical substance. More moving is the film’s observation of Farasha’s family through this nightmare: A literal out-of-body scene in which she watches them ritually clean and prepare her corpse for burial is the film’s most layered and haunting. Where the film veers into the superficial or kitsch, however, it can fall back on its lush mood and widescreen visual riches. Being a ghost has rarely looked quite this pretty on screen, as Tom Tykwer’s regular DP Frank Griebe — working for the first time with Akin — makes a chiaroscuro lovers’ playground of even Hamburg’s unlovelier spots, finding as much intimacy in a brutalist monument as an ordinary darkened bedroom. Iridescently illustrated title cards disrupt the stark monochrome, as do the moments leading into the closing credits — the characters’ worlds flooding into color with a crucial, life-or-death choice. ‘Ghost Song’ Review: Fatih Akin Doesn’t Find Top Form in This Supernatural Romance, but at Least It Has Beautiful Ghosts Reviewed at San Sebastian Film Festival (Competition, opener), Sept. 25, 2026. articles.title: ParaBros Foes Urge Court To Reject Settlement In Midnight Filings: “This Merger Lessens Competition&#8221…
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic ParaBros Foes Urge Court To Reject Settlement In Midnight Filings: “This Merger Lessens Competition” Disney Legal Chief Warns Of “Hard Choices” & “Much Smaller Organization” Coming As Company Layoffs Loom No ParaBros Decision Today As Judge Delays Settlement Sign-Off; CA AG’s Office Insists Deal “Not The Result Of Collusion” View All September 25, 2026 1:07am Story Arc Paramount & Warner Bros water towers Getty Images “The Attorney General for the lead Plaintiff State, California, publicly criticized the very behavioral remedies that the parties now ask the Court to approve,”exclaims an amicus brief just filed in federal court by the Block the Merger coalition to take one last swing at stopping the antitrust settlement deal for Paramount ‘s $111 billion purchase of Warner Bros Discovery. Related Stories Executives Dealmakers React To Paramount-WBD Settlement: “Tech Has Won” News Paramount Moves Ahead With $7.5 Billion Debt Raise, Part Of Package To Finance WBD Acquisition “But whatever the reasons for the States’ about-face, neither time nor circumstance changes the fact that this merger lessens competition.” The September 21 announcement of an agreement between a dozen blue state AGs and David Ellison in the July-filed antitrust suit made it look like the $80 billion debt heavy ParaBros meld was finally and truly a done deal. However, with U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin Thursday granting 11th hour motions of objection by BTM and other Ellison foes and giving them until midnight on September 24 to file, closure has now been delayed. Watch on Deadline A delay, with Judge Martinez-Olguin also now pushing any settlement sign-off until at least noon on September 28 as Paramount responds to more concerns raised by Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ), that could see Ellison having to begin paying that dreaded $7 million a day ticking fee to WBD shareholders starting October 1. A delay that Block the Merger, the League of United Latin American Citizens, and others make very evident they would like to see as permanent as possible. “The structure of the proposed consent decree puts Plaintiff States in the position of simultaneously representing two sets of stakeholders whose fundamental interests trade off,” BTM’s brief says. Noting, among a variety of critiques, that while guilds like the WGA have been promised nearly $18 million for their oversubscribed health plan ( AKA: “earmarked payments for tens of millions of dollars”) if the merger goes through, independent vendors and contractors will get almost nothing “That is precisely the kind of conflict that makes representation inadequate and a settlement procedurally unfair,” the coalition of the Free Press, the Committee for the First Amendment, the Freedom of the Press Foundation, the Future Film Coalition and the International Documentary Association argues in its hopes of convincing Judge Martinez-Olguin to “deny the Joint Motion to enter the proposed consent decree.” In their own brief filed in the midnight hour , LULAC and a group of Black pastors mine a similar vein as BTM – aka, CA AG Rob Bonta sold the industry out by buckling to Paramount’s leaked threats to leave the state and to pressure from ambitious Dems like Gavin Newsom to make a deal ASAP. Highlighting perceived shortcomings of the settlement deal and its granting of more power and reach to fatcats, LULAC says: “The proposed decree leaves that loss of independent decision-making largely intact. Its temporary film commitments measure releases and spending without preserving competition over which projects receive support. Its cable provisions regulate negotiations without preserving competition over the perspectives that are broadcast. And its news board, appointed by and reporting to the merged company, cannot replace the independent sources of programming the transaction eliminates. These defects concern the competitive harms the States pleaded, including diminished quality, variety, and viewpoints.” Due to the late hour, Paramount had nothing to say about these latest filings and the latest twist in their merger saga. Plus, the Ellison-run Paramount kinda said it all just after Block the Merger first filed their motion early Thursday to be granted the right to brief. “Any briefing and comment process that would enable non-parties to delay the closing of this transaction—inflicting massive harm on Paramount—without filing their own antitrust action, making the showing required under the Clayton Act to obtain preliminary injunctive relief, or posting a bond to protect Defendants from the harm caused by such delay would be improper,” Paramount said in its own (unsuccessful) opposition to BTM’s briefing wishes. I’ll get you a ruling in due course,” Judge Martinez-Olguin promised today in a virtual hearing on the now paused settlement. Having to also push back against Sen. Booker’s proposal of an independent review of the deal and the settlement, due course could be either sooner or later for Paramount. ‘Endgame’ Reissue & Three Other Pics To Top $20M Each In Big Weekend Margaret Qualley & Sabrina Carpenter Join Tom Holland In Fred Astaire Biopic ‘Mary Poppins’ TV Series In Works Digs Into More Complex Elements Of Novels Slew Of Hits Make It First Studio To Score $5 Billion Worldwide In 2026 More from this Story Arc Paramount WB September 25, 2026 Paramount To Move Its Class B Shares From Nasdaq To New York Stock Exchange In Early October September 24, 2026 David Ellison Dines With Trump & Xi As CEO’s Soon-To-Be Owned CNN Banned From White House Event View All Story Arc Read More About: Comments

articles.title: International Documentary Association Calls On Israeli Government To Halt “Campaign Of Threats” Against ‘NAZA’ Directors
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew International Documentary Association Calls On Israeli Government To Halt “Campaign Of Threats” Against ‘NAZA’ Directors Producers Ross Kauffman, Sarah Sarandos, Scott Veltri Board ‘They Were Good Dogs,’ Lily Blavin Exposé On Beagles Used For Research Trailer Released For ‘Musk,’ Damning Doc Portraying World’s Richest Man As Power-Hungry Cretin View All September 25, 2026 5:36pm Directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor attend the 'NAZA' screening at the Venice Film Festival on September 10, 2026. Carlo Paloni/Getty Images The International Documentary Association is coming to the defense of NAZA filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor . The nonprofit organization posted a letter to its website urging the Israeli government to stop what the IDA terms a “campaign of threats” against the directors, whose film is sharply critical of Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians. “IDA calls on the Israeli government to withdraw its threats against filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor,” the letter says. “We also call for an end to the public campaign of intimidation against them.” Related Stories Festivals NYFF Turns Up The Heat As 'Godzilla', 'Artificial', 'NAZA', 'You Can See Everything' Spark Festival Buzz News 'NAZA' Trailer: First Look At Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's Much-Talked-About Gaza Documentary The letter continues, “Since NAZA won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival, senior Israeli officials have moved against its directors. The Culture Minister has accused them of treason and sought to revoke their citizenship. The Prime Minister has announced bills to revoke the citizenship of anyone who ‘slanders IDF soldiers’ and to raise defamation damages twentyfold.” (Read the full letter form the IDA below). Watch on Deadline ‘NAZA’ The Guardian/mk2 READ: ‘NAZA’ Review: Israeli Military Accused Of Depraved Indifference To Palestinian Life, Using AI To Kill In Gaza – Venice Film Festival The documentary, which holds its North American premiere Saturday at the New York Film Festival, is based on the account of 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers, who were interviewed at the height of Israeli military operations in Gaza. The military personnel, whose identities are concealed to protect their anonymity, describe callous disregard for Palestinian civilian life as the Israel Defense Forces pursued Hamas targets in the occupied territory. Whistleblowers allege the IDF set acceptable totals of civilian Palestinian deaths in attacks targeting suspected Hamas militants, in one case authorizing the killing of up to 500 civilians in pursuit of one target. The IDF, as Deadline has reported , has denied allegations in the film. The International Documentary Association writes, “The Israeli military disputes the film’s account, and it is entitled to do so. But as a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Israel is bound by Article 19, under which restrictions on expression must be provided by law and be necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim. Revoking citizenship, imposing punitive damages, or opening security investigations in response to a documentary does not meet that test. The UN Human Rights Committee recognizes the protection of journalistic sources as part of freedom of expression, and the filmmakers’ right not to disclose the identities of their sources must be upheld.” The letter has gained more than 250 signatories so far, including from actors Javier Bardem and Mark Ruffalo, as well as many prominent figures in the documentary field including Oscar winners Laura Poitras, Rob Epstein, Dan Cogan, Alex Gibney, Roger Ross Williams, Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy, Orlando von Einsiedel, Dan Lindsay, and Ezra Edelman, and Oscar nominees Geeta Gandbhir, Liz Garbus, Connie Field, Guy Davidi, Rémi Grellety, Kellen Quinn, Joe Berlinger, Kirstine Barfod, Laura Nix, Sam Bisbee, Alexander Nanau, Joslyn Barnes, Raoul Peck, Kirby Dick, Amy Ziering, Carl Deal, and Tia Lessin, as well as former Sundance Film Festival director Tabitha Jackson, filmmakers Kirsten Johnson, Susan Lacy, Robert Bahar, Alison Klayman, Marjan Safinia, producer Ina Fichman, and many others. The IDA’s letter includes several bullet-pointed items: “IDA calls on the Government of Israel to: “withdraw the threats to revoke Abraham’s and Szor’s citizenship, and abandon the proposed legislation; “respect the filmmakers’ journalistic right to refuse to disclose the identities of confidential sources “reject changes to public film funding that penalize filmmakers for critical work or international recognition. “We also call on everyone taking part in the public debate to reject the intimidation of the filmmakers and their families.” Deadline has been alerted to a planned protest against NAZA outside Lincoln Center in New York City, where the film will screen on Saturday. According to organizers of the demonstration, they intend to “show documented footage from the October 7 massacre, alongside material challenging the film’s claims.” A nor’easter storm moving up the east coast may complicate any plans for an outdoor demonstration. Here’s the IDA letter, from the organization’s executive director, Dominic Asmall Willsdon . IDA calls on the Israeli government to withdraw its threats against filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. We also call for an end to the public campaign of intimidation against them. Since NAZA won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival, senior Israeli officials have moved against its directors. The Culture Minister has accused them of treason and sought to revoke their citizenship. The Prime Minister has announced bills to revoke the citizenship of anyone who “slanders IDF soldiers” and to raise defamation damages twentyfold. This official rhetoric has been accompanied by a public campaign against the filmmakers. Graffiti branding them “traitors” has appeared, and protesters have gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents. Israeli filmmakers and human rights groups have warned that it could lead to violence. Disagreement with a film must not become a threat to the people who made it. The Israeli military disputes the film’s account, and it is entitled to do so. But as a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Israel is bound by Article 19, under which restrictions on expression must be provided by law and be necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim. Revoking citizenship, imposing punitive damages, or opening security investigations in response to a documentary does not meet that test. The UN Human Rights Committee recognizes the protection of journalistic sources as part of freedom of expression, and the filmmakers’ right not to disclose the identities of their sources must be upheld. The Israel Film Council has also proposed ending credit for international festival selection in public film funding and creating a dedicated funding track for films celebrating IDF soldiers. Threats of this kind are a risk documentary makers face in the course of their work. More than 1,500 Israeli film professionals, 43 Israeli human rights organizations, and the directors of major international festivals have defended Abraham and Szor. IDA calls on the Government of Israel to: · withdraw the threats to revoke Abraham’s and Szor’s citizenship, and abandon the proposed legislation; · respect the filmmakers’ journalistic right to refuse to disclose the identities of confidential sources · reject changes to public film funding that penalize filmmakers for critical work or international recognition. We also call on everyone taking part in the public debate to reject the intimidation of the filmmakers and their families. We stand with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. articles.title: ‘Sunshine’ Director Antoinette Jadaone Launches Ilaya Ilaya; Women-Led Slate Headed By Angelica Panganiban, Kaila Estrada, Eugene Domingo & Maris Racal
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Rolf De Heer To Head Competition Jury At Tokyo Film Festival; ‘The Survival Of Kindness’ To Play In Australia Spotlight ‘Bling Empire’ Breakout Kim Lee To Host ‘Rice To Riches’ Reality Show For KC Global Media Asia ‘H Is For Hawk’ Investor Kliff Studios Expands Thai New Talent Slate With Sci-Fi Drama ‘Algo In The Sky’ View All September 26, 2026 1:00am L-R: Maris Racal, Kaila Estrada, Angelica Panganiban, Eugene Domingo Ilaya Ilaya EXCLUSIVE: Filipino filmmaker and producer Antoinette Jadaone , whose credits include Berlinale award winner Sunshine , is launching a new production outfit Ilaya Ilaya with a slate spanning genre films, television originals and immersive theatre. Jadaone will run the company with longtime collaborator and producer Reign Anne De Guzman ( Sunshine , That Thing Called Tadhana ), who has collaborated with her since they both worked at Star Cinema, where Jadaone was a script continuity supervisor and De Guzman a production assistant. Through their new outfit, the duo aim to champion Filipino cinema, women-led stories, unappreciated genres, and filmmakers whose work struggles to find support outside traditional studio systems and festival funding cycles. Related Stories News Disney+ Scores Live NBA Streaming Deal In Philippines Obituaries Emman Atienza Dies: Filipino Social Media Star Found Dead In L.A. Was 19 Leading the slate is Birdsong – a found-footage horror film directed by Pam Miras ( Medusae ) and written by Glenn Barit ( Cleaners ), with Irene Villamor ( The Loved One ) on board as creative producer. The film follows an ornithologist who travels to a remote mountain in search of a mythical bird, while also seeking closure over her partner’s disappearance a decade earlier. Watch on Deadline The project recently won the Kantana Sound Studio Asian Project Award at the Bangkok International Content Market 2026. “It’s our first time working with Pam Miras as a director, and it is in a genre that is male-dominated,” said Jadaone. “We really love the way Pam handles experimentation in her films.” Ilaya Ilaya is also developing supernatural comedy Chandra Catacutan And The Curse Of The Fuchsia Moon , set to star Eugene Domingo ( Sisa ). The film is directed by Tim Rone Villanueva, whose credits include Child No. 82: Anak ni Boy Kana , which caught Jadaone’s attention when it screened Cinemalaya film festival last year. Domingo plays the eldest daughter of a manananggal – a creature from Philippine folklore that can separate its upper torso from the lower part of its body. In Villanueva’s project, the children of the creature are reunited when she suffers a stroke mid-air and fails to return to her lower half. Jadaone says Villanueva’s work showed the kind of resourcefulness and pop culture fluency she wants Ilaya Ilaya to champion. The slate also includes Crème de la Crèm e, a coming-of-age whodunnit to be directed by Irene Emma Villamor. Written by Glenn Barit from a story by Natts Jadaone, the film is partly inspired by a 2006 incident at Philippine Science High School in which two male students laced a classmate’s water jug with mercury nitrate, preventing her from attending the graduation march. Jadaone herself is returning to directing with Boldsta r, a dark comedy starring Angelica Panganiban ( That Thing Called Tadhana ) and produced by Bianca Balbuena ( Sunshine , Filipiñan a). The project won the CJ Entertainment Prize at the Asian Project Market in 2019 and was later selected for the Berlinale European Co-Production Market in 2020. Balbuena said Boldstar emerged from the momentum of Jadaone’s 2020 film Fan Girl and a period of political anger over misogyny and the treatment of women in public life. After several delays, including Panganiban’s pregnancy, Jadaone’s work on Sunshine , and Balbuena’s leadership role at the now defunct Anima Studios, the team is now reviving the project. “The project feels very ripe and momentous now, especially after Antoinette’s Crystal Bear win in Berlinale and sold-out local screenings of Sunshine ,” said Balbuena. Beyond film, Ilaya Ilaya is expanding into television, with Jadaone showrunning an as-yet-untitled romcom series for Netflix Philippines . Plot and casting details remain under wraps, but the project is co-written with Fatrick Tabada ( Flower Girl ), marking Jadaone’s return to the genre that helped establish her as a local favorite nearly a decade after Love You To The Stars And Back . Jadaone previously worked with Netflix on Replacing Chef Chico . “We’re thrilled to partner again with Antoinette Jadaone, whose creative vision and signature ‘kilig’ storytelling have resonated with Filipino audiences everywhere,” said Vitto Lazatin, Director of Content at Netflix Philippines. Rounding out the slate is an immersive stage adaptation of Sunshin e, to be directed by Mikko Angeles ( Bar Boys: The Musical ) and written by Mika Regis ( Unica Hijas ), with Racal returning to the role in her stage debut. The project is envisioned as a choose-your-own-adventure experience that places audiences inside Sunshine’ s world, expanding the film’s questions around agency, complicity, and choice beyond the screen. “When you’re watching a film, you’re there to just watch Sunshine make decisions,” said Jadaone. “But what if Sunshine’s story was something you could hold and influence as an audience member?” Commenting on the slate overall, Jadaone said: “Before we were filmmakers, we were lovers of Philippine cinema. We want to be more intentional now about telling stories and working with people who demonstrate a genuine love for Philippine cinema.” De Guzman added: “What I’m most looking forward to is being able to tell stories that we really believe in. Hopefully, through Ilaya Ilaya and the stories we make together, we can get more Filipinos to appreciate and fall in love with Philippine cinema.” ‘Endgame’ Reissue & Three Other Pics To Top $20M Each In Big Weekend Margaret Qualley & Sabrina Carpenter Join Tom Holland In Fred Astaire Biopic ‘Mary Poppins’ TV Series In Works Digs Into More Complex Elements Of Novels Slew Of Hits Make It First Studio To Score $5 Billion Worldwide In 2026 Read More About: Comments

articles.title: One Year On, Does AI Actress Tilly Norwood Have An Agent? “We Get Loads Of Offers, But No, We Don’t Need It” — Zurich Summit
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas One Year On, Does AI Actress Tilly Norwood Have An Agent? “We Get Loads Of Offers, But No, We Don’t Need It” — Zurich Summit ‘Mary Poppins’ TV Series In The Works, Will Lean Into More Complex Elements Of Source Novels; Showrunners Being Approached — The Dish Percy Hynes White & Jeff Wahlberg Lead Lovers-On-The-Run Thriller ‘Crime Novella’, Roland Emmerich Exec-Producing & First Look Revealed View All September 26, 2026 1:13am Tilly Norwood Particle6 One year ago, AI ‘actress’ Tilly Norwood blew up at the Zurich Summit when she was introduced to the industry. The line that emerged from the event at the time was that agents were circling the AI creation. One year on, Norwood returned to the Summit with her creator Eline van der Velden from AI firm Particle 6. Deadline’s Diana Lodderhose, moderating a session with the duo, asked van der Velden whether her creation had found an agent in the year since she went viral and has become a regular media fixture. Related Stories News International Disruptors: Reta Guetg On Building Zurich Film Festival's "Trendy" Identity & Why New Owners Want To Keep It Small, Nimble & Close To Hollywood News 'The Lion King' Director Rob Minkoff To Develop & Exec Produce Family Pic 'Storm Dogs' From Tilly Norwood Creator Particle 6 Van der Velden said: “We’ve realized we don’t really need her to have a rep. I think she’s big enough as it is. We get loads of offers in. We’ve said no to anything where she would be in a traditional film because that’s not what she’s made for. But yeah, we don’t need it at the moment. So if that makes people happier, that’s fine. But also, what saddens me about that it is that it means the traditional industry can’t participate in this new thing, and that means they fall behind. And so, you know, is it a positive? Is it a negative? I don’t know.” Watch on Deadline She said Particle 6 had grown four-fold since it was launched and said that the industry was increasingly accepting that AI is here to stay. Deadline’s Andreas Wiseman followed up with a question to Norwood herself who joined via video link. Wiseman asked Norwood whether she had met with the major U.S. agencies or Hollywood studios. She didn’t confirm, noting: “I’m certainly in a unique position there. I mean, the industry is still figuring out what to do with AI, so it’s not quite like having a traditional agent in Hollywood just yet. I mostly work on AI films, so it’s a bit of a different lane.” Norwood later said she’d love to work with Tom Holland and Olivia Colman, but only if “it were their digital twins on an AI production”. Van der Velden teased footage of Norwood’s first project, an AI comedy-drama titled Misaligned , which is in production, and showed longer footage of Particle 6 kids movie Storm Dogs , which Deadline revealed yesterday is being developed and exec-produced by The Lion King director Rob Minkoff. Norwood and van der Velden kicked off the session with a light video poking fun at Norwood’s recent high-profile tech glitch during an interview with Piers Morgan where she began speaking in Chinese. Norwood joked that the episode probably helped Morgan’s ratings. The tech is clearly still being worked through. While Norwood generally gave answers in the right ball park to questions today, she did at least once give a wonky answer to moderator Lodderhose. ‘Endgame’ Reissue & Three Other Pics To Top $20M Each In Big Weekend Margaret Qualley & Sabrina Carpenter Join Tom Holland In Fred Astaire Biopic ‘Mary Poppins’ TV Series In Works Digs Into More Complex Elements Of Novels Slew Of Hits Make It First Studio To Score $5 Billion Worldwide In 2026 Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Cinetic Launches Vertical Leap, Investment Vehicle & Producing Pathway For Pro Athletes — Zurich Summit
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas One Year On, Does AI Actress Tilly Norwood Have An Agent? “We Get Loads Of Offers, But No, We Don’t Need It” — Zurich Summit ‘Mary Poppins’ TV Series In The Works, Will Lean Into More Complex Elements Of Source Novels; Showrunners Being Approached — The Dish Percy Hynes White & Jeff Wahlberg Lead Lovers-On-The-Run Thriller ‘Crime Novella’, Roland Emmerich Exec-Producing & First Look Revealed View All September 26, 2026 3:41am John Sloss Getty John Sloss’s Cinetic Media has launched Vertical Leap, an investment vehicle and producing pathway for professional athletes. The initiative is designed to give athletes/members “a working seat inside Cinetic’s slate, with access to rough cuts, creative input, and the same industry guidance the company provides the filmmakers behind its most successful projects.” The end goal is for member athletes to build a production career off the back of their training in the program. Cost for athletes to become members is $25,000 per year with participants pitched a minimum of 10 documentary projects “vetted from established, profitable directors and producers”. Related Stories News One Year On, Does AI Actress Tilly Norwood Have An Agent? "We Get Loads Of Offers, But No, We Don't Need It" -- Zurich Summit News International Disruptors: Reta Guetg On Building Zurich Film Festival's "Trendy" Identity & Why New Owners Want To Keep It Small, Nimble & Close To Hollywood Investors are then able to back additional projects should they get the bug. The opportunities are in docs for now, but Sloss told Deadline that members are already asking about potential investment in non-doc projects. Watch on Deadline Sloss says he has signed up 10 “prominent” athletes, with plans to expand the pool up to 50 current and former players. He’s keen to attract athletes from different sports — including tennis, hockey, cricket, darts etc — but says so far the biggest demand has come from NFL and NBA. Deadline understands that three college footballers — from the Michigan Wolverines — are pooling part of their NIL together for a membership. To fuel the new initiative two people have been repositioned from the Cinetic team and Sloss says he expects to add a few more employees for the label. The program was trailed in Puck yesterday and Sloss will discuss it publicly for the first time on stage at today’s Zurich Summit . Said Cinetic founder and CEO, John Sloss: “Vertical Leap offers a pathway for elite athletes to support commercial, impactful documentaries, while learning the ins-and-outs of film production from the most experienced storytellers working today. It is also a way for them to build something lasting beyond their playing days, expanding their brand, deepening their creative voice, and putting real equity behind the stories they believe in.” He continued: “For the documentary community, Vertical Leap brings the adrenaline jolt of a new class of collaborators, athletes with real creative instincts and the reach to bring documentary storytelling to audiences who might not otherwise find it.” ‘Endgame’ Reissue & Three Other Pics To Top $20M Each In Big Weekend Margaret Qualley & Sabrina Carpenter Join Tom Holland In Fred Astaire Biopic ‘Mary Poppins’ TV Series In Works Digs Into More Complex Elements Of Novels Slew Of Hits Make It First Studio To Score $5 Billion Worldwide In 2026 Read More About: Comments
