articles.title: ‘Backrooms’ Director Kane Parsons Distances $400M Hit From Horror Moniker: “I Don’t View It As A Horror Project”- Zurich Summit
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Tales Of Syria’s Disappeared; Lebanese Wartime Adoption & Palestinian Mental Health Set For Cinemed-Aflamuna Project Incubator Netflix-Acquired Animation ‘In Waves’ To Open The American French Film Festival In L.A. CAPA Deputy Director Unveils Sean Connery Doc; Talks Mission To Expand French Company’s International Reach View All September 26, 2026 6:41am Kane Parsons attends a 'Backrooms' special Screening on May 19, 2026 in London, England. Alan Chapman/Dave Benett/Getty Images for A24 Films Kane Parson’s $400M hit Backrooms , spinning off his web-series inspired by “creepypasta’ horror content on the internet, is invariably and understandably billed as a horror. The director told a panel at the Zurich Summit on Saturday, however, that he does not see it as being aligned with the genre. “I didn’t direct like a horror film. I don’t view it as a horror project. I think that’s just naturally been the path of least resistance from a marketing perspective and it’s what seems comfortable to people as a framing device,” he said, Related Stories News Cinetic Launches Vertical Leap, Investment Vehicle & Producing Pathway For Pro Athletes -- Zurich Summit News One Year On, Does AI Actress Tilly Norwood Have An Agent? "We Get Loads Of Offers, But No, We Don't Need It" -- Zurich Summit Parsons acknowledged that A24, which spearheaded the adaptation the web-series and distributed the movie, would not like his comments, but added he hoped to be able to avoid this sort of framing in the future. Watch on Deadline “I’m going to try to stay as oblivious to those labels as possible… I think I have more creative control now with future projects so those sorts of structures will probably be a little less forceful in the future,” he said. Parsons was talking on a panel on the $4.7 billion resurgence at the U.S. box office this summer, alongside Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences CEO Bill Kramer; President & Chief Content Officer Mattel Studios and Barbie producer Robbie Brenner and Sony Pictures Classics co-head Michael Barker. Kramer, Brenner and Barker all acknowledged the role played by Backrooms in the box office resurgence, alongside Obsession , which was also born out of the YouTube space. “ Backrooms was an amazing example… and speaks to one of the things that’s happening with our industry…. your fandom travelled from YouTube to the theaters,” said Kramer. “Young people want to go back to movie theaters. Fandoms shift. Theatrical can inform a fandom. YouTube can inform a theatrical fandom. It’s all connected in a way that I don’t think we thought was possible, and that for me was a big takeaway of this summer, and it gives me great hope for the film industry. ‘Endgame’ Reissue & Three Other Pics To Top $20M Each In Big Weekend Margaret Qualley & Sabrina Carpenter Join Tom Holland In Fred Astaire Biopic White House Blocks CNN From Air Force One Slew Of Hits Make It First Studio To Score $5 Billion Worldwide In 2026 Read More About: Comments

articles.title: SCAD Savannah Film Fest: Directors of 10 of 2026’s Top Documentaries Set for ‘Docs to Watch’ Panel (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All September 24, 2026 3:07pm (Top row, L to R) 'American Doctor,' 'Avedon,' 'Cookie Queens,' 'Everest: The Other Side' and 'The Last First: Winter K2'; (bottom row, l to r) 'My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile,' 'Once Upon a Time in Harlem,' 'One in a Million,' 'The Trial of Alec Baldwin' and 'You Can See Everything.' Ibrahim Al-Otia/Watermelon Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection; Susan Middleton/Netflix; Roadside Attractions/Courtesy Everett Collection; Jimmy Chin; Apple TV+; Venice Film Festival; Sundance Film Festival (2); Blue Ant; A24 The SCAD Savannah Film Festival and The Hollywood Reporter have announced the 10 standout 2026 documentaries that will be represented by their directors on the 13th annual edition of Docs to Watch, the fest’s panel that has become an important stop on the road to the Oscars for nonfiction films. This year’s selections: Poh Si Teng’s American Doctor (Watermelon), Ron Howard’s Avedon (Netflix), Alysa Nahmias’s Cookie Queens (Roadside), Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi’s Everest: The Other Side (Nat Geo), Amir Bar-Lev’s The Last First: Winter K2 (Apple), Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile (MUBI), William Greaves and David Greaves’s Once Upon a Time in Harlem (Neon), Itab Azzam & Jack MacInnes’s One in a Million (Frontline), Rory Kennedy’s The Trial of Alec Baldwin (Abramorama) and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything (A24). Related Stories Movies A24 Fixes Viral Typo in Elizabeth Holmes Documentary Trailer That Baffled Fans General News Elizabeth Holmes to Be Moved From Prison to Halfway House in 2027 Over the past 12 years, 27 films that were represented on the panel went on to receive an Oscar nomination for best documentary feature, and eight ultimately won that award: 2015’s Amy , 2016’s O.J.: Made in America , 2017’s Icarus , 2018’s Free Solo , 2019’s American Factory , 2021’s Summer of Soul , 2022’s Navalny and 2023’s 20 Days in Mariupol . The 2026 panel will take place over 90 minutes at the Lucas Theatre on the afternoon of Wednesday, Oct. 28, and will be moderated by yours truly. “This year’s Docs to Watch selections reflect a range of films that take us somewhere we didn’t expect to go, whether that’s into a hidden chapter of history, the life of an extraordinary individual, or a story unfolding in front of us right now,” Christina Routhier, the senior executive director of SCAD Theaters and Festivals, said in a statement. “We’re excited to partner with Scott Feinberg and The Hollywood Reporter to bring these filmmakers and their films to Savannah and give our students and audiences the chance to experience the work, meet the artists behind it, and be part of the conversation.” Here are some brief loglines about each of 2026’s Docs to Watch: • American Doctor , a film independently financed and directed by a Malaysian-born American journalist, follows three American physicians — one Jewish, one Palestinian and one Zoroastrian — as they volunteer at a hospital in Gaza amid the ongoing war • Avedon , from Oscar-winning director Ron Howard, explores the life, work and legacy of the American portrait photographer Richard Avedon, drawing upon unprecedented access to his personal archives and including never-before-seen stills and behind-the-lens footage • Cookie Queens , the year’s highest-grossing non-celebrity doc, is a heartwarming chronicle of four young girls’ efforts, in the face of varying forms of adversity, to meet their sales goals during Girl Scouts cookie-selling season • Everest: The Other Side , from the Oscar-winning directors of Free Solo , is another film about extreme outdoor athletes, in this case a man and a woman who fall in love and share a dream of climbing and then skiing down the north face of Mt. Everest • The Last First: Winter K2 follows a team of mountaineers as they strive to achieve something never previously accomplished, namely, climbing K2, the second-highest mountain in the world after Mt. Everest, in winter • My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile is the six-hour second installment, following a five-hour first, in an epic portrait of independent Russian journalists whose coverage amid Vladimir Putin’s authoritarian crackdown forces them to flee their homeland • Once Upon a Time in Harlem is a miraculous achievement, featuring remarkable footage of a gathering of Harlem Renaissance luminaries that was shot by one filmmaker in 1972 but not turned into a film until that filmmaker’s son completed it more than a half-century later • One in a Million , the winner of the Sundance Film Festival’s audience award, chronicles a tumultuous decade in the life of a young Syrian girl who, along with her family, flees her war-torn country and seeks refuge in Europe • The Trial of Alec Baldwin is the result of exclusive access to the titular star following a 2021 accidental shooting during the making of the film Rust , and includes powerful footage from the set, from Baldwin’s police interrogation and from the legal proceedings that followed • You Can See Everything , a film unlike any other, follows The Rehearsal ’s Nathan Fielder as he is welcomed into the home of Theranos’ Elizabeth Holmes over the 34 days before begins serving a prison sentence, and tries to figure out what she’s really about The 29th SCAD Savannah Film Festival will take place Oct. 24-31. Presented by the Savannah College of Art and Design, it is the largest university-run film festival in the world. Each year, some 75,000 people attend the eight-day event, which attracts some of the biggest names in Hollywood and world cinema, and which features exclusive screenings, panel discussions and workshops. Tickets for this year’s fest are now on sale . THR

articles.title: ‘Unabomber’ Review: Jacob Tremblay and Russell Crowe in a Facile Rendering of Ted Kaczynski’s College Days
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Richard Lawson Plus Icon Richard Lawson View All September 24, 2026 6:00pm Jacob Tremblay in 'Unabomber.' Philippe Bosse/Netflix While Netflix has Ryan Murphy busy investigating (or flat-out making up) the motives of killers like Jeffery Dahmer, the Menendez Brothers and Lizzie Borden, the streamer has enlisted director Janus Metz to tell the story of Ted Kaczynski , the math prodigy turned reclusive murderer known as the Unabomber — also the movie’s title. But Unabomber , written by Sam Chalsen and Nelson Greaves, is not some sweeping birth-to-death survey of Kaczynski’s life. It instead focuses on a young Kaczynski’s time at Harvard University, where he participated in a brutal psychological study that, in the movie’s framing, may have helped form the anarchic worldview that eventually led to his infamous deeds. Related Stories TV Felicia Pride on Capturing Innocence, Humanity in 'A Different World' Sequel and Revering the Original: "We're Not Replacing It" TV Keira Knightley, Ben Whishaw Reunite as Old Killers With New Enemies in 'Black Doves' Season 2 Trailer Never mind that Kaczynski himself has said that the study, conducted by psychology professor and sometime government operative Henry Murray, didn’t have much effect on his life. Unabomber presupposes that it did, that Murray’s cruel (and later condemned) experiment in breaking down the philosophical principles of test subjects, stoked a rage — at academia, at technology, at universities — so fierce that Kaczynski later decided to enact his revenge. Perhaps not figuring that argument compelling enough on its own, the film tacks on a 1990s-set plot covering the days leading up to Kaczynski’s capture in Montana. Unabomber The Bottom Line A faint sketch of a killer as a young man. Release date: Friday, Sept. 25 Cast: Russell Crowe, Jacob Tremblay, Shailene Woodley, Annabelle Wallis, Gus Halper Director: Janus Metz Screenwriters: Sam Chalsen, Nelson Greaves Rated R, 1 hour 37 minutes Both narratives concern people prying into Kaczynski’s psyche and finding only further questions. In the 1950s, in the hallowed, lacquered-wood halls of Harvard, we watch a perspicacious boy genius — Kacyznski was all of 16 when he started college — as his intellect, his curiosity and his naiveté are weaponized against him, hardening his most radical beliefs into ideology. In the 1990s section, we observe relative lay people as they try to divine specific clues from Kaczynski’s manifesto, markers that might give away something crucial. These twin analyses are both facile and unenlightening. The investigation arc is so boilerplate that it has an FBI agent placing a pile of documents on her desk and saying to them, “Talk to me.” The 1950s portion of the film is at least able to conjure up some mid-century moodiness, skulking around in the nervous temper of early Cold War days, as academia colluded with government agencies to buttress the country against the perceived Soviet threat. (At its best, the film calls to mind Robert De Niro’s unfairly maligned CIA origin story The Good Shepherd , which begins its postwar tale on the leafy quads of Yale.) And yet, the ultimate conclusions of that half of the film are just as unpersuasive as everything that happens 40 years later. That’s largely owed to starchy, frequently clichéd writing. But sadly one must put some of the blame on the actor playing Kaczynski, Jacob Tremblay , who long ago escaped the confines of Room and now, at 19, has found himself in this dark mess. His clean-cut boyish features do actually resemble Kaczynski at that age, but Tremblay otherwise has trouble evoking the volatile storms of Kaczynski’s mind. His voice cracking and eyes wide with alarm, Tremblay effectively communicates Kaczynski’s youth, but it all plays as bratty and insouciant rather than registering as the beginnings of true menace. Tremblay was a better fit for his other recent film about extremism, 2025’s Sovereign , in which his guilelessness served a more poignant purpose. As Murray, Russell Crowe has dusted off his A Beautiful Mind professorial duds and phones in a performance of avuncular appeal masking sinister motives. We believe that Murray cares, in some way, for Kazcynski — or, at least, that he’s impressed by the student’s prowess — but not enough to stop his predatory work. The portraiture is not very detailed beyond that. Part of the problem may be that, for the bulk of the experimentation, Murray is out of the room. Kaczynski is instead sparring with a fellow student, a haughty older boy played by the reliable Gus Halper, who did towering work as another collegiate monster in the under-seen 2016 frat-hazing thriller Goat . Had Tremblay and Crowe been given more opportunity to go toe to toe, something in the picture might have caught flame. Instead, Unabomber trudges through its motions, toggling between grim school daze and a tediously generic FBI manhunt. In the latter part, Shailene Woodley does her best to give some texture to her rogue agent character, Joanne, but she has precious little to work with. Perhaps cognizant of that, the filmmakers give Joanne a brief, humanizing button at the end of the film, a moment of solitude in which she has a cathartic cry as she processes all that she’s just experienced. The scene might register as thoughtful were it not such a blatant rip-off of the closing seconds of Zero Dark Thirty , in which a dogged investigator who’s finally caught her prey sheds tears of relief and exhaustion and something more ineffable. It doesn’t pack the same punch the second time around, and at the end of something so bland. Watching Unabomber , one longs for a smarter, more sophisticated, more probing version of this same double-act. A better film about what might have radicalized Ted Kaczynski that also delineates how he was eventually captured could be startling and revealing, complicating the public idea of Kaczynski as mere renegade madman. But this film serves up only the most basic, obvious version of that — try as it might, at times, to immerse us in murky psychological depths. In the end, it has all the markings of a final paper written by a student who got all the dates right, but failed to find the real meaning behind any of the history. Full credits Release date: Friday, Sept. 25 Cast: Russell Crowe, Jacob Tremblay, Shailene Woodley, Annabelle Wallis, Gus Halper Director: Janus Metz Screenwriters: Sam Chalsen, Nelson Greaves Cinematographer: Yves Bélanger Production designer: Michele Laliberte Costume designer: Veroniqué Marchessault Music: Marco Beltrami Editor: Zach Staenberg Casting: Christine Kromer Rated R, 1 hour 37 minutes THR

articles.title: Inside the Hollywood Home Studio That’s Birthed Several Pop Hits
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All September 24, 2026 6:12pm Leland in his home studio. Courtesy Situated in the hills of Studio City sits a home studio that’s birthed a slew of popular songs. “The first session I did here was with MUNA in 2019,” says Leland . The 39-year-old producer owns that home studio. It’s first iteration was situated inside the main house on his property and has since expanded into its own little oasis. Steeped in warm colors, with luxurious candles burning away, Leland’s current studio feels more like a chic getaway spot rather than a workspace. It’s become a home base for him and other creatives in his circle to collaborate. His dog, Crosby, is a frequent visitor and how he’s keeping track of the passing time — the MUNA session had to be in 2019 because he has a photo of one of the band’s members with the dog as a puppy. Related Stories Music Teyana Taylor, Charli xcx, Belmont Cameli Join 2026 MTV VMAs Presenters Lineup (Exclusive) Music MTV VMAs Producer Van Toffler Promises a "Kick-A**, Fast-Paced Show," Says Madonna's Performance "Will Make Your Head Spin" The actual studio only accounts for, at times, 50 percent of where the creativity’s happening when artist comes to Leland’s place. “The writing doesn’t have to happen in the studio. The recording can happen in the studio,” the producer explains. “I feel like a lot of it is just sitting out here having conversations.” Leland in his home studio. Courtesy An artist might be staying in the cottage on the property while they’re there working. “They can just walk down to the studio, which has been really nice,” says Leland. The Shards star Hayes Warner , another collaborator of Leland’s, stayed in his cottage while she was filming the Ryan Murphy show. Leland wrote music for the series, which is set to release a soundtrack next month . On a day where he’s welcoming an artist into the studio, the producer tends to start the day with a hike. He’ll walk to Fryman — if you ever see someone dangerously walking down Laurel Canyon Boulevard, it’s likely Leland. He’s only had one close call, he points out, and it was actually from a friend. “One of my best friends happened to be driving down Laurel Canyon, and he was like, ‘Girl, did I almost hit you?’ I was like, ‘Yes, but I would’ve wanted it to be a friend,'” he says cheekily. After his hike, hopefully without any close calls, Leland will get fresh flowers for the studio, along with a candle or incense. His routine tends to change depending on who he’s working with that day. “I love getting the studio ready for a session. I love that part of it,” the producer says. “Or cleaning up after a session, which is usually just Goop [Kitchen] bags, water and Coke Zero.” The space is meant to be a space of peace and quiet, even if that’s not always what’s happening in the studio itself. Leland, who’s also RuPaul’s Drag Race ‘s producer and songwriter, explains that it can range from longtime collaborator Troye Sivan to Charli xcx , who he says recorded some of the Wuthering Heights album in the studio, to Demi Lovato. A Drag Race executive producer or even RuPaul might be around while Leland’s tinkering on Sivan’s work, so they’ll share it. Leland in his home studio. Courtesy If Leland’s working with an artist for the first time, he’ll listen to their music on his morning hike — or he’ll listen to anything he’s anticipating will be a good reference point for the work that’ll happen later that day. No matter how familiar with the project or the artist, he wants to be prepared and have something in his back pocket. Some artists, however, have a good idea coming into their sessions with Leland. “When Rebecca Black came in, I was so excited to work with her and she had such a clear vision for what she wanted to make, and it was just so fun,” he says. The pair wrote the track “Corsetry” from her latest album in the space. “I have the same feeling about [Black] that I had when Adéla first walked into the room,” Leland says of the pop princess of the moment. The 22-year-old has been blowing up this summer. Leland and the pop star — who broke out as a contestant on the audition project Dream Academy that formed the girl group KATSEYE — worked together on songs from her first EP, “SexOnTheBeat” and “DeathbyDevotion.” Leland, by his on admission, loves working with women. “I love a pop girl,” he says. But by far, the producer’s most impactful collaboration, both professionally and creatively, remains Sivan. Getting to be part of a gay pop star’s career is something he’ll never take for granted. “So many songs that you love that are by the female pop stars that we love, a lot of the times there’s a queer person as one of the collaborators when you look up the credits,” Leland says. “I think now my ear is trained to where I can tell if a gay person was in the room or not.” He adds, “I really think for songs, you can tell. And not that every song needs to have a gay person in the room, obviously, but I think depending on what you’re going for, you can really hear if there was some queer energy in the room or not. I feel like it’s been so fun to sometimes be that person with the different artists that come through.” Leland in his home studio. Courtesy Leland and Sivan collaborated once again for the pop star’s upcoming album She’s the Best , set to be released next month. Many of the great pop stars of the past weren’t publicly out, so watching Sivan’s career get to the point it’s at now has been almost surreal for Leland. “People like Troye are allowed to be pop stars, and you’re allowed to have that experience, and maybe not allowed, you’re demanding it,” the producer says. “I always want the music to speak for itself. I don’t want opportunities because I’m queer. I want opportunities because I’m good. I don’t want opportunities for Troy because he’s a gay pop star,” says Leland. “I want opportunities for him and for our music because the music is good and the music videos are good and the team’s good and the energy is good.” He adds, “I want that support from the queer community because the music is great and the art is great. I want that support from the straight community because the music is great and the art is great, not just because any of us happen to be queer.” THR

articles.title: David Ellison, Tech Titans and Fox News Hosts Attend White House State Dinner Honoring China’s President
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 24, 2026 6:45pm President of China Xi Jinping clinks glasses with U.S. first lady Melania Trump as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House on September 24, 2026 in Washington, DC. Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Tech and media titans… as well as a small army of Fox News hosts descended on the White House Thursday evening to attend the state dinner honoring China’s president Xi Jinping. President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump hosted the dinner, which was heavy on corporate bigwigs. According to a guest list released by the White House, attendees included Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison , just days after his company inked a settlement to clear its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery … including CNN, which saw its reporters denied access to the state dinner even after a federal judge reinstated their press passes to the White House complex. But it was mostly tech giants in attendance, with photos showing Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk sitting at the head table with Trump and Xi, joined by Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Apple’s Tim Cook. Earlier this week, there were reports that Ellison may ask Musk to invest in Paramount as part of its WBD takeover. Other attendees included OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, OpenAI president Greg Brockman, Google co-founder Sergey Brin and CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, TikTok investor Jeff Yass, and LCMH CEO Bernard Arnault, along with a slew of other CEOs from finance, manufacturing and other industries. And there was also a Fox News contingent, with hosts Jesse Watters and Laura Ingraham as well as anchor Bret Baier all making the cut too. Podcast hosts, including Katie Miller (the wife of White House aide Stephen Miller) and David Sacks (tech investor and All-In co-host) were on the list, as was Cheryl Hines, who was there with her husband RFK Jr. THR

articles.title: Hannah Einbinder Shares Statement After Being Arrested at United Nations Netanyahu Protest
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 24, 2026 8:28pm Sarah Sherman, Hannah Einbinder and protesters against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his war in Gaza block a street next to the United Nations (U.N.) on September 24, 2026, in New York City. Spencer Platt/Getty Images Hannah Einbinder has released a statement after being arrested on Thursday during a protest ahead of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ‘s United Nations address. “If the pictures of my friends and me getting arrested in protest of Netanyahu’s shameful visit to New York draw attention to anything, let it be to the devastating genocidal war Israel is waging against people of Palestine and Southern Lebanon-to the settler attacks, the home demolitions, the bombing of people as they sleep; to the crimes that happen every SINGLE day but garner almost no international press coverage,” the actress wrote on her Instagram Story on Thursday. “The US government has the power to bring an end to all of this killing, pillaging, and land theft, yet instead it chooses to welcome the butcher of Gaza with open arms.” Related Stories General News Susan Sarandon, Hannah Einbinder Detained at United Nations Netanyahu Protest News Hannah Einbinder Defends Mark Ruffalo From Paramount "Antisemitism" Claim: "All of Us Artists Could Stand to Be More Like Mark" The Hacks actress, Susan Sarandon and Caleb Hearon were among those reportedly taken into custody alongside around 100 protesters before Netanyahu addressed the United Nations General Assembly. Cynthia Nixon and Sarah Sherman were also at the protest, with Einbinder being photographed with the Saturday Night Live star. Einbinder concluded, “The fact that the orchestrator of all this bloodshed is roaming freely in our cities is an indictment of BOTH REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS who enable and protect architects of genocide like netanyahu [sic]. Let us not mistake the spectacle for the story: genocide is the headline, and it is time for it to end.” In a second Instagram Story, she shared a link to donate to Pal Humanity. A spokesperson for the New York City Police Department told The Guardian that officers responded to “unscheduled demonstration” reports where an intersection was blocked. “Members of the NYPD Community Affairs Bureau issued … warnings, advising participants that they should leave,” the spokesperson told the outlet. “They continued to block the intersection. Multiple individuals who didn’t comply were taken into custody.” The actress-comedian has been a vocal supporter of Palestinian rights. At the end of her acceptance speech for supporting comedy actress at the 2025 Emmys, Einbinder said, “I just wanna say, finally, go birds, fuck ICE and free Palestine.” The Hollywood Reporter reached out to Einbinder’s reps for additional comment, but did not hear back. THR

articles.title: NASA Astronaut Victor Glover Signs With CAA (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 25, 2026 5:23am Artemis II NASA astronaut Victor Glover Courtesy of NASA NASA astronaut Victor Glover has signed with CAA for representation in all areas after he has retired as a space explorer. The Hollywood talent agency will look to expand opportunities for Glover in the unscripted TV and books and publishing spaces, as an event speaker and for brand endorsements and community impact. The signing follows Glover in spring 2026 piloting NASA’s Artemis II mission, and becoming the first Black astronaut to fly around the moon. That 10-day mission had Glover flying as far as 252,756 miles from Earth. Signing with CAA also follows Glover, a veteran naval aviator, test pilot and astronaut, stepping back from NASA to support future missions as part of the agency’s emeritus program. He has also joined the California Polytechnic State University, his alma mater, as an executive advisor. Glover received his Bachelor of Science in general engineering from Cal Poly, which along with Brown University awarded him honorary Doctor of Science degrees. Glover brings to the Hollywood talent agency a social media presence that includes around 532,000 Instagram followers and another 250,000-plus on the X platform. The retired U.S. Navy captain also piloted the first operational flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft, Resilience, to the International Space Station. He was first selected to become an astronaut in 2013 after serving as a test pilot for the F/A‐18 Hornet, Super Hornet and EA‐18G Growler aircraft. A native Californian, Glover also earned his Master of Science in flight test engineering and a Master of Military Operational Art and Science from Air University, and a Master of Science in systems engineering from the Naval Postgraduate School. THR

articles.title: Warner Music Names Val Blavatnik to Executive Team, Unveils Suite of Leadership Promotions
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All September 25, 2026 7:00am Atlantic Music Group CEO Elliot Grainge, and WMG managing director Val Blavatnik. Monica Schipper/Getty Images Warner Music Group announced a suite of leadership changes Friday morning that most notably has Val Blavatnik, son of the company’s majority shareholder Len Blavatnik, officially joining WMG’s executive team as managing director of North America, U.K. and corporate development. Industry insiders had been anticipating the younger Blavatnik’s entry into the company for years , and speculation of his impending appointment had been growing louder over the past several months. As managing director, WMG said Blavatnik, who is also on WMG’s board of directors, would “unify and drive business and operational strategy across these markets while guiding the company’s investment strategy to support growth.” Outside of Blavatnik’s new role, Atlantic Music Group CEO Elliot Grainge has also been named chairman of WMG’s distribution service ADA, and he is appointing Atlantic COO Zach Friedman as ADA’s vice chairman. With Warner Records COO Tom Corson recently being promoted to WMG COO, Aaron Bay-Schuck has been named sole chairman and CEO of Warner Records Group. Warner Music Latin America President Alejandro Duque, who had previously been named president of ADA last year, has been elevated to President of Warner Music International, where he’ll now also oversee the APAC and EMEA regions. Warner Music Iberia exec Guillermo Gonzalez has been upped to president of Warner Music EMEA, with Andrés Rothschild succeeding him as president of Warner Music Iberia. “To build upon our successful year in which we delivered on all three strategic priorities to grow market share, increase the value of music and increase our efficiency, these frontline executive changes enhance our best-in-class leadership team with diverse skill sets to execute on the next chapter of WMG’s growth,” WMG CEO Robert Kyncl said in a statement. “Elliot, Aaron, Alejandro and Guillermo are exceptional, dynamic and proven leaders who have transformed their domains, and elevating them allows us to further scale their success. I’m also excited to welcome Val to the executive team, where his operational and strategic focus will help us build our momentum across key markets.” As part of the shakeup, WMG executive Simon Robson, who’s been at the company for nearly 30 years, will step down in December to “pursue new opportunities.” “We owe a tremendous debt of gratitude to Simon Robson for his dedicated service, operational excellence and trusted leadership while expanding WMG’s global footprint over his remarkable tenure, and wish him the very best in his next endeavors,” Kyncl said. The wide swath of executive moves is just the latest in a particularly notable c-suite shakeup at WMG over the past several years. Former WMG CFO Armin Zerza confirmed he’d be departing from the company in July, with his eventual successor set to become the company’s fourth CFO since 2023. Meanwhile, earlier this week, WMG had announced that Warner Chappell COO and co-chair Carianne Marshall was departing as well , with Guy Moot set to become the publisher’s sole chairman. THR

articles.title: ‘American Horror Story’ Is Back With 13: Here’s How All the Seasons Connect (So Far)
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All September 25, 2026 7:27am Jessica Lange as Constance Langdon in 'American Horror Story: 13.' Eric Liebowitz/FX Logo text [This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the first three episodes of American Horror Story season 13 , “13,” 1:13 AM” and “Rauhnacht.”] As Madison Montgomery ( Emma Roberts ) says, “Surprise, bitch!” American Horror Story is officially back for its 13th season — and so are many of the franchise’s most memorable characters, with a plethora of superstitions to come. Thursday night debuted the first three episodes of the highly anticipated season 13, introducing new character Ben (Joey Pollari) as the audience’s entry point to this twisted, crossover story. Ben fittingly has triskaidekaphobia, a fear of the number 13, though he can’t seem to escape it. Related Stories TV When and Where to Watch 'American Horror Story' Season 13 Online TV Ryan Murphy Says He Finished 'Glee' Reboot Script Despite his debilitating triskaidekaphobia, his greater fear is that his relationship with his Taylor Swift-superfan girlfriend, Kira (Madelaine Petsch), will crumble if he doesn’t attend her birthday trip on the 13th with 13 of her best friends. He ends up taking the flight, but the plane crashes, killing Kira and 12 of her friends. Ben survives, as does another passenger who was sitting in 13B. Ben was sitting in 13F. The crash is the first indication that the number 13 is more than just a superstition in the new season. As the first three episodes unfold, the number keeps appearing in increasingly sinister ways — ultimately helping connect the season’s seemingly disparate characters and storylines. Before getting to what appears to be the main setting of the season — an apartment building called the Apollyon in New York City — the episode flashes to Miss Robichaux’s Academy for Exceptional Young Ladies, where Supreme Cordelia ( Sarah Paulson ) and Madison of season three’s Coven are helping newbie Ophelia (Avantika) work on her telepathy. This is where Madison makes her iconic grand entrance: “Surprise, bitch! This witch approves.” A storm is happening, however, hinting that we’re in the same timeline as the plane crash. Cordelia senses something sinister approaching. “So much vengeful death,” she says. “Something wicked this way comes.” With so many stars returning for the 13th installment and reprising their roles, Ryan Murphy had clarified to The Hollywood Reporter ahead of its release that this season is not a sequel; instead, “It’s a different story with characters that you love returning.” “They’re fighting a very big villain,” he said of the returning stars. “There has to be something big enough that even the ones who were villains before are now heroes — they’re united against a force that we’ve touched on in other seasons, but not in the way we are doing this season. There’s a big villain.” That villain remains a mystery after the first three episodes, but the story increasingly points toward the mysterious Mr. Nas. Fedor Steer as Mr. Nas. Eric Liebowitz/FX A month following the plane crash, Ben arrives at the Apollyon and meets the one-and-only Constance Langdon ( Jessica Lange ), who lives on the 13th floor and is apparently no longer tethered to the infamous Murder House from season one. She introduces Ben to Nas, played by Fedor Steer, who portrays the character in his older years. Paul Anthony Kelly plays Young Nas. Constance says Nas is 87, and Ben becomes his caregiver. Pollari told THR that Lange took him under her wing, as he’s a newcomer this season. “We are close off screen as well, and the scenes that we have together really developed a bond,” he said at the show’s New York premiere . “I learned a lot from her.” During the time of the plane crash, Nas is shown coughing up a strange black substance at the same time . Could Nas be the ultimate villain Murphy is referring to? The connection only becomes more suspicious in the second episode. After Ben discovers a series of strange references to the number 13 throughout Nas’ penthouse, including 13 figures in a depiction of The Last Supper , the episode cuts to Los Angeles, where Twisty the Clown (John Carroll Lynch), the serial killer clown from season four’s Freak Show , arrives at a clown school and proceeds to massacre 13 people at the school, including the teacher played by Tig Notaro. Back at the Apollyon, Nas vomits the same black, viscous substance again. The episode therefore appears to establish a connection between Nas and the deaths, though exactly what that connection is remains unclear. Ben also continues to question why Constance is caring for Nas. She reveals that all of her children are “alive and thriving,” which leads to one of the season’s biggest surprises: the return of her daughter Adelaide (Jamie Brewer), who is back “in this mortal coil.” The reunion becomes even stranger when Constance prepares for a dark holiday celebration, with Kai Anderson ( Evan Peters ) from Cult helping decorate a black Christmas tree topped with a pentagram. Constance’s son, Tate Langdon (also Peters), is there as well, with Peters playing both characters in the same scene. Joey Pollari as Ben, Jessica Lange as Constance Langdon. Eric Liebowitz/FX The gathering then grows into a supernatural AHS reunion in the third episode. Winter Anderson (Billie Lourd) from Cult arrives with a masked friend who is revealed to be Elizabeth Short, aka the Black Dahlia (Mena Suvari), from Murder House . Lourd — who first joined the Murphy-verse in 2015 for Scream Queens, which she hopes is revived — appeared in season seven’s Cult alongside Peters’ Kai. Of reuniting with the star, she told THR, “Evan is my brother from another mother. I love that man so much. We have so much fun together.” For the dark holiday scene, Lourd said she watched Peters put on his Rubber Man suit. “I did feel bad for him, having to be in that latex suit though. I watched him get lubed up and into it one day,” she said. During the reunion, Constance tells Elizabeth that she will become one of “13 lucky leading ladies,” adding yet another ominous reference to the number. Of season 13 bringing everyone together, Suvari told THR, “It’s really for all of the fans that have been so loving about this show along the way.” But the gathering has a larger purpose. The holiday is Rauhnacht, a period when the veil between Hell and Earth is at its thinnest. After Constance’s party, Winter, Kai, Tate and Adelaide take Elizabeth to a speakeasy called Club Hell. When they reach the basement of the Apollyon, Wilhemina Venable (Sarah Paulson) from season eight’s Apocalypse meets them, marking Paulson’s second character entrance, and welcomes them to what she calls a portal to Hell. The episode ends before revealing exactly what Constance and the others have planned for Elizabeth, though the references to sacrifices and the group’s plans for the 13 “leading ladies” suggest that she is being prepared for some kind of ritual. That leaves the first three episodes with a much larger mystery than simply why so many familiar faces have returned. The season appears to be building toward a supernatural conflict that connects the worlds — and timelines — of several previous American Horror Story installments. Evan Peters as Kai Anderson. Eric Liebowitz/FX As audiences wait for more episodes to drop weekly, Leslie Grossman, another regular in Murphy shows who is set to reprise Coco St. Pierre Vanderbilt from Apocalypse, explained how the seasons connect. “It is one big universe, but there’s many different timelines, and we have taken great care to make sure that all of the timelines intersect in a way that makes sense and is very satisfying for the fanbase,” she told THR. “So remember, all one universe, different timelines and they’re going to intersect in ways that are surprising.” She added, “I have to tell you, I read scripts and I was like, ‘No way! I had no idea that was going to happen.’ There are many Easter eggs and a lot of good payoff if you’ve been a fan of the show, but you can also have not watched it before, and I think you’re going to still enjoy this season.” After three episodes, big questions remain: Who exactly is Nas? Why does he seem connected to the deaths surrounding the number 13? Why has Constance brought these particular characters back together? And what exactly is waiting beneath the Apollyon? Oh, and is Ben really alive? *** New episodes of AHS: 13 premiere Thursdays on FX . Read all of THR’s coverage here . THR

articles.title: Dolly Parton’s ‘9 to 5’ Returns to Theaters With Ticket Sales Donated to Dollywood Foundation After Star’s Death
articles.full_text: Sep 25, 2026 6:22am PT Dolly Parton’s ‘9 to 5’ Returns to Theaters With Ticket Sales Donated to Dollywood Foundation After Star’s Death By Jordan Moreau Plus Icon Jordan Moreau Latest ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Adds 4 New Scenes Tying to ‘Doomsday’: [SPOILER] Fights Doctor Doom, [SPOILER] Travels to the Past and the Multiverse Collapses 18 hours ago ‘Black Doves’ Season 2 Trailer: Keira Knightley Investigates Spy Murders With a New Team in Netflix Action Thriller 23 hours ago George Lucas Says He Had Three More ‘Star Wars’ Movies to Make but ‘Decided to Retire’ From Directing Instead 3 days ago See All ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection Dolly Parton ‘s hit 1980 comedy “ 9 to 5 ” will return to theaters next month for one week in the wake of the country superstar’s death on Aug. 25 at age 80 . All U.S. ticket sales will be donated to The Dollywood Foundation to support its flagship program, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library. “9 to 5” will be back in theaters from Oct. 9-15. Disney made the announcement on Sept. 25, aka the new annual “Give Like Dolly Day.” The celebration, an homage to the film’s title, encourages people around the world to make a difference in a child’s life and honor Parton’s lifelong mission of inspiring kids to “dream more, learn more, care more and be more.” Since it was founded in 1995, Parton’s Imagination Library has donated more than 300 million books to children around the world, and each month it sends out 3 million books directly to kids’ homes. Children who are enrolled receive one book per month from birth to age five, at no cost to families. articles.title: Turkish Distributor Baska Sinema Boards AI-Generated Feature ‘A Woman Asleep’ for Theatrical Release (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 25, 2026 6:35am PT Turkish Distributor Baska Sinema Boards AI-Generated Feature ‘A Woman Asleep’ for Theatrical Release (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Turkish Distributor Baska Sinema Boards AI-Generated Feature ‘A Woman Asleep’ for Theatrical Release (EXCLUSIVE) 56 minutes ago ‘Percy Jackson’ Season 3 Stars Walker Scobell, Leah Sava Jeffries Set to Attend Italy’s Lucca Comics and Games 1 day ago Gaza Documentary ‘NAZA’ Set to Stream for Free on The Guardian Website After Global Release 1 day ago See All Turkish arthouse distributor Baska Sinema has acquired domestic theatrical rights to “A Woman Asleep,” an experimental English-language AI feature directed by pioneering artist and filmmaker Vikki Bardot. Bardot is considered one of the early practitioners of photographic AI art and video art. She delivered a TEDx talk on AI and art in 2023, and her artworks have been exhibited worldwide, including New York, Paris, London, Berlin, Rome and Miami. Her AI short “Dreamt by Another” screened in more than 40 festivals and was recently acquired by Mubi for Turkey . Related Stories 'Into the Breach' Review: Star-Studded British Theater Doc Needs More Time to Serve Its Sprawling Subject Matter 'Alpha Gang’ Review: Cate Blanchett, Chris Pine and an All-Star Cast Play Space Aliens in David and Nathan Zellner’s Endearingly Goofy Sci-Fi Spoof “A Woman Asleep” is inspired by the 1974 cult French film “The Man Who Sleeps,” directed by Bernard Queysanne and Georges Perec. That movie, in turn, was based on Perec’s novel “A Man Asleep.” Popular on Variety In a rare occurrence, Bardot’s 80-minute AI drama that, according to the synopsis, examines contemporary alienation and numbness in today’s world of hyper-connectivity, is set for a spring 2027 release across 20 cities in Turkey via Baska Sinema. “A Woman Asleep” is produced by pioneering Turkish AI production studio Spongeworthy that is also behind buzzy AI-generated doc “Post Truth,” directed by Alkan Avcıoğlu which made a splash on the festival circuit and also, similarly, got a theatrical release via Baska Sinema in Turkey. The narration for “A Woman Asleep” is generated using an AI voice clone trained on the director’s own voice. “This choice extends the film’s conceptual framework and dreamlike qualities, allowing the narration to exist in a space between the human and the synthetic, consistent with the world the film portrays,” the promotional materials say, citing the storytelling approaches of Alain Resnais, Michelangelo Antonioni, Chris Marker and Apichatpong Weerasethakul as references. Edited from a pool of 50,000 individual shots, the experimental film took two years to complete. “I have been focused on AI filmmaking for 5 years, before it was even a popular subject in cinema,” said Bardot in a statement. “The most interesting use of AI isn’t recreating Hollywood forms. It’s giving independent filmmakers the freedom to make personal, formally ambitious films that might otherwise never get financed,” the director added. Commented Baska Sinema director Armagan Lale: “What interests us is not the technology itself, but how filmmakers use new tools to expand the expressive possibilities of cinema.” “A Woman Asleep offers a distinctive, female-centred perspective on a society shaped by technological dependency and emotional disconnection,” she added. “What matters to us is that these tools serve a clear cinematic vision . “ Tim Blake Nelson’s ‘The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd,’ Jesse Eisenberg’s ‘The Debut’ Among Rome Film Festival Standout Titles Dakota Johnson on Being in Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Music Video: ‘We Respect Each Other’s Creative Minds’ Silver Lion Winner ‘Miss Violence’ Director Alexandros Avranas to Helm Greek Adaptation of Globoplay’s Hit Series ‘The Others’ (EXCLUSIVE) Oscars: Denmark Selects May el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion Winner ‘Woman Unknown’ for International Feature Race ‘Shrinking’ Season 4 Casts Judith Light (EXCLUSIVE) Tom Hiddleston Recalls Trekking to Everest for ‘Tenzing’ and Kevin Feige Telling Him ‘Thor’ Wasn’t ‘Going to Be the Only Film’ He Would Play Loki In Loading comments...

John is set to open the venue — a state-of-the-art, 600-capacity facility at Battersea Power Station — with a concert on Monday. Apple Music Hall’s lineup through the end of the year will include shows from Charli xcx, Burna Boy, Baby Keem, Skye Newman, Troye Sivan, Arlo Parks and Chase & Status. All performances will also be livestreamed globally on Apple Music. articles.title: Rio Fest’s RioMarket, Kicking Off Oct. 1, to Feature TikTok Program and Online Business Meetings
articles.full_text: Sep 25, 2026 6:59am PT Rio Fest’s RioMarket, Kicking Off Oct. 1, to Feature TikTok Program and Online Business Meetings Amid a strong presence of Asian countries, RioMarket is launching an app to connect international film markets By Marcelo Cajueiro Plus Icon Marcelo Cajueiro Latest Grace Passô’s ‘Our Secret’ Nabs the Best Film Kikito at the 54th Gramado Film Festival 1 month ago ‘Seduction,’ Helmed by Zelito Viana and Marcos Palmeira, to Premiere at the Inffinito Fest in Miami (EXCLUSIVE) 1 month ago Gramado Targets Next-Gen Talent as Permanent Growth Engine (EXCLUSIVE) 1 month ago See All Walkiria Barbosa Credit Eny Miranda RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — RioMarket , the business section of the Rio International Film Festival, will be held over Oct. 1-11, featuring for the first time a partnership with TikTok and online one-on-one business meetings. The event, taking place in a warehouse in Rio’s port area renovated for the 2016 Summer Olympics, will gather execs and talents of the local and international film industry, with a strong presence of Asian countries, and will launch an app to connect festival film markets around the world. Related Stories Spain’s National Film Prize Honoree Carmen Machi: ‘Acting Has Been the Driving Force of My Happiness and Also a Balm for My Darkest Moments’ Penélope Cruz Sobs and Kisses Javier Bardem as ‘Bunker’ Dazzles Venice With Record 15.5-Minute Ovation The first online one-on-one business meetings were held at RioMarket 2025 and proved successful, Walkiria Barbosa , the Rio Film Festival ‘s executive director and head of international marketing, told Variety . Popular on Variety “We ran a pilot last year, and we are going to expand it this year. During the pandemic, we learned that it is possible to do business online,” she said. “We received applications from companies in several countries, including film and television production companies, streaming platforms, distributors, and television networks,” she said. One of the new features of RioMarket 2026 is a partnership with TikTok, Barbosa said. The social media giant will hold at the event a three-day workshop for 40 TikTok content creators invited by the company from several states in Brazil. The program’s aim is to improve the quality of the content they produce through technical sessions on directing, lighting, editing, screenwriting, format development, filming, and other areas of individual content production. “The goal is to raise the quality of entertainment content production on TikTok by connecting creators with experienced audiovisual professionals. We believe Festival do Rio, which brings together the leading players in Brazil’s entertainment industry, is the ideal setting to launch this new model,” Luciana Galastri, head of entertainment partnerships at TikTok in Latin America, told Variety . Luciana Galastri. Courtesy TikTok Barbosa stressed the strong presence at RioMarket 2026 of Asian countries, particularly China, India and South Korea, as well as Russia. Over the past years, Brazilian companies are increasingly doing more business with players from these countries, while maintaining the traditional interaction with partners in the North and Latin America and Europe, she said. From China, one of the highlights is the lecture of Spike Liu, president of China Year Technology. He will present experiences on the use of AI in content creation and production processes in the audiovisual sector. RioMarket will profit from the presence of international players in the soft launch of its app, which aims to connect film festivals’ markets around the world. Tentatively named Connecting Screens, the platform is inspired by Cinando, the online networking and business platform for film and audiovisual professionals run by Cannes’ Marché du Film. Connecting Screens will facilitate business meetings and provide info about projects, among many other features, Pedro Souza, president of the Financing Committee of the Audiovisual Industry and Commerce Federation (FICA), told Variety . “While Cinando resembles Wikipedia, our app will be a sort of Tinder, Linkedin and Wikipedia. The idea is to match sellers and buyers of the audiovisual industry,” Souza said. Photo Ilda Santiago . Credit Phil Lavra Apple Photos Clean Up Ilda Santiago, Rio Fest’s exec director of programing and international projects, stressed the importance of forming a new generation of moviegoers for the festival. RioMarket 2026 will count with the presence of participants of the Generation Program, Rio Fest’s initiative dedicated to the use of films in fostering education for children and teenagers in Rio. Santiago also underscored the significance of RioMarket: “The market feeds the festival program, and the program, in turn, feeds the market. Today, no major film festival can afford to operate without a strong industry market.” One of the most promising panels of RioMarket 2026 is the one that will put, face to face, two of the most critically acclaimed film directors in the world: Iran’s Asghar Farhadi , of “Parallel Tales” (2026), “A Separation (2011)” and “About Elly” (2009), and Brazilian Walter Salles , of “I’m Still Here” (2024), “Central Station” (1998) and “The Motorcycle Diaries” (2004). Another important panel is the one on LatAm Content Meeting, the Brazilian version of the Sunny Side of the Doc. Fernando Dias, the event’s founder, will provide information for non-fiction content makers interested in participating in the next edition of LatAm Content Meeting, in September 2027 in São Paulo. There will also be two panels presenting successful cases of international co-production of documentaries resulting from deals initiated in the first two editions of LatAm Content Meeting in 2025 and 2026. In addition, content analyst Gustavo Martínez will host a workshop centered on his approach to conflict structure in screenplays, which is based on Newton’s Third Law of Motion and aims to create points of tension and release so the audience remains engaged. “We are holding an event on the scale of the markets at the world’s leading international film festivals,” said Barbosa, who is also the president of FICA. She believes there is an opportunity for the growth of the Brazilian audiovisual industry. “Our goal is to triple the industry’s share of Brazil’s GDP over the next five years. It currently stands at 0.6%. We aim to achieve this by strengthening our companies, increasing the number of movie theaters, advancing technological development and expanding exports of Brazilian productions,” Barbosa said. articles.title: New York Film Festival Boss on Scoring ‘Artificial’ and ‘Behemoth’ World Premieres and Why Movies Are ‘Unavoidably Political’
articles.full_text: Sep 25, 2026 7:00am PT New York Film Festival Boss on Scoring ‘Artificial’ and ‘Behemoth’ World Premieres and Why Movies Are ‘Unavoidably Political’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Paige DeSorbo on Leaving ‘Summer House’ Behind and Speaking Out About a Past Abusive Relationship: ‘Domestic Violence’ Can ‘Truly Happen to Anyone’ 2 days ago ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Could Top Box Office, Brad Pitt’s ‘Heart of the Beast’ and Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ Vie for No. 3 2 days ago ‘Evita’ on Broadway: West End Stars Diego Rodriguez, James Olivas to Reprise Roles Alongside Rachel Zegler (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All From the surprise election of mayor Zohran Mamdani to the Knicks winning the NBA championship, it’s been a time for underdog stories in the Big Apple. The New York Film Festival is continuing the trend, pulling off a coup by securing several major world premieres in a year that’s been frustratingly light on festival fanfare. NYFF starts on Sept. 25, and over the next two weeks, audiences will be the first to watch “ Artificial ,” Luca Guadagnino’s buzzy movie about OpenAI founder Sam Altman; “A Statement,” director Tom McCarthy’s starry drama about climate change; “Behemoth,” Tony Gilroy’s ode to film scores led by Pedro Pascal; “14th,” Ava DuVernay’s timely documentary about the 14th Amendment; and “Godzilla Minus Zero,” a kaiju sequel to Oscar-winner “Godzilla Minus One.” It’s an exciting change of pace for the small-but-mighty NYFF, whose lineup is often comprised of the buzziest movies from Cannes, Venice or Toronto. Related Stories Penélope Cruz Sobs and Kisses Javier Bardem as ‘Bunker’ Dazzles Venice With Record 15.5-Minute Ovation ‘Day Drinker’ Trailer: Johnny Depp's Hollywood Comeback Continues in a Twisty Thriller With Penélope Cruz and Madelyn Cline “Premiere status is never the be-all and end-all for us,” says NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim. “But I think we’ve proved in the last few years that we create a pretty interesting context for the launch of a film.” Popular on Variety Many of these films tackle hot-button issues that speak to these politically fraught times. But that’s not to say that everything on this year’s lineup is fire and brimstone. There are fun and joyous movies, too, Lim points out, citing Jordan Firstman’s heartfelt comedy “Club Kid” and Jesse Eisenberg’s musical drama “The Debut.” Ahead of this year’s festival, Lim spoke to Variety about lining up so many heavy hitters and whether festivalgoers should be prepared for any surprises. NYFF is hosting several buzzy world premieres. Was that a priority? There is more than usual this year. It’s just a confluence of factors. Timing is always part of it. We are a month after the major fall festivals: Telluride, Venice, and Toronto. We’re not a competitive festival. It doesn’t make sense for us to have world premieres be the majority of our program. But I’m very excited about each of the world premieres. How did you get “Artificial” on the lineup? There was chatter that it might skip the festival circuit entirely. That was genuinely an up-in-the-air situation. It was with a different studio until very recently , and it was an open conversation of whether this would do festivals. Luca is a filmmaker we have a relationship with, and I thought we would be a great launchpad for the film. This is a film that deals with a very pressing situation. AI is in the news practically daily. The film recaps this trajectory that we’ve been on with alarming clarity. And it does this in the form of an incredibly entertaining movie. It has a very dark humor, which is certainly one valid way of approaching the dystopian present. Tom McCarthy’s climate change drama “A Statement” wasn’t on many people’s radars. How did that come together? We knew the film might be ready. We saw it very late in the process. It fits exactly what I was saying about films that are tackling contemporary realities. We’ve just lived through some kind of climate apocalypse in most parts of the world this summer, and much in the same way that “Artificial” does with the AI crisis, this film is looking at a very specific moment in time with this climate conference from 1980. It explains why it’s so hard for action to be taken, despite very clear evidence. There’s been a lot of debate recently about the place of politics at film festivals. At Venice, jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal called films “fundamentally, unavoidably political.” What is your take? I’d agree with that statement. I think all films are political. Even to say that one is apolitical is kind of a political position to take. To be human, to be alive in the world, is political. Cinema of all the art forms is unavoidably political. We’re reflecting the world; we’re responding to the world. The most urgent, meaningful films today are engaged with the realities of contemporary existence. Which film on the lineup surprised you the most? That’s a really tough one. Maybe “Behemoth,” Tony Gilroy’s film, another world premiere, because even though he’s been very active, he hasn’t made a feature film in a while. It was so clearly a passion project, and it has such a clear point of view. This is a film that makes clear that music isn’t just an accompaniment in the background of a film but a narrative device. We also try to make room for what you might call smaller films in the main slate, and those are often, for me, the most surprising. There are a couple of titles that have really stayed with me. “The Loneliest Man in Town” by Tikovian Rainer Frimmel, an Austrian film that’s a really lovely character study, and Nicholas Pareda’s film’s “Everything Else Is Noise,” a Mexican film by I think one of the most interesting filmmakers working today. It’s important for us to create the possibility for discovery and surprise for the audience, so we balance out the higher profile films with these other titles. One of the buzziest moments of last year’s festival was the surprise screening of “Marty Supreme.” Will there be surprises for festival attendees? “Marty” was a very exciting moment for us. I think that might account for the larger-than-usual number of world premieres in the lineup. I don’t think we will or need to do a surprise every year. It has to be the right film. A surprise that ends up being anticlimactic doesn’t serve anyone. We’re not wedded to the surprise thing. It’s not an annual tradition. But I think we will have evenings this year that will certainly rival the excitement of the “Marty Supreme” night. NYFF doesn’t have jury prizes. Will that ever change? As long as I have any say, there will not be competitions. So many filmmakers have told me that one of the reasons they truly enjoy their time at New York is the instant removal of stress of not having a competition. That changes everything when you’re a filmmaker and you have this pressure of: Will you get called back? Will you win? What does it mean to win or not win? It makes sense for premier festivals to have competitions, but I don’t think, in the context of how we’re currently configured, a competition would add anything. How do you survive long festival days, or when you have to screen multiple movies in one day? I wish I knew… that would make it easier. [Laughs] . I’ve actually gone back to watch films multiple times because when I’m in that state, you have to acknowledge that you’re losing your perspective. You know what it’s like to be at a festival and have a three or four film day, and it’s like you don’t trust your judgement. [Laughs] . For me, not doing anything screen related is the only way to reset. Caffeine also helps. You were crowned by GQ as the best dressed man at last year’s festival. How much thought do you put into your outfits? It’s a long festival! It’s just about being aware that you’re on stage with people who have stylists and budgets, and you don’t want to look like a slob. But it is a long festival … 15 days. It’s something I should probably start thinking about soon. articles.title: Warner Music Group Names Val Blavatnik Managing Director of North America and U.K. Amid Other Executive Moves
articles.full_text: Sep 25, 2026 7:00am PT Warner Music Group Names Val Blavatnik Managing Director of North America and U.K. Amid Other Executive Moves By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Warner Music Group Names Val Blavatnik Managing Director of North America and U.K. Amid Other Executive Moves 6 minutes ago Music Industry Moves: Chvrches Sign With Futures Music Group; MSG Entertainment Names Josephine Vaccarello President 22 hours ago Bad Brains’ Earliest Studio Recordings to Be Released in November 2 days ago See All In a long-expected move, Warner Music Group has named Val Blavatnik Managing Director of North America, U.K. & Corporate Development amid several other top leadership moves. Blavatnik, 28, the son of Warner Music’s primary owner Len Blavatnik, will “unify and drive business and operational strategy across these markets while guiding the company’s investment strategy to support growth,” according to the announcement. In other moves, Alejandro Duque is elevated to President, Warner Music International, adding the APAC and EMEA regions to his remit; Elliot Grainge is named Chairman of the independent distribution company ADA in the U.S. in addition to his current role as Chairman and CEO of Atlantic Music Group, and appoints longtime associate Zach Friedman to serve as Vice Chairman of ADA in addition to his COO role at AMG. Courtesy of Maria Farinha Filmes Oscar-nominated Italian producer Donatella Palermo (“Fire at Sea,” “Caesar Must Die”) has boarded Eryk Rocha’s highly anticipated doc “ Elza ” as a production associate. The film will have its world premiere at the Rio Film Festival and its international premiere at the Rome Film Festival . “Elza” is the follow-up to Rocha’s “The Falling Sky,” which premiered to great acclaim at Directors’ Fortnight. The film is a comprehensive documentary about one of Brazil ’s most renowned singers and public figures, Elza Soares. Drawing on rare archival materials and intimate conversations between Soares and the director during the final years of her life, “Elza” traces the icon’s seven-decade career while revealing the many facets of the woman behind the legend. The project comes with the backing of high-calibre partners, including Aruac Filmes (“Cinema Novo”), Maria Farinha Filmes (“The Beginning of Life”), Globo Filmes (“I’m Still Here”), RAI Cinema and Gullane +. How Penélope Cruz Could Dominate Awards Season With 'La Bola Negra,' 'The Invite' and 'Bunker' Rocha, who followed Elza over eight years of filming, said: “Elza Soares is a beacon whose art and legacy continue to guide us. To tell her story is also to tell the story of our country. By allowing Elza to tell her story in her own voice, the film brings us once again into the presence of this immense woman and artist.” Popular on Variety “The film is also a way to honor her dedication to music and her commitment to everything she was, and everything she continues to represent,” he added. “I am deeply moved to share this film with audiences and to have Elza’s voice sing once again, for Brazil and the entire world.” Soares’s work intersected with some of the defining figures in international music, from Argentine tango composer and arranger Astor Piazzolla to jazz legends Louis Armstrong and Ella Fitzgerald. Soares met Armstrong in Chile in 1962, during a World Cup that would change the course of her life. Named BBC’s “Voice of the Millennium,” Elza transcended genres and national borders to become a global symbol of artistic freedom, resilience, and the enduring power of Black women’s voices. Her death in 2022 moved the entire country, with artists and fans paying lengthy homages to the trailblazer. “Elza” is produced by Aruac Filmes and Maria Farinha Filmes, in co-production with Globo Filmes and GloboNews. The film is distributed by Gullane+ and Maria Farinha Filmes. The film was produced in collaboration with Faber Produzioni and RAI Cinema. “Elza” is supported by the City of São Paulo, through Spcine, and by Itaú Cultural, and was produced with funding from the Brazilian Federal Government, through the Aldir Blanc National Policy for the Promotion of Culture (PNAB), in coordination with the National Culture System, with investment from the Audiovisual Sector Fund, and with institutional support from the Ministry of Culture and Ancine. International Co-Productions Point Towards a Strong Future 3 hours ago See All Courtesy of Zurich Film Festival Willem Dafoe , who is at the Zurich Film Festival presenting the opening night film “ Tenzing ,” spoke about the record-breaking 2026 box office while emphasizing the importance of watching the Jennifer Peedom epic in cinemas. The film, which opened to warm Zurich audiences last night, will have a limited theatrical release in the U.S. from Oct. 9 ahead of its global streaming debut on Apple TV on Oct. 16. “The only problem is that the audience comes mainly from three, four huge movies,” he said of this year’s record-breaking $4.76 billion U.S. summer box office, driven largely by Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and Destin Daniel Cretton’s “ Spider-Man : Brand New Day.” “A couple of smaller movies kind of catch on and do well, but it’s got to be spread out a little bit.” Related Stories Three Films, and a Second Oscar? How Penélope Cruz Could Dominate Awards Season With 'La Bola Negra,' 'The Invite' and 'Bunker' 'Bunker' Review: Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz Are Brilliant in Florian Zeller's Riveting, Slightly Overstated Thriller of Isolation and Invasion Dafoe himself is perhaps one of the actors who best treads the line between blockbusters and small festival darlings, having appeared in Sam Raimi’s first “Spider-Man” back in 2002 as well as collaborating with now-renowned auteurs early in their careers, such as Sean Baker, Wes Anderson, Yorgos Lanthimos and Robert Eggers. Popular on Variety Speaking about his turn in the comic book world, Dafoe said he became a part of it at the “start of business-as-normal making movies from comic books.” “When I was proposed this role, some of my friends were like: ‘Are you kidding? Are you going to play this green guy? That’s not cool! That sounds like a terrible movie!’” “I was not a big comic book fan; I didn’t know about this world, but Sam Raimi did,” he added. “I saw his attachment to it and saw how he saw it. I liked him so much that he really is what got me into it. Once I was in it, I had really fun things to do.” The actor said he “had done some movies that had found success” but that, to this day, the most consistent point of recognition from audiences is “probably the Green Goblin.” “For better or for worse,” he said. “Luckily, I do other things so I am not haunted by this mono-identity, but it’s pretty strong.” Dafoe enjoyed his experience in the Marvel Cinematic Universe both in the 2002 film and during his return as Green Goblin on “Spider-Man: No Way Home.” “They’re part of cinema. They are right up there with Bela Tarr,” he quipped. Apple Original Films “Tenzing” chronicles the story of the first-ever ascent of Mount Everest by Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary, played by Genden Phuntsok and Tom Hiddleston, respectively. Dafoe plays Colonel John Hunt, the leader of the 1953 British expedition team. Commenting on the experience of shooting on real mountains at high altitude, Dafoe said the entire film team had to be “very careful.” “We had great safety people,” he noted. “They’re checking for avalanches, for all sorts of things. There are 10 guys purely helping us slip in and making sure we’re safe, helping us if we struggle […] That’s the tension. Nature is the biggest partner you’ll have because it tells you what you have to do. There is no invented world. It’s a world that really exists; you’re not questioning [its] authenticity. You’re definitely on this mountain, and you’re definitely having a little hard time breathing, or you’re fatigued, or you’re hungry, or you have to go to the toilet, and there’s no toilet there… All kinds of challenges and, on top of that, you’ve got the scenes.” ‘The Musical’ Star Will Brill on His Dark, Surprisingly Delightful 9/11 Revenge Comedy ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Adds 4 New Scenes Tying to ‘Doomsday’: [SPOILER] Fights Doctor Doom, [SPOILER] Travels to the Past and the Multiverse Collapses ECAM Incubator Film Project ‘Our Raised Skin’ Explores the Male Body and the Fear of Its Touch Tom Hiddleston Recalls Trekking to Everest for ‘Tenzing’ and Kevin Feige Telling Him ‘Thor’ Wasn’t ‘Going to Be the Only Film’ He Would Play Loki In Turkish Distributor Baska Sinema Boards AI-Generated Feature ‘A Woman Asleep’ for Theatrical Release (EXCLUSIVE) Backers of U.S. Film Incentive See Window to Pass Bill This Year Loading comments...

articles.title: Shemar Moore Is Back in Action in Starz’s Solid Cop Drama ‘S.W.A.T. Exiles’: TV Review
articles.full_text: Sep 25, 2026 7:15am PT Shemar Moore Is Back in Action in Starz’s Solid Cop Drama ‘S.W.A.T. Exiles’: TV Review By Aramide Tinubu Plus Icon Aramide Tinubu Latest Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review 4 days ago ‘MobLand’ Season 2 Proves the Show Just Wouldn’t Work Without Tom Hardy 7 days ago Netflix’s ‘Monster’ Finally Delivers an Outrageously Engaging Season With ‘The Lizzie Borden Story’: TV Review 1 week ago See All Kit Karzen/Sony Pictures Televis Just one year after wrapping an eight-season run on CBS’ “S.W.A.T.,” Shemar Moore ’s stoic but righteous Sergeant II Daniel “Hondo” Harrelson Jr. returns on a new network in the spinoff series “ S.W.A.T. Exiles .” Created by Jason Nig, the Starz show is set two years after the original series ended, and Hondo is in a very different place. Divorced and alone, he has also been ousted from the LAPD following a botched raid that ended with the death of one of his young squad members. These days, Hondo is a reluctant bodyguard for some of Los Angeles’ most insufferable billionaire tech bros, but his luck changes when LAPD Commander Robert Hicks (Patrick St. Esprit, reprising his role) offers him the opportunity to command a new unit. Deeply resentful following his forced retirement, Hondo begrudgingly takes the new position, but soon realizes he’s being set up to fail. A solid sequel to a well-liked procedural, “S.W.A.T Exiles” uses many of the same tricks that made the original show so popular. Yet, with a brand-new team and a handful of compelling storylines, the show proves it can stand on its own. The 10-episode first season (four episodes were available for review) opens on an ordinary day in LA., where audiences get a glimpse of Hondo’s empty house. Aside from dirty dishes and a calendar covered in his young daughter’s doodles, there are few signs of life. He moves on autopilot, bitter about the past and working out his anguish with endless push-ups. Each day blends into the next, so when Hicks offers him the chance to suit up again, he decides he can’t pass it up. Yet almost as soon as he enters his new headquarters, Hondo recognizes this new role isn’t what it seems. It’s clear the LAPD has an image problem, and they’ve trotted him out yet again to fix it. Additionally, the short-tempered leader has been given an unpredictable Gen Z team who are difficult to corral. Among the new 44 Squad, which Hondo aptly calls the Exiles, is Sammy Bishop (Lucy Barrett), a gun expert and social media star who, much to Hondo’s horror, has no qualms about live-streaming from headquarters. Malik Henderson (Adain Bradley), a Marine veteran and devoted husband and father, appears most suited for the job, especially when Hondo makes him Scout, or the point person for missions. (Malik has some skeletons in his closet, though.) Ethan Cole (Freddy Miyares) is a neurodivergent tech savant who picks up on way more than people give him credit for. Cassidy Han (Zyra Gorecki) is intense, disciplined and determined not to let her prosthetic leg define her, but her reserved nature makes her a mystery to her colleagues. The recruits are rounded out by Jude Callan (Ronen Rubinstein), a charming, cocky bad boy with unexpected depth. At the start, Hondo flexes his rusty leadership skills and tries to get his ragtag crew to work as a cohesive unit. Still, despite the typical procedural formula with cases tied to gun smugglers, cartel assassins and kidnappings, the show remains topical enough to keep viewers engaged. When Hondo realizes his team is being undermined and someone on the inside is feeding information to the mayor’s office to take him down, the stakes for “S.W.A.T. Exiles” become more intriguing. While this conspiracy runs across the entire first season, the reveal of who’s behind it isn’t as straightforward as one might expect. “S.W.A.T Exiles” isn’t as fixed or formulaic as other action-dramas. Episode 4, “Get Clear,” is a gem in the season. Instead of taking audiences through yet another mission, Hondo and the team are called before the Force Review Board to testify about a prior bungled assignment. Cutting back and forth between the present and the past, each member of the unit reflects on a hostage situation turned ICE raid that went completely off track, leaving an unarmed civilian shot dead by Hondo’s hand. As the officers recall the incident, Hondo focuses on finding out who the mole is and how to proceed with this information. When it’s all said and done, “S.W.A.T. Exiles” doesn’t reinvent the wheel for its genre, or even from the previous series. But Moore is commanding and earnest as he steps back into Hondo’s shoes, this time, to shepherd a new generation of officers who are also trying to navigate their pasts and personal lives. And it looks like Starz believes in the franchise, since “S.W.A.T. Exiles” has already been greenlit for Season 2.
