articles.title: BBC Boss Matt Brittin On Expected Service Closures: “No Program Or Channel Will Exist Forever”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake BBC Boss Matt Brittin On Expected Service Closures: “No Program Or Channel Will Exist Forever” ‘Have I Got News For You’ Producer Torches BBC Investigation Into Victoria Beckham Joke As “Total Waste” Of Money BBC Rebukes ‘Have I Got News For You’ After Complaints About “Gratuitously Offensive” Victoria Beckham Joke View All September 25, 2026 5:12am BBC boss Matt Brittin on 'Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg' BBC News BBC director-general Matt Brittin has hinted that the broadcaster is preparing to close TV and radio networks as it looks to save money and better serve audiences online. In an interview that will air over the weekend, Brittin told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the BBC’s ambition to save £500 million ($662M) “may well mean” that services are shut. The former Google executive said the BBC “wouldn’t guarantee any program or any channel will exist forever. The tight financial situation means that we’re having to look at some of those decisions a bit sooner than we might like.” Related Stories News 'Have I Got News For You' Producer Torches BBC Investigation Into Victoria Beckham Joke As "Total Waste" Of Money News BBC Rebukes 'Have I Got News For You' After Complaints About "Gratuitously Offensive" Victoria Beckham Joke Brittin’s comments follow Deadline reporting on Wednesday that the BBC is expected to announce the closure of TV and radio networks as early as next week. There is speculation about the future of BBC Three, but nothing is confirmed at this stage. Watch on Deadline “We wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever” BBC Director General Matt Brittin has said that the BBC's financial situation "may well mean" that some channels and radio stations will have to close. #BBCLauraK https://t.co/JZziQESjYy pic.twitter.com/m6Iv4cWEsU — BBC Politics (@BBCPolitics) September 25, 2026 Brittin told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg : “We might have some channels and services where maybe 100,000 people are watching the broadcast service, but 500,000 are getting those programs on iPlayer. When’s the right time to migrate that service fully to being on demand? And part of my job is to safeguard value for money for the licence fee payer.” He added that the BBC had to go “in different ways to reach audiences and we’re locked into yesterday’s model of how people consume content and actually the audience is always already living in tomorrow’s world.” The BBC’s £500M target expands on a previous savings goal worth £1.5 billion. The bigger picture behind the cuts is that 94% of the UK population use the BBC every month, but fewer than 80% pay the £180 annual licence fee. The BBC is attempting to bridge this gap. Up to 2,000 jobs are at risk under the savings strategy, while the BBC is also involved in tense negotiations with unions over employee pay rises . articles.title: International Disruptors: Reta Guetg On Building Zurich Film Festival’s “Trendy” Identity & Why New Owners Want To Keep It Small, Nimble & Close To Hollywood
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Percy Hynes White & Jeff Wahlberg Lead Lovers-On-The-Run Thriller ‘Crime Novella’, Roland Emmerich Exec-Producing & First Look Revealed ‘The Lion King’ Director Rob Minkoff To Develop & Exec Produce Family Pic ‘Storm Dogs’ From Tilly Norwood Creator Particle 6 José Luis Rebordinos Reflects On His Final Year At San Sebastián: “What Surprises Me The Most Is How Much The Festival Has Grown” View All September 25, 2026 6:12am Reta Guetg Zurich Film Festival Welcome to Deadline’s International Disruptors , a feature where we shine a spotlight on key executives and companies outside of the U.S. shaking up the offshore marketplace. This week we’re talking to Zurich Film Festival Director & Co-Owner Reta Guetg about this year’s edition, her evolution at the festival and why she and fellow co-owners want to make it Europe’s trendiest festival. For someone who works in an industry that is constantly in flux, Zurich Film Festival Co-Owner and Festival Director Reta Guetg is resolute in her ambition for the young film event. Last year, she and ZFF CEO and Co-Owner Christian Jungen led a management buyout of the festival from newspaper publisher NZZ Group and this year the Swiss event is doubling down on a deliberately boutique identity, strengthening its relationship with Hollywood and positioning itself as a launchpad for awards contenders – all while using its industry flagship event, the Zurich Summit , to put emerging issues like AI at the center of the conversation. Related Stories News 'The Lion King' Director Rob Minkoff To Develop & Exec Produce Family Pic 'Storm Dogs' From Tilly Norwood Creator Particle 6 Festivals Zurich Summit 2026: FilmNation, AMPAS, Sony Classics, Mubi, Mattel, Komplizen, Mediawan, CAA, UTA, TikTok & YouTube Among Speakers At Swiss Conference “We’re not going to be an A-festival, that’s not our strategy,” Guetg tells Deadline. “We want to have the best films we can and push them to an audience, but also to the industry. We want to put them on the radar and be a relevant launchpad for awards contenders. We can be the perfect second home for a film to get visibility through a cool place like Zurich.” Watch on Deadline The 22 nd edition of ZFF kicked off on Thursday night with the European premiere of Mount Everest adventure Tenzing , starring Tom Hiddleston and Willem Dafoe and highlights in this year’s lineup include the European premiere of Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky as well as screenings of Naomi Watts starrer The Housewife and Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut . Further films set to screen at the 11-day event include Danny Boyle’s Ink , Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine , Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid , Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan starrer Josephine and Alexander Skarsgård and Olivia Colman rom-com Wicker . Talent in attendance this year include Hiddleston, Watts, McDonagh, Julianne Moore, Richard Linklater and John Turturro, all of whom are set to be feted by the fest. This weekend sees the return of its annual Zurich Summit, its flagship boutique industry conference that Guetg has been carefully building since she first joined ZFF in 2016. Running September 25-27, the summit is now renowned for attracting top Hollywood and international execs who descend upon the swanky Dolder Grand Hotel for the weekend to discuss current industry trends, issues and financing models. ZFF has dubbed it “the Davos of the film world” in reference to the annual World Economic Forum in the Swiss Alps. ZURICH, SWITZERLAND – OCTOBER 03: Christian Jungen, Amanda Seyfried and Reta Guetg attend the “The Testament Of Ann Lee” green carpet during the 21st Zurich Film Festival at Corso Green Carpet on October 03, 2025 in Zurich, Switzerland. (Photo by Joshua Sammer/Getty Images for ZFF) Last year, the event went viral when Tilly Norwood was introduced to the world during a Deadline-moderated panel with her creator Eline van der Velden. After reporting that a number of talent agents were circling the AI actress for representation , the story quickly sparked a global debate and firmly put Zurich at the forefront of the conversation. “The Tilly Norwood story really showed how Zurich can be relevant,” says Guetg. “We are a platform to launch a discussion for the industry that continued to be a discussion out of Zurich. That was really memorable and I think it was a sign that somehow, after all of these years, we are at the center of these important topics and ideas. It validated all that we have built over these years.” With wind in its sails, the Zurich Summit is ramping up its efforts this year. Attendees the 2026 event include FilmNation Entertainment CEO Glen Basner (who is receiving the annual Game Changer Award), Backrooms director Kane Parsons, AMPAS CEO Bill Kramer, CAA Media Finance Co-Heads Roeg Sutherland and Sarah Schweitzman, UTA Independent Film Group Partner and Head Rena Ronson, Mediawan Pictures CEO Elisabeth d’Arvieu and Mubi CEO Efe Cakarel. Van der Velden is also returning along with speakers from TikTok and YouTube. Guetg, who was first in charge of building the industry strand of the fest when she started at ZFF decade ago, points to its strong relationships with Hollywood – notably CAA – who have helped bring speakers to the confab each year. “We’ve had a lot of goodwill and help from Hollywood execs and agencies to help us grow this event – they are our soft power.” Its success, she says, is also down to its “boutique and bespoke” nature. “It’s one of the rare times, particularly in this busy fall season, where there’s less people,” says Guetg. “It’s very curated and it’s an environment where people really have time to sit down and talk to each other in different surroundings. I think this quality time makes a difference.” First steps Guetg’s route into the film business began in Bern in 2000 when she launched short film festival Shnit. “It grew quite quickly into a big thing in our hometown,” she says. “We built it from scratch, and our idea was to just show fun, short films in Bern. We had a very good community of really packed cinemas.” That festival quickly grew internationally, spanning to multiple cities including Cape Town, Bangkok and Cairo, among others, and Guetg said growing it was “intuitive.” “I learned so much by doing it and that’s really how I learned how to own my own business and be in charge of everything,” she says. “It was a super great school for me.” After a decade, Guetg felt it was time to move on and, after some production freelancing gigs, ZFF approached her to head up the festival’s burgeoning industry section. “Zurich had a similar history in terms that the founders just had an idea and went for it,” she says. “That felt so familiar to me. It was obviously a completely different size but this idea that nobody really waits for you and being a bit of an underdog – because Zurich did things differently to other festivals –, that felt very natural to me.” ZFF’s next phase It’s a pivotal time for ZFF now, which is notably entering a new chapter following a management buyout in July 2025. Guetg is one of the festival’s now five owners, alongside well-respected former artistic director Jungen (now ZFF CEO), entrepreneur and TV host Max Loong, longtime ZFF President Felix E. Müller and finance expert Marek Skreta. The move gave Guetg and her fellow owners greater control over the festival’s future after being owned by NZZ Group, publisher of Neue Zürcher Zeitung newspaper, for a decade. ZURICH, SWITZERLAND – SEPTEMBER 28: Reta Guetg, Tom Quinn, Christian Junger at the Zurich Summit Dinner during the 21st Zurich Film Festival at Restaurant Terrasse on September 28, 2025 in Zurich, Switzerland. (Photo by Andreas Rentz/Getty Images for ZFF) “It happened in July, almost three months before last year’s festival, so there was not much time to think about what it would really mean,” she says. “So, we had to regroup quite quickly after the festival with this new ownership and figure out where we wanted to go.” The response so far, she says, has been energizing. “It’s opened up a lot of motivation for all of us, including the team, festival friends or donors that support the festival – everyone liked the idea of having an independent group of people run it rather than a big corporation.” The priority is to retain what she describes as Zurich’s DNA: an ability to move quickly, experiment and take risks without becoming weighed down by its own scale. “We need to be so agile, and Zurich has always been quite adaptive, so it was important for us to keep the DNA of the festival.” She is clear that the ambition is not to scale up to the size of festivals like Cannes or Toronto. Instead, much like its summit, Guetg sees value in Zurich’s comparatively intimate scale. “That’s the idea – to keep it small. We don’t want to grow it into a huge event quantity-wise, that’s not the idea at all. We’re a very guest-friendly and talent-friendly city and we’re known for being good hosts.” ZFF has increasingly embraced its own position as a slightly unconventional European player. Guetg cites a 2022 Guardian article’s description of Zurich , which said: “If Venice and Cannes are the grandmothers of the European festival scene, ZFF is the trendy teenager.” The phrase, she says, has stuck. “This has become our vision – to be the trendiest film festival in Europe,” Guetg says. “And I think we’re quite near this.” She continues: “We’ve been lucky that people have been connecting us with people who are aligned with our vision of what we want Zurich to be. Looking ahead, I think it’s important that we try not to do everything, but we continue to try and get the right people. And also to continue to not be so risk averse, because that is more important than ever.” The 22 nd Zurich Film Festival runs September 24-October 4, 2026. ‘Avengers: Endgame: Encore’ & ‘Primetime’ Eye $3M Previews ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’, Meta Finale & Season 2 Judge Grants Suit Settlement Delay; Company Proceeds With $7.5B Debt Raise David Ellison Dines With Trump & Xi; WBD’s CNN, MS Now Denied Access To Event Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Scrubs’ Stars On Joel Kim Booster & X Mayo’s Departures, Ava Bunn’s Promotion, J.D.’s New Foe & Giving Interns Their Own Episodes In Season 2
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On Magic Of Returning To ‘Big Bang’ Stage, Going Multi-Cam In Meta Season 1 Finale & Season 2 Plans ‘The Beast In Me’ Renewed For Season 2 With Claire Danes Reprising Role; Howard Gordon Back With Netflix Overall Deal David Oyelowo & Viola Prettejohn To Star In ‘The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo’ TV Series For Sky View All September 25, 2026 7:00am Joel Kim Booster, X Mayo, Ava Bunn & John Higgins in 'Scrubs' ABC ABC’s Scrubs revival starring Zach Braff (John “J.D.” Dorian), Donald Faison (Christopher Turk) and Sarah Chalke (Elliot Reid) is undergoing some cast changes heading into its second season. Two prominent recurring players are leaving , Joel Kim Booster, who played scheming attending physician Dr. Kevin Park, and X Mayo as charge nurse Raymond. Meanwhile, as reported exclusively by Deadline, two actors are joining in major recurring roles: SNL alum John Higgins as Grant , the new Chief Resident, and Keyla Monterroso Mejia as surgical nurse Mimi . (Additionally, Tamera Mowry-Housley will guest star as Dr. Steffie, a pediatric doctor.) Related Stories Casting Tamera Mowry-Housley To Guest Star On 'Scrubs' Season 2 News Imagen Awards: 'Acapulco' Leads As 'Brownsville Bred,' 'Will Trent' & 'Scrubs' Take Top Prizes - Full List Braff explained to Deadline the rationale behind Park’s departure and Grant’s arrival as a way to replicate the dynamic between Braff’s J.D. and Dr. Cox (John C. McGinley) on the original series, crediting Scrubs creator Bill Lawrence with the idea for the change-up. “Joel was incredible,” Braff said. “I think that we wanted to try and find a nemesis for J.D. who was underneath him. Bill Lawrence had this idea that that, well, there’s no one above J.D. except an administrator, and we’ve seen that before. It might be fun if the person driving him nuts is coming from underneath him, a chief resident, and so that was rethinking where the thorn in J.D.’s side is. “Obviously JD needs conflict, right, for the story to work, things are going very well for J.D., that’ll get boring quick. We need some conflict for drama and comedy, and I think the notion was: what if we introduce a fun thorn in his side, who is actually underneath him and drives him nuts, in the same way that J.D. drove Dr. Cox nuts.” Enter Higgins’ Grant. Mayo’s exit was particularly surprising as charge nurses Dubois (Michael James Scott) and Raymond (Mayo) were two of the revival’s breakout characters in Season 1. Turns out the departure was not story-driven but logistical. “We would have loved to have X on more,” Braff said. “She’s just working so much and so busy, and wasn’t really fully available. But we are bringing in more nurses and more characters. Michael James Scott really just popped, we all love him so much. He’s so friggin’ funny. Every single line he says on the show makes us all laugh, and so he really, really is shining. The writers keep writing to him, and I can’t imagine an episode without him. He’s so lovely to be around, and such a good actor.” The reason Mayo’s schedule came into play is that she and most of the Scrubs cast are recurring guest stars. As such, they are not under contracts and their services are subject to availability. Bunn’s Promotion In Season 1 of the revival, only Braff, Faison and Chalke were series regulars. They are being joined in Season 2 by Ava Bunn , who has been promoted from a recurring. She plays one of the new interns, Sam Tosh. “I think the Ava Bunn storyline — she plays Tosh on the show — is something that needs to be explored,” Faison said. “I don’t know if you’re on social media, but we’re on social media, and a lot of my diagnoses come from the doctors on social media or the things that they say, and that’s something to talk about. That is a new wave of getting information. Google used to be the way to do it, I’m going to Google all of my ailments and see what happens. Now it’s a new era, and a lot of people get their information from things like Instagram or Meta or ChatGPT. So, adding her to the show as the fourth in all of this is, she popped last year, and so here we go, and we’re excited for her too. This is something new.” Added Chalke, “Yeah, she’s great. She comes in with such great ideas, she’s improving all the time, and never delivers the same line twice. She has such confidence in her own skin for such a young age. It’s really cool.” Changing Interns’ Narrative — But Not Series’ Narrator Bunn’s character Sam Tosh got more attention than other new characters last season as she emerged as a wide-eyed intern standout in the vein of J.D. from the first eight seasons and Lucy (Kerry Bishé) from Season 9. Does Bunn’s promotion to a series regular signal a handover of narrator duties from J.D. to Tosh like it happened with him and Lucy in Season 9? “No. It’s interesting. The old show was about the interns, right? Well, now the show is about us,” Braff said, “So, unlike that Season 9, the show is not going to pivot to being about a new cast of interns.” With returning Scrubs fan favorites taking the spotlight, the show has not been able to sufficiently service the new cast, with most interns yet to make an impression as we know very little about them. The series is looking to correct that in Season 2. “One thing we did last year was we tried to service all the interns in every episode, and I think what we learned was we didn’t have the time in 21 minutes to really give them enough story,” Braff said. “So this year, we’re not putting each intern in every episode, but giving them their own episodes to shine, and I think that’s a better strategy for the audience, getting their claws into them and getting to know them better and embracing them more. With the exception of Ava, who’s been made a regular and she’ll be in every episode.” Mentors & Mentees For medical intern Tosh and surgical intern Dashana Trainor (Amanda Morrow), main storylines have been their relationships with mentors Elliot and Turk, respectively. “For Elliot, she picks up again in Season 2, where she’s mentoring Tosh, and, obviously, they’ve all become such great doctors and are really looking forward to this new chapter of being mentors,” Chalke said about Elliot, J.D. and Turk. “Elliot had a bit of a journey last season trying to figure out the balance of how do you mentor this kid who’s way too hard on her, and then pulled back, and is now giving her some more rope and recognizing what a good doctor she is and is becoming.” Said Faison, “With Turk, Dashana is already an example of excellence, she’s already at the top of her game, she’ll have Turk’s job in a few years. She’s that good of a surgeon, that good of a doctor already. And so I think Turk is taking her for granted. She’s making his life a lot easier, and he’s not even paying attention to it because he’s so stuck in his own mental health issues. So he’s got somebody there who should be inspiring him like no other, but he can’t see past his own reflection in the mirror to see that this girl is everything that he’s been asking for, and so, whereas these guys are thriving, being mentors for their doctors, he’s not even paying attention to how good she is.” Scrubs Season 2 launches on Sept. 30 with a two-episode premiere on ABC and streaming next day on Hulu. ‘Avengers: Endgame: Encore’ & ‘Primetime’ Eye $3M Previews ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’, Meta Finale & Season 2 Judge Grants Suit Settlement Delay; Company Proceeds With $7.5B Debt Raise David Ellison Dines With Trump & Xi; WBD’s CNN, MS Now Denied Access To Event Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Dolly Parton, Lily Tomlin & Jane Fonda Film ‘9 To 5’ Gets One-Week Screen Return For Parton Charity
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Bowen Yang And Reece Weaver Extend Broadway Engagements In ‘Oh, Mary!’ And ‘Chicago’ Due To Popular Demand Macklemore Launches Free Palestine Tour; U.S. Dates To Be Announced Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Music Video Featuring Colin Farrell & Dakota Johnson To Debut At VMAs; Watch Teaser Clip View All September 25, 2026 7:02am 9 to 5 movie poster Courtesy A newly restored 9 to 5 , the hit 1980 workplace comedy starring Dolly Parton , Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin , will return to theaters for a special weeklong theatrical run beginning October 9, with Disney donating net proceeds from each U.S. ticket purchase to The Dollywood Foundation. The proceeds will be used to support Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library. Tickets to see the newly restored 20th Century Studios film in theaters are now on sale. The 9 to 5 theatrical re-release was announced today on “Give Like Dolly Day,” a new annual celebration encouraging the world to make a difference in a child’s life and honor Parton’s lifelong mission, inspiring children to “Dream More, Learn More, Care More and Be More.” Related Stories News Dolly Parton Tribute By Kacey Musgraves Set For Sunday's VMAs Legal Block The Merger & Elizabeth Warren Call Out AGs For Betrayal In Deal Talks With Paramount: "A Win Only For David Ellison" “Give Like Dolly Day” is observed annually on 9/25 – a date chosen as an homage to the film’s title. Watch on Deadline In 9 to 5, a group of female office workers – the all-knowing manager who trained the boss but can’t get promoted (Lily Tomlin), a befuddled newcomer (Jane Fonda) and an alluring personal secretary everyone presumes is having an affair (Dolly Parton) – all band together to seek revenge on the man (Dabney Coleman) who is making their lives miserable. Directed by Colin Higgins and produced by Bruce Gilbert from a screenplay by Higgins and Patricia Resnick, 9 to 5 received an Academy Award nomination for the hit title song written and performed by Parton. 20th Century Studios is releasing the newly restored film in theaters for a one-week engagement, from October 9-15. ‘Avengers: Endgame: Encore’ & ‘Primetime’ Eye $3M Previews ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’, Meta Finale & Season 2 Judge Grants Suit Settlement Delay; Company Proceeds With $7.5B Debt Raise David Ellison Dines With Trump & Xi; WBD’s CNN, MS Now Denied Access To Event Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Scrubs’ Stars On How Scott Foley & Rachel Bilson’s Arrival Changes J.D. & Elliot’s Relationship & Impacts Turk’s Marriage
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On Magic Of Returning To ‘Big Bang’ Stage, Going Multi-Cam In Meta Season 1 Finale & Season 2 Plans ‘The Beast In Me’ Renewed For Season 2 With Claire Danes Reprising Role; Howard Gordon Back With Netflix Overall Deal David Oyelowo & Viola Prettejohn To Star In ‘The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo’ TV Series For Sky View All September 25, 2026 7:30am Rachel Bilson and Scott Foley in 'Scrubs' Disney/Darko Sikman Exes J.D. ( Zach Braff ) and Elliot ( Sarah Chalke ) are both getting significant others in Season 2 of Scrubs ‘ revival on ABC, and for Elliot, it’s a blast from the past and someone J.D. was once jealous of. As Deadline revealed exclusively last month , Scott Foley is returning to the medical comedy, reprising his role as marine biologist Sean as he and Elliot rekindle their previous on-again off-again romance. And Rachel Bilson , whose hospital visitor Charlie hit it off with J.D. in the Season 1 finale , is also back for an arc as the duo hard launch their relationship that may be coming fast and furious for J.D. Related Stories News 'Scrubs' Stars On Joel Kim Booster & X Mayo's Departures, Ava Bunn's Promotion, J.D.'s New Foe & Giving Interns Their Own Episodes In Season 2 Casting Tamera Mowry-Housley To Guest Star On 'Scrubs' Season 2 “J.D. is going, as you said, a little fast and furious with her, and Turk’s giving him advice that he’s going way too fast and needs to calm down,” Braff said. Added Faison, “He’s a little rusty with his courtship, and he’s going all in a little too too much, but that makes Turk realize that he hasn’t been going in with the wife at all, as far as the romantic side goes. Like he’s just playing husband; I’ll come home, we’re gonna do the maybe watch a movie thing, and then let’s go to bed, and then I’ll go to work, and you go to work in the morning, and stuff like that. He’s not doing any type of romantic anything.” The first three episodes of Season 2 set up a “running storyline of the difference in all of our lives,” Braff said. “J.D. is a bachelor again, and he’s out there in a new exciting thing, Turk’s been in a long-term relationship for many years, and Elliot’s also dipping her toe in the dating waters,” he said. “The contrast between our romantic lives is something that’s really been funny. Scott Foley’s back to be a love interest for Sarah for some episodes, and Rachel’s been mine, and the dynamic with us all together is just hilarious, we’re having so much fun.” Besides revisiting a classic Scrubs love triangle (J.D., Elliot, Sean) that produced the signature “Nobody cares, Sean” line the jealous J.D. used to say, Foley’s return serves another story purpose. “The writers were like, ‘How do we bring back Elliot’s neuroses?’,” Chalke said. “And so they thought that Scott would be a good way to do that because now that Elliot’s more comfortable in her job and feels super confident as a doctor, this is kind of what shakes her and brings back a lot of her neurotic days.” This marks a character adjustment — and return to form — for Elliot. “One thing we overcorrected for a little bit in Season 1 was Elliot being this mature person, and not that she’s not mature, but I think I and Sarah and others and fans missed a little bit of batsh*t crazy Elliot. Said Chalke, “We brought some of the batsh*t back.” Added Braff, “So we’ve taken the batsh*t dial in Elliot and put it back to normal. And by normal, I mean her old batsh*t stuff. “Which has been super fun to do, I missed it,” Chalke said. Is Elliot getting back with Sean because she may be jealous of what J.D. has with Charlie, and what happened with her Season 1 romantic interest pilot Wes who doesn’t seem to be in the picture anymore? “We reference the fact that she’s still with the pilot at the beginning, but she doesn’t really realize, like Carla’s, like ‘Elliot, he’s so boring.’ She’s like, ‘He’s not boring, he’s just sending me pictures,’ and it was amazing the different alts of the jokes that the writers came up with for the photos that Wes was sending her. And then she realizes, she looks at what Charlie and J.D. have, and she’s like, ‘Huh, maybe I do want that’.” Braff applauded Elliot’s classy reaction to his new romance. “She’s being very mature about it, I have to say, because J.D.’s not being very tactful about his loving on Charlie. Added Chalke, “Yeah, it’s in her face, in the workplace and outside.” “Yeah, it’s not very respectful,” Braff continued. “But J.D.’s about to get a big wake-up call when TV’s Scott Foley shows up with his green eyes.” Added Faison, “He’s so handsome. He’s got like this salt and pepper thing going right now. It’s just dreamy.” Scrubs Season 2 launches on Sept. 30 with a two-episode premiere on ABC and streaming next day on Hulu. ‘Avengers: Endgame: Encore’ & ‘Primetime’ Eye $3M Previews ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’, Meta Finale & Season 2 Judge Grants Suit Settlement Delay; Company Proceeds With $7.5B Debt Raise David Ellison Dines With Trump & Xi; WBD’s CNN, MS Now Denied Access To Event Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Anthony Kim Documentary From ‘Cocaine Quarterback’ Director Set at Propagate Content (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 24, 2026 5:00am Anthony Kim Jordan Bank/Getty Images An Anthony Kim documentary film from Jody McVeigh-Schultz ( Cocaine Quarterback: Signal-Caller for the Cartel , Spy High ) is in the works at Propagate Content , The Hollywood Reporter has learned. And if you do not know who Kim is, well, his story is very much deserving of the… honor? Kim was a golf prodigy and rising star until a 2012 achilles injury derailed not just his career, but his life. What was supposed to be a 12-month recovery turned into a 12-year hiatus from the game — at any level. Along the way, Kim, who received a massive insurance payout for cashing in an insurance policy protecting against a career-ending injury, struggled with drugs and alcohol. Related Stories Business Ben Silverman's Propagate Content Lands $50 Million In Financing to Boost Creator Bets TV 'Made in Korea' Finale: Hyun Bin Reflects on the Message Behind Disney+'s Hit K-Drama Thriller “Anthony Kim was a golf prodigy destined for greatness before injuries, addiction, mental illness, and isolation led him to disappear from the sport, and the world, for more than a decade,” the doc’s synopsis reads. “Now, after an improbable return and a victory few believed possible, Kim tells his story for the first time, on his own terms. A deeply personal journey of recovery, redemption, and the search for what comes next.” The documentary is produced by Propagate Content. Executive producers include company founders Ben Silverman and Howard T. Owens, as well as Drew Buckley and Jack Katkavich. “Anthony’s story is one of extraordinary resilience, marked by some of the highest highs and lowest lows imaginable,” Silverman said in a statement. “We’re hopeful that by telling his story in all its complexity, we can inspire others to believe that a comeback is always possible.” Kim returned to professional golf in 2024 via a LIV Tour exemption. He struggled mightily before securing his first pro golf tournament win in 16 years in February 2026. Other Propagate documentaries include The Last First: Winter K2 for Apple TV, I’m Chevy Chase and You’re Not for CNN, Netflix’s sports documentary series Untold , Hillary for Hulu, LFG for HBO Max and Jerry West: The Logo for Amazon Prime Video. Propagate, founded in 2015, also produces the Chopped shows for Food Network, Fox comedy Best Medicine and Apple TV comedy Stick . Their next scripted project is Apple’s Protective Custody , a new comedy series starring Ben Stiller and Benicio del Toro. THR

articles.title: Judge Orders White House to Restore Access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 24, 2026 5:42am Journalists gather in the Brady Press Briefing Room before going into the Oval Office at the White House on Sept. 18, 2026. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images A federal judge has ordered the White House to restore access to CNN , MS NOW and Politico, just days after President Trump had banned the outlets from the complex. Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, released his decision overnight Wednesday into Thursday, meaning that the reporters could return to the complex as early as today. “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action,” said Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr, attorney for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter . Trump said last week that he was banning the three outlets from the White House, and subsequently justified it by citing vague concerns around national security. The White House TV pool has since been suspended, with CNN not able to participate. In the Temporary Restraining Order, Kelly wrote that after examining the facts, the plaintiffs made a strong enough argument to warrant the decision. For example, the White House had renewed CNN reporter Betsy Klein’s pass months after some of the reporting it cited to justify her ban had been published. “Plaintiffs are also likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process. The ‘general rule’ is that ‘individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them’ of a constitutionally protected interest.” he wrote in the ruling. “Defendants do not dispute that Plaintiffs did not receive notice and an opportunity to b heard before their hard passes were revoked.” He also poured cold water on the national security claims made by President Trump in recent days. “Nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns. Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ Plaintiffs from the White House—instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly Wrote. “And even the justifications provided to Plaintiffs after this case was filed are ambiguous about the true purpose of the revocations: while Defendants’ letters to Plaintiffs mention national security concerns, they purport to identify reporting that “threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods,” leaving open the possibility that all the stories fall into the later bucket, rather than the former.” THR

articles.title: ‘Real Housewives of Rhode Island’ Star Alicia Carmody on How the Bravo Series Changed Her Life: “I Never Knew I Could Work This Hard”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 24, 2026 6:00am Alicia Carmody of 'The Real Housewives of Rhode Island.' Noam Galai/Bravo Alicia Carmody’s life has done a full 180 since it was announced she joined The Real Housewives of Rhode Island cast not even a year ago. Five months after the show debuted on Bravo , the Housewife is deep into filming on the highly anticipated second season, but she squeezed in some time to chat with The Hollywood Reporter about her new partnership with Ferrero celebrating Adultoween. “I love Halloween . I love snacks. I love Ferrero. I love a Butterfinger. I love a Kinder Egg. So it kind of just like all worked out,” Alicia says when asked why she wanted to partner with the food company behind snacks such as Nutella, Kinder and Tic Tac. Related Stories TV Kim Kardashian Debuts New Reality Show 'Team Moms: Baseball': Where to Watch Online TV Khloé Kardashian on 'The Girls' Future, 'The Kardashians' Longevity and Her Sephora Fragrances Alicia adds of the partnership, “Halloween has always been one of my favorite times of year. It’s really about embracing that sense of play and not taking yourself too seriously. That’s exactly what Adultoween is about: Giving adults permission to be creative and have fun again, the way we did as kids. And honestly, snacking is such a huge part of that nostalgia for me — Ferrero has always been part of my Halloween memories, so partnering with them for this felt really natural.” Ferrero’s Halloween collection includes Kinder Joy x Stranger Things Eggs, Kinder Bueno Halloween Lay Down Bags, Butterfinger Skulls, Keebler Spookie Fudge Stripes, Mother’s Eerie Critters and Kinder Joy Glow in the Dark Halloween Eggs. When asked if partnering with brands is something she was looking forward to after becoming a Housewife, Alicia admits, “I actually really never thought I was going to even be a Housewife. I really didn’t know what to expect, to be honest.” Alicia Carmody for Ferrero. Courtesy Bravo revealed in May that Rhode Island was pacing as the network’s second-biggest series across platforms, behind only The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills , the longtime ratings winner of the franchise. Alicia says that the cast “had no clue” their show would be so well received, and she believes viewers resonated with her story because she “was so honest about my life.” Among the topics she discussed on season one were her 10-year engagement to Billy Kitsilis and her desire to be more involved in their business, Pizza Mamma. “I don’t know how to not be myself, and I think people could see that, you know,” she says when asked why fans resonated with her. “I shared my family, my aunts, building a business with my fiancé. I just think that I was so honest about my life.” Being a Housewife is a full-time job, and Alicia says it’s been hard work. “It’s a full-time job, but I didn’t know that. I was like, I’m gonna film going out to dinner with my girlfriends, having a cocktail, a drama here and there, you know,” she says. “I never knew I could work this hard, and it keeps you young. It keeps you moving. You’re always pushing yourself to different limits.” Alicia is partaking in Bravo Fan Fest Charleston this October, just ahead of Halloween. It will be her first fan event as a Housewife, and she’s preparing to “take up every moment that I can.” As for details about season two of The Real Housewives of Rhode Island , she remains tight-lipped, but hints at a potential story to come. “It’s a lot of work, to wedding plan,” she says. Would she ever let Bravo film her wedding? “You never know. I don’t even know what day it is right now, so you never know what [it will be] like when it actually happens. I mean, it’s been 10 years that we’ve been engaged.” With the launch of her partnership with Ferrero, Alicia gave her Instagram followers a peek into how she celebrates Halloween, while announcing a giveaway that will see a winner receive Ferrero Halloween goodies. Of what she loves most about the holiday, the Housewife said, “I love that Halloween, you can be creative and you can be whatever. You can make yourself into whatever you want.” “Adultoween started as an insight the Ferrero Group discovered and has grown into a cultural movement,” said Chad Stubbs, chief marketing officer of Ferrero North America. “We’re excited to see where this year’s trends land and how they’ll shape the way we engage and show up for our fans in bigger and better ways this Halloween and beyond.” THR

articles.title: How Bob Chapek’s Disney Dream Turned Into an Instant Nightmare: Bob Iger “Wanted to See Me Fail”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Former CEO Bob Chapek, right, with his predecessor and successor, Bob Iger. Courtesy Disneyland Resort/Christian Thompson Of all the stories and tales that Disney tells so well, perhaps none proved as fanciful, and lasted as long, as the fantasy that Bob Iger was going to retire. Sure, he thought about it. And he talked about it. Bob’s public contemplations of retirement became a Hollywood tradition, like the Oscars, only it occurred slightly less frequently. Still, it was something of its own production. On different occasions, including that first conversation in my office when he asked me who I thought should replace him (and I said “me”), Bob Iger dropped more breadcrumbs than Hansel and Gretel, but they never actually led anywhere. First he was going to enter politics, then, after some initial feelers, thought better of it. Then, two years later, he publicly flirted with bringing an NFL franchise to Los Angeles, which never gained momentum. Each time, the entire management class underneath him readied for what could be a moment of transition. A number of us felt like the slipper would fit on our feet, if only Bob Iger would take it off in the first place. Still, I did feel like I was being prepared for advancement. After that initial conversation about who his replacement should be, I started being invited to more functions, like board dinners, with corporate leadership. Those early engagements with the board also allowed me to participate in discussions about the company’s future. Bob’s long-standing relationship with many board members created powerful alliances for him, and he often used them to his advantage. As long as we were on the same team, those strong alliances were providing effective support for me as well. By the end of 2016, my two main competitors for the top spot, Jay Rasulo and Tom Staggs, were gone. I realized I was genuinely in the running for the role. Brooks Barnes of The New York Times had called Tom “the only obvious candidate for the job When Tom left, the chatter shifted, with some placing their bets on either Kevin Mayer or me crossing the finish line first. Kevin had also held key executive positions, including overseeing Disney’s acquisitions of Pixar, Marvel, and Lucasfilm, among others. The question of who Bob’s successor would be took another unexpected turn in 2017, and by then, a lot had changed for me. I now had an office in Burbank as chairman of parks and resorts. The successful completion of Shanghai Disney had elevated my standing with Bob, and talk of his retirement was heating up again. When he asked to meet with me shortly before Thanksgiving, I couldn’t help but wonder if this was the moment I had been waiting for. After a few years of waiting, working, and delivering profound value from my position in parks, I let myself fall into the trap once again. By the fall of 2017, Bob had indicated that he was preparing to retire, and this time, he seemed serious about it. Just before the Thanksgiving holiday, he visited the headquarters of Imagineering,, the creative design division that was one of my responsibilities as chairman of Disney Parks, Experiences, and Products. Around five o’clock, at the end of a fun but exhausting day, he asked if he could see me before he left the building. He followed me into my Imagineering office and shut the door. “Bob, I have some news,” he said, his gaze unwavering. My heart began to race. Could this be it? “Bob, we are buying Fox, and I’m staying three more years. Have a great holiday,” he said bluntly before getting up and walking out. It had happened again. I felt as if I were on a football team lining up on the fifty-yard line for a drive and making it all the way to the five-yard line, only to be pushed back by holding calls, sacks, or too many players on the field. In football terms, at the very least, I was dealing with false starts and delay-of-game penalties that seemed completely arbitrary. That holiday season, I felt dejected, thinking that I might never get my chance to truly achieve my dream. Still, I had a job to do. So I did what I always do: I kept my head down and worked harder. Parks was doing well, and the best way to get the role I wanted was to be great at it. Kevin, from the reports of many, was not so subtle in his efforts to ramp up his public relations campaign for his candidacy—and in some circles he was anointed as the favorite to be Bob’s successor. Nevertheless, Bob and other insiders repeatedly assured me that, despite Kevin’s maneuvers for the coveted position, they did not consider him a serious candidate. I had to push aside any thoughts of finishing as the runner-up, because I would consider that a great disappointment—or, as I had told my wife, Cindy, a failure. To be clear, pushing aside thoughts and frustrations is easier when you have one of the best jobs at one of the biggest companies in the world. There’s always plenty to do, and when you’re a competitor, you’re always looking for ways to improve your score, which, for me, meant Disney’s bottom line. Shanghai and Disneyland Paris were growing, and our new pricing systems in parks and cruises were paying dividends, literally. Our earnings report in November 2019 touted that revenues for the quarter increased 8 percent to $6.7 billion, and park operating income increased 17 percent to $1.4 billion. The next month, I was working in my office, getting ready to spend the holidays with my family, when Bob requested another meeting with me. I couldn’t help but think of the meeting years before when he had come in, also right before a holiday, to tell me he was staying. He did have news. In December 2019, he came into my office, closed the door, and this time delivered some different news. “Bob, I want you to know. I’m leaving.” I didn’t roll my eyes. At least, I didn’t mean to. In my mind, let’s just say I was less than convinced. Okay, Bob , I thought. Then he said the words that would change my life forever. “I’ve told the board you’re my replacement.” I barely said anything. It wasn’t until Susan Arnold, the board’s lead independent director, called me the next day that I started to think this long-imagined fantasy might be real. So, there I was one day in January 2020, sitting in The Rotunda, the company’s executive dining room located in Burbank atop Team Disney—the Michael D. Eisner Building. Susan Arnold had asked if I wanted to get lunch. While The Rotunda is a place reserved for executives whose titles grant them the privilege of entry, the seating arrangement is more reminiscent of a high school lunchroom, except that everyone is much wealthier and more powerful. Each table represents a level in the company’s hierarchy, and the seating is determined by each employee’s rank. If Bob Iger were in town, he would sit at his preferred seat at essentially the twelve o’clock of the circular arrangement of tables. If not, the next-highest-ranking person would take his place. It was the third week of January when Susan and I finally took our seats at this head table in the dining room. Unsure of what to expect, I wanted to be ready for anything. I had eaten at the head table many times before, but this was still an event for me. I was here with the head of our board. People saw. We ordered salads and made small talk. But in truth, I didn’t have much of an appetite. Before we started eating, Susan looked at me and said directly, “So I understand Bob has spoken with you.” I simply nodded in response. “Well, it’s going to happen, and it’s going to happen fast. Bob has decided relatively abruptly that he’s done, and the job is yours.” Suddenly, the clinking of silverware and murmurs of nearby conversations faded away as I tried to process what I had just heard. I couldn’t believe it; I had so many questions. However, I was extremely careful to avoid asking the wrong ones, which could lead to another setback. I had been toyed with for six years. It seemed like I was on the goal line. The last thing I wanted to do was draw a flag. “How fast are we talking?” I asked her. I suddenly started thinking about the logistics—not just of doing the job, but of the announcement, which I assumed would be a thoughtful, drawn-out process. I was envisioning engaging with board members and some press, followed by a publicity tour and some meet and greets with key stakeholders over the next few months. “It’s coming within two weeks, not months,” she said, her voice steady and firm. As soon as the lunch was over, I called Cindy. At the time, we’d been married for nearly forty years, and if anyone knew how much this meant to me, it was her. After more than a decade of waiting, I was, in fact, getting “it.” Finally. It was a victory for me, but it would come at a cost to others. Kevin Mayer, the presumed front-runner to some, announced he was leaving shortly after my appointment was made official. Kevin’s departure made him the third of Bob Iger’s top lieutenants over the last decade, along with Tom Staggs and Jay Rasulo, to leave. Each of them believed he was the front-runner to be anointed team captain, convinced the job was his. Instead, in the end, Bob had just been toying with them. During my follow-up conversations with Bob, he expressed a desire to remain involved and help me succeed in his former position. He also voiced his frustrations, saying, “I’m ready to leave, Bob. I’m sick of the earnings calls and all the board meetings.” Those familiar with the situation suspected there were other reasons behind his decision to leave. One possibility was that his compensation wasn’t meeting his expectations, despite his receiving more than $100 million in stock awards from the Fox deal. Although he was a top player in the industry, his pay was considerably less than that of executives at Universal, Paramount, and Fox, all of which have more concentrated shareholder control from a smaller number of influential large investors versus widespread retail investors like Disney. Later, I would discover there might be other reasons behind his “abrupt” decision. After all the years of uncertainty and playmaking, I was surprised by how quickly everything came to a head. The timeline of my appointment moved at such a breakneck pace that I didn’t have the opportunity to meet with a single board member on the matter of my ascension and the transition. As these events unfolded in a whirlwind, I learned that while Bob Iger would no longer be CEO, the board had agreed to allow him to stay on as “executive chairman of the board” and “creative director” for an additional two years. This meant I would have to report to both the board and Bob, although the interpretation of that varied depending on whom you asked. It certainly was confusing to me, as the story kept changing. Initially, I wasn’t too concerned about this arrangement. After all, Bob had always supported me. Why wouldn’t he continue to do so? My naiveté about my dream job was about to end rather abruptly. When Bob Iger released a statement naming me as his successor, the news stunned most people at the company, catching them entirely off guard. By the end of my first day on the job, I realized that I, too, had been caught off guard—and not in a good way. As part of the announcement and rollout, we had arranged an interview with CNBC, with interviews with other outlets to follow. Sitting in matching directors’ chairs on the Disney studio lot, Bob and I were only a few minutes into our first interview with CNBC when I noticed things weren’t going as expected. Bob usually appeared confident and optimistic in interviews, but he clearly didn’t feel that way during this one. I quickly understood I needed to do everything possible to avoid making the situation a fiasco. I could almost feel the daggers Bob was hurling my way. When he introduced me to the world as his successor, he initially had said we had worked “extremely well” together. Seconds later, he went out of his way to clarify that “Actually, our senior management team has worked together quite well.” That was it. In response, throughout the exchange, I made every effort to compliment him for all the magic he had created for the company and acknowledge what an outstanding mentor he had been to me. “I plan to follow in his footsteps and recognize I have some big shoes to fill,” I said. “We have a solid strategy, and I intend to continue implementing every part of that strategy.” Whenever I glanced in Bob’s direction, his expression was ice-cold, and his shifting body language spoke volumes about how miserable and uncomfortable he felt. There were moments when he even appeared angry, with his jaws clenched. Bob Iger was botching the handoff because I believe he didn’t want to let go of the ball. What I didn’t know then is that the reality of that truth would leave no room for recovery. It was so obvious that a reporter who had been covering the CEO transition shared his observation with me following the CNBC interview: it was apparent to him that Bob regretted everything and that the spotlight on me frustrated him. Why? Because I was now the one providing the play-by-play while he was relegated to adding color commentary. I didn’t respond to the reporter. He was right. The day after my announcement, I flew to New York to meet with investors and participate in more media interviews. I still hadn’t even been inside my new office at Disney, which I learned would not be the same one Bob had occupied as CEO. Famous for liking to get to the office early and working out, Bob had a private shower in his office. “You don’t need a shower in your office,” he told me. I didn’t want to make things any more awkward than they already were, so I readily acquiesced. I didn’t care about the trappings of a fancy office. I was just excited to have the job. I took a different office. The symbolism loomed large, as I would later experience. While I might have landed the position, it seemed like Bob was now doing to me what he had previously done to Kevin, Tom, and Jay: playing me. Two weeks later, the concerns I had during our CNBC interview began to play out openly. We were scheduled to hold our annual shareholder meeting in Raleigh in March, just before everything shut down because of COVID. On the plane, I had asked Bob how he wanted to handle the Q&A from the board. He was aware I had never run a television network before, let alone a number of them, between ABC, ESPN, and other cable channels. Given my quick appointment, he understood there were still aspects of the company’s operations that were unfamiliar to me. “How do you want to divide up these questions, Bob?” I asked, feeling increasingly anxious as my palms began to sweat. This was my first time addressing the shareholders as the new CEO. “Oh, no. I’m not getting up there,” he informed me. “It’s all you.” “I’ve had the job just two weeks, Bob,” I reminded him. “Well, you have a binder. Study it,” he responded dismissively. At that moment, I was 100 percent convinced he wanted to see me fail. Of course, the very first question was about TV. It came from a conservative activist who threw me a curveball. He wanted to know how I could sleep at night knowing the liberal bent of ABC News. He proceeded to provide example after example before basically ending with, essentially, “What do you think of that, new guy?” ABC News was a wholly owned subsidiary of Disney. So, as CEO, I was responsible for its operations and, apparently, alleged political bent. I responded that ABC held itself to the highest standards of objectivity and balanced coverage. I felt my answer hit his curveball satisfactorily. However, the feedback I received from both sides of the political spectrum within the company indicated neither side was totally satisfied. The liberal wing said I should have told him he was full of it, and those on the right thought I should have been more sympathetic. It seemed there was no way to win. In that moment, though, Bob Iger had let me down. Unfortunately, that wasn’t the last curveball that day. While flying back from the Raleigh meeting, our finance chief, Christine McCarthy, suggested, “Hey, why not have our first one-on-one meeting now?” Although it seemed like a normal request, Bob reacted explosively. “How could you dare disrespect me by having your first one-on-one in front of me?” he shouted, his face flushed and visibly upset. In all the years we had worked together, this was the first time I had seen him demonstrate anger. We rode most of the rest of the way in relative silence. As we flew above a country that was only beginning to confront a global pandemic, I, too, was realizing just how difficult my life was about to become. Copyright © 2026 by Robert Alan Chapek and Don Yaeger. From the forthcoming book BEHIND THE CASTLE WALLS: My Thirty Years at the Happiest Place on Earth by Bob Chapek with Don Yaeger to be published by Gallery Books, an Imprint of Simon & Schuster, LLC. Printed by permission. THR

articles.title: Terence Winter Teams With  ‘Age of Disclosure’ Director to Adapt UFO Insider’s Story
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 24, 2026 6:00am Terence Winter Brigitte Lacombe Emmy-winning writer Terence Winter is teaming up with the filmmaker behind the indie documentary hit The Age of Disclosure to adapt an upcoming memoir that purports to reveal the behind-the-scenes story of the U.S. government’s cover-up of UFOs. The Sopranos and The Wolf of Wall Street writer will tackle the forthcoming book Out of the Shadows by former senior U.S. intelligence official Jay Stratton, who is considered the senior-most former government official to come forward claiming the existence of non-human intelligent life. Related Stories TV Vincent Pastore, the Mobster "Big Pussy" on 'The Sopranos,' Dies at 80 TV 'The Sopranos' Creator Says Hollywood Is "Going Back to Greed and Fear" in Trump Era The project, which is seeking distribution, is spearheaded by Age of Disclosure director-producer Dan Farah. “For all of human history, mankind has wondered whether we are the only intelligent life in the universe,” Winter said in a statement. “Jay Stratton’s shocking true story answers that question and more as it delves into the world of the U.S. government’s investigation of UAP and non-human intelligent life. It’s a riveting journey into a world the public knows little about. Jay is the key-man in the U.S. government’s modern-day investigation of UAP. While his decades of work have been in the shadows, it has changed the course of history and I couldn’t be more excited to bring his story to the screen.” “ Out of the Shadows has the propulsive storytelling of a high-stakes political thriller,” added Farah. “It brings you behind the scenes of the U.S. government’s investigation of the biggest mystery of all time. At the center of the story is the deeply personal, harrowing toll Jay’s pursuit of the truth had on him and his family.” Stratton cofounded the Advanced Aerospace Weapons System Application Program (AAWSAP), the first official U.S. government program to investigate UAP since the closure of the Air Force’s Project Blue Book in 1969. For 16 years, Stratton reportedly investigated UAP and non-human intelligent life on behalf of the federal government. In Age of Disclosure , Stratton declared, “I have seen, with my own eyes, non-human craft and non-human beings.” “It’s time for the world to learn the truth,” Stratton said in a statement. “There is far too much at stake. UAP activity over our nation’s sensitive military and nuclear sites is an ongoing issue.” Out of the Shadows will be published in the U.S. by HarperCollins imprint William Morrow on Oct. 13. The project marks the latest in a wave of UFO-related projects, which earlier this year included Steven Spielberg’s film Disclosure Day . Public interest in the topic has surged in the wake of a succession of media reports, lawmakers and whistleblowers making claims about unidentified anomalous phenomena. THR

articles.title: Israel-Gaza War Documentary ‘NAZA’ Sets Global Theatrical Release Plans
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 24, 2026 6:20am 'NAZA' Naza/The Guardian NAZA , the Israel – Gaza war documentary, has set plans for a global theatrical release from Sept. 28 after picking up the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival. The film from No Other Land directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor will have a North American premiere at the New York Film Festival on Saturday, to be followed by a theatrical release starting Oct. 9 in the U.S. and now a global rollout. “We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. The threats from the Israeli government to revoke our citizenship and the death threats do not change that and will not stop the film. We thank our colleagues for the solidarity and look forward to sharing NAZA all over the world very soon,” Abraham and Szor said in a statement. Related Stories TV 'Made in Korea' Finale: Hyun Bin Reflects on the Message Behind Disney+'s Hit K-Drama Thriller Movies Rolf de Heer Named Jury President for Tokyo Film Festival For the film’s international release coming hot on the heels of the Venice premiere, The Guardian and partner mk2 Films have inked deals with theatrical distributors in 56 territories. Those markets include The Middle East, France, Canada, UK, Italy, Spain, Germany, Belgium, Netherlands, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Brazil and Central America. After the theatrical run globally, NAZA, executive produced by Jonathan Glazer ( The Zone of Interest ) and featuring testimony from 24 Israeli military officers outlining the systems and protocols they allege Israel uses to target and kill Palestinian civilians in Gaza, will stream on The Guardian website, for free. The film’s title, NAZA , comes from an acronym the Israeli military uses as a shorthand for civilian casualties. The film’s producers said the documentary has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel, and The Guardian was looking for ways to allow the film to be seen in Gaza and the West Bank. NAZA is produced by The Guardian and JW Films. Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent and a NAZA producer, in his own statement said: “ NAZA is grounded in rigorous journalism published over the past three years, but it is also a powerful piece of cinema that will soon be available on screens, large and small, around the world. The initial response from those who’ve seen it shows audiences are engaging deeply with the urgent questions the film raises. We’re working with MK2 and international partners to bring the film to global audiences as soon as possible.” THR

articles.title: YouTube Bets That a Slew of AI-Powered Features Can Maintain Its Video Domination
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 24, 2026 6:50am YouTube Custom Feeds YouTube YouTube may be the most-watched video platform on planet earth, but it is not wrestling on its laurels. The Google-owned platform this week announced a barrage of AI-powered features and tools, for both viewers and creators, that it is betting can help people make more content faster, and help viewers more specifically find what they are looking for. The company announced the tools at its annual Made on YouTube event in New York City, with CEO Neal Mohan taking the stage in Google’s office in a former shipping pier on the Hudson River. “Since the start of the year, we’ve launched over 3,000 product updates and improvements, keeping up with evolving viewer tastes and increasing creator ambitions,” Mohan said. “This is what it looks like to innovate in the YouTube era, an era where entertainment is built from the ground up by creators and the communities that fuel them.” For YouTube viewers, the biggest change will be the introduction of Custom Feeds, which will let users type what they are interested in in (think “help me find new DIY creators” or “witty podcasts for my 30 minute commute”), with the platform creating new tabs that will refresh with options in those defined areas. The platform is also adding new functionality to Ask YouTube, enabling followup questions and more specific search capabilities. On the creator front, some of the announcements drew applause and buzz from many of the creators in attendance. YouTube Studio can now suggest pacing and structure for videos, and help creators automatically A/B test thumbnails. Soon it will allow for A/B testing of videos, enabling different versions of content for different audiences. It is also rolling out a conversational editing assistant, letting users lean on YouTube’s apps to help it edit content using natural language prompts. Opt-in AI-powered comment moderation is also in the works, as is a voice detection tool that will join its current likeness detection program. “Our approach has always been to use AI to empower human creativity, and to do it responsibly,” Mohan told the crowd. THR

The Virtual Reali-Tea Awards will debut as part of Philo’s free channel lineup. Tune into the exclusive streaming premiere of the 2026 Virtual Reali-Tea Awards on October 9 and catch up on last year’s awards at Philo.com/VRTs . THR

articles.title: ‘The Swan’ Unmasked: Inside the Most Sadistic Reality Show Ever
articles.full_text: ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection The mere mention of “ The Swan ” is enough to send chills down one’s spine. Created by former Telemundo exec Nely Galán, the Fox reality series selected 16 female contestants — from over 250,000 applicants — who were so-called “ugly ducklings” and subjected them to a 90-day ordeal of extreme plastic surgery, dentistry, training and crash dieting (with a little bit of therapy thrown in) to transform them into what its panel of “experts” deemed “attractive” before making them compete in “the ultimate beauty pageant,” where the women vied against one another for the ultimate prize of being crowned The Swan. Related Stories Emmys in Talks to Move to Amazon Prime Video Under New Licensing Arrangement, as the Broadcast Wheel Deal Ends (EXCLUSIVE) Amazon's AWS Now Lets Streamers Deliver up to 10 Live Feeds on One Screen In a review for Entertainment Weekly, Gillian Flynn, the future author of “Gone Girl,” called it “a foul blend of condescension and self-obsession” and “a misogynistic mix of TV’s twin vices: commercialism and conformity.” Popular on Variety The show’s first season debuted in April 2004 and was a smash hit, attracting 9 million viewers across America. But ratings plummeted in Season 2 amid heavy backlash to the show’s inherent ugliness, and it was canceled. “The Swan” has since ranked atop most lists for the “Worst Reality TV Series in History” and represents the cultural nadir of the image-obsessed early aughts. Now, the new documentary “The Swan: Behind the Mirror” examines the notorious reality series and the carnival of horrors its participants endured. Directed by Erin Lee Carr (“I Love You, Now Die: The Commonwealth V. Michelle Carter”) and premiering Sept. 29 on Hulu, the film tackles the show from all angles, including interviews with a dozen former contestants, show producers, trainers, cultural commentators and even one of its plastic surgeons, painting it as an enterprise that preyed on those with self-esteem issues in order to chase ratings. “They were not looking for people that had their life together,” says Carr. “They were looking for people who were, in my mind, vulnerable, and when you isolate people for 90 days who have already expressed that they have mental health issues, it’s going to go sideways.” Kristy Garza was interested in “The Swan” because she was exiting the military and ready for a life change. “I’d always struggled with self-esteem issues not because of my ability, but my appearance,” she tells Variety. “I’d always been a tomboy and wanted to feel like the prettiest girl in the room.” Also, after Kristy gave birth she “had cow teats at 23 years old.” She applied and was accepted for its first season. But things seemed off immediately following her surgeries. “My alarm bells started going off when we got to the apartments in Marina Del Rey and they showed us that all the reflective surfaces were covered,” she recalls. “I’d signed my life away in this contract and you’re already giving me surprises, so what else is going on?” Indeed, the 16 women on the show were trapped in apartments with no reflective surfaces — even CDs were confiscated by producers — and would have to request permission to leave via their Nextel walkie-talkies. They came to call it “Pretty Prison.” “There were times that I would call on the radio and no one would answer, so you get stir-crazy,” Kristy remembers. Kristy Garza in “The Swan: Behind the Mirror.” Disney There was no seeing family or friends, contestants were forced to work out six days a week (sometimes twice a day) while recovering from myriad plastic surgeries and had to adhere to a strict diet of 800-1,200 calories a day, courtesy of Jenny Craig. “There were so many of us that didn’t shit for a week,” Kristy shares in the doc. “The Swan” boasted of shelling out $250,000 on each contestant to cover their cosmetic surgeries, training, dieting and therapy, and producers drilled that sum into their heads throughout the entire process. “We were constantly being told, ‘You can leave, but if you do you’ll owe us for everything we’ve done!’” claims Kristy. If that weren’t enough, the beauty pageant element of the show wasn’t even revealed to contestants until after their surgeries were performed, while they were in recovery. Carl Buehl, a senior producer on the first season of “The Swan,” says this mandate came down from Fox executives to up the ante, posing the question, “Aren’t you tearing down everything we’ve done for them?” This curveball felt particularly manipulative to Kristy. “I came in because I have self-esteem issues and now you’re going to make me compare myself to everybody on a national stage while I’m still building myself up?” she exclaims. “I’m super pissed to this day. We were grossly mishandled and disrespected. You can’t invite somebody to play a game with you and then change the rules in the middle of the game. It was bullshit .” Season 2 was even more exploitive. For its big twist, sisters Kari and Gina Bravata were pitted against each other as contestants — only Gina’s participation was kept secret from Kari. The siblings were given the code names “Mark” and “Greg” so as not to spoil the surprise, and if Gina happened to spill the beans her contract stipulated that she was liable for $5 million plus attorney’s fees. “It was mean and it was cold and it was heartless. I’m still so bitter and so angry,” Kari attests. “I think they ultimately tried to break our bond, which is never going to happen because we’re stronger than them.” Kari and Gina Bravata in “The Swan: Behind the Mirrror.” Disney Far and away the most odious talking head in the documentary is Dr. Randal Haworth, one of the show’s two plastic surgeons. “There are no victims in life, only volunteers,” he declares. The women recall Haworth summoning them to a garage where they were pressured to undress and have fully nude photos taken of themselves as rock ‘n’ roll music blared. Though done under the guise of “before and after” plastic surgery photos, Haworth reveals in the film that the nudes were really for a coffee table book he was cooking up that never saw the light of day. Kari only learned about the coffee table book idea during the making of the doc. “It was a shock and it makes me feel sick,” she asserts. “We were told we had to do it and I remember crying in the middle of it.” And then she almost died. Since production has never been transparent about exactly what went down during her surgery, Kari has only her blurry memory combined with the accounts of cameramen who were in the operating room documenting it — until they were removed. “From what I’ve heard, they tried to wake me up and take me off anesthesia, pulled the tube out expecting me to wake up, and I didn’t,” Kari recounts. “During me not waking up, my lungs filled with fluid and my oxygen started dropping. It got to a low enough point that all the cameras got icked out, and that’s the extent of what I know happened.” She shakes her head: “I don’t think I’ll ever know what happened. I would love, for my own medical history, to know the extent of what happened, but I have absolutely no idea.” While “The Swan: Behind the Mirror” contains loads of access, two key players are noticeably absent: its creator Nely Galán and the show’s chief plastic surgeon, Dr. Terry Dubrow . Carr says she had “many conversations” with Galán about participating in the doc, but her demands — an executive producer credit and a degree of editorial control — proved too much. Since Galán owned the footage to “The Swan,” Carr and her team were forced to get creative, having subjects comment on scenes from the show being played on an iPad so they qualified as fair use. As for Dubrow, Carr says he “wanted a sum of money that would never make sense for a documentarian to pay an expert,” adding it was “under $100,000 for one interview.” “The Swan” Season 1 beauty pageant. ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection Dubrow, whose name may sound familiar from his role as the husband to “The Real Housewives of Orange County” star Heather Dubrow, opened up about his “The Swan” experience during a recent appearance on the podcast “We Need to Talk With Paul C. Brunson.” According to Dubrow, the show had been approved for a third season that was poised to be even more outrageous than Season 2. “We’re casting the third season, and because reality TV was really pushing the envelope at the time, we were going to do some crazy casting. We were going to have triplets. And because there were two surgeons, I was going to operate on two, [Haworth] was going to operate on one, and we were going to see how different they looked,” explained a chuckling Dubrow. However, when Peter Ligouri took over as entertainment chairman at Fox, one of his first orders of business was canceling “The Swan.” A number of ex-“Swan” contestants in the documentary contend that they experienced health complications following the show, from veneers falling out and gum disease — the show’s resident dentist, Dr. Sherri Worth, had her license revoked in 2017 for scamming clients — to more serious ones. Kristy discovered that she had two large aneurysms on her aorta and had to have a pair of open-heart surgeries. “It turns out I was born with a bicuspid aortic valve, which somebody on the show should have noticed when I was going through the health screening,” she says. Kari was confined to a wheelchair and had to have her gall bladder removed. “They told me it was probably from starving myself [on the show],” she says. Kristy and Kari say they and the other “Swan” contestants haven’t thought about filing a class-action lawsuit against the makers of the show, but the two found solace during the making of Carr’s documentary, which gave them much-needed closure. The final sequence of “The Swan: Behind the Mirror” sees the 12 women who participated in the film reunite for a celebratory dinner, reveling in each other’s company. “The documentary has been the most healing I’ve been able to do in the past 22 years,” offers Kristy. “Erin made me feel valued and seen. I didn’t even know how much I needed this. I thought I’d gotten past it after all these years, but I’d just compartmentalized it. We went from trauma and drama to this awesome sisterhood.” “It was healing in a way that you can’t even put into words,” adds Kari. “The weight that was lifted through this, and the girls that I can lean on, was healing and strengthened this bond that we have. I can’t wait for everyone to hear our story.” Loading comments...
