articles.title: Donald Trump Just Told Ari Emanuel He’s Excited About a Vance-Rubio Ticket in 2028
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All September 23, 2026 12:47am Rachel Maddow grills Ari Emanuel at 92Y on Tuesday September 22, 2026 in New York Steven Zeitchik Donald Trump doesn’t want to stay in the White House past 2028, Ari Emanuel says — he’s too excited about JD Vance and Marco Rubio coming in instead. “I spoke to him three weeks ago,” the TKO chief told Rachel Maddow at New York’s 92Y Tuesday night, describing a call with the President about the federal tax credit. “And in that conversation … He thought JD and Marco Rubio would be a formidable group.” You mean as a joint ticket (presumably with Vance at the top), Maddow asked? “Yes,” Emanuel said. “That’s what he thought.” The best cable-news show Tuesday night wasn’t on the air. It was inside the New York venue, as Maddow interviewed her agent on the day of his memoir’s release, and despite their association repeatedly held his feet to the fire on a range of political and cultural topics. The (unstreamed) conversation went from convivial to feisty to testy and back again, as Emanuel sought to convince the audience, only sometimes successfully, that his friendliness with the White House and oligarchs like Elon Musk was for the greater good. “I don’t think it’s productive to say I’ve never changed him,” Emanuel said of Musk. “I do think I’ve changed him a little.” (Emanuel is notably friendly with Elon Musk, his company even investing in Musk’s Twitter.) Emanuel’s Roll the Calls tracks his time from a young apprentice in the CAA mailroom to his current status, at 65, atop the agency and UFC-WWE heap, with all the rage he (proudly) unleashed to get there. But at the event he showed a cannier side, one willing to play nice with power, as Emanuel praised moguls like David Ellison — whom the agent very publicly supported in his successful bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery. Though Emanuel allowed that he didn’t like how Paramount’s Stephen Colbert cancelation went down, he pointed to how Ellison has “let Matt and Trey do what they’re doing, and Jon do what he’s doing,” referring to South Park and The Daily Show , which regularly take aim at the President. “That’s like a cop pulling you over and you saying, ‘Look at all the people in the crosswalk I didn’t hit!’” Maddow said. “I appreciate the metaphor but I disagree with you,” Emanuel replied, as he talked up the (much-eyerolled ) oversight board charged with ensuring CBS News and CNN independence. “Do you worry about compliant billionaires taking over media?” Maddow asked. “You’re getting most of your news from your phone and social media,” Emanuel said, avoiding the question. Maddow was not done, noting how Ellison has “tanked the [CBS] morning show, the nightly news and is deep-frying 60 Minutes .” She called “the CBS News and 60 Minutes situation under Ellison” an “embarrassment.” She said she knew that for Emanuel there were “business reasons [to support the mogul] — he paid $8 billion to get UFC rights.” “7.4,” Emanuel corrected. “I wish it was eight.” The two spent some time in a lighter mode talking about such topics as Emanuel’s unusual longevity plays that has him doing cold plunges and eating live worms. (No, really.) But then one of the pricklier exchanges emerged when Maddow pressed the TKO leader on his 2018 meeting with Vladimir Putin (over potential UFC initiatives in Russia) and warming again to Saudi crown prince MBS after previously returning a $400 million investment in the wake of the Jamal Khashoggi murder. “Where’s the line?” Maddow asked Emanuel. “I’m sorry to say we’re adults … It’s not always black and white,” Emanuel responded, saying that he thinks MBS has now “done some incredible stuff.” “You’re getting frustrated,” Maddow said. “I’m not frustrated,” Emanuel replied, seemingly a little frustrated. Emanuel also defended his decision to hold a UFC event on the White House lawn in June (“there were incredible videos on American history”) and doubled down on Musk. “I don’t agree with Elon [on immigration],” Emanuel said. “On the other hand I was happy what he did in Ukraine blocking the Russians , happy what he’s doing with Neuralink, happy what he’s doing in space,” he said. Despite the support for some of the biggest business players around, Emanuel couldn’t resist a shot at the brass of rival CAA. “They have not handed the reins down,” he said of the top leaders, which includes Bryan Lourd, Kevin Huvane and several other longtime execs. “That’s bad leadership.” Emanuel also sought to downplay the singular threat of Trump’s presidency. “You don’t think people said at the time Nixon was the most dangerous president in all of U.S. history?” Emanuel asked, to demurrals from Maddow and some in the audience. “Shut the fuck up, stop,” he said, half-smiling. “He’s a different kind of cat,” Maddow pushed back on Trump, noting her belief that “I don’t think he’s going to leave [in 2028].” Emanuel said the Vance-Rubio comment indicated to him “that’s not a man trying to be in the White House forever.” (Rubio, incidentally, has indicated he won’t challenge Vance, which could pave the way to a VP selection. Of course, Vance would first have to win the nomination in what is expected to be a competitive primary, then deem Rubio enough of an asset in a post-Trump world to choose him. Also, an outgoing president hasn’t successfully joysticked the new one since the 1980’s.) Meanwhile, Emanuel’s own family may also be a factor in the race as Rahm Emanuel potentially positions himself to play centrist spoiler on the Democratic side. The younger Emanuel did nothing to cool the speculation about his brother when he said he would do “whatever I can” should he try to run, because “he’d be a great candidate,” as he talked up the former White House chief of staff and Chicago mayor. “Is there anybody more qualified than my brother?” Ari Emanuel asked. Maddow seemed most upset by Emanuel cozying up to Trump and oligarchs for what she suggested was his own benefit. “Is there anything about your relationships [with them] that has ever had a positive or mitigating effect on the harm they are doing to our country?” she asked. “I want to live in a society. You have conversations [in a society],” Emanuel answered. “When I’ve disagreed with the president, with Elon Musk, with a lot of the people you’ve mentioned, I have in my opinion swayed them. That might not satisfy you. I’m sorry,” he said. THR

articles.title: MIP London Ends After 2 Years, Replaced by London Book Fair Event
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 2:22am MIP London in 2025 Courtesy of Getty After two years, MIP London has ended and is set to be replaced by a new two-day conference taking place during the London Book Fair. On Wednesday, RX France confirmed the launch of MIP Talks from Mar. 16-17, 2027. The event will be backdropped by the London Book Fair, one of RX’s flagship events, bringing together leading voices from across the worlds of entertainment, media and culture to explore what is changing, what is breaking through and where new opportunities are emerging. MIP Talks will take place at London ExCel and is set to represent a “new expression of MIP in London, looking beyond traditional television and content to the wider cultural, creative, technological and commercial shifts reshaping global entertainment,” according to organizers. The inaugural MIP Talks will be built around the editorial theme ‘From IP to Fandom — and Fandom to Global Business,’ in which experts will explore an entertainment landscape where traditional boundaries are disappearing, audiences move across platforms and experiences, and IP can come from anywhere. Programming will be highly curated and editorially led, organizers added, spanning headline conversations, unexpected pairings, global trends and data, cultural insight and case studies from across the international entertainment business. Lucy Smith, director of the entertainment division, RX France, said: “The boundaries of entertainment have all but disappeared. IP can come from anywhere, audiences don’t think in sectors and an idea can travel further and faster than ever before. MIP has always been about understanding where the entertainment business is going next. MIP Talks at The London Book Fair takes that curiosity further bringing together the people shaping what breaks through, how fandom is built and where new global businesses are emerging.” THR

articles.title: Brad Pitt Says Indie Cinema “Feels as Strong as in the ’90s”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 4:08am Brad Pitt hits the 2026 San Sebastian Film Festival. Getty Images Spain Ahead of what will likely be a rabid San Sebastian Film Festival premiere, Brad Pitt joined his Heart of the Beast director David Ayer for a press conference on Wednesday. Journalists and attendees swarmed the room at the town’s Kursaal Theater, where a jovial Pitt made his first San Sebastian appearance since the 2009 presentation of Inglourious Basterds alongside filmmaker Quentin Tarantino. He delighted reporters by touching on man’s bond with dogs, the consolidation of Hollywood and the current independent film climate. Related Stories Business MIP London Ends After 2 Years, Replaced by London Book Fair Event TV 'The Remarried Empress' Special Look: Shin Min-a, Ju Ji-hoon Preview Disney+'s Lavish K-Drama Pitt was swiftly asked about his producing outfit and what he makes of the indie film landscape. The star was buoyant: “I think the current setup has actually been really conducive to independent [films], in a really cool way because more eyes are getting on these projects. It feels even as strong as in the ’90s,” he said, before asking Ayer for his own opinion. Ayer chimed in: “I think there’s new pipelines of discovery out there, new auteurs. We have people coming in off YouTube or the internet,” he said, referencing young horror directors Curry Barker and Kane Parsons, “but now we’re seeing what I believe may be the ascent of it, as we find filmmakers in that space, but also as young people matriculate into the industry. They have much different tastes, and they grew up on a different sense of media than we did. So I’m actually very excited about the future and future opportunities and future stories that are going to be told.” Brad Pitt makes his San Sebastian Film Festival entrance ahead of the premiere of David Ayer’s #HeartoftheBeast pic.twitter.com/EC3XYDgMpv — The Hollywood Reporter (@THR) September 23, 2026 Pitt was asked straight out of the gate about the consolidation of Hollywood, with the Paramount-WBD merger looming and in a climate where the streamers reign supreme. “What I love about what streaming has brought to us is so many more opportunities for actors, writers, directors,” replied Pitt. “And because of that, we have a greater plethora of really interesting stories and really interesting talents, and that’s been amazing. Of course, we had a dip — and we’re seeing that come back; we’re seeing the communal experience being embraced again.” He continued: “But what happened is movies got so expensive. We always talk about this. The very big tentpole movies were able to recoup, and the more independent, lower-budget, or anything in the middle ground — anything from maybe 30, 40, 60 [million dollars] — has a really difficult time getting made, even movies like ours, because it’s very difficult for the studio to recoup that middle budget. […] I’m hoping these movies still have a lot [of support], because that’s usually where I end up most,” he laughed. “The middle ground.” Pitt was also asked about the emotional bond between his character, James, and the dog, Odin, and why those bonds are so important in real life. He replied: “[The characters] James and Odin are both extremely capable creatures. They’ve been trained. They’ve been hardened. They’ve been proven. But it was more their bond between each other […] we would fight more for another than we would even for ourselves, and that kind of care and love and loyalty kept them both points in our film, and I think that’s also true love. When I think of the darker days, certainly my close relationships, I relied heavily on friends, dear close friends, handful of close family, and was very open about my growth.” For the final question (it’s a room full of European journalists, after all), Pitt was asked about how it’s possible to cope in a “sad world full of hate, wars, politics, and racism.” The U.S. star replied: “I think we could spend more time on where we are the same… What binds us, what connects us, and I think we can listen better through these divisional lines. But you know, maybe we just start taking care of the people that are around us and making sure they’re okay.” In Heart of the Beast the Oscar-winning star plays a former Special Forces officer who, accompanied by his retired combat dog, must survive in the Alaskan wilderness following a harrowing plane crash. Ayer’s credits include Training Day , Suicide Squad , End of Watch , The Tax Collector and Sabotage . His latest feature is written by Cameron Alexander and reunites him with Pitt (who starred in Ayer’s Fury ). The film’s cast also includes J.K. Simmons and Anna Lambe. Pitt produces the film alongside Olivia Hamilton, Marty Bowen and Ayer, with Damien Chazelle among its executive producers. The 2026 San Sebastian International Film Festival runs Sept. 18-16. THR

articles.title: Jesse Eisenberg Used to Have “a Negative Opinion” of Acting: “They Pay Us Too Much, We’re Vain”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 5:21am Jesse Eisenberg at the 2026 San Sebastian Film Festival Getty Images Spain Jesse Eisenberg regaled a room of journalists with brilliant — but slightly tragic — tidbits from his childhood and career while discussing his latest feature, The Debut . Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti, Halle Bailey, Havana Rose Liu, Bernadette Peters, Colton Ryan, Lilli Cooper, Maulik Pancholy and Bonnie Milligan join Eisenberg in The Debut , following a shy woman (Moore) who is unexpectedly cast in a local production of an original musical. Under the spell of the strong-willed and enigmatic director (Giamatti), she loses herself in the role and the high-stakes world of this community theatre production. Related Stories Movies Brad Pitt Says Indie Cinema "Feels as Strong as in the '90s" Business MIP London Ends After 2 Years, Replaced by London Book Fair Event The film is premiering at the San Sebastian Film Festival , where an extremely polite Eisenberg (“thank you so much,” he said after each question) appeared for a press conference on Wednesday. The actor-writer-director, whose last film A Real Pain was nominated for multiple Oscars, said The Debut is partially autobiographical as it pulls on his own experience joining community theater. “The movie takes place in 1990 in central New Jersey, and when I was in central New Jersey in 1990, I was like [Moore’s character] Mona Friedman. I was so shy. I was depressed, and I didn’t have friends. And then I walked into this community theater when I was seven years old, and suddenly everybody was so nice, and they hugged me,” he said, prompting giggles from the room. “Going from a kid who was made fun of in school because I have the same hair as you, curly hair, and the kids were saying mean things to me. And then I walked into the community theater, and everybody said, ‘Wow, your hair is so amazing! Come this way, you should play with me!'” Jesse Eisenberg is asked why he chose not to reprise his role as Mark Zuckerberg for Aaron Sorkin’s #TheSocialReckoning at the San Sebastian Film Festival: “It just didn’t feel like something I wanted to act in again. But that’s nothing to do with how great the movie is… Jeremy… pic.twitter.com/frYHOls2BF — The Hollywood Reporter (@THR) September 23, 2026 The experience was, to say the least, transformative. “Suddenly it was like I walked into an alien planet where everybody was nice, and then just like Julianne Moore’s character, I took it too far and became crazy. So really, the movie is charting my life when I was a child. But I just thought it would be so much better to make it about an older woman because Julianne’s amazing, and it’s more emotionally impactful to see a woman.” Such is his admiration for Moore — who starred in Eisenberg’s first directorial feature, 2022’s When You Finish Saving the World — that she changed his long-held view of acting. “I used to have this negative opinion about acting because I was an actor and I just thought, ‘This is just such a ridiculous job. They pay us too much. We’re vain,'” said Eisenberg. “We want to look pretty in the morning, we want to stay in the nicest places, and we want to not ever lift anything on movie sets, and then we want all the credit for the movie! I was always like, ‘This is a weird job, and it’s not fair.’ And then on my first movie, I saw Julianne Moore rehearsing for a scene.” He saw her on the monitor, preparing for an office scene. “She was going through a real, deep emotional process to get ready for the scene. I remember looking at it, and I go, ‘Oh, wait a second, that’s really hard.’ Like we’re all out here joking, and I’m having a donut, and she’s in there suffering. I realized, ‘Oh, maybe acting is actually a really valuable thing. Maybe difficult. Maybe it’s challenging. Maybe it takes a lot. And suddenly, in [one] moment, my entire opinion on acting changed because I saw somebody else doing it, and it wasn’t just about me.” Moore and Giamatti, he said, are two of his favorite actors. “And the movie has this element of a romance, which was not in the script at all,” revealed Eisenberg about Giamatti’s onscreen magnetism. “His character is not supposed to be romantically charming. He’s more supposed to be scary and mysterious. But he just brought this warmth to it, and it plays great in the movie.” Naturally, the filmmaker was also asked about his refusal to return to the role of Mark Zuckerberg in Aaron Sorkin’s hotly anticipated Social Network (2010) follow-up, The Social Reckoning , which will instead see Succession alum Jeremy Strong in the role. “It’s ironic because people associate me with this website, but they know way more about the website than I do, and I like to keep it that way,” replied Eisenberg about the Facebook founder. “I’ve talked about it a lot, and Aaron Sorkin’s talked about it a lot. I loved his script, and he’s a genius,” continued the star. “And the movie, I’m sure, is incredible. But for me, it just didn’t feel like something I wanted to act in again. But that has nothing to do with how great the movie is. The movie will be a great movie, and Jeremy Strong will be amazing in the movie. I’m sure. I just didn’t feel like it’s something I wanted to do again.” The 2026 San Sebastian International Film Festival runs Sept. 18-26. THR

articles.title: Cineplex Puts Up “For Sale” Sign as It Names New CEO
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 23, 2026 5:41am The main entrance of Cineplex's Scotiabank Theatre Toronto. Roberto Machado Noa/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Cineplex has put itself up for sale while unveiling former Landmark Cinemas head Bill Walker as its new CEO, replacing a retiring Ellis Jacob. “As part of the strategic review, the board will consider a range of alternatives, including, but not limited to, a potential sale of the company. The board has engaged Goldman Sachs and TD Securities as co-financial advisors in connection with the strategic review,” Cineplex, the Canadian exhibition giant, said in a statement via its board of directors. Cineplex operates around 1,606 movie screens at 156 locations across Canada, and is a major launchpad for Hollywood tentpoles and other films screening north of the border. Putting up a for sale sign gets Cineplex back to where it was the last time Jacob sought an exit from the exhibition giant in 2019. At that point, U.K. exhibition giant Cineworld Group unveiled a deal to acquire Cineplex for $2.1 billion to create a company with more than 11,200 movie screens globally. But a year later, as the pandemic took hold on the exhibition industry, Cineworld abandoned the movie theater deal to create one of the world’s largest cinema companies. Cineplex was subsequently awarded damages of $1.236 billion in lost synergies from the abandoned takeover deal, but was unable to collect those funds after Cineworld went through a Chapter 11 bankruptcy process in the U.S. That left Jacob and his executive team at Cineplex having to manage their balance sheet and greatly disrupted business in Canada during the pandemic. The latest attempt to possibly sell Cineplex comes amid better times for the Canadian exhibitor as it rides a Hollywood box office rebound. Jacob, a Canadian exhibition industry pioneer, in mid-2025 announced he will stay on at the movie theater chain until the end of 2016 to assist a transition to new leadership. That includes Walker being named as the new CEO. Walker previously served as CEO of Landmark Cinemas, Canada’s second-largest theatre exhibitor, which operates as part of Kinepolis Group NV, a publicly traded cinema company based in Belgium. Walker helped seal Landmark’s sale to Kinepolis in 2017, while continuing to run the company under Kinepolis’ public ownership. Jacob will become a special advisor to the Cineplex board as it looked to strategic alternatives to maximize returns to shareholders. “Bill brings a unique combination of industry expertise, operational leadership, transaction experience and strategic perspective. Given his deep understanding of the theatrical exhibition industry and proven leadership experience, the board is confident that Bill is exceptionally well positioned to lead Cineplex. At the same time, the board believes it is appropriate to conduct a comprehensive review of strategic alternatives available to the company,” Cineplex board chair Phyllis Yaffe said in a statement. Cineplex added no timetable for its strategic review process has been set as the company added “there can be no assurance” that a transaction will follow as the company continues to operate as usual. “Having spent much of my career in the exhibition industry, I have great respect for what the Cineplex team has built. I believe the company possesses an exceptional platform for growth, a powerful brand and meaningful opportunities to create value. I fully support the Board’s commitment to evaluating strategic alternatives and look forward to working closely with the board, management team and other stakeholders as the strategic review progresses,” Walker added in his own statement. THR

articles.title: Broadcast TV Bounces Back: More Orders as Network Fare Drives Streaming Ratings
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 6:15am Mike Colter and Rachel Keller in CBS' 'Cupertino.' Elizabeth Fisher/CBS Logo text The 21st century has not been terribly kind to broadcast TV. The DVR, a spike in cable original programming and, most recently and seriously, the rise of streaming to become the primary way people consume TV, have battered the network model for the past couple of decades. The stats don’t lie: Over the past year, broadcast networks have averaged only about 21 percent of all TV use in the United States, based on Nielsen’s Gauge measurement. The Oscars are moving to a streaming platform, and the Emmy Awards may follow. Late night shows are suffering deaths by a thousand cuts (or, in CBS ‘ case, one big one). Obviously, there’s a “but” coming, and here it is: Despite the structural forces weighing on the network business, there’s also a good deal of optimism among those who work there. Network shows don’t draw the on-air ratings they once did, but they make up a lot of the difference when they hit streaming platforms. The media giants that own both networks and streaming services seem to have figured out that the two platforms can support one another. And among the people who actually make the shows, there’s a growing sense that the network model of producing shows on a set schedule is a good way to do business. UTA partner and TV literary agent Mickey Berman, who represents several writers and showrunners, puts things pretty succinctly: “When you look at the combined package, the shows are working and people are watching them.” Part of the appeal of network TV, both for audiences and creatives, is its consistency: The expectation is that they’ll be on the air every year, usually with 12 to 22 episodes per season. The early years of the streaming boom promised a reprieve from the admittedly grueling schedule of a full network season — but as that model has moved from still fairly regular (if shorter) seasons to eight or 10 episodes every couple of years, the network model has come back into vogue (see also: The Pitt and HBO Max’s recently ordered How to Survive Without Me and FX and Hulu’s The Bear , among other streaming series that have approximated the network model). “I think for a while, people were a bit seduced by streaming and enjoyed some of the creative freedom and other things about it,” Lisa Katz, president scripted content for NBC and Peacock, tells The Hollywood Reporter . “But over time, broadcast shows have continued to show they’re consistent, and I think that they continue to be high in quality and bring in fans. There’s something about it — maybe the new thing felt great, but NBC is celebrating its 100th anniversary, and there’s a reason it’s had the staying power and the legacy that it has.” Berman also notes the “tremendous amount of stability” in working on a network series. For writers, actors, directors and other crew members, “They know that if a show works, they’re going to be shooting or writing for a certain period of time with more episodes and hopefully more seasons.” Michelle and Robert King, the creators and showrunners of The Good Wife, The Good Fight and CBS’ freshman drama Cupertino (among other shows), have moved back and forth between broadcast and streaming. The network business has its pluses, they say. “Selfishly, one thing about doing broadcast shows is they don’t get lost,” Michelle King says. “There are a few streaming shows that one hears about, but there are so very many that seem to just get lost that no one has heard of. Broadcast shows tend to get marketed. People have heard of them, and people get to see them. We’re super proud of Cupertino , so we’re thrilled that people are going to get to see it.” Robert King adds that he’s found — somewhat counterintuitively — that they have more control over a network show than they might on a streaming series. “You don’t have a lot of non-writing producers looking over your shoulder because of the speed with which everything needs to be done,” he says. “I mean, they talk about streaming doesn’t know how to do 20 episodes a year anymore. Writers do. It’s just the non-writing producers want to [sweat] everything. … I like doing 20 episodes because you can be intuitive in the writing and the stories you tell.” Amy Reisenbach, the president of CBS Entertainment who greenlit Cupertino , says she has fielded calls from creators and showrunners looking to return to a broadcaster after making streaming shows. “There is nothing like waking up the next day, from a writer’s perspective and executive’s perspective, in my mind, to getting the ratings and getting a [glimpse] into what you did last night,” she says. “And when you’re waking up to 8 million-ish viewers for Tracker and Marshals the next day … I don’t think you can underestimate the power in that and knowing how many people tuned in for your show the night before.” The stability of network TV extends to the number of scripted series at the networks as well: 56 shows are due to air on the big four broadcasters in the 2026-27 season, up from 50 (plus one limited series, Fox ‘s The Faithful ) last season. ABC , CBS, Fox and NBC combined canceled only six scripted series (ABC kept all 10 of its shows), while adding a dozen to their rosters. “There’s been a renewed interest from the talent base in broadcast because of the stability, because of the quicker turnaround, because of the opportunity for more episodes and more seasons, and that’s not just financial,” Berman says. “It’s also about building a relationship with the audience, where they fall in love with characters and can see them on a schedule that they expect. Grey’s Anatomy has been on the air for so long. People love those characters. But even [for shows that haven’t been on for as long], people want to grow with those characters.” NBC’s Katz also led the charge for a mini-revival of pilot season in the spring, making eight of them and picking up four (dramas Line of Fire and The Rockford Files and comedies Newlyweds and Sunset P.I. ). Networks continue to develop shows year-round and using various methods to develop shows, from smaller pre-pickup writers rooms to straight-to-series orders. But the pilot process has a lot of upside, from Katz’s perspective. “It benefits the show and gives us the opportunity to launch it in the most successful way possible, and to make some adjustments, whether it be in casting or a storyline, when we still have time to do it,” she says. “That’s one of the things I’ve loved about broadcast that’s really challenging in streaming. In streaming, the way that we’re doing it, you have maybe three weeks left of shooting when you’re seeing the first cut. It’s very hard to make adjustments.” One other key factor fueling the optimism around network shows is that in the past few years, media giants have recognized that broadcast and streaming can be complementary rather than mutually exclusive. That network shows bring in sizable audiences when they reach streaming is hardly new information, but better Nielsen measurement of streaming — and the public release of more data — has helped bring the point home. For the 2025-26 season, about half of the top 25 shows in cross-platform ratings originated on broadcast networks. Nine network series (not including sports and news programs) averaged 10 million or more cross-platform viewers, and four others came in just below that threshold. With ABC, CBS and NBC’s parent companies each owning a big streaming service (Hulu/Disney+, Paramount+ and Peacock, respectively), the broadcast-streaming symbiosis is good for both aspects of the business. (Fox has a next-day streaming deal with Hulu for its shows, and some are also available on its own platforms, free streamer Tubi and the year-old Fox One subscription platform.) “We have always considered Paramount+ and CBS parts of a larger ecosystem that includes Pluto as well,” Reisenbach says. “We have a great partnership with Cindy [Holland] and Jane [Wiseman]. They’re obviously working on their shows, which are very different than our shows, but we’re conscious of wanting to be complementary. I’m so appreciative of how grateful they have been for the next-day programming from CBS. They totally get what we do and the kind of shows that we make, and they have created this lane for us.” The network-streaming relationship and the uptick in series orders has Berman feeling good about the next couple of years for his clients, and for network TV. “I think in the next couple years, there’s going to be tremendous opportunity to capitalize on that [momentum], and hopefully new models come from that about how our clients participate,” Berman says. “I’m really optimistic. I feel like the worst is definitely behind us, and I’m glad we have a four-year [labor] deal so that we can really build some momentum toward the future.” THR

articles.title: Meet One of the Key Republicans Championing a Federal Film and TV Tax Credit
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 6:25am Rep. Brian Jack (R-GA) speaks to supporters of President Donald Trump at an event hosted by Vice President JD Vance on August 21, 2025 in Peachtree City, Georgia. Megan Varner/Getty Images Hollywood is stereotypically seen as an industry beloved and supported by liberal politicians, but the current push for a federal film and television tax credit is complicating that typical portrait. Even before President Donald Trump ordered Congress to “get this done!” on Aug. 31, a few key conservative backers of the incentive idea, working alongside Jon Voight , unions and studios alike, emerged in the legislative branch, U.S. Rep. Brian Jack (R-GA) among them. A 38-year-old freshman Congressman representing an area of Georgia that stretches from the suburbs of Atlanta to the border with Alabama, Jack is in some ways a natural ally to the industry. His district includes Trilith Studios, the sprawling production complex in Fayetteville that has hosted Moana , Superman and multiple Marvel shoots in past years, but was impacted by the latter Disney-owned brand’s recent relocation of major shoots to the U.K. Jack is also, as The Hollywood Reporter learned in a recent interview, a movie props collector. In his possession include several props from his favorite TV show, Entourage , the credit card that Daniel Craig’s James Bond swiped in 2006’s Casino Royale (a gift from Pawn Stars ’ Rick Harrison, Jack is careful to note, before he was elected to Congress) and a business card used by Sebastian Stan’s Bucky Barnes in Thunderbolts* , which was filmed in part at Trilith. “As you may recall, he [Barnes] served as a congressman in Thunderbolts , so I have his congressional business card,” Jack says. Make no mistake, Jack is also an unambiguous Trump-era Republican. Before being elected to the House, Jack served as Trump’s political director during and following his first term in the White House, then joined the office of former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy as a close advisor. Main issues listed on his re-election campaign website include ending illegal immigration, cutting taxes, supporting American energy including oil and gas and ending “the weaponization of justice” against former President Joe Biden’s “perceived enemies.” To understand his interest in a federal tax credit, THR sat down with Jack at his office in Capitol Hill’s Longworth House Office Building, once the domain of former President Lyndon B. Johnson when he was a House representative. Jack explained what the film and television production caucus will do, responded to criticism of the federal tax credit and revealed how he plans on getting more Republicans on board. Why did you decide to take a leadership role in creating and film and television caucus as well as supporting the tax incentive? Well, first and foremost, I am proud to represent Trilith Studios, one of the largest movie production studios in the country. And it’s very special for my district because it not only has generated many, many jobs across my district from craftsmen to carpenters to electricians, but it also is a source of pride for many of us. Many of the movies we see on the big screen are filmed literally in my backyard, so to speak. I grew up in Fayette County, live in Peachtree City, and many of these movies were produced at Trilith Studios in Fayette County. Unfortunately, we’ve seen over the last three to four years, a mass exodus of film production to other countries. I’ve been told, unsure if this is the specific statistic, but I’ve been told that at its peak, occupancy on the lots was 98 percent or close to 100 percent when they were filming Avengers: Endgame . And today occupancy is extremely low, perhaps in the single digits. So it certainly has made an impact on my district and I’m eager to revitalize American film production. I, like President Trump, believe that our country is well served by having a robust film production industry. From everything I’ve heard, you’ve been interested in the incentive idea for a while. Why is an incentive important, in your view, as opposed to more punitive measures like tariffs? Well, I will say from the outset, I have long supported an all-above approach because I think ultimately our common shared goal is for American film production to flourish. And if a punitive measure and action is the most constructive way to achieve that, then I would be supportive of that. If it’s incentives to film in states and generate jobs and grow the economy of communities and states we represent, then I’m also supportive of that. But it seems that, including the President, many have agreed that an incentive would be the most constructive way to achieve this goal. But that having been said, I will never take any option off the table. I’m curious what you’ve heard from constituents in your district about the phenomenon of production moving out of the country and the impact it’s had on them. Well, frankly, many of those affected are people I interact with and engage and they’re now onto second, third or fourth careers, and the common theme across many of those interactions with my constituents is they wish they were back filming movies. And though I’ve never been involved in movie production, as somebody that’s been involved with politics for some time, I can understand the excitement that’s connected to making a film and seeing it on the big screen and having that pride and having a community be excited about some of the locations at which films were made. So I certainly hear it from my constituents as it relates to them wishing they could be back in the movie industry and wishing they had the stability that they enjoyed many years ago. And I’m eager to deliver wins for my constituents as any member of Congress should be. Earlier this month, the Wall Street Journal editorial board came out with a piece that questioned the tax incentive, calling it “handouts for Hollywood.” What is your response to this kind of criticism? Well, I certainly respect their perspective. I think that, as I mentioned before, an all-above approach is the most constructive way, I think. I should reread their editorial, but I suspect that they too share the objective that we all have, which is to ensure we have a robust film industry in America. We view that as a soft power export, a cultural export. We certainly want Americans to enjoy American film as they grow up just as you and I did when we were growing up. So I respect their perspective and ultimately we’ll watch this legislation continue to move and grow within the United States Congress. And ultimately I think it’s up to our constituents to convey to us what they determine as necessary for a robust film industry, especially in many of these districts where film has made a big impact. So I think you can go around each congressional district and see district impact by film production in previous years. Turning to the caucus now, I’m curious what some top items on the agenda might be for that group. Well, I think first and foremost, you’re going to see an effort to educate members about the benefit. We saw the study that you reported on yesterday. Those are very encouraging numbers, $250 billion projected over eight years to generate growth in the American economy, over 140,000 jobs to be created. And frankly, the best legislation comes out of very informed members of Congress debating issue sets. And we have thousands of issues on Capitol Hill in which we deal with every month. So I am eager to partner with our caucus members to educate members of Congress about the benefits of film production. And I can speak to it from my own congressional district as to how it’s been beneficial for my own. There are a lot of caucuses out there. What sort of pragmatic things can a caucus accomplish in this case? It can be an opportunity, especially as we break for the election, for members who are interested in the topic. The caucus is a wonderful way to learn more about the topic and we’ll have quite a few weeks before Congress returns to session. So I’m hopeful that members want to join the caucus or take interest in the caucus. And though there are many caucuses, the effectiveness rate of caucuses is usually connected to the engagement level from the leadership. How do you plan on convincing your Republican colleagues who may not come from states where there’s a ton of production to get behind this idea? First and foremost, I think the underlying effect on the economy, $250 billion over the next eight years if we see movement and action on this topic, is persuasive. I think the President has very much laid out the case as well that he thinks it’s a national security priority for us to ensure that American entertainment is made by Americans, filmed by Americans, produced by Americans. So I think there’s certainly an element of that as well, but ultimately it’ll be incumbent upon not just members of Congress that are interested in it like myself, but also it’s important for constituents to chime in. And by the way, I think if you go around many districts across the country, there are going to be stories — maybe it was 10 years ago, maybe it was 15 years ago — but a movie being filmed in a certain area, maybe that had a big impact that members of Congress today should know about. Favorite movie? The Godfather. Favorite TV show? Entourage. What are you watching right now, if you’re watching anything? Well, a lot of college football and a lot of professional football. I love The Odyssey . I saw it a few times this summer. I was going to ask; I read that you were a Christopher Nolan fan. Big time. I saw Spider-Man: Brand New Day , which was good. I’m not currently watching a show, but I often re-watch… if you’re inclined to include this, I was a massive fan of Lost way back when. But I saw By Any Means this past weekend, and I’m a big fan of Mark Wahlberg. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. THR

articles.title: ‘Digger’: Tom Cruise’s “Brave Gorgeous Misfire” Gets Very Mixed First Reactions
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 6:26am Tom Cruise in 'Digger.' Courtesy of Warner Bros. Tom Cruise ‘s Digger is being called a very big swing of a dramatic satire that’s provoking mixed-to-negative reactions after the film’s first press screenings. In Digger , Cruise — nearly unrecognizable in makeup and prosthetics — plays an oblivious oil tycoon whose drilling in Greenland dislodges an ice shelf from a glacier that’s going to cause a global disaster. He must race to prove that he’s humanity’s savior before the ecological accident wreaks havoc on the planet. The film also stars Riz Ahmed, Sandra Hüller, John Goodman, Michael Stuhlbarg and Jesse Plemons. Related Stories Movies Tom Cruise Reveals How He Cut 'Digger' Transformation Time From Six Hours to Under One Business Tom Cruise Blesses Paramount's Deal to Buy Warner Bros., in the Name of Movie "Abundance" The apocalyptic film from Alejandro G. Iñárritu is being called everything from “brave” to “baffling” to an outright “misfire” after screenings were held in New York and Los Angeles. The story, which is also drawing comparisons to Dr. Strangelove , also includes a very big reveal — which we won’t spoil — that is getting strong reactions from the crowd. Still, many critics expect Digger will be a strong awards contender, particularly for Cruise’s performance and the film’s production design, but also expect Warner Bros. and Legendary to have a very tough time recouping their estimated $130 million investment (“I expect a HORRENDOUS CinemaScore,” one critic predicted). Here are some of the first reactions: Anne Thompson (IndieWire): “A.G. Iñárritu’s Digger is a brave and gorgeous art film that will not score with mainstream audiences but will play best for the Academy, especially crafts and actors. But critics will divide on Cruise. The tour-de-force amphitheater scene might put him across. Riz Ahmed is fab.” Ryan Lattanzio (Screen Talk): “The problem with continuing to make statements about your own art and reflect on your own legacy is that you’ll eventually ruin both. A self-indulgent miscalculation from end to end.” Mike Ryan : “Tom Cruise, as you probably expect, is *going for it* in DIGGER, which makes me want to like it. Though I find some plot choices baffling. There are very interesting moments in a meta, Cruise’s career way, but MAVERICK did them better. (It’s also kind of generally unpleasant.)” Edward Douglas (The Weekend Warrior Show): “I cannot say that Digger is very good, although I could tell what Iñarritu and Cruise were going for. There is a major reveal (not a twist) towards the end that almost justifies the craziness… but it will be a tough movie to review, and I expect a HORRENDOUS CinemaScore.” Chris Gore (Film Threat): “ Digger is the biggest swing of Cruise’s career. It’s either going to blow your mind or you’ll have other thoughts when you learn what is really happening in Iñárritu’s masterfully directed film.” Hoai-Tran Bui (Inverse): “Very mixed on DIGGER which had things I liked (Cruise’s performance included) and things I found absolutely insufferable. I wasn’t a devoted Inarritu hater before this but now I kind of get it!” Matt Neglia (Next Best Picture): “This is Tom Cruise’s most dynamic and interesting role in years, and it provides him plenty of space to preach to the back row but not enough to dig deeper and deliver a performance that could’ve had far more power and nuance had Alejandro González Iñárritu’s ambitious split narrative not been so imbalanced in favor of its zany but empty theatrics. Nobody else is given enough material to fully flesh out their characters … Less of a bang and more of a hollow misfire.” Joey Magidson (Awards Radar): “Digger is a mess. Tom Cruise and Alejandro G. Iñárritu are taking a massive swing here, but despite some great production design and a commitment to their big choices, not a whole lot works here. Cruise is good and Riz Ahmed is a highlight, but man this wasn’t enjoyable.” Scott Menzel : “Alejandro González Iñárritu continues to take big swings and make bold choices as a writer and filmmaker. While this film certainly won’t work for everyone, I found the pairing of Iñárritu and Tom Cruise to be an engaging and one of a kind experience. Cruise really does have a knack for comedy, and while not all the jokes land, he fully commits to his performances and the material…This is very much the type of film that will take a bit of time to process after you see it … Digger is ambitious, messy and strange, but it is also a film that will be incredibly divisive and get people talking. It does what good art should do so even if it’s not a perfect film.” Clayton Davis ( Variety ): “ Digger is not what people are expecting — and how audiences react may be the ultimate test of Tom Cruise’s star power. I respect the swing and what Alejandro González Iñárritu is going for. Tom Cruise and John Goodman are delivering stellar work (Sophie Wilde might be best in show for me), and the production design and cinematography are impressive (we’ve missed you, Chivo). In the end, not all the dots connect, and I wish the film leaned harder into the absurdity and satire it kept reaching for. Shocker! The divide on this one is going to be wide.” Jack Hamilton ( Good Day Chicago ): “DIGGER is my favorite film of ‘26 — I avoided spoilers, so the surprises had an incredible impact. A bit Kubrick, a bit BLACK MIRROR but also feels original — a surreal, weird, funny study on (human) nature and storytelling. Tom Cruise’s performance ranks among his career best.” Kristen Lopez (The Film Maven): “DIGGER is a very mixed bag. You’ll get what it’s saying, and the concept is interesting, but it doesn’t trust the audience enough not to hold its hand. Riz Ahmed is great. The Cruise performance is solid. Hard to do satire when the absurdity is so prominent in reality.” Digger opens in theaters Oct. 2. THR

articles.title: Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc Drops Full Trailer — and You Will Want to See Everything
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 23, 2026 6:37am 'You Can See Everything' A24 In Nathan Fielder ‘s documentary film about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes , you can see everything — including Holmes shed a(t least one) tear. On Wednesday, A24 released the full-length trailer (below) for You Can See Everything from Fielder ( Nathan for You , The Rehearsal ) and Lance Oppenheim . It’s crazy, it’s confusing, it’s uncomfortable — but that’s Nathan for you. The new film will release in theaters on Oct. 16 following its brief festival tour. You Can See Everything has joined the New York Film Fest Spotlight Lineup , where it will debut on Sept. 30. The film already enjoyed a surprise world premiere at Telluride — that’s where all of those critics’ pull quotes came from. Related Stories Movies Inside NYFF's Splashy Lineup: Landing 'Artificial,' Weighing a Secret Screening and Opening on the "Miraculous" 'Paper Tiger' (Exclusive) TV 'Crystal Lake' Trailer Sends Linda Cardellini's Pam Voorhees Over the Edge The trailer is a bit more revealing than what we got last time from a brief teaser, but like Fielder and Holmes, everything here still presents as an enigma wrapped in a mystery. The Hollywood Reporter ‘s critic, Angie Han, wrote that You Can See Everything “begins as a fascinatingly intimate portrait of a deluded or disingenuous scammer reveals as something even wilder, more ambitious and less predictable, until we’re left to ponder what value a personal truth has at all.” You Can See Everything is a film in two parts, Han wrote out of Telluride. Its second half kicks into a second fifth gear. “Its abrupt turns are so deliciously surprising I’m loath to give away too much detail,” Han tip-toed. “But I’ll say broadly that it gets excitingly meta and almost surreal in confronting the fact that Holmes is now in prison, and therefore unable to speak for herself in any length or depth. Control of her narrative has once again slipped outside her hands, and in her absence, the void gets filled by other means.” You Can See Everything , created in secret over four years by the directors, provides the billionaire-turned-convicted-fraudster a platform to share her side of the Theranos story. Holmes continuously professed her innocence alongside partner Billy Evans before being hauled off to prison to serve an 11-year sentence. Boiled down to basics, Holmes hyped up her company Theranos as having the ability to run hundreds of health and medical tests using a single drop of blood from a finger prick. Founded in 2003, Theranos eventually reached a $9 billion valuation, but it was almost all smoke and mirrors. Holmes’ proprietary miracle machine, The Edison, could never reliably do what she claimed it could, and the company dissolved in 2018. THR

articles.title: ‘Variations on Violence’ Wins Best Film at Oldenburg
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 6:42am 'Variations on Violence' Courtesy of the Oldenburg Film Festival Zachary Nichols’ Variations on Violence won the German Independence Award for Best Film at this year’s Oldenburg Film Festival, Germany’s leading indie film festival. The film follows a military drone operator whose remote-controlled violence follows him home, along with his sister Mary, who is caught in a cycle of unstable relationships as Johnny’s grip on reality deteriorates. Nichols originally developed the project as an art installation before expanding it into a feature. Boris Mojsovski’s Foreign Tongue received the Spirit of Cinema Award, which is determined by festival audience vote. The Canadian film, in its German premiere, stars Steve Byers, Cynthia Aspherger and Greg Bryk. It centers on Kathy (Kim Sue Murray) a single woman who falls into a coma after a fall at a speed-dating event and wakes up speaking with a Bosnian accent — a change that alters how she is perceived and treated, and that connects her with a hospital cleaner who introduces her to a new social world. Related Stories TV Jeff Probst Reveals Major 'Survivor 51' Twist -- and It Could Change the Game for Years (Exclusive) TV New Documentaries-Only Streamer DocuStream Sets Launch Plans (Exclusive) Marjorie Conrad’s The Joyless Economy won the German Independence Award for Originality, Daring and Audacity. The 58-minute film is built from the video collection of an unnamed woman and follows her sexual history and infidelities in a split-screen structure, pairing her cinematic tastes, particularly her growing porn obession, on one side of the frame with her life story on the other. The Oldenburg jury called the film “hypnotic and ethically complex.” The Joyless Economy premiered in Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight section. Matthew Osubor’s Big Daddy’s Flowers received the Hans Ohlms Award for Best Debut Film. The jury noted the film, which had its world premiere at Oldenburg, was made without a budget and praised the resourcefulness that constraint produced, comparing its tone to the irreverence of 1990s comedies. Osubor, who also stars, made the film under the mentorship of 90s indie film stalwart Alexandre Rockwell ( In the Soup ) follows an ambitious flower-delivery driver (Osubor) who gets drawn into the orbit of a powerful local figure called Big Daddy. Matthew Osubor in Big Daddy’s Flowers. Courtesy of the Oldenburg Film Festival The Seymour Cassel Award for acting went to Frank Mosley for Jackrabbit and Gia Crovatin for Murderous . Mosley was recognized for his role as T.A. Diamond in Jared Hogan’s film, set in 1930s Utah, about a miner disabled in an accident who leaves his family under false pretenses with a hidden revolver. The jury called the performance non-performative, saying it reflected honesty and authenticity within a bleak setting while retaining the character’s humanity and humor. Crovatin was honored for her role as Marian, a filmmaker accused of creative theft by a former classmate, in Neil LaBute’s Murderous , a psychological thriller LaBute has said drew on Joseph L. Mankiewicz’s Sleuth and Alfred Hitchcock’s Rope and Dial M for Murder . The jury noted the difficulty of embodying dialogue-driven material and called the performance an achievement within that tradition. The 107-minute film, co-starring Thomas Sodaski and Jordan Baker, had its world premiere at the Globe Oldenburg. Gia Crovatin in Murderous . Courtesy of the Oldenburg Film Festival Michele Leonardi’s White Whiter Whitest Black won the German Independence Award for Best Short Film. The jury praised the 15-minute film’s restraint, saying it trusted its audience without over-explaining, and described it as addressing themes of innocence and guilt through a betrayal the jury called difficult to reconcile morally, handled with simplicity. This year’s retrospective was dedicated to LaBute , who attended alongside Crovatin. The festival screened LaBute’s In the Company of Men (1997), Your Friends & Neighbors , Nurse Betty (2000), Some Velvet Morning (2013) and House of Darkness (2022) in conjunction with the retrospective. Stunt performer Zoe Bell received a tribute in recognition of more than three decades of work in the field; the festival screened Double Dare (2004), Death Proof (2007), Angel of Death (2009) and Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019) as part of the program. THR

articles.full_text: Sep 23, 2026 6:10am PT ‘You Can See Everything’ Trailer: Nathan Fielder Lives With Elizabeth Holmes, Makes Her Cry and Interrogates Her Husband in Documentary By Isabelle Farina Plus Icon Isabelle Farina Latest ‘Crew Girl’ Renewed for Season 2 at Netflix 18 hours ago Ke Huy Quan Says His $100,000 ‘Indiana Jones’ Residual Check Was ‘Life-Changing’ As a Child Actor: It ‘Didn’t Make Any Sense’ 3 days ago Ben Affleck Almost Cast Ex-Wife Jennifer Garner in ‘Animals’ Before Deciding ‘We Don’t Wanna Do That’: ‘You Just Get Baggage’ 3 days ago See All A24 A24 has released a new trailer for “ You Can See Everything ,” the mysterious and highly anticipated documentary that’s heating up awards season. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim ’s top-secret doc is 174 minutes and follows Theranos founder and fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in her final days of freedom and first few weeks of imprisonment. The official logline reads: “Thirty-four days before she’s sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss.” Related Stories Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’ The highly anticipated documentary premiered to a full crowd at the Telluride Film Festival, followed by the reveal of a short teaser and an Oct. 16 release date announcement. Leaving much to be discovered, the minute-long teaser showed Fielder and Holmes staring intensely into each other’s eyes as Holmes promises she’s being genuine. Popular on Variety “I don’t have anything to deceive you on,” Holmes tells him. “Of course I’m not deceiving you. I’m engaging with you as a human being. Why would I deceive you? There’s no reason for me to do that.” Variety’s film critic Owen Gleiberman saw the film at the festival and described it as “a one-of-a-kind reality-TV-as-hangout-movie psychodrama circus. Yet it’s been made with a spirit of true inquiry, driven by Fielder’s acidly quizzical personality (as an onscreen interviewer, he’s got the most drop-dead deadpan since Steven Wright), and it gets its hooks in you.” Similarly, Variety’s own Clayton Davis concluded that the film “keeps escalating in strangeness across its three-year span and lands a final movement that had Telluride’s most seasoned attendees walking out shell-shocked. ‘Wild’ and ‘WTF?’ were the words circulating on the gondola line, and they were compliments.” Watch the trailer below. articles.title: Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs
articles.full_text: Sep 23, 2026 6:16am PT Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs 49 minutes ago Dolly Parton’s Manager Files for Restraining Order Against Fired Nephew, Alleging Ex-Security Head Sent ‘Terrorizing’ Texts and Threatened to ‘Destroy the Entire Brand’ 11 hours ago Taylor Swift Announces New Single, ‘Patient Zero,’ Coming This Week 20 hours ago See All TAS Rights Management No surprise here: “Patient Zero,” the song Taylor Swift announced Tuesday, is not an orphan or a one-off. The pop superstar followed news of the single a day later with her Wednesday morning reveal for a release that includes four new tracks and will also be out this Friday — “ The Life of a Showgirl : The Encore.” A visit to pre-order pages shows that the new songs, besides the already announced “Patient Zero,” are “Cleveland!,” “Pink Clouding” and “Babylon,” listed as tracks 13-16 on the newly expanded version of her 2025 “Showgirl” album. On social media, Swift wrote, “About a year ago, you guys did a truly unfathomable thing. Something that completely blew my mind… You gave ‘The Life of a Showgirl’ the biggest first week for an album in history. I took a trip to Sweden to celebrate with Max and Shellback , my two collaborators on this album. Really we just wanted to reflect and take in how grateful we were for the moment we were in, but there was a studio there and we did what we do when we feel anything at all: We wrote more songs. I hope you love them, because they were born out of pure gratitude for your exuberance for and celebration of the album we made. ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ including four new songs is out on Friday and available to pre-order and save now.” Swifties had long assumed there would be no deluxe or bonus-filled edition of 2025’s “The Life of a Showgirl” because, at the time, Swift had assured fans that she felt pleased with the exact 12-song configuration she was putting out and did want to augment it with anything she might have left on the cutting room floor. But, as fans now learn, that didn’t preclude coming up with additional material after the fact, which the singer is saying came out in a spontaneous explosion of post-release exhilaration with her two collaborators on that album. View this post on Instagram Prior to “Showgirl,” she hadn’t worked with the dynamic duo of Max Martin and Shellback since 2018’s “Reputation,” but clearly the reunion took in a big way. Popular on Variety Related Stories Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’ Eagle-eyed Swifties noted that Swift had quietly teased this project some time ago, by including the phrase “Patient for the encore” to the side of the frame in her music video for the “Showgirl” single “Opalite.” Much more recently, she had given fans Easter eggs in puzzle form with a pre-taped sketch that aired as part of the Emmys telecast. There; Swift, in character as a “Law & Order: SVU” detective, said, “I think what we’re going to be looking for is hiding in plain sight.” She then stared into the camera and uttered several seeming nonsense phrases or words: “Saccharide. Aries. From the vineyard. North or south.” Fans eventually figured out that if you took the third letter from each of those utterances, they gave up the letters that form the word “encore.” The announcement of the “Encore” edition also settles another point of trivia that had come up when Swift revealed the “Patient Zero” single was imminent on Tuesday. Many pointed out that Swift was not lately in the habit of releasing a stand-alone single ahead of an album actually coming out; the last time she had done so was with “Me!” being released months ahead of “Lover” in 2019. Now that everyone knows the “Encore” collection is coming out the same hour as the single, it’s clear she’s not breaking with that recent pattern after all. The new release features cover photography by the team of fashion photographers Mert Alas and Marcus Piggott, continuing the imagery they created ffor the original “Showgirl” album. No physical release has been announced for the expanded project, which hits DSPs as Thursday night turns into Friday morning. The streaming service Apple Music does show the track list as being broken down into Disc 1 (the original 12 tracks) and Disc 2 (the four newly released songs), but it’s unclear if that augurs for a two-disc vinyl or CD edition. Spotify has the 16 tracks listed in a single running order. For now, the release of the four “Showgirl” addenda puts to bed previous widespread conjecture that Swift was certain to put out “Taylor Swift (Taylor’s Version)” this fall to celebrate the 20th anniversary of her debut album. But setting that aside for newly written songs is a tradeoff most fans will be happy with. So, “Our Song (Middle Aged Version)” can wait. articles.full_text: Sep 23, 2026 6:19am PT ‘Heated Rivalry’ Star Callan Potter, Cobie Smulders, Iris Apatow Joined by Colin Mochrie, Andrea Martin in ‘Any Way You Want Me’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Heated Rivalry’ Star Callan Potter, Cobie Smulders, Iris Apatow Joined by Colin Mochrie, Andrea Martin in ‘Any Way You Want Me’ (EXCLUSIVE) 32 minutes ago Bong Joon Ho Has ‘Two or Three’ Ideas for Crime and Horror Movies After Animated ‘Ally,’ Which He Hopes to Debut at a Festival Next Year 58 minutes ago ‘Ah Girl,’ ‘The Sea Speaks His Name’ to Bookend Jakarta Film Week 4 hours ago See All Helen Tansey/Jeff Vespa/Maxime Coté/Tyler Patrick Henry/ Taylor Hill Comedy veterans Colin Mochrie (“Whose Line Is It Anyway?”) and Andrea Martin (“Evil,” “My Big Fat Greek Wedding”) have boarded “Any Way You Want Me,” joining Callan Potter (“Heated Rivalry”), Cobie Smulders and Iris Apatow in Rana Strazza’s romantic drama, which is now shooting in Toronto. Strazza writes and directs the film, which takes place in 1950s New England and is designed to play like a picture from that period. Fina Strazza stars as Billie Blake, who comes back to her hometown after her mother comes into a dress shop through an inheritance. Next door is a diner run by Calvin Wilkes (Brian Altemus), her boyfriend from high school. Thrown together with him again, Billie has to confront the honesty and the deception that brought their relationship to an end. Related Stories Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’ Smulders’ credits include “Shrinking,” “How I Met Your Mother,” “The Lincoln Lawyer” and the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Apatow appears in Alexandra Pechman’s Toronto title “Magazine” and has “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” on the way. Altemus is known for “Brilliant Minds” and Harlan Coben’s “Shelter.” Popular on Variety In keeping with the classic Hollywood pictures it draws on, the film has assembled a cast steeped in stage as well as screen work. Martin, a Broadway veteran, has won two Tony Awards from four nominations. She is also an alum of “SCTV” and has worked opposite Steve Martin, Catherine O’Hara, Eugene Levy and John Candy. Mochrie likewise came up through theater before improv made him an international name. Fina Strazza made her Broadway debut at eight, playing the title role in “Matilda.” In 2025 she landed a Tony nomination for best performance by a featured actress in a play for “John Proctor Is the Villain,” in which she appeared with Sadie Sink. Smulders won the 2017 Theatre World Award for her debut performance in Noël Coward’s “Present Laughter,” opposite Kevin Kline. “It’s great to get a chance to return to my stage roots with the pathos of this film, which started when I studied at Studio 58 in Vancouver, and of course at Second City,” Mochrie said. “Improv and theater are closely related, and there’s something incredibly exciting about bringing that experience into Rana’s world. I’m thrilled to be working with Andrea, Fina, and the rest of this wonderful cast.” Marium Carvell, Rebecca Ablack, Jennifer Hui, Michaela McGowan, Robert Fulton and Joseph Daly complete the ensemble. First Magnitude Films and Stagg Forrest Films are producing. The shoot is set to wrap in mid-October. Fina Strazza is repped by Paradigm, Mara Entertainment and Jackoway Austen Tyerman. Smulders is repped by UTA and Gang, Tyre, Ramer, Brown & Passman. Altemus is repped by Innovative Artists and Linden Entertainment. Potter is repped by The Talent House and David Dean Management. Apatow is repped by UTA, 3 Arts Entertainment and Ziffren Brittenham LLP. Mochrie is repped by The Characters, and Martin by Play Management and Gary Gersh at Innovative. articles.title: Kerry Washington Expands ‘Street You Grew Up On’ Interview Series Into Weekly Ongoing Podcast From Her Simpson Street Production Company and Daylight
articles.full_text: Sep 23, 2026 6:30am PT Kerry Washington Expands ‘Street You Grew Up On’ Interview Series Into Weekly Ongoing Podcast From Her Simpson Street Production Company and Daylight By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Kerry Washington Expands ‘Street You Grew Up On’ Interview Series Into Weekly Ongoing Podcast From Her Simpson Street Production Company and Daylight 30 minutes ago Judge in Paramount-State AGs Case Still Has Questions, Schedules Hearing on Settlement Terms 14 hours ago White House’s Trump TV 24-Hour Livestream, Launched After His Ban on CNN and MS NOW, Slammed by Critics as ‘Literally State-Run TV’ 18 hours ago See All Getty Images Kerry Washington is turning her “ Street You Grew Up On ” interview show, which she has run in four discrete seasons over the last several years, into an ongoing weekly podcast. The actress, producer and director, best known for her role on ABC’s “Scandal,” first launched the show as a digital series in 2021 during the COVID pandemic. Now she’s expanding the interview series to a weekly, full-length audio and video podcast under a partnership between her production company, Simpson Street, and creator-services company Daylight. Related Stories Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’ The expanded format gives Washington “more room to follow the memories, relationships and stories that emerge from the show’s deceptively simple question: What street did you grow up on?” according to her company. In each episode, she invites a guest to revisit the people, places and experiences that shaped them before they became famous, exploring how childhood, family, community and belonging continue to influence their identities. Popular on Variety Washington’s guests on Season 5 of the weekly show include Ben Affleck, Dwayne Johnson, Demi Lovato, Colin Kaepernick and Chelsea Handler. Past guests on “Street You Grew Up On” include Michelle Obama, Jane Fonda, Queen Latifah, John Legend, Issa Rae and Jay Shetty. “My company Simpson Street is named after the street in the Bronx that my mother grew up on. I have always been curious about how our origin stories impact who we become,” Washington said in a statement. “’Street You Grew Up On’ allows me to continue to explore this idea by engaging in conversation with people whose journeys fascinate us all. I’m excited to expand the series into a podcast and spend more time with our guests exploring the people, places and experiences that have shaped their lives.” Season 5 of “Street Your Grew Up On” premieres Wednesday, Sept. 30. New episodes will be released every Wednesday. Audio will be available on all podcast platforms, with full video on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube. Daylight’s services span distribution, audience development, marketing, IP expansion and technology. The company’s studio arm, QCode, is a premium content studio that has produced a slate scripted podcasts. articles.title: Production Surge in Spain Confirmed by Olsberg SPI Study, but Headwinds Approach
articles.full_text: Sep 23, 2026 6:45am PT Production Surge in Spain Confirmed by Olsberg SPI Study, but Headwinds Approach Said Spain Film Commission's Juan Manuel Guimeráns: ‘If the U.S. introduces a federal tax credit, I expect production there to grow. I don’t think that’s necessarily negative for other territories. If production in the U.S. increases, labor and other costs may rise, which could still push some production elsewhere’ By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest ‘Fluorescent, Dirty and Sexy’: Eire Cid’s ‘The Imaginary Kings’ Presented at Madrid Film School (ECAM) Incubator 9 hours ago Queer Horror Explored in ECAM Incubator Title ‘The Unmoving Hands’ 21 hours ago El Sol Ermitaño Launches at San Sebastián Festival With WIP Title ‘Lovers Go Home’ (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago See All (l-r) Marta Moretto, Olsberg SPI; Kayleigh Hughes, Olsberg SPI; Jesus Cambra, Pablo de Olavide University; Xiomara Garcia, Film Madrid Region; Rodrigo Diaz, SEDIA; Juan Manuel Guimeráns, Spain Film Commission Courtesy of Spain Film Commission Spain’s audiovisual sector is continuing to expand, with production spend expected to reach €5.68 billion ($6.6 billion) in 2025, up 45% from 2022, according to a new study by U.K.-based consultancy Olsberg SPI , commissioned by the Spain Film Commission . At a presentation held at the San Sebastian Festival, Kayleigh Hughes of Olsberg SPI said the study expands on the consultancy’s 2024 analysis of incentivized international production, taking a broader look at Spain’s audiovisual production sector from 2023-25. Related Stories Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’ The research uses Spanish Statistical Institute data to measure production expenditure across film, video and television, including spending on goods, services and personnel. However, it excludes exhibition, distribution, broadcasting and video games, while post-production will be included in the full report, she added. Popular on Variety The sector is expected to generate €4.98 billion in gross value added (GVA) for the Spanish economy in 2025. That includes €2.72 billion in direct activity, alongside indirect activity generated by suppliers and service providers and induced activity linked to employee spending. Hughes said the figures underline the audiovisual sector’s growing economic footprint beyond production companies themselves, supporting a wider ecosystem of businesses and workers. The study also points to broader benefits including screen tourism, cultural visibility, technical innovation and sustainability. Spain has also recorded strong growth in film and co-production volumes in recent years, according to European Audiovisual Observatory data, reinforcing its position as both a domestic production hub and an international filming destination. A panel comprising Spain Film Commissioner Juan Manuel Guimeráns, Madrid Film Region Coordinator Xiomara Garcia, Olsberg SPI’s Marta Moretto and Jesus Cambra of the Pablo De Olavide University held forth on the current state of affairs. Moretto said the figures in the Olsberg study reflect substantial public and private investment and underline the growing scale of Spain’s production ecosystem. The sector’s economic impact extends well beyond production companies. Jesús Cambram of Pablo de Olavide University noted that almost half of the roughly €5 billion in value generated around the audiovisual industry is created outside the sector itself, demonstrating its wider “tractor effect.” The employment multiplier is similarly significant: for every 10 jobs directly linked to audiovisual production, another 11 are generated outside the sector, Cambram asserted. Those jobs include electricians, carpenters, hair and makeup professionals, transport workers and hospitality staff. “We’re not talking only about production,” Cambram said. “There are many more activities that benefit from the positive momentum of the audiovisual industry.” He argued that workforce training should reflect those needs, with skills shortages in areas such as electrical work and carpentry potentially affecting production while also creating opportunities across the wider economy. Guimeráns, meanwhile, stressed that the sector’s impact extends to wages and working conditions beyond the audiovisual workforce. “Touching this sector is either doing good or doing harm to other sectors,” he said, urging policymakers to consider those knock-on effects when designing measures affecting production. The territorial impact is particularly visible in Madrid, where the regional audiovisual industry generates around 30,000 jobs, according to Garcia of the Madrid Film Regional Office. She said productions increasingly depend on local infrastructure, suppliers and services, making municipalities important parts of the production ecosystem. She cited a shoot at a protected 18th-century theater that required specialist carpenters and technicians while also benefiting local restaurants. In another example, “The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon” used an 8,000-square-meter production hub and hired a specialist vintage-car restoration company to prepare vehicles for the production. Guimeráns said Spain is now among the leading audiovisual markets in the E.U. in absolute terms, but faces competition both internationally and between its own regions. “The producer moves very easily,” he said. “The territories and sectors that have better conditions attract more activity.” He singled out the potential impact of new U.S. production incentives and warned that even policy announcements can influence production decisions. For Spain, he argued that any reform should improve incentives while preserving the mechanisms that are already working. “We have to improve Spanish incentives — not only in percentage, but also in procedures, legal certainty and timing,” Guimeráns said. “Let’s do it, but let’s do it with a clear head.” Spain’s growing production base, he added, is producing films, series and television formats that are increasingly traveling internationally. “What we have to do is push that forward,” he said. “The study’s 2025 estimates show investment stabilizing after significant growth between 2022 and 2024,” Guimeráns later told Variety, adding that the slowdown reflects intensifying international competition. “The jump from 2022 to 2023 coincided with Spain’s improved tax incentives,” he said. “Since then, other countries have been changing their incentives too — Italy, Portugal, France and the U.K. We’re all fishing in the same pond. It’s a big pond with room to grow, but we’re all fishing in it.” But incentives are only one factor in production decisions. “Production doesn’t move from one territory to another for a single reason,” Guimeráns said. “Incentives are important, of course, but so are labor and production costs and how easy it is to shoot in a particular territory.” He said historical data suggests incentives tend to expand the overall production market, even if activity shifts between territories. “If the U.S. introduces a federal tax credit, I expect production there to grow,” he told Variety. “I don’t think that’s necessarily negative for other territories. If production in the U.S. increases, labor and other costs may rise, which could push some production elsewhere.” Among recent major productions in Spain, Guimeráns highlighted “The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon” calling it “a very powerful, very large production” with filming spread across the country.
