articles.title: David Ellison: Me, Move? I Love L.A.
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 3:17pm Paramount CEO David Ellison Valerie Macon / AFP via Getty Images Fresh off brushing past California attorney general Rob Bonta with a settlement in which arguably only minor concessions were made, David Ellison is ready to re-commit to the idea of keeping his Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery empire in Los Angeles. “Now that we reached and announced a settlement, we’re eager to get to work building a stronger Hollywood,” Ellison said in a statement. “Let me be clear: the newly merged company will be headquartered in Los Angeles. We aren’t going anywhere. Our history is here and this is where our future is being built.” This brings the mogul back in line with his tune circa February of this year, when he was making promises to California politicians about how he would boost local production and bring back glory to Hollywood’s hometown. Then California attorney general Rob Bonta and his posse of 12 states filed a lawsuit in July that seemingly had Paramount on the ropes. And then the whispers started. You know, Ellison and his family have deep ties to Tennessee , he could pull up stakes and move Paramount there. Texas officials want the state to be the corporate headquarters capital of the United States, plus they have lower taxes — how does Austin sound for a Paramount base? Even at the time, these hints were chalked up to a game of high-stakes chicken over the summer between Ellison and California. Bonta himself, in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter in August when he struck a more defiant tone about the lawsuit, characterized it as a “ Hail Mary ” move and said “it seems like they’re grasping at straws.” But with each passing day, and with the threat of a $7 million-per-day ticking fee that Paramount would have to pay starting in October, the threat of a relocation kept feeling a bit more serious. Also, other states appeared to start taking the rumors seriously, too, which probably helped kick up the dust even more. Now there’s a legal settlement in place between the 12 states and Team Ellison dictating some terms for what “Stay in L.A.” means. Per the consent decree, the Warner Bros. and Paramount lots in L.A. County can’t be sold during the commitment period, which is five years. (Right now the Warner Bros. lot sits on about 140 acres, including the Ranch, while Paramount’s Melrose Ave footprint is about 65 acres.) It’s worth noting that up until Ellison’s buy, Paramount had been headquartered in New York (Paramount has an office in Times Square), and only last year had moved to L.A. And outside of the studio lot infrastructure itself, there are no commitments in the consent decree for, say, having a new office complex in another market outside of L.A. WarnerMount (ParaBros?) is a sprawling empire, after all. For example, does a combined company that owns both CBS News and CNN need office space in L.A., New York and Atlanta? Paramount owns 14 properties totaling 2.1 million square feet of space while Warner Bros. owns 14 properties totaling around 9.5 million square feet globally, per a June report commissioned by L.A. County. There are plenty of real estate scenarios to walk through that have yet to be sorted. But the question was never really about the fine-print of where the corporate HQ was. It was about intent. Through this summer of leaks, the implied message from Team Paramount was that Ellison would be ready to potentially do damage to the Los Angeles entertainment economy if things didn’t go his way in the court battle. There were plenty of locales that would be happy to greet Paramount and set up a water tower and some soundstages. Just look at the production flight that had been plaguing L.A. for years on individual feature films and television series. Local officials feared that a Paramount move would be the straw that broke the camel’s back, despite California doubling its tax incentive annually to $750 million and pledges to cut red tape and make it easier to shoot in state. Now that things did go the way that Paramount hoped as far as the settlement, it may prove tougher to just hit rewind to when Ellison was writing letters in March to California lawmakers saying, “my expectation that the commitments I have made will preserve and expand good-paying film and television jobs in the area.” But as of this settlement Monday, we’ve now hit full circle in that regard. Next up, if the deal closes as expected in a couple weeks, is the plan to start finding those $6 billion in cost synergies between the companies while fulfilling the rules-of-the-road in the consent decree. If L.A. County’s own commissioned report in June is any indicator, there will be a lot of redundancies up ahead as the studios start integrating. “The merger places about 2,495 jobs in Greater Los Angeles County and about 6,000 globally at potential risk,” it estimates, “mainly in corporate, tech, real estate, and other shared functions due to duplicative roles across the two companies.” THR

articles.title: Clavicular Charged With Rape, Drugging Person for Sex in Massachusetts
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 7:44pm Clavicular Francois Durand/Getty Images “Looksmaxxing” influencer and streamer Clavicular , whose real name is Braden Peters, has been charged with one count each of rape, drugging a person for sex and providing alcohol to a minor in Massachusetts, according to new court documents obtained by The Bulwark . The charges, filed by prosecutors in a Cape Cod courthouse on Sept. 8, are reportedly connected to an incident that happened on May 23, 2025. The 20-year-old’s arraignment is set for Oct. 14. The Bulwark wasn’t able to access additional records on the case, but the timeline appears to match a civil lawsuit filed in April against the streamer in Florida. Related Stories General News D4vd Murder Case: Victim's Family Demands Justice as Indigent Claim Draws Scrutiny Music Tupac Murder Trial Begins as Prosecution Calls Rapper's Death "An Act of Revenge" CBS 4 Miami previously reported that 18-year-old Alorah Ziva, whose real name is Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, accused Peters of battery, fraud and sexual misconduct, according to the complaint. She alleged the influencer injected her with Aqualyx, a fat-dissolving substance not approved by the FDA, during a livestream in 2025 without her consent. The lawsuit also accused Peters of nonconsensual sexual encounters at his parents’ home in Cape Cod while Mendoza, who said she was a minor at the time, was intoxicated. In July, Peters filed a motion to dismiss several counts of the civil lawsuit. In response to The Bulwark report, Peters’ rep wrote in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter , “Clavicular has not been physically served. As usual, the Bulwark is exaggerating the status of a case to boost traffic. We appreciate the Hollywood Reporter for fact checking.” Later on Monday, Peters took to X to share a letter that he claimed Mendoza sent him after the alleged incident, appearing to thank him for “helping me as much as you have been.” The streamer also shared a video of Mendoza, where she appeared to call the Aqualyx injection “fun,” and said Peters was “super nice” and “sent me an Uber home right after.” It’s unclear when the video was filmed. “Trying to get my attention in anyway possible, a lawsuit? Seriously… really petty of you,” Peters wrote in the X post. He added in a separate post Monday, “Lmao was literally trying to work at Bacara as a bottle girl… how about dont finance cars you cant afford. Happens to all successful young men, people try to come for your money. Greed is evil.” In another video that’s been reposted on X , allegedly from the 2025 livestream, Mendoza also appeared to say she was 18 years old at the time. If convicted in the Massachusetts case, Peters faced a maximum sentence of twenty years in prison on the rape charge. This isn’t the first time the streamer has faced criminal charges. In April, Peters was charged with unlawfully discharging a firearm after he was seen in a video shooting an alligator in the Florida Everglades. At the time, Peters’s lawyer Jeffrey Neiman said the group was “following the instructions of a licensed airboat guide.” He added that the streamer “relied on that guidance” and that “no animals or people were harmed.” Earlier this year, Peters was also hospitalized after appearing to overdose during a livestream in April. After being released the following day, he wrote on X , “Just got home, that was brutal. All of the substances are just a cope trying to feel neurotypical while being in public, but obviously that isn’t a real solution. The worst part of tonight was my face descending from the life support mask.” THR

articles.title: Elliot Graham, Oscar-Nominated Film Editor on ‘Milk,’ Dies at 50
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes , Carly Thomas September 21, 2026 8:12pm Elliot Graham Joe Maher/Getty Images Elliot Graham, the film editor who received an Oscar nomination for Milk and cut films including Steve Jobs , Captain Marvel and No Time to Die , has died. He was 50. Graham died by suicide Saturday in Los Angeles, according to the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner. The biopic Milk (2008), directed by Gus Van Sant and written by Dustin Lance Black, starred Sean Penn as Harvey Milk, the first openly gay man to be elected to public office in California. The film was nominated for eight Oscars including best picture and won for best actor and original screenplay. Related Stories Movies Anjanette Comer, Actress in 'The Loved One' and 'The Appaloosa,' Dies at 86 TV James Sloyan, Actor in 'The Sting,' 'Xanadu' and 'Oh Madeline,' Dies at 85 On Facebook, Oscar-nominated Milk producer Dan Jinks wrote that his movie “wouldn’t have come together in the way it did without [Graham’s] amazing work.” Graham then reunited with Van Sant on the romantic drama Restless (2011), starring Mia Wasikowska. Graham also won a BAFTA award (shared with Tom Cross) for editing the James Bond film No Time to Die (2021), directed by Cary Joji Fukunaga in what would be the film editor’s final credit. And he produced and served as film editor on the 2018 FX series Trust , about the 1973 kidnapping of teenager John Paul Getty III. Born on June 8, 1976, in Claremont, California, Graham got his first credit for editing the thriller The Last Minute (2001), directed by Stephen Norrington. Next, he handled additional editing chores on X2: X-Men United (2003), then worked again for director Bryan Singer as film editor on Superman Returns (2006). In addition to Danny Boyle’s Steve Jobs (2015), starring Michael Fassbender, and Anna Boden and Ryan Fleck’s Captain Marvel (2019), starring Brie Larson, Graham served as film editor on Bill Paxton’s The Greatest Game Ever Played (2005), Robert Luketic’s 21 (2008), Stephen Daldry’s Trash (2014) and Aaron Sorkin’s Molly’s Game (2017). He also did additional editing on films including The Amazing Spider-Man 2 (2014), I Am Michael (2015) and Beasts of No Nation (2015). THR

articles.title: New Book on MGM Classic ‘The Women’ Reveals Extent of Joan Crawford and Norma Shearer’s Feud (Exclusive Excerpt)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Illeana Douglas Plus Icon Illeana Douglas View All September 22, 2026 5:00am 'The Women' LMPC via Getty Images Illeana Douglas ’ new book Jungle Red! The Making of MGM’s The Women , published on Sept. 15 by Lyons Press, delves into the titular 1939 classic which boasted an all-star cast of actresses — among them Joan Crawford , Norma Shearer , Rosalind Russell, Paulette Goddard and Joan Fontaine — and provided a template for modern female-driven projects like Sex and the City and The Real Housewives. In the following exclusive excerpt from the book, Douglas makes the case that the greatest Hollywood “feud” of all time did not involve Crawford and Bette Davis or sisters Olivia de Havilland and Fontaine, but rather Crawford and Shearer. Related Stories Movies Ann Blyth, the Evil Daughter in 'Mildred Pierce,' Dies at 98 Movies Casey LaLonde, Grandson of Joan Crawford, Dies at 54 Joan Crawford and Norma Shearer in a promotional portrait for The Women (Screen Archives/Getty Images) If MGM had been primed to sell The Women as “the Catfight of the Century,” they didn’t need to invent antics or drum up stories of feuds. Everyone knew that Norma Shearer and Joan Crawford really didn’t like each other. In March of 1939, before Crawford had even set foot on set, Howard Strickling had approved a Look cover promoting The Women that depicts Shearer and Crawford glaring at each other, with a headline that reads, “They Don’t Like Each Other… Inside Stories of 31 Hollywood Feuds.” On April 25, 1939, MGM’s production, listed as #1091: The Women , began shooting. A movie based on the stories of what happened behind the scenes might make a good sequel. When director George Cukor was asked whether he was fearful that longtime rivals Shearer and Crawford would try to upstage each other, he laughed, saying, “They’re too smart for those antics.” He was being optimistic. The best publicity angle, since there were no men in the cast and no juicy romances, was to exploit their longstanding “feud”. How much each actress fueled their “feud” is a matter of opinion, but since every squabble — the billing, the dresses, the trailers, and their eventual showdown because of Crawford’s knitting needles — was dutifully reported on, you have to imagine someone was spilling the tea. Anita Loos, screenwriter of The Women , said, “Norma and Joan could never have been personal friends— they came from different worlds. Norma thought Joan crude and pushy and Joan considered Norma overbearing and uppity — but they both knew the ‘feud’ was good copy, and so they helped it along.” When Shearer hosted a wrap party luncheon, chiefly to show the press how well they were getting along, Crawford skipped it. She seemed delighted to let the bad feelings percolate, telling gossip columnist Hedda Hopper, who was cast in the film, “So many people say Norma and I don’t like each other. Who are we to disagree with the majority opinion?” Shearer then refused to attend the premiere and penned an open letter to the trades downplaying her role and casting shade on the one actress she had least wanted to work opposite, Crawford. “I’m asked about the so-called power and influence I had at the studio. I don’t think anyone acted more like an employee than myself. Just because of my marriage to Mr. Thalberg, and as a consequence of my friendship with the other executives, there have been any number of times when I did not put up as stiff a fight as another actress would have. I didn’t want to appear to be taking advantage. For instance, I didn’t want to make The Women . I did make it, for the reason I just explained, and partly because I was taught by Mr. Thalberg to think of what is good for the picture as a whole rather than what is good for me as an individual.” Crawford had her reply teed up. She praised Russell for walking away with the film. Of her other co-star, Shearer, Crawford said, “Norma Shearer, as usual, played the perpetual virgin, the wronged wife.” She did give her one compliment. “I love playing bitches, and Norma helped me tremendously with this part.” When Cukor came on board to direct The Women in February of 1939, only one queen, Shearer, was attached, set to play the leading role of Mary Haines. She had seen the play on Broadway in 1936, and it was inevitable she would star in it. But when Shearer spoke to Hopper, who reported on every casting decision — including her own — Shearer distanced herself, saying, “You know, I hesitated a long time before playing this part. Then I decided that fighting to hold a husband is every woman’s problem.” Shearer referencing holding on to a husband when talking to Hopper was significant. After her husband Irving Thalberg’s death, she was in the process of reinventing herself. Doing a comedy about a bunch of bitter, funny wives complaining about men, when her husband was gone, was not in sync with her carefully crafted image of herself as the grieving widow of a man who was already gaining mythological status. She could also read the newspaper. The Women was no longer a Norma Shearer vehicle but, courtesy of Hunt Stromberg, “George Cukor’s The Women .” Every day, names were being mentioned: “Suzanne Kaaren gets a role in an MGM picture on the strength of a single test. George Cukor picks her for The Women ” ( Hollywood Diary ). Shearer waited on the sidelines, nervously wondering who her co-stars would be. The stable of talent at MGM was vast, and with 135 roles up for grabs, Cukor was auditioning all viable options except, it seems, Crawford. In March, the press was reporting that Crawford had been turned down for the role of Crystal, while it was announced that eighteen-year-old Lana Turner had been cast. Hairstylist Sydney Guilaroff wrote, “When Norma was cast as the jilted wife, Joan Crawford set her sights on Crystal. She relished the notion of going head-to-head with Queen Norma, now without the protection of her late prince.” Crawford was resentful that even in Thalberg’s absence, Shearer was still getting all the plum roles. Stromberg promised Crawford that Idiot’s Delight would be her next film, but then Mayer decided to give the part to Shearer. “‘No tits Shearer,’” Crawford complained, “could neither dance nor sing and had no experience playing fast women.” Crawford had been looking forward to working in Idiot’s Delight with Clark Gable, and perhaps rekindling their on-again/off-again romance. Instead, it was Shearer he held in his arms. “She had no chemistry with Gable, and that’s what the picture was all about.” Crawford was envious that Shearer had just received, with the studio’s backing, her fifth Oscar nomination — for Marie Antoinette . MGM consistently threw their voting bloc to Shearer, while Crawford had never even been nominated, despite standout performances in Paid (1930), Grand Hotel (1932) and Sadie McKee (1934). She was not about to let The Women slip through her fingers — even testing for the role, something unheard of for an actress of her stature. Eventually she won over Cukor, convinced Stromberg the picture needed her, and beat out teenager Turner by telling Mayer, “The woman who steals Norma Shearer’s husband can’t be a nobody.” Crawford may have, as she said, “resented the hell out of Shearer,” but playing Crystal only made sense if she appeared opposite Shearer. Without her, Crawford would be left playing a supporting part, a “heavy,” as Mayer called it, and for nothing. Shearer was pragmatic. She may have feared working with Crawford, but she knew The Women would garner more attention if Crawford was in the film, but only if Shearer could control the narrative, like later claiming it was her idea to cast Crawford. In the opening credits of The Women , Cukor had the cheeky idea of depicting each actress on-screen as some kind of animal. Crawford is a leopard. Shearer is a young deer. An innocent little deer does not do Shearer justice. A more accurate representation would be a lioness, for Shearer persevered in the jungles of Hollywood, marrying the boss, becoming “the first lady of MGM,” picking up six Academy Award nominations, even winning Best Actress for The Divorcee (1930). But Shearer was threatened by Crawford from the day she was hired as Shearer’s body double in Lady of the Night (1925). As for Crawford, Shearer’s marriage to Thalberg solidified the rivalry. Less than a year after Shearer’s wedding, Our Dancing Daughters (1928) was released, making Crawford a breakout star in the public’s eyes, but not at MGM, and not with Shearer, who called Crawford “an ambitious upstart” and referred to her as “common.” Crawford’s chief resentment was that Shearer got the best female roles at MGM only because of Thalberg. After Crawford was relegated to a succession of dancing films, like Hollywood Revue of 1929 , and Untamed (1929) — an unhinged, “jungle-themed” musical — Crawford confronted Thalberg. “Why do you save all your good roles for your darling Norma?” she asked. “Don’t you think I deserve some consideration?” Thalberg punished her for impertinence and put her in Montana Moon (1930), a low-grade musical Western. In 1938, after being labeled “box office poison,” Crawford needed a hit badly and lobbied hard for Idiot’s Delight . The part of a former showgirl masquerading as a Russian countess, opposite Gable, seemed tailor-made for Crawford. Stromberg told her that Shearer wanted to play the part. Of all the slights, this was perhaps the biggest grudge Crawford carried into The Women . “I cried buckets over Idiot’s Delight ,” she said. After The Ice Follies of 1939 . Crawford was at a low point professionally. She needed a hit. Her philosophy of going after the role of Crystal was simple. “It’s going to be a good picture. I need a good picture. If I can’t get one of my own, let me sneak into someone else’s.” She convinced Stromberg to talk Cukor into testing her. Though intrigued by the idea of an on-screen rivalry, Cukor was not a fan of Crawford’s acting, which he felt was mannered. After testing her for Crystal, though, Cukor consented and told her the part was hers. What changed? Crawford was not shy about her open and persistent dislike of Shearer. Once, years before, when she was asked what she thought of Shearer, she smiled and said, “Well . . . I’m an actress . . . and she’s married to the boss.” Cukor may have decided, possibly with the influence of Stromberg, that the competition with Shearer would make their scenes sizzle. Crawford was excited, telling the press after she won the part, “Even people who didn’t like me admitted I had intestinal fortitude, taking my career in both hands and gambling.” When Hopper asked Shearer what she thought about Crawford being cast, Shearer graciously said she was looking forward to it, and that The Women was “going to be a fascinating experience for her.” Butter wouldn’t melt in her mouth, as they say, but before shooting began, she made sure her contract stipulated that only she would have top billing, with her name above the title. It was a battle she would later lose, first to Crawford, then Russell. Shearer arrived early her first day to check the set and saw that there were three star trailers parked side by side. In accordance with being number one on the call sheet, Shearer had been assigned dressing room number one, nearest to the camera. It had been redecorated for her in coral, pink and cream. It was also air-conditioned. Inside there was an upholstered floral lounging sofa where she could rest and practice her lines, with fresh orchids on her dressing table. Shearer noticed that one of the trailers — dressing room three — was sticking out one foot further than the other two. When she inquired as to who was in dressing room three, she learned it was Crawford. Russell had been assigned number two. Shearer demanded Crawford’s trailer be moved back one foot in accordance with the others. Crawford’s arrival had been accompanied by glowing stories from reporter Harry Mines in his Raves and Raps column. “ The Women has been before the cameras at MGM,” he wrote, “but not until yesterday did Joan Crawford start work. Joan has a new and fancy portable dressing room, decorated in mauve. It was difficult to get a peek at the quarters, as baskets of flowers took up most of the space. Miss Crawford’s friends have deluged her with posies and telegrams on her first day in production.” Crawford stepped out of her limousine that first day of filming accompanied by her maid. Her uniformed chauffeur carried her record player and records, and one of her beloved dachshunds, Pupchen, acquired during her marriage to Franchot Tone. Crawford had a special clause in her contract allowing her to bring Pupchen to the studio when filming. An insurance policy protected the company in case the dog ever bit anyone or barked during a take. Cukor did not have to worry about a barking dog. It was Crawford’s vocalizing to opera that could be heard loud and clear during Shearer’s rehearsals. Though the set was not far from her dressing room, Crawford insisted she be driven to it via limousine. Shearer later followed suit, always making sure her limousine arrived after Crawford’s. Hairstylist Sydney Guilaroff recalled that Cukor’s greatest challenge was not directing on-screen but trying to keep the peace off-screen. He wrote that one solution was to always keep the actresses busy, separating them whenever possible. If one was rehearsing, then he could send another one to a fitting, or have them get a hair and makeup test. That way they were unlikely to be in the same space at the same time. “This worked well,” he said, “until Shearer and Crawford had their one face-to-face scene together.” To rattle Shearer, Crawford called in sick, and Cukor had to rearrange the schedule. Harry Mines, in the Los Angeles Daily News , ran a story that Crawford was under doctor’s orders not to work, and was ill from a combination of “intestinal flu and arsenic poisoning.” It’s hard to believe Crawford came across arsenic on the set, unless someone slipped it in her tea! (Hmm…) After two days, however, it was reported that she had made a remarkable recovery — or at least was well enough to continue. “On her sickest morning,” Mines wrote, “Joan had to do her most important scenes with Norma Shearer. Despite the tough break, Miss Crawford sallied through, doing such a good job that few realized how bad she was feeling.” The scene in question takes place after the fashion show in Crystal’s dressing room. Mary Haines (Shearer), Sylvia (Russell), Peggy (Fontaine) and Edith (Florence Nash) discover Crystal is trying on dresses and has asked the saleswoman (Frederika Brown) to charge the clothes to Mr. Stephen Haines’s account. Mary crosses the hall to confront Crystal and enters Crystal’s dressing room. Cukor began to rehearse. What happened next has been written about and reported from so many angles it’s like the film Rashomon (1950). Every bystander recalls what happened with slight variations, but all agree on one thing: Crawford, after years of perceived slights at the hands of Thalberg and Shearer, saw an opportunity to get even, and she did. Without Thalberg, there would be no repercussions. Crawford perhaps even sensed there was a bit of schadenfreude from Cukor, the cast, and the crew, knowing this moment would come, and wondering which cat would draw the most blood. THR

articles.title: ‘R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2’ Trailer Teases Cassandra Peterson’s New Role and the Curse’s Return (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Abbey White Plus Icon Abbey White Contributing Writer View All September 22, 2026 6:00am R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2. Tubi Something wicked this way comes in the new look at R.L. Stine ’s Pumpkinhead 2 . Ahead of its Tubi premiere on Oct. 9, The Hollywood Reporter can exclusively debut the sequel’s first full trailer. Helmed by Jem Garrard, the filmmaker behind the franchise’s 2025 installment, Pumpkinhead 2 once again follows kids Sam (Bean Reid) and Becka (Adeline Lo) as a new curse awakens in Redhaven. While still struggling with the fact that his family doesn’t remember him — a consequence of stopping the harvest curse — Sam and his friend Becka begin to notice strange things around town. To get to the bottom of this series of unsettling occurrences, the duo reteams and, in the process, discovers there’s a new crop of cursed pumpkin entities, conjured up by an ancient ritual book, just like the one that nearly took Sam’s brother Finn (Seth Isaac Johnson). Related Stories Beyond the Book Inside 'The Love Hypothesis': How Director Claire Scanlon, Star Lili Reinhart and More Adapted BookTok's Biggest Obsession Movies Nicole Wallace Joins Josh Heuston in Amazon MGM's 'Throttled' Adaptation This time, the friends are facing a series of child-like pumpkin-headed monsters, seemingly victims of the previous curse, called up from the ground of Redhaven. “I would like to go back to when one murderous scarecrow was the problem,” an exasperated Becka is seen telling Sam in the upcoming film’s two-minute trailer. Their investigative trail leads them to the town sheriff (Bob Frazer), who was responsible for keeping the first child-stealing curse alive. He reveals to the duo that he stole the cursed book from a woman named Cassandra, seemingly a local who lives on the edge of the town’s forest. Portrayed by Cassandra Peterson, best known by horror fans as Elvira, this wise witch has powers that may be key to helping the kids stop their Pumpkinhead uprising. “I can end the curse,” she tells Becka and Sam. “The magic is strongest on the harvest moon.” Working with others from the town, the duo once gears up to take on the powerful and deadly Pumpkinhead children to ensure no more kids are forgotten. “We don’t get to forget,” Sams says. Inspired by Stine’s The Haunting Hour , the Tubi film is written and directed by Garrard, and also stars Matty Finochio, Sebastian Billingsley-Rodriguez, and Kendra Anderson. Pumpkinhead 2 is executive produced by James Mattagne, Joan Waricha, Harvey Kahn, Yvonne Bernard, Dan Bernard, Jem Garrard, Allen Lewis, and Rama Diallo, and produced by Front Street Pictures. R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2 is part of the “Terror on Tubi” lineup. Timed to its release, Garrard and Stine will be joined by Tubi Chief Content Officer Adam Lewinson and drag queen and actor Jimbo ( RuPaul’s Drag Race UK and All Stars ). THR

articles.title: VFX House 22Dogs Launches New Facility at Pinewood Toronto Studios (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 22, 2026 6:00am Pinewood Toronto Studios Courtesy of Pinewood Studios 22Dogs VFX, the visual effects studio behind work on Apple TV’s The Morning Show and the Netflix heist thriller Here Comes the Flood, has opened a new base in Toronto as its North American headquarters. The Milan-based international studio, with VFX credits also on Netflix’s Outer Banks, Lionsgate’s Day Drinker and Prime Video’s The Greatest, already has a Los Angeles commercial office in its global footprint. The new North American headquarters at Pinewood Toronto Studios will be the third production studio for 22Dogs VFX after facilities in Milan and Tenerife. 22Dogs VFX joins other global studios in Toronto doing visual effects magic for major studios and streamers chasing digital tax breaks, currency savings and lower labor costs in Ontario. The Pinewood Toronto Studios facility will be led day-to-day by Samara Melanson, head of studio, who will work closely with Andrea Marotti, 22Dogs partner and executive producer, based in the Los Angeles commercial office. “Since founding 22Dogs, our vision has always been to build a studio where creativity, innovation, and collaboration come together to support filmmakers at the highest level. Toronto is a natural next step in our global journey, and we’re excited to welcome new artists, partners, and clients as we continue to grow our international footprint,” Carlo Tosi, founder of 22Dogs VFX, said in a statement. The Los Angeles office will continue working closely with major studios and streamers and international producers, many of which bring film and TV series work to Canada for production and post-production. Pinewood Toronto Studios already serves as a Canadian production hub for Netflix and Amazon MGM Studios. “Toronto attracts leading creative companies from around the world, and we’re pleased to see 22Dogs VFX establish its Canadian home at Pinewood Toronto Studios. Their investment reflects the reputation of Ontario’s screen industry and further enhances the collaborative ecosystem our studios are known for,” Sarah Farrell, general manager of Pinewood Toronto Studios, said in her own statement. THR

articles.title: ‘Heart of the Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt and His Canine Co-Star Earn Your Tears in David Ayer’s Tense, Tender Survival Thriller
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All September 22, 2026 6:00am Brad Pitt in 'Heart of the Beast.' Paramount Pictures If you’ve seen the trailer for Brad Pitt ’s new movie, you probably think that it’s a harrowing tale of survival in a dangerous wilderness. Don’t be fooled. Heart of the Beast is actually a love story, and one of the most moving to come along in a long time. That it’s a love story between a man and his dog doesn’t at all detract from its emotional impact. Indeed, Pitt displays an engagement with his co-star that may be his most resonant yet. Although to be fair, that isn’t really saying much since two of his most notable cinematic romances are Meet Joe Black , in which he played Death, and Mr. and Mrs. Smith , in which his character spent most of the film trying to kill his wife. Related Stories Movies Netflix's 'Cliff Booth' Trailer Has Brad Pitt Taking a Playful Poke at Leonardo DiCaprio Movies 'World War Z' Sequel Back on With Brad Pitt Returning, Edward Berger Directing Heart of the Beast The Bottom Line Packs a surprising emotional punch. Release date : Friday, September 25 Cast : Brad Pitt, J.K. Simmons, Anna Lambe Director : David Ayer Screenwriter : Cameron Alexander Rated PG-13, 1 hour 41 minutes The film, reuniting Pitt with his Fury director David Ayer , features the actor as James Belmont, retired after a 30-year stint with Special Forces that saw him facing combat in Iraq and Afghanistan. Now he lives a quiet, solitary life. Well, not entirely solitary, since he shares it with Odon, his beloved German Shepherd combat dog, with whom he experienced many dangerous missions. Odon bears the physical and emotional scars of his years in combat, sporting titanium teeth and an artificial leg, and suffering from PTSD-induced nightmares. The story begins with James flying his Cessna plane into the Alaskan wilderness (convincingly and gorgeously played by New Zealand) for a few days of camping and fly-fishing. The happy solitude is briefly interrupted by a stranger who happens by and spends the evening chatting away with the mostly silent James before taking off in a canoe early the next morning. He’s played by J.K. Simmons , making a strong impression in a brief amount of screen time and demonstrating yet again that he’s one of the most invaluable character actors in the business. An impending storm forces James and Odon to leave early, leading to the first of several surprises in the screenplay by Cameron Alexander. The plane winds up crashing into the water, not because of the weather conditions but rather James suffering a heart attack that renders him unconscious. Both he and Odon, who was thrown from the plane before it went down, miraculously survive, and when we later see James scarfing down aspirin by the handful we realize that he was well aware of his heart condition. Thus begins the survival part of the story, with James and Odon having to traverse 58 miles of wilderness to reach the nearest road. Along the way they encounter a variety of life-threatening situations, including a massive grizzly bear, a treacherous tree-bridge crossing over a gorge with rapids below, and an attack by a pack of CGI wolves. Both man and beast suffer an array of debilitating injuries along the way. But what makes the film special are not the survival elements, as grippingly and (mostly) convincingly filmed as they are, but rather the relationship between James and the loyal Odon, both of them constantly risking their lives for the other. Pitt makes his character’s feelings for his dog touchingly palpable, most notably in a quiet scene in which he removes Odon’s artificial leg and gently massages his stump. And while Odon doesn’t have much in the way of dialogue (he does have a very expressive bark), the way he looks at his co-star is so adoring and non-judgmental you may find yourself reevaluating the relationships in your life. Odon is mostly played by Uber (we can forgive the name), who would be the instant frontrunner for the PATSY Award if that worthy honor still existed. Credit must be given to his trainers, handlers, and Pitt himself, who reveals so much chemistry with his canine fellow actor that his previous female co-stars might be jealous. For certain scenes Uber is doubled by three other dogs, all of them his sons, which must have made for an especially harmonious set. Heart of the Beast sometimes feel repetitive in its pile-up of perilous moments, but Ayer’s expert direction and the fast-paced 101-minute running time prevent monotony from sinking in. And if the film’s ending leaves you dry-eyed, you’re clearly not an animal lover and someone I have no desire to meet. Full credits Production: Domain Entertainment, Gulf Stream Pictures, Wild Chickens, Temple Hill, Kino World Distributor: Paramount Pictures Cast: Brad Pitt, J.K. Simmons, Anna Lambe Director: David Ayer Screenwriter: Cameron Alexander Producers: Olivia Hamilton, Marty Bowen, David Ayer, Brad Pitt Executive producers: Damian Chazelle, Scott Lumpkin, Cameron Alexander, Chris Long, Pete Chiappetta, Anthony Tittanegro, Andrew Lary, Sophie Cassidy, Zack Conroy Director of photography: Mauro Fiore Production designer: Greg Berrry Editor: Dody Dorn Composer: Jared Michael Fry Costume designer: Amanda Neale Casting: Tricia Wood Rated PG-13, 1 hour 41 minutes THR

articles.title: Neon Sets ‘Paper Tiger’ Awards Categories, Plans First Real Push for a James Gray Film (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All September 22, 2026 6:00am Adam Driver in 'Paper Tiger' Cannes Film Festival Paper Tiger , James Gray ’s crime-thriller starring Miles Teller , Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson , which premiered to strong notices at May’s Cannes Film Festival — including a rave from The Hollywood Reporter — and is set to open the New York Film Festival on Friday night, will be given a full-fledged awards push this fall by its U.S. and U.K. distributor Neon , The Hollywood Reporter can exclusively report. THR can confirm that as part of the campaign, Neon will promote Teller for best actor, Driver for best supporting actor and Johansson for best supporting actress, ending months of speculation about where the trio of A-listers would wind up. Related Stories Movies Inside NYFF's Splashy Lineup: Landing 'Artificial,' Weighing a Secret Screening and Opening on the "Miraculous" 'Paper Tiger' (Exclusive) Movies Korean Director Na Hong-jin on the Meaning Behind 'Hope' and His Sequel Plans: "Don't Be Surprised if He Crosses Over to the North" Paper Tiger , like many of Gray’s films, is semi-autobiographical. It tells the story of how a blue-collar family man (Driver) is enticed by his more ambitious brother (Driver) into an ill-advised business enterprise that ends up landing the two of them, as well as the man’s wife (Johansson) and children, in the crosshairs of the Russian mafia. Made on a $15 million budget cobbled together from a wide variety of sources (it has 24 executive producers listed in its credits), Paper Tiger is the sort of mid-range budget, adult-targeted American movie that almost never gets made anymore. Since its debut in Cannes, enthusiasm for it has been cultivated at the Locarno Film Festival, where Gray collected a special achievement award; and at numerous private screenings in Los Angeles, Manhattan and the Hamptons, which have attracted dozens of Academy members. Paper Tiger ‘s entire principal cast and all of its department heads will join Gray at its big Alice Tully Hall premiere on Friday night, and then on Saturday afternoon Gray will participate in a Walter Reade Theater conversation about the film moderated by a fellow chronicler of New York and one of his vocal admirers, Martin Scorsese. After that, the film will play at a host of fall film festivals — among them Mill Valley, Hamptons, London, Newport Beach, Chicago, Virginia and Savannah, with Gray set to collect directing honors at Mill Valley, Virginia and Savannah — en route to its U.S. theatrical release in select theaters on Nov. 13 and wider release on Nov. 20. Will it all be enough to finally land Gray — a longtime darling of critics and Cannes, but never a nominee of the Academy — and/or his film in the Oscar race? For a variety of a reasons, none of Gray’s prior films with awards potential received a fully-realized awards push. 2013’s The Immigrant , which was highlighted by a standout Marion Cotillard performance, was buried by Harvey Weinstein after Gray, who had final cut on the film, refused to acede to Weinstein’s demands for edits. 2016’s The Lost City of Z played on the closing night of the New York Film Festival, but then Amazon and Bleecker Street released it not that fall or the next, but rather the following spring, and it promptly disappeared. Gray did not have final cut on 2019’s Ad Astra , a big-budget studio film starring Brad Pitt, and it was taken away from him and re-edited by 20th Century Fox, resulting in a version that Gray has disavowed. (It did become the only Gray film to land an Oscar nom, best visual effects.) And Focus largely scrapped its campaign for 2022’s Armageddon Time after it underperformed commercially. Neon, which acquired the film last April, after it was completed but before Cannes, is said to be firmly committed to breaking that streak. A full breakdown of the awards categories for which Paper Tiger will be pushed appears below. BEST PICTURE James Gray, p.g.a. Anthony Katagas, p.g.a. Rodrigo Teixeira, p.g.a. BEST DIRECTOR James Gray BEST ORIGINAL SCREENPLAY James Gray BEST ACTOR Miles Teller BEST SUPPORTING ACTRESS Scarlett Johansson BEST SUPPORTING ACTOR Adam Driver BEST CASTING Douglas Aibel, CSA BEST FILM EDITING Scott Morris BEST CINEMATOGRAPHY Joaquin Baca-Asay BEST PRODUCTION DESIGN Happy Massee, Production Designer Kendall Anderson, Set Decorator BEST COSTUME DESIGN Amy Roth BEST ORIGINAL SCORE Christopher Spelman THR

articles.title: California Vowed to Stop Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger. Why Did It Fold?
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Winston Cho Plus Icon Winston Cho View All September 22, 2026 6:16am California attorney general Rob Bonta. Getty Images Logo text For months, California attorney general Rob Bonta told anyone who would listen that Paramount ‘s $111 billion bid for Warner Bros. Discovery would ruin Hollywood and that he could stop the merger. Then, when his leverage appeared the highest, the political and economic realities surrounding the showdown became impossible for him ignore. That pressure came from the top. Gov. Gavin Newsom had expressed concerns about the state’s lawsuit, particularly in relation to employment levels. He had inserted himself into negotiations to encourage a settlement. “I’m very mindful of what this means to the state — our reputation,” he said at a press appearance last month, adding that he took CEO David Ellison’s threat to move out of California “seriously.” Indeed, Newsom’s fingerprints were all over the announcement of the settlement. Paramount thanked him “for his support throughout this process.” Read between the lines and the picture comes into focus: Newsom wanted a deal, and Bonta fell in line. Newsom leaning on Bonta — along with Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and gubernatorial nominee Xavier Becerra — put the state’s top prosecutor in an increasingly untenable position. California had sued to stop the merger, but it also faced the prospect of losing Paramount regardless of the outcome of the lawsuit if a deal wasn’t struck ahead of an Oct. 1 deadline when the so-called $7 million-per-day ticking fee starts accruing. That dynamic offers insight into how a case that once threatened to derail the biggest Hollywood marriage in decades ended with a whimper that stood in stark contrast to the political furor that spun off from it. This was always the likeliest outcome for the states challenging the deal. The government had signed off on the acquisition, and merger cases are tough to win in court. The states, especially California, were being asked to gamble on a trial whose outcome was far from certain. Still, that didn’t make the terms any less striking. While the settlement is broad in scope, it doesn’t require any divestitures that are typical of enforcer-friendly deals. Instead, it appears to be a five-year operating agreement imposed through a consent decree. Under the agreement, Paramount and Warner Bros. must release at least 30 theatrical films a year for the first two years and 32 for the following three, maintain minimum numbers of wide and independent releases and ensure that at least half of the films are produced or jointly produced by the combined company. They must keep 45-day theatrical windows and a 90-day SVOD holdback for qualifying films. A $30 million per film penalty is assessed for missing the annual quota, with divestiture of Paramount’s stake in Miramax in play if the shortfall remains unaddressed. The company also has to spend an additional $300 million annually on U.S. production (or $1.5 billion above its 2025 baseline over five years). Separately, the Paramount and Warner Bros. studio lots in Los Angeles must remain open and operate for the duration of the decree. Other notable terms: Keeping Paramount and Warner Bros. basic-cable negotiations separate and creation of a five-member independence board overseeing editorial standards at CBS News and CNN (selected by Paramount). A violation of the former term could see an order forcing the studio to divest from BET, VH1 and Comedy Central, among other channels (blue-chip assets like CNN or New Line Cinema are not on the table in these divestiture scenarios). If you said the settlement doesn’t go far enough, Bonta would probably agree. “I don’t think these two companies should merge,” he said at Monday’s press conference, titled “Attorney General Bonta Makes Announcement to Keep California Vibrant.” So why blink now? Here, the timing of the settlement is key. For California, the worst case scenario wasn’t only the merger being allowed to proceed but also Paramount moving its headquarters and hundreds of employees out of California while the case progressed. Call the threat a bluff if you want, but Ellison had been in talks with Tennessee and Texas officials leading up to the deal, with a decision expected at the start of next month. State politicians were clearly rattled as Los Angeles sees historically low filming levels. For Newsom, the departure of one of Hollywood’s most public-facing companies under his tenure as he teases a presidential run would’ve been a particularly unwelcome outcome. In the end, that risk outweighed a chance to stop the merger. The states certainly had a viable antitrust case, but it was a coin flip. They faced some of the best lawyers in the country too, including antitrust powerhouse Jeffrey Kessler, who most recently secured a landmark win for states suing Live Nation, Beth Wilkinson, who guided Microsoft’s bid to acquire Activision Blizzard across the finish line, and former U.S. Solicitor General Paul Clement, perhaps the most experienced Supreme Court litigator in the country. On the appeals front, it appears Paramount found sympathetic ears among the justices. The Supreme Court earlier this month told Bonta to respond to a challenge by Iowa and Montana looking to stop the antitrust lawsuit, signaling a potential review of the case that saw the government side with the studio at various points. Leading up to the settlement, it appears factions within alliance emerged on whether to accept the deal, with New York, Connecticut, Minnesota, Nevada as the holdouts. Ultimately, convincing California proved enough to overcome pushback from some of the other states, which faced the prospect of continuing to pursue the case without the state that would’ve been at the center of the trial. In a statement, Connecticut Attorney General William Tong expressed concern about the deal. The state “wanted and demanded full divestiture of CNN and CBS News. We wanted to save ethical and independent journalism and news,” he said. “We fought aggressively for that remedy. I am deeply disappointed that we could not do more.” Newsom also stressed at the press conference last month that Bonta is “not just representing the state of California, he’s also part of this coalition with a dozen other states.” The WGA’s statement illustrated the complexity navigating incentives and goals from each of the plaintiffs in the alliance while emphasizing the weight of the states’ decision to settle. “As a nonprofit, the WGA must contend with the reality of forging ahead alone, with no backing from government enforcers, with a complex antitrust lawsuit that would cost millions of dollars to pursue through trial,” it said. So now, Paramount is positioned to acquire Warner Bros. in a deal will create Hollywood’s next media and entertainment colossus. Faced with that reality, the rank-and-file are confronting an uncomfortable question: What good is all the talk about fighting consolidation if the political and economic costs become too high when the moment actually arrives to oppose one of the biggest mergers in industry history? THR

articles.title: Mike Leigh Explains Why “It’s More Than Probable” That ‘Tender Loving Care’ Is His Final Film
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 22, 2026 6:29am Mike Leigh at TIFF 2026. Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for IMDb Beloved British auteur Mike Leigh has explained to the San Sebastian Film Festival why it’s “more than probable” his latest drama-comedy, Tender Loving Care , will be his last. The filmmaker appeared via video link at a press conference for the competition title, alongside producer Georgina Lowe and cast members Alice Bailey Johnson, Paul Jesson and Marion Bailey, who is the mother of Bailey Johnson and Leigh’s real-life partner. Their co-star Kate O’Flynn , who just won an Emmy for her scene-stealing performance in Widow’s Bay , was unable to travel to the film festival in northern Spain. Related Stories Business VFX House 22Dogs Launches New Facility at Pinewood Toronto Studios (Exclusive) Movies Red Sea Film Festival Cancels 2026 Edition, Vows to Return Next Year With "Renewed Vision" “It’s quite straightforward,” said Leigh when asked whether Tender Loving Care will indeed be his last film. “I have a medical condition [myositis], which affects my muscular movement, and it’s quite difficult to move around. [It’s] certainly more difficult than it should be for a filmmaker, and therefore it’s more than probable that this film will have to be my last film. That’s all,” he explained. “It’s a practical matter to do with my medical condition — a physical condition.” Leigh has touched on struggling with the condition — a disease affecting the immune system — a few times this year, as Tender Loving Care made its debut at Telluride, TIFF and now San Sebastian. If it is to be his last, The Hollywood Reporter called it “a lovely addition and likely conclusion to an exceptional career,” as Leigh, who was here in San Sebastian just two years ago with Hard Truths , once again shows his knack for gently gut-wrenching storytelling. In the film, O’Flynn plays a social worker, Amy, who moves in with her university pal (and fellow social worker), Rosie (Bailey Johnson). Amy is particularly close with her parents (Jesson and Bailey), who live nearby and are muddling through on lots of cups of tea. When a family health crisis strikes the characters later in the film, Leigh deftly tells us that much of British stoicism is actually courage, solidarity, and unspoken fear in the face of adversity. “Humanity is humanity,” said Leigh to the room of journalists about “reflecting positivity” and resilience amid “tough times.” He continued: “We haven’t stopped being human. The quality of life hasn’t gone away just because we’re in tough times — on the contrary, all the more reason to reflect positivity the way we can. Obviously, I hope that Tender Loving Care wouldn’t be misunderstood as a piece of romantic escapism because it isn’t. It’s a hard look at realities, but it is about compassion, and compassion is as important in these times as many other times.” With the film’s confrontation of post-War decline in Britain, as well as debilitating cuts to health and social care services, the director and his cast were asked about staying optimistic in the current climate, where, as Jesson eloquently put it, “people with lots of money […] run their countries brutally.” Leigh replied: “It’s a question with no black and white answer. One wants to be optimistic. One wants to see light at the end of the tunnel. I have children and grandchildren, and my youngest grandchild is actually two years of age. If everything goes as it should, he will be my age in the 22nd century, and I want that world to be a good world. I want his life to be positive,” he said. “On the other hand, it’s not difficult to be pessimistic because, as has already been referred to, so many things are happening in the world which are frightening and limiting. And really, that’s all I can say.” Bailey jumped in, explaining that she grew up in an age where she and her peers believed they were changing the world. She added: “I would say we have a moral obligation to try to be optimistic, but it’s very hard. But unless we are optimistic, we fail. And I’ll just point out, Alice is actually my daughter in real life,” she said, smiling. “So, of course I am concerned. I’d be concerned in any case about the future. I’m of the same generation as [her character] Birdie, and certainly when we were in our 20s, we thought we were going to change everything. We thought it was going to get better — that we were breaking down all sorts of horrible taboos and repressions that were around after the war, and that working people would have a better life. I would have been astonished to have known then what I see happening now.” In a lighter moment, Leigh was asked about the abundance of wine drank in the film — O’Flynn and Bailey Johnson’s characters have a few bottle-induced dance parties — to which he responded: “Drinking is part of our culture — certainly in the West or indeed in many cultures. As far as I’m concerned, it’s about making films about how we live at all kinds of levels in real life. Part of that is that people drink, so there’s a sort of symbolism in it. […] It’s not a comment about the pros or cons of drinking. It’s just the fact that it is part of the texture and fiber of everyday life.” Jesson added: “There is also a lot of tea [in the film]. I don’t think you should run away with the idea that most Brits are drunkards.” The 2026 San Sebastian International Film Festival runs Sep. 18-26. THR

articles.title: ‘Resident Evil’ Reboots at No. 1 as ‘Shaun the Sheep’ Bounds to No. 3 at U.K., Ireland Box Office
articles.full_text: Sep 22, 2026 5:01am PT ‘Resident Evil’ Reboots at No. 1 as ‘Shaun the Sheep’ Bounds to No. 3 at U.K., Ireland Box Office By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Resident Evil’ Reboots at No. 1 as ‘Shaun the Sheep’ Bounds to No. 3 at U.K., Ireland Box Office 1 hour ago Juliet Stevenson, Olivia Williams Join Tim Crouch’s ‘An Oak Tree’ at the Other Palace (EXCLUSIVE) 5 hours ago Parvathy Thiruvothu on Playing a Police Officer in ‘Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar’ and Speaking Out About Misogyny Despite Scrutiny: ‘I Enjoy Watching Patriarchy Fall Apart’ 5 hours ago See All ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Sony’s franchise reboot “ Resident Evil ” stormed to the summit of the U.K. and Ireland box office, debuting in first place with £4.2 million ($5.6 million) across its opening frame. articles.title: ‘Gangs of London’ Producers Claim They’re Owed $20 Million From Vice Over Pulse Films Sale
articles.full_text: Sep 22, 2026 5:05am PT ‘Gangs of London’ Producers Claim They’re Owed $20 Million From Vice Over Pulse Films Sale By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Sees Mary Embark on Married Life in First Images 3 days ago Lego’s ‘Ninjago Legends: Duskfall’ Anime-Style Shorts Premiere in Korea Ahead of YouTube Release 3 days ago King Charles Denies Bombshell Book Claim That He Said World Would ‘Forget’ Princess Diana 5 days ago See All Courtesy of AMC/SKY The founders of “Gangs of London” producer Pulse Films claim they are owed more than $20 million over the sale of the studio to Vice Media in 2021. Thomas Benski and Marisa Clifford, who founded Pulse Films in 2005, allege Vice still owes them $20.43 million after acquiring their 22% stake in the company for $53.24 million. At the time of the acquisition, which brought Vice’s shareholding to 100%, the duo received $10 million in cash as well as a secured loan note for the remaining $43.24 million. Vice paid the initial installments but in September 2022 missed a payment of $5 million as well as subsequent payments, leaving a debt of just over $20 million. Popular on Variety Related Stories Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago Maria Bartiromo Out at Fox News, Fox Business Under the terms of the secured loan note, Benski and Clifford were entitled to force a sale of Pulse in order to reclaim the money. However, they claim Vice misled them into waiving their rights after fraudulently promising the parent company was solvent and about to be sold for a significant sum, which would enabled their debt to be repaid. The “true state of affairs,” they claim, was that Vice was “financially distressed” and “no genuine sale process capable of generating full repayment was underway.” Vice media filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy the following year. Benski and Clifford have not yet filed suit but earlier this month their motion for pre-action discovery, filed against Pulse Films, was denied by a judge in London’s High Court, who said the request for discovery before a lawsuit was even filed placed a “disproportionately heavy burden” on the company. Pulse Films said complying with the request would have cost more than £440,000 ($588,000) and involved reviewing over 264,000 documents. The judge said in his decision that while “it is not obvious to me that there is concrete evidence of dishonesty” this was effectively a question for a court to decide once a lawsuit has been filed. Variety has contacted reps for Benski, Clifford, Pulse Films and Vice. articles.full_text: Sep 22, 2026 6:00am PT Billy Bush to Join Fox News as Contributor By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest MS NOW, CNN, Politico Allege Trump, White House Staffers Violated First Amendment in New Suit 1 day ago ‘This Week’ Executive Producer Ready to Scramble for Midterms 5 days ago CookUnity Serves Gourmet Meals in New York City Bodegas With Spicy Promotional Recipe 5 days ago See All Getty Billy Bush , the longtime entertainment-news correspondent, is expected to join Fox News Media as a contributor, a potential sign that the outlet is growing more eager to cover the worlds of celebrity and popular culture with more depth. Bush’s new role is expected to be unveiled Tuesday, and he is slated to appear on Fox News Channel ‘s “Jesse Watters Primetime” in the 8 p.m. hour. He is expected to appear across multiple Fox News Media platforms. Related Stories Maria Bartiromo Out at Fox News, Fox Business Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago Bush has covered Hollywood for years, most famously as the East Coast correspondent for “Access Hollywood,” but also as a host for “Extra.” He had a short stint as a co-host of the third hour of NBC’s “Today.” In recent years, he has gone the independent route, hosting “Hot Mics with Billy Bush,” a digital program that looks as sports, politics, entertainment, technology and popular culture. He is expected to continue with his own ventures. Popular on Variety “I’m excited to join Fox News Media and its loyal audience to share my perspective on the people, ideas and moments shaping today’s culture…. as well as the ones trying to undo it!” Bush said in a statement Bush has grappled with notoriety and cancel culture. He found himself out of work for three years after a surreal incident in which a 2016 “Access” outtake was released showing then-Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump telling Bush about how he was able to sexually assault women. Information about the incident leaked from NBCUniversal and broke in The Washington Post , and Bush, who by then had moved over to NBC’s “Today,” lost his job . Bush has covered major live entertainment events, including the Golden Globes, Grammys and Academy Awards. He covered the Olympics from 2004 to 2016 on NBC and reported live from Prince William’s wedding to Catherine Middleton for NBC News. He has made several appearances in movies and TV shows. Bush is the nephew of the late President George H.W. Bush and the cousin of former President George W. Bush and former Florida Governor Jeb Bush. articles.title: ‘Heart of the Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt Is a Veteran Stranded With His Combat Dog in David Ayer’s Stirringly Crafted Survival-in-the-Wild Saga
articles.full_text: Sep 22, 2026 6:01am PT ‘Heart of the Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt Is a Veteran Stranded With His Combat Dog in David Ayer’s Stirringly Crafted Survival-in-the-Wild Saga In spirit it's not far removed from an old Disney movie, but Pitt gives a true performance, and so does the canine actor playing his trusty companion. By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest ‘Heart of the Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt Is a Veteran Stranded With His Combat Dog in David Ayer’s Stirringly Crafted Survival-in-the-Wild Saga 41 minutes ago ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name 3 days ago ‘Resident Evil’ Review: Zach Cregger’s Reboot Is Funky Monster Fun, a One-Man-Against-the-Squish-Zombies Lark That Never Gets Bogged Down in Video-Game Sludge 6 days ago See All Scott Garfield In “ Heart of the Beast ,” Brad Pitt does something a lot of actors might not quite bring off in a man-and-his-dog-in-the-wilderness saga: He gives a true performance. His character, James Belmont, is a retired Special Forces officer who has been through a great many deployments. (There are combat flashbacks to what looks like Afghanistan, though the war isn’t named.) In the opening sequence, he’s piloting a small plane through the spectacular Alaska mountains, his trusty German Shepherd, Odin, by his side. Odin is battle-scarred, with titanium teeth and only three legs (he wears a prosthetic one). He’s a combat dog, raised by James since he was a puppy; having been through so much war together, the two have an animal closeness you can just about touch. Pitt shows you the love and trust James and the dog share, and also the veteran James is: alert, grizzled, taciturn, resourceful, a little too content to be by himself — but he’s that way because war has formed him, and how many others would understand? Related Stories Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago Billy Bush to Join Fox News as Contributor “Heart of the Beast” opens on a note of disquiet: Odin, standing alone in the middle of a road, as a young woman (Anna Lambe) approaches in a pick-up truck. So something happened along the way. The film then flashes back a week, to when the Alaska trip starts off as a bit of low-key R&R. For a while, we revel in the roughneck pleasure of it all. The grandeur of the skies and forests and lakes and snow-capped cliffs (the film was shot in New Zealand), the surreal quietude, the hiking through the woods, the serenity of pitching camp on a shore under the stars, the coziness of the campfire, the cooler of Belgian ale, the catching and eating of fresh salmon, the pouring of steaming coffee out of a tin pot — we could almost be watching a biopic about the Marlboro Man. All that’s missing is the lantern. Popular on Variety Pitt, in a beard and a buzzcut and camouflage shirt and aviator shades, with a compass tattoo under his left ear, is playing a man out of Hemingway by way of L.L. Bean. His James is so centered in this wilderness that he makes us feel at home too. It’s a telling feature of the movie that the character exhibits no overt war trauma; there’s almost a political layer to it, an undermining of the inevitability of the damaged vet. At the same time, you feel James’ war experience in the very premise of the film: his craving for isolation. Early on, he meets a stranger who looks like an old prospector (he’s played by J.K. Simmons), but after a few friendly minutes of light banter the stranger goes on his way. The only buddy in this movie is the dog. If it’s a surprise to see Brad Pitt holding down the center of a wilderness drama this tranquil and wholesome, the other surprise of “Heart of the Beast” is that it was directed by David Ayer, a specialist in reckless tales of urban violence and underworld nihilism (“The Beekeeper,” “The Tax Collector,” “End of Watch”). In a dramatic change of pace, Ayer and Pitt (both producers on the film) have teamed up to make something that isn’t so far removed, in form and spirit, from an old-school Disney movie. That said, the real surprise of “Heart of the Beast” is how well-made it is. Ayer draws on his logistical talent, and even his taste for violence, to craft a tale of survival that makes us feel the pain, the fear and the hardship, the stakes of what it takes to battle nature. We know something is going to go wrong, and without giving too much away, let me just say that James and Odin wind up stranded, without the plane, 58 miles from the nearest road. To survive, they’ll have to trek to that road, through the forest and the mountains and the plains — and since they start off by covering 8 to 10 miles a day, the journey seems eminently doable. They have supplies, and they can forage for food. But in this saga of man vs. nature, nature is not forgiving. The first obstacle is a grizzly bear, which approaches out of nowhere. The beast has been created with digital effects, which is the sort of thing that critics tend to pick at, but I’m interested in how scary and convincing the encounter is, and in this case the answer is: plenty. Ayer stages it with an awesomely meticulous danger. There are howling wolves. There’s a cliff that joins to the one across the white-water river below with a bridge made of two tree trunks. There’s a treacherous fall through the rapids. There is bone popping out of skin. Throughout, Brad Pitt projects a tensile strength, and a survivor’s moxie, that’s heroic but never superhuman. We see the physical anguish he refuses, and how the accumulation of wounds, even as he shakes them off, start to stack up. At one point, he thinks Odin is gone from this world, and when that turns out to be not the case, he weeps with gratitude. There’s a way to sum up “Heart of the Beast,” and that’s by saying, “This is a terrific performance — and Brad Pitt is extremely good too.” Because Uber, the dog who plays Odin, does one of the most affecting pieces of canine acting I’ve seen since the days of “Old Yeller” and “Lassie Come Home.” You feel Odin’s weariness, his intelligence, his dogged loyalty. The bond he shares with James emanates from the heart of both beasts, and that makes the film a journey stirring in its primacy. ‘Heart of the Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt Is a Veteran Stranded With His Combat Dog in David Ayer’s Stirringly Crafted Survival-in-the-Wild Saga Reviewed at AMC Empire, Sept. 17, 2026. MPA rating: PG-13. Running time: 101 MIN. Production: A Paramount Pictures release, in association with Domain Entertainment, Gulfstream Pictures, of a Wild Chickens, Temple Hill, Kino World production. Producers: Olivia Hamilton, Marty Bowen, David Ayer, Brad Pitt. Executive producers: Damien Chazelle, Scott Lumpkin, Cameron Alexander, Chris Long, Pete Chiappetta, Anthony Tittanegro, Andrew Lary, Sophie Cassidy, Zack Conroy. Crew: Director: Dave Ayer. Screenplay: Cameron Alexander. Camera: Mauro Fiore. Editor: Dody Dorn. Music: Jared Michael Fry. With: Brad Pitt, J.K. Simmons, Anna Lambe. articles.full_text: Sep 22, 2026 6:31am PT Oscar Best Picture Category Will Soon Be Dominated by International Films, Claims ‘I’m Still Here’ Producer Rodrigo Teixeira The RT Films boss was speaking at the Creative Investors' Conference in San Sebastian By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Will Record Summer Box Office Save Indie Cinema? Not Quite, but Cannes Might, Say U.S. Producers 3 hours ago U.K.’s National Film and TV School and Sean Connery Foundation to Establish Permanent Base in Edinburgh (EXCLUSIVE) 5 hours ago Netflix Partners With British Library, Sets Talks Series With Florence Pugh, Zoe Kazan and More 15 hours ago See All Credit: Alile Dara Onawale - Globoplay U.S. films will soon be the minority among the nominees for the top Academy Award, claims one of South America’s most successful producers. Rodrigo Teixeira , who through his RT Films banner has produced the likes of “Frances Ha,” “Call Me by Your Name,” “Ad Astra” “Bergman Island” and “I’m Still Here,” building up long-standing relationships with filmmakers such as James Gray in the process, made the claim at the San Sebastian Film Festival ‘s Creative Investors’ Conference, co-organized by CAA Media Finance. Related Stories Maria Bartiromo Out at Fox News, Fox Business Billy Bush to Join Fox News as Contributor “We are [now] seeing at least three-four international films in the best film category,” he said, speaking on Tuesday. “And in five years from now, I believe international films will make up 60% of the category for best film. I truly believe that. Because we can talk more. We have freedom of speech, and in the U.S., without freedom of speech, it’s difficult to get financed. But outside the U.S. we have it, and I believe in five years the international films are going to be bigger than American films.” Popular on Variety Teixeira is an Oscar nominee himself, having produced Walter Salles’ Brazillan smash hit “I’m Still Here,” which in 2025 was nominated for best picture and best actress (for Fernanda Torres) and won the Oscar for best international feature. The film would also earn more than $36 million (from a budget of around $9 million), becoming the highest-grossing Brazilian film since COVID. “I’m Still Here,” claimed Teixeira, was part of a wave of cinema from Brazil made in the wake of the “very hardcore, right-wing” Bolsonaro government and served as as “an act of hope” that helped “change the self-esteem of the country.” Teixeira was recently in Cannes with his latest Gray collaboration and competition title “Paper Tiger,” which he said he originated, and Director’s Fortnight entry “La Perra” from Dominga Sotomayor, which would win the Palm Dog Award. Coming up for RT is Gray’s next project and Mia Hansen-Love’s Mary Wollstonecraft biopic “If Love Should Die,” starring Renate Reinsve and now shooting in Sweden.
