articles.title: Muse Entertainment Unveils ‘Doula: A True Crime’ Trailer As Boat Rocker Studios Boards CBC Doc
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Muse Entertainment Unveils ‘Doula: A True Crime’ Trailer As Boat Rocker Studios Boards CBC Doc ‘Stuff The British Stole’ Producer WildBear Entertainment Reshuffles Top Team To “Get Ahead” Of Industry Transformation BBC Drama ‘Ministry Of Time’ Adds Adeel Akhtar, Ciaran Hinds & Eight More To Cast View All September 21, 2026 9:01pm EXCLUSIVE: Here’s a trailer for Doula – A True Crime , a Canadian doc series from The Walrus and the Whistleblower filmmaker Nathalie Bibeau about a bizarre criminal case of a woman who faked pregnancies. The three-parter, which will premiere on Canadian pubcaster CBC on October 7, looks into the story of Kaitlyn Braun, who aged 24, reached out to more than 40 doulas with the same shocking story: that she had been sexually assaulted and was in her third trimester carrying a stillborn child. We can reveal Boat Rocker Studios has acquired the international distribution rights to the Muse Entertainment -produced show and will launch it at MIPCOM Cannes next month. Related Stories Trailers 'Coven Academy' Trailer Reveals A Forbidden Love Triangle & Explosive Powers In Supernatural Witch Series News A+E Global Media Backs Lifetime Korea Series 'Oh! My Guard' Starring K-Pop Performer Jung Yong-hwa & Hong Seung-hee The doc is notable for including the first interview with Braun, who was hit with 53 criminal charges after doulas, who had helped her and provided pro bono services such as hours of phone and video calls and round-the-clock in-person care, began to question her narrative. Watch on Deadline After piecing together the pattern that had formed over nine months between June 2022 and February 2023, many found others like themselves and started a grassroots campaign for to alert authorities through a viral TikTok counter-offensive. In the trailer, we hear from several doulas shaken by their experience. “I can’t tell you I was assaulted, that’s not really what happened and I can’t tell that I was scammed, that doesn’t encompass what she did to me. I have to tell you the whole story so you understand,” says one. “I have no felt fear like that in my entire life,” says another later in the trailer. The one-minute clip ends with a camera making its way up a porch, where it is met by Braun, who smiles as she opens the door and says, “Hello!” The film was made over several years, and attempts to go beyond the sensationalist reporting that followed the story at the time. Braun conversed with Bibeau several times over extensive interviews and phone calls, offering insight into her actions and motivations. “Everyone knew that Kaitlyn Braun had committed crimes. I wanted to understand why,” said Bibeau, writer, director and producer of Doula: A True Crime . “The deeper I went, the less the story yielded to easy conclusions. Kaitlyn’s deception played on empathy, and the harm it caused was real. “But the very thing that made the harm possible was also what I needed to understand her. I’m drawn to the places where human behaviour resists a clean moral frame. And this story lives in one of those places – where empathy doesn’t get in the way of truth, but brings us closer to it.” Jonas Prupas, Managing Director of Unscripted and executive producer at Montreal-based Muse, said the story “could easily be reduced to its more sensationalist elements,” but that Bibeau had made it “into something nuanced, surprising and deeply human.” Mellany Welsh, SVP and Global Head of Distribution & Brands at Boat Rocker Studios, added the doc offered international buyers “a story they won’t find anywhere else.” Muse – known for the likes of Sullivan’s Crossing , The Kennedys and Nose Deep – made the show for CBC and CBC Gem, with the series premiering on October 7 at 8am ET on CBC. Prupas and Courtney Dobbins are exec producers for Muse. For CBC, Sally Catto is General Manager, Entertainment, Jennifer Dettman is Executive Director of Unscripted Content, and Michelle McCree is Senior Director and Commissioning Editor of Documentary. articles.title: Brixton Community Cinema Creator Abiba Coulibaly On Why She Decided To End The Popular London Film Club
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: Brad Pitt Revisits The Character That Won Him An Oscar In David Fincher’s Latest Movistar Plus Announces 2027 Slate, Including JA Bayona & Fernando León Projects, At San Sebastián Naomi Watts Says She’d Like To Work With Paul Thomas Anderson & Praises The Advancements Older Women Have Made In Hollywood — San Sebastián View All September 22, 2026 1:02am Abiba Coulibaly Next month, the Brixton Community Cinema , the roving cinema project that has quickly become one of the UK’s most admired film communities under the stewardship of independent programmer Abiba Coulibaly , will close. Coulibaly announced the cinema’s farewell season in August on Instagram . “The closure of Brixton Community Cinema is not to give up and abandon either, just to recalibrate,” she wrote in the statement. Coulibaly launched the BCC in 2022 as a pay-what-you-can pop-up cinema club. She programmed a wide variety of titles, but the cinema’s central focus was international repertory and arthouse films. Past screenings featured titles like The First World Festival of Negro Arts by William Greaves, Abdellatif Kechiche’s La Faute à Voltaire , and Sarah Gomez’s One Way or Another . Related Stories News Muse Entertainment Unveils 'Doula: A True Crime' Trailer As Boat Rocker Studios Boards CBC Doc News 'Trump TV' Promo Uses Clips From 'The Simpsons,' 'Seinfeld,' 'Friends,' 'The Dark Knight' & Many More The eclectic programming made the BCC a must-visit film destination for cinephiles in London. In turn, the cinema’s audience grew and so did its reputation. BCC pop-up screenings moved from small non-arts spaces in Brixton to venues like London’s Cinema Museum. Criterion’s Ashley Clark described Coulibaly as “fantastic” during an interview with Deadline earlier this year . So why end things now? Watch on Deadline Speaking with Deadline ahead of her final screening on October 6, Coulibaly explains that the BCC project simply grew at a pace that was impossible for one person to maintain. “The project had grown more than I ever expected,” she explains. Below, Coulibaly speaks with us in depth about how she built Brixton Community Cinema, what she learned about audiences during the BCC’s successful run, and what she has planned next. Films set to screen as part of the BCC’s final season include Margarida Cardoso’s Kuxa Kanema: The Birth of Cinema (2003) and Sanaz Sohrabi’s essay film An Incomplete Calendar (2026). Legendary artist and filmmaker John Akomfrah will also sit for a discussion with Ish filmmaker Imran Perretta. Scroll down to see the full lineup. DEADLINE: Abiba, you’re closing the Brixton Community Cinema. Why? ABIBA COULIBALY: I always knew it wouldn’t last forever. I was actually adamant from the start that it wouldn’t, because I knew the limits of the “pay what you can” model. So I think it was always more of an experiment. But it all came to a head, I’d say, a year to 18 months ago, because the project had grown more than I ever expected. I then felt I needed to do things like register as a CIC, get a business bank account, and start paying for domains. As I tried to scale up, I realized I didn’t have the time or money to handle all the admin and bureaucracy. I actually ended up losing a lot of time and money in the process. It was too much for just one person. DEADLINE: The cinema did really grow. I did a piece with Ashley Clark at Criterion about his great book on Black cinema, and he name-checked you and the cinema. I was surprised he’d heard of it considering he isn’t based in the UK. Did no bigger institutions or funders come along to invest or support your work? COULIBALY: I read that interview and was really surprised and flattered to see my name mentioned. Ashley and I actually grew up on the same road, opposite each other, but he’s a decade or so older. But in terms of people coming along, honestly, no. Firstly, the question of who you work with has been difficult. It has very rarely been possible to align values and access to resources. I never envisaged having to deliberate so much about working with organizations. Sometimes it would be that they aren’t based in Brixton or Lambeth, or maybe I didn’t agree with their political stances. But in terms of one-off project fees, yeah, sure, I’ve been approached; it would be something like £500. But never any big, long-term support. Generally, money and business aren’t my strengths. For this final season, a friend volunteered to raise some money, and they managed to get £2500 from WeTransfer. That has been our only major partnership or collaboration. DEADLINE: I’ve been to your screenings, and they were always very well attended. What did you learn about what audiences want from cinemas in 2026? COULIBALY: I felt my audience was seeking cinema experiences that could address their real-world concerns. They weren’t really seeking an escapist moment, but rather the space to discuss and engage with relevant things happening around them. I started the project in late 2022. The genocide in Palestine began in late 2023, and I tried at times to speak to that through my programming alongside other things going on in various other countries. I always got the impression that those were the events audiences really wanted to attend. But I also had many difficulties with myself as a programmer. I began with a lot of enthusiasm about the power of cinema. Over the years, that has dampened in some ways. That is also why I want to take a step back. I also got the impression from audience members that they’ve had so many weird institutional failings from both cinemas and arts institutions. It’s really got to the point where there are very few large galleries, museums, or cinemas in London that don’t have some kind of problematic scandal or history. I think people are really searching for cultural spaces which don’t feel so compromising, when it feels impossible to boycott and divest from every single cultural institution in London. Abiba Coulibaly at the BCC’s open-air cinema during the 2023 London Festival of Architecture. DEADLINE: Talk to me about this final lineup. You’re focusing on a large geographical area; there are films from Madagascar, Pakistan, and Malaysia. COULIBALY: To end this run, I felt I needed to choose a theme or location. I’ve always tried to steer clear of regionally focused programming. I sometimes find it a lazy way of attracting audiences. I’m also slightly resistant to labels. I actually saw that BFI Future Film created a little zine for its Young Programmers’ Festival, and inside they said, “Go to Brixton Community Cinema if you want to see Black cinema.” They probably thought it was a really nice way to shout me out, and I’m sure they’re sweet people. But that’s so funny because I show films from all over the world. Ultimately, I believe I’m from the best city in the world. When I was growing up, there was so much mixing between all groups of people. With this final season, I was thinking very clearly about the question: How do you reflect a city back at itself? DEADLINE: You’ve actually done a lot of really important work here. Screening films that people otherwise would never see or even hear about. Have you ever thought about consolidating it all in a book or publication about the cinema? COULIBALY: From the very start of Brixton Community Cinema, I focused heavily on printed material. I used to do a lot of program notes and zines designed by some very talented friends behind the publishing studio Em—Dash, who do all of the graphics for the project. I produced those less over time because it was so labor-intensive. But I have this amazing archive of essays, texts, and interviews that I’ve always thought would make a really great anthology that could also speak to the political moment. For instance, the third or fourth screening I ever did was Jafar Panahi’s Offside , during the 2022 World Cup. When the screening came around, the protests in Iran had really taken off. So, I commissioned a Tehran-based film journalist to write about what it would mean to rewatch the film in this moment. There are so many interesting texts like that that are not only great films but also speak to the social and political context of making the Brixton Community Cinema. It’s really just a case of money. All of the material is there; all of the ideas are there. DEADLINE: You’re not going away completely. You programmed parts of the BFI’s Sarah Maldoror season. Where will people be able to find you? COULIBALY: I’m freelance, so who knows. I’m also a programmer for the Open City Documentary Festival. That’s my one regular programming gig. I will also continue to programme independently. articles.title: Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Princess Diana’s Brother Over “Bulls***” Claim In Bombshell Memoir
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Princess Diana’s Brother Over “Bulls***” Claim In Bombshell Memoir Tom Cruise Earns Applause With Six-Minute Monologue On Why Art Beats AI In Filmmaking: “There Is Nothing Like Human” BBC Removes Blackface Sketches From ‘That Mitchell And Webb Look’ View All September 22, 2026 1:53am Piers Morgan and Charles Spencer Getty Piers Morgan has received an apology from Charles Spencer, brother of the late Princess Diana , over an inaccurate claim in the Earl’s bombshell memoir. Spencer’s book, Swan Song , has dominated the headlines in the UK for days following his explosive allegation that King Charles III said Diana would soon be forgotten in the aftermath of her death. Morgan drew attention to another section of Spencer’s book, in which the Earl claimed that Morgan published “intrusive” images of Diana in a gym while he was editor of The Daily Mirror. “I come across in the despicable manner imaginable,” Morgan said of Spencer’s book. “There’s just one problem — it’s all bulls***. And very easy bulls*** for me to prove it.” Related Stories News Princess Di Returns To 'SNL UK' As "Deeply Intelligent, Autonomous, Neurokinetic Android" In Cold Open Skewering King Charles, Ed Sheeran & AI News Tilly Norwood Malfunctions During Piers Morgan Interview: "Seems I Had A Little Hiccup" Speaking on his YouTube show Piers Morgan Uncensored , the former CNN anchor continued: “The photographs, which he says that I published, were printed by The Sunday Mirror on November 7, 1993. I joined The Daily Mirror in October 1995. In fact, at the time of the gym pictures, I was doing a showbiz column on The Mirro r’s arch rival, The Sun .” Watch on Deadline 'It's all bullsh*t… you'll be hearing from my lawyers.' BREAKING: Piers Morgan plans to take legal action against Earl Spencer over “fabricated inaccuracies” made about him in his bombshell book on Diana. Watch more 👇 📺 https://t.co/ZWOoVI5C3O @piersmorgan pic.twitter.com/3w66CTrwZc — Piers Morgan Uncensored (@PiersUncensored) September 21, 2026 Morgan added that Spencer had printed “fabricated inaccuracies” that strike “at the heart of his credibility.” He said: “If Earl Spencer can be so incredibly defamatorily wrong about such basic facts involving me, well why should we believe anything else that he puts in this book?” In a statement, Spencer acknowledged the error. “As an historian, accuracy is important to Earl Spencer. He therefore wishes to clarify that his assumption was incorrect. Earl Spencer apologises to Mr Morgan for this error,” a representative of the Earl said. Spencer added, however, that he was correct in his recollection of a phone call he had with Morgan, in which he informed the journalist that he could not attend Diana’s funeral. “Earl Spencer’s account of his conversation with Piers Morgan is accurate. Mr Morgan was surly and annoyed when Earl Spencer called personally to tell him that he was not welcome at his sister’s funeral,” the statement continued. On his show, Morgan addressed Spencer directly. “You will be hearing, and your publishers, from my lawyers because I would like the complete lie you have published about me and those photographs to be removed from your book. And I would like a donation to be made to the King’s Trust for the damage that you have caused with your lie.” It is not yet clear if Morgan will accept the apology. In his book, Spencer recalled a conversation he had with King Charles in 1997 over whether Princes William and Harry should walk behind the coffin of Diana ahead of her funeral. Spencer said his reservations were met with a “stream of anger” from Charles. He writes that the then Prince “unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. ‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough.’” In response, Buckingham Palace said last week: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.” ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Diana’s Brother Over Memoir Which Midnight Madness TIFF Pic Could Become The Next Box Office Obsession? ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $108M WW Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M From Sale Of Pulse Films
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Princess Diana’s Brother Over “Bulls***” Claim In Bombshell Memoir Tom Cruise Earns Applause With Six-Minute Monologue On Why Art Beats AI In Filmmaking: “There Is Nothing Like Human” BBC Removes Blackface Sketches From ‘That Mitchell And Webb Look’ View All September 22, 2026 3:38am 'Gangs of London' Sky/Vice Studios EXCLUSIVE : Thomas Benski and Marisa Clifford , founders of Gangs of London producer Pulse Films , are suing Vice Media , claiming they are owed more than $20 million. Vice took a majority stake in Pulse Films in 2016 before acquiring Benski and Clifford’s remaining 22% shareholding in December 2021 for $10M in cash and $43.24M in loan notes. Soon after, Vice ran into serious financial difficulty, with Benski and Clifford alleging that the company failed to pay loan notes totalling $20.4M, breaking the terms of their sale agreement. The producers — who exited Pulse in 2022 — claimed that they were persuaded not to exercise their contractual rights by former Vice executives, who they accuse of making fraudulent misrepresentations about the company’s financial health and failed sale to Antenna Group. Related Stories News Could 'Gangs Of London' Be About To Move To Miami Or Johannesburg? Vice Studios Boss Amy Powell Says She Is Mulling Franchise Expansion News Pulse Films Exits TV & Film Game After 20 Years As Vice Makes Layoffs In London Vice Group entered Chapter 11 bankruptcy in May 2023. Three months later, a consortium of former lenders — led by Fortress Investment Group, Soros Fund Management and Monroe Capital — acquired the company after a bankruptcy auction. Watch on Deadline Vice Media’s position is that Benski and Clifford’s allegations are baseless and lacking in evidence. The company intends to vigorously defend its position. Details of the dispute emerged for the first time in a UK High Court ruling earlier this month, during which Benski and Clifford failed in their efforts to get Vice to disclose thousands of documents relating to their grievance. Judge Peter MacDonald Eggers dismissed Benski and Clifford’s pre-action disclosure application, but did not reach any conclusions on the merits of their case. Deadline understands that the producers will continue to pursue action against Vice and are currently assessing their legal options. The duo, who now run Magna Studios, declined to comment. A Vice Media spokesperson said: “Vice Media is pleased to note that the London High Court has dismissed an application for pre-action disclosure by Thomas Benski and Marissa Clifford in relation to allegations concerning events prior to Vice Media’s Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023. “Those allegations are groundless. In dismissing the application, the court relied on the vague, inconsistent and unsatisfactory way in which the allegations have been advanced. We will continue robustly to defend any claim, to the extent it is pursued.” Benski and Clifford’s pre-action disclosure application named four defendants, including Pulse Films and Nancy Dubuc, the former CEO of Vice Media. Pulse Films’ intellectual property, including Sky series Gangs of London , now sits under Vice Studios. Summarizing Benski and Clifford’s claims, Judge Peter MacDonald Eggers wrote that they have “advanced serious allegations of fraudulent misrepresentation and unlawful means conspiracy against the respondents [at Vice]. In particular, the applicants’ case is that they were induced not to exercise valuable contractual enforcement rights by alleged repeated and false assurances by the respondents as to the valuation, solvency and an imminent sale of the Vice Group.” He continued: “Whether the allegations of fraud and conspiracy can be established will be an issue in any substantive proceedings which may be issued by the applicants in respect of their claim and will turn on the respondents’ knowledge about the Vice Group’s financial position and the failure of the sale process at the time they were allegedly giving assurances to the applicants.” The judgment added: “The respondents deny the allegations of fraud and conspiracy, which they state are couched in ‘unacceptably nebulous terms, based on unwarranted inferences, and without any sufficient evidential foundation.'” Vice’s position is that its executives were not obliged to keep Benski and Clifford abreast of the company’s financial position and that they dealt with duo with “honesty and integrity” at “all times.” ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Diana’s Brother Over Memoir Which Midnight Madness TIFF Pic Could Become The Next Box Office Obsession? ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $108M WW Read More About: Comments

articles.title: MIPCOM Bets On Creators, Brands & AI As International TV Business Readies For Cannes Get-Together
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart MIPCOM Bets On Creators, Brands & AI As International TV Business Readies For Cannes Get-Together Dhar Mann, Sean Atkins Set For MIPCOM’s First-Ever Pre-Opening Keynote Princess Diana Documentary Featuring Unheard Tapes Set For International Launch At MIPCOM View All September 22, 2026 5:06am MIPCOM in Cannes RX France MIPCOM boss Lucy Smith wants the world to know that October in Cannes is now about more than buying and selling TV programs. “Our biggest challenge is changing the perception,” she says, with this year’s event just weeks away. “You don’t come to MIPCOM just for your distribution deals anymore. You’re coming because you’ve got to find valuable IP, or you want to find out more about what’s going on in branded entertainment, or you’re looking at what’s happening in vertical drama or AI.” Distribution remains the spine of MIPCOM, but as the international TV industry has changed, so has its biggest annual get-together. “We are a marketplace, but it’s not just a buy-and-sell market anymore,” Smith says. Related Stories News Muse Entertainment Unveils 'Doula: A True Crime' Trailer As Boat Rocker Studios Boards CBC Doc News Dhar Mann, Sean Atkins Set For MIPCOM's First-Ever Pre-Opening Keynote That wider remit for MIPCOM means embracing the creator economy, brand partnerships and tech. Watch on Deadline Put simply, it had to change to stay relevant. Consolidation and industry shifts are impacting its core distribution business. For example, Warner Bros. and Paramount may have separate stands and spaces in Cannes this year, but that is unlikely to be the case when MIPCOM 2027 kicks off. The same is true of Banijay and All3Media. The medium-sized and small distributors, meanwhile, are feeling the pinch. Acquisition execs still attend MIPCOM in healthy numbers, but often with reduced buying power as their budgets come under pressure. Smith’s first MIPCOM was in 2006 and she now runs the market, which is organized by RX France. She says: “We evolve with the changes in the industry. We came out of probably ‘24 thinking, ‘This whole industry is just changing so much, and there’s less funding from traditional sources, so what does all that mean?’” The change under her leadership is visible. First, there was a heavy push into co-production and FAST channels, and then into brands and the creator economy. “We really wanted to make sure we were bringing more of the creative conversations around funding and IP. That was the first step, and then we brought the MIP Innovation Lab, so we could address streaming in a broader way. “And then, the big push had to be the creator economy.” YouTube had its biggest-ever presence at MIPCOM in 2025. It will be even more visible this time. Smith says partnering with the Google-owned company was “the right way to really make a mark and to say MIPCOM would be focusing and pivoting to the creator economy.” This year, Dhar Mann Studios kicks off MIPCOM, with a pre-market headline session on Sunday, before proceedings start in earnest on Monday. Powerhouse digital producer Mann and DMS CEO Sean Atkins will jointly keynote. “We all know that you know creator-led businesses are reshaping the global media landscape and we knew that that was that was something we needed to address,” Smith says. “We were getting calls from studios saying, ‘Hey, we want to meet all these creator-led businesses.’ And these businesses are really at that intersection of creators, brands and branded entertainment.” Having partnered with BrandStorytelling last year, RX France launches MIP BrandWorks this time to cover off its branded entertainment activity, with denstsu the headline partner. “We want to become the home of branded entertainment because we see ourselves as the gateway to the global entertainment content and media business. If you want to be working in content, and obviously brands need to be embedded in content to be culturally relevant, this is where you come and do that.” Artificial intelligence is also on the menu. A new conference and market will run under the MIP AI Entertainment Forum banner, with Versos AI and Protégé the partners. “Companies involved in AI and entertainment have a specific need to be part of the content industry conversations,” Smith says about the reason for launching the new forum. “You’ve got the studios and producers, the production side of things, you’ve got the workflow piece, and you’ve got the licensing part; those will be the pillars.” While the focus is shifting, MIPCOM’s USP remains bringing a critical mass of people together. In a world of Zoom meetings and with pressure on travel budgets, the numbers are not as big as in yesteryear, but no other international TV event gathers 10,000 people. “We know that bringing people together at one time in one place gives them the opportunity to work together on what these new businesses are,” Smith says. “We wanted to bridge the gap in the conversations between traditional media companies, who remain hugely important, and these newer creator-led studios.” Glitz and glamor are in the DNA of Cannes. The film festival and Cannes Lions lean into that with starry photocalls and A-lister parties. MIPCOM has the same setting and its own share of photo moments, but as it expands its focus, the event is still really all about dealmaking. “If you really want to do business and understand these new ways of doing business, this is where it’s going to be happening, and this is where things will start moving forward,” Smith says. ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Diana’s Brother Over Memoir Which Midnight Madness TIFF Pic Could Become The Next Box Office Obsession? ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $108M WW Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Heart Of The Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt And A Soulful German Shepherd Struggle To Survive The Wilderness In An Emotional Journey That Will Have You Sobbing
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Forgotten Island’ Review: H.E.R. And Dave Franco Give Life To Gorgeously Animated And Frenetic ‘Toon ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Oscar-Predictive Toronto Film Festival People’s Choice Award ‘Magazine’ Review: Lily McInerny And Bright Young Cast Give Flavor To Pre-Digital Vanishing Era Of NY’s Literary World – Toronto Film Festival View All September 22, 2026 6:00am Brad Pitt and Odin in Heart Of The Beast Paramount Pictures Going to see Heart Of The Beast is a dangerous proposition if you don’t want to be seen crying uncontrollably in public. This man and his dog story is an emotional roller coaster that lays it all out there, and I lapped it up just like I did in My Dog Skip, Turner & Hooch, K9, Marley & Me, Old Yeller, and countless others. But there was something visceral about this one, a largely dialogue-less film where the story is told in the eyes of Brad Pitt playing opposite a loyal and tough German Shepherd named Odin. This is a story of a 30 year military veteran and the dog who stood with him in Iraq and Afghanistan only to finally find peace in the Alaskan wilderness until the unthinkable happens and it becomes an even greater tale of survival against all odds. It stays with you, won’t let go, and gives you new appreciation for those who serve, whether on two feet or four paws. Related Stories News Post-Merger Paramount May Overdeliver On Settlement Terms With 36-Film 2027 Slate Amid Speculation About Duplication & WB Leadership News Paramount Settlement Protects Pluto TV, Sets BET & Comedy Central As Potential Divesture Targets While Omitting Premium Channels & TV Studios David Ayer who directed Pitt in the terrific 2014 tank movie, Fury, here gets perhaps the most moving performance the actor has ever given. He plays Sgt. Major James Belmont whose military service is behind him and has come to the peace and solitary serenity of the wilderness, flying his plane, his dog, aka Canine Commander Odin by his side. It is as if this pair simply survived hell on earth to one day find heaven together. Watch on Deadline We see them all alone among nature’s wonders, until one day a stranger just appears out of nowhere. James hoists his gun but isn’t necessary. The man, Watkins (nicely played by J.K. Simmons ) is a friendly guy just looking for a little company before rowing off on his boat down the river. It turns out to be a welcome interlude, brief but meaningful. He will be the only human being James and Odin encounter together on their journey. Both suffer from bouts with PTSD, and James comforts Odin after disturbing nightmares shake him. It gets real when James suffers a heart attack and the plane careens out of control, finally landing in the water and sinking. Odin is thrown out before that, and somehow James survives and struggles to go back frantically trying to find his dog. He does even as Odin shows little signs of life, but after a night willing him to live, Odin, who wears a prosthetic leg and has few teeth due to another cruel war injury, clearly has a knack to survive and the next morning he is miraculously back to his old self. Using his expertise with a map and a compass, James and Odin set out to somehow find a semblance of civilization but the trip becomes one harrowing hazard after another including a frightening confrontation with a grizzly bear, a fight with a pack of wolves, James being swept away down the river, and more things most people could never live to tell. This is a pair that survived the worst of war (brief flashbacks briefly show that aspect of their past shared life) and now are unexpectedly in survival mode once again. His heart failing, James inherently knows his own days may be numbered, but he is going to make sure they find the road for reasons he doesn’t share with Odin, or Odie as he calls him. Heart Of The Beast is one of those movies that, with great dignity and little fanfare, shows the true connection between man and animal just as countless movies have done since Rin Tin Tin starred in silent pictures. That Ayer, with a heart wrenching screenplay by first time writer Cameron Alexander, has found a way to make it all feel fresh is why this director should be applauded. The success of the film is also due in no small part to Pitt who makes us believe this animal is his soul brother, much more than just a pet, or even a partner in combat. Odin is all he has left and he will honor him no matter what it takes. No spoiler but Pitt will simply break your heart in doing just that. As for Odin, has any dog ever won an Oscar? Lassie, Benji, anyone? Well, it is high time. Odin delivers one of the best performances by an actor this year, hands down. Actually the truth is he is played by four canines, the main star being Uber, with strong support from his own sons, Ryker, Zika , and Hondo. Give much credit to their trainer, Andrew Simpson. Other than Simmons and of course Pitt, the only other human on board is Anna Lambe as a woman driving her truck when in the distance she sees a dog sitting in the middle of the road. That is the opening image of the film, and then the story flashes back a week. I will leave it at that. New Zealand stands in for Alaska, quite convincingly, with stunning cinematography and camerawork from Mauro Fiore. As pretty as the natural landscape all is to watch it is still the gut wrenching emotional reach of this simple story of humanity at its finest, loyalty and friendship at its most meaningful, and above all the heart of a ‘beast’ and the man standing at his side. There will not be a dry eye in the house. If this one doesn’t move you, there is no hope. Producers are Pitt, Ayer, Olivia Hamilton and Marty Bowen. Damien Chazelle is among the Executive Producers. Title: Heart Of The Beast Distributor: Paramount Release Date: September 25, 2026 Director: David Ayer Screenplay: Cameron Alexander Cast: Brad Pitt, J. K. Simmons, Anna Lambe, Odin. articles.title: Elliot Graham Dies: Oscar-Nominated ‘Milk’ Editor Was 50
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38 Cate Blanchett Asks London Audience To Stop Filming Play, Says Stage Is Place “Where We Can Simply Be Together And Be Present” Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic” View All September 22, 2026 6:53am Elliot Graham (2022) Joe Maher/Getty Images Elliot Graham, the Oscar-nominated film editor for Milk whose credits also included Steve Jobs, No Time To Die, Superman Returns and Captain Marvel , died Saturday, September 19, in Los Angeles. He was 50. Graham died by suicide, according to the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner . Born in Claremont, California, on June 8, 1976, Graham launched his show business career in the early 2000s with the feature film The Last Minute (2001) and the TV series House (2004). He moved into big-budget feature projects with 2006’s Superman Returns . Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries News Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38 Two years later he was hired by edit Milk , the Harvey Milk bio-pic written by Dustin Lance Black and directed by Gus Van Sant. Starring Sean Penn, Milk was nominated for eight Oscars, including for Graham’s editing. (Black and Penn won their categories). Watch on Deadline “The movie Milk wouldn’t have come together in the way it did without the amazing work of our editor Elliot Graham,” Milk producer Dan Jinks wrote in a tribute on Facebook . “He was nominated for an Oscar for his role.” “I have so many thoughts and feelings about this sweet, kind and quirky man,” Jinks continued. “For now, I’ll just say rest in peace Elliot.” After Milk , Graham worked again with Van Sant on the 2011 film Restless starring Mia Wasikowska. He also edited an episode of the Kelsey Grammer series Boss that year. Additional credits include Steve Jobs (2015), Molly’s Game starring Jessica Chastain (2017), Captain Marvel (2019) and No Time To Die , the 2021 James Bond film starring Daniel Craig. Graham and editor Tom Cross shared a BAFTA award for their work on the film. In addition to his editing credit for the 2018 FX limited series Trust , the Danny Boyle-directed project about the kidnapping of John Paul Getty III, Graham also served as producer. Graham also provided additional editing on X2: X-Men United (2003) and The Amazing Spider-Man 2 (2014). Information on survivors was not immediately available. ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Diana’s Brother Over Memoir Which Midnight Madness TIFF Pic Could Become The Next Box Office Obsession? ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $108M WW Read More About: Comments

articles.title: “It Fills Me With Pride”: How the Basque Country Is Nurturing Its Next Generation of Filmmakers
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 3:00am Nitya López Saitua on the set of 'Family Drill.' San Sebastián Film Festival It’s no longer a secret that Basque cinema is getting some overdue time in the spotlight. Thanks to an almighty production boom in the region, powered by a whopping 60 percent tax rebate (increasing to 70 percent for projects shot in the Basque language, Euskera), the Basque Country’s film and TV output has never looked so healthy. And the proof is in the pudding: The Hollywood Reporter took an in-depth look at the record 45 nominations for Basque projects at this year’s Goyas, also known as “the Spanish Oscars,” after a decade of concentrated investment. Related Stories Movies Red Sea Film Festival Cancels 2026 Edition, Vows to Return Next Year With "Renewed Vision" Movies San Sebastian Winner Yesim Ustaoglu Returns to Competition With 'What Remains' (Exclusive Clip) With San Sebastián’s profile rising exponentially every September, the people working behind the scenes to make sure Basque cinema is capitalizing on every single success are already pushing the next generation of original voices into the festival hot seat. At the 74th edition, a total of 31 titles with Basque production ties — including David Pérez Sañudo’s hotly anticipated competition title The Harvester — will screen across the festival’s many selections. Twelve are documentaries, marking a real moment for Basque docs at this installment. But with award statuettes firmly on the mantel, the Basque region now sets itself the task of sustaining this run of form long-term. The answer? Find and nurture the next generation’s emerging talent. For example, the debut feature from Nitya López Saitua in Zinemira, Family Drill , a project fuelled by word-of-mouth buzz across northern Spain . “He’s been doing great as a first AD and second AD for so many years,” begins Mar Izquierdo, coordinator of Zineuskadi, a non-profit operating at the epicentre of the Basque film and TV industry, “and everyone was like, ‘But he’s got it. He’s not going to be an AD.’ And we really do hope that with this film, everyone else will be able to see it.” Izquierdo’s company works strategically to promote the Basque audiovisual sector, partnering with every production output in the region, working alongside the Basque government’s culture department and public broadcaster ETB Basque to help facilitate co-productions, distribution and sales deals, as well as earning key projects coveted slots at the globe’s biggest film festivals and plotting awards campaigns. One young talent they’ve thrown their support behind is the 30-year-old López, who was in such a hurry to capture the creative process practically spilling out of his head that Family Drill — a co-production with Mubox Studio, who are distributing the film — was shot with just 10 people across three days in his childhood home on the Basque coast. He tells THR : “Iraia Elias and Miguel Garcés [play] my mom and dad and we recreate my parents’ relationship, [leading up to] the last argument that broke the relationship when I was four years old.” It is as deeply personal as it sounds. “This was a way to recreate memories that I didn’t have,” says López, firmly out of AD mode and in full-fledged director mode. “And I think it was very important to free-work on the scenes, without a script.” Family Drill San Sebastian Film Festival López’s determination to start the shoot before he lost that powerful sense of direction in chronicling his parents’ split speaks to the strength of the Basque Country’s storytelling. “We have really great directors here in the Basque Country, and internationally they are [getting] more recognized,” continues the first-time filmmaker. “I have the opportunity of working with many of them, and I love their work, and I’m very proud to be part of the next generation making movies. I think that we are in a great moment [compared to] making movies here 20 years ago.” It used to be the case that, “if [creatives] want to direct, they must go to other places, go to Madrid,” he explains. Here in the region López calls home, there have never been so many reasons to put roots down. One of his countrymen, Javier Giner, also arrives at the San Sebastián Film Festival with his first movie. This Solitude is premiering in the New Directors section. A debut feature it may technically be, but director-writer Giner has known global success with the International Emmy-winning I, Addict series, based on his own life and struggle with drug addiction. With This Solitude , Giner, who grew up in Bilbao, reacts to the unprecedented impact of that show. “ I, Addict was a huge hit in Spain and it dealt with a part of my life where I suffered [with] the illness of addiction,” he says. “After that explosive TV series where I presented myself to the world with no mask, I needed to go back to my childhood, to a very intimate place, a very silent place — much smaller than I, Addict .” Giner suddenly found himself shooting where he grew up, Bilbao, back to the places and locations that he says “have an emotional resonance” for him. The film, starring Oriol Pla, Marina Salas, Gemma Martínez, Kai Etxaniz and Itziar Lazkano, is a Balance Media Entertainment production, with The Embassy TV and Basajaun Filmak as co-producers, and Filmax handling distribution. “We meet two young people who live in Bilbao, Leo and Lorea, and we follow them through the grief process after they break a five-year-long relationship,” Giner explains. “And I use that journey as an excuse to talk about a lot of things like class, the housing [crisis]. […] Those moments in our lives everyone goes through, in a sense of reconstructing yourself because nothing works around you and you don’t quite grasp who you are [or] what you want.” He speaks with as much gusto as López, who also, in some way, depicts his Basque youth on screen — a common theme running through many of these films — and seeing fellow regional filmmakers make a name for themselves in recent years only speaks to the urgency of the stories coming out of the Basque Country, according to Giner. “To be honest, it fills me with pride,” he says. “I think movies and filmmakers, when they’re honest with their upbringing and their roots, there’s something very beautiful in it. As an audience member, I love when I discover London through Mike Leigh’s eyes, for example, or I discover parts of the world that I don’t know about through some filmmaker’s eyes.” Giner says that in the last 10 years, especially, Basque stories have been “very important to tell.” He continues: “I jokingly call This Solitude my very Basque movie, because there’s a reflection of identity in the movie… It tells [you] a lot about the place. And the Basque Country, it’s beautiful. It has beautiful landscapes. It has great possibilities. It is filled with really talented people, both in front of and behind the camera. So, I mean, it fills me with total pride if someone considers me the representation of the Basque Country at this year’s festival.” He is admittedly still pinching himself that he’s here: “It’s incredible. To be honest, a lot of my film education has to do with the San Sebastián Film Festival because when I was a teenager, I used to go from Bilbao to San Sebastián and watch movies.” López concurs that Basque cinema has its own culture, but also lauds the region’s directors for still being able to make “really universal movies.” And Izquierdo says the variation across the projects this year is particularly exciting for her. “The best thing is we are covering every possible subject,” she says. “We have a biopic for a musical group. We have culinary cinema. We have a French co-production, a coming-of-age [film] within a school. We have everything.” Basque filmmaker Javier Giner. San Sebastian Film Festival And naturally, the festival also serves as something of a springboard for those nail-biting awards runs. “It’s the most important film festival in Spain and one of the [category] A film festivals in the world,” says Giner about what a premiere in San Sebastián can do for one’s Goya hopes. “So it’s definitely a great trampoline. But it’s something that I don’t want to think about because I don’t want to get lost in that narrative and it take away from the pure pleasure of putting a film out there and sharing it with the public.” Of course, it’s not just Basque filmmakers travelling to shoot here. Taiwan’s Tsai Ming-liang is presenting Dust in San Sebastián, a short film and exhibition piece as part of his Walker series, which is a Basque co-production. Nanni Moretti made the most of those tempting tax incentives, too, with his last movie It Will Happen Tonight filming in the region before its recent Venice Film Festival premiere, and the Catherine Zeta-Jones starrer Kill Jackie — releasing Oct. 2 — shot extensively across Bilbao. “It’s not only that we continue to have emerging talent, but we are able to co-produce and have A-class films as minority co-producers,” beams Izquierdo. But she maintains that the most rewarding part of her job is platforming the next generation of Basque filmmakers, who are carving out a path by leading with instinct, leaning into personal storytelling, and celebrating each milestone. “The big names know how to [make] their way through the other festivals,” says Izquierdo. “But some of them need this in order to get the next one — it’s a window of opportunity for them, because otherwise maybe their documentary or small film would be just another small fish in the pond. Here,” she adds, “they get the chance on the big screen, where exhibitors and distributors will be able to notice them.” The 2026 San Sebastián International Film Festival runs Sep. 18-26. THR

articles.title: Red Sea Film Festival Cancels 2026 Edition, Vows to Return Next Year With “Renewed Vision”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 3:43am Johnny Depp at the 2025 Red Sea Film Festival closing ceremony Courtesy of Getty The sixth edition of the Red Sea International Film Festival has been postponed, the event’s Foundation has confirmed. A note released to press on Monday explains that this year’s installment, originally set for Dec. 3-12 in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, has been pushed back to the fourth quarter of 2027. It comes as the entire region deals with ongoing military tension amid the U.S.-Israeli-Iran war, with the threat of missile and drone strikes active and Saudi Arabia dealing with targeted attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis. Related Stories Movies "It Fills Me With Pride": How the Basque Country Is Nurturing Its Next Generation of Filmmakers Movies San Sebastian Winner Yesim Ustaoglu Returns to Competition With 'What Remains' (Exclusive Clip) The decision follows “a comprehensive review of a range of considerations relating to the timing of the next edition, including the logistical requirements involved in staging an international event of this scale,” said the statement. “It reflects the Foundation’s commitment to ensuring the Festival takes place at the right time and under the right conditions to deliver the experience for which the Red Sea International Film Festival has become known,” it continued. “As part of this continued commitment, the Foundation will introduce year-round programming at Culture Square in Historic Jeddah beginning in November 2026, establishing it as an ongoing destination for film screenings, cultural events and specialised film-industry programmes.” Organizers have vowed that the festival will return in 2027 with a “renewed vision and a programme that continues to celebrate cinema and filmmakers from Saudi Arabia, the region and around the world.” The Red Sea Film Festival has gone from strength to strength in recent years and funnelled much of its investment into attracting Hollywood A-listers to Jeddah, as well as its Red Sea Fund, Red Sea Labs and wider initiatives, which will continue to operate within the Foundation’s “year-round ecosystem.” Among the attendees last year were Michael Caine, Johnny Depp, Sean Baker, Juliette Binoche, Adrien Brody, Kirsten Dunst, Jessica Alba and Queen Latifah. THR

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico Sue White House for Revoking Press Credentials: “Patently Unconstitutional”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 5:03am The White House Briefing room, on September 19, 2026 in Washington, DC Photo by Graeme Sloan/Getty Images CNN , MS NOW and Politico are suing the Trump administration after the White House revoked their press credentials, effectively banning them from the White House complex and making it a challenge to cover the President and his staff. “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the three news outlets said in a statement early Monday morning. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” Related Stories Business Sylvester Stallone Learned About Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship While Watching TV: "It Won't Work" TV Alan Ritchson Reveals Which 'Reacher' Season Got Canceled After "Someone Got Re-Elected" In fact, CNN had been slated to be the primary TV press pool Monday, a day in which President Trump is slated to fly to New York for meetings with Mayor Zohran Mamdani and French President Emmanuel Macron on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. In a memo later Monday morning, the White House TV pool had been suspended given CNN’s banishment. CNN splits the primary pool duties with ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News. “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government,” a joint statement from TV pool companies said. “No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.” In their lawsuit (led by famed First Amendment litigator Ted Boutrous), the news outlets argue that Trump’s decision was in profound conflict with the law. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the suit states. “Presidents from the earliest days of the Republic have disagreed with and complained about the tenor and content of press coverage of their administrations. But as the Supreme Court has recognized, the First Amendment, including its guarantee of a free press, reflects “a profound national commitment to the principle that debate on public issues should be uninhibited, robust, and wide-open, and that it may well include vehement, caustic, and sometimes unpleasantly sharp attacks on government and public officials.” The suit states quoting a passage from the landmark case, New York Times Co . v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254, 270 (1964). “And the Constitution protects the liberty and property interests that news organizations and White House reporters have in their press credentials and the access those credentials afford them to cover the White House for the benefit of the public,” it continues. “No official can deprive Plaintiffs of those interests on a whim—with no notice, no process, and no warning—as the President did here.” Trump announced his ban in a post Friday , causing some confusion in the White House as crews from the outelts remained onsite. However, on Saturday morning journalists from all three outlets trying to enter the White House complex found that their credentials had been revoked . In an Oval Office appearance, Trump said that the decision followed cumulative coverage over the past few years, and wasn’t driven by any story in particular. “The President repeated his straightforward rationale for targeting these three news organizations, calling it ‘wrong’ to ‘allow people to write purposely negative stories,'” the lawsuit recounts. “The President complained about coverage he considers ‘one-sided’ and ‘never good,’ and at one point even referred to his own unprecedented act as the ‘ban on the free press.'” He also suggested that he knew his move would end up being litigated, suggesting that the outcome would depend on the judge that gets the cse. In his first term the White House banned CNN correspondent Jim Acosta from the White House, but a judge ordered his pass returned, citing First Amendment protections. The AP had also sued after it was barred from covering certain events after its style guide declined to refer to the body of water as the Gulf of America. THR

articles.title: Kit Harington Credits Harry Potter With Helping Him Through Sobriety Struggle
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 6:03am 'Game of Thrones' Courtesy of HBO Logo text Kit Harington is feeling warmer — a bit — towards the idea of reprising his iconic fan-favorite role of Jon Snow, and discussed his return to HBO in the upcoming Harry Potter TV series. The actor first told the Happy Sad Confused podcast Monday that he actually feels more comfortable with the idea of reprising the reluctant Game of Thrones warrior than he did in the past. The topic was raised when Harington was asked about HBO’s Snow spinoff sequel that was developed several years ago and then shelved. Related Stories TV 'A Tale of Two Cities' Review: Kit Harington Has Done Far, Far Better Things Than This Bland MGM+ Dickens Adaptation Lifestyle 'Game of Thrones: The Mad King' Play Sets London Transfer “We developed it two years or so,” Harington said. “I still think there’s a world in which something could work. I wouldn’t have gone into it in the first place if I didn’t. But I was very insistent at the start — as was HBO and George R.R. Martin — of like: ‘If we don’t find the right thing, let’s not do it. It’s much better if we don’t.’ After a little while of of thinking about it — it kind of was me — [I said], ‘This isn’t quite the right [story].'” Continued Harington: “[But] now I’ve gone and done all these other things and now I feel more comfortable with that character and that world again and where it sits in my life.” Yet it was another franchise headed to HBO that helped Harington with his sobriety struggles — Harry Potter . Harington told the podcast that the Potter audiobooks were helpful in the wake of ditching alcohol. “My brain is incredibly busy, especially at night, and I’ve always found going to bed very difficult like and my brain doesn’t turn off,” he said. “When I got sober that got especially bad. So I started listening to Harry Potter audio books, and now they’re the thing I listen to every night.” THR broke the news of the Snow development in 2022. In our cover story profile of Martin in January, we reported the initial idea was a tale of Snow living alone as a broken man with PTSD, having chased off his direwolf Ghost and thrown away his sword Longclaw. Harington wanted Jon to eventually die and to avoid being a hero. The story echoed, in some respects, Harington’s personal struggles — entering rehab following an intense shooting experience on Thrones. Last year, a new writer (Quoc Dang Tran from Drops of God ) came aboard to attempt to revive the sequel idea, possibility shifting the drama to the Mediterranean-like land of Essos. Harington was cast as Gilderoy Lockhart in the Full Cast Audio editions of the Potter books, which were released last year. Last month, Harington was cast to join HBO’s live-action Harry Potter series, where he’ll play the dangerously narcissistic Defense Against the Dark Arts professor in season two. “Lockhart is addicted to himself,” Harington quips. “It’s just a tiny step to my left [for me].” Harington is currently promoting his role in a four-part TV adaptation of Charles Dickens’ A Tale of Two Cities on MGM+, which was released Sept. 6. THR
