articles.title: Netflix’s ‘Cliff Booth’ Trailer Has Brad Pitt Taking a Playful Poke at Leonardo DiCaprio
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 7:06am 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' Logo text The first full trailer has dropped for Netflix ‘s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth . The new footage (below) has Brad Pitt ‘s former stuntman now working as a Hollywood fixer, while also bartending and working as a projectionist. The trailer also includes a playful joke at the expense of his Once Upon co-star Leonardo DiCaprio . Booth explains he no longer doubles for DiCaprio’s character Rick Dalton because “Rick got too fat.” Related Stories TV 'Sweet Magnolias' Canceled at Netflix After Five Seasons Business Netflix Stock Falls After Wells Fargo Downgrade: "Engagement Trends Look Worrying to Us" The film marks a unique collaboration — written by Quentin Tarantino with David Fincher taking over as director. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth gets a two-week exclusive run in Imax theaters globally starting Nov. 25 and then will debut on Netflix on Dec. 23. Here’s the detailed official description and trailer: “Murder, blackmail, theft, extortion — just another summer in Hollywood. It’s 1977, eight years since Cliff Booth (Pitt) encountered the Manson family in Quentin Tarantino’s parallel history of 1969, Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood. In The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , directed by David Fincher from a new script by Tarantino, the fairytale is over. Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s great and, sometimes, not so good.” Continued the description: “He’s curious when he gets a call from talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), on behalf of her client, TV megastar Charlie Peters (Scott Caan) — a man known for doing his own stunts. And he’s further entertained and intrigued when he meets other characters in Charlie’s world, from his knowing wife Toni (Carla Gugino) to pro football champion turned screen star Roderick ‘Hot Rod’ Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II). Then there are the Verdusco brothers (Matt Groove and JB Tadena), mysterious gangsters causing mayhem across the city. What was once a fairytale is now a crime story — a cocktail of violence, ambition, and desire that could only happen in L.A.” THR

articles.title: Movie Theater Advertising Giant Closes $275 Million Deal to Expand to Offices
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 7:12am National CineMedia's Noovie pre-show, hosted by Maria Menounos, features trivia, ads and promo interviews. National CineMedia National CineMedia , the in-theater advertising company that works with AMC Theatres, Cinemark and Regal for pre-show commercials content, has closed a major deal to venture outside of the cinema. The firm, led by Thomas Lesinski, has sealed an agreement to acquire Captivate Holdings, which powers tens of thousands of small screens in office buildings, lobbies and elevators that show short ads and content as people walk by (or when waiting for your floor in an elevator). The deal is valued at $275 million. National CineMedia already has a foothold in this business through all of its screens showing ads in movie theater lobbies (it had 17,000 screens in over 1,300 theaters, as of its annual report). Now it wants to bring that formula to office buildings and residential properties, too. And with Captivate’s platform, the company says it’ll have 48,000 digital screens to do so. Its primary vehicle to sell ads is its Noovie pre-show which is hosted by former Today correspondent Maria Menounos and features movie trivia, junket-style interviews with celebrities and Hollywood flashback moments mixed in with commercials. Since emerging from bankruptcy in 2023 — just as the COVID years were particularly brutal to theaters, they also wreaked havoc on in-theater advertising — National CineMedia has been positioning itself for a rebuild. The company spent $8.2 million last November to buy Spotlight Cinema Network, an ad network which caters to boutique, luxury and drive-in theaters like Cinépolis Luxury Cinema, Landmark Theatres and more. The restructured firm, once co-owned and launched by the major theater chains as a joint venture, also disclosed in its annual report that it now has no ownership interest from AMC and Cinemark as of the beginning of this year. Now it’s looking to become a national player in the advertising game, but is taking on debt to do so in the form of a $275 million senior secured first lien term loan facility. National CineMedia bought Captivate from growth equity firm Generation Partners, which had owned the advertising platform since 2013, when it purchased the company from newspaper giant Gannett. “The acquisition of Captivate is a key step in advancing NCM’s strategy to build a broader premium video and digital out-of-home advertising platform,” stated National CineMedia chief Lesinski on Monday, adding: “With the transaction now closed, our focus turns to bringing these capabilities together and executing on the opportunities we see across the combined business.” THR

articles.title: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Daisy Edgar-Jones and George MacKay Are Standouts in a Jane Austen Redo That’s Fine if Not Strictly Necessary
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 8:00am Esmé Creed-Miles (left) and Daisy Edgar-Jones in 'Sense and Sensibility.' Courtesy of Focus Features Pity any director who undertakes to remake a beloved literary property previously seen on screen in what is widely regarded as an unimprovable adaptation. That’s the daunting task faced by Georgia Oakley, who landed on the map with her assured 2022 debut feature, the politically personal queer character study Blue Jean . But the director’s take on Sense and Sensibility seldom steps out from the long shadow of Ang Lee’s enchanting 1995 retelling of the Jane Austen classic, scripted by Emma Thompson with endless amounts of verve, wit, emotional perspicacity and exquisite romantic yearning. Related Stories Movies Inde Navarrette: I Didn't "Want to Make Any Friends" During 'Obsession' Shoot to Focus on Film Movies Why 'Sense and Sensibility' Star George MacKay Still Hasn't Watched Ang Lee's Oscar-Winning Classic No disrespect to Oakley’s cast, all of whom are more than capable actors, but in almost every familiar beat of the story I found myself thinking back fondly to the actors who filled those roles for Lee — chief among them Thompson, Kate Winslet, Hugh Grant, Alan Rickman, Gemma Jones and the priceless Elizabeth Spriggs. I get it that this is intended as a fresh spin on Austen’s 1811 Regency romance, aimed at a new generation of movie lovers who have no great attachment to earlier versions. But for those of us who adore the 1995 film, unfavorable comparisons seem inevitable. Sense and Sensibility The Bottom Line Glum and glummer. Release date : Friday, Oct. 16 Cast : Daisy Edgar Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe, Bodhi Rae Breathnach, Frank Dillane, Herbert Nordrum, George MacKay, Fiona Shaw, Stacy Martin, Tom Brooke, Turlough Convery, Chloe Pirrie, Eliot Sumner, Bethany Slater, Ceara Coveney Director : Georgia Oakley Screenwriter : Diana Reid, based on the novel by Jane Austen Rated PG, 2 hours 11 minutes One subtle shift in first-time screenwriter Diana Reid’s adaptation is the firmer centering of the quarrelsome but inextricably bonded older Dashwood sisters, Elinor ( Daisy Edgar-Jones ) and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles). Of course this was always the case in Austen’s novel, right down to the way the title reflects the two sisters’ contrasting characters, with Elinor’s rationality and restraint representing “sense” and Marianne’s unguarded passion and unbridled emotionality signaling “sensibility.” Theirs is the paramount love story here, which works well in some ways but less so in others, somehow diminishing the stakes of their respective longing for Edward Ferrars ( George MacKay ) and Willoughby ( Frank Dillane ). Part of the brilliance of Thompson’s screenplay for the 1995 adaptation is that it foregrounded the sisters while also making the world they inhabited and its characters equally vivid. Here, there’s too little relief from the sisters’ downbeat moods to make us care about them. Oakley and Reid lean so heavily into Elinor and Marianne’s crushing disappointments and the forces holding them back in a period of vast gender inequity, that their sorrows shove the characters’ more captivating qualities to the side. Sense and Sensibility is a book with its fair share of melancholy — starting when Elinor, Marianne, their younger sister Margaret (Bodhi Rae Breathnach) and their mother ( Caitríona Balfe ) are forced after Mr. Dashwood’s death to vacate their Sussex home, Norland Park, due to stringent primogeniture laws. But I can’t recall another adaptation, either for film or television, that made the story so overwhelmingly morose and its protagonists such a joyless pair. Casting John (Tom Brooke), the eldest Dashwood offspring, who inherits the estate, as a spineless weasel yields little tension because it’s obvious from the minute we meet his avaricious wife Fanny (Stacy Martin) that she will talk him down on any annual stipend he proposes allocating to his stepmother and half-sisters, in compliance with his late father’s wishes. Austen’s mean-spirited vipers — Caroline Bingley and Lady Catherine de Bourgh in Pride and Prejudice and Mrs. Elton in Emma , as well as Fanny — are as memorable as her heroines. Martin plays Fanny with the right brittle calculation, but she’s a standard-issue rich bitch. I missed the outrageous malice of the character in Lee’s version, hilariously evil in Queen of Mean Harriet Walter’s delicious turn. Humor is often a casualty here, even in the book’s most dependable source, wealthy widow Mrs. Jennings, the mother-in-law of a distant cousin of the Dashwoods, who offers them a cottage on his estate in Devonshire. Sublime English character actress Spriggs made this raucous, gossipy matchmaker a spark plug who brought fresh fizz to Lee’s film every time she appeared, as did a marvelous Imelda Staunton as her complete twit of a daughter, Charlotte. Fiona Shaw ’s work here as Mrs. J is colorless by comparison, loud and abrasive and so unable to read the room that we never get much sense of the kindness and generosity beneath the character’s overbearing manner. She just seems to require an audience. Other characters blend into the wallpaper, among them Mrs. Dashwood, wasting the considerable talents of Balfe (so wrenching as the unhappy mother in Andrew Haigh’s upcoming A Long Winter ); and Lucy Steele (Ceara Coveney), whose confidences are a form of torture for Elinor though here she’s barely around long enough to make an impression. That leaves the men, who fare well enough. Playing Edward as the courtly and compassionate polar-opposite of his awful sister Fanny, MacKay brings a gentle diffidence that syncs beautifully with Edgar-Jones’ delicate reserve. Their climactic scenes near the end, once all the obstacles have been removed, are lovely — and not just because Austen’s prose in their outcome is so indestructible. Dillane, superb in Harris Dickinson’s Urchin , has presence but is somewhat shortchanged by the script’s one-dimensional grasp of Willoughby, the dashing romantic hero revealed to be an opportunistic cad who breaks Marianne’s heart. And as the self-abnegating Colonel Brandon, Norwegian actor Herbert Nordrum (one point of the triangle in The Worst Person in the World ) is touching as he takes several steps back when he sees that Marianne’s affections lie elsewhere, then steps forward with heroic devotion when her health is in grave danger. Nordrum didn’t quite rip out my heart the way Rickman did 31 years ago, but his watchful intensity gives him one of the most moving character arcs. The performance likely to have the most fervent admirers in Creed-Miles’ as Marianne, the reckless romantic who lets her heart lead her, with devastating results. Oakley and costume designer Grace Snell break from the traditional pristine elegance in period films set in this era, making Marianne a free-spirited child of nature whose dresses and hair look consistently bedraggled, starting when she is first seen lying in long grass in the opening scene. The director certainly gets a lot of raw feeling out of the actress, but should the character really seem almost feral? The emphasis on naturalism perhaps removes some of the emotional barriers for young contemporary audiences, but it also gives the movie a low-energy feel and a drab look, with flat light and a dreary color palette. Historical sticklers will roll their eyes at all the free-flowing tresses in place of tidy updos, though the element that made me groan the most was the ball scenes. Does every post- Bridgerton period piece now have to mix traditional dance with expressively stylized modern touches? That kind of flourish has become as much a cliché as the buttoned-up starchiness of old-school costume dramas, especially when it’s as inorganic as it is here. The women just appear to have gotten lost on their way to quadrille practice and stumbled into a Pina Bausch class. Still, I suppose we should at least be grateful that Oakley for the most part held back from the gimmicky Emerald Fennell approach . Full credits Release date: Friday, Oct. 16 Production companies: Working Title, in association with November Pictures Distribution: Focus Features Cast: Daisy Edgar Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe, Bodhi Rae Breathnach, Frank Dillane, Herbert Nordrum, George MacKay, Fiona Shaw, Stacy Martin, Tom Brooke, Turlough Convery, Chloe Pirrie, Eliot Sumner, Bethany Slater, Ceara Coveney Director: Georgia Oakley Screenwriter: Diana Reid, based on the novel by Jane Austen Producers: Tim Bevan, Eric Fellner, India Flint, Jo Wallett Executive producers: Thea Paulett, Angela Moneke Director of photography: Arnaud Potier Production designer: Francesca Di Mottola Costume designer: Grace Snell Music: Roger Goula Editor: Izabella Curry Casting: Kharmel Cochrane Rated PG, 2 hours 11 minutes THR

articles.title: There’s a Deal, Now It’s All About the Details. Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Fight
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Alex Weprin , Winston Cho September 21, 2026 8:03am Paramount CEO David Ellison and 12 states led by California AG Rob Bonta have agreed to terms. Getty Images Logo text They have a deal. After days of marathon negotiations, Paramount Skydance and the state attorneys general have settled the blockbuster antitrust lawsuit over the $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed. The agreement is expected to be announced later Monday (on Yom Kippur, no less). But it also clears Paramount to close the deal, which had a so-called $7 million-per-day ticking fee set to begin Oct. 1. The settlement allows the studio to avoid paying those costs assuming it can close in the next 10 days or so. The agreement comes after months of what has been a bitter and public back and forth, with threats by Paramount to leave the state of California (Texas and Tennessee both courted the company), accusations of antisemitism levied at some critics of the deal and a political undercurrent running just beneath the surface of the whole thing, given the Ellison family’s relationship to President Donald Trump, Rob Bonta’s own political ambitions and the hyper-politicized nature of dealmaking today. The state attorneys general, led by California’s Bonta had sued to block the deal, alleging that the merger would give the combined Paramount-Warners too much control over basic cable TV and the theatrical film business. The Writers Guild of America later joined the fray, with a lawsuit that argued the merger would suppress wages and worsen working conditions for writers by creating a single mega-buyer of film and television programming. Earlier this year, consumers had also filed a complaint challenging the purchase. Ellison, for his part, promised to release a minimum of 30 films per year theatrically, though many in the industry remain skeptical about how long the company can sustain that level of production. Bonta had maintained he’ll only accept structural remedies, which typically involve companies selling off parts of the combined business. It’s believed a sticking point for the states in any settlement involved Paramount operating the two studios as independent businesses and selling off parts of its cable business. For Ellison, parting ways with CNN was a no-go. Still, the specifics of a deal are still TBA, including any potential divestitures. The legal and public message jockeying in the court battle was contentious. Leading up to the deal, Paramount had said it would leave California if an agreement wasn’t struck by Oct. 1, when the so-called ticking fee starts accruing, regardless of the outcome of the lawsuits — a move Bonta had called “blackmail.” This came after the studio came to terms with Bonta and the WGA in a joint agreement to hold off on consummating the merger until a trial had determined whether it violated antitrust laws, though it was scheduled for next year. Across the litigation, Paramount had been rankled that the government and dozens of foreign regulators cleared the purchase. In June, the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division found that the acquisition would actually increase competition across media and entertainment. The decision cleared the way for Paramount to become among the largest theatrical distributors in the country and own a top five streamer by subscriber count, until the deal was challenged by the states. Notably, the green light didn’t require any divestitures, behavioral remedies or concessions. Paramount has framed the merger as one that will boost competition, arguing it’s necessary to compete against tech giants like Netflix, Amazon and Apple. Hollywood will soon see whether that’s true. THR

articles.title: James Sloyan, Actor in ‘The Sting,‘ ‘Xanadu’ and ‘Oh Madeline,’ Dies at 85
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 8:37am James Sloyan Carsey-Werner / Courtesy Everett Collection James Sloyan, the busy character actor who appeared in films including The Sting and Xanadu and played Madeline Kahn’s husband on her short-lived 1980s ABC sitcom, has died. He was 85. Sloyan died July 22 at his home in Sherman Oaks, his family announced over the weekend. Star Trek fans know him for his five appearances as a member of four species across The Next Generation , Deep Space Nine and Voyager in the 1990s, and he served as the voice of Toyota’s luxury brand Lexus in commercials for 18 years starting in 1989. Related Stories Music Chad Gilbert, New Found Glory Guitarist, Dies at 45 Movies Gerrit Graham, Actor in 'Phantom of the Paradise,' 'Pretty Baby' and 'Used Cars,' Dies at 77 In George Roy Hill’s The Sting (1973), winner of the Oscar for best picture, Sloyan helped set the plot in motion with his turn as Mottola, the numbers runner who works for racketeer Doyle Lonnegan (Robert Shaw) and falls victim to a “pigeon drop scam” perpetrated by Johnny Hooker ( Robert Redford ) and Luther Coleman ( James Earl Jones ). And in the Olivia Newton-John musical fantasy Xanadu (1980), he played Simpson, the tyrannical boss of Michael Beck’s artist Sonny Malone at AirFlow Records. Sloyan landed the role of Kahn’s husband, a guy who writes steamy romance novels under the pen name Crystal Love, but the 1983-84 show — the first produced by Carsey-Werner Productions — lasted just 18 episodes. The youngest of four kids, James Joseph Sloyan was born in Indianapolis on Feb. 24, 1941. His father, James Sr., was a construction engineer. When he was 4, he “discovered the delights of the Indianapolis State Fair, wrangling an appearance with [Western movie actor] Lash LaRue and his traveling Western Show,” his family said. After spending time living overseas and in Albany, New York, Sloyan graduated from the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York and served three years in the U.S. Army before returning to New York, where he acted and was a choreographer for fight scenes for Joseph Papp’s New York Shakespeare Festival. He made it to Broadway in Arthur Kopit’s Indians in 1969, had the lead in such off-Broadway productions as Irv Bauer’s A Dream Out of Time and made his onscreen debut in the 1970 film The Traveling Executioner , starring Stacy Keach. Sloyan, who moved to California in 1973, appeared in The Gang That Couldn’t Shoot Straight (1971) and on episodes of The Doctors , The Streets of San Francisco , Kojak and Delvecchio before landing a regular role on the 1977 ABC drama Westside Medical . He played a Romulan admiral and then the son of the Klingon Worf (Michael Dorn) on Next Generation , the Bajoran scientist Dr. Mora on Deep Space Nine and the Haakonian scientist Ma’bor Jetrel on Voyager . His TV résumé also included the telefilms The Disappearance of Aimee , starring Faye Dunaway and Bette Davis, and The Billionaires Boys Club and stops on Wonder Woman , Buck Rogers in the 25th Century , Lou Grant , Falcon Crest , Knots Landing , Cagney & Lacey , Moonlighting , Murder, She Wrote , Quantum Leap , The X-Files and NYPD Blue . “Friends and colleagues remember him always present, always curious, courageous, inventive and loyal as well as brash, mouthy and very urban. He was one-of-a-kind,” his family said. Survivors include his wife, actress Deirdre Lenihan ( Needles and Pins , The Waltons ), whom he married in 1973, and their children, Daniel, a musician, and Samantha Sloyan, an actress ( The Life of Chuck , Dr. Penelope Blake on Grey’s Anatomy ). His brother, author and Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Patrick Sloyan, died in February 2019. THR

articles.title: Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 6:15am PT Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review By Aramide Tinubu Plus Icon Aramide Tinubu Latest Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review 2 hours ago ‘MobLand’ Season 2 Proves the Show Just Wouldn’t Work Without Tom Hardy 3 days ago Netflix’s ‘Monster’ Finally Delivers an Outrageously Engaging Season With ‘The Lizzie Borden Story’: TV Review 4 days ago See All NBC For decades, law-enforcement procedurals have been staples on television, and when they are done well, these series build loyal fanbases that stick with them for years. NBC ’s newest drama, “ Line of Fire ” is from “Quantico” creator Joshua Safran and loosely based on executive producer Jenna Bush Hager’s experiences with the United States Secret Service. The show has all the makings of becoming a classic in the canon of beloved police procedurals. “Line of Fire” follows the Hollingsworth family: Secret Service Agent Mike Hollingsworth ( Peter Krause ); his estranged wife, U.S. Marshal Jane Hollingsworth ( Hope Davis ); and their three adult children, FBI Agent Clare Hollingsworth (Kat Cunning), Secret Service Agent Mike “Micah” Hollingsworth Jr. (Tommy O’Brien) and DOJ analyst Russ Hollingsworth (Taylor Bloom). Mike, Jane and their children try to keep things professional, but continually cross personal boundaries because of their agencies’ proximity. Boasting intense family dynamics and several truly intriguing cases, “Line of Fire” has a depth, intensity and a hint of soapiness that works perfectly within the genre. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony The 10-episode first season (two episodes were available for review) opens in Crozet, Virginia. A U.S. Marshal, under the guise of being a delivery driver, attempts to track down a missing fugitive. Unfortunately, before the morning breaks, both the Marshal and the outlaw lay dead in the woods. The next day, Jane arrives at the crime scene, determined to figure out what happened. Needing a bit more reach than the Marshals can offer, Jane calls in her daughter, Clare, for her expertise and for the FBI’s resources. Though Clare is eager to help, Jane’s team is not exactly pleased that the FBI is encroaching on her territory. For her part, Clare isn’t thrilled when her mother badgers her about bringing her mysterious new boyfriend to dinner to finally meet the family. Popular on Variety Back in Washington, D.C., Mike is set to finish out his final week at the Secret Service Headquarters before retiring. Yet, he’s increasingly concerned Micah is skirting his professional duties for a personal relationship with Sydney (Savannah Lee Smith), the president’s college-age daughter. Elsewhere, Russell is ready to get his feet wet at the DOJ, but his family’s constant requests complicate his role. Chaos and dysfunction are par for the course for the Hollingsworths. But when a seemingly standard case unearths long-buried secrets that threaten the family’s safety, each person must decide whether their jobs are worth more than the people they love. From bank robberies to cartel killings and even contending with the First Family’s drama in the White House, all of the cases the Hollingsworths handle are interesting. Still, the Hollingsworth family dynamic anchors “Line of Fire.” Though they’ve been long separated, Jane and Mike have a solid friendship; one that can only be formed after knowing and loving someone intimately for half your life. Not only do the former couple share children, but Mike and Jane also share secrets — shocking ones they keep close to their chests. The siblings, each with unique relationships with their parents and each other, are also well mapped out. Though only two episodes were available to screen, the family feels well lived-in: a boisterous clan with varied personalities becomes the ecosystem that shapes the series. In the pilot, Mike and the siblings arrive at Jane’s house for a chaotic and hilarious family dinner to meet the beau Clare has avoided introducing them to. Immediately, the audience gets a full sense of who these people are and how this family functions. Yet, that doesn’t make any of the cases sprinkled within the show any less worthwhile. In fact, it makes the conspiracy sitting at the center of “Line of Fire” even more gripping. “Line of Fire” has all of the essential elements that make procedural dramas so fun. With a stellar cast and some detailed mysteries which will likely stretch across the season (and into the next, assuming there is one), changing the Hollingsworth family dynamic as we know it, it’s clear NBC has a gem on its hands. “Line of Fire” debuts Sept. 21 on NBC, with the remaining episodes airing weekly on Mondays. articles.title: Kit Harington Says Joining ‘Harry Potter’ Series Was a ‘Very Simple “Yes, Please!”’: ‘I’m a Bit of a Nerd for It’
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 7:10am PT Kit Harington Says Joining ‘Harry Potter’ Series Was a ‘Very Simple “Yes, Please!”’: ‘I’m a Bit of a Nerd for It’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Kit Harington Says Joining ‘Harry Potter’ Series Was a ‘Very Simple “Yes, Please!”’: ‘I’m a Bit of a Nerd for It’ 1 hour ago ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: Brad Pitt Reprises His Oscar-Winning Role in David Fincher’s Tarantino Sequel 3 hours ago ‘SNL U.K.’ Brings Back Princess Diana as King Charles’ AI Assistant: ‘It’s That Woman From the ’90s!’ 1 day ago See All 2026 Getty Images / ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection Kit Harington didn’t think twice when he got the call to join HBO’s “Harry Potter” series as Gilderoy Lockhart , admitting that he’s “a bit of a nerd” for the wizarding world. Speaking on Josh Horowitz’s “Happy Sad Confused” podcast, the “Game of Thrones” star revealed the personal connection he has to the “ Harry Potter ” books — and why saying “yes” to the show was a no-brainer. “I listen to the Stephen Fry audiobooks. And I do that because my brain is incredibly busy, especially at night, and I’ve always found going to bed very difficult. My brain doesn’t turn off,” Harington said. “When I got sober, that got especially bad. And so I started listening to ‘Harry Potter’ audiobooks, and now they’re the thing I listen to every night. So they have a very special place in my heart.” Popular on Variety Related Stories Chile Film Industry Surges 20.5% Compared to Previous Season, New Catalog Reveals (EXCLUSIVE) Where Is Spain Heading? María González Veracruz, Secretary of State for Digitization, Unpacks Roadmap In fact, Harington was recently part of Audible’s “Harry Potter” audiobooks as the voice of Lockhart — a famous yet arrogant wizard who becomes the new Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher at Hogwarts — before the TV series came his way. “When I knew they were doing this show, I was like, ‘I think that’s a brilliant idea, I think they can really delve into it further than the films did.’ I’m fully supportive of it,” Harington said. “And then I got called to be in it, and that was just a very simple, ‘Yes, please!'” Harington took over the role of Lockhart, who will first be seen in Season 2, from Nicholas Hoult after he exited the series due to scheduling conflicts. Harington joked that it “wasn’t hard” for him to step into the shoes of the self-centered professor. “He’s addicted to himself. He’s just a tiny step to my left,” Harington said with a laugh. With filming on Season 2 already underway, Horowitz asked Harington if he had started discussing his character’s look yet. “Yes, and I’m going to say highly little about anything because it’s very secretive,” Harington said. “But yes, I’m engaging with that as we speak.” Harington went on to say that stepping onto set for the first time will be special for him as “I’m a bit of a nerd for it and I love it like I do.” And when Horowitz enquired what Hogwarts house Harington identifies with, he replied: “I’m Gryffindor, obviously!” The British actor said he is especially excited because filming the “Harry Potter” series at the Warner Bros. Studios in Leavesden allows him to stay present for his two young children. “[‘Harry Potter’] films down the road from me. So I get to be a dad; I get to go play in a world I love,” he said. “Genuinely, right now I’m very content.” Watch Harington’s full interview on “Happy Sad Confused” below. ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day,’ ‘The Odyssey’ Extend Battle Atop U.K. and Ireland Box Office as ‘Insidious’ Makes Strong Debut ‘Practical Magic 2’ Casts a Spell Over U.K., Ireland Box Office as Oasis Doc Rocks No. 2 China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Crosses $300 Million ‘The Odyssey’ Translator Emily Wilson Slams Christoper Nolan’s ‘Abysmal’ Screenplay: ‘I Would Be Ashamed to Have Written Any Part of This Script’ Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Overwhelms ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ as Admissions Top 10 Million Elliot Page Is ‘Not Really’ Getting Casting Calls After ‘The Odyssey’: ‘If Someone Wants to Call Me…I’d Love to Do Good Work’ Loading comments... articles.title: Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 7:26am PT Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban 1 hour ago Paramount Settlement Talks With States Progress but Some AGs Push for Tougher Terms 14 hours ago White House Blocks CNN and MS NOW Journalists From Entry and Confiscates Their Badges After Donald Trump Bans Networks 2 days ago See All Getty Images In an unprecedented move, four of the five TV networks that provide White House pool coverage of President Donald Trump — ABC News , CBS News , NBC News and Fox News — have joined in solidarity with CNN , which is the fifth TV pooler, announcing they are suspending coverage of the president because of his ban of CNN. “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government,” the five networks said in a joint statement Monday. “No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.” Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast The blackout of White House pool coverage by the networks comes after the Trump administration suspended CNN as the designated TV pool provider on Monday, Sept. 21 — leaving no TV pooler for the day. It also follows CNN, MS NOW and Politico announcing that they are suing Trump and three White House officials over his unilateral ban of the news outlets, alleging it violates the First Amendment. Popular on Variety The suspension of the TV news pool means that, for the time being, no major television network will provide coverage of Trump’s events, including his scheduled appearances Monday at the White House and his visit to the United Nations in New York City. Bryan Boughton, Fox News’ Washington bureau chief and the current White House TV pool chair, wrote in an email to the other networks Monday, ”This is to advise that, effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President. This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties. There will be no replacement pool put in place.” The White House designates secondary TV news pool providers (as well as those for print, radio and new media outlets). However, the secondary TV networks do not have any obligation to provide content to third parties. Trump said on social media Friday, Sept. 18, that he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico “effective immediately” from the White House , citing his familiar allegation that they propagate “fake news.” The White House barred entry to staffers from the three outlets on Saturday and revoked their press passes. At an Oval Office briefing Friday, Trump indicated that there was no single story that triggered him to ban the news outlets, but was rather a cumulative effect of their “purposely negative” coverage. He also suggested that the New York Times and the Washington Post would be next in line to be barred from the White House. ‘Superhero Fatigue Is Real. articles.title: Paramount Settles Antitrust Case With State AGs, Removing Obstacle to Warner Bros. Deal
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 7:56am PT Paramount Settles Antitrust Case With State AGs, Removing Obstacle to Warner Bros. Deal By Gene Maddaus Plus Icon Gene Maddaus Senior Media Writer @GeneMaddaus Latest Paramount Settlement Talks With State AGs Reach Critical Stage as Merger Opponents Rally and Urge Rob Bonta ‘Do Not Cave’ 1 day ago Gavin Newsom Signs Bill Creating $10 Million Post-Production Tax Credit 2 days ago Paramount and California AG Bonta Reportedly in ‘Advanced Talks’ to Settle Antitrust Suit 3 days ago See All Getty Images Paramount has reached a deal with 12 state attorneys general that removes a major obstacle to closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The deal comes just before the company was to begin accruing a $7 million daily “ticking fee” on Oct. 1, which was seen as an important milestone in the case. Bloomberg was first to report the news, followed by the Wall Street Journal. A source also confirmed to Variety that a deal is done. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony The merger was on hold pending the outcome of the states’ antitrust lawsuit, which was set for a trial on March 2, 2027. The $111 billion merger is the largest in Hollywood history. Popular on Variety Details of the agreement have yet to be made public. An official announcement is expected to come later Monday. The two sides spent the weekend in tense discussions over Paramount’s commitments to remain in California and over guarantees for its production levels. The discussions also focused on editorial oversight of CBS News and CNN, a key concern for East Coast attorneys general. Sources said the settlement does not require Paramount to make any major divestitures. California Attorney General Rob Bonta led the 12-state coalition, which sued to block the deal in July despite prior approval from the U.S. Department of Justice. Since then, Bonta has insisted on “robust structural remedies” — which has been taken to mean significant divestitures. Opponents of the deal were quick to blast Bonta for “caving” to Paramount’s pressure campaign. “Today, billionaires have yet again bribed, censored and bullied their way to the top,” said Alvaro Bedoya, a senior advisor at the American Economic Liberties Project, who also expressed disappointment with California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Xavier Becerra, who is running for the governor’s seat. “People want champions who are not afraid of rich bullies. Newsom, Becerra and Bonta did not meet that mark. The people who work in the film and TV industry and the small businesses who support it will suffer as a result. And so will everyone who values dissent in our democracy.” The Writers Guild of America filed a separate suit to block the merger in July, and that case was set to be heard along with the states’ case in March. The WGA is expected to sign on to the settlement agreement. Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin, who is overseeing the states’ antitrust case, granted a 28-day restraining order in July, finding that the states had put forward a strong case that the deal would harm competition in the basic cable and theatrical markets. Paramount then agreed to pause the transaction until a trial on the merits, rather than fight a motion for a preliminary injunction. The states argued that the merger would lead to higher prices and fewer options for theaters and cable and satellite providers, who would in turn pass on higher costs to consumers. Paramount has argued all along that the deal is pro-competitive and will result in more content production as the company seeks to take on streaming giants like Netflix and Amazon. In recent weeks, Paramount has sought to ratchet up the pressure on Bonta to abandon the case, including by threatening to leave California and move to Texas or Tennessee. Paramount has also enlisted state Democratic lawmakers to urge Bonta to settle, while IATSE and the Directors Guild of America have also pushed for a deal. Cinema United, the trade group representing theaters, had initially strongly opposed the merger. But as its three largest members — AMC, Cinemark and Regal — came out in favor of a settlement one-by-one, the group also reversed itself and called for a deal. That left Bonta and the other attorneys general in the position of trying to prove economic harm to exhibitors without the support of many of them. articles.title: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Georgia Oakley Puts a Moody, Naturalistic Spin on the Jane Austen Classic
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 8:00am PT ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Georgia Oakley Puts a Moody, Naturalistic Spin on the Jane Austen Classic The British director’s follow-up to her BAFTA-winning “Blue Jean” brings Daisy Edgar-Jones, George MacKay, Esmé Creed-Miles, and a scene-stealing Frank Dillane together in a romantically earthy 18th-century England. By Beatrice Loayza Plus Icon Beatrice Loayza Latest ‘Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ Review: Alex Gibney Profiles the Controversial Author During His Harrowing Hospitalization 3 days ago ‘Hombre al Agua’ Review: Gael García Bernal Directs and Stars in a Sputtering, Screwball-y Dramedy About One Man’s Identity Crisis 1 week ago ‘A Good Little Soldier’ Review: Alba Rohrwacher Goes Corporate Drone in Stéphane Brizé’s Lukewarm Workplace Drama 2 weeks ago See All Screenshot courtesy YouTube/Focus Features It’s been over 30 years since Ang Lee’s “ Sense and Sensibility ” became (for this critic, as for many) the Platonic ideal of the Jane Austen adaptation. Lush but controlled, dryly funny (thanks to Emma Thompson’s Oscar-winning script) in that chatty, cheeky, keenly perceptive Austen way, Lee’s classic also boasted a formidable cast to unleash a floodgate of big, ugly-cry-inducing emotions by its finale. All of which is to say that Georgia Oakley had a tough act to follow in taking on the beloved tale of two sisters navigating matters of the heart in two vastly different ways. Though slightly muted (in both feeling and color palette) by comparison, Oakley’s moody, naturalistic spin on the Austen touchstone is a solid undertaking. It’s also a confident, bigger-budget follow-up to her BAFTA-winning debut “Blue Jean,” a poignant Thatcher-era queer drama; that film’s restrained yet tactile intimacy translates well to a late 18th-century England of stifled desire and pastoral exuberance. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony There’s an earthy romanticism to Oakley’s vision of the times, with shots of quivering cattails, dew-spotted spiders, and floating lilypads complementing the roiling inner lives of sisters Elinor ( Daisy Edgar-Jones ) and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles) Dashwood. The younger Marianne is the more daring and vivacious of the two — a lightly shaky camera is on her heels as she adventures through the forest and receives news of their father’s death — and thankfully Oakley avoids the corny Mother Earth symbolism (à la “Hamnet”) that woodsy women amid sun-dappled pastures can so easily invite. The film’s natural splendor is pleasing, of course, but Oakley makes a point to show the grit and exhaustion of scaling hills and taking multi-day journeys by horse carriage — tough physical realities matched by the cruel social conventions that upend the Dashwoods’ lives. Popular on Variety Hewing close to the novel’s major plot beats, Diana Reid’s script efficiently lays out the stakes, as mother Dashwood (Caitríona Balfe) finds herself penniless and powerless against the takeover of her family’s estate by John Dashwood (Tom Brooke), her dead husband’s only male heir from his first marriage. Before she and the girls relocate to a modest seaside cottage in Devon, they suffer insults from John’s comically stingy wife Fanny (a wonderfully catty Stacy Martin) while Elinor meet-cutes with Fanny’s brother Edward ( George MacKay ), their mutual affection growing over wholesome nature walks and portrait sessions. (In a sweet reversal of the typical gendered gaze, it’s Elinor who draws Edward.) Sadly, Edward is too spineless and, er, sensible to follow his heart and lets a confused Elinor slip away when her family finally retreats to their new isolated home, courtesy of the kindly but coarse Mrs. Jennings (Fiona Shaw). For her part, the blunt and free-spirited Marianne finds her match in the dashing Willoughby ( Frank Dillane , the face of Harris Dickinson’s “Urchin”), brushing off the endearingly awkward advances of Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum, from “The Worst Person in the World,” speaking in a placid baritone). In Devon, Marianne and Willoughby enjoy a rustic romance of piano dueting and cliffside snuggling, and though he makes quite the statement in giving her a white steed, he never commits before heading back to London and remaining there for the foreseeable future. London is where Edward is, too, so when Mrs. Jennings plans a trip to the capital, Marianne and Elinor eagerly tag along. The girls’ weathered white gowns and tousled, stallionesque manes confer a cottage-core modernity that’s set in contrast to the gilded interiors and tightly-wound updos of their London acquaintances. Between the two sisters, Elinor’s prudence and Marianne’s joie de vivre are charted out via Holly Blakey’s enchanting choreography: In the country, Marianne and Willoughby partake in a riotous, rollicking folk dance, while Elinor and Edward cross paths at a buzzy London ball where they dance a comparably restrained, yet slinky, sensual waltz. Oakley’s beautifully textured worldbuilding — of soft, candlelit interiors; hunted game hanging on wall hooks; and so very many neat dogs (pugs, sheepdogs, mastiffs, whippets!) — is paired with a quivering psychological realism. Low-angle close-ups betray the fragility of Elinor’s self-composure when Edward tells her that he is engaged to another woman; and Marianne is a jittery bundle of broken idealism when she finds Willoughby arm-in-arm with a wealthy fiancé. These lovers’ quarrels unfold with a touching sincerity to Roger Goula’s wistful score, though Oakley’s more grounded drama also feels oddly safe, with a seriousness of tone that strips away some of the wit and comedy that makes Austen’s work, well, Austenesque. And though players like Edgar-Jones and MacKay make for perfectly tender lovebirds, they don’t exactly breathe new life into their characters. This might be the difference between being a gifted actor and a real star, which Lee’s “Sense and Sensibility” had across the board. Creed-Miles’ sharp-tongued, twinkle-eyed Marianne comes close to that inexplicable magnetism, though the script, which makes her sound like a broken record with the number of times she goes on about passion and passionate men, renders her a tad clichéd. In terms of casting, what Oakley’s “Sense and Sensibility” does confirm is that Dillane’s recent breakthrough was no fluke. His Willoughby is a slouching, smug-faced scoundrel — a rake all his own, and perhaps the only major presence in the film that brings an unstudied lightness and humor to this world of breath-held decorum. ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Georgia Oakley Puts a Moody, Naturalistic Spin on the Jane Austen Classic Reviewed at Universal Screening Room, New York City, Sept. 18, 2026. MPA Rating: PG. Running time: 132 MIN. Production: (U.K.) A Focus Features presentation of a Working Title production. Producers: Tim Bevan, Eriv Fellner, India Flint, Jo Wallett. Executive producer: Thea Paulett, Angela Moneke. Co-producer: Jane Frazer. Crew: Director: Georgia Oakley. Screenplay: Diana Reid. Camera: Arnaud Potier. Editor: Izabella Curry. Music: Roger Goula. With: Daisy Edgar-Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, George MacKay, Herbert Nordrum, Frank Dillane, Fiona Shaw, Stacey Martin, Tom Brooke, Caitríona Balfe. articles.title: Reza Rahadian, Dian Sastrowardoyo Starrer ‘Descendants of the Sun’ Heads to Busan Market as Barunson E&A Launches Sales
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 8:00am PT Reza Rahadian, Dian Sastrowardoyo Starrer ‘Descendants of the Sun’ Heads to Busan Market as Barunson E&A Launches Sales By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Reza Rahadian, Dian Sastrowardoyo Starrer ‘Descendants of the Sun’ Heads to Busan Market as Barunson E&A Launches Sales 31 minutes ago ‘A Teacher’s Gift’ Lands U.K. Distribution Deal With Peccadillo Pictures (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Bestselling Japanese Novelist Maha Harada Says ‘If This Is a Dream, I Hope I Never Wake Up’ About Her San Sebastian – and Busan – Bound Directing Debut ‘In My Father’s Room’ 6 hours ago See All Barunson E&A Barunson E&A will launch international sales for “ Descendants of the Sun ,” a big-screen version of the landmark Korean series that first aired in 2016, at the Asian Contents & Film Market in Busan, running Oct. 10-13. The Seoul-based company, known for producing Bong Joon Ho’s Academy Award winner “Parasite,” is making the film alongside Dapur Film, Tobali Putra Productions, NEWKO and Barunson C&C, its own subsidiary production arm. NEW (Next Entertainment World), owner of the original intellectual property, has come on board as a co-production company. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony Production has wrapped on both parts of the film, which were shot back-to-back. Part One is aiming for an Indonesian theatrical bow by mid-2027. Popular on Variety The adaptation arrives at the original series’ 10th anniversary, a show many credit with helping bring K-drama to global audiences. The original drew a 38.8% rating in its home market, marked the first instance of a Korean drama airing simultaneously in China, where iQIYI logged upward of two billion streams, and eventually found distribution in more than 30 territories, among them the U.S., the U.K., France, Germany, Japan and Russia. The series was similarly popular in Indonesia a decade ago, fueling anticipation for the new version before any footage had surfaced. The Indonesian film relocates the central romance to a setting and cultural backdrop specific to Indonesia while retaining what the studio describes as the emotional core of the original. Hanung Bramantyo, one of Indonesia’s leading box office directors, helms the project. He previously directed “Miracle in Cell No. 7,” an Indonesian version of the identically titled Korean film that ranks as the country’s eighth-highest-grossing domestic release. Reza Rahadian and Dian Sastrowardoyo lead the cast. Rahadian’s credits include “Vengeance Is Mine, All Others Pay Cash,” which won the Golden Leopard at Locarno, and Sastrowardoyo has appeared in Netflix’s “Cigarette Girl” as well as “The Fox King,” a Toronto Film Festival premiere. “Ten years on, ‘Descendants of the Sun’ is still one of the titles people point to when they talk about the start of the K-drama wave,” said Barunson E&A CEO Yoonhee Choi. “We see the strength of the Korean IP as a starting point, not an endpoint. This adaptation places that globally recognized story under a different sun, in an Indonesian landscape with a local sensibility all its own. It retains the familiarity of a story audiences already know and love, while opening it to a new context and, we believe, audiences beyond Indonesia.” “As the producer behind the original series, I deeply admire how the director has honored its spirit while creating a truly Indonesian story that I believe will translate just as powerfully wherever it’s seen,” added Woosik Seo, CEO of Barunson C&C and an executive producer on the film. “Descendants of the Sun” heads an ACFM slate for Barunson E&A that also includes “Satan’s Slaves: Origin,” a prequel to Joko Anwar’s horror franchise, whose first two entries are among Indonesia’s highest-earning local films; “Stoneborn,” an occult mystery from the “Exhuma” creative team starring Jongseo Jeon of Cannes title “Burning” and Sul Kyung-gu of Venice title “Possible Love”; and “Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng,” a comedy debuting at the Busan International Film Festival ahead of an Oct. 28 theatrical release. ‘The Odyssey’ and ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Power $239 Million U.K., Ireland July Box Office Korea Box Office: Local Comedy Remake ‘The Intern’ Leads Weekend Admissions as ‘The Odyssey’ Retains Revenue Crown Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Eclipses ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Continues Dominance ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day,’ ‘The Odyssey’ Continue Tussle Atop U.K., Ireland Box Office John Carpenter, Colman Domingo and Charlize Theron to Be Honored at Academy Museum Gala Loading comments... articles.title: Carly Rae Jepsen on How Marriage, Motherhood and the Joy of Pop Music Fueled Her Ambitious Double Album ‘Day and Night’: ‘I Knew What Colors I Was Playing With’
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 8:00am PT Carly Rae Jepsen on How Marriage, Motherhood and the Joy of Pop Music Fueled Her Ambitious Double Album ‘Day and Night’: ‘I Knew What Colors I Was Playing With’ By Steven J. Horowitz Plus Icon Steven J. Horowitz Senior Music Writer speriod Latest Jhené Aiko Scores First No. 1 on Albums Chart With ‘Westside Whimsy’ 20 hours ago Chad Gilbert, New Found Glory Guitarist and Backing Vocalist, Dies at 45 20 hours ago Jay-Z Revisits the Ghosts of Lyrics Past in the Illuminating (and Possibly Too Thorough) ‘Jay-Z in 8’: TV Review 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Mikayla LoBasso It sounds like an obvious approach, but Carly Rae Jepsen began working on her new double album “Day and Night” with a simple ethos: make the type of music she would want to listen to. “Like, what do I have to offer to the musical landscape right now?” the 40-year-old tells Variety over Zoom, just weeks before her sixth album released this past Friday. “And that began with how I always begin every project, which is, what am I attracted to? What music am I listening to that I love?” Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony As evidenced by the album’s two-dozen tracks, split evenly between Laurel Canyon coffee pop and synth-glittered bops, “Day and Night” is an amalgamation of self-professed influences — a “mixed bag of chips,” she says — inspired by artists and styles spanning Blossom Dearie and Minnie Ripperton to ABBA and house music. The “Day” section of the album is decidedly folksy, packed with organic instrumentation across tracks like acoustic ballad “Wild Child” and shimmying “After All,” while “Night” slips into something a bit more mischievous on the smoky “Amalfi Coast” and effervescent “Don’t Leave Me on the Dance Floor.” Popular on Variety For anyone who’s followed her since her explosion into mainstream pop with 2012’s “Call Me Maybe,” it’s clear that Jepsen is a creature of creation, consistently amassing songs until they start to take shape as a project. (She famously recorded 250 songs for her seminal sophomore album “Emotion,” which she recently celebrated with a 10th anniversary show at Los Angeles’ Troubadour.) With “Day and Night,” Jepsen had been working on material and was a quarter of the way through the process when she presented her work to her guitarist, Tavish Crowe, who realized that she was making music in two distinct lanes. “He said, ‘What if it’s like a house party, and as a thought experiment, we make this the upstairs and the downstairs?'” she recalls. “So we started doing that for fun. And then ‘Day and Night’ was born when I was just driving in my car here in LA. I loved its simplicity. It perfectly described this organic kind of dreamy thing, and then the nighttime, you immediately feel things get heightened and a little darker and more experimental. So then I would show up with sessions with a bit more intention and it became really fun because I knew what colors I was playing with.” “Day and Night” is also a diary, of sorts, as Jepsen began to fall in love with her now-husband Cole Marsden Greif-Neill, known to the music world as Cole M.G.N., whose credits include Beck, Wallows and Christine and the Queens. They had previously worked together on “So Right,” included on her 2023 album “The Loveliest Time,” and on “Day and Night,” he contributes to a handful of tracks — some of which are directly inspired by their burgeoning romance. Throughout the record, Jepsen sings of surrendering to this newfound love, of basking in the resplendence and joy that it brings. Mainly, she says, there’s an element of “how shocked I am that this is all happening.” She explains that she’s always thought of herself as an artistic observer of life, as opposed to a participant, and that in the past, she’d written about relationships that may have been doomed because she loved “an impossible situation.” “I think that the idea of really engaging, saying yes to the whole thing — a baby, a child, a family, a forever — that felt like big stuff,” she says. “So it wasn’t until I really met Cole that I — and probably even before I met Cole — that I had done some of my own personal work to get to a place where I was ready to meet a man like Cole, where I was like, okay, this is wild. I want all the things. And even the first time I might have even admitted that to myself was when I was writing ‘After All,’ which is how I decided to open the album so boldly. Like, alright, here we go!” Jepsen lights up when talking about the very first day she met Greif-Neill, when they ended up in the studio to write “Day and Night” cut “No Labels, I Love You.” “I was driving home from that session and I thought, cute guy, but [only] in there. Not gonna touch that hot stuff. And you know, don’t kiss the producer. Rule number one,” she says with a laugh. She pulled to a stop sign and saw he had texted her with questions about the song’s second verse and decided to save his number under a combination of his name and the track they had just worked on. “I put ‘Cole I Love You’ in my phone. Lo and behold, five years later, we’re married with a baby, and I’m like, oh. Well, that worked out. He’s still saved as ‘Cole I Love You’ because of that day.” Shortly after marrying in October 2025, Jepsen and Greif-Neill welcomed their first child in March amid the completion of “Day and Night.” She had been prepping for the baby’s arrival while balancing the demands of being a pop star — at the “Emotion” anniversary show in August 2025, she says she was four months pregnant and wore a dress with “distracting lines” in hopes of making it an “optical illusion” — and is gradually learning how to delineate between family and career. “I’m more of a planner than I’ve ever been before,” she says. “A big part of getting ready for this double album and mixing it and putting the art together and even preparing like what videos were shot when was all around the idea of like, baby’s on the way. It was like a different meaning for the word deadline… And there was a conversation of, am I doing this before the baby comes or after the baby comes? It was like, before, because after the baby comes, I’m gonna be focused. So it’s changed that in a really wild way that I didn’t expect. It was so obvious what the priority was, which was building a career around a life, not the other way around.” That includes making time for the Broadway adaptation of the 1999 rom-com “10 Things I Hate About You,” set for previews in August 2027. Lena Dunham is adapting the musical’s book with Jessica Huang, while Jepsen is writing the music and lyrics with Ethan Gruska, whose credits include Ryan Beatty, Fiona Apple and Phoebe Bridgers. “We wanted to handle with care, but not trepidation,” she says of the musical. “We wanted to feel emboldened to think about what would cause these characters to feel like words are not enough and they need to break into the song. So we began with playlists for each character. Bianca had like her ’90s playlist. And it became really fun to sort of think about, you know, what the message of our show is.” Jepsen stops short of giving too much away: When asked about how she plans to handle the iconic scene where Heath Ledger’s character sings Frankie Valli’s “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You,” she demurs. “That one you’re gonna have to come and see. I know, disappointing answer, but I gotta leave some for the show.” For now, Jepsen is enjoying the spoils of motherhood as she releases one of her most ambitious projects to date. In the past, she’s complemented her studio albums by releasing full companion records of B-sides, something she’s not entirely counting out for “Day and Night. “In a very elusive way, in a very non-sexy way, I’ll say I consider myself sort of like a chipmunk,” she jokes. “I like to store my ideas in my cheeks, save them for later. Who knows.” But, as always, she’s looking for the next spark of inspiration. “A big part of my nature is to be in constant creation. I like to be making things. I don’t find it tiring,” she says. “It fuels and excites me. One of my greatest joys, even when I’m on the road is to pull up with Tavish and be like, hey, like late night tonight, let’s go to like your hotel or my hotel and we’ll get the office space and pull up some sound and just jam. That’s going to be different with a baby, but we’re going to figure out how to make that happen and fit it in between the cracks.” ‘The Odyssey’ Becomes Universal’s Highest-Grossing Film of All Time Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Bests ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Box Office: ‘Practical Magic 2’ Conjures Up $13 Million on Friday as ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Nears All-Time Domestic Box Office Record ‘The Odyssey’ Leaked on X: High-Quality Bootleg Seen by Millions in Hours Before Takedown ‘The Odyssey’ Sets 20,000 Screen China Release, Including Near-Total Imax Commitment (EXCLUSIVE) China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Continues Dominance Loading comments...
