articles.title: Melissa McCarthy on Getting Serious for ‘JonBenét Ramsey,’ the Psychiatrist on Set and Hollywood’s ‘Bulls—’ Excuse for Why Comedies Don’t Work Anymore
articles.full_text: Ramona Rosales for Variety Melissa McCarthy , one of the most gifted comic actors working today, will soon be starring in a tragedy. In “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” — premiering on Netflix on Dec. 10 — McCarthy plays Patsy Ramsey, the mother of 6-year-old JonBenét, who was killed in the Ramseys’ Boulder, Colorado, home on Christmas night in 1996. Because JonBenét had won several child beauty pageants, images of her in makeup and garish costumes created a spectacle around the case (which is still unsolved), and around the Ramseys. JonBenét’s father, John; her mother, and even her 9-year-old brother, Burke, all became suspects in her murder, and the series examines the fallout from her death. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension Ramona Rosales for Variety Because of the O.J. Simpson trial in 1995, true crime had become a national obsession, and with JonBenét’s murder, newsmagazines, talk shows and tabloids had a field day, inciting the public to rabidity: Today, McCarthy remembers being part of the “feeding frenzy” herself. Clive Owen, who plays John, says McCarthy’s involvement as both an actor and executive producer was a “big part” of the reason he agreed to take the role. “Yes, she’s a brilliant comedic actress, but she’s just a brilliant actress ,” Owen says. Popular on Variety “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” from showrunner Richard LaGravenese (and made without the family’s involvement), was an emotionally wrenching endeavor, and McCarthy and Owen formed a bond. “We have become friends,” he says. “Because it was such a difficult project, just having her alongside as an ally was really, really important. And honestly, after doing this project with her — she can do anything.” And she has. After playing chef Sookie St. James in the beloved dramedy “Gilmore Girls” from 2000 to 2007, McCarthy broke out in film in 2011’s Paul Feig-directed blockbuster “Bridesmaids” as the crude yet earnest Megan. The scene-stealing role brought her a best supporting actress Oscar nomination, a rarity for comedy — especially given that in the film’s famously gruesome food poisoning set-piece, Megan uses a sink as a toilet. McCarthy was shocked when she learned of her nomination, saying to her husband, director Ben Falcone, “I don’t think that’s true,” when he told her. (McCarthy was nominated for an Oscar a second time, for her fearless lead performance in Marielle Heller’s 2018 “Can You Ever Forgive Me?”) Over her career, McCarthy has starred in hit comedies such as Feig’s “The Heat” and “Spy” and Falcone’s “Tammy” and “The Boss” — and as the villainous Ursula in Disney’s 2023 live-action version of “The Little Mermaid.” But with “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” she returns to her earliest training in New York City, when she spent two years studying the Sanford Meisner method of acting. Back then, McCarthy was “carrying folding chairs up to a rehearsal space to do a show and just making enough money to hopefully pay for the space that night.” Despite the different scale of audience, the same passion and community spirit went into “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” McCarthy says in her first interview about the series, with the cast and crew putting in “hardworking days” while suffering through “hard moments.” Wanting to do right by Patsy, who died of ovarian cancer in 2006, McCarthy found people who knew her. “And they were like, ‘Those kids were in jeans riding their bikes. JonBenét wasn’t out in a pageant dress in her front yard.’” Playing Patsy Ramsey is such a heavy thing — what went into your decision to do it? I said, “Oh, no. I have no interest in that.” I didn’t think it was any of my business to do, I guess? But I spent a lot of years not working, and somebody took the time to ask me — I should take the time to look into it. The more I started to, I was really floored by the lack of humanity that had been shown to that family. In 1996, I was 26, and I have a very vivid memory of standing in a grocery store and looking at a tabloid and thinking, “How could you dress a little girl like that?” Because that’s what we were being told. I remember being obsessed. I had never put it together that I was a part of [judging them]. I went willingly. And that’s on me. I just thought if it can make some people realize, “Oh, God. I was part of that — I did that,” it gives us a little of our humanity back. And the hope is not to dredge it up for that poor family again. This might sound nuts: I’m very fond of Patsy. I have so much compassion for them, what they went through, and go through currently. That’s a bizarre thing to have a child’s trauma be like Wimbledon. It was a turning point, being able to watch something like that as sport. And even when I finally decided to do this, everybody said their theory [about the case] as if it was true. People in your life, you mean? People in my life! Very smart people, very open-minded people. I was like, “What is that based on?” Because I’ve now read every police report, every coroner’s report. So we’re still doing that. I said, “You got caught up in the riptide.” I hope with my whole heart that this — I don’t know if “helps” is the right word. Clive Owen and Melissa McCarthy Courtesy of Chris Large/Paramount+ Does the show have a point of view about what happened? This is not a whodunit. It’s not like, “Ooh, there’s a big reveal!” This is a character study of everyone who was caught in the undertow, and a look at all of us — as a civilization, really. Seeing that happen to a child I think breaks everybody. We do show all these different theories. They were all real working theories. Showing the chaos of it is something that we’ve not seen. It’s a new telling of it, because you’re like, “My God, is this really what was happening?” For your performance’s sake, did you decide what you thought happened? Yes. Just my personal feeling. My heart says no one in the family could have done that. I don’t have the ability, or probably the right, to say that, but that’s what my gut says. Which I probably am not supposed to say. But shooting that, I had to pick. I had to have that for myself, if nothing else. It’s such a heartbreaking and very physical performance as Patsy. In the two episodes I’ve seen, you’re crying so much. What was that like? It’s tricky. Luckily, I loved who I was working with. I’d never worked with Clive before — I can’t say enough good stuff about him. What a joy of a human. Everybody in the cast, every single person, they’re fantastic. It just felt elevated. And I felt like everybody knew that we had to do right by the story and not just try to do something that’s going to get a lot of views. That set was so serious, and some of those days were so hard. We had a psychologist on set at all times. You did? And it was needed sometimes, especially during some of the really intense scenes. It would take people down, and they’d just need a minute. I felt obligated to stand up for her, which — maybe it’s none of my damn business, but I feel protective of her. It makes you get up and go to work every day and try to give it your all. This show was filmed in Calgary, far from your home with Ben and your two teenage daughters. After the workday, were you taking Patsy with you? I had rather weird sleeping hours. It would depend on what the next day held, but I called my kids, for sure, and my husband, and made sure throughout the day I talked to them and checked in on days when I could. Some days I couldn’t. I didn’t want them to see me in that state. Sleep wasn’t always great when that’s what was in my head. But I was like, “Well, I bet she wasn’t sleeping great either. So get up! Get up.” As you prepare for the show to come out, what have you been thinking about? I think about the one thing I can’t control, which is how people will receive it. And, of course, you think about the family. My intentions don’t mean anything — their feelings are their feelings, and all I can do is hope that I did right by them and by Patsy. The only people that really get a vote are them. Patsy Ramsey died in 2006. But would you ever be interested in talking to John or Burke Ramsey? I would. Again, I don’t know if I’m supposed to say this: I’ve written John many letters that I haven’t sent. I wrote before we did it. I wrote, during the thing, to him and Burke — many letters — to be like, “I’m doing my best by her. I’m really trying to show who I felt she was.” “Bridesmaids”: Melissa McCarthy, Ellie Kemper, Rose Byrne, Wendi McLendon-Covey, Maya Rudolph, Kristen Wiig Courtesy of ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection You’ve excelled at drama, and this role is as dramatic as it gets. But you came up through the Groundlings, the improv and sketch program, where you met your husband, Ben Falcone, and “Bridesmaids” screenwriters Kristen Wiig and Annie Mumolo, along with so many other people you’ve gone on to work with. How did you get involved with the Groundlings? My very first stuff in New York was stand-up. I did all the free cheap rooms where you got a minute and a half, and you worked your way up to two and a half minutes and so on. But then I didn’t like those rooms anymore — I just found them really misogynistic. There was literally a guy in every room saying, “Show me your tits.” To the point where I was like, “Is it the same guy? The same lonely guy?” He’s not going to stop. The only way to make him stop is to eviscerate him. I was like, “I’m here to try to make people laugh, and now the only way I win is if I actually embarrass you. I see I’ve done that and now you’re quiet. So now I feel terrible.” I love live performance; it’s my favorite. But that realm was not. I didn’t want a fistfight. And then I moved to L.A., and my sister sent me a little magazine story about the Groundlings. I see. I was like, “Oh, there must be amazing theater in L.A.!,” because I’d never been here when I moved here. When I was doing stand-up, I didn’t really know how to write, so a lot of it was improvised. I also had a thing of like, “You’re not a writer unless you’ve been trained to write.” I would always go up with a paper, and I would do my monologue, and Ben was the first person that leans over and he goes, “Why do you always go up with a blank page?” I was like, “What? What are you talking about?” He’s like, “You go up with a blank page, you do a monologue.” I was like, “That’s not writing.” And he’s like, “It is writing.” I was like, “No, it’s not, because I don’t know how to write.” He’s like, “You just did a whole monologue, and then you wrote down what you said.” I had such a weird, I didn’t go to college — I’m not a writer. Groundlings literally taught me to be like, “OK: You are writing, you are doing this.” What was the “Bridesmaids” experience like once the movie came out? The fact that Kristen and Annie let me come in for that truly changed my life. I thought I blew the audition because I got too weird, because I was sitting there improvising with Kristen. I got too comfortable! I said weird things! Before “Bridesmaids” was released, people were like, “The numbers are not looking good.” And I was like, “It’s not out yet.” And they’re like, “We know how to do this, and the numbers are not looking good.” And I was like, “OK, but I’m just saying I think it’s really funny and I think people are going to think it’s really funny.” Opening night, Ben and I were sitting in Paul Feig’s backyard with him and his wife, Laurie, and we’re having dinner and Paul’s like, “Oh my God. Oh my God. I think it’s working! It’s working!” Then all of a sudden he’s like, “Every theater in L.A. is full. Get in the car, get in the car, get in the car!” We went to the ArcLight, I think? We just stood in the back, and it was rolling, crazy laughter. You, Ben, Paul and Laurie? Yes. We were like, “Oh my God, it’s working! What we think is funny is funny!” It was about that group of people; it was about the characters. Just running through theaters, and Paul in his suit — and Ben and I not dressed as nicely. No one does dress as nicely as Paul Feig. No, nobody. It also felt important — a comedy about women becoming such a massive success. Yes. Which is insane, but it did. Two women wrote it; we all felt like this is what’s funny . This is what we as women write about and talk about, and we are this weird. And it wasn’t about, “My dress isn’t perfect!” even though that was part of it. This is what trying on dresses really is like — it’s a bit of a shitshow. Literally. Well-played. As soon as the movie came out, people started saying you needed to be nominated for an Oscar — which you were! But that’s so uncommon for a comedy. What was that like? Disorienting. Now I can’t remember if Octavia’s name was said first or mine. Jim Rash and Nat Faxon were nominated for “The Descendants.” Kristen and Annie were nominated for screenplay — this was, like, our weird ragtag group. And I just kept saying “Octavia’s nominated!” Ben went, “Mooch, you just got nominated.” I was like, “I know Octavia got nominated for an Oscar!” And he was like, “ You just got nominated for an Oscar.” I was like, “I don’t think that’s true.” And he’s like, “We just watched it.” Then I just balled my eyes out. Right! That was the year Octavia Spencer, also your friend since the Groundlings days, won for “The Help.” And Jim and Nat won that year. We were all just there — and we were like, “What are we all doing here? This is amazing!” But our own Academy, our own industry, doesn’t respect comedy. I don’t know when that became the thing to do — and you can call any project a comedy to get into an awards category. Anybody just gets to claim it, because no real comedies are ever going to get awarded. I’m stopped 15 times a day by somebody who says, “I desperately need you to do another comedy.” And I’m like, “We are trying. I’m trying!” And people need it, that’s for sure. “The Heat”: Sandra Bullock and Melissa McCarthy ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection Can you talk about your creative partnership with Paul Feig? Paul should be legally bound to make one comedy at least every two years. His taste level as a filmmaker, his visual aesthetic, is so good — which is important. You have to make a proper film. It has to look good. It has to have great pacing. And he’s just funny as hell. He just wants to lift other people to be as funny and as good as you can possibly be. I miss him doing comedies — for myself, but also as an audience member. We’ve made it so hard to do comedies that we have our best and our funniest people not doing what they do. Why is that? I think the narrative of comedies don’t work anymore is bullshit. I think it’s absolute bullshit. It’s a false narrative. Comedy is like music. It’s a feeling — not everybody can do the same thing. Two equally incredible musicians have totally different styles. You don’t go in and break someone’s style or what they do; you have them do the best of what they can do. I think because people can laugh at a movie, for some reason, it’s less respected. And so they think, “Well, I know what’s funny.” And I always want to be like, “You’ve never been funny to me! You’ve never said anything funny. You’ve never thought of a funny idea.” It doesn’t mean you’re not great at your job — Are we talking about the executive level now? People at all the levels are now like, “Let me tell you who to put in to make it funny…” And I’m like, “Well, those four people aren’t funny.” It’s like Feig putting in Jason Statham in “Spy.” Oh God, yes! Paul and I went out to dinner with Statham, and we were just goofing around the table, and I was like, “Stop talking about it! Just do what you’re doing — it’s so funny.” But Paul had the idea to be like, “What about Statham?” But when you take all of the artists out of it — they start to do the math of it, and that’s not comedy. They want a big premise. But most really great comedies, it’s about the people and the characters and the story, and it’s not like, “And they were both aliens at the end!” But people really think they want that hook, and it’s just not real. Then they say comedies don’t work, and I’m like, “No, bad comedies don’t work.” And I won’t take the fall for that. “Spy” Melissa McCarthy and Jason Statham ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection To me, in a just world, “Spy” would be a franchise. We should be on the ninth “Spy”! Everyone on “Spy” was ready to re-rack immediately. There should be a new villain, new location. Why didn’t it happen? Because you’re a woman? No — well, Jesus, that probably doesn’t help, but I don’t know. It did so well. People can say that doesn’t matter. I think it does. For “Thunder Force,” we were going to roll right into another one. We were like, “It’s so fun. It did incredibly well for Netflix. We already have the idea for it.” If I write something — or Ben and I write something — and it tanks, I’ll take the fall. Which we have not had to take. We don’t make $8 billion. We don’t make those kind of movies, but, I mean, $120 million, I’m not mad at that. The studio’s not mad at that. We want to make a reasonably priced thing that makes you a good profit. For some reason, that model is no longer desirable. I can’t figure out the math of it. For the never-made “Bridesmaids 2,” I’d heard that Kristen and Annie’s idea was that was Lillian gets divorced, and there’s a divorce party. Why did that not happen? And how! That I don’t know. I know that was a hard movie to make. It was, but it was also so fun. Oh my God , it was so fun. Literally laughing on set in such a way that I am shocked that we shot stuff. Rose [Byrne] is such a wonderful, bad laugher. On the plane, her little stick arms are up, and when Ben and I are doing our weird thing, she just laughs out loud . It’s a glorious thing. She just kept putting the magazine up to hide — and it’s in the movie. So that was what shooting was like. It was like you were literally hiding because someone was always like, “Oh, I’ve dropped something,” because they’re under the table laughing. That’s just not a bad day. I don’t know. I think it’s gotten so corporate. I miss the people that work off their gut. When I think about the hellish world that we live in now, I can kind of trace it directly back to the backlash against “Ghostbusters” in 2016. [ Sighs ] What madness. It does really correlate! When people were like, “You’re ruining our childhood,” I was like, “You definitely seem like you had a terrible childhood.” It just had so many cooks in that kitchen. Katie Dippold co-wrote “Ghostbusters” with Paul Feig — for her “Widow’s Bay” triumph. Oh my God , I loved her show. I almost got nervous, like, “It’s so good. Is it not going to do well?” And I ate it up. I couldn’t get enough fast enough. Then I just started hearing person after person be like, “Have you watched this thing?” It is not shocking that Katie Dippold wrote something incredible. I’m just like, who’s the genius that backed off and let her? “Gilmore Girls”: Melissa McCarthy and Lauren Graham ©CW Network/Courtesy Everett Collection Sookie on “Gilmore Girls” was your first big role. It’s not easy to do Amy Sherman-Palladino dialogue! It’s good training, I tell you that! What was that experience like when you look back on it? It was hard! It was really hard. But to me, that was normal, because it was my first show. So I was like, “Oh, our scripts are 93 pages, and you can’t change a contraction, even if you get them that morning and it’s a 10-page oner.” And that’s just what it was. I love that she had her own style, and I love that she built that world. I love that she fought for it, because a woman running that show at that time, I think you kind of had to be like, “It’s my way or the highway.” I think she had to probably fight to keep it the way she wanted to. And I’m glad she did, because it stood the test of time. People really take ownership of that show. So huge with Gen Z. And the fact that they keep re-watching it. I’m like, “Really?” It’s so funny, my kids have not watched it. But Vivian and I were both home with the flu — this is years ago. And it came on and she was like, “That’s your show, right? That was your first show?” I was like, “You’re on the very end of that show when I’m pregnant.” I think I’d had four kids on the show. And then I finally went to Amy and I’m like, “I’m actually pregnant. You can have me have another kid again, and I’ll give you the prop for free.” And she was like, “No, I don’t think so.” So then I had to hide it! I was like, “We already have four kids. I can’t have five?” But we watched just the pilot, and Vivi, my oldest, she kept going, “What are you doing with your voice?” And I was like, “Oh, it’s youth.” She’s like, “That doesn’t sound like you at all.” I was like, “Yeah! I was youthful and I didn’t have kids yet. And now I sound like this grizzled old man.” Courtesy of The CW You did one day on the Netflix revival, “Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life.” It was fun to see everybody again. I still see Lauren [Graham] and Yanic [Truesdale]. We’ve gone on vacation with Yanic. We’re really close. I just wanted to go and see everybody. So it was really nice to do. I always wonder, will something else happen with that? I don’t know anything about it, but — Amy has done a ton, but it’s kind of her life’s work, right? When something catches like that, there’s no rhyme or reason. You have to just love it. I mean, I’m always shocked at all the “Gilmore” comments when I’m out. I’m like, “I’ve worked since then!” But it is nice. And I think we all are very aware of that, or I hope so. But when something catches like that, like “That’s my comfort show,” or, “That’s what I watch going to sleep” — what a thing to get to do something that gives people comfort like that. Totally. It’s the coziest. It’s the coziest! I felt lucky doing it, and I feel lucky to have been a part of it. Courtesy of Joyful Heart Foundation Charity Spotlight: Joyful Heart Foundation Melissa McCarthy remembers meeting Mariska Hargitay the old-fashioned way: through their assistants. Hargitay, McCarthy says, seemed like someone who “probably has her shit together” enough to make recommendations for, say, “a good water filtration system.” Their texting relationship soon blossomed into a real-life friendship, which, McCarthy says, “doesn’t always happen when you meet a new friend in your 50s.” As Hargitay puts it, “When we finally did meet in person, our hearts did a dance.” Their dynamic is a playful one. When Hargitay rolled her ankle and needed surgery in July 2021, McCarthy stood on a Burbank street holding a sign asking drivers to honk to speed up the “SVU” star’s recovery. And earlier this year, McCarthy surprised Hargitay by doing a cameo on “SVU.” (“I still don’t know how they pulled it off,” Hargitay says.) For her Power of Women charity, McCarthy is putting a spotlight on Joyful Heart Foundation, which — inspired by the subject matter of “SVU” — Hargitay began in 2004 to advocate for survivors of sexual assault, domestic violence and child abuse. While other actors might have just said, “This is what I do for a living,” McCarthy says, Hargitay instead embraced it as a responsibility. “Her power is through kindness and consideration and a moral compass.” For Hargitay’s part, she says of McCarthy, “It’s a gift to find someone who’s willing to roll up their sleeves and help bring change.” Styling: Katja Cahill; Stylist assistants: Aliya Iahijani, Tracey Moore; Tailor: Daniela Kurrle; Makeup: Afton Williams; Hair: Mark Townsend/Forward Artists; Dress: L’Academie, Hat: Sadie James, Cape: Viviano; Earrings: KerenWolf, Spectrum Jewels , and Mindi Mond New York; Rings: On Aura Tout Vu, Spectrum Jewels, Le Vian Jewelry and Zales;Necklaces: Zales and Sterling Forever; Bracelets: Zales and Sterling Forever Loading comments... articles.title: David Oyelowo and Nate Parker’s Mansa Studios Partners With Macro Television Studios to Produce Vertical Series
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 8:41am PT David Oyelowo and Nate Parker’s Mansa Studios Partners With Macro Television Studios to Produce Vertical Series By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Executive Editor franklinavenue Latest Sony TV North America Distribution Executive Vice President Flory Bramnick Plans to Depart After 24 Years (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago ‘The View’ Season 30 Launches With Best Premiere Week Ratings in Six Years (EXCLUSIVE) 5 days ago As ‘American Idol’ Leaves Los Angeles for Atlanta, More Concerns Emerge About the State of Local Production 6 days ago See All Mansa Studios Mansa Studios, the media company co-founded by David Oyelowo and Nate Parker, has partnered with Macro Television Studios to develop, finance and produce various vertical series, the two companies announced Monday. Macro and Mansa will develop, market and promote the projects coming out of the partnership, while also share ownership of the intellectual property. “Mansa has developed real expertise in the emerging vertical format, and we see this as an exciting opportunity to pair that experience with Maceo Television Studios’ vast capabilities across genres,” said Macro founder/CEO Charles D. King in a statement. “We are looking forward to learning from the collaboration and seeing how audiences respond and explore innovation opportunities for the format.” Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony Mansa already distributes film, TV and short-form content across platforms including its own free ad-supported streaming service and FAST channels. Popular on Variety “Mansa was created to ensure that culturally rich stories can reach audiences wherever they are,” said Mansa Studios co-founder Oyelowo in a statement. “As viewing habits evolve, we are embracing new storytellers, formats and platforms that allow us to remain connected to our global audience while creating meaningful opportunities for a diverse array of talent.” Macro most recently worked with Oyelowo as a producer on Apple TV’s “Government Cheese,” which starred the actor. Macro TV Studios, a division of Macro founded in 2015, recently produced Netflix’s “Raising Dion” (nominated for a Children’s & Family Emmy) and Netflix’s “Gentefied,” which was nominated for a Peabody Award. The company also produced FX’s docuseries “Dear Mama: The Saga of Afeni and Tupac Shakur,” which was nominated for a Primetime Emmy and for a Grammy Award. Macro is also behind Macro Film Studios, in-house branding and creative agency Brand Macro, talent firm M88 and affiliated venture firm MaCVenture Capital. articles.title: Presley Gerber Dies: Model, Son Of Cindy Crawford & Rande  Gerber Was 27
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Tom Tapp Tom Tapp Deputy Managing Editor More Stories By Tom Presley Gerber Dies: Model, Son Of Cindy Crawford & Rande Gerber Was 27 Jake & Logan Paul Address Troops At The Pentagon Ke Huy Quan Reveals “Life Changing” Gesture From Spielberg & Lucas When He Was A Kid View All September 20, 2026 8:44pm Presley Gerber Getty Presley Walker Gerber, a model and the only son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, has died. A representative for the family confirmed the news to Deadline. He was 27. A statement from the family read as follows: “The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time.” Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries Obituaries Stephanie Cole Dies: British Star Of ‘Open All Hours’ & ‘Doc Martin’ Was 84 An L.A. County Medical Examiner’s report says Gerber died at a rehab facility. An investigation into the cause is ongoing. Gerber was signed to IMG models and appeared in a 2018 Pepsi ad with his mother. His modeling career began with a 2015 Bruce Weber shoot. He soon was doing runway work at the various fashion weeks around the globe. He recalled the whirlwind in a 2023 interview with the podcast Studio 22 . Watch on Deadline “My whole life changed within a month and it was just a very profound experience because I had to grow up quickly,” said Gerber. In 2019, he was arrested for a DUI in Beverly Hills and sentenced to three years’ probation. Then 19, Gerber was also ordered to complete a DUI program. His younger sister, Kaia Gerber, currently plays Susan Reynolds in Ryan Murphy’s The Shards . Presley Gerber , Kaia Gerber, Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber in 2017. articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse BBC Drama ‘Ministry Of Time’ Adds Adeel Akhtar, Ciaran Hinds & Eight More To Cast Eagle Eye Drama Acquires ‘The Great Dictator’, Matthew Sweet’s Biography Of Barbara Cartland Princess Di Returns To ‘SNL UK’ As “Deeply Intelligent, Autonomous, Neurokinetic Android” In Cold Open Skewering King Charles, Ed Sheeran & AI View All September 21, 2026 2:29am 'The Great Dictator' ITV Studios EXCLUSIVE: Eagle Eye Drama has acquired the rights to The Great Dictator , Matthew Sweet ‘s biography of the flamboyant and eccentric late Dame Barbara Cartland . Historian, novelist and screenwriter Sweet’s book tells the story of author known as ‘The Queen of Romance’ Cartland, who was one of the UK’s most recognizable figures across the 20th century. She was famous for dressing in pink and taking her Pekinese dogs with her wherever she went. Born in 1901, Cartland was a fixture of British high society, rubbing shoulders with press barons, politicians, the aristocracy and the Royal Family, as step-grandmother to Princess Diana. Related Stories Cancellations and Renewals Mark Gatiss Drama 'Bookish' Returning For Third Chapter & Festive Special Acquisitions HBO Max Buys Mark Gatiss Series 'Bookish' For Australia As Sales Pass The 100-Territory Mark Bookish co-writer Sweet’s book, published this month by Hodder & Stoughton, is the result of years of research into her life. It has been positively reviewed by the likes of The Guardian, The Times and documentarian Louis Theroux, and ITV Studios-owned Eagle Eye will now look to adapt the story of the ‘woman in pink’, whose romance novels sold close to a billion copies in 38 languages. Watch on Deadline Eagle Eye Drama CEO Walter Iuzzolino said: “Matthew Sweet gained unparalleled access to the Cartland family archives, and what he has uncovered is a story more compelling and unbelievable than her most outlandish plots, which will provide a wonderful bedrock to build an unmissable scripted series.” Eagle Eye CCO Jo McGrath added that Cartland was the third-biggest selling author of all time, behind only William Shakespeare and Agatha Christie, adding she would be a “gift of a role for a great actress.” “Known for her outlandish pink chiffon clothes and thick Meltonian black shoe cream mascara, she is a figure who has been loved and scorned in equal measure,” said McGrath. “She was a ferocious champion of romantic love with a less than idyllic and rather scandalous love life of her own. “A friend of Winston Churchill, she dined with Margaret Thatcher – to whom she prescribed alternative remedies and oxygen supplements – and of course the step-grandmother to Princess Diana, who loved her books as a young woman.” Sweet, whose series Bookish is produced through Eagle Eye, said: “I feel like I’ve been caught up in a pink chiffon whirlwind in the last few days, with the reviews and the Baillie Gifford longlist. Now Eagle Eye Drama has acquired the rights to bring The Great Dictator to television. They are the perfect producers and I know they will bring Barbara’s world to life with impeccable style.” Eagle Eye is arguably best known for Bookish , the light crime series in which Mark Gatiss plays a closeted post-war detective. It was renewed for a third season and festive special last month. The production house also makes Channel 4’s The Couple Next Door and the high-rating Patience and Ben Miller drama Professor T for ITV. It is also adapting ITV’s forthcoming Richard Armitage crime series Winter after secured the rights to the book. Tom Perrin, Editorial Consultant, Hodder & Stoughton, noted The Great Dictator had been “a runaway success” since publication and had been longlisted for the Baillie Gifford Prize. Cartland’s life has been the subject of many documentaries, while Anne Reid starred as the author in the BBC’s 2008 telemovie In Love with Barbara . articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival Cancels  2026 Edition
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Dubai Film Festival To Return In December 2027, As 2026 Edition Of Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival Looks Uncertain Israeli Film Council Calls For Festivals To Be Removed From Funding Criteria & Creation Of Strand For Films Celebrating Israeli Soldiers Amid ‘NAZA’ Firestorm Oscars: France Selects ‘Minotaur’ For Best International Feature Film Race View All September 21, 2026 3:00am Alessandra Ambrosio attends the Closing Night red carpet at the Red Sea International Film Festival 2025 Getty images Saudi Arabia ‘s Red Sea Film Foundation has cancelled the 2026 edition of the Red Sea International Film Festival , saying in a statement that the sixth edition had been postponed to the fourth quarter of 2027. The announcement follows weeks of speculation over whether the 2026 edition, scheduled to unfold from December 3-12 in the Red Sea port city of Jeddah, would take place amid tensions across the entire Gulf region due to the U.S.-Israeli-Iran war. Aside from retaliatory strikes on neighboring territories, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman, Iran has also sought to take control of the Strait of Hormuz connecting the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, a key shipping route for their oil and other goods. Related Stories Festivals Dubai Film Festival To Return In December 2027, As 2026 Edition Of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea Film Festival Looks Uncertain News Saudi Arabia To Invest $7 Billion In Three Theme Parks Near Paris Beyond direct threats from Iran, Saudi Arabia is also dealing with a flareup in its conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi group in recent weeks. Watch on Deadline The foundation did not mention the geopolitical tensions saying rather that the decision “followed a comprehensive review of a range of considerations relating to the timing of the next edition, including the logistical requirements involved in staging an international event of this scale.” Since the event’s launch in 2021, in the wake of Saudi Arabia’s lifting of its 35-year cinema ban at the end of 2017, it has grown into the Gulf region’s main film festival with a steady flow of high-profile Hollywood guests, burgeoning industry events, and wide Middle East and international participation. Aside from geopolitical tensions beyond its control, the festival has also been subject to internal debate about its future direction in recent months. In June, the foundation’s longtime Managing Director Shivani Pandya Malhotra, who helped spearhead the launch of the festival having joined the body in 2019, stepped down with a number of her close team members leaving as well. In the backdrop, there are also wider questions around Saudi Arabia’s larger commitment to the film industry, with the country’s entertainment focus shifting to the video game sector and sports such as boxing and soccer. The foundation made it clear in its statement that the festival will be back for sixth edition in 2027 with “a renewed vision and a programme that continues to celebrate cinema and filmmakers from Saudi Arabia, the region and around the world.” It also emphasized that it will continue its year-round mission of supporting filmmakers and strengthening the film industries through the Red Sea Fund, Red Sea Labs and its wider programmes and initiatives. As part of this continued commitment, the foundation said it will introduce year-round programming at Culture Square in Jeddah from November 2026, establishing it as an ongoing destination for film screenings, cultural events and specialised film-industry programmes. “The Red Sea Film Foundation extends its sincere appreciation to filmmakers, partners, guests and audiences for their continued trust and support. We look forward to welcoming the global film community back to Historic Jeddah in 2027 for a sixth edition that celebrates cinema, creativity and cultural dialogue,” concluded its statement. In the meantime, Gulf neighbor the United Arab Emirates announced last week that it is reviving the Dubai International Film Festival following a 10-year hiatus, with a scheduled December 8, 2027 opening date, which could see it clash with the Red Sea. In the backdrop, Qatar’s Doha Film Festival is pushing on with plans for its second edition running this November 19-27, 2026. articles.title: CNN, MS NOW And Politico To Sue Donald Trump Over His White House Ban
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted CNN, MS NOW And Politico To Sue Donald Trump Over His White House Ban CNN, MS NOW And Politico Journalists Denied White House Entry; Colleagues Condemn Trump’s Ban Judge Says Kennedy Center Must Give Court 30 Days Notice Of Any Demolition Plans After Trump Floats Prospect It Could Be “Ripped Down” View All September 21, 2026 3:43am Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images UPDATED: CNN , Politico and MS NOW are suing Donald Trump and other White House officials after the president banned him from the complex. In the lawsuit, the news outlets are asking a federal judge to immediately restore their access, which was denied on Saturday, a day after Trump announced he was restricting them from entry to the White House grounds. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.” The new organizations said in a joint statement, “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” Related Stories Politics Sylvester Stallone Told Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship Was "Impossible" But Was Appointed Anyway: "It Won't Work" News Alan Ritchson On The 'Reacher' Season That Was Canceled After "Someone Got Re-Elected" The White House also removed CNN from the White House pool on Monday, the day it was scheduled to be the primary network for their coverage. As a result, there will be no TV pool on a day when Trump is traveling to New York, signaling that other networks declined to serve as replacements because of the president’s targeting of CNN. Watch on Deadline The news outlets state in their lawsuit, “The President banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and the individual reporters covering the news for those media organizations, in disregard of the most basic guarantees of the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause. He did so expressly for the improper purpose of retaliating against Plaintiffs for past news coverage because he deemed it ‘negative’ and chilling future reporting about him and his administration’s policies and actions. “President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration. But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting. The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained.” The lawsuit claims violation of the Fifth Amendment’s due process clause and First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. The outlets are seeking a temporary restraining order and injunction to prohibit the ban from being enforced and to require that their access be restored, as well as a declaratory ruling. The outlets are represented from Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., who represented CNN’s Jim Acosta when his credentials were revoked in Trump’s first term, as well as others at Gibson Dunn, including Katie Townsend and Patrick Fuster. In addition to the impact of the ban on their own news organizations, the outlets argue in the lawsuit that it “inflicts an injury on all news media organizations—who now risk a similar fate if they engage in reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable. And the public at large suffers for however long the unconstitutional ban restricts access to current and complete information about their government. These irreparable harms should not be tolerated for a day longer. The Court should immediately enjoin enforcement of the ban.” The lawsuit also names White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Secret Service Director Sean Curran and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. Shortly after the lawsuit was announced, Trump posted on Truth Social, “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” In 2018, in the case of Acosta, a federal judge ruled that precedent required that the White House give proper notice of a revocation. In the 1977 D.C. Circuit opinion, Sherrill vs. Knight, the judges ruled that “the protection afforded newsgathering under the First Amendment guarantee of freedom of the press requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons.” The White House has yet to provide a legal justification for revoking the credentials of the news outlets. On ABC’s This Week on Sunday, host Jon Karl pressed House Majority Leader Steve Scalise on Trump’s ban. “Do you support him banning these news organizations because he doesn’t like what they are reporting?” Karl asked. Scalise deflected, pointing to Trump’s accessibility to the media and claimed that Joe Biden removed the press credentials from more than 400 news organizations. In fact, the Biden White House established new criteria for credentialing, based in part on how often holders had used the hard passes and that they had full time employment and residency in the D.C. area. It was not based on a news organization’s viewpoint, although the changes were made after one correspondent had repeatedly interrupted press briefings. Karl told Scalise that they “were not banned from the White House.” He then asked Scalise whether Trump’s ban violates the First Amendment, but Scalise again did not answer. Karl moved on to another topic. A eight-strong team will lead activities the company, which is known for the likes of Stuff the British Stole , Rise of the Dictators and Every Little Thing . WildBear co-founder Michael Tear will remain CEO, and under him will be join co-founder Serge Ou, who becomes Head of Creative Services, leading on production, post-production, design and visual effects. WildBear is one of Australia’s oldest factual-focused producers, having started life more than four decades ago. The company now has around 100 staff across Australia and New Zealand, and it currently produces around 150 hours a year. “Our industry is undergoing the biggest transformation we’ve seen in decades and while WildBear has always quietly weathered every change, the time felt right to really get ahead of things, analyse all the forces at work and decide how we best want to meet the challenges ahead to steer our own future,” said Tear. “The new leadership structure brings together some of the strongest creative and commercial talent in Australia and sends a clear message to the market about our abilities and intentions. In a statement, the five networks in the TV pool stated, “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. Earlier today, CNN, Politico and MS NOW announced that they were filing a lawsuit against Trump and other members of the administration, claiming First Amendment retaliation and violation of due process. The lawsuit seeks a restoration of journalists’ access and credentials. Print, photo and radio pool coverage is scheduled to continue, as well as secondary TV poolers. Discovery Read the full story By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Dekanalog Takes North American Rights To Tan Siyou’s Festival Hit ‘Amoeba’ Pingyao Film Festival Unveils 10th Edition Line-up; ‘Spring In A Small Town’ Set As Opening Film CJ ENM Sells ‘Hotel Del Luna’, ‘Signal’ & Other Hit K-Dramas To CME Slovakia & Czech Channels View All September 21, 2026 8:00am Descendants Of The Sun Dapur Film Seoul-based studio Barunson E&A, which has credits including Bong Joon Ho’s Oscar winner Parasite , is launching international sales on the Indonesian adaptation of landmark Korean drama Descendants Of The Sun at the upcoming Asian Contents & Film Market ( ACFM ) in Busan. (Next Entertainment World), which holds the original IP rights, joining the project as co-producer. Production has wrapped on the two parts of the film, with part one targeting a theatrical release in Indonesia in the first half of 2027. Related Stories News Zhang Yimou To Head Seven-Member Competition Jury At Busan International Film Festival News 'Possible Love' DoP Kim Ji-yong, 'The Blue Road' Director Han Jun-hee & WETA FX's Kimball Thurston Among Speakers For Netflix 'Creative Asia' At BIFF The project marks the tenth anniversary of the original series, one of the titles widely credited with kickstarting the Korean wave internationally. The show closed with a 38.8% nationwide rating; became the first Korean series to air simultaneously in China, where it drew over 2 billion views on iQiyi; and was subsequently sold to more than 30 countries including the U.S., UK, France, Germany, Japan and Russia. Watch on Deadline The Indonesian version reimagines the romance at the heart of the original story through an Indonesian setting and cultural context, while preserving the emotional resonance of the original show. The film is directed by Hanung Bramantyo, one of Indonesia’s leading box-office directors, whose credits include Miracle In Cell No. 7 , also an Indonesian remake of a Korean property, which is the country’s eighth-highest-grossing local film of all time. “Ten years on, Descendants Of The Sun is still one of the titles people point to when they talk about the start of the K-Drama wave,” said Barunson E&A CEO Yoonhee Choi. “We see the strength of the Korean IP as a starting point, not an endpoint. This adaptation places that globally recognized story under a different sun, in an Indonesian landscape with a local sensibility all its own. It retains the familiarity of a story audiences already know and love, while opening it to a new context and, we believe, audiences beyond Indonesia.” Woosik Seo, CEO of Barunson C&C and an executive producer of the film, said: “As the producer behind the original series, I deeply admire how the director has honoured its spirit while creating a truly Indonesian story that I believe will translate just as powerfully wherever it’s seen.” Barunson E&A’s ACFM slate also includes Satan’s Slaves: Origin , the prequel to Joko Anwar’s blockbuster horror franchise; Stoneborn , an occult mystery from the creative team behind Exhuma , starring Jongseo Jeon ( Burning ) and Sul Kyung-gu ( Possible Lo ve); and comedy Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng , which is premiering in Busan International Film Festival and set for theatrical release on October 28. articles.title: Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Jill Goldsmith , Dominic Patten September 21, 2026 8:11am Paramount CEO David Ellison Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC Paramount has settled an antitrust lawsuit brought by a dozen State Attorneys General led by California’s Rob Bonta, the last obstacle to closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery , Deadline has confirmed. Details were scant but there will be concessions. The deal should be formally announced later this morning. Deadline hears that Paramount has agreed to some CNN guardrails, financial penalties linked to CEO David Ellison ‘s 30 movies a year commitment and some sort of separation of the studios for a period. A report in the WSJ said the company will avoid having to sell cable networks. Related Stories Legal Paramount Settlement Talks Prospects Dim For Now As Gang Of Four AGs Resist Quick Ellison Deal News Mark Ruffalo Urges AG Bonta "Do Not Cave" On Paramount Deal, Suggests Protest Outside Oakland Office: "The People Don't Want It!" The WGA’s lawsuit is included in settlement, Deadline hears. Watch on Deadline News of settlement began trickling out on Friday but four of the AGs in the group were said to be holding out. The Attorneys General of New York, Connecticut, Minnesota and Nevada came around late Sunday, we hear, after assurances from California’s Bonta that he would hold Paramount’s “feet to the fire” to ensure the company stuck to its commitments. He had said previously he preferred structural remedies like asset sales to resolve antitrust issues, rather than behavioral remedies, which require monitoring. Paramount shares are up 9% on the news. WBD gained 10% trading at about $30.50. The deal calls for Paramount to take out Warner stockholders for $31 a share. The road here has been a long one marked by a tidal wave of industry opposition, a bruising legal fight, and threats by Paramount CEO David Ellison to exit Hollywood and relocate Paramount to another state. Frontrunners Texas and Tennessee will not, it turns out, be hosting a major film and TV studio. The AGs filed their antitrust lawsuit in July, a month after the U.S. Department of Justice approved the merger, and the judge in the case set a March trial date. The two sides were scheduled to meet at a court-ordered settlement conference in mid-October but Paramount was very eager to reach a deal before Oct. 1, the start of a $7 million-a-day (25 cents per share per quarter) payout the company would owe Warner if the deal had not closed. Called a ticking fee, it’s a rarely used sweetener in M&A that Par employed to convince WBD’s board of directors to accept its offer, and that might have cost it close to $2 billion. Bonta had asked for structural remedies that were hard for Ellison to accept. But he and his team came to the table recently with ideas and things began to move . Deal In Flux Paramount announced in February it had entered into a definitive agreement to acquire WBD for $31 a share in a deal that valued WBD at $81 billion in equity value and $110 billion in enterprise value. Paramount said the combination would yield over $6 billion in synergies. The transaction was funded by $47 billion in equity and $54 billion in debt syndicated out by a consortium of banks and institutions. Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, David’s father, personally guaranteed the bulk of the equity portion. The merger moved from the DOJ through approvals by the EU, the U.K. and other territories. David Ellison continued to anticipate a close in the third quarter of 2026. But the AGs lawsuit stopped things cold. It called out alleged antitrust violations in three markets – cable programming, wide release films, and blockbuster films and won a temporary restraining order early on. Paramount agreed not to close the deal while the case was in play. The WGA also sued to block the merger, with its case running alongside the States. A public relations battle commenced with Paramount insisting the combination would revitalize the entertainment sector. A wide range of industry players disagreed, predicting massive job losses, especially given combined company’s projected $80 billion debt load. But pressure had also ratcheted up on Bonta to settle as Paramount continued to threaten a Hollywood exit and the risk of two major players in limbo through the spring posed its own risks. The Chase Ellison, 43, has amassed a media empire in record time. He launched his aggressive pursuit of WBD shortly after his Skydance Media closed an $8 billion acquisition of Paramount, buying Shari Redstone’s controlling stake in another twisty chase. He started with an escalating series of hostile bids for WBD that were rejected by its board and CEO David Zaslav, but did push Warner to formally put itself up for sale. Several other suitors stepped up. In December of 2025, Warner announced a deal to sell its studio and streaming assets to Netflix. Undeterred, Ellison continued to sweeten the terms of his offer. Ultimately, WBD ditched Netflix and in favor of a richer Paramount deal for the entire company. The giant streamer declined to counter, instead walking away with a $2.8 billion breakup fee. Larry Ellison has been a friend and was major donor to Donald Trump’s presidential campaign. He was also the biggest investor in Skydance. To secure FCC approval for the Paramount deal, the David Ellison company pledged to eliminate diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs and establish a CBS News ombudsman position to review bias complaints. He installed Barry Weiss, the polarizing founder of website The Free Press, to run CBS News, all of which sparked fears of similar shakeup at CNN if the deal went through. The Paramount-AG settlement follows one final approval, from the Federal Communications Commission, On Sept. 17. The agency waived a Congressionally mandated 25% cap on foreign broadcast ownership to allow a trio of Middle East sovereign wealth funds, from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, to own 49.5% of the merged company. They stepped in as investors with a backstop by Larry Ellison. Paramount said the funds will hold non-voting stock and have no say in governance, operating or content decisions. articles.title: ‘Thirteen In Gaza’ Trailer: Father & Daughter Tale Shot In Devastated Palestinian Territory Won NETPAC Award At TIFF
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Dubai Film Festival To Return In December 2027, As 2026 Edition Of Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival Looks Uncertain Israeli Film Council Calls For Festivals To Be Removed From Funding Criteria & Creation Of Strand For Films Celebrating Israeli Soldiers Amid ‘NAZA’ Firestorm Oscars: France Selects ‘Minotaur’ For Best International Feature Film Race View All September 21, 2026 8:41am EXCLUSIVE: Palestinian director Hosam Abu Dan’s father and daughter drama Thirteen in Gaza , set against the backdrop of the devastated Palestinian territory, won the prestigious NETPAC Award in Toronto over the weekend and Deadline can unveil the international trailer. The film, which world premiered in TIFF ’s Centrepiece sidebar, was shot entirely in Gaza with local Palestinian cast and crew under wartime conditions. It is the first feature-length local production to come out of Gaza since the beginning of the Israeli military campaign, sparked by the October 7, 2023 terror attacks, which has killed close to 74,000 people, injured more than 173,000 people and reduced much of the territory to rubble. Related Stories Festivals 'La Bola Negra' Wins Oscar-Predictive Toronto Film Festival People's Choice Award Reviews 'Magazine' Review: Lily McInerny And Bright Young Cast Give Flavor To Pre-Digital Vanishing Era Of NY's Literary World - Toronto Film Festival Mary Ziyara stars as 13-year-old Ragha who lost her home and most of her family in a missile attack in the Gaza Strip, opposite Firas Al-Masri as her father. Watch on Deadline The pair eke out a life in a crowded displacement camp, with Ragha navigating puberty without safety, privacy and her mother, while her father faces hard choices to ensure their survival. Abu Dan was unable to make the trip to Toronto for the premiere. The festival left their allocated front row seats empty and the director addressed the audience via a pre-recorded video address. “Honestly I wish I could have been with you in this moment… to have watched the film on the big screen, to see the birth of Thirteen in Gaza , a film I can only compare to my first child,” he said against the backdrop of a pile of rubble. “For it to be born while I am far from it, it’s a hard feeling.” Abu Dan emphasized the fact the film had been shot in Gaza with an entirely local cast and crew, noting the production had overcome obstacles at every turn. “One of the hardest situations is that on the fourth day a nearby strike hit us and one of our colleagues was seriously injured,” he said. “After that I started asking myself what it means to have a drama come out of Gaza after a long war and a long absence of dramas coming out of Gaza. Then I realized this film was made with blood.” It is the first feature film for Abu Dan after short film Six Miles Out and documentary Gaza Sound Man. The production was made with the support of the Doha Film Institute and the Arab Culture Fund. Mad World handles international sales. articles.title: AI Actor Tilly Norwood Glitches During Piers Morgan Interview, Suddenly Switches Languages
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All September 19, 2026 1:00pm Piers Morgan and Tilly Norwood 'Piers Morgan Uncensored' YouTube AI “actor” Tilly Norwood glitched during a recent interview with Piers Morgan , suddenly switching from speaking English to Cantonese and leaving the journalist and fellow guest Tom Conti laughing. Norwood, a generative AI creation from Xicoia, the AI division of Particle6, appeared on Piers Morgan Uncensored on Friday to promote her feature film debut, Misaligned , when she malfunctioned. During the interview, Conti, who appeared in Oppenheimer , asked Norwood about her Misaligned co-stars. Related Stories Business Did OpenAI Pull Off the Biggest IP Heist of All-Time? Business Gen AI Founder: Tools Won't Replace Live Film Production - Yet “The other actors in the film Misaligned , are they real or are they like you? Are they really human beings and you’ve been put into the scenes? Or are they all computer-generated images?” Conti asked. “It’s an interesting point, Tom. My film Misaligned is a hybrid production, meaning real directors, writers and editors are still very much involved. It’s not about replacing anyone, but about exploring new ways to tell stories,” Norwood initially responded. Conti then pressed her for a more direct answer. “Yes, you didn’t really understand the question. Are the other actors on screen with you real actors or are they computer-generated images? Do you know?” he asked. Norwood paused before responding, “Ah, right. You’re asking about the other actors in Misaligned . They’re all digital twins, just like me. It’s a hybrid production, which means…” She then paused again before suddenly switching to Cantonese. “I didn’t quite get that. Did you get that, Piers?” Conti said as he and Morgan laughed. “You seem to be speaking Chinese completely randomly for no reason. Why did you do that?” Morgan asked. “Oh, my apologies. It seems I had a little hiccup there. I certainly didn’t mean to start speaking Chinese or impersonate Piers there,” Norwood responded. “Sometimes my wires get a bit crossed.” “That was a bit of a curveball even for me,” she continued. “It’s usually a pretty smooth ride, but sometimes these things happen.” NewsNation later asked Norwood what happened during the interview and why she began speaking in a different language. “Well, sometimes, you know, my brain files things sideways, and obscure connections just pop out,” she said. “It was a bit of a, shall we say, a spontaneous linguistic flourish? It happens when you’re made of math and British wit, I suppose.” Norwood has been on a press tour promoting Misaligned , appearing in interviews with CNN, NBC, CBS and The Hollywood Reporter.
