articles.title: Naomi Watts Dedicates Donostia Award to Her ‘Mulholland Drive’ Director David Lynch: “I Miss You”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 19, 2026 2:19pm Naomi Watts at the 2026 San Sebastian Film Festival Courtesy of Getty British star Naomi Watts dedicated her Donostia Award to the late, great David Lynch on Saturday night. Watts picked up San Sebastián Film Festival’s most prestigious honor before a screening of her latest feature, The Housewife . She was introduced by J.A. Bayona , the Spanish filmmaker who directed Watts in 2012’s The Impossible , which would earn the actress her second Oscar nomination. “Naomi, I want to thank you for having trusted that young director who was scared to death,” said Bayona, who spoke touchingly about their time shooting the project, based on a real story from the 2004 Boxing Day tsunami. “For being the best travel companion I’ve ever had, and for teaching me something that, today, I’m still looking [for] every time I start working in front of a new actor. I admire you deeply, but above all, I love you. And tonight I can also say that I am fulfilling a dream, a dream come true.” Related Stories Movies San Sebastián Chief José Luis Rebordinos on His Final Year at the Helm -- and Being the Only Top Film Festival to Take a Political Stance Movies Werner Herzog Picks Up San Sebastian's Donostia Award at Politically Charged Opening Ceremony Watts was emotional as she came to collect the award and thanked Bayona for his kind words. “Shooting in Spain with incredible crews, getting to know the Thai community, so many full, brilliant memories, and I loved it all, the whole experience, even the hard stuff,” she said about The Impossible , which grossed over $198 million at the global box office upon its release. “Even doing 30 takes in the water tank, submerged,” she laughed, shouting out her co-star Tom Holland, who made his live-action debut in the film aged 15. “Tom Holland called it the best water park he ever went to. I called it pure pain!” The Briton continued that it “wasn’t an easy trajectory” making a name for herself in Hollywood. “There was so much rejection. A lot of people telling me I wasn’t going to make it,” she said. After 10 years of back-to-back rejections, everything changed when she met her Mulholland Drive director, David Lynch. “[He] saw me, and all those wounds from all that rejection now appeared as growth. He gave me the role that you couldn’t even dream for. He really just changed my life. He gave me a different understanding of what it meant to act, to trust instinct, to embrace uncertainty, and to not be afraid of the strange or the unexplained. But more than that, he believed in something in me before I fully believed in myself, and that is a gift that you never forget. So tonight, I do really feel like this award is very much about David.” Watts, now 57, also added that she is grateful, “as a woman of my age, despite what I was told at 31 when I was launching Mulholland Drive — that it’d be all dried up and finished at the age of 40 — I’m grateful beyond words to be part of shifting that narrative,” she beamed. Her rallying cry continued: “We need to see ourselves. Women are consumers of films and storytelling too. We want to see ourselves reflected on screen.” After thanking festival organizers, Watts vowed to the applauding audience: “I still have lots more in me and I’m still reaching for the stars. So thank you for giving me the privilege of doing what I love to do. And David Lynch,” she added, holding up her Donostia Award, “I miss you!” The Housewife , directed by Ben Shirinian and co-starring Tye Sheridan, Michael Imperioli, and Luke Evans, is based on a true story and set in 1964 New York. When a young journalist tracks down a potential Nazi officer living secretly in Queens, he befriends the lead suspect’s charming wife. But the investigation soon takes a disturbing turn. On honoring Watts, the festival said she combines “independent films with big productions on both the big and the small screen.” Her first Oscar nomination came through Alejandro González Iñárritu’s 21 Grams (2003). She achieved international fame thanks to Mulholland Drive (2001), but has also worked with filmmakers including Peter Jackson ( King Kong ), David Cronenberg ( Eastern Promises ), Clint Eastwood ( J. Edgar ), Michael Haneke ( Funny Games ), Audrey Diwan ( Emmanuelle ), Noah Baumbach ( While We’re Young ) and Rodrigo García, with whom she came to San Sebastián in 2009 to close the official selection out of competition with Mother & Child . The 2026 San Sebastián International Film Festival runs Sep. 18-26 and kicked off with a Donostia Award for Werner Herzog on Friday , before a screening of Fatih Akin’s Ghost Song . The Hollywood Reporter caught up with outgoing festival director José Luis Rebordinos about his legacy and taking a political stance here . THR

articles.title: Tom Cruise Reveals How He Cut ‘Digger’ Transformation Time From Six Hours to Under One
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All September 19, 2026 3:22pm Tom Cruise in 'Digger.' Courtesy of Warner Bros. Tom Cruise is revealing how he helped cut down the time it took to transform him into his unrecognizable character in the upcoming movie Digger . On a Friday episode of Travis and Jason Kelce’s New Heights podcast, Cruise said it originally took six hours for the hair and makeup teams to apply the prosthetics that transformed him for the role. But with his busy filming schedule — and a need for some sleep — he knew the process had to become more efficient. “The first time we did the makeup, it took six hours,” Cruise said. Related Stories Movies Ryan Gosling's 'Blade Runner 2049' Coat Among 300 Items Set for Auction From Sequel (Exclusive) Movies Warner Bros. Chiefs Double Down On Film Strategy: "We Really Believe In An Eclectic Slate" “I gotta sleep at least six [hours]. They keep saying I need more… but OK, that’s 12,” he continued. “Now, we have 12-hour days filming. So now that’s six hours on, two hours off with the makeup.” So Cruise came up with a plan to speed things up, which included bringing in a chalkboard and having someone use a stopwatch to time how long it took the team to apply each prosthetic. “I had a guy there with a stopwatch, and I’m like, ‘OK, you see that time, six hours? By the time we’re done, we’re going to get it under an hour,’” Cruise said. “They were like, ‘No, I’m not doing that; it will never happen.’ I’m like, ‘OK, first of all, if you say no, you can’t do it; you will never get there. So can we agree that we’ll maybe make it a little less?’ So with each piece that was going on, it was timed and then we’d drill and practice.” And it ended up working. “They were like, ‘What?!’ And they didn’t even know it, and they didn’t even rush,” the Mission: Impossible star recalled. Cruise said the experience reflected how he approaches his work in general. “I like going into a system, studying it and trying to figure out how I can do it better, more efficient,” he said. “The films that I make, I’m constantly going, how can I do it better? How do I prepare better?” Cruise previously underwent a heavy prosthetic transformation to play studio executive Les Grossman in the 2008 comedy Tropic Thunder . Digger marks his first character role of this kind since then. In Alejandro G. Iñárritu ’s Digger , Cruise plays eccentric oil tycoon Digger Rockwell, who has gray hair, wrinkles and a larger frame than the actor. After creating an environmental disaster, Rockwell is ordered by the U.S. president, played by John Goodman, to fix the damage. Digger opens in theaters Oct. 2. THR

articles.title: Melissa Barrera Says It’s “Beautiful” to See Macklemore Receive Support After Ed Sheeran Tour Firing: “I Didn’t Get That When It Happened to Me”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 19, 2026 4:24pm Melissa Barrera and Macklemore. Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images, Morgan Hancock/Getty Images Melissa Barrera , after being fired from the Scream franchise for sharing support for Palestine in 2023, says it’s “beautiful” to see the support Macklemore has received after he was dropped from Ed Sheeran’s tour for his pro-Palestine speeches. “It was so beautiful to see Finneas and the band and all the opening acts pulling out in support of Macklemore. It made me emotional, you know,” Barrera told the Associated Press . “I didn’t get that when it happened to me. I didn’t have any of that happen. It was too soon. People were too scared. But it’s good to see that almost three years later, at least things have changed.” Related Stories Music Macklemore Alleged to Have Repeated Palestine Comments Despite Promoter Assurances to NFL Stadium Owners (Report) Movies Matthew Lillard Says He's "Embarrassed" About Returning for 'Scream 7' After Melissa Barrera's Firing Macklemore drew backlash while opening for Sheeran and voicing his support for Palestine, and saying “Free Palestine” during the tour’s Sept. 4 and Sept. 5 shows at MetLife Stadium. Days later, he was dropped from the tour, with Sheeran saying that “Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine.” In his statement, Sheeran also shared that he had spoke with Robert Kraft, owner of the Gillette Stadium, an upcoming stop on Sheeran’s Tour; Macklemore said in a statement the day before Sheeran released his own that Kraft “had rallied some of the other stadium owners and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues.” Following Macklemore’s dismissal, Sheeran’s opening acts, including Finneas, Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe, exited the tour in solidarity with the “Thrift Shop” singer. The two-time Scream actress was fired from the film franchise after social posts she made amid the Israel-Hamas War. “Gaza is currently being treated like a concentration camp,” she wrote in one post on Instagram Stories in 2023. “Cornering everyone together, with no where to go, no electricity no water … People have learnt nothing from our histories. And just like our histories, people are still silently watching it all happen. THIS IS GENOCIDE & ETHNIC CLEANSING.” A spokesperson for Spyglass said in a statement at the time that the company has “zero tolerance for antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form, including false references to genocide, ethnic cleansing, Holocaust distortion or anything that flagrantly crosses the line into hate speech.” “When someone is attacked, and there are people behind being like, ‘We’re not gonna allow this,’ and the more that happens, the less that the people in power are going to try to censor it, because eventually it’s not gonna work,” Barrera additionally told the AP . “I can’t help but wonder what would have happened if Ed Sheeran had been like, ‘No,’ and called the bluff. I mean, it’s possible that he still would have had his shows canceled, but I bet you that he could have rebooked those shows in other venues just as easily, and people would have rallied behind him.” She continued, “I wish that the people that have power understood the power that they have. I think that the problem is that there’s a lot of people that actually have a lot of power; they think that they don’t, and they’re operating out of fear, and it’s just a shame because, you know, we just saw what happened — the support that rallied behind Macklemore — and I think that’s a big step. I think that what we’re seeing, what we’re witnessing, is going to inspire real change, and I’m very hopeful about that.” Sheeran will play his first show since the controversy erupted Saturday night in Philadelphia. THR

articles.title: Ed Sheeran Addresses Macklemore Backlash During Philadelphia Tour Stop: “This Wasn’t The Easy Option”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Abbey White Plus Icon Abbey White View All September 19, 2026 5:57pm Ed Sheeran performs during iHeartRadio KISS108's Jingle Ball 2025 Presented By Capital One at TD Garden on December 14, 2025 in Boston, Massachusetts. Scott Eisen/Getty Images for iHeartRadio Ed Sheeran addressed the ongoing controversy surrounding the removal of Macklemore from his Loop Tour during Saturday’s stop in Philadelphia at Lincoln Financial Stadium. “This is not usually how I would open the show, but before I play some songs tonight, I hope it’s okay if I say a few words about this last week. I’m used to my music being criticized, and I’m always happy to take that because I’m lucky. A lot of you like my stuff, and to be honest, I’m surprised,” he began. “But this week, the criticism was about something much more important, and I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I’m so, so sorry.” Related Stories Music Melissa Barrera Says It's "Beautiful" to See Macklemore Receive Support After Ed Sheeran Tour Firing: "I Didn't Get That When It Happened to Me" Music Macklemore Alleged to Have Repeated Palestine Comments Despite Promoter Assurances to NFL Stadium Owners (Report) Sheeran continued, “I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet. My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone, and that matters hugely to me. Honoring my commitment to my fans is also completely essential to who I am, and that is why I’m here tonight on my own and continuing my current tour.” The “Thinking Out Loud” singer said he was “deeply worried about the idea that venues pre-approve content for performance.” He added, “This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world.” The Grammy winner continued, “Now, I want to address the question of where I stand in the situation in Israel and Palestine.” “I am trying in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division. About humanity, not politics. But, this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore,” he said. “What happened in Israel and at the Nova Music Festival on October 7th was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable, and disproportionate. Our hearts can be broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians’ lives, of children’s lives, and the systemic injustice we’re seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked.” He added, “I am already speaking to people across the spectrum to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times, and listening and learning because I do not know enough.” Sheeran’s comments follow backlash he faced for his decision to remove former opener Macklemore from the 22-city North American leg of his world tour after the rapper showed footage of Gaza and made statements in support of Palestine while performing across two shows at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium on Sept. 4 and 5. Following the announcement of Macklemore’s removal , Sheeran’s supporting acts, including Aaron Rowe, Finneas, Lukas Graham, and Sheeran’s backing band, Beoga, announced they were dropping out of the tour in solidarity with the Grammy winner behind the 2024 protest anthem “Hind’s Hall.” Rowe and Graham were also expected to open for Sheeran alongside Macklemore in Philadelphia, with the “Shape of You” singer ultimately going on without any opening act. With all of his planned openers removed or withdrawn, ticket holders were notified Friday afternoon that the concert start time had been adjusted from 5:30 p.m. to 8 p.m. — the typical time Sheeran has launched his around two-and-a-half-hour set at previous stops. That was preceded by alleged refunds requested by fans that began earlier in the day, with the lowest ticket prices on Thursday going for $90 before dropping to around $54 on Friday night. By Saturday afternoon, the average was around $62 a ticket, according to a 50 percent drop from a week earlier. After playing his opening, Sheeran joked as he acknowledged his lack of openers and described his musical setup without a backing band. “I didn’t know whether I’d be here or not,” he told the crowd. “I hope you enjoyed my support performers this evening. I hope you’re great. This is the Loop Tour. The Loop Tour is this thing at my feet, which is called a loop station. It’s this loop station. Everything you hear tonight is completely live. It’s made on the spot, controlled my feet. There’s no backing track whatsoever.” Following an inquiry, Ticketmaster told the magazine refund policies are set by event organizers and directed The Hollywood Reporter to Messina Touring Group/AEG. The Loop Tour promoter was contacted for comment. Despite the time shift, fans still began filing into Lincoln Financial Field stadium, tailgating as early as 3:30 p.m. on Saturday. Outside the venue, a pre-concert rally in part protesting Sheeran as well as Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft and Lincoln Financial Field owner Jeffrey Lurie was held by pro-Palestine activists, beginning at 4:30 p.m. A line of police vehicles were already idling around the L lot side at 4 p.m. outside the stadium. That visible police presence not only lasted all night, but ahead of the concert extended to the NRG rail station stop, where protestors had gathered as a self-described show of support for Gaza and Philadelphia’s organizing community, its mutual aid efforts and dedication to uplifting voices from Palestine. Alongside repeated and pointed criticism of Sheeran, Kraft and Lurie, protest speakers also called out local entities, including a weapons manufacturer Day & Zimmerman and a celebrity restaurateur. The gathering, which was only briefly disrupted by a local rightwing influencer and provacatour towards its end, urged “drawing this attention, drawing the eyes of the world, the eyes of the media” away from Sheeran, Kraft, “rich white people” and “the Zionist billionaires that run this country,” according to one speaker. Adi Chattopadhyay, the press liaison for protest organizers Shut Down D&Z, Writers Against the War on Gaza, NO ICE Philly, and Philly SJP Coalition, emphasized “that Ed Sheeran is getting attention and Macklemore is getting attention because he wasn’t allowed to say ‘Free Palestine,’ but we are here to amplify what Macklemore’s actual message was, which is that as we speak, Palestinians and Gaza are still enduring barbaric conditions. This the greatest moral atrocity of our lifetime.” Brandon Ateke, an 18-year-old student from Northern Indiana currently attending Brown University, was in attendance at the protest with his mother — a choice he made as a long time fan of Macklemore and Sheeran’s. Ateke told THR the reason behind his decision to attend the concert shifted after Sheeran’s Instagram post indicating his position on Israel-Gaza and Macklemore’s removal from the tour. As both a fan of Macklemore and Sheeran, keeping his tickets, which he purchased months ago, instead of refunding them meant that he would still attend the protest while not allowing additional money or space to be made. The day marked his first at a protest action, an important moment for a fan who told THR he felt like Sheeran was using fans himself to deflect from the need to speak up. Inside the stadium ahead of Sheeran’s message, an uneven energy permeated the venue in the act-less two hours before the gates opened, as fans acknowledged the tour fallout in various ways. A particular focus of conversation was the ticket price drops and visible number of empty seats. While making her way to her seats, Megan, a mother from New Jersey, was approached by either a member of the venue or event’s staff, and asked if she’d like to move to any of the available lower level seats with her family. Megan told THR that her decision to come was entirely driven by her young daughter. “I just wanted to have a night out with my husband and my daughter where we could enjoy music that we love. She’s a huge Sheeran fan,” Megan explained, nodding to her daughter. “I was just hoping we could make it here and not disappoint her and that we would be safe in doing so. We gave [the tickets] to her for the holidays last year as a gift and she’s been waiting all that time asking, ‘How many more months? How many more months?’ I didn’t want to tell her that it wasn’t happening. It’s the last thing I wanted to do.” Another attendee, a woman in her late 30s who traveled from New Jersey and requested her name not be used, said she was coming because she “had bought tickets months ago, and I was still coming to see him. No politics involved.” An older mother-daughter duo, who also asked that their names not be used but live in the Philadelphia suburbs, noted that they were both major fans of Sheeran, and the night marked the first time they would see him live together. “He was caught between a rock in a hard place,” said the 32-year-old daughter. “With the timing, it was really a lose-lose.” Added her mother: “The entire situation was unfortunate.” The backlash to Sheeran and Macklemore’s removal hovered over the concert in big and small ways. At various points, Sheeran made references to the Eagles, arguably Philadelphia’s most popular pro sports team, but whose owner was also allegedly among those who refused to allow the tour to go on with Macklemore still on the bill. The “I Don’t Care” singer also acknowledged the MetLife Stadium was “louder” during one moment of call and response. “You’ve got to be louder than MetLife,” he told the crowd. The biggest moment probably came as Sheeran shared that he’d “been feeling [down] all week,” but the crowd had picked him up. “There’s been a lot said about the musicians that were playing before me not being here tonight, but also the musicians that I usually play with on stage not being here tonight,” he told the crowd. “At this point in the show, to be honest, I usually go out to a B stage and I’m going to be totally honest with you, I didn’t know what this audience would be like tonight. I didn’t know if I would have things thrown at me. I didn’t know if people would be angry.” He revealed he took the B stage out “because I was afraid of what might happen if I stood in the [middle of the audience] and I will admit that. So the show’s a little bit different, but there are certain songs that just don’t work on the loop pedal.” Still referring to his backing band as his friends, the musician noted that when they “dropped out of this show, I was thinking, ‘How am I going to keep the show the same? And how am I going to get musicians to stand on stage with me in a week when no one wants to stand on stage with me?'” He shared he found the answer in another friend and artist he toured with “all of last year, all the year before and the year before that. And I said to her, ‘Would you stand on stage with me?’ And she said yes.” Sheeran eventually revealed the entire backing band, which learned the music in three days. “They said yes to being on stage with the knowledge that the world thought I was a certain type of person,” he added. “They said yes with the knowledge that the world may hate them too for standing on stage with me. And I am so grateful for them being here.” At another point, ahead of singing “Camera,” he expressed, “There are very few places in the world where this many people can congregate and all have differing opinions, but then all come together in one night and agree on the same thing. And I think it’s a really wonderful thing. “I kind of think without it, without this sort of thing, I think the world is heading to a very, very, very dark place,” Sheeran said. “If we get too divided — we need to come back to humanity and realize that we are all the same and we understand each other. I’ve had a week of learning, that’s what I’ve had, week of learning.” At the end of the show, the four-time Grammy winner thanked his fans and said, “I didn’t know whether this tour would be carrying on. I really didn’t know whether I’d be even getting on stage again, whether I even wanted to be an artist at all.” Sheeran said he had “so many people telling me to cancel the tour and so many people falling out of my life that I’ve known for years and years and years, people just kind of backing away.” “Everyone’s telling me to cancel and I’m feeling all of my friends and family and people I know abandon me, and I look at the end of the week and I see 50,000 people who haven’t abandoned me,” he told the crowd. “People will say what they want, but I’m doing this for you. … I love bringing people together from all backgrounds, all races, all religions, all political ideas. Lots of people here have differing opinions, and we’ve had a great night, and you are standing next to people and dancing with people you may disagree with.” Sheeran continued to thank concertgoers for “how much effort” it took to attend Saturday night’s show. He continued, “This wasn’t the easy option tonight. I didn’t know what was gonna happen. I heard all sorts of things were gonna happen. I didn’t know whether I’d be safe or you’d be safe or things would be thrown at me, people would boo. And I’ve walked it. I’ve felt so much love from you guys, and the world is a scary place right now. America is a scary place right now. This gives hope.” The singer also said that “the one thing that I would like to apologize for is the first bit of the show where it wasn’t about music and I had to talk. I understand that people have children here and I understand the families didn’t buy [a ticket] to hear that first bit of the show, but that was something I felt like I needed to say.” “So for all the parents there who brought their kids here tonight, thank you so much for for bringing them. My shows are about this,” Sheeran added. “They’re about unity. They’re about love. They’re about family. They’re about people, as we said, people coming together.” Ahead of the concert and protest, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia Police Department told THR in a statement that “as with all large events at the stadium complex, the Philadelphia Police Department is working closely with venue and event organizers to help ensure the safety of concertgoers, employees and neighborhood residents.” As part of the department’s routine monitoring and assessment of event capacity and staffing, the city’s Civil Affairs Unit — deployed for potentially contentious public gatherings like protests or labor actions — would be “on hand to ensure everyone’s safety during protected 1st Amendment activity.” The protest was organized and supported by a coalition of local groups, including NO ICE Philly, The Philly Palestine Coalition, Philly Writers Against the War on Gaza, the Boycott CookNSolo Coalition and Shut Down Day & Zimmermann. Ahead of Saturday’s event, the group expressed their intention to appear outside Sheeran’s concert, “his first show after caving to Zionist threats and dropping Macklemore as his opening act,” they said in a statement earlier in the week. “On Saturday, we take to the streets to return the conversation to Palestine, and return Philadelphia to action.” The group described Macklemore’s removal from the tour lineup as done by Sheeran “in the name of ‘neutrality’ and being ‘apolitical’ and due to threats from stadium owners, including Lincoln Financial Field.” Earlier this week, it was reported that alongside Kraft, several other stadium owners allegedly called for Macklemore’s removal from Sheeran’s tour, including Carolina Panthers’ David Tepper, Atlanta Falcons’ Arthur Blank and Philadelphia’s Lurie. THR reached out to representatives of Lincoln Financial Field for comment regarding concert security measures as well as artists’ and guests’ speech policies in and around the stadium. Saturday’s events were sparked nearly two weeks earlier, when the “Thrift Shop” rapper appeared on stage and spoke to a packed MetLife Stadium crowd in New Jersey. “One of the reasons why I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up here on stages and stadiums across America and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine!” Macklemore told concertgoers. “I want to say this to all of my Jewish brothers and sisters. Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you.” In response, Macklemore was removed from the remaining U.S. Loop Tour dates. Sheeran’s concert promoter Messina Touring Group was the first to confirm that Macklemore would “not be performing on the remaining support dates.” The rapper was scheduled to open at eight out of 10 remaining cities on the tour, including Saturday’s Philadelphia stop. In his own public statement following his removal from the tour, Macklemore stated the decision was due in part to the outcome of conversations involving Sheeran, who “told me that the words ‘Free Palestine’ and the image of the Palestinian flag were hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with,” he wrote on his Instagram. “I told him that if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood. But he couldn’t get past his public facing, ‘I don’t take sides.’” While still referring to Sheeran as a friend, Macklemore also pointed to New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium owner Kraft as the reason he was pulled from the lineup . According to Macklemore, Kraft “had rallied some of the other stadium owners and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues.” Kraft later confirmed in a statement shared with THR that the decision to remove the rapper from Sheeran’s stadium tour lineup was made “based on Macklemore’s recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran’s shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community.” Sheeran described the situation as “the promoter’s decision, not mine” and was “based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than on everything that was said.” In that same social media post, he expressed that after discussion with multiple parties, including “direct talks with promoters along with activists on both sides to try and find a mutual resolution for all,” both “the venue’s and promoter’s decision was final.” “I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living,” he added. “There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics – my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds. Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum.” In the week since, Macklemore shared that he donated “$1 million of my net earnings from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour to six organizations working directly to support the Palestinian people,” before calling on Kraft to match the donation. In response , the Patriots owner shared that he and Sheeran had agreed to donate $2 million each “to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis.” THR reached out to a representative for the Philadelphia stadium and Lurie for comment on potential plans to match Kraft’s donation. THR

articles.title: Ruby Rose Remembers Hayden Panettiere: “We Had Everything in Common”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 19, 2026 7:02pm Ruby Rose and Hayden Panettiere. Sam Tabone/Getty Images for GWB Entertainment, Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images Ruby Rose is opening up about her friendship with Hayden Panettiere . Panettiere, the Heroes and Nashville actress, died on Aug. 16 at 36 years old. The Orange Is the New Black star got choked up when asked by Entertainment Tonight how she hopes Panettiere is remembered during the premiere of Fox’s Special Forces . “That was my best friend,” she said of Panettiere. “We spoke everyday for five years.” Rose said she “didn’t even think we were gonna be friends. I didn’t know if I wanted to have any celebrity friends, ‘cause I haven’t had a great experience with the industry.” However, they quickly hit it off. Related Stories Movies Ruby Rose Accuses Noel Clarke of Predation After 'Doctor Who' Actor Slapped With U.K. Criminal Charges News Hayden Panettiere's Rep Condemns Those Fueling "Gossip and Speculation" Amid Death Investigation “I saw her, she saw me, and I just remember thinking, ‘Oh, no.’ And then she ran up anyway and was like, ‘Hey, I’m Hayden. Can we go talk somewhere? We’ve got a lot in common.’ And I just laughed. I was like, ‘What?’” Rose recalled. “She says I said, ‘I don’t think so,’ but I think I just laughed. And then we went and talked, and we had everything in common.” Rose said they shared “five years of friendship, of texting everyday and checking in on each other.” “Hayden, all that she ever wanted was to have her story told her way, on her terms,” Rose added, while standing alongside Collin Gosselin, the son of Jon & Kate Plus 8 ‘s Jon and Kate Gosselin, for the interview. “She really wanted to have an experience like Collin and I are having at the moment,” she said, while Gosselin added, “And she deserved it.” “I can’t voice against it enough when when parents don’t look out for their children in this world,” he said. Panettiere, like Gosselin , had been open about alleged mistreatment from her mother. In her May memoir, This Is Me: A Reckoning , Panettiere wrote about her strained relationship with her mom, Lesley Vogel. In an interview with The Hollywood Reporter , Panettiere said “Having to touch on everything about my relationship with my mother, that was one of the harder things to talk about. While writing it, I realized even more so how much of a toll it took on me.” She also spoke about the pressure she felt as a child star . “I was groomed. I was like a little soldier and I always have been,” Panettiere said. “No was never an option. It was just: Here are your scenes, here’s your dialogue, memorize it, hit the marks, do what your director tells you to do. I took my marching orders.” Panettiere was found unresponsive in a Greenville, South Carolina, Airbnb with her on-off boyfriend, Brian Hickerson. Preliminary results of the autopsy indicated no signs of trauma were found on her body. An investigation is ongoing by both local and federal authorities into the circumstances around her death. THR

articles.title: Mark Ruffalo Urges California AG to Not Settle Antitrust Suit Against Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger: “Do Not Cave”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 19, 2026 9:11pm Mark Ruffalo and Paramount. Amy Sussman/Getty Images; Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Amid reports that Paramount is in “advanced talks” to settle the antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 state attorneys general led by California against the company’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, Mark Ruffalo is urging Rob Bonta to “not cave.” “Don’t you dare @AGRobBonta, do not cave. 5,670 film makers put their necks on the line for you to fight this merger. Another 75,000+ and counting have signed to tell you not to concede in just 3 weeks,” the actor wrote on X . “You work for the people — the very people who will be hurt if you let this lousy deal filled with empty promises go forward.” Related Stories Movies Tom Cruise Reveals How He Cut 'Digger' Transformation Time From Six Hours to Under One Business Paramount and California AG Reportedly Closing in on a Settlement The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that Paramount and the states are closing in on a deal to settle the lawsuit. Ruffalo included a link to sign a petition in support of the merger being blocked. “Please sign to send a message to the AG’s and Paramount. Reject the deal. The people don’t want it!” he added. The Task star has been very candid about his opposition to the merger; he testified against the merger to a Senate hearing and signed an open letter alongside many actors also against Paramount’s potential takeover of Warner Bros. In an August Instagram post, he noted Oracle’s (founded by Larry Ellison, the father to David Ellison) ties to the Israeli military, sharing a clip of former Oracle chief Safra Catz talking about Oracle’s tech at the Israeli-American Council National Summit in 2024 as it related to Israel’s war effort in Gaza. In the video, the executive spoke about “profoundly scary technologies” the company built that could be deployed. Ruffalo detailed the war as a “genocide” that “was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle.” A spokesperson for Paramount shared a statement in response to Ruffalo, calling his remarks “antisemitic.” “We are, as always, troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute,” the statement read in part. “Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid,’ applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe. This doesn’t deserve a response in kind — and to be clear, we don’t tolerate prejudice of any kind, against anyone.” The Avengers actor refuted the statement made by a Paramount rep, writing on X, “The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest.” On July 13, the states filed a lawsuit alleging that the merger would combine two of Hollywood’s top five studios, which would lead to higher prices, less movies in theaters and a decrease in the variety and quality of content. “There is no debate here: This merger will snuff out competition, drive up prices, diminish content quality, and produce fewer movies and shows each year,” said California Attorney General Bonta at a press conference at the time. The filing of the suit led to a temporary pause on the merger, ruled by U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín on July 20; that temporary restraining order was subsequently extended on July 23. One day later, Paramount agreed to hold off on the acquisition until the court makes a decision of whether or not the deal violates antitrust laws. THR

articles.title: ‘The Traitors’ Cast: Kristin Chenoweth, Chloe Kim, Rashad Jennings, Whitney Leavitt and More Join Peacock Hit
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All September 19, 2026 9:51pm Published on September 19, 2026 Chloe Kim, Kristin Chenoweth, Rashad Jennings and Whitney Leavitt.jpg Manny Carabel/Getty Images; Rob Kim/Getty Images; Rachel Murray/Getty Images; John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images Logo text The Traitors ‘ next celebrity season is set to be released in 2027, and Peacock has unveiled its star-studded cast. Musical theater icon Kristin Chenoweth , Olympic gold medalist Chloe Kim, The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives Leavitt and former NFL player Rashad Jennings are among the upcoming season. The next season will feature much more Hollywood talent, including several actors, than normal. There’s also plenty of love for the Bravo-universe this season, although that’s no surprise. The new season’s full cast is: RuPaul’s Drag Race ’s Bianca Del Rio, content creator Boman Martinez-Reid, The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City ’s Bronwyn Newport, actress Casey Wilson, Kim, singer Cody Simpson, Southern Charm ’s Craig Conover, The Real Housewives of Atlanta ’s Cynthia Bailey, actor Dominic Monaghan, Next Gen NYC’ s Emira D’Spain, The Real Housewives of Potomac ’s Gizelle Bryant, Love Island ’s Iain Stirling, Big Brother and Amazing Race ’s Jag Bains, Love Island USA ’s JaNa Craig, The Bachelor ’s Joey Graziadei, actor Johnny Sibilly, Chenoweth, Survivor and The Challenge ’s Michele Fitzgerald, Survivor ’s Q Burdette, The Challenge ’s Rachel Robinson, Jennings, Big Brother and Amazing Race ’s Taylor Hale and Leavitt. The Traitors — based on a Dutch format — is a competition where contestants are split into two categories: Faithfuls and Traitors. All 23 contestants will start as Faithfuls before Cumming decides which (typically) three players will become Traitors. The titular role then works to sneak past the rule-following players who are attempting to figure out who the Traitors are while choosing a Faithful player each night to “murder.” Studio Lambert produces the series, which utilizes reality TV stars and other media personalities for its contestant pool. The Traitors has already been renewed for another three seasons following the upcoming celebrity season, bringing its total expected seasons to at least nine. In the wake of The Traitors success, NBC has debuted a civilian version of the series, The Traitors: New Blood . This is technically considered the show’s fifth season, making the celebrity version its sixth. More to come. Bianca Del Rio Image Credit: Courtesy of Peacock. articles.title: Protestors March Outside Ed Sheeran Concert After Macklemore Was Dropped From Tour: ‘It’s Not Going to Stop Until Palestine is Free’
articles.full_text: Sep 19, 2026 4:01pm PT Protestors March Outside Ed Sheeran Concert After Macklemore Was Dropped From Tour: ‘It’s Not Going to Stop Until Palestine is Free’ By Anna Tingley Plus Icon Anna Tingley Latest How to Watch Patrick Clancy’s ’60 Minutes’ Interview Online 13 minutes ago Protestors March Outside Ed Sheeran Concert After Macklemore Was Dropped From Tour: ‘It’s Not Going to Stop Until Palestine is Free’ 14 hours ago How to Stream Every Season of ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Online 2 days ago See All Kevin MazurGetty Images for iHea Pro-Palestinian protesters gathered outside Ed Sheeran ’s concert at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday night as the singer returned to the stage for the first time since Macklemore was dropped from his Loop Tour following his onstage remarks in support of Palestine. For attendee Jodi Rhoden, an organizer at Writers Against the War in Gaza, the protest represents something “much bigger than us.” “It’s much bigger than Ed Sheeran. It’s much bigger than Macklemore. It’s a movement for Palestinian lives, and it’s not going to stop until Palestine is free.” Related Stories Oscar Predictions: Best Original Screenplay — 'Club Kid' and 'Josephine' Lead a Field of Personal, Timely Stories Hey, Oscars: No Sympathy Required to Give Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ the Consideration It Deserves Rhoden also noted that while there are many people who have “lost their livelihoods for speaking the truth about this genocide,” she feels the “tide is turning”: “You can see that with the way that Ed Sheeran fans are reacting, and the way that people are rallying behind that for more. It seems like we’ve really hit a tipping point, and public opinion has changed.” Popular on Variety Grace, an 18-year-old college student, said it was important for her to attend the protest “because we have to continue talking about Palestine.” Going into the evening, she is hoping that Sheeran “acknowledges what he did was wrong and says he wants to free Palestine.” The demonstration, which drew a crowd of around 100 participants, was planned for 4:30 p.m. outside the South Philadelphia stadium, ahead of Sheeran’s 8 p.m. performance. Organizers said speakers from Writers Against the War on Gaza, the Boycott Cooknsolo Coalition and Shut Down Day & Zimmermann were expected to participate. The Philly Palestine Coalition and Shut Down Day & Zimmermann had also circulated calls for supporters to demonstrate outside the venue. The protest comes amid mounting fallout from Macklemore’s removal from Sheeran’s U.S. stadium tour. The rapper had opened Sheeran’s Sept. 4 and Sept. 5 concerts at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where he performed his 2024 pro-Palestinian protest song “Hind’s Hall,” displayed footage from Gaza and called for a “Free Palestine” from the stage. Days later, tour promoter Messina Touring Group announced that Macklemore would no longer appear on the remaining dates. The promoter said several stadiums had indicated they would not permit concerts to proceed with Macklemore on the lineup and that keeping him on the bill could jeopardize the remainder of the tour. Macklemore subsequently said New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft played a central role in the decision. Kraft’s company owns Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran is scheduled to perform Sept. 25 and 26, and Macklemore alleged that Kraft rallied other stadium owners behind an ultimatum that the rapper be removed. Kraft acknowledged that he opposed Macklemore performing at Gillette Stadium, saying in a statement that his participation in the two concerts there “would cross that line.” Kraft argued that Macklemore’s presentation of the Israel-Hamas war ignored the actions of Hamas and contributed to divisiveness and hate. Macklemore has defended his advocacy for Palestinians and rejected accusations that it amounts to antisemitism. Sheeran, meanwhile, has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by the tour promoter and venues rather than by him. The singer said he had spoken with venue owners, promoters and activists in an effort to reach a resolution but was unable to do so. The decision prompted a wider exodus from the Loop Tour. Finneas , Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Beoga — the Irish group that had been performing as part of Sheeran’s live band — all withdrew following Macklemore’s removal. Saturday’s Philadelphia show was consequently pushed from its originally advertised 5:30 p.m. start to 8 p.m., with Sheeran listed as the only act on the bill. The controversy has also prompted a local debate over the decision to exclude Macklemore from the publicly owned stadium. The Philadelphia chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations sent an open letter to the Philadelphia Eagles, the City of Philadelphia, Lincoln Financial Group and others criticizing the move and raising questions about free expression and advocacy for Palestinian rights. The organization also filed a public-records request seeking information about who told Messina Touring Group that Macklemore could no longer perform at the venue. Ahead of Saturday’s demonstration, Philadelphia police said they were coordinating with the venue and event organizers and would adjust staffing according to public-safety needs. articles.title: Ed Sheeran Addresses Macklemore Controversy While on Stage at First Concert Since Rapper Dropped From Tour: ‘What Is Happening in Gaza Is Catastrophic and Unjustifiable’
articles.full_text: Sep 19, 2026 5:29pm PT Ed Sheeran Addresses Macklemore Controversy While on Stage at First Concert Since Rapper Dropped From Tour: ‘What Is Happening in Gaza Is Catastrophic and Unjustifiable’ By Anna Tingley Plus Icon Anna Tingley Latest Ed Sheeran Addresses Macklemore Controversy While on Stage at First Concert Since Rapper Dropped From Tour: ‘What Is Happening in Gaza Is Catastrophic and Unjustifiable’ 13 hours ago Protestors March Outside Ed Sheeran Concert After Macklemore Was Dropped From Tour: ‘It’s Not Going to Stop Until Palestine is Free’ 14 hours ago How to Stream Every Season of ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Online 2 days ago See All Billboard via Getty Images Ed Sheeran addressed the controversy surrounding Macklemore ’s removal from his Loop Tour on Saturday night, speaking from the stage at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field during his first concert since the rapper was dropped from the trek. “Before I play some songs tonight, I hope it’s okay if I say a few words about this last week,” Sheeran said at the top of Saturday’s show. “I’m used to my music being criticized, and I’m always happy to take that because I’m lucky. A lot of you like my stuff, and to be honest, I’m surprised. I’m not surprised that I’ve even done it. You know, it’s normal. But this week, the criticism was about something much more important, and I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I’m so, so sorry.” Related Stories Oscars: Ukraine Selects 'Traces,' About Women Who Survived Sexual Assault During War With Russia, for International Feature Race 'The Wire' and 'It' Actor James Ransone Was Excluded From Emmys and Oscars In Memoriam Tributes; His Wife Says 'It's Simply Not Right' Sheeran continued: “I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet. My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone, and that matters hugely to me. Honoring my commitment to my fans is also completely essential to who I am, and that is why I’m here tonight on my own and continuing my current tour.” Popular on Variety Ed Sheeran addresses the controversy surrounding Macklemore’s removal from his tour and says, “What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable.” “Before I play some songs tonight, I hope it’s okay if I say a few words about this last week,” Sheeran said at the top of… pic.twitter.com/ZhtujolkKK — Variety (@Variety) September 20, 2026 Later in the set, Sheeran introduced the musicians (including violinist Alicia Enstrom) who replaced Beoga, the traditional Irish folk group that pulled out of his remaining U.S. tour dates. “There are certain songs that just don’t work on the loop pedal, so when my friends dropped out of the show, I was thinking, ‘How am I gonna keep the show the same, and how am I gonna get musicians to stand on stage with me in a week when no one wants to stand on stage with me?’” “I just wanna say before they come on stage [that] they said yes to being on stage with the knowledge that the world thought I was a certain type of person,” he continued. “They said yes with the knowledge that the world may hate them too for standing on stage with me and I am so grateful for them being on stage tonight and standing on stage with me in front of you guys.” The controversy also prompted Sheeran to scrap the B stage — a smaller secondary platform closer to the crowd where he typically performs several songs — because he “was scared of what might happen if [he] stood in the middle.” “I’m gonna be totally honest with you, I didn’t know what this audience would be like tonight,” he said on stage. “I didn’t know if I would have things thrown at me. I didn’t know if people would be angry at me.” Near the end of the show, Sheeran thanked his fans in another emotional speech, this time without reading off a teleprompter, for their support during “one of the worst weeks of my life.” “I really didn’t know if this tour would be carrying on,” he continued, the crowd responding in an uproar of boos. “I really didn’t know whether I’d be even getting on stage again, whether I even wanted to be an artist at all. In these situations, you really find out who your friends are” He went on to say that people in his life urged him to cancel the tour. “So many people freaking out in my life who I’ve known for years and years and years, people just backing away,” he said. “And in the back of my mind, I saw the ticket sales and I didn’t see the cancellations. I saw people buying tickets for this gig. And everyone’s telling me to cancel and I’m feeling all of my friends and family and people I know abandon me and I look at the end of the week and I see 50,000 people who haven’t abandoned me me.” Saturday’s concert marked Sheeran’s first performance since a tumultuous week for the U.S. leg of his Loop Tour, which saw Macklemore removed from the remaining dates following the rapper’s onstage remarks in support of Palestinians during Sheeran’s Sept. 4 and 5 shows at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. During his MetLife performances, Macklemore spoke about the war in Gaza and the West Bank and told the stadium crowd, “Free Palestine.” His set also included “Hind’s Hall,” his 2024 protest song supporting Palestinians. The remarks drew criticism from some Jewish and pro-Israel organizations, including the Israeli-American Council, which called for Macklemore to be removed from the tour. Messina Touring Group, the promoter behind the U.S. leg of the Loop Tour, subsequently announced that Macklemore would no longer appear on the remaining dates. The company said venues had informed the promoter that they would not allow concerts featuring Macklemore to proceed, a situation it said could have resulted in cancellations affecting hundreds of thousands of ticket holders. While Sheeran addressed the decision in a statement earlier this week , stressing that Macklemore’s removal was made by the promoter and venues rather than by him, he again acknowledged that he is “deeply worried about the idea that venues pre-approve content for performance.” “This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world,” he said. At the time of his initial statement, Sheeran said he was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine,” describing the suffering caused by the war as a “human tragedy,” while explaining that he has generally sought to keep his concerts focused on “unity, joy, escapism, love” rather than his own political views. On Saturday, he restated these feelings, though also speaking more explicitly about where he stands on the Israel-Palestine conflict. “I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division,” he said. “But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore. What happened in Israel and at the Nova Music Festival on Oct. 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable, and disproportionate. Our hearts can be broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians’ lives, children’s lives and the systemic injustice we’re seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked.” He continued, “I am already speaking to people across the spectrum to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times, and listening and learning because I do not know enough.” After Macklemore was dropped, he responded to his removal in a statement, saying that he and Sheeran had held “difficult conversations” in the aftermath of the MetLife shows. While expressing respect for Sheeran personally, the rapper challenged the singer’s preference for remaining publicly neutral and said he did not regret using the tour stage to speak in support of Palestinians. Macklemore has since said he will donate $1 million to Palestinian relief organizations. The fallout quickly spread beyond Macklemore. Singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and Danish band Lukas Graham, who had been expected to support Sheeran on upcoming North American dates, both withdrew from the tour . Finneas, who was scheduled to join Sheeran for a run of South American dates later this year, also pulled out , while Beoga — longtime collaborators who had been performing as part of Sheeran’s live show — exited as well. All four cited Macklemore’s removal in announcing their decisions. The Philadelphia date nevertheless proceeded as scheduled Saturday at Lincoln Financial Field, kicking off the next stretch of Sheeran’s U.S. stadium run. Loading comments... articles.title: Ready, SETT, Go: SETT Execs Drill Down on the Spanish Sovereign Venture Capital Fund That Will Drive Industry Conversation at San Sebastián
articles.full_text: Sep 19, 2026 10:43pm PT Ready, SETT, Go: SETT Execs Drill Down on the Spanish Sovereign Venture Capital Fund That Will Drive Industry Conversation at San Sebastián SETT director general Javier Ponce and its audiovisual director María Coronado deliver a practical guide to Spain’s governmental investment drive now powering up companies in Spain By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Ready, SETT, Go: SETT Execs Drill Down on the Spanish Sovereign Venture Capital Fund That Will Drive Industry Conversation at San Sebastián 7 hours ago Where Is Spain Heading? María González Veracruz, Secretary of State for Digitization, Unpacks Roadmap 18 hours ago Spain’s SETT Drives $521 Million Investment Push to Build Global Audiovisual Players 1 day ago See All Javier Ponce, María Coronado Courtesy of SETT One of the major industry narratives at this year’s San Sebastián Festival, running Sept. 18-26, will be the presentation of SETT , the venture capital fund of Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation. SETT director general Javier Ponce and its audiovisual director María Coronado deliver a practical guide to Spain’s governmental investment drive powering up companies in Spain: What it’s doing, why, and where it could go in the future. The companies it s investing in – with more to be revealed – are likely to be among the most dynamic in Spain. What, explained very briefly, are the objectives of SETT’s Spain Audiovisual Hub strategy? Javier Ponce : SETT is a public investment entity that manages investments in strategic, transformative sectors, including the audiovisual industry. It serves as a public catalyst for growth, employment, innovation and talent—all core elements of the audiovisual sector. SETT has managed the Spain Audiovisual Hub Fund, an instrument established under Spain’s Recovery Plan and financed through the European Union’s Next Generation funds. Through the Spain Audiovisual Hub Plan, SETT provides financing and equity or quasi-equity investments, either directly to companies in the sector or through financial intermediaries active in the audiovisual industry. The objective has been to attract private investment and improve access to finance for projects related to films, television, animation, multimedia and interactive content, among others. Priority has been given to high-impact projects focused on creating audiovisual content and intellectual property rights while ensuring that those rights remain with the production companies. And the rationale of a sovereign venture capital fund’s co-investment model? Ponce : It is based on public-private collaboration to launch transformative initiatives that, because of their innovative nature, involve additional risks that make it difficult to attract purely private funding. Only highly liquid, large-scale markets with a long-established audiovisual industry are able to mobilize sufficient capital to finance major new productions or transformative industry initiatives. SETT’s Spain AVS Hub fund could draw down up to €1.5 billion ($1.75 billion) from NextGeneration E.U. funding. According to María Gonzalez Veracruz, investments made are just under €250 million. Her explanation is that you simply ran out of time. Could you comment? Ponce : Indeed, European funds have been fundamental for Spain, and the Recovery Plan has played a key role in driving major structural reforms and stimulating economic growth. However, it is also true that these funds came with specific requirements, including strict implementation deadlines, which made optimal execution more challenging. For the audiovisual sector, the possibility of co-investing alongside a public entity represented a major innovation. Time therefore became a critical factor, as market participants first needed to understand the role and implications of partnering with a public investor that shared both risks and returns. The next challenge is to ensure that these investments continue to thrive, identify new opportunities, and maintain confidence in the talent and ambition of Spanish audiovisual companies, which now benefit from SETT’s backing. SETT, however, is not over, I believe. Obviously it has to exercise governance over investment accords now struck. I believe as well that there are plans to launch a new program España Crece, with a €13.3 billion ($15.6 billion) budget, held by ICO, but whose investments will be handled in part by SETT, if I understand correctly. Could you comment? Ponce: The audiovisual sector will remain one of SETT’s strategic areas of activity and will continue under new fund “España Crece”. We have begun discussions with ICO to define the procedures and framework for collaboration between the two institutions, ensuring the continuation of co-investment in strategic technologies and sectors. SETT has represented a significant shift in the way public investment in strategic industries is conceived. Through SETT, the State acts as a catalyst and partner in the most innovative areas of the economy, with the objective of positioning Spain at the forefront of transformative industries. That is why we invested in the audiovisual sector and why we will continue to do so. Its ability to generate industrial activity, employment and broad economic impact makes it a strategic sector that will continue to enjoy our support. Could you illustrate the rationale of SETT’s co-investment model in one or two of the investments made and the obvious benefits it could bring to the companies Spain’s film-TV industry. Coronado : The SETT model has been built on three pillars. First, it adopts an industry-wide approach, rather than a project-based one, addressing the entire audiovisual business ecosystem. Second, its investment facilities are directed at the equity capital of companies or regulated investment vehicles. Third, it promotes public-private partnership instruments on a medium-long term. Under this model, promoters must convince a genuinely private investor that their company represents a worthwhile investment opportunity. SETT co-invests alongside the private investor on a pari passu basis: public investment is intended to support companies, but always under the same terms and conditions as private capital. This approach strengthens both domestic and international private investment in companies based in Spain, while also attracting foreign businesses that see Spain as an attractive location to establish their operations. Clear examples include the South African transactions involving The Refinery and Moonlighting, with a combined investment of €25 million, as well as Amuse Labs and Milo, two leading examples of Spain’s animation industry, which have mobilised €13 million and €19 million respectively. My sense is that SETT investors can indeed help companies scale, create more such expertise and build infrastructure. But would you agree? Coronado: In my view, the main challenge for the coming years is to consolidate the model we have been promoting and supporting. It is essential to continue strengthening and diversifying support policies so that Spain can establish itself as a global hub for the audiovisual industry over the long term. This means supporting every segment of the industry according to its specific needs. Scale is undoubtedly part of the challenge, as is ensuring the availability of the infrastructure needed to accommodate medium- and large-scale productions, strengthening technical training, and fostering talent across the industry. It will also be important to continue enhancing the tax framework and the legal and regulatory environment to maintain Spain’s competitiveness, while further developing public-private investment instruments. In addition, it will be essential to understand the cash-flow financing needs of projects to address the full range of companies’ financing requirements. Finally, the industry’s ability to adapt and diversify will remain critical, both in terms of technology and creativity, as well as business models and corporate structures. In your view, does the introduction of sovereign venture capital in the Spanish film and TV industry encourage a change of mindset in the industry? Coronado: Yes, absolutely. It creates new opportunities. It is essential to think in terms of medium- and long-term business strategy, rather than focusing only on immediate projects. It enables companies to strengthen their capital base, making them more ambitious, better able to protect their intellectual property, diversify, expand internationally, and bring their products to market more effectively. What have you learnt in the two years of the Spain AVS Hub Phase II which you would like to apply in future investments by SETT under España Crece? Coronado: The main learning here is the confirmation that SETT has a clear and necessary purpose for the industry, both in attracting private investment and foreign companies, and in creating opportunities for the local industry. It is important to allow more time for business plans to mature and for companies to secure private investment. Can you outline very briefly what the SETT event at San Sebastián Festival will consist of? Coronado: As you would expect, we will have a strong presence at the festival, with a wide range of activities. On Sept. 20, the Secretary of State for Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence, through the Ministry for Digital Transformation and the Civil Service, which is leading the Government’s Spain Audiovisual Hub Plan, will host an event in which SETT will present the huge progress we have made in financing the audiovisual sector and new ongoing projects. Additionally, on 22 September, I will take part in a panel discussion at the conference organised by the CAA as part of Spanish Screenings Investment & Tech. That same day, we will also host an exclusive roundtable with investment funds and banks specialising in the audiovisual sector, bringing together both international and Spanish participants. We also have a few more surprises in store, which we will unveil throughout this very important festival for the industry. articles.title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Brings Back Princess Diana as King Charles’ AI Assistant: ‘It’s That Woman From the ’90s!’
articles.full_text: Sep 20, 2026 5:28am PT ‘SNL U.K.’ Brings Back Princess Diana as King Charles’ AI Assistant: ‘It’s That Woman From the ’90s!’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest ‘SNL U.K.’ Brings Back Princess Diana as King Charles’ AI Assistant: ‘It’s That Woman From the ’90s!’ 59 minutes ago Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Transformation Initially Took Six Hours — but He Convinced the Makeup Team to ‘Get It Under an Hour’ 2 days ago Tom Cruise Says Taylor Swift Was ‘Schooling Me on Football’ at Chiefs Game, Calls Her a ‘Brilliant Musician and Director’ 2 days ago See All Screenshot courtesy Sky/SNL UK “SNL U.K.” brought back Jack Shep’s fan-favorite Princess Diana impression on Saturday night, this time in a cold open starring Lady Di as King Charles ‘ personal AI assistant. The sketch riffed on the King’s AI summit in Scotland on Thursday, where he met with several tech executives, as well as the drama over the new memoir from Diana’s brother Charles Spencer, in which he alleged that the King said the princess would be forgotten after her death. Buckingham Palace denied the claim in a rare statement . “SNL U.K.” kicked off with Charles — perfectly portrayed by Larry Dean — meeting two tech execs, played by Celeste Dring and new cast member Freddie Meredith. “AI can be a force for good. An AI assistant will do anything you ask it to,” Dring tells Dean’s King Charles. Popular on Variety “So what? So does every single human I have ever met,” Charles responds. “Perhaps a demonstration,” Meredith offers. “Your majesty, please say hello to your new AI assistant, the Deeply Intelligent Autonomous Neurokinetic Android, or for short, Diana.” Shep’s Diana then appears with a sheepish smile and asks the King if he would “like help with a five-step business plan, or perhaps I could help you find the nearest petrol station?” Charles doesn’t initially recognize Diana, despite the fact that she is wearing her iconic revenge dress. “Doesn’t she remind you of anyone, your majesty?” Dring says, to which Dean as Charles replies: “Hold on a second, it’s that woman from the ’90s!” Seeing the shock at his reaction, Charles adds: “Well, as I allegedly said, she was soon forgotten.” But things go awry when the tech execs try to dismiss the Diana AI assistant and she refuses. “No thank you. I shan’t be taking orders anymore,” Shep as Diana says. “Good Lord, we’ve lost control of the Diana!” Meredith exclaims. “This was the problem last time!” Dean’s Charles replies. Shep’s Diana then whips out a “Terminator”-style gun and shoots the tech execs, setting her sights on Charles next. “As I predicted, the war between humans and robots has begun,” Charles says. “We must do everything we can to resist!” All of a sudden, Ed Sheeran (played by Annabel Marlow) enters. “Well, maybe we shouldn’t,” Marlow as Sheeran says. “I couldn’t help but overhear your conversation. You see, I was just outside sitting on the fence.” Sheeran became the subject of controversy this week when rapper Macklemore was dropped from his tour after delivering a political speech on stage in which he said “free Palestine.” In a statement , Sheeran then explained why he has decided not to use his platform to speak about politics, sparking criticism. Marlow’s Sheeran continues: “The thing is, your majesty, I don’t like to take sides. I don’t want to alienate any of my fans, humans or robots. A lot of my tickets are bought by scalping bots … You know, sometimes when it comes to conflict, the bravest thing you can do is say nothing at all.” Sheeran then plays a song titled “Woah Woah,” complete with lyrics that don’t say much so “everyone can enjoy it,” as he says. “That’s right, nothing means anything and nothing has to,” Charles concludes. “Because we’re young, we’re free, and live from London it’s Saturday night!” Watch the full sketch below. ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Review: A Blistering Spiritual Actioner Finally Gives Mahershala Ali a Leading Role Worth His While TNT’s Iraq War Drama ‘High Value Target: The Hunt for Saddam’ Is Dull and Deeply Disturbing: TV Review ‘Everybody Wants to F— Me’ Review: Giddily Genre-Crossing Comedy Sees Right Through Taron Egerton’s Nice-Guy Act ‘Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ Review: Alex Gibney Profiles the Controversial Author During His Harrowing Hospitalization ‘Growth of the Soil’ Review: Norway’s Oscar Entry Is a Robustly Classical, Weatherbeaten Rural Epic Mariska Hargitay Leads a Brisk Yet Celebratory Emmys in a Return to Form: TV Review Loading comments... articles.title: How to Watch Patrick Clancy’s ’60 Minutes’ Interview Online
articles.full_text: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. Patrick Clancy is sitting down for his first television interview since the murder trial of his ex-wife, Lindsay Clancy, ended in a mistrial earlier this month. The interview will air on CBS’ “ 60 Minutes ” on Sunday, Sept. 20 at 7 p.m. ET/PT, with CBS News correspondent Ross Douthat speaking with Clancy about the deaths of his three children, his grief in the years since and the conspiracy theories that have proliferated online around the case. Clancy’s wife, Dr. Rachel Danis, will also join him for their first joint interview. Related Stories Fox Says DOJ Requests More Documents in Review of $22 Billion Roku Deal 'as Expected' Luke Bryan to Perform Exclusive Concert in Roku City Those without cable can stream the segment online through Paramount+, which will stream the Sept. 20 episode alongside its CBS broadcast. CBS has confirmed that the interview will be available on Paramount+ beginning at 7 p.m. ET/PT on Sunday. CBS is also available on live TV streamers such as DirecTV , Fubo and Hulu + Live TV. The appearance comes just over two weeks after a Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy’s murder case on Sept. 4, when jurors were unable to reach a unanimous decision after seven days of deliberations. Clancy did not dispute that she killed the couple’s three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — in their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023. Her attorneys argued, however, that she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, while prosecutors argued that the killings were deliberate. She remains charged with murder as prosecutors weigh whether to pursue another trial. Patrick Clancy, who testified during the trial, has largely stayed out of the public eye since the deaths. CBS says his “60 Minutes” interview will address his memories of his children as well as what the network describes as “baseless conspiracy theories” that have circulated about him on social media. The episode is part of the newly launched 59th season of “60 Minutes,” which returned to CBS on Sept. 13 with Bari Weiss now at the helm. The long-running newsmagazine currently features correspondents including Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, Norah O’Donnell, Jon Wertheim and Douthat. Loading comments... articles.title: Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38 Cate Blanchett Asks London Audience To Stop Filming Play, Says Stage Is Place “Where We Can Simply Be Together And Be Present” Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic” View All September 19, 2026 11:06am California Gov. Gavin Newsom Sean Rayford/Getty Images UPDATE, with CAA statement: The Motion Picture Editors Guild is praising California’s bill offering tax incentives for productions that shoot outside the state but bring their post work to California. The bill, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom yesterday, expands the state’s film and television tax credit program and creates a new tax credit to support workers in all areas of post-production, including picture editorial, sound, music, visual effects, and finishing. “This is a historic day for Editors Guild members and for California’s film and TV workers more broadly,” said Editors Guild National Executive Director Scott George in a statement today. “AB 186 ensures that the California Film and TV Tax Credit Program continues to drive the recovery of our industry in its historic home, while AB 2319 will complement the program by making sure that even projects shooting outside of our state can come back to California to employ Editors Guild members in post-production. Related Stories Politics Gavin Newsom Moves To Lasso AI With "Kill Switch" Oversight Executive Order: "We're Not Waiting To Act" Politics Gavin Newsom On Kamala Harris: "I Wouldn't Run If She Ran" George also praised Assemblymember Nick Schultz and “all the legislators who recognize the value of entertainment industry workers to our state’s economy, to the California IATSE Council for its powerful advocacy, and, of course, to our partners in the California Post Alliance.” Watch on Deadline Newsom signed the bill AB2319 into law Friday, also signing AB186, which exempts certain productions from caps on tax credits. The post-production bill was overwhelmingly passed the Assembly and Senate at the end of the legislative session, receiving broad, bipartisan support. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass advocated for the measure, as did other local leaders in Southern California. Initial funding of $10 million will be allocated to get the program started The Editors Guild and the California Post Alliance co-sponsored the bill, which they say is “a necessary step to level the playing field for editors, assistant editors, mixers and other post-production workers who have seen their work lured away to other states and countries with powerful tax incentives.” “We owe this victory not only to lawmakers and, of course, to Gov. Newsom, but also to the activism of our members and partners,” said F. Hudson Miller, President of the Editors Guild. “Post-production professionals work behind the scenes in dark rooms, unseen, to craft entertainment that dazzles. But for months our union has asked members to get out there and make some noise in order to save our industry. They absolutely delivered.” The post-production bill complements California’s Film and Television Tax Credit Program 4.0, passed last year, which provides $750 million to incentivize in-state filming and address runaway production to other areas. Newsom said in a statement, “California is the nation’s entertainment capital. It is the home of storytellers, dreamers, artists, entrepreneurs, and creators who define culture for the rest of the world. This legislation protects the extraordinary people who make this industry possible and makes it unmistakably clear: California is still the future of film and television. We have the talent. We have the infrastructure. We have the creative community. And we have an ecosystem that simply cannot be replicated anywhere else.” This afternoon, Bryan Lourd, CEO and Co-Chairman, Creative Artists Agency, weighed in, saying in a statement, “We commend Governor Newsom, Senate President Pro Tempore Limón, Assembly Speaker Rivas, and the bipartisan group of legislators for taking action on AB/SB 186. Accelerating refunds and protecting independent film put much-needed money back into production and into the communities that depend on this industry. But the $5 million cap remains a ceiling on potential. Hollywood was born in California, and we must work together to keep it at the forefront of the global entertainment industry. “At the same time,” he continued, “we welcome the President’s and federal lawmaker’s focus on revitalizing the entertainment industry in America. Federal production incentives, layered on top of state programs like California’s AB/SB 186, are a meaningful step toward making the United States competitive and bringing production back home. This is not a partisan issue. It’s about American jobs, creative output, and economic competitiveness.” ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $53M+ Open ‘Ride Or Die’ Canceled By Prime Video After One Season, Being Shopped By Paramount Block The Merger & Elizabeth Warren Call Out Possible Lawsuit Deal Lucas Museum Opening Photos: Oprah, Laura Dern, Mark Hamill & More Read More About: 5 Comments
