articles.title: Between ‘The Love Hypothesis’ and ‘Adults,’ Rachel Marsh’s Breakout Moment Is Here
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Marsh is set to star as Anh in 'The Love Hypothesis.' Photography by JJ Geiger, Styling by Katie Bofshever, Hair by Barb Thompson, Makeup by Hinako “I love anytime women are funny,” actress Rachel Marsh declares. Thankfully, the 34-year-old has been able to be in plenty of projects that showcase this, most recently Prime Video’s romantic comedy The Love Hypothesis . Marsh plays Anh, a graduate student and best friend to Lili Reinhart ‘s Olive in the streamer’s adaptation of the wildly popular Ali Hazelwood novel. The actress was not looking to become the quirky best friend character, a trope that director Claire Scanlon and writers Sarah Rothschild and Hazelwood were not interested in rehashing. Related Stories TV 'Adults' Defies Sophomore Slump With Ratings Growth Next Big Thing Xolo Maridueña Wasn't Planning to Be an Actor, But Has Been "Pleasantly Surprised by the Journey" “She is important in this story,” Marsh tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent Zoom. “She also is funny.” Marsh feels like the friendship between her character and Reinhart’s Olive is the foundation for the entire story, something that’s also true in Hazelwood’s book. The two women had a wonderful time finding that on — and off — screen friendship. “Building that trust was pretty easy. Lili is so amazing. She’s so sweet,” the actress says. “She’s such a good actor and a great scene partner. It was really fun for us to get to develop their best friendship over the course of the summer in Montreal.” The upcoming romcom is not the first time you’ve seen Marsh on your screen. Her turn as Carly, the girlfriend to leading player Samir (Malik Elassal), in Adults has gone viral over the last month. It’s mostly thanks to a ridiculously catchy fake K-pop song in the series — if you haven’t heard “Hiccups (Body Go Crazy),” it’s time to look it up . “When I was reading it, I was like, ‘You guys know this is too good,'” she says of the song. It all started when Marsh got a call from series co-creator Ben Kronengold telling her that the show was thinking about making Carly a K-pop star and wondering if it’s something she’d be comfortable with. “I was just tears in my eyes, full body chills,” she says cheekily. “No one’s ever asked me this before. My dream.” Former Saturday Night Live video director Paul Briganti directed Marsh’s turn as a K-pop star on Adults , helping bring some SNL music parody vibes to the scene where she shoots a music video for the song. The director cheered her on as she made “the stupidest hand moves or facial expressions,” something she loved. “It sparked something in me, which I think every single girl has. Where I wondered, ‘What if I can sing and I just haven’t been vocally produced in the right way,'” she says. There’s an entire choreographed version of the song that didn’t make the cut. Maybe it’ll be released, she muses. But “Hiccups” fans, don’t worry. Marsh is also pleading for a version of the song to be released on streaming platforms. “I really think they should put the song on Spotify or something,” she says. “I think people yearn for things like that, to just have a moment of joy.” *** It’s a busy release couple weeks for you. How are you feeling? I feel good. It’s been really cool. We had our first fan screening the other night for The Love Hypothesis and it went really well. It’s fun, this waiting period. The first batch of people saw it, and they really like it. Are they going to get spoilers? I’m just anticipating a lot, but I think it went really well and it made me even more excited for the 23rd when it comes out. Did you know about the book at all before you signed on? I did. I had seen it because it was a big book in airports and bookstores everywhere. It was a top seller for so long, so think I just saw the cover and it was on my list of books to read. I never got to read it. I feel like it was beautiful that I was able to read it when I booked the job and didn’t really have a preconceived notion of it before that, so I could find the similarities between the book and the script. That was really fun I feel so honored to be in it. It’s so beloved by so many people. (l-r) Jeremy (Nicholas Duvernay), Ahn (Marsh) and Malcolm (Jaboukie Young-White) in ‘The Love Hypothesis.’ Philippe Bossé/Prime Video How was it shooting in Montreal? Awesome. I’d never been. I was like, “What is this magical place?” It felt like Europe and Brooklyn. Like other cities but nicer people and beautiful streets and public transportation. I could go on and on, but I loved it so much. Part of it is being an actor is so fun is if you’re lucky enough to book a job in a place that you haven’t been, it’s like they put you up, they pay for things. You get to experience the world in this privileged sense, but it’s such a dream. I really had a blast and I tried to do all the Montreal things. We all did Cirque du Soleil as a cast. There was such a fun food scene in Montreal too. I tried to try all the food, and I love Canada. What is the ideal genre for you? Do you like that you get to dabble in different things? I really do. In acting — it’s interesting because you don’t really get a lot of agency in choosing your jobs — but I feel so lucky. I’ve had a lot of these roles that are drama, and I came from comedy. I had some imposter syndrome for sure doing them, but then the more I did it, I was like, “Oh, comedy and drama are so…” They’re so closely linked. I don’t know, it feels really fun for me to get to do both. As long as it’s feeling fun. Fallout also has an element of comedy, so I think that feels very familiar. But then the cool thing about them is they shoot on film, so that’s such a challenge for me, it’s totally new. With The Morning Show , there’s so many celebrities in that show. It’s a very high pressure job, and so that’s a challenge in a different way. The acting is fun, and I’m just mostly coming in and delivering bad news to Jennifer Aniston, and so it’s like, “How do I do that in eight different ways?” Does it all come back to comedy? For me, comedy has always been what I am trying to be really great at, and I think it’s the most challenging thing to do as an actor. Even though I’ve done some dramatic stuff, I still think the comedy is the hardest, and so I will always want to be doing that and pushing myself to be better at it. What’s the ideal day off for you look like? I’m being honest, an ideal day off — this sounds so basic, this is not going to be good. I try to go to a workout class in the city. In Montreal, I tried to go to a fun Pilates class or something, and then I’ll try to find a coffee shop because I used to co-own a coffee shop. I love pulling my own espresso shots. I have a little espresso machine. I just love coffee, and I love buying an $8 little drinkie. I don’t know why. I just have to buy it, so I will go to a coffee shop just read a book or be on my phone or just hang out and people watch. That’s really what I did a lot in Montreal, or even in Toronto, when we were shooting Adults and I had the day off. I’m not used to being by myself very much, so it’s nice to be forced to. I try not to try to do extra work like writing or whatever when I’m shooting something because it feels like just the work is enough. [I love] just going in and eating. I love to eat dinner by myself too. I love going to a new restaurant and sitting at the bar and getting a glass of wine. Some places it’s way more chill, but if you do it in L.A., people are like, “Whoa, this girl is in crisis.” That’s crazy. There’s so many people here, you’d think it’d be more acceptable. No, you can’t. Even I am judgmental of girls who do that, but in any other city, anywhere else in the world, I feel like it’s totally fine. I took advantage of that, and nobody even cares or bothers you. I would bring a book or just sit there and talk to people. I like to do that a lot or just watch TV. In Canada, they have a very interesting TV choices, so I got a VPN and had to do that to watch my shows. Just a chill day by myself is really nice. Marsh as Carly in ‘Adults’ season two. FX You used to co-own a coffee shop? Oh my God, girl. Please tell me more. Well, when I got out of college… I went to business school, and I didn’t even know I wanted to be an actor. I grew up pretty religious. I don’t know if you want to put this in there, but pretty religious and really wanted to do good in the world. I guess that’s not a religious thing, but I worked at a couple nonprofits and worked for an agency that worked for nonprofits. I was really in the nonprofit space, and then I got burnt out by that, which sounds so insane. I got burnt out by the nonprofit life and thought about what I wanted to do. I was already selling my homemade almond milk to this coffee shop here in L.A. Then I just became a co-owner. We worked at the coffee shop together, and we had regular customers. I still am friends with a lot of those people. I had worked in restaurants and stuff before, but never a coffee shop, which I think is a very specific thing for L.A. culture. The service industry, in current day, is rough. I know how specific I am with my coffee or my matcha, so I understand some people, but it was rough. I really did love it. I loved having a little business. Maybe one day, I’ll own another coffee shop or a little shoppy shop, something where I could sell stuff. We’ll see. Maybe I won’t act forever, or maybe I will and it’ll be a tax write-off. THR

articles.title: Chris Brown Turns on Texas Rep. as Congressional Honor Causes Controversy
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All September 18, 2026 6:46pm Chris Brown arrives at London court on July 24, 2026. Courtesy of Getty Chris Brown delivered divergent statements to Texas state Rep. Venton Jones and U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett , the two Texas Democrats who honored him and Usher at the Arlington stop on their co-headlining tour, as controversy swirls around the polarizing pop star’s official recognition by the two lawmakers. On Sept. 12, Crockett took to the stage during Brown and Usher’s stop on The R&B Tour at AT&T Stadium and announced that, for the multi-platinum singer’s separate contributions to music, both artists were being recognized in the Congressional Record. State Rep. Jones was also on stage at the concert to join Crockett in the presentation and presented Brown a separate legislative recognition. The decision lit up a major controversy online, with liberal Texas Democrats’ reaction to Crockett ranging from deeply confused as to why she honored a well-known domestic abuser to red-hot rage at a decision many found to be an embarrassment. Related Stories Music Chris Brown Pleads Guilty After London Nightclub Attack Music Usher Says Diddy Has Been "Misrepresented": "I Don't Have Anything Negative to Say About Sean Combs" “We are experiencing Black joy to the highest level,” Crockett said at the concert. “And I wanted to make sure we document that at the congressional level. So let’s give it up again for Chris Brown.” Crockett has not made a public statement this week regarding the event at AT&T Stadium. But speculation has run wild as to why a lawmaker known for taking President Trump to task and equating him to an abusive partner while advocating for abortion access and diversity, equity and inclusion would go out of her way to sing the praises of someone so associated with violence against women. A New York magazine article on Friday floated several potential explanations for her reasoning, from drumming up voter support before the midterms to her eye for a post-politics career as a celebrity. Brown opted to stir the pot of controversy on social media as the growing backlash against the two lawmakers brought his name into headlines this week — inevitably dredging up his dark history of domestic abuse and legal issues that still plague the hitmaker. On his Instagram page , Brown thanked Crockett but laid into Jones after Jones, in an appearance on Don Lemon’s show, apologized to domestic violence survivors and reframed the concert appearance as having been about voter mobilization ahead of the midterms — a framing Brown suggested contradicted what happened onstage, where the midterms went unmentioned. “Thank you so much,” Brown wrote to Crockett. “I apologize for any backlash you have to deal with for awarding me. I’m not political but I move off of frequency and energy and I’m so grateful. ONCE AGAIN, THANK YOU.” “I don’t want the award anymore my brother,” he wrote to Jones. “You went on with Don Lemon and started tap dancing for them folk. Y’all keep that st. “ On a now-deleted Instagram Story, he continued, writing, “Funny thing is… Y’ALL CAME TO ME WITH THIS! NOT THE OTHER WAY AROUND. I was minding my damn business. My shows in Dallas were already sold out. I ain’t [want] to be honored because I knew some st like this would happen…” Brown was probably correct to predict the political blowback. His track record of legal trouble has dotted his entire adult life. His first foray into the court system and the court of public opinion came in 2009, when he pleaded guilty to the felony assault of his then-girlfriend Rihanna, an incident that occurred when he was still a teenager. His string of legal woes has not definitively concluded since then; a case stemming from a 2023 incident at a London nightclub saw the singer take a plea in late July so prosecutors would drop charges of assault, attempted grievous bodily harm, and a weapons charge. Brown is currently awaiting sentencing in the case. THR

articles.title: The Best Films of the Fall Festivals: THR Critics’ Picks
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Clockwise from top left: 'Misty Green,' 'Possible Love,' 'The Debut' and 'You Can See Everything.' Courtesy of A24 (3); Courtesy of Netflix Along with Sundance in January, Berlin in February and Cannes in May, the fall festival trifecta of Venice, Telluride and Toronto almost invariably yields many of the films destined to keep percolating in the conversation from critics’ group awards in December all the way to the Oscars mid-March. This year’s crop was way lighter than usual on major contenders, but The Hollywood Reporter’ s hard-working reviews team nonetheless found plenty to love. Five of our top 13 picks are documentaries, with subjects as varied as the resistance of independent journalism in Putin’s Russia; an iconoclast of British queer cinema; a devastating new perspective on the war in Gaza; a sui generis portrait of a convicted fraud queen; and the struggles of delivery workers in New York City. On the narrative side, new vehicles for Julianne Moore, John Malkovich and Mahershala Ali gave those fine actors arguably their best roles in years, while the less widely known Rosalind Eleazar scored a star-making performance that should put her on every casting director’s radar; a giant of English realism crafted what will likely be the swan-song culmination of a glorious career; a debuting Lebanese director reinvigorated the heist genre; and a master of contemporary Korean cinema delivered a unique contemplation of the wealth and class divides. DAU (Venice) Image Credit: Phenomen Berlin At once immense and intimate, political, historical and personal, Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s loose biopic of Russian physicist Lev Lendau is the kind of shoot-for-the-moon feature that rarely happens anymore — and certainly not like this (the shoot relocated hundreds of actors and thousands of extras inside a giant simulacrum of the Soviet era, their daily interactions captured by a roving team of camera and sound technicians). Comparisons could be made to Oppenheimer or The Brutalist , but this is very much its own, highly original and cinematic labor of love, telling the tale of a brilliant man crushed by the weight of a totalitarian regime. — JORDAN MINTZER The Debut (Telluride, Toronto) Image Credit: A24 Blessed with swing-for-the-fences brio, the latest feature by Jesse Eisenberg makes for a frequently hilarious journey into the mind of an overly committed actor. Julianne Moore is a hoot as newbie thespian Mona, who starts like one of those disaffected housewives the Oscar winner has played so often in her career but turns out to be much stranger, while Paul Giamatti makes director Jerry ferocious but not monstruous. As the balance of power between them begins to shift, their scenes together are not just entertaining but thrillingly dynamic. — ANGIE HAN Furies (Venice, Toronto) Image Credit: RT Features Propelled by a raw, heart-pounding ferocity, Rami Kodeih’s Beirut-set first feature is a sharp fusion of personal desperation and political rage, as specific to Lebanon’s corruption-fueled economic crisis as it is generally, woefully recognizable. Following two sisters determined to reclaim their savings after the bank freezes their accounts, the movie infuses a time-tested genre with the offhand wiseass humor of siblings who know and love each other deeply, brought to messy, magnificent life in a pair of spectacular performances. — SHERI LINDEN Misty Green (Toronto) Image Credit: A24 Coming 12 years after Top Five , his terrific last feature as writer-director, Chris Rock delivers an enthralling character study and an insightful plunge into a milieu he knows intimately. In a star-making performance, Slow Horses ’ Rosalind Eleazar plays the title character, a Los Angeles-based actress and singer whose talent is as indisputable as her gift for self-sabotage. While attempting to restart her career, she navigates money troubles, a family crisis and an industry that rarely makes things easy. Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya, Anna Kendrick and Rock also star. — DAVID ROONEY My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile (Venice, Telluride) Image Credit: Venice Film Festival If part one of director Julia Loktev’s 12-hour chronicle of journalism under fire concluded with a cliffhanger, part two covers the painful aftermath of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. By that point, we’ve come to know the handful of independent reporters — most of them women accused of being “foreign agents” by Putin’s government — whom Loktev documented during the months leading up to the war, showing how they held fast to their beliefs while their homeland crumbled around them. In this second part, we watch the courageous, resourceful journos deal with forced exile, scattering across several countries and continents as the Russian state continues to pursue them for bogus offenses. It’s a gripping and essential study of persecution and resistance. — J.M. NAZA (Venice) Image Credit: Venice Film Festival It’s hard to describe all the feelings provoked by watching a film like the new documentary from No Other Land directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. Outrage, of course. Most certainly contempt, on a profound level, for the current Israeli regime and its prime minister, Bibi Netanyahu. Yet this sober and thoroughly reported bombshell of an exposé, in which two dozen IDF intelligence officers detail the systematic targeting of civilians in Gaza since October 7th — how it was carried out deliberately and with state-of-the-art precision — is above all a brave and indispensable act of bearing witness. — J.M. Possible Love (Venice, Toronto) Image Credit: Courtesy of Netflix Following the haunting 2018 masterwork that was Burning , Lee Chang-dong reaffirms his status as one of the greats of contemporary Korean — and world — cinema with this transfixing chamber drama about economic and emotional unease, throwing together two couples on opposite sides of the wealth divide. All four leads in the quiet powerhouse are superb, with especially memorable work from the wonderful Jeon Do-yeon, who won the Cannes best actress honors in 2007 for Lee’s Secret Sunshine . — D.R. Queer Edward II (Venice) Image Credit: Brenda Prince/Bishopgate Institute This wondrous documentary is comprised of footage from the set of Derek Jarman’s 1991 screen adaptation of the Christopher Marlowe play Edward II . Filled with vintage archival material that supplements the portrait of the irrepressibly charming Jarman and his talented collaborators, the film is guaranteed to induce swooning nostalgia in those who remember queer life, London and the filmmaking scene thereof in the early 1990s. But the doc also offers sadly timely history lessons about the necessity of resisting despotic, homophobic authoritarians — especially if you can do it with men dressed as nuns. — LESLIE FELPERIN Tender Loving Care (Telluride, Toronto) Image Credit: Courtesy of Joseph Lynn/Thin Man Films Ltd/Bleecker Street Revolving around a London woman ( Widow’s Bay Emmy winner Kate O’Flynn), her BFF and fellow social worker (Alice Bailey Johnson) and her aging parents (Marion Bailey and Paul Jessup), Mike Leigh’s new, and possibly last, film is warm and inviting, filled with giggles and gossip and gentle gallows humor. It’s also wrenching, with a topical urgency simmering just beneath the jovial surface: Leigh is tough-minded about what it means to look out for one another at this point in history — specifically in a country whose public services have been eroded by an ethos of self-reliance codified by Thatcher and further cemented, or perverted, by Brexit. — JON FROSCH Union Town (Venice, Toronto) Image Credit: Venice Film Festival Barbara Kopple, the documentarian laureate of the American organized labor movement, follows 1976’s Harlan County, USA and 1990’s American Dream with another complex and galvanizing film taking the temperature of the national workplace. Unsurprisingly, what Kopple witnesses in the gig economy is disheartening: a decentralized employee base at the mercy of nearly faceless ownership and mired in a struggle to get UPS, Amazon and various food delivery apps to do the right thing. It’s powerful and powerfully bleak, but Kopple always finds hope in solidarity. — DANIEL FIENBERG Wild Horse Nine (Venice, Telluride, Toronto) Image Credit: Searchlight John Malkovich does his best work in years in Martin McDonagh’s poignant, blood-dipped buddy comedy . He stars as a terminally ill CIA operative dispatched in 1973 to Santiago with the younger partner he mentored (played by a wired Sam Rockwell) to lay the groundwork for a coup to overthrow Salvador Allende’s Chilean democracy. On what seems like a whim but ends up being far more complicated, the two agents visit Easter Island, where the famous sentinel-like stone heads bear witness to violence and sorrow, summoning the CIA’s irascible head of South American operations (a plum role for Steve Buscemi). — D.R. You Can See Everything (Telluride) Image Credit: A24 In the first half of this fascinatingly intimate documentary portrait , filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim essentially embed with Elizabeth Holmes in the last weeks before her prison sentence — but it’s the second half that really kicks into gear, getting excitingly meta and almost surreal. What begins as a fascinatingly intimate peek at a deluded or disingenuous scammer reveals itself as something much more ambitious and less predictable, until we’re left to ponder what value a personal truth has at all. — A.H. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother (Toronto) Image Credit: Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios A perfectly cast Mahershala Ali finally gets a leading role suitable for an Oscar-winning actor of his stature, playing a devout Muslim and contract killer who finds himself forced to care for his three kids after his wife dies in Bassam Tariq’s achingly human Texas-set thriller . It’s a crime story with a large, beating heart, a loving portrayal of Islam, and — rarest of all — a movie that explores the possibility of a form of masculinity that allows for the full range of human emotion. — JOURDAIN SEARLES THR

articles.title: ‘Murderous’ Review: Neil LaBute’s New Film Is Undone by Its Overly Familiar Premise and Obvious Plot Machinations
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All September 18, 2026 7:57pm Neil LaBute's 'Murderous' Oldenburg International Film Festival Best-selling novels like Jean Hanff Korelitz’s The Plot and stage thrillers like Ira Levin’s Deathtrap , among many other works, have demonstrated that stealing another writer’s work can have fateful if not deadly consequences. Neil LaBute ( In the Company of Men , Nurse Betty ) delivers another variation on the familiar theme with his latest effort, receiving its world premiere at the Oldenburg Film Festival. Taking place in a single location and featuring but three lead performers, Murderous carries a strong whiff of such LaBute-cited influences as Joseph L. Mankiewicz’s Sleuth and Hitchcock’s Rope. Unfortunately, it doesn’t live up to those predecessors, feeling like an undernourished stage thriller whose plot machinations are far too obvious. Related Stories Movies Neil LaBute and Gia Crovatin on Making Hitchcock-Lean Indie Horror-Comedy 'Murderous' Movies Zoë Bell Is Ready for Round Two Murderous The Bottom Line Stagy and contrived. Venue : Oldenburg International Film Festival Cast : Gia Crovatin, Thomas Sadoski, Jordan Baker Director-screenwriter : Neil LaBute 1 hour 47 minutes The story, beginning with a first chapter titled “Him,” revolves around Marian (frequent LaBute collaborator Gia Crovatin), a filmmaker who made a splash with her debut effort, a femme-oriented horror film entitled “Murderous.” With her financial success signified by her gorgeously rustic home, a former mill, and the vintage red Porsche in her driveway, she’s surprised one day by the unexpected arrival of Norman ( Thomas Sadoski ), who announces that he wants to have a talk. And that he’s driven all the way from Iowa to do it. Clearly made uncomfortable by the intrusion, she eventually agrees to invite him in. It turns out that they were both students at the same time — he was a teacher’s assistant, he reminds her — and had a brief romantic relationship. He compliments her expensive new home, commenting that she seems to have no personal items or photographs. What she does have are valuable knick-knacks previously owned by such famed writers as Truman Capote and Willa Cather. Not to mention Shirley Jackson’s letter opener. It’s a wonder she doesn’t have Chekhov’s gun on display. After brief small talk in which Norman’s sorry lot in life is made clear — he has no job and no girlfriend, he admits — he finally gets to the point. “Did you think I wasn’t going to see it?” he asks about her film that won awards and put her on the map. It turns out that he had originally devised the film’s premise and the two had worked on the idea together and even collaborated on flipbooks of individual sequences, which he claims to still have “somewhere” in his possession. Needless to say, he thinks they need to come to some sort of agreement on compensation. Despite the tension, things, as they tend to do in LaBute’s works, turn sexual. When he reminds her that she cheated on him during their relationship, she takes it as a cue. “Is that what you want to make up for things? A blow job?” she asks. Norman thinks carefully for a moment before replying, “I wouldn’t hate it.” To reveal more about what happens next during the charged encounter would be too much of a spoiler. Suffice it to say that things end … abruptly. Another unexpected visitor, this time an older woman, arrives in the second chapter, “Her.” She’s Lila (Jordan Baker), who declares herself to be a big fan and simply wants some DVDs autographed, including one for her son. Again, Marian reluctantly invites the stranger in, and the two engage in a lengthy discussion about Marian’s film and the film business in general. It provides the opportunity for Marian to launch into a diatribe about the frustrations of working with clueless movie distributors and marketers, which, coming from LaBute, feels like the most personal and honest part of the film. The film drops hints about Lila’s true identity, or at least Marian’s perception of it, with the subtlety of a sledgehammer. Onstage, these plot machinations might have worked with a live audience eager to be manipulated. But they come across as forced and artificial here, and despite the best efforts of the performers Murderous feels more like an actors’ exercise than an organically plotted thriller. It never transcends its air of narrative claustrophobia and, considering its thin premise, would have benefited from a sharp cutting of its overlong 107-minute running time. Full credits Venue: Oldenburg International Film Festival Production: Hardball Entertainment, Bad Pelican, Big Time Decent Productions Cast: Gia Crovatin, Thomas Sadoski, Jordan Baker Director-screenwriter: Neil LaBute Producer: Daryl Freimark Executive producers: Gia Crovatin, Neil LaBute, Alexander Sablow Director of photography: Alexander Sablow Production designers: Rob Bissinger, Anita LaScala Editor: Bridget Durnford 1 hour 47 minutes THR

articles.title: Hudson Williams Shares How “Surreal” It Was for Him and Connor Storrie to Return to ‘Heated Rivalry’ Set
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All September 18, 2026 10:06pm Hudson Williams speaks onstage during "Making Waves With...Hudson Williams" during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Mathew Tsang/Getty Images for TIFF Logo text Hudson Williams is teasing what it’s been like on set for Heated Rivalry season two. The 26-year-old actor, speaking during a conversation at the Toronto International Film Festival , spoke about what it was like for him and co-star Connor Storrie when they went back to set on the hit queer hockey romance drama . “It was surreal to step into it,” Williams told the crowd. “We’re going to be kissing each other, brother. I’m going to be doing my fucking Russian accent to you,” he said, mimicking Storrie. Williams said it was hard for them to wrap their heads around going back and were concerned they wouldn’t be able to get right back into it. Williams pointed out that it was the first time he’d ever returned to a character on a big scale. Related Stories Movies 'The Face of Horror' Review: Kristine Froseth Sparkles, but Anna Biller's Medieval Tale Can't Stop Getting in Its Own Way Movies 'Masc' Review: A Neurodivergent Gay Man Navigates the World in a Striking and Distinctive Debut Feature Williams said much of their memory around the first season wasn’t just shooting but seeing the episodes, fans reactions and everything that’s happened in the last 10 months. But ultimately the pair decided to be “overconfident” and knew they knew their characters in and out. “We’re going to show up and it’s just going to be Ilya and Shane right back,” he said. Storrie ended up working on the first day, without Williams, and came back to tell his co-star about the experience. “He was like, ‘It was sort of weird. They were all so good that I was like, am I good? Am I in it? Am I doing the thing? Am I doing an impression of Ilya?'” Williams recalled Storrie saying. Williams told the crowd he was extremely confident that wouldn’t happen to him. “Then I showed up. I was doing the scene and there was some extras, who were clearly fans, and they’re just so perky. I was like, ‘Oh God. Oh God, am I doing a Shane impression?'” he questioned. Thankfully, Williams and Storrie were able to find their footing quickly. Williams pointed to the show’s creator Jacob Tierney continuing to the make the set feel just as small and intimate as he did when they were filming season one. It helped the the crew is still the same as the previous season. Williams also teased a bit of season two , which will mainly be based on Rachel Reid ‘s Heated Rivalry follow-up novel, The Long Game . “It’s a sad book,” he said. “If season one/book one is the yearning season, book two is external adversity and [relationship] communication problems that feel very real and human.” The actor added, “To be able to play those as Shane, [it’s] going to be frustrating and annoying to leave set [when] things are left unsaid, but hopefully it’ll make for really good TV.” THR

articles.title: Angelina Jolie and Salma Hayek Pinault on Their New Film ‘Without Blood’ and Spending ‘A Lot of Time Talking About Our Pain, Our Losses, Our Traumas’
articles.full_text: Sep 18, 2026 4:12pm PT Angelina Jolie and Salma Hayek Pinault on Their New Film ‘Without Blood’ and Spending ‘A Lot of Time Talking About Our Pain, Our Losses, Our Traumas’ The duo also talks about the possibility of making a comedy together. By Marc Malkin Plus Icon Marc Malkin Senior Editor, Culture and Events marcmalkin Latest Angelina Jolie and Salma Hayek Pinault on Their New Film ‘Without Blood’ and Spending ‘A Lot of Time Talking About Our Pain, Our Losses, Our Traumas’ 13 hours ago Orville Peck on His New Album ‘Mule,’ Battling Addiction and Making Out With a Pro Football Player 2 days ago Barbra Streisand Condemns Trump’s ‘Unchecked Ego’ Over Kennedy Center Name Battle: ‘Galling and Painful to Witness’ 2 days ago See All Getty Images In “ Without Blood ,” written and directed by Angelina Jolie , Salma Hayek plays Nina, a woman who spends her adult life looking for the three men responsible for the wartime murder of her father and brother when she was just a child. In two of the cases, her revenge is fatal. But then she meets the third accomplice, Tito (Demián Bichir), now a clerk in a newspaper kiosk at a train station. Related Stories TIFF Takeaways: A Chris Rock Crowd-Pleaser, Peter Farrelly's 'Rocky' Standing Ovation and Market Growing Pains ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Review: Takashi Miike’s Loose Remake Is a Complete Nonstarter The movie is in many ways a two-hander featuring Nina and Tito talking over drinks with flashback scenes chronicling both of their sometimes harrowing lives. “I was afraid that I couldn’t play this part, and also I was afraid to go so far every day at work and go into this really difficult place,” Hayek says during a joint interview with Jolie. “At the beginning, I wasn’t sure that Angelina was directing. I thought she was just producing. I’m like, ‘Oh no, I don’t want to suffer like that. I don’t want to.’ And then she started talking to me about the importance of the piece. And then you have to understand that Angelina is an extraordinary director.” Popular on Variety Salma Hayek Pinault stars in “Without Blood.” Courtesy Image “Without Blood” is an adaptation of Italian writer Alessandro Baricco’s novella of the same name. Like the book, the movie doesn’t specify the time or the location where the story takes place, nor identify the war at the center of the story. The characters speak English and Spanish. “I wanted it to be that anyone watching it from anywhere could identify with it,” Jolie says. “Even if it wasn’t an actual war or a conflict, there’s something beautiful in the book where it says, ‘We return to where we break.’ So part of the conflict and the idea of the film is that anybody can identify with something in your life where something happened where it broke you and changed you, and how much you wish you could sit across from that person and have answers and have some kind of say your piece and hope that they could see you and hope that it gives you some kind of healing or closure. Of course, sometimes it doesn’t give you what you think you’re looking for or doesn’t heal those.” This isn’t the first time Jolie has made a film about war and conflict. Her directorial debut was the Bosnian war drama “In the Land of Blood and Money” in 2011. “Unbroken” (2014) told the story of American prisoners-of-war during World War II. The life of Cambodian author and human rights activist Loung Ung under the rule of the Khmer Rouge was the subject of “First They Killed My Father” in 2017. “In ‘First They Killed My Father,’ we had trauma therapy tents because a lot of people there had been through war and I’ve learned that everybody’s been through some level of trauma,” Jolie says. “What we did on this was the time spent with everybody discussing it. We all ended up spending a lot of time talking about our pain, talking about our losses, our traumas. Obviously, community can be very, very healing.” Jolie and Hayek Pinault first worked together five years ago when they co-starred in the Marvel movie “Eternals.” Next, Jolie will serve as a producer on Hayek Pinault’s directorial debut, “Arena,” an epic romantic adventure that the “Frida” star also wrote. “In a way, she’s my partner,” Hayek Pinault says. “I’ve written two different scripts with two different pens that she gave me. It’s a really good, enriching and artistic relationship. That is hard to find. It’s such a gift.” I asked Jolie if she’s ever been tempted to direct lighter material like a comedy. “We’ve laughed a lot. We fantasized about making different comedies together,” Hayek Pinault says. Jolie laughs, “My comedies tend to be a bit dark. I think I have a dark sense of humor.” Hayek Pinault turns to Jolie and says, “You’re funny. So funny. She just keeps it a secret.” Jolie isn’t sure she has what it takes to helm comedy. “I don’t know how good I’d be. You have those things that we think, as an actress, you like to try everything and then you get to a point you realize other actors are good at certain things and there are many who are better at comedy than I am. But I do think I’m a pretty good straight person, like the ‘Maleficent.’ I’m a good straight.” “Without Blood” is in theaters now. articles.title: ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name
articles.full_text: Sep 18, 2026 7:02pm PT ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name Phil Spector made her name...and erased it. Barry Avrich's film tells Darlene Love's extraordinary story and pays tribute to her soul-stirring talent. By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name 11 hours ago ‘Resident Evil’ Review: Zach Cregger’s Reboot Is Funky Monster Fun, a One-Man-Against-the-Squish-Zombies Lark That Never Gets Bogged Down in Video-Game Sludge 3 days ago ‘The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd’ Review: Amanda Seyfried and Scoot McNairy Are Powerful in Tim Blake Nelson’s Twisty Dark-Side Prison Saga 4 days ago See All Courtesy of TIFF “Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been” is a documentary about one of the greatest singers in the history of pop music, but it’s also a stunning meditation on the issue of identity in pop. Darlene Love recorded her most defining songs in the early ’60s, when she was part of the Phil Spector hit factory. She led a group called the Blossoms, who Spector recruited, in 1962, to sing “He’s a Rebel,” the track that became the prototype for the Wall of Sound. The song was supposed to have been sung by the Crystals, but they were 3,000 miles away in New York, and Spector, eager to rush the song into production, figured it didn’t matter — he could just credit the Crystals (which he did), and no one would know. Related Stories Oscars: Ukraine Selects 'Traces,' About Women Who Survived Sexual Assault During War With Russia, for International Feature Race Oscars: Israel Selects HIV Drama ‘Tell Me Everything’ for International Feature Race Darlene Love sings “He’s a Rebel” with a saucy majesty that builds in power, until it becomes almost lordly in its reverence-for-the-bad-boy. (It’s no accident that Kenneth Anger, in “Scorpio Rising,” transposed the song so that she was singing about Jesus.) Her voice is as big as the Wall of Sound she helped to create. She sang lead on another Crystals track, “He’s Sure the Boy I Love,” did the background vocals on many other Spector songs — and, in 1963, sang “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home),” the greatest pop-music Christmas song ever recorded. She was credited on that one, but “The Phil Spector Christmas Album” had the misfortune to be released on Nov. 22, 1963, the day JFK was shot. The record fizzled; after a few weeks, Spector suppressed any further distribution of it. The album was essentially lost (until it was reissued by Apple Records in 1972). So even though Darlene Love had been billed on the album’s greatest track, her name remained lost as well. Popular on Variety Thirteen years ago, Morgan Neville’s documentary “20 Feet from Stardom” paid tribute to rock ‘n’ roll’s most fabled back-up singers (the majority of whom were Black), and to how they spent their careers standing in the shadows. Darlene Love was one of those singers, and she featured prominently in the film; when it won the Oscar for best documentary, it was Love who stood up at the Academy Awards and gave an indelible speech. “20 Feet from Stardom” captured a very particular situation: The artists it was about didn’t get to be stars, but the movie suggested that in an alternate universe they might have been. Darlene Love, however, has lived a special, heightened version of that conundrum. She hovered in the background, not getting the recognition she deserved. At the same time, she was a star. Not a maximal one, but if being a true pop singer means singing lead on some of the most magical recordings of the 20th century, Love did that. She was out there in front, spearheading the sound. It was her name that was erased, so in a strange way her identity got erased too. You knew that voice in your sonic bones, but it was in front of you and invisible at the same time. Darlene Love didn’t need an alternate universe (she lived in both universes), and “Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been” tracks the unique fusion of glory, injustice, fleeting opportunity, dashed dreams, resilience, and latter-day recognition that defines her story. The movie, like Love’s life and career, is a one-of-a-kind ride, and by the end you don’t just feel like you know and understand this remarkable artist. You feel closer to the center of the mysteries of pop. Love is 85 now, but in the documentary, which is built around a present-day interview with her (though there’s also a ton of great archival footage), she’s ageless. Under a wig of orange-blonde curls, her face beams, her smile dances, her laugh rings out, her personality is funky and vivid, and she simply doesn’t seem old . Love got to know Paul Shaffer when David Letterman fell in love with “Christmas (Baby Please Don’t Come)” and decided, in 1986, to feature Love singing it on his late-night show (a performance that became an annual ritual). The documentary presents Love along with Shaffer and his band in a studio of the Power Station, where she performs updated renditions of several of her key songs. Her voice is extraordinary, the force and quality of it undimmed. And Love proves a great narrator of her own legend. She knows what she was robbed of (not just credit but the life she could have had), yet she has transcended bitterness. The film’s director, Barry Avrich, takes us back to the age of radio (he pays nifty homage to it in the opening credits), when you would hear a voice coming out of that box, and the voice took hold of you. Love, born Darlene Wright in 1941, shuttled between Los Angeles and Texas and spent her first 15 years in church, dunked in gospel as much as Aretha or Ray Charles were. She joined the Blossoms in the late ’50s, and they sang backup on a host of classics, starting with Sam Cooke’s “Everybody Likes to Cha Cha Cha” and then on “Chain Gang” and “Rockin’ Robin,” “Monster Mash” and “Johnny Angel.” From there, they moved on to Phil Spector. They worked for him as back-up singers, in addition to being swapped in for the Crystals and Bob B. Soxx and the Blue Jeans, for whom Love sang lead on the sublimely lilting “Why Do Lovers Break Each Other’s Hearts.” Spector was a holy terror even then (though he was also a genius), and the name game he played with his female soul singers, moving them around as if they were interchangeable game-board pieces, was designed to do several things at once. It made Spector himself the star. (He was the first producer to do that.) It enabled him to withhold royalties. And in the largest sense, it was his (racist) way of treating all his talent like indentured servants. Love became a magnetic presence on “Shindig!,” the great rock ‘n’ roll TV show that allowed its performers to be wild and woolly (Shaffer offers a great reminiscence of it). She led the Blossoms in back-up vocals on pop songs from “Monday, Monday” to the Beach Boys’ “In My Room,” and she went on tour with the other Spector singers, falling into a serious relationship with Bill Medley of the Righteous Brothers. Onstage, she had a toothy insolence. Her career was a string of missed opportunities, including one that sounds like a conspiracy theory, though as presented in “I Know Where I’ve Been” it’s a fascinating one. Love was originally set to record “River Deep, Mountain High” for Phil Spector. At the last minute, he changed the singer to Tina Turner — and the song was, of course, a legendary commercial flop, the one that effectively ended Spector’s reign. The theory presented is that Turner’s rendition of it had too much R&B grit to succeed on the pop charts of 1966. Whereas Love, who had a much smoother pop-soul croon, would have made it a hit. Ah, the seduction of alternate-universe thinking! The documentary reveals how Spector became a creepier presence with the years and continued to shadow her, at one point buying out a contract she had with someone else. There’s no doubt that Spector’s great songs made her career, but the way he designed it they also nipped it in the bud. Love was still singing in the early ’70s (we hear her do a spellbinding rendition of “I’ll Be There”), but as the age of peak R&B wound down, so did her opportunities. She was married several times and had four children, two of whom got involved in the L.A. gang-banger scene and wound up in prison. (They have since emerged and triumphed.) Love wound up cleaning houses. Yet she was not forgotten. Bruce Springsteen and Steven Van Zandt, both fans from way back, took an interest in her (they are interviewed extensively). She wound up reviving her career by doing nostalgia-act performances on cruise ships. This ultimately led to the 1984 jukebox musical revue “Leader of the Pack,” which she was featured in as it began performances in the Greenwich Village club the Bottom Line; it became a sensation. The documentary hints that it was also successful when it moved to Broadway (which isn’t the case; it flamed out there), but Darlene Love was relaunched. And as much as that, she was recognized . The exultant Letterman performances of “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home),” featuring bigger choirs each year, helped a great deal, and so did her 2011 induction into the Rock ‘n’ Roll Hall of Fame. Suddenly, everyone knew who Darlene Love was. “I Know Where I’ve Been” completes the journey. It’s a film that leaves you staggered — at the soul-stirring splendor of her voice, at the forces of the time, both big and small, that marginalized her, and at our awareness of what might have been, which should never stand in the way of our awe at what was. ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name Reviewed at Toronto Film Festival (TIFF DOcs), Sept. 14, 2026. Running time: 115 MIN. Production: A Melbar Entertainment, TPH Entertainment production. Producers: Taraji P. Henson, Barry Avrich, Mark Selby. Executive producers: Jamila Jordan-Theus, Len Evans, Tim Drake, Randy Lennox, Jeffrey Latimer. Crew: Director, screenplay: Barry Avrich. Camera: Ken Ng. Editor: Dave Kennedy. With: Darlene Love, Bruce Springsteen, Cher, Dionne Warwick, David Letterman, Steven Van Zandt, Nancy Sinatra, Paul Shaffer, Lou Adler, Marc Shaiman, Robert Smigel, Jimmy Fallon. articles.title: World Premiering at San Sebastián, Igor Legarreta Describes His Third Film ‘The Blind Ants’ as a Coastal Western Set in the Basque Country
articles.full_text: Sep 18, 2026 10:00pm PT World Premiering at San Sebastián, Igor Legarreta Describes His Third Film ‘The Blind Ants’ as a Coastal Western Set in the Basque Country Based on the acclaimed eponymous novel by Ramiro Pinilla, 'The Blind Ants' is a story of survival in 1930s Biskaia By Roberto Prieto Plus Icon Roberto Prieto Latest Catalonia: A Dozen Highlights at San Sebastián, From a Time-Loop Thriller to a Singular Heist Tale and a Potential Arthouse Sleeper 1 day ago ‘Brother’s Keeper’ Director Ferit Karahan’s ‘Djinn Wedding’ Asks: ‘Can a Person Who Refuses to Acknowledge Their Own Darkness Ever Truly Change Their Fate?’ 5 days ago TIFF 2026: 20 International Titles to Track, From Feng-I Fiona Roan’s Shuhua Starrer to a Taxidermy Musical and a John Madden Parkinson’s Rom-Com 6 days ago See All 'The Blind Ants.' Photo Credit: Imanol Nabea “The Blind Ants” (“Inurri Itsuak”), the third feature by director Igor Legarreta (“All the Moons,” “When You Stop Loving Me”), had it world premiere on Sept. 18 at the 74th San Sebastián International Film Festival. Part of the Zinemira section, which is dedicated to Basque productions, the film is competing for the Irizar Award for Basque Cinema. It will be in Spanish theaters on Oct. 9, distributed by Buena Vista International Spain. Set in the Basque Country in 1930, the film tells the story of an English ship that is stranded on the shores of Biscay during a violent storm. Holding tons of valuable coal, the local people of Algorta scramble to rescue some of it in order to help them survive a harsh winter. The Jauregui family decides to risk it all and brave the unrelenting storm in order to keep some of the black gold. Their decision leads to tragic consequences that will change them forever. Related Stories Oscars: Hungary Selects Ildiko Enyedi’s ‘Silent Friend’ for International Feature Race (EXCLUSIVE) Andrew Scott Has Waited His Whole Career for a Role Like 'Elsinore.' Can Focus and the Bard Anoint Him With an Oscar? “We launched a production company in the Basque Country with a clear vision: to combine our strengths with local talent to create films that are artistically ambitious and uncompromising in their production values. We achieved this with “Inurri Itsuak”: a Basque-language film with international appeal and high production value that tells a story as deeply rooted in the local context as that of Ramiro Pinilla. Partnering with Playtime for international sales and Buena Vista for distribution in Spain will help the film reach the widest possible audience, Lazona Zinema producer Luis Ferrón told Variety . Popular on Variety ‘The Blind Ants.’ Photo Credit: Imanol Nabea “The Blind Ants” stars Urko Olazábal (Goya Award for Best Supporting Actor for “Maixabel,” nominated for Best Lead Actor for “Soy Nevenka”), Itziar Ituño (“Money Heist,” “Intimacy,” “Irati”), Josean Bengoetxea (“Balenciaga,” “Errementari,” “Loreak”), Miren Gaztañaga (“The Last Romantics,” “Ane,” “The Platform”) and Carlos Santos (“The Nuclear Bunker,” “Invisible,” “1992”). It is produced by leading Basque producer Lamia Producciones, Lamia Films, Lazona Zinema, Lazona Producciones, Buendía Estudios Bizkaia, Bruja del Norte AIE, and Sideral Cinema. It is co-produced with Caviar Antwerp. Igor Legarreta. Photo Credit: Esteban Delaiglesia Variety caught director Legarreta before the premiere. The film is based on Ramiro Pinilla’s book. Was it difficult to adapt it into a narrative film? Igor Legarreta: Adapting a novel is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, you have all the necessary materials: plot, characters, theme… But on the other hand, you have to transfer a literary universe to a very different world such as cinema. It is a long and complex process where you must try to separate yourself from the initial material, but without ever betraying it. I would like to point out that Pinilla’s novel conveys his love for both literary and cinematographic fiction, especially for the American fiction of the first half of the twentieth century. The film aims not to betray that love, and I truly believe that there are not many films with the character and visual strength of “Blind Ants.” What attracted you to the story? Legarreta: Undoubtedly, the experience that reading the novel provides. It is a literary gem that has not received the acclaim it deserves. I find many emotional connections with the story of the Jaureguis: life on the Basque coast, the small universe of the caserío [the Basque farmhouse], willpower as a weapon to continue fighting…. In the end, it is the story of a Basque family and its unwavering struggle not to lose its dignity. Did you shoot the film entirely in the Basque Country? Legarreta: Yes, the film was entirely shot in Bizkaia, in the Basque Country. We tried to preserve that coastal atmosphere. It is not for nothing that I have sometimes defined “Blind Ants” as a coastal Western. This is a big Basque period production co-produced with Belgium’s Caviar. Can you tell me about how the project came together? Legarreta: As often happens in cinema, travel companions are added little by little. The arrival of Robin (Caviar) and the subsequent incorporation of Kris and his entire team (Loom) helped us to grow the project in size and ambition. They are also part of the Jauregui family. You’ve worked with Itziar Ituño on some of your previous projects. Can you tell me about your working relationship with her? Legarreta: I’ve known Itziar since the time we were making short films at university, when she was taking her first steps as an actress and I as a director. Then, for some time, our paths separated until we met again in “All the Moons” (2021). Working with her is always a pleasure. She is a very close person, generous in her way of working, the kind of actress that is always part of the crew. Perhaps that’s why she has an enormous capacity to connect with real emotions and with real life. Tell me about the rest of the actors. Legarreta: It was a challenge to bring together a family as extensive and particular as the Jaureguis. We had to find a group of actors that could give us a real sense of family. And I think we succeeded. I had never worked with most of them, and in some way, they joined the project as we were making up that family. It has been a wonderful team that managed to take that bond beyond the filming. Any particular challenges while shooting the film? Legarreta: Half of the novel takes place during a stormy night on a cliff. When it came to filming, we decided to build a huge set to be able to shoot in the best conditions. We had to guarantee full safety in the scene, while we needed to have absolute control over all the elements. It was a real technical and creative challenge where the production design led by Mikel Serrano shines through in the film. articles.title: ‘It’s My Most Personal Film,’ Says Director Rodrigo García Saiz of His San Sebastian New Directors Title, ‘Morro’
articles.full_text: Sep 18, 2026 11:28pm PT ‘It’s My Most Personal Film,’ Says Director Rodrigo García Saiz of His San Sebastian New Directors Title, ‘Morro’ By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest Writer-Star Berto Romero, Director Javier Ruiz Caldera Unpack San Sebastian Buzz Title ‘5 More Minutes’: ‘Characters and Audience Should Feel Every Second’s Weight’ 4 hours ago ‘It’s My Most Personal Film,’ Says Director Rodrigo García Saiz of His San Sebastian New Directors Title, ‘Morro’ 6 hours ago James Gray’s ‘Paper Tiger’ Set to Open the 50th São Paulo Film Festival 3 days ago See All 'Morro' Courtesy of Calouma Films A dog is indeed a man’s best friend. A New Directors contender at the San Sebastián Film Festival, “ Morro ” explores the unlikely bond between a man and the dog he inadvertently adopts. It is Rodrigo Garcia Saiz ’s (“Lluvia”) sophomore feature and, by his own account, his most personal film to date. The titular Morro is a dog, reflecting Garcia Saiz’s own lifelong connection with the animal. Related Stories Oscars: Ukraine Selects 'Traces,' About Women Who Survived Sexual Assault During War With Russia, for International Feature Race TIFF Opens With Siân Heder’s Crowd-Pleasing ‘Being Heumann’ — and Apple Has Its Next Oscar Contender “I’ve always had a connection with dogs and I also wanted to reflect on the violence in Mexico since I left it,” says Garcia, who now resides in Madrid. “But not so much about showing the violence itself, but about what happens to the people who stay. And how an animal that doesn’t judge, that asks for nothing but love and gives love, could help.” Popular on Variety “Morro” revolves around Mateo, a vet in rural Mexico, who lives quietly with the unresolved guilt of losing his son. In a town where violence simmers beneath the surface, his fragile routine is disrupted when he treats Morro, the injured dog of a local drug lord. Caring for the animal sparks a wordless, judgment-free bond that slowly gives Mateo a renewed sense of purpose. “So the premise is really: Who saves whom? I started researching, went into conflict zones, and discovered this story, which is loosely based on the experience of someone I met through a friend.” “At first, he was a little hesitant because he didn’t really want to tell us the whole story. But little by little, he opened up. I gradually gained his trust, and he started telling me things, and I began putting the story together with another screenwriter [Carlos Armella] and some other collaborators. It was really exciting to realize that what I had in my head actually happens in real life. So I made the story very much my own and it became a story that really came from my heart.” He’s quick to point out that his film is not about drug trafficking and violence is never explicitly shown. “The violence is more in the moral and physical context.” Finding the right dog to fit the part was a challenge as he didn’t want a trained one, but as luck would have it, he found the right dog, which bonded with his lead actor, Gustavo Sánchez Parra (“Amores Perros,” Michael Rowe’s Cannes-winning “Leap Year” ), who even took him home. “He looked a little like the dog from the story I researched. And when I saw him, I fell in love with him because he had such a beautiful expression. He could also believably be a drug dealer’s dog, but at the same time, he’s such a gentle, sweet animal.” He also chose to film in 35mm with his DP Alfonso Herrera Salcedo (“Spectre”), a bold choice. “Shooting on 35mm was also a way of going back to basics. The set became almost like a church where everyone had to be quiet. There were no cell phones because the film stock is obviously very expensive, and you can’t just improvise, especially when you’re working with an animal and such a great actor. Everyone had to be completely focused and attentive. I’m really grateful that Kodak, PhotoKem and others supported me so much, because I feel the film has a very particular spirit – and that also comes from our decision to shoot it on 35mm.” His next project is even more personal: “I’m working on a film that deals with my relationship with my father, who died on my tenth birthday.” “Morro” is produced by Calouma Films , alongside Central Films and The 42 Film. Paola Cortés (“Lluvia”) Alberto Müffelmann (“I’m No Longer Here”), Julia Cherrier (“The Intruder”) and Pablo Guerrero (“New Order”) serve as producers. The 74 th San Sebastian Film Festival runs Sept. 18-26. articles.title: Portugal’s Queer Lisboa Celebrates 30th Anniversary With Vast Showcase of Latest LGBTQ Titles, Dose of Radical 1970s Counterculture and Family Fare
articles.full_text: Sep 18, 2026 11:44pm PT Portugal’s Queer Lisboa Celebrates 30th Anniversary With Vast Showcase of Latest LGBTQ Titles, Dose of Radical 1970s Counterculture and Family Fare Unspooling are films by Ira Sachs, Leah Nelson, Pedro Almodóvar, Jane Schoenbrun, Sally Potter, the Wachowskis and João Paulo Ferreira By Ed Meza Plus Icon Ed Meza @edmezavar Latest Portugal’s Queer Lisboa Celebrates 30th Anniversary With Vast Showcase of Latest LGBTQ Titles, Dose of Radical 1970s Counterculture and Family Fare 6 hours ago Don Palathara’s Indian Drama ‘Monkey Play’ Selected for Vancouver’s Inaugural Works-in-Progress Lab (EXCLUSIVE) 18 hours ago Canada’s BetterHalf Films Joins Indonesia’s Studio Amarana on Animated Film ‘Galeo of the Seawalkers’ (EXCLUSIVE) 18 hours ago See All André Godinho's 'Nothing Left' world premieres at Queer Lisboa. Courtesy of Terratreme Celebrating its 30th anniversary this year, Portugal’s preeminent Queer Lisboa – International Queer Film Festival kicked off Friday with a vast program showcasing the latest in LGBTQ cinema, from established filmmakers to new voices, and a look back at the underground counterculture and revolutionary works of activist filmmakers on both sides of the Atlantic. Lisbon’s oldest film festival, Queer Lisboa launched in 1997 at the Cinemateca Portuguesa as the Lisbon Gay and Lesbian Film Festival, opening with the 1950 short film “Un chant d’amour,” the only film ever directed by French novelist and playwright Jean Genet, whose works included “Querelle de Brest,” famously adapted by Rainer Werner Fassbinder. Related Stories Inde Navarrette Sets Best Actress Oscar Campaign for ‘Obsession’ as Focus Features Mounts Full Awards Push (EXCLUSIVE) Telluride Toasts Andrew Haigh as 'A Long Winter' Hands Fred Hechinger and Caitríona Balfe Awards-Worthy Roles Ana David and João Ferreira Credit: Joana Linda/Nuno Ferreira Santos The festival’s origins at the Portuguese Cinematheque is one of the factors that has distinguished it from other queer festivals across Europe, Queer Lisboa artistic director João Ferreira tells Variety . Popular on Variety “From the very beginning, I would say that the festival was not envisioned as a kind of niche or festival only for the LGBTQ community because of the institutional support that it already had from day one. So I think it’s a very particular case for a queer festival in Europe. It was certainly not the case with some festivals that started more or less at the same time, like Madrid or Paris. “The audience was from the very beginning, a very broad audience and an audience interested in film, a cinephile audience,” Ferreira adds. “But of course, also because in the first three years it was organized by the Portuguese chapter of ILGA [the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association], it also had this very important community aspect to it.” The Man I Love Courtesy of Cannes Film Festival The festival’s perception of queer cinema has never been based merely on narrative, Ferreira notes. “It was much broader than that. We were interested in a queer gaze at the world. We were interested in a camp aesthetic. So we were looking for very different kinds of films that could fit in this idea.” It was a view that shaped what the festival ultimately became, he adds. “Then the festival was called the Gay and Lesbian Film Festival, but the idea was already queer at the time, the way we looked at film.” With a total of 94 feature, documentary and short films, the 30th edition of Queer Lisboa takes place at its regular venues, the Cinemateca Portuguesa and Cinema São Jorge, running Sept. 18-26. Boasting a strong lineup that includes some of the year’s top LGBTQ titles, the festival opens with the Portuguese premiere of Rami Malek -starrer “ The Man I Love ” from Ira Sachs, whose previous films, “Passages” and “Peter Hujar’s Day,” likewise screened in Lisbon. Leah Nelson’s acclaimed animated drama “ Tangles ” closes the event. Papaya ‘Papaya’ was among the first films to receive Screen Brasil distribution support. Credit: Priscilla Kellen With nearly a dozen sections, including five competition categories and six non-competitive sidebars, the festival offers a broad showcase. New this year is Queer Family, dedicated to kids and their families, with a focus on culturally enriching independent films that explore themes of inclusion and identity. Two Brazilian features make up the program, Allan Deberton’s Berlinale award-winner “ Gugu’s World ” and Priscilla Kellen’s animated “ Papaya .” It’s been a long-standing goal to attract younger audiences, says Ana David, programmer and director at Queer Lisboa. Gugu’s World Courtesy of Jamille Queiroz The new section is aimed directly at families and the festival has already received positive feedback from interested parents. “We’ll see if it’s the kids bringing their parents, or if it’s the parents bringing their kids. It’s important for us to work with young audiences who will also become the adult audiences of the festival in the future,” David says. The new section also provides the opportunity for parents and their children to have an intergenerational experience and to even talk about things after the screening, she adds. The festival has already sold a large amount of tickets for the Queer Family screenings. “We think it’s going to work out really well,” David says. With the increasing growth and appeal of LGBTQ cinema, Queer Lisboa has sought to find a balance between popular mainstream works, new discoveries and the more radical experimental films that have long defined queer cinema. “We want this spectrum, the big films and very small films,” says Ferreira. “It’s part of our joy as programmers to discover these smaller and more independent, sometimes more DIY filmmakers and filmmaking, and we try to put all that in the program. It is challenging.” While it’s much easier now to acquire films than it was 30 years ago, it’s become more difficult to filter through the huge amount of available titles and curate the 90-plus films that the festival presents, Ferreira adds. Bound Courtesy of Queer Lisboa Offering a rare treat for its 30th anniversary is an expanded Retrospectives section with 19 titles, including such works as the Wachowskis’ 1996 debut film “ Bound ”; Sally Potter’s “ Orlando ” (1992), Lisa Cholodenko’s “ High Art ” (1998), Patrice Chéreau’s “ The Wounded Man ” (1983), Kim Longinotto and Jano Williams’ British doc “ Shinjuku Boys ” (1995) and, from West Germany, Frank Ripploh’s 1980 classic “Taxi to the Toilet” (“Taxi zum Klo”). This year’s showcase is especially interesting as Queer Lisboa is hitting 30 at the same time BFI Flare in London turns 40 and San Francisco’s Frameline turns 50, David notes. Those festivals, along with Paris’ Chéries-Chéris, “served as inspirations for the birth of Queer Lisboa.” “It speaks to the longevity of queer cinema, but also the festivals that have for a long time now been promoting and expanding on the knowledge and appreciation of queer cinema,” David notes. Orlando Courtesy of Queer Lisboa For Queer Lisboa, it was an opportunity to look back at early films that are rare exhibitions in Portugal even if they’re already considered canon films within queer cinema. “We wanted to offer some classic titles that people know and can engage with the retrospective, but then also offer something new for them to learn about and that can expand on their knowledge,” David adds. An important element of that is to present the films in restored or digitized versions. It’s the first time that “Orlando” screens at the Cinemateca Portuguesa, David points out. “And they actually have a 35mm print, so it’s amazing that we can offer an excuse for this film to be shown.” “And to take it out of the closet,” Ferreira quips. Fatucha Superstar Courtesy of Queer Lisboa Also presented will be a newly restored version of João Paulo Ferreira’s 1976 subversive queer musical comedy “Fatucha Superstar,” inspired by Andrew Lloyd Webber’s “Jesus Christ Superstar.” Made in the wake of the revolution that swept away Portugal’s authoritarian dictatorship, the film blasphemously ridicules in ultimate kitsch fashion one of the main pillars of the former regime, the apparition of Our Lady of Fátima and the Christian symbolism that surrounded it. Along with Óscar Alves, João Paulo Ferreira was part of the rebellious and independent gay filmmaking movement that produced the first queer films in post-revolution Portugal. Together they founded the film collective Cineground and screened their Super 8 films in Lisbon’s queer bars and night clubs in the 1970s. Maspalomas Maspalomas Film Factory Entertainment Among the returning talents and exciting discoveries this year are Portuguese filmmaker André Godinho and the world premiere of his debut feature “Nothing Left,” described as a Portuguese queer version of “Punishment Park”; and German artist duo Benjamin Ramírez Pérez and Stefan Ramírez Pérez with the world premiere of “Life Is About Losing Everything,” their hybrid doc on the life and work of Canadian poet Lynn Crosbie, likewise a first feature. Both films unspool in the Queer Art Competition, which showcases experimental, boundary-busting works that “explore the limits of cinematic languages, genres, and narratives.” Other highlights include Swiss-French feature “ Summer Drift ,” by Céline Carridroit and Aline Suter, and the European premiere of “Public Access,” David Shadrack Smith’s look at the people who transformed New York City TV into a groundbreaking space for self-expression during the 1970s and 80s. This year’s diverse lineup includes special screenings of Pedro Almodóvar’s “ Bitter Christmas ” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “ Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma ,” while the fest’s non-competitive Panorama sidebar presents such recent international festival hits as “ Jim Queen “; “ Maspalomas ;” “ Outerlands “; and “ Prosecution .” Strange River Courtesy of Queer Lisboa Competing in this year’s Queer Lisboa feature film competition are: “Black Burns Fast,” by Sandulela Asanda (South Africa) “ On the Road ,” by David Pablos (Mexico) “ Strange River ,” by Jaume Claret Muxart’s (Spain, Germany) “ La Gradiva ,” by Marine Atlan (France, Italy) “ Iván & Hadoum ,” by Ian de la Rosa (Spain, Germany, Belgium) “ Julian ,” by Cato Kusters (Belgium, The Netherlands) “ London ,” by Victor Di Marco and Márcio Picoli (Brazil) “Raging,” by Ryan Machado (Philippines) The entire Queer Lisboa program can be explored here . Yossman @KJYossman Latest Lego’s ‘Ninjago Legends: Duskfall’ Anime-Style Shorts Premiere in Korea Ahead of YouTube Release 6 hours ago King Charles Denies Bombshell Book Claim That He Said World Would ‘Forget’ Princess Diana 2 days ago Ozzy Osbourne and Black Sabbath’s Final Concert Film Sets October Release Date 3 days ago See All The LEGO Group “ Ninjago Legends: Duskfall” is premiering in Korea this weekend ahead of a worldwide release on Lego ’s YouTube channel. The anime-style shorts feature some of “Ninjago’s” most beloved characters as they encounter new challenges and new battles while bringing back some familiar voices from the original show as well as “Ninjago Dragons Rising.” The series of three interconnected shorts, each three-minutes long, premiered Friday at a “Ninjago Legends” Duskfall” fan event at the Park Mall Yongsan in Seoul. The shorts will be released on the Lego Group’s YouTube channel on Saturday, Sept. 19. Related Stories Oscars: Israel Selects HIV Drama ‘Tell Me Everything’ for International Feature Race TIFF Opens With Siân Heder’s Crowd-Pleasing ‘Being Heumann’ — and Apple Has Its Next Oscar Contender The three shorts are titled “The End Begins,” directed by David Cazeaux and Charles Lefebvre, “Terminus,” directed again by Cazeaux and Lefebvre, and “Epilogue,” directed by Cazeaux, Lefebvre and Hugo Cierzniak. Popular on Variety Andrew Francis reprises his role as Cole alongside Kelly Metzger as Nya and Vincent Tong as Kai. Also returning to the franchise are Brian Drummond as Diviner and Runt, Adrian Petriw as Scott and Sabrina Pitre (the voice of Sora in “Dragons Rising”) as a reporter. In a trailer for the shorts series, it opens with a female voice saying “Kai, if you make it out of this, promise me you’ll walk away.” It then cuts to plenty of action before Kai, in his red ninja outfit, says: “Save the Elementals, I’m coming.” The female voice then says: “We’re not fighting demons or monsters anymore, they call us warriors. Protectors. Ninja.” Created to mark the fifteenth anniversary of the “Ninjago” franchise, the shorts offer fans who’ve grown up the show an opportunity to watch the characters in a new way, with many hoping the anime-style shorts will be expanded into a full series.
