articles.title: Writer-Star Berto Romero, Director Javier Ruiz Caldera Unpack San Sebastian Buzz Title ‘5 More Minutes’: ‘Characters and Audience Should Feel Every Second’s Weight’
articles.full_text: Sep 19, 2026 1:38am PT Writer-Star Berto Romero, Director Javier Ruiz Caldera Unpack San Sebastian Buzz Title ‘5 More Minutes’: ‘Characters and Audience Should Feel Every Second’s Weight’ By Anna Marie de la Fuente , John Hopewell (L-R) Berto Romero, Javier Cámara, '5 More Minutes' Credit: Quim Vives World-premiering in San Sebastián main competition, Javier Ruiz Caldera’s time-warping drama ‘5 More Minutes’ (‘5 Minutos Más’) suggests one way an on-the rocks relationship may come closer together again: by plunging them into the makings of a global apocalypse. Writer-star Berto Romero (“The Other Side”) and Belen Cuesta (“The Endless Trench”) play a couple who are trying to repair their frayed marriage, retreating to an idyllic vacation home in Spain’s exquisite Girona countryside. There they are handed the keys by Carlos, a property manager, played by the ever-popular Javier Cámara (“Talk to Her”) in a rare, less simpático role. Not long after he hands over the keys, time jumps back five minutes. Related Stories John Turturro Has Waited 40 Years for an Oscar Nomination. ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Makes the Case 'I Play Rocky' Premieres at TIFF: A Movie About a Best Picture Winner That's a Best Picture Contender? Actor-writer Berto Romero and Belen Cuesta in ‘5 More Minutes’ QUIM VIVES As time continues to jump back for them, again and again, they grow increasingly paranoid. Catalonia has always looked to France for inspiration. This is a film which melds the great French and Catalan tradition of questioning the civilized manners of the bourgeoisie, rcast in a thouroughly modern genre blender, part excriciating comedy, part min-bending sci-fi, and part a shockingly violent thriller, driven by the logic of nightmares. Popular on Variety A potential breakout, “5 More Minutes” is produced by Movistar Plus, El Terrat, part of The Mediapro Studio, and Ikiru Films. Filmax handles domestic distribution in Spain and internatonal sales. Ruiz Caldera and Romero both spoke to Variety in the run-up to San Sebastian’s world premiere. What was it about this project that compelled you to take it on, particularly after your previous film? Ruiz Caldera: I always want my next film to differ from the previous one and present a new challenge. Berto Romero’s script offered that, combining the genres I love most: fantasy, thriller and irresistible humor. I immediately wanted to make it. The choice of music framing the film is striking. What informed the decision to open and close with Roy Orbison’s “In Dreams,” and what did you hope that musical motif would evoke? Ruiz Caldera : Finding the right song was difficult. We wanted something hypnotic and mysterious that signaled this wasn’t simply a comedy. Then “In Dreams” clicked. Many will remember it from David Lynch’s “Blue Velvet,” and I hope that association adds an intriguing layer. The performances feel remarkably spontaneous despite the film’s highly choreographed structure. How much latitude did you allow the actors to improvise, particularly Belén Cuesta, whose role is especially dialogue-heavy? Ruiz Caldera : We rehearsed extensively and improvised during preparation, but the actual takes were highly choreographed. The film consists of five-minute takes, so everything had to be timed precisely. Making it look spontaneous was the goal, and Javier Cámara, Belén Cuesta and Berto Romero made that possible. The film navigates an unusually delicate tonal terrain between black comedy, suspense and the fantastic. How did you calibrate those elements without allowing one to undermine the others? Ruiz Caldera : Humor helps release tension before catching the audience off guard again. Given the characters’ extreme situation, black humor also feels natural—a way of protecting themselves from anxiety and fear. The setting in Girona plays a significant atmospheric role. What drew you to this particular location, and how did its familiarity and natural beauty inform the film’s darker impulses? Ruiz Caldera : It was shot in a beautiful valley in Girona, Catalonia, at a friend’s house I’ve known since childhood. It’s a paradise – an ideal setting for a nightmare. The decision to construct the film around precisely five-minute takes presents a formidable formal and technical challenge. What motivated this constraint, and how did you coordinate the cinematography, production design, costume, sound, visual effects and production teams to sustain identical conditions across every sequence? Every sequence shot had to last exactly five minutes, no more or less. We wanted audiences to genuinely feel the weight of those five minutes without relying on editing. After months of testing, every sequence was filmed at exactly 6:35 p.m., with identical light. Close coordination between cinematography, art, costume, sound, visual effects and production made the technical feat possible. How has the involvement of Movistar Plus, a producer with El Terrat and Ikiru, helped to empower “5 More Minutes” in production terms. And how should it help its distribution potential in Spain? Romero: I have worked with Movistar Plus on several productions over the years and have built a strong relationship of trust with their creative and production teams. The same is true of El Terrat, with whom I have worked in film and television for more than two decades. Together with Ikiru Films, they have supported the project from the beginning and given us complete creative freedom. For distribution in Spain, having Filmax on board gives us great confidence. Their experience, knowledge of the market, and ability to connect films with audiences are a major advantage. Together with the support of Movistar Plus, El Terrat and Ikiru Films, we have a strong foundation to give ‘5 More Minutes’ visibility and reach a broad audience. “5 More Minutes” blends sci-fi, survival thriller and excruciating (in the best sense) comedy. What attracts you to genre mixes? I have always been drawn to stories that blend genres. Life itself is a good example: it can move from comedy to horror, thriller or drama in a matter of seconds. To me, that feels natural. I like to follow the story I want to tell and let the genres emerge organically. I come from stand-up comedy and television, where I have worked for 30 years, so my way of seeing the world is naturally influenced by humor. At the same time, I have always loved genre stories, especially horror, thrillers, science fiction and fantasy. I think my writing is a mix of everything I enjoy, filtered through my own view of life. With ‘5 More Minutes,’ I never set out to make a comedy. But in the end, humor, much like life in ‘Jurassic Park,’ found a way. A considerable number of top Spanish directors – Rodrigo Sorogoyen, Alberto Rodríguez – use genre. Is there something about Spain or Spanish cinema which explain this predilection in auteurs? I don’t feel qualified to speak for other writers or define a characteristic of Spanish cinema. For me, it is simply a personal preference as a storyteller. I find it fascinating to use genre conventions, subvert them and take audiences somewhere they don’t expect. I think this fascination with genre is more international than uniquely Spanish, though that may just be my own bias. In my case, it is a purely instinctive and irrational impulse when I write. articles.title: Naomi Watts Believes Standards Have Changed for Older Women in the Industry: ‘Look at the Emmys Last Week… That’s Heartening to See’
articles.full_text: Sep 19, 2026 2:48am PT Naomi Watts Believes Standards Have Changed for Older Women in the Industry: ‘Look at the Emmys Last Week… That’s Heartening to See’ The ‘Mulholland Drive’ star is at the San Sebastián Film Festival to screen Ben Shirinian’s ‘The Housewife,’ as well as to receive this year’s Donostia Award By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Naomi Watts Believes Standards Have Changed for Older Women in the Industry: ‘Look at the Emmys Last Week… That’s Heartening to See’ 3 hours ago Catalonia: A Dozen Highlights at San Sebastián, From a Time-Loop Thriller to a Singular Heist Tale and a Potential Arthouse Sleeper 1 day ago Boutique Filmes Lines Up Marina Ruy Barbosa, João Guilherme, ‘Strange Way of Life’ Breakout José Condessa for ‘The Mystery of the 5 Stars’ With Vera Egito to Direct (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago See All Naomi Watts Courtesy of JuanKR for PC British actor Naomi Watts , at the San Sebastián Film Festival to receive this year’s prestigious Donostia Award, spoke about opportunities in the industry for women over 50. Talking a week after Sarah Paulson told Variety about the lack of film offers following her spellbinding portrait of Marcia Clark in “The People v. O.J. Simpson: American Crime Story,” Watts said, “things have changed.” Watts recalled entering the industry late “by Hollywood standards,” starring in David Lynch’s lauded “Mulholland Drive” at 31 years old. “I was told at the beginning that I better get my skates on because it all finishes at the age of 40. And here we are today. I’m in my late 50s. Look at the Emmys last week [and] the number of women in strong categories over 50. That’s heartening to see.” Popular on Variety Related Stories Oscars: Philippines Selects Rafael Manuel’s ‘Filipiñana’ for International Feature Race Oscars: Hungary Selects Ildiko Enyedi’s ‘Silent Friend’ for International Feature Race (EXCLUSIVE) Nominees over the age of 50 included Rhea Seehorn (“Pluribus”), Jean Smart (“Hacks”), and Allison Janney (“The Diplomat”). “I do think things have changed,” she added. “Women are consumers of film and TV, and their stories should be reflected. That narrative had to be shifted. And I am grateful to be a small part of that shift.” The actor is also at the Basque festival with Ben Shirinian’s feature debut “ The Housewife .” The film, the Donostia Award Screening, stars Watts, Tye Sheridan, Luke Evans, Michael Imperioli and Lena Olin. Set in 1964 and based on a true story, the film tells the tale of a young journalist who tracks down a potential Nazi officer living secretly in New York and befriends the suspect’s charming wife. Prodded about the parallels between a film about World War II and the Holocaust and the ongoing wars today, specifically the ongoing war in Palestine, Watts said: “It’s a very, very scary time what is going on in the world globally.” “We must be vigilant, we must pay attention, and not let that happen again. Hopefully this film sparks a dialogue. We don’t give answers; we hopefully send you away with questions of how did this happen and, who do you relate with in this story, and how we can avoid this happening ever again.” “We have to tell these stories; storytelling is important, particularly now,” she reiterated, noting how she vows to continue supporting minorities and representation on screen. “I’m proud to be a part of the LGBTQ community. Minorities are being attacked right now, and it’s frightful and unacceptable. My heart is with these communities, particularly my family. I’ll do whatever I can to stick up for minorities.” As for playing an immigrant in the U.S. as an immigrant to the country herself, Watts said she “moved to America with hopes and dreams,” all of which she has already “surpassed.” “Hermine, the woman I play in this story, was there post-World War II, when things were much more sunny and bright. Her story was about trying to find a new place and erase the past, which she was able to do for a period of time.” “In terms of me, I have American children, I do love America, and what’s going on today is complicated and certainly nerve-wracking, but I have faith that things will work out in time,” she added about the U.S.’s current political climate. Watts noted how the role was “very complicated,” and she had a “huge amount of fear” when taking on the adaptation of the harrowing true story. “It was like nothing I ever played before: this duality of this woman who had done horrific things, heinous crimes, and yet blending into society as a normal person – very much a good citizen, a good wife, baking cookies, showing up to church. That duality and living with that secret was interesting to me as an actor.” “I am always looking to do new things even though I might have a repetitive theme in my work – grief and identity— things that are meaningful to me,” she continued. “This character is like nothing I’ve ever played. I’m at an age now when some might joke I’m in my villain era, but this is an extreme one and not a joke. I felt compelled to play this story.” When asked about the similarities between her role in “Mulholland Drive” and “The Housewife,” especially how both characters broach these notions of duality, Watts said both roles are “deeply psychological and confronting,” but while she didn’t particularly enjoy playing Hermine, she has nothing but wonderful memories of her time on set with the late Lynch, who died early last year. “‘Mulholland Drive’ was nothing but fun,” she said. “It was coming at a time in my life when I didn’t have any breaks after years of struggle, so every day on set was just a wonder. Getting to learn how Lynch works and directs was truly wonderful. I’ll never forget those days.” The actor called working with Lynch “an incredible break.” “I had been working to get a film role for a good 10 years before that lucky break came. I was very much a journeyman actor, working wherever I could, but I had a lot of rejection. really was quite shut down, not bringing good energy into rooms I was asked to audition in. It took someone like David Lynch to see through the veneers I had created. We had a beautiful conversation, and he gave me the role of a lifetime.” “I’m forever indebted to David Lynch; he is in my heart forever,” she went on. “This is a film that has remained in people’s consciousness for decades, and I think it really launched me because every great filmmaker saw this film.” The San Sebastián Film Festival runs Sept. 18-26. articles.title: Spain’s SETT Drives $521 Million Investment Push to Build Global Audiovisual Players
articles.full_text: Sep 19, 2026 2:55am PT Spain’s SETT Drives $521 Million Investment Push to Build Global Audiovisual Players Spearheading the Spain Audiovisual Hub Phase 2, SETT, a state-backed venture capital fund, represents new opportunities for Spain’s film and TV industries By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Writer-Star Berto Romero, Director Javier Ruiz Caldera Unpack San Sebastian Buzz Title ‘5 More Minutes’: ‘Characters and Audience Should Feel Every Second’s Weight’ 4 hours ago TV Operators Power Spain’s Global Breakout as the San Sebastian Film Festival Readies Launch: ‘Spanish Cinema Has Never Been So Powerful’ 19 hours ago Juan Andrés García Ropero ‘Bropi,’ the New Director of Contents of Movistar Plus, on Its San Sebastián Titles, Strategy 19 hours ago See All 'People of the Book,' the first film from Good Films Studios Spain Courtesy of GFSS No Spanish industry initiative is likely to drive more conversation at this year’s San Sebastián Festival than the latest moves by the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation ( SETT ). Over the past 12 months, state-backed venture capital fund SETT, the investment driver of the Spain Audiovisual Hub , has plowed €215.6 million ($252.3 million) into Spain’s film, TV, video game and new technology sectors, sparking matching private-sector investment of a further €230 million ($269.1 million), says María González Veracruz, Spain’s secretary of state for digitalization and artificial intelligence. That’s around four times the average budget of Spain’s core subsidy fund at the country‘s ICAA Film Board. Popular on Variety In other ways, SETT, which is part of Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation, also harbors a revolution. Since the 1940s, Spanish governments have offered subsidy grants and loans for individual films, and from around 2015, tax breaks on shoots in Spain. In contrast, SETT invests up to 10 years in companies with a portfolio of productions, requiring co-investment from private-sector partners, and looking to give them an edge in the international market. It also backs private-sector investment vehicles. “We are moving from an era of encouraging an ecosystem to consolidating a truly international audiovisual industry,” says González Veracruz. Eleven of 15 SETT investments have been made public to date, with beneficiaries including animation sector leaders ( Anima Kitchent , Amuse Animation, Planeta Junior), new Spain-based production companies ( Good Films Studios Spain , Ítaca Films Madrid, Moonlighting Studios Spain), post-production facilities ( Lazona Audiovisual Hub, the Refinery) and a full chain-of-value production-distribution player (Impulse Studio). Also underscoring the range of SETT’s portfolio, risk capital fund partners include Aurora Media Inversiones, led by the Secuoya Content Group, Culture CAP7, which targets small- to medium-sized enterprises, and elevated genre specialist Moby Dick Film Capital. Serving as a “public catalyst for growth, employment, innovation and talent, which are all core elements of the audiovisual sector,” SETT brings to the table the weight and power of the Spanish government and European Union backing, says SETT director general Javier Ponce. With the Spain Audiovisual Hub a key element of Spain’s post-COVID Recovery Plan, SETT’s funding is financed through the European Union’s Next Generation funds, Ponce notes. Its model has been built on three pillars, adds SETT audiovisual director María Coronado: “First, it adopts an industrywide approach, rather than a project-based one, addressing the entire audiovisual business ecosystem. Second, its investment facilities are directed at the equity capital of companies or regulated investment vehicles. Third, it promotes public-private partnership instruments in the medium to long term.” Companies must represent a “worthwhile business opportunity,” she adds. As global markets have contracted to some 75% of peak TV, according to Ampere Analysis, however, where are these opportunities? The key to SETT is its specific operations. SETT has taken a 46% stake for €19.8 million ($22.6 million), for instance, in Good Films Studios Spain, set up at Spain’s Ciudad de la Luz, one of Spain’s biggest studio complexes. It aims to make competitive English-language movies, budgeted at €15 million-€25 million ($17.5 million-$29.3 million) “with stars of international theatrical market value,” says GFSS head Miriam Segal, producer of “Good,” with Viggo Mortensen and “The Infiltrator,” starring Bryan Cranston. Attracting such stars, however, is ever more difficult, she adds. “So it makes making independent films at this level very, very hard. So to have a government body like SETT and hopefully new producer-driven tax incentives, it’s like I died and went to heaven,” says Segal. “In a world that’s receding, to have a country with the vision to support filmmakers, independence, training and creation of an industry is very exciting.” Established in Madrid by Roberto Butragueño and Andrés Sánchez Pajares and co-owned by SETT, Impulse Studio offers everything, from upstream development to financing, production, post-production, international sales and distribution. “When we talk with potential partners on projects or potential investors, we have the stamp of security of government backing,” says Sánchez Pajares. With SETT’s support, we can bring “hard equity” to the table, retaining part of the IP, “and offer all services at any phase of a project,” says Sánchez, Impulse Studio CEO. “I think that will allow us to sit at tables where we were not able to talk to date.” Further growth opportunities turn on scaling up animation projects aimed at the preschool audience. In another move, investing €9.2 million ($10.7 million) and partnering with Planeta Junior and Amuse Animation, SETT co-bought select distribution rights to hit preschool toon series “Milo,” sold to 186 territories, across multiple formats. “‘Milo’ represents a strategic opportunity in the field of technology development, particularly in software, video games and mobile applications,” says Coronado. “Spain has already established itself as one of Europe’s most attractive production hubs, thanks to its combination of creative talent, production incentives, and infrastructure,” says Maria Rua Aguete at London-based consultancy Omdia. “The next logical step is for Spain to transition from being a production destination to building globally competitive Spanish companies that own and export intellectual property.” EU Next Generation funds ran out on Aug. 30. SETT doesn’t aim to stop here, however. “The audiovisual sector will remain one of SETT’s strategic areas of activity and will continue under new fund, España Crece. We have begun discussions with [Spanish state bank] ICO to define the procedures and framework for collaboration between the two institutions, ensuring the continuation of co-investment in strategic technologies and sectors,” says Ponce. A Drill Down on Further SETT Investments “ The goal of the Hub’s second phase is clear: that Spain continues to be not only a great place to film, but also a great place to create, produce, finance, and export content, technology, and intellectual property to the world,” says González Veracruz. She adds: “ It’s a portfolio that reflects an industrial, technological, domestic and international view of Spanish audiovisual production.” A breakdown of announced SETT investments: *South Africa’s Known Associates Group and SETT have invested a joint €25 million ($29 million) to launch Moonlighting Studios Spain, a Madrid-based production company, and post-pro The Refinery, with facilities in the Basque Country and the Canary Islands. *Alongside DNEG , “The Odyssey’s” sole VFX partner, SETT has taken €24.9 million ($29.1 million) equity in the Canary Islands’ Anima Kitchen, behind pre-school animation series hits “Cleo & Cuquín.” Anima Kitchent is renowned for leveraging YouTube, where it has over 67 million subscribers, in order to launch and consolidate IPs. “The real edge is the combination: strong IP and production values paired with data analysis that tracks audience trends in real time. Producing quickly and at high quality is precisely what makes that IPs travel into new markets,” comments Pablo Hernández, executive president of the Canary Islands ZEC tax benefit zone. *SETT has put up €20 million ($23.4 million) of a total €45 million ($52.65 million), the rest coming from Mexico’s Ítaca Films and investor Omega Capital, to found Ítaca Films Madrid, an international content studio. “For Ítaca Films, SETT represents much more than financing. It’s an instrument which institutionalises the industry, strengthens producers and shows that creativity, when it counts on structure and solid bases, can grow and develop better,” says Ítaca’s Santiago García. *Focused on the creation, ownership and global distribution of kids & family IPs, Amuse Labs, a new Canary Islands animation company, has received a €6.4 million ($7.3 million) investment from SETT in return for a 48% equity position. Amuse Studios will become Amuse Labs’ second-largest shareholder. *SETT has taken a 46% equity participation for €1.1 million ($1.3 million) in Lazona Audiovisual Hub, along with Lazona (36%) and El Alamedia Estidios (13%), billed as a Madrid creation and post-production factory aiming to meet the large demand for post-production services in the Spanish capital. ‘Days of Thunder 2’: Jonathan Levine in Talks to Direct Tom Cruise in Paramount Sequel Nicole Kidman Got Warned About Marrying Tom Cruise but Fired Back: ‘I Don’t Care. articles.title: Headed to Netflix this fall
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi Book-To-Movie Adaptations Coming Out In 2026 Everything We Know About Netflix’s New ‘Pride & Prejudice’ Series So Far TV Show Book Adaptations Arriving In 2026 So Far View All February 24, 2026 7:00am The first teaser trailer for Netflix ’s Pride & Prejudice series, based on Jane Austen ’s classic novel, is here. The clip features Elizabeth Bennet (Emma Corrin) and Mr. Darcy (Jack Lowden). The six-part series will be a faithful, classic adaptation of the novel, written by Dolly Alderton ( Everything I Know About Love, Good Material ) and directed by Euros Lyn ( Heartstopper ), launching in fall 2026. Related Stories Casting ‘Pride & Prejudice’: Rufus Sewell & Freya Mavor Among New Additions As Netflix Series Sets Full Cast, Releases First-Look Image Of Bennet Women News ‘Pride & Prejudice’ Helmer Joe Wright Talks Film’s Internet Legacy — And How Emma Thompson Improvised Charlotte Lucas’ Meme-Worthy Speech Alongside Corrin ( Nosferatu, Black Mirror ) and Lowden ( Slow Horses, Benediction ), Olivia Colman ( The Favourite, The Crown ) will be Mrs. Bennet, Rufus Sewell ( The Diplomat, Scoop ) will be Mr. Bennet, Freya Mavor ( Industry, La Dame Dans L’Auto ) will be Jane Bennet, Jamie Demetriou ( Stath Lets Flats, Barbie ) will be Mr. Collins and Daryl McCormack ( Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery; Good Luck to You, Leo Grande ) will be Mr. Bingley. Rhea Norwood ( Heartstopper ) will play Lydia Bennett, Hopey Parish and Hollie Avery will play Mary and Kitty Bennett, Siena Kelly will play Caroline Bingley, and Fiona Shaw ( Bad Sisters , Harry Potter ) will play Lady Catherine de Bourgh. When the full cast was revealed during production, writer and executive producer Alderton said: “‘Once in a generation, a group of people get to retell this wonderful story and I feel very lucky that I get to be a part of it. Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice is the blueprint for romantic comedy – it has been a joy to delve back into its pages to find both familiar and fresh ways of bringing this beloved book to life. With Euros Lyn directing our stellar cast, I am so excited to reintroduce these hilarious and complicated characters to those who count Pride and Prejudice as their favourite book, and those who are yet to meet their Lizzie and Mr. Darcy.” Watch on Deadline Other executive producers include Laura Lankester, Will Johnston and Louise Mutter for Lookout Point, as well as Alderton and Lyn. Corrin is also an executive producer, marking their debut in the role. Austen’s beloved novels have enraptured generations for over 200 years. Her most famous and widely-read novel, Pride and Prejudice has inspired countless writers and filmmakers with its iconic characters, sharp social commentary and timeless love story. In the UK last week, the teaser played on the big screen ahead of Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights starring Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi. Austen’s Sense and Sensibility will get a new adaptation in film form later this year as well from Focus Features starring Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood, Esmé Creed-Miles as Marianne Dashwood, Catríona Balfe as Mrs. Dashwood and more. The 1995 film version of Sense and Sensibility starred Kate Winslet, Emma Thompson, Alan Rickman, Hugh Grant and more.

articles.title: Paramount Sets California Exit Plans Over Antitrust Battle With Blue States & Stymied $111B WBD…
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Paramount And State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of October Settlement Meetings Banned: CNN & MS Now Shut Out Of White House By Trump; POTUS Says “Other Fake News Media Outlets To Follow” Gavin Newsom Moves To Lasso AI With “Kill Switch” Oversight Executive Order: “We’re Not Waiting To Act” View All September 16, 2026 12:14pm Story Arc Paramount's Melrose Gate Eric Thayer/Getty Images David Ellison has let it be known that he is willing to take his Paramount ball and leave California if the state doesn’t ditch its effort to block the company’s pending merger with Warner Bros Discovery . Related Stories Executives L.A. County Projects Huge Job Losses If Paramount Exits California; Company Slams Antitrust Action By AGs & WGA In Official Rebuke News Judge Sets Date For Settlement Talks In Paramount-WBD Antitrust Case And now it looks like the CEO’s ball really could be in play. Paramount brass have told key officials and stakeholders the company is “deadly serious” about leaving California and the home of Hollywood after more than 100 years, sources tell Deadline. Among those told a deposit has been put down on the moving trucks is L.A. Mayor Karen Bass and state Attorney General Rob Bonta . The AG joined with 11 other states to file an antitrust lawsuit against the $110 billion merger. The Writers Guild of America has also sued. “Mayor Bass is focused on protecting and fighting for jobs in L.A., including critical jobs in the entertainment industry that have been a vital part of Los Angeles’ economy,” a spokesperson for City Hall told Deadline today. “She’s been engaged on this issue and will continue to fight to make sure L.A. is home to Hollywood,” the mayor’s office added. Watch on Deadline Thousands of jobs will be lost if Paramount’s corporate headquarters were to shift to Georgia, Tennessee or Texas, three sites reportedly floated by the company. Even without a move, a merged company would likely see layoffs as it looks to deliver shareholders $6 billion in promised cost savings. Bonta has over the past several months called out Paramount for engaging in “blackmail” in its efforts to sway the court of public opinion over the merger. He is likely to express that sentiment again on Thursday at a conference in New York City, where he is slated to appear on an antitrust panel along with AGs from Pennsylvania and New Hampshire. As the exit plan appeared to be taking more concrete shape on Wednesday, the AGs office again accused Paramount of saber-rattling. “We cannot comment on a company’s plans,” a spokesperson for AG Bonta told Deadline Wednesday over the moving notice. “It’s no secret that Paramount has been making this threat, despite its alleged commitment to California and Hollywood. What Paramount decides to do is Paramount’s choice alone. We’ll continue to apply the law without fear or favor and continue to be open to coming to the table for good faith discussions.” Paramount had no comment when contacted by Deadline about the current state of exit plans. TMZ first reported that the company had contacted city and state officials about an exit announcement. While the trio of red states are all under consideration, Tennessee has strong link to the Ellison family. In that, Paramount has been making inquiries about commercial real estate possibilities that could meet its needs, well-placed sources tell me. The limbo state of the merger since the mid-July filing of the lawsuits has ratcheted up anxiety levels in an industry already contending with the rise of Big Tech, production leaving the U.S. and other challenges. The trial date of March 2 feels like an eternity from now for an industry on edge. The parties will hold court-ordered settlement meetings next month and a hearing will be held next week on Paramount’s request for a $1.88 billion bond from the plaintiffs to cover “extraordinary losses” the company anticipates due to having to pay a “ticking fee” during litigation. Beyond that, it’s anyone’s guess. Ellison’s big move to move comes almost two weeks before the October 1 date when the ticking fee, which Paramount voluntarily added as a sweetener in its battle with Netflix over buying WBD, starts kicking in. At roughly $7.2 million a day, the fee would reach $635 million for the full quarter, paid directly to WBD shareholders. California Attorney General Rob Bonta left, Paramount CEO David Ellison Getty Images Despite the storm of speculation about the red state/blue state dynamic of the potential move, the fact is any exit will have little immediate impact on the antitrust suit’s route through the federal courts – at least for now. The optics would be very immediate if Paramount really does leave. One plus for the company, in theory, arrived Tuesday when the U.S. Department of Justice sided with Paramount on jurisdiction and the bond request and a possible SCOTUS intervention , the optics are very immediate if Paramount really leaves. The economic devastation of a move would be real, a recent report delivered to L.A. County warned. “At a minimum, relocating Paramount’s headquarters and other operations out of California would result in losses of 2,750 and 5,550 job-years in California across all industries and losses of between $1.01 billion and $2.03 billion in economic output between October 1, 2026, and September 30, 2031,” the county affiliated Economic Development Corporation wrote in a September 10 document. The third such report to the powerful Board of Supervisors last week is very similar to language in a Paramount statement of September 8 detailing harsh consequences if the merger falters – which makes sense as Paramount helped the non-profit EDC put the whole thing together. “Once Paramount completed the entire relocation of its headquarters and other operations out of California, the state would experience the permanent loss of approximately 28,990 to 57,980 full-time jobs statewide across all industries, and losses of between $10.6 billion and $21.2 billion annually in economic output,” the county document says. With a projected $80 billion in debt, the merged company is widely expected to cut its workforce, though Paramount execs have insisted to date that job losses would be minimal. Efficiencies, they say, will be realized through improved technology and other means. The EDC did identify one bright spot: Ellison’s repeated assurances that the merger would not reduce the collective theatrical release output of the legacy studios. Combined, they will release at least 30 films a year, executives have promised, winning praise from exhibitors and trade groups. “Paramount’s post-merger production commitment of 30 features a year for three years would generate a total of between 1,020 and 2,760 job-years in California across all industries and between $377.7 million and $1.01 billion in economic output between October 1, 2026, and September 30, 2031,” the county estimates. ‘Resident Evil’ Leveling Up With Franchise-Record $50M-Plus U.S. Opening Trump Bans CNN, MS Now & Others From White House, Says More To Follow Company & State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of Settlement Meetings Brad Pitt Returning For ‘World War Z’ Sequel; Edward Berger Directs For Paramount More from this Story Arc Paramount WB September 18, 2026 Paramount And State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of October Settlement Meetings September 18, 2026 Those Across The Paramount-Warner Bros. articles.title: AG Bonta Says Paramount’s California Exit Is David Ellison's Choice: "It Lies At Their Feet"
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill AG Bonta Says Paramount’s California Exit Is David Ellison’s Choice: “It Lies At Their Feet” Steven Paul Talks U.S. Production Incentive And “Uplifts” To Sweeten Deal As Draft Legislation Takes Shape James Cameron’s Lightstorm Vision Acquires Creative-Tech Collective Outsyders View All September 17, 2026 1:29pm Story Arc California Attorney General Rob Bonta Getty “We, respectfully, didn’t think that the United States DOJ did an adequate review, and we thought we needed to step in to make sure we were protecting consumers,” California AG Rob Bonta said of a lawsuit that’s rocking Hollywood after 12 attorneys general sued to block Paramount’s merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. Related Stories Legal Paramount Sets California Exit Plans Over Antitrust Battle With Blue States & Stymied $111B WBD Merger News Judge Sets Date For Settlement Talks In Paramount-WBD Antitrust Case He was dinging the Department of Justice, which blessed the deal in June . “When we looked at, it was and continues to be, a black-and-white, bread-and-butter case. We looked at the facts. We looked at the law. We did our own independent assessment of the law, the facts, and we decided that there was an antitrust violation in three separate markets we set forth in our complaint,” he told The Atlantic Festival in New York on a panel of state attorneys general. “We thought we needed to step in to make sure we were protecting consumers who are paying satellite bills and cable bills, consumers who are trying to enjoy one of the joys of life and go to the movies, and make sure that those costs aren’t raised, make sure that jobs are protected, make sure that those choices are in competition in the marketplace,” he said, appearing alongside New Hampshire AG John Formella and Pennsylvania AG David Sunday. They discussed how attorneys general have increasingly stepped up in antitrust and consumer protection fights across sectors with recent high-profile case against Live Nation-Ticketmaster, Nexstar-Tegna and Meta. articles.title: Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger Clears FCC Foreign Ownership Review
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Judge Says Kennedy Center Must Give Court 30 Days Notice Of Any Demolition Plans After Trump Floats Prospect It Could Be “Ripped Down” ABC Pushes Back On FCC’s Justification For Early License Renewal Order, Highlights “Substantial Evidence” Of Trump “Retaliatory Motive” Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger Clears FCC Foreign Ownership Review View All September 17, 2026 2:07pm Story Arc Getty Images The FCC Paramount ‘s proposed merger with Warner Bros. Discovery cleared an FCC review of its foreign ownership stake. Paramount has disclosed that total foreign ownership of the combined company would be 49.5%, including 38.5% from investment funds from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. Paramount had petitioned the FCC to sign off on the foreign investment, as any foreign ownership stake above 25% requires agency approval. In its declaratory ruling , the FCC said that it believed that the “public interest would be served by granting the Petition.” Foreign owners are restricted from holding broadcast licenses, so the FCC had a role in the regulatory review of the transaction because of Paramount’s holding of CBS stations. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Paramount's 'Crawl 2' Sets Summer 2027 Release, 'Heart Eyes 2' Going A Week Earlier In 2028 Commentary Those Across The Paramount-Warner Bros. Deal Aren't Considering The Impact On The Independent Business -- Guest Column Paramount contends that the foreign investments do not pose national security, law enforcement, foreign policy or trade policy concerns. They noted that the Ellison family will retain a majority of the voting interests and control, while the foreign investors will not have voting control or governance. The FCC ruling included a provision that the company said must obtain permission if “Paramount’s foreign voting interests in the aggregate exceed 25%, or if it proposes to change the voting interests of any of the approved Foreign Investors under this Declaratory Ruling.” Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the FCC, along with Democrats on Capitol Hill, have raised issues about the foreign ownership stake in the transaction. A Paramount spokesperson said, “When the proposed transaction with Warner Bros. Discovery closes, the Ellison family and RedBird will collectively hold the largest equity stake in the combined company and 100% of the voting shares, with no other equity participant having any governan ce rights.” The spokesperson noted that the ruling came after a national security review by the Committee for the Assessment of Foreign Participation in the United States Telecommunications Services Sector. Paramount submitted a letter of agreement related to protections for data and provisions that formalize restrictions on the rights and access of foreign investors. In a statement, Gomez said, “The FCC just let some of the most repressive governments in the world indirectly control nearly all of a combined Paramount-Warner Bros. An investment this large in one of America’s biggest media companies doesn’t just buy equity, it secures influence over what gets said and what gets made. “That’s why I called for this new and novel issue to go to a full Commission vote given what’s at stake. Instead, the FCC snuck this ruling out as a staff-level decision, with no public vote and no accountability for a call of this magnitude.” ‘Resident Evil’ Leveling Up With Franchise-Record $50M-Plus U.S. Opening Trump Bans CNN, MS Now & Others From White House, Says More To Follow Company & State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of Settlement Meetings Brad Pitt Returning For ‘World War Z’ Sequel; Edward Berger Directs For Paramount More from this Story Arc Paramount WB September 18, 2026 Paramount And State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of October Settlement Meetings September 18, 2026 Those Across The Paramount-Warner Bros. articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Stuart Ford Stuart Ford September 18, 2026 7:55am Story Arc Stuart Ford; Paramount Studios AGC Studios/Getty Editor’s note: AGC CEO and chairman Stuart Ford , a veteran of the independent film scene, trained as a lawyer before working for Miramax and then running IM Global and AGC, which has a busy slate of film and TV projects. Here, he considers how the independent business could be impacted by the Paramount -WBD deal and how the indie sector is conspicuous in its absence from the AG’s antitrust complaint. Related Stories Legal Paramount Sets California Exit Plans Over Antitrust Battle With Blue States & Stymied $111B WBD Merger Legal Paramount Warns CA AG Bonta & WGA Of WBD Merger Fallout & “Financial Consequences If Their Challenge Ultimately Fails” For anyone who hasn’t read the states’ entire antitrust complaint against the Paramount- Warner Bros . Discovery merger closely — HHI calculations, box office concentration ratios – I can tell you there’s important insight into what happens to a theater chain or a cable distributor when the number of people they negotiate with drops from five to four. What it doesn’t seek to do is confront any of the systemic issues that are hampering the industry’s vital organs of independent film and international television. That’s as big a worry as it is a missed opportunity. What I will say is this: I read all 38 pages looking for my own sectors — independent film and international television production — and found mostly their absence. Specifically, I found the absence of the risk-takers, the people and companies who put creative and financial capital on the line to get something made before any of the bigger corporations are willing or able to. For both solid policy and bona fide commercial reasons, I’m arguing that any path forward must do a better job than the antitrust lawyers have done so far at encouraging investment in these vital organs within the entertainment ecosystem. Watch on Deadline Let’s talk specifics. The complaint is built around theater chains and streaming and cable distributors. Independent film barely registers as a category worth naming, let alone protecting. International television doesn’t appear at all. That’s not a knock on the lawyers who wrote it — they built the case they think will win. But a shrinking circle of major buyers does real damage to independent film and international television. That damage runs on two tracks that reinforce each other. Track one is economic and structural. Right now, the biggest drag on these key sectors is the steady erosion of Pay-1 license fees for films and the collapse of independent television sellers’ negotiating leverage with U.S. streamers. Pay-1 — the deal that lets a streamer air a film after its theatrical window — used to be a reliable revenue line. It helped independent financiers underwrite risk up front, and independent distributors could price it into their economics. Fewer studios invariably means weaker Pay-1 arrangements. Internationally, the problem compounds: fewer major U.S. feature buyers means fewer of the validation signals that overseas broadcasters use to convince local exhibitors a project is worth backing. This chills the foreign presale market and the capital it generates. In television, the issue is an even simpler case of diminishing licensing appetite from U.S. streamers. This has triggered lower minimum guarantees from overseas distributors who in the past have been structurally key to deficit financing shows. So on the film and television fronts, less leverage, less revenue, less capital — a straightforward economic squeeze. Track two is creative, and it’s just as corrosive. Independent film and international television production are, at their best, the industry’s most vibrant forums for bold voices and genuinely original, authentic stories — stories made because they’re exciting, not because they fit a franchise slate. Christopher Nolan couldn’t get near a studio until he’d shot Following for a few thousand pounds. International television is structurally similar to independent film, with projects typically being co-productions anchored by one or two commissioning overseas broadcasters alongside a deficit-financing distributor willing to be a financial counterparty. Phoebe Waller-Bridge was writing Fleabag for BBC Three before she was rewriting a Bond film. Take away that structure, and you take away the on-ramp that built those careers. Here’s why both tracks matter not just to companies like mine, but to the very company this merger would create. A huge amount of “studio content” is developed and packaged by independent producers and financiers before a studio or streamer ever writes a check. Independent producers often find the book, attach the director, and build the financing plan, and only then does the project arrive looking viable and de-risked. There’s also the small circle of companies such as my own that prolifically commit mid-to-high eight-figure sums to fund film and television productions. By squeezing our economics and starving our ability to discover and back bold voices, the majors and streamers aren’t just hurting the independents — they’re throttling their own supply chain, shrinking the number of places where the next hit can be found and brought to their desks. There’s an obvious beneficiary, and it isn’t another studio. Every time Hollywood lets independent film and international television wither as a forum for outside investment and new talent cultivation, it hands the development of that talent, and the audiences that follow it, straight to YouTube and TikTok. These platforms are more than happy to be the farm system the industry no longer wants to fund. Here’s the good news. Audiences — younger ones especially — are palpably hungry for the authentic storytelling that independent and overseas markets so reliably produce, even in a landscape increasingly crowded with algorithmic feeds and AI slop. So as our studio environment continues to change, there must be strategic planning to empower the independent film and television systems. Hollywood wants to continue reaching audiences around the world and across generations. It can only do so if independent risk-takers are creatively and financially incentivized to stay in the system. articles.title: Everything We Know About Netflix’s New ‘Pride & Prejudice’ Series So Far
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi Book-To-Movie Adaptations Coming Out In 2026 Everything We Know About Netflix’s New ‘Pride & Prejudice’ Series So Far TV Show Book Adaptations Arriving In 2026 So Far View All September 18, 2026 3:20pm (L to R): Emma Corrin as Elizabeth Bennet, Freya Mavor as Jane Bennet, Olivia Colman as Mrs Bennet, Hopey Parish as Mary Bennet, Rhea Norwood as Lydia Bennet, Hollie Avery as Kitty Bennet in 'Pride & Prejudice' Ludo Robert The misty moors will be back on the screen — the small screen this time — in a new version of Pride & Prejudice by Jane Austen. Headed to Netflix this fall , the series stars a cast of some familiar and some young up and comers, with some well known creative names attached. Related Stories Books Everything We Know About Georgia Oakley’s ‘Sense And Sensibility’ Film So Far Trailers Netflix Unveils ‘Pride & Prejudice’ Series Teaser Trailer & Release Window For everything we know about the Netflix adaptation of Pride & Prejudice , read on. When will Netflix’s Pride & Prejudice come out? The show will arrive Dec. 3 on Netflix. Watch on Deadline How many episodes are in Netflix’s Pride & Prejudice ? There will be six episodes in the TV adaptation. Who is in the cast of the Pride & Prejudice show coming to Netflix? Along with the release date news, Netflix unveiled first-look photos of the cast in character . Emma Corrin ( Nosferatu , The Crown ) will portray Elizabeth Bennet , played by Keira Knightly in the 2005 film directed by Joe Wright. Jack Lowden ( Slow Horses , Benediction ) will step into the shoes Matthew MacFadyen left behind as Mr. Darcy. Olivia Coleman will portray Mrs. Bennet, previously played by Brenda Blethyn. Rufus Sewell ( The Diplomat, The Holiday ) will portray Mr. Bennet, played by Donald Sutherland in the 2005 film. Freya Mavor ( Industry ) will portray Jane Bennet, and Heartstopper alum Rhea Norwood will play Lydia. Newcomers Hollie Avery and Hopey Parish will play Kitty and Mary, respectively, in their debut roles. Louis Partridge ( Disclaimer , Enola Holmes ) will play Mr. Wickham, and Jamie Demetriou ( Stath Lets Flats ) will play Mr. Collins, previously portrayed by Tom Hollander known for his iconic line about boiled potatoes. Fiona Shaw, who will also appear in the upcoming Focus Features rendition of Sense & Sensibility (2026) , as Lady Catherine de Bourg. Daryl McCormack ( Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, Bad Sisters ) will portray Mr. Bingley, love interest of Jane, and Siena Kelly ( Black Mirror ) will play his sister Caroline Bingley .

articles.title: ‘Magazine’ Review:  Lily McInerny And Bright Young Cast Give Flavor To Pre-Digital Vanishing Era Of NY’s Literary World – Toronto Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews ‘All About Corinne’ Review: Isabelle Huppert Shines As Movie Extra With Bigger Ambitions In Delightful Take On French Film Industry – Toronto Film Festival ‘Up Against It’ Review: Antonio Banderas & Eva Birthisle In Trudie Styler’s Witty Comedy About Divorced Couple Forced To Conceive Baby To Save Their Daughter – Toronto Film Festival View All September 18, 2026 3:43pm Lily McInerny in "Magazine" Toronto Film Festival Perhaps the title of this Toronto Film Festival premiere says it all. Magazine is a period piece set in a pre-digital world as the long proud tradition of print publications is about to end in favor of quick hits and screen-reading in a new and strange universe ruled by social media, not the once smart and thriving intellectual world of New York City publishing. It is this period circa 2011 that debuting feature filmmaker Alexandra Pechman tackles here in a style reminiscent of movies made by Whit Stillman, some influences of Noah Baumbach, but I would go back even to 1977’s now nostalgic look at a struggling indie Boston newspaper, Joan Micklin Silver’s Between the Lines. There are echoes of all of them in this slight but well-cast story of the monthly New Yorker -lite magazine called Platen , a safe place for authors with audacious stories to tell, ruled by a staff of bright pseudo-elitists that viewed now look like a tribe long ago and far away. That it has been just 15 years since the setting of this movie, only shows how far we have — and haven’t — come in a rapidly-paced environment that no longer stops to smell the roses, value content over Kindles, words over hits. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Reviews Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Festivals ‘All About Corinne’ Review: Isabelle Huppert Shines As Movie Extra With Bigger Ambitions In Delightful Take On French Film Industry – Toronto Film Festival The focus of Pechman, though is all on the fresh faced, eager, non-paid summer interns getting their first taste of the then-real world of niche publications, because that is what Platen is all about. As in any movie like this we have our protagonist, Nora ( Lily McInerny ) as she stands eagerly in front of the building, checking her watch, careful not to be exactly on time for her first day as an intern. She clearly has visions of belonging in this place, and whatever college preparation there was, this is the real deal. She is welcomed by other interns including the warm and fun Tabitha ( Shrinking’s Lupita Maxwell) and nerdy Leonard (a funny Daniel Zolghadri ), along with the more colorful Daphne ( Iris Apatow ). And then at the corner desk in front there is the guy who clearly sets his sights on Nora almost immediately, editorial assistant Thomas ( Joshuah Melnick ), the kind of Lothario who eyes his prey instantly, although we don’t quite know that yet. We will. Nora finds out soon as she ends up in Thomas’ bed in no time, a new relationship that probably isn’t such a wise move for a young woman whose big hope is that a prized position might open up at Platen during her time there. She proves proficient at copy reading, correcting mistakes, menial work, but is it enough to stand out? Pechman sets this all up between the various characters, each with hopes of getting the gig that doesn’t yet exist, and then soon brings in the lively Greer (Ruby Cruz) to add to the mix as she and the others vie for the job that does eventually surface. She and Nora become friends but it is clear Greer may be a stronger candidate than any of them. Lording over everything is Mickey (an amusing Jake Lacy ), the publisher who offers wisdom to the newbies like, “a magazine is like a snapshot of a single moment in time, and then it’s gone.” It is a prophetic line considering how fast the world is leaving this kind of enterprise behind. Beyond the competition for full-time employment and the unfortunate sexual advances of Thomas (this is all clearly pre #MeToo) and the subplot of that relationship, what we have is a group of young hopefuls getting their first taste of a world they would very much like to live in permanently. Not all of them will, but you have the feeling this bunch, especially Nora, will find their own path after a memorable summer and a taste of the realities of being a tiny fish swimming upstream in the big city. In the meantime, why not just dance? Pechman has made a handsome-looking, well-appointed film for her first feature, one that in style feels oddly out of time as much as the subject matter does. What it undoubtedly will be remembered for its engaging young cast. It is nice to know this kind of independently made small slice of life is still getting financed. It is like a little antidote to The Devil Wears Prada, but it works on its own modest terms. Producers are Pechman, Anne Alexander and Tess Cohen. articles.title: John Wilson Lays Down ‘The History of Concrete’ With ‘The Weight’, ‘Shaun The Sheep’ In Packed Indie Weekend – Specialty Preview
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill AG Bonta Says Paramount’s California Exit Is David Ellison’s Choice: “It Lies At Their Feet” Steven Paul Talks U.S. Production Incentive And “Uplifts” To Sweeten Deal As Draft Legislation Takes Shape James Cameron’s Lightstorm Vision Acquires Creative-Tech Collective Outsyders View All September 18, 2026 4:15pm The Weight and A History Of Concrete and Shaun the Sheep- The Beast of Mossy Bottom Vertical/John Wilson/Ardman It’s a busy specialty weekend with fewer new studio releases. Well-reviewed Depression-era western The Weight starring Ethan Hawke and Russell Crowe in wide release joins comedic doc The History of Concrete by John Wilson in an exclusive engagement. GKids opens Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom and Johnny Knoxville stars in R-rated Tiny Fugitives . From TIFF come Angelina Jolie’s drama Without Blood and doc You Had to Be There (full title below), about how a 1972 Toronto production of the musical Godspell changed the comedy world. Related Stories News The 65 Movies That Have Made More Than $1 Billion At The Global Box Office News 48 Of The Most Anticipated Movies Of 2026 The Weight from Vertical opens in wide release on 1,504 screens. Director Padraic McKinley’s feature film debut stars Ethan Hawke and Russell Crowe. Certified Fresh at 93% on Rotten Tomatoes, it premiered at Sundance, see Deadline review . Opened the Deauville Film Festival this month, with Hawke receiving the Deauville Talent Award celebrating exceptional artists in cinema. Watch on Deadline Referenced as harkening back to classics such as William Friedkin’s Sorcerer and John Huston’s Treasure of the Sierra Madre , The Weight is set in 1933 Oregon as Samuel Murphy (Hawke) is torn from his daughter and sent to a brutal work camp. Warden Clancy (Crowe) tempts him with early release if he smuggles gold through deadly wilderness, but betrayal festers within the crew, and Murphy questions how far he’ll go to see his child again. Preview events this week included an AMC Dolby Cinema Early Access screening program at 200+ theaters and an Alamo Drafthouse simulcast screening across the chain’s markets followed by a live Q&A with Hawke, co-star Julia Jones and McKinley from the Brooklyn location. Magnolia Pictures drops Sundance-premiering The History of Concrete by the host of HBO series How To with John Wilson at the IFC Center in New York. The comedic documentary is loosely structured around and inspired by cement, the world’s most widely used building material and the bedrock of Wilson’s beloved New York City. He bounces from Rome to check out the Pantheon, built in 126 AD (the world’s largest unreinforced concrete dome), to a concrete convention in Vegas, with long digressions into Hallmark moviemaking, tattoo taxidermy and New York’s underground music scene — interspersed with musings on his career path and Zoom meetings with perplexed potential investors in the project. Wilson’s HBO series ran for three seasons from 2020-23. The History of Concrete sits at 100% RT score (off 41 reviews). Based on presales, it’s looking like the best opening for a documentary in IFC’s 21-year history, per Magnolia. The distributor went heavy on the NYC premiere Wednesday with a concrete truck wrapped in the film’s title treatment parked outside the theater, and a 125-pound poster made entirely from concrete in the lobby. Expands to 20 markets including Los Angeles next week. Greenwich Entertainment is out with You Had To Be There: How the Toronto Godspell Ignited the Comedy Revolution, Spread Love & Overalls, and Created a Community That Changed the World (In a Canadian Kind of Way ) by Nick Davis at Film Forum in NYC. Eugene Levy, Martin Short, Jayne Eastwood and others reminisce about the 1972 Toronto production of the musical Godspell , where Short, Levy, Gilda Radner, Victor Garber, Paul Shaffer and other entertainment icons got their start. Premiered at TIFF. See Deadline review. Executive produced by Judd Apatow. Adds L.A. and other markets next week. Without Blood from Brainstorm Media, directed by Angelina Jolie and starring Salma Hayek and Demián Bichir, opens on 350 screens. Jolie also produced and penned the screenplay based on the book by Italian writer Alessandro Baricco. A young woman seeks a reckoning decades after surviving the brutal murder of her family during a wartime conflict. Premiered at TIFF, see Deadline review . Moderate/wide : GKids is releasing StudioCanal and Aardman production Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom on 2,173 screens. The film is currently Certified Fresh at 98% on RT. Official synopsis: The residents of Mossy Bottom Farm are looking forward to Halloween – until the clumsy Farmer trashes the Flock’s beloved pumpkin patch. When Shaun turns mad scientist to fix the problem, things rapidly spiral out of control… With The Farmer missing and a wild beast roaming the woods of Mossingham, all the ingredients are in place for a monstrously fun family adventure. Indie distributor Inaugural Entertainment opens the raunchy R-rated comedy Tiny Fugitives , starring Johnny Knoxville, in about 300 theaters. Co-written and directed by Michael Lewen, it follows a reckless, fiercely determined group of 12-year-olds who hatch a chaotic plot to escape reality and spend the rest of their lives at sleepaway camp. Standing between them and permanent freedom is Bob (Knoxville), the camp’s deranged, relentless, 50-year-old lifer counselor. With Aaron Harris (Matlock) , Isa Bernal Steiner, Jai Soundar, Alyssa Gervasi, with Blake Anderson (Workaholics) and Jay Baruchel (How to Train Your Dragon) . Sundance-premiering The Musical by Giselle Bonilla, written by Alexander Heller and starring Will Brill (Tony winner for Stereophonic ), Gillian Jacobs and Rob Lowe (who also produces), is out on 250 screens. Convinced he’s a big fish stuck in a small pond, bitter playwright Doug Leibowitz has been marking time as a theater teacher until he can get to New York. But when he finds his ex has been dating the person he hates most in the world, the school principal, his plans shift to secretly staging the most inappropriate play possible at the middle school. Unapologetic Partners, Blue Harbor Entertainment and Variance Films are partnering on the release. Live-action biblical drama Daniel and the Fiery Furnace from EKKL Entertainment arrives on 1,493 screens this weekend. Written and directed by Matthew and Daniel Kooman, it’s the origin story of the prophet Daniel against the backdrop of exile in Babylon. Limited: Watermelon Pictures opens Traces of Home by Colette Ghunim at the Angelika in NYC. The doc follows the filmmaker on a journey of self-discovery as she sets out to reunite her parents with the ancestral homes they were forced to flee as children in Palestine and Mexico. Filmed over five years and featuring animation and archival footage. Executive produced by Melissa Barrera and John Leguizamo. Winner of the Grand Jury Prize in U.S. Competition at DOC NYC last November and Best Documentary Feature at San Diego Latino Film Festival. Expands to Laemmle Royal and Laemmle Glendale in L.A. next week. As Alex Gibney’s Musk makes headlines, the Oscar-winning documentarian has another film out this weekend — Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie opens in 18 theaters via Abramorama. Featuring the writer and his wife Rachel Eliza Griffiths and inspired by Rushdie’s memoir Knife: Meditations After an Attempted Murder , it explores his recovery from a 2022 attack at a speaking engagement where was stabbed 15 times. With personal footage that has never been seen by the public, the doc follows the writer on his physical and spiritual recovery. Quiver Distribution debuts Berlin-premiering coming-of-age drama Sunny Dancer on about 20 screens. A group of teenagers finds friendship at a summer camp for cancer survivors. Stars Bella Ramsey, Neil Patrick Harris, James Norton and Jessica Gunning with a score by Este Haim. Fourth Act Film opens SXSW-premiering documentary First They Came for My College , directed and produced by Patrick Bresnan about a right-wing takeover of liberal arts school the New College of Florida orchestrated by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis. World premiered at True/False and screened at DC/DOX, IFF Boston, SFFILM and the Florida Film Festival, where it won the Feature Documentary Audience Award. Starts at the Hippodrome in Gainesville, FL, and rolls out to about 30 markets, hitting DCTV in New York City on Sept. 25. ‘Resident Evil’ Leveling Up With Franchise-Record $50M-Plus U.S. Opening Trump Bans CNN, MS Now & Others From White House, Says More To Follow Company & State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of Settlement Meetings Brad Pitt Returning For ‘World War Z’ Sequel; Edward Berger Directs For Paramount Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Paramount And State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of October Settlement Meetings
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten , Dade Hayes September 18, 2026 4:44pm Story Arc L-R: Rob Bonta and David Ellison Getty Images They’re talking! Or are they? And what are they actually talking about? Does everyone need to chill out? Paramount and state attorneys general are talking, we are told. However, the discussions that are occurring over coming to a deal in the battle over Paramount’s $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery are far from advanced. Related Stories Legal Paramount Sets California Exit Plans Over Antitrust Battle With Blue States & Stymied $111B WBD Merger News Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger Clears FCC Foreign Ownership Review In fact, sources tell us, the conversations that are occurring between David Ellison ’s team and California AG Rob Bonta ’s crew are centered on laying out the agenda for their already scheduled mid-October court ordered settlement discussions. “This is part of the process before you get the principals onboard, it’s pretty straightforward,” declares an individual with direct knowledge of the state of affairs. “The end is not nigh.” Earlier this week, a federal judge made it official and ordered Para, WBD and the AGs to appear for a two-day settlement conference October 14-15 in a San Francisco courtroom. Watch on Deadline Core to the discussions will be scenarios like Paramount potentially operating the film and TV studios of Paramount and Warner Bros. separately, at least for a period of time after the close. Bonta has said a “behavioral remedy” like the company agreeing to release at least 30 films a year, will not satisfy the plaintiffs. Along with studio consolidation, cable network concentration is a key part of the states’ complaint, with speculation centering on some way of moving some of the 50-plus cable networks out of the combined portfolio to avoid running afoul of antitrust limits. Eyebrows (and hopes) were raised late Friday about a potential resolution of Paramount’s legally waylaid WBD merger. The Wall Street Journal reported tonight that Paramount is in “advanced talks” with California’s Bonta over a settlement of the antitrust suit being brought by the Golden State AG and 11 other states. Shares in Paramount, which are down 23% in 2026 to date amid mounting uncertainty about the fate of the merger, jumped 5% in after-hours trading. WBD stock, which is also underwater for the year, rose 6% after hours. After Donald Trump’s DOJ and other major jurisdictions approved the mega-merger with no conditions, the dozen attorneys general filed a much-expected antitrust suit against Para and WBD on July 13. The case, set to go to trial on March 2, 2027, has seen an explosion of threats that Paramount would move to a red state , “blackmail” accusations by Bonta and a media war in the court of public opinion. It could also cost Ellison and his Oracle founding father Larry Ellison some sweet cash with a $7 million a day ticking fee set to WBD shareholders to start on October 1. In that context, talk of advanced talks is just another piece of that PR puzzle. “I get why some want this to look bigger than it is, there’s a lot of pressure here,” an insider notes. “This is too big, too much on the line for anyone to rush a deal,” the source added. “Hold your horses. No one wants to waste anyone’s time.” As with initial talks last month, it is mid-level staff that are in communication as the brass stay above the fray, as it is, we hear. Paramount had a blunt “no comment” on whether negotiations with the AGs were going on and what the status of them are at present. Having called out Paramount previously for alleged leaks that scuttled the last set of behind the scenes talks, Rob Bonta’s office today were 100% by the book. “Potential settlement talks are confidential,” a spokesperson for the CA AG told Deadline In the non-answer answer they added: “We cannot confirm or deny whether settlement talks are occurring or their alleged substance.” Interestingly, Bonta’s office did not complain of leaks or bad faith on the part of Paramount like they did last month when planned settlement talks were cancelled on claims the company was playing the press. While there appeared to be reason for optimism (mild as it is at this stage) there are many caveats to consider — and not just because there is a big Paramount+ streamed UFC fight out of L.A. this Yom Kippur weekend. Getty Images The latest word of discussions follows an ill-fated sequence in August. Bonta canceled negotiations hours before they were set to take place, accusing Ellison of “playing games” ahead of those meetings. “Not only did Paramount leak the alleged substance of settlement discussions, but they misrepresented these discussions, demonstrating a lack of good faith,” Bonta said at the time. Even as recently as Thursday of this week, when Bonta made an appearance at the Atlantic Festival in New York, the top cop of California said the fate of the deal “lies at the feet” of Ellison and the Paramount team. A follow up sit-down on MS Now, Democrats’ favorite cabler newser, contained much of the same even as Paramount leaks tried to up the ante on the Melrose lot packing up for Tennessee, Texas or Georgia. Sources tell us Bonta had a “conversation” with fellow ParaBros antitrust plaintiff NY AG Letitia James while out on the East Coast this week. To that, it is not clear if AG Bonta is back on the West Coast tonight. The leverage has been heavily on the side of the AGs since a string of rulings in the case by a federal judge favored the plaintiffs. Even when it came to setting a date for the antitrust trial, the judge landed on early March, which was a lot closer to the AGs’ preference of April than to Paramount’s stated desire for November. Despite momentum in the case, high-profile Democrats in California, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and L.A. Mayor Karen Bass, have publicly pressured Bonta multiple times to settle the case. The ambitious Newsom and reelection-fighting Bass fear damage to the industry, L.A. and the state if the deal remains pending for several months. At the same time, of course, a damning August report delivered to L.A. County from the region’s Department of Economic Opportunity says the $80 billion debt ladened merger will likely cause the loss of thousands of jobs , adding to the pain for a region already facing a downturn in production and other headwinds. The job loss and economic pain could be much greater if Paramount makes good on their threat to leave L.A., says a September 10 report to the County from the Economic Development Corporation. On the flip side, that same leaked EDC report, which Paramount commissioned, also told the powerful Board of Supervisors that ailing Hollywood would be boomtown if ParaBros went though with jobs and productions galore. As well, the ParaBros court calendar is looking pretty full even before those official settlement talks of next month and the spring 2027 trial. A hearing will be held next week in Oakland on Paramount’s request for a $1.88 billion bond from the plaintiffs to cover “extraordinary losses” the company anticipates due to having to pay those pricey ticking fee during litigation. articles.title: ‘VisionQuest’ Creator Terry Matalas Says No GenAI Was Used In Making Of Show: “There Hasn’t Really Been A Need”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘VisionQuest’ Creator Terry Matalas Says No GenAI Was Used In Making Of Show: “There Hasn’t Really Been A Need” Cody Fern Recalls Filming ‘House Of Cards’ When The Kevin Spacey “Nuclear Bomb Hit” Maisie Williams Played ‘Practical Magic 2’ Character As “Sapphic Icon” Despite Sequel Omitting Book’s LGBTQ Plot View All September 18, 2026 5:40pm Paul Bettany in 'VisionQuest' Marvel Despite VisionQuest ‘s subject matter as the first solo outing of the title artificial intelligence, the Marvel series kept things strictly human-made. Series creator Terry Matalas recently confirmed there was no GenAI used in the making of the Disney+ series, which debuts Oct. 14 on the streamer, noting there wasn’t “a need” for the tech. “No, not at all. There hasn’t really been a need,” Matalas told ScreenRant . “All the designs nod to how our current form of AI processes things… That felt like a fun way for us to comment on it.” Related Stories News Marvel Mastermind Stan Lee’s Voice & Likeness Resurrected By AI Company ElevenLabs News VisionQuest’ Trailer: First Look At Disney+ ‘WandaVision’ Spinoff Starring Paul Bettany – D23 Production designer Will Hughes-Jones explained that his team employed human creativity to emulate the flawed look of AI software renderings.
