articles.title: ‘Resident Evil’ Racing Toward Healthy Box Office Haul for Zach Cregger’s Reboot
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All September 17, 2026 6:38pm Austin Abrams in 'Resident Evil.' Courtesy of Everett Collection Logo text Resident Evil looks to get off to a running start in its opening weekend at the box office . Sony Pictures releases writer-director Zach Cregger ‘s horror-survival video game adaptation on Friday in roughly 3,500 North American theaters, with the studio projecting a debut frame of $40 million for the three-day weekend. This is in line with third-party tracking services, although some of those have upped their expectations in recent days as interest heats up, with the possibility that the opening gets close to $50 million or higher. It carries a $75 million production budget. Related Stories Movies Zach Cregger on Revamping 'Resident Evil' and Why He Doubts He'll Ever Return to Comedy Movies 'Resident Evil' Review: Zach Cregger Gives a Fatigued Franchise an Exhilarating Shot in the Arm A launch of $40 million would give the new Resident Evil the distinction of the highest-grossing opening in the history of the franchise. The series’ previous titles have collectively grossed more than $1.2 billion worldwide. Hailing from TriStar Pictures, Constantin Film and Davis Film, Resident Evil stars Austin Abrams , Zach Cherry, Kali Reis and Paul Walter Hauser in the story of a medical courier (Abrams) attempting to deliver a precious item in the midst of a deadly viral outbreak in Raccoon City. The movie looks to continue the hot streak for Cregger, whose most recent release was Warner Bros.’ Oscar-winning horror film Weapons , which hit theaters last summer, and before that was his well-received Barbarian . Resident Evil reboots the film franchise adapting Capcom’s video game series that launched in 1996. The first live-action feature adaptation came with director Paul W.S. Anderson’s 2002 movie Resident Evil , with the Milla Jovovich-led project opening to $17.7 million domestically and going on to surpass $100 million globally throughout its run. Jovovich starred in five sequels before Kaya Scodelario led the 2021 reboot attempt Resident Evil: Welcome to Raccoon City , which underperformed at the box office. Director Zach Cregger (right) and Austin Abrams on the set of Resident Evil. Dušan Martinček/Sony Pictures While the Resident Evil movies have not been known as critical darlings, the latest one is a very different story, as it holds an eye-popping 96 percent approval rating from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , critic Frank Scheck noted that Cregger “crafted a propulsive, simultaneously terrifying and hilarious thrill ride that showcases both his cinematic chops and perverse sense of humor.” As for Cregger, he told THR at the Los Angeles premiere that he had high hopes for the movie’s reception. “I felt pretty confident,” the director said. “We’ll see. Maybe I’m delusional, but I don’t think so. I’ve seen the movie, and I like it.” This should provide more of a jolt to the early days of fall than the previous frame, which saw Warner Bros.’ Practical Magic 2 take the top spot in a subdued debut that ended the six-weekend winning streak for Sony’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day . Earlier this week, the Tom Holland-led Spidey movie swung its way to No. 1 on the all-time domestic chart, toppling Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens . Also opening in wide release is stop-motion animated sequel Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom , hitting theaters stateside from GKIDS. THR

articles.title: Barbra Streisand Slams Trump’s “Unchecked Ego” Amid His Kennedy Center Demolition Threats
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All September 17, 2026 7:35pm Barbra Streisand onstage at the 2026 Oscars. Kevin Winter/Getty Images Barbra Streisand is criticizing President Donald Trump over his controversial handling of the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C. The EGOT winner released a statement on her official website Thursday, a day after an image that photojournalists captured through the windows of Air Force One showed Trump examining a poster board that appeared to display the words: “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.” “In 2008, I was deeply honored to be included in the 31st annual class of Kennedy Center Honorees. For me, and for so many artists, that honor represented something larger than a career recognition. It represented a belief in the importance of art to the life of a democracy,” Streisand wrote. “That is why what is happening to the Kennedy Center is so galling and painful to witness.” Related Stories Business Jon Voight Explains What He's Up to as Trump's Special Ambassador to Hollywood News Kennedy Center's Abrupt Plan to Shut Down May Spark Further Legal Battles Her comments came as a district judge in Washington instructed the Kennedy Center on Thursday to provide at least 30 days’ notice before carrying out any significant changes to their renovation or construction plan, “including but not limited to any ‘demolition’ of the center’s main building,” The New York Times reported . The Kennedy Center has been at the center of a legal battle as Trump has slammed a court decision to block his name, two times now, from being added to the building’s exterior. On Wednesday, the president told reporters that the arts institution may be “ripped down” if his name does not appear on the building, CNN reported . Streisand continued, “When Donald Trump attempted to put his name alongside the late President Kennedy’s on the building’s entrance, the move was met with widespread opposition from artists and much of the public. A federal judge subsequently ruled that the Kennedy Center’s name could not be changed without an act of Congress, and Trump’s name was removed from the building’s façade. “Yet the fight continued. After his name was removed, a humiliated Trump ordered a large tarp placed over the façade, where it remains today. The Trump-aligned board then relentlessly lobbied again to add his name, prompting another federal ruling that blocked their effort,” she said. “And now, a thoroughly defeated Trump has announced that the Kennedy Center is being closed for what the completely stacked board describes as a major renovation. Oddly, when Trump’s name was still on the building, there was no discussion of closing it! “You can easily imagine my indignation at seeing this revered institution become the subject of such a bitter struggle over one man’s name and unchecked ego,” Streisand added in her statement, which also included a photo of her and John F. Kennedy in 1963, as well as an image of her and Morgan Freeman at the 31st annual Kennedy Center Honors in 2008. Read Streisand’s full statement below. In 1964, in the aftermath of President John F. Kennedy’s shocking assassination, Congress passed legislation designating the National Cultural Center as a living memorial to him. The Kennedy family and other American leaders wanted a meaningful way to preserve his legacy. Re-naming the Cultural Center in JFK’s honor was a fitting choice, because he was a true champion of the arts. Since then, the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts has stood as one of America’s great cultural venues. Many of the world’s most accomplished actors, musicians, singers and dancers have graced its stages. In 2008, I was deeply honored to be included in the 31st annual class of Kennedy Center Honorees. For me, and for so many artists, that honor represented something larger than a career recognition. It represented a belief in the importance of art to the life of a democracy. That is why what is happening to the Kennedy Center is so galling and painful to witness. When Donald Trump attempted to put his name alongside the late President Kennedy’s on the building’s entrance, the move was met with widespread opposition from artists and much of the public. A federal judge subsequently ruled that the Kennedy Center’s name could not be changed without an act of Congress, and Trump’s name was removed from the building’s façade. Yet the fight continued. After his name was removed, a humiliated Trump ordered a large tarp placed over the façade, where it remains today. The Trump-aligned board then relentlessly lobbied again to add his name, prompting another federal ruling that blocked their effort. And now, a thoroughly defeated Trump has announced that the Kennedy Center is being closed for what the completely stacked board describes as a major renovation. Oddly, when Trump’s name was still on the building, there was no discussion of closing it! You can easily imagine my indignation at seeing this revered institution become the subject of such a bitter struggle over one man’s name and unchecked ego. It is difficult not to think about what President Kennedy himself would have envisioned for the Center: not a monument frozen in time, but a living place where artists could challenge, inspire, provoke, and bring Americans together through the transformative power of the arts. The Kennedy Center was meant to pay tribute to a beloved president, and to advance his philosophy that artistic achievement was proof of a free society. He believed that when the creative impulse cannot flourish freely, a society loses its vitality. Yet another reason why it is so important that Americans exercise their right to vote in the upcoming midterm elections! THR

articles.title: ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Review: Shun Oguri and Lily James in a Meandering Franchise Entry From Takashi Miike That’s Semi-Coherent at Best
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 17, 2026 9:05pm Shun Oguri (center) in 'Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo.' Courtesy of NEON The first in a planned series of international sequels, Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo gets things off to a mostly inauspicious start, despite enlisting the magnetic Shun Oguri as the latest incarnation of the seedy, morally hollow detective to whom the films owe their title. It’s closer in terms of plot machinations to Abel Ferrara’s 1992 original with Harvey Keitel than to Werner Herzog’s wildly eccentric 2009 follow-up, Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans , a snug fit for Nicolas Cage’s gonzo extremes. But that doesn’t mean the choppy narrative ever gathers much steam. What’s surprising is that prolific Japanese cult director Takashi Miike , known for explosions of operatic violence, gore and perversion in breakthrough films like Auditon and Ichi the Killer , delivers a franchise entry that aspires to be a hardboiled crime thriller but lacks the electricity to build suspense or even tension. While devout Miike-heads might feel sated by the one or two amped-up set pieces and the characteristic strain of dark humor, this is by far the weakest of the three Bad Lieutenant s. Related Stories Movies 'The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd' Review: Amanda Seyfried and Scoot McNairy Bring Raw Intensity to Tim Blake Nelson's Death Row Drama Movies 'Re/Pair' Review: David Schwimmer, W. Kamau Bell and Van Jones Lead Pragmatic Doc About the Past and Present of Black-Jewish Relations Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo The Bottom Line A sluggish neo-noir oddly lacking in tension. Venue : Toronto International Film Festival (Special Presentations) Cast : Shun Oguri, Lily James, Shotaro Mamiya, Liv Morgan, Jun Kunimura, Hiroshi Tachi, Shuhei Nomura, Nanase Nishino, Yuka Kouri Director : Takashi Miike Screenwriter : Daisuke Tengan Rated R, 1 hour 48 minutes The characters played by Keitel and Cage in previous installments both experienced a drug-fueled spiritual crisis. A cynical cop with a long history of investigating the yakuza underworld, Yabuki (Oguri) doesn’t appear to have much on his mind beyond feeding his meth habit, playing ping pong and doing drugs with a couple of giggly Korean sex-workers, and keeping the loan sharks at bay as he attempts to pay off — or recklessly increase — his gambling debts. He is occasionally troubled by guilt over his role in the death of a partner 15 years earlier, but those thoughts surface in surreal dream states rather than serious self-reflection. Yabuki’s marriage is already in such a shambles that even his preteen kids are losing their faith in him. He scarcely blinks when he comes home and finds a note from his wife saying she has left with the children and telling him not to try to find them. With the yakuza syndicates in a transitional state as old clans dissolve and new ones are formed deeper underground, his colleagues in law enforcement call on Yabuki’s expertise when a naked body turns up, an extensively tattooed young gangster whose neck has been neatly snapped. Yabuki recognizes the victim but withholds that information from the cops, instead using it to chip away at his debts. While that investigation is ongoing, another spate of murders comes to light as Ishizuka (Shotaro Mamiya), a disenfranchised yakuza soldier fresh out of prison, wanders around town with a hefty machete delivering payback to anyone who betrayed him. He starts with his wife, chopping her up and then rolling her remains into meatballs, served up in planter boxes on the terrace for crows to feast on — inarguably the movie’s most quintessentially macabre Miike touch. More criminal than cop in the eyes of many, including himself, Yabuki is an outsider at the precinct. But he hangs around long enough to be roped into assisting American FBI agent Gwen Birgssen ( Lily James ) in an investigation. Gwen has been dispatched to Tokyo to track down Megan (current Women’s World Champion WWE wrestler Liv Morgan), the missing daughter of a prominent U.S. congressman who came to Japan to study the art of sushi and got sidetracked by drugs and thugs. It later emerges that in addition to crack and raw bar cuisine, Megan has a thing for short dudes with impressive body ink. It’s this thread more than anything that derails any plot momentum, partly because James is so woefully miscast, assuming an unconvincing Southern Fried drawl you might expect to find in a regional theater staging of Tennessee Williams. The Brit actress has obviously put in time on the fight training, demonstrating nimble moves in a nightclub brawl with no bearing on the plot. It does serve, however, to get both Gwen and Yabuki so sexually charged that they tumble into bed together. The old fight-and-f*ck combo never fails. Miike appears to have minimal interest in dialogue-driven scenes. That’s too bad because Gwen and Yabuki have a few of them in which key information is possibly shared. Between James’ garbled twang, Oguri’s unsteady command of English (the actor fared better in that regard in Godzilla vs. Kong ) and a muddy sound mix, much of their conversation is incomprehensible. Which might be for the best considering the increasingly bonkers twists of the script by Daisuke Tengan, who collaborated with Miike on Audition and the hit samurai epic, 13 Assassins . The two investigations do eventually intersect of course, which happens when another slender tatted-up young gangster turns up dead and the victim’s father (Jun Kunimura, immortalized as Boss Tanaka in Kill Bill: Vol. 1 ) cuts Yabuki a deal to clear all his debts with the Chinese mob if the cop delivers the killer to him. The inevitable bloodbath happens, along with lots more meatballs for the hungry crows and revelations about how Megan gets her freak on. But the cases are resolved too haphazardly to make us care much, especially when it involves Gwen, the least persuasive gunslinger in the history of movies, snarling “Motherfucker” as she plugs a mobster full of lead. Like much of Miike’s work, the visuals are equal parts slick and rough-edged, and the Shinjuku setting, specifically the red-light Kabukicho district with its warren of back alleys, bars and brothels, supplies plenty of shadowy atmosphere, often stained with neon. But the movie is way too busy to keep all its plates spinning and if not for the fact that Oguri is so watchable with his mop of unruly hair and sleepy deadpan delivery, there would be very little here to recommend. But Miike fans might even give Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo a stamp of approval just for one scene of major mayhem, in which Yabuki does some virtuoso driving, plowing through yakuza scum while protecting the lives of … a bunch of cute kids? Don’t even ask. Full credits Venue: Toronto International Film Festival (Special Presentations) Production companies: Pressman Film, Recorded Pictures Company, OLM Distribution: Neon Cast: Shun Oguri, Lily James, Shotaro Mamiya, Liv Morgan, Jun Kunimura, Hiroshi Tachi, Shuhei Nomura, Nanase Nishino, Yuka Kouri Director: Takashi Miike Screenwriter: Daisuke Tengan Producers: Jeremy Thomas, Sam Pressman, Naokai Kitajima, Misako Saka Executive producers: Paula Paizes, Ivan Kelava, Peter Watson, Yuzo Kuwahara, Nobuyuki Iinuma, Tetsu Fujimura, Max Loeb, Mike Apgar, Tom Quinn, Sarah Colvin, Kristen Figeroid, Laurel Charnetsky Director of photography: Nobuyasu Kita Production designer: Akira Sakamoto Costume designer: Yuya Maeda Music: Koji Endo Editor: Naoichiro Sagara Sound designer: Jun Nakamura Rated R, 1 hour 48 minutes THR

articles.title: ‘Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story’ Review: Ryan Murphy’s Latest Netflix Serial Killer Saga Is Faux-Feminist Nonsense
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All September 17, 2026 9:30pm 'Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story' In the final hour of Netflix’s Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story , the titular murderess, having finally made her peace with the act of violence that has defined her life, turns to the loyal companion who’s been by her side through it all. “Okay,” she says. “Let’s make it mean something.” Lizzie (Ella Beatty) is talking about her wealth and notoriety, which she wishes to channel into a force for good. In the moment, though, all I could hear was showrunner Ian Brennan muttering that sentiment to himself. The latest addition to his and Ryan Murphy ’s murder-verse tries desperately to draw something, anything meaningful out of Borden’s saga, with all the finesse of a college freshman trying to crank out a 15-page term paper in the two hours before deadline — and with all the same power of persuasion. Related Stories TV Homer Gere Shares His Theory About 'The Shards' and Robert Mallory TV 'Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story' Team on Painting a Portrait of Female Rage -- and Leaning into Lesbian Theories Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story The Bottom Line Lots of killers, tons of filler. Airdate: Thursday, Sept. 17 (Netflix) Cast: Ella Beatty, Vicky Krieps, Charlie Hunnam, Rebecca Hall, Sarah Paulson, Jessica Barden, Joey Pollari, Billie Lourd Creators: Ryan Murphy, Ian Brennan As the subtitle indicates, Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story is first and foremost a retelling of the real events you probably first heard of as a playground chant (one whose melody becomes a recurring motif), or perhaps saw depicted in more detail by Chloë Sevigny and Kristen Stewart in 2018’s Lizzie . While the real-life Borden has always denied responsibility for the August 1892 deaths of her father and stepmother, the series wastes no time playing coy; it takes as settled fact that it was indeed Lizzie who wielded the axe. As for why , there, too, the series has a clear-cut answer: because they’re emotional sadists whose sole pleasures in life are tormenting the help and insulting their daughter. Playing Abby and Andrew, Rebecca Hall and Charlie Hunnam gorge on the scenery like they’re trying to make themselves sick; one dinner sequence even ends with them spewing geysers of vomit. There’s zero nuance to their performances, and also nothing unique about them to make them memorable. But as a way to get you to sympathize with the devilish Ms. Borden, I can’t say their cartoonish villainy is ineffective. The only real question left is the how , and that too is more or less established in the Max Winkler-directed premiere. Vicky Krieps plays Maggie, a new housemaid who makes an immediate impression on the family with her skill, her work ethic and her anachronistic style (punk shags in Manic Panic shades, literally a century before they’ll be cool). Lizzie falls in love practically at first sight, and Maggie seems charmed right back. Under Maggie’s guidance, the sweet, shy, sheltered girl who’d never so much as heard of la petite mort blossoms into one confident enough to start rattling the gilded cage her parents have trapped her in. At Maggie’s suggestion, she begins to wonder if killing them might not be her only way out. Then, having put together so many puzzle pieces so quickly, The Lizzie Borden Story finds itself with the problem of having eight hours’ worth of content to fill. I wish I could say that the series has an easy solution for that, too. Instead, it flails about for a number of stalling tactics, none of them particularly satisfying. One is simply to slow down the pace of the storytelling. Bits of exposition are repeated in rapid succession (“It’s the culmination of my life’s ambitions, really,” says a character of a completed project, and then, a few minutes later, “It’s everything I ever dreamed of, really,” just in case you weren’t paying attention the first time). Lizzie and Maggie indulge in dreamy nature idylls that clumsily evoke historical lesbian dramas like Portrait of a Lady on Fire or Ammonite , only, for some reason, with way less sex. Intriguing tangents are brought up to go nowhere — no sooner has the show finally started to explain why Abby sucks so much than it’s done her off, thus nipping in the bud any interest we might have taken in her. The other method, more successful at padding that run time but even more annoying in its spirit, is to insist that The Lizzie Borden Story is actually about something much, much bigger than itself. That Borden is in fact part of a whole historical lineage of female killers, all of whose tales are linked together by some lazily nebulous concept of What It Means to Be a Woman in Society, and that there’s therefore something pretty Female Empowering about the fact that Lizzie has decided to axe-murder her parents, if you really think about it. The show attempts to do all this by braiding Lizzie’s story with those of arguably the only other female killers as famous as she is. In the late 19th century, Lizzie and Maggie spend long hours reading each other the story of Elizabetta Báthory, the 16th-century countess accused of bathing in the blood of virgins. Krieps plays Elizabetta in flashbacks, which adds nothing significant to our understanding of either Elizabetta or Maggie but does provide the actor an opportunity to don another anachronistic hairstyle (this time, it’s severe bangs and tomato-red streaks). Meanwhile, in the 20th century, Lizzie has in turn captivated Aileen Wuornos (played by Sarah Paulson in a broad performance more suited for Saturday Night Live ). The series lavishes much more attention on Aileen than it did Elizabetta — like, to the point where one wonders if what Murphy and Brennan truly wanted was to do Monster: The Aileen Wuornos Story , and were only stopped by the existence of 2003’s Monster , the Aileen Wuornos story. In this Monster ’s telling, Aileen worships Lizzie to the point of booking an overnight stay at her old home and hallucinating interactions with her. To this sex worker turned killer of johns, Lizzie is a role model, a spiritual sister, someone who just gets how the pressures of womanhood can drive a gal to violence. Never mind that none of these three killers have anything in common — not their backgrounds, not their motives, not their methods, not their outcomes. Never mind that The Lizzie Borden Story ’s further attempt to reframe Lizzie as not just a self-actualized independent lady but an outright icon of the women’s suffrage movement comes out of nowhere. Or that for a show supposedly so in tune with the struggles of womanhood, it has no sympathy to extend an embittered wife and mother like Abby (who, for all her abuses, was not a literal murderer ), and no curiosity to offer a rebel like Maggie (whose goals or desires or even personality traits always seem to be changing at the whims of the plot). All of these people, you see, are female. For Monster , that’s reason enough to lump them together — even if, in the end, it has nothing more substantial to say than, “Women be choppin’.” THR

articles.title: Macklemore Alleged to Have Repeated Palestine Comments Despite Promoter Assurances to NFL Stadium Owners (Report)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All September 17, 2026 10:18pm From left: Ed Sheeran, Robert Kraft and Macklemore. Paras Griffin/Getty Images for for iHeartRadio; Aaron J. Thornton/WireImage; Allen Berezovsky/Getty Images The Macklemore controversy rumbles on, with new reporting alleging that assurances were given to a group of NFL stadium owners that the rapper would not repeat any comments on the issue of Palestine during Macklemore’s second, and ultimately final, stint as the opening act on Ed Sheeran ‘s tour. In a story published in The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday , the newspaper revealed more details of alleged communication between Sheeran, the promoters of Sheeran’s Loop Tour and NFL stadium owners, including New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft , after concerns were raised over Macklemore declaring “Free Palestine” on stage before performing “Hind’s Hall”, his pro-Palestinian song at the MetLife Stadium concert on Sept. 4. Related Stories Music Robert Kraft Responds After Macklemore Invites Him to Match His $1M Donation to Support Palestinian People Music Ed Sheeran Openers Finneas, Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe Depart Tour in Solidarity With Macklemore After the incident, the WSJ reports that representatives of Kraft and other NFL stadium owners — including Carolina Panthers owner David Tepper, Atlanta Falcons owner Arthur Blank and Philadelphia Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie — reached out to Loop Tour promoters Messina Touring Group about Macklemore’s overtly political comments. The owners were alleged to have been told that Macklemore, who was initially set to feature on 10 dates for Sheeran, would not bring up the issue of Palestine again during his performances. At the Sept. 5 concert at the MetLife Stadium, however, the Grammy-winning artist said: “One of the reasons why I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up here on stages and stadiums across America and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine! I want to say this to all of my Jewish brothers and sisters. Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you.” Macklemore’s comments on the second of the two Metlife Stadium concerts were picked up by news outlets after the Israeli-American Council petitioned for Sheeran to remove the rapper from his tour. Other pressure groups such as StopAntisemitism and Combat Antisemitism Movement as well as the singer Pink also called for the rapper’s removal. The WSJ reports that behind the scenes, Kraft and Sheeran had a 40-minute phone call about the Macklemore controversy. Kraft is claimed to have told Sheeran that while he had sympathy for the Palestinian people, Macklemore’s comments in his estimation constituted hate speech, and was not a free speech issue. After days of media scrutiny and with concerns about the future viability of the Loop Tour without access to NFL stadiums, Messina released a statement on Sept. 14 that Macklemore was dropped from the remaining eight U.S. tour dates. In a statement to Rolling Stone , Messina said: “As the concert promoter for Ed Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour, we have been notified by venues on the upcoming U.S. tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans. After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.” After being dropped, Macklemore released a lengthy statement about the controversy . “Before I get into it, I want to say something that should be obvious. In this moment I think it matters. I am not a victim,” Macklemore wrote on Instagram. “Ed Sheeran is not a victim. Pink is not a victim. We have careers, money, opportunities, safety and audiences around the world. Whatever consequences any of us face for what we say, we get to go home to our families. The victims are the Palestinian people.” Sheeran also released a lengthy statement after Macklemore’s removal . “After Macklemore’s performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting. I was informed that this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than on everything that was said. I spoke with the venues at length all week to try and build a bridge. One of those people was Robert Kraft. I was also involved in direct talks with promoters along with activists on both sides to try and find a mutual resolution for all, but the venue’s and promoter’s decision was final.“ Sheeran then reiterated, “Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine. Macklemore’s contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.” Macklemore’s removal set off a fire storm, with Sheeran’s other support acts Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and his backing band Beoga all pulling out of the remaining tour dates in solidarity with the “Thrift Store” rapper. On Sept. 16, Macklemore announced that he would donate his earnings from the Loop Tour, approximately $1 million , to six organizations supporting Palestinians and called on Kraft to match his donation. Kraft responded by donating $2 million. THR

articles.title: ‘Resident Evil’: What Critics Are Saying About Zach Cregger’s New Horror Film
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All September 18, 2026 12:09am Austin Abrams in 'Resident Evil.' Dušan Martinček/Sony Pictures Logo text Zach Cregger ‘s Resident Evil has arrived — and the critics are embracing the latest reimaginging on the long-running video game franchise. Based on the popular Capcom video games, Resident Evil stars Austin Abrams as Bryan, an outmatched medical courier who becomes trapped in a monster outbreak in Raccoon City during a single night of chaos and has to try to survive. The Sony Pictures ‘ film reunites Abrams with his Weapons director Cregger, who also co-wrote the script. The cast also features Zach Cherry, Kali Reis and Paul Walter Hauser. Related Stories Movies 'Resident Evil' Racing Toward Healthy Box Office Haul for Zach Cregger's Reboot Movies Zach Cregger on Revamping 'Resident Evil' and Why He Doubts He'll Ever Return to Comedy While Cregger’s take on Resident Evil is the eighth installment in the live-action franchise, it’s also a reboot and serves as a fresh start. Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter earlier this week, Cregger defended his decision to scrap the games’ legacy characters. Responding to online pushback, he said, “I know that when you dive into an IP you’re going to get flack, a certain degree, from the fandom. It would be weird if I were shocked that that was happening. But I think that when the people who love these games the way I do see the movie, my hope is that they feel seen and they feel like this movie is paying homage to the games, because it is, it’s obvious.” As of publication, it has an 96 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes and a 91 percent audience score. As the movie enters theaters , THR has rounded up what critics are saying, below. THR’s Frank Scheck, wrote in his review , “Abrams’ shaggy appeal as the everyman hero who somehow manages to overcome every obstacle thrown in his way, including the most monstrous creatures Cregger and his talented creative team could devise, is a key factor in the film’s success. Filled with baroque gore and wildly imaginative set pieces delivered at a feverish pace, Resident Evil transcends its simplistic premise with the sort of cinematic wit and flair for which the filmmaker has been justly acclaimed.” IGN’s Tom Jorgensen wrote, “Whatever your idea of what a good Resident Evil movie should be, I have to recommend to the skeptical to put that to one side and lock in for what Zach Cregger delivers with this new adaptation of the Capcom games. With a clear appreciation for odds stacked against the protagonist and all manner of freaky foes to stand against them, Cregger ably adapts the spirit, if not the letter, of the Resident Evil games into a jet-fueled horror experience that has room for lots of tension, some great laughs, and a strong central performance from Austin Abrams.” He added, “With a tendency towards celebrating the feel of the games and not the specifics of the plot, Resident Evil succeeds in amplifying classic gameplay moments into horror movie beats in a way that goes far beyond simple fan service.” The New York Times’ Brandon Yu praised the tone, writing, “It’s a thriller that’s as funny as it is jumpy, with a remarkable number of jokes rooted simply in Abrams either shrieking in fear or muttering with incredulity. Cregger weaponizes comedy not only as an irrepressible reflex, but as a tool: If horror is about tension and release, he sees the relief of a laugh the same way he might a scream. But it only works because of Abrams. The movie is essentially a one-man show.” Meanwhile, YouTube critic Jeremy Jahns said the humor “they could have pulled it back a little bit to make the last act a little smoother.” Overall, however, he added, “I actually really enjoyed it. The nods were there without feeling like nostalgia bait. The vibe, the fish out of water scenario that grows bigger and bigger as the film goes on does decidedly feel like Resident Evil. Also, it is decidedly and works well as a Zach Cregger horror film. I guess these two concepts just work well together. And I thought Austin Abrams did a great job carrying us through it. This movie being a Resident Evil dark horror comedy was a surprise to be sure, but a welcome one.” Inverse’s Chrishaun Baker explained that the movie, “playfully engages with the first, is totally uninterested in the second, and cashes all in on the third. For a movie and a filmmaker to have spent months at ground zero of a battle over what form video game adaptations should take, it’s ironic that Resident Evil would end up being one of the best video game films ever made. By bucking the cloying attempts at “pleasing fans” that have sunk so many other movies of this kind, Zach Cregger has made the platonic ideal of what a video game movie should be: a cinematic experience that approximates the medium-specific idiosyncrasies of the game, while offering something new and satisfying for fans and newcomers.” The Guardians’s Jesse Hassenger compared it to Cregger’s prior film, writing, “ Weapons had a creepy, evocative aversion to simple metaphorical reads that ultimately increased its effectiveness; the same isn’t quite true here. Resident Evil foregrounds one obvious bit of character change for Bryan, but after doing a great job making us care about him for more than 90 minutes, Cregger seems to abandon him a few steps shy of completing any real journey. Is he awaiting a level up that never arrives? Hard to say. But maybe bringing a video game sensibility to the big screen while keeping any gamer cheesiness on the margins is journey enough.” THR

articles.title: “This Is So Uncomfortable”: Douglas Booth on Putting Britain’s Police Misogyny Problem on TV
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 18, 2026 3:00am Douglas Booth in 'The Blame' Courtesy of ITV Logo text Douglas Booth has, admittedly, always been drawn to rather eccentric characters. The English star has been in this business for almost two decades — “so old now,” he laughs over Zoom, mussing up a famously good head of hair — and in that time has portrayed rock stars ( The Dirt ), poets ( Mary Shelley ) and fairies ( The Sandman ). “It’s really hard to go and play Boy George or Nikki Sixx or Dan Leno,” Booth tells The Hollywood Reporter . “Certain actors can’t do that, but I thrive on that.” As thrilling as thriving is, Booth, who was undoubtedly part of an unofficial 2010s “Brit Pack” of 20-something actors with his Riot Club co-stars Sam Claflin and Max Irons, found himself gunning for a part that would involve less fantasy and more familiarity. “I very much love playing people that are just so far removed from myself,” he says. “[But] this was a good time to play a modern bloke. Does that sound silly?” Related Stories Movies Tokyo Film Festival Unveils Gala and Anime Selections, Featuring Cate Blanchett, Tony Gilroy, 'Wild Horse Nine' and 'Grotesqqque' Movies Alfonso Cuarón to Make First Korea Visit for Busan Film Festival The product of Booth’s self-set challenge to take on “normalcy” is anything but silly. In ITV ‘s six-episode The Blame , premiering Sept. 20, he stars as Tom, a detective in a run-of-the-mill English town trying to be a good guy. His professional partner, Emma ( Michelle Keegan ), is a headstrong presence in the force and consistently confronts the everyday sexism that permeates the office. But a teenage ice-skater’s murder soon draws Emma and Tom down a dark, twisty path, forcing them to investigate their own team. In what will almost certainly shock viewers tuning into The Blame , adapted from Charlotte Langley’s book of the same name, the show depicts actual text messages from the real-life Metropolitan Police group chat scandals, in which multiple investigations exposed deep-rooted and systemic racism, homophobia and sexism — dismissed as “banter” — poisoning the country’s top police force. Such was Booth’s discomfort finding out these texts were sent by U.K. police officers that he felt confident The Blame could send Brits an important message. “I remember reading [and thinking], ‘No woman would ever [write this]. This is just so uncomfortable and shocking.’ And then, yes, on the script, it came up: ‘These are all real text messages from members of the Met Police who’ve now been dismissed,'” he recalls to THR . “It lands really well in this series and anchored it for me. It’s also the reason why we’re making a big commercial series that, I felt, is one of the first to really delve into the problems we have with misogyny in the police force.” Below, Booth discusses what he hopes The Blame can achieve and why Tom is caught “in a moral bear trap.” He also touches on the career he’s built, the U.K.’s adoration of a gripping police procedural and whether he’d ever be up for playing a particular fictional spy dominating a lot of the current headlines: “I would sound disingenuous if I said that playing such an iconic character wouldn’t appeal to me.” I know this story is adapted from a book. Did you know much about it before the show came up? I didn’t know anything about the book. I got a message from my agent and a message from [Quay Street Productions] founder Nicola Shindler, who’s an amazing producer. I’d actually worked with her on my first-ever lead performance when I played Boy George [in Worried About the Boy ]. She [sent] an email saying, “You may remember me,” which I very much did. I had an amazing experience working with her before. I mean, she’s been nominated for like 13 BAFTAs or something ridiculous. So instantly, my ears pricked up. And then I read the script and absolutely loved it. I stupidly read it right before I went to bed, and then I couldn’t get to sleep because of the twist at the end of episode one. And I was like, “What?!” It really was a page-turner. I also think it had something important to say. From the beginning of episode one, I was immediately suspicious of a couple of characters. At its core, it’s a whodunit set within a police station, right? But you will be guessing until the very end of the last episode. Everyone comes under suspicion at some point for different reasons. One could call them red herrings, but I don’t necessarily think they are. It’s the fun of watching a thriller — if you’re sat there watching something like, ‘I think it’s that [person], or that [person].’ It’s quite a complex story with a lot of things going on. As you get into it, there is a tangled web of things that all get resolved the right way, but everything that happens happens for a reason. You’ll find out more about Tom and Emma’s past and how they’ve leaned on each other. British star Douglas Booth says he liked the idea of playing “a modern bloke.” Yellow Belly Photo How would you describe Tom as a character for audiences coming into this show? He is a man very much trapped between two worlds . Ultimately, Tom is someone who wants to be a good person. He’s got himself trapped in this toxic work culture, and he’s very much trying to do the right thing. But along the way, he’s probably got himself into a bit of a moral injury and made some compromised decisions — as does Emma, as do many people in that department. In my head, when I was playing him, I kind of imagined that he’d got his foot stuck in a moral bear trap, and he just couldn’t quite get himself free. He’s wrestling with that, and it’s corroding his internal core a little bit. To take a step back and [give] an outside view of Tom, he’s a detective at this police station. He’s very close with Emma. I feel, in certain ways, he feels isolated from the rest of the department. He’s in a constant wrestle with his principles, but also his ambition and drive to be promoted and do well in life… His eggs are very much all in one basket. And sometimes I feel that about myself in this career. ( Laughs .) All my eggs are very much in this basket. I always try to understand the humanity behind it, you know […] if you find out something compromising that could derail the whole thing right before you get across the finish line — do you say something or do you not say something? It was that wrestling with inner human greed and the want to progress alongside your principles. I read that this series uses the actual text messages from multiple real-life cases of toxic police group chat scandals in the U.K. Were you shocked when you found that out? That is one of the most shocking moments of the series, apart from some of the twists and turns towards the end, and probably the most sickening. It’s absolutely awful, and it’s really shocking. And I was like, “I can’t believe [the show writers] have written this.” I remember reading [and thinking], ‘This can’t be no writer… no woman would ever [write this]. This is just so uncomfortable and shocking.’ And then, yes, on the script, it came up: “These are all real text messages from members of the Met Police who’ve now been dismissed.” It lands really well in this series and again, it anchored it for me. It’s also the reason why we’re making a big commercial series that, I felt, is one of the first to really delve into the problems we have with misogyny in the police force. When we were filming, it was the [BBC] Panorama Charing Cross film [about the] WhatsApp group — it came out the year we were shooting. It is shocking and disgusting behavior. You can’t quite believe the misogynistic, racist things that these people are saying. [The show] very much reflects the problems that we have with some of our systems and institutions, the police that are supposed to be protecting us that are potentially letting us — and specifically women — down. Is the hope very much among writers and producers of this show that The Blame prompts discussion and stays with viewers? As you said, it’s a big commercial series, so hopefully a lot of eyeballs on a very important story. I hope so. First and foremost, it’s a gripping thriller about a murder, and then it quickly becomes more complex. I think we obviously want the themes of the show to stay with people, and I think hopefully by the end of the series they will have. But yeah, there were definitely conversations about it, and there was a lot of sharing. I was always sending the producer the constant BBC News headlines about the failure of the police. But at the same time, I also have a lot of respect for the police. It’s a really difficult job that they do. So the aim definitely wasn’t to go out there and be police bashing in in any way. They do a really tricky job, but there are systematic failings that just don’t seem to be fully addressed. We’d be thrilled if it started a conversation or at least made however many of the — hopefully — millions of people that watch it… If it makes a small amount of them, particularly men who have acted inappropriately or [people who] have been acted inappropriately upon, to sit up and think about their position within that, then could only be a very good thing. It was refreshing to see all of this explored through such a strong character in Emma. Have you and Michelle crossed paths before? No, I’ve literally never crossed paths with Michelle before, which is rare because I’ve been doing this almost two decades. So old now. ( Laughs. ) Over half my life. But yeah, she’s famously one of the nicest people in the industry. I’ve only heard incredible things, and she’s the nation’s sweetheart. When you’re around her, people just love her wherever you go — from all walks of life. She’s so grounded and down-to-earth. And we just got on like a house on fire. Also, she’s not in loads of things. She’s in things that run for a while. She’s in good things. It was a real pleasure to work with her and that really helped our chemistry throughout the series. Michelle Keegan and Douglas Booth for ‘The Blame’ ITV You have been in this industry, as you say, for nearly two decades. I think I first saw you in Great Expectations or The Riot Club , over a decade ago. How does The Blame capture this chapter of your career and which roles are talking to you at the moment? It sounds silly to say but it was the chance to play a very normal person — to play a detective my own age in a six-part show where I could really just explore that human element and that complex character. That was a real draw for me. The job I just did before, I played a fairy in The Sandman for years, so I’d been getting up, having prosthetic ears put on my face at 3.30 every morning. When you’re younger, you try to pretend that you have some great master plan for your career, making choices like you’re Leonardo DiCaprio. But not everyone is blessed like Leonardo DiCaprio to work with Martin Scorsese from the age of 20 or whatever. You’re always trying to do the best work that’s available to you. And this was a really exciting script, with a producer I really trusted, and Michelle was great. […] You make independent movies and you go to film festivals and 150 people see them and that’s it. ( Laughs .) So I guess if there was any strategic thinking in the choice, it was to be in a commercial show that had lots of eyeballs on it and just play a man. I’m often drawn to playing fairies or rock stars or poets. I love playing musical performers like in The Limehouse Golem and I very much love playing people that are just so far removed from myself. This was a good time to play a modern bloke. Does that sound silly? Not at all. It’s really hard to go and play Boy George or Nikki Sixx or Dan Leno. Certain actors can’t do that, but I thrive on that. And I think it was a challenge for me, for over a good six-hour stretch, to just play a bloke. I want to ask about The Sandman and the Netflix of it all. At this moment, in an industry with a very saturated market, where the streamers are dominating and the broadcasters are a little more cash-strapped, the police procedural continues to do very well. Can you speak a little bit about that and why they’re so important here? It’s funny you say the traditional broadcasters are more cash-strapped, but when you do this show [ The Blame ], I can’t walk through the city without being on a 30-foot-high billboard in every single train station. If [the broadcasters] think they’ve got a good horse, they’ll back it, and then you make a massive Netflix show, and they don’t do a single bit of promotion for it because they don’t feel they have to. So the way they spend the money is quite interesting. On the importance of it, I can only answer it from my own experience of doing this and having one coming out, but the amount of people that want to talk to me about it or are excited for it in my day-to-day life… My mates don’t normally give a crap about anything I’m in. ( Laughs .) That’s why I love it. They couldn’t care less whether I’m in this movie or doing that, but the amount of people who say, “I can’t wait to watch [ The Blame ].” There’s something about it. I don’t know whether it’s going back to school, that autumn feeling. It’s pure comfort food [in] entertainment. A quick note on what you’ve got coming up: The Way of the Wind . Can we talk about that? That’s a Terrence Malick movie. I filmed it a couple of years ago now. It was a really beautiful moment in time. My agent said, “Oh, Terrence Malick wants to speak to you. You need to call his assistant.” I called his assistant and got through to Terrence and he said, “Oh, Douglas, it’s so great to speak to you. I don’t think I’ve seen you since you were on stage with McKellen…” I was like, ‘This is all a mistake. They think I’m someone else! I’ve told my friends I’m going to do a Terrence Malick film.’ And I said, “I don’t think I was born then, Terrence. [You’re] talking to Douglas Booth.” And he was like, “Oh, Douglas. I thought I was talking to Douglas Hodge,” who he’d also offered a part in the film to. Luckily, it wasn’t a mistake. He’s seen the Mary Shelley movie I made with Elle Fanning and my wife, Bel Powley. I can’t actually say too much, but that film made him want me to play a part in this film. I would love to see it, but he’s been editing it for a very long time. He is an absolutely wonderful man to work with. He didn’t sit down once on set — he’s always by the camera, still like a young child, still so hungry, and communicates with you through old, typewriter-print letters. He’s so inquisitive. Apart from Terrence, do you have a dream director you’d like to work with? You’ve already done so much, so I also have to ask: Bond? Does that appeal? You’re in the right age range and you’re British. ( Laughs .) I would sound disingenuous if I said that playing such an iconic character wouldn’t appeal to me. But I’m definitely not the one making the decisions on whether I will or not. I’d love to work with Denis Villeneuve. He’s fantastic. Paul Thomas Anderson, Quentin Tarantino, if he ever makes movies again. Chris Nolan. I’m saying very basic answers! I’ve worked with Darren Aronofsky and the Wachowskis and when you work with these filmmakers who make such big, iconic movies, there is a thrill about it. The Blame premieres in the U.K. on ITV Sept. 20. THR

articles.title: How Fatih Akin Breathed Life Into San Sebastian’s Haunting Opener ‘Ghost Song’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 18, 2026 4:00am 'Ghost Song' San Sebastian Film Festival Fatih Akin is no stranger to the festival circuit, having wowed Berlin with his Golden Bear-winning Head-On in 2004 and nabbing best screenplay in Cannes for The Edge of Heaven in 2007. The German-Turkish filmmaker, also a Golden Globe winner for 2017’s In the Fade , has sent a couple of movies to San Sebastian over the years. “I don’t remember which films it was,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter on Zoom. “But I always wanted to go.” Akin is getting his chance and then some with this year’s haunting opener Ghost Song , following two students who meet in a Berlin nightclub and immediately fall head over heels in love. Farasha (Mariam Dawoud) and Faris (Eren M. Güvercin) are struck by a deep-rooted connection that they can’t wait to untangle, but the cord is abruptly cut short when Farasha is killed. For the next 40 nights, she visits Faris in his dreams, where their mutual infatuation slowly drives him to the brink of insanity. Related Stories Movies Tokyo Film Festival Unveils Gala and Anime Selections, Featuring Cate Blanchett, Tony Gilroy, 'Wild Horse Nine' and 'Grotesqqque' Movies Alfonso Cuarón to Make First Korea Visit for Busan Film Festival The Warner Bros. film, co-written with Ruth Toma and set for release in Germany Nov. 5, is actually inspired by Akin’s own discovery of anime and manga, and bolstered by his desire to make Ghost Song for a younger audience. “I’m not a boomer, but I’m Generation X, and Gen Z is very different,” he says. “They work with very different tools and worlds, and you have this influence [that] is not coming from Hollywood. You have this influence coming from Asia, from Japan, China, Korea.” The black-and-white feature is both tender and harrowing, the anime influence palpable in the beautifully illustrated title cards marking the remaining nights Farasha and Faris have together. The story also deftly draws on spirituality rooted in the Islamic tradition — a nod to Akin’s religious upbringing. “It’s my form of dealing with that,” he tells THR , “or using it as storytelling.” Below, ahead of its glitzy red carpet premiere on Friday as Spain’s most prestigious film festival officially gets underway, Akin unpacks the making of Ghost Song . He talks about its depiction of teen suicides — “everybody knows somebody in the generation of my kids who [took their own life] or who tried to” — as well as his decision to keep the film in black-and-white, its similarity to Demi Moore and Patrick Swayze’s Ghost , and why he’s vowed to never relive this particular process again: “This is the very last time I do it this way.” When did this journey start, and why this story? It all started about 10 years ago. It was basically an idea [from] my son. He had this idea of me doing a film for kids, and it was a story about two friends, and one is a ghost — two boys and they’re best friends. I liked the idea of doing something for children, which was very different than what I did before. And I gave it to this writer, Ruth Toma, who I had worked with before. And she wrote the screenplay for this children’s movie. But then I turned to doing In the Fade and other stuff. We never stopped developing the screenplay in the meantime. And what happened was, with the growing up of my children, the age of the characters had changed. That happened [naturally], and so the focus shifted as well and it became a romantic [film]. My kids really taught me or showed me the world of anime. I was very much in manga and graphic novels before… But I was wondering, can I combine it with my take on cinema? So there’s an anime influence on this film? Very much. Anime films often have this romantic touch. They are in this fantasy world, you know? Like parallel universes, rebirth, dying and coming back — this is very popular in the anime world. But also social matters. A Silent Voice is a film about mobbing and suicide in the teenage world or in the young adult world, and so anime is a tool or a window for a younger generation than I am. I’m not a boomer, but I’m Generation X, and Gen Z is very different. They work with very different tools and worlds, and you have this influence [that] is not coming from Hollywood. You have this influence coming from Asia, from Japan, China, Korea. I was very much influenced by Western cinema, by American cinema. Filmmaker Fatih Akin at the 2025 Cannes Film Festival. Courtesy of Getty Are there any particular directors from that region that you’re a fan of? Hayao Miyazaki, the guy who won the Academy Award with Spirited Away . All his work is pretty influential, and of course, the guys who made Suzume , Your Name and Belle , these are incredible pieces of work, in a very visual way. I had the opportunity to do [that] with this film: combine it with that world [and make] a spiritual film. When you think about spiritual films, you end up with Kundun or The Last Temptation of Christ stuff, but I see more the desire and need of doing such a film for a director. Spirituality, the supernatural… I’m interested in this stuff in a private way, but how can you make a film about it that’s still for a wider audience? Ghost Song gave me the opportunity to do that — to do a spiritual film, but to do it as much [for]… I don’t know. Pop culture. It’s interesting that this started as a children’s film because it really is quite morbid. It’s not a children’s film anymore. It started as a children’s film, but then it became […] [for] young adults. And what we found out when we worked on this is that suicide is the highest reason for dying between 15 to 25-year-olds in the whole world. I didn’t know that, and it was scary. Suicide is a theme which has always popped up in my work. I don’t know why these things pop up in my work, but it’s here [in Ghost Song ] again. And everybody knows somebody in the generation of my kids who [took their own life] or who tried to. COVID was a very depressing period for this generation. So I observe that, in a way. I deal with that. I think the film is for everybody in a way — not too young — but sometimes I can understand that people of 60 years, if they don’t have kids or if their kids are grown up, that they cannot connect with such a film. But a younger audience can. And I’m 53 now. I’m thinking about getting old, and to do such a film and to connect with a younger audience… It keeps me young. ( Laughs. ) This film tackles so much: suicide, mental health, young love. I want to ask about the mythology of this film, if that’s the right word. The lore, and Farasha haunting Faris for 40 nights. Is that rooted in a certain tradition? Yes, the Islamic tradition. But we discovered that Orthodox Christianity has that too. […] I have this Islamic background. I grew up in an Islamic family, a very faithful, religious family. It’s my form of dealing with that, or using it as storytelling. It was beautiful. I don’t know if I saw the final version of the film — I saw a black and white version? That is the final version. I have two versions. That happened because the anime world was influencing this film, so when you do a film, you have reference films. The only reference films I had for this one, which I gave to my DP, were the anime films. Your Name , A Silent Voice , maybe Ghost , the Patrick Swayze film. ( Laughs .) But nothing else on a visual level comes to mind. So this was the influence, and the colors and the color grading was very important. For the first time, I really, really, really worked with strong colors. It starts with the costume and goes through the set design and the lighting, but very much the grading as well. And the grading is a process in filmmaking that comes at the end, after the film is edited and done. [But] with the fast rush and to not get distracted by it or not lose the faith in the visuality of the material, what did I do? I switched off the colors in the editing process. And what happened is we got used to it. The whole film was a long journey and very difficult to edit. I was in the editing room [for] almost six months. What do you do when you edit six months in black and white? You get used to it, and that’s like a relationship. You fall in love with it. So [we were] like, “Okay, let’s keep it in black and white.” It’s beautiful in black and white, and it’s existential in black and white. And this film is about existentialism, and it’s manga, and manga and anime are in black and white because the colors are too expensive to print. It became this art form. It’s so strong and so unique. So which one will you screen in San Sebastian? The black and white. I’m asking that they also show a color version of the film. I’m not sure if I have convinced the festival committee yet. But we have the opening in black and white, and I hope that I can get a second screening in color because you have to see both versions of the film to have the complete picture. This is also very much an immigrant story. And we see glimpses of Farasha’s journey to Europe. I wanted to ask whether that’s rooted in anything personal for you? I am always looking for heroines and heroes who are not that common in Western cinema, but [are] part of the Western world when you go out on the street. I’ve always done that since my very first film. I don’t know if it’s just personal. It’s something I observe on the street in daily life. Syrian migration in Germany since 2015 has become very visible in Germany, and these people somehow adapted to so much and so fast, as well. I mean, they’re in the medical sector and the care sector. They’re in all sectors, and they changed this country. The Turks have been here since the ’60s of the last century, but the Syrians came 10 years ago. It was an opportunity to put that in the story as well. To give more texture. I don’t have these typical rock-and-roll kids [as] heroes. Faith is important for [Farasha] in a way. Maybe her faith, her religion, makes her otherworldly. You have to believe in that… If you deal with life and death and past life, you automatically end up in a spiritual film, and so it was a way or an opportunity to use my personal biography in this spirituality of the film. How do you hope the audience reacts after watching Ghost Song ? I’ve seen some reactions [already]. Some reactions really shocked me — some people, they’re very much emotionally shaken by the film. I had never seen that before, or in other works I did. Usually, it’s not so much a young audience who’s like that. It’s more like 30 and up, you know? For them, this is a roller coaster, and I always try to give the audience a physical experience as well. I think if a film reaches a physical level — laughing, crying, whatever it is… If this two-dimensional medium can create that, can create goosebumps, but on the other hand, console. […] I hope this film could be a friend for a lot of young people. It deals with life and death, but in a life-positive way. It’s a tragic love story — we don’t have that too much these days in the cinema, especially a lot in German cinema. It’s catharsis. It’s a troubled world. Everybody has a lot of issues all over the world, and you get sidetracked from that escapism. If a film can give you catharsis, it can be very helpful. What does it mean to be opening the San Sebastian Film Festival ? It’s my first time at San Sebastian [Film Festival]. I think in the past, I sent films there and they passed [on them]. I don’t remember which films it was. But I always wanted to go to San Sebastian. It has that great name and good food and [it’s a] sophisticated festival in a way. I was very, very curious always about that because I have a lot of friends in Spain, and I think I have an audience in Spain, so I have a good relationship [with] that country. To get to that festival with this film and opening it, it means a lot to me. It’s also good to know that there aren’t just the usual suspects to present a film. I mean, Cannes is great, and it did a lot for me. And so did Venice and Berlin. But there are other parts of the world, other festivals in the world. It’s not just that I want to support them, but they also support you. I feel very humble and and very honored that they picked up the film for opening. You know, in [the World Cup], I wanted Spain to win. ( Laughs. ) How were you able to get Ghost Song funded? We got government funding. But our biggest supporter, and I’m very thankful that I have them, was Warner Brothers. [Around] half of the budget is coming from Warner Brothers., I’m not sure. My producers know it better. ( Laughs. ) It was very difficult to finance this film. Very, very, very difficult. On the one hand, films have become more and more and more expensive, especially in Germany. That’s why a lot of German filmmakers move somewhere else to do their films. The cost, everything gets so high here. And you never get the full budget for any film. Here, and also for [my] last two films, [including Cannes-premierer] Amrum , we went into the risk. We said, “Okay, we are not [at] full budget,” but we still greenlit the film. This is becoming more and more dangerous. This is the very last time I do it this way. Life is too short. It’s heart attacks and cortisol and sleepless nights! It’s not like when I started doing films. I was this young filmmaker in another time, in another country. You had some kids, you had some employees and a company and you’d do a film and fulfill that. It doesn’t work like that anymore. As someone who has been working with Warner Bros. recently, and with a lot of European creatives speaking about the proposed Paramount takeover, can I ask: do you have an opinion? Nobody knows. As a rule in filmmaking, nobody knows shit. And I don’t know about tomorrow. […] I don’t have an opinion about that. I can just say I work with the team in Germany and the U.K., and they’re very supportive. I have to say, a brilliant, professional, great team, and a lot of fun to work with. This interview has been shortened and edited for clarity. The 2026 San Sebastian International Film Festival runs Sep. 18-26. THR

articles.title: MGA Entertainment Debuts New Music Video, Single Tied to Mirror Mi Doll Line (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All September 18, 2026 6:00am Mirror Mi music video MGA Entertainment MGA Entertainment has debuted a new music video and single tied to a new line of dolls dubbed Mirror Mi. MIrror Mi features six fashion dolls, each of which embodies “a signature emotion and brought to life through a distinct personality, point of view and style.” The dolls feature fashionable clothing, long rooted hair and collective accessories, among other features, that represent their particular emotion. They are: Blaze Maxx (electric), Amora Valentina (love), Luna Skye (dreamy), kiko Kittyama (crazy), Shai Meadows (sheepish) and Suki Goldpetal (fragile). Related Stories TV A 10-Year-Old Budding "Hollywood Reporter" Gets Her First Red Carpet Experience, Interviewing the Stars of 'L.O.L. Surprise! The Next Headliner' TV L.O.L. Surprise! Dolls Getting Their Own Live-Action Scripted Series (Exclusive) The cinematic music video “takes those personalities and emotions beyond the dollhouse and into an elite performing arts academy, where the characters (live-action) pursue their creative passions while navigating friendship, self-expression and change, ultimately discovering the power within every emotion,” the company said, adding that the launch “reflects MGA’s broader vision for Mirror Mi: using dolls as the first point of connection, then deepening character development and emotional relatability through music and storytelling.” The video was produced in partnership with London Alley Entertainment and directed by Grammy-nominated filmmaker Colin Tilley. MGA said that additional projects in the works for the Mirror Mi line include stop-motion films and an animated short-form series launching later in 2026. “With Mirror Mi, we set out to create a world as layered and expressive as the fans it was created for,” said Josh Hackbarth, chief marketing officer at MGA Entertainment. “The dolls are the first point of connection, but music and storytelling allow us to reveal so much more about who these characters are and the emotions that shape them. Every look, lyric and storyline uncovers another side of their personalities, giving fans another opportunity to connect and see themselves reflected in these characters.” The Mirror Mi dolls Mirror Mi dolls are currently available at retailers. The product line will expand with four-inch Mini Mis that can be customized, posed and displayed. “We didn’t begin Mirror Mi with a trend, a color palette or a silhouette. We began with emotion and feelings,” said Paula Garcia, chief design officer at MGA Entertainment. “That idea guided every creative decision, from the sculpt, expression and articulation to the hair, fashion and accessories, allowing each character’s personality and the emotion she embodies to shine through. To us, great character design does more than create something beautiful; it is about creating an immediate and meaningful connection. Every detail is intentional and every element has purpose, revealing something about each character’s identity, perspective and unique way of expressing herself. Mirror Mi represents our vision for the future of doll design: emotionally resonant, creatively fearless and unmistakably original. Watching these characters evolve from an initial idea into fully realized dolls and now seeing the world we imagined expand beyond the product and come alive through music and cinematic storytelling has been truly breathtaking.” The news follows on the heels of MGA, the company behind such brands as Bratz, Rainbow High and L.O.L. Surprise!, premiering a new live-action TV series tied to the latter, titled L.O.L. Surprise! The Next Headliner. The Mirror Mi music video is streaming on YouTube and the song also will be available on Spotify . Watch the video below. THR

articles.title: Why Matthew McConaughey Doesn’t Want to Take a DNA Test — Despite Woody Harrelson’s Insistence — to See If the Two Stars Are Really Brothers
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All September 18, 2026 6:00am Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey attend the premiere of Apple TV series 'Brothers' at the Hammer Museum on Sept. 17. Eric Charbonneau/Apple TV via Getty Images You may know the story — Matthew McConaughey ‘s mother once told him that she knew Woody Harrelson ‘s father right around the time McConaughey was conceived, creating a possible scenario where the two may be half- brothers . The rumor is now being taken to the next level with Brothers , an Apple TV comedy where McConaughey and Harrelson play versions of themselves who uncover a family secret that they may be related. There is, of course, an actual way that the two could find out the truth, as The Hollywood Reporter asked at the show’s L.A. premiere on Thursday if they would ever take a DNA test. Related Stories TV 'Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story' Team on Painting a Portrait of Female Rage -- and Leaning into Lesbian Theories Movies Zach Cregger on Revamping 'Resident Evil' and Why He Doubts He'll Ever Return to Comedy “I’ve been wanting to but he refuses,” Harrelson explained, as McConaughey replied, “I’ll probably come around to it” but added, “If it’s true, I got a lot to unpack. If it’s not true, he’s not gonna be near as fun to hang out with.” Harrelson admitted, “I’m going to be really sad for a while if it’s not true,” which seems to be McConaughey’s main deterrent to the test, as the Interstellar star joked, “Let’s just keep floating this idea, because I don’t want him being all upset.” Harrelson was quick to reply, “I don’t think that’s going to be a problem because I think we’re brothers;” McConaughey confirmed, “He’s fully convinced, I’m not. There we go.” #MatthewMcConaughey and #WoodyHarrelson share why they haven’t gotten a DNA test to prove if they’re actually related at the L.A. premiere of their new show, #Brothers pic.twitter.com/thzj17dLeH — The Hollywood Reporter (@THR) September 18, 2026 The two stars — who previously shared the screen on season one of True Detective — also mused on playing themselves on camera for the first time. McConaughey said it was “More of an adjustment than I expected” and Harrelson explained it was “much harder than you would think, really. I was doing some weird, giggly, stupid performance and then I saw it and I was like ‘Oh my god, I hope we do reshoots.’ We did, so that was good,” teasing he told the director, “I don’t like that me, can we do it again?” Lee Eisenberg, who was behind Jury Duty and Lessons in Chemistry , serves as showrunner for the series, which sees Holland Taylor playing McConaughey’s mother and the pair’s wives and children also recast. “Their families would be there on the set, just hanging out at Video Village, watching versions of themselves. The whole thing was very surreal,” Eisenberg recalled, while also emphasizing that “I never wanted this to feel like a documentary” and the actors took some liberties to play up their personas. As for if he believes the two are actually brothers after working on the show, Eisenberg admitted, “I go back and forth. When you see the pictures of the two of them [from growing up] side-by-side, it feels a little uncanny.” Brothers starts streaming Sept. 23 on Apple TV. THR

articles.title: ‘Tenzing’ Actor Tenzin Dalha Unveiled as Male Lead in Bengali Thriller ‘Chheledhora’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 17, 2026 11:08pm PT ‘Tenzing’ Actor Tenzin Dalha Unveiled as Male Lead in Bengali Thriller ‘Chheledhora’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ 3 hours ago ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’ 5 hours ago Alfonso Cuaron to Make First Korea Visit at Busan as Festival Also Spotlights European Women+ Filmmakers 7 hours ago See All Getty Images Tenzin Dalha , at the Toronto Film Festival with Jennifer Peedom’s Apple original Film “ Tenzing ,” has been revealed as the male lead in Bengali-language thriller “ Chheledhora ,” opposite Swastika Mukherjee. His casting had been withheld when the Indo-American production was first announced earlier this year, with producers naming only Mukherjee at that point. “Tenzing,” a gala presentation at TIFF, features Genden Phuntsok as legendary mountaineer Tenzing Norgay, with Tom Hiddleston, Willem Dafoe and Caitríona Balfe also in the cast. A limited theatrical run begins Oct. 9, with global streaming on Apple TV following Oct. 16. Popular on Variety Related Stories MoreThan Films Acquires Serville Poblete’s Buzzy Toronto Hangout Comedy ‘Sunburn’ (EXCLUSIVE) 'I Play Rocky,' 'Elsinore' and 'Tangles' Signal an Oscar Season About the Craft of Acting and Memory In “Chheledhora,” written and directed by Shieladitya Moulik – whose credits include “Sweater” and “Surjo” – Dalha and Mukherjee anchor a story set off by an act of parental defiance. Mukherjee plays Brishti, a divorced mother who “steals” her own daughter for a birthday outing, only for the child to be genuinely abducted. The discovery then draws a group of deeply flawed adults and their children into an erratic journey through Northeast India, where the youngest characters gradually emerge as the moral compass for the adults around them. Filmed extensively in Arunachal Pradesh’s Ziro Valley, the production combines family drama, thriller elements and dark humor with the cultural texture of India’s Northeast. It is currently in post-production. “We made a very conscious decision not to announce Tenzin when we first revealed ‘Chheledhora,'” said Ann Mukherjee, founder of Indo-American production company Sita22 Films. “We knew he had this extraordinary international moment ahead of him with ‘Tenzing,’ and TIFF felt like exactly the right time for audiences to discover another side of him. Tenzin possesses a quiet emotional intelligence and restraint that makes him a fascinating counterpoint to Swastika’s tremendous emotional force. Their chemistry is central to the film.” Mukherjee described “Chheledhora” as a film that makes both a physical and emotional journey into India’s Northeast. “We want to tell stories that are deeply rooted in India but aren’t constrained by conventional ideas of language, geography or identity,” she said. Dalha said it felt “particularly special” to be discussing one project while at the festival for another. “They are completely different films, yet rooted in human grit, empathy, the lengths to which humans are capable of going for people they love,” he said. “What drew me to ‘Chheledhora’ was Shieladitya’s writing. His understanding of humans as imperfect complex beings and looking at life beyond the dichotomy of individuals as good or bad. He wrote these beautiful broken young adult characters making questionable choices for their loved ones.” The actor described Mukherjee as “a force of nature in frame and a force of joy on set,” adding that the Arunachal landscape shaped the film’s atmosphere from the outset. “Shooting in Ziro and Arunachal Pradesh provided the perfect backdrop for a thriller, and the weather set the tone right for the ambience,” he said. The film is produced by Ann Mukherjee for Sita22 Films, with Jitin Hingorani as co-producer and creative producer, Dhanraj Sawant as executive producer and Priyangi Borthakur as supervising producer. Italian cinematographer Vincenzo Condorelli shot the film. “The idea was never to make a Bengali film that simply happens to travel to the Northeast,” said Hingorani, who also heads content and development at Sita22 Films. “The journey changes these characters, and the Northeast becomes part of the film’s emotional language. Pairing Swastika and Tenzin gives us two performers coming from very different cinematic and cultural energies, and that tension is part of what makes the film so exciting. At Sita22, our mandate is to find stories that can be hyper-local and super-global at the same time, and ‘Chheledhora’ embodies that philosophy beautifully.” Director and Producer James Wan on YouTube Filmmakers: ‘You Don’t Even Need to Be in the System Anymore to Get Something Made’ Dr. Orna Guralnik Gives Ciara Miller, Dylan Efron and Carl Schmidt a ‘Couples Therapy’ Session in New Samsung Galaxy Spot Paranormal Comedy ‘Don’t F — k With Ghosts’ Premieres On Demand, Launches Original YouTube Channel (EXCLUSIVE) Tom Cruise Says Taylor Swift Was ‘Schooling Me on Football’ at Chiefs Game, Calls Her a ‘Brilliant Musician and Director’ ‘Fortnite’ Launches ‘Kingdom Hearts’ Crossover (Gaming News Roundup) Fan Bingbing, Pedro Pascal, John Malkovich, Javier Bardem Films Lead Tokyo Festival’s Gala Selection Loading comments...
