articles.title: Netflix, YouTube and Amazon Launch a Streaming Public Policy Group
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 14, 2026 7:01am The sun sets behind the U.S. Capitol Dome on September 4, 2026 in Washington, DC. Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images A new public policy group has been formed in Washington D.C., one that will represent the interests of streaming platforms. The Streaming Access and Choice Alliance (SACA) launched Monday, with Netflix , YouTube and Amazon as its founding members. TechNet, the tech public policy group, is leading the new venture, with Mike Ward, TechNet’s senior VP of federal policy and government relations also leading SACA. “Americans want more content choices and flexibility in how and where they watch their favorite programming, including sports and other live events,” said Ward in a statement. “Streaming and digital entertainment companies offer audiences better features and value for their money. The industry and its customers deserve a dedicated voice in Washington, D.C., advocating for policies that enable innovation and address the needs of today’s consumers.” While Big Tech and Big Hollywood are well-represented in D.C., streaming services are not currently well represented in D.C. The Motion Picture Association looks out on behalf of entertainment companies and studios, while TechNet and other groups work on behalf of tech giants. A previous lobbying group, the Internet Association, shuttered a few years back. SACA meanwhile will “advocate for policies that expand consumer access to high-quality content, preserve choice, and support the innovative viewing experiences consumers value.” Streamers, after years of growth, are facing fresh pressure from the public and from government officials, as prices continue to rise and with programming splintered across so many platforms. Sports have become a particularly big boogeyman, with Prime Video and Netflix each hosting exclusive NFL games this season, and with the FCC and broadcasters lobbying for regulators to require sports to be available for free on broadcast stations. Indeed, the SACA website certainly suggests that the sports push will be a top priority for the group. “Streaming provides audiences and sports fans more choice and more control. SACA makes sure Washington hears them,” the group’s website states. David Ellison, the CEO of Paramount, has argued that his quest to secure Warner Bros. Discovery is being done in part so that his company can compete with the tech giants. THR

articles.title: Ridley Scott Reveals Directing Secrets to Fellow Helmer Jimmy Chin: “Don’t Listen to Anybody”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Jimmy Chin Plus Icon Jimmy Chin View All September 14, 2026 7:15am Ridley Scott on the set of 'Black Hawk Down.' Columbia/Courtesy Everett Collection In climbing, we have a word for talking up your own accomplishments — spraying . You’re not supposed to do it. The rule makes things awkward for someone promoting a documentary about climbing, which is what I was doing in early 2016. But that’s how I wound up at an awards-circuit luncheon in New York City seated next to Ridley Scott and across from Matt Damon. The whole point of luncheons like that is to convince members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences to give your film an Oscar. It’s all very uncomfortable. Publicists handle the choreography, making sure you meet the right people and sit next to the right people. I was there for Meru , which had come out the summer before. Ridley and Matt were on the campaign trail for The Martian . I already knew Matt because one of his trainers is a close friend of mine. I’d worked out with Matt while he was training for his film Elysium . I’d never met Ridley Scott. Related Stories Movies 'Everest: The Other Side' Review: A Frustrating, Guiltily Compelling Portrait of the Triumph and Tragedy of Extreme Mountaineering Movies 'Coyote vs. Acme' Snags No. 2 With $15.4M as 'Spider-Man' Nears 'Avatar 2'; 'Dog Stars' Put to Sleep I was intimidated. One of the first movies I’d ever seen was Alien — back in the early eighties, when I was about 10 years old and hanging out at my friend Chris’s house in Mankato. We watched Alien together and it blew my mind. I wasn’t thinking about who was directing the movie, and I certainly didn’t know who Ridley Scott was. All I could think about was the alien exploding out of John Hurt’s chest. Years later, when I was an undergraduate at Carleton, I took a film class and we all joined the professor to go see Blade Runner (The Director’s Cut) at a theater in Minneapolis. When I put two and two together and realized that this guy named Ridley Scott had directed both, he suddenly became an icon in my mind. By the time I found myself next to him at that awards-campaign luncheon, I knew that his body of work was vast and brilliant, packed with other timeless titles like Thelma & Louise, Black Hawk Down, Hannibal, Gladiator, Prometheus, Robin Hood — and thirty other unforgettable features. Ridley Scott was that rarest of beasts in Hollywood, a guy who could make one riveting blockbuster after another while maintaining absolute creative integrity. Nobody else had a body of work that large in which every frame was handmade. Sitting next to him, the question I had was not what he knew. It was how he had stayed in motion at that level for this long. This interview is excerpted from ‘Rules to Live By: How Extraordinary Lives Define What Really Matters’ by Jimmy Chin (out Sept. 29) Celadon Books I barely spoke to Ridley at that luncheon; I was too scared. A few years later, when I started making Nyad , I found myself thinking about Ridley because of the sheer number of decisions that a director has to make every day during production, from which framed picture you want hanging on one wall of one room on one set — How about this picture? Or this one? Or maybe this one? — to which fifty out of a hundred possible extras should appear on the beach and whether one particular extra should wear the red shirt or the blue shorts. On and on: Every single detail goes through the director. The people running every production department — art, camera, lighting, wardrobe, stunts — are constantly coming to you with options inside of options inside of options. Yes or no? What do you think? I wound up loving the sheer intensity of directing Nyad . It also drove my admiration for Ridley to a new level. Nyad is a relatively contained story, set entirely in the present day and with only a handful of characters. Compare that to Blade Runner or Alien or Robin Hood , for which the set designs alone were vastly more complicated than anything I’ve ever contemplated; then add the vast landscapes and thousands of extras for Kingdom of Heaven, Black Hawk Down , and Prometheus . In the decade since that lunch, he’s directed seven more features — Alien: Covenant, All the Money in the World, The Last Duel, House of Gucci, Napoleon, Gladiator II and The Dog Stars. Seven films in ten years, in a stretch of life when most directors have long since stopped working. Years later, while I was working on my new book of interviews with people I admire, I reached out to Ridley. Of all the directors I might have asked to talk to, he was the one I wanted most. To my surprise, he said yes. “My parents were great,” Ridley said. “There was no strange upbringing. Nothing odd happened. By the end of the war, my father was an acting brigadier general dealing with D-Day and then with the Marshall Plan rebuilding Germany. I spent 1947 on a troop ship in my little overcoat with my name on the label in case I got lost, and my own little gas mask, going down the Rhine to be met by my father’s driver. I was there for five years, from 1947 to 1952. My parents would turn me loose every morning and say, ‘Out you go, be back by five. Don’t kill yourself and don’t die.’ My mom was four foot eleven. She said she was five feet. But Dad was away so often that Mom was the man of the house. Tony Scott, my younger brother, was thirteen or fourteen and already rock climbing on granite when he said to me, one day, ‘Hey, you want to go climbing?’ We hit the Yorkshire Dales on bicycles. We went to this granite tower and Tony says, ‘I’ll go up first.’ So Tony nips up the wet granite with a rope. It’s probably eighty feet, it’ll kill you if you fall. And he lobs the rope over the top in the fog, so I can’t see him, and he says, ‘Ready? I’ve got you, up you come.’ I struggled up about fifty feet. Then I said, ‘My arms are giving out!’ He said, ‘You’re using too much arm! You got to use balance.’ I peeled off and swung like a dead spider on a rope. My fourteen-year-old brother saved my life. “My mother taught me to be relentless, too. If you do what we do for a living” — make movies — “you better be relentless. You better not take no for an answer. Deal with life as it comes at you. I’ve just spent months working on a project and then the studio suddenly said, ‘It’s not the right time.’ I said, ‘What?’ So I will now bypass them and take it somewhere else. That’s the job. And very parallel to the importance of being relentless is a cool assessment of what you’re going to do.” *** Ridley went to school in the 1950s at the Royal College of Art in London, where one of his classmates was the young David Hockney. After college, Ridley designed sets for the BBC and directed television commercials. He says he made more than two thousand commercials before he was done, and he credits that commercial work for his later success. Art school taught him what he wanted to say; commercials taught him how to make an audience listen. The film I most wanted to ask Ridley about was Black Hawk Down . I’ve watched it twenty-five times. I should have probably asked about Blade Runner, Alien , or Gladiator , too, but I love Black Hawk Down . I’d always wondered how Ridley shot it, how he made everything feel so visceral. He somehow put you simultaneously inside and outside the action and maintained continuity through it all. The cameras seemed to be everywhere all at once. When I asked him how he came to make it, Ridley said, “My best friend, the person I’ve known the longest in Hollywood, is Jerry Bruckheimer. When Jerry was an advertising-agency producer doing commercials, I’d just finished shooting one with him in San Francisco and we were driving to the airport and he said, ‘I’m going to get out of this business. I’m going to go into the movies.’ I said, ‘Yeah, sure.’ Then he did four movies with my brother, Tony Scott — Top Gun, Beverly Hills Cop II, Days of Thunder and Crimson Tide. Somehow the films Jerry was doing were not for me, I wasn’t interested, but then he came to me with Black Hawk Down and I said, ‘OK, I’ll do this.’ The story covered a simultaneous eighteen-hour action” — the Battle of Mogadishu, involving 160 U.S. soldiers in multiple helicopters and ground vehicles across an entire city — “so it took a lot of sorting out visually.” Ridley told me this came out of something he had learned by shooting all those commercials: how to have multiple cameras shooting at once from different angles without any of those cameras appearing in any other camera’s shot. For Black Hawk Down , Ridley decided that he would, in essence, stage the entire sprawling Battle of Mogadishu, with all its moving parts, as a series of simultaneous actions, and have eleven camera units capturing everything together. “Simultaneous insanity,” he called it. “But it meant that I could crosscut between all these simultaneous events — from when the Black Hawk helicopters come into base, take off again; cut to the High Street, helicopters passing over, scattering chocolates; Night Hawk helicopters coming into base, landing, taking off; guys running into the building. Cut. That’s one take of eleven cameras but it gets every component of the action and lets me cut it all together.” I could not imagine running a production that complex, much less walking into a financing meeting and saying, “Oh, and by the way, for my next movie, I’m going to need eleven cameras and eleven camera crews.” Ridley wasn’t having it. “Shooting with eleven cameras simultaneously makes it cheaper,” he said. “Because it takes fewer than half as many days. That allowed me to shoot Napoleon in 42 days instead of 130. Gladiator II in 47 days instead of 120.” *** When I was out raising money for Nyad , I kept running into the classic concern about anyone making the jump from directing documentaries to directing narrative — I’d never worked with actors before. People knew I could tell a story, that I knew how to frame a shot and move people through it, and that I had my own personal visual language. But still: Will he be able to get the best performance out of the actors? Intuition told me it wouldn’t be so different from working with elite athletes, which I’d done for years. Once we got the financing to make Nyad with Annette Bening and Jodie Foster , I reached out for advice from the handful of actors I knew. They all said the same thing: “The biggest tell of a first-time director is that they won’t stop directing.” An inexperienced director is constantly saying things to the actors like “I want you to feel this, or really bring out that sense of conflict between you and her.” In other words, a first-time director just can’t shut up. One friend after another told me, “If you do that, you will lose your actors, you will likely lose everybody on set too because they will all feel it and you probably won’t make your day.” Director Jimmy Chin, far right, on the set of Nyad in 2023. From left: Karly Rothenberg, director Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, Annette Bening, Jodie Foster, Diana Nyad, Bonnie Stoll, Rhys Ifans. Kimberley French/Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection Ridley mostly affirmed what I’d heard from friends. “Actors don’t want the history of life between every fucking take. They want ‘faster,’ ‘slower,’ or ‘louder.’ So, ‘Jodie! Faster!’ Because an actor at that level has already thought about what they’re going to do. So my biggest compliment to an actor might be, ‘Wow, where the fuck did that come from?’ And they’ll say, ‘What, you don’t like it?’ And I’ll say, ‘No, I love it! That’s me being blown away! You got it! Want to go again?’ And when they reply, ‘No,’ I say, ‘Exactly.'” Ridley made it clear that, to his way of thinking, this level of trust has to apply to every member of a team — any team, trying to accomplish anything extraordinary. “You can’t do shit by yourself. You need help, and the better I get at my trade, the better the people helping me need to be so that we can all go to the next level together. You cannot do what I do without a handpicked team. Even the final stuff like editing is an art form. It’s the final rewrite. I pick my team little by little. You find out who works well with you, and cameramen who don’t mind if I position the cameras, who won’t get pissed off.” “My unit on Napoleon was twelve hundred personnel. It’s a fucking town. Two hundred horses, five hundred extras. There’s wardrobe, makeup. One morning, I got there and they told me, ‘Joaquin [Phoenix, who played Napoleon] is in the trailer and won’t come out.’ I found him and said, ‘What’s up?’ Joaquin said, ‘Who’s all this for?’ I said, ‘It’s for you dude.’ He went, ‘Oh God,’ and then he passed out. Or take Gladiator II. We built the Roman Colosseum full scale. Paul Mescal comes on and looks around at this gigantic set with hundreds of extras and I get out in front of it. I said, ‘Forget it. It’s only a fucking set.’ I will not let him dwell in terror.” Ridley talks a lot about decisiveness: faster, alone, less consultation with others. “As a director,” he told me, “I always have everything planned, but even now I might show up in the morning with a new thought. Another direction. You have to listen to yourself and then just say, to everyone else, ‘This is where we’re going, no questions.’ Once you’re driving the car and doing 205 miles per hour, you can’t take advice. But watch out, too. Do not lose your temper. I’ve got a real fucking temper, and I learned to rein it in pretty early. Kicking doors and punching walls doesn’t work because people don’t respect it and it makes them nervous, so they won’t perform properly. You have to be calm, ideally humorous, and always determined and sure of yourself and your vision. If you’re sure, they’re not going to question it. I worked with a very good actor recently. He said, ‘How are you so sure?’ I said, ‘I’m not.’ You gotta hide your fear. “There’s only one critic. Yourself. It’s a bit like being a painter. Do not listen to the fucking tutor. You’re on your own with the canvas. You make the assessment, you make the decision. Blade Runner got torn apart by Pauline Kael in The New Yorker . I’d never even met her, and her article was so destructive. But now I have those four pages framed and hung on the wall so I’ll never forget: ‘Don’t listen to anybody, just yourself.'” “The thing that’s taken me the longest to learn is, ‘Make your mind up faster.’ Ridley said that, after the production of Alien , his eldest brother, Frank, got a terminal diagnosis of melanoma. “That damaged me quite heavily. While he was dying, I was working on an adaptation of Dune . I prepped it with the company, and we were going to shoot in Mexico City, and I went to Mexico City and said, ‘I don’t want to spend the next ten months here.’ I went back and stayed with my brother. So I had a big gap before the next movie. It took me too long to decide what to make next.” Five years elapsed before Ridley made his next film, Blade Runner . After that, though, his pace accelerated — and he has now made twenty-nine features. “Just make the movie,” he said. “Don’t overthink it. If you like it, do it. And then, ‘Next.’ And, ‘Next.’ You’re not going to make the meaning of life. I mean, you might eventually, but you’ll only do that when you climb to it.” *** I told Ridley that part of my motivation for working on this book was turning fifty and looking at life’s back half. So he had advice for me there, too. “Early on,” he said, “my idea of success was an E-Type Jaguar, but now I drive a Prius that I’ve had for ten years. People say, ‘What’s the matter, you bankrupt?’ I say, ‘No, I’m trying to save the world.’ Less is more. You can get your Rolls-Royce and your Porsche and your Land Rover, and then you stare at them in your garage and think, ‘Why have I got three cars?’ Once that thought hits you, you get sensible. But if it never hits you, then you carry on being an idiot.” I told Ridley this was a climber’s mentality. Ridley said, “I think of a climb in terms of a beginning, middle, and end. There’s a parallel there with life. You tend not to think about the end. I’m 88 now, and I tend not to ever think about what happens next. I really don’t dwell on it, and I just consider my good fortune about being healthy in full mind and body. That’s an incredible stroke of luck. So I just carry on with that, see how long it’ll take me. At the same time, though, it’s a bit like a climb: The nearer you get to the top is really when you got to watch that you don’t get careless. Alex Honnold visualizes every move on El Cap before he ever leaves the ground. Ridley does the same thing on paper. On a final note, I once asked Ridley what he knows now that he wished he’d known as a younger man. His reply stuck with me: “Nothing. I did OK. Just never forget the steps you took. It’s called experience. Little by little, you’re making decisions intuitively. Everything I do now is intuitive — even controlling my anger on my way into a meeting that’s going to be stupid. I once kicked a wall in a trailer. My foot went through the wall and I fell on the carpet. I lay there, incredibly embarrassed. I’ll never do that again.” From Rules to Live By: How Extraordinary Lives Define What Really Matters by Jimmy Chin Copyright © 2026 by the author and reprinted by permission of Celadon Books. THR

articles.title: SkyShowtime May Be Sold or Shut Down, Board Warns In Memo Shared With Staff (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 14, 2026 7:15am SkyShowtime CEO Monty Sarhan Photo by Pablo Cuadra/Getty Images for SkyShowtime Comcast and Paramount Skydance are launching a “review of strategic options” for their European joint venture streaming service SkyShowtime , The Hollywood Reporter has learned. While no decisions have been made as of yet, shutting down the business is one of the options on the table. The board of the JV informed SkyShowtime CEO Monty Sarhan of the strategic review Monday in a letter, which was viewed by THR . Sarhan subsequently shared it with staff at the company. “SkyShowtime operates in one of the most competitive markets in our industry. Despite the excellent work of the team and the strength of what you and the team have built, the landscape continues to evolve rapidly, and remains highly challenging,” the board’s letter stated. “Against that backdrop, SkyShowtime’s shareholders are commencing a review of strategic options for the business, which includes the possibility of a wind down. No decisions have been made, and all options remain under consideration.” SkyShowtime combines content from NBCUniversal and Sky Studios as well as Paramount, effectively offering a service with the combined programming might of Peacock and Paramount+ in the U.S. The service was first announced five years ago, and serves more than 20 different countries in Europe. In his note, Sarhan noted that SkyShowtime currently has “several million subscribers and stand in scale alongside the most established players in the market.” However, with a rapidly changing media environment (when the JV was formed, David Ellison had not yet acquired Paramount, and he is currently seeking to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery), and with media giants reexamining their streaming strategies, the experiment may well be nearing its end. In his note to SkyShowtime employees, Sarhan wrote that: “I know this news creates uncertainty and, as we work through what comes next, my priority and that of the leadership team, is to be there and support all of you. Together, we have created a community and culture with empathy, opportunity, and innovation at its heart. Whatever comes next, we will all continue to be there for one another.” SkyShowtime’s board, in its letter, noted that the companies are taking their time to figure out what the best path forward will ultimately be. “We know the most important question this raises is what it means for the SkyShowtime team. This update is the beginning of a dialogue, not the end of one,” the board wrote. “The service continues to operate as normal for customers and partners, and every role continues unchanged today. At this time, we ask that the team remain focused on bringing our audiences the quality of service and programming you have all expertly delivered over the years, and maintaining momentum of the operating business into 2027. “Where any proposal could affect employees, we will follow the information and consultation processes required in each of our markets,” it continued. “Final decisions will be made after those conversations have taken place.” THR

articles.title: ‘The Last Photograph’ Review: Zack Snyder Tries Indie Filmmaking on for Size, With Painfully Ponderous Results
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Michael Rechtshaffen Plus Icon Michael Rechtshaffen View All September 14, 2026 7:22am 'The Last Photograph' Toronto Film Festival After an extended sojourn working in the DC Extended Universe, successful filmmaker Zack Snyder casts off those studio shackles and goes full-on indie with The Last Photograph , a highly personal, long-in-gestation, self-styled Western that trades lavish studio sets for the wide-open spaces of Colombian location shoots. But while the change of pace undoubtedly felt liberating, the end result comes across as a leaden misfire. Overstuffed with pretentious symbolism and flatly delivered, vapid dialogue that constantly overstates the obvious, the ultraviolent film — about a rogue government agent who enlists the help of a heroin-addicted shutterbug to take revenge on the murder of his brother and sister-in-law and rescue their abducted kids — is certain to be regarded as a major disappointment by Snyder’s rabid fan base. Related Stories Movies Six Years After Starring Father Died Soon After TIFF Short Premiere, 'Strong Son' Director Returns With Grief Drama Movies 'Seventeen' Director Justin Ducharme Talks Portraying Struggling Sex Workers as BFFs in Gritty Vancouver The Last Photograph The Bottom Line Small canvas, big misfire. Venue: Toronto International Film Festival (Special Events) Cast: Stuart Martin, Fra Fee, Constanza Andrade, Marlon Moreno, Quique Mendoza, Gustavo Angarita, Ed Hughes, Pedro Calvo-Anca, Mia Calvo, Jackie Kay, Jose Restropo Director: Zack Snyder Screenwriter: Kurt Johnstadt 2 hours, 15 minutes Positioned as a premium centerpiece for TIFF’s inaugural market, where it is hoping to secure a distribution deal, the 135-minute slog was given Special Event status, meaning there will be no repeat screenings beyond its world premiere on Sunday evening. Many of those who exited the theater shared the same expression of disbelief over what they had just experienced. We don’t know it when we’re first introduced to him, but Ethan Black (Stuart Martin), who would appear to be a loner sheep herder, is actually an ex-DEA agent who thought he had left his more violent ways behind him. That is until his young niece and nephew are kidnapped at a birthday party following the fatal shooting of his diplomat brother and the latter’s wife (Constanza Andrade). Regarded as something of a God-like presence by the locals, Black turns avenging angel as he teams up with Joe Wallace (Fra Fee), a junkie war photographer — when he’s not shooting conflict, he shooting heroin — who snapped a photo of the children’s mother at the moment she was shot in cold blood. Wallace is instrumental in Black identifying and tracking down her killer and hopefully bringing home those missing kids. And so, the two men with very different life philosophies proceed to journey ever deeper into the South American heart of darkness, with a little bit of The Searchers thrown in for good measure. A whole lot of very intense blood-spilling ensues, but to be honest, it often comes as a welcome distraction from screenwriter Kurt Johnstadt’s monotonous dialogue and clunky expository character motivations that are needlessly underscored by redundant flashbacks. Who would’ve thought, for example, that Wallace was constantly hiding behind the lens of his trusty camera as a way to numb himself to the horrors of the world? And when he tells Black, “I’m not good at being noble,” was that a deliberate nod to the Humphrey Bogart line in Casablanca ? And, if so, why? Saddled with characters that play more like memes than fully inhabited human beings, both Martin and Fee , let’s just say, have made a better impression elsewhere. Mexican actress Andrade, whose character happens to be the love of Black’s life, fares somewhat better, but still isn’t quite let off the hook by the film’s overall tendency to portray its female characters in the same misogynistically objectified light. The xenophobic portrayal of the area’s indigenous population is a whole other, uncomfortable issue. To be fair, Snyder, who’s also credited as the film’s cinematographer, captures no shortage of admittedly stirring images throughout, especially those involving flickering light and brooding shadows. The constant intrusion of yellow butterfly imagery, on the other hand, begins to border on the overindulgent long before one final, eyeball-rolling appearance. In the absence of the filmmaker’s trademark super-sized canvas, the usual techniques can’t help but feel forcefully out of scale here. Still, one might justifiably argue that Snyder at least deserves credit for going out on a limb — even if it can’t help but snap under the weight of all that affectation. Full credits Venue: Toronto International Film Festival (Special Events) Production companies: Stone Quarry, Hollywood Gang Cast: Stuart Martin, Fra Fee, Constanza Andrade, Marlon Moreno, Quique Mendoza, Director: Zack Snyder Screenwriter: Kurt Johnstadt Producers: Zack Snyder, Deborah Snyder, Gianni Nunnari, Wesley Coller Executive producers: Alessandro Salem, Kurt Johnstadt, William Doyle, Juan Pablo Solano, Simon Beltran Director of photography: Zack Snyder Production designer: Diego Garcia Costume designers: Stephanie Porter, Johanna Buendia-Para Music: Hans Zimmer, Omer Benyamin, Steven Doar Editor: Melissa Remenarich-Aperlo Sales: CAA 2 hours, 15 minutes THR

articles.title: Gerbil: Inside Hollywood’s Most Unkillable Rumor
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close Richard Gere’s early image in films like 1980’s American Gigolo, and his reluctance to be interviewed about anything personal, left people wondering about his sexuality. Courtesy Everett Collection When the White House was looking for a way to attack Richard Gere this summer, they went low. Very low — even for this administration. Gere, the politically active 77-year-old actor and philanthropist, had criticized President Trump’s “ignorance” for cuts to the U.S. Agency for International Development. At an event promoting an educational partnership on migration, Gere remarked, “He has idiots around him.” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, fired back in a July 21 post on X, “Not going to listen to a guy who may have put a gerbil up his ass.” Related Stories Opinion Maybe Paramount-Warner SHOULD Leave L.A. Lifestyle Could the Galliano Met Gala Fiasco Mark the End of Anna Wintour's Reign? And there it was. Again! That those in Trump’s orbit would traffic in the tawdry is hardly news. But the choice of this particular angle of attack reveals the almost supernatural staying power of a rumor, or urban legend, that started roughly four decades ago. I was not surprised to see the White House post. Nothing about the gerbil rumor, not its longevity nor its continued impact, surprises me. You see, I have been investigating everything about it for six years. The Hollywood Reporter is releasing the first two episodes of my podcast series, Gerbil , on Sept. 17, and installments will be released weekly on Thursdays after that. The gerbil legend may be the most essential rumor in Hollywood history because it perfectly reveals how the products of the entertainment industry, deliberately and, more importantly, accidentally, express fears, yearnings, nightmares and dreams that worm themselves eternally into our brains. Or, as Stanford communications professor Fred Turner told me, “This is Richard Gere, an American icon. And so in some sense, the gerbil is not just up Richard Gere’s ass, it’s up America’s ass.” Comedian Sam Kinison, among the first to refer to the story in his act. John Atashian/Getty Images The basic version of the rumor — and it is a rumor, not something for which proof has been publicly produced — is that sometime in the 1980s, Richard Gere showed up at the emergency room of Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles with a gerbil lodged in his rectum that he had inserted for sexual pleasure. Somehow this unsubstantiated story became internationally known with almost no major media explicitly reporting it, and before the modern version of the internet. Barely a decade after the word “meme” was coined to refer to things or ideas that can be imitated and culturally transmitted, and before the concept of memes going “viral” had become known outside academia, the gerbil rumor caught on and caught fire. The first stand-up comedian to ever mention Gere and a gerbil in his act appears to be the late Sam Kinison, who was already noticing how widely it had spread in May 1990. At a Las Vegas show, Kinison’s bit went, “I hope it’s a rumor. I was in Miami last night, the fucking crowd there went nuts. Everybody in the country knows supposedly because … I don’t want to get in trouble, but supposedly — supposedly — I guess he was in the hospital. … How good could this fucking feel?” Calling it a rumor is a kind of shorthand because the gerbil thing is far more than simple gossip about, say, who is dating whom. Jan Harold Brunvand, author of numerous books cataloging urban legends, considered the gerbil rumor “modern folklore.” Brunvand noted that Nobel Prize novelist Gabriel García Márquez was fascinated with trying to discover the origins of what he called “lost stories,” often untraceable tales that keep evolving new details such as one about the man who supposedly discovered a large diamond in the stomach of a fish he caught. Or was it a person who found a gold ring in their order of fried chicken? Or a Bible story about a fish with a coin in its mouth? When exactly the gerbil story started is one of the mysteries I aimed to solve. It also has many variants — although none in the Old Testament. (But maybe in Freud!) Some versions mention the use of a cardboard paper towel roll to guide the gerbil inside. Others insist duct tape or condoms were tools. Still others say the ER visit happened at St. Vincent’s in New York or Hollywood Presbyterian. The gerbil is freed and runs around the ER. The gerbil dies and somewhere are X-rays showing it. It’s not Gere, it’s some other celebrity. A reply from the NSA to the author’s Freedom of Information Act request seeking information on the gerbil hearsay. Courtesy To save you a trip, your AI machine will tell you the Gere gerbil rumor isn’t true. But this is part of what drew me to the story. The machines only know what they can search: digitized magazine articles, Reddit threads and fact-checking sites. I decided to figure out what, if anything, might be true about it and why this particular rumor never seems to die. As an investigator, it was my duty to explore the possibility that he did what people said he did. But even if Gere did not do the deed, what might be learned from the undeniable existence of the urban legend? I used old-school journalism. I interviewed doctors, film directors, actors, talent agents, nurses, would-be witnesses, reporters and many others who were there when the story started. I traced everything that had been written, much of it nondigital, dating back to the story’s murky origins. I studied emergency room records, police reports, criminal case files and filed Freedom of Information Act requests. No one had done this thorough a job to trace the legend’s origins and find out what is true and what is demonstrably false about it — and, more importantly, why the damn thing has outlasted nearly every other gossip item in the history of Hollywood. It has been said that we are living in a “post-truth era,” where people decide what is real based not on facts but on how they feel about an idea. Into this factual breach rush memes that reflect ideas of how the world works, ideas that exhibit what Stephen Colbert called “truthiness” rather than truth. As I was starting the project, I would say the word “gerbil” to anyone I met and record their reactions. One person free-associated revealingly that the idea that celebrities are engaged in weird sexual stuff just feels true. “There’s a sinister underbelly to what really goes on in Hollywood,” they said. Not only does the weirdness make sense to outsiders who assume celebrities are not just like us, the details are so odd, it seems no one could ever make this stuff up, so it must be true. “Conspiracy theories are renowned for making a kind of sense that appeals far more than the truth,” says Susan Blackmore, author of the influential 1999 book The Meme Machine. You don’t have to be over 40 to know the rumor is still everywhere. When the gossip merchant known as Deuxmoi appeared on the Taste of Taylor podcast in November 2024, host Taylor Strecker gushed, “Like the first-ever celebrity conspiracy theory is that [Gere] used to shave gerbils, inject them with cocaine, put Vaseline on them and stick them up his butt. And use them as little vibrators …” The anonymous representative of Deuxmoi replied, “I’ve had people message me and be like, ‘My mom’s friend is a nurse, and he really did come in’ … I think people started to believe it for real. … I don’t believe it, but if I have enough glasses of wine, I might, like, start to believe it.” Young, old or whatever, you could also have heard recent tell of the gerbil legend in one form or another on the podcasts of Joe Rogan, Tig Notaro and Mae Martin, Dax Shepard, and Conan O’Brien; on Family Guy , South Park , Curb Your Enthusiasm and Family Feud ; on TikTok posts that garner hundreds of thousands of views, on Lady Bunny’s Instagram feed, and on Tom Green’s recent stand-up special. I could go on. Lemmiwinks the Gerbil, a character inspired by the Gere rumor, on South Park. Courtesy Why has it lasted? When exactly did it start? Why did it start? Perhaps most importantly as a service both to a country weary of lies and to the widely beloved Richard Gere, is there any chance it’s true, and if it’s not true, is there any way to stop it? I took on this project not to dredge something prurient up, but because it actually struck me as important. Mike Rothschild, who has written books about QAnon and antisemitic conspiracy theories, says that he is sometimes criticized for platforming these things. But he believes that the only way to fight them is by reporting whatever truth can be found. If you believe that truth matters, and that a journalist’s job is to fight lies wherever they arise, you have to ask questions of these theories, rather than being baited into easy criticisms that don’t work to stop conspiracy theories. “So much of it is just the weirdness and the salaciousness and the pointing and laughing,” Rothschild says, “rather than really trying to develop a deeper understanding of the psychological forces behind these movements. Because psychological forces don’t get clicks. Pointing and laughing at weirdos waiting for JFK Jr. to come back gets clicks.” Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, the setting of most renditions of the tenacious gerbil rumor. Myung J. Chun/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images This is the essence of the gerbil investigation. What psychological forces gave rise to all this in its moment and why does the gerbil persist? To paraphrase the great poem: What rough beast, its hour come round, slouched toward Cedars-Sinai to be born? There is little doubt that the gerbil rumor was a form of homophobia. Gere’s early image in films like American Gigolo and plays like Bent , and his reluctance to be interviewed about anything personal, left people wondering about his sexuality. And the death of Rock Hudson from AIDS in 1985 left the public skeptical about which stars in Hollywood were telling the truth about their preferences. This is part of how Hollywood helped make the gerbil legend, shaping stars to deliver fantasies but telling lies along the way. (There’s more. I’m not spoiling the whole series for the sake of this little article!) In a time now when memes like the Coldplay couple or some celebrity’s too-thin thighs run across your screen only to be overwhelmed by the next hourly outrage or craze, the gerbil rumor comes from a slower time and thus can be slowly examined, its rise teased apart, its makers and its impacts exposed, its truths revealed. The rumor was never harmless. In a pioneering early 1990s academic study of the rumor, ethnographer Norine Dresser reported on an 11-year-old girl telling her that she heard the Gere rumor on the playground and believed it to be true. Rock Hudson, then 29, and his new bride, Phyllis Gates, 25, in 1955. The death of the actor from AIDS in 1985 left the public skeptical about which stars in Hollywood were telling the truth about their preferences. Bettmann/Getty Images Dresser noted that, “Through the acceptance of this legend as truth, the children are internalizing a stigma that will be difficult to destroy. As they grow older and learn more about homosexuality, it will remain linked with lurid bestial behavior. As a result, when these children go through their own sexual awareness and ambivalence, these ideas will remain forever connected, and their own self-images and development may conceivably be damaged.” The 11-year-old in 1993 is 44 now. There is no way Gere could have had any idea the rumor would go as far and last as long as it has. As the years have gone on and his hair has whitened, Gere has become nearly as famous for his charity and his spirituality as his acting. As I’ve dug deeper, I’ve come to believe he might be convinced to see that the gerbil rumor, which has bedeviled him for so long — and my reporting shows it has bothered him — could become a tool for enlightenment. Too grand? After six years on this story, I can tell you the gerbil legend has become my teacher, and I think it can help all of us. My initial request to speak to Gere was denied. “Due to his schedule at this time, Mr. Gere will be unable to participate,” emailed a representative for Gere. The most cogent comments he ever made about the rumor were in a 1991 television interview with Barbara Walters. She asked, “Do you have any idea why anyone would want to hurt you, or embarrass you, or try to smear you?” After some back-and-forth, Gere said, “Does any of this bother me personally? No. People have their own motivations for doing crazy things, you know, and it has nothing to do with me. You know, if I’m a cow and someone says I’m a zebra, it doesn’t make me a zebra.” I expect that as the episodes roll out and Gere and his people have a chance to hear what I’m up to — an attempt, finally, to bring the full truth to bear on the rumor — I will get a call from them. As Tom Hanks did by coming on the podcast Dead Eyes to unravel an old mystery about him, I expect Gere will see this project as something that is of service. Perhaps if, instead of pretending that it has not hurt him, he speaks movingly about the fact that it has, that this is not a victimless little joke, something else new and true will be brought to the story. You’ll have to listen to find out if that’s how it turns out. This story appeared in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Macklemore Dropped From Ed Sheeran Tour After Pro-Palestine Comments During Performances
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All September 14, 2026 8:34am Macklemore performing May 2024 in Melbourne, Australia. Morgan Hancock/Getty Images Macklemore has been dropped from Ed Sheeran ‘s Loop Tour as the rapper drew major headlines for his pro-Palestine speeches during his opening performances on the trek, with Sheeran’s promoter stating Monday that venues set to host the tour threatened to pull out if Macklemore was on the bill. “As the concert promoter for Ed Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour, we have been notified by venues on the upcoming U.S. tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans,” Messina Touring Group, Sheeran’s longtime concert promoter, said in a statement provided to The Hollywood Reporter . “After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.” Related Stories Music Pink Issues Statement Following Backlash for Critiquing Macklemore's Pro-Palestine Comments: "Standing Up for My Own People" Music Macklemore Responds to Backlash Over "Free Palestine" Plea: "Wanting All Humans to Be Treated Equal Should Never Be Controversial" Reps for Sheeran and Macklemore didn’t immediately respond to request for comment. The news was first reported by Rolling Stone. The move comes over a week after Macklemore, who’s long supported the Free Palestine cause, garnered significant backlash from pro-Israel groups after giving pro-Palestine speeches during performances at MetLife Stadium on Sept. 4 and 5. “A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine,” he told the crowd during his first performance. “I said, ‘Free Palestine!’ I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them.” The Israeli-American Council launched a petition calling to remove him from the tour. The rapper doubled down, telling addressing Jewish members of the crowd during his next show to clarify that “criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.” He also shared a post on social media last Monday writing that “wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial.” In its statement, Messina Touring Group didn’t specify which venues objected to Macklemore’s spot on the bill, or if it was all of them. He was slated to perform at all of Sheeran’s upcoming North American stadium dates except for the Miami shows on Oct. 29 and 30. Per Rolling Stone, the venues that objected included Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field, Foxbourough’s Gillette Stadium, Atlanta’s Mercedes-Benz Stadium, Indianapolis’s Lucas Oil Stadium, Charlotte’s Bank of America Stadium, Arlington’s AT&T Stadium and Tampa’s Raymond James Stadium. Messina’s statement didn’t specify why the venues pushed back on Macklemore’s performance, though as Rolling Stone noted, a removal from the publicly owned and operated venues (which include all but Gillette Stadium and Bank of America Stadium) due to his previous statements could raise issues a of first amendment rights. Aside from the groups, others who’d voiced out against Macklemore’s actions included Pink, who reposted a call to remove Macklemore from the tour, drawing significant backlash of her own. Days later, she posted a lengthy statement clarifying her views, stating that she was “standing up for my own people, and I thought I knew going in how lonely that would be. And it’s lonelier than that.” THR

articles.title: Netflix and Sega Set ‘Crazy Taxi’ Game-to-Film Adaptation
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 14, 2026 8:45am 'Sonic' Courtesy of Fortyseven Communications Netflix is expanding its video game adaptation slate with Sega . The streaming giant is at work on a feature film treatment for Crazy Taxi t o be written by Dan Gregor and Doug Mand, the duo behind the 2025 reboot of The Naked Gun. Neal H. Moritz and Toby Ascher of Original Film and Toru Nakahara, head producer at Sega, are producing the adaptation of the Crazy Taxi game that since a 1999 arcade launch has put players behind the wheel of a fearless cabbie racing the clock through chaotic city streets. Netflix and Sega are also adapting the Sonic game as a new animated series in development with Carlos Stevens and Nakahara, and the Stranger Than Heaven game from RGG Studio and set in early 20th-century Japan to become a live action film, with Nakahara again producing for the video game maker. The Sonic action game franchise began in the 1990s and has sustained strong sales. Related Stories Business Netflix, YouTube and Amazon Launch a Streaming Public Policy Group Movies Netflix to Stream Lee Chang-dong's Films Globally as 'Possible Love' Awards Campaign Heats Up The new multi-title collaboration will look to live-action comedy, kids’ animation and live-action crime adaptations to reflect the range of Sega’s library and expand Netflix’s track record in turning game worlds into scripted and unscripted, live-action and animated films and series. “Great games already have what every adaptation is chasing — characters people love, worlds they know by heart, and fandoms that show up. With Crazy Taxi, Sonic, and Stranger Than Heaven , we get to work across three completely different eras of Sega’s catalog, celebrating everything fans love, while introducing them to new audiences,” Brandon Riegg, vp of nonfiction and transmedia at Netflix, said in a statement. For Sega, the aim is bringing the fan base for its popular games to a new streaming platform, with an eye to franchises. “We’ve watched Netflix take on stories across every kind of format and treat each one with real craft, and seeing that same dedication applied to Sonic, Crazy Taxi and Stranger Than Heaven is something we at Sega are incredibly proud to be a part of,” Shuji Utsumi, president and COO of Sega, said in another statement. Netflix’s earlier video game adaptations include a live action series based on Assassin’s Creed, a live action movie based on the Gears of War game and animated series adaptations for Minecraft, Magic: The Gathering and the Clash of Clans games. THR

articles.full_text: Sep 14, 2026 7:30am PT ‘Emily in Paris’ Star Lucien Laviscount Joins Daisy Ridley in ‘The Good Samaritan’ as Action-Thriller Secures Key Deals (EXCLUSIVE) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture 9 minutes ago ‘Emily in Paris’ Star Lucien Laviscount Joins Daisy Ridley in ‘The Good Samaritan’ as Action-Thriller Secures Key Deals (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Tessa Thompson and Michael Shannon Join Mads Mikkelsen in Death Row Drama ‘Last Meals’ From Ramin Bahrani (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago See All Credit: David Burlacu Lucien Laviscount , the “Emily in Paris” breakout recently seen in the rom-com “People We Meet on Vacation,” has joined fellow Brit Daisy Ridley in upcoming action-thriller “The Good Samaritan.” From “Taken” director Pierre Morel and based on an original screenplay by “Rambo: Last Blood” screenwriter Matthew Ian Cirulnick, the film also stars Josh Duhamel (“Ransom Canyon,” “Shotgun Wedding”) and Sharlto Copley (“Monkey Man,” “District 9”). Production set to begin this fall. Related Stories Jimmy Kimmel in Talks to Renew Late-Night Show at ABC Jeff Corwin to Return to Television With Wildlife Conservation Series ‘Jeff Corwin’s Southern Wild' Meanwhile, Highland Film Group — which is handing international sales and has “The Good Samaritan” on its TIFF market slate — has unveiled a number of key deals for the title. Popular on Variety Highland has sold rights to Splendid Film for Germany, Vertigo Releasing for the U.K., Key 2 Media for Spain, Blue Swan Entertainment for Italy, Three Lines Pictures for Benelux, Spentzos Film for Greece, Cinemundo for Portugal and Mediasquad for Eastern Europe. Other deals include ATV for Turkey, Falcon Films for Middle East, Lionsgate for India, Prima Entertainment for Indonesia, MovieCloud for Taiwan, California Filmes for Latin America, VVS Films for Canada, Filmfinity for South Africa and PictureWorks for Airline Rights. CAA Media Finance and UTA Independent Film Group are co-representing U.S. domestic rights. “The Good Samaritan” follows successful entrepreneur Dr. Rosalind Carver (Ridley) and her husband Matt (Lucien Laviscount) after they rescue a wounded man drifting off the coast of Indonesia, unaware that they’re stepping into a deadly conspiracy. Within hours, their yacht vanishes, Matt is abducted by a gang of ruthless pirates led by Langbore (Copley), and paradise becomes a trap. Imprisoned by corrupt officials, Rosalind crosses paths with Sean Fuller (Duhamel), a battle-hardened ex-mercenary with his own reasons for taking down the pirates. In a desperate race against time, Rosalind and Sean are forced into an uneasy alliance, fighting to save her husband and expose a global trafficking empire that eliminates anyone who tries to stop it. “The Good Samaritan” is produced by Mark Canton (“300,” “Power,” “Den of Thieves”) of Canton Entertainment. Also producing are Oakhurst Entertainment (“Canary Black,” “The Fix”), Renee Tab (“Freelance,” “Sound of Freedom”) of Sentient Entertainment and David Lipper and Bobby Daly of Latigo Films (“The Fix,” “Not Without Hope,” “Neglected”). Executive producers include Morel, Matthew Ian Cirulnick, Ryan Winterstern, David Hopwood, Jeff Kranzdorf for Latigo Films, Ralph Brescia, Dorothy Canton for Canton Entertainment and Delphine Perrier and Arianne Fraser for Highland Film Group, with Canton Entertainment’s Karley Ferlic serving as a co-producer. The film is financed by Robert MacLean for Tribune Pictures. Highland Film Group’s current slate also includes Andy Tennant’s comedy “The Fun Lady” starring Jessica Alba; Nimród Antal’s sci-fi action thriller “Bluefly” starring Russell Crowe and Priyanka Chopra Jonas; Lisette Feliciano’s “Iron Jane” starring Eiza Gonzalez and Brandon Sklenar; Neil Burger’s action thriller “Barracuda” starring Anthony Mackie and Dafne Keen and Justin Chadwick’s action spy-thriller “The Mark” starring Jessica Alba, Tom Hopper and Elsa Pataky. articles.title: ‘Mr. Irrelevant: The John Tuggle Story’ Trailer: ‘Superman’ Star David Corenswet Plays NFL Player Diagnosed With Cancer in Real-Life Story
articles.full_text: Sep 14, 2026 7:55am PT ‘Mr. Irrelevant: The John Tuggle Story’ Trailer: ‘Superman’ Star David Corenswet Plays NFL Player Diagnosed With Cancer in Real-Life Story By Mya Copeland Plus Icon Mya Copeland Latest ‘Mr. Irrelevant: The John Tuggle Story’ Trailer: ‘Superman’ Star David Corenswet Plays NFL Player Diagnosed With Cancer in Real-Life Story 44 minutes ago African American Film Critics Association Donates $25,000 to Black Film Hall of Fame – Film News in Brief 6 days ago ‘The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon’ Final Season Reveals First-Look Teaser (TV News Roundup) 6 days ago See All Sarah Enticknap Paramount released the trailer for “ Mr. Irrelevant : The John Tuggle Story,” a sports biopic about the final pick in the 1983 NFL draft. The sports drama tells “the heartfelt story of the inspiring, enduring impact John Tuggle had on his team and teammates after being drafted by the New York Giants,” the logline says. “Superman” star David Corenswet stars as John Tuggle, who was drafted by the New York Giants in 1983 as the last selection in the NFL draft, a position nicknamed “Mr. Irrelevant.” Tuggle made the roster and played the following season on special teams before being promoted to starting fullback after Rob Carpenter was injured. His teammates voted him special teams player of the year. Related Stories FCC Asks Court to Throw Out ABC's Lawsuit Alleging TV License Review Violates First Amendment, as Agency Repeats Claim the Action Is Unrelated to Jimmy Kimmel or 'The View' Jimmy Kimmel in Talks to Renew Late-Night Show at ABC During the offseason, Tuggle underwent minor surgery for a knee injury and was involved in a car crash. Following the crash, he went to see a doctor for shoulder pain and was diagnosed with cancer. The Giants did not keep him on the team after the 1985 season, but paid for his health insurance until his death in 1986 at age 25. The team wore his number 38 on their helmets for the 1986-87 season, which ended in a Super Bowl win. Popular on Variety The film also stars Isabel May as Katie, Michael Shannon as Giants head coach Bill Parcells and David Krumholtz as Julius “Whitey” Horai. “Mr. Irrelevant: The John Tuggle Story” was written by Nick Santora and directed by Jonathan Levine. Santora and Levine also produced the film, along with Gillian Bohrer. The film is slated for theatrical release on Dec. 25. Watch the full trailer below. articles.title: How to Watch the 2026 Emmys Live Online
articles.full_text: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. TV’s biggest night is here. The 78th annual Emmy Awards take place Monday, Sept. 14, bringing together the casts and creators behind the year’s biggest shows — from “The Pitt” and “Hacks” to “Pluribus,” “Widow’s Bay” and “Beef.” The ceremony airs live coast-to-coast from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles beginning at 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT on NBC, with Peacock serving as the official streaming home of the Emmys . Related Stories Jimmy Kimmel in Talks to Renew Late-Night Show at ABC FCC Asks Court to Throw Out ABC's Lawsuit Alleging TV License Review Violates First Amendment, as Agency Repeats Claim the Action Is Unrelated to Jimmy Kimmel or 'The View' STREAM THE EMMYS ON PEACOCK The easiest way for cord-cutters to watch the Emmys online is with Peacock , which will livestream the complete ceremony alongside its NBC broadcast. Peacock Premium currently costs $12.99 per month, while Premium Plus runs $19.99 per month. Both plans include access to the live Emmys telecast; Premium Plus removes ads from much of Peacock’s on-demand library, though commercials can still appear during live events. Viewers can also watch NBC online through live-TV streaming services that carry their local NBC station. Options include Hulu + Live TV, DirecTV , Fubo and Sling TV. Hulu + Live TV. Hulu + Live TV offers a three-day free trial for eligible new subscribers. Availability of local NBC stations can vary by market. STREAM ON SLING Variety and CNN are also joining forces for live coverage from the Emmys red carpet. “CNN & Variety Red Carpet Live: TV’s Biggest Night” begins at 5 p.m. ET and will stream on CNN.com/Watch and the CNN app for CNN streaming subscribers, giving viewers three hours of arrivals, interviews and fashion coverage before the main ceremony. CNN correspondent Elizabeth Wagmeister and Variety co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh will host the special live from the carpet, with Melissa Rivers joining throughout the evening to weigh in on the night’s fashion and biggest arrivals. The appearance marks Rivers’ first return to an awards-show red carpet in nearly 20 years, following the years she spent covering Hollywood alongside her mother, Joan Rivers. “Law & Order: SVU” star Mariska Hargitay will host this year’s ceremony, becoming the first woman to solo-host the Emmys since Jane Lynch in 2011. Hargitay is already an Emmy winner herself for playing Olivia Benson on the long-running NBC procedural and enters Monday’s ceremony fresh off Creative Arts Emmy wins for her documentary “My Mom Jayne.” “The Pitt” enters Monday night as the most-nominated show of the year with 25 nods, as the HBO Max medical drama looks to repeat its success from last year. Noah Wyle is again among the acting contenders, while Katherine LaNasa and Taylor Dearden are among the show’s heavily nominated ensemble. On the comedy side, “Hacks” earned 24 nominations for its fifth and final season, setting a new record for the most nominations received by a comedy series in a single year. Jean Smart is once again up for lead comedy actress, while Megan Stalter scored her first Emmy nomination for the show. But “Hacks” has some serious competition. Apple TV’s “Widow’s Bay” picked up 19 nominations, while “Pluribus” scored 18, including a lead drama actress nomination for Rhea Seehorn. Netflix’s second season of “Beef” follows with 16 nominations. There could also be some career milestones. Harrison Ford is in contention for his first Emmy win for “Shrinking,” while Smart has a chance to continue her dominant awards run with “Hacks.” The ceremony will also include television-history tribute s marking the 30th anniversary of “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” and the 50th anniversary of “Charlie’s Angels.” The 78th Emmy Awards air Monday, Sept. 14 at 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT on NBC and stream live on Peacock. articles.full_text: Sep 14, 2026 8:10am PT Oasis Announce 2027 Tour Dates By Steven J. Horowitz Plus Icon Steven J. PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades! The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel’ – and we will continue to do so!” Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account Monday. We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE! Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP” Popular on Variety Trump’s comments came after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday, Sept. 12, posted a 3,815-word essay online warning about the dangers of AI. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he wrote. articles.full_text: Sep 14, 2026 8:28am PT SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest ‘Emily in Paris’ Star Lucien Laviscount Joins Daisy Ridley in ‘The Good Samaritan’ as Action-Thriller Secures Key Deals (EXCLUSIVE) 59 minutes ago Tessa Thompson and Michael Shannon Join Mads Mikkelsen in Death Row Drama ‘Last Meals’ From Ramin Bahrani (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Sydney Sweeney’s Naked Sports Betting Ad Ignites Backlash From Olympic Athletes: ‘Stop Sexualizing Women in Sport’ 3 hours ago See All Getty Images for SkyShowtime SkyShowtime , the European streaming service co-owned by Comcast and Paramount Skydance, could be shuttered. This was the warning in a letter from the board of the joint venture to SkyShowtime CEO Monty Sarhan, which said a “review of strategic options for the business” had begun. Sarhan subsequently shared the letter — which has been seen by Variety — with staff at the company. Related Stories Jimmy Kimmel in Talks to Renew Late-Night Show at ABC FCC Asks Court to Throw Out ABC's Lawsuit Alleging TV License Review Violates First Amendment, as Agency Repeats Claim the Action Is Unrelated to Jimmy Kimmel or 'The View' “SkyShowtime operates in one of the most competitive markets in our industry. Despite the excellent work of the team and the strength of what you and the team have built, the landscape continues to evolve rapidly, and remains highly challenging,” the letter stated. “Against that backdrop, SkyShowtime’s shareholders are commencing a review of strategic options for the business, which includes the possibility of a wind down. No decisions have been made, and all options remain under consideration.” SkyShowtime was launched in late 2022 and gradually rolled out across more than 20 European territories, combining content from Peacock, Paramount+ and Sky. But the impending Paramount-WBD deal has led to uncertainty at the company, with reports in the media of plans to quietly fold the service into Paramount+. Popular on Variety I know this news creates uncertainty and, as we work through what comes next, my priority and that of the leadership team, is to be there and support all of you,” Sarhan said in his message to SkyShowtime employees. “Together, we have created a community and culture with empathy, opportunity, and innovation at its heart. Whatever comes next, we will all continue to be there for one another.” The letter from the SkyShowtime board underlined that, with much still undecided, the service continued to operate as normal. “We know the most important question this raises is what it means for the SkyShowtime team. This update is the beginning of a dialogue, not the end of one,” it said. “The service continues to operate as normal for customers and partners, and every role continues unchanged today. articles.title: Stagecoach 2027 Lineup: Garth Brooks, Riley Green, Zach Top to Headline
articles.full_text: Sep 14, 2026 8:30am PT Stagecoach 2027 Lineup: Garth Brooks, Riley Green, Zach Top to Headline By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Stagecoach 2027 Lineup: Garth Brooks, Riley Green, Zach Top to Headline 10 minutes ago Lil Durk Acquitted in Murder-for-Hire Trial 3 days ago Jay-Z Brings Justin Timberlake Onstage in Paris 4 days ago See All The annual Stagecoach festival will return to the Empire Polo Club in Indio, Calif. next April, and as usual it has a powerful set of headliners: Garth Brooks , Riley Green and Zach Top, with a reunited Florida Georgia Line set for a special late-night set at the festival, marking the duo’s first officially announced performance since teasing a reunion earlier this year. Other artists on the bill include Hardy, Willie Nelson & Family, Kelly Clarkson, Brothers Osborne, Shaboozey, Dasha, Stella Lefty, Stephen Wilson Jr, Journey, Pitbull, Carín León, Matchbox Twenty, Cameron Whitcomb and more. The festival continues Stagecoach’s tradition of male-dominated lineups, with just Clarkson among the top-billed performers. Lainey Wilson was one of last year’s headliners, since the festival’s 2007 debut, Miranda Lambert has headlined three times, Carrie Underwood twice and Shania Twain once. Related Stories Jimmy Kimmel in Talks to Renew Late-Night Show at ABC FCC Asks Court to Throw Out ABC's Lawsuit Alleging TV License Review Violates First Amendment, as Agency Repeats Claim the Action Is Unrelated to Jimmy Kimmel or 'The View' The festival takes place April 23-25, 2027. Tickets go on-sale starting Friday, September 18 at 11am PT, with payment plans offered at only $49 down. Popular on Variety Of the headliners, Riley Green’s new album “That’s Just Me” is set for release on September 18; Zach Top recently earned two more nominations at the 60th Annual CMA Awards and is currently in the midst of an extensive headline tour; and Garth Brooks, who’s currently on the road with his acclaimed “Blame It All On My Roots” arena tour. Of his upcoming performance, Green says, “Let’s do this again. We’re excited to make it back out to the desert after a wild ride last year. We’ll probably stay all weekend and catch the other sets so come join us.” Top recalls, “When we played Stagecoach in 2024, it was one of the very first festivals where we really drew a crowd for our set. We packed out the Palomino stage and I remember feeling like we were really doing something. Now to be back in 2027 as a headliner is just something truly special.” “Stagecoach is a guaranteed good time,” Brooks adds, “I was shocked by how personal everything there is…from the people working the venue to the people singing along. A MUST if you’re a Country music fan!” Additionally, Late Night on Mustang Stage, presented by Boot Barn, returns with Sean Paul, Florida Georgia Line and Flo Rida, shifting into full-throttle mode after dark with big singalongs and familiar hits that keep the party going after the main stages wrap. “The last time we played Stagecoach was back in 2018, and a whole lot of life has happened since then,” Florida Georgia Line says. “There’s something really special about getting to come back to the desert together, step on that stage again, and share these songs and memories with the fans who have been with us through it all. We couldn’t think of a better place to do it.” Two of Stagecoach’s attractions, Diplo’s HonkyTonk, now in its fifth year, and Guy Fieri’s Stagecoach Smokehouse, return for 2027. Amazon Music is returning as Stagecoach’s exclusive livestream destination for the fifth year in a row. Fans will be able to stream live performances from artists on Amazon Music, Prime Video, Twitch, Amazon Live, and the Amazon Music app on Fire TV. Fans can also listen to the Official Stagecoach Playlist streaming now exclusively on Amazon Music here. articles.title: ‘Crazy Taxi’ Comedy Movie Coming From Netflix and Sega, New ‘Sonic’ TV Series and ‘Stranger Than Heaven’ Film in the Works
articles.full_text: Sep 14, 2026 8:45am PT ‘Crazy Taxi’ Comedy Movie Coming From Netflix and Sega, New ‘Sonic’ TV Series and ‘Stranger Than Heaven’ Film in the Works By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Trump Says He’s the Only AI ‘Guardrail’ Needed and Mocks Anthropic CEO’s Call for AI Slowdown: ‘Pretending to Be a Perfect Little Angel’ 27 minutes ago FCC Chairman Slams James Talarico as Running a ‘Hoax’ With Jimmy Kimmel Interview, Which ABC Punted to YouTube, to Get ‘Clicks and Donations’ 1 day ago Gary Oldman Predicts HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Series Will Be ‘More Satisfying’ for Fans Than the Movies 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Sega Netflix has hit the start button on multiple adaptations of Sega hit gaming franchises. The first project under the companies’ new multititle deal is a feature-film adaptation of “ Crazy Taxi ,” Sega’s long-running racing game. The movie will be written by Dan Gregor and Doug Mand — the writing duo behind the 2025 reboot of “The Naked Gun” — with Original Film’s Neal H. Moritz and Toby Ascher and Sega’s Toru Nakahara, the producers behind the Sonic franchises, on board to produce. Related Stories FCC Asks Court to Throw Out ABC's Lawsuit Alleging TV License Review Violates First Amendment, as Agency Repeats Claim the Action Is Unrelated to Jimmy Kimmel or 'The View' Jimmy Kimmel in Talks to Renew Late-Night Show at ABC Netflix and Sega also announced two other adaptations in development: a new animated “ Sonic the Hedgehog ” kids’ series and a movie based on action-adventure game “Stranger Than Heaven.” Popular on Variety “Great games already have what every adaptation is chasing — characters people love, worlds they know by heart, and fandoms that show up,” said Brandon Riegg, VP of nonfiction and transmedia at Netflix, in a statement. “With ‘Crazy Taxi,’ ‘Sonic’ and ‘Stranger Than Heaven,’ we get to work across three completely different eras of Sega’s catalog, celebrating everything fans love, while introducing them to new audiences.” Toru Nakahara, head producer at Sega, commented: “Expect something cute yet cool for ‘Sonic,’ hilariously crazy for ‘Crazy Taxi’ and a badass action drama for ‘Stranger Than Heaven,’ because we’ve got some amazing creative ideas lined up and we are just getting started. The whole team is absolutely thrilled!” In “Crazy Taxi,” which made its arcade debut in 1999, players sit in the driver’s seat as a “fearless cabbie racing the clock through chaotic city streets — flying off ramps, dodging traffic and chasing tips with punk-rock energy that became the series’ signature,” per Sega. The latest title in the franchise, “Crazy Taxi: World Tour,” is scheduled for release in 2027. “We couldn’t be more excited to continue our longstanding relationship with Sega and bring ‘Crazy Taxi’ to life with our partners at Netflix,” Original Film’s Moritz and Ascher said in a statement. “This film is for anyone who’s spent hours behind the wheel of a yellow cab on their Dreamcast, with the music cranked up, smashing through everything in sight just to make the next fare.” Meanwhile, a new animated “Sonic” series is currently in development with Carlos Stevens and Toru Nakahara. The show will present Sonic and his friends as heroes for an upper pre-school audience, touted as a “high-voltage, comedic, yet emotionally grounded series built for kids who want to feel a little edge, a little attitude, and a lot of ‘that’s my crew’ wish fulfillment,” per Sega. Three seasons of Netflix’s “Sonic Prime” 3D animated series are currently available to stream only on Netflix. “Stranger Than Heaven” hails from RGG Studio, developer of the bestselling “Like a Dragon: Yakuza” series, with over 30 million copies sold. The game, set to be released in January 2027, is set in early 20th century Japan, following a foreigner who claws his way from destitute stranger to feared yakuza to entertainment tycoon. Toru Nakahara is set as producer on the film. “We’ve watched Netflix take on stories across every kind of format and treat each one with real craft, and seeing that same dedication applied to ‘Sonic,’ ‘Crazy Taxi’ and ‘Stranger Than Heaven’ is something we at Sega are incredibly proud to be a part of,” said Shuji Utsumi, president and COO of Sega. “The fandoms of these games deserve storytelling that honors what makes each title special, and we know Netflix shares that commitment. This is just the start of what these titles can become.” The new Sega titles will join Netflix’s growing slate of video game adaptations. Those include a live-action “Assassin’s Creed” series; a live-action “Gears of War” film; animated series adaptations based on “Minecraft,” “Magic: The Gathering” and “Clash of Clans”; the “Overcooked” competition series; second seasons of “Cyberpunk: Edgerunners” and “Splinter Cell: Deathwatch”; and the third and final season of “Devil May Cry.” Chris Rock Says Scott Rudin’s ‘Hard Coaching’ Made Him a Better Filmmaker: Some Creatives Don’t ‘Respond to a Hug’ Sara Bareilles on ‘Good Grief’ and Finding Joy in the Tough Stuff: ‘Grief Is the Mothership of This Record, but It Carries Release, Hope, Optimism and Connection’ Lisa Uncensored: On ‘Always Lalisa,’ Blackpink, Leaked Videos and Bond Girl Dreams Javier Bardem to Be Honored by Rome Film Festival With Lifetime Achievement Award ‘Mr. Irrelevant: The John Tuggle Story’ Trailer: ‘Superman’ Star David Corenswet Plays NFL Player Diagnosed With Cancer in Real-Life Story ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Review: A Blistering Spiritual Actioner Finally Gives Mahershala Ali a Leading Role Worth His While Loading comments... articles.title: Former Tubi Production Exec Ashla Soter Joins Post House Digital Sword
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse ‘Nightsleeper’ Season 2: Colin Morgan, Madeleine Mantock & Christian Cooke Lead Return Of BBC Thriller Drama International Insider: European TV In Peril; Venice & TIFF Latest; Mercedes Ron Interview Cricket Legend Virender Sehwag To Host ‘Rise And Fall’ Season 2 For Prime Video View All September 14, 2026 7:00am Ashla Soter Digital Sword EXCLUSIVE: Post house Digital Sword has hired former Tubi production exec Ashla Soter. A month after exiting the streamer, she’s been named Executive Producer and SVP of Production at Digital Sword, where she will assume oversight of production across the company’s full slate, working with studios, brands, and agencies alongside Digital Sword’s global editorial, color, VFX, and finishing teams. Soter will also continue to produce select projects independently. At Tubi, she was the first production hire for the streamer’s originals push and spent three years there. She was in charge of original content production and oversaw more than 150 scripted and unscripted titles, including Sidelined: The QB and Me , which was a big seven-day ratings hit and grew into a three film franchise. Related Stories News Playhouse Studios Buys Halo Post Assets & Launches Playhouse Post News Adobe Previews AI-Powered Video Editing System 'Project Frame Forward' Besides being a production exec, Soter is an independent producer and over the past decade has worked on the likes of feature doc The Chainsaw Artist . Watch on Deadline “We needed someone who could run a full slate and hold the standard on every job,” said Cal Laird and Joan Pabon, founders of Digital Sword, in a statement. “Ashla has done exactly that, at the highest level.” “This team cares about making great work more than anything else, and it shows in everything they touch,” added Soter. Founded by Laird and Pabon, Digital Sword represents editors and artists and works across film, television, advertising and music.
