articles.title: ‘Casket Girls’: First Look At Gabrielle Union In Supernatural Horror — TIFF Market
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Dove Cameron & RJ Mitte Thriller ‘Cassi’ Gets Sales Launch At TIFF Market ‘One Piece’ Star Taz Skylar Returns For Crime-Thriller ‘Villains’; Double Dutch Selling At TIFF Market ‘House Of The Dragon’ Actress Maddie Evans Leads Brit Horror ‘Pendle 1612’ About Notorious Witch Trials View All September 14, 2026 8:35am Casket Girls Aura Entertainment EXCLUSIVE : Here’s your first look at Gabrielle Union in supernatural horror-thriller Casket Girls , in which she stars with Mike Colter. The film follows “Detective Shay Williams (Union) and her partner Galpin (Colter) as they investigate a child’s supernatural encounter and accidentally release the legendary ‘Casket Girls’ from beneath a centuries-old New Orleans church. Trapped inside, they and a handful of survivors must outwit the bloodthirsty vampires before they’re picked off one by one.” Aura Entertainment recently acquired the U.S rights to the film, which Capture is selling internationally at the TIFF market. Directed by Justin G. Dyck (Creepshow), pic is produced by QC Entertainment, best known for Jordan Peele’s Oscar-winning Get Out and Spike Lee’s BlacKkKlansman . The film also stars Raúl Castillo, Matt Frewer and Thomas Lennon. Watch on Deadline The film was originally written by Thomas Lennon and Robert Ben Garant, with revisions by Keith Cooper and Justin G. Dyck. Sean McKittrick and Raymond Mansfield produce for QC Entertainment, with Edward H. Hamm Jr., Jameson Parker and Gabrielle Union serving as executive producers. Aura’s slate also includes Code 3, K-Pops! , Trap House , and recent releases Icefall, Hungry , and upcoming The Beast . ‘Prima Facie’, ‘Wilson Shedd’, ‘Evil Genius’ Reviewed; Deadline Studio Vids Jeremy Thomas Tributes: Producer Remembered By Industry ‘Adolescence’ Scribe Says Writers Using AI To “Cheat” ‘Practical Magic 2’ Brews Up $46M WW & $30M In U.S. Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Paramount & Comcast Streamer SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Board Says
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max ‘Lupin’ Part 4 Trailer: Is The Titular Character Up To His Old Tricks Or Is There Really A New Lupin? ‘Sunday In The Park With George’ Revival Delayed After Ariana Grande & Jonathan Bailey Exit ‘Heated Rivalry’ Distributor Sphere Abacus Buys Digital Outfit Rocket Rights View All September 14, 2026 8:39am 'Landman': available on SkyShowtime in some European territories Emerson Miller/Paramount+ The future of Paramount and Comcast ‘s international streamer SkyShowtime is in serious doubt amid the Paramount-Warner mega-merger. A note from the SkyShowtime board to CEO Monty Sarhan informed him that it has kicked off a strategic review, “which includes the possibility of a wind-down.” “No decisions have been made, and all options remain under consideration,” added the note, which Deadline has obtained. SkyShowtime was launched as a JV streaming service four years back between Paramount and Comcast as a way of entering European territories that didn’t have access to their own streamers Paramount+ or Peacock. It combines shows from those two streamers plus Sky Studios and local originals, and has steadily grown its subscriber base across 22 European markets over the years. Related Stories Executives L.A. County Projects Huge Job Losses If Paramount Exits California; Company Slams Antitrust Action By AGs & WGA In Official Rebuke Legal They're Talking! Paramount & AGs Settlement Talks Set For Next Month; Bonta Downplays Significance As "Standard Course" The board’s note to Sarhan said the update is “the beginning of a dialogue, not the end of one” and “where any proposal could affect employees, we will follow the information and consultation processes required in each of our markets.” Watch on Deadline “We recognise this is difficult news and that it creates uncertainty,” it added. “We are grateful to you and to everyone at SkyShowtime for all that has been achieved.” Sarhan relayed the note to staff, adding: “I know this news creates uncertainty and, as we work through what comes next, my priority and that of the leadership team, is to be there and support all of you.” The news comes amid the Paramount-Warner mega-merger, which we have already reported could create complications for SkyShowtime. In May, industry sources told us Paramount’s proposed ownership of Warner Bros. Discovery’s HBO Max would likely put the David Ellison-run company in breach of its JV agreement for SkyShowtime. A person familiar with the matter, however, told Deadline the review revealed today is “entirely unrelated” and is a “joint review by both shareholders.” THR was first with today’s news. ‘Prima Facie’, ‘Wilson Shedd’, ‘Evil Genius’ Reviewed; Deadline Studio Vids Jeremy Thomas Tributes: Producer Remembered By Industry ‘Adolescence’ Scribe Says Writers Using AI To “Cheat” ‘Practical Magic 2’ Brews Up $46M WW & $30M In U.S. Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Netflix and Sega Set ‘Crazy Taxi’ Film; ‘Sonic’ & ‘Stranger Than Heaven’ Adaptations Also Part Of New Slate Partnership
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt Jon Cohen Named President Of Lipovsky & Stein’s Wonderlab Banner Comedian Mojo Brookzz Bringing Debut Special ‘I Know You Lying’ To Netflix In October ‘The Family Stone’ Sequel Set At Searchlight With Claire Danes, Rachel McAdams, Sarah Jessica Parker & Many More Returning View All September 14, 2026 8:45am 'Crazy Taxi' scribes Dan Gregor & Doug Mand Gregory Wallace/Sela Shiloni Netflix has set a new slate of projects with video game company Sega , including film adaptations of their titles Crazy Taxi and Stranger Than Heaven , and a new Sonic children’s series. Dan Gregor & Doug Mand , the screenwriting duo behind 2025’s reboot of The Naked Gun , are penning Crazy Taxi . First released in arcades in 1999, the game puts players behind the wheel of a fearless cabbie racing the clock through chaotic city streets — flying off ramps, dodging traffic, and chasing tips with punk-rock energy. The next installment in the series, Crazy Taxi: World Tour , releases next year. Producers on the film include the Sonic franchise’s Neal H. Moritz & Toby Ascher (for Original Film) and Toru Nakahara. Related Stories News 'Lupin' Part 4 Trailer: Is The Titular Character Up To His Old Tricks Or Is There Really A New Lupin? News Netflix To Stream Lee Chang-Dong's Previous Works Following 'Possible Love' Silver Lion Win In Venice Netflix’s animated Sonic series, in development with Carlos Stevens and Nakahara, is targeting “an upper pre-school audience,” per the streamer — “a high-voltage, comedic, yet emotionally grounded series built for kids who want to feel a little edge, a little attitude, and a lot of ‘that’s my crew’ wish fulfillment.” Watch on Deadline From RGG Studio — developer of the Like a Dragon / Yakuza series — Stranger Than Heaven takes place in early 20th-century Japan, following a foreigner who claws his way from destitute stranger to feared yakuza to entertainment tycoon. Nakahara is producing the live-action feature take. Netflix and Sega come to their new partnership after working together on the animated series Sonic Prime , which ran for three seasons. Sega’s Head Producer Nakahara said, “Expect something cute yet cool for Sonic , hilariously crazy for Crazy Taxi , and a badass action drama for STRANGER THAN HEAVEN , because we’ve got some amazing creative ideas lined up and we are just getting started. The whole team is absolutely thrilled!” Netflix’s Brandon Riegg, VP of Nonfiction and Transmedia, said: “Great games already have what every adaptation is chasing — characters people love, worlds they know by heart, and fandoms that show up. With Crazy Taxi , Sonic and Stranger Than Heaven , we get to work across three completely different eras of Sega’s catalog, celebrating everything fans love, while introducing them to new audiences.” Sega’s President and COO, Shuji Utsumi, stated: “We’ve watched Netflix take on stories across every kind of format and treat each one with real craft, and seeing that same dedication applied to Sonic , Crazy Taxi and Stranger Than Heaven is something we at Sega are incredibly proud to be a part of. The fandoms of these games deserve storytelling that honors what makes each title special, and we know Netflix shares that commitment. This is just the start of what these titles can become.” Sega’s trio of games joins a growing slate of video game adaptations at Netflix that includes a live-action Assassin’s Creed series; live-action Gears of War film; animated series adaptations based on Minecraft , Magic: The Gathering and Clash of Clans ; competition series Overcooked ; second seasons of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners and Splinter Cell: Deathwatch ; and the third and final season of Devil May Cry . ‘Prima Facie’, ‘Wilson Shedd’, ‘Evil Genius’ Reviewed; Deadline Studio Vids Jeremy Thomas Tributes: Producer Remembered By Industry ‘Adolescence’ Scribe Says Writers Using AI To “Cheat” ‘Practical Magic 2’ Brews Up $46M WW & $30M In U.S. Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Misty Green’ Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is a Revelation in Chris Rock’s Sharply Observed Love-Hate Portrait of the Hollywood Hustle
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 12, 2026 8:30pm Rosalind Eleazar in 'Misty Green.' Courtesy of TIFF The title characer in Chris Rock ’s sure-footed fourth feature as director, Misty Green , is having a rough week. An actress still best known for a TV series that ended years back, she’s about to be evicted, her bipolar brother is fresh out of a psych ward and in need of both emotional and financial support, a pimpy former colleague dangles a lucrative sex-work gig, and while her undeniable gifts might very well help her book an acting job, the many axes she has to grind in the entertainment industry keep getting in the way. In a star-making performance, Rosalind Eleazar — best known as the tough MI5 operative grieving for her partner on Slow Horses — bites into this gift of a role with grit, tenacity and zero-fucks-given scrappiness. It’s a revelatory turn in a sensitively observed drama that depicts Los Angeles as both a shimmering beacon of fame and success and a soul-sucking grind of constant rejection, where disparities of race, class and gender are as much an obstacle as that casting director who seems to hate you. Following its premieres at the Toronto and New York film festivals, A24 will release the movie Oct. 9. Related Stories Movies 'The Surgeon' Review: Michelle Yeoh Plays a Kidnapped Doctor Trying to Outwit Her Captors in Deliriously Fun Genre-Bender Movies Mahershala Ali Reveals He Was "Yearning" to Perform Action On-Screen Before Filming 'Your Mother, Your Mother, Your Mother' Misty Green The Bottom Line Simultaneously breezy and steeped in melancholy. Venue : Toronto International Film Festival (Gala Presentations) Release date : Friday, Oct. 9 Cast : Rosalind Eleazar, Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya, Anna Kendrick, Chris Rock, Topher Grace, Alexandra Shipp, Amy Landecker, Tracie Thoms, Necar Zadegan, Rich Sommer Director-screenwriter : Chris Rock Rated R, 1 hour 44 minutes Coming 12 years after Rock’s last feature as writer-director, Top Five , a highly entertaining account of the quest to be taken seriously of a standup comic with a history of substance abuse issues, Misty Green is both an extension of certain themes explored in the 2014 film and a departure. While Andre Allen, Rock’s character in the earlier movie, had a fear of not being funny when sober, Eleazar’s Misty is more of a dabbler than an addict. But her problems with impulse control make it hard for her to say no to a night of hard partying, which tends to mess with her professional obligations. The biggest difference, however, is that Misty Green is a significantly more mellow and thoughtful movie, the work of a mature director who knows what he wants to say and has full command of the tone of voice in which to say it. The film is frequently funny, but Rock and his actors never push for comedy. The wry humor is undergirded by melancholy, darkness, despair — by an awareness that even when you appear to have made it in Hollywood, maintaining that perch on the success ladder is not a given. Talent alone often is not enough. Misty appears to have been floundering for years, bristling every time some young up-and-comer tells her how much their mom and dad loved her in her Emmy-winning role on a show called Red Eye . She’s handed a deadline to pull herself out of her rut when Celine (Amy Landecker, hilariously caustic) bursts in unannounced to kick Misty out of her late husband’s apartment. Dazed and hungover, Misty protests that Celine’s husband gave her the apartment, but the unmerry widow is not buying it, giving her a week to find new digs. The industry town’s monomania makes it seem almost normal when Celine starts running audition lines with her before begrudgingly agreeing to the seven-day grace period. With no money and no friends or exes willing to help her out, Misty needs to book a role, pronto. But given her abrasive reputation — she was once fired off a film for punching the wardrobe woman in the face — that’s not easy. Things are further complicated by the reappearance of her loose-cannon brother Jay ( Daniel Kaluuya ), released from a psych ward but still only tenuously in control of his mental health. Her occasional hook-up, the slick and insincere Zach ( Adam Driver ), tempts her out on the town the night before an important audition, offering her a chance at big money if she’s willing to put aside her moral qualms and be part of the “entertainment” for a frisky emir at a lavish party in Dubai. Driver has often been fearless about playing unlikable characters, but Zach takes him to new lows of douchiness when he’s tossing Birkin bags, jewels and cash to a screaming crowd of paid models. Her least complicated relationship is with straight-talking bestie Naomi ( Anna Kendrick ), with whom she works out at a gym near the Santa Monica Pier. Naomi serves as a sounding board and support system for Misty’s anxieties. That’s more than she gets from her agent Randy ( Topher Grace ), who throws up his hands in defeat after another abortive audition, telling her, “No one wants to work with you. You’re too difficult!” While this is very much an ensemble piece, with a bright constellation around Eleazar’s blazing supernova, Rock gives himself a choice suporting role as the one person in the industry who might not have given up on Misty. Jordan is a director who was forced to fire Misty some years back for her anger issues. He’s now staying in her apartment building while holding auditions for a Dreamgirls remake, and while he’s wary about working with the volatile Misty again, he doesn’t rule it out. That remains true even after she gets high with Zach while on an impromtpu date with Jordan, getting them both banged up in a car accident. She goes back to her apartment — where the eviction clock keeps ticking — and tips her stash of booze and pills down the drain, probably not for the first time, but maybe the last? Jordan often gets to channel classic Rock humor (“All civil rights movies suck, you wanna know how I know? Because white people like them!”), but the character is also notable for his sensitivity, even soulfulness. Jordan is an industry veteran with genuine empathy for people like Misty, coughed up and spat out while trying to sustain a career in the face of endless closed doors. The chemistry of Eleazar’s scenes with Rock is sublime. Eleazar’s layered, brittle but also vulnerable performance makes Misty’s depths as a performer apparent, notably in two songs. She sings with moving expressiveness on a torchy version of “One Night Only” in her Dreamgirls audition and a stunningly heartfelt take on Radiohead’s “Creep,” in a Hollywood Roosevelt lounge bar gig. Naturally, her propensity for self-sabotage means her path is one step forward, two steps back, through no fault of her own when Jay loses his cool after being pulled over twice by the same Black cop (Anthony Anderson, one of a handful of cameos) in both cases with no cause beyond racial profiling. When Jay lands in prison, the fiercely protective Misty feels obligated to come up with his exorbitant bail, prompting desperate choices that nudge her career goals aside. Throughout all this, Eleazar keeps us firmly in Misty’s corner in a bold performance that simultaneously pushes the audience away while pulling us in. The tenderness with which Rock has built this vehicle around character, actress and a milieu he clearly knows intimately imbue the material with an aching depth of feeling that stayed with me for days. Misty Green is a poignant snapshot of one woman sweating on the showbiz treadmill, in a town where glittering dreams, crushing defeat and emergency compromise solutions often walk in tandem — the latter echoed in constant local crime news reports heard on car radios. Misty’s personality flaws are what make her so captivating in a smart, refreshingly understated movie that’s very much an insider’s view — jaded, but also clear-eyed — and a credit especially to Rock and Eleazar. Full credits Venue: Toronto International Film Festival (Gala Presentations) Release date: Friday, Oct. 9 Production company: A24 Films Distribution: A24 Cast: Rosalind Eleazar, Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya, Anna Kendrick, Chris Rock, Topher Grace, Alexandra Shipp, Amy Landecker, Tracie Thoms, Necar Zadegan, Rich Sommer, Kelli Garner, Nicole Parker, Ice-T, Anthony Anderson Director-screenwriter: Chris Rock Producers: Peter Rice, Chris Rock, David Worthen Brooks, Victoria Thomas Executive producers: Nelson George, Shaum S. Sengupta, Miles Alva Director of photography: Kira Kelly Production designer: Michelle Patterson Costume designer: Neishea Lemle Music: Marcus Miller Editor: Adam Dicterow Casting: Victoria Thomas Rated R, 1 hour 44 minutes THR

articles.title: Toronto Awards Analysis: ‘I Play Rocky’ Channels Namesake, Could Follow in Its Oscar Footsteps
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All September 12, 2026 10:18pm Anthony Ippolito in 'I Play Rocky' Claire Folger/Amazon Content Services Sometimes, history repeats itself. Exactly a half-century ago, in the year of the American bicentennial, a low-profile film — the story of a small-time boxer who, against all odds, went the distance against the champ — became a gigantic hit and ended up vanquishing the likes of All the President’s Men , Network and Taxi Driver to win the best picture Oscar. That film was John G. Avildsen’s Rocky , which was written by and starred Sylvester Stallone . Eight years ago, another film with a low-profile premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival , where it polarized critics but played through the roof with festivalgoers and ended up winning the TIFF audience award en route to several Oscar nominations, including one for best picture, which it ultimately won. That film was Peter Farrelly ’s Green Book . Related Stories Movies Anthony Ippolito on Speaking to Sylvester Stallone Before Filming 'I Play Rocky': "Very Overwhelming and Daunting" Movies Mahershala Ali Reveals He Was "Yearning" to Perform Action On-Screen Before Filming 'Your Mother, Your Mother, Your Mother' On Saturday night, Farrelly returned to TIFF for the world premiere of I Play Rocky , a film about the inspiration for and making of Rocky . Like Green Book , it polarized critics, but delighted festivalgoers — indeed, it generated numerous instances of mid-film applause, as well as a lengthy standing ovation at the end — and it will probably follow in the footsteps of Rocky and Green Book to a best picture Oscar nom, if not a win. If nothing else, I Play Rocky will catapult its little-known star, Anthony Ippolito , who plays Stallone, into the thick of a crowded best actor Oscar race. The 27-year-old eerily channels Sly’s unconventional but iconic appearance and manner of speaking, and, as was the case with Stallone 50 years ago, the story of his path to his career-changing part will have many rooting for him as much as the character he plays. Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky’ Claire Folger/Amazon MGM Studios The biggest hazard for I Play Rocky , which Amazon/MGM is set to begin rolling out in the U.S. on Nov. 6, is Stallone himself. In THR ’s TIFF lounge , Ippolito said he had spoken with Stallone before playing him and Farrelly said he had shown Stallone the finished film and Stallone was pleased with it. And during remarks from the TIFF stage just before the film unspooled, Farrelly gave a shout out to Stallone. But Stallone was not directly involved with — nor does it seems he will financially benefit from — I Play Rocky . And if the recent past is any indication, he believes he deserves a cut of anything Rocky -

articles.title: ‘Look Back’ Breakouts Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada on Growing Up on a Hirokazu Koreeda Set
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada Courtesy of Getty Images Like the characters they would ultimately play, child actors Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada could easily have become rivals when they first arrived on the set of Japanese auteur Hirokazu Koreeda ‘s latest acclaimed drama, Look Back . Both 11-year-old fifth graders when filming began, the two actresses came to the film with opposite levels of experience and very different dispositions. Okada had been appearing in Japanese film and TV projects since she was an infant. “I’ve been working in this business since before I could even understand things, so it’s like everyday life to me now,” she says. The young veteran was chosen for her role for her layered poise and Koreeda’s confidence that she was up to the task of mastering the dialect of Japan’s remote Akita prefecture, the place her character would call home. Nanase, meanwhile, was a total newcomer to the screen who had been scouted and picked purely on the basis of her natural, bubbly charisma and seemingly boundless confidence. Related Stories Movies Toronto Awards Analysis: 'I Play Rocky' Channels Namesake, Could Follow in Its Oscar Footsteps Movies 'Misty Green' Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is a Revelation in Chris Rock's Sharply Observed Love-Hate Portrait of the Hollywood Hustle “I remember looking at her on the first day and thinking, Hmm, is she really so good?” says Nanase. “But then we were introduced and started talking, and I was like, wow, this girl is really interesting!” The pair, who later shared their 12th birthdays on set just one day apart, became instant best buds. By the time of Look Back ‘s well-received world premiere in Venice last week, they had grown inseparable. As a duo, they landed on various fashion outlets’ best-dressed-of-the-festival lists, thanks to their stylishly retro outfits and adorable antics on the red carpet, where they struck coordinated poses and jumped in the air in unison. The Hollywood Reporter caught up with Nanase and Okada on the Lido the following day for what amounted to their very first interview with the international press. “I can’t imagine how I could have gotten through this whole experience without her by my side,” says Okada. “I think I would have been really scared, but instead it has been so fun together.” Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada in ‘Look Back’ Among Japan’s most decorated contemporary directors, Koreeda’s great hallmark, aside from the gentle humanism of his storytelling, is the unforgettable work he consistently gets from child actors. His 2004 breakthrough, the child-abandonment drama Nobody Knows , would see its 12-year-old star Yuya Yagira take home the Cannes Film Festival’s best actor award, making him the youngest winner in the festival’s history. Much of the director’s most feted work that has followed has hinged upon delicately naturalistic performances from kids, from the switched-at-birth saga Like Father, Like Son (Cannes’ jury prize winner in 2013) to his Palme d’Or triumph, Shoplifters (2018), and recent best screenplay winner, Monster (2023). Nanase says she wasn’t sure what to expect for her audition with Koreeda and his producers, because they hadn’t sent her any scenes to prepare. Instead, they said she should just come to the meeting and be herself. “The moment he entered the room, he had this aura of someone who takes his time and has everything under control, which was very comforting,” Nanase remembers. “He spoke to me like I was a grown-up person, but he was very kind and gentle.” Later, on set, Koreeda would explain each scene to his inexperienced star and then give her the dialog shortly before rolling cameras. “He would share the main idea behind the scene and tell me what he would like me to do,” she says. “But then he would say, ‘What do you think about this? Do you think it’s a good idea? Is there anything else you want to try?'” Nanase adds: “Before we started, I was a little worried about how everything would feel on set, but it never once made me nervous.” Before preproduction, Koreeda’s only request to his actors was that they not read the manga (Japanese comic) on which Look Back is based, nor watch the popular anime of the same name that was previously adapted from it. Instead, Koreeda’s team suggested they watch Shoplifters and Monster with their parents, to give them a sense of the endeavor they were joining. “Both films had something in them that sticks in your heart, something that you don’t find in normal movies,” says Okada. “I thought they were beautiful.” Look Back is a feature adaptation of Japanese artist Tatsuki Fujimoto’s wildly popular manga of the same name. A coming-of-age drama of delicate simplicity, the story follows Fujino (played by newcomer Nanase), a vivacious grade-schooler whose gift at drawing comic strips has made her a minor celebrity at her small-town elementary school in remote northern Japan. Fujino’s budding drive to become a great artist is further inflamed when she sees the drawings of Kyomoto (Okada), a reclusive classmate who rarely leaves home but whose work has a surprisingly adult-like sophistication. What begins as a fierce rivalry between the two eventually blossoms into an adoring friendship and manga-making partnership — Fujino draws the characters, Kyomoto does backgrounds — as the story follows the two girls over 13 years as they come of age, get a first taste of professional publishing success, and eventually experience a heartbreaking falling out that sends them down separate paths. Shot on location in Japan’s northern Tohoku region over the course of a full year, the film is positively Studio Ghibli-esque in its reverent portrayal of childhood innocence in the Japanese countryside — amid the shifting beauty of the seasons and the halting wonders and dramas of growing up. Midway through the film, adult actresses Natsuki Deguchi and Aju Makita, who bear an uncanny resemblance to the kids, step in to play the more mature Fujino and Kyomoto. The only in-depth preparation the project required of its younger stars, aside from dialect coaching for Okada, was intensive drawing practice. As in the film, Nanase was trained to draw figures, while Okada learned to sketch backgrounds and panoramas. Koreeda brought the two on a shopping outing to a bookshop in Tokyo where they bought loads of drawing books and materials, and later they took online drawing classes and met regularly with a professional manga artist. “All of the directors I’ve worked with so far have always been very nice to me, but director Koreeda is on another level,” says Okada. “He is so good at giving advice. I remember when we were shooting one of the first drawing scenes together, he told us to focus all our attention on the sound of our pens scratching the paper, like it’s music, and that was somehow very helpful.” Above all, Look Back is a story about the making of artists, and the film’s two young leads say they intend to carry some of that spirit into the next stage of their careers. “My character, Fujino, has so much determination once she decides she wants to become a manga artist, and that’s how I want to be too,” says Nanase. “I’ll be carrying her with me when I go to my next audition — absolute confidence!” Okada, despite her lifelong acting background, says Look Back has similarly changed how she thinks about her path. “Kyomoto is able to look inside herself and think deeply about what kind of artist she wants to become,” says the 12-year-old. “I want to try to do that too — so I can try to reach higher and higher with my acting.” THR

articles.title: ‘Happily Ever After’ Star Shuhua Yeh Makes the Leap From K-pop Idol to Actress: “It’s Really Happening”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close Shuhua stars as Kitty in 'Happily Ever After.' Courtesy of Cube Entertainment Happily Ever After star Shuhua Yeh might be a fresh face in the acting world, but she’s no stranger to the global stage. Making her acting debut in Feng-I Fiona Roan’s sophomore outing, which is having its world premiere in Toronto, she’s finally achieving a goal that’s been in the cards for her since her high school days. “I was aiming to become an actress at first,” she tells The Hollywood Reporter on a late night — actually, early morning — Zoom call from her home in Seoul. Yeh, who grew up in Taoyuan, Taiwan, and attended an arts high school in Taipei, where she majored in drama. She spent much of her young life believing her career in entertainment — which was always a certainty — would begin with acting and then she’d branch out. Things didn’t quite go to plan. Related Stories Toronto Rising Stars 'Look Back' Breakouts Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada on Growing Up on a Hirokazu Koreeda Set Movies Toronto Awards Analysis: 'I Play Rocky' Channels Namesake, Could Follow in Its Oscar Footsteps Yeh ended up moving to Korea and began training to become a K-pop idol under Cube Entertainment. She debuted in the girl group I-dle, formerly known as (G)I-dle, in 2018. The group found quick domestic success and has continued to rack up hit after hit in Korea and beyond. Despite her brief interlude from acting while amassing international success as a pop star, Yeh hasn’t found the transition to be that difficult. K-pop tends to lean into plot-based album concepts, so she had the opportunity to develop her craft while working on music videos. “It somehow feels like picking up something from my childhood,” Yeh says. “It feels exciting rather than very challenging. I can finally demonstrate the things I have in my toolbox.” In Happily Ever After , Yeh plays Kitty, one of the two sisters at the center of this family-focused film. Kitty’s the younger sister and the ideal daughter — depending on your definition — alongside Xuan Chen’s Claire. When a stray cat wanders into their lives, long-dormant tensions bubble up to the surface. The film explores the burden of expectations that families can place on young people. Yeh as Kitty in ‘Happily Ever After.’ Splash Pictures, Inc When Yeh first read the script, she wasn’t sure which of the two roles was intended for her but felt that Kitty’s personality was quite the opposite of her own — a prospect she found exciting. She wanted, she says, a bit of challenge and more room to play with. Yeh initially met up with Roan and a producer to discuss the film, where the director shared the story of her family and her sisters. Sisterhood sits at the center of the film and Yeh, herself the middle child of three sisters, found it easy to relate the material to her own life. Throughout the process of making Happily Ever After, Yeh not only drew from her own family experiences — she also came to see her own family in a new light. “I sometimes find that I’m not used to straightforwardly facing my own family issues,” she says. “Sometimes I just move forward through life. During this process, I saw the different perspectives of the different sisters, the younger one and the elder one, and also myself, my own perspective.” The new outlook is a continuation of her ever-evolving view of her own sisters as she’s grown into adulthood. She’s started to see her sisters as their own individuals, outside of her own perspective as merely younger and older sisters. It’s an observation she likely wouldn’t have made in her younger days: “In the past, when I was still a student, I think I was more egocentric and more of a rebel.” Yeh went to work in Korea a decade ago, still a teenager, having trained for two years before she made her K-pop debut. She says working at such a young age made her grow up faster than her sisters. “Sometimes when I go back to see my elder sister, I sometimes feel like she’s kind of childish,” she says, lovingly taking a jab at her older sibling. “Growing up brought me a different way of perceiving my sisters.” She’s noticed that her younger sister, on the other hand, has changed in the years she’s been away. “I can see she’s also becoming more mature and more considerate to other people,” she says. Yeh’s still active as a K-pop idol, even if she’s about to make her TIFF debut as an actress. She and I-dle released new music earlier this year, and the group experienced one of the most significant stages of their career this summer, performing at Chicago’s Lollapalooza. The other women of I-dle — Miyeon, Minnie, Soyeon and Yuqi — have been by her side throughout every major moment of her career, including her move into acting. “My members know that taking part in a film has been one of my deepest wishes, and they always wish me the best of luck,” Yeh says. The other members of I-dle will often ask to see clips of the movie or anything she can share with them. Yeh’s a bit nervous for them to see the final product, especially since at the time of this Zoom conversation she had yet to see it herself. Yeh performs onstage during Lollapalooza at Grant Park on July 31, 2026. Joshua Applegate/WireImage Yeh’s quick to admit she’s not afraid to be in front of the camera or in the spotlight — it becomes second nature when it’s part of your daily life, one has to imagine. But the thought of standing onstage at her own movie premiere has her feeling something new. “When I start to imagine that I’m standing on the ground of TIFF, I don’t actually feel nervous,” she says. “But as the days are coming closer — I’ve started to see all the marketing and the press talking about this — it’s been a constant reminder that it’s happening. It’s really happening.” Still, “nerves” isn’t quite the word she would use to describe how she’s feeling. “Instead of being nervous, I would say my heart’s pounding for it. I feel excited, and I really would like to embrace this experience.” Yeh’s hoping audiences at TIFF and beyond will embrace Happily Ever After too. This film and this story, she says, have deeply touched her and the rest of the cast and crew. She’s hoping that will resonate with a global audience. She also has a more selfish wish — that audiences will see more than just Shuhua the K-pop idol and be open to the fact that she’s trying something she loves. Says Yeh: “I hope, of course, that the audiences can finally see me as an actress. I constantly encourage myself to grow in terms of self-discovery and challenge myself. I won’t let myself down.” THR

articles.title: Inside ‘NAZA,’ the Bombshell Exposé on IDF’s War in Gaza
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close 'NAZA' Naza/The Guardian NAZA , which won a Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival Saturday night , is already one of the most shocking and controversial documentaries of the year. It may also prove to be one of the most indispensable. The exposé, from Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, features testimony from 24 Israeli military officers outlining the systems and protocols they allege Israel uses to target and kill civilians in Gaza. The film’s title, NAZA , comes from an acronym the Israeli military uses as a shorthand for civilian casualties. Related Stories TIFF RISING STAR 'Happily Ever After' Star Shuhua Yeh Makes the Leap From K-pop Idol to Actress: "It's Really Happening" Toronto Rising Stars 'Look Back' Breakouts Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada on Growing Up on a Hirokazu Koreeda Set Abraham and Szor, part of the director collective behind the Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land , which documented the destruction of a village in the occupied West Bank by Israeli soldiers and settlers, shot NAZA clandestinely over three years, doing the interviews under the cover of night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv. The duo used VFX to alter the voices and faces of the officers. Their allegations and revelations are harrowing. One describes hacking into the phone of a 12-year-old girl to identify when her father, a target, comes home, and ordering the bombing that kills the whole family. Another describes how snipers gun down Palestinian civilians as they desperately scramble to reach a food distribution site. NAZA was enthusiastically received in Venice with a 25-minute standing ovation, an all-time record. Jonathan Glazer, the Oscar-winning director of The Zone of Interest , executive produced the film. Mk2 Films is handling worldwide sales. In a statement, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it “categorically rejects” the film’s allegations and criticized the use of anonymous testimonies, which it said “cannot be verified.” It repeated claims that “the IDF strikes military targets and makes unprecedented efforts to minimize harm to civilians.” Abraham and Szor spoke to The Hollywood Reporter on the making of the film, fighting the “complicity of silence” and whether their film can bring about real-world change. “Because this is not something of the past. It’s still ongoing.” The film builds on investigative work you did with The Guardian , the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine , and Hebrew-language outlet Local Call between 2023 and 2025. How did that collaboration come about? Yuval Abraham: The film is built on investigative work that I’ve done together with colleagues at The Guardian , like Harry Davies and Emma Graham-Harrison and others, who — we’ve been looking at the way the Israeli targeting systems work, Israeli mass surveillance over Palestinians, and how mass killing works. And me and Rachel, of course, we worked on No Other Land together with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, and we realized that we wanted to make a film that is in this intersection between cinema and journalism. I think a film allows us to examine the system, the systemic nature of the killing in Gaza — and we knew that we wanted to have a very rigorous process of journalism, of fact-checking, of scrutinizing the work that we were doing, and The Guardian and The Guardian ‘s investigations desk were very valuable in that sense, to partner with us on this. How did you find these 24 officers who speak to you so openly in the documentary, and how did you convince them to speak? Abraham: It was a process. It took months, and in some instances years, to find people and to speak with them. For some of them, it took a long time until they decided to agree to speak in front of a camera. I think people were aware that what they are exposing is quite damning information on the Israeli state crimes that were perpetrated in Gaza. And if you think about the fact that Israel, to this day, is not letting international journalists enter Gaza to witness what human rights organizations across the world are calling a genocide — much of the burden is placed on Palestinian journalists, who have been killed. You know, 200 of them have been killed. So I think it’s obviously for this reason that people were afraid, because it’s clear that the Israeli government is trying to block these attempts at accountability, whether it’s through assassinating and killing Palestinian journalists or through other means, by preventing international journalists from coming in. So it was a challenge, but ultimately, when you’re an investigative journalist, you build a network of sources. You move from one person to the next. You have to be patient sometimes and let people make up their own minds. It was important for us that the people participating give their informed consent, and we knew that we would have to rely on a large group of sources — because this film is making quite heavy claims about how Israel’s system of targeting works, about the fact that attacking civilian spaces, family homes, is something that is built into the system by design. It’s looking for targets when they come back to their homes. ‘NAZA’ directors Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham Barol/Anadolu via Getty Images The fact that there were protocols that soldiers operated by, of shooting and killing anybody they saw on the ground in large areas, including women and children — I don’t know if this was a written protocol, but many, many soldiers said that this was the logic they were operating by. So to credibly make those claims in a documentary, we knew we would need many sources. So this is why we also had to get two dozen of them for this film. The other thing that I would want to add is that I think these policies, and the truth of these policies, should have been evident without relying on Israeli soldiers. Palestinians have been documenting this on the ground from the very first day. You don’t have to be a genius to realize that when children come into hospitals with sniper wounds, and Palestinians are documenting it, that they’re being intentionally shot by soldiers. Between May and late October 2025, Palestinians were documenting massacre after massacre happening at the food sites, the GHF sites — you didn’t have to wait for the soldiers who appear in our film, describing how they would see snipers shooting at unarmed civilians running toward food in front of the camera, to know that this is true. That truth should have been evident from the very start, and I think, because so many people — especially Israelis, and people in the United States and in Germany and other places — are still denying those crimes, and because the denial of those crimes allows them to persist, we felt it was important to also bring insider testimony from the people who design those systems, from the people who operated those systems. Because it’s ongoing. It’s not something of the past. It’s something that’s very much rooted in the present, and we hope will not continue more and more into the future. What did the people who agreed to speak with you say were their reasons for doing so? Rachel Szor: In the film there are 24 different people speaking, so there’s a range of reasons why people want to speak. We also talked about it between ourselves: what is their motive to come to us? The film touches on it a bit. There are some people that perhaps feel some sort of responsibility, and they also wanted to speak about it in Hebrew so that more Israelis will hear about it. Some people in the film, you see, feel some sort of pride [in what they did]. We don’t really know what the psychological reasons are. I feel that perhaps it’s also because not many people are asking these questions. In Israel, in the mainstream media, no one really talks about it. There are a few journalists who investigate those things, but no one really gives those soldiers the stage. It’s really like a secret topic, especially the intelligence around it, no one really talks about it. So it was kind of the first time they could speak about it was when they spoke about it with Yuval. The film is less about trying to solve the question of why they spoke out, or how Yuval got to them; it’s really more about them describing the systems they use for the mass killing. (L to R): Jonathan Glazer, Rachel Szor, Yuval Abraham and producer James Wilson attend the “NAZA” photocall at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival Aurore Marechal/Getty Images How did Jonathan Glazer get involved in this project as an executive producer? Abraham: We met Jonathan for the first time with No Other Land . He hosted a Q&A, and we connected afterward. We were really influenced by The Zone of Interest . I remember hearing Jonathan say that in that film, the victims were out of sight, but they were never out of mind for a second. That really, I think, informed how we were thinking of the cinematic language and the way we structured NAZA — the fact that we are looking at an Israeli city, Tel Aviv, we are looking at Israelis involved in mass killings, and the victims, for most of the film, are out of sight. But they’re never out of mind, in the sense that the reason for being of this film is the crimes committed against the Palestinians in Gaza. This was our motivation, and this is also what we were interested in exploring — how those systems look, and what allows people to participate in them. You’ve both been investigating these types of crimes for some time, in different forms, including with your last film. Was there anything surprising or shocking for you that came out of these interviews and this investigation? Abraham: I’m not sure if it was surprising, again, because the truth of what is happening in Gaza could have been evident, and should have been evident, from the start. If you listen to the openly genocidal statements of Israeli ministers, senior figures in the government, senior military officials — I mean, just recently, our defense minister, Israel Katz, said that the only solution for Gaza is migration, and the government is ready to do it by air, by land, or by sea, in any way possible. This kind of rhetoric makes clear that the intent is the removal of Palestinians, and the dehumanization has been on the table. It could have been clear from the start, if people listened to Palestinians, to civilians in Gaza, to journalists who have been documenting it. So I can’t say there was a surprise at the revelations in the film. I think what was striking was hearing how much these tools are already built on a logic that is extremely deadly for civilians. We look at one kind of protocol of operation, a tool called Where’s Daddy, which is a system that, by spying on family members of people the Israeli military wants to kill, waits until a family member says the person is home, and the system is built on bombing those individuals when they are in their family homes, when they are sleeping, at night. What was really striking about this to me is that you so often hear the way the international media and the Israeli media frame this killing as ‘okay, we are bombing them because Hamas is using them as human shields.’ You imagine that Hamas is firing rockets out of those civilian houses, and this is why they are bombed. And we have soldiers in our film saying Hamas uses human shields in some cases, but the majority of the killing — this mass slaughter of civilians inside their homes — is not because the homes are used as human shields. It’s because this is how the Israeli targeting system is built. It’s because the goal — a genocidal goal, in my mind, from the start — was to destroy these so-called targets, with AI involved in selecting those targets, and that civilian spaces are routinely bombed by design. These are practices and methods that existed already before the massacre of October 7, but afterward they were applied and pushed to such an extreme that the inevitable, pre-calculated, premeditated results are, as we know, that more than 2,900 families in Gaza, multiple generations, were just completely erased, all the members of the family murdered. This was part of the logic of how the Israeli system operated. What was it like, personally, to conduct these interviews with people admitting to war crimes? Abraham: Yeah, it’s a challenge, because I know that as an interviewer, you don’t really need to push the person talking in order to get to the truth. All you have to ask, really, once the person is sitting in front of you, is: describe to me what you did, how did systems work? Because the truth of what happened in Gaza is so horrible, just asking is sometimes enough. I actually think you need to use quite a lot of manipulation if you want to obscure that truth, if you want to reframe it in a way where it is not clear — that is the difficult task. The film is based on more than 100 hours of interview material, and every story or claim that is made in the film is something that we heard again and again, from multiple people and multiple sources. I felt it was important to interview them in that way so that the audience feels this film is as factual, as objective as possible, because it is also some kind of document. Of course, we have our personal opinions. We’ve made them clear. But I know that the people I want to reach, the people who need to change, the people whose silence or complicity is allowing the crimes to persist, are maybe people who don’t agree with my conclusions. There are Israeli elections coming up — do you expect this film and its revelations to affect the debate, or even the result of the elections? Szor: Yeah, we really don’t know. Of course, we hope that it will be shown in Israel and will have as much influence as possible. But unfortunately, in this election, what’s happening in Gaza — still ongoing every week — and what’s happening in the West Bank is just not a topic, an issue, in the elections. So it’s a big question for us as well, how the film will be received in Israel. But we hope that the fact that it’s soldiers from the system speaking in Hebrew will perhaps have some sort of influence. ‘No Other Land’ Courtesy of Sheffield DocFest Will it be released in Israel? Do you have a distributor there? Abraham: We don’t have a distributor yet, but it’s definitely our intention to release it as widely as possible in Israel, and in the United States, and in Germany. As I said, I think it’s our responsibility — we are Israelis, we come from that society, and we are citizens of the country that is committing these grave crimes, and we want to confront that, and show and share this with people from the place we come from, and also around the world. We will try. We can’t know if there will be mainstream platforms in Israel, but we want to take this film there. I think it’s definitely important for us, because I feel it’s our responsibility to do this work. Your last film No Other Land had difficulty getting distributed in the U.S. and other territories. Do you expect similar resistance from mainstream distributors with this film? Abraham: I don’t know — it’s kind of too early to tell. My gut tells me, and I hope I’m wrong on this, that it will be just as difficult. I know there are important public opinion changes in the United States. I think there will be a big audience for this film, especially in the United States, since the killing was carried out with weapons that were created in the U.S., funded by U.S. taxpayer money — $21.7 billion worth of arms and equipment sent to Israel since October 7, which is still being carried out. Just this week, a seven-year-old girl in Gaza was killed with her father in her car. This is all being done thanks to the support of the United States, and the refusal of consecutive U.S. governments to condition or suspend completely the arms they send to Israel. So it’s so important for us that people in the United States really listen to the Israeli officers and soldiers describing how their weapons were used. And I hope there will be a mainstream distributor that takes this film and carries it into the United States. I don’t know that it’s going to happen, but I hope it will. More generally, what level of risk is there — for you, and for the people who participated in this film — of being prosecuted or targeted by the Israeli government because of these revelations? Abraham: There is someone in the film who says they want to hide their identity because they are afraid of retaliation and imprisonment by the Israeli government. Israel’s government is a far-right government, and we know that they are not letting international journalists into Gaza, and they’ve killed so many Palestinian journalists there. So it’s clear there is an intent to obscure or hide the truth, and there’s something about that truth appearing through the voices of people inside that system that I’m guessing the state will be very unhappy about, and will try to block from coming out. But at the same time, I can speak for myself and Rachel — I think there is nothing wrong in what we are doing. I think it’s what we should be doing as journalists, and what we should be doing as humans, and as citizens of a country that is committing such crimes. So I hope that we will not have to pay a certain kind of price for it. (L to R): The directors of ‘No Other Land’: Basel Adra, Rachel Szor, Hamdan Ballal, and Yuval Abraham Mike Coppola/Getty Images Given the backlash you faced after your last film, and given that Gaza and the occupied territories aren’t playing a major role in this election, does that discourage you? Rachel Szor: I think the question is less about the backlash and more about the impact. With No Other Land , we won the Oscar, as a collective, and it’s the biggest award you can get, and we felt so many people watched it — but still, this week, two villages were destroyed in a-Safai al-Tahta, and that’s exactly what the film was about — this policy of removing and destroying the houses of Palestinians in that area — and it’s still happening. So, in a way, you ask yourself what kind of impact it can have. But so many people, greater than us, are doing things, and you’re never sure what impact it will have. We have this privilege as Israelis to bring these testimonies in the film. It was less a question of whether we despair or not and more the feeling that we have to do it. Yuval Abraham: I think Rachel and I think realize we are operating in a system of Jewish-Israeli supremacy and privilege. When our Palestinian journalist colleagues in Gaza are really paying with their lives — so many have been killed and murdered by Israel for documenting what is happening around them — to me, it’s clear that there is an importance to documentation. In our film, No Other Land , Basel is still continuing to document what was happening to his community. He says that change can sometimes be like water dropping — drop after drop after drop — and eventually there will be a change. We hope so. For me, I think a lot of this change has to start with a change in U.S. foreign policy, and I hope that the film can contribute to that somehow. This interview was edited for length and clarity. THR

articles.title: ‘Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom’ Review: The Third Time’s Charming, Just Like the First and Second
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All September 13, 2026 4:00am 'Shaun The Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom' It’s a little early for Halloween, but that hasn’t stopped the creators of Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom from delivering their creepiest feature yet. Not to worry that it will scare youngsters, however, since this third film in the hit franchise spun off from Aardman Animation’s Wallace & Gromit series is just as delightful as its predecessors. Delivering the same sort of droll, deadpan British humor via stop-motion animation as 2015’s Shaun the Sheep Movie and 2019’s A Shaun the Sheep Movie: Farmageddon , this installment could easily become the third to receive an Oscar nomination for best animated film. Related Stories TV Pokémon Stop-Motion Series Set at Disney+ as Part of Larger Distribution Deal Movies A Hairy Monster Threatens The Flock in Trailer for New 'Shaun the Sheep' Movie The story is set a few days before the holiday, when the farmer and his flock are eagerly preparing for the Halloween Hoedown, with Shaun the Sheep (Justin Fletcher) proudly hanging up his offspring Timmy’s drawing of a pumpkin. The farmer (John Sparkes) has a big crush on the local veterinarian (Nina Sosanya, voicing a new and welcome human character), who keeps finding strange objects in her patients’ bodies. But he’s afraid to ask her to the hoedown because he’s embarrassed about his encroaching hair loss. Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom The Bottom Line As usual, a drolly amusing delight. Release date : Friday, Sept. 18 Cast : Justin Fletcher, John Sparkes, Kate Harbour, Dani Dyer, Roman Kemp, Nina Sosanya, Paul Whitehouse Directors : Steve Cox, Matthew Walker Screenwriters : Mark Burton, Giles Pilbrow 1 hour 20 minutes When the farmer accidentally destroys his flock’s beloved pumpkin patch, Shaun attempts to remedy things by conducting a few experiments after he reads an introductory science book. While he succeeds in restoring the pumpkins, the well-meaning sheep’s efforts go awry, causing the farmer’s hair-growth lotion to have the unintended effect of making him sprout hair in inappropriate places and eventually covering his entire body with thick, matted orange fur. Needless to say, the farmer’s attempts to rectify the situation with his electric razor are for naught. As the Beast of Mossy Bottom roams the countryside spurring fear and panic, the intrepid veterinarian attempts to solve the mystery, convinced that the creature she’s tracking is Bigfoot. The farmer’s loyal canine sidekick Bitzer (Sparkes), desperate to find his missing master, gets involved as well. Meanwhile, the farmer’s attempt to remove his excess hair with duct tape proves painful enough to produce monstrous howls. It’s all sheer silliness, of course, and that’s the point, with the dialogue-free storyline providing the possibilities not only for endless cuteness — these painstakingly moved puppets, representing both human and animal characters, are truly adorable — but also a series of witty visual and sound gags that will please children and adults alike. The former will delight in the big-eyed animal shenanigans, while the latter will enjoy a great gag about the unintelligibility of parking signs and the amusing sight of a particularly large sheep proudly erasing a blackboard with her wool. One of the film’s funniest scenes features the Beast taking refuge in a Halloween shop and trying to blend in with life-size figures of the Mummy and Dracula. Much as its predecessor riffed on sci-fi movie themes and clichés, this installment finds fodder in horror films with jokes inspired by everything from Frankenstein to the “Thriller” video to Psycho (there’s a shower scene, with the sounds of a sheep flossing replacing Bernard Herrmann’s piercing strings). While not everything works, the gags come at such a fast pace that you’re never bored. And unlike the frenetic, in-your-face style of so many American animated films, the charmingly low-key Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom always feels understated, as if slightly embarrassed when the humor becomes lowbrow. The fun isn’t just in the images. The performers’ non-verbal voice work, the inventive sound effects and the amusing musical selections add greatly to the fun as well. Full credits Production: Aardman Animations Distributor: GKIDS Cast: Justin Fletcher, John Sparkes, Kate Harbour, Dani Dyer, Roman Kemp, Nina Sosanya, Paul Whitehouse Directors: Steve Cox, Matthew Walker Screenwriters: Mark Burton, Giles Pilbrow Producer: Richard Beek Executive producers: Sarah Cox, Peter Lord, Andrew Orr, Nick Park, Carla Shelley, Julia Stuart Director of photography: Charles Copping Composer: Natalie Holt 1 hour 20 minutes THR

articles.title: ‘Words Are Weapons’: Michaël R. Roskam on Turning a WWII Fake-Newspaper Prank Into a Heist Movie
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 13, 2026 5:00am 'Le Faux Soir' Frakas-Productions-Rectangle-Productions-_-Goodfellas-RTL-Belgium In November 1943, a group of Belgian journalists and printers pulled off one of the great stunts of the occupation: they intercepted the Nazi-controlled newspaper Le Soir (The Evening) and replaced it with a satirical counterfeit, Le Faux Soir (The Fake Evening), mocking the occupiers. It was the world’s first media hack. In his film version, Belgian director Michaël R. Roskam ( Bullhead , The Drop , Racer and the Jailbird ) tells the story as a caper — “ Ocean’s Eleven , but with a newspaper” — featuring a cast of Belgium and France’s funniest actors. Le Faux Soir has its world premiere at TIFF and is being sold by Goodfellas worldwide. Related Stories Movies Inside 'NAZA,' the Bombshell Exposé on IDF's War in Gaza TIFF RISING STAR 'Happily Ever After' Star Shuhua Yeh Makes the Leap From K-pop Idol to Actress: "It's Really Happening" Roskam spoke to THR from Brussels about researching 1940s jokes and linotype machines, why authoritarians can’t stand being laughed at, and the limits of satire. When did you first hear about Le Faux Soir , and how did you decide to make a film about it? That’s actually my co-writer, Bernard Falaise. He’s about my age, and he decided that he wanted to do film studies, so he went back to university. At some point, he had this course about piracy in media and satire. In that course, they had been talking about Le Faux Soir. All of a sudden, their phones started buzzing — the ones who had them still active got notifications — it was the attacks in Paris, on [French satire magazine] Charlie Hebdo. A year later they had a choice: either write a thesis or write a script. He wanted to write a script on the Le Faux Soir story. He came to me because we’re friends and he really helped me with casting on Bullhead . He’s French-speaking, I’m Flemish-speaking. He’s like, “Dude, I want to make the script. It’s tough. You want to give it a read?” And he told me the story, and I was like, “That’s a movie. This is amazing. I’ve never heard of it.” No one on the Flemish side [of Belgium], with very few exceptions, had ever heard of this story. Even on the French-speaking side, it was mostly the subscribers of Le Soir , because every year they do a kind of article about it. I’m like, “Dude, if you manage to write this, I’ll direct it.” So he tried, and his script was fairly cool. But I said, “You already told me the story, and I see images, how I would direct it, and your script is not what I see.” But I wouldn’t want to steal the project from him so I said “Let’s write it together, and I’ll direct it.” Michaël R. Roskam talking with actors on the set of ‘Le Faux Soir’ Maxence-Dedry What was the hardest thing about cracking the script? The hardest problem was the text [of the fake newspaper] because the text is funny. It’s a satire. The text is funny, but the text is also old, it’s from the ’40s. A few of the jokes still hold up, but a lot of them refer to people or things where it’s more “I feel it’s funny, but I don’t get the joke, because I don’t know what they’re talking about.” And I was way more fascinated in how they pulled the thing off. Because writing a satire isn’t the dangerous bit, it’s publishing it. How they did it felt to me like a heist movie. Ocean’s Eleven , but with a newspaper. That’s what I said: we need to be very disciplined about the humor, to make it funny without making a satire movie, like Life is Beautiful — which is fantastic — or Taika Waititi’s Jojo Rabbit . I didn’t want to make a satire. I wanted to make a realistic movie about very realistic, very funny people risking their lives. How did that shape the casting? Even at the script stage, I said: “Dude, we need to cast people with funny bones.” I needed François Damiens, I needed Arieh Worthalter, I needed Bouli Lanners. They’re big names in the French-speaking community, the funniest guys on the planet. Bouli is funny and poetic. Arieh is a great, sensitive and funny actor. François Damiens is a funny clown who does everything to hide that he’s actually a fantastic actor. And then you have Mélanie Thierry, who is very poetic, serious, but she also has a little something, a twinkle in the eye. When I had my Ocean’s Eleven together, it was also about holding them back, or they’d turn the film into a full-blown comedy. What’s compelling is that the heroes here aren’t the typical resistance fighters planting bombs. They’re people making jokes, puns and silly poems as a way to resist fascism. I see this film as right in between something like Chaplin’s The Great Dictator and Inglourious Basterds. For me, it was not about doing what Chaplin does, making that kind of satire. It was about showing how Chaplin does it. Michaël R. Roskam holds up a copy of the fake ‘Le Soir’ Guillaume-Van-Laethem I’m a print guy, so I was geeking out on the mechanics — where they get the paper, the presses, how they copy it. How deep did you go into the research? My way of working is to learn everything about the subject I’m making a movie on. From Bullhead , I still know how to raise cattle and bring them to the meat market, illegally and legally. I know the holdups I staged in Racer and the Jailbird would work in real life. Here, I know how to print a newspaper using 1940s technology. I could be a project manager of a newspaper in the ’40s. I went to museums and started finding people, retired people in their 80s and 90s, who told me how it was. Then younger people who learned from the older people, who are rediscovering the old techniques. La Démocrate in France is a museum, but they still print a newspaper, La Démocrate, using the old methods. And they’re young guys. It’s so amazing. Discovering the linotype was one of the most magical things I have ever encountered in my career. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a machine I didn’t know existed that is still alive only because of the passion of people keeping it alive. It’s literally a wonder. I still get goosebumps when I see it. I can look at it for hours. Just the sound of it. For your readers: the linotype is a machine that automates typing, where the letters are melted into a mold, instead of setting every letter by hand. It’s an automatic process, but still mechanical. It’s nothing digital. When I saw this, I knew: this is what we need. We need to evoke those moments. There’s something about the physicality of it. If you were doing a story about social media satire today, visually you’d just have people looking at their phones. Some little text appearing on screen, yeah. What does this story have to say to audiences at this moment? Well, the reason why we tell historical movies is always in the now, in the moment when you decide that the story is important. It came to Bernard at one of the craziest, most horrific events of the last 10 years: the shooting at the Charlie Hebdo editorial offices. This act of terrorism against satire. And because of the issue of fake news. Fighting fake news today is dangerous, but during the Second World War, you could get a bullet in your head for making the wrong comment, the wrong joke. I hope that young people will watch this film with their grandparents, and see that there have always been people fighting against fake news, against how the truth has been bent throughout history. It was done with weapons and violence, but very often it was also done with words. One of our characters says: “Why do the Nazis burn books? Because words are weapons.” And he means it. It’s always been like that with satire. It’s like making fun of the king. It’s forbidden, but it’s the only way you can hurt him. That’s what I wanted to do. Although it’s almost ironic that today, so much of the spoofing is coming from authoritarian regimes. Russia famously has farms that copy Le Monde or Der Spiegel — the exact websites — and promote their own fake news within them. They’re doing exactly what Le Faux Soir did, but for the opposite purpose. Exactly. Isn’t that ironic? If an alien were to look from space at the modern day, he might think that we, the establishment, are the Nazis of the time, and that the ones on the right hacking us are the resistance of the ’40s. We’re defending democracy, but there are some people who are victims of that situation, and they want this system to be dismantled, and they’re using everything they can. I believe that I’m fighting for the right thing. I’m for democracy. But I don’t know. Maybe I’m on the wrong side. I don’t know. It’s a terrible thought to think that I’m on the wrong side, man. It also raises the question of how effective satire really is against authoritarianism. Those famous Berlin cabaret artists who mocked Hitler were all either shot or exiled. Le Faux Soir doesn’t topple the Nazis either. The satirists are rounded up and shot. Satire is not like blowing up a bridge. But if it works, if you can make it work, you can plant the seeds in the heads of the people. It has a toppling effect. Satire has a mental effect. It is the first button of the emperor’s clothes being opened, and then the next one. And if you continue doing it, at some point he’s naked on his throne and everybody’s laughing, and that’s when he loses. That’s why authoritarian regimes hate satire. They can’t stand it. They come back with falsification, with fake news, which is not the same as satire. This interview has been edited for length and clarity THR

The deal with Rai Cinema International Distribution is for Dionisio’s second narrative feature that stars Tecla Insolia and Romana Maggiora Vergano and is being shopped at TIFF: The Market in Toronto. IDDA follows childhood friends Adele and Sofia, now in their thirties, whose lifelong bond is challenged during a journey through the volcanic landscapes of Sicily’s Mount Etna. Roskam on Turning a WWII Fake-Newspaper Prank Into a Heist Movie Movies Inside 'NAZA,' the Bombshell Exposé on IDF's War in Gaza Andrea Curti, CEO and head of acquisitions at FilmClub Distribuzione, a Minerva Pictures’ company, in a statement on Sunday said: “We’re extremely proud to have the chance to bring one of the most awaited titles of the season to the Italian audience. IDDA is first and foremost an amazing journey with wonderful people: Irene Dionisio, Giovanni Pompili and the whole production team, and the amazing cast with three of the most talented voices of our contemporary cinema.” Dionisio made documentaries before moving into narrative filmmaking with Pawn Street, which debuted at Venice in 2017. Strazza will play Billie Blake, who returns home when her mother inherits a dress shop next to her high school sweetheart Calvin Wilkes’ diner. Forced to face Calvin, Billie must contend with the truth, and lies, that ended their romance, according to a synopsis from the producers. Strazza joins an ensemble cast that includes Cobie Smulders, Iris Apatow, Brian Altemus and Callan Potter. Anyway You Want Me , set in 1950s New England and now shooting in Toronto, is also being shopped this week to international buyers at TIFF : The Market. articles.title: ‘Back in Black’ Director on Lovable Serial Killer Doing “Bad Things for the Right Reasons” in Christopher Walken-Starrer
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 13, 2026 6:15am Back in Black Toronto Film Festival Back in Black , as a darkly funny crime drama, is no whodunnit. Ron Murphy’s satire about a failing funeral home has Christopher Walken starring as family patriarch Clyde Mortimer who is staring down bankruptcy. But his business enjoys a sudden rebound in fortune when Sam, his quiet granddaughter played by Ella Ballentine, triggers a suspicious rise in the number of small-town murders that leaves local police stumped and a trail of cadavers arriving on his doorstep. All of which begs the question: what is it about benevolent serial killers that’s expected to have Toronto Film Festival audiences cheering Sam on as an antihero while her town’s local kill count rises? “It’s a bit of a trick, isn’t it? Most people in test screenings that we’ve done are rooting for (Sam). And meanwhile, what she’s doing is morally reprehensible,” Murphy tells The Hollywood Reporter ahead of Back in Black , his debut feature, having a world premiere at TIFF. Related Stories Movies Fina Strazza to Star in, Produce Romantic Drama 'Any Way You Want Me' (Exclusive) Movies Toronto: Irene Dionisio's 'IDDA' Lands at FilmClub Distribuzione for Italy (Exclusive) It turns out Sam, an embalmer by day and cold-blooded killer by night, is preying on local townsfolk because she doesn’t want to see Mortimer and his wife, played by Jane Curtin, fight over finances and be denied a dignified retirement. “I’m asking the audience, how far would you be willing to go for someone you love,” Murphy adds about his morality-bending psychological drama that has Fargo meets Six Feet Under vibes. Not that Walken’s Mortimer character, for his devotion to his family and its generational business, isn’t himself cunning and ruthless. Murphy recalls getting on the phone with the Hollywood legend with his prolific film resume and Oscar-winning role in 1978’s The Deer Hunter soon after he read his Back in Black script. “I think he was testing me because he said, ‘Ron, I’ve played these dark characters for 50 years, these morally questionable characters,’” and Walken was suggesting that, at his age, actors just want to play normal people. After insisting Clyde Mortimer was not a bad man, but in service to people he loved during tough times, Murphy added with an Avis, Try Harder sales pitch: “By the way, I didn’t write this for you. Nick (Torokvei) and I wrote it for Jack Lemmon. And he’s not available. You’re our second choice.” Murphy is also with the layers of moral contradictions in Back in Black , urging audiences to explore how, in a world filled with injustice and inequity, serial killers can help as well as harm — even if that helps Mortimer cash in on bereaved relatives by upselling them on pricey caskets. “It’s important that a bad person gets their comeuppance. But if they’re doing bad things for the right reasons, then an audience’s morality bends, as we’ve seen in the screenings. That’s very upside down, because innocent people are being harmed,” the director argues. For Murphy, while Back in Black is his first feature, he has deep roots in the TV business. He began as an assistant to the late John Candy, and from there directed episodic comedies that starred Steve Carell, Leslie Neilson, Tim Conway, Snoop Dogg, and even Michael Cera and Drake in early small screen roles. His Canadian TV directing credits include Trailer Park Boys, Heartland, Lost Girl and Wynonna Earp. But with his first feature, Murphy has looked to offer, via satire, his own take on our wider economy and politics. “There’s definitely a sort of darkness in the culture that we all feel, certainly since the pandemic. And it’s disorienting, and I feel I want to reflect that darkness in a comic way,” he explains. Another anomaly in Back in Black is Sam, as played by Ballentine, a child actor graduating to adult roles, has no lines to speak as she and her grandfather quietly share a language of love and loyalty. “In film school, I was obsessed with Buster Keaton, and I’ve always wanted to make a silent film. I just think there’s an elegance to telling a story with no words,” Murphy says. Having made his first feature long after he left film school, Murphy adds he’s looking forward to connecting, with his TIFF world premiere, to a theatrical audience after long working on TV sets and in edit rooms where viewers are well out of sight. But as to how Toronto audiences greet Back in Black , whether with laughter, gasps or silence, Murphy has no expectations to avoid opening night distress: “I’ve learned during my television career to be very Buddhist about the material and to abandon your attachment to outcomes. If you think it’s going to be funny and they don’t laugh, your heart is broken. Or you’re surprised they laugh at something else you didn’t think was funny.” Instead, Murphy is looking to Toronto for fresh eyes for a movie he and his team have long been working on. “As soon as it screens at TIFF, it belongs to the audience, and they can do with it whatever they want, respond to it however they want, and I’m really good at just letting go,” he adds. THR
