articles.title: Shuhua’s Acting Debut and Breaking Free From the ‘American Girl’ Label: Director Feng-i Fiona Roan on Toronto Title ‘Happily Ever After’
articles.full_text: Sep 13, 2026 4:11am PT Shuhua’s Acting Debut and Breaking Free From the ‘American Girl’ Label: Director Feng-i Fiona Roan on Toronto Title ‘Happily Ever After’ By Lin Ying-Hsuan Plus Icon Lin Ying-Hsuan Latest Taiwan Strengthens Global Co-Production Presence at Toronto Film Festival With ‘Happily Ever After,’ ‘The Age of Goodbyes’ and ‘Arrested Memory‘ 24 hours ago Sam Worthington, David Duchovny and Ke-Xi Wu’s ‘The Exiles’ Inspired by Joseph Conrad’s ‘Heart of Darkness,’ Director Midi Z Reveals (EXCLUSIVE) 2 months ago Wu Jing Honored at MIFFest, Says Hong Kong Action Cinema’s Influence Still Runs Through Every Wuxia Film Today 2 months ago See All Happily Ever After Toronto Film Festival “ Happily Ever After ,” the follow-up feature from Taiwanese director Feng-i Fiona Roan , is bowing in the Toronto Film Festival ’s Special Presentations lineup, arriving amid heightened attention following the success of her acclaimed debut, “American Girl.” “American Girl” premiered in the Asian Future section of the Tokyo International Film Festival before earning seven Golden Horse Award nominations and winning three prizes, including best new director. During the Golden Horse celebrations, Roan received a gentle but prescient warning from Oscar-winning filmmaker Ang Lee. Related Stories ‘Stuffed’ Review: Jodie Comer and Harry Melling Sing the Body Eccentric in an Odd, and Oddly Touching, Taxidermy Musical 'NAZA' Review: Two of the 'No Other Land' Filmmakers Deliver a More Devastating Exposé of Israeli Genocidal Policy, This Time in Gaza “Director Ang Lee reminded me that the second film is always the hardest,” Roan tells Variety . “Being able to present my second feature at TIFF as its first stop is very meaningful to me. I also hope it can open up more conversations and opportunities.” Popular on Variety Drawn from Roan’s childhood and family history, “American Girl” earned widespread acclaim but also prompted some observers to question whether the filmmaker could move beyond autobiography. “From the development stage of ‘Happily Ever After,’ I was determined to break away from that label,” Roan says. “I was entering a different phase of my life and was even planning my own wedding at the time. This fictional story went from nothing to a complete screenplay within a year, but it also captured the emotional shifts that my friends and I were experiencing at different stages of our lives.” “Happily Ever After” closely examines the subtle emotional dynamics between two sisters. The story initially placed greater emphasis on the younger sister, played by Shuhua, before evolving into a dual-protagonist narrative. “While developing the screenplay, I watched ‘Frozen’ for a second time and suddenly realized how remarkably well it balances the narrative arcs of its two sister protagonists,” Roan says. “I went back and analyzed the screenplay for that reason, then used what I learned to refine the rhythm of my own script.” Beyond the expectations surrounding Roan’s second feature, the film has attracted attention across the film, television and music industries for casting K-pop star Shuhua in her film debut. “When we met Shuhua, we only asked her to read two scenes,” Roan says. “Her confidence and personality came through so naturally that we decided on the spot.” During production, Roan sought to create an authentic sense of family among the cast. Rather than addressing Shuhua by her real name or her character’s name, everyone on set simply called her “little sister.” Before filming began, Shuhua was also invited to name the cat that appears as the family pet. Shuhua’s own experience as the middle child in a family of three daughters gave her a deeper emotional connection to the role, according to Roan. “I gave her only one note: Before making any movement or delivering any line, she had to have a motivation,” Roan says. “Only after you have convinced yourself can your performance move the audience.” Asked how she hopes international audiences will view contemporary Taiwanese cinema, Roan draws on her experience living in the U.S. and her observations from attending international film festivals. “Filmmakers from the previous generation, such as Hou Hsiao-hsien and Edward Yang, naturally still have enormous international visibility,” she says. “Their particular time and circumstances allowed them to pursue their artistic practices to an extremely high degree, and those achievements have secured their place in film history.” Roan believes her own generation brings a stronger awareness of genre and a greater willingness to experiment with different forms. “Every festival feels a little like a social experiment,” she says. “We bring different stories to international audiences and observe how they respond and what kinds of thoughts those stories provoke.” Alongside the classics of Taiwanese cinema, Roan cites French New Wave pioneer Agnès Varda as a formative influence. She also points to Ozu Yasujirō’s cycle of films about fathers marrying off their daughters, Kore-eda Hirokazu’s family dramas and Greta Gerwig’s explorations of women’s inner lives. “My favorite film this year is ‘The World of Love,’ by South Korean director Yoon Ga-eun,” Roan says. During the early development of “Happily Ever After,” Roan immersed herself in reading, including Taiwanese author Kevin Chen’s novel “Ghost Town.” Stories exploring family, identity and self-worth fed into her new fictional direction while allowing her to retain the emotional honesty of her earlier work. As the film meets its first international audience in Toronto, Roan is eager to exchange ideas with filmmakers from around the world. Above all, she hopes “Happily Ever After” will spark a conversation around the question embedded in its title: What does it mean to be happy on your own terms? articles.title: ‘Masc’ Review: A Sensitive Character Study Where Identity is Found in Imitation and Observation
articles.full_text: Sep 13, 2026 4:20am PT ‘Masc’ Review: A Sensitive Character Study Where Identity is Found in Imitation and Observation Filmmaker Bertil Nilsson creates a grammar for masculinity in collaboration with his lead actor Joshua Griffin. By Murtada Elfadl Plus Icon Murtada Elfadl Latest ‘Masc’ Review: A Sensitive Character Study Where Identity is Found in Imitation and Observation 2 hours ago ‘What Will I Become?’ Review: Transmasculine Lives Take Center Stage in a Poignant Portrait of Loss 4 weeks ago ‘Bouchra’ Review: Animated Memoir Explores Diasporic Queer Identity and the Fraught Bonds Between Mothers and Daughters 3 months ago See All Duktiga Ltd In “ Masc ,” director Bertil Nilsson pulls off a nifty trick: He observes an observer. Usually a film’s protagonist has the dominant POV, but here, Robin (Joshua Griffin) is trying to find his personality by observing other men in his orbit. He almost never initiates the action and is mostly reticent about his reactions, but he takes note of everything. This makes for a fascinating watching experience for the audience, as they find themselves in Robin’s shoes, trying to figure out how to behave. In the process “Masc” becomes a thoroughly unique experience. Related Stories 'Boatbuilders' Review: A Mellow Maine Boatyard Study That Offers All the Quiet Rewards of Fine Craftsmanship in Action ‘The Fire Within You’ Review: An Insufferable Christmas Eve Family Drama in Which the Corrosive Rants Are as Noxious as the Dyspeptic Images Robin is queer, biracial and neurodivergent, so society forces multiple identities on him. In the span of a year, he changes his appearance five times and tries on different jobs, places and people to hang out with. He works as an apprentice handyman and lab assistant, tries to immerse himself within a therapy group and seeks camaraderie with different guys his age. In the process, he takes on their mannerisms and models his personality on them, tries to figure out why they behave the way they do. It’s an intense journey that’s also internal; the strength of the film, and of Griffin’s performance, lies in how tangible and visceral they make that progress. Popular on Variety Nilsson wrote “Masc” based on a story he crafted with Griffin, and it plays as an organic collaboration between filmmaker and actor. Whether or not they improvised the situations that they put Robin in together, those play so naturally that the film sometimes has the feel of an observational documentary, which is exactly as it should be with such a sensitive character study. But “Masc” is also clearly a work of fiction. Not only does Nilsson place the audience in Robin’s purview, he also creates scenes that tell us how he imagines things, how he wishes situations would transpire. In one immaculately crafted and tenderly portrayed scene, Robin stays overnight with a friend, Benji (Tega Alexander). The audience is privy to his vacillating feelings about his friend, how he hopes the night will go, and what he fears it might become. It is a vivid portrait of his innermost feelings and anxieties. Griffin is tremendous, carrying the film on his shoulders as he appears in almost every frame. He has amazing physical control, making even the solitary scenes captivating; his presence, both jittery and grounded, conveys the complexity of Robin’s constant observation and recording of other people. When he is alone, there’s clear relief in the easier, more rhythmic way he moves. In closeup, his eyes broadcast all that the character is feeling; always watchful, always taking note of everything and everyone. The performance makes a moving and empathetic endeavor of the character’s search for a blueprint of life and personality. Griffin’s vulnerability is most pronounced in a long scene where Robin spends time with his father (Lincoln Conway) — finally, he is not observing and just being, even if he’s not entirely comfortable. He still has fears of being unloved, but he’s at his most unguarded. Perhaps this familiar form of masculinity is the one he’s been searching for all along. What makes “Masc” compelling is the way Nilsson turns observation into a mode of self-construction. Robin studies the men around him as though they might offer a grammar for being, borrowing their gestures, routines and affect in an attempt to locate something stable within himself. Yet the film understands identity not as something waiting to be discovered, but as something continually negotiated through imitation, desire and rejection. “Masc” shows that for those who exist outside prescribed ideas of masculinity, becoming oneself can first require learning how to read everyone else. ‘Masc’ Review: A Sensitive Character Study Where Identity is Found in Imitation and Observation Reviewed online, Sept. 9, 2026. In Toronto Film Festival (Platform). Running time: 83 MIN. Production: (U.K.) A Duktiga production. Producer: Bertil Nilsson. Executive producer: Joanne Michael. Crew: Director, camera: Bertil Nilsson. Screenplay: Nilsson, from a story by Nilsson, Joshua Griffin. Editor: Anna Meller. With: Joshua Griffin, Tega Alexander, Reece King, Ed White, Lincoln Conway, Robbie Bellekom, Hi Ching. (English dialogue) Music By: Daniel Sonabend. articles.title: Yoon Dan-bi’s Toronto and San Sebastian Film ‘The World Before’ Gives Its Camera a Soul and Its Island a Voice
articles.full_text: Sep 13, 2026 4:21am PT Yoon Dan-bi’s Toronto and San Sebastian Film ‘The World Before’ Gives Its Camera a Soul and Its Island a Voice By Ophélie Surcouf Plus Icon Ophélie Surcouf Latest Stephanie Ahn’s Seven-Year Road to ‘Bedford Park’: ‘You Never Know What Can Make Your Film Better’ 2 days ago Hyun Bin and Woo Do-hwan Turn Against Each Other in Hulu and Disney+’s ‘Made in Korea’ Season 2 2 weeks ago Cortis and Airbnb Color Outside the Lines With Immersive Seoul Hideout 5 months ago See All 'The World Before' Courtesy of the Toronto Film Festival Seven years after “Moving On,” Korean filmmaker Yoon Dan-bi returns with “ The World Before ,” a coming-of-age film about desire and first love. Speaking with Variety ahead of the film’s Toronto Film Festival Platform world premiere, Yoon discusses how capturing the authenticity of change worked its way at every stage of the production. “I want to make films about things that can’t be described in one sentence,” says Yoon. “In my previous movie I wanted to capture nostalgia, here I wanted to capture the restlessness, that fever you experience when innocence turns into desire.” Related Stories ‘Back to Buenos Aires’ Review: Marco Bechis’ Return to the Screen Covers Similar Ground to Earlier Works but is Only Fitfully Effective Netflix’s YA Rowing Drama 'Crew Girl' Capsizes and Sinks: TV Review The coming-of-age story follows 17-year-old Jin and her unexpected reunion with childhood friend Du-jae, who returns for his grandmother’s funeral on a remote Korean island. For Yoon, narrating the chapter that marks the end of childhood and the beginning of adulthood required focusing on her character’s inner turmoil, but also very much on their physicality. Popular on Variety “As well as emotion, I’m very keen on observing people’s movement,” she explains. “When the feeling of desire is born, how does it affect movement? How do they let their guard down when they love, hug each other, unexpectedly hold hands? I wanted to portray that desire in a very realistic way, without being overtly sexual.” That attention changed drastically how she used the camera. While ‘Moving On’’s stationary and observational lens blurred the line so well between reality and fiction that many commented it felt it was a documentary, Yoon tried another technique in “The World Before.” “The camera moves around a lot as if it had its own soul,” says Yoon. “I wanted to move it unexpectedly to create a rhythm. For example, there’s a scene on the beach with Jin and Du-jae where you see the light coming in, then the sun goes behind the clouds and comes out again. It was all natural light when we were shooting,” she pauses to laugh. “My crew told me this effect can be done in post production, but I tend not to believe them and I prefer to wait.” Yoon is grateful to her crew, who she says had a hard time rescheduling shoots, staged across two islands during the hot, humid months of the Korean summer, when a typhoon came around. They also had to carry all the equipment without cars as Soan-do, one of the islands located in Wando County off the southern coast, had no bridge connecting to the mainland. “We wanted rain scenes,” she adds, “but it didn’t rain that summer.” Still, Yoon loves the aesthetics of this period which she describes as the season of growing up. Lulled by the chant of cicadas, the island’s bright stillness offers the perfect contrast to the movement Yoon chases – light inching on naked skin and leaves blowing in the wind. “Soando feels very much like how the countryside used to be in Korea,” Yoon notes. “The main labor there is fishing abalone and seaweed, they’re pretty much self sufficient. The villagers offered help and invited us for food, which helped the actors to adapt to island life quickly. But looking back, I realized I went with a sort of prejudice, I thought everyone would want to escape but it turns out they all wanted to stay there.” The correction found its way into the character: “Jin likes living on the island and doesn’t even consider leaving,” Yoon says. Other surprises made it into the film as well – a local grandmother was cast for the opening scene after the villagers pronounced her the best singer among them ; an improvised moment between the young leads watching ants by the roadside, became one of the movie’s authentic snippets of life. But those additions are only possible because the script is written to accommodate them. “I tend to revise my script a lot while shooting, and I write it with that process in mind,” Yoon says. “That’s why I prefer to film in chronological order so I can really connect to the following scene. Of course, it doesn’t always work as I intend to,” she laughs. Another ingredient of her movie’s authenticity is her casting process. She found the central pair, Sim Su-bin (“Teach You a Lesson,” “Filing for Love”) in the role of Jin, and first timer Kim Eo-jin as Du-jae through auditions. Both are relatively unfamiliar faces, even to Korean audiences, so Yoon built the surrounding ensemble to help them carry the film. “I was worried that if the older actors were too famous, they’d take the focus away from them, so I needed to balance this,” she says. Once shooting began, she made a point to let her young leads embody the material. “As in my previous film, an emerging actor was playing the protagonist, so if the actor prefers to do a scene in a different way than I envisioned, I try to adapt,” Yoon explains. “I encourage the actors to find the intimacy that feels right for them. I know how they talk and behave, I don’t want them to stick to the script but use their own words.” Only the second Korean film selected for the section after Yoon Ga-eun’s “The World of Love” last year, “The World Before” will be headed to the San Sebastian Film Festival ‘s New Directors competition later this month. articles.title: Tom Nicoll Looks Beyond Male Influencer Culture in TIFF Title ‘Salvation’: ‘I Don’t Think Anyone’s Ever Been Insulted Into Changing Their Mind’
articles.full_text: Sep 13, 2026 4:24am PT Tom Nicoll Looks Beyond Male Influencer Culture in TIFF Title ‘Salvation’: ‘I Don’t Think Anyone’s Ever Been Insulted Into Changing Their Mind’ By Callum McLennan Plus Icon Callum McLennan Latest ‘I Don’t Know’: Kenneth Branagh on Directing, ‘Harry Potter’ and How Christopher Nolan Had Him Speaking Russian Backwards 4 weeks ago Director Frieda Luk on Olivia Luccardi’s ‘Sacred Creatures’ Role and the Fine Line Between ‘Crazy’ and ‘Enlightened’ 4 weeks ago ‘How the F— Would You Get This Movie Made in America?’ Christine Vachon, Film4, BBC Film Put ‘Trainspotting,’ ‘Ratcatcher’ and ‘The Wicker Man’ Through the 2026 Greenlight Test 4 weeks ago See All Liam Harkins as Danny in Salvation Scottish writer-director Tom Nicoll is unveling at Toronto his buzzy debut “Salvation.” It tracks an aspiring online life coach whose attempt to reinvent himself and then sell that transformation to others pulls him in increasingly desperate directions. The psychological and blackly comic thriller world premieres in TIFF ’s Discovery section, having already been selected for the BFI and British Council’s Great 8 showcase at Cannes. MetFilm Sales recently boarded world sales on the film, which stars Liam Harkins, Stephen McMillan, Kathleen McDermott and Conor McCarron. Related Stories 'Snowfall' Spinoff 'The Drop' Is an Evocative, If Uneven, Portrait of South L.A. in the Gangsta Rap Era: TV Review ‘Back to Buenos Aires’ Review: Marco Bechis’ Return to the Screen Covers Similar Ground to Earlier Works but is Only Fitfully Effective Set largely in Greenock, a post-industrial Scottish town, “Salvation” follows Danny Carlton, played by Harkins, as he emerges from a self-improvement retreat convinced he has found the way forward. Having been transformed, at least in his own mind, by charismatic guru Marshall Allison (Kevin O’Loughlin), Danny sets off to build a life coaching business of his own. The problem is that virtually nobody wants what he is selling while the money he has spent and borrowed pursuing it grows. Popular on Variety For Nicoll, the film was never primarily about finding easy targets in the world of male influencers. “I suppose, in general, in my life, I’m interested in that idea of what people find purpose in, what people choose to do with their lives, what they find value in, what they choose to put their energy into,” he told Variety . With Danny, that became a question of “what is lacking” to compel someone’s move towards a culture offering answers, status and self-optimization. “I don’t think anyone’s ever been insulted into changing their mind,” Nicoll explained. “It’s easy to point and laugh at someone.” A sweeping satire of the influencer sphere might provide “easy jokes” for five or ten minutes, he argues, but understanding why somebody is susceptible is the harder and more interesting motivation to pursue. We see Danny’s excitement and defence of his new found answers among a doubtful circle of family and acquaintances. His confidence might be misplaced, but he isn’t cynical. When he tells Scott, a depressed young man played by Stephen McMillan who comes to see him, all he’s learnt and how he wants to help he’s genuine. “He really means that when he’s saying that Marshall saved him from a very dark place,” says Nicoll. “That is, I think, a crucial part of the character.” Over the course of the film, “the economic imperative kind of takes over,” altering the relationship between Danny and Scott as the former discovers the wordplay he absorbed as self-help can turn into a tool for manipulation. The result is a chain of unequal relationships: Marshall has power over Danny, while Danny gains power over Scott. For Nicoll, that dynamic goes beyond any single strain of digital culture. “Most people could probably relate to the idea of when you go online and someone’s telling you how to eat better or exercise better or be happier, be in a better relationship,” he said. At a moment of insecurity, the promise that somebody else knows how to sort it can prove hard to resist. Nicoll had previously directed Liam Harkins in short “Lighting Tests” and wrote Danny around a rare combination he saw in the actor: an outwardly conventional masculinity alongside vulnerability, sensitivity and comedic timing. “I had the idea for the story and thought he would be perfect for the role,” said Nicoll, who sent drafts back and forth to Harkins roughly a year before shooting. “I knew that on a production standpoint, he would just be the rock that could build the production around.” The relationship at the film’s centre needed warmth as well as exploitation. The director recalls nervously arranging a Zoom between his two leads prior to filming, preparing questions in case conversation petered out. “I think I probably said about three things in the hour,” he says. “They were just chatting, getting to know each other, and then just talking about the characters.” A later read-through of three key scenes confirmed the chemistry: “It was an amazing one of being like, ‘Oh, we’ve got something here.’” That closeness is gradually squeezed by the film’s visual language. Working with cinematographer Alex Grigoras, Nicoll chose a 4:3 frame. “We always knew it was going to be a film of faces,” he says. The format offered intimacy and, as Danny’s choices reduce, claustrophobia. Centering him clarifies his self-absorption. He is initially, “the centre of his own world.” The use of long lenses compress the spaces around him, particularly in the interiors, while stillness releases giving way to unsettled camerawork as the predicament deteriorates. Composer Salla Luhtala’s score pushes in almost the opposite direction. At the start, as Danny leaves the retreat filled with new conviction, the music enlarges his modest circumstances matching the way he sees himself. “It’s like the world is his oyster. That’s what he feels like,” Nicoll explained. “It should feel like he’s reborn. It should feel like new momentum. It should feel like the new life is calling him.” Rather than standing outside Danny and mocking the fantasy, Nicoll wanted audiences pulled into it. “Salvation” is as Indie as it gets assembled through self-financing and crowdfunding, with Screen Scotland boarding late and providing £45,000 ($60,750) through its Production Growth Fund. Shot around Greenock and Glasgow, the production initially completed 15 days before returning months later for a few more days. “That’s the nature of independent filmmaking, I suppose,” he says. But the enforced pause became “an amazing opportunity,” allowing a chance to clarify the story and add “scale and cinematic scope at the right moments.” Nicoll looked to an American independent tradition for ways of making those limitations feel like choices. Sean Baker’s “Red Rocket” and earlier work were reference points, as was Kelly Reichardt’s “Old Joy”: films capable of retaining a distinct voice without requiring vast resources. And what of that word “Salvation”? “It’s the kind of underpinning, I think, of a lot of these self-help ideas,” says Nicoll. “You can be saved from this thing, and you can move into a kind of hallowed place, or a place free of this previous pain or this previous deficiency. And I don’t know if I believe in that.” The film isn’t interested in providing a clean, moralistic conclusion. The director prefers films that resist “easy answers,” leaving open the question of whether Danny is capable of deep reflection or likely to place explanations for everything that has happened to him elsewhere. For a film that Nicoll describes as “an independent film in its bones,” there is buzz around it. MetFilm Sales’ acquisition adds a strong international sales push to a run that has included Great 8 and selection as one of Screen International’s Rising Stars Scotland 2026. “It’s been pretty wild,” Nicoll said. “It’s pretty much close to best-case scenario” for a film made this way. More importantly, he adds, “it is the film I wanted to make.” The recognition offers the possibility of scaling up, something the writer-director is keen to pursue as he looks to move beyond the indie and micro-budget level. He has several scripts in various stages, including larger-scale thriller and horror projects. “Ambition can be talked about just as it relates to budget, but I think it’s about your approach to characters and characterisation, and how deep you’re willing to go in terms of excavating what it is to be human,” he says. “That’s what ambition is about in filmmaking to me, and that’s what I would want to take going forward, no matter the level of budget.” Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit ‘Congo Boy’ (EXCLUSIVE) Cannes’ Critics’ Week Reveals Lineup of Armenian Filmmakers Taking Part in Next Step Studio Program (EXCLUSIVE) Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie ‘Red Rocks’ Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) Wim-Wenders Produced ‘I’ll Be Gone in June’ Bought for North America After Cannes Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Sundance Prizewinner Blerta Basholli on Kosovar War Drama ‘Dua’: ‘Teenagers Growing Up in Conflict Zones Are No Different From Any of Us’ France’s National Film Board to Reduce Funding for Productions That Fail Gender Equality Targets Loading comments... articles.title: ‘Girl Group’ Review: Rebel Wilson’s Bawdy Pop Comedy Is All Fizz and Little Substance
articles.full_text: Sep 13, 2026 4:52am PT ‘Girl Group’ Review: Rebel Wilson’s Bawdy Pop Comedy Is All Fizz and Little Substance Wilson stars as a coach to a crew of singing misfits whose harmony as an ensemble is the movie’s greatest asset. By Natalia Winkelman Plus Icon Natalia Winkelman Latest ‘By Any Means’ Review: Mark Wahlberg Teaches the Virtues of Violence in Elegance Bratton’s Bluntly Drawn Historical Thriller 1 week ago ‘The Accompanist’ Review: Susan Sarandon Shines as a Problematic Foster Parent in Zach Woods’ Unsteady Directorial Debut 3 months ago ‘The Breadwinner’ Review: Nate Bargatze Bumbles Through a Domestic Comedy That Thinks Incompetent Dads are Still Funny 4 months ago See All TIFF Toward the end of Rebel Wilson ’s “ Girl Group ,” a fizzy, gaudy clone of “Pitch Perfect” sculpted from the mentor formula of “Bad News Bears,” the movie spirals into an interminable sequence of pop music performances. The song-and-dance numbers are so awkwardly endless that they call to mind the denouement of a very different pop spectacle: Brady Corbet’s “Vox Lux,” in which Natalie Portman’s megastar becomes a tragic emblem of the emptiness of the celebrity industrial complex. Related Stories ‘The Stunt Driver’ Review: Jay Baruchel Takes a Leap into Tepid Biopic Territory 'Practical Magic 2' Review: Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman Don't Quite Cast a Spell in an Overlong, Predictable Sequel “Girl Group,” which follows a band of misfits competing to become signed music artists, could not be further removed from that type of cynicism if it were set on a different planet, and Wilson, starring as the group’s coach, seems hardly to know the meaning of the word. A comedy whiz who became famous for playing — as she wrote in her memoir — “the fat funny girl,” Wilson has little on her mind here beyond sparkly merriment, and “Girl Group” is an accordingly flamboyant extravaganza designed to have audiences humming and nodding along without thinking a single thought. Popular on Variety There are occasions that call for this sort of broadly comforting trifle, on airplanes or in late-night popcorn sessions. “Girl Group” seems even to nod to its position on the feel-good shelf when, after a trying day, a character suggests to her sister that they head home to snuggle and rent “Pitch Perfect.” This movie — despite performances from a veritable diva corps d’elite, including Nicole Scherzinger and Ashley Roberts of The Pussycat Dolls, the Spice Girls’ Mel C, and All Saints’ Shaznay Lewis — never reaches the emotional heights of that rewatch-ready franchise, nor does it really strive to. It’s instead at ease as a second-stringer, a congenial romp that exists only as it unspools before you, then dissipates like stage fog the moment it’s over. The story opens in 1997, as five friends at a London girls’ school prepare to perform in their auditorium. Backstage, a member of the crew frets to her teacher (a brief but keen Sally Hawkins) about the pressure, before the pals — who perform under the name Gurlfriends — head onstage and bring the house down. The overture gives way to a whirlwind montage of the group’s ascent, culminating with a member named Tassie (played in the present day by Wilson) ditching the gang to try and make it as a solo act. The effort fails, and Tassie sinks into an alcoholic stupor from which she emerges, years later, to find that she’s been replaced for the reunion tour by a warbling prima donna. This is where the real story starts, and where Wilson might have been better off centering the movie all along. Sentenced to community service at a youth center, Tassie meets a group of Gen Z-ers whom she’s assigned to mentor ahead of an upcoming competition. The washed-up star sees their talent as a chance to rehabilitate her own image, but the peppy, ambitious teens have aspirations of their own, and as Tassie sets about molding them into a glossy vision of millennial pop stardom, her narcissism increasingly becomes a liability to their success. There are feeble gestures at a generational divide over female sexuality and pop-star image, as when one of the younger crew exclaims that Gurlfriends were “totally playing into the male gaze.” But such moments are so few and far between that it feels as if Wilson forgot about the theme halfway through, or, more likely, found it too thorny to properly unpack. Fair enough: prickly questions about how famous women can or should display themselves are unlikely to be settled by a broad comedy more interested in cramming in mile-a-minute jokes. Much of the film’s humor consists of bawdy clowning, with a handful of contemporary reference-laden jokes thrown in for good measure. And despite Wilson’s frank discussions of weight and weight loss in her memoir, there’s a curious abundance of size-related gags. At one point, a child accuses Tassie of looking like she “ate” Sabrina Carpenter. Elsewhere, Jennifer Coolidge, gamely playing Gurlfriends’ manager, encourages Tassie to promote Splurt, a nutrition bar with a laxative effect. Its potential to induce sudden bowel urgency in front of a crowd does not go unnoticed. Amid the slew of tired gags, the harmony among the younger cast is the film’s greatest asset, and their easy rapport and naturalism help cut against the run-of-the-mill story. The standouts are Chabely Ponce, as an acoustic guitar-slinging crooner, and Lilah Pate, who excels as the group’s leader, despite having to suffer through one ill-conceived scene involving an aggressive, nonconsensual kiss. Their enthusiasm as an ensemble suggests a warmer movie, one in which the nonconformists take center stage as they blossom into more confident versions of themselves. But lost in the surrounding muddle and often eclipsed by Wilson’s relentless mugging, their stories wind up playing second fiddle. Their vivacity may be enough to break through Tassie’s vanity, but it can’t wholly elevate the movie around them. ‘Girl Group’ Review: Rebel Wilson’s Bawdy Pop Comedy Is All Fizz and Little Substance Reviewed at Toronto Film Festival (Gala Presentations), Sept. 11, 2026. articles.title: ‘The Stunt Driver’ Review: Jay Baruchel Takes a Leap into Tepid Biopic Territory
articles.full_text: Sep 13, 2026 5:12am PT ‘The Stunt Driver’ Review: Jay Baruchel Takes a Leap into Tepid Biopic Territory Baruchel takes the lead for a period comedy about a hapless stunt driver that isn’t as funny as the documentary it’s based on. By Vadim Rizov Plus Icon Vadim Rizov Latest ‘Le Faux Soir’ Review: Fake News Tells the Truth in an Earnest, Slow-Paced Period Piece 2 days ago ‘The Sun Never Sets’ Review: Dakota Fanning and Jake Johnson Split, Maybe, in Joe Swanberg’s Unsatisfying Romcom 2 weeks ago Many Tarantino projects never happened 17 years ago See All Jay Baruchel in "The Stunt Driver," courtesy Film Cardinal In “ The Stunt Driver ,” Jay Baruchel reteams with his “Goon” director Michael Dowse and takes on a showy lead part as stunt driver Ken Carter, who’s best remembered for a jump he didn’t make: a proposed mile-long leap over the St. Lawrence River in a rocket-powered car. The five years spent on that ill-fated project were captured in the 1981 documentary “The Devil At Your Heels,” which “The Stunt Driver” credits as source material but doesn’t improve on. While the technical aspects of the period recreation are impressive, this remake never finds its own reason to exist. Related Stories 'Bunker' Review: Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz Are Brilliant in Florian Zeller's Riveting, Slightly Overstated Thriller of Isolation and Invasion 'Snowfall' Spinoff 'The Drop' Is an Evocative, If Uneven, Portrait of South L.A. in the Gangsta Rap Era: TV Review As in the doc, Carter is introduced executing a stunt jump which leaves him injured and begging the crowd not to leave, addressing them from the stretcher before being carried off. That naked lust for the adulation generated by danger is more bluntly stated when Carter repeats variations on “I gotta jump, people like me” as sufficient justification for his extremely dangerous stunt, the requirements of which include constructing a 90-foot ramp to launch the car. The documentary’s archival footage is seamlessly intercut with staged recreations as Carter assembles a small team of enablers: engineer Dick Keller (Ed Helms), sports agent Bill Wilkins (Dan Bakkedahl), goofy Quebecois protege and hype-man Danny Lafortune (Marc Beaupré). In standard biopic fashion, Ken’s wife Gloria (Laurence Lebouef) is relegated to worrying and suffering in the background. Popular on Variety Granted interviews with surviving friends and access to unused footage from the documentary, Dowse takes particular advantage of a forgotten radio interview in which Carter was hypnotized. While the additional insight from this rediscovered artifact provides the foundation for a degree of vulnerability and self-revelation that the documentary couldn’t tap into, Carter’s fears remains one-note even when grounded in reality. Carter’s naked craving to be liked and the class-based chip on his shoulder take on sinister connotations at moments when Baruchel sounds strangely like Richard Nixon, further muddying the emotional waters. When not mired in pathos, Baruchel plays Carter as an eccentric showboater, especially in his elaborate dialogue, which is far beyond the quotable but comparatively low-key man shown in the documentary; the final scene’s slow dissolve fade from Baruchel to the real subject only heighten the oddities of the actor’s performance. Speaking to the trade-war tensions of the present moment, “The Stunt Driver” also makes Carter a zealous Canadian patriot who derides rival stuntman Evel Knievel (Ben Foster) as an unwelcome “yankee doodle dandy” and later yells, “I eat Americans like you for breakfast!” Besides the additional psychologizing and final 20 minutes, which address Carter’s years after the jump, the film makes one major alteration to the source text. Presumably because the name of the American stunt driver who took Carter’s place on the jump, Kenny Powers (as in the protagonist of “Eastbound & Down”), would be a distraction for many viewers, both name and personality have been changed to Quebecois comic relief Lafontaine. While both the casting and location choices honor Kane and Baruchel’s shared Quebec background, the change of Powers’ nationality omits another logical place to heighten the anti-American angle. (In a very specific feat, the film’s most notable performance is arguably given by Joe Coben as “Devil” director Bob Fortier; the actor’s speech patterns are eerily like the real ‘70s thing to a degree unheard since Jon Voight channeled Howard Cosell in “Ali.”) The first 80 minutes toggle between restaging scenes from the documentary while matching its academy ratio, and alternately providing additional context in widescreen, with a third aspect ratio thrown into the mix at the climax. The idea is clear: the documentary shows some but not all of the truth, so the new film is supplemented by a glossier but more emotionally truthful format and complemented at the end by a new format to heighten Carter’s anxiety. DP Sara Mishara does a bravura job of using numerous formats (digital and actual 16mm, as well as 35mm stock, among others) and rendering them period-plausible as well as handsomely lit and colored in their own right. “The Stunt Driver” is, nonetheless, slow going, and less enjoyable than the funnier, springier documentary it takes great pains to expand on. ‘The Stunt Driver’ Review: Jay Baruchel Takes a Leap into Tepid Biopic Territory Reviewed at Toronto Film Festival (Special Presentations), Sept. 11, 2026. articles.title: Variety and Chanel’s Women in Film Bash: Ayo Edebiri, Lily-Rose Depp, Michelle Yeoh, Courteney Cox and More Light Up TIFF
articles.full_text: POUPAY JUTHARAT / CHANEL Variety and Chanel ‘s annual Women in Film dinner was the place to see and be chic at the Toronto Film Festival on Friday night. The hottest invite of the festival gathered prominent women and nonbinary filmmakers, where the legendary fashion house co-hosted an evening to remember with Variety co-presidents Ramin Setoodeh (also co-editor-in-chief) and Dea Lawrence. When Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh entered the bar for the evening cocktail hour, Emmy winners Sarah Paulson and Colman Domingo greeted her with hugs. Soon, Patricia Arquette breezed in, pulling in her fellow Oscar winner for a quick photo. Related Stories 'Burgundy' Review: An Attractive, Light-Bodied Wine Doc With a Good Nose but No Legs 'Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing' Review: A Handsome Ode to an Oft-Disrespected Sport That power quartet — plus Chanel ambassadors and actresses Ayo Edebiri and Lily-Rose Depp, Noomi Rapace, Luke Evans, David Harbour, India Amarteifio, Rosalind Eleazar, Cole Sprouse, Amber Midthunder, Jessica Henwick, Charlie Heaton, “I Play Rocky” breakout Anthony Ippolito , Cooper Raiff, Mariana di Girolamo, Emanuela Postacchini, Mackenzie Davis and more — epitomized the top-tier talent who assembled to celebrate the achievements of women and nonbinary filmmakers in this year’s lineup. Popular on Variety While the term “filmmaker” generally refers to directors, the event saluted many powerful multihyphenates, like actor-director Fala Chen (“Bloodline”) or Courteney Cox, who launched her directorial debut “Evil Genius” out of the fest. “At Variety , we’ve made a commitment to cover parity in the entertainment industry and the importance of female representation on the big screen. And while there have been significant strides, there’s still much room for improvement,” said Setoodeh, kicking off the event. While Hollywood is having a banner year at the movies, Setoodeh noted, none of the top 15 films at the box office were solely directed by women. “That’s why this dinner is so important. It’s an opportunity for you all to network, to come together, to brainstorm,” he said, asking the female filmmakers and producers in the crowd to raise their hands high. “If you’re an executive, here’s who you need to talk to.” Lawrence drove that point home, quoting the late Gloria Steinem: “Representation is not just who gets to appear in the story. It’s about who gets to tell the story. And so tonight we celebrate the women who are doing exactly that: creating, directing, writing, producing, and leading the way, opening those doors for the next generation of women.” Sarah Paulson, Michelle Yeoh and Colman Domingo POUPAY JUTHARAT Ayo Edebiri POUPAY JUTHARAT Chung Suet Ying and Fala Chen POUPAY JUTHARAT Luke Evans POUPAY JUTHARAT Seth Rogen and Lauren Miller Rogen POUPAY JUTHARAT This year’s TIFF lineup proves progress is possible, as 35% of the official selection is directed or co-directed by women, like “Love of Your Life” from Rachel Morrison or “Josephine” by Beth de Araújo. That impressive figure — a goal that TIFF leadership set for 2028, but reached two years early — is made possible when organizations like Chanel and publications like Variety hold Hollywood’s decision-makers to account, said TIFF’s Chief Business and Marketing Officer Jennifer Frees. “Chanel and Variety share TIFF’s passion for supporting the remarkable creators who continue to shape the future of culture and of cinema,” Frees said. “So with that in mind, this evening is a celebration of world-class creativity and the community that it fosters.” One such initiative is the Chanel Women Creators’ Network, an extension of the TIFF Share Her Journey’s annual Writers’ Lab. “At Chanel, it’s nothing new for us to support women — because our founder was a woman,” said Gregoire Collignon, president of Chanel Canada, referring to Coco Chanel. “Since the ’30s, she was designing and supporting women in film.” This program, established in 2020, continues that legacy, he added, and “reinforces the house’s commitment to championing women in the arts and to creating opportunities for their artistic and personal development.” Carol Nguyen is a 2025 fellow whose documentary “Still Night, Burning House” is also debuting at this year’s fest. The 2026 fellows are Shannon Walsh, Hannah Vastinsalo, Shannon Welby and Amelia Eloisa. “These four exceptional creators represent the vision, the originality and the artistic excellence that define the next generation of filmmaking,” Frees said. “Through their work, they’re expanding perspectives, they’re challenging conventions, and they’re reminding us why diverse stories matter so much.” After the speeches, the mingling continued: “Being Heumann” director Sîan Heder and star Ruth Madeley fielded congratulations for how well their film played as the festival’s opening night selection. Next to them, Lauren Miller Rogen (“Babies”) and Seth Rogen chatted with Ziwe Fumudoh. When the party moved upstairs for an intimate, seated dinner, Rogen’s signature laugh rang out above the din of conversation and the clanking of forks and knives. This fashionable crowd was ready to let their hair down and have some fun amid the business of the fest. articles.title: ‘Much Ado About Nothing’ Gets Modern War-Zone Update From Lakeem Rose (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 13, 2026 6:15am PT ‘Much Ado About Nothing’ Gets Modern War-Zone Update From Lakeem Rose (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Cannes Prize-Winning Nepal Oscar Entry ‘Elephants in the Fog’ Sells Wide for Best Friend Forever (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Trans Pregnancy Drama ‘Aman’ Boards Parallax Films for Global Sales Ahead of Toronto and London Premieres (EXCLUSIVE) 5 hours ago Inside ‘Ah Girl,’ the Singapore Drama Built From a Director’s Own Childhood: ‘We Can’t Fly Without First Learning How to Walk’ 20 hours ago See All Fast Motion Films British writer-director Lakeem Rose, is developing his feature debut, a contemporary adaptation of William Shakespeare’s “ Much Ado About Nothing ,” with Canadian producers Plato Fountidakis and Paul Rapovski and Hong Kong-based producer and casting director Mike Leeder. In Rose’s version, the story shifts to a world just after a modern-day war, centering on four returning soldiers who reunite at the house of a family friend. Old grudges resurface alongside fresh romantic entanglements and a scheme that threatens to unravel everyone involved. Related Stories 'Alpha Gang’ Review: Cate Blanchett, Chris Pine and an All-Star Cast Play Space Aliens in David and Nathan Zellner’s Endearingly Goofy Sci-Fi Spoof ‘A Common Story’ Review: A Stunningly Played Study of a Couple Whose Inability to Articulate Their Emotions Drives Them Apart The dialogue stays true to Shakespeare’s Early Modern English, paired with subtitles in contemporary English, even as the setting and visual world around the text are reconstructed for today’s viewers. Rose is also folding sequences styled after silent cinema into the modern-day military backdrop. Popular on Variety “As always, we have to edit these texts to flow as a screenplay. I’ve been studying how filmmakers and performers like Kenneth Branagh and David Harewood bring this language to life,” said Rose. “The language has survived for 400 years for a reason. Our experiment is to change the context around it and see what happens when these characters, relationships and ideas are placed in a world that feels immediate to people now.” Fountidakis is producing, with both he and Rapovski steering the project in their roles as managing partners at Fast Motion Films; Clever Creature handles the film’s international sales and distribution. Between them, the two Canadian producers have spent decades working in genre film and television, having contributed to “Enhanced,” “Believer,” “Mutant X,” “Bullet Proof Monk,” “The Chronicles of Riddick,” “Scott Pilgrim vs. the World” and “Lost Girl.” That background in action design and production is expected to inform the look of the film’s military setting, from its locations to its physical action sequences. “Independent cinema depends on backing new voices with bold tastes,” said Fountidakis. “This modern adaptation has the opportunity to introduce Shakespeare to audiences who might never otherwise engage with his work. Lakeem has a distinctive perspective on the material, and the combination of Shakespearean language, contemporary genre filmmaking and a post-conflict setting gives the project a very fresh identity.” Red Packet Media’s Leeder rounds out the producing team. He has been based in Hong Kong since 1990 and has built his career around Asian and international genre titles, having worked on “Rogue One: A Star Wars Story,” Jet Li’s “Fearless,” “Man of Tai Chi,” the “Ip Man” franchise and “The Raid” films. “What interests me is the collision of traditions,” said Leeder. “The language remains Shakespeare’s, but the world around it belongs to contemporary genre cinema. Setting ‘Much Ado’ in the aftermath of such immediate conflict gives the romance, humor and deception a new tone, while the silent visual passages allow parts of the story to be told entirely through image. Plato’s genre experience and Lakeem’s background in theatre and music make this a genuinely unusual way into the material.” Rose’s path into filmmaking began with an English degree at the University of Oxford, where he appeared in a staging of Shakespeare’s “Love’s Labour’s Lost” under the guidance of Shakespeare scholar Jonathan Bate. His work outside narrative film spans music, visual media and documentary projects. A separate documentary series, “Reinventing Shakespeare,” is tracking the film’s progress, following Rose and his collaborators as they work through what Shakespeare’s writing can offer a new generation of viewers. Rose and Fountidakis plan to take meetings around the project at the Toronto Film Festival market. The adaptation is in development now, with a 2027 release targeted. articles.title: Melissa Rivers on Her Glorious Return to the Emmys Carpet, Remembering Her Mom Joan and Why ‘It’s Been Really Hard’ to Watch ‘Hacks’
articles.full_text: Sep 13, 2026 6:25am PT Melissa Rivers on Her Glorious Return to the Emmys Carpet, Remembering Her Mom Joan and Why ‘It’s Been Really Hard’ to Watch ‘Hacks’ By Daniel D'Addario Plus Icon Daniel D'Addario Chief Correspondent DPD_ Latest Courteney Cox on Her TIFF True-Crime Drama ‘Evil Genius’: ‘The Story Is So Unbelievable’ 21 hours ago Antonio Banderas, Trudie Styler and Eva Birthistle on the Sorrow and Joy of TIFF Medical Dramedy ‘Up Against It’ 22 hours ago Lee Pace on Romancing Sandra Bullock in ‘Practical Magic 2,’ Life as a Leading Man and His 6-Foot-Five Star Power: ‘I’m a Monster!’ 3 days ago See All Chris Pizzello/Invision/AP/Shutt Melissa Rivers is returning to the red carpet. Fashion expert and author Rivers — who rose to fame reporting outside awards-shows with her late mother, the comedian Joan Rivers — will be joining Variety co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh and CNN correspondent Elizabeth Wagmeister at the two brands’ Emmys pre-show broadcast. On “CNN & Variety Red Carpet Live: TV’s Biggest Night,” streaming live beginning at 5 p.m. ET on Monday, Sept. 14 at CNN.com/Watch and on the CNN app for CNN’s streaming subscribers, Rivers will provide interviews and commentary. Related Stories 'Being Heumann' Review: Siân Heder's First Film Since 'CODA' Is a Bold and Stirring Dramatization of the Protest That Launched the Disabled-Rights Revolution 'A Good Little Soldier' Review: Alba Rohrwacher Goes Corporate Drone in Stéphane Brizé’s Lukewarm Workplace Drama Her presence promises to be both a nostalgic look back and a turning of the page, as Rivers insists she wants to strike a tone that’s been absent for a while: As a duo, the Riverses broadcast for E! and for the TV Guide Channel before, in 2007, their association with the red-carpet ended. In 2011, the elder Rivers declared “We’ve done that. It’s not fun anymore.” Melissa agrees, and is hoping to bring a spirit of joie de vivre to the proceedings. The pair continued to host E!’s “Fashion Police,” which Melissa continued after her mother’s 2014 death until the show’s final episode in 2017. Popular on Variety A few days before her hosting gig, Rivers spoke to Variety about the spirit of “fun” she feels has been missing from the carpet, what she thinks of Jean Smart’s performance as a groundbreaking female comedian and what Joan Rivers would say about celebrity style in the age of Ozempic. You’re back on the red carpet after a long absence. What does it mean to get to come back? Well, first of all, it’s my first time back in 20 years. It’s crazy. I’m going to give you the timeline: I was originally supposed to join in via Zoom, and do some color — some fun. Then I got a call either Saturday or Sunday [Labor Day] weekend, and they said, “Would you be interested in being on the carpet?” Without really thinking about it, I said “Sure.” And then 10 minutes later, I was like, “Oh my God!” Suddenly, it dawned on me, I haven’t stood on a red carpet for coverage in 20 years. It became very overwhelming, because I realized I had so much to do. What does your preparation look like? Luckily, I’ve seen most of the shows. CNN gave me a huge briefing book, and I’m going through the storylines, the actors, the different categories, finding interesting facts. The other day, they’re like, “And here are the presenters!” and I’m like — Oh, God, they have to put more in my brain. How I used to do it came back: By storyline, category, and then individuals. Matthew Rhys has won for [“The Americans”], and this is his first time for “Widow’s Bay.” If I end up talking to him, I’m like, “Is there one that you’re more emotionally attached to?” You’ve won, and here you are with your hat in the ring. And with you and Keri Russell — who gets more mirror time? Right — they’re prepping together. Do you do your fittings at the same time? For my wedding, trying to get my husband, my son, and his two sons coordinated for a fitting, it might as well have been D-Day. But I’ve been really outspoken about this: The fun has been gone. The lightness has been gone. It’s not going to be the same as me and my mom; it’s never going to be that again. But there’s a whole new lane for just being fun and lightening up. I’m going to be the shallow end of the pool. Don’t come to me if you’re going to want to make statements. I want to know who you’re wearing, and fun stuff. I want to know, was there ever a performance you really thought you were going to get nominated for, and you didn’t? It felt as if in some point since you and your late mom left the red carpet, the tone of coverage did get more serious. I’m curious what you made of that as an observer. Yeah, it got very, very serious. The one with #MeToo and all the women wore black [the 2018 Golden Globes, at which all female attendees wore black garments in an organized protest], that was great, because there was a theme. Everybody was wearing black, and you got to see actual personalities come through, because of the decisions that the women made. That would have been the greatest “Fashion Police” ever. But that’s really where it turned very serious and statement-oriented. The world has become so much more serious in the last 20 years. The social reckonings, the political landscape: The world is going to hell in a handbag. But let’s call it what it is. It’s a bunch of beautiful, talented, successful people, walking into a building to see if they won something. The consequence is, Does someone like your dress? And you’ll be the judge of that! Of course I will. One of the things people used to love was — as my mom used to say, when you sat on your couch at home, you didn’t say everybody looked wonderful. We were just giving voice to that. We tried to be the viewer. That’s why I’m saying: If you want to make a political statement, go to another position. Don’t stop. Because that is not my vibe. Let’s bring fun back. Are there any attendees whose style you tend to really like? Keri Russell always looks amazing. I’m going through, in my head, who the women are. Jean Smart always looks appropriate and yet glamorous. Who else do we have? Hannah Einbinder. Zendaya. Oh, forget it. Zendaya — okay, we’re all running for number two. It’s almost like, “Why bother?” Speaking of Jean Smart, though, I’m curious if her performance on “Hacks” ever called your mom to mind. Many people think Deborah Vance is based in part on Joan Rivers. Yes, of course. And my mother would be so happy that if there was anyone playing someone lightly based on her, that it was Jean Smart. She would be so happy. Not only is Jean so talented, but she is tall and elegant and blonde. My mother always joked that Cate Blanchett would play her in a movie. She got Jean Smart, which would thrill her to death. In the fifth season, an Emmy nominee this year, Deborah and her daughter D.J. have a real breakthrough in their relationship. Did you recognize this as true to life, or see yourself in Kaitlin Olson’s performance as D.J.? I actually haven’t watched it yet. I’ll sum it up: We leave the relationship in a really positive place overall. It’s really hard for me to watch these things. I can’t speak intelligently about it because I haven’t watched enough of the show for a multitude of reasons. When someone snuck me the pilot, I was not thrilled by how I was portrayed. But I do appreciate that there was an evolution of the relationship. Do I think where my character started was accurate? No. Do I love the fact that they portrayed evolution — which is a true theme between mothers and daughters? I love that. Speaking of mothers and daughters, have you ever re-watched the perennially viral clip of your mom and you walking out of “The Celebrity Apprentice” together after you were fired? Oh, God, no! I’m not sure if that was one of my greatest moments or one of my worst moments. Hell, no! I wonder what your mom would have made of the current landscape, where stars are more open about the work they’ve had done and Ozempic has redefined the red carpet. I think she would say, “Thank God — everybody’s caught up! And admitting it!” Back in the day, we would be looking behind people’s ears for fresh scars. Now, everyone’s like, “Look what I’ve done!” It’s clear you missed the red carpet, even as the prep is a bit stressful. What was it like walking away from awards-show reporting? We chose to walk away because… It’s like anything — you show up and you kind of don’t care. That was when my mom and I had the conversation. We both came to it separately that it was time to walk away. I was never planning on this. If you had asked me two weeks ago, “Would I ever go back?,” I would say no. And I still can’t believe I just said “Sure” without really thinking about it. I hate making this more serious than it is — I have a goal, which is to make it fun again. I’m going on my own personal campaign to bring fun back. articles.title: Venice Golden Lion winner May El-Toukhy
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie May El-Toukhy’s ‘Woman Unknown’ Wins Golden Lion For Best Film At Venice Film Festival – Full Winners List Iranian ‘A Bit Of Light’ Filmmakers Discuss Timely Venice Contender: “We Have To Talk About The Reality… Of The Mass Killing That Happened” Jeremy Thomas Dies: Legendary UK Producer Of ‘The Last Emperor’ & ‘Crash’ Was 77 View All September 12, 2026 9:56am May el-Toukhy receives Venice Film Festival's Golden Lion on Saturday Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images) Danish-Egyptian director May El-Toukhy ’s Woman Unknown has won the Golden Lion for Best Film at the 83rd Venice Film Festival. The post-World War II psychological thriller was one of just two films directed by women in the running for the Golden Lion this year. Set in Denmark in the summer of 1945, the picture stars Mathilde Arcel as nanny and housemaid Marie who is on the cusp of marrying her wealthy, older, widowed employer. Related Stories News May El-Toukhy, One Of Only Two Female Directors In Venice’s Competition: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings” Festivals May El-Toukhy On Venice Golden Lion Win & Riccardo Scamarcio Remembers Jeremy Thomas — Winners Press Conference There is dark side to the jubilation of the liberation as women who fraternized with German soldiers are tracked down and publicly shamed. Marie’s past threatens to catch up with her. “The film tells the story of invisible women,” said El-Toukhy Saturday on receiving the prize. “Women who go unseen and unheard. My thanks go to my amazing cast for the passion you poured into portraying these characters.” Watch on Deadline

articles.title: interview with James Talarico
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Anthropic CEO Calls For Slowing Down AI Development, Warns Of “Swarm” Taking Over Internet In 6-12 Months CBS Wants Ex-‘Matlock’ Writer’s Racial & Sexual Harassment Suit Dismissed; Says Claims Are “Fabrications & Outright Lies” Jimmy Kimmel’s James Talarico Interview Posted To YouTube As Host Calls Out Trump And FCC: “They Want To Make Our Editorial Decisions For Us” View All September 10, 2026 9:09pm Story Arc James Talarico and Jimmy Kimmel Screenshot Jimmy Kimmel ‘s interview with James Talarico was posted to YouTube on Thursday evening rather than the late-night host’s ABC broadcast amid concerns over an FCC enforcement action. “Why are they so scared of you?” Kimmel asked Talarico at the outset of the 20-minute interview, noting that Stephen Colbert also posted a sit-down with the Texas U.S. Senate candidate in February over concerns it would invoke the rule. Related Stories Late Night TV James Talarico Calls FCC Pressure On Jimmy Kimmel Interview “The Most Dangerous Form Of Cancel Culture” Late Night TV Jimmy Kimmel “Play-Acting” Over James Talarico Interview & FCC Threats, White House Claims “They are worried that we’re going to win this race in Texas,” Talarico said. “But we are the underdogs until the last vote is counted.” For decades, daytime and late-night TV talk shows have operated on the assumption that they were exempt from the FCC’s equal time rule, which requires broadcasters who feature candidates to provide comparable time to their rivals, if it is requested. Watch on Deadline But in January, the FCC under chairman Brendan Carr , appointed by Donald Trump , issued guidance to broadcasters that TV talk shows may not be exempt, a move that critics saw as a regulatory effort to crack down on daytime and late-night hosts the president does not like. Weeks later, the FCC started an investigation of The View after it featured Talarico as a guest. The equal time rule includes an exemption for news coverage and news interviews. ABC has pushed back against the FCC’s actions , releasing a 2002 letter from the FCC affirming that The View was exempt. The network also has argued that the FCC is selectively enforcing the rule, as its January guidance did not address talk radio, where conservative hosts routinely feature political candidates, including Talarico’s Republican opponent, Ken Paxton. Kimmel opened his interview by noting that, until recently, the FCC has long recognized that late-night talk shows have been exempt, pointing to Donald Trump’s guest spots. “When he was running, he was on the show two times, but now I guess he doesn’t like me anymore, or the First Amendment, and so the FCC has threatened me or threaten my show, our network, even our local ABC stations, because they want to make our editorial decisions for us, which of course we cannot accept,” Kimmel said. “And so tonight we’re bypassing the public airwaves and hosting this YouTube interview on YouTube, even though our government would clearly prefer that we not do it at all.” The FCC does not regulate streaming platforms. In a statement earlier on Thursday, a White House spokesman claimed that Kimmel was creating “a false narrative about this administration’s policies. “Chairman Carr has not threatened him regarding interviewing James Talarico, or any other candidate,” a spokesperson said. Carr has not commented, but previously said that the TV talk shows are free to feature political candidates, but they may be on the hook to offer time to their competitors. He also suggested that the Colbert interview was a publicity stunt designed to drive up fundraising for Talarico. In his monologue on the Jimmy Kimmel Live TV broadcast, Kimmel challenged the White House’s statement. He told the audience that he would be interviewing Talarico but viewers would not see it. He called the threat of FCC action “yet another attack on free speech, something that is all too familiar for the show for us.” Kimmel also said that he would “love” to interview Paxton, but the rule would not just apply to Talarico’s GOP rival. “Our affiliates in Texas would have to give equal time to as many candidates as there are on the ballot. There’s about 10 candidates on the ballot,” Kimmel said. ABC’s legal team has argued that offering all candidates such time is untenable. The interview was otherwise a pretty standard sit-down for Talarico, giving him the opportunity to repeat some of his campaign themes, including how his life has been shaped by religion and Jesus Christ. It was also clear that Kimmel was a fan of Talarico, and he even ran a portion of one of his campaign ads. He said, “I’ve been following you for a long time. I’ve been watching your videos. I think what you’re doing is great. I really do. … You hit on something that used to be on all of the bumper stickers. ‘What would Jesus do?’ I think Jesus has been co-opted by this MAGA enterprise in this way. It makes no sense when you really think about it. Would Jesus be throwing people into vans and separating them from their children? Would Jesus be taking kids off food stamps? … This is not the Jesus that I learned about growing up. And you bring it right back to the Bible, to the real teachings of Jesus, and it is very authentic.” If the past is any guide, the Kimmel interview may ultimately draw more attention than Talarico would have gotten via a standard broadcast. His interview with Colbert has drawn 9.5 million views on YouTube, far more than the show’s average. ‘I Play Rocky’, ‘Misty Green’ & ‘The Surgeon’ Reviewed; Deadline Studio Vids FCC Charr Accuses James Talarico Of Running “Hoax” With Kimmel Sit-Down ‘Practical Magic 2’ Conjuring $30M U.S.; NFL Week 1 To Impact Holdovers May El-Toukhy’s ‘Woman Unknown’ Wins Golden Lion; Full Coverage More from this Story Arc ABC vs. FCC August 21, 2026 What’s Next For ABC Vs. articles.title: May El-Toukhy On Venice Golden Lion Win & Riccardo Scamarcio Remembers Jeremy Thomas — Winners Press Conference
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas ‘Twilight’ Star Kellan Lutz Leading Faith-Based Survival Thriller ‘The Rescue’; Sales Launch At TIFF ‘Starship Troopers’ Duo Denise Richards & Casper Van Dien Reunite For Thriller ‘No Free Lunch’ — TIFF Market Saban Acquires & Dates Sharks Vs Whales Thriller ‘Alphas’ With Martin Henderson, Teagan Croft & Charlotte Vega View All September 12, 2026 2:59pm L-R: May el-Toukhy and Mathilde Arcel with the Golden Lion for the Best Film Award and the Coppa Volpi for Best Actress for 'Woman Unknown' on Saturday Getty Venice Golden Lion winner May El-Toukhy is not surprised that some pundits considered her win a shock Saturday evening. Speaking at the winners’ press conference this evening, the Danish director of Woman Unknown responded to a question about her win being called a “surprise” by some in the media: “It doesn’t surprise me that some people would say, ‘Oh, did she get it?’ Because that’s part of everyday life as a woman in this industry.” Related Stories Festivals Venice 2026 Winners: May El-Toukhy’s ‘Woman Unknown’ Wins Golden Lion For Best Film – Full List News May El-Toukhy, One Of Only Two Female Directors In Venice’s Competition: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings” El-Toukhy added that she is used to being counted out, and that before the lineup was confirmed, she was very low on Venice prediction lists. “I was far down on predictions,” she said. “There were like 40 films predicted, and I was 39 or 40 every time. By now I’m pretty used to that. That’s a systemic issue. When I look to those lists, we would be four women, and I would feel that I had to compete with those four women and not my male peers, and that’s a systemic issue, and that’s something that all of us need to think about, including journalists, the media, my male peers. How can we make it easier for women to be part of this industry? I don’t have the feeling that my male colleagues aren’t interested in having women in the industry, but still, there are structures in place that we haven’t found a way to solve.” Watch on Deadline Venice jury head Maggie Gyllenhaal was asked by one journalist whether the jury’s decision to award one of only two Competition films by a woman with their top prize was a “political decision.” Gyllenhaal batted away the suggestion and instead described the winning film, about sexual shame and political paranoia in postwar Denmark, as “a brilliantly made movie that felt like a laser beam.” Danish actress Mathilde Arcel scored the festival’s Best Actress prize for her turn in the well-reviewed drama-thriller as a woman with secrets to hide who desperately tries to avoid mob justice. It’s rare at the Venice festival for the same film to win the top prize and an acting award, but Gyllenhaal explained that it’s possible when the jury votes unanimously for the Golden Lion winner’s lead actor or actress to get the acting prize, which happened in this case. Elsewhere this evening, the filmmakers behind Special Jury Prize winner NAZA , the hard-hitting film about the IDF’s killing of Gazans, said they hope the film will reach an audience in Israel, before also touching on the IDF’s (Israeli Defence Force) comments criticizing the film.

articles.title: L.A. County Projects Huge Job Losses If Paramount Exits California; Company Slams Antitrust Action By AGs & WGA In Official Rebuke
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic They’re Talking! Paramount & AGs Settlement Talks Set For Next Month; Bonta Downplays Significance As “Standard Course” Macro CEO Charles D. King & WME’s Courtney Braun Added To Deadline’s L.A. Law Summit CBS Wants Ex-‘Matlock’ Writer’s Racial & Sexual Harassment Suit Dismissed; Says Claims Are “Fabrications & Outright Lies” View All September 12, 2026 3:56pm Paramount Skydance's David Ellison at Donald Trump's 2026 State of the Union address Getty Images There will be harsh job losses and severe economic pain if Paramount carries out its threat to leave California over the antitrust action a coalition of blue state attorneys general are pursuing to stop David Ellison ‘s $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery, an internal L.A. County report estimates. “At a minimum, relocating Paramount’s headquarters and other operations out of California would result in losses of 2,750 and 5,550 job-years in California across all industries and losses of between $1.01 billion and $2.03 billion in economic output between October 1, 2026, and September 30, 2031,” L.A. County’s Economic Development Corporation says in a leaked September 10 document. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News The ParaBros Backlash: Threats To Leave L.A. & An AG Who Won’t Back Down Divide Hollywood Legal They’re Talking! Paramount & AGs Settlement Talks Set For Next Month; Bonta Downplays Significance As “Standard Course” Simultaneously, as Paramount brass are scheduled to sit down for Potemkin court-ordered settlement talks with AGs next month, a filing in federal court late Friday made clear Ellison’s crew thinks their debt-heavy acquisition of WBD shouldn’t even be up for discussion — antitrust , employment-wise or otherwise. However, it is the report from L.A. County that likely carries much more weight as Gavin Newsom, IATSE, Karen Bass and more line up to advocate for a settlement in this increasingly personal fight between California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Ellison. No two ways about it, sounding in parts like it was penned down on Melrose, the report hurts. It might save special pain for Supervisor Lindsey Horvath and her four fellow board members who unanimously voted in July to support the AGs’ antitrust lawsuit. With leaks out of the Melrose lot that Ellison is contemplating a move to the redder horizons of Tennessee, Georgia or Texas if the AGs don’t holster their legal pistols and start negotiating by October 1, this week’s EDC document from the county offers zero anesthesia for a region that has already suffered the loss of nearly 50,000 jobs and scores of productions over the past six years. “Once Paramount completed the entire relocation of its headquarters and other operations out of California, the state would experience the permanent loss of approximately 28,990 to 57,980 full-time jobs statewide across all industries, and losses of between $10.6 billion and $21.2 billion annually in economic output,” the document says in language that sounds much like Paramount’s own ominous protests of just a few days ago. Any serious contemplation of Paramount storming out of the Golden State has been downplayed by Paramount. Yet, that October 1 date that’s been floated is no accident: That’s the day Team Ellison have to start forking out $7 million every 24 hours to WBD shareholders if the deal crashes. Cited as “extraordinary losses” by Paramount in an attempt to secure a $1.88 billion bond out of the blue states and WGA plaintiffs, that potentially poisonous ticking fee in the WBD contract adds up to more that $635 million a quarter for Ellison. Real money, no matter who your Dad is. In that context, and in an even more terse tone that a previous LA. County missives, the latest four-page jobs report adds: “Note that since this employment would be lost to California permanently, these figures are more appropriately expressed as full-time jobs instead of job-years.” Then, as a spring 2027 trial looms, there is also the real estate and ancillary blast radius of Paramount and WBD leaving town. A shuttering of soundstages, closing of vendors and more that would result in “permanently” decimating the physical and economic foundations built up over 100 years of Hollywood. It’s bleak, to say the least. Even more so when one considers the EDC’s own math figure on the upside of one big ParaBros. “Paramount’s post-merger production commitment of 30 features a year for three years would generate a total of between 1,020 and 2,760 job-years in California across all industries and between $377.7 million and $1.01 billion in economic output between October 1, 2026, and September 30, 2031,” the finding (first reported by Politico) asserts, with a spotlight on Ellison’s big-screen promise. Rob Bonta and Letitia James Getty Images At the same time, in the mix of the AGs long-anticipated July 13-filed antitrust action, Paramount’s September 11-filed Defendants’ Answer to Complaint and Defenses basically insists that Bonta, New York AG Letitia James and pals just get outta ParaBros’ corporate way and stick to their side of the street. Slicing the AGs as being out of their jurisdiction, the presumption pitched here is the antitrust suit “amounts to a series of attempted shortcuts and assumptions that collapse under scrutiny.” Supercharging the usual litany of agreements and disagreements that characterize such perfunctory responses, lawyers for Oracle scion Ellison use the filing to pre-argue (bordering on pre-relitigating) their POV on ParaBros ahead of a March 2, 2027 trial and a September 24 bond hearing, a pricey ticking fee kick-off and a possible SCOTUS intervention. “Paramount’s proposed merger with Warner Bros. (the ‘Merger’) will enhance competition, not diminish it,” they state in the 25-page document, citing the AGs as using “cherry-picked data from the past.” In language we’ve heard over and over since the AGs took to the legal barricades, Paramount’s Beth Wilkenson-led legal SEAL team continued: “The Merger will benefit movie theaters by bringing more films to the big screen. It will benefit cable companies by providing more high-quality content on TV in the face of declining cable subscriptions. It will benefit content creators by increasing investment in, and production of, films and TV shows. And for all these reasons, it will also benefit consumers, not only with more high-quality content in theaters and on cable, but also with a better combined streaming offering to create real competition against dominant tech giants like Netflix, Disney, and Amazon.” That sounds a lot like Paramount’s declaration of July 13 that the AGs’ big move “distorts settled antitrust law and is based on a misrepresentation of competition in the entertainment industry today,” doesn’t it? There’s that, and then there’s the real blade being unsheathed in the September 11 filing: “Plaintiffs’ entire theory of leverage falls apart — models that ignore the real world have no basis in a court of law.” A sentiment stuck in further with: “Day by day, the weak case against this Merger gets even weaker.” Bonta’s usually media quick and to the point office was silent when Deadline reached out for a response to Paramount’s official response. As for that L.A. County report… no one was saying nuthin. ‘I Play Rocky’, ‘Misty Green’ & ‘The Surgeon’ Reviewed; Deadline Studio Vids FCC Charr Accuses James Talarico Of Running “Hoax” With Kimmel Sit-Down ‘Practical Magic 2’ Conjuring $30M U.S.; NFL Week 1 To Impact Holdovers May El-Toukhy’s ‘Woman Unknown’ Wins Golden Lion; Full Coverage Read More About: 19 Comments
