articles.title: ‘Babies’ Review: Lauren Miller Rogen Film Is A Witty, Heartfelt Exploration Of Childless Adulthood & Chosen Family – Toronto Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘The Face Of Horror’ Review: Anna Biller’s Medieval Ghost Story Is A Technicolor Fever Dream Of Love, Betrayal & Vengeance — Toronto Film Festival Courteney Cox Is Ready To Direct A ‘Scream’ Movie: “I Think I Should” Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews View All September 12, 2026 5:17pm 'Babies' with Lauren Miller Rogen, Anna Kendrick, Seth Rogen and Kate Berlant Roadside Attractions/Vertical After years of fielding questions about whether she wants to be a mom, Lauren Miller Rogen gives the definitive answer in the form of her witty, heartfelt comedy Babies . Written and directed by Miller Rogen, Babies stars Anna Kendrick and the auteur’s husband Seth Rogen as the happily married Aaron and Annie, a couple without kids of their own who are constantly asked about why they don’t have any. When their friend Eliza (Kate Berlant) leaves her husband Luke (Dan Stevens), she and her young daughter move in with the couple, giving them a chance to test drive being parents. Rogen’s Aaron hilariously compares the opportunity to receiving a Baskin Robbins sample. Rogen and Kendrick share the kind of onscreen chemistry that makes you think they could be pretty great parents — or if you are a parent, it might make you jealous of their child-free dynamic. Either way, they swap quips back and forth in the same effortless way they express love and care for one another. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Reviews Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Acquisitions Roadside Attractions & Vertical Make First TIFF Acquisition This Year With Seth Rogen & Anna Kendrick Pic ‘Babies’ Berlant and Issa Rae play their longtime friends Becky and Eliza, both at different stages of parenthood with very different parenting styles. As Eliza, Berlant gives a hilariously high-strung performance of a recently single mom trying to figure out her divorced life. Rae plays the seemingly perfect working mom, who has her hands full with a snarky teen daughter, a baby on the way and a gallery she’s starting with Annie. Stevens and Zach Cherry complement their onscreen spouses with their own unique takes on fatherhood — Stevens as the unreliable co-parent who adores his daughter while neglecting his wife, and Cherry as the constantly reliable dad who is cooler than his daughters can admit. The talented ensemble of seasoned actors is adequately matched by their child co-stars, each brimming with personality. It’s safe to assume the film came from a personal place for Miller Rogen, who along with her husband has taken numerous questions from the media over the years about their decision not to have kids. “What f*cking business is it of yours?” Rogen asks in one voice-over, a question he’s likely been holding in during many an interview over the years. The film also deals with the pain and uncertainty of a sick parent, mirroring the filmmaker’s own experience with her late mom’s Alzheimer’s, which inspired the couple’s Hilarity for Charity nonprofit. A sincere comedy about the ups and downs of life, Babies offers a balanced critique of parenthood that gives good parents their due while also celebrating the beauty of chosen family, as well as the joys of being able to go to the movies alone in the middle of the day, smoke a joint in your own home, and have sex whenever you want with the bedroom door unlocked. articles.title: ‘NAZA’ Review: Israeli Military Accused Of Depraved Indifference To Palestinian Life, Using AI To Kill In Gaza – Venice Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew ‘NAZA’ Review: Israeli Military Accused Of Depraved Indifference To Palestinian Life, Using AI To Kill In Gaza – Venice Film Festival ‘Black Sunflowers’ First Look: Ukraine’s Youth Live Life On The Edge In Propulsive Doc From EP Sean Penn – Toronto Film Festival Doc Talk Podcast: ‘Remake’ Director Ross McElwee On Love, Loss And Grieving For His Son View All September 12, 2026 5:56pm Filmmaker Yuval Abraham (right) interviews a source in 'NAZA' The Guardian/JW Films The devastating documentary NAZA , an investigation into Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was shot at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, in part to avoid potential Israeli eavesdropping, presumably, and to facilitate shielding the identities of participants. Those participants are 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers who reveal, in almost matter-of-fact tones, chilling details of a program that has caused catastrophic destruction of residential areas in Gaza, and massive loss of life among Palestinian civilians, including women and children. The sources – “whistleblowers” seems an appropriate term – come forward on condition of anonymity; they are filmed in silhouette, and their voices, as noted at the beginning of the film, have been digitally altered to conceal their identities. Related Stories News Gaza Doc ‘NAZA’ Gets 25-Minute Venice Ovation, Setting New A-List Festival Record As Palestinian Flags Fly In Sala Grande Festivals ‘No Other Land’ Co-Directors Yuval Abraham & Rachel Szor Lift Lid On New Bombshell Doc ‘NAZA’ Exposing Israel’s Deliberate Targeting Of Civilian Homes In Gaza – Venice One of the participants says that if he doesn’t hide his identity, “Israel will put me in jail for what I expose.” Watch on Deadline NAZA , a late addition to the competition lineup in Venice , on Saturday night won the festival’s Special Jury Prize . The film is directed by Israeli Jews Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor , two of the four directors of the Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land . Abraham appears on camera, interviewing his subjects on the rooftop; they explain that “NAZA” is a Hebrew acronym used by the Israel Defense Forces to signify collateral damage (נזק אגבי, or Nezek Agavi, per an interview included in press notes), in other words, an acceptable loss of civilian life incurred while trying to kill suspected Hamas militants. The film suggests the number of “NAZA” considered acceptable in each attack was elastic. In some cases, it would be under a dozen, but in others it could be 200 or even 500 people deemed permissible collateral damage, according to Israeli military personnel interviewed in the film.

articles.title: ‘The Surgeon’ Review: Michelle Yeoh Goes All John Wick Taking Her Scalpel To The Bad Guys – Toronto Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Misty Green’ Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is The Whole Show In Chris Rock’s Sizzling Hollywood Portrait Of A Down-And-Out Emmy Winner Whose Career Is On The Skids – Toronto Film Festival ‘The Surgeon’ Review: Michelle Yeoh Goes All John Wick Taking Her Scalpel To The Bad Guys – Toronto Film Festival ‘Closing Night’ Review: Killer Cast Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts And Dianne Wiest As Mothers On The Edge – Toronto Film Festival View All September 12, 2026 7:05pm Michelle Yeoh in 'The Surgeon' Toronto International Film Festival After supporting roles in blockbusters like Wicked , Michelle Yeoh has her first all-out starring role since winning the Best Actress Oscar for Everything Everywhere All at Once three years ago. Considering her expertise in martial arts and kick-ass action ( Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon for starters), her latest effort in the genre is a lot of fun but not for squeamish stomachs since The Surgeon makes The Pitt look like PAW Patrol. This medical thrill ride holds nothing back in exploring the human anatomy as weaponry that even John Wick would envy. Maybe we should call this one John Sick ? Who needs a gun when you bring on instant death just by pulling out the colon and squeezing for 30 seconds. This movie from writer-director Dr. Roshan Sethi (A Nice Indian Boy) is a manual for turning bad guys inside out – literally. There can be no doubt what attracted Yeoh, a supreme action star as well as serious actor, to the role of Eliza, a world-renowned surgeon who has followed her Monastic code of medicine for 40 years and now is retiring. Early on a phone call from her insurance company says it all: “Should we continue insuring your hands?” and the answer is no, no longer necessary. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Reviews Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Festivals The Obsession For The Next ‘Obsession’ At TIFF: Festival Hot List Includes Pics For Sale With Cynthia Erivo, Chase Infiniti, The Maras, Dave Bautista & More But those plans to take it all easy are rudely interrupted when she is abducted at gunpoint by criminals and ordered to operate on their gravely ill leader, Sean ( Martin Freeman ). Apparently she is the only hope this crime boss has, and his henchmen, notably Cole (Yuri Kolokolnikov), an imposing Russian bad guy, is watching closely to make sure she does what she is ordered to do as she cuts him open, starts removing organs, and proceeds to make the weakest among us want to reach for the barf bag. Prosthetics supervisor Suzi Battersby leaves little to the imagination. Congratulations, Suzi. Eliza senses once she has done the job she will be killed, but they have come to play with the wrong doc. She does make one demand: that they crank up the Thin Lizzy songs, her preferred music to cut by. It doesn’t take long before she uses her exceptional ability to turn every key body part into a death sentence, particularly in a clock-ticking demonstration of how lethal her hands can be when she sets about slicing and dicing with her scalpel. Yeoh’s martial arts skills really come into play in battling these guys by manipulating their mobility in delightfully paralyzing ways. We get a little more info on Sean in a flashback to her initial meeting with him where they talked about his dire diagnosis and knew she was likely his only ticket to live. So how could he accept she had hung up her scrubs? In the tight 92-minute running time, Sethi shows his own bona fides by making a truly original action flick that may be the most informative trip inside the body since Fantastic Voyage. Although Freeman creates a fairly dimensional character while the other baddies are strictly stereotypes, it is Yeoh that makes this enterprise worth watching. She not only still have the action chops, she is completely believable and authentic as a doctor who has seen it all and possesses extraordinary talent in the profession. Her last stand in the operating room is one to behold. Shout-out to fight choreographer Laurent Demanioff for the dazzling moves. There can be no doubt this film, which had its world premiere tonight at the Toronto Film Festival, is a tailor-made vehicle guaranteed to turn up the temperature for Yeoh fans everywhere all at once. Producers are Basil Iwanyk, Erica Lee, Diarmaid McGrath, Tim Headington, Lia Buman, Neil Shah, Steve Klinsky, Adam Kolbrenner, John Schoenfelder and Russell Ackerman. articles.title: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr Accuses James Talarico Of Running A “Hoax” With Jimmy Kimmel Sit-Down; YouTube Interview Nears 7 Million Views

For one, when it passed the statute, Congress applied it to broadcast tv stations—not cable programs like GameDay. For another, Congress stated that the statute only applies to… https://t.co/r3KP7RvQL8 pic.twitter.com/m5IbEl8Ngr — Brendan Carr (@BrendanCarrFCC) September 13, 2026 A Talarico campaign spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Kimmel interview had drawn 6.8 million views as of Saturday evening. In February, Stephen Colbert posted an interview with Talarico to YouTube, telling viewers that he was warned by network executives about featuring the candidate on the broadcast. That interview generated 9.6 million views on YouTube. Like the Kimmel interview, the YouTube views were well over the average audience for the actual late-night broadcast. In an interview this week, Talarico characterized the Kimmel incident as government censorship and a form of “cancel culture.” He also posted the interview to X, calling it “the interview Trump’s FCC doesn’t want you to see.” For decades, daytime and late-night TV talk shows have operated on the assumption that they were exempt from the FCC’s equal time rule, which requires broadcasters who feature candidates to provide comparable time to their rivals, if it is requested. News coverage and news interviews have been exempt from the requirements, and the rule also does not apply cable or streaming, where the FCC’s authority is limited. But in January, the FCC under Carr , appointed by Donald Trump , issued guidance to broadcasters that TV talk shows actually may not be exempt, a move that critics saw as a regulatory effort to crack down on daytime and late-night hosts the president does not like. Within weeks, the agency launched an investigation of ABC’s The View after it featured Talarico as a guest. Until now, Carr had yet to weigh in on Kimmel’s latest criticisms and the decision to move the interview to YouTube. The late night host called the FCC’s equal time enforcement threats an effort to “make our editorial decisions for us, which of course we cannot accept.” On Thursday, a White House spokesperson said that Kimmel was “play acting” to “create a false narrative,” and that Carr “has not threatened him regarding interviewing James Talarico , or any other candidate.” Carr has denied that the FCC’s stricter enforcement of the equal time rule was an attempt to censor guests. On X, Carr posted, “The Equal Time statute does not prohibit anyone from interviewing anyone on broadcast tv. It is about more speech, not less. Congress wanted to ensure that voters would decide elections, not media gatekeepers picking winners and losers by providing preferential airtime to some candidates and not others. Indeed, when the statute applies, it simply requires broadcast stations to offer comparable time and placement. And comparable does not necessarily mean an interview by the same person on the same program either.” Carr’s comments were in response to a post from University of Texas Democrats, who noted the appearance of Sen. Ted Cruz (D-TX) on ESPN’s College GameDay on Saturday. The group posted on X, “So I can’t watch Talarico on Kimmel but I have to watch Ted Cruz on GameDay?” The FCC chairman noted that the equal time rule would not apply to Cruz’s appearance because it was on a cable network and because the regulation covers only legal qualified candidates, or contenders who are in the midst of an election campaign. Cruz is not up for reelection this year; Talarico’s Republican rival is Ken Paxton. ABC is challenging the FCC’s enforcement of the rule when it comes to The View, pointing out that the agency affirmed its exemption from the regulation in a 2002 letter. The network also has sued the FCC on First Amendment grounds. It claims that the agency’s order that its eight owned stations submit to early license renewals is a form of regulatory retaliation, due to the Trump administration’s dislike of its news coverage and other content including The View and Kimmel. In his post, Carr again defended the FCC’s regulatory efforts as within the bounds of the agency’s authority. He wrote, “In exchange for that free and exclusive right to use spectrum, broadcasters made a deal with the American people. They agreed to operate, not in their own narrow interests, but in the public interest. There are various rules and policies that they must follow. This sets them apart from newspapers and cable shows and podcasts. But some broadcasters want to break their deal with the American people. They want to keep their free access to billions of dollars worth of spectrum, of course. They are less eager these days to abide by their public interest obligations.” ABC’s legal team has argued that the FCC is engaging in selective enforcement, as its January guidance did not target conservative talk radio, and wrote that the equal time rule is unworkable for shows like The View as it puts network stations on the hook for time to potentially dozens of candidates on the ballot. Kimmel said this week that he would love to interview Paxton, but “our affiliates in Texas would have to give equal time to as many candidates as there are on the ballot. There’s about 10 candidates on the ballot.” ‘I Play Rocky’, ‘Misty Green’ & ‘The Surgeon’ Reviewed; Deadline Studio Vids FCC Charr Accuses James Talarico Of Running “Hoax” With Kimmel Sit-Down ‘Practical Magic 2’ Conjuring $30M U.S.; NFL Week 1 To Impact Holdovers May El-Toukhy’s ‘Woman Unknown’ Wins Golden Lion; Full Coverage Read More About: 9 Comments

articles.title: ‘Misty Green’ Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is The Whole Show In Chris Rock’s Sizzling Hollywood Portrait Of A Down-And-Out Emmy Winner Whose Career Is On The Skids – Toronto Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Misty Green’ Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is The Whole Show In Chris Rock’s Sizzling Hollywood Portrait Of A Down-And-Out Emmy Winner Whose Career Is On The Skids – Toronto Film Festival ‘The Surgeon’ Review: Michelle Yeoh Goes All John Wick Taking Her Scalpel To The Bad Guys – Toronto Film Festival ‘Closing Night’ Review: Killer Cast Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts And Dianne Wiest As Mothers On The Edge – Toronto Film Festival View All September 12, 2026 8:30pm Rosalind Eleazar in 'Misty Green' A24/Youtube. I have to confess I am a sucker for down-on-your-luck Hollywood stories, especially movies about actresses who once had success and are now scraping the bottom. Of course there is the classic of classics, Sunset Boulevard, but there are many more. A personal favorite is The Star, which got Bette Davis an Academy Award nomination as a has-been who walks around Hollywood carrying her Oscar saying things like “Come on Oscar. Let’s go get drunk.” Jane Fonda got nominated as well playing a down-and-outer in Hollywood in The Morning After. For sleazy fun, there’s Connie Stevens in The Sex Symbol, Kim Novak in The Legend of Lylah Clare (“Tell them Lylah is coming!”), and a great Natalie Wood in a real favorite Inside Daisy Clover to name just a handful. The lure of Hollywood and the dark side of those who chase the dream has been fascinating subject matter for filmmakers throughout Hollywood history and now it is Chris Rock ‘s turn. Rock was doing a group voice-over session and noticed a couple of once successful actresses from hit sitcoms who were now doing this kind of day work to keep the lights on and it got him thinking about a scenario that eventually became his latest idea for a film, Misty Green . It has been 12 years since his last and most critically acclaimed turn behind the lens with 2014’s Top Five. Earlier this century he tried his hand directing 2003’s Head of State and 2007’s I Think I Love My Wife (I quite liked that one), though neither of those two were box office hits. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Reviews Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews News How Meditation, Hope And Hard Work Brought Rosalind Eleazar Her “Long Shot” Dream Lead In Chris Rock’s ‘Misty Green’ Now he is back, and if Misty Green will be remembered for anything it is the remarkable performance of British actress Rosalind Eleazar , a co-star currently on Slow Horses but soon who will be known as well for playing the title role in this story of an L.A.-based television actress, a once-upon-a-time Supporting Actress Emmy winner, now going through tough times, various addictions, family problems and standing in her own way of reviving her career because she won’t lower herself to audition. This is the kind of material that could lend itself to show business clichés (we have seen it a hundred times), but Rock has created a character, specifically a Black actress on the skids, the kind we don’t get to see portrayed on screen as opposed to the long list of similar stories listed above with white stars. This is all about Misty. We meet her best friend Naomi ( Anna Kendrick ), who tries to encourage her, even helping with a self-tape audition Misty resists; we meet her frustrated agent Randy ( Topher Grace ), who complains because on the last job she punched a co-star; we meet friend and would-be filmmaker Zach ( Adam Driver ), whose drug-induced invitations and sleazy job ops are not what Misty needs but can’t resist because she needs the cash; and we meet her brother Jay ( Daniel Kaluuya ), whose is in and out of jail, a mess, but someone she loves and wants to help. These are the people around her and they also include Jordan (Rock plays him), a working director with whom she has a past, and with whom she might have a future dream role if she can get her act together. Misty Green is also a pretty depressing portrait of L.A., the land of the haves and the have nots as Rock sees it, a fairly empty place dreamers head towards with no idea how to navigate a life worth living. Really this scenario isn’t particularly fresh, but I have to say when I heard the brief synopsis I was all in. It is a bit uneven though in execution, and Rock, in his role, plays it seriously until resorting to some dialogue and use of the N-word that resembles his old stand-up rather the guy he’s playing here. But is all lifted way up high by Eleazar, who makes this all worth the ticket. She’s mesmerizing in one of the best performances by an actress this year. You believe her; you may even know her. Among the rest of the cast the standout is Kaluuya, who is heartbreaking as a young man who simply has never been able to get out of his own way, despite the best intentions. Driver gets the sleaze of his role just right, though it is a one-dimensional character. In the large cast there are some familiar walk-ons such as Anthony Anderson as a cop, and even Ice T as himself. The Los Angeles locations are well chosen, giving a sense of what the city really is behind the fake glamour. Rock is a very smart performer, you can’t have doubts about that, and he has a keen eye for the underbelly of showbiz. So even in a movie that is not the sum of all its parts, many of those parts are pretty good and he has delivered a film that will be remembered as the one that gave us a glimpse of the movie star Rosalind Eleazar is about to become. Producers are Peter Rice, Rock, Victoria Thomas and David Worthen Brooks. Title: Misty Green Festival: Toronto (Gala Presentations) Distributor: A24 Director-screenwriter: Chris Rock Cast: Rosalind Eleazar, Anna Kendrick, Adam Driver, Chris Rock, Daniel Kaluuya, Topher Grace, Rich Sommer, Amy Landecker, Anthony Anderson Rating: R Running time: 1 hr 44 mins ‘I Play Rocky’, ‘Misty Green’ & ‘The Surgeon’ Reviewed; Deadline Studio Vids FCC Charr Accuses James Talarico Of Running “Hoax” With Kimmel Sit-Down ‘Practical Magic 2’ Conjuring $30M U.S.; NFL Week 1 To Impact Holdovers May El-Toukhy’s ‘Woman Unknown’ Wins Golden Lion; Full Coverage Read More About: 1 Comments

articles.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Peter Farrelly’s Sensational Biopic Of The Making Of Stallone’s Classic Is Just As Inspiring As The Original Movie – Toronto Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Misty Green’ Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is The Whole Show In Chris Rock’s Sizzling Hollywood Portrait Of A Down-And-Out Emmy Winner Whose Career Is On The Skids – Toronto Film Festival ‘The Surgeon’ Review: Michelle Yeoh Goes All John Wick Taking Her Scalpel To The Bad Guys – Toronto Film Festival ‘Closing Night’ Review: Killer Cast Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts And Dianne Wiest As Mothers On The Edge – Toronto Film Festival View All September 12, 2026 9:30pm Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone in 'I Play Rocky' Amazon MGM It is no spoiler to say I am going to reveal the final moments of Peter Farrelly ‘s fantastic crowd-pleasing biopic I Play Rocky , chronicling the making of the 1976 classic Rocky , which not only made Sylvester Stallone a major star but also became one of the greatest behind-the-scenes stories in Hollywood history. Stay all the way through the very last of the credits and you will be rewarded with the only scene in this saga not re-created for the movie. Introducing Stallone for the first time on The Tonight Show to promote Rocky, Johnny Carson tells a bit of the incredible backstory of Stallone turning down hundreds of thousands of dollars for his screenplay in order to insist he star in the movie he wrote for himself (even though he was completely unknown at the time). “If someone were to actually make a movie about the making of Rocky nobody would believe it,” Carson prophetically said. Related Stories Reviews Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Festivals The Obsession For The Next ‘Obsession’ At TIFF: Festival Hot List Includes Pics For Sale With Cynthia Erivo, Chase Infiniti, The Maras, Dave Bautista & More Well, someone has done that, and the film that has resulted is a winner in every way, a movie that in fact manages to carry the same emotional wallop as the original Rocky and containing a performance from Anthony Ippolito that is so uncanny I didn’t for a minute think he was anyone but the actual Stallone. It feels like they just used de-aging technology so Stallone could play himself a half-century younger. But make no mistake, Ippolito’s powerful, moving and inspiring portrayal is not mere imitation. This guy inhabits Stallone in every way, delivering an authentic portrait that will blow you away. Watch on Deadline Farrelly has said he would not have made the film without Stallone’s blessing, which he got, and he has, with Peter Gamble’s beautifully structured and crafted screenplay, made one of the best movies ever made about Hollywood moviemaking and the sheer mechanics of getting anything made. Certainly it is one of the most entertaining. In a year that marks the 50th anniversary of Rocky, a film that spawned five sequels and three more films in the Creed spinoff series with Michael B. Jordan, I Play Rocky brings us full circle right back to the beginning and manages to slyly recapture the fresh spirit that birthed it. This film has turned the making of Rocky into its own Rocky-like moment of triumph. Starting with Ippolito on screen as “Mike Stallone” auditioning for a nameless role, one of those aspiring actors working any menial job he can to support his dreams of making it in the industry, Gamble’s script shows us in linear fashion exactly how this impossible dream happened. From scraping the bottom of the barrel, even doing soft porn (a hilarious audition scene that really happened), finding a puppy he names Butkus, meeting his eventual wife Sasha (a perfect AnnaSophia Robb) at the movie theater where he works, and finally getting a break to meet big-time producers Irwin Winkler (PJ Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbell) who sadly inform him Jan Michael Vincent got the job so the role of his brother has to go to someone else, all the ups and downs of the life of an actor trying to just get by and keep going are here. On his way out the door of their office he tucks a script he wrote called Paradise Alley (eventually a movie Stallone got made) under a pile that says “weekend reading.” Their assistant knew the ruse but read the script and praised it, which caught the producers’ attention. They tell him he has real talent as a writer and to come up with some ideas. Sitting at a bar wondering how he was going to get by he sees a Muhammed Ali fight and bingo, the idea for Rocky comes pouring out of him, written in longhand in only three and a half days and handed to Sasha to type. Chartoff/Winkler (Byrne and Kebbell are really wonderful in these parts) sparks to it and manage to sell to a skeptical studio head, Sandy Maddux (a terrific and scene-stealing Tracy Letts in a composite of studio execs at the time). “Boxing pictures? Nobody makes boxing pictures,” he barks. The only hang-up is Stallone won’t sell it to them unless he stars in it. In a series of scenes where the price keeps going up with seemingly no ceiling, Sly holds his ground. “I won’t sell it for $1 million. Not $10 million,” he swears, and you can see the passion of a man who believes in himself, willing to “go the distance” just like Rocky to prove it. Finally, after knocking the budget down to just $1 million with clauses designed to get Stallone fired so they can get Ryan O’Neal or an actor on that level when it inevitably falls behind schedule, the saga of the actual filming begins and it has all been re-created with tender loving care, from the cinematography to production design, costume, music, editing and one riotous scene after another. It is not just about the making of this one film against all odds, but rather it is really about the making of just about every film, a love letter to movies that in its own way is on par with Truffaut’s Day For Night. A scene in Philadelphia at the meat-packing plant where they find the local union head has gotten wind they are shooting without permits turns into an amusing nail-biting moment where all the equipment and cast and crew has to be immediately hidden before he gets there. Another scene, the re-creation of the iconic run up the Philly steps, show us one of the first uses ever of the now indispensable Steadicam (using the original, I am told) as it reinvented that aspect of moviemaking. But the emotional knockout is delivered in the filming of a scene with Burgess Meredith (played by Robert Morgan) as Mickey, who tells Rockey he will agree to train him, after first rejecting him. The key scene just wasn’t working, and director John Avildsen (a great Jay Duplass) tells him they have to do it again, but how? It needs a stronger emotional hook or it fails. Stallone then proceeded to completely make up a five-minute take on the spot that is masterfully delivered. Ippolito brought me to tears watching him play it, quite tricky since this improv is now scripted but has to feel spontaneous. The entire cast with Ippolito is ideal, with special shoutouts to Keki Seto as Talia Shire and Stephan James as Carl Weathers, both taking on Stallone’s iconic Rocky co-stars in style. There are so many highlights in a movie that pulls off a tall task in bringing the same feeling we got the first time we saw Rocky. Farrelly, who won and deserved a couple of Oscars including Best Picture for Green Book, a film that tugs at the heartstrings without ever being anything less than simply human, has now made another film that makes us feel good about life and ourselves. Like Frank Capra used to do, he has made a movie that gives us hope. It couldn’t come at a better time. Producers are Toby Emmerich, Christian Baha, Farrelly, Paul Currie and Michele Weiss. Title: I Play Rocky Festival: Toronto (Special Presentations) Distributor: Amazon MGM Studios Release date: November 6, 2026 Director: Peter Farrelly Screenwriter: Peter Gamble Cast: Anthony Ippolito, AnnaSophia Robb, Toby Kebbell, P.J. Byrne, Jay Duplass, Matt Dillon, Stephan James, Tracy Letts, Kiki Seto Running time: 2 hr 8 mins ‘I Play Rocky’, ‘Misty Green’ & ‘The Surgeon’ Reviewed; Deadline Studio Vids FCC Charr Accuses James Talarico Of Running “Hoax” With Kimmel Sit-Down ‘Practical Magic 2’ Conjuring $30M U.S.; NFL Week 1 To Impact Holdovers May El-Toukhy’s ‘Woman Unknown’ Wins Golden Lion; Full Coverage Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘60 Minutes’ to Tackle Trump Pardons in Season Premiere
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 11, 2026 4:51pm '60 Minutes' correspondent Lesley Stahl with Donald Trump. Courtesy of CBS News/'60 Minutes' The 59th season premiere of 60 Minutes will dedicate a segment to Donald Trump’s controversial use of the presidential pardon. The segment is the third and final segment to be revealed from the premiere episode, following Jon Wertheim’s profile of the Los Angeles Rams and coach Sean McVay, and Norah O’Donnell’s exclusive interview with the U.S. pilot who was shot down and rescued in Iran. But it is Lesley Stahl’s segment, “The Pardon Economy,” that may end up raising the most eyebrows. “Presidents have pardoned criminals since the time of George Washington. It’s a constitutional power that has been controversial from the start — but perhaps never more so than during the Trump presidency,” the description states. “Lesley Stahl and 60 Minutes investigate the world of lawyers and lobbyists who have created a new pardon economy. Shachar Bar-On and Michael Kaplan are the producers.” 60 Minutes is in flux. New executive producer Nick Bilton is working with returning correspondents Stahl, Bill Whitaker, Wertheim and O’Donnell, as well as a handful of new hires, to try and get the season off the ground following an exodus of talent, both voluntary departures and forced ones. Former CBS News chief Wendy McMahon predicted that the season premiere will be a “banger” this week, betting that the show will put its best foot forward to try and set the tone, but that “shows three, four, and five could get quite interesting, I think.” Any segment targeting Trump, who sued CBS over a 60 Minutes interview with Vice President Kamala Harris, is sure to attract extra scrutiny. While the first show will be familiar, Bilton is expected to change things over time, with hidden camera investigations, and perhaps end-of show segments featuring commentary or debate, all cited as potential additions. For now, however, the show is leaning on the familiar: Stahl, O’Donnell and Wertheim are all veterans of the program. The new faces and other changes will wait until future episodes. THR

articles.title: Pink Issues Statement Following Backlash for Critiquing Macklemore’s Pro-Palestine Comments: “Standing Up for My Own People”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All September 11, 2026 6:08pm P!NK attends The 79th Annual Tony Awards at Radio City Music Hall on June 07, 2026 in New York City. Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for Tony Awards Productions Pink issued an extensive statement on Friday addressing the backlash she faced for resharing a post calling out Macklemore for his pro-Palestine comments and demanding he be removed from Ed Sheeran’s ongoing tour. In a lengthy post on Instagram Friday, the singer-songwriter said that the post she had shared “said things in words I didn’t write, and I wouldn’t have chosen all of them,” further stating that “I’d rather be disagreed with for what I actually said than hated for what anybody else wrote, so let me say it.” “I was born a Jew. I didn’t pick it, and I’ve never hidden it,” she wrote. “And this week a whole lot of people decided what I believe without asking me, without checking a single thing I’ve ever said or done, because a repost and the word ‘Jew’ were apparently enough to fill in the rest. But let me fill it in… myself.” Related Stories Music Snoop Dogg Tapped to Host the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards Music Noah Kahan Drops "Orbiter" Music Video on Spotify View this post on Instagram “Of course I don’t speak for Israel, or for any government,” she continued. “I never have. What I said in October 2023 is still exactly what I believe: Hamas is a terrorist organization. Palestinians deserve a future that honors their humanity and their aspirations. Protecting innocent life comes first, everywhere, and nobody should ever celebrate the death of a child. Anybody’s child. I’ve spent a decade as a UNICEF ambassador for kids who didn’t choose the country or the war they were born into, and I have grieved every one of them, on both sides of that fence. I didn’t do it from behind a screen; I went to those children and held them. I’m not going to litigate a complex war in an Instagram caption, and I’m not going to recite anybody’s slogan to earn back a follower.” P!nk responds to backlash after she shared a post labelling Macklemore as “anti-Israel” for spreading awareness about Palestine: “Last Sunday I reposted somebody else's post about Macklemore's set at Ed Sheeran's show. It said things in words I didn't write, and I wouldn't have… pic.twitter.com/tAixSCFTRG — Pop Base (@PopBase) September 11, 2026 She continued her post in her comment section, though it appears much of her statement was removed after she limited comments on the post. Her statement in full is still available in screenshots online, including in the X post above. Regarding Macklemore specifically, she recalled the rapper wearing a costume during a performance back in 2014 that was widely criticized at the time as antisemitic. He apologized, saying that “I respect all cultures and all people.” “Every Jew I know knew exactly what it was,” Pink wrote Friday. “But he apologized, and I let it go, because that’s what we do. We let it go. Then last weekend he stood in front of a stadium full of music -loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens, dedicated a song to the movement of his choice, and then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn’t about them. You don’t get to decide that for us.” “That’s what prompted my repost,” Pink continued. “Not ‘Free Palestine,’ and not anyone’s right to say it. I have never asked for another artist to be silenced and I’m not asking now. I don’t need anyone fired, and I don’t need a refund. What I need is to be able to say, as a Jewish mom, that scared me, and it scared people I love, without being told our fear is just propaganda, and without being told I’m somehow cool with genocide because I noticed?” Pink further said she was “standing up for my own people, and I thought I knew going in how lonely that would be. And it’s lonelier than that. But I’m doing it anyway.” She wrote that the phrase “zionist” has become a “slur by people who couldn’t tell you the details of what I believe.” She concluded her post in remembrance of today’s 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks and for the start of Rosh Hashanah, finishing with a “shana tova” for the Jewish new year. Macklemore courted controversy last week during his opening set on Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour for his Free Palestine messaging, with the Israeli-American Council subsequently sharing a petition calling to have him removed from the tour. During his set last Saturday, the rapper further continued with his Free Palestine message, further saying on stage that “to all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you.” The rapper doubled down further on Monday, writing on social media that “wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial.” Wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial. pic.twitter.com/BOJ9xMoIZn — Macklemore (@macklemore) September 7, 2026 THR

articles.title: Lady Gaga Welcomes First Child With Fiancé Michael Polansky
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 11, 2026 6:22pm Lady Gaga attends the world premiere of The Devil Wears Prada 2 at Lincoln Center in New York, New York on April 20, 2026. Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images for 20th Century Studios Lady Gaga is a mother! The Grammy and Oscar winner has welcomed her first child with her fiancé, Michael Polansky, sources confirmed to People and Page Six . The “Born This Way” singer got engaged to the entrepreneur in April 2024. She dished on the proposal during a an appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live! in October of the same year. “He proposed to me right after my birthday, so my birthday passed and I was like, ‘Oh, I thought he was going to propose,’” she told host Jimmy Kimmel. Related Stories Lifestyle Hotel Cipriani Books Chic New Guest: Dior Spa Music Lady Gaga Teams Up With Apple Music for Reimagined 'Mayhem' Filmed Live Performance She further explained that they went on a rock climbing trip, and Polansky had a sweet surprise for her. Gaga said, “We climbed to the top, we looked around, took some photos. And then went back down and we were just walking back to the room, talking. And he actually — it was very Michael — he asked me if he could ask me. He wanted to know if it was OK to propose before he proposed. And I was like, ‘Yes, it’s so OK!’” The Hollywood Reporter reached out to reps for Gaga, but did not immediately hear back. The couple has worked together professionally, with Polansky being credited as a writer on her 2025 Grammy-winning record Mayhem . He’s also listed as a writer on her song “Glamorous Life” from The Devil Wears Prada 2 soundtrack, which Gaga also made a cameo in. Gaga has been candid in her desire to become a mother one day. During a 2025 appearance on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert , the singer said she hoped her “next starring role” would be taking on the title of a mom. “I would like to do many things,” she said of what’s next for herself. “What I really want is to be a mom. That’s my next starring role, I hope.” Page Six was first to report the news. THR

articles.title: Josh Hartnett Reveals He Was “Actively Not Looking to Do a TV Show” Before Joining ‘Below’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Mariel Turner Plus Icon Mariel Turner View All September 11, 2026 6:25pm Logo text Josh Hartnett was happy to continue his career on the big screen before Below came his way. The Oppenheimer actor revealed on Friday that was “actively not looking” for television roles before reading the script of the Netflix thriller miniseries, created and written by Jesse McKeown. “Can I just say I was actively not looking to do a TV show?” Harnett shared at The Hollywood Reporter ’s Studio at 1 Hotel during Toronto International Film Festival , presented by sponsor Canada Goose. “Like, I was actively not looking for this. I’d just came off a movie and wanted to do another movie. I was going to go do another movie, and then I read this [script], and I was like, ‘Wow, this is amazing.’” Related Stories Movies Sorry, Caleb Hearon Is Not Your Clown in 'Trash Mountain' Grief Dramedy Movies Courteney Cox Says She Decided to Direct 'Evil Genius' After Chance Encounter at the Beverly Hills Hotel: "I Made a Lot of Deals There" Set in a remote Newfoundland fishing village, Below follows Hartnett’s Calvin as he fights to protect his family and community from a mysterious, terrifying sea creature. The series, which also stars Charlie Heaton, Mackenzie Davis and Natasha Henstridge, has been compared to Apple TV’s comedy horror hit Widow’s Bay , but Hartnett sees a distinct difference between the two shows. “ I saw Widow’s Bay and I really liked it, but there’s a totally different tone in this show,” he explained. “It’s much more sort of human-oriented and less sort of overtly comedic, but very funny in its own way.” Below was filmed on location in St. John’s, Newfoundland, Canada, where Hartnett learned the unique Canadian accent and lived like a local. The Verity actor told THR that he often frequented restaurants in town (“I love The Duke. It’s a great pub”) and did his best “not to hit [a] moose” while driving. Hartnett and Heaton worked with a dialect coach to perfect the Newfoundland accent. “ Charlie and I play father and son, and we are clearly from the same place. We had to find the specific sounds that we were gonna use for our family accent,” the actor said. “Newfoundland is not — there’s not a lot of people, but it’s a very large land mass, and there are lots of people that have been there for generations in one place. [They have] very specific dialects, and there’s many of them. We had to choose which one was gonna work best, I think, for the family, and then all work together … We were able to do that, which was really cool, and we had a great dialect coach.” Hartnett added that he listened to The Broadcast , a long-running radio show on CBC, “almost every day” to master the accent “because [there] was so many regional dialects.” While his character in Below may be fearless in the water, Harnett has a decidingly different view. “I was born in 1978, like [when] Jaws [was popular],” the actor dished. “[I’m] terrified of the water.” Below debuts on Netflix on Oct. 8. articles.title: Sydney Sweeney Faces Backlash for Sexualized Novig Ad: “Exactly Why Women in Sports Aren’t Taken Seriously”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 11, 2026 6:50pm Sydney Sweeney’s Novig ad Novig More than a year after her American Eagle ad controversy, Sydney Sweeney is facing backlash for another campaign: her sexualized promotion for sports trading app Novig. The Euphoria actress partnered up with Novig on Wednesday to support the new platform, which launched last month. She not only starred in the ad but also joined Novig as a strategic partner and equity holder. Novig’s “platform combines the mechanics of modern financial exchanges with a sports-first experience, creating a more efficient and transparent way for fans to trade on sports outcomes,” per a release. It’s also dubbed “the only prediction market to maintain a 21+ age requirement,” which the brand argues “[sets] a higher standard for responsible participation as the category continues to grow.” Related Stories THR + Sportico: Game Recognize Game Belmont Cameli and NHL Phenom Macklin Celebrini Talk 'Off Campus,' Olympic Heartbreak and Handling the Hype Lifestyle Sydney Sweeney Stars in Provocative Ad Campaign for Novig Sports Trading App Some users are arguing Sweeney’s ad for the age-restricted platform could have used an R-rated rating as well. “I couldn’t believe when that ad came on the tv. I had my 2 children in the living room I had to yell at them to look away from the TV. I don’t understand WHY they would need to create such a [vulgar] ad,” a TikTok user commented on a post made by Marissa Womack, manager of game day promotions and programming for minor league baseball team the Harrisburg Senators. Others took to Sweeney’s Instagram comments , including one user who called out Instagram’s inconsistencies with taking down potentially sexualized content. “Love how @instagram allows for stuff like this but the moment I post something in a bikini , the post is removed,” they wrote, while another added, “22.4 million views but not even 1 million likes… why? Because this is not what we want for our sports ads. ESPECIALLY when kids like and follow sports as well.” Other descriptors for the ad in the Anyone But You star’s comments include “disgusting,” “pathetic,” “sad” and “inappropriate.” The Hollywood Reporter reached out to reps for Novig and Sweeney for comment but did not hear back by the time of publication. Womack explained her frustration with the ad in her TikTok video, calling out the representation of women in the sports industry. “This [criticism] isn’t about me being jealous or insecure of [Sweeney]. … it’s about the fact that this is already a male-dominated field where we are constantly having to prove why we belong. it’s about having passions and joy working in this industry and when the only representation is sexualization, you see less and less young women wanting to pursue this industry!” The campaign, in Sweeney’s own words, “was about embracing a fun idea.” She added in a statement, “The concept is simple: cut through the noise and put the focus entirely on sports. The campaign brings that idea to life with confidence, humor and a playful edge.” The only “sports” that are featured in the ad, however, are different balls and uniforms placed provocatively on top of Sweeney’s mostly naked body. One TikTok user directly criticized the sexualization of the actress in the ad in the comments of a video shared by Sam Tirelli, a studio/field director for a Maryland-based sports network: “There is 0 reason to have somebody naked just saying sports over and over again. You can make amazing ads and content without constantly having women be sexualized.” Many users also slammed the ad for being “exactly why women in sports aren’t taken seriously,” one TikToker argued. They also called out the notion that “they probably knew it was going to be controversial too,” with The Housemaid star being known to spark controversy through brand advertisements. Most prominently, her viral 2025 American Eagle jeans ad caused widespread backlash , partly due to a piece of the advert where Sweeney said, “Genes are passed down from parents to offspring, often determining traits like hair color, personality and even eye color. My jeans are blue.” Some people argued that the campaign tagline “Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans” was a play on the term “great jeans” versus “great genes” and claimed the ad promoted eugenics. The ad garnered so much online backlash at the time that it prompted American Eagle to respond , releasing a statement that read in part, “Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans is and always was about the jeans. Her jeans. Her story.” Sweeney has addressed the controversy numerous times, saying that “the reaction definitely was a surprise.” She later commented on the cultural conversation that arose with the American Eagle ad, with a Cosmopolitan interviewer asking her about being labeled “MAGA Barbie,” as she’s repeatedly said she does not want to address her personal politics. “I’ve never been here to talk about politics. I’ve always been here to make art, so this is just not a conversation I want to be at the forefront of,” Sweeney said. When asked in the same interview if she sees herself confirming her political beliefs in the future, she said, “No.” Sweeney added, “I’m not a political person. I’m in the arts. I’m not here to speak on politics. That’s not an area I’ve ever even imagined getting into. It’s not why I became who I am. I became an actor because I like to tell stories, but I don’t believe in hate in any form.” Sweeney also made sure to note that politics were not to be bet on when trading on Novig. “No betting on wars or deaths, and no politics,” she said, before a clip of her from behind and masking her breast with only her hand was shown, as she adds, “Just you, your takes and sports.” A mini logline provided in a press release for the Novig ad reads, “Ahead of football season, Sydney Sweeney is putting the focus exactly where it belongs, on ‘Just Sports.'” However, that “focus” is now anywhere but sports and instead back onto another conversation-starting ad led by the two-time Emmy nominee. THR

articles.title: Courteney Cox Says She Decided to Direct ‘Evil Genius’ After Chance Encounter at the Beverly Hills Hotel: “I Made a Lot of Deals There”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Mariel Turner Plus Icon Mariel Turner View All September 11, 2026 7:25pm Evil Genius Courtesy of TIFF Fans may have the Beverly Hills Hotel to thank for Courteney Cox ’s newest project. The Friends alum revealed that she was approached about directing Evil Genius , her first feature film as a director in 12 years, after accidentally running into Barbara Schroeder, who directed the Netflix documentary of the same name, at the iconic hotel in Beverly Hills. “I was at the Beverly Hills Hotel sitting at the counter; my favorite spot in the corner. I saw [Schroeder], and I was like, ‘Oh my God, I love Evil Genius . You did such a great job,’” Cox said at The Hollywood Reporter ’s Studio at 1 Hotel during TIFF , presented by sponsor Canada Goose. “She said, ‘It’s available to direct.’ She goes, ‘You should run with it.’ We had a good relationship before. … I made a lot of deals there [at the Beverly Hills Hotel], and made a lot of money there. It’s just interesting.” Related Stories TV Josh Hartnett Reveals He Was "Actively Not Looking to Do a TV Show" Before Joining 'Below' Movies Sebastian Stan Says "Invitation to Be Negative" in Society "Starts at the Top": "It's Just So Lazy" Cox jokingly added that those deals were always “at the counter”: “I can’t get inside the poker room.” Cox’s chance encounter sparked the idea to direct, but it took years to get Evil Genius off the ground. The Scream star told THR that the film was in development for “eight years” through the COVID-19 lockdown and the 2023 WGA and SAG-AFTRA strikes before going into production in 2025. Despite facing significant obstacles, Cox “couldn’t let [the story] go because I loved it.” The film, which stars Patricia Arquette, David Harbour, Michael Chernus, Garret Dillahunt and Danielle Macdonald, follows the true crime story of the 2003 “pizza bomber” case that resulted in the death of Brian Wells. “We got these two amazing actors,” Cox said, referencing Arquette and Harbour, who also visited THR ’s studio on Friday. “I knew there was a story beneath the headlines that was really emotional and touching and terrifying and all of the things, and I’ve got the best actors to play the parts.” Cox was joined by her daughter, Coco, and Arquette’s daughter, Harlow, who both have small parts in the film. The Shining Vale actor told THR that Coco loves to perform. “Coco, she’s got a little scene in the movie, and Harlow, Patricia’s daughter, is young Marge,” Cox said. “Coco’s really sweet, too. … Coco loves acting so much that she was so happy to be there. It’s amazing.” “She’s been studying since she was so little, and doing shows and plays,” Arquette added of Coco. “She’s the only one… well, her and David, who did a lot of musical theater, and all of this. She just finished her first other movie. So, it’s very exciting. They’re fifth-generation actresses, our little daughters.” Evil Genius premieres at TIFF on Saturday, Sept. 12. THR

articles.title: Sorry, Caleb Hearon Is Not Your Clown in ‘Trash Mountain’ Grief Dramedy
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 11, 2026 7:32pm Trash Mountain Courtesy of TIFF Comedy helped Caleb Hearon process his own father’s unexpected death. So when the comic and actor co-wrote Trash Mountain with Ruby Caster, Hearon had to consider how much to lean into comedy as tears roll down his cheeks while starring alongside Zooey Deschenal in Kris Rey’s dramedy about love and grief. “No. If anything, I’m eager to prove that I’m not just a clown,” Hearon, the star of The Devil Wears Prada sequel and an HBO Max comedy special, told a Toronto Film Festival audience on Friday night after the world premiere of his comedic weepie. Related Stories Movies Courteney Cox Says She Decided to Direct 'Evil Genius' After Chance Encounter at the Beverly Hills Hotel: "I Made a Lot of Deals There" TV Josh Hartnett Reveals He Was "Actively Not Looking to Do a TV Show" Before Joining 'Below' Caster told the Scotiabank audience she was wary with Hearon as a skilled comedian in writing the wrong joke that crossed a line between drawing laughter and tears around grief. That led Hearon to break the tension by joking: “You stepped across a lot of lines. And I want to talk about that, here, tonight.” In Trash Mountain , Hearon plays Gavin, a young gay Chicago man forced back home to rural Missouri after his hoarder father died. Once there, Gavin, who appears to have walked away from everyone he has ever loved in life, has an emotional reunion with his half-sister Abbi, played by Deschanel. “This was a really complicated guy, and he didn’t have a perfect son either,” Hearon said of his real-life father whose inspired character doesn’t appear onscreen in Trash Mountain . But the late father is ever-present as Gavin and Abbi pick through the detritus of his life and which grows in the front yard of his home as a mountain of rubbish to be hauled away. And as the siblings pick through mess their hoarder father left behind, one man’s trash becomes keepsakes that Gavin and Abbi must consider holding onto or leaving behind as junk. Deschanel decided after an early wardrobe call to bring one of the scarves her late grandfather wore before his death on set as a prop. “I have them in my closet, and every time I see them I think of my grandfather. These objects can be conduits for people that have passed,” Deschanel, best known for roles in All The Real Girls and The Good Girl, told the TIFF audience. Trash Mountain also stars Jackie Weaver, Jaboukie Young-White, Kyle Martin and Holmes, and Lilly Wachowski is among the executive producers. The Toronto Film Festival continues through to Sept. 20. THR

articles.title: Almodóvar’s Deep Dive Into … Almodóvar
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By David Canfield Plus Icon David Canfield Senior Entertainment Writer View All September 12, 2026 2:25am Pedro Almodóvar Courtesy of Getty Images Bitter Christmas is Pedro Almodóvar ’s 24th feature film over the course of 46 years. There’s never been more than a three-year gap between his releases. He won Cannes’ best director prize in the 1990s ( All About My Mother ), an Oscar for best screenplay in the 2000s ( Talk to Her ) and the Venice Film Festival’s top prize, the Golden Lion, just two years ago ( The Room Next Door ). With his latest movie, Bitter Christmas , the 76-year-old Spaniard remains on that restless trajectory, pushing himself deeper into uncharted territory — this time, by turning the camera back on himself. Related Stories Movies Sorry, Caleb Hearon Is Not Your Clown in 'Trash Mountain' Grief Dramedy Movies Courteney Cox Says She Decided to Direct 'Evil Genius' After Chance Encounter at the Beverly Hills Hotel: "I Made a Lot of Deals There" In fact, he does this within several sections of his cinematic nesting doll of a drama. The main plot follows Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia), a highly regarded filmmaker in the present day — and resembling Almodóvar in more ways than the spiked silver hair — writing a screenplay inspired by a period of his life from two decades earlier. Bitter Christmas shifts between Raúl’s day-to-day, centered on his real-life bonds with assistant Mónica (Aitana Sánchez-Gijón) and boyfriend Santi (Quim Gutiérrez) seeping into his fiction, and the evolving action of Raúl’s movie (also called Bitter Christmas — yes, we’re getting very meta here). That latter arc follows a director named Elsa (Bárbara Lennie) who begins suffering panic attacks while feeling out her relationship with her new boyfriend, a kindly stripper and firefighter named Bonifacio (Patrick Criado). Raúl ruminates over how much to pull from reality in telling Elsa’s story. At one point, he is confronted by a loved one about inserting a vulnerable, private moment from their life for his own script’s ending. He considers the overlap between Santi and Bonifacio. It can feel like you’re watching some sort of Almodóvar documentary — but of course, the director himself is the third layer. Raúl, too, is told through his lens. This made for an emotional process for Almodóvar, a master of melodrama who’s gone richly personal with modern classics like Bad Education and Pain and Glory . “This is a film in which I really expose myself a lot,” he says. “I have always been attracted to the very mysterious relationship between reality and creation. I didn’t want to pull back in being critical of myself and my own creative process.” Fans of Almodóvar can read into Bitter Christmas as much as they’d like — the lines between fact and fiction are blurry and ambiguous, and in conversation, Almodóvar shares key autobiographical reference points without diving into the specifics. Yet the introspection remains fascinating, especially for a director who’s never been afraid of big feelings rooted in aching truth. The dynamic between the ailing, short-tempered Elsa and the sweet, hunky Bonifacio is drawn directly from Almodóvar’s own relationship with a boyfriend from the early 2000s. (The director’s long-term partner is actor and photographer Fernando Iglesias.) “Migraines had accompanied me through a good chunk of my life, but the panic attacks were new to me, and this person, who I was only at the beginning of a relationship with, really saved me that first terrible weekend when it happened,” Almodóvar says. As Elsa’s story unfurls under the line-by-line command of Raúl’s typewriter, though, Bonifacio fades from that part of the narrative. There is deliberate “silence” here, as Almodóvar puts it: Is Bonifacio pining for Elsa? Frustrated with her being so preoccupied? Happy to wait for her return? The director will not say. “You don’t really know that much — like the relationship between Raúl and Santi,” he says. “You don’t know whether it’s a very joyful and shared physical partnership or whether one of them is much more in love than the other one. There’s not a lot of information that is shared.” Almodóvar is implicitly sharing here, of course, that he knows what he wants to hold back in interviews, too. What we don’t know of the characters, we don’t know of him. Bitter Christmas takes a thornier turn when Raúl, arguably, goes too far in his exploration of autofiction. This weds the film’s two timelines with a tensely electric current sourced all the way back to their creator. Almodóvar had to think about how far to push this line of storytelling — and perhaps, as a result, where he’d set his line for imagination to more explicitly take over. “It’s more of an ethical intuition than anything else because the genre of self-fiction doesn’t really set any limits, right?” he says. “The line for me is that I don’t want to harm the people that I use for inspiration. So far, I think I have succeeded. But when you’re dealing with reality and fiction, it’s always an ambiguous line — the limits are very porous.” Almodóvar reexamines this as we talk more, speaking frankly about how hard it can be for any subject, however loosely defined or camouflaged by remixed characteristics, to stay out of an artist’s way. “When an author is writing about the reality that is most proximate to them, you have to think that writers are always going to be selfish,” Almodóvar says later. “Once they have an idea for a story, they’re not necessarily going to think about who they are going to harm or not. Once you have that story, that inspiration, it’s quite powerful and valuable — as a writer, you don’t let it go.” That notion is clearly on Almodóvar’s brain these days. Bitter Christmas will make its North American premiere at the Toronto Film Festival on Sept. 13, before hitting select U.S. theaters on Nov. 13 — and so far, Almodóvar has been pleased to see audiences take the movie on its quirky terms. Meta-storytelling is in the air: We happen to be talking on the publication day for Life of M , Rachel Cusk’s novel widely alleged to center on a thinly veiled (and not always flattering) version of Natalie Portman. The reality is more complicated, certainly — Cusk has declined to comment on the rumors at all — but the media frenzy has already dominated the narrative around it. “This is one example in which using an inspiration perhaps did some harm,” Almodóvar says, eager to learn more about Cusk’s book. “It’s a danger of self-fiction — that it then just becomes gossip.” Almodóvar’s goal was the opposite: to look inward — to offer, for a filmmaker with a body of work as deep and accomplished as anyone of his generation, a rare and dishy window into how and why he does what he does. And maybe negotiate, in real time and for all to see, his dramaturgical boundaries. Indeed, above all, Bitter Christmas reveals Almodóvar’s profound, enduring love for making movies and why he’s not stopping anytime soon. “I’m invested in the force of the story, making sure that the story works, that the story interests people — the script is my focus,” he says. No matter the degree to which a movie like this becomes an exercise in veiled memoir, “It’s never with any kind of thought about my well-being. For me, the very fact of making films is the psychological support.” It’s no coincidence he’s begun to find a cinematic shape for these more cerebral ideas so much later in his career: “You lose the fear of exposing your intimacy,” he says. The result, inevitably, is one of Almodóvar’s bravest works — even as, or maybe because, it only raises more questions for the viewer along the way. THR

articles.title: Canadian Auteur Matthew Rankin Had a Fever Dream About Canadian History
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 12, 2026 4:00am Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney Toronto Film Festival Matthew Rankin’s films about Canadiana tend to have theatrical audiences rubbing their eyes. In his 2024 cinematic mashup Universal Language , marveling viewers could hardly believe a Canada onscreen where Persian and French are the two official languages and a local Tim Hortons becomes an Arabic tea lounge. With Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney — set for its world premiere on Sept. 15 as part of the Midnight Madness program at the Royal Alexandra Theatre in Toronto, Rankin’s genre-bending collage of archival footage, special effects and animation becomes a digital docufantasia of politics and pop culture, chronicling the journey to power for Canada’s 18th prime minister, Brian Mulroney. Related Stories Movies Sorry, Caleb Hearon Is Not Your Clown in 'Trash Mountain' Grief Dramedy Movies Courteney Cox Says She Decided to Direct 'Evil Genius' After Chance Encounter at the Beverly Hills Hotel: "I Made a Lot of Deals There" Rankin tells The Hollywood Reporter that his English- and French-language film looks to combine the two things his producer, the National Film Board of Canada, does best: documentary and animation. The result is a kaleidoscopic manipulation of moving images, backed by abstract language about the generational machinations of the then-Progressive Conservative Party over which Mulroney ultimately triumphed to become Canadian PM in 1984. “I don’t think of [the film] as a biopic. It’s the history of an image, how that image was created and how to mobilize his story to create a brand, to create a package that would ultimately become the brand of the Conservative Party,” Rankin explains. His fever dream of political maneuvering north of the border portrays ambitious men campaigning for power less as a series of contests by candidates seeking public office and more like TV wrestlers seizing the championship belt by unseating rivals after brutal title matches and aggressive storylines. “It’s like a blood sport,” the director says of the political environment that produced the joyfully combative Mulroney, who in one mixed-media collage wears a sequined and feathered robe like the ones boxers or professional wrestlers don to enter the competitive ring. ‘Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney’ Toronto Film Festival Behind the surface charm and inner furnace of ambition, Rankin portrays a Mulroney haunted by the early success of John Diefenbaker, Canada’s 13th prime minister, and the disembodied voice of Pierre Elliott Trudeau, another Canadian leader and father of the 23rd Canadian PM, Justin Trudeau. And as he won over Canadians, the director captures how Mulroney accomplished the Progressive Conservative dream: winning over Quebec, uniting a fragmented country and delivering economic gains coast to coast. “The Conservative Party is a bizarre coalition,” adds Rankin. “Mulroney had to unite disparate factions like disappointed Quebec separatists, Alberta rednecks and elderly ladies in Atlantic Canada, in addition to business leaders in Toronto and environmentalists on the West Coast.” The film also has a distinct parallel to today: the eventual fracturing of the Mulroney coalition led to the current Canadian political landscape, where Quebec and Alberta have separatist movements and the Conservative Party has moved further to the right than the former Progressive Conservatives. “The whole idea of the political center is more and more problematic, more and more tense, and this film does set a compass to where the center was 40 years ago,” Rankin argues. “Certainly, conservatism meant something very different in 1984 than it means in 2026. Donald Trump didn’t emerge out of the ether. There was a process at work, and it began then,” he adds. Rankin portrays that triumph over Canada’s political center ground by combining found footage with music and cultural elements because the director, like most Canadians back then, came to know Mulroney as a creature of TV. “He was the first to really create a sophisticated propaganda by seeing the potential in television and the packaging of his message in television. He really delivered,” Rankin insists. And to show Mulroney as the triumph of political performance over policy, the film blends archival footage, 16mm animation, pixilation and other experimental filmmaking techniques to play with vintage footage like analog-era TV commercials, political propaganda, as well as campaign buttons and brochures. In all, Rankin remixed and reimagined around 80,000 pieces of archival material to arrive at a portrait of Mulroney that is more video art installation than sober political biopic. ‘Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney’ Toronto Film Festival In one scene, Rankin offers an animated train steaming ahead with the giant brain of Diefenbaker as cargo, in an echo of fellow surreal Winnipeg director Guy Maddin and his use of brain models and motifs in films like Brand Upon the Brain! and Rumors . The director puts that satirical take on Canadian conservative politics down to his upbringing in Winnipeg. “The way I look at a thing, I always end up sort of seeing the thing and its opposite simultaneously,” Rankin explains. “Winnipeg is a very ironic place to live. It’s full of contradictions and hypocrisy and bizarre tensions, and when you live in a place like that, things become funny.” The same double vision extends to the film’s subtle nods toward current U.S.-Canada tensions: In archival footage, Diefenbaker is seen meeting U.S. President John F. Kennedy, while Rankin scrolls at the bottom of the screen “51st State?” while Diefenbaker, in a thought bubble, thinks, “Yankee go home.” Rankin’s visual layering and collage wastes little time in showing Diefenbaker and other Conservative Party politicians falling out of favor with Canadians, only for Irish Catholic Mulroney — famed for singing “When Irish Eyes Are Smiling” off-key — to emerge from the wings and win power in an eventual landslide, at a time when like-minded conservatives like Margaret Thatcher led Britain as prime minister and Ronald Reagan sat in the White House as the U.S. president. In the end, Rankin’s Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney chooses neither a hagiography or a curb-stomping critique, instead portraying an ambitious, risk-taking politician who managed to charm Canadians until he fell out of favor at the ballot box. For Rankin, the moral murkiness is the point. “I feel when we see Mulroney being kind of duplicitous or ruthless or superficial or whatever, these things that are typically lobbed at him honestly make me like him a little bit more.” THR

articles.title: Carla Woodcock Joins Kate Beckinsale, Katherine McNamara in ‘White’ (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 12, 2026 5:00am From left: Katherine McNamara, Carla Woodcock, Kate Beckinsale Daniele Venturelli, Jemima Marriott, Araya Doheny Carla Woodcock (Starz’s Outlander ) has signed on to play the lead in White , the upcoming shark survival thriller from horror director Jake West ( Evil Aliens ), The Hollywood Reporter has learned exclusively. Woodcock will play Willa Harba, which the film’s press copy describes as “a struggling actress trying to catch her big break” who is traveling overseas for a shoot with a self-obsessed star when their private jet crashes into the Pacific. Willa is the sole survivor, stranded on a broken wing in the middle of the ocean with only a satellite phone to link her to the outside world. But when she calls her demanding studio boss (played by Kate Beckinsale ) for help, she brushes her off. Her signal gets picked up by a marine biologist Sam Swatek ( Katherine McNamara ), who has some bad news: Willa has crashed landed in the middle of White Shark Café, a stretch of ocean where great whites gather to feed. Related Stories Movies Canadian Auteur Matthew Rankin Had a Fever Dream About Canadian History Movies Almodóvar's Deep Dive Into ... Almodóvar West is directing White from a screenplay by Dan Schaffer, the writer and illustrator of the cult comic book series Dogwitch . Highland Film Group, which is co-financing White and handling world sales on the title at TIFF, has pre-sold multiple international territories, including to Splendid Film in Germany, IIF in Italy, Three Lines Pictures for Benelux, Cinemundo for Portugal, Falcon Films for the Middle East, Latin America to California Filmes and Rialto Distribution for Australia / New Zealand, among others. White is being produced by Yariv Lerner, Dominic Burns, Crawford Anderson-Dillon and Sky Morfopoulos. Kate Beckinsale is executive producing together with Highland Film Group’s Arianne Fraser and Delphine Perrier, Patrick Wintersgill, Kevin Glynn, Pauric Duffy and Hannah Leader. Highland Film Group’s current slate includes Nimród Antal’s sci-fi action thriller Bluefly with Russell Crowe and Priyanka Chopra Jonas; Neil Burger’s action thriller Barracuda starring Anthony Mackie and Dafne Keen; and Pierre Morel’s action thriller The Good Samaritan starring Daisy Ridley, Josh Duhamel and Sharlto Copley. Woodcock is repped by Sarah Camlett at Independent Talent Group. THR

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel’s Pulled TV Interview With James Talarico Hits 5 Million Views in 24 Hours on YouTube
articles.full_text: Sep 11, 2026 8:15pm PT Jimmy Kimmel’s Pulled TV Interview With James Talarico Hits 5 Million Views in 24 Hours on YouTube By Selome Hailu Plus Icon Selome Hailu Latest Jimmy Kimmel’s Pulled TV Interview With James Talarico Hits 5 Million Views in 24 Hours on YouTube 9 hours ago ‘Sheriff Country’ Sets Backdoor Pilot for Medical Spinoff Starring ‘Schitt’s Creek’ Actor Noah Reid 18 hours ago ‘Ransom Canyon’ Canceled After Two Seasons at Netflix 22 hours ago See All Jimmy Kimmel ‘s pulled TV interview with James Talarico , the Texan Democrat running for the U.S. Senate, has crossed 5 million views in the 24 hours since it was posted to YouTube. It was revealed during Wednesday night’s episode of “ Jimmy Kimmel Live !” that the interview would not air on his ABC show because of threats from Donald Trump’s FCC against the network’s affiliate stations. “Out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” Kimmel said on air. “It will be posted on YouTube instead. It will not be on TV.” Related Stories Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie 'Red Rocks' Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit 'Congo Boy' (EXCLUSIVE) This, of course, is not Kimmel’s first conflict with the FCC. Chairman Brendan Carr’s threatened ABC after the host’s comments about the assassination of Charlie Kirk in 2025, and the network later suspended him for nearly a week. Popular on Variety Talarico is no stranger to FCC feuds either. In February, the agency told “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” that it couldn’t broadcast an interview with him. The segment was posted to the show’s YouTube Channel instead, where it reached more than 9 million views. The pulled TV interview between Kimmel and Talarico started with the late night host asking the Texas senate candidate why Trump and the FCC are so scared of him. Talarico responded: “Well, they’re worried that we’re going to win this race in Texas. But we are the underdogs until the last vote is counted. We’re not just going up against the most corrupt politician in Texas. We’re going up against this entire corrupt system.” Watch the full 20-minute interview in the video below.
