articles.title: How Meditation, Hope And Hard Work Brought Rosalind Eleazar Her “Long Shot” Dream Lead In Chris Rock’s ‘Misty Green’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Baz Bamigboye Baz Bamigboye Columnist/International Editor At Large @BazBam More Stories By Baz How Meditation, Hope And Hard Work Brought Rosalind Eleazar Her “Long Shot” Dream Lead In Chris Rock’s ‘Misty Green’ Breaking Baz: Léa Seydoux Talks ‘Gentle Monster’s “Complexity” And “Contradictions” & Why She Wants To Take More Risks — Telluride Film Festival Kenneth Branagh Hosts Judi Dench, Anthony Hopkins, Ian McKellen, Gary Oldman & Helen Mirren In Telluride-Bound Doc ‘Into The Breach’ View All September 12, 2026 5:00am Rosalind Eleazar Stanley Morgan Slow Horses star Rosalind Eleazar says she fights hard for roles that “people don’t immediately assume I could play.” The latest example of this is her titular role in Misty Green , the new film from director-writer-producer Chris Rock , in which he also stars. Misty Green is a Hollywood actress who no longer has the town at her feet. A fast and loose substance abuse lifestyle has knocked her down from acclaim to disdain and forced her to beg for even minor auditions. Yet, Misty is like “a jaguar” — to use Eleazar’s term. She swirls around Los Angles with a swaggering brio that belies her penurious circumstances. Related Stories Reviews Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline's Reviews Reviews 'Girl Group' Review: Rebel Wilson's Musical Comedy Is Fun Spiritual Sequel To 'Pitch Perfect' -- Toronto Film Festival “If someone was to give you a breakdown of Misty Green I wonder if they would immediately go, ‘Rosalind Eleazar for that part?’” she tells me via Zoom from the Dolomites region of the Italian Alps. “I think people may associate me more with, I don’t know, something like being a lawyer,” she says. So Eleazar felt going after the role was “a long shot”, but she connected to Misty the moment she read Rock’s script. More importantly, she wanted the part. “It’s a dream role,” she says. Watch on Deadline Bigger names than hers were chasing it too. Having seen her work on stage and screen since the beginning of her career — which includes appearances on stage with the likes of Matthew Broderick and Ralph Fiennes; holding her own playing a memorable Yelena opposite Toby Jones, Richard Armitage, Aimee Lou Wood and Ciarán Hinds In Uncle Vanya at the Harold Pinter Theatre in the West End, and in The House of Bernarda Alba with Harriet Walter at the National Theatre and many TV films and series — Misty Green is undoubtedly the outstanding performance of her career, and by far one of the year’s best. The East-London-based actor admits “there were tears. I was crying when I thought I didn’t get it… As an actor, one thing I do share with Misty is that you go on this roller-coaster of emotions after you’ve auditioned and it’s out of your hands now, and the next day, you’re like, Oh, I think today I might get a call, and you just live in this endless hope. Then three days go by… So your emotions are constantly going like that,” she says. She’s in the Dolomites on a hiking holiday with her producer and actor husband Gabriel Lo Giudice ( The Wanderer: Destinations Unknown ) ahead of arriving in Toronto for TIFF , where she’s planning to meet up with Gary Oldman and some of the acting team behind the motley crew of Apple TV’s Slow Horses . Then, on Saturday, September 12th, comes Eleazar’s big night — Misty Green will have its world premiere at Roy Thompson Hall. Rosalind Eleazar in ‘Misty Green’ A24 Next month, the movie will have galas during the BFI London Film Festival and A24 will give Misty Green a limited release from October 9th. Daniel Kaluuya , Adam Driver, Anna Kendrick also star. Looking back over the whole auditioning process, Eleazar is incredulous over what she put herself through. Still waiting to hear whether or not she’d landed the role, she was in her London apartment “meditating, and I was trying to connect and talk to Chris in my mind,” she reflects with a rueful grimace then a smile. “At one point I genuinely thought I had connected to him, and then whilst I was on set, I said to Chris, ‘Do you remember? Did you ever at one point feel me talking to you?’ He just looked at me and went ‘ No ,’” she sheepishly divulges. ”You’re lucky if roles like Misty Green come once in a lifetime,” she says, “and I’m so happy that that somehow has worked out for me.” After two auditions over Zoom in London, the London Academy of Music & Dramatic Art graduate flew to Los Angeles for chemistry tests with Rock, who plays a director who understands that hidden beneath Misty’s armor of pain is an artist with proper talent. Once the part was hers, Eleazar sprang into action. She took singing lessons — performing “One Night Only” from Dreamgirls is one of the movie’s many highlights — and Rock tasked her with watching some movies, including Klute with Jane Fonda and Donald Sutherland. An aspect of Eleazar’s performance that fascinates me is the sultry physicality with which she infuses Misty. “I move very differently to Misty,” she says, explaining how the 5Rhythms method played a significant role in developing her walk for the movie. The 5Rhythms practice is a movement and dance practice created by Gabrielle Roth intended to liberate the mind and body. Eleazar played around with where she felt Misty’s natural tempo stood. Rosalind Eleazar. Photo: Will Aldersley “Obviously, throughout the day and through the course of whatever, her tempo changes,” she says, noting that Misty “has quite a lot of sexual energy to her.” The way Misty moves, Eleazar remarks, marks her as “someone that is also wanting to be noticed and someone that is wanting to be respected.” Eleazar broke out the Misty walk on the streets of LA. “It has to become like second nature, rather than something that on the day of film you suddenly feel self-conscious with because it’s not in your body,” she says. The street test helped her pare down the walk to what she describes as “a floaty staccato,” which allows Misty to “turn corners incredibly fast.” That means, Misty can catch you off guard, giving her a quite languid quality until she springs like the “jaguar” label Eleazar gave her. Eleazar, who studied Spanish, Mandarin and psychology at the U.K.’s Nottingham University, says she has “a lot of compassion generally for people that come out into the world punching and surviving, and they have these layers upon layers of protection because of whatever’s happened early on in their life, and they’re not immediately likable or lovable, and it takes time to love Misty. She’s not someone that you necessarily easily warm to.” Eleazar is generally drawn to larger-than-life characters, she says. In all her parts, from her Jacky Bast in Kenneth Lonergan’s 2017 television adaptation of Howards End onwards, she suggests there’s a commonality. “They’ve all been quite big in some way,” she says. “They’re eccentric and sort of Shakespearean, and I find that I enjoy looking for the humanity in those sort of larger-than-life characters.” Two days prior to auditioning with Rock in LA, she’d read with Ralph Fiennes in London for Rebecca Lenkiewicz’s play Small Hotel , which premiered at the Theatre Royal in Bath with Fiennes and Francesca Annis in the fall of 2025. There’s a slim chance of it transferring into the West End in 2027, if scheduling doesn’t get in the way. Rosalind Eleazar in ‘Small Hotel’ Marc Brenner For some reason Judi Dench becomes a topic in our conversation. When I remark that I still replay in my head the Cleopatra the great dame performed opposite Anthony Hopkins in Shakespeare’s Antony and Cleopatra at the National Theatre in 1987, Eleazar’s eyes light up. “Cleopatra is my dream role!” she cries. She’d love to play Medea and Elektra too. Surely working with Oldman, Saskia Reeves, Jack Lowden, Kristin Scott Thomas, Ruth Bradley, Christopher Chung, Aimee-Ffionn Edwards, Kadiff Kirwan and others on Slow Horses is like being in a theatrical repertory company, because they all come from theater backgrounds? Nodding admiringly, she says that the cast often takes tea with Oldman who “sort of watches over all of us and is interested in you and what you’re doing and is always a champion of your work.” She connected with Kaluuya in part because they both hail from the theater, although Misty Green is the first time they’ve worked together. “We would take lots of long walks together and discuss our shared history for the characters and also sharing our own stories. And he’s just an insane actor… I love dangerous actors — Anna [Kendrick] and Adam [Driver] too — you feel you can jump off together and see where you land,” she says, adding that her scenes with Kaluuya were incendiary. “Every take was so different and that beautiful trust you have with someone…” In the film, Rock’s character raises questions about racism and sexism in Hollywood but those subjects are not the film’s main concerns, a point that Eleazar concurs with. “Misty Green isn’t about race,” she says. However, she and Rock did have a conversation about it. “I think that there are places for different types of films, and this character was able to just exist, and there’s a universality to her. It didn’t matter that she was my skin color, that’s not the leading narrative of the film,” she says. And off screen whenever she has “potentially experienced certain things” related to race “I privately deal with it, and I kind of think to myself, well, let my work do the talking. I would love to be known as someone that is a solid actor rather than other things. But it doesn’t mean that I’m unaffected by it. Let’s say I’m not unaffected by sexism and racism in our industry,” she says. If Misty Green takes off for her the way I feel it will, then Eleazar’s going to be very busy. Could she move to Hollywood for work? She has an American passport. “I can I can work there if I started doing a lot more American projects and if it made sense. I do love living in London though, and still loads of shows are made out of the U.K. and in Europe.” Smiling, Eleazar looks directly at me and says: “This sounds incredibly cheesy, but when part of your dream is starting to become true, it’s actually also quite frightening, because you’re like, oh my gosh, I have portrayed this character in this movie, and I’m incredibly proud of all of our work. And it’s now at the stage of sharing with other people, and it feels exposing. But at the same time, I’m incredibly excited by it, and I’m feeling grateful. What an opportunity I had. And Chris giving me that opportunity — it was a long shot.” Misty Green will premiere 9.30pm, September 12th at Roy Thompson Hall at the Toronto Film Festival. ‘Practical Magic 2’ Conjuring $30M U.S.; NFL Week 1 To Impact Holdovers Company & State AGs Set Antitrust Suit Settlement Talks For October Noah Reid To Headline CBS’ ‘Sheriff Country’ Medical Spinoff, Will Guest On Cop Show ‘Onwards And Sideways’ Chat; ‘Girl Group’, ‘River’, ‘Stuffed’ Reviews; WB Chiefs Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Female-Led Producer Candid Broads Is Proud to Stand for New Voices, Impact and Representation
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 11, 2026 2:00am 'Swim Sistas' film still Courtesy of Candid Broads Productions Naomie Harris narrates Swim Sistas , a short documentary directed by actress and author Catherine Joy White that was designed as a “poetic and visually rich love letter to water, sisterhood, and the resilience of Black women across generations.” Hannah Congdon’s short doc The Long Away Game tells the story of a female Afghan refugee soccer player finding a home and community in Yorkshire, England. And Julie Magnaudet’s comedic short The Contraception Fair , starring Alex Rider ‘s Ronkẹ Adékọluẹ́jọ́, Derry Girls ‘ Kathy Kiera Clarke and The Baby ‘s Amber Grappy, follows a young woman who wants to stop taking the birth control pill, only to find herself at the “Female Contraception Fair,” an imaginary place where female contraceptive methods compete for her attention and pressure her to make a choice. Related Stories Movies How 'Obsession' Rewrote TIFF History Movies The Don of Hollywood North Takes His Final Bow Three films by three female directors, backed by one female-led production company that is focused on character-driven narratives that want to surprise audiences. And that production company has one badass name: Candid Broads Productions . Founded in 2020 in London by French-British actress and producer Oriane Pick, who serves as CEO and founder, the company’s team also features producer Anaïs Ferrato. The goal, as Candid Broads says on its website, is “to bring unspoken truths from underrepresented communities to the forefront of the entertainment industry” and “ensuring diverse female representation both in front of and behind the camera.” And it does so by combining “warmth, energy, and cinematic flair” and championing emerging filmmakers. With a slate of shorts that has made waves under its belt, the production company has started to transition into feature-length filmmaking and is eyeing a move into series, while continuing to make shorts. Pick and Ferrato talked to THR about Candid Broads’ vision, its move into new areas, and why they aren’t afraid to highlight the importance and value of diversity and inclusion at a time when there has been a political backlash against them, especially in the U.S. Candid Broads Productions CEO and founder Oriane Pick Courtesy of Kim Hardy How did the company’s name come about? “We wanted to make sure to highlight that the company is really female-centric, and we didn’t want to call it ‘chick,'” Pick recalls. “But we thought ‘broads’ seemed cool. And ‘candid’ came because we’re both French, so we’re very blunt sometimes, probably a bit too much at times. But we love being honest, and we thought having ‘candid’ in there would really work. So we’re essentially the honest chicks.” The Candid Broads brand is also meant as a signal to creatives and creative partners. “There are a lot of people who are not saying things the way they are, or hiding a little bit what the reality is,” Pick tells THR . “But we say to every writer and director who works with us. It is a very tough industry. We need to have a really thick skin. We’ll get lots of nos, but then we’ll get a yes, and the yes that we’ll get will just make up for all of the nos. So, one of the reasons we were so keen on that name for the company is because we never give up. We’re always very honest about what we do, how we do it, and we take people along the journey with us on this magnificent ride.” Female-focused doesn’t mean that Candid Broads won’t do stories about men. “We like casting a bit of a wider [net],” Ferrato tells THR . “We are female-centric, but also did a short film not so long ago called Punching Bag that follows a male protagonist. It’s really all about finding distinctive voices and taking a chance on emerging writers and directors, or sometimes a duo if they’re not the same person.” Candid Broads is all about new impulses or different approaches. “It’s all about perspective for us,” explains Ferrato. “When we read a script, we [want to think], oh, we haven’t seen that before. It may be something that has been explored, but the voice of that director or writer is bringing something that feels different.” Anaïs Ferrato, courtesy of Inès Leila Hachou Courtesy of Inès Leila Hachou After all, making an impact and taking audiences outside their comfort zones is key to Candid Broads’ mission. “It’s about stories that feel uncomfortable or difficult,” Ferrato notes, adding with a laugh. “We like making things difficult for ourselves.” After all, “it’s about impact. That’s something that we’re really interested in. Whether it’s opening a conversation, breaking stigmas, or eventually contributing to some kind of change. Of course, the impact will change depending on the film. But it has to be organic. We can’t invent it. Nine times out of 10, the story either feels urgent or very personal to the creators. And that’s what we are drawn to.” Asked about the recent political backlash in the U.S. against such ideas as representation and inclusion, the Candid Broads team is unfazed. “For us, it’s really important that everyone does their duty on it, and that we all make sure that it’s part of every film,” Pick tells THR . “Whether it’s behind the camera or in front of the camera, or the kind of story that we tell, all of that needs to be cohesive. We’re obviously Caucasian women, but we’ve been telling a lot of stories through the eyes of a Black filmmaker about a Black character. Any kind of representation is really, really vital.” Bottom line: “It’s about finding that gem and pushing stories so that we really make sure that representation is not just a word,” she emphasizes. “It’s something much bigger.” Adds Ferrato: “There’s a discourse against it at the moment, but for us, it’s always been something quite simple. When you look at who traditionally has had the opportunity to tell stories and who we’ve seen traditionally on screen most of the time, it was the same people or the same type of protagonist. But how much talent and how many stories are we missing when the opportunity isn’t there? So for us, the idea is to provide that opportunity.” ‘The Contraception Fair’ film still, courtesy of Candid Broads Productions Candid Broads actually requires at least gender parity on its sets, but most of the time, it ends up with around 60 percent women without even forcing it, the duo shares. So, what does Candid Broads have on its slate? The company has recently wrapped production on its first feature film, which is also Kieran Bourne’s feature debut, the romantic drama Arthur & Clara, starring CJ Beckford and Mirren Mack. “When a filmmaker and an actress unknowingly run away to the same rural farmhouse hoping to find themselves, they discover they only needed one person to truly see them,” its synopsis reads. Speaking of debut features, the company has been casting for the coming-of-age comedy Underdogs from writer-director Fabia Martin ( The Rev , Six for Gold ). Alisha Weir ( Abigail , Matilda the Musical ) is will star in the story, told through the eyes of disillusioned but determined teens. Underdogs follows two teenage girls in foster care who find themselves on the run in a stolen ambulance in search of family and freedom – only to end up illegally competing at Crufts, the world’s largest annual dog show, held in Birmingham, England. Grappy plays a strung-out social worker who is tasked with getting the girls back home. Also on Candid Broads’ slate is the first full-length film from Amy Hodge, entitled Am I Nervous , a feature adaptation of her and the company’s short The Date, which earned writer Bethan Marlow a 2024 BAFTA Cymru Breakthrough Award nomination. The short, which starred Millie Kiss, Sinead Matthews and Precious Scott, told the story of Sasha, “a loud-mouthed 13-year-old who goes on her first date but when she gets turned on and takes charge of her own sexuality, it reveals the confusing nature of what girls are allowed to want.” The feature, which the writer and director are co-writing, is in early development with Ffilm Cymru and “follows a teenager and a grandmother as they both embark on their own journey of reclaiming their sexuality,” Ferrato says. ‘The Date’ film still, courtesy of Candid Broads Productions Courtesy of Candid Broads Productions Also in the works is Loud & Clear , the next feature written by Kieran Bourne, which Pick is producing with Alexa Waugh ( Cielo ). More shorts are also in the pipeline. Among them is the dark comedy Vag , which will also be executive produced by Slick Films. “It’s a film about vaginismus and the politics of female pleasure and dating, written and directed by Lily Britton,” shares Ferrato. “Vaginismus is a condition that we haven’t really heard about. It’s still something that is quite taboo, and we wanted to offer a much-needed representation of it when it comes to that film.” A synopsis for the short reads: “Marianne is 27. She’s successful, vibrant, and – thanks to vaginismus – unable to have penetrative sex. When a promising romance turns sour, she’s forced to explore her own pleasure – something she’s never dared to before.” Candid Broads is also in development on its first TV series, which is being written by Ali Hughes ( Dreaming Whilst Black ), but the team isn’t ready to unveil its title or plot details yet. Mischief International is co-producing it, with its founder Maria Ishak as executive producer. The Candid Broads Productions team behind the scenes of the shoot for ‘Punching Bag,’ courtesy of Inès Leila Hachou Courtesy of Inès Leila Hachou One thing is for sure. The Candid Broads team isn’t sitting on its laurels. “We’re moving into features, bridging the gap between what we know or what we believe the audience wants, but also what the industry thinks they want and the safer choices,” highlights Ferrato. “So, right now it’s about trying to see how we can push that further. And because we have a lot of projects, we want to make sure that we have enough capacity and don’t spread ourselves too thin.” Concludes Pick: “There are a lot of different things on our slate right now, which is so exciting. We love working on very different stories at different stages, so that we just keep busy, we keep learning and we keep challenging ourselves. A main thing for us is to never get bored.” THR

articles.title: Toronto Builds Its One-Stop Shop
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 11, 2026 3:45am Geoff Macnaughton Courtesy of TIFF As the Toronto Film Festival this year launches TIFF: The Market , its official bazaar for global film, TV series and immersive content, fest organizers have also rolled out an accompanying financing and co-production forum, the International Financing & Project Market (IFPM). That’s part of a bigger plan, says Geoff Macnaughton , vp market programming and theatrical and programmer of Primetime at TIFF. Macnaughton explains that offering two markets — one for film, series and immersive projects in development, and another for completed and varied media content — is intended to provide the wider industry with what it needs to survive and thrive in an increasingly global and multiplatform media business. Related Stories Movies Female-Led Producer Candid Broads Is Proud to Stand for New Voices, Impact and Representation Movies 'Being Heumann' Review: Siân Heder's Drama About the Fight for Disability Rights Strikes Familiar Notes but Gets the Inspirational Uplift Job Done The TV series showcase at TIFF includes Mike Flanagan’s Carrie , a reimagining for Prime Video of Stephen King’s classic novel; American Hostage , the psychological thriller series for MGM+; and Yaga , the Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson Williams supernatural mystery series. The IFPM, as a cornerstone of The Market, has TIFF taking over the International Financing Forum (IFF), a co-production market that for 20 years was run by Ontario Creates during TIFF’s 11-day run. Ontario Creates remains a presenting partner of the IFPM, with Karen Thorne-Stone, president and CEO of the provincial media support agency, welcoming TIFF expanding on the success of her longtime IFF event. “Together, we look forward to creating new opportunities for Ontario and international producers to connect, finance and bring compelling projects to audiences around the world,” she says. The Hollywood Reporter spoke to Macnaughton ahead of the Toronto Film Festival about becoming both a film and talent showcase and having two content markets in its quiver. Toronto will become a market-first festival this year. How does a returning International Financing & Project Market fit into that offer to the industry? When building the market, some of the important things for us were: How do we create a future-thinking market; another question we were asking ourselves was how do we create more opportunities for producers; the third question was how do we make sure that what we’re developing on the programming side of things is as impactful as possible? And so we kind of wrapped our brains around, if we want to support producers more, do we necessarily come in and invent something completely new? Or do we work with some partners and evolve something that’s established? And Ontario Creates has had great success with their international financing forum in past years. So instead of building a market and having the international financing forum sit outside of it, we approached the leadership team there and discussed the idea of what it might look like if this fell under the overarching market umbrella. Most IFPM projects are movies, but you’ve also included six TV series and five “innovation” projects. Is that a nod to an increasingly cross-platform and digital industry? Really, the vision of the market was very much kind of a one-stop shop for global industry professionals. The other part that was really important to us was the types of projects that were presented — that it was not only a film market, but a market that welcomed those working in film series and immersive to broaden our definition of who has access, but also bring in decision-makers and creatives who are across all of those platforms. Because among indie content makers looking for elusive financing, there’s more debate on whether a project is a film or a TV series? Yeah, exactly. And in the project market, there will be a mix of all of those. For creators and IP holders, there are more options out there than there have been. But the businesses all have various challenges and opportunities. So the idea of someone developing a film that might make more sense as a series, or someone developing a series that may make more sense as a film, or the idea I’m developing something, but it has a life across these other elements — as an IP holder, I want to take full advantage of that. With most IFPM projects being films, are movies still the engine driving TIFF and the industry’s long tail? The festival is very much the welcome party phase of a film’s life and introducing it to a public audience or a press audience or an industry audience for the first time. Obviously, the films are being acquired at various stages in their development. But we’ve seen over the last years, that finished films at film festivals are not the instant acquisition they once were. Those acquisitions take time. So, instead of trying to change how the industry works, it’s more about leaning into what the industry needs. And if what the industry needs is to showcase more projects at an earlier development stage, that’s what we’re going to lean into and offer. Where once indie film producers looked to streaming platforms for financing and acquisitions, the streamers now have their own original film pipelines. Does that leave the streamers to premiere their titles at TIFF, and indie producers to look beyond Netflix to the IFPM and your Content Market to fully finance and shop their own titles? On the streamer side of things — and I can tell by the attendance numbers and what the data is telling us — the streamers are sending their acquisitions team in a big way. The acquisitions teams are utilizing festivals, and specifically TIFF, in different ways than maybe five years ago. But they’re picking up projects at earlier stages of development. You’re seeing them pick up content out of market screenings. The streamers have a big pipeline to fill, and Toronto being the audience-friendly festival and audience-friendly market, we continue to allow for that. And how are indie producers adapting? A handful of years ago, it felt like certain companies kind of took over and were the ones that were moving the needle in terms of acquisitions. And everyone else had to kind of wait until those acquisitions were done to see what remained. That’s leveled out a bit. If you look at the last few years and the types of companies that have had the biggest acquisitions out of markets, it’s a more diverse mix. Whether it’s Focus with Obsession or theatrical distributor players like Sony Pictures Classics, they’re very active. There’s a bit more of a level playing field than there was maybe just after the pandemic. That should be an encouraging sign for producers. Besides titles, the industry is also eyeing emerging talent. Back to the point about the streamers having their own content pipelines, they’re looking in markets for talent and future talent to tie to what they’re developing. The Focus example with Obsession is a good one. A company is not only acquiring Obsession and the global hit that it became, they’re also looking to work with a Curry Barker or [ Obsession star] Inde Navarrette on their next project. That’s what a lot of theatrical or streamers or distributors are doing in Toronto, because all the markets and festivals have a plethora of emerging talent that is being showcased, not only in films with official selection, but also through our development labs and different places. To those who inevitably ask why TIFF didn’t launch an official market 10 years ago, is your answer that the IFPM and the inaugural Content Market aren’t about legacy content? It’s more about what the industry needs now and into the future? Building the market was a long-gestating decision. It wasn’t something we took lightly. We took our time with it because building a market is a big step for a festival. The idea of throwing two massive, large-scale global events at the exact same time is a feat. And over the last 25 and even 50 years, TIFF has had an industry infrastructure in some way. That’s included national agencies, that’s included talent development programs, that’s included a conference. Now to become an efficient market is to put our flag in the sand and say, “We are invested in growing our support for the global screen sector,” and it allows us to be nimble to industry changes. How people watch content is always going to evolve. But the thing that stays consistent is to get a film made, to get a series made, to get an immersive project off the ground, the business side of things needs to happen. THR

articles.title: The Don of Hollywood North Takes His Final Bow
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 11, 2026 4:00am 'The Martini Shot — 50 Years of Hits, Hustle & Hollywood North' Courtesy of Don Carmody Having racked up 130-plus movie credits over a 50-year producing career, Don Carmody has long been known as the Don of Hollywood North by studio bean counters who crunched the numbers and chose to save money by shooting in Canada. Now Carmody, at 75, is ready to leave the stage — or at least Canadian film sets — with a lavish sendoff planned for the 2026 Toronto Film Festival. “The days of me freezing my ass off at 2 o’clock in the morning on a film set are behind me,” Carmody tells The Hollywood Reporter . Related Stories Movies Toronto Builds Its One-Stop Shop Movies Female-Led Producer Candid Broads Is Proud to Stand for New Voices, Impact and Representation That’s after Hollywood catapulted him to the status of its most bankable producer in Canada, as he brought over $2 billion worth of American production north by, in effect, opening the floodgates to Los Angeles runaway production, starting in the 1980s. Carmody traces his start shepherding studio films to Canada to his time matching Hollywood production values with lower budgets as a co-producer at Cinepix Film Properties, on genre fare like David Cronenberg’s Shivers (1974) and Rabid (1976) and comedies like Ivan Reitman’s summer camp romp Meatballs . “They looked good, and people didn’t go, ‘Oh, that’s a weird-looking movie’ or ‘It’s got really bad production values.’ That opened the door for me,” Carmody recalls. The studios noticed just how much Carmody put onscreen despite tight budgets. “The studios found out how little we were spending on them and asked, ‘How do you do that?’ ” he says. He also leveraged the low Canadian dollar against the American greenback and took advantage of early tax breaks. The other unseen draw for the major studios in Canada was its creatives and crews, and local actors aligned with ACTRA, the country’s performers union. “They said, ‘Well, can you do that for us?’ So I started bringing up pictures brought to me by the studios,” Carmody explains. “Canada had a large talent pool and you could count on bringing in fresh faces. And it was important to [Hollywood] producers and directors that they see people that spoke and looked American and were really good actors.” For helping make Canada Hollywood’s backlot, the studio’s top man up north is cementing his legacy at TIFF by endowing $100,000 to establish the CMPA Don Carmody International Production Mentorship Program, putting another $100,000 into creating the CFC Don Carmody Producer Residency at the late Norman Jewison’s Canadian Film Centre and doing a Sept. 13 keynote at the TIFF market. He also screened a career documentary, The Martini Shot — 50 Years of Hits, Hustle & Hollywood North , on Sept. 9 at the Hot Docs Theatre. Of course, some Hollywood directors early on likened shooting in Canada to “being sent to Siberia,” while others welcomed how the distance from Hollywood offered more creative freedom. An early convert was the late Sidney Lumet, who knew Canada from shooting select scenes for his 1977 psychological drama Equus across the U.S. border. But when Disney’s Touchstone Pictures lost a producer, they flew Carmody to New York City to meet with Lumet and ultimately start a five-picture collaboration that included titles like the erotic thriller Guilty as Sin in 1993 and the 1997 medical satire Critical Care , both of which had Toronto doubling as New York City. “[Lumet] loved everything up here, except the bagels,” recalls Carmody. In 1997, Carmody received a call from newly hired Miramax Films head of production Kevin Hyman, who offered him the 1998 Sharon Stone title The Mighty , which shot in Toronto after a tightfisted Harvey Weinstein insisted on a budget that ruled Hollywood out. “I flew down, met with Harvey and convinced him we could make the picture look good by shooting it up in Canada, and that I would be able to handle Sharon Stone,” who wasn’t happy about heading up north, he recounts. Don Carmody, courtesy of Rafy While working on The Mighty , Carmody got another call from Hyman. Carmody remembers the conversation word for word: “OK, we have another for you. It’s very tricky. These two guys from Boston wrote this script we’d like to make, and they want to make it in Boston,” which was too costly a location, he remembers. So, with Weinstein promising a greenlight if Good Will Hunting could be done in Canada, Carmody — who spent time in Boston as a young man and could muster a convincing “Southie” accent — greeted a decidedly reluctant Matt Damon and Ben Affleck as they came through airport customs in Toronto to be shown that Canada’s biggest city could double as South Boston. “I said, OK, what do you want to see first? The duck boats? Or do you want to see the Swan Pond?’ ” Carmody recalls saying to the two stars, a reference to locales in Toronto that could double for popular land and sea tourist sites in Boston. “They couldn’t believe that existed in Toronto.” As ever, keeping a lid on the movie’s budget proved key for Carmody. “Just because I’m from Boston, that would have meant nothing if we had gone way over budget, or I couldn’t deliver the proper locations on Good Will Hunting ,” he says. An Oscar trophy eventually came Carmody’s way with Rob Marshall’s Chicago in 2002, but only after Weinstein said he would not go over a $40 million budget on the musical drama. Going forward, Carmody says the attraction of the Canadian talent pool and film tax credits (which he insists need a hike in Ontario) will keep Hollywood studios and streamers shooting in Canada. If something “amazing” comes his way, he adds, he may get back into producing, but these days Carmody is looking to exploit his original IP with sequels and adaptations, which means mostly talking to lawyers. And while being a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and other industry guilds, Carmody also works with their Canadian counterparts, including the Canadian Media Producers Association, representing indie producers, along with the Academy of Canadian Cinema & Television and the Canadian Film Centre. “It’s important to support the incoming and up-and-coming producers, because Canada needs its own base of well-trained and smart producers,” he says. And if he has any advice for young producers, it’s that making movies requires patience — and stamina. Asked about the most fun he ever had making a film, Carmody says: “Probably a sequel. They’re easier,” before adding, “Making a movie is like banging your head against the wall. It feels so good when it stops.” THR

articles.title: How ‘Obsession’ Rewrote TIFF History
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 11, 2026 4:30am Inde Navarrette in 'Obsession.' Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection There has probably never been a worse moment to open a film market in Canada. The country is locked in a grinding trade war with its largest partner and closest neighbor; tariff threats have crept from steel and lumber into the entertainment conversation, and the independent film business — the actual product on offer in Toronto this week — is in the middle of its own slow-motion restructuring. The class of buoyant new distributors who arrived at TIFF two years ago with fresh cash and big talk has thinned out considerably. Streamers are buying less and paying less. Theatrical is a coin flip. Related Stories Movies The Don of Hollywood North Takes His Final Bow Movies Toronto Builds Its One-Stop Shop And yet TIFF: The Market, which runs Sept. 10-16 at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre alongside North America’s largest film festival, opens with something no first-year market has any right to: momentum, and a founding legend. A legend called Obsession . Twelve months ago, a 25-year-old YouTube sketch comedian walked into the Royal Alexandra Theatre with a horror movie he had shot for $750,000 with a cast of unknowns. He walked out with the biggest TIFF acquisition in history — an estimated $15 million worldwide deal with Focus Features — and the film went on to gross $513 million globally, becoming the top-grossing festival pickup of all time. In fact, the story of Obsession ’s TIFF triumph actually started on the Croisette. Capstone exec Ruzanna Kegeyan — who had sold 2010 Midnight Madness breakout Insidious worldwide — ambushed TIFF programmer Peter Kuplowsky the minute he landed in Cannes. “She said, ‘Have you heard of Curry Barker ?’ Initially, I blanked,” Kuplowsky says. Then she mentioned the YouTube sketches, and a long-held theory clicked into place. “I’ve long had the belief that sketch comedy writers make terrific horror filmmakers,” he says, citing Zach Cregger applying setup-and-payoff structure to Barbarian . Kegeyan sent a rough cut; Kuplowsky watched it a week later and emailed her before it was even finished. Then came the phase no market can manufacture, only host: the whisper campaign. Nobody was screening the film. So the calls came to the programmer instead. “It was constantly, ‘How good is it? Is it this?’ ” Kuplowsky says. “And I was like, ‘Well, I’m invoking Barbarian in my note, so I think it’s as good as Barbarian .’ And they’re like, ‘What does that mean, that it’s going to make $40 million?’ And I’m like, ‘I would hope so. I think it depends on who buys it and how they release it.’ ” Days before the premiere, Jason Blum, Weapons producer Roy Lee and Paranormal Activity producer Steven Schneider preemptively greenlit Barker’s follow-up project, Anything but Ghosts , alongside Divide/Conquer’s Adam Hendricks and Greg Gilreath. In hindsight, it was the best marketing spend of the festival: three of horror’s shrewdest operators publicly betting on a filmmaker whose movie no one had seen. By the time Obsession made it to TIFF, the buzz on social media had become deafening. “I remember coming out onstage for the screening, and there were people in the audience that were already chanting Curry Barker’s name,” Kuplowsky says. “Then TIFF Next Wave came out and read their introduction, describing why they connected to this film. And I pointed to them and said, ‘Buyers, this is your audience. Pay attention.’ ” Blum sprinted in during the preshow. Kuplowsky stood at the back the whole time, watching the crowd more than the film. “So electric. Every moment was working. The big jump scares got everyone out of their seat.” Christian Mercuri of Capstone, which financed the film, had felt it in the room. “You can tell during the screening,” he says. “And then — it’s not that we said 100 percent we’re selling it. We had to sit with everybody that was interested and determine that that was the right path. It was a couple of days of negotiations, and then we felt we had the right partner.” Barker’s team spent the next 24 hours in meetings, landing at roughly 1 a.m. Sunday on Focus, which beat A24 and Neon largely on the strength of a global distribution apparatus its rivals don’t have. CAA and Capstone closed it. Obsession was not a triumph of the traditional system. It was a triumph around it. The film cost less than a studio spends on a trailer, was made by a director whose audience was built for free on YouTube, and was launched by buzz, word-of-mouth and the magic of a Midnight Madness crowd. At a time when the traditional indie model — established IP, star-driven packaging, presales stitched together territory by territory — looks shaky, Obsession offers an alternative. The lesson of Obsession , Mercuri says, is to bet on “original content, original ideas and strategies that “push the envelope and take risks. As an industry, it’s sort of our responsibility to listen to some new voices, not always do the same old, same old. The core of it is original fare.” Nobody expects this week to turn a $750,000 negative into $513 million. That was never the bet. The bet is that what happened in the Royal Alexandra last year — a room full of professionals watching a debut feature work, in real time, on an audience — is worth building a market around. Not because it can be repeated on schedule, but because it proved the thing everyone had started to doubt: that an original idea, made cheap and launched smart, can still detonate. A market has to be built on something. Worse foundations have held. THR

articles.title: With ‘Trash Mountain,’ Caleb Hearon Becomes Your New Favorite Indie Darling
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Mia Galuppo Plus Icon Mia Galuppo Senior Entertainment Reporter miagaluppo Follow Sign Up View All September 11, 2026 5:00am Caleb Hearon Sandy Honig Caleb Hearon grew up in a small town in rural Missouri with a population under 10,000. It’s the kind of locale that can — especially for a young queer person — leave lasting scars and simultaneously build up an enduring sense of humor. The comedian and performer has long excavated his Midwestern roots for his stand-up. Now, Hearon’s life acts as the inspiration for the TIFF -bound indie Trash Mountain , Hearon’s most personal project to date. Directed by indie vet Kris Rey, Hearon co-wrote and stars in Trash Mountain as Gavin, a gay man who lives in Chicago but is called back to his small Missouri town by his half sister — played by Zooey Deschanel — after the death of their hoarder father, each of them tasked with cleaning up the emotional and literal mess left behind. Related Stories Movies 'Being Heumann' Review: Siân Heder's Drama About the Fight for Disability Rights Strikes Familiar Notes but Gets the Inspirational Uplift Job Done Movies 'Rapinoe' Review: Doc Portrait of American Soccer Icon Is Engaging and Inspiring, if Necessarily Incomplete Several years ago, Hearon‘s own father unexpectedly died. “We had a really complicated relationship — but a beautiful one,” says Hearon. “I feel lucky that we got to a really good place before he passed.” Along with his family, Hearon, who was working in a writers’ room in Los Angeles at the time, was confronted by the not-oft-talked-about logistics that come with a loved one’s passing: locating paperwork, cleaning out homes and jumping through a seemingly endless number of bureaucratic hoops. He started writing the screenplay for Trash Mountain as a cathartic exercise: “I never thought we would honestly make a movie about it.” But after sending it to filmmaker friends Colin Trevorrow and Lilly Wachowski — who each signed on as producers — the production process began in earnest. Typical of indie filmmaking, there were years of false starts, with funding and casts periodically materializing and disappearing. Hearon has built a career that spans prestige TV ( Fargo , Mr. & Mrs. Smith ), a well-regarded podcast ( So True with Caleb Hearon ) and stand-up, with his debut special, Model Comedian , released by HBO in 2025. It was during a small break in the middle of filming The Devil Wears Prada 2 — his biggest project to date where he stars alongside Meryl Streep and Anne Hathaway — that Hearon got a call from Trevorrow saying that they finally had the money to make Trash Mountain but that they would have to pick up cameras the next month. “I was like, ‘What the hell?’ ” he recalls. “Because you’ve got so many years in your career of dreaming of scenarios like where you’re at a job, and you’re talking about me having another one.” The backbone of Trash Mountain is the relationship between Hearon’s Gavin and his sister, Abbi. It’s the kind of effortlessly funny dynamic that makes the heartaches that come with having a sibling look truly worth it. Hearon shares an agent with Deschanel at CAA, and the rep told him that the actress happened to be looking for a new project and was available during Trash Mountain ’s small — very small — production window. “I was like, ‘Look, if the job is pretending to love Zooey Deschanel, it’s gonna be like the easiest acting job in the whole world,’ ” Hearon says with a laugh. At a lunch in Los Angeles with Deschanel, Hearon remembers: “I swear to God, I said, ‘Why would you do this?’ I knew everyone was going to have to do it for like $7 and a handshake in rural Illinois in the winter.” Deschanel was sold nonetheless. Trash Mountain Courtesy of TIFF Production on Trash Mountain was only 18 days and came with all the stories you would expect from true indie filmmaking, stealing locations and chasing light. One day, filming in a local big box store, Hearon kept overhearing a loud conversation from the next aisle between who he thought were members of the crew. Unbeknownst to him, they were local shoppers trying to decide which T-shirt to buy. He remembers, “I was in the middle of the take going, ‘I’m so sorry. Can we cut? People are being really loud.’ And [director Kris Rey] was like, ‘Yeah, we couldn’t afford to shut down the place, and we have about an hour left, sorry!” Trash Mountain also marks Hearon’s first time at the top of the call sheet. “During filming, I kept joking, ‘You know what this film needs? 30 pages where you don’t see Caleb.,’” he laughs. But it was also a position he didn’t take lightly, saying, “There’s this thing I’ve learned through the years of not being number one on the call sheet where I watch the people who are, and they have so many other jobs. Everyone’s energy, everyone’s tone, everyone’s gratitude flows from the director and the leads.” For already established fans of Hearon’s comedy or for audiences watching him onscreen for the first time, Trash Mountain is the kind of discovery people travel to a film festival hoping to see. A true indie with craftsmanship and heart that is bigger (much, much bigger) than its budget. “I was acting before I was ever a presence on the internet. It’s funny because sometimes I do feel that pressure of wanting people to know that I’m an artist,” says Hearon. “I do want people to know that, sure, I have a popular podcast that I’m very fucking grateful for, and I appreciate that so much, but this is what I got into all this for.” THR

articles.title: Toronto’s Best Hotel Lobbies
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Melinda Sheckells Plus Icon Melinda Sheckells Contributor View All September 11, 2026 5:15am 1 Hotel lobby in Toronto Courtesy of 1 Hotel Toronto During TIFF, a hotel lobby is rarely just a hotel lobby. It is a meeting room, holding pen, cocktail bar, talent corridor and, when the timing is right, one of the easiest places to see who has just arrived in Toronto. For 2026, the action stretches from the Ritz-Carlton and BISHA near TIFF Lightbox to Ace and 1 Hotel farther west, while Four Seasons keeps Yorkville firmly in the festival conversation. These are the lobbies worth knowing — whether you have a room key or not. The Ritz-Carlton, Toronto 181 Wellington St. W., Toronto, ON M5V 3G7 The Ritz-Carlton runs two shifts during TIFF. Mornings start with juice shots and a collagen bar before the lobby changes gears for Champagne, a bespoke cocktail bar, theatrical presentations and live music during opening weekend. EPOCH stays open until 2 a.m. on weekends, with DJs Thursday through Saturday. The hotel is also an official TIFF: The Market hotel partner, hosting private exhibitor suites. Come early to regroup between screenings; come back when the festival moves from premieres to nightcaps. Related Stories Movies Toronto Builds Its One-Stop Shop Movies Female-Led Producer Candid Broads Is Proud to Stand for New Voices, Impact and Representation The Ritz-Carlton, Toronto BISHA Hotel 80 Blue Jays Way, Toronto, ON M5V 2G3 During TIFF, BISHA becomes the House of BISHA, bringing filmmakers and talent through the hotel during the festival’s crucial opening stretch. That makes the lobby at 80 Blue Jays Way an unusually efficient place to catch the TIFF ecosystem in motion without staking out a red carpet. The location helps: TIFF Lightbox is barely a block away, while Mister C gives the lobby its own built-in cocktail scene. BISHA Hotel Ace Hotel Toronto 51 Camden St., Toronto, ON M5V 1V2 Ace returns as an official TIFF hospitality partner for 2026, with private festival events including an invite-only filmmakers’ lounge. Downstairs remains resolutely public — and arguably more interesting. Shim-Sutcliffe’s triple-height lobby hangs beneath massive poured-concrete arches, with an oak-lined bar suspended above Patrick Kriss’ Alder; Evangeline handles rooftop duty. TIFF Lightbox is about a 10-minute walk away, close enough to stay connected but far enough to escape King Street between screenings. Come here when you want TIFF energy without feeling trapped inside TIFF. Ace Hotel Toronto 1 Hotel Toronto 550 Wellington St. W., Toronto, ON M5V 2V4 The Hollywood Reporter Green Room takes over Flora Lounge Sept. 11-20, with film-inspired Don Julio cocktails and live piano on select nights. The setting trades red-carpet polish for reclaimed Toronto timber, greenery and the hotel’s nature-driven design vocabulary, while Casa Madera downstairs and Harriet’s on the roof keep the night moving without leaving the building. It is west of the Lightbox crush, but during festival week, Flora serves as the industry’s living room. 1 Hotel Toronto Four Seasons Hotel Toronto 60 Yorkville Ave., Toronto, ON M4W 0A4 King West may have the red carpets, but Yorkville remains one of TIFF’s most reliable off-camera stages. Four Seasons returns as an official festival hospitality partner, with a TIFF photography exhibition running through the lobby, a Sept. 8 kickoff at d|bar and the invite-only Road to the Golden Globes on Sept. 12. The hotel is nowhere near TIFF Lightbox, which is precisely why the crowd here feels different: less premiere-line chaos, more industry meetings, talent arrivals and drinks that turn into dinner. During TIFF, Yorkville plays the long game. Four Seasons Hotel Toronto THR

articles.title: Toronto: Ex-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau Launches Film, TV Production Banner Hope & Hard Work
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 11, 2026 5:32am Justin Trudeau and Katy Perry at the Tribeca Festival's world premiere of 'Katy Perry: The Lifetimes Tour - Live from Paris' on June 8, 2026 in New York. Stephanie Augello/Variety/Getty Images Former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau has found time away from new romantic partner Katy Perry to launch his own film and TV production banner at the Toronto Film Festival on Friday. Hope & Hard Work, to be run alongside co-founder Katie Telford, also unveiled a film and TV scripted and unscripted slate with a focus on Canadian stories for global export. “At a time when the world can feel increasingly divided, we believe in the power of great storytelling to bring people closer,” Trudeau and Telford said in a joint statement. Related Stories Lifestyle Toronto's Best Hotel Lobbies Movies How 'Obsession' Rewrote TIFF History “As a Canadian company, we have an opportunity to bring values including kindness, optimism, openness and a belief in one another to everything we make, wherever the story comes from and wherever it ultimately finds its audience,” they added. Projects already in development include Closer by Sea, an adaptation of the Perry Chafe book; and another adaptation of novelist Uzma Jalaluddin’s Detective Aunty book to be produced by Neshama Entertainment as Trudeau and Telford executive produce. The new banner will develop and produce projects across film, TV, audio and live experiences for exploitation at home and abroad by optioning popular literary works and original concepts. Hope & Hard Work also has a strategic partnership with Earth Tones, a media company run by Aliya Jasmine and Aliza Sovani, as they lead the unscripted division and produce documentaries and docuseries. Pop star Perry has been busy on the media front herself, having just premiered her upcoming documentary, Katy Perry: The Lifetimes Tour – Live from Paris , at the Tribeca Festival. Directed by Paul Dugdale, the full-length concert film captures Perry’s The Lifetimes tour, which supported the singer’s sixth studio album, 143 . Trudeau and Perry, as a couple, have made more red carpet and social media post appearances of late after the pair first sparked romance rumors in July 2025. Hope & Hard Work and its principals are represented by 3 Arts Entertainment. THR

articles.title: ‘9/11: Reunited’ Firefighter on Giuliani’s Mamdani Attack: “Leave Politics Out of It”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Seth Abramovitch Plus Icon Seth Abramovitch Senior Writer SethAbramovitch Follow Sign Up View All September 11, 2026 5:45am Bill Spade and his wife during their reunion with Carol D'Allara in 9/11 Reunited. National Geographic/Virginia Sherwood Bill Spade, one of the first responders featured in National Geographic ‘s new docuseries 9/11 : Reunited , has a message for those seeking to turn today’s 25th anniversary commemoration into a political battle: “Leave politics out of it.” Spade, the only member of Staten Island’s FDNY Rescue Company 5 crew to return home on Sept. 11, 2001, spoke to The Hollywood Reporter after former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani called on current Mayor Zohran Mamdani to stay away from the ceremony at Ground Zero. “As firefighters, we always got a call, and if it was a fire, we responded into a building,” Spade says. “Most of the time, you couldn’t see your hand in front of your face, and we were searching for victims and survivors. We never asked the color of their skin, their nationality, their beliefs or anything like that, political affiliations. We just went in and tried to save a life and help people.” Related Stories TV 9/11 Programming Guide: Everything Airing and Streaming for the 25th Anniversary Movies Six Movies Show How Hollywood Has Grappled With 9/11 “The same thing on 9/11,” he continues. “You didn’t know who you were saving or who you were helping, and it wouldn’t have mattered anyway. You were just trying to help people.” Giuliani, who led New York during the attacks, said during a Newsmax appearance that there was “no question” Mamdani should skip the commemoration and that his attendance offended him. He also drew a connection between the Muslim mayor’s faith and the ideology of the 9/11 hijackers, claiming Mamdani was concealing a desire to make Islam the country’s dominant religion. Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor, has confirmed that he will attend the ceremony and other anniversary events. He has said the focus should remain on the families “whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago” and the first responders who tried to save them. “I just try to stay out of politics with it and keep it as a day of memorializing all 2,977 people,” Spade continues. “They were killed. They didn’t die. They were killed. So leave it for a day of remembering all those people, and let’s leave politics out of it.” Spade will not be at Ground Zero on Friday. He traditionally leaves the ceremony to the victims’ families and instead accepts speaking engagements elsewhere, often accompanied by his wife and sons. This year, he will participate in a firefighters’ memorial in Coppell, Texas, before appearing in Behind the Lines: A 9/11 Story , a touring stage production in which he recounts his experience alongside Army veteran Jaymes Poling and trumpeter Dominick Farinacci. In the three-part 9/11: Reunited , survivors are brought together with people whose lives became bound to theirs during the attacks. For Spade, participating offered the chance to complete something he had wanted to do for nearly 25 years: tell the sons of NYPD Emergency Service Unit officer John D’Allara about their father’s final moments. Spade and D’Allara met in the darkness inside the North Tower, where they worked together to help trapped civilians escape. Although they knew each other for only about half an hour, the two men spoke about their wives and young sons as the catastrophe unfolded around them. D’Allara was killed when the tower collapsed. Spade met D’Allara’s widow, Carol, several years later and told her what had happened, but her sons were still young. In 9/11: Reunited , he finally sits down with the now-adult brothers and recounts the conversation he shared with their father. “It was something I felt I had to do,” Spade says. “It was always lingering in my mind that I wanted to tell them about the last moments of their dad.” The meeting, he says, “lifted” a weight he had carried for decades. D’Allara’s eldest son, John, became a Marine reservist and a nurse, while his younger son, Nicholas, followed his father into the New York Police Department. Spade has told his own story at least 500 times, including during more than 300 walking tours. He now volunteers as a docent at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, where he also speaks to graduating FDNY recruits and teachers developing classroom curricula. His two sons attended New York public schools, but Spade says their formal observance of the attacks seldom extended beyond a moment of silence. “That really bothered me, that we can’t do more in our schools than have a moment of silence,” he says. With a growing portion of the population born after the attacks, Spade believes preserving the individual stories has become more urgent. Spade says he experienced survivor’s guilt only briefly, reasoning that although he missed the men of Rescue 5, he would have missed his family even more had he died. For years, however, he had the same recurring dream. “I was in a school, and they were outside playing, all those guys,” he recalls. “I would always think, ‘Hey, I want to be outside with them playing and not here in the school.'” Then one night, his friend Mike Fiore, one of the Rescue 5 firefighters killed that day, approached the window. “He gives me the thumbs-up, like, ‘We’re okay,'” Spade says. “Since then, I’ve never had that dream. I kind of realized to move on and that they are okay.” 9/11: Reunited is streaming on Disney+ and Hulu. THR

articles.title: Toronto: Global Media Producers Urge Stronger Local Content Laws to Fend Off Streaming Domination
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 11, 2026 5:48am CEO Neal Mohan speaks onstage during the YouTube Brandcast event at Lincoln Center on May 13, 2026, in New York City. Noam Galai/Getty Images for YouTube A coalition of international media organizations has urged governments to support local producers against the “ubiquity of global streaming services” that puts commissions for diverse storytelling at risk. The call, issued at the Toronto Film Festival , comes as countries internationally have urged politicians to compel foreign streaming platforms to subsidize local media production as Netflix , Amazon and YouTube reshape the global film and TV markets. “Streaming has upended the way content gets commissioned, produced and seen, but domestic policies have not kept pace,” Reynolds Mastin, president and CEO of the Canadian Media Producers Association, representing indie producers, said in a statement that comes as TIFF kicked into gear on Friday. Related Stories Movies Toronto: Ex-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau Launches Film, TV Production Banner Hope & Hard Work Lifestyle Toronto's Best Hotel Lobbies “Canada, like so many countries around the world, needs updated laws and regulations for the digital world, and we each look to our respective governments to stand up for our cultural sovereignty,” he added. The 23 screen sector organizations signing the joint statement include European Audiovisual Production, Screen Producers Australia, Screen Producers Ireland, Animation Ireland, Swedish Film & TV Producers and AnimFrance. The call from groups representing around 750,000 workers across Canada, Australia and Europe cautioned that domestic content rules are required to shore up the production of local stories. Canadian producers recently repeated a call on the government in Ottawa to restore plans to force American companies to help subsidize domestic film and TV production as part of the larger cross-border tariffs and trade war with the U.S. The story in Europe has legacy broadcasters looking to get bigger with local government support and legislation to fend off the dominance of Netflix and Amazon on the audience side, and YouTube, Facebook and TikTok on the advertising side, or risk losing their competitive edge. The Toronto Film Festival continues through to Sept. 20. THR

articles.title: Freeze Turkey! 50 Years Later, the Wild True Story Behind ‘Charlie’s Angels‘
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The OG Angels, from left: Jaclyn Smith, Kate Jackson and Farrah Fawcett. Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Courtesy Everett Collection Once upon a time, there were three little girls who came to Hollywood — two from Texas, the other from Alabama — to become famous. And they were each, at first, assigned very captivating roles, including a nonspeaking ghost in a vampire soap opera and a pitchwoman in shaving cream and shampoo commercials. But then along came a producer who took them away from all of that, and they went to work for him. His name was Aaron. From its debut on Sept. 22, 1976, Charlie’s Angels was a phenomenon, drawing at its peak as many as 40 million viewers an episode — a massive crowd even back then, even for an Aaron Spelling show. The general opinion was that men tuned in for the bikinis and short shorts — especially when breakout star Farrah Fawcett was wearing them — while women watched for the other clothes. A few might have even turned it on just to follow the Angels’ wacky undercover assignments. Like the time they infiltrated a Roller Derby. Or the time they infiltrated a pro football cheerleading squad. Or a beauty pageant. Or a woman’s prison. Related Stories Movies Toronto: Global Media Producers Urge Stronger Local Content Laws to Fend Off Streaming Domination General News '9/11: Reunited' Firefighter on Giuliani's Mamdani Attack: "Leave Politics Out of It" Critics hated it. “When the publicity started, there was all of this criticism leveled about the show, that it was ‘jiggle TV,’ ” recalls Spelling’s widow, Candy. “Aaron didn’t take it personally, he really didn’t. He said, ‘Oh, good — more publicity.’ “ “You have to remember that ABC was like the Fox of its time,” adds David Bianculli, a veteran television critic and a co-host of NPR’s Fresh Air . “It was the youngest, smallest network. And the idea was: How do you get an audience as fast as possible? You do it by appealing to young people with attention-getting programming.” While maybe not what anyone would call a feminist show, Charlie’s Angels did come along right when women were first being liberated on network TV. In 1974, Angie Dickinson took the title role in NBC’s Police Woman ; Lynda Carter debuted in Wonder Woman in 1975, followed by Lindsay Wagner in The Bionic Woman , a spinoff of ABC’s popular The Six Million Dollar Man , in January 1976. Charlie’s Angels would transcend them all — and still, 50 years later, stands as an odd yet enduring pop cultural force that continues to bounce and jiggle back onto screens. Drew Barrymore launched two blockbuster movies based on the show in the early aughts, while Elizabeth Banks attempted a somewhat less successful relaunch in 2019. Just this past February, Sony announced it had hired The Proposal scribe Peter Chiarelli to pen a new Angels script. Half a century since its premiere, young women — and a fair number of gay men — are still doing the iconic “Angels pose” on their social media feeds, while the show remains the subject of a million memes and TikToks. Its plotlines still get endlessly dissected by feminist scholars, critics and influencers who continue to mine its fluffy 109 episodes for the deeper meaning behind such dialogue as “Freeze, turkey!” “This wasn’t Shakespeare,” admits Jaclyn Smith, who, of course, played Kelly Garrett, one of the original Angels. “It was make-believe. And you know what? The audience needed illusion. They loved illusion. We need escapes. And Charlie’s Angels was an escape.” Clockwise from top left: Cheryl Ladd signed autographs on set during season two; Fawcett’s ubiquitous red bathing suit poster; Prince Charles visited the Angels on the Fox lot in 1977; Fawcett infiltrated a Roller Derby team in season one; Fawcett showing a bad guy her foot; a season three episode with Fawcett (second from left) in a guest star role alongside her replacement, Ladd. Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Courtesy Everett Collection; Getty Images *** Spelling was already riding a wave of success during the early 1970s, having launched a series of well-rated television films and an ABC police procedural titled The Rookies . Over the course of the next two decades, into the 1980s, he’d dominate the airwaves like no other producer, with such signature frothy fare as Fantasy Island , Hart to Hart , The Love Boat and, most notably, the blockbuster primetime soap Dynasty . With The Rookies ending in early 1976, Spelling and his producing partner Leonard Goldberg were on the hunt for a starring vehicle for Kate Jackson, who had arrived on The Rookies after a small but notable part on the early ’70s horror drama Dark Shadows . They landed on a concept titled The Alley Cats , about three gorgeous dominatrix- telegraphing detectives named Alison, Lee and Catherine (as in Al-Lee-Cat). When Spelling pitched the idea to ABC’s then-vp primetime, Barry Diller, he told Spelling, “You should be ashamed of yourself.” But when freewheeling Fred Silverman took over the network a year later, the concept got a green light, with some minor adjustments. The reconceived idea now revolved around three comely policewomen who ditch their dead-end jobs to go work as private eyes for a boss they never see. “I thought it was a terrific idea,” says Robert Wagner, now 96, who ended up partnering on the show as part of the deal Spelling and Goldberg struck with ABC. “I thought the character of Townsend hiring these three ladies — it all had great possibility.” The Alley Cats became Charlie’s Angels . Husky-voiced Jackson would play Sabrina Duncan, the trio’s wiry leader and ersatz brain; Fawcett was cast as Jill Munroe, the quintessential California beach girl, sporty and evincing a million-watt smile. Rounding out the crew was Smith as smoldering ingenue Kelly Garrett (Smith originally was cast as Sabrina, until Jackson decided the role was better for her). For the never-seen Charlie, the producers hired Oscar winner Gig Young, who lost the part when he showed up to his taping drunk; John Forsythe stepped in to voice the wolfish detective agency owner. Rounding out the cast: David Ogden Stiers as the agency’s stuffy attorney, Scott Woodville, and then, later, David Doyle as the doughy, frog-voiced comic relief, assistant John Bosley. Test audiences hated the pilot, a shambolic, overly convoluted mess about a missing heiress. ABC, convinced the show was going nowhere, dispatched it as a throwaway TV movie in March 1976. Except the telefilm proved to be a smash: 30 million people tuned in, a whopping 49 percent of viewers. The network brass was shocked, but Jackson wasn’t. “I had never heard of anything like it before. And it seemed like it might work,” she says today. “Obviously, when you start a show like that, you have no idea whether it’s going to hit or not. But I always thought it was going to be successful.” The freshman show finished its initial 1976-77 season ranked fifth in the Nielsens, a breath behind CBS’ powerhouse M*A*S*H . The Angels landed on the cover of Time , and Fawcett landed in a red bathing suit on one of the most ubiquitous posters of all time. It sold 7 million copies and helped launch a whole industry of ancillary Charlie’s Angels products — dolls, trading cards, lunch boxes, hair care sets — that raked in tens of millions of dollars. But then, disaster. Just before production on season two was scheduled to begin, Fawcett announced she was quitting the show. To this day, there isn’t complete clarity on why she decided to leave. But there is no shortage of theories. Mike Pringel, who served as Fawcett’s assistant and publicist and has written two books on Angels history, says she wanted more money, “what she was worth,” as he puts it. (Fawcett and Smith earned just $5,000 an episode that first season, while Jackson made $10,000). It’s also likely that at that point Fawcett had bigger screen ambitions (although her first film after leaving Angels was Somebody Killed Her Husband with Jeff Bridges, which was such a bomb that Hollywood nicknamed it “Somebody Killed Her Career”). Jackson, though, blames Spelling, whose onerous work schedule kept his Angels locked in a gilded cage. “He didn’t want us to leave the lot. We waited all day because he didn’t want us to meet a producer and be offered something and think we were movie stars. We sat in our trailers, hours and hours,” she says. “It didn’t have to be that way.” Smith had spied trouble brewing — she remembers Fawcett kept casually telling her that she had never actually signed her contract — but was still taken by surprise. “When we had the [first-season] wrap party, we were all like a team and having fun and talking,” she says. “She never brought it up that she was really going to carry through. I guess I thought at the last minute she was going to change her mind.” Jackson says that while there was blame “on both sides” for the split — Fawcett’s failing marriage to Lee Majors undoubtedly played a role, as did Spelling’s sometimes staggering greed — “For Aaron to want a piece of that poster …” Jackson says with disbelief, citing Spelling’s desire for a cut of Fawcett’s bathing suit image profits. “Not want it, but demand it. She wasn’t going to say yes.” Spelling responded to Fawcett’s resignation by taking her to court in a breach of contract case that was splashed all over the tabloids; it was eventually settled when Fawcett reluctantly agreed to return for six guest appearances spread out over seasons three and four. But well before all of that, Spelling knew he’d need to find an actress who could replace Fawcett in season two. He homed in on spunky Cheryl Ladd, whose most notable credit to that point had been voicing one of the band members on the kiddie cartoon Josie and the Pussycats . Ladd didn’t want the job at first. But Spelling made his pitch and Ladd ultimately signed on to play Kris Munroe, bubbly kid sister of the flown-the-coop Jill. “Trying to replace Farrah? I don’t know who’s going to be brave enough to try that,” she says, recalling how she was a wreck on the first day of shooting. “I said to myself, ‘Oh man, I hope this works.’ “ Even without Fawcett, ratings stayed high in season two, possibly because Spelling kept reducing Ladd’s wardrobe to a series of diminishing bikinis. “He really, really liked my bod,” she says, laughing. “What can I say? I mean, it’s not a terrible thing. But at the same time, I said, ‘OK, Aaron, fine. I’m fine with a bikini. But only if we’re on a beach or on a boat. You have to give me that much.’” The other Angels, though, were growing increasingly restless, and not just about the outfits. Jackson was particularly vocal in her criticism of the show’s shallow scripts, which featured plotlines about them going undercover as French maids, showgirls, lifeguards and, perhaps most infamously, prison inmates. Also, Jackson couldn’t hide her deep disappointment at Fawcett’s departure, which Ladd says she took out on her. “She wasn’t warm to me,” Ladd says. “I was hoping things would get better. But I was not her favorite. She wanted Farrah. And I think she was really pissed off that Farrah left. So she had some issues there with all that change. I just kind of did my work and was pleasant.” “Oh, boy,” Smith says when I ask about the rift between Jackson and Ladd. “It was not a relationship. It was never the camaraderie of the first three. And I love Cheryl. I think she did a great job. But it was very intimidating. Those were very difficult shoes to fill.” Jackson, for her part, sounds like she might finally be ready to bury the hatchet. “The first year was just fun,” she says. “We all got along so well. And Farrah and I had the same sense of humor. And I was just disappointed that we weren’t all going to be together another year or two or three. But it worked out fine.” *** Jackson on set for the “Circus of Terror” episode, which aired in October 1977; Tanya Roberts (left), Smith and Ladd; Ladd (left), Smith and Shelley Hack in 1979; Gene Barry with Roberts in season five’s “Hula Angels,” which aired in 1981; and David Doyle as assistant John Bosley with Hack in 1980’s “Dancin’ Angels” episode. Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Courtesy Everett Collection; Getty Images As it turned out, Fawcett wasn’t the only one with big-screen dreams. Jackson was thinking about making the jump to features as well. And she had a pretty spectacular offer, from Dustin Hoffman no less. Hoffman wanted to cast Jackson in a theatrical film about a searing divorce titled Kramer vs. Kramer , and he made assurances that she could film her part around her Angels commitment. Indeed, Kramer producers revised the film’s production schedule “either four or five times” to accommodate her Angels commitment, Jackson remembers. But each time, Spelling found a reason it wouldn’t work. “Until finally Dustin called and said, ‘He’s not going to let you do it,’ ” says Jackson. A relatively unknown actress by the name of Meryl Streep ended up getting the Kramer vs. Kramer role — and won her first Oscar for it. Jackson, not surprisingly, was devastated. “I said to myself, ‘I’ll finish the season. But that’s it. I’m leaving after this.’ I pretty much let Aaron know. He said, ‘You can’t quit. You’re fired.’ “ By that time, Spelling may have had his own reasons for letting Jackson go. By the end of the 1978-79 season, Charlie’s Angels had dropped out of the top 10, tumbling from fourth to 12th. He may have seen Jackson’s departure as a chance to revive interest in the series, an opportunity to refresh the franchise. And he could think of no better way to do that than with a big, splashy hunt for a new Angel. Indeed, he would undertake the biggest actress search since Scarlett O’Hara. Not everyone was enthusiastic. “When Kate left, it was never the same for me,” says Smith. “I adored Aaron, and I wanted to uphold my contract. But all the changing Angels … the show wasn’t as fresh. They kept thinking a new Angel would bring it. They should have concentrated more on the scripts.” Amazingly, though, Spelling’s Angel hunt actually worked, at least for a time. Some 5,000 actresses were considered amid months of hysterical media prognosticating on who would wear the invisible halo next. “Aaron loved the attention,” says Candy Spelling. Henry Winkler and Cheryl Ladd co-hosted the Emmy Awards in 1979. Fawcett, Jackson and Smith fete Aaron Spelling at a tribute for the producer. Things went south, though, when Fawcett left Charlie’s Angels right before production on season two began. Says Jackson: “When we had the [first-season] wrap party, we were all like a team and having fun. Farrah never brought it up that she was really going to carry through. I thought at the last minute she was going to change her mind.” Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Getty Images *** Among those 5,000 wannabe Angels were some then-unknown actresses with such names as Michelle Pfeiffer, Barbara Bach, Melanie Griffith, Kathie Lee Gifford and Connie Sellecca. But the one who landed the role of Tiffany Welles was a perfume model by the name of Shelley Hack. Lithe, confident and oozing breezy elegance, Hack was best known as the face of Revlon’s Charlie perfume in a series of ads in which she whirled her way through various cityscapes while being serenaded by jazz pianist Bobby Short. The show’s designer, Nolan Miller, lobbied hard for Hack, whose casting offered him a chance to ditch Jackson’s turtleneck-and-jeans sensibility for high fashion. The style in season four remains the most dazzling of the series. The problem was that the clothes proved far more interesting than the plots. That’s because Spelling’s star search — and his desire to wring it for publicity for as long as he could — meant the show’s writers had no idea who they’d be writing dialogue for as they prepared the new season. As a result, for the first 10 episodes, Hack barely spoke a word. Her Tiffany was largely a vacant, immaculately tailored mannequin serving as Townsend agency décor. Another issue: Smith and Ladd, both going through divorces, wanted more time off. Apparently having finally learned his lesson, Spelling accommodated them. But that meant the narrative approach of the show had to focus more on one Angel per episode, with the other two sidelined as window dressing. It was the complete antithesis of the show’s premise. “Aaron’s concept was three girls on the screen at all times.
