That was the power of our show,” Smith says. “The sisterhood dwindled.” Carrying the expectations of a ratings rebound on her slender shoulders, Hack found herself isolated — and an easy target for haters who blamed the series’ continued ratings slide on her. Recalls Candy Spelling, “I’m the one that kept saying to Aaron, ‘Shelley Hack isn’t going to work.’ She wasn’t really an actress. She was a model. And the audience didn’t like her.” Adds Ladd: “She didn’t get enough to say. And I think it was a lot for her to just jump in there. It just all started crumbling around us, and I could feel it. I felt bad for her.” Fawcett skateboarded in season one; Smith filming in Vail, Colorado; Ladd still signing autographs; the Angels joined a chain gang during season one; Spelling with Ladd, Jackson and Smith in 1978. Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Courtesy Everett Collection; Getty Images Hack rallied in the latter half of the season, with the writers finally rounding her into more of a three-dimensional character. But she was abruptly dumped toward the end of the season, anyway, with three episodes still left to film. She was not happy about it and wasn’t shy about saying so in public. “I feel like I’ve been sunbathing on Three Mile Island,” she told People after the sacking was announced. “I met her and we talked about it,” Jackson recalls. “She said it felt personal. There’d be some event and the three of them were invited, but they sat her behind a big concrete post or something. She’s really smart and funny. There was no reason to treat her that badly.” Another Angel casting call was launched. This one would be quicker — only 2,000 considered. The winner this time was Tanya Roberts, a former Clairol and Ultra Brite model whom Spelling once again squeezed into ever-more-microscopic bikinis. Roberts proved to be a hurricane in heels. “She was a pistol,” Ladd says. “She had a foul mouth and would just say the most outrageous crap.” But she wasn’t Farrah. Or Kate. Or even Cheryl. By 1981, the show’s novelty had also largely worn off and the culture had mostly moved on. “When you think about its structure, the Angels were still responsible to this unseen pimp-like boss who would send them off on an assignment that would require at least one of them to be a prostitute or a porn star or a showgirl,” Fresh Air ‘s TV critic Bianculli recontextualizes the series. “It was at least equally exploitation as it was power.” Whatever it was, by the end of season five, the show fell to 59th in the ratings — out of 65. ABC canceled it, sending the Angels to network TV heaven (also known as syndicated reruns). “It had lost the magic,” Smith says wistfully. “But the magic at first was pretty amazing and pretty special.” And, it turns out, pretty durable, too. Spelling is gone — he died in 2006 — and so, of course, is Fawcett, who died three years later, as well as Roberts, who died in 2021. Weirdly, though, the show they and all the other Angels made together a half century ago — that came to define not only their careers but the entire era — somehow keeps finding its way back to our screens in one incarnation or another. Apparently, as so many polyester-clad bad guys discovered on ABC all those decades ago, Angels can’t be killed. Jaclyn Smith, Farrah Fawcett and Kate Jackson. Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Courtesy Everett Collection This story appeared in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: ‘Krux’ Director Tony Vahl Combines Practical Magic With Post-WWII Taboo: ‘A Belief Can Help You – or It Can Destroy You”
articles.full_text: Sep 11, 2026 5:33am PT ‘Krux’ Director Tony Vahl Combines Practical Magic With Post-WWII Taboo: ‘A Belief Can Help You – or It Can Destroy You” By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest ‘Krux’ Director Tony Vahl Combines Practical Magic With Post-WWII Taboo: ‘A Belief Can Help You – or It Can Destroy You” 31 minutes ago ‘Viva Carmen’ Reveals Clip Featuring Singer Silvia Pérez Cruz – and Brand New Song – Ahead of North American Premiere at TIFF (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Venice Final Cut Winner Machérie Ekwa Bahango on ‘Madi Makambu’ and Why She Wants Congo to Be Seen: ‘We’re a Great Nation That Needs to Write Its Own History’ 3 hours ago See All 'Krux' ©Lucasz_Bak The “Practical Magic 2” press tour might be taking over the world, but Tony Vahl ’s impressive feature debut “ Krux ” also finds space for the supernatural. Set in the final days of the WWII and premiering at TIFF and San Sebastián, it portrays a German village waiting for the inevitable: the arrival of Soviet troops. Some of its inhabitants look for ominous signs and listen to prophecies. Others don’t want to wait for a destiny they believe would be worse than death. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro “My grandmother was very superstitious. She used to tell me that you shouldn’t hang laundry on New Year’s Eve because someone might then hang themselves. I was really fascinated by this,” Vahl tells Variety . Popular on Variety “In the film, the priest has his religion. The mayor – his Nazi cult. People always need something they can hold onto. A belief is such a powerful thing. It can help you – or it can destroy you.” While Vahl leaves certain things unsaid – “I didn’t want to say ‘Russians’ or limit it to just one nation” – the fear is real. “There’s something in the air and you can’t define it,” she says. “When I was little, I would go to the riverbank with my grandmother. At that time, people didn’t talk much about the war. But my grandmother was different. She told me that in the old days, corpses would float down the river. Then she said: ‘People would go in the water.’ I didn’t understand what it meant. It sounded like a fairy tale – and a horror movie. But I remember how it made me feel. It never left me.” As the Third Reich collapsed, mass suicides claimed the lives of thousands of Germans. For the longest time, nobody talked about it. “It was a taboo. Then, about 10 years ago, Florian Huber wrote about it [in ‘Promise Me You’ll Shoot Yourself’]. I realized: ‘Oh, it’s not a unique story. It was happening all over Germany’.” In the film, starring Jella Haase, Frida-Lovisa Hamann, Clemens Schick and Lukas Miko, mass panic ensues and the unthinkable happens. “I would ask myself: ‘How could parents kill their own children?’ But they really believed that the future would bring nothing good,” says Vahl. “I wanted to find an ethical way to tell this story. If I’m being honest, all my movies are about death, but I didn’t want to exploit it. I wanted to keep certain things in the shadows because our imagination can make things even more terrifying.” Interestingly enough, Vahl doesn’t care much for war movies. “I’m not a fan, and we have a lot of them in Germany. I never wanted to make a typical war movie with explosions and soldiers. I studied psychology, so I’m more interested in people’s mentality and how we operate in extreme situations. This film is not a historical lesson, but rather a story about humanity and morality.” Keeping this in mind, she set out to uncover lesser-known secrets from that time. Just like the so-called “steel helmet wedding” (pictured) where a helmet stood in for the absent – or dead – groom. “It really happened, even though there aren’t many photos left,” she says. “I have so much respect for history and at the beginning, I focused on that more. But I’m also a big genre fan and yes, I like having some secrets. These characters have no backstories, and things just keep getting darker, like a spiral.” “I’m a big Steve McQueen fan and he used to talk about ‘body cinema’. You feel it in your gut. That was my main approach, too. I know this movie isn’t easy to watch, but I wanted to leave people with the same feeling I had after ‘Hunger,’ ‘White Ribbon’ or even ‘ The Zone of Interest .’ You are asking yourself: ‘What is this film doing to me’?” Fittingly enough, “The Zone of Interest” producer Ewa Puszczyńska is also behind “Krux” – as are Martina Haubrich, Claudia Schröter and Peter Hartwig. A Cala Filmproduktion, Extreme Emotions and Kineo Film production, it’s sold by Global Constellation. Vahl still did her research, however. For over a year. “I was always in the library, but it wasn’t easy to find information about that time. Then, I read Ian Kershaw’s ‘The End: Hitler’s Germany, 1944 – 45’ and he described the Germans as ‘dead inside’,” she says. “They didn’t question these things because they were brainwashed. There was this death cult, this hero cult. They had odd words like kadavergehorsam , which means ‘cadaver-like obedience’. The government, or the state, trained people to be without will, without a body, and without the freedom to ask questions.” She adds: “This is what happens in dictatorships. For some people, it’s easier – at least they have someone to follow. They need this kind of leadership. It happens again and again, and now we have the same situation in Germany.” Just before the interview, the far-right party AfD [Alternative für Deutschland] won big in German regional election. “It makes me really nervous,” she admits. “There’s a nice quote from Ingeborg Bachmann: ‘History teaches but has no pupils’.” Hansal Mehta, Siddharth Bodke on ‘Scam 2010’ as First Look Unveiled for SonyLIV Series: ‘A Story About Ambition, Influence and Arrogance’ (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Shark Tank India’ Sets Season 6 With Parrot Campaign on SonyLIV (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... articles.title: Def Leppard Documentary ‘Long Live Def Leppard’ Coming to Theaters in 2027 From Bleecker Street’s Crosswalk
articles.full_text: Sep 11, 2026 5:45am PT Def Leppard Documentary ‘Long Live Def Leppard’ Coming to Theaters in 2027 From Bleecker Street’s Crosswalk By Angelique Jackson Plus Icon Angelique Jackson angelique814 Latest Def Leppard Documentary ‘Long Live Def Leppard’ Coming to Theaters in 2027 From Bleecker Street’s Crosswalk 31 minutes ago TIFF Opens With Siân Heder’s Crowd-Pleasing ‘Being Heumann’ — and Apple Has Its Next Oscar Contender 9 hours ago Andrew Scott to Receive Mill Valley Film Festival’s Acting Award for ‘Elsinore’ (EXCLUSIVE) 20 hours ago See All Ross Halfin Def Leppard ‘s epic journey from Sheffield to global rock superstardom is getting the documentary treatment from filmmaker Jeff Feuerzeig (“The Devil and Daniel Johnston,” “Author: The JT LeRoy Story”). “Long Live Def Leppard” is the first authorized feature-length documentary about the British band, which has sold more than 110 million albums worldwide and been inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Bleecker Street’s event cinema division Crosswalk has acquired the North American rights to the doc and slated the film for an early 2027 theatrical release. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro “In the summer of ’81, after reading about Def Leppard in Creem, I saw the not-yet-famous band open for Ozzy Osbourne on his first Blizzard of Ozz tour at Asbury Park’s Convention Hall,” Feuerzeig said in a press release announcing the acquisition. “These young lads from working-class Sheffield were punching far above their weight and playing for keeps. I was smitten, a fan for life. It has been an honor to collaborate with the guys and bring their unique, heartwarming, and often humorous underdog story to the screen. This is not your typical sex, drugs, and rock ’n’ roll tale. Long live Def Leppard, indeed!” Popular on Variety Produced in close collaboration with the band, the documentary aims to “take fans on a wild ride into the world of this iconic English rock band, with never-before-seen footage and unparalleled access to its members”: Joe Elliott (vocals), Phil Collen (guitar), Rick Savage (bass), Vivian Campbell (guitar) and Rick Allen (drums). “After exploding onto the global rock scene with their hit albums ‘Pyromania‘ and ‘Hysteria,‘ the band faced two devastating chapters: drummer Rick Allen’s life-altering accident, which cost him his arm, and the loss of guitarist Steve Clark, whose anthemic and dynamic riffs earned him a permanent place among the guitar legends of all time,” a synopsis explains. “Those tragedies became defining moments in the band’s history, as Def Leppard rebuilt themselves and went on to become one of the most enduring forces in rock.” “Def Leppard is a once-in-a-lifetime rock band, whose story and live performances demand to be seen and heard on the big screen,” adds Bleecker Street CEO Kent Sanderson. “Longtime fans and those just being introduced to the group are going to be blown away by this high-energy, compelling, and ultimately moving look into this legendary band.” Sobey Road Entertainment served as lead financier on “Long Live Def Leppard.” The film was executive produced by Nigel Sinclair and Cassidy Hartmann (of White Horse Pictures); Stuart Goldstein and Rosie Taylor (Vice Studios); Andrew Trapani (Sobey Road Entertainment); Emmerson G. Farrell; David Sze; David B. Kirk; Bruce Resnikoff and Adam Barker (Universal Music Group); Lawrence Mestel; Natalia Nastaskin and Robert Dippold (Primary Wave Music); Todd Lieberman (Hidden Pictures); Brian Monaco (Sony Music Publishing); and Mike Kobayashi (CSM Management). Vice Studios’ Amy Rattray serves as line producer. articles.full_text: Sep 11, 2026 5:45am PT 9/11 News Broadcasts: How the ‘Today’ Show, NY1, Fox News and More Covered the Attacks in Real Time By William Earl Plus Icon William Earl @beautifulbill Latest 9/11 News Broadcasts: How the ‘Today’ Show, NY1, Fox News and More Covered the Attacks in Real Time 31 minutes ago Is ‘Vintage Violence’ the Future of Movies? Inside the Frantic Chase Movie Built for Phone-Addicted Audiences: It’s a ‘New Approach to Viewing’ 19 hours ago How ‘River’ Director Joshua Giuliano Made a ‘Beautiful, Brutal’ Slasher With Two Modern Scream Queens and a ‘Terrifying’ Villain 21 hours ago See All Courtesy of NY1 On the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11, YouTube serves as a fascinating time capsule for news coverage from that day, during which shocked anchors documented the national tragedy in real time. American Airlines Flight 11 was flown by a terrorist into the North Tower of the World Trade Center at 8:46 a.m. ET on that day, and it was the first signal for news broadcasters to pivot to live coverage. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro On New York’s local NY1 , Pat Kiernan had just wrapped his popular “In the Papers” segment when the feed switched to a live shot of the smoking World Trade Center. During CBS’ “The Early Show,” Jane Clayson hosted the show’s “Week of Wishes” segment before Bryant Gumbel broke in to share his first news update. Popular on Variety NBC had “ Today ” anchors Katie Couric and Matt Lauer spearhead breaking analysis. “Fox and Friends” coverage was preceded by a backstage look at Matchbox 20 on tour, a sobering reminder that the day began just like any other. Nearly 3,000 victims were killed in the attacks, with thousands more estimated to have died as a result of health issues tied to the aftermath. For the 25th anniversary of the tragedy, networks are planning comprehensive coverage and tributes, including a special edition of “Fox and Friends” with Brian Kilmeade, Ainsley Earhardt, Steve Doocy and Lawrence Jones; CNN is planning live commemorative coverage; ABC News will have segments from David Muir, Robin Roberts and Diane Sawyer; Michael Strahan hosts Hulu documentary “ 9/11 : United We Stand — 25 Years Later”; and NBC News will present never-before-seen footage from its 9/11 coverage in a documentary special on “Dateline.” Watch the Sept. 11, 2001, broadcasts below. articles.title: New Zealand Set to Unveil Tri-Nation Indigenous Co-Production Initiative at Toronto (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 11, 2026 5:45am PT New Zealand Set to Unveil Tri-Nation Indigenous Co-Production Initiative at Toronto (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest New Zealand Set to Unveil Tri-Nation Indigenous Co-Production Initiative at Toronto (EXCLUSIVE) 31 minutes ago Oscars: Singapore Selects Anthony Chen’s ‘We Are All Strangers’ for International Feature Race 4 hours ago San Sebastian Competition Title ‘Border’ Boards Reel Suspects for Global Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago See All New Zealand Film Commission New Zealand is set to announce a first-of-its-kind Indigenous co-production initiative at the Toronto Film Festival , New Zealand Film Commission CEO Annie Murray tells Variety . The pact will bring together Māori filmmakers from New Zealand, Aboriginal filmmakers from Australia and Indigenous Canadian filmmakers in a program of collaborative storytelling that none of the three countries could mount alone. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro “They’re not beginning filmmakers, these are mid-career filmmakers who will collaborate together on stories, working in wānanga, we call them, but very intensive workshops together in each country,” Murray says. Popular on Variety The announcement is expected on Saturday, the same day NZFC head of funding Ainsley Gardiner — a filmmaker and Oscar nominee who served as a co-producer on the first Indigenous Canada-New Zealand co-production, “Night Raiders” (2021) — participates in the From Pitch to Partner: Global Co-Production Showcase alongside reps from Telefilm Canada and Eurimages. For Murray, the initiative reflects a clear creative principle. “The real base of successful co-production is a shared creative purpose,” she says. “A strong base of mutual trust, creative alignment — it’s about creating something together that neither party could do on their own.” New Zealand arrives at TIFF with three projects spanning a wide range of scale and approach. Debut feature “God Bless You, Mr. Kopu,” from filmmaker Alex Liu, is presented by Murray as evidence of a new generation of confident, culturally specific New Zealand voices. “What it gives you is a really unique take on modern New Zealand through a cultural lens,” she says. “It shows you very clearly on screen how super diverse New Zealand is culturally.” “Man of Valor,” directed by Tearepa Kahi and screening as part of TIFF: The Market, follows Māori World War II hero Sgt. Haane during the Battle of Takrouna in Tunisia. Murray points to the film’s authenticity as the source of its power. “It works because it’s authentic,” she says, “and authenticity resonates locally and internationally.” The third project, “ Tenzing ,“ which tells the story of how Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first reached the summit of Mount Everest, represents the international co-production end of the spectrum, produced through New Zealand’s screen production rebate and filmed across multiple countries. Across all three, Murray sees a common thread: the projects most likely to travel are those most confident in their point of origin. “The strongest stories come from a cultural confidence and a cultural pride,” she says, “and you find that in New Zealand.” On the policy front, NZFC’s recent changes to the New Zealand Screen Production Rebate are generating early traction. The minimum qualifying spend threshold for the 20% cash rebate was reduced from NZ$15 million ($8.7 million) to NZ$4 million ($2.3 million) — opening the incentive to independent and mid-budget productions that had previously found New Zealand out of reach. Murray says the first qualifying project under the new settings has already been secured, with others in advanced consideration. “It’s creating opportunities, too, for our actors,” she says. “These are films in the kind of anything from $15 million to $30 million U.S. dollars that wouldn’t have the budget to bring everybody in with them that the bigger-budget productions can do, so they are looking to source locally.” Murray frames New Zealand’s broader international appeal in terms that go beyond logistics and locations. “We have a way of doing business that is very inclusive, and celebrates diversity, and a warmth that makes it a really, really fantastic place to make creative works,” she says. “They always want to come back to do more.” ‘Shark Tank India’ Sets Season 6 With Parrot Campaign on SonyLIV (EXCLUSIVE) Hansal Mehta, Siddharth Bodke on ‘Scam 2010’ as First Look Unveiled for SonyLIV Series: ‘A Story About Ambition, Influence and Arrogance’ (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... articles.title: ‘In Alaska’ Producer Tyler Hagan Wins CMPA’s Feature Producer Indiescreen Award at Toronto Film Festival
articles.full_text: Sep 11, 2026 5:45am PT ‘In Alaska’ Producer Tyler Hagan Wins CMPA’s Feature Producer Indiescreen Award at Toronto Film Festival Anthony Cauchy scoops emerging producer award, KOTV takes TV producer award By Jennie Punter Plus Icon Jennie Punter Latest ‘The Stunt Driver’ Helmer Michael Dowse on Working With Jay Baruchel, Building a Ramp and a Rocket Car: ‘It Wasn’t for the Faint of Heart’ 1 hour ago Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: ‘We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Toronto’s Indigenous Film and Industry Slates Aim to Grow Audiences and Spark Biz by Reflecting the Diversity of Global Screen Culture 1 day ago See All L-R: Tyler Hagan (Experimental Forest Films), Louis Morissette (KOTV), Anthony Cauchy (Locomotive Media) Tyler Hagan of Experimental Forest Films has won the Canadian Media Producers Association ’s (CMPA) 2026 Feature Film Producer Indiescreen Award. The plaudit was announced Sept. 10 at the Indiescreen Awards, held at a packed industry event and ceremony at the Sutton Place Hotel on the opening evening of the 51st Toronto Film Festival . The award, which recognizes a producer’s filmmaking accomplishments over the course of their career, comes with a C$20,000 (US$14,461) cash prize and is presented in partnership with Telefilm Canada . Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro Recognized by the jury for his dedication to mentorship, sustainable production and community-building, as well as his passionate advocacy for emerging and underrepresented filmmakers, Hagan elevates exciting new Canadian cinema artists by nurturing talent and presenting their films at prestigious international festivals and markets. Popular on Variety Hagan’s most recent producing credits include “In Alaska” and “Seventeen,” both of which are premiering at this year’s Toronto Film Festival. He was the recipient of the Kevin Tierney Emerging Producer Indiescreen Award in 2022 for “Until The Branches Bend.” Anthony Cauchy (Locomotive Media) scooped the CMPA’s 2026 Kevin Tierney Emerging Producer Indiescreen Award, which recognizes the impressive potential of an up-and-coming producer and comes with a C$10,000 prize (US$7,230). Cauchy was recognized for his ambition in bringing French-language storytelling with impressive craft and production value to Western Canada. Through “Surf Bay, Côte Ouest,” the first francophone series filmed in British Columbia, the Vancouver-based producer showcases strong storytelling instincts and a drive to create Canadian work that crosses linguistic and regional boundaries. KOTV, headed by president Louis Morissette, took the CMPA’s 2026 TV Producer Indiescreen Award. Founded in 2011, the Quebec-based company was recognized for the depth and versatility of its body of work, which spans English and French-language productions across an array of genres and formats. “Plan B,” an innovative psychological drama starring Patrick J. Adams that has run multiple seasons and been successfully adapted for English-language audiences, was cited as a testament to that creative ambition. Morissette accepted the award and $20,000 (US$14,461) prize, which was presented in partnership with the Canada Media Fund. “At a time when cultural sovereignty has never mattered more, this year’s Indiescreen Award winners are seizing the moment,” CMPA President and CEO Reynolds Mastin said. “Each winner represents what makes Canadian independent production so exciting right now, from ambition and versatility to a willingness to push Canadian stories further than ever before. Thank you for reminding us of what we’re fighting for at this critical moment in our nation’s history.” The award winners were selected by three national juries, chaired by last year’s winners. The CMPA is the country’s leading member-based advocacy organization for independent producers. articles.title: Global Africa Hub at TIFF Market Seeks to Boost Visibility — and Deals — for African Filmmakers in Toronto: ‘It’s Our Moment’
articles.full_text: Sep 11, 2026 5:55am PT Global Africa Hub at TIFF Market Seeks to Boost Visibility — and Deals — for African Filmmakers in Toronto: ‘It’s Our Moment’ By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest Telekom Srbija’s Content Head on Blueprint for Turning Serbian Production Powerhouse Into Global Player 1 day ago Serbian Sci-Fi Epic ‘Sanctuary,’ Starring ‘The Handmaid’s Tale’s’ Nina Kiri, Acquired for U.S. Distribution (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Lav Diaz on the Hunt for Truth in ‘An Entry Into the Sadness of a Portuguese Woman,’ Third Chapter of His Acclaimed Hermes Trilogy (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago See All Courtesy of Neon, Cannes Film Festival The first-ever Toronto film market, running as part of the Toronto Film Festival , will have a robust contingent of African filmmakers, executives and industry professionals on the ground. Producers at TIFF: The Market look to capitalize on the festival’s historically strong position as a platform for some of the continent’s most diverse and exciting talents. Charles Tremblay, who heads up the market, says the event is “is designed to build on the festival’s legacy of creating access and opportunities for global content to be discovered and relevant topics to be explored. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro “We’re excited to continue our long-standing and fruitful relationship with the African continent through a variety of market initiatives for companies and creatives,” he says. “We’re very interested in the financing, production and distribution landscape in the continent at the moment … [and] our Summit programming echoes this interest.” Popular on Variety Anchoring the activities will be the Global Africa Hub, a pavilion for African creatives sponsored by Canex Creations, the pan-African initiative launched by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) to finance, support and promote Africa’s creative and cultural industries. The hub is presented in partnership with Nigerian private equity firm MBO Capital, South African genre powerhouse Gambit Films, Nigerian production outfit Narratives Entertainment, and leading Nigerian production and distribution company FilmOne. Also exhibiting will be the International Salon for Audiovisual Content (SICA), a burgeoning trade fair and business hub that takes place every year in Ivory Coast. Toronto has long been one of the international industry’s leading platforms for African cinema, and this year is proving to be no exception, with new titles from South Africa’s John Trengove (“The Smell of Apples”) and Jenna Cato Bass (“Future Tense”), as well as the latest from Nigerian mogul Mo Abudu ’s EbonyLife Films (“The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives”), among the anticipated African titles set to debut. The festival will also host the North American premiere of Nigerian directing duo Arie and Chuko Esiri’s “Clarissa,” the star-studded, Lagos-set adaptation of Virginia Woolf’s “Mrs. Dalloway” that was acquired by Neon and premiered in Cannes. For Canex Creations CEO Osahon Akpata, the inaugural TIFF bazaar offers an opportunity for the pan-African investment platform to “create a bridge” between African filmmakers and the global industry. “Access to markets remains a challenge [for African filmmakers],” Akpata tells Variety . “Navigating these markets is not always something that we’re well-prepared for, and it affects our ability to get good outcomes.” One of the ways in which the TIFF partnership looks to give filmmakers a boost is through market screenings of African titles for key North American acquisition and distribution executives. “We will do as much as we can to connect them to commercial opportunities,” says Akpata. Among the works in progress to be featured are “The Black Book 2: Old Scores,” director Editi Effiong’s sequel to his blockbuster Netflix action hit, and “I’m Coming for You,” the fiction debut of Rotterdam-winning filmmaker Cyrielle Raingou (“Le Spectre de Boko Haram”). There will also be a special buyers screening of “Muganga — The One Who Treats,” the advocacy-driven drama inspired by the true story of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dr. Denis Mukwege, directed by Marie-Hélène Roux and co-produced by Angelina Jolie. Key executives will also be on hand for a TIFF market panel on new models for financing and distributing African film, including Canex Creation’s Akpata, Gobez Media producer Tamara Dawit, MBO capital executive director Adekunle Adebiyi and Janet Brown, COO of Tribeca Enterprises. In addition, EbonyLife’s Abudu will join production and distribution veteran Moses Babatope, of the Nile Media Entertainment Group, for a session on the global success of the Nigerian film industry. Abudu is a long-time fixture at the Toronto Intl. Film Festival, where “Baba Segi’s Wives” marks EbonyLife’s fifth selection. Commenting on the prospects for African filmmakers at TIFF: The Market, she pointed to a string of sold-out screenings for the film — an adaptation of Lola Shoneyin’s 2010 debut novel — as proof that audiences are clamoring for more African stories. “I think that gives you a clue as to the appetite for our content,” she says . “The world is beginning to appreciate us for who we are. It’s our time. articles.title: Venice Film Festival Takeaways: Malkovich Storms the Oscar Race, Political Movies Dominate Buzz and More
articles.full_text: Sep 11, 2026 6:00am PT Venice Film Festival Takeaways: Malkovich Storms the Oscar Race, Political Movies Dominate Buzz and More By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest ‘Hawaii Five-O’ Movie in the Works From ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Director Destin Daniel Cretton 19 hours ago ‘Now You See Me’ Live Show Sets Broadway Debut 23 hours ago ‘& Juliet’ to Close on Broadway After Four Years 1 day ago See All Getty Images Is Venice still vibrating from all the rounds of applause? It’s become customary for audiences at the festival’s premieres to clap and cheer for a seeming eternity after the credits roll. (Often to the visible discomfort of the actors and filmmakers, who look like they don’t know what to do with themselves when the hurrahs rage into double digits.) Call it a Champagne (or Aperol spritz — we’re in Italy, after all) problem for stars John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell and director Martin McDonagh, whose dark comedy “Wild Horse Nine” was embraced with a rousing 13-minute standing ovation inside the Lido’s famed Palazzo del Cinema. But that didn’t turn out to be the festival’s biggest reception — later in the week, Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem received 15.5 minutes of applause for their marriage-in-crisis drama “Bunker, and on Thursday, Gaza documentary “NAZA” was greeted with a massive 24.5 minutes, the longest of any recorded ovation at a major film festival. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro And for all the complaints that Hollywood has basically abandoned film festivals, there was no shortage of celebrities to elicit big reactions from crowds. Robert Pattinson (“Primetime”), Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem (“Bunker”) and Oasis’ Liam and Noel Gallagher (“Don’t Look Back in Anger”) were among the boldface names hoping to turn festival kudos into awards chatter or box office plaudits. Popular on Variety As Venice wraps up and festivalgoers take their last bites of pasta and sips of spritzes, here are takeaways from the floating city. George Clooney Steals the Show Only Clooney could become the talk of the fest without even having a movie to promote. The A-lister traveled to Venice not for a new project but to receive the prestigious Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement. (If that has a familiar ring, Clooney played a movie star who accepts a career honor in Italy in last year’s “Jay Kelly.”) Indeed, Clooney was everywhere this year, making appearances at a press conference, the opening-night ceremony and a master class. He had a lot to say about the power of art in times of turmoil, the importance of free speech and the fraying state of democracy. And he found time to teach festivalgoers a new term: “There’s a great word, kakistocracy, which is a country run by the least qualified people. I think maybe we have a kakistocracy right now, but we’ll get through it.” We believe you, George! Malkovich Storms Into the Oscar Race Get ready to see a lot of Malkovich. The beloved character actor is drumming up awards buzz for “Wild Horse Nine,” in which he plays an eccentric CIA agent reflecting on his life. McDonagh has a pretty good track record of getting his actors from the Lido to the Academy Awards. Rockwell and Frances McDormand won Oscars for 2017’s “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri,” while Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson were nominated for 2022’s “The Banshees of Inisherin,” both of which bowed in Venice. Recognition feels long overdue for Malkovich, whose last nomination was more than three decades ago, for 1993’s “In the Line of Fire.” Matt Damon and Tom Cruise, you might have some competition… Politics, Politics, Politics Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera wasn’t exaggerating when he called this year’s lineup “the most political ever.” The 83rd edition was packed with films about hot-button issues like right-wing media barons (“Ink”), right-wing trolls (“Musk”), conflict in the Middle East (“NAZA”) and ICE (“They’re Here”). Offscreen, it’s become de rigueur to probe actors and directors at film festivals about the state of the world — a conversation that escalated at Berlin after jury president Wim Wenders said filmmakers should “stay out of politics.” Maggie Gyllenhaal, who is presiding over the Venice jury, disagrees. At the jury press conference , she called movies “fundamentally, unavoidably political” and challenged people to “hear stories about the most corrupt, most perverse people.” Her reasoning? “It opens up the opportunity to find empathy.” A Record-Breaking Embrace Audiences, for their part, seem just fine with politics at the forefront. “NAZA,” a devastating exposé about the systems behind the Israeli military’s remote killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, elicited the longest standing ovation in film festival history. (Or, at least since journalists began reporting on the trend.) The documentary was met with 24.5 minutes of applause, surpassing the ovation for last year’s Gaza-set drama “The Voice of Hind Rajab” and that of Guillermo Del Toro’s “Pan’s Labyrinth” at Cannes in 2006, both of which clocked in at 22 minutes. Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor are two of the four filmmakers behind 2025’s Oscar-winning doc “No Other Land.” Given the warm reception for and timeliness of “NAZA,” will the duo find themselves back in the awards conversation? Where Are the Women? Gyllenhaal may be jury president, but she’s just as confused as everyone else about the dearth of women-directed films in the main competition lineup. (She didn’t select the movies, after all.) Only two titles up for the Golden Lion — “Woman Unknown,” a drama by May el-Toukhy, and “NAZA,” with Szor co-helming — were directed by women. “I guess it’s finally become clear that men make better movies than women do,” Gyllenhaal deadpanned at her press conference. In all seriousness, though, she puts the blame on the powers that be. “There’s a systemic problem,” she said. “It’s harder for women to get films financed.” A Star Is Born Lance Oppenheim, the 30-year-old director known for non-fiction work like “Some Kind of Heaven” and HBO’s “Ren Faire,” emerged as a major talent to watch. A24’s “Primetime,” his debut feature film, was one of the buzziest of the festival, scoring an enthusiastic seven minutes of applause as audiences embraced Pattinson’s immersive performance as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen. And that was just the fanfare on the Lido. The next day in Colorado, Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder unveiled their top-secret documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, titled “You Can See Everything,” which became the talk of Telluride Film Festival. It’s safe to say Oppenheim will be getting plenty of use out of his tuxedo over the next few months. Feeling Hot, Hot, Hot This year’s hottest accessory? Electronic and handheld fans. Temperatures on the Lido were sweltering , which left A-listers on the verge of overheating on the red carpet. At their respective premieres, Jack O’Connell (“Ink”) had to take off his thick Dunhill coat before blotting the moisture on his face and shirt; Parker Posey (“Wild Horse Nine”) continuously waved herself with a decorative fan while mouthing about the brutal heat during the movie’s long standing ovation; and Pattinson (“Primetime”), wearing a suave all-white suit, dabbed the sweat off his forehead with napkins before posing for a cast photo. articles.title: Thailand Bets on Film Tourism to Turn Movie Locations Into Travel Destinations
articles.full_text: Sep 11, 2026 6:15am PT Thailand Bets on Film Tourism to Turn Movie Locations Into Travel Destinations By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest New Zealand Set to Unveil Tri-Nation Indigenous Co-Production Initiative at Toronto (EXCLUSIVE) 30 minutes ago Oscars: Singapore Selects Anthony Chen’s ‘We Are All Strangers’ for International Feature Race 4 hours ago San Sebastian Competition Title ‘Border’ Boards Reel Suspects for Global Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago See All HBO The Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT) has launched “Amazing Locations: From Scene to Scenic,” a campaign built to convert the country’s rising profile as a filming destination into lasting tourism, as productions ranging from “ The White Lotus ” to “The Challenge” Season 42 continue to draw international attention to Thai locations. TAT deputy governor Nithee Seeprae says the campaign grew out of watching how quickly the “set-jetting” trend has taken hold among travelers who plan trips around what they have seen on screen. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro TAT frames the push as part of a broader strategy to make Thailand a top-of-mind choice for global productions, pointing to the strength of its local crews, production infrastructure, studio facilities and incentive programs as the pillars of that pitch. The campaign’s specific job, as Seeprae describes it, is to bridge filmmaking and travel: encouraging filmmakers to turn Thailand’s varied landscapes into cinematic backdrops while steering travelers toward the real places they recognize from the screen. Popular on Variety “We have seen firsthand how tangibly it benefits destinations and local communities when a film or series puts a place on screen,” Seeprae says. “It genuinely inspires people to travel, and we have seen that pull firsthand, audiences putting Thailand at the top of their must-visit list simply because they fell in love with it on screen first.” The numbers back up the strategy. Seeprae says the country’s cash rebate program has drawn in upward of 100 foreign productions to date, funneling more than THB20 billion ($608 million) toward Thai crews and local economies. The rebate program itself is administered by Thailand’s Dept. of Tourism rather than TAT, though the agency promotes it as part of the country’s broader pitch to filmmakers. He points to Koh Samui as a case study: after the island appeared in the third season of “The White Lotus,” online interest in the destination jumped 88% and hotel reservations there grew 44%, figures he says have been echoed by titles including “The Hangover Part II” and “Jurassic World: Rebirth.” Recent Thailand shoots also include the Bollywood blockbuster “Dhurandhar,” Sam Raimi’s “Send Help,” the survival sequel “Fall 2: Deadpoint” and “John Rambo.” Seeprae says this year’s push doubles down on undiscovered locations rather than simply revisiting places already familiar to international audiences. He points to Isan provinces such as Nong Khai, Bueng Kan and Ubon Ratchathani, along with Nakhon Si Thammarat in the south, as places with striking scenery and a distinct sense of place that international productions have yet to explore. He cites director Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s body of work as proof that cinema can give an entire region “a place in the world’s imagination.” As part of the campaign, TAT is running trips that bring filmmakers, producers, influencers and cultural figures into these locations along both a B2B track focused on production logistics and a B2C track aimed at travelers. The push comes as Thailand’s production sector matures well beyond service work. Nicholas Simon, founder and producer at Indochina Prods., has watched the local crew base grow from working transportation on shoots to running productions worth well over $100 million. “Crew who were working 15 years ago as transport coordinators are now line producing $100 million projects,” Simon says, pointing to Thai nominees at the Creative Emmys for “The White Lotus” and “ Alien: Earth ,” and a Thai costume designer from “The Creator” who is now a voting member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. “Jurassic World: Rebirth” behind the scenes Everett Collection Simon credits “The White Lotus” and “Alien: Earth” with changing how Hollywood sees the country itself, rather than as a stand-in for somewhere else. Those productions, he says, also introduced the industry to Thailand’s art department talent, and “the film incentive has driven a new wave of productions scripted Thailand for Thailand.” Simon adds that under-filmed regions such as Songkla, Ranong and the natural rock formations of the north and northeast still hold plenty of unexplored ground, noting that “The Creator” alone shot across 17 of Thailand’s 76 provinces. That maturity has pushed Indochina into original content through its new venture, TSixtySix. Producer Cod Satrusayang, head of studio at TSixtySix, says, “We think given the right support and the right stories, Thailand can become the next Asian wave following in the footsteps of South Korea,“ adding that clients who once came to Thailand purely for service work are increasingly asking about local stories too. Satrusayang says the biggest remaining gap is screenwriting talent able to work within structure, and that streamers willing to back genres beyond horror and romance are reshaping what gets developed. TSixtySix has a heist film releasing early next year and a coming-of-age drama shooting in late January, with Satrusayang predicting demand for Thai content will keep rising. The country’s reputation as a source of acclaimed auteurs reinforces its appeal as a location, according to Raymond Phathanavirangoon, producer and founder of the SEAFIC Script Lab. Wong Kar Wai shot much of “In the Mood for Love” in Thailand because, Phathanavirangoon says, “there are locations in Thailand that seem untouched by time since the 1950s-1960s.” He notes that European filmmakers have told him Bangkok’s futuristic skyline could support a science-fiction film in the vein of “Alphaville,” and points to the local production “A Useful Ghost” as an example of a film built around unusual local settings. Phathanavirangoon says specificity, not international polish, is what makes Thai stories travel, citing “9 Temples to Heaven” and the Burmese Busan winner “Ma — Cry of Silence” as films that succeeded by staying rooted in local culture rather than chasing a global audience. Phathanavirangoon says independent filmmakers are often the ones expanding what audiences associate with Thailand beyond its best-known landmarks. He points to Udon Thani, near the Phu Phra Bat Historical Park, and a growing contemporary arts scene anchored by museums such as Dib and MAIIAM, as the kind of settings independent directors are now drawing on. Director Chantana Tiprachart’s upcoming “Esarn Seven,” shot north of Udon Thani, is one example he cites of a film built around a region rarely seen on screen. Producer Cattleya Paosrijarern, whose work centers on independent and auteur cinema, says international shoots and homegrown storytelling can coexist without one undermining the other. “Even with line production, we always push to be creative partners, not just vendors,” Paosrijarern says. She says international funding is welcome but “the money must serve the artist’s vision,” and argues that hyper-local Thai stories only resonate abroad “when it’s backed by quality,” pointing to knowledge, vision and sustained policy support as the real drivers of that continuity. Her upcoming slate includes “Tremble Like a Flower,” the debut feature from visual artist Pathompon Tesprateep, and “Esarn Seven.” Thailand’s location appeal extends into unscripted television. “The Challenge” Season 42 shot across Bangkok, Pattaya and the Chonburi region, and executive producer Justin Booth says the decision came down to more than scenery. “Thailand has some of the most professional and polished art department personnel anywhere in the world, and you’re able to access that level of talent at a better price,” Booth says. He adds that the range of environments within a compact area gave producers flexibility to design challenges they could not have built elsewhere, comparing the local infrastructure favorably with other countries that have hosted the franchise. Season 42 also splits its 24 competitors into three teams competing for a share of $500,000, reviving the “Cutthroat” format the show first used in 2009. Booth says the cast made the timing right for the format’s return, and that viewers should watch how team dynamics evolve after a run of seasons built around pairs and individual competition. Asked whether he’s conscious that viewers might want to visit places the show has featured, Booth says that outcome isn’t the production’s primary goal but is one it keeps in mind. “The whole point of turning ‘The Challenge’ into an international competition show was to showcase these locations while also reaching a new or different audience,” he says. Host T.J. Lavin says Thailand delivered some of the most memorable moments he has filmed for the show, from a season-opening challenge staged in downtown Bangkok to the daily rhythms of life in the country. “It was one of the most incredible and fun places that I’ve ever been,” Lavin says. “Not to mention, foot massages on the daily were amazing.” He says the humidity added real physical difficulty to the competition, thickening the air enough that “even some of the easiest tasks become difficult.” Thailand’s locations are also central to “Inherit,” the horror feature set to premiere as a gala presentation at the Toronto Film Festival . Director Banjong Pisanthanakun says finding the right physical spaces shapes his films as much as the scripts do. For “Inherit,” he says the main family house “actually combined three real locations plus a sound stage to create a single location that matched the exact mood we wanted.” Pisanthanakun says Thailand’s horror tradition, which he calls part of the culture’s “modern cultural heritage,” continues to travel internationally alongside newer genres such as the family drama “How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies” and the thriller “Bad Genius.” Star Davika Hoorne, who plays a centuries-old demon matriarch in the film, says she hopes international audiences take away more than scares. “For audiences around the world, ‘Inherit’ is more than just a horror film, it’s also a glimpse into Thai culture,” Hoorne says. “I hope people feel both the thrill and the heart, and walk away pleasantly surprised.” Several of these voices are set to share a stage in Toronto. TIFF is hosting a summit panel titled “From Scenic to Scene: How Thailand Shapes Global Cinema,” billed as an exploration of how landscape, local culture and incentives turn the country into what organizers describe as “a global story engine.” Pisanthanakun and Satrusayang are the featured guests, with Phathanavirangoon moderating and Seeprae delivering opening remarks. For TAT, the ambition extends well past any single title. Seeprae says success five years from now would mean Thailand being recognized as “a prototype destination for filmmaking,” with productions returning to explore regions beyond the familiar and the resulting tourism sustained rather than a brief moment of interest. articles.title: ‘Rojo’ Director Benjamín Naishtat on Awaited Toronto, San Sebastián Title ‘Glaxo,’ the Impunity of Power and Connecting via Genre
articles.full_text: Sep 11, 2026 6:25am PT ‘Rojo’ Director Benjamín Naishtat on Awaited Toronto, San Sebastián Title ‘Glaxo,’ the Impunity of Power and Connecting via Genre Noting that ‘Glaxo,’ from São Paulo-based RT Features and Rei Pictures in Buenos Aires, is set entirely in Argentina but shot in Brazil, Naishtat laments: Argentina is 'a country with a great filmmaking tradition and it is now in very serious danger' By John Hopewell , Roberto Prieto Lali Espósito in 'Glaxo' Courtesy of RT Features, Rei Pictures “At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?” Nobel Prize winning author Mario Vargas Llosa famously asks at the beginning of “Conversation at The Cathedral.” In “ Glaxo ,” one of the most awaited of Latin American films this year, director Benjamín Naishtat charts what he describes as the whole of Argentina’s loss of innocence, which again has its origins in 1950s dictatorship and is equally pervasive. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro After the lighter turn of co-directing “Puán,” a “deliciously droll” makeover movie, said Variety , in “Glaxo,” which world premieres in Toronto’s Special Presentations, Naishtat returns to the disturbing collective psychology portrait of “Rojo,” charting the impunity of power — a cop, and the Glaxo corporation — and a tale of betrayals in its central coming of age section. Popular on Variety Set along three timelines — Florida, outside Buenos Aires, on June 6, 1956, and then Chivilcoy, a town in the sticks also outside the Argentine capital one year later and then in 1984. Esteban Bigliardi as Flaco in ‘Glaxo’ Courtesy of RT Features, Rei Pictures In the first, with Argentina under military dictatorship, based on historical facts depicted by Argentine writer Roberto Walsh in a trailblazing example of a non-fiction novel — police commissioner Folcada arrests 12 men listening to a boxing match, and then is leaned on by his boss to make an example of them. One year later, now a civilian and a wealthy ranch owner, Folcada has moved to Chivilcoy with his stunning wife, Negra Morcada (Lali Espósito, notable), dazzling four teen friends — Miguelito, Verdemann, “Bicho” and Lucio. “This is the story of a betrayal,” says narrator Miguelito. In fact it’s the story of multiple endemic betrayals driven by the exercise of unaccountable power and the misjudgment of adolescence, under the weight of which four teens’ seemingly “Stand by Me” friendship unravels. If “Rojo” was a “witheringly provocative examination of temporary moral eclipse becoming permanent moral apocalypse,” as Variety noted , “Glaxo” delivers a broader historical take on the same Argentinean dark ages. It delivers a pedigree producer package as a production of Brazil’s RT Features (“Paper Tiger,” “I’m Still Here”), produced by Argentina’s Rei Pictures (“Zama,” “The Settlers”). The film is inspired by novel “Glaxo,” from the film’s co-writer, Hernán Ronsino, which was partly inspired in turn by Walsh’s “Operation Masacre.” This deep concern for heritage – historical, literary, cinematographic – is one of the film’s sources of emotion. Variety talked to Naishtat before the Toronto world premiere of “Glaxo,” after which the film segues for its European bow in main competition at San Sebastián. Two first questions. At the beginning of the “Conversation in The Cathedral,” Mario Vargas Llosa famously asks: “At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?” It seems that to a certain extent Hernán Ronsino and you in “Glaxo” are asking the same question about Argentina. Also Miguelito, the narrator, says “This is the story of a betrayal. It seems to me that this is the story of many betrayals…. Benjamin Naishtat : I think that’s a very good analysis of the film, and basically this reading is obviously connected to Hernán Ronsino’s novel. When I read the novel for the first time, two things struck me. First, its very austere style, almost like an American police crime novel, but also closely related to Argentine writer Rodolfo Walsh, the author of “Operation Massacre,” a book that has a strong connection to “Glaxo.” The film “Glaxo· also has a string connection to “Operation Massacre,” an underground film from 1973 by Jorge Cedrón, a filmmaker who isn’t very well known but who is very important in the mysterious history of Argentine cinema. I wanted to mention that because it’s important. But going back to your point, yes, I think it really is an open question for the audience. To what extent does “Glaxo” suggest any answers? Naishtat: I don’t think the film tries to give us an answer but it simply presents us with the question. As an audience member, I’m more interested in leaving with more questions than with simple answers. That’s what we tried to do with this project: generate questions in a historical echo going backwards, but posing possible hypotheses about when Argentina got screwed and also about Argentina’s present. I think we tried to analyze the current state of Argentina from a different angle and from a different perspective. One possible hypothesis comes in the prologue, set on June 9, 1956, turning on Police Commissioner Folcada, which suggests the terrible impunity of power. The other might be the terribly limited prospects of people like Miguelito living in Chivilcoy, a town outside Buenos Aires, where the two latter parts of the film is set. Naishtat: The impunity of power is a good point. It relates to your earlier question and is a good starting point in relation to what impunity means in Argentina. In fact, the historical episodes depicted in the prologue — historical episodes that occurred in 1956 — remain unpunished to this day. Those responsible for that massacre never had to pay a price for what they did. Regarding Miguelito and his life opportunities, I do share your view, but it’s also related to the film being not only a thriller but melodrama and also a coming-of-age story. I personally love the coming-of-age genre. What’s fascinating is that it connects you to an age we’ve all lived through — adolescence — in which love, and even more so, falling in love, has a devastating power over you. Without knowing who we are, we already have the capacity to fall in love in a way that we will never again experience. And that’s dangerous. So I tried to play with those themes a little bit by telling a story about adolescent love. You’ve mentioned genres. The film plays with their different registers and has multiple echoes from other films. Naishtat: This is my second collaboration after “Rojo.” with cinematographer Pedro Sotero. “Rojo” was a language exercise in relation to thrillers and television from the ‘70s. “Glaxo” has three different languages in the same film. So we have a prologue, which relates to clandestine Latin American films from the ‘70s, filmed as if it was shot on Super 16mm, with texture, like using only a single lens, and with very precarious shooting and lighting conditions. Courtesy of RT Features, Rei Pictures Then we have the main 1950s section, which tries to play with Italian and American melodrama, like films such as “A Place in the Sun” or “Giant” by George Stevens, which were strong points of reference for the images in that section. Then we have the film-noir section set in the 1980s, shot in CinemaScope with anamorphic lenses to generate maximum atmosphere, which honestly, was a lot of fun. We’re both huge cinephiles. Pedro and I love genre cinema, and I think we’re convinced that the future of cinema, if there is one, is a popular future, let’s say within the popular genres — being able to talk to the audience and bring complexity to popular genres. In other words, recovering the complexity that popular genres used to have in other eras. The credits say that “Glaxo” is a production of Brazil’s RT Features produced by Argentina’s Rei Pictures. That speaks volumes of the comparative current state of the two countries’ film industries. Naishtat : Yes. This is very important. As the film’s credits say, the producer of the film is Rodrigo Teixeira and his Brazilian production company RT Features and Rei Pictures is a minority co-producer on the Argentine side. The film was shot entirely in Brazil, which is very strange, because it’s set entirely in Argentina and so it was a very difficult decision for me. Rodrigo and I wanted to shoot it in Argentina, but the current state of Argentina made that impossible. The cuts and the freezing of public funding for the film industry have been brutal for Argentine cinema. There are fewer productions now and less of a presence in the major markets and the major festivals. And perhaps what will become even more evident in the coming years will be the total lack of promoting new talent and new voices. There used to be a very interesting generation making their first features not only in Buenos Aires, but in Córdoba, in other cities, in Patagonia — genuinely interesting voices. This government, which is waging an open war on culture in general, is, in my opinion, a fascist government, an enemy of culture, one that has no cultural politics whatsoever. It doesn’t even have conservative politics, it has no politics at all; the politics is that there are no cultural politics and this is derailing the life plans of many people. I personally can keep working because, as you know, this is my fifth film and I’ve been able to secure financing in Brazil with Rodrigo Teixeira, or in France, or in other places. But if I had to start my career today, I’d have to work somewhere else. I wouldn’t be able to work in cinema, and this is what’s happening in Argentina, which is very sad. I think it’s important to call this out, because as you know, we’re a country with a great filmmaking tradition and it is now in very serious danger. ‘Shark Tank India’ Sets Season 6 With Parrot Campaign on SonyLIV (EXCLUSIVE) Hansal Mehta, Siddharth Bodke on ‘Scam 2010’ as First Look Unveiled for SonyLIV Series: ‘A Story About Ambition, Influence and Arrogance’ (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... articles.title: the official opening-night film
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony ‘Practical Magic 2’ Sparks $3.5M+ In Previews On Thursday – Box Office Update The Obsession For The Next ‘Obsession’ At TIFF: Festival Hot List Includes Pics For Sale With Cynthia Erivo, Chase Infiniti, The Maras, Dave Bautista & More Netflix Unveils U.S. Market Rollout For ‘La Bola Negra’ Theatrical Release View All July 7, 2026 7:00am TIFF The Toronto Film Festival said Tuesday that Apple Original Films’ Being Heumann from Oscar-winning CODA filmmaker Siân Heder will be the opening-night film of TIFF ‘s 51st edition in the fall. In addition, two other world premieres — Prima Facie from British director Susanna White starring three-time Oscar nominee Cynthia Erivo, and The Assassin(s) from Korean filmmaker Hur Jin-ho ( A Normal Family , TIFF ’23) — have been set for this year’s TIFF, which runs September 10-20. Related Stories Festivals Details Of Toronto Film Festival’s C$23M Market Revealed: Name & Dates Set As More Heavyweight Industry Advisors Join Ahead Of 2026 Launch Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More Being Heumann stars BAFTA Award nominee Ruth Madeley ( Don’t Take My Baby ) as famed disability activist Judy Heumann in what is a feature take of her bestselling memoir. Being Heumann follows Heumann as she leads more than 100 disabled people to take over the San Francisco Federal Building, kicking off a 28 day sit-in in 1977. The protestors form a tightly bound community, refusing to leave until the government enforces section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which required all federal spaces to become accessible. Heder and Rebekah Tussing adapted the memoir. Mark Ruffalo, Dylan O’Brien, Jon Beavers, Rob Delaney, Ray Fisher and more star in the pic. David Permut, Heder, John W. Beach, Kevin Cleary and Kevin J. Walsh produce. Watch on Deadline ‘Prima Facie’ Prima Facie is the feature adaptation of the West End and Broadway play (which originally starred Jodie Comer). Erivo plays a British defense barrister who exudes enviable brilliance in navigating the ruthless and gladiatorial London courtrooms. She is formidable in her defense of men charged with sexual assault; but just as she is fast-tracking to stardom, the tide turns to crisis, and she must fight to define herself. Playwright Suzie Miller adapted her Olivier-winning and Tony-nominated play for the big screen. Deadline first told you about the project at Cannes 2025, when Embankment Films handled global sales with UTA Independent Film Group and CAA Media Finance co-representing domestic. The Assassin(s) is set in 1974 and follows the attempted assassination of Korean president Park Chung-hee on August 15 of that year — one of the most consequential days in the country’s history. Yoo Hae-jin, Park Hae-il and Lee Min-ho star. Park portrays a news editor who delves into unanswered questions surrounding the attempted assassination. Yoo is the police inspector, and Lee is a journalist both of whom witness the assassination. “We’re thrilled to open this year’s festival with Siân Heder’s inspiring follow-up to her Oscar-winning CODA ,” TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey said. “ Being Heumann features an electric performance from Ruth Madeley in the story of Judy Heumann, a world-changing advocate for accessibility. We’re also glad to reveal the news that Toronto audiences will be the first to see Cynthia Erivo in Susanna White’s searing legal drama Prima Facie , and that the South Korean power duo of director Hur Jin-ho and superstar Lee Min-ho will launch their thriller The Assassin(s) at our 51st festival. Lots more to come.” Being Heumann will debut on Thursday, September 10 at Roy Thomson Hall. Last year’s TIFF drew 700,000 attendees. articles.title: Cricket Legend Virender Sehwag To Host ‘Rise And Fall’ Season 2 For Prime Video
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Cricket Legend Virender Sehwag To Host ‘Rise And Fall’ Season 2 For Prime Video Spain’s Mediapro Group To Become Imagina After Reorganization K-Drama Day Returns For Fourth Time On Rakuten Viki With Park Ji Hoon, Bae In Hyuk & More Involved View All September 10, 2026 11:25pm EXCLUSIVE: Indian cricket legend Virender Sehwag is swapping the bat and pads for a suit and microphone. The sporting superstar, known as the Sultan of Multan, has been unveiled as host for Season 2 of Rise and Fall , Prime Video India’s reality series to replace Ashnee Grover. This marks the first time he’ll front a streaming TV show. Sehwag’s role was revealed in a trailer that you can watch above. The 1-minute 44-second trailer sees him playing versions of Albert Einstein, a doctor, a teacher and a karate yellow belt in a series of vignettes before a skyscraper building flashes on screen and the retired batsman switches to a sharp suit. “In Rise and Fall , the game of up and down is going to be very twisted,” he says to camera. Related Stories News Stephen King Calls Mike Flanagan's 'Carrie' Miniseries "Brilliant" Casting Danny Huston & Sofia Black D'Elia Among 5 To Join Kristen Stewart In Prime Video's 'The Challenger' Sehwag has long been eyed as an on-screen presence thanks to his sharp wit and straight-talking style. He retired from cricket in 2015 after a glittering career in which he became one of India’s most destructive opening batsmen and the country’s vice-captain for large portions of his international career. Watch on Deadline Numerous Indian cricketers have taken the TV pathway as their careers wound down with former Test team captain Rohit Sharma recently announcing a show, Family Full House , for Sony Entertainment Television and the likes of Ajay Jadeja and Shikhar Dhawan also fronting shows. Sourav Ganguly is the current presenter of Bigg Boss Bangla , the Bengali-language version of Big Brother , which kicked off its most recent season on August 30. Rise and Fall Season 2 was announced in March after the first run became a huge hit for Amazon’s MX Player , which has since been subsumed into Prime Video. The show is a remake of the Studio Lambert format for UK network Channel 4, though that version was cancelled after one season due to low ratings. The Indian show, from Banijay Asia , has been the breakout for the format. Set across the contrasting worlds of a penthouse and the basement in the same highrise building, the game brings together 15 celebrities, who are divided into two groups, the Rulers and the Workers. While the Rulers enjoy the privileges of the penthouse, the Workers navigate the realities of the basement. Should the Rulers. Over the course of challenges, members of the Workers are able to replace Rulers in the penthouse, changing their fortunes and the tide of the game. “The love and excitement audiences showed for Rise and Fall i n its first season gave us the perfect reason to take this unique power game forward,” said Amogh Dusad, Director and Head of AVOD Content, Prime Video India. “Season 2 brings a fresh set of personalities into a format where power is always in motion, and every decision carries a consequence. “With Virender Sehwag stepping in as host, we’re bringing a whole new energy to the show; his wit, spontaneity, and fearless personality make him an exciting fit for the game. We’re excited for audiences to experience the drama, strategy and entertainment in Rise and Fall Season 2, and watch it on Prime Video for free.” Sehwag compared the gameplay to a professional match. “Cricket has taught me one thing – no match is won before the final ball, and Rise and Fall Season 2 takes that unpredictability to another level,” he said. “As a host, what excites me about this game is that there are no easy wins and no fixed positions. The biggest challenge isn’t just getting to the top but knowing how to stay there. You have to know when to attack, when to defend, and, most importantly, when to read the game before it reads you.” Deepak Dhar, Founder and Group CEO of Banijay Asia, said the “overwhelming response that Rise and Fall received in its debut season reaffirmed the strength of its unique premise, where power, strategy and human behaviour come together to create an unpredictable game.” No launch date or contestant casting as been revealed yet, but the show will stream free on Prime Video and the MX Player Android app, which is still available under a a new identity – MX Player by Prime Video. ‘Practical Magic 2’ Weaves $3.5 Million In Thursday Previews Trudeau Company; Reviews For ‘Being Heumann’, ‘The Housewife’; Photos Netflix Cancels Josh Duhamel-Minka Kelly Series After Two Seasons ‘Muppet Show’ Special Got Viewership & Emmys – Where’s The Disney+ Series Order? articles.title: Pierce Brosnan Says Tom Hardy ‘MobLand’ Feud Was “Storm In A Teacup”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake BBC Stokes Anger By Curbing Cab Rides For Night Shift Workers… As Senior Managers Spend $17,000 On Taxis In Three Months Pierce Brosnan Says Tom Hardy ‘MobLand’ Feud Was “Storm In A Teacup” Channel 4 To Combine Drama & Comedy Teams Under Historic Jobs Cull View All September 11, 2026 1:34am Pierce Brosnan, Helen Mirren and Tom Hardy at the 'MobLand' premiere Getty Pierce Brosnan has said that it is all happy families on the set of Paramount +’s MobLand . At the Season 2 premiere in London, Brosnan was asked about the behind-the-scenes drama involving Tom Hardy , who reportedly clashed with showrunner Jez Butterworth and had timekeeping issues on set. “Oh my God, it was a storm in a teacup, really,” the James Bond star told Press Association. “I love the dude. I love Tom Hardy. I’m a massive fan of the man’s work. Truly. “We are rock solid as a company, as a family. Everyone shows up for work, and everybody’s just there on the spot. It moves very fast so it’s not like we go out and socialise and go to the pub or anything like that.” Related Stories News 'Avatar: Seven Havens': Paramount+ Drops Official Trailer For Next Chapter In Franchise Legal September Showdown! SCOTUS Orders Blue State AGs To Respond To ParaBros Merger Antitrust Suit Objection From Iowa & Montana Hardy added that it was a “privilege” to work with Brosnan and Helen Mirren . “In many aspects, of course, I look up to them. Coming up, these are actors that came before me,” he told PA. Watch on Deadline “So to be able to work with them is a privilege, but also to be able to enjoy them, watching them spread their wings with their range now as well, and play against their type in some aspects, and really enjoy that is a beautiful thing to watch as a human being.” Mirren also joined the chorus. “The relationships are amazing. Obviously, Pierce and I have an extraordinary chemistry on-screen and off-screen. We’re very, very fond of each other. We respect each other enormously,” she said. The actors are set to be reunited in Season 3, which was confirmed by Paramount earlier this month after a meeting in London between Hardy, Butterworth and series executive producer David C. Glasser, where they hashed things out In Season 2 of MobLand , produced by Paramount Television Studios and 101 Studios, the Harrigans struggle to show a unified front as rising rivals threaten their fractured criminal empire – and Harry Da Souza (Hardy), their street-smart and formidable ‘fixer,’ must walk a dangerous tightrope when tensions within the family intensify. As violence spills into every corner of their lives, loyalties snap, safety proves temporary, and the battle for power leaves no room for mercy. Alongside Hardy, Brosnan and Mirren, Season 2 also stars Paddy Considine, Joanne Froggatt, Lara Pulver, Anson Boon, Mandeep Dhillon, Jasmine Jobson, Teddie Allen, Emmett J. Scanlan, Johnny Flynn, Ophelia Lovibond, Janet McTeer, and Toby Jones. MobLand is executive produced by Glasser, Ritchie, Butterworth, Hardy, Ivan Atkinson, Dean Baker, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari and Keith Cox. articles.title: BBC Stokes Anger By Curbing Cab Rides For Night Shift Workers… As Senior Managers Spend $17,000 On Taxis In Three Months
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake BBC Stokes Anger By Curbing Cab Rides For Night Shift Workers… As Senior Managers Spend $17,000 On Taxis In Three Months Pierce Brosnan Says Tom Hardy ‘MobLand’ Feud Was “Storm In A Teacup” Channel 4 To Combine Drama & Comedy Teams Under Historic Jobs Cull View All September 11, 2026 1:37am BBC boss Matt Brittin Getty EXCLUSIVE : The BBC has sparked unrest among staff with plans to slash taxi usage for night shift workers. Bosses at the UK broadcaster want to change the qualifying time for expensable cab fares, meaning employees would have to leave work 30 minutes later or start 30 minutes earlier for the BBC to foot the bill for a car journey. Bectu and the National Union of Journalists are fighting the taxi changes, which the BBC has put forward as part of its 2027 pay offer. The BBC’s improved offer of a basic 1.5% pay rise was rejected by the unions , with further talks set to take place over the coming weeks as the spectre of industrial action looms. Related Stories News 'RuPaul's Drag Race UK' Canceled By BBC Amid "Financial Pressures" News 'RuPaul's Drag Race UK All Stars' Sets Fall 2027 Global Premiere On WOW Presents Plus BBC employees are unhappy about the below-inflation pay rise, and the cab curbs have only exacerbated unease. BBC journalists, who contribute to 24-hour news coverage, are particularly exercised about the proposals, with one insider describing them as “unreasonable.” Watch on Deadline Another accused the corporation of “pissing about around the edges” as it seeks to save £500 million ($674 million) over the coming years. Critics have also raised concerns about the safety of women who need to travel to and from work at night time. A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster is “looking at all our operating costs” as it seeks to make savings. They added: “The safety of our staff remains paramount, and the changes have been designed to bring the BBC more in line with others in the industry and reflect the greater availability of public transport, particularly in London.” The cab curbs come as the BBC recently published senior management expense claims for the first quarter of its 2025/26 financial year. The BBC’s highest-paid staff claimed more than £13,000 ($17,600) on taxi journeys in the three months from April to June 2025. This was up 6% on the same period in 2024, according to an analysis by Deadline. The expense claims were made before the BBC introduced new cost control measures in April 2026, cracking down on travel costs and other outgoings, including attending conferences, awards, and events. A spokesperson said the BBC has “strict guidelines” for taxi usage, which apply to all staff. BBC director general Matt Brittin told staff this week that he was unimpressed by some of the expense claims, which pre-dated his arrival. “When I look at it, there are some things there that don’t make any sense to me, and I wouldn’t want to happen under my watch,” he said. “We have to spend our money very carefully, and I think we’re all very conscious of that.” Brittin added that pay talks had been a “pretty difficult process for everyone” and he acknowledged that strike action was a possibility. Any industrial action would be subject to a ballot of union members. ‘Practical Magic 2’ Weaves $3.5 Million In Thursday Previews Trudeau Company; Reviews For ‘Being Heumann’, ‘The Housewife’; Photos Netflix Cancels Josh Duhamel-Minka Kelly Series After Two Seasons ‘Muppet Show’ Special Got Viewership & Emmys – Where’s The Disney+ Series Order? articles.title: French TV Disruptor Jeremy Zag Talks Building ‘Miraculous’ Universe, Plans For A Live-Action Series & Latest On Katy Perry Animated Movie ‘Melody’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart Ross Butler & Marc Evan Jackson Join Sayani Gupta In ‘Arya’ Pablo Larraín’s ‘My Sad Dead’ Trailer: “The Dead Start To Make Themselves Present” International Sales Of French TV Programs Crash To A Ten-Year Low View All September 11, 2026 2:00am Fans of Miraculous: Tales of Ladybug & Cat Noir can expect a live-action version of the animated series, its co-creator Jeremy Zag has said. Meanwhile, his studio, Zag Entertainment, is also making headway on Melody , an animated feature film with Katy Perry . Zag co-created French animated show Miraculous through Zag. He was feted as Deadline’s 2026 French TV Disruptor this week at Unifrance’s Rendez-Vous market, recognizing his work creating animated series and movies that have travelled the world. He received the accolade in the historic surroundings of the Montivilliers Abbey in Normandy, France. Ahead of being presented with the award, the animation boss sat down with Deadline to talk about his work, and tease some of what’s next. Related Stories News International Sales Of French TV Programs Crash To A Ten-Year Low News French TV In Focus: Screenings & Shows To Watch At The Unifrance Rendez-Vous Zag explained how with Miraculous and other work he always sets out to create a whole universe, spanning TV and film as well as games and merch. “I really believe in the power of a brand, and I believe that from a little drawing, you can create a giant franchise,” he said. Zag decamped to L.A. to build Miraculous into a global franchise. He took creative inspiration from U.S. superhero culture, but also learned some American business smarts to create a universe of characters. The Zag team has a raft of new superheroes ready to join Ladybug, and Zag also teased a live-action Miraculous series. “We’re going to keep the DNA of what people love about Miraculous ,” Zag said about the project. “We are moving forward now. Based on Mark Behr’s eponymous 1993 Booker Prize-nominated novel, the film follows a young boy growing up in a white utopia in Cape Town in the 1970s at the height of the racial segregation imposed by the Apartheid system. On the surface his family leads a charmed life, but the complex family drama will expose the brutality beneath the idyllic façade. Related Stories Festivals Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline's Reviews Reviews 'Being Heumann' Review: Siân Heder & Talented Disabled Ensemble Recount Historic Protest That Paved Way For ADA -- Toronto Film Festival “We were deeply touched and very impressed by the strength, the emotional power and the sheer beauty of the film,” remarked Michéle Halberstadt, co-founding chief of the Paris-based distribution company, the upcoming slate of which also features TIFF titles, Le Faux Soir by Michaël R. Roskam and We Are All Strangers by Anthony Chen. The film is produced by Eric Abraham, Jack Sidey (Portobello Productions), Cait Pansegrouw (Cadence) and Frank Hoeve (BALDR Films). It is the second South African film produced by Abraham and Sidey, whose credits include the Academy Award-winning films Kolya and Ida .
