articles.title: Anchor Access, Original Shows and a Real-Life Lounge: Inside MS NOW’s Membership Push
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Uniting the biggest names in Hollywood with the athletic stars they admire most close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 10, 2026 6:00am A rendering of the MS NOW Members Lounge in Dallas MS NOW Latr this month a few thouand of MS NOW ‘s biggest fans will descend on College Park Center at the University of Texas at Arlington for what the news brand says will be its biggest event yet: “MS NOW Live: Together in Texas.” The event comes at a critical moment for MS NOW, which this week launched its first subscription offering, the MS NOW membership. The Texas event, it turns out, will be a testing ground, in more ways than one. MS NOW members attending the live event will discover a dedicated members lounge, with a bar, comfortable seating, and the opportunity to mingle with other super fans as well as some of the channel’s talent. “As a long timer in our business, I feel like it’s really, really different,” says Marcus Mabry, MS NOW’s senior VP of content strategy, “I’ve never had anything like this in any other news space I’ve been in, we actually want to emphasize people being together, and that’s really powerful.” “We’ve ignored humanity for some reason,” he adds. “So even down to the decor, the offerings of food and beverage, even down to that, it’s about warmth and celebration, and it celebrates of our democracy, which we don’t often do that much these days in our country.” Mabry says that MS NOW intends to pop up member lounges throughout the year, likely tied to live MS NOW events or news events, a real-life benefit to a digital subscription, and one of many features that executives at the cable channel hope will help it stand out in a crowded space for subscriptions. “Our challenge is to prove to our audience, which is many million strong, that this is worth their time and this is worth their wallet, and we are pretty humble about the task in front of us, and we know that it’s a busy, crowded marketplace,” MS NOW president Rebecca Kutler says, when asked by The Hollywood Reporter in the company’s New York headquarters about entering a crowded market. “We think through our research that we have found a white space that’s meaningful. We think we are creating something that doesn’t currently exist, and now it’s on our team to deliver on that and earn, earn our members, earn the community.” The membersip will have plenty of video content, of course. All the MS NOW shows are there, as are a slate of originals, including interview programs hosted by Rachel Maddow and Claire McCaskill, a data-centric program led by Ali Velshi, The Very Last Word with Lawrence O’Donnell, and a legal show led by Andrew Weissmann. But the company is leaning into the other stuff even more: Live Q&A’s with anchors and correspondents, twice per day, including standing Q&A’s every week with the likes of Rachel Maddow and Joe Scarborough. The talent has fully bought in. “For us on the talent side, we all raised our hands because we also know what the future looks like, right?” says Stephanie Ruhle, who will also do weekly Q&As. “This wasn’t a question of, do we want to enter into a new venture with Rebecca? We make great shows and we feel great about it, but it’s not a secret that linear TV is going in one direction, and so none of us are saying, ‘well, we’re going to jump off this ship.’ We’re saying we are part of an amazing machine. We see where the future is. Why don’t we maintain what we have and now jump into this new venture? That’s not a giant financial investment for our company, that’s an investment for all of us in our collective futures.” There will be news, but not too much news, and at the end of the day’s top stories, there will be a dedicated mindfulness experience, in partnership with Calm. In their research, executives found that consumers “said they were overwhelmed by the sheer volume of news. They said they were isolated, either because they were blue dots in red states, or because they were afraid to wade into the cesspool that is social media. And they told us they were anxious, either about the state of the country, or the state of the world, or frankly the future of our democracy,” says Mabry. “So what we’ve done in the MS NOW membership and app is we’ve built a product designed to confront overwhelm with concise curation, to defeat isolation with connection, both to our journalists and to each other, and to confront anxiety by giving our members agency,” he adds. “I don’t know whose idea was to put wellness into this thing, but it’s brilliant because that is literally the antidote to everything I hear,” quips Velshi, speaking to reporters in MS NOW’s office this week. The mindfulness content will include meditation exercises, but also content from doctors, therapists and psychologists, not to mention former ABC News correspondent Dan Harris, who left ABC five years ago to focus on his meditation company. “I think there’s a huge opportunity here, and there’s a real service that can be provided,” Harris says. “A lot of people feel like they need their anxiety and anger in order to do anything in this environment, and I get that. I’m not trying to deny you your anger, I just don’t think it’s the cleanest burning fuel. I think the cleanest burning fuel is a regulated nervous system that allows you to respond wisely with maximum effectiveness.” But getting together in real life will be a big piece of it, through big events, members lounges, and even live tapings of episodes like The Weeknight, which will also be heading to Texas. “I think this is actually very transformative,” says Weeknight co-host Symone Sanders. “It is no small thing that a news organization, especially in this economy, is investing in their folks going on the road, but also investing in in-person experiences. It feels kind of BravoCon-ish, if you will.” “It is building on the connections, the parasocial relationship, frankly, that we build with our audience for the people that tune in with us every night. But I think this kind of investment is the future, and we’ve clearly got something going,” she continued. “We are inviting people to our table, and so we want folks to feel like they are literally sitting down having dinner with us every night. And the in-person aspect of that just allows us to magnify it even more.” If CNN’s subscription is for news junkies, and Fox Nation is for Fox fans, MS NOW thinks it can carve out a slice of the business that is distinct, and less dependent on a linear TV brand that is sliding in one direction. “We believe, and you’ll hear me say this over and over again, our brand is to be pro-democracy, and if you are pro-democracy, kind of subhead A of that is strong, free, and fair press, and that is a huge part of what we are building, both for our DTC community and for the overall MS NOW brand,” Kutler says. . THR

articles.title: Belmont Cameli and NHL Phenom Macklin Celebrini Talk ‘Off Campus,’ Olympic Heartbreak and Handling the Hype
articles.full_text: Skip to main content THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Uniting the biggest names in Hollywood with the athletic stars they admire most close Macklin Celebrini (left) and Belmont Cameli were photographed Aug. 17 in Vancouver. Cameli styling by Sydney Lopez. On Cameli: Saint Laurent shirt, pants; Calvin Klein tank; IWC watch; Jack Spade belt. Celebrini styling by Courtney Mays. On Celebrini: Won Hundred shirt; Madewell tee. Photographed by Amanda Pratt; Cameli hair: Rexford Bangle; Celebrini grooming: Erin Klassen; Fashion assistants: Bea Crane and Tallulah Crane “I’m not a hockey player, but I play one on TV,” could be the calling card for several of today’s hottest young actors. Belmont Cameli , the 28-year-old star of Prime Video’s Off Campus , falls into that group — but more impressive is how quickly he’s distinguished himself within it. Ask any Hollywood casting director to name the top up-and-coming talents, and Cameli will almost certainly be near the top of that list. Still, playing a sexy hockey player on TV and being an actual player in the NHL are very different jobs, performed by very different types of guys. That’s what we assumed, anyway, when we brought together Cameli and Macklin Celebrini , the San Jose Sharks’ wunderkind center, for THR ‘s Game Recognize Game video series. As their conversation reveals, the pair have a lot more in common than we could have expected. Related Stories Lifestyle Sydney Sweeney Stars in Provocative Ad Campaign for Novig Sports Trading App THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue The Athlete Is the Studio On Cameli: Saint Laurent shirt, pants; Calvin Klein tank; IWC watch; Jack Spade belt. On Celebrini: Won Hundred shirt; Madewell tee. Photographed by Amanda Pratt Of course, we did know that both are in the midst of meteoric rises. Off Campus is hardly Cameli’s first project — the Chicago-area native has worked alongside Robert De Niro and was a series regular on the Saved by the Bell reboot — but his role as college hockey star Garrett Graham has completely changed his career trajectory. He’s currently shooting the show’s second season in Vancouver. Celebrini also has been spending his summer in his hometown of Vancouver, much of it at a training rink. Only 20, Celebrini is already a bona fide NHL superstar. He earned his first Olympic medal this year, winning silver with Team Canada after falling to the U.S. in the gold medal game. And in July, he inked a five-year, $94 million contract extension, making him the highest-paid player in the league at the time (a one-of-a-kind version of his rookie trading card recently sold for $1.28 million at auction). While this is the first time Cameli and Celebrini have met, they had a previous close call. Celebrini was asked to make a cameo appearance in Off Campus . “Can you tell me why the shoot time was from midnight until 3 a.m.?” asks Celebrini, jokingly incredulous. Learning about the brutal production schedule of an actor has him wondering whether he actually has it easy. Cameli is quick to set him straight: “Nobody’s hitting me at full speed.” “Every day, there are kids around watching the practice,” says Celebrini. “They want their stuff signed, and for me that’s really cool because I was that kid hanging around.” Won Hundred shirt; Madewell tee; Our Legacy track pants; Celebrini’s necklace. Photographed by Amanda Pratt “I ALWAYS BELIEVED THAT I COULD SORT IT OUT” BELMONT CAMELI Do you know that we share a common trainer? Barb [Underhill]. MACKLIN CELEBRINI She’s teaching you how to skate? She’s great. CAMELI We came here for two weeks in March for a boot camp during the offseason, and that’s when we met Barb. We have a few mutual friends, actually, because you know [New York Rangers defenseman] Vincent Iorio. CELEBRINI He’s your double. I played with Vinny on the San Jose Sharks for a couple of months. CAMELI I want to ask you the same question I like to ask anyone who plays hockey. What’s the greatest in-game moment you’ve ever had? CELEBRINI Stepping onto the ice at the Olympics was one of the coolest things I’ve ever done. Representing Canada, knowing how global that is and how big that tournament is. That was one of the most special moments for me. CAMELI I feel that when we’re shooting, and I got the Garrett Graham jersey on, I step out and it’s a mostly empty rink that they will fill in with fans later with special effects. ( Laughs .) It’s kind of something like that. Maybe not completely. CELEBRINI Very similar. Lots of cameras. CAMELI What is something people constantly assume about you that is completely wrong? CELEBRINI I think hockey players in general have a bad rap of not having much personality. It’s just what the culture has always been with hockey, but if you meet some of the guys that play in the NHL, they’re some of the funniest guys. I feel like that really doesn’t get portrayed very well on camera. CAMELI There’s something about the locker room interviews in hockey that are pretty fucking serious. We have tons of doubles who’ve grown up playing hockey and they are a bunch of goofballs. You were drafted first overall. What was draft day like? CELEBRINI I thought I was going to be super nervous and a little panicked. You walk up in front of all those people, and it’s a real raw moment for you. The thing that surprised me most was that I was very calm. When I got picked, it was more exciting than anything. Mine was at the Las Vegas Sphere. It was such a big production that I think it was one of the coolest drafts that they’ve had. CAMELI When did you start playing hockey? How old were you? CELEBRINI I was 3 years old when I put on skates and started skating around the rink. Not long after, I started playing hockey. CAMELI I was 27. CELEBRINI Really? You were 27 when you started acting? CAMELI No, when I started skating. ( Laughs. ) I was 20 or 21 when I started acting. I hadn’t been a performer. I was an athlete before that. I played football, wrestling and volleyball. When you were a kid, was your dream always to go to the NHL? CELEBRINI That was always my dream. Growing up here, watching the NHL all the time, put it in my head that it was bigger than something that I could do. I was just dreaming about it. When did you know you could act professionally? For sports , it’s a little bit easier because you see all the guys you’re playing against and there’s rankings. “You can say whatever you want about me or people in my life, but it’s not going to affect me because I’m fully aware of what my reality looks like and feels like,” says Cameli. Saint Laurent shirt, pants, loafers; Calvin Klein tank; Maor ring; Cameli’s necklace; IWC watch; Wander socks; Jack Spade belt. Photographed by Amanda Pratt CAMELI Full honesty, I thought I could act professionally before I ever acted. I was a college student and was studying business. I realized that’s not what I wanted. I arrived very quickly at the dream of being a filmmaker. I hadn’t done it before, but I thought I could figure that out. I didn’t know for certain that I would have success, and I imagined it would take quite some time, but I always believed that I could sort it out. But the first time I actually felt like a professional actor was when I shot a horror film in Budapest. It was a really fun shoot for a movie called Until Dawn , which was based on a video game. When was the first inkling that you could get drafted and could compete in the NHL? CELEBRINI I did a lot of interviews from when I was 14 and on. The biggest question was if I thought about playing in the NHL one day. My answer was always that I didn’t think about it very much because I was trying to focus on what I was doing. Obviously, I thought about it. I watched NHL games and dreamed of playing in the league and achieving that goal. But I think juniors — I was 16, so two years back from my draft year — was the first time I started thinking I could actually play in the NHL. CAMELI How old were you when you got drafted? CELEBRINI I turned 18 on June 13, and then the draft was June 30. I played my first NHL game three months later. That summer was insane. It moved so fast. Photographed by Amanda Pratt “NOBODY IS KNOCKING ME OFF MY FEET” CELEBRINI Have you ever had to cry on set? How do you make yourself cry? CAMELI Yes, I’ve had to cry on set. The thing about Off Campus is that it gets pretty heavy. We deal with some pretty serious themes. For me, I don’t have a real good hack beyond the text, so if the script is written emotionally enough, it’ll move me. Some people are better at it than others. There are some actors on this show who are just like, boom. I’m not there. I need to believe it. CELEBRINI Your shoot days are 14 hours sometimes. Do you get coffee or do you do something else to kind of get you through? CAMELI Last year, Ella [Bright] and I were really working close to 80 hours every single week, so when I have big full weeks like that, it’s no coffee in the morning. I’ll probably end up with one or two coffees in a day, but I don’t do the first one until hours into the day. If I start with it right away, I’m going to need another one in two hours. Then I’ll end up having five or six more. Sugar-free Red Bulls are popular on our set. You were almost on our show, right? CELEBRINI Yeah. Can you tell me why the shoot time was from midnight until 3 a.m.? Would that be on a Saturday or what? It was an absurd time to film. CAMELI There is no absurd time to film. You could be filming at any given moment. CELEBRINI Talking about how long your days are, I think being an athlete’s pretty easy. It might be the best job in the world. CAMELI Yeah, but nobody’s knocking me off my feet and hitting me full speed. CELEBRINI That’s true, you could get hurt. CAMELI What does your offseason regimen look like? Is it up to you? Are you designing it? CELEBRINI My dad specializes in sports medicine and science. For the past eight years, he’s worked with the Golden State Warriors. I also have a strength and conditioning coach that my dad worked really closely with, so they put their heads together and come up with a program based on whatever I feel like I need to work on and get better at. I trust them. CAMELI Are you on a pretty strict diet? CELEBRINI I try to eat as good as I can. Obviously, I cheat on it a little bit. Throughout the week, it’s more [about the] routine. In the morning, I’ll make eggs and sourdough toast. I bring a smoothie with me, so I always have something. The days are long. I usually get the same stuff because it’s routine, and I like it. It’s healthy. CAMELI What part of your game are you most focused on getting better and growing over your offseason this year? CELEBRINI Last year, with the Olympics, we played a lot of games. It was the first year where I played way more games than I practiced. In the second half of the year, I didn’t really skate unless it was a game, which was the weirdest thing ever. I’d get off the ice, and I wouldn’t touch the ice until warm-ups of the next game. It was [about] energy. You just don’t have enough energy to even get dressed and get out there. It takes a lot. Especially after the Olympics, that kind of drained you a little bit. That impacts my top speed. CAMELI What’s your top speed? CELEBRINI Last year, I think it was like 22 miles an hour, 21, 20 something. I feel like I got caught, especially with how many games I played. It was tough to feel fresh every night. I’m balancing some of that conditioning with speed work and trying to get faster and have a little bit more pop. CAMELI What I love about hockey is how individual it is in play style. I’m still developing mine. CELEBRINI If this show runs for 10 seasons, you’re going to get real good. Photographed by Amanda Pratt CAMELI The best thing that would help my game right now is being able to transition from skating forwards to backwards and backwards to forwards while having some speed. Not quite there yet. And stopping. I can skate so fast, but I can’t stop so good. I hit the boards at least once a day. At full speed. CELEBRINI Get Barb on that. That should be the first thing. Starting and stopping. CAMELI I can stop on my right pretty good, but I don’t even really have the left at all. Sometimes we’re shooting, and for the camera, I have to do it on the left side. I’m like, “You guys have to move the camera to the other side because I can’t do that.” I want to ask you about the Olympics. In four years when you win, we’ll do this again. What was it like? You’ve lost other big games, but how did you deal? CELEBRINI Obviously, because of the magnitude of the game — USA and Canada, that rivalry, and then the history that went into it. I don’t know if you saw it, but I had a lot of chances in that game. I had a breakaway. I had a couple chances. Their goalie played unbelievably. [When it comes to losing,] I have a very short memory because I’m not really thinking about anything except for what I’m doing. I forget to text people back. It’s just the way I am. Honestly, I haven’t watched the game back. I can’t really let it eat at me just because in two years we have the World Cup of hockey and then another Olympics. CAMELI Is there a part of you using it as fuel? CELEBRINI That’s the way a lot of people have brought it to me, but you may never get that opportunity again. When COVID happened, NHL players weren’t in the Olympics, and also there was a lockout that made the NHL players not play in the Olympics. For 12 years, those guys that would’ve played in the Olympics didn’t get the chance. You never know what’s going to happen. I think about it all the time. I wish there was a better outcome, but to your point, there’s a reason for everything that happens. I’m a big believer in that. There was some stuff to learn from that. It’s like, you do a lot of auditions, how did you handle hearing “no”? CAMELI You can’t really let the “no” affect you because it’s just part of the job. My real job is to procure more work. The job happens when I’m at home shooting self-tapes, memorizing lines, reading scripts, building out characters for auditions. You hear “no” on most of those. “THERE’S ANOTHER LEVEL TO FANDOM THESE DAYS” CAMELI Hype is interesting. You went No. 1 overall, you’re leading the team down there in San Jose. You probably started getting attention pretty young. CELEBRINI Hockey’s a little different than other sports in that way. There’s attention around you, but some of the top basketball prospects or football prospects, there are cameras at every high school game. It’s just a different level. I didn’t have that very much. Then you just kind of get used to it. People are always talking about you, and you can’t really pay attention to it because there are so many opinions out there that don’t matter. CAMELI Especially in sports. You get people critiquing your game, and then on and off the ice. It’s kind of the same with us, too. Being an actor, everybody has something to say about your performance, but then they also have everything to say about what’s happening in your personal life, too. CELEBRINI I feel like that’s a big thing for actors. Do you feel like people are too invested in your personal life? How do you feel about that? Do you have paparazzi following you around? CAMELI There’s been some paps around. That’s all new and kind of strange. Look, if you’re a fan of the show — the thing that I’m so proud of and pour my heart and soul into — then that’s fucking awesome. But the way our show popped, there’s another level to fandom these days, especially with the internet. Sometimes there’s a real venom to the way people put you under microscopes. You feel constantly observed. I’ve been pretty good with handling that. You can say whatever you want about me or people in my life, but it’s not going to affect me because I’m fully aware of what my reality looks like and feels like. A lot of people have really nice things to say, and a lot of people have mean things to say. To me, it’s just all noise. When I see people out, and they come up to say they love the show, that’s always really enjoyable. It doesn’t always go that way. Some people will just run up with a camera in your face and ask for a picture. I’ll be like, “No, hello?” People get excited. Usually, they’re really sweet. What about you? Photographed by Amanda Pratt CELEBRINI While you were talking, I was relating to everything you were saying. Maybe not as much as you, but it’s a different feeling when it’s kids or the people who look up to you. I get that a lot with younger kids around the rink. Usually, every summer I skate at a private rink, but this summer I’ve been skating at a very public rink. Every day, there are kids around watching the practice. They want their stuff signed, and for me that’s really cool because I was that kid hanging around. My dad worked for the Canucks for four years, so I was around some of the professional players. I know how much it meant to me. That’s something that I’ll never really get sick of. But there are some incidents where it gets a little weird. CAMELI Have you ever searched your own name? CELEBRINI I have. Just to see what’s going on. I can’t say I do it very much, but I have done it before. CAMELI Check the temperature. I’ve done it before, too. Right when we started to do press for this show and the noise started up, I did it. It was mostly good and some bad. I haven’t done it since. I’m really protective of making sure that the choices I make, the things that I do and the people I surround myself with are things that serve me. That type of thing doesn’t always accomplish that task. You signed a new contract lately. What was that for? CELEBRINI Five years, $18.8 million a year, $94 million total. CAMELI What was that like for you when you signed that big contract? CELEBRINI It was exciting. The entry-level contracts in the NHL aren’t quite as big as other sports, so this is the first time you make real money. Well, in terms of professional sports. Obviously, a million dollars a year is a lot of money. In terms of the actual contract, it still feels weird because that’s not really why I’m playing. It was a long negotiation trying to figure out what worked best for our young team. Making sure everyone gets paid and where the [salary] cap is going. [It was] figuring out all that data and figuring out what makes the most sense, and we landed on that. CAMELI Has your spending gone up? CELEBRINI No. I mean, it’s been a couple weeks. CAMELI No, me neither. What’s the first big thing you want to buy? Boat? House? Houseboat? CELEBRINI A houseboat would be great. That’d be awesome. Probably a house. I don’t really need anything else. CAMELI I’m there too, honestly. I still have the same closet of clothes. I probably will still have that same wardrobe for a long time. I drive my Honda, the first car I bought. I’ll drive that puppy until the wheels fall off. Having opportunities to make a good living, doing what I love doing, I’ll never take that for granted. I’m just grateful to be in a greater position to help other people. CELEBRINI Did you get a bump from season one to season two? CAMELI Yeah. When you sign an X amount of years for a TV show, there’s one baked in there. It’s commonplace to renegotiate at a certain point. CELEBRINI How many seasons do you think Off Campus will run for? CAMELI That’s a question that, from you, I really like. From a journalist, I’d be like, “You’re trying to dig.” My business answer is Amazon optioned all the books a couple of years ago. There are five books in the first [series]. There are another four [in the second series]. In success, it could run for a long time. We all hope so. Does the kind of money you’re making add pressure? CELEBRINI It’s cliché, but I have expectations for myself with the way I prepare and how much confidence and belief I have in myself. I want to do as good as anyone else wants me to do. I already put that pressure on myself to perform. [We went] into last year with higher expectations on our team, and then going into this year with higher expectations on our team — it’s just going to keep building. But it doesn’t really change what we do on the ice. I’m never going to change what I do because of outside circumstances. That doesn’t affect the game at all. This story appears in The Hollywood Reporter’s September 2026 Sports issue .

articles.title: Musical ‘& Juliet’ Will End Broadway Run In January
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Uniting the biggest names in Hollywood with the athletic stars they admire most close By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All September 10, 2026 6:00am The Broadway production of '& Juliet.' Matthew Murphy Musical & Juliet will end its Broadway run in January, after more than four years on Broadway. The show, created by David West Read, reimagines the Shakespearean tragedy so that Juliet lives and is set to a pop score from Max Martin, with songs including “Since U Been Gone,” “Roar,” and “I Want It That Way.” The musical, which is set to close Jan. 3, 2027, is the last remaining show on Broadway from the 2022-2023 season. The show began in the UK before opening on Broadway at the Stephen Sondheim Theatre on November 17, 2022. The Broadway musical recouped its $17 million capitalization in 2024 (and the tour recouped in 2025), and has since grossed more than $175 million. Though capacity has remained fairly strong throughout its run, grosses have begun to trend downward over the past two years. It joins Six , another longer running musical which opened in 2021, in announcing a January closing date. Related Stories Lifestyle Broadway Box Office: 'Hamilton' Leads Labor Day Weekend Grosses Lifestyle Scott Rudin Plans Two New Broadway Shows, Including One With Julia Roberts and Paul Rudd Throughout its run, the musical has welcomed a number of celebrities making their Broadway debuts, including Chrissy Metz and Joey Fatone, both currently in the cast, as well as Charli D’Amelio, Laurie Hernandez, Kandi Burruss and Cheryl Porter. Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson also had a one-night, walk-on role in the musical. Before the show ends on Broadway run, it will welcome Kenzie Ziegler, Aly Michalka, Spencer Sutherland, Anthony Gargiula and more. The musical is produced on Broadway by Max Martin, Tim Headington, Theresa Steele Page, Jenny Petersson, Martin Dodd and Eva Price. THR

articles.title: Monica Dolan Shares How She Prepared to Portray the Woman Who Uncovered an Irish Mass Grave Scandal in ‘The Lost Children of Tuam’: TIFF
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Uniting the biggest names in Hollywood with the athletic stars they admire most close By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 10, 2026 6:01am Monica Dolan in 'The Lost Children of Tuam' Courtesy of Element Pictures Monica Dolan ( Mr Bates vs The Post Office , Pride , Wolf Hall , Black Mirror ) is quietly having a banner year. At the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), the English character actress is pulling triple duty, appearing in no fewer than three films. In the real-life The Lost Children of Tuam , produced by Liam Neeson and directed by Frank Berry, Dolan stars as history enthusiast Catherine Corless, who researched the Bon Secours Mother and Baby Home in Tuam, Ireland, only to uncover that as many as 796 children had been buried in unmarked graves on the property. The movie world-premiered at the Galway Film Fleadh in July, where it won the best Irish film award, and will screen in the Centerpiece Program at Toronto, beginning on Sunday, Sept. 13. Related Stories Movies Oscars: Australia Picks 'First Light' as International Feature Contender (Exclusive) TV 'RuPaul's Drag Race UK' Dropped by BBC Also at Toronto, you can see Dolan in the world premiere of John Madden’s Onwards and Sideways , starring Laura Linney and Rhys Ifans as two people with a lot in common – a great sense of humor, a love of dance, and, as just diagnosed, Parkinson’s. Dolan plays the sister of Ifans’ character. And then there is Simon Stone’s Elsinore , which is already attracting awards season buzz after its Venice world premiere before it heads to Toronto. Starring Andrew Scott as British actor Ian Charleson, who throws himself into playing Hamlet while succumbing to AIDS, the film’s ensemble cast features Dolan as the sarcastic receptionist at the National Theatre in London. If you needed any more proof of Dolan’s versatility, earlier this year, she also featured in the supporting cast of season 2 of BBC comedy series Smoggie Queens . Her role: the ex-wife of the drag queen character Mam, played by Mark Benton. Dolan studied drama at the Guildhall School in London and then went into television, soon turning heads, including with characters who have darker sides. Among others, she played a real-life stalker in U Be Dead and serial killer Rosemary West in Appropriate Adult opposite Dominic West, a role for which she won the BAFTA TV Award. More recently, she drew praise, nominations and awards for her portrayal of a real-life woman in charge of a local post office branch in ITV drama Mr Bates vs the Post Office . You may also remember her for portraying George Mackay’s bigoted mother in the 2014 film Pride . On stage, she won the 2019 Laurence Olivier Award for best supporting actress for playing Karen Richards in the West End production of All About Eve . Rhys Ifans and Monica Dolan in ‘Onwards and Sideways’ Courtesy of BBC/Hilltop Screen Dolan talked to THR about her TIFF films, needing a coach to nail the right Irish regional accent in The Lost Children of Tuam despite having Irish parents, how she chooses roles, and why she likes to explore a wide range of human behavior. How does it feel to have three films at the Toronto festival? Or is this something you do regularly? (laughs) No, I’ve never had this before. It is really incredible. Actually, I was very, very excited when I heard I’d got two, and my agent and I were trying to organize all the logistics. And then I just got another little one-line email saying, “By the way, Elsinore is in there as well.” But really luckily, they all fall over the same weekend, so I can be there for all three. I’m really happy about that. In The Lost Children of Tuam , you are the protagonist, while in the other two films, you’re part of great ensembles. Is the work much different for you when leading a project? Yes, they’re quite different skills. I’m quite lucky in that I’ve played lots of lead roles in the theater, and when you do that, you’re leading the whole company for quite a long time. It is sort of a marathon rather than a sprint. But when you’re in an ensemble, the important thing to remember, always, is that you’re telling a story. And when you’re in an ensemble, part of your job is to support and just to treat that seriously. It’s quite uncommon for me to lead a film, but I absolutely love the experience, and I’ve been watching other leading actors closely. So, hopefully, I didn’t make too much of a mess of it. Well, I didn’t know Catherine Corless before The Lost Children of Tuam , but I was captivated by her as portrayed by you. Did you get to spend much time with her in preparing for the role and what did you look for? I was really, really lucky with Catherine because she’s a beautiful person. She’s incredibly approachable, and she just thinks in a very unusual way. If I asked off-the-wall questions at whatever time of day or night, it never really fazed her. I might go from asking something very specific about maps and death certificates to saying, “Do you wear your jewelry at night?” Because you’re creating a whole person. She was really wonderful. I visited their small [agricultural] holding. I met Aidan, Catherine’s husband. I met their dogs. And I met some of her family, and I was there when the cows ran into the garden, so that was fun. Catherine also made a physical model of the Mother and Baby Home. There were so few photographs, and she wanted to be able to visualize it. And she wanted the survivors to be able to visualize it as well. So she showed me that and talked me through that. That was quite illuminating. Once I started talking to her about the model, everything became a bit more three-dimensional. And I realized that I actually just wanted to know what she cared about and what was important to her. And they got a wonderful field at the back, and we went for a walk around there, and I think maybe that was my most valuable time with her. Information about herself just flowed more freely, and it was also more two-way because I was talking about myself as well. I think we went on the walk because I asked, “What’s your favorite thing?” and she said, “my garden.” So I got a real sense of what she really cares about. I don’t think I’ve met anyone who has more care and value and love for living things. Monica Dolan in ‘Mr Bates vs the Post Office,’ courtesy of ITV PBS/ITV/Masterpiece Theatre / Courtesy Everett Collection That’s fascinating! Are there any things you always ask when portraying a real-life person? One thing that I’ve developed, which I’ve found really useful, is to ask the person, if it is a real person, and if they don’t mind – I wouldn’t ask everyone – to record just 15 minutes of their life story. What’s really good about that is that you get their voice and you get their background in one. And if it is about 15 minutes, you can listen to it on your way from the unit base to the set. Also, if you’re asking somebody to tell you about themselves, they’re not thinking about their voice as much. If you’re asking them something that they know a lot about, and they can hopefully get involved in, and they’re obviously emotionally involved in because it’s themselves, they [don’t think and worry too much] about their voice. How else do you get into a character, especially when she is not based on a real-life person? We also had a really terrific script here. Rebecca Lenkiewicz ( She Said , Ida ) spent a lot of time with Catherine. It might sound like quite a radical thing to say, but most of the time when I’m reading a script, I mainly look at the behavior of the people and not really at what they’re saying. One of the characters I played actually was at her most chatty when she was about to do something really awful, but didn’t say very much otherwise. If I were speaking to younger people at drama school, I think I’d tell them that as a tip – to look at the character’s behavior. Catherine, early on, really found it very hard to believe that once people knew the truth, they wouldn’t act on it. She spends a lot of the film being quite bewildered, and she did spend a lot of her time being quite bewildered about that in real life. She realizes that they’re purposely ignoring her, and that creates an enormous amount of anger and depression. With anything where you’re pursuing a cause or request, most of the time the person or the character has something that makes them very personally invested. I think that in her darkest moments, that was what kept her going. Catherine did speak to me about her relationship with her mother, and their relationship wasn’t the easiest. After her death, Catherine and her husband researched her mother’s background and discovered that she was illegitimate [and had been raised by foster families]. So, it’s about her personal motivation and also how she’s trying to do the right thing, while it’s becoming really apparent that nobody else is. I think she’s an extraordinary woman in that. I think other people, practically anybody else, could have had all of the information that she had, but wouldn’t have been able to put it together in the way that she did and wouldn’t have been able to even notice what she did notice. Gillian Anderson and Monica Dolan in ‘All About Eve’ Jan Versweyveld I read that your parents are Irish. Could you tap into their Irish for the role of Catherine? My mum’s from Enniscorthy in County Wexford, and my dad’s from Swords in Dublin, neither of which accents [is from] the West of Ireland, so I sort of had to start from scratch. I had a really wonderful coach, Paul. Why did you become an actress in the first place? I’ve always been quite nosy and sort of gossipy. You must have that as a journalist as well. (laughs) So, I like doing detective work about people. I don’t always notice it at the time, but I realize it later. I think it’s partly because I was the youngest of four, and I was five years younger than the next one up. So I needed to do quite a bit of showing off to get any attention. Everyone else was very academic and very clever in my family. With acting, you can behave in the most extreme and appalling and exciting ways, and there aren’t any consequences because it’s all a game. I mean, hopefully there are not any personal consequences, but you’re sometimes dealing with quite extreme things. You’re exploring sides of human nature and putting yourself in someone else’s skin, experiencing that. I think it creates more empathy in oneself. And I’d go as far as to say I’ve definitely learnt from each of the characters I’ve played, and hopefully they sort of stretch you as a person. You’ve played some really dark and scary characters in dramas, and then I saw you earlier this year in the BBC comedy Smoggie Queens , about the chosen family and lives of a group of LGBTQ+ friends. How do you choose roles, or how did that comedy role come about? A lot of it depends on what I’m offered. With Smoggie Queens , I saw the first [season] and I absolutely loved it. My friend Mark Benton, who I’ve known for years, was in it playing Mam. So, I texted him and said, “Oh my gosh, I love this series. If there’s ever a part for me, can you let me know?” And so, then, in the next [season], I was playing his ex-wife Paula. That group of people and that production is incredibly well organized and incredibly humane and enormous fun. It was just wonderful being around those people. They are so big-hearted and witty. At this stage in your career, do you have any preference for film, TV or theater? The atmosphere and the production on every series and every film will be different. And the dynamic of every production is different, be it theater, film or television. I really enjoy variety. THR

articles.title: AI Is Deflating Hollywood’s Microdramas Scene
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Uniting the biggest names in Hollywood with the athletic stars they admire most close By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All September 10, 2026 6:05am China pioneered the microdrama industry as we know it, with the duanju format exploding in popularity during the pandemic. So when AI -generated verticals began flooding the Chinese market and reports emerged that production workers were scared for their jobs, it was an ominous sign for the burgeoning industry in the U.S. Now, it’s become clear that companies serving the American market are very much testing the appeal of these bite-sized, AI-generated stories. Not every firm is going the route of My Muse or Inkitt Ironblood, apps that exclusively release AI verticals, often fantasy, period and action stories that would require some serious budgets if they were filmed in live action. But some major players, including DramaBox, DramaWave and FlareFlow, have increasingly been embracing synthetic actors and settings and showering their apps with prompt-generated, sometimes uncanny fare, no human actors required. For entertainment workers in the Los Angeles area, that shift has come with consequences. In the wake of the 2023 Hollywood strikes, verticals became a lifeline for cast and crew as traditional jobs evaporated. Now, L.A.-based microdrama workers tell The Hollywood Reporter that jobs in the once-reliable industry have become scarcer, while unscrupulous use of the tech on the work of creatives is on the rise. It’s a tough pill to swallow for an underemployed Hollywood workforce that once saw the field as a job-saver. “People who’ve been working full-time in this space for years are going back to their day jobs, going home, and that’s cast, crew, producers,” says Candace Mizga, an actor in the vertical space and co-founder of the microdrama platform Chera TV, which does not use AI. “It has been a huge, huge jump, especially this past couple of months. It’s been pretty wild to see.” It will come as no surprise that AI microdramas can individually be made cheaper, faster and with fewer workers. While budgets for live-action microdramas tend to fall in the $100,000 to $300,000 range, pro-looking, feature-length AI microdramas can cost $60,000 to $100,000, according to AI verticals production studio Axis AI Studios. (Think that’s a bargain? The app TrueShort has claimed its 20- to 30-minute AI projects can be made for as little as $1,000 to $3,000.) In terms of the production schedule, these projects can be completed in two weeks as compared to 12 weeks for a live-action story, per Holywater Tech, which owns the all-AI My Muse app. Owl & Co. And though a live-action shoot might require 50 workers for seven days, “now we would need five people for seven days to make one show,” says Guy Shimoni, the CEO and co-founder of the platform Shortical, which releases both live-action and AI verticals. While microdrama firms have been dipping their toes into AI for some time, the release of the Seedance 2.0 AI video generator tool in February accelerated adoption of the tech, says Shimoni. Once Seedance 2.0 released, enabling that viral video of Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise fighting, “The technology was really there to tell a good story, a good narrative, the art effects weren’t too bad,” Shimoni says. “We all started adopting when Seedance 2.0 came out.” While it’s unclear how much AI is to blame, microdrama insiders say work opportunities at large have recently been slowing. Maddie Grove, a talent manager at LEWK Management, has some 15 actor clients in the verticals space. “June hit and all of a sudden we went from having 15 to 20 different shows casting on breakdowns a day to maybe four,” she says, noting there has been a “significant drop” in employment opportunities. She’s not alone in seeing a larger change afoot. “Last year, I was getting anywhere between five to 15 vertical auditions a week,” says Chera TV co-founder and verticals actor Kylie Karson. “I would say I’m getting two a week [now].” Other cases are more obviously tied to the embrace of the tech. Lucia Lopez is a production designer and director who for half a year worked with a production company in Atlanta to produce a microdrama a month for the platform DramaShorts. The production company’s contract with DramaShorts abruptly ended in July when the company went “fully AI.” She adds, “They don’t want anything as live action. And it was in the blink of an eye.” Now she’s back in L.A. and says outreach to producer contacts hasn’t yielded new work. THR has reached out to DramaShorts for comment. “The sheer speed with which apps have basically shut down entire productions, completely pulled out, completely transitioned over to AI is quite spectacular,” says Jen Cooper, the founder of Vertical Drama Love, a media brand that closely tracks the industry. Still, some companies claim they can create more employment opportunity through AI, not less. Shortical’s Shimoni, who notes that individual AI microdramas might use five employees instead of 50, says platforms can now make many more microdramas, rather than produce the same number with fewer people. He adds, “The business is more efficient. So actually we’re understaffed, we’re recruiting more, we’re missing people.” A makeup artist on the CandyJar microdrama ‘Fight Dirty’ gets star Carter Harvey — who plays a street fighter in the romance series — ready for his close-up during a Los Angeles shoot. The Hollywood Reporter Beyond employment concerns, the rise of AI microdramas has sparked issues for creatives around consent. Vertical actors including Ashley BeLoat and Evan Gambardella spoke to Business Insider in July about platforms allegedly using performances and likenesses from live-action microdramas in fully AI projects without human performers’ permission. The publication also reported on platforms allegedly posting sexualized ads for microdramas that used AI to engineer scenes and dialogue that were never filmed or cleared with the actors involved. Some actors are now negotiating AI language into their contracts. But even for those who have written protections, the paperwork doesn’t always matter. Grove — who is BeLoat, Karson and Mizga’s manager — says that, since June, she’s seen platforms breach actors’ contracts four times when it comes to AI. Sometimes, platforms will hire a third-party ad company with which actors don’t have a contract; that company will “take many creative liberties that are overtly sexual, rage-baiting, clickbaity” for advertisements, Grove adds. Lack of leverage may be one reason why this is happening — companies may bank on the idea that burgeoning performers aren’t going to raise a stink or bankroll expensive lawsuits. But unauthorized use of AI isn’t just impacting niche creatives in the vertical space. Vertical Drama Love’s Cooper and social media users have pointed to the visual similarities between characters in DramaWave’s The Rise of the Lycan Queen and DramaBox’s Deny Me, Dragon King and actor Henry Cavill’s character in The Witcher . Flowing white hair? Check. Broad shoulders? Check. Very square jaw and dark brow? Also check. “I like to play a game of where is Henry,“ wrote one social-media user on Reddit. “Sometimes multiple characters look like him in one drama and they use his witcher voice a lot.” THR has reached out to representatives for Cavill, DramaWave and DramaBox for comment. Unscrupulous use of AI can also affect screenwriters. Writer-actor Tess Dinerstein sold a pirate-themed microdrama script to DramaBox in 2025, before she says AI was on the radar of many companies in the U.S. market. Around the same time as she finished revisions for the drama in 2026, she remembers telling an exec that she wouldn’t like the script being made into an AI show. A few months later, that exec had exited the company, and Dinerstein learned that the show had been released as an AI project. Dinerstein acknowledges that DramaBox owns the full rights to the script, but she won’t watch or publicize the adaptation because she doesn’t approve of it. “When I spend so much time on a script and fall in love with the characters and feel like it could be done really well with people, [the use of AI] takes a lot of the heart and soul out of the piece,” she says. THR has reached out to DramaBox for comment. Where is all this headed? In China, more than 95 percent of microdrama titles in the first three months of 2026 were reportedly made using AI. Across the Pacific, viewer demand will ultimately determine whether AI verticals become a short-term curiosity or a staple of the format. “You have to remember whoever’s running this, they’re running numbers. They don’t care about your face, my face,” says actor Eli Jane, who has appeared in about 30 verticals. “If the audience doesn’t show up for AI, then they’re going to stop making that content.” Worried about the AI invasion, actor Martina Monti — who has some 40 microdramas under her belt — began counting the number of vertical acting jobs posted on the digital casting platform Actors Access in seven-day samples across multiple months to determine if a slowdown was reflected there. (She says it was — Actors Access, which is a go-to platform for microdrama acting jobs, did not respond to a request for data for this story.) Says the performer: “Some people have a more positive expectation for the future. They’re like, ‘Hey, we hope that this AI bubble is going to just pop.’ And other people, we don’t know.” She adds, “It’s not going well for now.” This story appeared in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Malachi Kirby Takes the Lead in ‘Uncle’ as Revenge Thriller Gets First Look (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 10, 2026 5:15am PT Malachi Kirby Takes the Lead in ‘Uncle’ as Revenge Thriller Gets First Look (EXCLUSIVE) WestEnd Films is showing footage in Toronto and has already announced the first wave of distribution deals. By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Malachi Kirby Takes the Lead in ‘Uncle’ as Revenge Thriller Gets First Look (EXCLUSIVE) 48 minutes ago Noel Clarke Charged With Sexual Assault, Voyeurism and Exposure 1 day ago Toby Kebbell Joins Prime Video’s U.K. Crime Thriller Series ‘Dirty’ Alongside Samantha Morton and Phoebe Dynevor (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All Mark Hilton Malachi Kirby , the BAFTA-winning “Small Axe” star recently seen as the lead in the Disney+ series “A Thousand Blows,” is starring in revenge-thriller “Uncle,” Variety can reveal. The film, from writer-director Joe Marcantonio (“Kindred”) and which recently wrapped production, also stars newcomer Freya Harvey. WestEnd Films , which is handing world sales, has released a first look image featuring Kirby and Harvey, and has announced the first wave of distribution deals, including for the U.K. (Sky), Portugal (NOS), Bulgaria (Beta) and Poland (Galapagos). Related Stories AI Filmmaking's Future Debated by Alibaba, Sonilo, PROMPTR Executives at TapNow and HappyHorse's Venice Production Bridge Panel Studio TF1 Launches Medical Drama ‘Dr. Seylan & Cindy’ at Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre “Uncle” follows teenage Millie (Harvey) and her uncle John (Kirby) who are thrown together on a relentless mission for revenge and retribution after the brutal murder of their family. Still grieving and struggling to find her place, Millie is drawn into John’s dangerous world — one driven by guilt, anger, and a pull toward violence he can’t escape. But as they close in on the people responsible, their bond deepens, and, as per the synopsis, Millie must decide whether she’s ready to follow her uncle down the “bloody path of revenge — and the violent, premature journey into adulthood that comes with it.” Popular on Variety The film also stars BAFTA Cymru winners Mark Lewis Jones (“Star Wars: The Last Jedi,” “The Crown,” “Baby Reindeer”) and Gabrielle Creevy (“Amadeus, The Guest,” “Black Doves”). Kirby replaces Micheal Ward in the film, which was already in production when the “Top Boy” actor was accused of sexual assault in mid 2025. Ward was recently cleared of all charges in a London court. Written by Marcantonio and Owynne Dawkins, “Uncle” is produced by Auroral Pictures’ Rebecca Knapp (“Rollin’ with the Nines,” “Popcorn”) and Matthew Wakeham (“Two for Joy,” “The Facility”) and Delta Pictures’ Adam Partridge (“Chuck Chuck Baby”). Nicola Pearcey (“Military Wives,” “Madfabulous”), EP at Picnik Entertainment and CEO at Facilities by ADF plc, is executive producing alongside Play House Studios’ Lorcan Kavanagh, Peggy Cafferty, Deepak Sikka, Mark Foligno and Sire Ramos, Principal Film Finance’s Tom George and Jon Gosier of FilmHedge. “Joe is an exceptionally talented filmmaker and he has brought a real confidence and intensity to ‘Uncle,'” said Maya Amsellem, managing Director of WestEnd Films, which will reveal the first footage of the film to buyer at the market in Toronto. “It’s a visceral revenge thriller with a strong emotional core, exploring family, grief and the cycle of violence in a way that feels both gripping and deeply human. We’re excited to unveil this first look ahead of sharing footage with buyers at TIFF .” “Uncle” was developed and produced with the support of Ffilm Cymru Wales with funding from the Arts Council of Wales and Creative Wales using proceeds from the National Lottery and the Welsh Government. Kirby is repped by Identity Agency Group and UTA. articles.full_text: Sep 10, 2026 5:45am PT Thai-Taiwanese Horror Slate Unites Fearfolks and Studio76 in Three-Picture Deal (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Ted Lasso’ Star Nick Mohammed to Host ‘The Traitors’ Stage Play in London 2 hours ago Okada Junichi-Hosted ‘The Floor’ Quiz Format Returns to Nippon TV for Season 2 in Japan (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Yami Gautam Dhar’s Amazon MGM Studios, Colour Yellow Film ‘Nayyi Navelli’ Unveils Teaser (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago See All Fearfolks/Studio76 Bangkok-based horror distributor Fearfolks and Taipei’s Studio76 have signed a three-picture Thai-Taiwanese horror development deal, which was unveiled at the Toronto Film Festival Market. The pact will see the companies co-develop, produce and distribute a slate of genre films for theatrical release. Leading the slate is “Cher,” a supernatural horror-thriller drawing on Thai folklore surrounding mythical forest nymphs. The project recently became the first Thai project to qualify for and win a top prize at the Frontieres Co-production Market in Montreal, and it has also qualified for the Tokyo Gap-Financing Market. Related Stories How 'The Pitt' Production Designer Expanded the Emergency Room for Season 2 How Did the Emmys’ Documentary Category Get So Star-Studded? “Cher” stars Mim Rattanawadee Wongthong, known for the “ Death Whisperer ” franchise, alongside Pae Arak and Weir Sukollawat of “4 Tigers.” Cinematographer Vikash Nowlakha has also joined the production; his work on the “Dhurandhar” duology helped drive a $330 million global box office. Popular on Variety The second title, “Blur Blur Ghost,” takes a lighter, comedic turn. A ghost with poor eyesight wrongly pins her own killing on an unfortunate insurance agent, driving the film’s dark humor. The third project will be selected through the RisingStories International Story Pitching Competition, an annual contest jointly hosted by Fearfolks and Studio76 to find new voices in Asian genre filmmaking. The 2026 edition is backed by Hong Kong’s Emperor Motion Pictures, Singapore’s August Pictures and Taiwan’s Candy Stage and Scloud, with additional support from the Screenwriters Guild of Taiwan and the Taipei Film and Drama Occupational Union. Dennis Yang, CEO of Studio76, said, “Our goal is to dismantle language barriers and provide creators with a seamless trajectory toward global distribution.” Hans Audric Estialbo, CEO of Fearfolks, said the cross-border deal would let Thai and Taiwanese stories tag-team, adding that it would let them “take on the global stage together.” Fearfolks, backed by Benetone Films, has previously distributed Neon’s “Hokum” and “Leviticus,” as well as A24’s highest-grossing film of all time, “Backrooms.” Studio76, backed by the KKBOX Group, Taiwan’s National Development Fund and Japan’s Asahi Broadcasting Group Dream Ventures, specializes in incubating local Taiwanese intellectual property and financing digital movies and drama series for global audiences. articles.title: Toronto’s Indigenous Film and Industry Slates Aim to Grow Audiences and Spark Biz by Reflecting the Diversity of Global Screen Culture
articles.full_text: Sep 10, 2026 5:45am PT Toronto’s Indigenous Film and Industry Slates Aim to Grow Audiences and Spark Biz by Reflecting the Diversity of Global Screen Culture 'Predator' series alumni Amber Midthunder and Dimitrius Schuster-Koloamatangi and 'North of North' stars Anna Lambe and Zorga Qaunaq lead the celeb cohort lighting up Toronto's Indigenous screens By Jennie Punter Plus Icon Jennie Punter Latest Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: ‘We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us’ (EXCLUSIVE) 28 minutes ago ‘Wolf of the North’ Snares Verve Ventures for North America Ahead of Toronto Market (EXCLUSIVE) 1 week ago Frontières at TIFF The Market Unveils Lineup, Featuring a ‘Dim Sum Western,’ Newlywed Night of Terror and Wolf-Tracking Dark Comedy (EXCLUSIVE) 4 weeks ago See All Zorga Qaunaq as Sesi and Anna Lambe as Yura in 'In the Heart of the South,' courtesy Mixtape VR Inc. and Sphere Media Toronto With enticing acquisition titles, rising talent and supercharged industry presence at the market, the Toronto Intl. Film Festival’s 2026 Indigenous lineup delivers the creative and collaborative screen projects that are increasingly attracting global partners, buyers and audiences. “We’re seeing contemporary Indigenous cinema telling stories within broad historical or present-day contexts but without centering those aspects,” international programmer of U.K., Ireland, Australia and New Zealand and global Indigenous cinema Jason Ryle tells Variety . Related Stories How Did the Emmys’ Documentary Category Get So Star-Studded? 'Widow's Bay,' 'DTF: St. Louis' and 'Spider-Noir' — Despite Its Cancellation — Dominate Creative Arts Emmys Night 2 Winners (FULL LIST) For “How We Stand,” Marie Clements adapts her stage play about separated sisters — played by Amber Midthunder (“Prey”), Alyssa Wapanatâhk (“Little House on the Prairie”) and Isabel DeRoy-Olson (“Dark Winds”) — navigating 1970s political and cultural changes in L.A. Popular on Variety “These are modern Indigenous young women trying to figure their way, just as we all do,” Clements says. “We learn who we are, and who we want to become, through living.” Nyla Innuksuk’s “In the Heart of the South,” one of three Indigenous titles in TIFF section Platform, is a sharp turn from her sci-fi horror “Slash/Back.” Set in the uptight art world, the films stars “North of North” series lead Anna Lambe as an Inuk filmmaker and Zorga Qaunaq (also “North of North”) as the estranged friend who arrives uninvited and rattles her plans. “It’s a sophisticated thriller that critiques arts institutions in Canada from the perspective of an Indigenous person,” says international programmer of Canadian features Kelly Boutsalis. “Brace Your Heart,” Amanda Kernell ’s Sápmi-set Platform feature, follows a young woman who inherits her late father’s reindeer herd and is pressured to accept a local leader’s courtship. “Most of the actors, including the leads, are reindeer herders,” says Ryle. “Amanda has a gift for drawing out performances from people with the smallest suggestions.” Theja Rio’s “Angh” (Platform) centers on a Naga family in a Indo-Burma border village and what happens after the arrival of a Christian missionary. “As far as we can tell, this is the first feature from the Naga people, who are building their own screen culture, as is happening elsewhere in the world, with different means,” Ryle says. The film‘s DP is Adam Pietkiewicz, the recipient of the Variety Artisan Award at TIFF. In his social satire “God Bless You, Mr. Kopu,” Alex Liu casts Dimitrius Schuster-Koloamatangi (“Predator: Badlands”) as a Tongan man drifting from his family while working for an American traveling salesman. The cultures of queer sex workers, hockey players and hip-hop artists are expressed, respectively, in Justin Ducharme’ s chamber drama “Seventeen,” actor-director Cody Lightning’s underdog dramedy “Smudge the Blades” and Alexandra Lazarowich’s doc feature debut “Turtle Island Rap.” “My film explores why it’s hard to be a rapper or beat-maker, and why people still choose to become one,” Lazarowich tells Variety . “The artists are a snapshot of what’s happening in youth culture. The nuances of their Indigenous identity are reflected in the people listening to their music.” Leo Matthew Temela in “In Alaska,” courtesy of IJswater Films, Experimental Forest Films, Uuktumiaq Studios Inspired by a true story, “In Alaska” follows Woody (newcomer Leo Matthew Temela), a depressed teen who is pursued as an eco-terrorist by an FBI agent (Noomi Rapace) after accidentally shooting a hole in an oil pipeline. During an early stage, filmmaker Jaap van Heusden met Inuit actor-director Vinnie Karetak for script notes. They became co-writers and co-directors. “We had to be fearless to keep the heavy subject of suicide in the film and make sure it was never glorified,” Karetak says. “There is a deep sense of loss already from the previous generation that is handed down to human. “When it came to Inuit characters, we collaborated. We talked about every scene, every character, every extra.” Karetak, who acted in “North of North,” says people in the community where the show was flmed helped out on “In Alaska.” “We cast Vinnie’s dog, his son and one of his close friends,” van Heusden recalls. “And we used my ex’s snowmobile,” Karetak adds. Below are the Indigenous directors and their world-premiering features, screening in various programs at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. “2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback,” dir. A Germany-France co-production from Soilfilms and Soldats Features, the psychological drama stars Soma Pysall (HBO Max’s “Para – We Are King,” Disney+’s “City of Blood”) as Tian, a young dancer trying to break free from a violent, controlling relationship. She trained at the Northern School of Contemporary Dance in Leeds before studying directing at Berlin’s German Film and Television Academy. articles.title: Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: ‘We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 10, 2026 5:48am PT Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: ‘We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us’ (EXCLUSIVE) Rising Indigenous talents Amber Midthunder, Alyssa Wapanatâhk, and Isabel DeRoy-Olson star as sisters on disparate paths in 1970s L.A. in Marie Clements’ Toronto premiere 'How We Stand' By Jennie Punter Plus Icon Jennie Punter Latest Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: ‘We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us’ (EXCLUSIVE) 30 minutes ago ‘Wolf of the North’ Snares Verve Ventures for North America Ahead of Toronto Market (EXCLUSIVE) 1 week ago Frontières at TIFF The Market Unveils Lineup, Featuring a ‘Dim Sum Western,’ Newlywed Night of Terror and Wolf-Tracking Dark Comedy (EXCLUSIVE) 4 weeks ago See All Amber Midthunder as Jessie in 'How We Stand,' courtesy of Tombs Production Inc. Writer-director Marie Clements, who premiered “Bones of Crows” in 2022, returns this weekend to the Toronto Film Festival for the world premiere of her latest feature, “How We Stand,” as her new three-part documentary series, “Reclaim My Skin,” waits in the wings for its premiere next month at the Vancouver International Film Festival. Both projects reveal stories of Indigenous women and the power of their actions and voices to bring about necessary change in the world, their communities, and their own lives. Related Stories Remembering the 2006 Emmys, When the Clock Ran Out for Network TV Emmy Overachiever Jason Bateman on Whether He Considers Himself an Actor or Director First “There’s a moment when you’re in the room with matriarchs when everything stands still,” Clement recently told Variety , talking about the doc series for the first time. Popular on Variety “I had the honor to interview Gloria Steinem with Indigenous activists Louise Wakerakats:se Herne and Michelle Schenandoah together in New York last year—even at their most passionate they never spoke over each other,” she said. “They gave space and listened, acknowledging differences while also understanding that we have more in common than what works to divide us.” “Reclaim My Skin” is produced by Marie Clements Media, Screen Siren Pictures and Rezolution Pictures. The series was commissioned by British Columbia’s Knowledge Network in 2024. “How We Stand,” which Clements adapted from her 2011 stage play “Tombs of the Vanishing Indian,” reflects both harsh truths and positive currents of the eras in which it is set. It’s produced by Marie Clements Media and Screen Siren Pictures. Myriad Pictures is handling international sales. Photon Films is the Canadian distributor. Three young Oklahoma sisters and their single mother (Cara Jade Myers, “Killer of the Flower Moon”) travel to L.A. in a 1950s relocation program for Native Americans that promises jobs in big cities. But they were sold a bill of goods. After finding community in the city’s cemented riverways, a tragedy separates the sisters, whose lives take different paths on the shifting cultural landscape of 1970s L.A. “There’s a vibrancy to being alive at any time,” Clements said. “These are modern Indigenous young women who want to grab their futures. They are looking at the world and having a point of view that may or may not land, but are learning who they want to become.” That vibrancy is enhanced by casting of stellar screen stars in the roles of the adult sisters. Amber Midthunder (“Prey,” “Novocaine”) is a doctor who starts a new job at her white husband’s clinic, Alyssa Wapanatâh (“Peter Pan & Wendy”) plays an outspoken activist who starts auditioning for Native American roles in Hollywood movies, while Isabel DeRoy-Olson (AMC’s “Dark Winds”) has the role of a young women adrift and in distress after a traumatic experience she’s trying to figure out. “It was incredible to watch these actors lean in and embody these characters,” Clement says. The stage play was originally commissioned by the Native Voices series at the Autry National Center in L.A. Clements spent time looking through the Autry’s collections in its museums. A colleague’s aunt, who had lived 30 years in the city, told her about the so-called tombs of the riverways where Indigenous people used to meet. “It started me thinking about the underground – where we can go to be together? – as well as the underground policies that were happening at this time,” she continues. The screen adaptation allowed Clement to more deeply explore the worlds suggested in her play. “Starting in Oklahoma with the Technicolor beauty of childhood and this young family and the feeling of possibility – what might happen to a family when they’re given a chance? “But I was also interested in the systems that were happening at the time,” she continues. “We don’t always know that that our lives are being designed by something that we don’t have control of.” While her new film is set in the past, present and future realities ran through the creation and production of “How We Stand.” “I want things to change, I think we all want things to change,” Clement says. “And I found myself thinking about children who are being taken away from their families right now, because our families understand being separated and what that does to the core of a family for generations. “Whether it’s residential school or immigration policies, it’s a profound act to take a member of someone’s family, especially children, away from mothers and fathers. And we’re witnessing that in our time right now. “The fight in the ’70s was around women’s bodies and women’s rights. And that’s trying to be reversed as we speak, so it really does kind of hit you. “Things can feel downtrodden but, you know, there are cool women out there who are still working for change, and that is not going to change.” “How We Stand” has its world premiere at the Toronto International Festival on Sept. 13. articles.full_text: Sep 10, 2026 6:00am PT James Marcus Haney’s ‘Black Sunflowers’ Boarded by Charades and CAA Media Finance Ahead of TIFF Docs Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Sean Penn is an executive producer on "Black Sunflowers," a documentary feature portraying Ukrainian youths. By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie ‘Red Rocks’ Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) 20 hours ago ‘Call My Agent! The Movie’ Premieres in Paris as Ted Sarandos Touts Netflix’s ‘Vital’ Role in France Amid Regulatory Fight 21 hours ago Penélope Cruz Sobs and Kisses Javier Bardem as ‘Bunker’ Dazzles Venice With Record 15.5-Minute Ovation 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Charades Charades and CAA Media Finance are launching sales on “ Black Sunflowers ,” the timely new feature documentary directed by James Marcus Haney (“No Cameras Allowed”) which will premiere at Toronto. Slated to premiere in the TIFF Docs section, “Black Sunflowers” portrays a young generation of Ukrainians, soldiers and civilians, whose coming of age is shaped by martial law and duty on the front lines. As another year of conflict stretches on, Haney captures the ordinary moments amid the war, moving between fast cars, underground clubs and conversations about the future. Related Stories French Drama Series 'The Red and the Black': Passion, Power, Political Intrigue and Victor Belmondo’s Anti-Romantic Hero Underwater Life Breaks New Comedy Ground in 'Submarine Jim,' Xilam's Latest Animated IP The American filmmaker closely collaborated with a Ukrainian production team led by Volodymyr Yatsenko at Limelite (“To the Victory!”), alongside a local crew. Popular on Variety The film is produced by Pedram Rezaee and Vlad Bolyelov and co-produced by Yevhenii Zdorovylo, Samy Mosher, Eric Maldin, Volodymyr Yatsenko and Anna Yatsenko, with Mikayla Jean Miller serving as creative producer. Sean Penn has joined the film as an executive producer, alongside Jay and Cameron Bush, Adam Tudhope, Anna October and Dianna Agron. Charades handles international sales and co-reps North America and global rights with CAA Media Finance. The film boasts a powerful soundtrack with music from British record producer Fred again.. and Brian Eno’s Secret Life project, as well as an original score by Brad Oberhofer and Ukrainian electronic composer Koloah. Also featured in the soundtrack are Aphex Twin, Four Tet, Idles, Sega Bodega, Nastya Vogan, Два Два Дев’ять, Ann Annie and Morwan. The film closes with a version of Morphine’s “Do Not Go Quietly Unto Your Grave” sung by a traditional choir based in Kyiv. “Upon arriving to Ukraine, I was surprised to see how much normal life carried on, despite the war,” Haney said. “While the scenes we see in Western media (bombed out villages, injured soldiers, etc) are true and must be seen by the world, I couldn’t help but think that mainstream media is missing half of the story.” “While the front lines footage is harrowing and necessary to show, the things, places, and people worth fighting for, and their everyday stories in extraordinary circumstances, are generally omitted from Western news,” he continued. Emphasizing the universality of their experiences, he said young people, who’ve already gone through the pandemic, are now forced to join the front lines to protect their own. “I’ve met an electronic DJ who enlisted in the army and still performs back home when he is on leave. A nature photographer turned war journalist. Teenagers who now already have 2.5 years of combat experience at the zero line. Lovers pulled apart to different battlegrounds. And as I looked into these faces, I couldn’t help but see parts of myself,” he said. Haney said he recognized himself in many of the young Ukrainians he met, who shared the same dreams, musical tastes and youthful impulses as people elsewhere their age, even as they faced both the realities of war and its psychological toll. He said he hoped the film would bring a more human dimension to the conflict and remind audiences how much people across the world have in common. Charades’ co-founders Carole Baraton and Pierre Mazars said, “Black Sunflowers shows us with stunning subtlety a reality that we, as Europeans, tend to forget: the portrait of a generation of young people whose lives are being shaped — and sacrificed — by the war in Ukraine.” “We are proud to support the film and to see the resonance it is already generating across the international art scene,” added the pair. A music photographer and filmmaker, Haney is best known for the 2014 documentary “No Cameras Allowed,” which grew out of his experiences sneaking into major music festivals including Coachella and filming artists backstage. articles.title: ‘& Juliet’ to Close on Broadway After Four Years
articles.full_text: Sep 10, 2026 6:00am PT ‘& Juliet’ to Close on Broadway After Four Years By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Ellen Burstyn Wipes Away Tears, Hugs Taika Waititi and Pamela Anderson as Heartfelt Drama ‘Place to Be’ Earns 6-Minute Venice Ovation 20 hours ago Box Office: ‘Practical Magic 2’ Aims to Dethrone ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ With $40 Million Debut 23 hours ago Ellen Burstyn Was ‘Sure’ Her Career Would Be ‘Finished by 40’: ‘The Fact That I’m 93 and Working Is a Miracle’ 1 day ago See All Matthew Murphy “& Juliet,” a revisionist jukebox musical about Shakespeare’s star-crossed lovers, is closing after four years on Broadway . The upbeat take on “Romeo & Juliet,” which uses Swedish music producer Max Martin’s chart-topping hits to imagine what would happen if Juliet didn’t stab herself with Romeo’s dagger and join in him death, has set its final performance for Jan. 3, 2027. By then, the show will have played 1,723 regular performances and 20 preview performances, putting it among the 50 longest-running Broadway musicals of all time. Luke Sheppard, who is returning to the Great White Way with “Paddington,” directed “& Juliet” while “Schitt’s Creek” alum David West Read wrote the musical’s book. Related Stories Nathan Lane to Be Honored Following 'The Birdcage' 30th Anniversary Screening at Virginia Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE) Studio TF1 Smashes Doc Records With ‘Leon Marchand: Beyond Gold,’ Rolls Out ‘Surface’ “& Juliet” opened on Broadway in 2022 after an unsuccessful stint on London’s West End, where the musical’s run was cut short by COVID and had to close without turning a profit. In New York, “& Juliet” broke multiple box office records at the Stephen Sondheim Theatre and became one of the rare post-pandemic musicals to recoup its investment. And the show has translated beyond Broadway with productions in 34 states and nine countries including Germany, Canada and Singapore. The tour has also become profitable, recouping in 2025. Popular on Variety Although “& Juliet” didn’t win any Tony Awards, the musical remained a hot ticket through fun casting choices like TikTok star Charli D’Amelio, ‘N Sync’s Joey Fatone, “Real Housewives” alum Kandi Burruss and Chrissy Metz, as well as special guests like Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. Fatone’s involvement was particularly fitting because “& Juliet” features ‘N Sync songs like “It’s Gonna Be Me.” Martin’s pop anthems, such as, Kelly Clarkson’s “Since U Been Gone,” Britney Spears’ “I’m Not a Girl, Not Yet a Woman” and “Overprotected,” Katy Perry’s “Roar” and Demi Lovato’s “Confident” also help to score Juliet’s new lease on life and love. “& Juliet” ends on a celebratory note, and producers estimate that 8,447 pounds (more than four tons) of confetti have been sprinkled into the audience of the Stephen Sondheim Theatre. “From the very beginning, ‘& Juliet’ has been winning over audiences and critics alike, shattering every stereotype about jukebox musicals to deliver a smart, funny, heartfelt story — all while sparking true joy in everyone who sees it,” producers Theresa Steele Page and Eva Price said. “We’re incredibly proud of the run we’ve had on Broadway, and the story of inclusion, acceptance and second chances we’ve been able to share with more than 1.5 million people in our four years on Broadway.” Louis Messina, Taylor Swift’s Tour Promoter, Urges Judge to Reject Live Nation/Ticketmaster Antitrust Settlement: ‘I Could Go Out of Business Like Other Promoters Who Have Fallen Victim to Live Nation’ Roxette Cancels 40th Anniversary Tour of North American Amphitheaters, Citing ‘Hugely Increased Touring Costs’ Live Nation Posts Continued Growth in Second Quarter With $7.7 Billion in Revenue Loading comments...
