articles.title: Spain’s Mediapro Group To Become Imagina After Reorganization
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Royal Period Drama ‘Queen Silvia’ To Get World Premiere Screening At MIPCOM Cannes Channel 4 To Combine Drama & Comedy Teams Under Historic Jobs Cull Kayleigh Llewellyn Adapting Sarah Waters Novel ‘The Paying Guests’ For BBC Studios Fiction View All September 10, 2026 6:26am Mediapro Executive Chairman Sergio Oslé and CEO Carlos Núñez Grup Mediapro Spain ‘s Grup Mediapro will relaunch as Imagina on January 1, 2027, following a major company review. The decision to relaunch comes after “several months of reorganization” and was announced internally yesterday at an all-staff meeting. “The change revives a name the group has used before across its more than 30-year history, reflecting its intent to look ahead while staying grounded in its past,” the company said in a note to press. Imagina was previously the parent company of Mediapro, following the latter’s 2006 merger with producer Globomedia. Related Stories News Woody Allen To Start Shooting Next Project In Spain In October Executives HBO Max Names Movistar Plus+ Film Chief & 'Sirat' Producer Guillermo Farré As Original Production Chief In Spain The news follows a tumultuous 2026 for the Spanish sports media and entertainment giant, during which it cut 189 staff. Senior execs such as General Manager Laura Fernández Espeso, The Mediapro Studio’s international content chief, Ran Tellem, and business chief Miguel Cardenal all left. Watch on Deadline Mediapro’s new management, Executive Chairman Sergio Oslé and CEO Carlos Núñez, said the company expects EBITDA to grow between 50% and 60% against 2025, along with positive cash flow generation. This was thanks to the company-wide review that took place over the first months of 2026 and ultimately “brought its resources in line with today’s market realities.” “The next step is to drive new projects that deliver unique experiences to audiences around the world, funding this growth with more than €100 million [$116 million] the company itself will generate over the next three years,” the company stated. Oslé and Nũnez were installed following the departures of founding partners Jaume Roures and Tatxo Benet. They are now presiding over a business that handles production of numerous major sporting events, sells broadcast rights to the likes of Spain’s La Liga outside of North America, MENA and India, and has a content production unit that is behind the likes of The Head . Southwind Media Capital, which is part of China’s Orient Hontai Capital, owns Mediapro, which has its main offices in Madrid and Barcelona. Southwind bought a majority stake in February 2018, with former bosses Roures and Benet retaining minority stakes. articles.title: Prime Video‘s ‘Carrie’ Trailer: Mike Flanagan Reimagines Stephen King’s Horror Classic
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lexy Perez Plus Icon Lexy Perez Senior Digital Editor and Producer View All September 9, 2026 6:00am Summer H. Howell in Prime Video’s ‘Carrie’ series. Robert Falconer/Prime Logo text Mike Flanagan is ready to give his take on Stephen King‘s classic, Carrie . Prime Video released the official trailer for the upcoming series adaptation of King‘s bestselling novel on Wednesday, “offering a revealing glimpse at how the series expands the world” and will bring “new depth and complexity to its beloved characters while exploring the forces that shape Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) as she navigates the cruelty and pressure of the modern world — building toward a single, shattering night.“ “How much do we really know about Carrie — or what happened in Chamberlain?“ the streamer teases of the Amazon MGM Studios production. Related Stories Movies 'Remain' Teaser Trailer: Jake Gyllenhaal, Phoebe Dynevor Star in M. Night Shyamalan and Nicholas Sparks' Supernatural Romance Movies Josh Heuston to Star in Amazon MGM's 'Throttled' Adaptation of Lauren Asher's Bestselling 'Dirty Air' Series Carrie stars Summer H. Howell as the titular character Carrie White, a high school girl with telekinetic powers, and Samantha Sloyan as Margaret White. Siena Agudong, Alison Thornton, Joel Oulette, Josie Tota, Arthur Conti, Thalia Dudek, Amber Midthunder and Matthew Lillard also star. The upcoming reimagining from Flanagan marks the first time the story has been adapted for television. King’s Carrie was published in 1974, spent 14 weeks on The New York Times bestseller list and has been translated into more than 35 languages. Brian De Palma’s 1976 film adaptation of Carrie , which starred Sissy Spacek and Piper Laurie, earned Academy Award nominations for Spacek and Laurie. The show synopsis reads: “Misfit high‑schooler Carrie White (Howell) has spent her life hidden away inside the walls of her home with her fiercely protective mother, Margaret (Sloyan). After her father’s sudden, untimely death thrusts her into the unforgiving ecosystem of public high school, Carrie is forced to navigate a viral bullying scandal that tears through her community, the relentless pressure and casual cruelty of the social‑media age, and the awakening of mysterious telekinetic powers that rise alongside her adolescence.” Carrie is written and executive produced by showrunner Flanagan ( Midnight Mass , The Haunting of Hill House ), with King also serving as executive producer. Among the directors for this season are Flanagan, Kate Siegel ( The Exorcist: Martyrs ), Axelle Carolyn ( Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen ), Kyra Sedgwick ( Family Movie ) and Hiromi Kamata ( Shogun ). All eight episodes of Carrie will be released on Oct. 7. Watch the trailer below. THR

articles.title: John Oliver to Host Comic Relief Live’s 40th Anniversary Show
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All September 9, 2026 6:00am John Oliver Theo Wargo/Getty Images Forty years after Billy Crystal, Whoopi Goldberg and Robin Williams headlined the original Comic Relief telethon, the charity is set to return to New York’s Carnegie Hall this fall with John Oliver hosting and a slew of funnymen and funnywomen lined up to take the stage. Nonprofit Comic Relief US announced on Wednesday the return of its annual “Comic Relief Live” benefit, which will take place Monday, Oct. 19. Oliver is returning as the event’s host at Carnegie Hall’s Stern Auditorium/Perelman Stage, following his hosting duties at the 2025 benefit. Related Stories TV John Oliver Takes a Close Look at Sean Duffy's "God-Awful" New Reality Show: "We've All Been Taken for a F***ing Ride" TV John Oliver Says Taco Bell Has the Moral High Ground Over Trump Administration Amid "Explosive Diarrhea" Parasite Crisis “Comic Relief puts comedy to work where traditional approaches fail, lowering defenses around difficult issues and bringing people together to be part of the solution,” the nonprofit said in a press release. Through this and other events, the nonprofit uses the power of comedy to drive positive change toward its vision of a just world, free from poverty. The nonprofit also announced several performers on Wednesday. Oliver’s fellow Daily Show alumni Roy Wood Jr. and Josh Johnson are set to appear, along with Indian American stand-up Zarna Garg and Overcompensating actress Mary Beth Barone. This year’s benefit also marks the 40th anniversary of the original HBO special and Comic Relief’s new satirical “Not Our Problem” PSA campaign. At the event, Comic Relief will present its 2026 Visionary Award, an honor established to recognize leaders and organizations who use their platform, innovation, and resources to advance systemic change for children and families facing poverty. This year, the award will be given to ServiceNow for its work empowering young people and investing in youth-led projects at the intersection of technology and social impact. Ticket packages and individual tickets for the Oct. 19 event go on sale Thursday. THR

articles.title: ‘The Uprising’ Review: Andrew Garfield in Paul Greengrass’ Intense but Monotonous Medieval Actioner
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All September 9, 2026 6:00am Andrew Garfield in 'The Uprising.' Focus Features Suffering from severe financial inequality and oppressed by the yoke of dictators and oligarchs, the people rise up and storm the seat of government. No, it’s not the latest Democratic Socialist manifesto, but rather the subject of the new historical drama written and directed by Paul Greengrass . The Uprising concerns the Peasants’ Revolt that occurred in medieval England in 1381, an event that’s probably more familiar to British than American audiences (we can barely bother to learn about our own brief history). In this case, a lack of foreknowledge may be helpful, since there are dramatic plot twists as the story unfolds that demonstrate that, when it comes to historical dramas, ignorance may be an advantage. Related Stories Movies Andrew Garfield Explains the Robin Hood Energy in 'The Uprising' -- and Why Marketing Noise Doesn't Faze Him Movies 'Artificial' Trailer: First Look at Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman in Creepy Biopic The Uprising The Bottom Line Skillfully made and acted, but exhausting. Release date : Friday, September 11 Cast : Andrew Garfield, Jamie Bell, Stephen Dillane, Tom Hollander, Cosmo Jarvis, Thomasin McKenzie, Jonny Lee Miller, Woody Norman, Stanley Townsend, Katherine Waterston, Sky Yang Director-screenwriter : Paul Greengrass Rated R, 2 hours 7 minuteds Ruled by a teenage King Richard II ( Woody Norman , C’mon C’mon ), the peasants are still suffering the effects of the Black Plague and onerous taxation incurred by the monarchy to pay for the country’s never-ending war with France. Among them is a simple farmer (a terrific Andrew Garfield ) whose miserable, solitary life is illustrated by his relentless plowing of his fields and the three graves, marked by one large and two small crosses, that occupy his land. Faced with the dictate of paying yet another tax, the farmer, who refers to himself only as “The Ploughman” — “I am what I do,” he says by way of explanation — erupts in a violent rage and suddenly finds himself at the center of a rebellion whose leaders include the real-life figures of radical cleric John Ball ( Jamie Bell ) and former soldier Wat Tyler ( Cosmo Jarvis ). Also figuring prominently in the proceedings is the cleric’s acolyte Alyce ( Thomasin McKenzie , Jojo Rabbit ), a fictional character representing the many women who took part in the movement. In typical action-movie leading-man fashion, the Ploughman demonstrates remarkable fighting abilities for someone who’s been working the fields instead of at war. To emphasize the present-day parallels, the film includes early scenes in which the king’s oligarchal counselors — including Treasurer Robert Hales ( Tom Hollander ), Archbishop Simon Sudbury (Stephen Dillane), Chief Justice Bealknap (Stanley Townsend), and London Mayor William Walworth ( Jonny Lee Miller ) — take advantage of the power vacuum caused by their overwhelmed teenage king and decide to take the necessary funds not from the rich merchants but rather the common people. From that point on, things get very, very violent. (During his publicity tour, Garfield has stated, “I hope that if any billionaires watch it, they’re scared shitless.” Somehow, I don’t think Elon Musk is quaking in his boots.) In typical Greengrassian fashion, The Uprising proves intense from first minute to last, the director utilizing his familiar handheld camera and frenetic editing style to an at times exhausting degree. The stylistic approach works well enough during the many and extremely bloody action sequences, but eventually proves so relentless and lacking in modulation that the film becomes a grueling and sometimes tedious experience. The director also tends to overdo the swooping drone shots, either real or CGI-generated, to convey the expansive scope of the uprising. Still, there’s no doubting the commitment of everyone involved, from the superb cast that seemingly includes every notable British character actor to the technical craftspeople who evoke medieval England with such vividness that you can practically smell the church incense (and much less appealing aromas). Pal Ulvik Rokseth’s gritty cinematography, featuring the sort of muted color palette endemic to historical dramas of this type (there was apparently no sunshine until at least the 18th century), fully immerses you in the action. Production designer Nikolaj Danielsen takes full advantage of the ancient Bavarian locations standing in for England, while costume designers Andras Daniel Toth and Attila Godena-Juhasz clearly worked overtime to create innumerable period outfits. The performances are first-rate across the board, with Bell and Jarvis outstanding as the lead conspirators. Katherine Waterston shines as King Richard’s mother despite not having much in the way of dialogue, while Sky Yang makes a strong impression as the Scribe who plays a pivotal role in the proceedings. But it’s Norman who steals the movie as the trauma-scarred teenage king who proves surprisingly cunning, the young actor proving mesmerizing every moment he’s onscreen. Briefly and confusingly marketed with the tagline “The Rise of Robin Hood,” the film merely hints at the possibility that it’s the origin story of the mythical figure whose onscreen death we already suffered earlier this year. Full credits Distributor: Focus Features Production: Blumhouse Atomic Monster, Thank You Pictures, Supernix Cast: Andrew Garfield, Jamie Bell, Stephen Dillane, Tom Hollander, Cosmo Jarvis, Thomasin McKenzie, Jonny Lee Miller, Woody Norman, Stanley Townsend, Katherine Waterston, Sky Yang Director-screenwriter: Paul Greengrass Producers: Jason Blum, Paul Greengrass, Gregory Goodman, Joanna Kaye, Joe Neurauter, Lars Sylvest Executive producers: Philipp Kreuzer, Chance Wright, Jay Taylor, Kwesi Dickson, Alastair Burlingham, Gary Raskin, Matt Murphie, Deborah Acoca, Cliff Lanning Director of photography: Pål Ulvik Rokseth Production designer: Nikolaj Danielsen Editor: William Goldenberg Composer: Volker Bertelmann Costume designer: András Dániel Tóth, Attila Godena-Juhász Casting: Dan Hubbard Rated R, 2 hours 7 minuteds THR

articles.title: Mahershala Ali and 76ers Star Jaylen Brown on Rejection, Rebirth and Refusing to Be Boxed In
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Mahershala Ali & Jaylen Brown on Aug. 9, 2026, at PMC Studios, Los Angeles. Styling by Van Van Alonso. On Brown: NB44 top; Oakley glasses; Jacquie Aiche jewelry. On Ali: Dunhill suit; 18 East shirt; Garrett Leight glasses; Jacquie Aiche jewelry. Photographed by Beau Grealy; Tailoring by Erin Castle; Mahershala Ali grooming by Tasha Reiko Brown; Jaylen Brown grooming by Saisha Beecham; Fashion Assistants Robi Morales, GYA Assistants Jaylen Brown is nervous. At least, that’s what he says. There’s certainly little outward indication of anxiety as the five-time NBA All-Star preps for the inaugural taping of Game Recognize Game , THR ‘s new series uniting an actor — in this case, Mahershala Ali — with one of his favorite athletes. With the sports and entertainment ecosystems intersecting more than ever, we thought it was time to bring stars at the top of each industry together for raw and candid conversations on everything from the pressures of fame to coping with failure. And we’ll count any butterflies as a win — though neither man is easily rattled. Related Stories TV Netflix Circling Andres Cantor For 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup Coverage THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue The $100 Billion Race to Build the World's Next Sports Mecca On Brown: NB44 top; Oakley glasses; Jacquie Aiche jewelry; Prada shoes. On Ali: Dunhill suit; 18 East shirt; Garrett Leight glasses; Jacquie Aiche jewelry; Thom Browne shoes. Photographed by Beau Grealy Brown, 29, is as famous for his off-court fearlessness as his on-court ferocity. From questioning NBA officiating and league politics to calling out ESPN and Nike, the 2024 NBA Finals MVP has never been one to shy away from saying what he thinks — and he thinks about a lot more than basketball. He has spoken at Harvard, was an MIT Media Lab fellow and is the first active NBA player to launch a fully independent performance brand, 741. When Boston recently traded him to the Philadelphia 76ers (where he will earn $183 million over the next three years), Brown held his introductory news conference not in the safe confines of an arena press room but at a community rec center, immediately placing him on the right side of his new city. Publicly imploring LeBron James to join him in Philly — and then seeing him do just that — didn’t hurt either. When we asked Ali, 52, what athlete he would most like to sit with for this new series, it’s not shocking Brown was at the top of his list. If Brown is on edge about the taping, it’s because Ali has the type of résumé that could reasonably intimidate any performer. He’s a two-time Oscar winner and Emmy-winning producer, with a new film ( Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother ) about to hit theaters and a new role on the second season of HBO’s hit Task . Ali also played basketball. Maybe not at Brown’s level, but well enough to land a scholarship at Saint Mary’s College before embarking on the path that would lead him here today. Before this, the two men had never met. Yet it didn’t take them long to get comfortable and candid on issues beyond sport and screen — from the weight of Black trauma to how their shared commitment to faith guides them at the top of their respective games. — David Katz Jaylen Brown wears NB44 top; Dzojchen pants; Oakley glasses; Jacquie Aiche jewelry; Prada shoes. Photographed by Beau Grealy Mahershala Ali wears Dunhill suit; 18 East shirt; Garrett Leight glasses; Jacquie Aiche jewelry; Thom Browne shoes. Photographed by Beau Grealy “IT’S ALWAYS ME VERSUS ME” MAHERSHALA ALI I’m a lot older than you, but I have to say, in so many ways I look up to you. I think you are just a profound talent and a really important person in the world. What you mean to the culture, I think, to the culture of sports, and specifically speaking as a former athlete and a Black man, just how important you are as a disrupter. We live in a world that has seen us in such limited ways for so long, and I think the biggest thing that makes me a fan, for lack of a better word, is just seeing how well you’ve embraced the fullness of yourself. JAYLEN BROWN Thank you. I appreciate you for sharing that. The people that come before are also the people that paved the way. ALI Right now, I’m working in Philadelphia [on Task ], and the announcement of you coming from Boston to Philly — to be there while that happened — was pretty remarkable. On top of that, LeBron deciding to join you. Tell me about how you’re feeling about that transition. BROWN Obviously it was disappointing, to some degree, in terms of how things transpired at the end in Boston. But I’m also very excited for the opportunity. You know, I’m more focused on that excitement. The past is the past. ALI Yeah. BROWN I’m putting all my energy toward that. It’s a lot, you know, moving all your stuff, your family, looking for a new place. Parting ways with the things that I grew comfortable with in Boston. Now I gotta find new things in Philadelphia, which is just rebirth. It’s just another form of transformation. ALI I love that. Transformation. I would love to be, when it’s all said and done, considered a transformational actor. I don’t know if I’ll always achieve that, but that is my baseline goal. I don’t ever want to repeat a character. I would like to eliminate character bleed from role to role. Meaning, “Oh, I saw him do that same thing in that part and that part and that part.” And I’m still learning. I’ve been doing this since 1993. But I really feel like I just started, on some level. What about you? How are you experiencing transformation? BROWN For me, growth and transformation are synonymous. So for me — I’m a Scorpio — I’ve had to transform many times. Once you recognize areas of your life where you need to grow, something has to die. ALI Yeah. Photographed by Beau Grealy BROWN So it’s always me versus me, that’s what it comes down to at the end of the day — you versus you. I’m my greatest opponent. When you say being a transformational actor, it resonates highly with me, because I would consider myself a transformational athlete. ALI So much of how I look at acting comes from the years I spent playing ball. It’s almost as if the career before my career has had such an influence and impact on me. In terms of preparing, in terms of embracing the work, in terms of telling stories and taking on character, being in service of something bigger than myself — so much of that, for me, was informed by my time playing sports. Discipline, hard work, sacrifice, integrity, selflessness, the best qualities that athletes can learn how to embrace, all of those things transfer over into the arts and performing. I would actually say you would be better prepared as an actor if you’ve had some real serious background in team sports. Because you can get tricked very quickly into thinking that acting is all about me . It’s about me and my character. The camera’s on me . It really doesn’t work, not only without that other actor, but without everybody on the other side of that camera. BROWN Well, I got some background in playing ball. So what I’m hearing is that for the next movie that you produce … I got a shot. ALI You got a shot. BROWN Y’all heard it here first. ALI I played four years undergrad at Saint Mary’s College. And then I took a year off and got into the graduate acting program at NYU … BROWN I just wanna say, at Saint Mary’s, man — I went back and found joy in watching clips of you playing. Because when you played, you didn’t just play, like, “I’ma just come out here, shoot some threes or da, da, da.” Nah, you, you played hard. ALI Thank you. BROWN You played with a level of tenacity … you played defense. You were a two-way player. You got after it, man. Watching how you played the game before I came to this interview told me a lot about you. You weren’t trying to be cool, make friends, none of that. You were like, “I’ma put my shoulder through somebody’s chest if I got to.” ALI ( Laughs .) I tried. I tried, man. Thank you, brother. That means a lot coming from you. “I DON’T KNOW WHAT I’M DOING HALF THE TIME” ALI When I was playing ball, something I quietly struggled with was beating other people. The emphasis on winning. And how you could win but not actually be your best. And then I got into grad school, and I and everyone else in the room were doing the same monologue that day. Everyone sort of brought their own thing to it, and it began to change my relationship around competition. That’s when, at the age of 23 or something like that, it dawned on me why I felt a more natural fit in the artist space. There was something in that space that allowed the conversation around competition to be more about you being your best self. BROWN I think most people think winning is one-dimensional. They think it’s black and white. I disagree. Obviously, there’s a result at the end of each game. But I think winning has context. Winning has dimensions. One is how I felt about myself. About my output. About how I interacted with my teammates. You know, did I do my job? Was I afraid? Was it a leadership moment where I could’ve stepped up? ALI When someone like yourself does so much at such a high clip and success rate — how does that shape embracing new things? Do you have this expectation or pressure that you put on yourself to excel? BROWN Good question. Nobody has ever asked me that. I rarely ever show things publicly that I’ve not already spent some time on. For the most part, it bothers me when I’m not good at things. The other day, my teammate Tyrese Maxey had a golf outing. I’ve never played golf before. Inside, it was hurting me to know that these guys were better than me. You know what I mean? ALI Yeah, yeah. BROWN Like, a lot better than me. And even though they were like, “It’s cool, man. We’re just vibing, having a good time, building chemistry with your teammates,” it was eating me alive. ALI I’m in pain for you right now. I feel it. Photographed by Beau Grealy BROWN It’s eating me up. So in my brain, I’m like, “Man, I’m about to go hire a golf instructor. I’m about to go grind for two months straight, come back, act like I didn’t do that at all. A lot of things do come naturally to me, but like the stuff that doesn’t, it frustrates me. So I will go behind the scenes and put in the work. Hire an instructor, whatever it is, and then come back and pretend like none of that happened. ALI I love that. BROWN And they be like, “Oh, man, like, what happened?” I’m, like, “Yeah, yeah.” ALI That’s great. BROWN We’re talking about winning and losing. Are there any rejections in your career that kind of stick out in your mind? ALI There’s a lot of examining that happens when I feel attached to something and it doesn’t go my way. I’ve had enough experiences, though, in life where I feel like with some patience and maybe grace, I got somewhat of an answer in time as to why that thing was not for me. I try as best as I can to tolerate the feelings around disappointment. And try not to internalize it too much. There is that thing around rejection being you’re closer to the “yes.” Like, I’m closer to the thing that actually is for me — and if I allow that “no” to stop me, that’s more about me. Am I worthy of the next thing if I’m going to allow this to stop me? For Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother , I got to unite with a director by the name of Bassam Tariq. We were originally supposed to work on Blade together. That didn’t happen, but we were able to use that training and the time we spent together and put it to good use on Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother . I’m playing a character that had sort of required me to immerse myself in some martial arts training. I also got to bring some qualities from my faith into this character in a very overt way, because this character is a Muslim assassin who is dealing with searching for breast milk for his child. BROWN What’s your relationship with faith? ALI I would say it makes the experience of being an actor so much richer because it allows me to be honest about my lack of talent or lack of skill in certain areas. Because I don’t know what I’m doing half the time. I take jobs and I show up and I’m like, “I’m here. I don’t know what I’m doing.” BROWN That’s hard to believe … ALI ( Laughs .) I swear! I kid you not. I’m like, “I don’t know what I’m doing. All right, we gonna have to figure this out.” So to me, acting is all faith. I don’t walk out on set and have not prayed, like, “Need help today.” Whether I feel like I got it or not. Because I would like to avoid any arrogance around storytelling. I’m so aware of my responsibility to reflect life and to work to extract a truth out of these characters that can impact people. I’ve had people just come up to me weeping, you know. When we first shared Moonlight in Telluride … BROWN Great movie. ALI Thank you. I kid you not, I saw people holding [director] Barry Jenkins, shaking — it so impacted their lives. I see a lot of actors sometimes throw away the importance of this work, and it’s sort of a false humility. This work is important. It can really impact lives, and I think it’s important that we look at it that way so that we’re responsible with it. So I take the work really seriously. BROWN I feel the same way about faith. I am completely faith-driven. I don’t need to see the staircase to take my next step. Faith is the basis of who Jaylen Brown is. ALI Let me ask, what were the priorities of your household growing up? BROWN It’s making me smile, ’cause it’s my mom. Like, she used to always say, “If you lie, you’ll cheat. If you cheat, you’ll steal. If you steal, you’ll kill.” It’s just engraved in my brain. Probably so many Black families grew up hearing that. So the worst thing you could do in our household was to lie. Like, if I got in trouble at school, it wouldn’t even matter the crime I committed, if I lied to my mother about it, that would be worse than the punishment of what I actually did. ALI Mm-hmm. Yeah. BROWN So as I got older, as I entered spaces and made mistakes, it was just part of my character development. I always would hear my mother and my grandmother’s voice. ALI For so many youths, sports is considered a way out. Did you relate to sports as “my ticket out”? Or did having a route to get an education — and forgive me if I’m making assumptions — but did that remove any kind of pressure you felt to use basketball as a tool to get somewhere? BROWN Not at all, to be honest. Like, obviously the overarching reality is that to make it to a high level of success, it was my greatest option. Like, I didn’t have a father, I didn’t have a family office, or another pathway that would’ve led me to reaching a certain level of success. But in reality, I just love the game. I just love the game so much that I was like, “I’m gonna be the best.” I learned to walk by chasing after a ball. So I wasn’t thinking, at 2 years old, “This is my ticket to making it out.” ALI Right. BROWN It’s just in my design. It was always just, “I love this game so much, I wanna play it at the highest level.” And in that thought, I made it out. ALI And is it still play for you? Because I know it changes. BROWN The NBA is a little different from just the altruistic love that you develop. It becomes work. ALI Yeah. BROWN And then there are politics that exist within the game. There’s things that get emphasized for entertainment, for bottom lines, for metrics. Yes, that sometimes takes the love away a little bit. But I love it so much, it could never really take the love away. ALI Just all the things on top of the reality of that love, right? BROWN As you climb industries, and you get to the top, it just gets more … ALI More cutthroat. BROWN Yes. ALI Right? It’s so important for those who do have moral fiber to be in those spaces. Because those highly competitive spaces tend to be spaces that end up impacting the rest of the world. BROWN So how do we normalize that? How do we make that the example versus the exception to the rule? ALI We need people like yourself. You know, the first thing that you did upon getting this crazy contract was speak about what you wanted to do in the community, right? And so now, years later, you have this to show for it in these communities in Atlanta and Oakland and Boston and, God willing, Philadelphia now. BROWN That’s the goal. ALI I was asking you a little bit earlier about your upbringing, and I was curious about some of the things that you may have had — or didn’t have — that are now sort of inspiring you to do certain work. Photographed by Beau Grealy BROWN The thing that I wish that I had around me more often was discipline. You know? Because if you lack discipline — a man who can’t say “no,” he’s susceptible to a lot of the distractions in the world. And I feel like if I had a son — or daughter — that would be one of the greatest tools that I can give. How to say no to all the distractions and everything that’s pulling at you in the most distracting era maybe in human history. How do you say no when the algorithm is placing everything in front of you? How do you have a strong enough discipline where you can still have control? ALI Yeah. And was this something that you learned from a certain coach? BROWN For me it was Islam. You know, when I started to dive into that. ALI And how old were you? BROWN I think like 13, 14, 15 — I had some good people around me that shaped the type of man that I wanted to be. But ultimately, for me it was Islam. For somebody else, it may be something else. What motivates you? ALI I think the motivation is to resonate. To leave you vibrating afterward. That’s it. If you can accomplish that, you moved a mountain that day. That’s a miracle, bro. To make somebody feel and think and consider. “THEY ONLY WANT YOU TO BE THE ENTERTAINER” ALI There’s real resistance in the sports world to athletes that have any real interest beyond the sport itself, especially as Black men. BROWN Yep. I would say this, it might be a little controversial, but I think it’s rooted in fear, even within our own community. There’s pushback, or almost like a hesitancy, rooted in the trauma of slavery. At one point, to do anything outside of being a slave was problematic. Reading, writing, anything. It’s similar when you think of an athlete doing anything out of what you’re just supposed to be doing. ALI Right. BROWN You’re supposed to just be entertaining me. Right? You’re not supposed to be doing anything else outside of that. And some people firmly still believe that. But I disagree. My responsibility is not to entertain you. My responsibility is to be influential. I think that fear is projected onto us in order to make us smaller, to make us more digestible, for the people who only … ALI Who are uncomfortable around us … BROWN Who only want you to be the slave. They only want you to be the entertainer. ALI Right. BROWN I think it’s a fear that’s instilled in talented people’s brains that if I use my abilities beyond what people are comfortable with, there’s going to be major pushback. ALI Right. BROWN And for me, the reason why I’m comfortable doing it is because I just don’t care. ALI Yeah. I feel like that is going to be your legacy on some level — how effective you’ve been able to be in spaces that go beyond the sport itself. BROWN When it’s all said and done, I want to break down that fear. That fear that I’m speaking to that is still instilled within our community. It’s in our parents, in our grandparents — because of the trauma and experiences that they’ve had. I want to break that fear down for the next generation. My legacy will be, hopefully, inspiring the next generation to be fearless. Photographed by Beau Grealy This story appears in The Hollywood Reporter’s September 2026 Sports issue .

articles.title: Why and How ‘Manhunt’ Depicts Hell as a “Colorful Candy World”: A Chat With DOP Jonathan Glendon
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 9, 2026 6:05am 'Manhunt' Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival A competition film of the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival that left audiences rattled and talking well past the lights came on after the movie was Wayne Wapeemukwa ‘s sophomore feature, Manhunt . Inspired by real-life murders in Canada in 2019, the film follows two young men who try to escape dead-end lives by embarking on a road trip through the country’s northern frontier, which ends up as a journey with much, much bigger – and darker – consequences for people around them and themselves. Related Stories TV 'Doctor Who' Star Noel Clarke Charged With Sexual Assault, Voyeurism and Exposure Business Channel 4 to Slash Workforce by 28 Percent as Broadcaster Unveils "Long-Term Transformation Strategy" Manhunt caused much debate among Locarno audiences by not compiling facts but offering a parable and diving into what Wapeemukwa described in a THR interview as the “nihilism at the heart of these boys’ lives. Online, we call it being blackpilled.” The film picked up an honor in Locarno’s Junior Jury Awards . Also turning heads in Manhunt , which Wapeemukwa wrote with Anna-Lena Theobald, were Canadian newcomers Harris Lowe and Landon Tunold, discovered by the team of Vaka Street Casting, which was also behind the Canadian hit Blue Heron , as the young male protagonists, along with L.A.-based Austrian twins Bianca and Dilara Foscht. And then there is the cinematography , courtesy of Toronto-based Jonathan Glendon in his feature film debut. Sensory and visceral, mesmerizing and unsettling at the same time, the movie’s visuals mirror the state of mind of the two guys at its center, earning the DOP all sorts of questions during a discussion after the Locarno world premiere of the film. Cinetic Media holds North American sales rights, while Aspect Ratio is handling international sales. About a month after the film’s premiere, THR caught up with Glendon in between all sorts of work projects to discuss how he approached the cinematographic look and feel of Manhunt , inspirations from Dutch cinematographer legend Robbie Muller and The Wrestler , the use of saturation and infrared light, and why he and Wapeemukwa imagined hell as a colorful candy world. This is your first feature film. How did you end up coming on board as cinematographer for it? There were a few things happening all at once. I knew the casting director of the movie, Katrín Braga – we have been friends for almost 10 years now. She specializes in street casting and sometimes sends me amazing photos of people she comes across for photography or film projects. Before Manhunt , she sent me a photo of Harris and Landon without saying anything, and I responded with: “Who are these guys? They look amazing and so interesting.” They had this crazy look, and their chemistry just in this photo was obvious. There was so much energy in it. ‘Manhunt’ Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival And she responded by asking: “What are you doing in August?” And I said: “Nothing. What do you mean? So, sounds good – [whatever you need].” And then the next day, the producer of Manhunt called me and said he would get the script for the film over to me, and it would be amazing if I could call the director, Wayne. I didn’t know what he was talking about, so he said: “Oh, you were recommended by Jeremy Cox, [the DOP on the likes of Backrooms and Longlegs ], who was going to shoot the film, but he can’t and suggested you, and Katrin suggested you as well.” Of course, I said: “I would love to talk to the director.” I ran home from a cafe because I felt I needed to read the script and prep in my office. Because this is my first feature, I really wanted to be as prepared as I could. When I called Wayne, it was just supposed to be a 15-20 minute chemistry call to discuss our approach and interests. But we ended up talking for an hour or an hour and a half and just immediately clicked. We had so many ideas to share about how we could approach some of the subject matter in a way that made it powerful, while being conscious of the world and the politics around the film. While watching Manhunt , I felt the film quite intensely. It was more of an all-around experience – there was a chemistry and physicality to it. How important was that to the creative team? And did you have any cinematic references for that? I’m so happy that you use the word “feel” for how the movie is interacting with you! I love that. Let’s talk about color in that context. I don’t think you should ever notice color in a movie, unless that’s a story beat. But it’s really important for the color to be felt. I was really inspired by the way that Robbie Müller shot Breaking the Waves , the Lars von Trier film. I remember watching that movie for the first time and for the first five minutes wondering: Why is the movie this sepia, this brown thing? And five minutes go by, and you completely forget about the color, but you still feel it, and the feeling is this bubbling, horrible anxiety. It’s like poison, like rot. It’s not loud, but your eyes are so good at adjusting to the world that when your eyes adjust to rot, you stop seeing it and you start feeling it. So, when we made Manhunt , we really wanted that feeling of an unsettledness to be felt. So, for Act 1 and Act 2, we are very referential to Breaking the Waves . The colorist, Dave Tolmiak, and I funneled the color away. It starts off quite muted and a little bit brown, and then we take a little bit more color away, a little bit more color away, a little bit more color away, a little bit more color away, until the moment before Act 3 starts, where there’s a pivotal moment in the movie where the two characters decide the way they want their life to be. They have the choice of acting upon evil, or of stepping back from the edge. ‘Manhunt’ Courtesy of Manhunt Productions At that point, the movie has almost zero saturation, and you don’t see it, but you feel it. You feel that there is no life left in the image. And this also works narratively within the film because there is a forest fire. And then there are some wild-looking colors in the final act. Where does that come from? We talked quite intensely about the ways in which hell could be represented, which is the third act of the film. That’s when the colors come – these crazy red skies and yellow trees and strange skin tones. It’s like we’ve gotten so used to the color being gone and to having this horrible feeling inside. I have described it as wanting Act 2 to feel like sand in your mouth – that textural feeling of grittiness and dryness, this unquenchable desire to change something, but you don’t know how. And then, I wanted Act 3 to be this candy-like hellscape. That was something that Wayne and I connected on early on. I’m fascinated by this idea of hell being a bright candy world… Can you tell me more about that? Working on Manhunt brought up a lot of philosophical questions and made me think a lot about what hell is. I realized that hell is actually different for everybody. Traditionally, there’s this rendering of hell as a dark cave with fire, and there’s the devil with a pitchfork poking everybody with it. That’s the sort of hell that we accept in media. But I realized that hell, just like heaven, is an incredibly personal experience – one person’s heaven is not another person’s heaven, and the same is true for hell. For our two main characters, their version of hell is kind of awesome in some ways. They make this choice willingly, and by doing so, they are, for a moment, in this bright, colorful candy world – this Monster Energy drink-, Mountain Dew-like pornographic space where everything is in full saturation, full brightness, full energy, full excitement. But when you eat too much candy, you get this headache, and you can’t sustain that sort of explosion. So, we wanted to represent hell in this brighter way. Jonathan Glendon behind the scenes of the ‘Manhunt’ shoot Courtesy of Jonathan Glendon How did you achieve that psychedelic look and feel? When Wayne initially suggested that hell was like candy, I thought about how we could use cameras that saw outside the visible spectrum. So all the colors that you see were from an infrared camera, and we got multiple effects from doing that. On the surface level, you get these incredible skies because infrared light is invisible to us. There’s far more infrared light on Earth than there is visible light, so you just get these bright vistas. And everything has a different relationship with infrared light. Trees, for example, have their chlorophyll interacting with infrared light in a very special way that makes it glow. So, with in an infrared camera, you get trees with vibrant purple or bright orange. I really love the work that Greig Fraser did on Dune: Part Two with the Colosseum scene, this black-and-white fight that uses infrared cameras and sees under the surface layer of the skin. I was really curious as to how that would look in color because black and white looks really beautiful. With color, it sort of makes people look like a newborn – their skin becomes wrinkleless and slightly translucent. And because we all produce heat, we also all produce a small amount of light, and it creates this very strange skin texture of a newborn baby mixed with a snake. And I thought that was very fitting for these characters, born again into hell. You mentioned photography before. Were there any inspirations from that or other creative fields that you brought to Manhunt , especially when it comes to the use of infrared light? I was initially really inspired by photographer Richard Mosse, who did this project on color infrared film stock that I really loved. I saw it in university and have always really admired it. It is called The Enclave . But that’s the only infrared color project that is in a narrative space that I was aware of. There are also a couple of music videos that have done it and a dance film from Montreal that I found that used infrared mixed with thermal imaging. But this is a camera technique that is more popular with photographers who shoot landscapes. So, there’s a novelty to it. ‘Manhunt’ Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Our director Wayne and I were just really interested in creating very visceral spaces, showing the deadness in the world. Since this isn’t a big studio project, how did you and the rest of the creative team on Manhunt get all this stuff done on a small budget? So many things came out of our nimbleness in filmmaking. We didn’t have very large lighting setups, so we really chose the time of day when we wanted to shoot. And for the last part of the film, the director, myself, the first First Assistant Camera, the actors, and the producer, we all actually camped for a week. We had a tent set up that had the camera in it overnight, and we had giant batteries that would charge smaller batteries. We did that so that we could gain access to these locations that were four or five hours away from any hotel in the middle of nowhere in the Rocky Mountains of Canada. I recall that you also mentioned during a Locarno Q&A that Darren Aronofsky’s The Wrestler was an influence for parts of Manhunt in some way. Could you share how? That film was shot by Maryse Alberti, and it’s some of the best handheld camera work I’ve ever seen. I really think it’s so perfect. I love the aspect ratio and the physical space that Mickey Rourke takes up in the movie. A lot of the movie is shot from behind, showing Mickey Rourke’s character move through the world, and so we see the world in front, but we don’t always get to see Mickey’s face in it. His physicality is his relationship with the world. So, you don’t fully get to know his character. And then the moments where you do get to come around, and you do get to see him from the front, you get a close-up, and it feels like a gift. When Wayne, the director, and I were talking about Manhunt , we talked a lot about the visual language and how we could create rules to confine us. We both really believe that creativity shouldn’t be limitless. Creativity actually lives most powerfully when there is some confinement, some restriction. Jonathan Glendon behind the scenes of the ‘Manhunt’ shoot Courtesy of Jonathan Glendon One of the rules that we made was to restrict the visibility of Joey and Kit in the first two acts. We wanted to see them from behind and obstruct them a little bit. We wanted to see their relationship with the world, and only in some instances do we show them fully. In the third act, when they make this terrible choice of who they want to be, that’s when we fully get to meet them. That’s when the movie stops being handheld, and the film fully becomes static on the tripod with wides. And we slowly get further and further away from them, as if nature and the environment are consuming them. We show the scale of nature to show how minuscule they are. Manhunt also includes video game segments, which take us inside the digital world, where key ideas and thoughts of the main characters form. How did you guys approach that? That part of the film was done by a really talented, recently graduated video game developer I had met at a party in Toronto. We always knew that there was going to be a Manhunt video game that they’re playing for the relationship between the two of them, and to have the game rendering their life, and their life rendering the game. There is this foreshadowing as to who they’re going to be in the video game; the skies in it even resemble the skies in Act 3. We shot the film first and gave this developer scenes and stills from it, so he could model the video game after the forest and the color palette we shot in. Before I let you go back to your work, will we see more feature film work from you – or are you at least open to it? And any genres or so you are particularly interested in? Yes, the narrative space is definitely where I want to be working. Since Locarno, I’m really happy that I’ve been in contact with people about projects. ‘Manhunt’ Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival I think the movies that I’m drawn to and that I hope to connect with are about spaces and approach, not genres. I really want to work on films that don’t fully know yet what they are. I want there to be a little bit of room where hopefully the director and I can create something together. I also love working with non-actors. I love films that are approach-driven, and I love directors who are open to creating rules. That’s really important for me. So, I’m very grateful to be interviewing for some movies right now, because I want to keep it going. THR

articles.title: Chris Hansen Calls ‘Primetime’ an “Insult,” Has No Regrets About ‘Predator’ Sting That Ended in Suicide (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Seth Abramovitch Plus Icon Seth Abramovitch Senior Writer SethAbramovitch Follow Sign Up View All September 9, 2026 6:15am Chris Hansen Jason Mendez/Getty Images Chris Hansen has not seen Primetime , and has no plans to sign anything in order to do so. But following the news out of the film’s Venice Film Festival premiere , the former NBC correspondent has read enough about Robert Pattinson ‘s performance and the film’s fictionalized depiction of his work to know that he objects. Directed by Lance Oppenheim in his narrative feature debut — who’s also grabbing headlines for co-directing with Nathan Fielder the Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything — and written by Ajon Singh, Primetime dramatizes the 2006 boom year of Dateline NBC ‘s To Catch a Predator , when Hansen’s hidden-camera stings became a ratings phenomenon and, eventually, a legal liability. Related Stories Movies Telluride Awards Analysis: Nathan Fielder's Off-the-Wall Elizabeth Holmes Doc Could Click with Academy -- and Land Picture and Acting Noms Movies 'You Can See Everything' Review: Elizabeth Holmes Doc From Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim Is Fascinatingly Slippery, Dizzyingly Clever Pattinson, who also produces Primetime , plays a version of Hansen consumed by the segment’s success and hungry for a primetime slot; Merritt Wever plays his producer; Skyler Gisondo and Phoebe Bridgers play decoys; and former NBC chief Jeff Zucker appears as himself. The film premiered in competition at Venice on Sept. 5 to a roughly eight-minute standing ovation . Pattinson emerged with strong notices and early Oscar talk , while reviews of the film itself were more mixed . A24 opens it in select theaters Sept. 25 before expanding in October. Lance Oppenheim and Robert Pattinson attend the red carpet for the ‘Primetime’ premiere during the 83rd Venice International Film Festival. Laurent Hou / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images Hansen’s dispute with the studio began well before Venice. In August, he said A24 would screen the film for him only if he signed a nondisclosure agreement that, by his account, would have been unacceptably restrictive. Studio sources called it a standard screening NDA meant to prevent plot leaks. But legal experts shown the agreement by The Hollywood Reporter say that the prohibitive legal language went far beyond that of a boilerplate NDA. Hansen decided to skip the screening and, as first reported by THR , bought ad space for his true-crime streaming network, TruBlu, to run before every screening of Primetime for at least the first four weeks of its release. Talking for the first time since Primetime ‘s unveiling in Venice, Hansen, 66, called THR from Chicago, where he was presenting at the annual conference of the National Center for Victims of Crime. He called the film an “insult,” compared Hollywood’s conduct to the predatory behavior it depicts — citing Harvey Weinstein in the process — and responded, with little hesitation, to questions about the controversial death of a sting target that serves as Primetime ‘s dark climax. The film has now premiered in Venice, and Pattinson is receiving Oscar talk for playing you. How would you feel if he were nominated? There wouldn’t be a movie if I hadn’t created the Predator investigative series, so that would not be possible without my work. Robert Pattinson has said that he hopes the movie adds to my legacy, and I appreciate that. But you still have something that is a complete work of fiction attached to a real name. Based upon what I’ve seen in the trailer and my understanding of what has been written about the film, they wanted to create something much darker and way more dramatic. I think it’s an insult to the thousands of men and women who work hard every day to protect children from predators. They turn something that is very positive, very challenging and not without risk into what is essentially a horror film. I guess it’s not surprising that a Hollywood studio would act in such an exploitive or predatory manner. We’re talking about an industry that was led by perhaps one of the biggest predators to walk the planet, Harvey Weinstein. They’ll all pat each other on the back and say, “What a great job. This is really dark and mysterious and intriguing.” But at the end of the day, it is a completely made-up work of fiction. Why would they not contact or consult me? Because they don’t care about the real story. And the irony is that the real story is pretty darn dramatic on its own. Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen in ‘Primetime’ BFI London Film Festival A24 did not officially approach you until shortly before releasing the trailer. What bothers you most about how the studio handled this? Obviously, we knew something was in the works. I’ve been a reporter for 45 years. You hear things. But to come to you at the last minute and say, “We’ve done this, and we didn’t feel that we had to come to you to discuss it,” seems sneaky and somewhat disingenuous, especially because the project is so largely a work of fiction. You look at the trailer, and there’s nothing in it that actually happened in real life. That raises the question: Why use somebody’s name, image and likeness? They do that because it has commercial value. The name is a brand, and the brand brings people into theaters, just as it does to my podcasts, my network and everything else we do. I have no issue with Robert Pattinson. I think he’s a great actor and a nice guy, and he has been very gracious in his comments about me. But they put him in a difficult position. He’s going to be asked, “Did you actually meet with Chris Hansen?” And he has to explain why, as an actor portraying me, they never reached out even to have a discussion. I think it’s because the studio and the director didn’t want to know the truth. They had a notion of the film they wanted to create, and they wanted to benefit from the use of my name. Has A24 offered you any explanation for not consulting you? In the correspondence we had back and forth, they essentially said, “This is loosely based on Chris’s work, so we didn’t have any compelling need to reach out to him, consult him or get permission.” But they used the name, and they never want to answer that question. But the filmmakers did consult Jeff Zucker, and he plays himself in the movie. What do you make of that? Maybe Jeff is a Hollywood insider. I haven’t talked to Jeff in some time. I learned later that he was going to be in the film, and I saw him in the trailer. But I never had the conversation that Robert Pattinson has with Jeff Zucker [depicted] in the trailer. Again, it’s totally fiction. Jeff Zucker and Chris Hansen at a party in 2008. NEIL RASMUS/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images You still haven’t seen the film? No. They wanted an NDA and said it was their standard procedure. It may be a very standard NDA for them, but it’s not standard if you’re Chris Hansen, and it would have been restrictive. I said, “I’d love to see it. I’m happy to agree not to give away the plotline or anything like that, but I don’t think I need to sign an NDA.” We came to an impasse, and that was that. I will see the film at some point, I assume when it comes out, and I’ll be able to judge it based upon that. The reviews suggest the film depicts the investigations as having crossed a line, becoming exploitation in which the public good was secondary to ratings. How do you respond to that? It’s just not true. From the beginning, we were transparent about what we did, how we did it and the results. The film’s timeline, scenario and conversations are completely made up. It just didn’t happen. I pitched [the stings] because I thought it was a critical issue, and Dateline approved it. It was never meant to be its own series. It was one of the many stories I did for Dateline and NBC. We hit on something incredibly compelling, so we continued to do it, and we continue today. The film apparently portrays the Predator investigations as your consuming obsession and suggests you were desperate to turn them into a primetime franchise. Was that true? I’ve won 10 Emmys for various reporting. None are for the Predator series. My understanding is that the film’s character has invested his whole world in this, doesn’t feel he gets enough respect for it and thinks it should be a primetime show. It was never the only thing I did. It was part of my repertoire as a reporter. It was compelling television because you had a felony being committed in real time, the person confronted with evidence, interviewed by me and then facing criminal justice. There’s never been anything quite like it. People keep asking me whether you’re furious about this or happy about the attention it could bring to TruBlu and your current work. Is it a mixture of both? I’ve never been angry about it. Don’t portray me as some angry guy. I understand how the media world works. I’m less schooled in the Hollywood world, but I understand my media world. And of course we will benefit from this in any way we can, because this very important work continues. We produce Takedown on TruBlu and have several documentaries in the works, including I’m Chris Hansen , which was underway before we knew about the film and is nearing completion. You participated in David Osit’s documentary Predators last year, which questioned the methods and legacy of the franchise. Was there anything objectionable to you about that film? It was one director’s point of view, and he left a lot of important things out. He was out to raise questions. It was almost like, “Have you hugged your neighborhood predator today?” He had a sociologist analyze whether it was appropriate to expose these guys and whether we’re too rough on them. It got a little silly at some point, and I think people saw that when they watched the documentary. Chris Hansen appeared in David Osit’s 2025 documentary ‘Predators.’ Everett Collection [Primetime ‘s final act centers on Louis William “Bill” Conradt Jr., a 56-year-old chief felony assistant district attorney in Rockwall County, Texas, and a former Kaufman County DA. During a November 2006 sting in Murphy, Texas, Conradt exchanged sexually explicit messages with a Perverted Justice volunteer posing as a 13-year-old boy but never went to the sting house. On Nov. 5, police obtained warrants and sent a tactical team to his home in nearby Terrell; he fatally shot himself as officers entered while members of the Dateline crew, Hansen among them, waited outside to film his arrest. Hansen and NBC have maintained that law enforcement and Dateline conducted parallel investigations. Collin County’s district attorney subsequently declined to prosecute any of the 23 other men arrested in the Murphy sting. Luke Dittrich’s September 2007 Esquire investigation is the principal account on which Primetime is based. ] Reviews confirm that Primetime depicts Bill Conradt’s death. How do you feel about the case being reexamined this way? We were completely transparent about what happened from the moments after it happened. This was no secret. It was unfortunate that somebody chose to take his life rather than face criminal consequences. You can draw your own conclusions as to why. They found child pornography on his computer. He had sexually explicit conversations with two different decoys posing as 13-year-old boys. I can’t speak for the police, but they decided to arrest him, apparently concerned about the possible destruction of evidence. He chose to take his life rather than face the consequences. We reported what we knew the next day on the Today show and continued to be transparent throughout the story. There are certain things you can’t control. Obviously, you don’t want anybody taking their own life, but that was a decision made by that individual. They’ll ramp it up in the film, I’m sure, and make it more dramatic than it really was. It was based upon an Esquire article that came out years ago that was a bit of a hit piece then, and apparently it’s part of the narrative in the film. According to the Esquire account, this was the first time you went to someone’s home after he did not come to the sting house. Do you regret that decision? We were covering what the police were doing. We didn’t have a role in the decision. The police decided to do it, and we covered it like any other arrest we would cover in the course of reporting the story. So you’ve never had sleepless nights, second thoughts or a change of heart after that incident? No. We continued to conduct investigations after that. [ Conradt’s sister, Patricia, sued NBC for $105 million. In February 2008, U.S. District Judge Denny Chin allowed the principal claims to proceed, writing that a jury could find NBC had “crossed the line from responsible journalism to irresponsible and reckless intrusion into law enforcement.” The ruling did not establish NBC’s liability, and the network settled with the family that June for an undisclosed sum. ] From left: Chris Hansen, Josh Macikoiewicz, Hoda Kotb, Keith Morrison and Dennis Murphy attend the ‘Dateline’ 20th Anniversary Mystery Party on Oct. 4, 2011. Eugene Gologursky/Getty Images Your theatrical ad buy was a clever response. What are you hoping comes from it? I want people to know that we do this important work every day and that they can see it on my streaming network, TruBlu, where we have the freedom, the independence and the control of our content to continue doing it. I think its importance is reflected in how many people continue to follow it. [ Hansen’s comments to Fox News and Dan Abrams’ SiriusXM show in late August produced a wave of headlines saying he was “weighing legal action” against A24. As a matter of law, his path is narrow. Public figures face a high bar in defamation cases, and courts have afforded dramatizations of real people broad First Amendment protection. In the 2018 case De Havilland v. FX Networks , a California appeals court threw out Olivia de Havilland’s suit over Feud . Daryl Hannah raised a similar objection in March , when she published a New York Times op-ed denouncing her portrayal in FX’s Love Story as “not even a remotely accurate representation of my life” and questioned whether real people have any recourse when a series takes liberties with their names. ] Are lawyers still examining whether you could take action against A24? I have lawyers looking at it, the best guys there are in this part of the world. But what do you get out of that besides making a statement? Is there something to be done? Is there some justice to be served? I don’t know. It’s an interesting legal question. Daryl Hannah raised a version of it in her New York Times op-ed about Love Story . I don’t know if you saw that. I sure did see that. Obviously, I’m a public figure, and the threshold for defamation is high. A number of things have to be shown. Are there other, more creative legal theories that could hold them accountable? Maybe. Is it identity theft? What separates this from identity theft? If somebody takes your name and image and makes money from it in a commercial enterprise, is that stealing somebody’s identity? I don’t know. It’s a question for our legal system, I suppose. Is legal action something you’re actively exploring? Somebody asked me that, and I said, “Well, I can’t rule it out until I see the film.” Obviously, nobody would. And then suddenly there’s a headline: “Hansen Weighing Legal Action.” It got the Page Six treatment. So no, you can’t rule anything out until you see the film. I’ve got some very well-schooled lawyers and advisers who keep an eye on it for me. But I don’t get up every morning and obsess over this. We just finished [a sting] in Louisiana, worked until 3:45 a.m., got on a plane at 6 a.m. and flew to Chicago for my niece’s wedding. Then I came back to New York and watched the U.S. Open. Now I’m at this conference helping survivors of these crimes get justice. I’ve got work to do. It’s a full-time job being the real Chris Hansen, much less worrying about a fictional movie. We’re not going to be taken advantage of or rolled over. But I don’t spend sleepless hours on it. One thing that’s become a lot more known because of Primetime : You’re still producing new Predator investigations. And they’re still resulting in arrests . It’s very active. TruBlu has around 270 episodes from the last four years, and we drop a new episode every Thursday. People get caught up in their feelings one way or the other about the franchise, and I understand that. But the positive effect of it way, way outweighs any negatives. I’ve often said jokingly that I wish we’d have a year when nobody showed up. I’d love to do a Southern cooking show in Florida, visit all the barbecues and work my way through the state. That would be a great way to spend some time as a journalist — but I don’t see it in my near future. THR

articles.title: The 50 Most Powerful TV Producers of 2026
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Illustrated by Neil Jamieson; Meriwether, lawrence: Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images. Brunson: Robin L Marshall/Getty Images. lee, rogen: Araya Doheny/Getty Images for SAG-AFTRA Foundation. Lindelof: Emma McIntyre/Getty Images. fey: Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images. Ignore that deep, existential AI dread for a moment — “It’s the devil’s tool,” cautions Damon Lindelof — and you’ll find that showrunners actually do have plenty to feel good about these days. Original concepts are selling again ( Widow’s Bay ! Pluribus !). Commercial success with the old model is still possible (see: High Potential or The Pitt ). Young people are watching more than just MrBeast attempting not to die on camera: Just look at Prime Video’s YA triumvirate of The Summer I Turned Pretty , Off Campus and Sterling Point . Hell, a Canadian import with zero marketing and a whole lot of gay sex turned two unknown actors into The Beatles. TV is so back! And even as creatives brace for the Warner Bros.-Paramount merger as if the moon herself were barreling toward the Southland to incinerate us all, THR ‘s annual poll of the most powerful writer-producers in TV dives into all the good stuff like show envy, the trends they’re glad to see die and the execs who impress them the most. And, yeah, sure, AI is coming for all our jobs. But it hasn’t yet. So take a breath and take note of Michelle King’s advice for aspiring TV scribes who might one day join the ranks of this storied list: “None of the sensible professions — lawyer, engineer, doctor — are safe from AI either. So, you might as well become a writer.” METHODOLOGY THR selected the Most Powerful TV Producers from all writing producers with live-action scripted series that aired original episodes in the U.S. between August 2025 and August 2026. With acknowledgment that roles and duties can vary significantly from show to show, each entrant is judged relative to slates, deal size, ratings, value to platform and studio, cultural impact, awards and, pivotally, who can actually sell a show in this bizarre and uncertain climate.
