But I’m staying optimistic because I’ve been around long enough that I’ve seen the death of the comedy, the death of the drama, the death of the comedy again, reality TV is going to replace everything… and yet good stories keep coming out and grabbing people. So, I’m going to stick with content is king.” Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past “True crime. I’m joking because everything is true crime and it’s all my wife ever watches, but man, I’d like it to be over.” Bill Lawrence at his office on the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank. Photographed by Roger Kisby Lee Sung Jin Where’s the Beef ? Likely on most of the top 10 lists you’ll be reading when 2026 comes to a close. Lee’s follow-up to his lauded 2023 anthology upped the star power (Youn Yuh-jung!) and delivered on incredibly high expectations. Publicly, he’s been noncommittal about the future of the Netflix franchise — up for another 16 Emmys. But he’s got other things going, like working on the script for the X-Men movie that had every actor under the age of 30 war-calling their agent. The scariest part about the TV business today “The industry made almost 50 percent fewer shows this year. Meanwhile, more and more writers rooms have become a room of one. That being said, there will always be a need for storytelling, and I’m hopeful there will be healthier cycles somehow on the horizon, much like the movie business this year.” Star I’m still dying to work with “Tied between Tom Cruise and Cate Blanchett.” My advice for any baby writer “Be yourself while perfecting your craft. Having a point of view is the most important, as you are the rare 1 in 8 billion commodity, but it will go further if you spend time perfecting your craft on the technical side.” Louisa Levy For anyone who hadn’t heard of Levy’s work before May, that changed the minute her adaptation of the spicy YA hit Off Campus premiered as the third-most-watched debut in Prime Video history with 36 million viewers in less than two weeks. In lieu of a victory lap, Levy went right back to work. She’s already filming season two in Canada, which is great news for its rabid, albeit slightly creepy, parasocial fan economy. A song I love and just can’t clear “Hannah’s original karaoke song in season 1 was AC/DC’s ‘You Shook Me All Night Long”’ but we couldn’t get it! I’m not mad though. It opened the door for us to use Warrant’s “Cherry Pie.” The scariest part about the TV business today “How few jobs there are. It was tough to have such a big boom and then such a constriction. Especially in Los Angeles. So many talented folks are out of work.” My advice for any baby writer “Study the craft of writing but also learn how to participate in a room. Eighty percent of TV writing is talking, 20 percent is writing, and 50 percent is navigating relationships. How does that add up to 100 percent? Figuring out the math is producing.” Chuck Lorre The sitcom king is still turning out personalized vanity cards after every episode of every series he produces — of which there are currently three: CBS’ Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage , Netflix’s Leanne and HBO Max’s Stuart Fails to Save the Universe . He’s Chuck Lorre … what more do you want us to say? Seth MacFarlane MacFarlane might still make more money than you can fathom from his enduring animated hits Family Guy and American Dad! , but his live-action output is enviable, too. The folks at Peacock have got to be pleased with his comedy double header of The ’Burbs and Ted — and his coup in scoring the rights to the viral Dungeon Crawler Carl book series, potentially one of the most consequential TV deals done this year. Leon Bennett/Getty Images Liz Meriwether Just when you think you’ve got the New Girl creator showhorned — get it? — in sitcoms, she delivers an epic string of prestige hits ( The Dropout, Dying for Sex and, now, Hulu’s Furious ) and then signs on to write Jon M. Chu’s Britney Spears biopic. But Meriwether’s return to features isn’t full time. On top of ample development, the wildly versatile scribe just secured a second season of her Emmy Rossum collab. If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “A blanket. Always. I can’t write without a blanket covering at least half of my body.” Song I love and just can’t clear “I’m still sad that we couldn’t clear Tori Amos’ song ‘Little Earthquakes’ in the New Girl pilot. A good portion of my teenage years was spent blasting that cassette tape and driving around suburban Michigan thinking that no one understood my pain.” The scariest part about the TV business today “That streaming platforms are not making as much TV, which means that people aren’t taking as many chances. New voices are getting lost in the process. Writing and shooting a failed pilot was my way into producing my own writing at a large scale. It was how I got my sea legs, and I just don’t think new writers are getting that chance to try and fail and try again. New voices will always find a way to appear, but it’s increasingly not through television, which feels like a huge loss.” Ryan Murphy He may not always have the critics on his side, but nobody knows how to launch a show like Murphy. After giving the world the most unhinged press tour (Hulu’s All’s Fair ), he heralded FX’s The Shards with so many L.A. billboards that Kaia Gerber briefly outpaced the German shepherd from Veronica’s Insurance. The American Love Story producer simply knows how to get stuff on air and in people’s faces, which is why you can’t currently hide from the fact that his American Horror Story is back for lucky season No. 13. Jonathan Nolan, Geneva Robertson-Dworet Together, Nolan and Robertson-Dworet manage one of the most ambitious, expensive and, to everyone at Amazon’s relief, popular series going right now. The second season of Fallout reached more than 83 million pairs of eyeballs worldwide in its first 13 weeks of release. Season three is set to wrap production in September, hopefully freeing up star Walton Goggins to bank a few more Walmart commercials. Song we love and just can’t clear Nolan “‘Is That All There Is’ by Peggy Lee.” Robertson-Dworet “‘The Wanderer” by Dion. One of the best songs in the history of the Fallout games.” The scariest part about the TV business today Nolan “Fear of fear itself. The rumors of the industry’s demise are greatly exaggerated.” Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past Robertson-Dworet “Not disparaging any trend, but I’m personally glad Fallout doesn’t have an aftershow so I don’t have to be on it.” Megan Park, Stephanie Savage and Josh Schwartz What do you get when you combine the YA Midas touch of Savage and Schwartz with an ascendant filmmaker like Park? Arguably the series of the summer. It was a late entry for Sterling Point , but within two weeks of its Aug. 5 launch, Prime Video says it took in 36 million viewers. A sophomore season was quickly ordered, one Savage and Schwartz will work on when they’re not busy with their recently ordered Paramount+ update of Clueless . Star I’m still dying to work with Park “Sandra Bullock. She has always been my all-time favorite. I’m working on trying to make that one happen …” Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past Savage “Thinking that YA wasn’t a viable genre anymore …” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … Schwartz “More flights please! With so many shows shooting out of town, you end up spending months away from your family.” A song I love and just can’t clear Park “‘Sundown’ by Gordon Lightfoot. I have wanted to put it in everything I’ve made. It reminds me of my childhood summers in Canada.” Tyler Perry Extending his TV partnership with BET Media Group through 2028, the Atlanta-based producing giant is by no means limited to his many, many Paramount offerings. Netflix original Beauty in Black has proved so popular for the streamer, it recently reversed course and uncanceled the series with the announcement of a fourth season. In this economy? Shonda Rhimes The reigning monarch of Shondaland renewed her Netflix megadeal for a second time in August. This new five-year pact will keep her overseeing Bridgerton , the Regency drama that’s logged 610 million views since its 2023 bow to become one of the streamer’s defining hits. And while she may no longer be hands-on at ABC’s Grey’s Anatomy , it’s worth noting that her creation heads into season 23 as one of the most watched broadcast and streaming series. If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “If? Girl, get you a team that fights for a rider.” 2026 series I’ve most admired “Pluribus.” The scariest part about the TV business today “AI is used to take jobs from hard-working craftspeople who work on sets. Also, the consolidation of studios will mean the narrowing of options for writers and producers. Devastating.” Star I’m still dying to work with “BEYONCÉ KNOWLES CARTER.” Mike Schur Known for his serial collaborations, Schur, who also executive produced Hacks , has two reunions of note in the queue. There’s a third season for Netflix’s Man on the Inside , starring his Good Place collaborator Ted Danson, and Peacock’s forthcoming Dig , a Parks and Recreation reteam with Amy Poehler. The latter drops all 10 episodes Thanksgiving week. A song I love and just can’t clear “’Ghost’ by Neutral Milk Hotel.” The scariest part about the TV business today “The scariest thing about the TV business is how scared everyone is about the TV business.” Rachel Sennott She may have co-created Big Mistakes with Dan Levy, but Sennott seems to make very few of her own. She spends her day-to-day creating and starring in her HBO comedy vehicle, I Love LA , which has been called Gen Z’s answer for Girls or S ex and the City . One could also call it a Gotham TV award winner and one of HBO’s fastest-growing comedies. 2026 series I’ve most admired “ Industry . Insane performances and incredible writing. And Dianna Agron just joined the cast for season five? I’m freaking out …” A song I love and just can’t clear “There’s a remix of the song ‘La Musique’ that I couldn’t get for season one. If anyone hears this, I’ll do anything please and thank you!” The TV executive who’s really impressed me … “Amy Gravitt. She always picks up the phone and gives me the real immediately. We talk at like 5am all the time.” Rachel Sennott, creator and star of I Love LA . Kenny Laubbacher/HBO Taylor Sheridan Yeehaw! When he’s not minting new hit (CBS’ Marshals ) after hit (Paramount+’s Dutton Ranch ) after hit ( The Madison ) or tending to his ongoing series ( Lioness, Mayor of Kingstown, Tulsa King, Landman ) or writing his first book ( How to Not Die in Prison: A Survival Guide ), Sheridan is going on podcasts to talk about how much Hollywood doesn’t like him. Taylor, Universal just bet the farm on you with that landmark deal to swipe you from David Ellison. Hollywood likes you just fine. Charlotte Stoudt Stoudt is tasked with landing one of the biggest planes in streaming history with the upcoming conclusion of The Morning Show . Apple TV’s megawatt drama, starring Reese Witherspoon and Jennifer Aniston, wrapped filming on its fifth and final season this summer. That will air in 2027, when you could say it’ll return to the streamer’s Top 10 — but that would suggest it had fallen off it. The TV executive who’s really impressed me … “Dana Walden should ditch Disney and run for president.” 2026 series I’ve most admired “ Mr. Scorsese – a complex protagonist with an incredible story arc.” A song I love and just can’t clear “John Brion’s ‘Little Person’ from Synecdoche, New York . Devastating.” Jason Sudeikis What seemed highly unlikely just a few years ago became reality in August when Sudeikis unveiled the rebooted fourth season of his pandemic-defining Emmy winner Ted Lasso . The feel-good comedy, aided by new co-showrunner Jack Burditt, won back viewers who helped set an Apple TV record with 296.6 million minutes streamed in just two days. Believe, I guess? Jacob Tierney It’s hard to remember the last time a project so completely seized the pop culture discourse as Heated Rivalry did when the Canadian import got a U.S. run on HBO Max. Tierney, previously known for his work on Letterkenny and Shoresy , turned the quiet December drop into an 11 million viewer phenomenon that platformed gay narratives like never before and minted generational stars out of leads Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams. The star I’m still dying to work with | “I love Chris Evans. He’s an old-fashioned movie star, and I love movie stars.” The scariest part about the TV business today “That we are back in the time where there are only four or five places to take your shows to, and, if they don’t want them, you’re kind of out of options.” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “A good napping situation, instead of falling asleep in a chair I find on set that I’m not supposed to be in. Someone is always telling me that if I sit in a chair that says ‘please do not sit,’ then everyone else will think they can sit in it.” Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams in Heated Rivalry . Crave/Bell Media Jonathan Tropper The list is almost over, so you know how much it pained us to wait this long to describe someone as having “a banner year.” Well, it was worth the wait. Because what a nice run Tropper is enjoying. The novelist and filmmaker has seen his Jon Hamm vehicle Your Friends & Neighbors become a prototype for a serial streaming drama — and it finally broke into the Emmy race. Tropper also ran Lucky , the Apple TV thriller from Reese Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine. As for 2027, there’s just the small matter of his friggin’ Star Wars: Starfighter screenplay. If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “Don’t let me drive. I will be on the phone, and I will crash.” Star I’m still dying to work with “Scarlett Johansson.” Dick Wolf At 79, Wolf has five series on NBC ( Law & Order, Law & Order: SVU and his trio of Chicago dramas), two series on CBS ( FBI and CIA ) and, in our dreams, nightly calls to gossip with Mariska Hargitay. He is a titan. He is a TV legend. And, just saying, he probably has the sway to get most platforms to pony up for a series to be shot in Los Angeles. We have cops and courtrooms, too, Dick! This story appeared in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: The Athlete Is the Studio
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Justin Birnbaum, Sportico Plus Icon Justin Birnbaum, Sportico View All September 9, 2026 6:30am LÆMEUR Coco Gauff has something to confess: She’s been nervous. But the 22-year-old tennis phenom, speaking over the phone after an early August training session, isn’t referring to the National Bank Open in Toronto, where in a few days she would begin a run to the semifinal. Nor is she talking about the U.S. Open at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, a tournament that will eventually pit her against Mirra Andreeva in a highly anticipated quarterfinal matchup on Wednesday, Sept. 9. In 2025, Gauff launched a production company called iROC Media Group and shortly thereafter partnered with Religion of Sports , the Los Angeles-based studio founded by Tom Brady, Michael Strahan and Gotham Chopra, to produce a range of projects. The joint venture a few weeks ago released its first original offering: a pair of shortform documentaries for the Tennis Channel covering the history of fashion in the sport and the story of Zina Garrison, the first Black woman to reach a Grand Slam singles final in the Open era. Related Stories THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue The $100 Billion Race to Build the World's Next Sports Mecca THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Esports Was Supposed to Be Bigger Than the NBA. What Happened? The addition of “executive producer” to Gauff’s résumé — alongside two-time Grand Slam singles champion, U.S. flag-bearer at the 2024 Paris Olympics and the youngest player to ever qualify for the Wimbledon main draw at just 15 years old — has caused some jitters. “I didn’t know how people would perceive it, to be honest,” she says. “But a lot of people were excited about it, and, obviously, I have to wait for feedback in September. That’s the hardest thing.” There are plenty of sports stars who can relate. Over the course of the past two decades, some of the most popular athletes on the planet have established similar businesses to service their creative ambitions, spanning documentaries, TV shows, feature films, podcasts and across multiple genres. (C) Jayden Daniels in Quarterback : Season 3. Courtesy of Netflix LeBron James co-founded the earliest form of the SpringHill Co. in 2007, which has since merged into Fulwell Entertainment. Stephen Curry helped create Unanimous Media in 2018, and Peyton Manning’s Omaha Productions emerged two years later. A 2025 study by USC Annenberg’s Norman Lear Center identified 33 athlete-owned production companies that have generated more than 370 media properties, led by other notable names like Naomi Osaka, Kevin Durant and Tony Hawk. More recently, Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen entered the fold last week by launching Out of Pocket Studios with Skydance Sports. What all these enterprises have in common is that they’re underpinned by a desire for more control. The modern athlete wants a larger say in how they’re perceived, how their intellectual property is used and how they’re compensated. That’s exactly what Gauff, the world’s highest-paid female athlete at $31 million in 2025 , was after when last year she formed a namesake company to house all her business ventures in partnership with powerhouse agency WME, with the media business underneath. “I don’t want to just promote a brand or a product,” she says. “I really want to be a part of it.” It’s also how James, the first active NBA player to achieve billionaire status , framed some of his own moves. “I got sick and tired of the media changing the narrative or picking their narrative about what I was doing,” he said in a 2022 Sports Illustrated cover story. Endeavoring to build a media empire is easier said than done, though. Many of these upstarts have historically been quick to parlay a buzzy name and big bankroll into an initial slate of projects, generally centered around its athlete founder. Giannis Antetokounmpo, for example, rolled out Improbable Media in 2024 with a feature-length documentary about his life story. And, for a time, that would be enough to get a business off and running, especially with the demand for sports-related content booming. Hollywood has changed. The fallout of the COVID-19 shutdowns and the concurrent writer and actors strikes of 2023 has left an indelible mark on the entertainment industry. Studios have shrunk budgets, major production houses have cut staff, and fewer projects are reaching the finish line. That’s not to say there isn’t opportunity — Netflix and Amazon spent about $40 billion combined on video and music content last year — but the degree of difficulty, especially for the sports stars dabbling in unfamiliar territory, has intensified. “Any athlete can walk a project in and have it sell, quote unquote,” says Josh Pyatt, the former co-head of WME Sports who joined Patrick Whitesell’s investment firm WTSL as a partner earlier this year and now runs WIN Artists, its media, content and brand partnerships division. “Getting it made, getting multiple projects made and creating real enterprise value is something that not many can actually do.” (L to R) Kauchani Bratt as Jimmy, River Rayne Thomas as Tyson and Jojo Jackson as Warlance in Rez Ball. Lewis Jacobs/Netflix LESSONS FROM KING JAMES Gauff can’t take credit for the idea to push into the media business. That belongs with her father, Corey. In 2020, amid the COVID quarantine and the absence of sports, the elder Gauff was inspired by watching The Last Dance , an eight-part docuseries that chronicled Michael Jordan’s legendary career. He thought it would be cool to one day produce something similar about his then-16-year-old daughter if she could continue to win in the years to come. Gauff agreed, even though to this day, she still hasn’t seen the documentary. “It’s really bad that I haven’t watched yet,” Gauff says with a laugh. The irony is that while Jordan never founded his own media and production company, some industry insiders suggest that it’s hard not to see his imprint on this era. The basketball legend’s first Nike deal, which landed him a royalty on the sale of every sneaker bearing his name, set a new standard for athletes looking to take ownership of their futures. The repercussions would reshape the signature shoe business and later trickle into other areas. To Pyatt, Strahan and Shaquille O’Neal “were the first” to define the modern athlete production company movement, with the former building SMAC Entertainment alongside entertainment executive Constance Schwartz-Morini since 2010, as he transitioned from pro football player to daytime television talk show host. O’Neal, meanwhile, long has excelled at attracting opportunities and weaving them together, like becoming the president of Reebok’s basketball division in 2023 and then later selling a show to Netflix about revitalizing the brand through his production outfit, Jersey Legends. But much of the oxygen of the era belonged to James. In 2020, he formed the SpringHill Co. with his business partner Maverick Carter, raising $100 million from backers like Guggenheim Partners and Elisabeth Murdoch and consolidating three of his businesses — SpringHill Entertainment, Uninterrupted and the Robot Co. — into a new juggernaut. The joint enterprise had produced TV shows like Survivor’s Remorse , The Wall and The Shop , as well as such films as Space Jam: A New Legacy , Hustle and What’s My Name: Muhammad Ali . With the growing demands of streamers pushing Hollywood toward a TV production peak of 600 shows in 2022, investors poured into the space. The SpringHill Co. a year earlier had sold a minority interest to a group that included Nike, Fenway Sports Group and RedBird Capital Partners at a $725 million valuation. The enthusiasm extended beyond just athlete-led businesses, with Blackstone-backed Candle Media buying a majority stake in Reese Witherspoon’s media company, Hello Sunshine, for $900 million in 2021. Kevin Hart’s firm, Hartbeat, raised $100 million at a $650 million a year later. The proverbial gold rush didn’t last. The aftermath of the pandemic forced the industry to rethink its compensation models, and the bets investors were making on upside gave way to a more fundamentally sound approach. The strikes of 2023 only heightened that strain. “We used to have an economic climate where it was prioritizing growth as opposed to profit,” says Leonard Armato, the former CMO of Skechers who helped O’Neal launch his footwear brand and currently advises the No. 1 pick in the 2026 NBA Draft, AJ Dybantsa. “And that came sort of to a screeching halt around the time of WeWork.” Since then, media companies led by some of the biggest names in Hollywood, like Hart, Jordan Peele and J.J. Abrams, have undergone layoffs. Hello Sunshine reportedly missed its profit projections in 2023, and parent company Candle Media later restructured its business to cut costs . That same year, the Springhill Co. eliminated 10 roles, though it described the move as a pathway to hiring 24 new jobs. In 2024, Bloomberg reported that James’ enterprise had never turned a profit in its four-year life span, having lost a combined $45 million in 2022 and 2023. The SpringHill Co. did rev up its growth plans last year by merging with James Corden’s Fulwell 73, raising a war chest of $40 million from existing investors. For those soldiering on, the industry shift taught at least one valuable lesson. “Every project has to be undeniable,” says Erick Peyton, the co-founder of Curry’s Unanimous Media. Coco Gauff in Tennis Story Serve Fashion Tennis Story Serve Fashion & Tennis Courtesy of Tennis Channel A LITTLE HELP FROM FRIENDS Gauff has full creative control over iROC, but it’s not a day-to-day gig. She picks the projects, gives notes and, in some cases, appears on camera. On the two upcoming short films, Gauff estimates she put in about five to seven hours of work. That’s understandable, considering her tennis schedule. Yet it does stress the gravity of finding the right partner. Gauff chose Religion of Sports, which produced documentaries like Shut Up and Dribble , Man in the Arena and Simone Biles Rising . “I’m kind of creative, but not in the things of finding the right people, cameras, angles and the right person to do the interview,” she says. “Just like so many little things I’ve learned that it takes to create a short.” It’s a commonality among athlete-led production companies. James has Carter. Curry has Peyton. O’Neal has Michael Parris and Authentic Brands Group, which bought a share of his entire business interests in 2015. Strahan has Schwartz-Morini. And Manning has Jamie Horowitz. The duo behind Omaha Productions met in 2019 and formed the business a year later, rattling off hit shows like Peyton’s Places and Monday Night Football With Peyton and Eli . It didn’t take long for outside money to arrive. Peter Chernin’s North Road content studio invested $10 million at a $400 million valuation in 2023, and WTSL, the firm Pyatt would later join, entered Omaha Productions’ cap table two years later in a deal that valued the company at more than $750 million. That success starts at the top, according to Pyatt. “Peyton appeals to red states, and he appeals to blue states, which is very rare,” he says. “Then you have someone like Jamie, who can activate it with Peyton.” But while Omaha Productions or any other talent-led media business can launch off the popularity of its central figure, it must evolve to achieve long-term sustainability. “We used to call it the ‘What happens if that person gets hit by a bus?’ ” Pyatt says. Peyton and Eli Manning now only appear in about a quarter of Omaha Productions’ projects as opposed to more than 70 percent at the beginning. Some of Peyton Manning’s critical contributions to Netflix’s Quarterback docuseries came behind the camera, as the Pro Football Hall of Famer, who does briefly appear in the show, used his personal relationships to help the streamer secure “some of the marquee quarterbacks in the league,” according to Brandon Riegg, vp nonfiction series and sports at Netflix. Chasers-TOM BRADY Remembers EVERYTHING! episode Courtesy of Chasers Riegg, who has worked with James, Curry and O’Neal, in addition to Manning, adds that any production company has to be held to the same standard of developing and executing projects, even if a famous figurehead can lift some of the industry’s typical barriers to entry. When athletes do learn just how hard it is to operate in Hollywood, prolonged success in entertainment becomes a question of their “appetite, ambition and tolerance.” “This is a marathon; this isn’t a five-year thing,” Riegg says. “This is a business. It’s not like hitting the lottery. It’s like you have to do idea creation at a regular cadence.” To offset the challenges of Hollywood production, some media companies use branded content and commercial campaigns. Omaha Productions has shot commercials for the Mannings, as well as Baker Mayfield, Brock Purdy and Jordan Spieth. It also put together a show for the PGA of America starring Colin Jost that was paid for by T-Mobile. The branded content and commercial campaign vertical now accounts for roughly a quarter of Omaha Productions’ revenue, the highest percentage in the company’s brief history. Pyatt doesn’t see that changing, especially with industries like gambling upping their content spends. Gilad Haas, who co-founded production studio and marketing agency Shadow Lion with Brady, says his firm previously struck a deal with FanDuel that produced both a miniseries about the Boston Celtics 2024 championship and hundreds of man-on-the-street, social-style posts. The progression of production companies to full-fledged media businesses has also resulted in other moneymaking endeavors. The Shop , SpringHill Co.’s popular barbershop-style talk show, launched its own line of men’s grooming products. Unanimous Media’s Peyton says his firm wants to play a bigger role in financing projects and funneling creators and other non-traditional talents to larger studios. Many companies in the space are figuring out how to push into live events, if they haven’t already, as the AI age places a stronger emphasis on social gatherings and human connection. Gauff has her own designs on where she wants iROC to go, including producing a movie with a theatrical release. She’s got time, though. Her entertainment journey is starting much earlier than those of James, Curry or Manning. “I’m 22 years old, so there’s still going to be a lot of eyes on me when I’m playing,” she says. “Hopefully, by the time I retire, we build something that can sustain itself without me promoting it as an active player.” This story appears in The Hollywood Reporter’s September 2026 Sports issue .

articles.title: Fox Says DOJ Taking Closer Look at Roku Megadeal
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 9, 2026 6:34am Fox Corp chief Lachlan Murdoch Drew Angerer/Getty Images The U.S. Department of Justice is taking a closer look at Fox Corp .’s $22 billion megadeal for Roku , the media company said Wednesday, potentially signaling regulatory scrutiny on a deal that would turn it into a digital video power player. In a securities filing Wednesday, Fox said: “On September 8, 2026, as expected, each of FOX and Roku received a request for additional information and documentary material (the ‘Second Request’) from the U.S. Department of Justice (the ‘DOJ’) in connection with the DOJ’s review of the Mergers.” “Issuance of the Second Request extends the waiting period under the HSR Act until 30 days after both FOX and Roku have substantially complied with the Second Request, unless the waiting period is terminated earlier by the DOJ or FOX and Roku otherwise agree to extend the waiting period,” the filing continued. “FOX and Roku will continue to work cooperatively with the DOJ in its review of the Mergers.” Fox says it still believes the deal is on track for a first half of 2027 close for the deal, which was announced in June. While the company says the second request was expected (indeed, they are not at all unusual for major deals), it nonetheless signals that there could yet be some regulatory scrutiny on the merger. It’s also hard to ignore the political elephant in the room: President Trump has frequently weighed in on major deals, and there has been a perception in the marketplace that companies with close ties to the White House are getting different treatment than companies perceived to be at odds with them. Paramount’s deal for Warner Bros. Discovery, for example, was given the green light by the DOJ despite some staff attorneys expressing concern around the deal. In the case of Fox, while it may be seen as being closely allied with the White House, Fox News late last week said that it “parted ways” with Maria Bartiromo, sparking some anger from White House officials like Peter Navarro, and a post from President Trump commending her for her work there. But as the Paramount-WBD merger shows, with the deal now held up because of an antitrust suit brought by state AGs, any wrench in the process can become a major holdup to dealmaking. While the DOJ request may be standard for something of this size, it could portend a more challenging path forward than the companies originally anticipated. THR

articles.title: Jenny Slate and Christian Slater Act Out Their Hectic New York City Morning Routines in New Cole Haan Campaign
articles.full_text: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. Cole Haan is putting Christian Slater and Jenny Slate in its shoes for fall. The footwear and accessories brand has tapped the two actors to star in “Comfortable Anywhere,” its fall 2026 global campaign, which rolls out Wednesday morning. The campaign centers on the idea that getting dressed shouldn’t require choosing between looking polished and actually feeling comfortable. Shot in a day-in-the-life format, the campaign features Slater as an unfazed host preparing for dinner guests (and attempting homemade pasta for the first time) while Slate is shown confronting a looming deadline and looking for inspiration just about everywhere except her desk. Related Stories Susan Sarandon Says She's 'Still Had Movies Taken Away Recently' Over Palestine Support: 'There Are Agencies That Are Telling People Not to Hire Me' Stefano Knuchel Premieres Final Chapter in 20-Year Hugo Pratt Trilogy With ‘Hugo in Venice’ “I grew up in New York, so I’m used to moving fast,” Slater tells Variety . “I’ve also been lucky enough to spend most of my life doing what I love. Along the way, I’ve learned to go with the flow and trust where I am.” “That’s what connected me to Cole Haan and the idea of Comfortable Anywhere” he adds. “Being comfortable enough with yourself to take things as they come.” ØriginalGrand SkyWeave Everarc Buy Now $205 Both stars wear the brand’s GrandPrø FlexCraft sneaker throughout the campaign, marking the first time Cole Haan has brought its FlexCraft technology to a sneaker. articles.title: Ellen Burstyn Was ‘Sure’ Her Career Would Be ‘Finished by 40’: ‘The Fact That I’m 93 and Working Is a Miracle’
articles.full_text: Sep 9, 2026 5:11am PT Ellen Burstyn Was ‘Sure’ Her Career Would Be ‘Finished by 40’: ‘The Fact That I’m 93 and Working Is a Miracle’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Ellen Burstyn Was ‘Sure’ Her Career Would Be ‘Finished by 40’: ‘The Fact That I’m 93 and Working Is a Miracle’ 1 hour ago Casey Affleck and Nick Nolte Get Emotional as ‘Company’ Debuts in Venice; Ben Affleck Shows Up to Support 15 hours ago Elon Musk’s MAGA Shift, Self-Driving Cars, Myths About Mars and More Get Examined in New Documentary: 5 Biggest Revelations 21 hours ago See All Ellen Burstyn , an Oscar, Tony and Emmy winner for projects like “Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore,” “Same Time, Next Year” and “Political Animals,” marvels that she’s still able to act as a nonagenarian. “When I was in my 30s and I thought about how long my career would last, I was sure I’d be finished by 40. I didn’t think it would go on much longer than that,” Burstyn said during a press conference for “ Place to Be ,” a quirky drama that debuts at Venice Film Festival on Wednesday. “The fact that I’m 93 and still working is a miracle of some kind that I’ve attracted into my life. I’m totally amazed, and at the same time, deeply grateful.” Related Stories The Next James Bond Has Been Picked, Says Gary Oldman, Whose 'Fingers Are Crossed' for 'Slow Horses' Co-Star Jack Lowden 'Star Wars' Heads to Imax 70mm for First Time With 'Starfighter' and 'A New Hope' 50th Anniversary Re-Release “Place to Be” stars Burstyn and Taika Waititi as a no-nonsense elderly woman and arrogant divorced man who form an unlikely friendship as she ventures from New York to Chicago to return a lost racing pigeon to its owner. Pamela Anderson and Murray Bartlett play Brooke’s concerned children, while Edgar Ramirez and Lena Waithe have cameos. Anderson skipped the press conference, which was attended by Burstyn, Waititi and Hungarian director Kornél Mundruczó. Burstyn has been using a walker because she recently took a fall, so Waititi gently helped her to her seat before the presser began. Popular on Variety Mundruczó said he developed the role of Brooke for Burstyn and noted that he rewatched much of her filmography as he wrote the part. “It was very beautiful to create a love story for her,” Mundruczó said of the platonic relationship between Burstyn and Waititi’s characters. Pigeons play a central role in “Place to Be,” and Mundruczó hopes the film will change the perception around a bird that he feels “get a bad rap.” “Pigeons are the losers of history. At the beginning, they were so important as messenger birds during war, and [they delivered] a ton of love stories,” Mundruczó said. “And then they became city rats. I found something very touching from these little birds.” Waititi swears he’s fond of pigeons, but he had one complaint about working with the birds. “They shit a lot. Every minute. And that’s a scientific fact,” Waititi said. “Physiologically, there’s something not right with them.” Producer Jomon Thomas revealed the filmmaking team had a meeting, where they considered using diapers for the 30 pigeons that appear in the movie. However, they decided against it because “it was tricky to take them off with visual effects.” Plus, Waititi chimed in, “nobody wants to take off a pigeon’s diaper…” “Place to Be” continues a career resurgence for Anderson. The former “Baywatch” star made her Broadway debut in 2022 as Roxie Hart in “Chicago” before earning some of the best reviews of her career for Gia Coppola’s drama “The Last Showgirl.” Anderson parlayed those raves into roles in “The Naked Gun,” “Rosebush Pruning” and “Place to Be.” Burstyn admits she was surprised at first when Pamela Anderson was cast as her daughter in “Place to Be.” “And then I met her and thought, ‘Oh, for sure, she could be my daughter.’ I felt immediately loving toward her,” Burstyn said. “She’s a wonderful person.” Burstyn is having a busy festival. The acting legend was in Venice for two movies (the other was Maggie Gyllenhaal’s Marilyn Monroe-inspired short “Flesh Impact”), and she received the prestigious Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement. At the ceremony for her career honor, Burstyn got emotional and broke down in tears as the audience greeted her with a standing ovation. “You can’t imagine how meaningful this is to me. It’s one thing to win an Oscar, a Tony or an Emmy — all of which I’ve won,” Burstyn said on Monday at her Golden Lion tribute , prompting laughter from the crowd. “But this … it’s a lot.” ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Is Both a Promising Reboot and a Tedious Sequel: TV Review Loading comments... articles.title: The ‘Sterling Point’ Muskoka Cottage Is Officially Available to Rent on Airbnb (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. Gordon Bay Cottage is officially taking reservations. Airbnb is opening up the historic Muskoka property featured as the exterior of Gordon’s lakeside home in “ Sterling Point ” for three limited stays this October. Beginning Sept. 15 at 9 a.m. ET, guests can request to book the cottage for Oct. 2-5, Oct. 9-12 or Oct. 16-19 for $180 CAD per night. Built in 1902, the waterfront property sits in Ontario’s Muskoka region, the picturesque cottage country that serves as both the setting and one of the biggest visual draws of “Sterling Point.” Guests will have private access to the cottage and dock, along with its expansive screened porch, fireplace and waterfront, where they can paddle across the lake or otherwise attempt to recreate the show’s considerably more dramatic version of cottage life. Related Stories 'Star Wars' Heads to Imax 70mm for First Time With 'Starfighter' and 'A New Hope' 50th Anniversary Re-Release The Next James Bond Has Been Picked, Says Gary Oldman, Whose 'Fingers Are Crossed' for 'Slow Horses' Co-Star Jack Lowden Gordon Bay Cottage on Airbnb BOOK ONLINE The series is executive produced by Josh Schwartz and Stephanie Savage, the team behind teen-TV staples including “The O.C.” and “Gossip Girl,” alongside Margot Robbie and Tom Ackerley’s LuckyChap Entertainment. Its cast also includes Jacob Whiteduck-Lavoie, Bo Bragason, Daniel Quinn-Toye, Mabel Strachan and Jeffrey Dean Morgan. While Sterling Point itself is fictional, much of the series was filmed in the real Muskoka Lakes region, including around Lake Muskoka, Lake Rosseau and Lake Joseph. Gordon’s cottage is among its most recognizable locations: exterior and waterfront scenes were shot at the historic Muskoka property, while the cottage interiors seen in the series were recreated on a Toronto soundstage. The cottage plays a central role from the show’s opening episodes. Annie’s trip begins after she learns that her late grandfather Gordon left her and her brother the island, with his home quickly becoming the base for the family mystery that drives the season. Rubin has said that seeing the real cottage helped make Gordon — a character whose presence hangs over the story even after his death — feel more tangible. Annie Jacobson (Ella Rubin) and Oona (Bo Bragason) in the Gordon Bay Cottage in Sterling Point Sabrina Lantos/Prime “Sterling Point” has also given Muskoka something of a tourism bump. According to Airbnb, searches for stays in the region from travelers outside Canada, for check-ins through November 2026, have risen nearly 110% year over year. Including Canadian travelers, searches are up more than 30%. The show arrives amid a particularly camera-ready moment for the Ontario getaway. Muskoka has increasingly found its way onto screens, including Park’s 2024 coming-of-age film “My Old Ass,” while the region also doubled for the Quebec cottage setting in the breakout hockey romance “Heated Rivalry.” (also briefly available to rent on Airbnb earlier this year). Park, who grew up spending summers in Muskoka, has said she wanted “Sterling Point” to depict the region as more than a generic scenic backdrop, incorporating its cottage culture as well as tensions around development and the increasingly eye-watering cost of owning property there. The “Sterling Point” getaway also continues Airbnb’s years-long push into pop-culture tourism. The platform has previously turned on-screen worlds into bookable experiences with Barbie’s Malibu DreamHouse, a recreation of Shrek’s swamp and the “Home Alone” house. In 2024, Airbnb formalized the strategy with its Icons category, which included stays and experiences inspired by Disney-Pixar’s “Up,” Marvel’s “X-Men ’97,” “Inside Out 2” and Prince’s “Purple Rain.” Those who would rather skip the inheritance drama can request a stay at Gordon Bay Cottage through Airbnb beginning Sept. 15. articles.title: ‘The Uprising’ Review: Andrew Garfield and Paul Greengrass Go Medieval on the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, With Uneven Results
articles.full_text: Sep 9, 2026 6:00am PT ‘The Uprising’ Review: Andrew Garfield and Paul Greengrass Go Medieval on the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, With Uneven Results Scuppered by the marketing department, this upscale actioner applies the director's signature documentary-inspired technique to a grim chapter of 14th-century history. By Michael Phillips Plus Icon Michael Phillips Latest ‘In the Grey’ Review: Jake Gyllenhaal, Henry Cavill and Eiza Gonzalez Magazine-Cover Their Way Through Guy Ritchie’s Attractive Time-Killer 4 months ago See All Focus Features Among medieval hand-held farming tools, the sickle is your best bet for reaping. It’s also just the thing for deadly weaponry in times of a peasant revolt, especially one momentous enough to earn capital letters and its own year marker — the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, for instance. In “ The Uprising ,” which doesn’t quite come together but has its earnest compensations, a stoic Andrew Garfield is first seen in a field against a smudge of gray sky, his farmland barely producing a crop. Garfield’s character is the Ploughman, no stranger to grief. His family has been wiped out in the Plague, along with half of England. Gaunt and spent, he speaks little and has less. But in the brave heart of this fictional protagonist, there lurks a righteous threshing machine, ripe for a Great Rebellion in writer-director Paul Greengrass ’ latest feature. This is a filmmaker whose high-end work has meant a great deal to many over the last generation. The clear-eyed, masterfully chaotic docudramas “Bloody Sunday” (dramatizing the 1972 massacre of peace protesters in Londonderry, Northern Ireland) and “United 93” (recounting the 9/11 terrorist attacks, painfully and indelibly); “Captain Phillips,” nearly as good, with Tom Hanks in charge even when he falls apart at last — these films look better every year. Related Stories ‘Look Back’ Review: Once Past the Over- Preciousness of a Child’s World, Hirokazu Kore-eda's Manga Adaptation Becomes a Moving Tribute to Friendship Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’ The visual instincts at work in Greengrass’s movies have never not been controversial, starting and ending with his documentary-honed “shaky-cam” framing, across various cinematographer-director collaborations. That visual attack is certainly present in “The Uprising.” Some have never liked it, and won’t like it here, either. Greengrass has made period projects before, including the 19th century-set Western “News of the World,” but this one goes further back, in two directions: one toward a documentary stylization of the real, the other toward newfangled folklore and bloody, bloody myth. Popular on Variety For much of “The Uprising,” Garfield’s Ploughman is primarily reactive — the audience’s entry point to a time, a place and a mess of a ruling class. Slapped with a fresh round of taxes, the underclass has had enough. Around the same time the Ploughman gets off the sidelines to save a neighbor about to be killed by a short-tempered poll-tax collector, Greengrass’s screenplay positions the punk kid on the throne, 14-year-old Richard II (Woody Norman), as a contrasting study in leadership training. The king is a distorted mirror image of the Ploughman. Garfield’s character grows into his destiny, once the ad hoc rebellion he soon joins in earnest hits London; meantime, the boy king is discreetly pushed around by the handler-oligarchs in charge. Skillfully insinuating actors on the order of Tom Hollander (Treasurer Robert Hales) and Stephen Dillane (Archbishop Sudbury) add some spice to the film’s periodic seminars in court scheming and skulking. It’s Katherine Waterston , as the wary Countess with a majorly disappointing son, whose penetrating gaze and ambiguous emotional currents show us glimmers of “The Uprising” that might have been. It’s a smallish part, but it doesn’t feel or play that way. Garfield does all he can to fill in the sketchier pieces of his largely non-verbal role. He’s at his most effective in his scenes with Thomasin McKenzie, fierce and affecting as a fellow rebel with a cause. Jamie Bell plays the priest John Ball, man of God and man of revolutionary action, and he too does well. Outside the court of Richard II, “The Uprising” isn’t really an actor’s movie; it’s more of a panoramic mosaic of uneven dramatic impact, as filmed by a 14th-century documentary filmmaker who somehow got ahold of a few Paul Greengrass movies. Does Greengrass really have his heart in the digital effects on display here? So many faux-drone overhead flights across the Thames, dotted with pretty little boats! All the CGI London-in-flames-under-siege locator shots! Yes, yes, they’re there for geographic and storytelling clarity. But they’re pure, clinical generica as filmmaking, and when they appear, they make “The Uprising” look like no one in particular made it. And the under-fire camerawork aesthetic seems off in this historical context. Now for the Robin Hood question. Perilously close to the release date, the Focus Features marketing team pulled a fast one, adding a subtitle to the film’s title: “The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood.” To be sure, Greengrass’ script implies as much. But the subtitle’s Hail Mary overtones hit everybody wrong, everywhere, all at once, and the movie quickly retracted it. And now one feels sad for Robin Hood, whoever he is. He’s hardly the same character we knew a few Robin Hoods ago. He’s swung from gorgeous Technicolor exuberance (“The Adventures of Robin Hood,” 1938) to bittersweet revisionism (“Robin and Marian,” 1976) and worse (“The Death of Robin Hood,” earlier this year, with Hugh Jackman). “The Uprising” has more to offer audiences than “The Death of Robin Hood,” but it’s a well-acted blur of fits and starts — right up to an epilogue suggesting a possible franchise about an avenging-angel-farmer, blood-streaked sickle at the ready. Paging Eli Roth. ‘The Uprising’ Review: Andrew Garfield and Paul Greengrass Go Medieval on the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, With Uneven Results Reviewed at AMC River East 21, Chicago, Aug. 31, 2026. articles.title: Amazon’s Prime Video Is Using AI to Lip-Sync Actors’ Mouths in Dubbed Titles, Starting With German Series ‘Maxton Hall’
articles.full_text: Sep 9, 2026 6:00am PT Amazon’s Prime Video Is Using AI to Lip-Sync Actors’ Mouths in Dubbed Titles, Starting With German Series ‘Maxton Hall’ By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Amazon’s Prime Video Is Using AI to Lip-Sync Actors’ Mouths in Dubbed Titles, Starting With German Series ‘Maxton Hall’ 32 minutes ago Paramount Repeats Demand That States and WGA Post $1.88 Billion Bond Over Warner Bros. Merger Delay, After AGs Argue Company Is Trying to ‘Offload Its Responsibility’ for Ticking Fees 16 hours ago Tom Rothman on Sony’s ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Blockbuster Success, Being Outbid for ‘Obsession’ and More 2 days ago See All Stephan Rabhold, Prime Video Amazon’s Prime Video is promising to make English-language dubs look more natural by using AI to sync up the way the actors’ mouths move on screen. The feature will be available first on “Maxton Hall,” the German-language romance that is Prime Video’s most-watched international original series to date. Lip-sync dubs are available starting Wednesday on “ Maxton Hall ” Seasons 1 and 2 globally in English and will also be included when the third and final season of the show releases on Prime Video on Dec. 9. The upcoming Season 3 is based on the 2018 novel “Save Me” by Mona Kasten. Related Stories ‘Possible Love’ Cast Sobs as Lee Chang-dong’s Epic Embraced at Venice With 6-Minute Standing Ovation Kore-eda Hirokazu on Adapting Fujimoto Tatsuki’s Manga for Venice Competition Film ‘Look Back’ The Prime Video team worked with a combination of AI and VFX technologies to develop the feature, but the company is not sharing specifics on what AI tools it used. Amazon said it Prime Video plans to expand the technology to additional titles in the future. Popular on Variety Prime Video’s AI dub-syncing feature synchronizes actors’ lip movements with human-dubbed audio, which creates “a seamless viewing experience that allows audiences to remain fully immersed in the story,” according to Amazon. “At Prime Video, we’re constantly innovating with new tools that enhance the viewing experience for our customers,” said Raf Soltanovich, VP of technology at Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios. “With lip-syncing, we’re creating a more seamless and immersive way for customers to enjoy global content. articles.title: AI ‘Could Kill Us All,’ Warns Anthropic Researcher as He Quits the Company: AI Companies Are ‘Gambling With Our Lives’
articles.full_text: Sep 9, 2026 6:35am PT AI ‘Could Kill Us All,’ Warns Anthropic Researcher as He Quits the Company: AI Companies Are ‘Gambling With Our Lives’ By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Suno Tries to Break Into Music Mainstream With New Label-Backed Model ‘v6’ 5 hours ago Suno Kills Controversial Mary J. Blige Ad Where She Seems to Endorse the AI Music Generator (EXCLUSIVE) 6 days ago AI Giant Nvidia to Buy Hugging Face for $12.9 Billion 6 days ago See All Getty Images for HubSpot Multiple current and former Anthropic employees warned — and admitted — on Tuesday that the researchers building new AI models believe the technology could lead to humanity’s destruction by the end of the decade, reflecting the industry’s frenzy over reining in rapid development. Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher at Anthropic, wrote on X that he resigned from the company on Tuesday because he believed the Dario Amodei-led company and OpenAI , his former employer, were “gambling with our lives” in how they improved the technology. Related Stories Lav Diaz on the Hunt for Truth in 'An Entry Into the Sadness of a Portuguese Woman,' Third Chapter of His Acclaimed Hermes Trilogy (EXCLUSIVE) ‘September 5’ Director Tim Fehlbaum Working on a ‘Historical Film’ Set in Berlin as Swiss Filmmakers Take on Challenges and Opportunities of Shooting in English “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon wrote. “This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.” Popular on Variety Anthropic did not respond to an immediate request for comment, but Coxon’s warnings were surprisingly affirmed by Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s alignment scene lead, and Samuel Marks, who runs the company‘s scalable oversight division. Hubinger wrote the company did “earnestly believe AI could kill all humans” and that he thought it was a greater than 10% risk “within the next desk.” “I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” he wrote on X. Marks’ own X post , which he said he wrote in his personal capacity, said that AI researchers continue building the technology despite the risk of “human extinction” because of a financial incentive and the fear the technology would be developed by AI developers who may abuse its capabilities. “Many AI developer staff desperately want to slow down to figure out how to build AI more safely,” he wrote. “I work on safety research at Anthropic because I hope my work will reduce the chance of these extinction-level bad outcomes.” The comments from Anthropic employees reflect a broader public tonal shift among AI companies, many of which entered the market touting the transformative potential of AI models but now warn that those models risk escaping human control. Anthropic as a company has called for a development slowdown since June, while OpenAI paired its debut of GPT-6 Astra last week, which it claimed pushed the world into an era of artificial general intelligence, with several warnings by company leaders and researchers that a slowdown was needed to improve safety conditions. “No one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence,” wrote Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, in a blog post on Sunday that was later reposted by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on X. Still, the industry sentiment has received pushback from the Trump administration, which has argued that slowing down development risks ceding the AI arms race to a rapidly evolving China. “There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Breitbart on Tuesday. “Like everything, a trillion-and-a-half-dollar defense budget, the Iron Dome. If they were to pull ahead of us on AI, then nothing else matters.” Ellen Burstyn Was ‘Sure’ Her Career Would Be ‘Finished by 40’: ‘The Fact That I’m 93 and Working Is a Miracle’ Bruce Davis, Longtime AMPAS Executive Director, Dies at 83 Noel Clarke Charged With Sexual Assault, Voyeurism and Exposure San Sebastián Festival Gets Spanish Government Industry Boost Stefano Knuchel Premieres Final Chapter in 20-Year Hugo Pratt Trilogy With ‘Hugo in Venice’ Suno and Believe Music Announce Strategic Partnership Loading comments... articles.title: Netflix South Africa Slate Includes Latest ‘How To Ruin’, ‘Seriously Single’ & ‘Disaster Holiday’ Editions
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Netflix South Africa Slate Includes Latest ‘How To Ruin’, ‘Seriously Single’ & ‘Disaster Holiday’ Editions International Revenues Of $2.1B Boost British TV Makers, Census Finds, As Pact Warns BBC Must Avoid “Managed Decline” Prime Video Adds ‘The Test’ Season 4 & True-Crime Docs On Backpacker Poisonings And Killer Trio To Australian Slate View All September 9, 2026 3:30am 'Love is Blind South Africa', 'Seriously Single Too' 'Another Disaster Holiday, 'Tuiskoms' and 'How to Ruin Diwali: Meet the Parents' Netflix Netflix ‘s How to Ruin , Seriously Single and Disaster Holiday franchises are getting new editions as part of the streamer’s latest South African slate. Following the launch of Blood Legacy Season 2 on September 25, Netflix will debut Seriously Single Too , Another Disaster Holiday later this year, with Tuiskoms Season 2, Marked Season 2 and Meet the Khumalos 2 also in production. How to Ruin Diwali : Mee the Parents launches on October 30 and Dineo and Zothile ‘Solo Ntsizwa’ Langa have been confirmed as the hosts of Love is Blind: South Africa . Docuseries Stars & Vows: Anele and Buzza is another debuting in 2026. Related Stories News Netflix Orders 'Lonesome Dove' Series From Zoe Kazan & Jeb Stuart Based On Larry McMurtry's Novel News 'The Gentleman' Returns To 45% Audience Decline For Season 2 Debut On Netflix How to Ruin Diwali: Meet The Parents comes from Burnt Onion Productions in collaboration with producer, Jayan Moodley. The show takes an irreverent look at an interracial couple whose engagement brings together two very different families and cultures. Moodley’s comedy The Kandasamys drew on similar South African Indian family tropes. Watch on Deadline Per the synopsis, it follows overachieving perfectionist Mmabatho Nkomo meeting her fiance’s traditional Indian family for the first time as her desperate attempt to impress backfires when she accidentally exposes her future father-in-law’s secret affair. With Diwali only days away, Mmabatho must navigate unfamiliar cultural territory and reunite the family she has torn apart without causing even more chaos. Rosemary Zimu-Mnguni, Kyle Clark, Jailoshini Naidoo, Koobeshen Naidoo, Sonia Mbele, Meshack Mavuso, Luthando ‘BU’Mthembu, Denise Zimba and Ashish Gangapersad star. Another Disaster Holiday, directed by Rethabile Ramaphakela, sees Joseph Ngema (Kenneth Nkosi) preparing to become a dad again at 50 and fighting to prove he is still father of the year. Per the preamble, “Under the guise of a romantic Sun City babymoon with a heavily pregnant Nandi, Joseph sets out to crash his children’s holiday with his ex-wife Dora and the hot younger boyfriend stealing his thunder. Enter Kay Sibiya, who joins the returning star-studded cast as Dora’s new bae and Joseph’s newest competition. Naturally, disaster follows.” Seriously Single Too , also directed by Ramaphakela, sees Dineo (Fulu Mugovhani) and Noni (Tumi Morake) return, though their friendship may not last their latest trip. The pic follow what is supposed to be a wild bachelorette getaway in Cape Town for the now-estranged friends turn into a disastrous chain of events that leaves them on the brink. Also starring are Buntu Petse, Keke Mphuthi, Yonda Thomas and Thabiso Rammusi. Romcom series Tuiskoms ‘s second season sees Fleur (Amalia Uys) and Werner (Armand Aucamp) preparing for their wedding, before their carefully planned future takes an unexpected turn. Per the synopsis, “At the same time, a free-spirited woman with a complicated past returns to Wilderness after years away, hoping to reconnect with the family she left behind. Across the town, old wounds, new beginnings and unexpected connections reshape the lives of those who call it home.” Uys and Aucamp star alongside Kim Syster, Jane de Wet and Clint Brink. Netflix recently found a hit out of South Africa in the shape of The Polygamist, which generated over 24 million views in its first weeks, reached the Top 10 in 62 countries and ranked first in 22 countries. The streamer is this week celebrating ten years in the country, and has trotted out several stats backing its performance there. During a press showcase in Rosebank, Johannesburg, where Netflix executives, filmmakers and on-screen talent gathered to mark the occasion, the streamer claimed to have supported 8,000 jobs through partnerships with more than 30 local production companies. Its local originals have included Blood and Water , Silverton Siege , Fatal Seduction and most recent Umthetho , and have been filmed in 20 cities across eight provinces. Netflix claims to have offered more than 300 local titles in total over the past decade, including acquisitions. “Ten years ago, we set out to share South African stories and voices with the world and today, we are proud to strengthen our partnership with the local creative industry and continue creating exciting stories that will entertain our members in South Africa and around the world,” said Ben Amadasun, VP of Content for Netflix Middle East and Africa. “Our slate ahead keeps that ambition alive with the addition of established names alongside bold new production partners across genres from unscripted to thrillers, family dramas and comedy.” Netflix also teased a new scripted series from Shaka iLembe maker The Bomb Shelter Film Productions and a multi-title partnership with The River producer Tshedza Pictures for four scripted series. articles.title: Channel 4 Confirms Plans To Cut More Than A Quarter Of Its Workforce
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake ‘Doctor Who’ Actor Noel Clarke Charged With Sexual Assault, Voyeurism & Exposure BBC Boss Matt Brittin Asked News Unit To Examine Jason Arday Coverage After Cambridge Professor’s Death ‘SNL UK’ Sets Amelia Dimoldenberg & Jamie Demetriou As Guest Hosts View All September 9, 2026 4:00am Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra Channel 4/Getty Channel 4 has announced the deepest round of layoffs in its 43-year history. The British network, home to shows including The Great British Bake Off and Taskmaster , is planning to cut 340 jobs by the end of 2026, meaning its workforce will shrink by more than a quarter. Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra announced the layoffs on Wednesday after spending recent months overseeing a strategic review of the commercial broadcaster. She told employees that the redundancies — equivalent to 28% of Channel 4’s 1,276-strong workforce — will ensure that more of C4’s £1 billion ($1.3 billion) income is spent on screen. Related Stories News International Revenues Of $2.1B Boost British TV Makers, Census Finds, As Pact Warns BBC Must Avoid "Managed Decline" News Channel 4 "Deeply Saddened" By Death Of Employee Lolita Visa The scale of the cuts has shocked insiders and others close to Channel 4. One source described it as a “very bad” day for the British broadcaster. Watch on Deadline Channel 4 finds itself increasingly isolated in a world in which it is dwarfed in size by some of its production suppliers, rival networks, and digital giants like YouTube. The state-owned broadcaster is grappling with these forces at the same time as reckoning with ad market contraction and rising production costs. Dogra has designed a new organizational structure, aimed at reducing management layers, removing duplication, and simplifying decision-making. She is positioning the changes as “owning our future,” building on the work of her predecessor Alex Mahon in growing digital sales to 34% of Channel 4’s revenue. Channel 4’s announcement was, however, light on details about the new structure, including how it will impact commissioning and the network’s fledgling in-house production plans. A consultation process with staff will begin shortly. Channel 4 said further details will be announced about the plans in the coming months. Dogra said: “Channel 4 is a precious asset which plays a unique role in the UK. We need to secure and own our future so we can continue to make shows others won’t, reach audiences others can’t, and thrive as a distinctive and disruptive British voice for future generations. “Today marks the first phase of our transformation, ensuring Channel 4 is the right shape and size to deliver its future strategy and focus investment in the programmes audiences love. “The challenges we face require a fundamental transformation in how we work. I know the proposals we are announcing today will be very difficult for many colleagues and will have a significant impact across the organisation. Many talented people who have made an enormous contribution to Channel 4 will be leaving as a result. “These decisions have not been taken lightly, but I strongly believe they are necessary to create a simpler, more focused and more sustainable Channel 4 that can invest a greater proportion of revenues into distinctive content, back British creativity and deliver impact for audiences long into the future.” Channel 4 chair Geoff Cooper added: “The proposals announced today are intended to secure Channel 4’s future as a trusted, independent British broadcaster. “By taking action now, it can build a more sustainable and resilient organisation, maximise investment in content and strengthen its ability to deliver public value for audiences, the creative industries and the UK for the years ahead.” Caroline Dinenage, chair of UK Parliament’s Culture, Media and Sport Committee, said the jobs cull was “deeply worrying” for Channel 4’s employees. “Channel 4 is a unique asset and must find ways to maintain independence and distinctiveness while capitalising on efficiencies and opportunities for collaboration,” she added. Channel 4’s job cuts follow similar redundancies at the BBC, which has committed to reducing its workforce by 10%, equating to around 2,000 layoffs. Channel 4’s last major round of redundancies came in 2024 when 200 roles were closed. Channel 4 cuts often spark conversations about the broadcaster’s executive pay, which reached record levels during Mahon’s tenure. Despite leaving Channel 4 in June 2025, Mahon’s total pay stood at £566,000, which is more than the BBC director-general earns in a year, despite running a considerably larger organization. PRIYA DOGRA EMAIL TO CHANNEL 4 STAFF: Thank you for joining the All Staff meeting today and I know many of you will now be in follow-up meetings with your ExCo member to understand what the announcement means for your role and your area. I appreciate this is a significant and unsettling moment for many of you, but particularly for those whose roles will be affected by the changes we are proposing. I want to be clear that we have not made these proposals lightly. They will affect many talented people who have contributed enormously to our success. Our intention is to support people through the process with care, respect and transparency. A lot of detail was covered in the All Staff, so I want to briefly summarise the key points. What I presented today is the first stage of our transformation strategy. This work is designed to help us prioritise investment in content, grow our impact and secure our long-term sustainability. We have proposed a new organisational design that will significantly decrease non-programming spend by reducing our overall headcount by approximately 340 roles, equivalent to 28% of our workforce, by the end of the year. These proposals are intended to create a simpler, more focused organisation and allow us to direct a greater proportion of our revenues towards distinctive British content. That investment is what allows us to have impact. But this transformation is not just about reducing costs. It is also about creating the platform for future growth, strengthening our revenues so that we can invest more in the content, creativity and public value that set Channel 4 apart well into the future. I explained why these changes are necessary: · The market around us has changed faster than expected. Audiences and advertisers are increasingly moving towards global platforms, while many of our competitors are becoming larger and better funded. Advertiser investment in UK television has fallen by more than £400 million since 2019 and is expected to decline further over the next five years. · At the same time, as a publicly owned, commercially funded broadcaster, we have fewer levers than many other organisations. We cannot simply cut profits to absorb financial pressure. Since 2019, while our revenue has remained broadly stable, our operating costs have increased by 25%. That means operating costs now account for a greater proportion of our revenue. In 2019, running Channel 4 cost us around 32p for every £1 of revenue we generated. Today that figure is around 40p. That means less of our revenue is available to invest in programmes, and as that declines, so does our ability to drive audience and revenue growth. That is not sustainable, and it is not what Channel 4 is here to do. · The challenges we face require a fundamental transformation in how we are organised and how we operate. The proposed changes have been developed through a comprehensive review of roles, structures and ways of working across the organisation. They focus on reducing management layers, simplifying decision-making and removing duplication, so that we can build a leaner, more efficient operating model ready for the future. · Our overall goal is to spend more of our revenue on content, because content is how Channel 4 delivers impact. Our purpose matters more than ever: to tell stories others don’t, provide trusted news, represent the UK in all its diversity and remain a distinctive British public service broadcaster. By making difficult decisions today and reshaping our organisation now, we can create a more sustainable cost base so we can protect and strengthen that impact and secure Channel 4 as a distinctive and disruptive British voice for years to come. Work on our future strategic direction is well advanced and will be shared in the coming months. At its heart, the transformation’s theme is ‘owning our future’: reshaping how we reach audiences through distribution, partnerships and platforms; enabling greater investment in distinctive programmes that set Channel 4 apart; and ensuring resources are allocated to maximise long-term value, sustainability and public impact. Today’s announcement is the first stage of that transformation and is an important step towards delivering those goals. I know that the next few weeks are going to be very difficult, particularly for those directly impacted, but also for those of you whose teammates will be going through the process. We will continue to share updates throughout this process, and I will also be travelling to each of our offices in the coming weeks to meet with you, hear your views and answer questions – details will follow. I want to thank you in advance for the professionalism and care I know you will show to each other, and for everything you will continue to do for Channel 4. articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Wicked’ & ‘Wicked: For Good’ Live-To-Film Concerts To Kick Off 2027 Tour In San Francisco & New York ‘Harry Potter And The Cursed Child’ Posts Big Gain As Summer Slips Away – Broadway Box Office Jim Geoghan Dies: ‘Suite Life Of Zack & Cody’ Co-Creator & Producer Was 79 View All September 9, 2026 4:30am Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo in 'Wicked: For Good' Universal/Everett Collection EXCLUSIVE: A series of live-to-film concerts of Wicked and Wicked: For Good , with film screenings accompanied by a live symphony orchestra, will officially premiere at Radio City Music Hall on January 23, 2027, with a special preview set for January 16 in San Francisco. The first event will be Wicked: Part One In Concert . The concerts are a collaboration between Universal Film and Universal Destinations & Experiences. See the announced tour dates below. The “concert experiences” will feature the films projected on an HD screen while orchestras perform Stephen Schwartz’s songs and Schwartz’s and John Powell’s underscore live-to-picture. Universal Film has partnered with Justin Hurwitz’s company Hurwitz Concerts, which has toured La La Land in Concert and Whiplash in Concert since 2023, and which now makes its entry into producing concerts of films not scored by Hurwitz. articles.title: ‘Joie de Vivre. Notes, Thoughts, Words, Reflections, Faces, And Visions Concerning Bernardo Bertolucci And The Cinephilia Of The 20th Century That No Longer Exists’ Review: So Long, Maestro! – Venice Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Telluride Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews ‘The Spiral’ Review: Valeria Bruni Tedeschi Is The Devil In Disguise In Paolo Strippoli’s Fiendishly Fun Horror-Thriller – Venice Film Festival View All September 9, 2026 5:31am Luca Guadagnino's 'Joie de Vivre'. Venice Film Festival. Ostensibly a tribute to the late Bernardo Bertolucci (1941-2018), the one-time giant of Italian cinema whose star has waned somewhat in recent years, Luca Guadagnino ’s 426-minute docu-essay — nearly twice as long as Alex Gibney’s Musk — is the endurance test of this year’s Venice Film Festival. Surprisingly, however, watched in two sittings, it is less of an ordeal than it might appear, partly thanks to the director’s forthright views: from the outset, Guadagnino admits that certain titles in the late maestro’s filmography are just too rubbish to bother with. No Beseiged . No Little Buddha . No Stealing Beauty . Hooray! Related Stories Trailers 'Artificial' Teaser Trailer Shows Andrew Garfield As Sam Altman In Luca Guadagnino Film News Hanway Boards Luca Guadagnino's Bernardo Bertolucci Doc 'Joie De Vivre' There’s a roundabout quality to Joie de Vivre that works best in first half, which is much stronger than the second. Guadagnino’s approach is very personal, snooping around the director’s former home in Rome — Via della Lungara, 3, if you’re planning a pilgrimage — he seems to be actively trying to summon the late auteur’s ghost. The house is just as Bertolucci left it (and therefore just as his widow, Clare Peploe left it, before she died in the summer of 2021). Somehow, the house still feels alive with his presence, and one wonders if he might come barging into his study at any minute, furiously denying that the DVD copy of Promising Young Woman on display in any way belongs to him. Watch on Deadline Guadagnino comes at Bertolucci from many angles, even claiming to have fancied him as a younger man, but facts and figures don’t really seem to enter into his concept of biography. Bertolucci just bursts onto the screen, fully formed, with his first ‘official’ feature film, Before the Revolution (1964). Technically, this was actually his second film after 1962’s The Grim Reaper , but Guadagnino will return to that later. The director, it transpires, has pressganged a lot of his friends and peers to help him out, and to discuss Bertolucci’s first international breakout hit, he wheels out a big gun: Martin Scorsese. Scorsese was an early convert to Bertolucci’s reinvention of Italian cinema, having caught a screening of Before the Revolution at the New York Film Festival . “The new voice had arrived,” he says. “And I was there .” Scorsese leads an impressive cavalcade of directors that are as perceptive as they are surprising: Catherine Breillat, Alfonso Cuarón, David Cronenberg, Abderrahmane Sissako and… wait a minute, is that James Gray ? (It is.) Guadagnino’s next stop is The Conformist (1970) swiftly followed by Last Tango in Paris (1972), the one-two punch that set him up as a major player in world cinema. The former made him an arthouse deity, the second brought him notoriety and very nearly jail time. At this point, Guadagnino drafts in friends from the other side of the divide — critics and media commentators such as Jay Weissberg, Scott Foundas, Murielle Joudet, Oyku Sofuoglu and… wait a minute, is that “contrarian analyst” Armond White? (It is.) The debate about Last Tango is the chewy center of this otherwise freewheeling production, and this also where the film starts to find its feet. Last Tango is perhaps the perfect film to hold up to the light, since it has accrued many meanings in the half-century since release. Its sexual politics once seemed so liberal, and now they very much do not, a paradox Guadagnino digs into: Has the world changed or have we changed? He also has the director’s back, defending Bertolucci from misguided allegations that the film’s famous butter scene was somehow done for real and improvised without the actress’s knowledge. Nevertheless, there’s a fascinating discussion about the imbalance of power on set, and it’s probably just as well the interval occurs here. The second half begins with Bertolucci’s masterpiece, the self-explanatory 1900 (1976), a period epic featuring, together for the first time, Robert de Niro and Gerard Depardieu. There’s a scene of front-frontal male nudity (or rather there was in the festival cut) that’s still an eye-opener today, and, as special guest star Margot Robbie points out, “The greatest cocaine scene ever”. Which brings us swiftly on to La Luna (1976), the jaw-dropping — and thus almost impossible to see nowadays — story about an incestuous mother and her junkie son (“It approached heroin in a joyfully unexpected way”). Guadagnino spends a surprising amount of time on Bertolucci’s almost completely uninteresting last film, Me and You (2012), before barging into Jeremy Thomas’s house and talking all over him, as the latter tries to discuss his two films with Bertolucci, The Last Emperor (1987) and The Sheltering Sky (1990). The Dreamers (2003) gets no coverage at all — even though Bertolucci’s affection for the nouvelle vague is catalogued in the first half — and Guadagnino ends his film with a forlorn elegy for the past (“The cinema I grew up with is gone”). Which is true, but then people said that in 1927, when sound arrived. The ostensible subject matter of the film, Bernardo Bertolucci, often gets pushed aside by Guadagnino and co., even while the speakers onscreen complain that Bertolucci was often pushed aside as a filmmaker. (It happens; we know that.) Those digressions are interesting, for sure, but it makes for a frustrating experience; one minute Guadagnino is in Marty’s screening room, bowing at the altar, the next he’s being dragged round a desolate field, talking philosophy by a woman with a very stern expression and even more forbidding hair. Bertolucci was “taking reality and making it eternal”, says a talking head, in a film that takes reality and, at times, simply makes it seem eternal. Title: Joie de Vivre.
