London’s Metropolitan Police announced on Wednesday that Clarke has been charged in connection with alleged offenses that took place between 2007 and 2016 involving five women. The 50-year-old faces two charges of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism, and one count of exposure. He will appear in Westminster Magistrates’ Court on October 21. Detectives have been investigating Clarke for a year, arresting the actor on September 25 , 2025. A file of evidence was presented to the Crown Prosecution Service, which authorised charges. The arrest followed Clarke being defeated in his libel lawsuit against The Guardian after the newspaper detailed allegations of sexual misconduct by more than 20 women in 2021. Clarke has always denied wrongdoing. Watch on Deadline Clarke has not worked in any substantial capacity since the allegations were published. He played Mickey Smith in Doctor Who , while his last series on UK television was ITV’s Viewpoint in 2021. Clarke created hit indie movie Kidulthood and had roles in other productions, including Star Trek Into Darkness and Bulletproof. articles.title: ‘The Uprising’ Review: Andrew Garfield Leads A Revolt Against King Richard ll In Paul Greengrass’ 1381 Epic With Political Relevance To Now
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews ‘Company’ Review: Nick Nolte And Other Notables Are In It, But Director Casey Affleck’s Son Atticus Makes Biggest Impression – Venice Film Festival ‘Bunker’ Review: Penélope Cruz And Javier Bardem’s Marriage Is In Crisis In Florian Zeller’s Drama Of Isolation And Fears – Venice Film Festival View All September 9, 2026 6:00am Andrew Garfield in 'The Uprising' (2026) Betina La Plante/Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection On the heels of this summer’s darker, more dour and reflective, deliberately meditative, if bloody new take on the Robin Hood legend, The Death Of Robin Hood with Hugh Jackman portraying the famous icon’s last days, comes another film set in the same milieu, this one around 1381, that chronicles events that helped inspire the Robin Hood myth, if not the man himself. But make no mistake, this is not another movie in that vein, but rather a more rip-roaring journey into the era and, as the title suggests, an uprising of the peasants against the corrupt government and tax policies and tyranny of King Richard II. And even though this is set 600 years ago, it feels remarkably relevant for today’s divided world between the haves and have nots with a government in both instances largely ignoring the plight of the poor citizens in favor of enriching themselves all in the false claim of caring for the people . Related Stories Trailers 'Artificial' Teaser Trailer Shows Andrew Garfield As Sam Altman In Luca Guadagnino Film News Andrew Garfield Hopes 'The Uprising' Makes Billionaires "Scared Sh*tless": "They're The Most Soul Sick" Writer/director Paul Greengrass ( Captain Phillips, United 93, The Lost Bus) , who often makes socially conscious films mixed with high entertainment value, has gone way back in time to make a crackerjack action film, but one with uniquely chilling connections to current times. ‘The more things change, the more they stay the same’, as the old saying goes. Watch on Deadline Like the recent Covid pandemic, 600 years ago it was the Black Death or Plague sweeping the planet and setting up disdain for the government that started whirling out of control. 50 years on, Andrew Garfield ‘s unimposing Ploughman becomes leader of the rebellion against the king in a fight for true justice and he must fight to save England, where half the population is already dead, thus an army is formed to make their voices heard. He has motivation too, as his family is also dead. That is a powerful tool against the King’s court, a group of uncaring Oligarchs who basically surround the impressionable king (Woody Norman), a mere teenage boy who lets them run the shop. Their plan is to quietly impose a devastating tax on those who can afford it least, and they are now enforcing it with collectors demanding the money. The violence that has been simmering with the Ploughman now erupts into a revolution joined by thousands and thousands of peasants. However to their surprise, their demands may actually be met with word that the King will meet with the rebels and address their concerns but cowards that they are they reverse course when they perceive their lives to be in danger. Shortly after the invasion of London begins, the capital is under rebel control, so what is this previously quiet and sullen teenage King to do? He takes matters into his own hands, defying the wishes of those who think they control him, and rides right into the heart of the mob with a shocking list of concessions. The rebels win, or so they think, but have they actually won? This thing is just getting going. Greengrass knows how to stage action, how to keep this pace roaring, and that makes this film a blast to watch, but also one that feels not just of its time, but of our times. We can feel the same rage right now about those not just in power, but those around them (think Stephen Miller, RFK Jr, and so many others) who pull the strings with no concern for the little guy. This rebellion, though led by a modest farmer, was also powered by John Ball ( Jamie Bell ) here the most idealistic and fierce believer in the cause for justice, along with Wat Tyler (Cosmo Jarvis). Even women are part of this, notably Alyce played with heart by Thomasin Makenzie. In this movie you really find yourself rooting for these people, and certainly against the conniving Treasurer Hale ( Tom Hollander ) and Archbishop Sudbury ( Stephen Dillane ). The entire cast is well chosen, with nice turns also from Katherine Waterston as the somewhat sympathetic Countess, Jonny Lee Miller as Mayor Walworth, and Sky Yang as Scribe, among others. Woody Norman, basically silent with indifferent facial expressions for much of the early going, is as it turns out a bit more powerful and manipulative than we could have imagined as King Richard ll. Garfield carries the film though with a quiet dignity and simple determination to do what’s right, a man whose moment whose time has come. The production values, as you might expect, are top drawer with special shoutouts to cinematographer Pal Ulvik Rokseth, composer Volker Bertelmann, and editor William Goldenberg who keeps this moving with an urgent pace that doesn’t quit. Producers are Jason Blum, Greengrass, Gregory Goodman, Joanna Kaye. Jason Blum, Joe Neurauter Lars Sylvest. articles.title: Ellen Burstyn Talks Working Into 90s with Starring Role In Unexpected Love Story ‘Place To Be’; Pays Tribute To Gloria Steinem – Venice
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie LevelK Posts U.S. & Euro Sales Haul For Karlovy Vary Prizewinner ‘The Guest’ Casey Affleck’s ‘Company’ Earns 4.5-Minute Ovation At Venice World Premiere Javier Bardem & Penélope Cruz Talk Playing Fictitious Arguing Couple In ‘Bunker’: “We Are Very Good At Creating Fiction & Reality” – Venice View All September 9, 2026 6:18am Murray Bartlett, Taika Waititi, Ellen Burstyn, Pamela Anderson and Director Kornél Mundruczó attend Place To Be Photocall at the Venice Film Festival Aurore Marechal/Getty Images Oscar-winning actress Ellen Burstyn addressed shifting attitudes to older woman in Hollywood ahead of the world premiere of Kornel Mundruzcó’s Place To Be , in which she co-stars opposite Taika Waititi , at the Venice Film Festival on Wednesday. The Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore and The Last Picture Show star revealed that she had started to question how long her career would last when she was in her 30s. “I was sure I’d be finished by 40. I didn’t think it would go on much longer than that. The fact that I’m 93 and still working is a miracle of some kind that I’ve attracted into my life somehow, and I’m totally amazed,” she said. Related Stories News Damilola Orimogunje On Making Venice Giornate History & Prioritizing African Distribution With His Sophomore Feature 'Dear Ajayi' News Casey Affleck's 'Company' Earns 4.5-Minute Ovation At Venice World Premiere “At the same time, I’m deeply grateful… to all the women who worked on changing the consciousness for the world in regard to women and all of the work that they did that made that possible for us to continue to have longer life lives as artists.” Watch on Deadline Ellen Burstyn talks working into later life with role in #VeniceFilmFestival film ‘Place To Be’: "When I was like maybe in my 30s, and I thought about how long my career would last. I was sure I'd be finished by 40… The fact that I'm 93 and still working is a miracle" pic.twitter.com/mPPFzFuibF — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 9, 2026 She paid tribute to American feminist icon and founder of Ms. Magazine Gloria Steinem , who died at age 92 in early September . “Gloria Steinem is the one I’m thinking of… she started Ms. Magazine back then. What influenced me was Ms. Magazine,” she said, acting out with passion a line in Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore in which her character declared, “It’s my life. It’s not some man’s life that I’m helping him out with”. “That really was the way it was before the change, and thank God, thank God, the world changed and allowed women to be full human beings,” she continued with a mischievous smile to applause and laughter: “Was that a comment?” Burstyn stars in light-hearted road movie Place to Be opposite Waititi as an elderly widow who forges an unexpected deep connection with a middle-aged man she meets while travelling from Chicago to New York to return a lost racing pigeon to its owner. The chance meeting and connection helps them confront personal disappointments, to rediscover a sense of purpose and wonder at a time when both thought it was no longer possible in the stages of their respective lives. Burstyn and Waititi are joined in the cast by Murray Bartlett and Pamela Anderson who did not participate in the press conference. Kornel Mundruczó on wanting to create a love story for Ellen Burstyn with ‘Place to Be’ #VeniceFilmFestival pic.twitter.com/FMfMkjEpzo — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 9, 2026 Mundruzcó told the press conference that he had first hit on the idea of developing a film for Burstyn after working with her briefly on his 2020 Oscar-nominated drama Pieces of a Woman. “I was totally fascinated by her, and I find I definitely wanted to make a movie for her, specifically for her. So, we started to develop it, and we watched all of her movies, although obviously we knew many of them,” said Mundruzcó, who directed the film from a screenplay by longtime collaborator Kata Weber. He said he quickly came to the conclusion that he wanted to create a love story for Burstyn. “That idea stayed all the way. How can I create a love story for her and other women at that age, in which the tone is kind of light and tender and kind of easy, but at the same time telling a very deep story.” Alongside accompanying Place to Be, Burstyn is also an honorary guest of the Venice Film Festival this year as a recipient of its Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement earlier this week . articles.title: Pablo Larraín’s ‘My Sad Dead’ Trailer: “The Dead Start To Make Themselves Present”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart International Sales Of French TV Programs Crash To A Ten-Year Low Prime Video Gathers YA Stars For Alpine Retreat & Drops First Looks At ‘Boys of Tommen,’ ‘Our Fault: London’ & ‘Love Me Love Me 2’ Freya Allan & Kodi Smit-McPhee Star In Nick Hamm’s Jack The Ripper-Era Thriller ‘Black Palace’ — First Look View All September 9, 2026 6:32am EXCLUSIVE: Here’s the trailer for Pablo Larraín’s Netflix miniseries My Sad Dead . Based on stories by acclaimed Argentine author Mariana Enriquez, the psychological horror will play in competition at the San Sebastian Film Festival later this month. Produced by Larraín’s Fabula, the much-anticipated series tells the story of Ema, a retired doctor grappling with grief after her mother’s death. She can see and speak with the dead around her, including her own mother. Mercedes Morán, Dolores Fonzi, Alejandra Flechner, and Carolina Álvarez star. Related Stories News Netflix South Africa Slate Includes Latest 'How To Ruin', 'Seriously Single' & 'Disaster Holiday' Editions News Netflix Orders 'Lonesome Dove' Series From Zoe Kazan & Jeb Stuart Based On Larry McMurtry's Novel Per the synopsis, the arrival of Ema’s niece, Julie, and the murder of three local teenagers trigger a strange phenomenon that breaks the fragile balance between the living and the dead. What had been Ema’s burden then begins to spread throughout the neighborhood: the dead start to make themselves present, and no one will be able to escape the sound of their own ghosts. “Living can sometimes be a truly terrifying experience; reality can induce sheer panic. Everyday life holds moments of terror, a quiet, unshowy kind of terror, stemming from things that are constantly close to you and, for that very reason, can be the most dangerous,” Larraín said. “ My Sad Dead shows us a city, poverty, violence, and people and social classes that have been forgotten. There is abandonment, death, and love, but at its core, the terror lies in the everyday.” The miniseries will run to four parts. The cast is rounded out by Carlos Portaluppi, Germán de Silva, and Chilean actress Luz Jiménez. It drops on Netflix on September 24. articles.title: Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller on Making ICE Doc ‘They’re Here’ Like a “Horror Movie”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 8, 2026 1:00am (L to R): 'They're Here' directors Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller at the 83rd Venice Film Festival Stefania D'Alessandro Life under ICE is like a horror movie. That’s the message of Oscar-winning documentarian Laura Poitras , whose new short documentary They’re Here chronicles how Immigration Customs Enforcement troops invaded and occupied Minneapolis last year, and the anonymous residents who resisted. Poitras co-directed They’re Here with Minneapolis-based journalist and documentarian Rachel Lauren Mueller. Using dashcam footage, ground-level filming and crowdsourced data visualizations, they reconstruct the resistance network and their tactics to track, document, and combat ICE’s masked agents. Related Stories Movies Why Andrew Garfield Says Billionaires Should Be "Scared Sh**less" by 'The Uprising' Movies Venice Home Crowd Gives Italian Horror 'The Spiral' 9-Minute Standing Ovation Stylistically, the film draws from horror and sci-fi cinema to depict how a picturesque American Midwestern city is turned into a dystopian nightmare. Men in balaclavas in unmarked cars drive down quiet snowy streets. At the Minneapolis airport, American vacationers gaze out the windows at shackled prisoners being dragged onboard planes nearby. A husband and wife hide in the trunk of a car as their son tries to sneak them past ICE officers. They’re Here is Poitras’s first project since her Nan Goldin documentary All the Beauty and the Bloodshed , which won the festival’s Golden Lion in 2022 and later earned an Oscar nomination. Poitras previously won the best documentary Oscar in 2015 for Citizenfour , her landmark account of Edward Snowden and his NSA surveillance disclosures. They’re Here is screening in Venice Open – Out of Competition, the festival’s nonfiction and special-presentation strand. Submarine Entertainment Sales is handling U.S. sales. Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter , Poitras and Mueller talked about going where the news cameras weren’t, using horror film tropes to capture the horrific reality of an ICE invasion, and how they hope their film will shock Americans into taking action. Let’s start with the origin story. How did the collaboration come together? LAURA POITRAS: So we have a mutual colleague and dear friend of Rachel’s, Adam Mellion, who has worked with me as a researcher on my last two films. He was in New York City in January, the day that Renée Good was executed, and lives in South Minneapolis, which is where Rachel lives. We all had this sense of urgency, this need to document what’s happening. The fact that both Rachel and Adam are based there made it something that I felt it was really important to be involved with. And you two immediately connected? POITRAS: We have a lot of things in common. We’re both, like, director-shooters and journalists, so we were totally in sync from the very beginning. Rachel and I just started talking about how we were going to approach it, what was going to be different from the news. Source protection was also the very top of our list. How do we do this safely? How are we encrypting information? Did you already have the connections to the groups that were organizing to track ICE agents and warn people? RACHEL LAUREN MUELLER: I live six blocks from where Renée Good was executed. I live right in the thick of where a lot of ICE activity happens, and the neighborhood groups were organically popping up. I was in some of the groups that were remnants of what came up during George Floyd’s murder, so there was some infrastructure that existed beforehand that then very rapidly transitioned into these neighborhood surveillance groups or mutual aid groups. ICE loads prisoners onto flights for deportation in ‘They’re Here’ Courtesy of Tim Evans My position as a neighbor was really essential to us getting access to some of these other groups. People were understandably very nervous about being on camera, letting a camera into the room. But I think the combination of me being from the city and understanding in a very visceral sense what this occupation felt like, in addition to Laura’s experience and understanding of surveillance and what was at stake, allowed people to be like, “All right, yes, you can come. You can come and film with us.” Access felt very slow, but it actually happened over a very quick amount of time, and we were filming every day from the beginning of January through March, and then some of the footage in the film is from December. So it really covers a large time period. What did you do to protect the people you were filming? POITRAS: We used Encryption, anonymization, redaction, a review process, releases that allowed people to opt out before the film was locked. All that. In a way, the use of concealing the identities of the protagonists becomes also part of the kind of how the film communicates the risks involved, right? And hopefully, it puts the audience in their perspective. Why did you think it was necessary to do this type of documentary, given that there was a massive amount of news coverage at the time? POITRAS: I think we felt really, like, a strong belief that working from a cinematic approach can communicate in a different way than what the news is doing. There is a sense that the news is kind of normalizing this violence by repeating the same clips over and over. I don’t know that that is productive, and we felt that we could do something different with it. And we have a belief in cinema and what it can do, and also a belief in documenting resistance. Pretty early on, we also started talking about genre. I was talking to Rachel and we were watching what was happening, and it was like a horror film — but it was also the reality of what was happening. So when we started cutting, we started using [elements of] that genre to communicate what was really happening. Not to get away from the reality, but to get us closer to the reality. ‘They’re Here’ uses imagery that evokes horror films and sci-fi dystopian movies. Courtesy-of-Jack-Califano- The visual style does have elements of a horror film. But also of sci-fi dystopia . POITRAS: Totally. I mean, I’m thinking of Children of Men , where you’re, like, rounding up of immigrants. Dystopian cinema always tells something about today, right? That’s what sci-fi is always doing. It’s always about the present. We were trying to change the lens or the perspective to reflect back on a reality that’s happening. So we were interested in those genres, but always in order to get us closer to the reality of the situation, which is one about terror and menace and a hidden, almost alien force that is abducting people and shooting them in broad daylight. What was your experience with ICE and the police while you were making the film? Did you come into any direct conflict? MUELLER: The Minneapolis police were told they should not be involved with ICE at all, so they were not present. But the federal agents absolutely were around all the time. I awoke to the sounds of whistles, which was the alert system — it’s like, ICE is in the area — multiple times. They were on my small residential street all the time. There are many moments where ICE was there, and I’m present, and I’m filming. But also, we were very clear about not being where the news cameras were, and so thinking about how to create a frame where things are happening, unfolding in real time, so you can understand the kind of dystopia of it in a different way than the news does. POITRAS: There’s a scene at the end when we’re in a car, and then somebody says, “ICE is here,” and the car door opens. That’s Rachel going out of the car and confronting ICE. That was the reality. You’re just driving, and then all of a sudden you’re in the middle of a war zone. MUELLER: I mean, it was almost every day that I would encounter them, whether I was filming or not. You would see them on the street. They were everywhere. Was there anything you discovered in the making of it that surprised you? MUELLER: Having lived there, I would say it wasn’t so much making the film that was the shocking part. It was just existing in that city, it felt like every day a new horror was kind of revealed. I remember when there was a memo that was leaked that said that ICE agents could break down doors without a judicial warrant. I’m not actually sure if they did or not. But that information was disseminated really rapidly. To live in city where this could happen, where ICE could just knock down my door, and they were given permission to do that. That felt shocking. For me, one of the most shocking things was the data visualization screens which show ICE activity everywhere across the country. That was the first time I’ve seen the scale represented that way. POITRAS: We were really interested in, how do we represent the scale? There were two [visualizations]. The first one is the ICE flights, and that is crowdsourced data that was being collected by people on the ground. It’s not like the government was telling the public how many flights were taking off. It was somebody actually going to the airport — Nick Benson is his name — and writing down how many shackled prisoners were being boarded onto these planes at Minneapolis International Airport, which is the same airport that the public uses to go on vacation. We had his database, which was more of a spreadsheet, and then we had another database from Human Rights First, and then worked with Josh Begley, who’s a data visualization [artist], and he then created, this graph that actually just shows a tiny slice of time. If we were to show the whole thing, you’d be watching for hours, or for three months or something. But we wanted to communicate the sense of scale, and that sort of shock of it. It was really important, to juxtapose the intimacy of the [victim’s] experience with the scale of it. What impact do you hope this documentary has? MUELLER: There’s two things that this film is holding at the same time. There is the optimism and hope that resistance can be effective and that the people have power and are able to take care of one another. And there is what the federal government is doing. Giving this visceral sense of what a paramilitary occupation of a U.S. city looks like. So I hope for both impacts, that we activate people into a sense of awareness that they might not have had, because the news media captures things in a very different capacity, and also a sense of optimism that this can be used, that other communities can look at this, be inspired, and use it as a tool. POITRAS: We’re interested in the process and the sort of blueprint of it, and then also how to denormalize the violence. Simply that, like, we should not be living in this world; this should not be happening. Hopefully that gets communicated through the cinema and the use of that kind of translating of a reality [to the] screen. Going back to what you said at the beginning about what the news media wasn’t capturing — what do you think is missing in the way traditional news media frames this story? POITRAS: I think we’re often failed by the news media over and over and over again. I mean, I can go back — I made a film about the war in Iraq that we were walked into [2006’s My Country My Country ]. The news media cheerlead for that war. We were walked into it. I think repeating images of violence endlessly — I don’t think that that is adding to anyone’s understanding. There are great journalists doing great investigative reporting, and that lives alongside this kind of news cycle that just repeats endless reels of violence that I don’t think adds depth or context. I feel like the news cycle is reactionary. It’s responding in a way that lacks depth and time and nuance. You guys approach this in a very different way, and you show things that haven’t been seen. But the facts of what was happening on the ground are well known and well documented. The resistance stopped the full occupation of Minneapolis, but ICE is still there and they’re occupying other cities now. How optimistic you are that recording the truth, showing the truth, presenting it in a dramatic way that evokes emotion, can have a real-world impact that convinces people to take action ? POITRAS: I hear you and all of that, but I still believe in it. There’s a difference between knowing something and actually understanding it on an emotional level. I’m thinking about the film I did about Nan Goldin [ All the Beauty and the Bloodshed ] and what she was able to do with her direct action organization, PAIN. The fact that the Sacklers were selling OxyContin and making billions of dollars and killing hundreds of thousands of people was not news, but they made it so that this family was going to be shamed and drummed out of museums, etc. And that is a victory, and yet still there’s an overdose crisis. So I feel similarly about this film. We want to show the community coming together and just resisting. Because I think, what’s the alternative? The alternative is just to let it happen. To me, that’s not an alternative. THR

articles.title: ‘Musk’: Alex Gibney Shares His Take on Elon Musk’s “Global Right-Wing Agenda” and the “Almost Existential Fear” of Talking He Encountered: Venice
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 8, 2026 4:33am Zoë Schiffer, Alex Gibney and Ashley St. Clair (left to right) Courtesy of Kate Green/Getty Images Elon Musk took the spotlight at the Venice Film Festival on Tuesday. Well, not in person! But he and his influence took center stage as filmmaker Alex Gibney discussed his new doc, simply called Musk , during a press conference around lunchtime. The film about the owner of X and CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, world-premiering in the Italian fest’s Venice Open – Out of Competition program, comes from producers Jigsaw Productions (Gibney, Jessie Deeter, Erin Edeiken), Closer Media (Zhang Xin), Anonymous Content (Nick Shumaker, Jessica Grimshaw) and Double Agent (Dana O’Keefe). Related Stories Movies Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller on Making ICE Doc 'They're Here' Like a "Horror Movie" Movies Why Andrew Garfield Says Billionaires Should Be "Scared Sh**less" by 'The Uprising' Despite its 225-minute running time, the Venice synopsis of the doc is brief and to the point: “An incisive look behind the legend of Elon Musk, the world’s most heralded ‘inventorentrepreneur’ who exerts an enormous influence on the world in which we all live.” Gibney shared how the doc team reached out to Musk for the film, without success, and how the focus of the project changed once the tech mogul “got wrapped into Donald Trump” and his story. The result is a mix of “the reality of what he has done and the unreality of his narrative,” the filmmaker said. “In the service of that, we created this formulation that came out of Musk’s own ideas about the notion that we’re living in a simulation or in some kind of existential video game, to convey in formal terms, through a kind of avatar, which speaks with Musk’s actual words, and video game imagery” both sides, the reality and the unreality. Of course, a member of the press asked if Gibney is concerned about a potential legal backlash by Musk. “We consulted our lawyers, and they gave us a sign-off to go forward,” when the doc team decided to use Musk’s words and visualize the mogul as an avatar, he replied. Asked if there has been any retaliation against the filmmakers, the director shared that he encountered a “tremendous sense of fear of talking, really almost existential fear,” among many of the people that the film team reached out to. So, how dangerous is Musk, especially for the future of democracy? “Extremely,” Gibney concluded. “Very dangerous.” A couple of questions focused on the tech mogul’s support for political parties on the right flank of the political spectrum in such countries as Germany, where the far-right AfD just won a regional election in Saxony-Anhalt this weekend. In fact, Musk congratulated the party on the victory via a “Well done!” on his X. Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in the region, thanked the billionaire in return, posting: “Thank you, @elonmusk , for your support and for your clear and highly important perspective on the political developments of our time — including here in Germany. If we take responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation. Germany would once again be a place worth investing in.” So, what does this all mean? “I hope I showed in the film that he’s involved in right-wing political parties all over the globe – in Germany, in the United Kingdom, in Brazil, in Turkey, and I think there are a number of reasons for that,” Gibney told the Venice press conference. “That seems to be his ideology at the moment. But in addition to that, many of these right-wing governments tend to be more pliable, and it’s easier to buy the results you want for administrations that are utterly corrupt and venal and have no sense of restraint or internal checks and balances.” Gibney’s takeaway: “So, I think he’s pursuing a global right-wing agenda, both for ideological and for very practical and monetary reasons.” Suggesting that these players are “more pliable,” the filmmaker emphasized the “crony capitalist aspect to his political aspirations” during the press conference. “With Trump suddenly, and with many other right-wing leaders around the world, he sees the possibility of being able to buy influence that’s unprecedented, because they’re much more amenable to the crony capitalist idea.” Gigney’s conclusion was that Musk is “always pragmatic” and “moves where the money is.” Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk walks to the stage to speak alongside Republican presidential nominee former President Donald Trump at a campaign event at the Butler Farm Show, Saturday, Oct. 5, 2024, in Butler, Pa. Alex Brandon/AP Images Gibney was joined during the press conference by political commentator and author Ashley St. Clair, who has a baby with Musk, and technology journalist and author Zoë Schiffer. The latter pointed out that at his companies, Musk tends to ensure “loyalty” at the highest levels,” while treating other people “pretty harshly.” At X, “he has tweaked the algorithm both to suppress mainstream journalism and to augment some of the more inflammatory comments and voices on that platform,” she said. St. Clair mentioned her past claim that “I was offered the opportunity not to speak for $40 million” in the form of a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) when she had her baby with Musk. “I got involved with Republican politics when I was 18, after I met Charlie Kirk, and there was an air of ignorance,” she explained. “But that ignorance does not excuse any role in that. I hope the risk that I’m taking now in speaking out and trying to fight back at least helps a little bit.” She also shared her take on his work with X and political parties around the globe. “His most complicated relationship is with the truth,” she said. “He is stoking flames that don’t exist in the real world, and he is creating something that is causing real-world effects. … I do believe that he is causing deliberate division that may be catastrophic if it’s not regulated or tamed, or if we don’t do our part in putting it down.” Gibney and St. Clair both mentioned what the former called Musk’s “very difficult and traumatic childhood” as a potential driver for him and his focus. “I think to some extent he’s now playing out that trauma on the rest of us.” All in all, he called Musk “a cautionary tale” that tries, among a “bewildering world of inputs” in the social media age, to stitch together a narrative to show the forest amid all the trees. In a director’s statement on the Venice website, Gibney shares: “In Musk , I chose to re-tell a familiar biographical tale but to forgo the master. Instead, I explored it from different angles that showed the master shot to be an illusion, and revealed a more disturbing truth. Musk reframes the story of the tech titan as the 21st century reincarnation of the confidence man. By subverting Musk’s favorite tropes of video gaming and simulations, the film conveys the dangers of becoming like the Game Master in Ready Player One . It’s a tale of power and its abuse.” THR

articles.title: ‘Musk’ Review: Alex Gibney’s Mammoth Elon Musk Doc Is a Poleaxing Portrait of the Tech Titan as a Con Man Given Way Too Much Power to Be Stopped
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 8, 2026 5:05am 'Musk' Courtesy of the Venice Film Festival Not long after news first emerged three years ago that Alex Gibney had begun work on an in-depth study of Elon Musk , the uber-tech bro went on the defensive on his social media platform, Twitter. Sorry, I mean X. “It’s a hit piece,” he cried, before switching to the totally mature “Gibney is a douche.” It must have been no surprise to the filmmaker that his subject would decline to make himself available for Musk , a whopping documentary think piece running close to four hours, which traces in dense detail the dizzying ascent to stratospheric wealth and influence of the man who dreams of colonizing Mars. Related Stories Movies Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller on Making ICE Doc 'They're Here' Like a "Horror Movie" Movies Venice Home Crowd Gives Italian Horror 'The Spiral' 9-Minute Standing Ovation Gibney’s solution to that key absence turns out to be a stroke of creative genius. After having his team pull together a data base with every statement Musk had ever made and every interview he had ever given, the director’s digital effects crew set about developing a CG avatar to address the camera as if in a sit-down chat from a gaming chair, sticking strictly to the billionaire business mogul’s own words. Musk The Bottom Line A provocative combo of indignation and alarm. Venue : Venice Film Festival (Out of Competition) Release date : Friday, Oct. 16 Director : Alex Gibney Screenwriters : Alex Gibney, Michael J. Palmer 3 hours 45 minutes What could be more appropriate for a subject who has hypothesized that we could all be living in a computer-generated base reality, a simulation controlled by some future power, as if all of humanity might be player characters in a video game? Gibney digs into the extent to which Musk’s ambitions were shaped early on by vintage sci-fi movies and books, though many have pointed out that he seemed to miss the anti-capitalist satire of one of his key inspirations, Douglas Adams’ The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy , instead treating it like a manual for technological advancement at any cost. This is the man who wants to ensure the survival of human civilization while our own planet teeters toward the abyss? If you buy that, Gibney seems to suggest, he has a bridge in Brooklyn to sell you. The filmmaker has likened his perspective in this project to that of Dorothy’s dog Toto in The Wizard of Oz , alert to the shuffling feet beneath the curtain rather than being bamboozled by the shyster title character’s techno showmanship. With a clarity that makes his conclusions hard to refute and a wealth of visual material, spiffy graphics and insightful interviews to keep it interesting throughout the epic run time, Gibney pulls back the curtain, charting the path of the South African whiz kid, who grew up under apartheid and has never denounced the racially discriminatory regime. The film hopscotches from Musk’s first U.S. software company, Zip2 — the sale of which netted him $22 million despite the enterprise never having turned an operational profit — through the key business ventures that helped consolidate his power and multiply his net worth. Those steppingstones include the purchase of Twitter, which soon cratered in value but became a crucial bullhorn to legitimize his partly illusory personal narrative for a devoted cult, sweeping the stated goal of promoting free speech under the rug. This was a logical extension of what Musk’s first wife, Justine Wilson, considers his strategic gaslighting skills, allowing him to shape exactly the image he sought to project, not of an investor but of a visionary inventor. That’s why it was so important to Musk to be credited as the founder of Tesla , which would come as news to engineers Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning. Gibney paints Musk as an unabashed megalomaniac. He ventures outside the professional sphere to touch on the “legions of children,” as someone describes them; the disposable “breeders”; the drug use; and the father who seems like a nightmarish piece of work. But the gossipy tidbits almost pale next to the eye-opening shadiness of some of the business strategies. The Tesla chapter is compelling less for the success of launching electric vehicles on the market than the more inconvenient factors that somehow went ignored — from falsehoods about the time required to swap out a battery pack to the playing down of fatalities that resulted from glitches in self-driving cars, reported to have caused at least 65 deaths. Around the same time, Musk mastered the art of stock manipulation, as well as securing government handouts and energy credits. He’s now inextricably linked with Republican Party politics and more specifically Donald Trump. But the film notes that although foundational funding for Musk’s SpaceX rocket program came from the George W. Bush administration, along with a $1.6 billion contract that reportedly rescued the division from looming bankruptcy, it was the Obama administration that honored and expanded on the initiative through NASA. In retrospect, that now looks like an uncharacteristically laissez-faire decision. Gibney lays out the shift by which Musk turned away from the Democrats to align himself for personal gain with Trump, in what many believe was a case of him buying the 2024 election, funneling close to $300 million into the campaign. That opened the door to the infamous DOGE purge. Musk unleashed a team of 19-to-22-year-old Silicon Valley bros to kneecap government agencies of which they had zero understanding. But crucially, they did understand those agencies’ IT systems, giving them access to classified programs and Americans’ personal information. Some of the tech reporters interviewed maintain that all that data has been used to link pension funds and 401ks to SpaceX, creating a precarious balance. While the formation of DOGE, during which Musk bounced around the Oval Office like a kid in a candy store, was positioned as a cost-cutting measure and an assault on fraud and waste, by decimating the IRS, the department substantially increased the federal deficit. DOGE’s primary achievement now appears to have been hobbling government agencies to block all investigations of Musk’s companies. While the entire section of Gibney’s film on DOGE has the sobering effect of a corruption exposé and the fear factor of a ‘70s conspiracy thriller, the cruelest part of it all is the dismantling of USAID, the independent government department for international development founded by JFK in 1961. It’s estimated that 14 million lives in developing countries will be lost because of DOGE cuts, 4.5 million of them kids under 5. “USAID is a criminal organization,” Musk says at one point. “Time for it to die.” His stunt with “the chainsaw for bureaucracy” now looks like the most juvenile theatrics, especially given that hundreds of federal workers had to be rehired when their departments stopped functioning, in some cases receiving back-pay for the interim months. One of the most sinister examples of cause and effect in this culling is the immediate suspension, after Trump signed the executive order, of medical and nutritional aid for children. An emotional former USAID employee recounts how 500 pounds of food destined for starving children was already on the ground but could not be distributed because of the government veto, meaning it was allowed to pass its expiration date and then be destroyed. Musk himself provides the key to comprehending how people in power could be so heartless when he calls empathy “a bug in Western civilization.” His rants about the “woke-mind virus” are both disturbing and tiresome, and his flair for self-dramatizing outrage is illustrated by comments about his trans daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson. “My son Xavier is dead,” Musk famously said, using his now-estranged offspring’s birth name. “Killed by the woke-mind virus.” Perhaps the loudest alarm set off by Gibney’s movie is the section devoted to Musk’s complete turnaround on AI. After initially coming out as a skeptic, he pivoted to full-steam-ahead with minimal regulation once he established his xAI offshoot — which quickly landed a contract with Pete Hegseth’s ignominiously renamed “Department of War.” Then there’s his chatbot Grok, which malfunctioned and self-generated an anti-Semitic, pro-Nazi rebrand dubbed “MechaHitler,” not to mention generating nude images of real women and girls. Of course, Musk’s distance from the project — which Bleecker Street will release Oct. 16 with a 10-minute intermission, ahead of its HBO premiere some time next year, provided Larry Ellison doesn’t run interference and have it shelved — means there’s no rebuttal here. articles.title: AMC Global Media Settles ‘Walking Dead’ Profit Participation Lawsuit for $120 Million
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 8, 2026 5:22am Andrew Lincoln as Rick Grimes in 'The Walking Dead.' Jackson Lee Davis/AMC Logo text The Walking Dead lawsuit saga may finally be over. AMC Global Media said Tuesday that it had settled the lawsuit brought by Walking Dead creator Robert Kirkman and the show’s other producers, including Glen Mazzara, David Alpert, Charles Eglee and Gale Anne Hurd. The lawsuit, initially filed in 2022, was about the profit participation rights for the original Walking Dead series, and its first spinoff series Fear the Walking Dead . AMC says that it will pay $120 million to resolve the lawsuit, including $85 million this month, with another $35 million next year. Related Stories TV Netflix and AMC Global Media Ink $500 Million 'Walking Dead' Streaming Deal TV Jack Quaid to Voice Gravitator in 'Invincible' Animated Series The $35 million will also serve as an advance against future profit participation rights. The settlement was reached on Friday, Sep. 4. The Walking Dead is the most successful franchise in AMC’s history (the company just inked a $500 million streaming deal with Netflix for the franchise in July), and the company has been battling lawsuits related to it since 2013, when Frank Darabont and CAA filed a profits suit about the program back in 2013. Darabont and CAA’s suit was settled in 2021 for $200 million, but it helped spark the new challenge from the franchise’s other producers, who filed the lawsuit now being settled in 2022. At issue in the suit is how the company calculates and collects profits for the franchise, and in turn how much the show’s creatives would be owed. “Robert Kirkman, Robert Kirkman, Inc., Gale Anne Hurd, Valhalla Entertainment, Inc., David Alpert, Circle of Confusion Productions LLC, New Circle of Confusion Productions, Inc., Charles Eglee, United Bongo Drum, Inc., Glen Mazzara and 44 Strong Productions, Inc., on the one hand, and AMC Global Media, on the other hand, are pleased to announce the amicable resolution of all their remaining claims and litigation related to The Walking Dead television franchise,” the two sides said in a statement Tuesday. “The parties look forward to sharing in the continued success of the franchise for many years to come.” THR

articles.title: Omaha Pulls Off a Star-Studded Hollywood Heist for the ‘Manningcast’ Schedule Release (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 8, 2026 5:35am 'Manningcast: Heist' Omaha Productions The Manning brothers may have pulled off their biggest heist yet. Sure, that’s the theme of this year’s Manningcast schedule release from Omaha Productions : An Ocean’s 11-style heist film, culminating in the reveal of the games they will be calling this coming season (including the Super Bowl), but the biggest heist of all may be what the former NFL stars pulled off onscreen in a 15-minute short film unveiling the schedule. The film, titled Manningcast: Heist , features some 40 cameos, spanning A-list movie stars to current and former NFL stars, and even a starring role by the NFL commissioner Roger Goodell himself. The result is high-energy, surprising and funny, with stars like Anne Hathaway, Jon Hamm, Paul Rudd, Larry David and Jason and Travis Kelce securing unexpected roles for themselves. Related Stories THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Padel Spanks Pickleball: Inside the Rise of the New Celebrity Sports Obsession TV When and Where to Watch F1 Italian Grand Prix at Monza Watch: “The tone of the heist is sort of a larger metaphor for the show itself,” says Omaha Productions president Jamie Horowitz, in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter . “The Manningcast is meant to be a safe space, a show where everybody can just come on and talk about a love of football. And you may have heard this before, but Omaha has very pure brand values — we try to uplift and unify — and we hope you see that in everything we do. And we also hope that people feel those values in that piece. This video is trying to be just a joyride of fun.” According to Therese Andrews, the head of production at Omaha, planning for the reveal started in late 2024, and they began production in early 2025 at the Pro Bowl, where they could secure the first round of cameos. “We map out the cameo roles early on when we do the script, thinking about what kind of people we want, and then we chip away throughout the entirety of the year to see how to build into that,” Andrews says, crediting Omaha writer and producer DJ Gallo with building out the heist concept. “The process with the creative is both scripted and it’s also sort of improv as we go. So as we book certain people, we’re reshaping the creative based on who we think is gettable, who might be interested in it, and then we rework every time we film with somebody.” Omaha executives credit the Manningcast itself as being a helpful piece of that puzzle. In fact, they see the over-the-top promotion of the NFL altcast as serving as a virtuous circle. “I think part of the reason that Paul Rudd, Kevin Hart, or David Letterman appears on the Manningcast is because we do things like this,” Horowitz says. “If the Manningcast was just a football show, Peyton and Eli probably could still recruit lots of great people. But the more you see these types of projects from Omaha outside of Monday night, the more likely creative people want to be part of our little world.” ESPN surely doesn’t mind if Omaha goes hard on promotion either, especially with the sports media giant’s first Super Bowl coming at the end of this season. The result is a piece of content (a promo video no less!) that levels up their ambitions and brings a whole host of stars along for the ride. “The Mannings work the same way they played football; they’re just always sort of eye on the prize of what’s the next play, and how do we evolve and figure out how to make things bigger,” says Andrews. “That’s part of our process throughout the whole journey. As much as this is about the Manningcast , it’s really a collection of talent, and finding a way to make something that’s dynamic and fun for people to watch and just celebrate the fact that football is coming back.” THR

articles.title: John Turturro “Grateful” to Zurich Film Festival for Golden Eye Award Honor
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 8, 2026 6:00am John Turturro Primož Korošec John Turturro will be honored with the Golden Eye Award at this year’s Zurich Film Festival . The Emmy-winning U.S. star is being recognized for his performance in Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , a project that is already garnering awards buzz . In the film, Turturro plays Harry, a seasoned pickpocket whose carefully controlled life is thrown into turmoil when a job goes wrong, setting off a tense chain of events that unfolds over the course of 36 hours. Turturro will accept the award in person at the Swiss film festival on Sep. 26, and share insights into his colorful acting and filmmaking career during a Zurich Film Festival Masters session the following day. Related Stories Movies 'Musk': Alex Gibney Shares His Take on Elon Musk's "Global Right-Wing Agenda" and the "Almost Existential Fear" of Talking He Encountered: Venice Movies Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller on Making ICE Doc 'They're Here' Like a "Horror Movie" “I am grateful to the Zurich Film Festival for this honor,” said the actor. “I was immediately drawn to Noah’s script and to the world he created in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York . There’s a sense of tension as the clock works against Harry, balanced by a finely drawn character-driven story set in a particular time and place in New York. As a lifelong New Yorker, the world felt rich and evocative, and there was a delicacy about it that felt almost radical about the story Noah was telling,” he added. Turturro’s career spans four decades, having worked with acclaimed directors such as Spike Lee, the Coen brothers, Martin Scorsese, Robert Redford, Robert De Niro, Nanni Moretti and Pedro Almodóvar. He first gained international recognition through his collaborations with Lee, appearing in Do the Right Thing and Jungle Fever . With Joel and Ethan Coen, he acted in Miller’s Crossing , Barton Fink , O Brother, Where Art Thou? and The Big Lebowksi , in which Turturro created the iconic Jesus Quintana. For his lead performance in Barton Fink , he won best actor at the 1991 Cannes Film Festival. Other credits include The Truce , Quiz Show , The Color of Money , The Good Shepherd , The Room Next Door and The Batman . On television, Turturro is best known for roles in Monk , for which he won an Emmy, as well as The Night Of , Mr & Mrs Smith and Severance . He received the Camera D’Or Award at the Cannes Film Festival for Mac , in 1992. Other films as a writer and director include Illuminata , Romance & Cigarettes , Passione and Fading Gigolo . CEO of Zurich Film Fest Christian Jungen said Turturro carries The Only Living Pickpocket in New York from the first minute to the last, “while also turning it into a deeply personal love letter to his hometown.” He continued: “Even though he portrays the antihero, we find ourselves rooting for him right until the end. That’s exactly what John Turturro is characterized by: he creates characters that are exaggerated for the screen yet feel completely true to life at the same time. With the Golden Eye Award, we honor an actor who has left his unmistakable signature on cinema for decades.” The Golden Eye Award honors actors and actresses who shape the current cinematic year while also ranking among the most significant performers of their generation. Previous recipients of the award include Jude Law, Kristen Stewart, Dakota Johnson, Jake Gyllenhaal, and Benedict Cumberbatch. Julianne Moore is set to receive Zurich’s Golden Icon Award this year.
