articles.title: Carly Rae Jepsen Could’ve Been a One-Hit Wonder or a Mainstream Megastar. Instead, She Became Far More Interesting
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Carly Rae Jepsen was photographed July 29 at PMC Studios in Los Angeles. Styling by Sophie Hardeman. Open24hrs vintage Jean Paul Gaultier top; vintage silk garter belt; Greta Garmel skirt; her own jewelry. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion; Hair: Summy Layo; Makeup: Pircilla Pae It’s early afternoon in West Los Angeles and Carly Rae Jepsen is a kid again. Dressed in a delicate sheer skirt with bright green socks popping under stiletto heels for her Hollywood Reporter photo shoot, she turns to her stylist to politely verify that she can get her loaned shoes dirty. The millisecond she gets that go-ahead, Jepsen’s jumping into a tree on the deck of The Hollywood Reporter ‘s headquarters, red hair streaming as she adjusts and mugs for the camera. Her tendency to throw herself into creative endeavors without overthinking has made her the artist she is today, allowing her to sidestep the pitfalls of one-hit-wonderdom. Jepsen shot to fame nearly 15 years ago at the age of 26 when her song “Call Me Maybe” became an early exemplar of modern virality. Living under a rock would hardly have prevented you from hearing the ubiquitous monster hit — and replaying it in your head ad nauseam. (You’re hearing it now, aren’t you?) Related Stories Movies Liam and Noel Gallagher Lock Arms at Venice Premiere of 'Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger' Movies Gallagher Brothers Skip Venice Press Conference for Concert Doc Now, 40 years old and just months after the birth of her first child, Jepsen has arrived at a place few might have predicted back then: neither a Taylor Swift-level megastar nor fading into obscurity by limply chasing another pop smash. “Where I’ve landed now in my career is the sweet spot,” the singer tells THR . “I can live a life, go to the grocery store, have a family, tour music that I love and have an audience,” she says. “That’s a very hard-earned, balanced thing that we’ve had to work at.” Initially released in 2011, “Call Me Maybe” became a global sensation in 2012, earning her two Grammy nominations and a spot atop the Billboard Hot 100. “In the moment, it was all happening rather fast,” Jepsen says. Her career moves after skyrocketing to success were less strategic than instinctual, she says: “If I’m being honest, I felt a little voice from inside screaming at me to hold on to why I started.” Her longtime friend and collaborator Tavish Crowe, who co-wrote the breakout song, was there to remind her that “Call Me Maybe” was just a “flavor” of Jepsen’s range as a singer. “I’ve always been blown away by how deep she can go on a song,” he says. “She’s always pushing the needle of what someone might expect or doing things that feel like they haven’t been done before.” With the hit song came a difficult period of adjustment and self-reflection. “It was so overnight that I feel like I understand what it must be like for some people who live in that space consistently, and my heart goes out to them,” Jepsen says. Maybe some celebrities feel they’re better at managing sudden success, she muses: “I’m just not very good at it.” Fame didn’t just happen to her, it happened to everyone in her orbit. But her main way of processing what happened back then is to simply think back and reflect. “I’m giving shit away, but I don’t care,” she says. “On a future song, that’s coming out after this album… There’s a song called ’16 and Rising.’ [It’s] about my coffee shop days and a guy I was dating back then, and what happened as I moved through this,” Jepsen says. “[It’s about] why I couldn’t quite settle for this beautiful life that was ahead of me because I was pining for something that I didn’t quite know what it was.” Greta Garmel top; The Frankie Shop skirt; vintage shoes. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Since the release of her breakthrough album, Kiss , Jepsen has kept one foot in the door of mainstream pop success and another in a more avant-garde space. Jepsen’s latest release, Day and Night, is a feat of balance, a double album that reflects the yin-yang equilibrium she’s striven for throughout her post-“Maybe” career. It’s divided thematically into Day, filled with sun-soaked psychedelic pop anthems, and Night, dripping in synth-heavy electropop. Jepsen hadn’t set out to make a bifurcated album; as with many of her most ambitious projects, it grew organically out of a back-and-forth with Crowe. She was heading on a trip to New York and was planning to show him the music she’d been working on. “He and I share music kind of like brother and sister in a very deep way,” she explains. Jepsen presented her friend one song from Day and one song from Night, and he suggested they think of them as contrasting material for a single project rather than two separate albums, as she’d originally imagined. She continued to mull the concept back home in L.A. until one day, driving around the city (once again with Crowe), the idea of Day and Night came to her. “As we were listening to stuff, it just felt like a song would naturally slot itself into the Night section or the Day section,” Crowe says. “Even before they were fully produced, too, you could still tell.” In the beginning, there were many pushes to divide the songs into two albums, but Jepsen says she “passionately disagreed” with that idea. “I wanted them together. They felt like two sides of the same thing,” says Jepsen. The duality of the album mirrored Jepsen’s own upbringing. “I grew up in two different houses because my parents divorced when I was quite young and remarried to incredible stepparents,” she says. It was a “very modern idea of co-parenting,” where she and her brother would switch houses every two days, both within 10 minutes of each other in the town of Mission, British Columbia. Her parents, all four of them, would have monthly meetings to discuss rules for the children. But the houses were very different. Night and day, you might say. “My mom’s a little bit more free spirit, hippie-ish, and my dad’s a little bit more the opposite of that,” she says. “I feel like musically there was a connection. They all love James Taylor, they all love Joni Mitchell, but they also had different flavors in terms of what my stepparents brought to the table with their musical tastes.” That duality made its way into Jepsen’s live shows, a mix of hits old and new. She considers it a win that “Call Me Maybe” isn’t the focal point of her concerts anymore, slotted within the set instead of as the closer. “I don’t think it’s a place to sit and hold resentment — what a useless waste of energy,” she says of the obligation to play the song she’s best known for. “If it’s a calling card that makes a couple of people happy, it’s not really about me anymore.” Left: Vintage bicycle tee; Kimberly Corday skirt; vintage hosiery; Prada shoes. Right: Open24hrs vintage Jean Paul Gaultier top; vintage silk garter belt; Greta Garmel skirt; her own jewelry. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion (2) After the whirlwind release of “Call Me Maybe” and Kiss , Jepsen took a break and headed to Broadway. She’d spend her nights doing Rodgers and Hammerstein’s Cinderella , while her days were occupied by her follow-up album, 2015’s Emotion , which would become a critical success. In the clearest indication of her abiding cultural clout, the video for the album’s biggest single, the bouncy earworm “I Really Like You,” featured an ebullient, fully committed Tom Hanks and included a cameo by Justin Bieber. The album solidified Jepsen as much more than a one-note artist, pushing the boundaries of what mainstream pop could be with risky sonic choices. She didn’t know whether it would be what her legion of fans wanted and, to an extent, didn’t care. In hindsight, she’s thankful for her “obliviousness” to the mechanics of fame and believes she was better off for her relative cluelessness about how to handle it. Among her most naive assumptions, she says, was that she would continue writing her own material. “Around that time, the idea of you being a pop writer for your own project was sort of like, it was cute,” she explains. “I had to learn how to know who my people were.” In another possible sign of her ingenuousness, Jepsen has maintained the same label and team at Interscope for her entire career, something of a rarity in the music industry. She counts herself lucky, gushing about the “incredible relationships” she’s had with her A&R. But she did make notable changes in her management. “I’ve had some good experiences with people, and I’ve had hard ones too,” she says. “It’s taken a second to figure out the right team for my management, and now I’m happier than I’ve ever been.” To anyone who has followed her career, it’s hard not to wonder whether “the hard ones” is a reference to Scooter Braun, the high-profile former manager and music executive who signed her in the wake of “Call Me Maybe.” There has been plenty of speculation about the circumstances in which they parted ways — as there has been with several other former Braun clients — but Jepsen claims to hold no ill will toward him. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion “I knew that I was on a different journey than he understood,” Jepsen says. “I wanted to do something a little bit less mainstream, and I liked what he had offered, but I didn’t necessarily think it was what I wanted anymore. I felt like it was just going to be a little bit easier to shake hands, walk away and go let my freak flag fly, so to speak.” The singer didn’t leave empty-handed, however. “I took one of his employees with me,” she admits, cheekily. Jepsen feels more freedom to explore with her current managers and says Interscope has always done well by her. “I wouldn’t say I had complete agency from the beginning, but not because they were trying to take it away,” she explains. “But I didn’t know how to take it.” The broad, extensive rollout that Interscope is giving Day and Night is a clear indication that the label trusts Jepsen’s instincts. The album is a collaborative mashup of all her “favorite people,” as well as newcomers introduced through friends. One of those newcomers is playwright, actor and social butterfly Jeremy O. Harris, who directed the music video for one of the album’s prerelease singles, “Don’t Leave Me on the Dance Floor,” starring Alden Ehrenreich. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion “She’s such an artist,” Harris says. “She understands her audience and her own work incredibly well but is also excited for someone who can show her another lens.” People are lining up to work with Jepsen. Fellow Canadian treasure Jacob Tierney shared that he’d been eager to get Jepsen to write an original song for the first season of his hit hockey romance series Heated Rivalry , but it wasn’t in the budget. Jepsen hasn’t heard from him yet about the second season but admits that writing a song for it would be a “dream” for her. “It was an incredible show. Ilya is the name of my son. Maybe, not maybe because of that show,” she says, referring to the character played by Connor Storrie. Perhaps the most significant collaboration on Day and Night has little to do with the music. The album was made against the backdrop of one of the most transitional times in Jepsen’s personal life. While making Day and Night , she was falling in love with the man who would become her husband, musician Cole M.G.N., one of her collaborators and a producer on the album. Later in the process, as the album was being mixed, she became pregnant with their son. When it’s suggested in our interview that the album has effectively served as a time capsule for this time in her life, she asks, “Can I steal that?” “I don’t want to say that my album’s only sunshine and rainbows and happiness because if I’ve done my job right, there’s some depth to it,” she says. But she’s not going to lie about how she’s feeling: “I’m the happiest I’ve ever been.” Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion This story appeared in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Inside ‘DAU,’ the 20-Year Soviet Simulation That Became Cinema’s Strangest Ghost Story
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content 'DAU' Ilya Khrzhanovsky On a cold night in November 2011, in a field outside Kharkiv in northeastern Ukraine, a gang of thugs stormed a Soviet scientific research institute, beat and humiliated the staff and burned the place to the ground. None of it was real. Well, some of it was. The institute was a film set — a working re-creation inspired by the Moscow institute run by the pioneering quantum physicist Lev Landau. It claimed, at the time, to be the largest set in European cinema history. Some of the thugs were actual neo-Nazis, led by real-life Russian fascist Maksim Martsinkevich, who would later be imprisoned for posting racist videos, investigated for murder and, in 2020, found dead in his cell of an apparent suicide. Related Stories Movies John Turturro "Grateful" to Zurich Film Festival for Golden Eye Award Honor Movies 'Musk' Review: Alex Gibney's Mammoth Elon Musk Doc Is a Poleaxing Portrait of the Tech Titan as a Con Man Given Way Too Much Power to Be Stopped Cameras rolled as the building burned. They continued to roll as the crew held a party on location, amid the ashes, with an open bar and music courtesy of electronic musicians Peaches and DJ Spooky. For three years before that night, the set had functioned less like a traditional backlot than a sealed micro-state. If you believe the rumors — and much of what is known about this project is only speculation — participants were required to wear authentic 1930s to 1960s-era clothing, right down to their underwear. They ate Soviet-style food, bought bread from the institute cafe with newly minted Soviet-era rubles and smoked Soviet cigarette brands. Anachronisms were banned: No mobile phones, no internet, no laptops. Women were reportedly forbidden to use modern tampons. All news came from a fully staffed on-set newspaper and radio station. The KGB officers were played, in some cases, by actual former KGB officers, and they could detain and interrogate other cast members. Not everything was filmed and recorded, but a lot was. Some 700 hours of footage, shot on 35mm film, and around 8,000 hours of recorded dialogue. None of that was the original plan, however. The initial idea, when a 29-year-old Russian director named Ilya Khrzhanovsky pitched it in 2006, was for a fairly conventional art house biopic of Landau — the recipient of the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physics, who was nicknamed “ Dau ” — financed by the European Union funding body Eurimages with German and Swedish support. What it became instead was Dau : a two-decade multimedia leviathan that has so far yielded more than a dozen experimental films, art installations in Paris and London, an aborted plan to rebuild the Berlin Wall, a ban in Russia for creating “pornographic propaganda,” accusations of abuse and exploitation, and a mythology so dense that the work itself all but disappeared behind it. ‘DAU’ Ilya Khrzhanovsky The Dau project became one of cinema’s great ghost stories. Akin to Orson Welles’ The Other Side of the Wind or Terry Gilliam’s The Man Who Killed Don Quixote — films that traded for decades on the mystique of never quite existing. For 20 years, the tales and whispers have circulated about the “mad Russian” director and his experiment. Some called it a “Stalinist Truman Show ” or “ Big Brother in period costume.” Some of the rumors, and a few of the reports at the time, paint Khrzhanovsky as a tyrant who went mad with power, like Colonel Kurtz in Heart of Darkness (or maybe Francis Ford Coppola making Apocalypse Now ). But Khrzhanovsky’s original idea, for an epic biopic on the life of Landau, never completely disappeared though. The filmmaker kept the footage he shot in Kharkiv between 2008 and 2011 — all 700 hours of it — and left it in a fridge for more than a decade. Now, 20 years later, the “mother film,” as Khrzhanovsky calls it, the biopic that spawned the leviathan, is finally finished. The 165-minute movie, titled simply DAU , premieres in competition at the Venice Film Festival this month. “[The new film] is more or less the model I wrote almost 20 years ago and that we filmed, starting from 2008,” Khrzhanovsky, now 51, explains via video call from Paris, where he’s completing postproduction with characteristic last-minute intensity. “[But] I didn’t really touch this movie from the moment when I finished the shoot [in 2011] until December 2023, when I started to edit and reorganize the material and find a new cinematic language for it.” Lev Landau makes for an unlikely epic hero, but his life offers up plenty of cinematic drama. A prodigy who started college at 14 and published major works on quantum theory before his 20th birthday, Landau worked with pioneering physicist Niels Bohr and, in 1937, was named head of the theoretical division of the secretive Institute for Physical Problems in Moscow. He was reportedly as experimental in his private life as in his physics, including practicing polyamory. At the height of the Soviet Terror, he was arrested for comparing Stalin to Hitler but dodged the Gulag. Rehabilitated, he worked on the project to build the Soviet atom bomb. In 1962, in the same year he became a Nobel Laureate, a crippling car crash left him bedridden until his death in Moscow in 1968. Compared with the other films to have emerged from the Dau shoot — the more experimental films DAU. Natasha and DAU. Degeneratsiya were screened at the Berlin Film Festival in 2020 — the mother film DAU promises to be almost mainstream: a Doctor Zhivago -style epic, albeit with discussions of quantum mechanics and a fair bit of explicit sex thrown in. It also arrives burdened by an entirely new scandal. Ahead of the festival, the Ukrainian government took the unprecedented step of formally complaining to Venice for selecting the film for competition . “At the time when Russia is continuing its war of aggression against Ukraine, systematically destroying cities, cultural heritage and national identity, offering one of the world’s most prestigious cultural platforms to a project linked to the Russian state and its networks of influence sends a deeply worrying signal,” reads the joint Aug. 17 statement from Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Culture and the Ukrainian embassy in Italy. The statement goes on to list the film’s alleged connections to Vladimir Putin’s Russia, including Khrzhanovsky’s Russian identity; and that of lead actor Teodor Currentzis, the Greek-Russian classical conductor who plays Dau in the film. There is also the connection to Sergei Adoniev, the Russian oligarch who bankrolled the original shoot, and who has been sanctioned by both Ukraine and the U.S. for his alleged ties to Putin. Khrzhanovsky took to Facebook on Aug. 20 to post a point-by-point rebuttal of the criticisms, noting that “ DAU is not an instrument of Russian state cultural policy. It is an artistic statement about the nature of totalitarian evil.” But speaking with The Hollywood Reporter, he says he understands the Ukrainian position. “The war is the war, and I cannot judge the position of Ukrainians who are suspicious of a Russian who spent time in Ukraine,” he says. “I wanted to correct the lies because things like saying I represent the Russian state is literally not true. I think it was misunderstanding and misinterpretation. But I don’t want to judge. They should do whatever they need to do to win this war.” The objection reflects how radically the perception of Khrzhanovsky’s Dau experiment has shifted over the course of two decades — from transcendent art project to exploitative scandal to, now, geopolitical lightning rod. The Stalinist Truman Show To understand the mythology of Dau , you have to go back to 2006. The year before, Khrzhanovsky had won a Tiger Award at Rotterdam for his first feature, the hallucinatory drama 4 . In that film, three strangers — a meat merchant, a prostitute and a piano tuner — meet up in an all-night bar in Moscow. They all invent fake biographies and spend the evening telling made-up stories from their imagined pasts. After they separate, these fantasy realities begin to dominate their everyday lives. Off the success of 4, Khrzhanovsky secured his European funding for what still looked like a straightforward Landau biopic. Everything changed when he met Adoniev and persuaded the Russian oligarch to bankroll the project. Adoniev had made his fortune in the mobile phone business; Forbes in 2017 estimated his wealth at $800 million. Freed from budgets, schedules and the ordinary logic of film financing, Dau the modest European art house movie mutated into a massive experiment designed to plunge participants — and, eventually, audiences — into the re-created horrors of the Stalin-era Soviet Union. The filmmaker’s own audit reveals the staggering numbers behind the project, listing “392,000 auditions, 40,000 costumes, 12,000- square-meter set, 10,000 extras, 400 principle roles. 700 hours of 35mm film, 8,000 hours of recorded dialogue, 500,000 set photographs.” ‘DAU’ includes massive set pieces not shown in the earlier movies, including a sequence involving “70 tons of cabbage.” Ilya Khrzhanovsky The project attracted remarkable participants beyond its massive cast of extras. Currentzis, the acclaimed classical conductor, agreed to play Dau after meeting Khrzhanovsky socially in Moscow in 2005. Performance artist Marina Abramović and opera director Peter Sellars took on roles. Real Nobel Prize-winning physicist David Gross and acclaimed mathematician Shing-Tung Yau took working residencies in Kharkiv, conducting real science in period costume. The idea behind the casting was to recruit to match the characters. So cleaners to play cleaners, academics to play scientists, even criminals and former KGB agents to play their Soviet equivalents. The Movie That Ate Itself In the three years of filming, only a handful of journalists were allowed inside “the institute.” Michael Idov spent several days there for a piece in GQ . He was allowed to move on and offset, given the official status of a “visiting foreign dignitary,” but required to dress in a three-piece suit and fedora and engage in period-appropriate small talk. In his 2011 piece, Idov described Khrzhanovsky as “unhinged,” portraying him as a dictatorial director who turned his set into an oppressive totalitarian microsociety. Actors were not just expected to perform but to physically experience life under the Soviet regime. “The real world was like a set to us,” Currentzis recalled in an interview with The Guardian in 2019. “We were sleeping and waking up and working in the clothes we had worn inside. When we were out, it was like visiting another time.” According to Currentzis, the reality of the Dau set was not always pleasant. “If the ‘KGB’ grabbed me, they could send me to jail. They could behave really badly to you,” he recalled. “I felt very uncomfortable many times, but it’s the same discomfort I feel in my own life. If we want to make something that is real, it has to be like real life.” Not everyone experienced it as art. Matthias Ganghofer, who worked as a first assistant cameraman on the Kharkiv shoot, would later stand up at a Berlin Film Festival press conference and say he found the experience on set “humiliating.” When he was caught using a cellphone, a violation of the project’s rules of historic authenticity, his name was marked on a blackboard for all to see. He claimed he left the project after three months. Khrzhanovsky says he fired him. “I fired a huge amount of people,” he adds. Speaking to THR , Khrzhanovsky speaks of the periods on set where there was no filming but life in the institute continued as a kind of “extended rehearsal.” He downplays the more extreme elements of the experience, noting that, for example, KGB arrests and interrogations were always agreed upon in advance. THR reached out to Currentzis, Ganghofer and several other members of the original Dau shoot for comment. Lol Crawley, one of the three cameraman on DAU , was not on the Kharkiv shoot, but he remembers a demanding but happy production, and a director who never resembled the tyrant of the rumors. “Ilya was in control, like any good director, but was such a warm and generous person to work with,” he says. (From L): Ilya Khrzhanovsky and cinematographer Jürgen Jürges instruct an actor on the set of ‘DAU’ Ilya Khrzhanovsky The GQ article was headlined “The Movie Set That Ate Itself.” But it didn’t. Eventually the money simply ran out — Khrzhanovsky estimates Adoniev spent around 25 million euros, about $40 million in today’s money, before pulling the plug — and the set burned in that staged massacre of November 2011. What survived was footage. Rather than cut one film from it, Khrzhanovsky began cutting many, along with a series of increasingly elaborate live installations built around the material. The first, in Paris in 2019, spread across the Théâtre du Châtelet and Théâtre de la Ville, immersing visitors in screening rooms, re-created Soviet interiors and hours of unseen footage. “I’m absolutely, 100 percent sure that what we’re experiencing here will be in the history books of Paris, of art history, of scientific innovation, of cinema history,” said Ruth Mackenzie, artistic director of Théâtre du Châtelet, of the 2019 Paris exhibition, describing the multi-site project as a once-in-a-generation “game-changer.” There was a plan to go further still, re-creating the Dau project in Berlin with an interactive exhibit that would have involved building a replica Berlin Wall in the German capital, creating a walled-in “city within a city.” Visitors would be required to purchase “visas” to enter and, once inside, it was promised, would experience life as it was in the old GDR. The project would end with a ritualistic tearing down of the wall on Nov. 9, 2018, 29 years to the day after the historic event in 1989. Chinese dissident artist Ai Weiwei was set to build the wall. Artists like Abramović and Run Lola Run director Tom Tykwer were involved. Brian Eno and Robert Del Naja of Massive Attack also signed up. “It’s the most extraordinary and multilayered art project I’ve ever heard of,” said Eno at the time. “You often hear things described as ‘ambitious.’ Nothing I’ve ever encountered comes close to the ambition of Dau .” It never happened. Berlin authorities objected on safety grounds to the project. There were also complaints from locals at the cost — reportedly close to $8 million — and the idea of using taxpayer money to re-create a dictatorship. There was talk of a “Disneyfication” of Stalinism. Over the years, bits and pieces of the Dau project have continued to emerge, in different forms. Last year, at the San Marco Art Centre in Venice from Sept. 5 to Nov. 23, Khrzhanovsky hosted the Dau exhibit The Quantum Effect , which featured footage shot in Kharkiv of scientists debating quantum and string theory. The Scandals Begin The first Dau films to emerge from the Kharkiv material, DAU. Natasha and DAU. Degeneratsiya — the former just over two hours, the latter more than six — screened at the Berlin Film Festival in 2020. DAU. Natasha , in competition, won a Silver Bear for outstanding artistic contribution for cinematographer Jürgen Jürges, the man responsible for most of those 700 hours of footage. Both films sparked an uproar. The controversy was hottest around DAU. Natasha . The film focuses on a cafeteria worker, played by Natalia Berezhnaya, and her colleague Olga (Olga Shkabarnya). They gossip, flirt with customers, and go out and get drunk. One evening after a roaring party, Natasha goes to bed with one of the institute scientists. She’s called in for questioning and torture by the KGB. The interrogation scene was the source of most of the controversy. Hatchet-faced officer Azhippo (played by Vladimir Azhippo, a former KGB officer) belittles and humiliates Natasha. In a particularly grim scene, he forces her to strip and insert a bottle into her vagina. Critics, assuming the scene wasn’t simulated, accused the production of sexual assault. ‘DAU. Natasha’ Courtesy of Phenomen film At the Berlin press conference, Khrzhanovsky was cagey and evasive when asked what in the film was “real” and what was staged for the camera. But the actors all supported him. Everyone on set, Berezhnaya told reporters, was “in charge of our own senses and emotions. We were well aware of what we were doing.” She denied the rape charges unequivocally. Cinematographer Jürges agreed. “In those scenes, we always had a safety vow. If somebody did not want to go along, we could stop at any time,” he says. “We didn’t work according to a screenplay; we were living our lives,” says Berezhnaya, though she reminds everyone that “we have amazing directors and amazing editors, and we are amazing actors.” That didn’t stop the outrage. A letter, published on now-defunct Russian feminist film website KKBBD.com and signed by five Berlinale-accredited Russian journalists, called out the festival for including, in the wake of #MeToo, a film that “contains scenes of real psychological and physical violence against nonprofessional actors.” Khrzhanovsky finds the allegations, particularly that of actual sexual assault, patently absurd. “[Berezhnaya] said it, she repeated it, and you can see it, if you just understand anything about anatomy, you see it isn’t real. But that story was there and got repeated and repeated,” he says. “Of course, it was an unusual way of filming, and having people play characters close to themselves [helped] them go further emotionally. But the whole time, you are on a set with a cameraman, a focus puller, a boom operator.” Berezhnaya was nominated for a European Film Award for best actress, but the controversy around the movie meant “she couldn’t celebrate, couldn’t be celebrated,” according to Khrzhanovsky. “Monica Bellucci came up to her and said what an incredible performance it was,” he recalls, but such praise was drowned out by scandal. Russia banned the film as “pornographic propaganda,” while Western press largely dismissed it. Then COVID struck, and the film barely saw a release. Looking back, it’s striking how the Dau films shown in Berlin were viewed through the lens of the #MeToo movement that had transformed Hollywood and cultural discourse. Stories that might once have been framed as the excesses of an avant-garde visionary — actors staying in character for months on end, living in Soviet-era quarters in period costume — now appeared as potential acts of exploitation and misuse of power. Interesting, too, how the project’s warnings about Russian totalitarianism, particularly stark in DAU. Degeneratsiya , and its discussions of art, philosophy, religion and quantum physics were largely overlooked at the time. Now, the “mother film” DAU arrives with yet another interpretive framing: that of current Ukrainian politics. The Political Context The protests against DAU by the Ukrainian government ahead of this year’s Venice Film Festival highlight a dramatic shift in geopolitics, one that makes the project’s original context almost unrecognizable. All the filming for DAU in Ukraine took place between 2008 and 2011, more than a decade before Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. At that time, Russian-Ukrainian cultural collaborations were not only common but actively encouraged, with co-productions regularly receiving support from both countries’ film funding bodies. Adoniev, the project’s main private funder, left the project years before he was sanctioned by Ukraine in 2022, and later by the U.S. in 2023, for his ties to Putin. “When we started to make this project, it was a completely different reality,” Khrzhanovsky notes. “Russian-Ukraine co-productions were everywhere. People would move from here to there. It was a completely different reality.” Khrzhanovsky’s own position vis-à-vis Russia has shifted just as dramatically. He has renounced his Russian citizenship in protest of the invasion of Ukraine, and holds British, German and Israeli passports. He set up the XZ Foundation with journalist Mikhail Zygar to counter Russian propaganda, mocking Putin’s description of the invasion as a “special operation.” As a result, he has been labeled a “foreign agent,” a designation used to target critics of the Putin regime. In Russia, Andrei Lugovoi, a member of the Duma and a former KGB agent, has called him a “master traitor” and accused him of “sabotage against Russia.” The Ukrainian objections also focused on Currentzis, who lives and works in Russia as artistic director of the Perm State Opera and Ballet Theatre. He took Russian citizenship in 2014 and has never publicly denounced Putin’s war on Ukraine — factors that make him particularly controversial in the current climate. “However one may judge his decision not to make such statements [against the war], judging a person on the basis of the citizenship they hold — and, even more so, using citizenship acquired years after most of the filming as evidence of the film’s current connection to the Russian state — is not justified,” Khrzhanovsky wrote in his Facebook post. Speaking to the political turmoil around the film, the director takes the long view. “Right now there is an emotional reaction mixed in with a need to protest the war, which I understand,” he says. “They need to stop the war, and if they want to destroy monuments, or forbid certain storytellers, that’s not my business.” History, he suggests, has a way of changing the narrative. “My Jewish mum was born in Ukraine and grew up there,” Khrzhanovsky says. “She was a Holocaust survivor and then moved to Uzbekistan, went back to Ukraine, then Moscow, and then Israel. Now she lives in Berlin. I grew up in the Soviet time when, in the movies about the Second World War, we didn’t say ‘Nazis,’ it was always ‘Germans.’ Now I hold a German passport. My mum too.” “I believe soon we will see a more multidimensional picture of who we are, what we did, and what kind of world we live in,” he muses. “That was part of my task with this project — to create this picture, to create this model.” Dau Phenomen Berlin Return of the Mother Film Khrzhanovsky returned to the “mother film” three years ago, going back into the editing suite with funding from Germany, France and Sweden, plus Rotterdam’s Hubert Bals Fund. Adoniev’s involvement with Dau , he says, ended in 2019. He still had the original material, and the original idea — Lev Landau and the Soviet Union from the 1930s through the 1960s — but his take on it had changed. “[Returning to] the material, the way I describe it, is like cognac. The cask is time,” he explains. “The style of the movie, its language, how I edited it, has changed because of the 20 years in between.” Of course, he adds with a smirk, “a 20-year cognac could still be a shitty one.” Ilya’s original idea of making a biographical film about Lev Landau had already changed after he cast Currentzis in the lead. His quantum physicist became Greek and his story started to diverge from Landau’s biography. The entire second half of the new film, Khrzhanovsky says, has “no connection whatsoever” to the life of the real Landau. DAU is structured in three parts, each shot by a different cinematographer, representing different periods of Landau’s life. Revisiting the footage, Khrzhanovsky realized he had assembled, back in 2008, a team that would go on to define contemporary art cinema: veteran German cinematographer Jürgen Jürges, best known for his work with Rainer Werner Fassbinder, in Kharkiv and Moscow; the then-up-and-coming Brit Lol Crawley, later an Oscar winner for The Brutalist , in Saint Petersburg; and Manuel Alberto Claro, who would go on to shoot Melancholia and Nymphomaniac for Lars von Trier, in Kharkiv. Crawley, the first cinematographer to shoot on the project, says the design was deliberate from the start: “Three different cinematographers, three different production designers, three different looks for the three different sections of the film,” Crawley tells THR . What he mostly remembers is the scale — “incredibly ambitious,” he says — and “these amazingly complex handheld sequences, where we had to reset and reset over and over again.” All 700 hours of 35mm footage were kept in climate-controlled storage — “many years in Switzerland, then moved it” to a “fridge in Berlin.” It was all Fuji 400, a stock the company discontinued in 2010, which should have made the pickups he needed in 2023 impossible. But Khrzhanovsky had anticipated that. Fuji agreed to produce the stock for one more year “just for us, just for Jürges,” he says. “I took that remaining stock and put it in the fridge with the rest of the 700 hours.” In 2024, he took out the reels and shot his additional scenes. “We filmed everything, down to the last meter.” The aged stock had lost two stops of sensitivity, meaning the image on the old film was substantially darker, which had to be compensated for with additional lighting. Khrzhanovsky refuses to disclose which scenes come from the original shoot and which are the add-ons. Khrzhanovsky, if you haven’t realized by now, is an obsessive. Dau hasn’t made him rich — he’s racked up huge debts, not least for storage — or particularly famous. He’s been called an abuser, a pornographer, a dictator and an agent of the Russian state. But he can’t let Dau go. The Quantum Artist In some ways, Khrzhanovsky was born for this. He comes from a film family — his father, Andrey, was an acclaimed director whose 1968 animated short, The Glass Harmonica , has the distinction of being the first animated movie banned in the U.S.S.R. (The film depicts a bleak, gray city controlled by greedy, corrupt authorities. Censors felt this was a bit too close to the reality of the ’60s Soviet Union.) Khrzhanovsky’s godfather was Soviet screenwriter and dramatist Sergei Yermolinsky, who was imprisoned and then sentenced to internal exile in Kazakhstan for “anti-Soviet activities” for offenses, including his friendship with dissident novelist Mikhail Bulgakov, and only freeed after iconic Soviet director Sergei Eisenstein ( Battleship Potemkin , Ivan the Terrible ) successfully petitioned for his release. For Khrzhanovsky, the Soviet past he re-created in DAU is “part of my DNA.” Returning to the story of Landau, the physicist whose experiments changed our notion of the reality of time and space, felt, he says, like he was creating a “quantum picture” — where multiple realities — past, present and possible future — exist simultaneously. “I started thinking about the me who began thinking of the project 20 years ago,” he says. “Then there are the real 20 years of my life, and of the lives of all the characters, the actors,” Khrzhanovsky reflects. “My life and the life of other characters are also part of the story of this process.” The whole Dau project, he says, “is much bigger than me,” but the film DAU , “this fictional story about society, about the relations between people,” he says, “belongs to me. I’m the author of this film.” Khrzhanovsky’s “mother film” is clearly a different beast from his other Dau features. It’s more conventionally structured, more obviously cinematic. It includes massive set pieces not shown in the earlier movies: a hypnotic sequence of women on an assembly line, smashing up an endless stream of clay rabbits; huge crowds in period costume crossing a re-created St. Isaac’s Square in St. Petersburg/Leningrad; a gigantic Soviet propeller plane trudging across a vast field; piles and piles of rotten cabbages — Khrzhanovsky has said he used 70 tons for the single scene. Crawley remembers one such sequence vividly: following Currentzis, as Dau, through the streets of Saint Petersburg carrying a red balloon, before he emerges into a square filled with dogs and fish, trams crashing, soldiers pouring out and destroying paintings and artworks. “It was incredibly ambitious,” he says. Khrzhanovsky still wrestles with the mythology surrounding the Dau project. The reports and rumors, the endless stream of shifting scandals, have developed their own momentum, often overshadowing the actual work. “That’s why I prefer to talk about this new movie, not the Dau project or the other films, and not about this or that rumor,” he says. “Just discussing or denying these things leads them to repeat and repeat. All the work gets dissolved in the lake of rumors.” If the “mother film” DAU , so obviously a work of cinema and not a “Stalinist Truman Show ,” had been the first work released, he admits, “the whole conversation would have been different.” But he says he cannot look back or be concerned about how he or his films will be judged in the current historical moment. He knows too well how quickly that moment can change. “The historical perception is always changing,” he says. “We see it with Israel. I hold an Israeli passport, and I still have the Israel flag on my Facebook. But I know what Israel is doing in Gaza and the West Bank. My son [the journalist and activist known as Andrey X] is one of the most influential bloggers on the West Bank, fighting with the state of Israel. That’s what I mean about a quantum picture.” Whether Venice audiences will embrace this “quantum approach” to narrative remains to be seen. The film demands patience. “It’s not an easy movie. It’s not easy to watch. It’s long. It’s mostly in Russian language,” says Khrzhanovsky. “And it’s a complex story, but I think there are still a lot of people around the world who may be interested in watching this movie.” The Feast That Never Ends Khrzhanovsky insists he won’t be “doing Dau for the rest of my life.” But he is also, at present, still doing Dau . Eight Dau films are available on his bespoke VOD platform, dau.com, with five more listed as “upcoming releases.” Many share the same characters and the same events, approached from different angles. DAU. New Man follows an institute experiment to engineer “perfect soldiers” by weeding weakness and empathy out of the new Soviet man. DAU. Sasha Valera is a May-October love story between two of the institute’s janitors. That is the logic of the whole enterprise: 14 features to date (including the “mother film”), plus the installations and exhibitions — Khrzhanovsky mentions the possibility of a Dau book or books — all from a three-year shoot in Kharkiv. One set of events recut again and again into parallel worlds. This is what is meant by a “quantum project”, the same material suspended in several states at once, resolving only when somebody finally looks at it. For 20 years, almost nobody has. DAU has existed as rumor rather than reality, scandal rather than art, shelved alongside cinema’s great ghost stories. Other movie ghosts, Gilliam’s The Man Who Killed Don Quixote or Welles’ The Other Side of the Wind , eventually surfaced – in forms no one quite expected. In Venice, on Sept. 7, so will DAU . THR

articles.title: How to Write Chad Powers: Go With “Your First, Stupidest Thought”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 8, 2026 6:09am Glen Powell in season two of 'Chad Powers.' Disney/Daniel Delgado Jr. Logo text Chad Powers ( Glen Powell ) should probably attend class a bit more. The Chad Powers title character is known around the Southern Georgia University campus for the “athlete” suffix of his student-athlete status. What I’m saying is he’s dumb — but in the most endearing possible way. That’s the way the Hulu comedy’s showrunner Michael Waldron ( Loki ) likes it. Waldron says the “most joyful stuff” to write in Chad Powers is the (prosthetically) masked man’s bizarre, roundabout answers to personal questions that could otherwise out Powers as Russ Holliday — or at least as not a real person. The exchanges that spark joy for Waldron do the same for viewers, and they’re not as difficult to write as you might think. Related Stories TV Meet Wynn Everett, the (Delightful) "Gus Fring" of 'Chad Powers' TV Taylor Frankie Paul Returning for 'The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives' Season 6 “That’s why I’m writing this show because, in some ways, it’s whatever your first stupidest thought. You don’t actually even have to be funny. The character is a real cheat because he just says stupid shit, and and the comedy comes from the great actor from how Glen sells it and then everybody’s reaction to it,” Waldron told The Hollywood Reporter . “I mean it is a precise thing and it’s like, ‘Well how stupid is it?’ It was fun this season to interrogate it a little bit. It’s like, as Russ says to Ricky, ‘Chad is stupid. I’m making deliberate creative choices.’ Now, I think that’s probably just [Chad] retroactively justifying a crappy performance.” “I could write Chad as a character forever,” he added. “I’ll be really sad to not get to write him.” With just six 30-minute episodes per season (by design), some of these idiotic run-on stories inevitably hit the cutting room floor. “In [the season two premiere ], there was a thing that we cut out where he’s in the trainer’s room when he gets brought back, and he’s— it’s so stupid,” Waldron said. “He’s talking about how he’s like having to manually beat his heart. How all of his automatic body processes are no longer automatic. So he says, like, ‘I’m controlling the individual enzymes in my gut.’ It’s just so self indulgent and stupid. So we cut it. But to watch Glen perform it on the day was hysterical.” Should Waldron and Powell get their way, and they probably will, Chad Powers will get one more season from Hulu. If season two is Russ/Chad in a Bruce Wayne/Batman parallel, as Waldron told his writing staff, season three, the College Football Playoffs, will explore more of a Peter Parker/Spider-Man duality. Those relationships are more different than they might first appear. “This season Russ is actually much more comfortable because he’s kind of had that catharsis at the end of the first season, where he’s like, ‘I’m happier as Chad,'” Waldron said. “The emotional arc of this season I would say is about him starting to take steps toward the idea of well, can you ever be okay being Russ again? That’s what Ricky is challenging him with, reminding him they’re the same guy.” That’s the DC Comics parallel from the Marvel writer. “In a third season… do you have to do Peter Parker and Spider-Man, where Chad has to say that Russ is part of his life in some way? Will we have to embrace that convention?” Waldron posed. “Maybe. We’ve always talked about that.” Tom Holland in Spiderman, Glen Powell as Russ Holliday on Chad Powers, and Robert Pattison as Bruce Wayne. Chuck Zlotnick/Columbia Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection; Disney/Daniel Delgado Jr.; Jonathan Olley/Warner Bros./Courtesy Everett Collection It is rare the co-creators of a series want said show to end after just 18 episodes, but that “was always the intent ” for Chad Powers , Powell told THR . “One of my pet peeves on TV is when people don’t stick the landing,” he continued. “When people draw things out. I’m like, ‘Come on!’ When you have a story that ends perfectly, it just makes me so happy.” For someone with roughly zero free time on his hands, the busy movie and TV star (and University of Texas student!) has given the Chad Powers timeline a ton of thought. “The lie” of Chad Powers the character could not possibly make it through an entire college football offseason, he realized pretty early on. “When you have the amount of eyeballs on this one man at the center of this team in South Georgia, as sort of the legend of Chad Powers grows, this lie becomes harder and harder to pull off in front of the world,” Powell said. “You want to honor that. It’s kind of the fun of the show.” So Waldron will be sad to no longer write Chad poorly tap-dancing around inquiries into his background, and whatever happens in the Natty (National Championship) — assuming we get that — the conclusion of Chad Powers will be bittersweet for fans. Powell asks you to trust the process. “We have a very exciting culmination in mind. So that’s the plan,” he said. “I’m really happy with where it’s all heading.” THR

articles.title: Javier Bardem Feels a “Responsibility” to Speak Out on Political Issues: “I Have You Guys Listening to Me”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 8, 2026 6:20am The 'Bunker' cast hit Venice Courtesy of Getty Naturally, real-life couple Penelope Cruz and Javier Bardem were immediately quizzed on how much their marriage spilled into Florian Zeller ‘s Venice competition feature, Bunker , at the movie’s press conference on Tuesday afternoon. Ahead of the movie’s red carpet premiere, Zeller, Bardem and Cruz were joined by co-stars Stephen Graham, Paul Dano and Patrick Schwarzenegger on the Lido to promote the film, following a renowned architect (Bardem) offered the chance to secretly design a survival bunker for a billionaire who is convinced that the end of the world is near. As he lets himself be seduced by this morally ambiguous project, his wife (Cruz) begins to question their marriage. Related Stories Movies Inside 'DAU,' the 20-Year Soviet Simulation That Became Cinema's Strangest Ghost Story Movies John Turturro "Grateful" to Zurich Film Festival for Golden Eye Award Honor Zeller confessed he was inspired to write the screenplay after reading an article about Meta tech billionaire Mark Zuckerberg building an underground bunker in Hawaii. “It was a secret project, meaning that everyone involved in this project had to sign an NDA, to make sure no one would know,” said the French filmmaker. “For some reason, the information went public, and I thought it was a fascinating paradox because this man who made a fortune based on the idea of connecting people together [through Facebook and Instagram], was working on a plan B to isolate himself from the rest of the world.” Questions around isolation, human connection and morality drive Bunker , as does an authentic wife-and-husband performance from the Spanish A-listers. Zeller said he coaxed the pair on board the project because he “adores” them, but also because he needed that legitimacy. “I think they are among the greatest actors working today, and so obviously it was an honor for me to work with them,” he continued. “But I have to say that from the very beginning, I was also interested into in having them together on screen, because I thought it would be a unique way to capture something special as a real couple — to give layers to all the scenes of this film, to blur the line, of course, between reality and fiction, but to try to approach something that I’m interested in, which is the burning authenticity of the truth.” He added: “To do that for actors, you have to be very bold, you have to be very fearless and ambitious, and this is what they are, and that’s why they are such great artists.” Bardem, who is particularly outspoken on a slew of political issues, including his support of Palestine, was asked during the presser about actors being told to “stay in your bunker, stay in your lane.” How important does he think it is to tell stories “outside of our own yard”? The Oscar-winning actor responded: “Well, I think as an artist, you have a responsibility to make a story happen and to tell the story that the director, the author, wants. And then you, as an individual — it doesn’t matter if you’re an artist, an actor, a plumber, or a taxi driver — you have the right to expose your truth or what you think is important.” He continued: “Obviously, I have more resources to do it than a taxi driver because I have this thing [gesturing to microphone] and I have you guys listening to me. So, the responsibility is a different one, and that’s what I think is important: to have a responsibility toward the world that we live in, and I don’t take it for granted.” He told the press conference that this movie speaks on those themes, especially “how much we are willing to see, feel, welcome [each] other” and “how much we are going to isolate ourselves and criminalize and dehumanize each other.” Cruz and Bardem were both probed on starring in Oscar-worthy films this year, Bardem’s The Beloved and Cruz’s Olivia Wilde hit The Invite , and conceded they were proud to represent their country on an international scale. But the Spanish actress also talked about being a woman in the industry and feeling pulled to intriguing female characters when reading a screenplay: “This woman says precisely the things that I usually think, and so I really wanted to be able to express these things and these feelings in public. This is why I wanted to be a part of this film,” she said. Cruz added that sometimes women “are used as puppets, and this is very sad.” She told the room: “There are few women who take very important decisions in the world, and I think this is a very sad reality. We are sort of manipulated, and I have to say that I’m usually quite optimistic. [But] when it comes to the role of women in the world, I am slightly worried. However, I do think that younger generations are realizing our importance, and so they’re starting to think this way, and they are opening their eyes. And maybe young people are more interested in politics now than they have ever been in the past.” Graham, Dano and Schwarzenegger weighed in on being a part of Zeller’s project, gushing over the filmmaker and his script. But the married Spaniards were the heroes of the presser, and even joked about arguing over their work: “No, no, never!” replied Bardem, prompting laughs from the room. Cruz chimed in: “I’ve known you for more than 30 years… Imagine if we never argued!” The 2026 Venice Film Festival runs through Sept. 12. THR

articles.title: Levan Koguashvili Brings ’90s Georgia to Venice With Comedic Drama ‘Guria’
articles.full_text: Sep 8, 2026 4:25am PT Levan Koguashvili Brings ’90s Georgia to Venice With Comedic Drama ‘Guria’ By JD Linville Plus Icon JD Linville Latest Thomas Heise’s Final Documentary ‘Übergang,’ a Potential Locarno Highlight, Reflects on Time and Transience 1 month ago Low Light Films Boards Locarno Competition Thriller ‘O Jacaré,’ Basil Da Cunha Celebration of Lisbon’s Vibrant Reboleira District (EXCLUSIVE) 1 month ago Annecy Young Audience Award Winner ‘Into the Forest’ Finds Freedom Through Imagination 2 months ago See All 'Guria' Courtesy of Venice Film Festival Levan Koguashvili ‘s “Guria” will world premiere in Venice’s Spotlight section on Sept. 9. The black-and-white tragicomedy, set in the western Georgian Guria region, follows Zuriko, a 45-year-old widower and farmer as he struggles to find love, as well as a fair price on hazelnuts. “Guria” is a co-production between Georgia ‘s Kino Iberica, Switzerland’s Cineworx, Luxembourg’s Tarantula and Bulgaria’s ArtFest, with support reaching further afield, including Turkey’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism, Norway’s SoRFond Film Fund and Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Fund. Related Stories Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers' Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: 'We Are the Opposite of Politicians ... We Are the Antidote' It’s the director’s fourth feature, following “Street Days” (2010), winner of a Tiger Award at Rotterdam; “Blind Dates” (2013), which scooped the Special Jury Award at Abu Dhabi, and “Brighton 4th” (2021), which took prizes at Tribeca and Cottbus. “Guria” was written by Koguashvili with Boris Frumin, a former professor and longtime collaborator. Popular on Variety Variety spoke with Koguashvili in Venice about “Guria” ahead of the film’s premiere. This project is a seven-country co-production with global financing. Can you discuss how Guria came to interest so many parties in telling a Georgian story? Koguashvili : Basically, the idea of bringing in so many parties came from financing. We had to look for many co-producers. In our case, you get a little bit of money from different places. Of course, it’s harder to manage a production when so many people are involved, but on the other hand, it makes for a very international crew. You have a sound guy from Switzerland, an editor from Luxembourg… it’s fun. I was really grateful that people got interested in this crazy story about friendship and love in Guria and found support in different countries. And Saudi Arabia came in at the very last moment. We were still raising money for some pickup shoots, and we brought the film to the Red Sea industry park and showed 20 minutes. We won a couple of awards there, and that’s how the Saudi co-producers came on board. It was a really great help, at the very last moment. Can you talk about co-writing the film? What did that collaboration look like, and what did each of you bring to the story? Koguashvili : Boris was my professor at NYU’s graduate program, and we ended up becoming friends and working together after school. There’s a an age difference (he’s almost 80 now), but we started collaborating during my first film there, and it’s kept going ever since. The way it works: I bring the material, Georgian scenes, life situations, characters, protagonists, and we discuss what to do with it, how to connect the story. What matters most is having strong scenes. You need a handful of very strong, cinematic scenes, and the rest can be good around them. So I lean hard on that. Boris is great at organizing and constructing material. He’s very much a teacher in that sense, about the logic of story development, and that’s what I learned from him. I loved his classes, in terms of how he approaches structure. What about Georgia and Guria in the ’90s make it the time and place to anchor this story? What has changed about that world? Koguashvili : I like Georgian provinces very much because they still have an authentic feeling. Big cities look alike everywhere now, but the provinces have their own flavor, and Guria especially has a very strong character. So it was already somewhere in my mind. Then I happened to read a book, “Gurian Diaries.” It was melancholic, about the poverty and the humor of that time, but there wasn’t really a story in it, just a guy remembering his childhood. I liked the atmosphere, so I called the author and asked if he had a concrete story. He didn’t, but he suggested we go to Guria together and see what we’d find. I spent maybe two or three months there. Once I felt I had enough material, I took everything to Boris, and in about three days we had the shape of a story, a plot. Your work tends to straddle this line of hardship and comedy. What draws you to that place, finding light in the darkness? Koguashvili : Several things, maybe, but mostly, this is how I see life. I don’t see even tragic moments as complete tragedy; life is always full of dimensions. By introducing irony and humor, you don’t make a tragic story less tragic. It just gets a different feeling, it becomes more human, and it’s easier to digest. It also gives the story a kind of lightness and lyricism, which I love. I believe tragedy and drama have to be told with some comedy in them. You try to find levity or humor even in the darkest, most dramatic situation. It’s also a way of working against cliché: when you think of the ’90s in a post-Soviet country, you picture a very dark movie, right? But I think that’s become a cliché too, and working against it is its own challenge. Also, Georgian character isn’t simple. Georgian life in that period was extremely difficult, but there was also a kind of absurdity to it, even a charm. So many things, but usually the films I love have that quality. They’re all comedies about tragedies. It’s a very tragic story, but the telling of it is full of comedy. How did you come to use singing and song as such an important narrative tool in Guria? Can you talk about the songs the characters sing through the film? Koguashvili : Georgia has a very strong tradition of folk singing, and Georgian singing is polyphonic. Usually there are three voices, but depending on the region, some songs have five, six, sometimes seven parts. It’s very complex, almost like Stravinsky, in a way. If you listen closely, it’s an absolute improvisation, done by people with no formal musical education, just peasants improvising, but creating enormously original music. Singing is also very much part of Georgian culture more broadly, of the Georgian dinners we call supra, when people gather around the table. I grew up in a family where we had those dinners often, 20 or 30 people coming to the house, drinking wine, and singing. So for Guria, I met a very interesting composer, the head of a folk center who works with traditional folk musicians. I told him I wanted to do something in the Georgian tradition but approached differently, not polyphonic, but a single voice, because a single voice felt more intimate to me. He’s from Guria himself, so he understood what I meant. articles.title: Elon Musk’s Ex Ashley St. Clair on Rejecting a $40 Million NDA and Participating in ‘Musk’ Doc: ‘I Hope the Risk in Trying to Fight Back Helps a Little Bit’
articles.full_text: Sep 8, 2026 4:37am PT Elon Musk’s Ex Ashley St. Clair on Rejecting a $40 Million NDA and Participating in ‘Musk’ Doc: ‘I Hope the Risk in Trying to Fight Back Helps a Little Bit’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Elon Musk’s Ex Ashley St. Clair on Rejecting a $40 Million NDA and Participating in ‘Musk’ Doc: ‘I Hope the Risk in Trying to Fight Back Helps a Little Bit’ 2 hours ago Summer Box Office Breaks All-Time Record With $4.67 Billion 19 hours ago Ellen Burstyn Cries as She Gets Venice Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement: ‘It’s One Thing to Win an Oscar, Tony or Emmy — All of Which I’ve Won. But This Is a Lot’ 23 hours ago See All Michael Buckner Elon Musk ‘s ex Ashley St. Clair spoke about her decision to reject a $40 million non-disclosure agreement after the influencer gave birth last year to Musk’s 13th child. By turning down the alleged payday, St. Clair was able to sit for an interview in “Musk,” a new documentary from Alex Gibney that seeks to make sense of the controversial billionaire who has outsized influence on the world in which we live. “When you are offered something like that, it creates a debate about what your speech means and how valuable that is,” St. Claire said at a Venice Film Festival press conference for “Musk,” which premieres on Tuesday. “Why do they want to offer me this amount of money to not speak?” Related Stories Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers' Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: 'We Are the Opposite of Politicians ... We Are the Antidote' St. Claire participated in the doc to “set the example for my kids that we should never take being materially comfortable that we’re speaking the truth,” she said. St. Clair gained prominence as a right-wing political commentator who advocated for conservative and anti-trans politics. She is now expressing her regret for platforming those beliefs, which she chalked up to her youth and confidants at the time. Popular on Variety “I got involved with Republican politics when I was 18 after I met Charlie Kirk, and there was an air of ignorance,” said St. Clair, who is now 28. “But that ignorance does not excuse any role in that. I hope the risk that I’m taking now in speaking out and trying to fight back at least helps a little bit.” Gibney, an Oscar-winning documentarian, has investigated corrupt corporations (“Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room”), sexual abuse coverups in the Catholic Church (“Mea Maxima Culpa: Silence in the House of God”), Scientology (“Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Disbelief”) and alleged Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election (“Agents of Chaos”). Gibney began working on a film about the tech titan and world’s richest man, with an estimated net worth of $900 billion through ventures including SpaceX and Tesla, back in 2023. “The thing that struck me most, particularly early on, there was a tremendous sense of fear of talking — both among people who were his critics, colleagues and friends,” saidGibney said. “I talked to many, many, many people. Many declined to speak.” Gibney and St. Clair were joined at the press conference by another interview subject, tech journalist Zoë Schiffer. “Musk,” which premieres at the festival on Tuesday, is nearly four hours long — and Gibney joked he didn’t set out to make such a long movie. “We intended to make a shorter film before Musk became wrapped in the career of Donald Trump and the United States,” Gibney said, adding the first thing he did was reach out to Musk, who declined to be interviewed. “Musk” promises to reframe all we know about him, “revealing that the so-called ‘visionary genius’ is little more than the 21st-century reincarnation of a confidence man,” according to the synopsis. Musk himself has said that perceived reality may be nothing more than a simulation, and Gibney argues “even his most heralded accomplishments are rife with illusion and misdirection.” Musk’s recent ventures include buying Twitter (and renaming the social media platform X) and starting xAI and its chatbot Grok. Although Musk didn’t participate in Gibney’s doc, he long ago called the film a “hit piece.” Gibney called Musk a “very dangerous” man and expressed a deep worry about Musk’s unwillingness to show concern about other people. “I would say he has a very difficult time with empathy, especially cognitive empathy, which is putting himself in the shoes of others,” Gibney said. “He seems incapable of doing that.” Added St. Clair, “He makes a conscious choice to not put himself on other people’s shoes. It is a deliberate rejection of empathy.” Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’ Berlinale Title ‘Members of the Problematic Family’ to Open Indian Film Festival of Melbourne (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... articles.title: ‘Musk’ Review: Alex Gibney’s Definitive Documentary Puts the Pieces of Elon Musk Together — It’s a Lacerating Portrait of Technocratic Brilliance, Power Lust and Crackpot Delusion
articles.full_text: Sep 8, 2026 5:05am PT ‘Musk’ Review: Alex Gibney’s Definitive Documentary Puts the Pieces of Elon Musk Together — It’s a Lacerating Portrait of Technocratic Brilliance, Power Lust and Crackpot Delusion Once you start lining up Musk’s scandals and cut corners, you see that he’s a creator of mirages who promises more than he delivers. By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest ‘Musk’ Review: Alex Gibney’s Definitive Documentary Puts the Pieces of Elon Musk Together — It’s a Lacerating Portrait of Technocratic Brilliance, Power Lust and Crackpot Delusion 1 hour ago ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: Nathan Fielder’s Documentary About Elizabeth Holmes Is a Shameless, Fascinating, Reality-TV-Eats-Its-Tail Look at Entitled Duplicity 1 day ago ‘The Debut’ Review: Julianne Moore Is Astonishing in Jesse Eisenberg’s Funny and Dizzying Community-Theater Comedy 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Venice Film Festival When a subject has been as exhaustively covered — and as infamous — as Elon Musk , the electric-car-entrepreneur-turned-rocket-man-turned-richest-billionaire-in-the-universe-turned-Twitter-disruptor-turned-DOGE-destroyer-turned-God-only-knows-what-he’ll-do-next, reviews of a documentary about him tend to lead by plucking out the film’s incendiary bits of investigative reportage, the ones that feel worthy of a news headline. “ Musk ,” Alex Gibney ’s 3-hour-and-45-minute documentary about the tech bro who would be king, has a handful of those. Related Stories Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers' Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: 'We Are the Opposite of Politicians ... We Are the Antidote' The biggest revelation, to me, was the film’s detailed history of Musk’s attempt to put a self-driving car on the market — a technology that’s sure to be here at some point, though Musk, in his race to be first, was far too eager to announce that it had already happened. Tesla released its Autopilot driver-assist system in 2015 (and then the Full Self-Driving Beta program in 2020), marketing the new technology with ads that exaggerated the car’s powers. And so people were suckered. From the outset, there were accidents. More than 60 fatalities have been linked to Tesla’s driver-assistance systems. Talk about something that could put a dent in your image! But Musk, for the most part, succeeded in hushing up the lawsuits, the federal investigations, and the fatal crashes, which were evidence of a recklessness that should have given the whole world pause. Popular on Variety There are other places where Gibney colors in sides of Elon Musk you knew in a cursory way. It’s well-known that Musk has fathered many children — at least 14, though the people around him say it’s many more. He believes his progeny to be part of a larger war against population decline. The documentary, which features a highly illuminating interview with his ex Ashley St. Clair, goes into the details of how Musk, apart from his two spouses, would zero in on young women he thought would make good “breeders” and get them pregnant, dropping all interest in them after the babies were born. (They were required to sign NDAs.) The film also goes into details of his alleged drug use (ketamine, Ecstasy, psychedelic mushrooms). Yet what makes “Musk” such a lacerating and important watch, grounded in Alex Gibney’s supremely insightful but user-friendly mastery of the documentary form, is that it takes this flamboyant and in many ways elusive figure, with his tech ambitions and cosmic dreams and malignant megalomania, and puts him together, letting us see how one chapter of his life led to the next, and how the Musk dream wasn’t always so grandiose. You can see it evolve right along with his look. In the mid-’90s, at his first company, the relatively modest Zip2 (which essentially put the yellow pages onto the Internet), he looks just like the tech geek he was inside, skinny and unthreatening, with receding hair and a rabbity grin. But it’s not long before his Ayn Rand ambitions start to poke through. The hair fills in, the body thickens, and the smile gets elevated into a kind of aggro leer, as Musk makes himself over into his version of a tech-head Nietzschean superman. Gibney plays around a bit, creating a synthetic “interview” with Musk (who, of course, wouldn’t cooperate with him) by putting verbatim quotes of his into the mouth of an AI Elon. Late in the movie, when Musk is wreaking the havoc of DOGE, we see him killing off bureaucrats as if in a first-person-shooter video game. From the start, Musk has three obsessions: the Internet, energy, and space exploration. He first tried to purchase old Russian ICBM rockets (minus the nukes they were built to carry) for $3 to $5 million, and Gibney shows a fitting admiration for the innovation of Musk’s space dreams. He was leading a movement that was organic: the privatization of space exploration, which resulted from the U.S. government having lost all passion for it. The thrill was gone — for NASA, and maybe for the public. But Musk rekindled that (working in cooperation with President Obama). Sending up rockets was his original and driving obsession. Musk thought of himself as an engineer-magician in the mold of Steve Jobs. With SpaceX, even Musk’s failures (i.e., the first three launches) were spectacular. But he might have gone bankrupt if the fourth launch hadn’t connected. In a way, you could say that the first semi-scandal of Musk’s career was the way he took over Tesla, a sports-car company co-founded by Martin Eberhard in 2003, and then erased Eberhard out of the narrative of the company. Instead, it would all be his, with Musk showcased as the sole visionary — the Henry Ford — of the electric-vehicle revolution. His genius was marketing the Tesla as less a car than a shiny new tech gizmo on wheels. Yet this required a lot of smoke and mirrors, like the Tesla battery fraud: the claim, sold in advertisements, that you could just swap a new battery into a Tesla (it would be as easy as replacing two double-AAs!), when in fact the Tesla battery weighed 1,000 pounds. What Musk was selling was pure fiction. When people started having problems with the cars, Musk established a boiler room full of scammers who took the calls and lied about how the cars could be fixed. In essence, he was gaslighting his customers. The second scandal, according to the movie, is the way he gaslit his first wife, Justine Wilson (who is also interviewed), after their first child died of SIDS-related causes. “Musk” opens on something that’s not new ( I wrote about it five years ago ), namely Musk’s ardent belief in simulation theory — the notion that we are all very possibly living in a giant simulation, an idea bolstered for Musk by his love of video games, which became more and more sophisticated in their creation of simulated realities. The way he saw it: Who’s to say that we’re not all just part of a digital dream landscape, and that there isn’t some cosmic force out there playing us? While it doesn’t spend a lot of time on this idea, “Musk” uses it make a point: that anyone who truly believes this — and thinks it’s the higher wisdom — may not be in complete possession of his marbles. It’s not that Musk is less than brilliant. It’s that it’s his very brilliance that leads him to invest in the idea that his fruitiest fantasies are reality — like the one he began to evolve out of SpaceX that said we were on the verge of colonizing Mars. There was no truth to it. But Musk, like his future frenemy Donald Trump, was starting to think that he had the power to create his own reality. Once you start piecing together Musk’s scandals and cut corners and slipshod management, you see that he’s a creator of mirages who promises more than he delivers. There’s no question that the Tesla, as he finally designed it, is a strong and beautiful car, and that Musk’s early advocacy of electric vehicles was a positive force in the world. But his rocket program is increasingly mired in a kind of sci-fi stasis. (His fixation on Mars is right out of the cheesy ’50s.) And when Musk took over Twitter, which he had to borrow so much to buy that he wound up slashing the company to ribbons, it was a lesson in atrocious management (which he camouflaged as a testament to free speech), and he then applied that experience — as if it were a positive prototype — to his slashing of the government under Trump. He was out to make destruction look cool. Increasingly, though, his ventures began to seem like they were about little more than Elon’s simulated glory. Musk, as the documentary makes clear, is a genuine if flawed technocratic visionary, a messianic opportunist, and something of a crackpot. Around the time he was given a cameo in “Iron Man 2,” he’d begun to think of himself as a Tony Stark figure: a superhero right out of the comics. He used his Starlink satellite technology to influence the war in Ukraine (not necessarily in a good way), and he became a mega-donor and collaborator of Trump’s, in no small part, to squash the federal investigation into the Tesla Auto-Drive fraud. In doing so, he demonstrated that tech fascism doesn’t need to be a form of government; it can do an end run around government to control people’s lives by reducing them to cogs. That, “Musk” argues, is the world Elon Musk has been building up to, not intentionally at first, but once he got a taste of power. The film says that what should scare us about him is how he coddles his own interests by passing them off as the world’s. ‘Musk’ Review: Alex Gibney’s Definitive Documentary Puts the Pieces of Elon Musk Together — It’s a Lacerating Portrait of Technocratic Brilliance, Power Lust and Crackpot Delusion Reviewed at Bleecker Street Screening Room, New York (Venice Film Festival, Out of Competition), Aug. 31, 2026. Running time: 225 MIN. Production: A Bleecker Street release, in association with HBO Documentary Films, Ronan Production Group, of a Jigsaw Productions, Anonymous Content, Closer Media, Double Agent production. Producers: Zhang Xin, Joey Marra, Nick Shumaker, Jessica Grimshaw, Dana O’Keefe, Ronan Farrow, Lawrence Wright, Jessie Deeter, Erin Edeiken, Alex Gibney. Executive producers: Executive Producers: William Horberg, David Levine, Richard Perello, Yariv Milchan, Michael Heimler, Natalie Lehmann, Emily Selinger, John Friedberg, Kent Sanderson, Tyler DiNapoli. Crew: Director: Ales Gibney. Screenplay: Alex Gibney, Michael J. Palmer. Camera: Benjamin Bloodwell. Editor: Michael J. Palmer. Music: Daniel Pemberton. With: Elon Musk, Justine Musk, Ashley St. Clair.
