articles.title: Javier Bardem & Penélope Cruz Talk Playing Fictitious Arguing Couple In ‘Bunker’:  “We Are Very Good At Creating Fiction & Reality” – Venice
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Renate Reinsve, Johnny Flynn & Vicky Krieps Set For Mia Hansen-Løve’s Mary Wollstonecraft Picture ‘If Love Should Die’ As Goodfellas Boards Sales – TIFF France & Korea Pledge $1.16B For Global Screen Industries At South Of France Cinema Summit Gaza Cinema Academy Launches At Venice Film Festival To Help Gazans Tell Their Own Stories View All September 8, 2026 6:25am Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz attend Bunker Photocall at Venice Film Festival Kate Green/Getty Images A-list couple Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem touched down at the Venice Film Festival on Tuesday for the competition world premiere of Oscar-winning French director Florian Zeller ’s highly anticipated thriller Bunker . Bardem plays an architect who takes on an ethically questionable project to build a survivalist bunker for a tech billionaire, in a move that will lead his wife (Cruz) of seventeen years to question their relationship. It marks the first time the stars who wed in 2010, and share two children together, have shared the big screen together in the role of a fictitious married couple. Related Stories News Casey Affleck On 'Company': "I Was Responding In Part To Raging Conflicts In The World, And To Things Inside Myself" -- Venice Documentary 'Musk' Review: World's Richest Man, And His Digital Avatar, Thrashed In Damning Alex Gibney Doc - Venice Film Festival The couple were asked at the press conference for the film whether they had put any of their real-life marriage into the roles, and whether they sometimes argued about work. Watch on Deadline “We are very good at really creating fiction and reality; otherwise, we won’t survive in this job,” replied Bardem. Cruz said it would be unimaginable that they had never argued once over the course of their 30-year relationship but that they rarely got heated over work. “We both really love this profession, but it’s true that there is a good balance in terms of how much you are speaking about work,” she said. “Obviously, if you are preparing a movie together, obviously that is going to be very present in the conversations. But we haven’t done this very often… it has appeared like every five years because all the things that we were offered, we didn’t think they were for us, or for us at that specific moment.” “But with this, there was no question because it was with Florian. When we had the first meeting with him about it, because we both loved the script, we knew that we were going to be protected.” Cruz suggested Zeller had a way of getting an actor to bring their life experiences to their performances, without bringing in their personal life. “Have somebody like him in the middle, you feel safer because you know there are going to be days that are more tricky, big arguments in the movie… emotional scenes… and I’m very grateful to Florian because he was always watching us, always feeling and seeing everything, without invading, he was a real protection for us in that way, and it was really beautiful to have that.” Zeller said he had approached the couple for the film simply because he “adored them” but also admitted he was intrigued as to how the fact they are a real couple would impact the film. “They are among the greatest actor actors working today, and so obviously it was an honor for me to work with them,” he said. “But I have to say that from the very beginning, I was also interested in having them together on screen, because I thought it would be a unique way to capture something special as a real couple, to give layers to all the scenes of this film, to blur the line, between reality and fiction, but to try to approach something that I’m interested in, which is the burning authenticity of the truth, and to do that for actors, you have to be very bold, you have to be very fearless and ambitious, and this is what they are, and that’s why they are such great artists.” Trump Admin Attacks UK Plan To Boost BBC Content On YouTube Apple TV & HBO Max Set Primetime Showdown After Early Wins; Winners List; More U.S. Summer Record In Play As Spidey No. 1; ‘Odyssey’ Wins Global Battle Surprise Movie ‘You Can See Everything’ Reviewed; More Pics In Focus Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Ellen Burstyn on Being “Recognized” by Marilyn Monroe, Changing Roles for Women With ‘Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 3:25am Ellen Burstyn Tiziana FABI / AFP via Getty Images Ellen Burstyn never met Marilyn Monroe. Not properly, anyway. By the time she walked through the doors of the Actors Studio in New York, Monroe was already dead. But the two women did see each other once, across a nightclub table, and Burstyn has been carrying the moment around for the better part of six decades. “I was enchanted just looking at her. She was such a magical creature,” Burstyn recalled, speaking to reporters at the Venice Film Festival, where she is presenting two films this year and will receive an honorary Golden Lion for lifetime achievement at a ceremony this evening. “And then she looked at me and nodded at me. I was very early in my career, and I thought: I’ve just been recognized by Marilyn Monroe. I carried that in my heart.” Related Stories Movies Gary Oldman Says a James Bond Has Been Picked -- and He's Hoping It's Jack Lowden TV Catherine Zeta-Jones' Real Swansea Accent Is Loud and Proud in Trailer for AMC+'s 'Kill Jackie' Burstyn plays a version of Monroe, an imagined projection as if the legendary actress had lived into her 90s, in Flesh Impact , a new short film from director Maggie Gyllenhaal ( The Bride! ). Dakota Johnson plays the younger Monroe in flashbacks. She also appears in Kornél Mundruczó’s drama Place to Be , which screens out of competition in Venice, as an elderly woman who strikes up an unlikely friendship with a middle-aged divorced man (played by Taika Waititi). “He’s the most talented, funny, nice, charming, adorable human being I’ve ever worked with,” said Burstyn. “The movie is about our relationship, and of course he’s a young man compared to me, and I’m much older, so it’s not a sexual relationship, but it is a love relationship [and] that’s what I think people are going to respond to.” Asked how the role of women in Hollywood has changed since she started out, the actress didn’t hesitate: “Oh my goodness. Enormously.” “When I first started working, which was 150 years ago,” the 93-year-old added, drawing a laugh, “there were no women on the set. There were no women in the crew. Nobody. It was all men. If a woman was on the set, then she was an actress.” The change, she said, came slowly and incrementally, one job at a time: first a script supervisor, then a camera assistant, then more. “Slowly that changed, until finally it’s gotten to the point where women are handling heavy equipment without even thinking about it, and they’re integrated into the crew.” The roles themselves took longer, and Burstyn had a hand in forcing that particular door open. The origin story of Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore , the 1974 road movie that won her the Academy Award for best actress, begins on the set of The Exorcist . John Calley, then running Warner Bros., called her agent and said the studio wanted to make another film with her. The scripts started arriving. “Every one of them was this old-fashioned idea of what women represent,” she said. “I didn’t recognize any of the characters as anything like the women I knew, or myself. Their husbands would go out and save the world, and when they came home, the women would hand them a cup of tea. It was that kind of supportive role.” So she made a counteroffer. “I said, ‘Well, I’d like to make a film about women as I know women to be.'” For a director, she picked “an unknown director” with a single feature to his name: Martin Scorsese . His working method, she said, shaped the film as much as the screenplay did. At the end of each shooting day, the company would rehearse the following day’s scene — and improvise through it. “That script grew into a film that I think is credited with helping to change the consciousness of women worldwide.” The Exorcist , by contrast, she described as both transformative and brutal. William Friedkin was “an extremely talented director,” she said, “but he was also one of those directors who would do anything to get a shot” — including, in her case, a back injury she says she should never have sustained. “It was a life-changing experience, but it was painful physically.” Asked about the through-line in her memoir — the way her discovery of herself as an actress ran parallel to her discovery of herself as a woman — Burstyn credited her decades studying with Lee Strasberg at the Actors’ Studio. “When you study with a master, it changes your life,” she said. “It changes who you are to yourself, because it brings you into areas not only of your art but of your own being and your own understanding. And it changes what you do forever.” The work never stopped, either. Even after winning the Oscar [for Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore ], and after Strasberg had put her in front of a classroom to teach, she was still turning up as a student. “I was still working for him,” she said, “bringing in scenes, bringing in difficult things.” The octogenarian mainly avoided politics during the talk, with only a side mention that “my country right now is providing a lot of material to be explored artistically and politically.” Asked if she had any advice for younger actresses coming up, Burstyn recounted her own encounter, early in her career, with a screen legend of her youth. “I met Bette Davis. She said, ‘the only thing that’s important is your work. Anybody tries to get in the way of you and your work. They’re your enemy’,” Burstyn recalled. “So that was my advice from the older generation.” THR

articles.title: Ira Sachs, Jordan Firstman and Diego Luna Among San Sebastian’s Film Talks Lineup
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 3:41am Jordan Firstman in 'Club Kid' Courtesy of Zurich Film Festival This year’s San Sebastian International Film Festival has unveiled a slew of top talent for its Film Talks slate. Among the high-profile names reflecting on their creative processes and films in a sit-down discussion will be San Sebastian jury president Ira Sachs , Club Kid director-star Jordan Firstman and Josephine ‘s Beth de Araújo. Filmmaker and Andor actor Diego Luna will also make an appearance, alongside Argentine filmmaker Benjamín Naishtat, Naëmi Ada, Fernando Postigo, Peter Decherney, Angelica Cantisani, Vanja Kaludjercic, Andrea Queralt, Maialen Franco, Beatriz Mbula, Dagmary Olívar Graterol, Wendy Espinal, Lucía G. Romero, Daysi Cruz Cid, Eva Montoya, Xixi Sofía Yen Chen, Herminia Loh, Cecilia Barriga, Antxón Gómez, Enric Pastor, Fran Araújo, Aina Clotet, Javier Ferreiro, Tiagx Vélez, Lluís Garau, Afioco Gnecco, Gloria Saló, Fleur Dopheide and Victoria Cazalla. Related Stories Movies Ellen Burstyn on Being "Recognized" by Marilyn Monroe, Changing Roles for Women With 'Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore' Movies Gary Oldman Says a James Bond Has Been Picked -- and He's Hoping It's Jack Lowden “The talks will also look at issues such as inclusion and anti-racist attitudes in the audiovisual world, the new narratives and authorships, creative residencies and international creation labs, the transformative power of the cinema and design and art direction,” said the festival. “They will also analyse the new ways of narrating family relationships, the body as a narrative device and the challenge of audiences, algorithms and audiovisual distribution.” San Sebastian’s opening film is Ghost Song from Fatih Akin. A number of buzzy projects are premiering in and out of competition, such as from Mike Leigh ( Tender Loving Care ), Pablo Larraín ( My Sad Dead ) and Jaime Lorente ( The Bad Son ). Competition highlights include Milo from director Nicole Garcia ( Oran ), a French drama featuring Marion Cotillard and Lurker star Théodore Pellerin; and In My Father’s Room , the directorial debut of Japanese novelist Maha Harada. Prolific German filmmaker Werner Herzog and British star Naomi Watts are receiving the fest’s Donostia Awards this year. THR

articles.title: ‘SNL UK’ Adds ‘Such Brave Girls’ Star Freddie Meredith
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 4:30am Freddie Meredith for 'SNL UK' Sky/Publicity Logo text Such Brave Girls star Freddie Meredith has joined the cast of Saturday Night Live UK ahead of its season two premiere. Fresh off his Edinburgh Fringe Festival debut with comedy show Need a Light? , nominated for the best newcomer award, the Brit joins the returning SNL UK ensemble: Hammed Animashaun, Ayoade Bamgboye, Larry Dean, Celeste Dring, George Fouracres, Ania Magliano, Annabel Marlow, Al Nash, Jack Shep, Emma Sidi and Paddy Young. Meredith, also known for his performance in Channel 4’s Big Boys , most recently featured in Kat Sadler’s twisted female-driven comedy Such Brave Girls on the BBC. He plays Josie’s embarrassingly needy and oblivious husband, Seb. Related Stories Movies Ira Sachs, Jordan Firstman and Diego Luna Among San Sebastian's Film Talks Lineup Movies Ellen Burstyn on Being "Recognized" by Marilyn Monroe, Changing Roles for Women With 'Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore' Among his comedy heroes are Jamie Demetriou, Tim Key, Tina Fey, Nathan Fielder, Kristen Wiig, Steve Coogan, Steve Carrell and Julia Davis. Meredith said about joining the show: “It will undoubtedly inform everything I do for the rest of my career, and I can’t wait for the experience.” “I trained at drama school and began working professionally in theater,” Meredith added about his background. “Over time, I found myself increasingly drawn to comedy and started doing stand‑up alongside my acting work, and that naturally led me into making short sketches online.” The next season of SNL UK is set to kick off on Sep. 12 with host Jeff Goldblum and musical guest CMAT. Broadcast live each week, the U.K. spinoff of NBC’s hit sketch series will once again welcome a different celebrity host and musical guest for every episode, alongside topical sketches, live music performances and a British take on the iconic Weekend Update segment. Last season’s celebrity hosts included Tina Fey — in a premiere that accrued an audience of over 220,000 — as well as Jamie Dornan, Riz Ahmed, Jack Whitehall, Nicola Coughlan, Aimee Lou Wood, Hannah Waddingham, and Ncuti Gatwa. SNL mastermind Lorne Michaels serves as executive producer on the show, and James Longman is lead producer. THR

articles.title: Laura Poitras Shares the Desperate Vision Behind Her ICE Documentary ‘They’re Here’: “What’s Happening in the United States Is a Nightmare”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All September 7, 2026 4:53am 'They're Here' Courtesy of Jack Califano Oscar-winning filmmaker Laura Poitras spoke bluntly at the Venice Film Festival Monday about the motivations behind her latest project, They’re Here , a 25-minute documentary that viscerally chronicles the Minneapolis resistance movement to ICE’s paramilitary occupation last year. “We believed in a sense of urgency in documenting this,” Poitras said of the film origins. “What we’re seeing in the United States is a nightmare, and we feel what’s happening in the mainstream media is that this kind of violence is being normalized. We believe very strongly in the power of cinema to denormalize this violence and to show what’s happening, so that you can feel the sense of terror.” They’re Here is Poitras’s first project since her Nan Goldin documentary All the Beauty and the Bloodshed , which won the festival’s Golden Lion in 2022 and later earned an Oscar nomination. Poitras previously won the best documentary Oscar in 2015 for Citizenfour , her landmark account of Edward Snowden and his NSA surveillance disclosures. Related Stories Movies 'Woman Unknown' Review: A Sharp, Haunting Portrait of Denmark's Post-War Reckoning Movies 'Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People?' Review: A Vietnam Vet Reckons With PTSD in a Heavy-Handed Trauma Drama Poitras co-directed They’re Here with Minneapolis-based journalist and documentarian Rachel Lauren Mueller. Told in the style of dystopian sci-fi cinema, the film starts in a picturesque wintry American Midwest landscape — but this is Trump’s America in 2025, where masked men are soon shown abducting children, as residents hide in the trunks of cars to safely get to work. Elsewhere, everyday American vacationers mill about at Minneapolis’ airport, gazing out the windows at shackled prisoners being dragged onboard planes nearby. They’re Here draws on dashcam footage, crowdsourced data visualizations and ground-level footage to reconstruct the resistance network and the cat-and-mouse surveillance tactics used by residents and ICE’s masked agents. “We were using the genres or language of dystopian cinema or horror to take us closer to reality, not to take us further away, and not to make fiction from reality,” Poitras explained in Venice. “This actually is the reality — the reality is a nightmare. The entire country is under attack, and immigrants are living in fear throughout the United States right now.” “Over the two Trump terms, we’ve seen that things have gotten more extreme, but people become used to certain things,” added Mueller. “So I think the real role of this film is to shake that up a bit — to change things from a space of intellectualization about these numbers and these images that we see, and to have it become more visceral again.” Poitras explained that the doc, like the resistance movement at its heart, emerged from a sense of solidarity with the immigrants who had made Minneapolis their home. “It came from a real sense of, ‘These are our neighbors, and we don’t want them stolen from us. We want these people to stay safe,'” she said. She also sees causes for both hope and despair in the Trump administration’s response to Minneapolis’ resistance, which she described as a “great success.” “At the end of the film, we say how these tens and hundreds of thousands of residents responded, and that ICE removed 80 percent of its agents. So there was a real response to this kind of resistance, which I think we can all take hope from,” she explained. “At the same time, ICE has a budget of $70 billion, which is just an astronomical amount of money. Additionally, in the last two months, 90,000 people were abducted. So it’s this is a record high that has happened in June and July. So ICE is absolutely still active. Their tactics just look very different now.” They’re Here is screening in Venice Open – Out of Competition, the festival’s nonfiction and special-presentation strand, and will have its world premiere in the Sala Grande on Monday afternoon. The film was produced by Mueller, Poitras and longtime Poitras collaborator Yoni Golijov, with ARTE France serving as co-producer. Submarine Entertainment Sales is handling U.S. sales. THR

articles.title: Ciara Miller Gets a Reality Check
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 7, 2026 6:00am “It’s what I would call a mindfuck at times, where I’m so happy about all of the opportunities, and I’m quite literally living my dream,” says Ciara Miller. She was photographed Aug. 24 at PMC Studios in New York. Styling by Eliza Yerry. Carolina Herrera sweater, skirt; State Property ring. Photographed by Nina Westervelt; Makeup: Kasey Spickard.; Hair: Weezy If you watch reality TV , Ciara Miller has been almost impossible to avoid lately. If you don’t watch reality TV, allow us to introduce the woman who apparently has been cast on all of it. There’s Summer House , the Bravo series she joined in 2021. Last year came Peacock’s The Traitors . This summer, she flew to Fiji to co-host Love Island USA: Aftersun . And on Sept. 15, having apparently exhausted the available supply of reality shows on NBCUniversal, she’ll turn up on ABC for season 35 of Dancing With the Stars . Related Stories TV Adele Zaikman on Winning 'DWTS: The Next Pro' and Daniella Karagach's Advice for Season 35 TV Alix Earle Finally Unpacks What Happened With Alex Cooper: "I Am Scared of Her" “The last couple months from Love Island to Summer House to Dancing With the Stars , that’s obviously insane,” Miller says. “It’s still kind of what I would call a mindfuck at times, where I’m so happy about all of the opportunities, and I’m quite literally living my dream.” Miller has been everywhere but to-her-self all at once: She’s careful about what she puts on plate, and she won’t say yes to every opportunity. “I’m just not that type to say yes to everything,” she says. “I also don’t want people to be so sick of me either. There comes a point where I’m like, you know what? I’m sick of seeing myself. So I’m sure maybe some people are sick of seeing me too. Take a little bit of a break, space things out.” It’s not exactly the career path the 30-year-old Miller envisioned growing up in Atlanta. She modeled as a teenager but went on to earn a nursing degree in 2018, eventually working as a traveling ICU nurse. When COVID hit, she found herself treating patients at a Brooklyn hospital. Cult Gaia top, skirt; Marie Mas earrings, bracelets (right hand); Christian Louboutin shoes. Photographed by Nina Westervelt Her route from intensive care to reality TV was surprisingly direct: through a boyfriend. She’d been dating Luke Gulbranson, then a castmember on Summer House , Bravo’s long-running series about a group of attractive young New Yorkers who spend their weekends drinking, hooking up and occasionally screaming at each other in the Hamptons. In 2020, Gulbranson invited her to join him in the house for season five. She never really left. Six years later, Miller has become one of Bravo’s more recognizable faces, parlaying Summer House into appearances on Winter House and The Traitors , then the Love Island hosting job and now Dancing With the Stars . She’d been trying to land that last one for a while. “I have talked to the Dancing With the Stars team for the past two years,” she says. “So when they wanted to have a call this year, I was like, ‘Absolutely, let’s do our yearly call because I’m obviously trying to be on the show.’” This time, the answer was yes. And as it happens, DWTS may be the one reality show Miller has been inadvertently preparing for most of her life. Long before the ICU or Bravo, she studied ballet, jazz and hip-hop. Miller calls herself “the show pony of my family” and remembers constantly staging homemade music videos for her grandmother, who took her to see Alvin Ailey performances. “I was always choreographing a music video for my grandmother to watch. Poor her — I mean, she would be proud of me picking up a pencil, literally anything,” Miller says. “[ DWTS ] is really a full-circle moment, coming back to my dancing roots and being able to perform on a stage this big.” Of course, there is a downside to spending six years turning your life into television: Eventually, your life becomes television. Miller learned that rather spectacularly this spring. She had been romantically involved with fellow Summer House castmember West Wilson when Wilson and Amanda Batula — one of Miller’s closest friends on the reality series — announced they were together. The very public betrayal left Miller wondering whether she wanted to return for season 11 and spend another summer under the same roof with the people involved. Wilson and Batula subsequently exited, while Miller stayed. “I definitely was very much on the fence about coming back to Summer House , full disclosure,” she says. But walking away would also have meant letting what happened determine what she did next. “I also felt like I’ve been in that house since I was 24, and these are my friends. Why wouldn’t I spend my summer how I’ve been spending my summer?” Miller says. “And to let a situation dictate where I’m going to be, I wasn’t willing to do that.” Wiederhoeft top, skirt; Marie Mas jewelry. Photographed by Nina Westervelt So she went back. And now, with Dancing With the Stars about to start, Miller is heading into yet another reality show — albeit one where, for once, all the drama is supposed to happen on the dance floor, but somehow always makes its way online. Reality TV can be a breeding ground for negativity, on- and off-screen. Miller has experience navigating the viciousness that can be the Bravo audiences, but she also was faced with criticism this summer from Love Island fans for her Aftersun hosting style. Dancing With the Stars fans are no angels either, and oftentimes, viewers’ pessimism centers mainly around a celebrity’s dance capabilities. Being judged on by performance rather than personality on a reality show “will be a whole different experience” for Miller. She also knows that’s “part of the experience” of Dancing With the Stars , but it won’t define her time on the series. “I don’t think you’re ever really prepared for the fandom, but I’ve been warmed up with the Bravo crowd, and honestly, even the Love Island fans, because they are a whole type of breed,” Miller says. “I’d like to say that I’m a little accustomed to fan feedback, and that’s great. We welcome it. Here’s the thing: You say thank you when you need to, and put your head down when you also need to.” Miller “love[s] to hear” viewer’s opinions, because “sometimes you can’t take their input and kind of tweak it and put your own spin on things.” But part of staying in the unscripted business is not paying mind to that negativity. “I don’t really ride the waves of what the fan response is typically, and that’s, a lot of times, how I get through it on Summer House and even Love Island ,” she says. “I like to see what everyone has to say, and I love that people will be talking about it. And hopefully, they’re nice. You just pray.” On Summer House , Miller knows she’s known for lounging in bed, so much so that her friend group was dubbed “Bed Bugs.” But on Dancing With the Stars , she’s ready to show off her competitive side. “I know part of my persona is being horizontal and in the bed, so people are really going to see me out of the bed,” Miller says. “People can only call me lazy for so much longer.” Much of Miller’s career has been dominated by reality TV. Her heart and soul are concentrated on Dancing With the Stars right now, but that doesn’t mean she’s not thinking ahead about a career away from cameras. “My wheels are always turning in terms of where I want to land and what would make sense for me as a landing pad post-reality TV. Because look, I’ll be honest, I’m not the reality TV girl that’s gonna get married on TV and have my kids on TV,” Miller admits. “The chances of that happening are slim to none. I’m a Capricorn. I’m always thinking five years ahead. But at this point in time, at this juncture, I’m not quite sure. I’m still figuring that out.” Photographed by Nina Westervelt This story appears in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: How a Sweet, Horny Hockey Show Rewrote the Rules of Independent TV
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content (L to R): Accent Aigu co-founders Brendan Brady, Jacob Tierney Ted Belton The story of Accent Aigu Entertainment, the Canadian production company behind 2026’s global TV breakout Heated Rivalry , began with a love story — between two dogs. Jacob Tierney was directing and showrunning on Letterkenny , the cult comedy he co-created with Jared Keeso, which aired on Crave in Canada and Hulu in the U.S. Brendan Brady had been brought on as a line producer. Both Tierney and Brady had dogs: Graham, a Lab/hound mutt, and Murphy, a black Labradoodle. “Murphy’s a boy. Graham is a girl. I know that’s confusing, but that’s crucial,” says Tierney. “We brought them together, and our dogs fell in love. That’s our meet-cute. For the next season, when we came back to do more Letterkenny , they got us a place where we shared a backyard so the dogs could play together.” Related Stories Movies Lee Chang-dong's 'Possible Love' Emerges as Venice Film Festival Sensation Movies Venice's Lone Female Competition Director May el-Toukhy on Gender Gap: "I've Never Heard a Female Director Being Called a Genius" “That was basically our lake house,” jokes Brady, referencing a much-memed scene from the season one finale of Heated Rivalry . “We decided to take it to the next level.” In 2023, after finishing Letterkenny and working on the first two seasons of its spinoff, Shoresy , Tierney and Brady left to launch Accent Aigu Entertainment. (The name, a tongue-in-cheek reference to Tierney’s Quebecois Francophone roots, was chosen “after several libations,” Brady admits.) The plan was to make independent TV in a new way that was both faster and cheaper without sacrificing creative vision. Cutting-edge TV on a budget. “The cost-effective element was what we were really excited about,” Brady says. “With Jacob’s amazing ability as a director and my experience as a line producer, we understood we could change the way production is made.” Three years and one low-budget Canadian queer hockey romance later, Tierney and Brady are more than just the flavor of the moment. Accent Aigu Entertainment stands as a model for something the international TV business is scrambling to figure out: how to make premium, globally competitive scripted television when the big streamers are no longer writing blank checks for it. Tierney and Brady applied their cost-saving strategies on the low-budget Letterkenny to Heated Rivalry. Lindsay Sarazin/Hulu The Accent Aigu method was honed on Letterkenny and its legendarily tight shoots. “People talk about how low-budget Heated Rivalry was,” notes Tierney, “but we shot six episodes of Letterkenny season one in 18 days. As a director-showrunner, my task was to create an aesthetic where we could do that and have it still be creative and visually appealing.” It starts with the scripts. On Letterkenny , Tierney and Keeso wrote “long scenes that were very still, not a lot of entrances and exits. Not a lot of movement,” says Tierney. “You can cover that in an aesthetically pleasing way so that the limitations turn into a choice. It’s a big master, you cover the close-ups, and then you’re done. Eight pages, eight minutes of the show, in like an hour and a half.” Hudson Williams, who plays Shane Hollander on Heated Rivalry, recalls the same approach on that show. “Jacob would use these long ‘oners,’ which are technically harder to achieve but if successful do save time over standard coverage,” he says. “They also look more cinematic than most TV shows.” The standard model of making television involves having multiple directors shoot each season, hired guns who come in to do one or two episodes each. Accent Aigu likes to lock in one or two directors for a whole season. (Tierney directed all six episodes of Heated Rivalry season one and will direct all of season two.) “The benefits are that you are not shooting blocks of TV, going back to the same locations over and over, which is how things are normally done,” says Tierney. “We shoot more like an independent film, location for location.” (L to R): Heated Rivalry stars Connor Storrie, Hudson Williams, director Jacob Tierney, producer Brendan Brady on the set of season 1. Sabrina-Lantos Adds Brady, “If you have an actor who you only need in one location or two locations, you can get them in for a day or two, as opposed to having them come in once a week for five weeks. It’s a model —especially in the Canadian system where budgets are restricted — that’s a very smart way to get television made. An independent film model for independent TV.” The original plan was to apply the Accent Aigu model to comedy. Then Tierney, who during the pandemic had become a voracious audiobook listener, discovered the hockey-romance subgenre and Rachel Reid’s Game Changers novels. The sweet and smutty tales involving same-sex romances between professional hockey players were below the radar of most television producers, but they were exploding on BookTok and had a fiercely devoted fan base. Tierney slid into Reid’s Instagram DMs and asked if anyone had optioned the rights. Nobody had, and Reid, a Letterkenny fan, was in. Jacob Tierney and Brendan Brady honed their “quality TV on a budget” style on cult Canadian sitcom Letterkenny . Courtesy of Lindsay Sarazin/Hulu Tierney adapted Reid’s second novel, Heated Rivalry , which follows two Major League Hockey stars, Canadian Shane Hollander (Williams) and Russian Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie) — fictional stand-ins for actual on-ice rivals Sidney Crosby and Alexander Ovechkin — who are drawn together into an intense, sweaty love affair. Tierney wrote the script on spec and pitched it to Bell Media, the owner of Crave, Letterkenny ‘s home network. Following the success of Bridgerton and The Summer I Turned Pretty , he knew Bell Media was looking for a romance series. But Heated Rivalry , with its queer storylines and graphic sex, felt risky — especially for Bell, which in addition to being the home of HBO in Canada, is the home of hockey broadcasting. “I read the first script and thought, ‘This is going to be special — [either] an insane flop or a real thing,’ ” Justin Stockman, vp content development and programming at Bell Media, told the Toronto Star . “Reading the second episode, I was sure I was going to get fired because it’s probably the most racy of all the episodes. But I thought, ‘This is worth getting fired over.’ “ Produced for roughly CA $3 million (about $2.2 million) an episode — a fraction of comparable HBO-level drama budgets — Heated Rivalry shot for 36 days in and around Toronto and Hamilton in spring 2025, doubling Ontario soundstages for Moscow, New York and a Las Vegas hotel room. The show leaned in on Accent Aigu’s playbook of long, unbroken takes and efficient indie film-style production. (L to R): Jacob Tierney and Brendan Brady share a laugh on the set Heated Rivalry. Sabrina-Lantos “Their approach was always, ‘Test it with less, and if it’s not enough, do more,’ ” Williams recalls. “In episode two, there’s the ice cream scene [set in Sochi, Russia]. At first it was just some chairs and tables on the volume stage, with the LED volume doing everything else. [But] it looked so fake that they scrapped the shoot. When we came back, they’d built a cafe and used longer lenses to make the background more out of focus. They tried less, and when it didn’t work, they added more.” Adds Storrie: “They prioritized the people, the connection and the world-building over having millions of resources. They played to their strengths — they were fast, precise and prepared.” On set, Brady kept morale up by periodically wandering into tense scenes in character as an invented superfan of Shane and Ilya. “He’d show up in the shower scene,” says Williams. “He’d do this dumb-jock-guy voice and say something like, ‘Hell yeah, fellas, I’m feeling it too!’ in relation to a certain excited appendage.” Tierney and Brady’s bet with Heated Rivalry was the old indie adage of producing for an underserved audience. In this case, that meant both queer fans hungry for a sexy romance story that doesn’t end in tragedy, and the large female demographic, the “wine mums” who make up the core contingent of Reid’s readership. “What we knew from the fans of the [ Heated Rivalry ] books is that they’re evangelical,” says Tierney. “They knock on doors, they tell their friends. They spread the good news online and on social media.” The show was designed to serve the superfans. Instead of a conventional will-they-or-won’t-they relationship drama, Tierney follows the books and gets straight to the sex. The approach annoyed some critics, but the fans loved it. When the first steamy 90-second trailer of the show dropped late last year, it exploded online, spawning a thousand TikTok memes. They knew they had something special. Connor Storie and Hudson Williams in Heated Rivalry. Courtesy of HBO Max/Photo Illustration by The Sporting Press Taking the series global, however, was a different challenge. Tierney and Brady held the IP for the show and had presold Canadian rights to Bell, so Heated Rivalry was less attractive for the global streamers — Netflix, Amazon or Apple — which like to buy all rights worldwide. And, outside Canada, few networks saw the commercial appeal of a horny hockey show featuring a lot of gay sex. “We were given a comically low offer, like $200,000,” says Tierney. “It was either 200 grand an episode or 200 grand for all six. For the world! And we’d have to pay for the dubbing and subtitles. Basically, it would have cost us to do the deal.” The show was saved by a buyer with a different appetite: HBO, which acquires territory by territory rather than insisting on the whole world. Jason Butler, HBO and HBO Max senior vp global content planning and programming, was an early booster and brought Heated Rivalry to HBO CEO Casey Bloys, who snatched it up for the main U.S. network as well as Australia. HBO would later take the show for most of Europe and Asia, with separate deals for Sky in the U.K., Movistar Plus+ in Spain and Neon in New Zealand. When the U.S. and Australia deals were finalized, HBO decided to go day-and-date with the Canadian premiere — with three weeks’ notice. “We could not believe the level of speed we were dealing with,” Brady says. “Between Nov. 1, when the show premiered, to Dec. 26, we were literally still finishing episodes.” “I was in the editing room, saying, ‘That music cue is wrong,’ while things are exploding online around the show,” Tierney recalls. “Ten days after the finale aired, we were at the Golden Globes party.” The explosion, when it came, was fast and total. Heated Rivalry was Crave’s biggest original series debut on record, with viewership up nearly 400 percent in its first week; a second-season renewal followed within days. On HBO Max, the show reached an average of 10.6 million viewers per episode in the U.S., making it the platform’s most watched acquired scripted series in history. Streaming minutes grew from roughly 30 million in its first week to more than 300 million by the season finale. Weeks after Heated Rivalry premiered, Storrie and Williams were presenting at the Golden Globes. Rich Polk/2026GG “When we acquired it, I had some sense that it would make some noise,” Bloys tells THR . “But over the course of two to three weeks, it was just steady growth. It was growing on the platform, growing online, growing in media … like a hockey stick, you know, up and to the right.” (Or just like, Brendan and Tierney might add, an accent aigu .) “I think what people responded to is the combination of the sex and the sweetness; I can’t think of another show that has that combination,” says Bloys. “There’s a sweetness to the story of Hudson and Connor, seeing them go from being waiters to walking red carpets in designer clothing … these sorts of stories don’t happen all the time.” If there’s a single lesson Accent Aigu wants the industry to take from all this, it’s about paying attention, early and seriously, to underserved audiences who are already organizing themselves online. “For years, TV executives have assumed certain genres only appeal to niche audiences,” says Brady. “What’s happening here proves otherwise.” Accent Aigu has since formalized its growth spurt into an actual company: Tierney and Brady, formerly co-presidents, have become chief creative officer and CEO, respectively, adding an entire C-suite, including Jayme Alter Wilson as president and Craig Merritt as CFO, with Lori Fischburg as the new head of production and Liane Cunje as development executive and producer. It’s built to scale up a slate rather than shepherd a single show. Heated Rivalry’ s Christina Chang, Brady, Robbie G.K., Tierney and Nadine Bhabha at the 2026 GLAAD Media Awards. Vivien Killilea/Getty Images The global success of Heated Rivalry , Tierney admits, “is not necessarily replicable.” What is, he argues, is the Accent Aigu approach of trusting a genuinely weird, specific creative vision and producing for the most passionate fans. “If you want to break through the noise, trust somebody to do something weird,” he says. “Whether it’s Taylor Sheridan or the guy that created Squid Game in South Korea, or Richard Gadd with Baby Reindeer or us with Heated Rivalry . If you let a weird person do a weird thing, people might pay attention to it. You might break through the noise and get that big return.” If Heated Rivalry has a lesson for executives or the industry writ large, that’s it, Tierney says. “It’s definitely not, ‘Let’s do more hockey shows.’ “ This story appeared in the Sept. 2 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Streaming Is Raising Prices Faster Than Cable Ever Did
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 6:05am Illustrated by Brian Taylor Yup, you’re getting screwed. The cost to simply watch new TV shows is up — way up — with streaming services delivering one wearisome price shock after another that rival the worst of the cable and satellite price hikes of yesteryear. Since 2022, streaming prices have risen more than three times as much as inflation (which is also too high). Behold some not-so-fun facts: · The price of Apple TV has tripled. The streamer launched at just $4.99 in 2019. It’s jumped 200 percent despite having the thinnest library — in terms of quantity, at least — of the major streamers. · Disney+ is right behind Apple TV. The service launched at $6.99 with no ads in 2019 and has since jumped to $11.99 with ads — or pay a whopping 172 percent more than its launch price. · Paramount+ ’s cheapest tier is up 80 percent in five years. Netflix Premium is up 125 percent since 2013. · If you want all eight major streamers without ads or bundle commitments, it’ll cost you about $151 a month. Four years ago, the comparable lineup cost about $90. So you thought you cut the cord, but now you probably have four, five or six cords — and each is auto-drafting from your bank account so you can keep watching Love Island and Tulsa King . The outlier here is HBO Max, having only climbed 23 percent over six years. HBO has been priced as a premium product for decades, however, and launched its streaming service in 2020 at a higher price point than the other services. And these numbers hide some recent drama. Apple TV went up 50 percent just in the past year. Peacock’s tiers likewise leapt about 50 percent. (It’s a bit wild that HBO Premium is only $3 more than Peacock Premium Plus, especially when the former gives you dragons and Hogwarts and the latter offers The Miniature Wife and Married at First Sight. ) Over the course of the past 12 months, streaming rates have collectively risen 11.8 percent. The biggest year of increase was 2023, when the streamers shot up an average of 17.7 percent. A Hollywood Reporter analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows cable and satellite prices, by comparison, rose an annual average of 3.9 percent — excluding a deregulation surge of the late 1980s, when the index peaked at 14 percent. But that was a seismic shift provoked by a federal intervention rather than, say, because Widow’s Bay is a good show, or “we’re pretty sure we can get away with this.” It’s worth pointing out that streaming hikes have wildly outpaced inflation — even with inflation wildly outpacing what should be inflation. Consumer prices have climbed an average of 3.84 percent annually since 2019, double the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent target. That number might still seem small, but it’s added up to a 33 percent increase in the cost of consumer living, which is why everything besides a Costco hot dog has gotten noticeably more expensive. This is also why streaming price hikes are such a gut punch — annual bumps of 10 or 15 percent compound fast. At this point, you might be wondering: Does this mean cable TV is now a better deal by comparison? Not at all, not unless you’re a massive sports fan or are really into the Hallmark Channel (hey, My Christmas Cowboy debuts in December). Fully loaded bundles from the likes of Spectrum and DirecTV cost north of $170. So what’s the solution? Just quietly suffer? Yes — in one way or another. You could do what your uncle commenting on this story on Facebook will suggest (perhaps in all caps): Buy an over-the-air antenna for $25 and tune into whatever the broadcast gods are willing to give you. But that way lies entertainment despair. Our TV past wasn’t actually better — you were just younger, so everything seemed better. The best hack comes courtesy of Gen Z, who have reportedly embraced streaming cycling. You

articles.title: ‘Primetime,’ Chris Rock’s ‘Misty Green’ and Latest Paul Thomas Anderson Movie Join London Film Festival Lineup
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 7:00am Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen in 'Primetime' BFI London Film Festival Hot off its Venice Film Festival premiere, Robert Pattinson ‘s Primetime is set to take on the BFI London Film Festival next month. The Oct. 7-18 event has unveiled even more additions to its starry, jam-packed lineup, including the U.K. premiere of Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall , the Oscar winner’s intimate recording of the Geese frontman’s solo piano performance at the legendary New York concert hall. The previously announced Artificial , starring Andrew Garfield and directed by Luca Guadagnino, is getting a Gala premiere with talent expected to attend. The movie chronicles the consequential days leading up to the sudden firing and reinstatement of Sam Altman as CEO of OpenAI. Related Stories TV How a Sweet, Horny Hockey Show Rewrote the Rules of Independent TV Movies Laura Poitras Shares the Desperate Vision Behind Her ICE Documentary 'They're Here': "What's Happening in the United States Is a Nightmare" From director-screenwriter Chris Rock is Misty Green in the fest’s “Journey” strand, starring Rosalind Eleazar, Adam Driver and Daniel Kaluuya. The comedy follows Eleazar as the titular character, stuck in the throes of a fading career, who has an old acquaintance re-enter her life. Also set to screen in London Film Festival ‘s “Create” strand is the latest documentary from Oscar winner Jonathan Glazer, titled Joy of Joys . The project intersperses clips from Abbey Road, where London schoolchildren film recording sessions with artists including Olivia Rodrigo, Arctic Monkeys and Jarvis Cocker, with daily recordings from kids in Gaza, Sudan, Ukraine and Yemen. Another doc, Everest: The Other Side , joins LFF’s “Journey” strand, following a mountaineering couple with a shared passion and ambition for the near-impossible from directors Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin. Finally, Inherit , from Banjong Pisanthanakun about a rich Thai family who fall apart with the arrival of a distant relative, will premiere in the “Cult” strand. The horror features a magnetic performance from Davika Hoorne. The BFI London Film Festival added sit-down discussions with Javier Bardem, star of the festival circuit’s Bunker , and Robert Eggers, gearing up to release the hotly anticipated Nosferatu follow-up Werwulf , to their Screen Talks slate. Check out the full Screen Talks lineup with Andrew Scott, Cynthia Erivo, Mahershala Ali, Jesse Eisenberg and more here . The world premieres from this year’s BFI London Film Festival include Brad Bird’s Ray Gunn and Travis Knight’s Wildwood , as well as star-powered screenings of Ink , Wild Horse Nine , Club Kid , Paper Tiger , Possible Love , Bunker , Tender Loving Care and more. The festival will open with Elsinore and close with The Debut . THR

articles.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: Elizabeth Holmes Doc From Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim Is Fascinatingly Slippery, Dizzyingly Clever
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 7:36am 'You Can See Everything' A24 Elizabeth Holmes would like you to know that she has never lied. Not just about Theranos — about anything ever, she insists, her startlingly large eyes shining with conviction. She’s only been misunderstood because she thinks so differently, or misrepresented by outside parties pushing their own cynical agenda. You Can See Everything , a new documentary about the billionaire turned convicted fraudster, is ostensibly her attempt to change all that. In the spirit of radical transparency, she intends to finally get her real story out there, once and for all. Related Stories Movies Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's Elizabeth Holmes Doc 'You Can See Everything': First Reactions Movies 'Carl Sagan: We Are Made of Star Stuff' Review: Nanette Burstein's NatGeo Doc Prioritizes the Human Over the Intellectual, for Better and Worse You Can See Everything The Bottom Line Smart, funny and full of surprises. Venue: Telluride Film Festival Directors: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim 2 hours 54 minutes But if you’ve ever seen anything by its directors, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim , you’ll already know better than to expect something so simple. What begins as a fascinatingly intimate portrait of a deluded or disingenuous scammer reveals as something even wilder, more ambitious and less predictable, until we’re left to ponder what value a personal truth has at all. The nearly three-hour film, which had its world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival, splits cleanly into two halves. In the first and more straightforward, Fielder (and Oppenheim, and their crew, though of that contingent it’s only Fielder we see regularly) essentially embed in the beachside San Diego rental where Holmes, her partner Billy Evans and their two young children are enjoying the last weeks before Holmes is due to report to a Texas federal prison for an 11-year sentence. There, You Can See Everything is only too happy to satisfy the voyeuristic curiosity that probably brought you here in the first place. Fielder seems to be lurking behind every doorframe and around every corner, taking in every emotional conversation or casually intimate moment. (The couple’s very different approaches to scrambling eggs turns out to be weirdly telling.) His high tolerance for awkwardness means he’s willing to ask the questions we’re all thinking but might hesitate to pose ourselves — like “ Why ?” when Evans speaks about choosing to be a part of Holmes’ life essentially at first sight, despite the very public and sordid details of her then-recent downfall. Fielder’s presence in front of the camera (and eventually in their guest room, which comes with no mattress because Evans claims to prefer sleeping on bare bedframes) also means You Can See Everything dispenses with any pretense of “objectivity.” What it aims for, instead, is a kind of authenticity — the sense that it’s earnestly trying to understand Holmes’ mind and motives, even if the filmmakers don’t appear to believe for a second that she’s as innocent as she says; that Holmes really is trying her best to communicate her line of thinking, even if it requires Olympic-level mental gymnastics to justify it. The documentary’s time with the family is fruitful, in that they reveal Holmes’ psychology as a fleeting paparazzi photo or a carefully managed puff piece never could. And were You Can See Everything just a profile of Holmes on the eve of her sentence, it would be a captivating if slightly baggy document in itself, with no shortage of moments to make you groan or goggle your eyes. But it’s the second half, which picks up two years later, where the movie really kicks into gear. Its abrupt turns are so deliciously surprising I’m loath to give away too much detail. But I’ll say broadly that it gets excitingly meta and almost surreal in confronting the fact that Holmes is now in prison, and therefore unable to speak for herself in any length or depth. Control of her narrative has once again slipped outside her hands, and in her absence, the void gets filled by other means. One is Evans, who’s all too happy to speak on his partner’s behalf, down to posting as her from her verified X account. He doesn’t even need to consult with her to say what she thinks about this or feels about that, because their souls are just that united — never mind that he’s clearly an angry boor with controlling tendencies, or that he disregards her actual, previously-stated-on-the-record opinions whenever they’re inconvenient. Remember what I said about this film not pretending to be objective? It makes no bones about the fact that it absolutely loathes this guy. Another sticky version of Holmes’ narrative is the Hulu show The Dropout ; though it came out before Holmes’ incarceration, it continues to shape the public’s perception of her to a degree that all the other articles and books and podcasts about her have not. Just ask the barber who explains the plot of the miniseries to Billy during a cut and shave. But yet another, You Can See Everything is shrewd enough to realize, is itself. Even as Holmes has tried to explain herself, our understanding of her has already been filtered through the questions Fielder asks, through his and Oppenheim’s impression of her level of sincerity, through the choices they’ve made about which interactions to leave in and which to cut out. There’s also the barest suggestion that Fielder may have an eensy crush on Holmes — though the fact that the picture hints at said crush without stating it outright could just be another pointed example of how easily we can be manipulated into inferring the thoughts and feelings of other people. An increasing reliance on simulacra (supposedly necessitated by Holmes’ absence, but you’re not going to convince me the guy behind The Rehearsal wasn’t just dying to reenact some conversations in a recreation of the Bryan Federal Prison visitors room) adds another giddy layer of artificiality in this ostensible search for truth — as does the introduction of a third co-conspirator who lightly interrogates Fielder in the way he once did Holmes, and finds he’s as capable of evasiveness as anyone else. In one scene, this new colleague and Fielder find themselves outraged on Holmes’ behalf that a crass X response posted by Evans through her account “does not sound like her.” They’re almost certainly right, based on what we’ve seen of Holmes — and they also have about as much authority to determine what Holmes would or would not say as anyone who isn’t Holmes herself does. You Can See Everything reaches for accuracy in its portrayal of a much talked-about figure. It ends up asking, with plenty of humor but no small amount of wisdom, what “accuracy” would even look like in the first place. Full credits Venue: Telluride Film Festival Distributor: A24 Production companies: Blow Out Productions, To Be Formed Productions Directors: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim Producers: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, Tatiana Bears, Maggie Ambrose, Jack Davis Executive producer: Emily Osborne Director of photography: David Bolen Production designer: Alex DiGerlando Editor: Adam Locke-Norton Music: Ari Balouzian 2 hours 54 minutes THR

articles.title: Tokyo Film Festival Adds New Initiatives, Kashiko Kawakita Award to Honor Women in Cinema
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 7:39am Sahoko Hata Tokyo International Film Festival The Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF) is adding a series of new initiatives for its 39th edition. The festival is adding two new awards for the Nippon Cinema Now section; launching a new section titled Crosscut Asia +; and establishing the Kashiko Kawakita Award to honor women in cinema. The festival says the new initiatives “aim to enhance the global reach of Japanese cinema, foster next-generation talent and co-creation across Asia, and promote the preservation and continuation of diverse film cultures.” The two new awards linked to Nippon Cinema Now include best film and a special jury prize. The festival is looking to draw more attention to local talent and “provide stronger support for undiscovered Japanese talent— from promising newcomers to visionary veterans—and to bring their work to worldwide audiences.” Related Stories Movies 'Primetime,' Chris Rock's 'Misty Green' and Latest Paul Thomas Anderson Movie Join London Film Festival Lineup TV How a Sweet, Horny Hockey Show Rewrote the Rules of Independent TV “Through the establishment of a new competition within the Nippon Cinema Now section, we will shine a spotlight on exceptional new Japanese talent and introduce them to the world,” Takeo Hisamatsu, TIFF’s festival director, said in a statement. “We hope to give creators the courage to take on their next challenge while empowering them to advance to the global stage. By serving as a platform for emerging talent to take flight, the Tokyo International Film Festival aims to contribute to the growth and development of the Japanese film industry.” Crosscut Asia+ will be a new section at TIFF for 2026 is a joint initiative with the Japan Foundation, and highlights Southeast Asian cinema. The section carries on the work of a former Tokyo section, the Japan Foundation Asia Center presents Crosscut Asia, which ran from 2014 to 2019. Crosscut Asia+ “will feature a curated selection of films jointly chosen by vibrant film programmers from both the region and Japan, centered around a unique, annual theme from their distinct perspectives.” For the inaugural edition of Crosscut Asia+, programmers Raslene (Indonesia) and Ueda Masayuki (Japan) will present six films under the theme ‘Side by Side,’ featuring a lineup that ranges from timeless classics to recent releases. Included in the lineup are Rafael Manuel’s Filipiñana , Kamila Andini’s Four Seasons in Java , Polen Ly’s Becoming Human , Bachtiar Siagian’s Turang , Daniel Hui’s Small Hours of the Night , and Hafiz Rancajale’s Behind The Flickering Light: The Archive . For 2026, TIFF is also establishing the Kashiko Kawakita Award to honor women in cinema, and the organizer’s revealed that Sahoko Hata will be the inaugural honoree. The award was established by the Kawakita Memorial Film Institute and was conceived as a recognition “by women, for women“ as an “achievement award [that] honors individuals who have been advancing film culture both in Japan and internationally.” The award pays tribute to Kawakita Kashiko — affectionately known as “Madame Kawakita”— a trailblazing woman who bridged East and West through cinema and who played a pivotal role in founding the Japan Film Library Council and the National Film Archive of Japan. Honoree Hata, is an acclaimed Japanese critic who fostered filmic links between her country and France. The now 95-year-old began her career in the 1950s and was a key figure in Japanese film culture, who helped purchase and bring landmark French New Wave films such as Breathless , Purple Noon and Mon Oncle to Japan. “When I was first approached about receiving the 1st Kashiko Kawakita Award, my initial decision was to decline,” said Hata in a statement. “Throughout the pre-war and post-war eras — a time when women were not even permitted to participate — Mme. Kawakita was active with her own distinct eye for importing, exporting, and above all, selecting films. Her legacy remains a page in film history, as well as a chapter in the history of women. On one occasion, Mme. Kawakita whispered to me: “As women, there are so many moments where we must endure, aren’t there?” They were profound words indeed. It is precisely because I felt a compelling desire to pass this story on that I resolved to accept the award.” The Tokyo Film Festival runs from Oct. 26 to Nov. 4. THR

articles.title: Tom Rothman on Sony’s ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Blockbuster Success, Being Outbid for ‘Obsession’ and More
articles.full_text: Sep 7, 2026 4:13am PT Tom Rothman on Sony’s ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Blockbuster Success, Being Outbid for ‘Obsession’ and More By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Tom Rothman on Sony’s ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Blockbuster Success, Being Outbid for ‘Obsession’ and More 4 hours ago Tetris Company Distances Itself From Trump White House’s ‘Build the Wall’ Game, Says ‘We Take Copyright Very Seriously’ 3 days ago Digital Creator Skyelar Chase Signs With Innovative Artists Entertainment 3 days ago See All Getty Images Sony’s Tom Rothman took a bit of a victory lap with the studio’s boffo success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which has become the highest-grossing film of 2026 to date. Rothman, chairman and CEO of Sony Pictures Entertainment ‘s Motion Picture Group, spoke Monday at the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, an international film and entertainment conference hosted by the French government. He was interviewed at the event by Variety co-editor-in-chief Cynthia Littleton. Related Stories Telluride Festival Lineup: 'The Debut,' 'Elsinore' and 'Tender Loving Care' Set for Premieres, Tributes for John Malkovich, Sandra Hüller and Andrew Haigh Nathan Fielder Drops Weird Trailer for Secret Elizabeth Holmes Doc ‘You Can See Everything’ Since its July 31 release, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” has spun up a whopping $2.4 billion at the global box office, including $923 million domestically. About the success of the film, Rothman joked, “First of all, I can’t be wrong all the time. It’s against the law of averages.” Popular on Variety More seriously, he said, “For a result like that to happen, everything has to work perfectly.” Rothman praised the “incredibly talented” team that worked on the films, including star Tom Holland, who “has been our partner in this for over a decade now,” as well as the support of Disney and Marvel. Why have audiences turned out in droves to see it? Rothman said “Brand New Day” is “not so much a superhero film, but ‘super-person’ film. The reason that movie has resonated all around the world is because it’s about a lonely guy… It’s like yeah, it’s about friendship. It’s very human. It’s very emotional.” He said, “It’s got plenty of whiz-bang, but that’s not what the secret is. The secret is it’s a relatable story that almost everybody has related to.” Referring to the opening session at the Lumière Summit, at which French President Emmanuel Macron and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung unveiled a $1.16 billion entertainment industry financing partnership , Rothman said, “We had three presidents today: The president of France, the president of Korea. And you have Mr. Clooney , the president of Hollywood” — gesturing to George Clooney, who was sitting in the front row. Alluding to Mark Twain’s famous quote, Rothman said this summer in particular has demonstrated that the death of the theatrical business has been greatly exaggerated. This summer, “movies were cool,” Rothman said. “They became cultural again… because they were culturally significant.” In particular, Rothman called out “Obsession,” the low-budget horror film reportedly made for $700,000 that has banked nearly $510 million at the global box office. He said the success of “Obsession” shows that “it’s a misnomer that young people won’t go to movies.” Sony Pictures was outbid for Curry Barker’s “Obsession” by “a couple million dollars” by Universal’s Focus Features, which reportedly paid $14 million for the rights . When Sony was outbid, Rothman joshed, “I was outraged.” But, he added, “I would like to have that moment back. I congratulate the worthy opposition.” Speaking about Sony’s global film business, Rothman said that Netflix “was brave enough at the time” to finance animated musical movie “K-Pop Demon Hunters,” which has become the streamer’s most-viewed film ever. “That is a deeply Korean, culturally relevant film,” he said. The key having a globally resonant film or TV show, Rothman said, is to have it be specific to a time and place. “Specificity leads to universality,” he said. “I have seen it many times in my career.” Sony, for example, now has a big Japanese anime business, “and it does great.” “Stories are the things that… become our cultural heritage,” said Rothman. Rothman joined Sony Pictures in 2013 as chairman of TriStar Pictures before being promoted to chairman of Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group in February 2015 and then chairman/CEO in 2021. Previously, he was head of Fox Filmed Entertainment from 2000 to 2012. Starz’s U.K.-Set Boxing Crime Drama ‘Fightland’ Is a Knockout: TV Review Loading comments... articles.title: The Next James Bond Has Been Picked, Says Gary Oldman, Whose ‘Fingers Are Crossed’ for ‘Slow Horses’ Co-Star Jack Lowden
articles.full_text: Sep 7, 2026 4:35am PT The Next James Bond Has Been Picked, Says Gary Oldman, Whose ‘Fingers Are Crossed’ for ‘Slow Horses’ Co-Star Jack Lowden By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest The Next James Bond Has Been Picked, Says Gary Oldman, Whose ‘Fingers Are Crossed’ for ‘Slow Horses’ Co-Star Jack Lowden 3 hours ago ‘The Inbetweeners’ Original Lead Cast Confirmed for Netflix Reunion Movie as Production Kicks Off in U.K. 7 hours ago KJ Apa, Isabel May and Archie Renaux YA Romance ‘Falling’ Getting North America Theatrical Release From Brainstorm Media (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All Getty Gary Oldman ‘s connection to the world of James Bond may be unknown, but the actor claims to have some key information about the casting of the next 007. According to the Oscar-winning acting icon, the hotly-disputed and widely-debated hunt to find the next superspy is over, and he’s hoping his “Slow Horses” co-star Jack Lowden is the name ready to be unveiled. “It’s been rumored that [Lowden] is on the shortlist,” Oldman said in an interview with Canada’s “The Morning Show.” “We’re going to find out pretty soon, aren’t we? Because they have picked him. They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet. So my fingers are crossed for Jack.” Related Stories Jordan Firstman's 'Club Kid' Hits Telluride, and Colleen Camp Could Be Its Secret Oscar Weapon How John Malkovich’s 30-Year Oscar Drought Could Finally End With ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Wild rumors have swirled for years over who is set step to step into the blood-splattered brogues of Daniel Craig, but with the next film set to go into production next year, speculation has ramped up considerably. Popular on Variety While nothing has been confirmed as the casting is kept under arguably the tightest wrap of any film production, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson and Lowden have all been reported as among those in the final running. Variety wrote that there had been interest in Louis Partridge, while stage star Tom Francis had reportedly auditioned. Amazon MGM has repeatedly refused to discuss anything about who has or hasn’t been considered for the role. Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next Bond film, which is being written by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. Last month, Lowden’s wife Saoirse Ronan threw down the gauntlet to Bond producers about her being involved in the next film, telling Empire that she was “dead serious” about playing a Bond villain. “I think it would be really interesting, having a young female villain,” she said. “Especially for girls and women, to see someone who can just take all that pent-up anger and direct it somewhere, there’s something interesting in that dramatically. So I would love to do more of that.” Starz’s U.K.-Set Boxing Crime Drama ‘Fightland’ Is a Knockout: TV Review Loading comments... articles.title: Belgian Royalty Series ‘King of Hearts’ Secures Key VRT Backing (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 7, 2026 4:46am PT Belgian Royalty Series ‘King of Hearts’ Secures Key VRT Backing (EXCLUSIVE) By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest ‘Plaza Catedral’ Director Abner Benaim, Chile’s Daniela Vega and Alfredo Castro Board Fiction Series ‘School of the Americas’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Belgian Royalty Series ‘King of Hearts’ Secures Key VRT Backing (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago ‘Strawberry and Chocolate’ Star Jorge Perugorría and Brazil’s Thiago Lacerda Lead Havana-Set ‘Hotel Nacional’ (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago See All 'King of Hearts' Courtesy of De Wereldvrede Enterprising Flemish broadcaster VRT has boarded the historical coming-of-age drama series ‘King of Hearts’ from Giles Coulier, whose company, De Wereldvrede , is behind such hits as 2019 series “War of the Worlds” and Prix Europa winner, “Albatros.” As continental royalty series hit ratins and sales – think “Maxima” – “King of Hearts,” currently in development, has been selected to participate in the inaugural Euro-Atlantic Co-Pro Pitch program to be held at the Iberseries & Platino Industria confab in Madrid. Related Stories At Telluride Film Festival, Bill Gates Compares Lack of Control Over AI to HAL in '2001': 'You Could Say "Please Shut Down," and It Would Say, "OK, I Took That Under Advisement, But..."' Telluride’s Julie Huntsinger on Her 20 Years Leading the Festival, Chasing ‘Digger’ and ‘Dune 3’ and a ‘True TBA’ Film Hidden Until Patrons Walk Into the Theater Based on real events, the drama centers on Baudouin, introverted and insecure, who is made King before he is ready for the task. As Belgium descends into crisis and his family fractures around him, he is forced to confront the man and leader he wants to become. Under mounting pressure, he learns to make difficult choices, challenge his father’s influence and forge his own beliefs. But with power comes a darker temptation: to control others as he himself was once controlled. Popular on Variety Later in life, he tries to protect his nephew Filip from the same painful path he went through. But he slowly realizes how hard it is to become a better man than the father who raised him. “We are thrilled we can once again work on a fiction series that sheds light on an important chapter in our recent history. As a public broadcaster, we believe it is essential to tell these stories, but always through emotionally compelling, surprising and strong storytelling,” said Elly Vervloet, VRT international drama expert. “’King of Hearts is the coming-of-age story of King Baudouin, who, as a young and unprepared prince, had to ascend the throne at a politically very delicate moment for our country and the whole world. We see him struggle to find his own voice, torn between power and responsibility, manipulated by people around him with their own agendas. We are thrilled that the producers and creators of De Wereldvrede approached us with this story, so that we can develop it further together into an ambitious and emotionally resonant series. We hope to bring some strong international partners on board to bring this fascinating story to audiences far beyond Belgium.” For producer Gilles De Schryver, who co-founded De Wereldvrede with Coulier in 2013, “King of Hearts” is by nature an international story. “It moves between Brussels, Leopoldville, Rome and Madrid, intertwining Belgium’s monarchy with Congolese independence, Cold War geopolitics and Catholic influence. It is designed as a high-value prestige drama with global story reach and appeal only an international co-production can deliver.” The project has secured script funding from the Flanders Audiovisual Fund (VAF), with a further VAF application pending. According to the partners, De Wereldvrede’s “mission is to produce high-quality fiction for an international market, with a strong emphasis on the creator’s vision and a bottom-up production approach.” The company broke through with the TV series “The Natives” (CANVAS), followed by Coulier’s feature film “Cargo,” which screened at numerous international festivals. Their short films have also earned recognition, including “Stephanie,” an official Cannes selection and winner of the Ensor for Best Short Film, and the series “Lockdown,” which won an award at Canneseries. “Roomies” (2022) received international acclaim. In 2024, the features “Holy Rosita” and “Julie Keeps Quiet” premiered internationally, earning numerous festival selections and awards. “Julie Keeps Quiet” premiered at Cannes Critics’ Week and was selected as Belgium’s official Oscar entry. Both films won five Ensor Awards. In October 2025, the second season of “Roomies,” by Kato De Boeck and Flo Van Deuren, premiered at Film Fest Gent to five-star reviews. Nathalie Teirlinck’s second feature, “Jonah Was Here,” is currently in post-production, while Pieter Van Hees’ latest film, “Alors on Danse,” is in advanced development and scheduled to shoot in summer 2027. De Wereldvrede is also developing several other projects, including the feature films “Harvest,” “The Right to Say Goodbye” and “Dirty Kids,” as well as the fiction series “Recidive” and “Beats of Love.” The 6 th Iberseries & Platino Industria runs September 29 to October 2, 2026.
