articles.title: Vertical Video Studio LoveHit Launches With Adaptations Of Literary Classics Starring Microdrama Regulars & Eric Roberts
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse ‘SNL UK’ Adds Comedian & ‘Big Boys’ Actor Freddie Meredith To Season 2 Cast Dori Media Wants Buyers To Hunt ‘New Love’ At MIPCOM Dvizhon Studios Launches With Sex Education Series ‘The First Time’ A Featuring Puppet Presenter, Ukraine War Veteran & Social Media Star Tumazar View All September 7, 2026 7:15am Ethan Vaughan and Jean Evans in 'Wuthering Heights' Aleksandar Sekulic EXCLUSIVE: Literary classics such as Wuthering Heights and Jane Eyre are getting the microdrama treatment. This is through the latest entrant into the microdrama field, LoveHit , an L.A.-based studio and app focused on originals based on classic literary adaptations. LoveHit, which launches this month, has a vertical video slate built entirely from classic novels in the public domain. At launch, this will comprise Wuthering Heights , Pride and Prejudice , Jane Eyre , The Great Gatsby and Beauty and the Beast . More are in post-production, including Dangerous Liaisons , The Scarlett Letter and Les Misérables . Related Stories News David Oyelowo & Nate Parker's Mansa Studios Debuts Slate Of TikTok Microdramas News Kevin Hart's Hartbeat To House Vertical Originals On Microdrama Platform aTwist Each has been written, shot and edited as both a vertical series and a horizontial features, with the latter being readied for TV and streaming buyers worldwide attending MIPCOM on October 12-15 in Cannes. Series will last roughly 50 episodes running between one and three minutes, with the films at 90 minutes. Watch on Deadline Actors appearing in the titles include microdrama regulars Meg Bush, Tyler Harlow and Sophie Swiszcz, along film, television and stage stars. These include Academy Award nominee Eric Roberts, who appears in Jane Eyre , which stars Raina Silver and Tyler Harlow. Ethan Vaughan and Jean Evans will star in Wuthering Heights , which is relocated to a present day American ranch. A vertical cut of the show launched on the LoveHit app on August 27 ahead of the full launch. Other plotlines see Dangerous Liaisons adapted in a story where a Manhattan socialite hires the anonymous author of a scandalous blog to destroy her ex-fiancé’s reputation. The Scarlett Letters follows a woman who believes her husband died overseas only to fall for the young pastor helping her rebuild, while Les Misérables moves the story into college, following a student who loses everything before finding anonymity and income behind a webcam, only for someone to recognize her. “There isn’t a market in the world where these titles need much of an introduction,” said Lenny Levi, CEO of LoveHit. “Every generation has adapted them, and every generation finds its own reason to connect with them. That’s what makes them evergreen.” We hear LoveHit has been privately financed, with a group of investors supportive of the company’s growth and content strategy. Levi is an L.A.-based film and media producer with more than 15 years across production, business affairs, international distribution and emerging media. He has worked at Sony Pictures Entertainment, CBS Television Studios, Paramount Television Studios and Riot Games. He has produced multiple feature films and currently focuses on film and vertical storytelling. He was closely involved in building and launching Squad.App, an AI-powered influencer marketing platform for brands and creators. He has also produced feature films. “We framed everything for both formats and cut two versions: the vertical version is made specifically for mobile devices and has its own way of telling the story, while the horizontal version goes to Cannes, where we’re already seeing interest in romance from television and streaming buyers around the world. I’m especially proud that we shot all of it in Los Angeles, using local casts and crews.” There have been a spate of L.A.-based microdrama businesses launching over recent weeks, and LoveHit’s launch comes less than a week after aTwist , which is led by a trio of former network execs, debuted. aTwist debuted on September 3 with titles such as Buried Alive, Back For Revenge , Cash Out , Hollywood Starlet , I Fell in Love with a Dragon Prince , I Swiped Right on a Serial Killer , My Billionaire Kidney , My Book Boyfriend Came to Life , Pretty Hurts and So Do I , Something is Alive in My Attic and Strangers, a Plane and a Deadly Game . It also has a production partnership with Kevin Hart’s Hartbeat, a deal with BET and the first microdrama from The Bold and the Beautiful ‘s creative chief, Bradley Bell. articles.title: Ben McKenzie Says He’d “Be Up for” a ‘The O.C.’ Revival: “It Was a Great Show”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All September 5, 2026 5:53pm From left: Adam Brody, Rachel Bilson, Ben McKenzie and Mischa Barton in 'The O.C.' season three. Courtesy Everett Collection Logo text California, here we come — again… possibly? hopefully? Ben McKenzie is weighing in on whether he’d be interested in returning to The O.C. In a new interview with on KIIS 1065, McKenzie was asked by the host if he would be open to “re-doing” The O.C. by returning as “one of the dads,” referencing Peter Gallagher’s Sandy Cohen role. “I don’t know that there has ever been serious talks, but I’d be up for it, sure,” he responded. “Yeah, I think so, under the right circumstances. It was a great show. We had a great time. I learned a lot. I was so young. We were all young.” Related Stories TV 'Modern Family' Duo Christopher Lloyd, Danny Zuker Land Comedy 'Mammoth' at Fox TV 'Sterling Point' Renewed for Season 2 at Prime Video He added that his 10-year-old child, whom he shares with actress Morena Baccarin and briefly appeared in three episodes of season three, “loved it.” “I now have kids come up to me, teenagers, and they talk about what a fan they are of the show. ‘You weren’t even alive when it came out,’” McKenzie continued. “They watch it with their parents.” The 47-year-old’s comments come after Mischa Barton , who played his on-again, off-again love interest, Marissa Cooper, recently teased that a possible reunion might be coming. During the Fox teen drama’s four-season run from 2003 to 2007 — named one of the best teen dramas of all time by The Hollywood Reporter — McKenzie played Ryan Atwood, a troubled teen from Chino, California, who is taken in by his public defender Sandy and his family. Ryan becomes like a brother to Seth Cohen ( Adam Brody ) and is part of the show’s central group alongside Summer Roberts ( Rachel Bilson ) and Marissa. McKenzie went on to lead the TV series Southland and Gotham following The O.C. He is currently promoting his documentary about the crypto industry, Everyone Is Lying to You for Money . View this post on Instagram THR

articles.title: Alanis Morissette Sues Former Tour Manager Over Alleged “Calculated Blackmail Campaign”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 5, 2026 6:42pm Alanis Morissette attends the Songwriters Hall of Fame 55th Annual Induction and Awards Gala. Alanis Morissette Alanis Morissette is reportedly suing her former tour manager, alleging that Keren Urinov led a “calculated blackmail campaign” against her, per People . The “Ironic” singer filed the suit on Tuesday, stemming from her working relationship with Urinov in 2025. “Plaintiff Alanis Morissette is the victim of a calculated blackmail campaign orchestrated by a disgruntled former tour manager,” the lawsuit reads, per People . “Morissette will not agree to work with an incompetent blackmailer for the next 15 years or pay her a ransom under the gun.” Related Stories Music Olivia Rodrigo's Inaugural Daisy Chain Fields Draws Massive Crowd to SoCal for a Day of Music and Empowerment Music Alanis Morissette, Ella Langley to Perform at Spotify's SXSW Showcase (Exclusive) According to the documents obtained by the outlet, Morissette’s legal team alleges that Urinov was “flagged for inspection and detained at a U.K. airport” when she was traveling with the singer to Spain. Urinov told Morissette and her team she was arrested and authorities issued a seizure notice, alleging there was marijuana and xylazine in her bag; she showed officials her Israeli medical marijuana license and was released, per People . The suit claims that the tour manager and her own legal team sent Morissette “increasingly extortionate” letters, where she threatened to sue. Urinov allegedly told the seven-time Grammy winner that she could “end to the matter” with a 15-year, full-time employment contract comprised of “an income equivalent to that of a tour director with annual increases and bonuses.” After Morissette did not comply with the “brazen demands,” Urinov and her lawyer allegedly sent her a letter “implying she would accuse Morissette of drug trafficking,” People added. The singer is suing on allegations of civil extortion, fraud and negligent misrepresentation. Morissette was previously embezzled by her former manager Jonathan Todd Schwartz. He admitted to embezzling more than $7 million from Morissette and other celebrity clients in 2017. Schwartz penned an apology essay for The Hollywood Reporter at the time, where he wrote, “To say I am incredibly ashamed and disappointed in myself is an understatement.” THR

articles.title: Alan Cumming Lands Third Straight Emmy for Best Reality TV Host
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All September 5, 2026 7:00pm 'The Traitors' Euan Cherry/Peacock Alan Cumming has extended his reign as the ruler of reality TV. Cumming took home the 2026 Emmy for outstanding host for a reality or reality competition program, which was handed out at Saturday’s Creative Arts Emmys ceremony in downtown Los Angeles. The Traitors host was nominated in the category against RuPaul (host of RuPaul’s Drag Race ), Kristen Kish ( Top Chef ), Ariana Madix ( Love Island USA ) and Jeff Probst ( Survivor ). He was not in attendance to accept his award, and presenter Johnny Bananas — a former contestant on The Traitors — took the trophy on his behalf, joking that he wasn’t going to hand over the Emmy “until you bring me back on the show” after he got kicked off early. Related Stories TV Creative Arts Emmys, Night One: Winners List (Updating Live) Movies Telluride Film Fest Kicks Off with Brunch, 'Wild Horse Nine' North American Premiere Cumming has won the category the previous two years, after breaking RuPaul’s eight-year winning streak in 2024; among the group of veteran hosts, Madix is the newcomer to the category, landing her first nom this year as face of Peacock’s mega hit dating show. The Traitors is up for seven Emmys this year, including reality competition program, production design, cinematography, costumes, picture editing and directing, and picked up several wins during Saturday night’s ceremony; the show has 17 total nominations over the course of its history. The Creative Arts Emmys are a two-day affair that see over 100 mostly below-the-line Emmys handed out between the dual ceremonies at the Peacock Theater. These awards are not televised, and take place ahead of the Primetime Emmys show on Sept. 14. The 78th Emmy Awards , hosted by Mariska Hargitay, will air live on NBC and stream on Peacock. THR

articles.title: Creative Arts Emmys, Night One: Winners List
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba , Hilary Lewis September 5, 2026 7:32pm Stephen Colbert, Bad Bunny and Mariska Hargitay. Scott Kowalchyk/CBS, Chris Graythen/Getty Images, Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for Tribeca Festival The first night of the Creative Arts Emmys is in the books. The annual two-day event — taking place ahead of the Primetime Emmys on Sept. 14 — will see over 100 awards handed out, mostly for below-the-line categories. Statues presented on Saturday include honors for variety programming, reality and documentary/nonfiction. Saturday’s big winners included The Late Show With Stephen Colbert , The Muppet Show , Love on the Spectrum , The Traitors , The Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny and My Mom Jayne: A Film By Mariska Hargitay , which each took home multiple trophies. Octavia Spencer also took home her first Emmy for narrating Lost Women of Alaska , and The Traitors ‘ Alan Cumming extended his winning streak for best reality tv host. Related Stories Movies Telluride Film Fest Kicks Off with Brunch, 'Wild Horse Nine' North American Premiere TV Norman Lear Awards to Honor 'Abbott Elementary,' 'The Morning Show,' 'Grey's Anatomy' and More (Exclusive) Hargitay, who is hosting the Primetime Emmys, has extra reason to celebrate this year, as she landed two statues — for the emotional documentary centered on her mother Jayne Mansfield — for directing for a documentary/nonfiction program and outstanding documentary or nonfiction special. The dual ceremonies, which are taking place at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles, are not televised live; on top of the competitive prizes, Creative Arts weekend is also celebrating the winners in juried categories for animation, costume and innovation in emerging media programming. Night one was full of reality-centered presenters, starting with Wanda Sykes to kick off the evening, followed by Lisa Rinna, Ariana Madix, Julianne Hough, ex- Summer House star West Wilson, Sean Wilson, Stassi Schroeder, Julie Chen Moonves and Jaleel White. Night two will feature buzzy categories including the guest actor and actress awards and a handful of limited series prizes. Coming into the Emmys, The Pitt leads the pack with 25 total nominations , followed by Hacks (with 24 nominations, a comedy series record ), Widow’s Bay (19), Pluribus (18), and Beef (16). articles.title: Mariska Hargitay Lands Two Emmys for ‘My Mom Jayne’ Ahead of Hosting Gig
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All September 5, 2026 8:00pm Mariska Hargitay, winner of the Outstanding Documentary Or Nonfiction Special award for "My Mom Jayne: A Film By Mariska Hargitay", poses in the Winner's Walk during the 78th Emmy Awards Night 1 at Peacock Theater on September 05, 2026 in Los Angeles, California Amy Sussman/Getty Images Mariska Hargitay is going into her Emmys hosting gig as a winner. The star, who is helming the Primetime Emmys on Sept. 14, took home two prizes at the Creative Arts Emmys for My Mom Jayne : A Film By Mariska Hargitay . She landed wins for directing for a documentary/nonfiction program and for outstanding documentary or nonfiction special; the night brings Hargitay’s career Emmy total to three, after she won best actress for Law & Order: Special Victims Unit in 2006. “It feels extraordinarily new and it’s deeply meaningful for me to have gone into a completely different arena, and to be recognized like this is really beyond my wildest dreams,” she told reporters backstage of how these two trophies compare to her one from two decades ago. Related Stories TV Creative Arts Emmys, Night One: Winners List TV Alan Cumming Lands Third Straight Emmy for Best Reality TV Host Hargitay also spoke about this particular moment in her career, where she’s living by the motto of “I just say yes. I said yes to Broadway and I said yes to hosting the Emmys — when they called me, I thought it was a joke, and then I went, ‘Why not?'” “It’s a year of firsts and a year of saying yes and not limiting myself or not being governed by fear. Like, what would I do if I wasn’t afraid? What if it all works out?” she continued. “I’m in that place right now of going, ‘I’ll figure it out.’ I’m really happy right now.” She also gave a hint at her mindset heading into the main show , admitting, “It’s been a big week, this hosting the Emmys is no joke,” teasing that NBC “undersold it to me” and told her it would just be two days of rehearsal, which was “a lie.” However, she expressed how excited she was to be working with The Late Show with Stephen Colbert writing team on her material and added, “I just can’t believe at this place in my life — my third act is starting and it’s pretty awesome.” THR

articles.title: ‘A Tale of Two Cities’ Review: Kit Harington Has Done Far, Far Better Things Than This Bland MGM+ Dickens Adaptation
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Daniel Fienberg Plus Icon Daniel Fienberg Chief Television Critic TheFienPrint Follow Sign Up View All September 5, 2026 8:43pm François Civil and Kit Harington of 'A Tale of Two Cities.' MGM+ Logo text MGM+ and BBC One’s A Tale of Two Cities is neither the best of adaptations nor the worst of adaptations, but Daniel West’s take on the Charles Dickens classic may well be the meh-est of adaptations. The four-part series benefits somewhat from the lack of an instantly identifiable definitive filmed interpretation of A Tale of Two Cities (depending on how you feel, I suppose, about the best picture-nominated 1935 feature) — a minor oddity given that the novel is in many ways Dickens’ most streamlined, featuring one of his best beginnings, best endings and most approachable narrative hooks. Related Stories TV Kit Harington Cast in 'Harry Potter' Season 2 as Gilderoy Lockhart, Replacing Nicholas Hoult TV Kit Harington Gets Caught in Love Triangle in 'Tale of Two Cities' Trailer A Tale of Two Cities The Bottom Line Fails to stand out as a romance, thriller or period piece. Airdate: Sunday, September 6 (MGM+) Cast: Francois Civil, Kit Harington, Mirren Mack, Roxane Duran Creator: Daniel West It’s a love triangle and a thriller set against the backdrop of the French Revolution. It features the usual Dickensian melange of colorful characters, breathless cliffhangers, shocking twists (not Oliver) and trenchant social commentary. It’s very much the epitome of a ripping yarn. Ultimately, though, freedom from negative comparisons to previous adaptations is not enough to prevent this take on A Tale of Two Cities from being a bland disappointment — one of the least Dickensian adaptations of a Charles Dickens work since Steven Knight adapted A Christmas Carol around the question, “What if Ebenezer Scrooge could say ‘fuck’?” It’s still a love story, but with virtually no passion between any of its three principals; and while it may be a tale of two cities, they both look like nearly identically designed stages in a warehouse in some affordable Eastern European country. For those who haven’t read A Tale of Two Cities or seen one of the forgettable previous adaptations — none, apparently, since a 1989 take that aired in the States under the Masterpiece Theatre banner — the plot is at once simple and convoluted. After a brief prelude in Paris in 1764, in which a young Lucie Manette watches her father apparently be killed, the action jumps forward 18 years. Lucie ( Mirren Mack ) is now living in London hoping to follow in her late father’s footsteps as a doctor. Lucie’s concrete interest in medicine is not, if memory serves, a part of a book in which she’s a more nebulous “healer,” nor is it all that relevant to the series after a strange introduction in which she’s practicing surgery on a corpse. It’s a nearly pointless choice, one of many. Lucie is living with Mrs. Lorry (Sharon Duncan-Brewster) and doing just fine for herself when her life is turned upside down with the arrival of Charles Darnay (François Civil). Charles is working on behalf of French revolutionaries, embodied by Roxane Duran’s Madame Defarge, to smuggle a generally irrelevant woman to safety in England. He’s also bearing a letter that suggests that Lucie’s dad (Yannick Renier) isn’t actually dead. The letter contains the evocative words “recalled to life,” which are potent on the page and nearly meaningless in the series. At the English border, Charles is wounded, which lets Lucie utilize her medical knowledge briefly. Then he’s arrested as a spy. Lucie seeks out legal representation for the heroic Charles, but finds only the generally drunk and uncouth Sydney Carton ( Kit Harington ). Both Charles and Sydney immediately fall in love with Lucie, because she’s somewhat the protagonist of the story and she’s pretty. Lucie, for her part, falls in love with both Charles and Sydney, which makes a little bit of sense since they look almost identical (assuming they aren’t standing next to each other, allowing one to see that Civil is a lot taller) and they’re both in constant need of chaste undressing. It makes less sense, though, because nothing in her interactions with either man comes across as the least bit romantic and the chemistry between Mack, Civil and Harington is wholly lacking, regardless of the permutation. As Lucie is reunited with her father, seriously psychologically damaged by his two decades in the Bastille, she learns shocking truths about Charles and his lineage and about the revolutionary motivations of Madame Defarge, whose general intransigence has caused her to be viewed as the villain of the piece, regardless of logic. Watching A Tale of Two Cities , it’s almost impossible to gauge what attracted West and the producers to the book, other than the IP and the reality that there are only so many times one can adapt Great Expectations , David Copperfield , Oliver Twist and A Christmas Carol before it becomes necessary to cycle back into the Dickens catalogue. The inspiration is nowhere to be found here. And A Tale of Two Cities is, as I’ve already said, a ripping yarn, featuring doppelgängers and surprises and the French blooming Revolution — featured in one thoroughly lifeless scene — plus it’s eternally timely since the story is one of those reliable Dickens screeds in which the impoverished masses are on the verge of toppling the heartless elite. Madame Defarge is — whether or not you buy her as a villain — one of fiction’s great adversaries, and her backstory is, itself, both eternally timely and specifically timely at a historical moment when you might have noticed one or two headlines about immoral wealthy men preying on defenseless young women. One could certainly adapt A Tale of Two Cities in a way that steers into the complications of Madame Defarge as a character, resulting in something that might almost resemble Hulu’s summer hit, Furious . She is, as a character, at best a righteous crusader and at worst a rigid zealot, but she’s hard to make uninteresting. Duran captures Defarge’s rage and, in a series plagued by thinly sketched characterizations hers comes closest to rising to the level of interesting. But her cause and her connection to that cause are mechanical pieces of the plot here, making it impossible to hate her or empathize with her. She’s just the person stirring up trouble whenever we go to Paris. Plus, it’s hard to know when we’re in Paris. As directed by Richard Clark, A Tale of Two Cities is temporally choppy and fails to build any emotional or geographical momentum. Though two cities are in the title, we’re treated to maybe a block or two of London and a block or two of Paris, visually interchangeable in a way that offers no real tangible connection to either staged location. Presumably, making Paris and London interchangeable is intentional, a parallel to the similarities between Charles and Sydney? Except that the entire purpose of the story’s arc is that one should be able to chart the life Charles was born into and the changes he made (all before the start of the story, since he’s pretty much stagnant onscreen throughout) and compare that to Sydney’s journey from the man he is when we meet him to the man he becomes by the end of the tale. In this case, though, since Harington and Civil are comparably solemn and earnest throughout — the actors do, if nothing else, look as similar as the story necessitates — there isn’t much evolution to trace. There are supposed to be comparable parallels to the arcs of Lucie and Madame Defarge, one as a force of optimistic good and the other as a force of all-consuming vengeance, but neither progression is all that engaging. Like Duran, Mack brings a little fire to the series, but Lucie is one of those Dickensian women who are unexplained rays of light who exist mostly to fuel the growth of the main male characters. As for the supporting ensemble from the page, from the bloodthirsty revolutionaries collectively known as Jacques to Sydney’s partner Mr. Stryver (a wasted Fehinti Balogun) to the figure known as The Vengeance, they’re either gone entirely or written so thinly here as to leave no impression. A Tale of Two Cities is in such a hurry to get from that memorable opening (rendered poorly as a voiceover at the end of the first episode) to that tremendous closing (rendered poorly as another voiceover) that the adaptation might as well have been as a two-hour movie. Certainly the cliffhangers at the end of each episode lack the urgency that Dickens himself understood so well how to evoke. The story itself is probably good enough to pull some viewers along from episode to episode, but the telling definitely is not good enough to inspire anybody to seek out MGM+. Regardless, there’s a far, far better adaptation of A Tale of Two Cities than has ever been done. This is not it. THR

articles.title: ‘The Debut’ Review: Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti Are Dynamite Together in Jesse Eisenberg’s Entertainingly Offbeat Theater Comedy
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All September 6, 2026 12:25am The Debut A24 When Mona ( Julianne Moore ) tells a friend she’s auditioned for a production of a show called Nosy Neighbors at their local theater, he admits he’s never liked musicals. They just don’t feel authentic, he explains, the way the characters are always bursting into song. Who does that? Well, no one, not even in the musical-loving The Debut . But among the first of the film’s sly tricks is that it builds a world in which it feels like people could , where in fact it feels more unnatural that they don’t. Blessed with swing-for-the-fences brio and, in Moore and Paul Giamatti , a leading duo capable of navigating every one of those wild turns, the latest feature by Jesse Eisenberg makes for a frequently hilarious journey into the mind of an overly committed actor — even if, in the end, it seems unsure quite what it wants to say about the self-destructive pursuit of artistic perfection. Related Stories Movies 'The Debut' Features Seven Original Songs, All Written by Jesse Eisenberg, and One Is Getting an Oscar Push (Exclusive) Movies 'The Row' Review: 'Icarus' Director Bryan Fogel's Doc Takes Viewers on a Gripping, Question-Raising Solo Voyage Across the Pacific The Debut The Bottom Line A very good time, if not necessarily a profound one. Venue: Telluride Film Festival Cast: Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti, Halle Bailey, Jesse Eisenberg, Cara Buono, Craig Bierko, Eldar Isgandarov, Bernadette Peters Director-screenwriter: Jesse Eisenberg Rated R, 1 hour 45 minutes At first, Mona would seem an unlikely candidate to go Method in the way of certain prestige actors or comic book movie stars . When we meet her, she’s a meek suburban housewife who’s never acted a day in her life, and whose audition is so mediocre she doesn’t even realize how mediocre it is. Once she lands a relatively minor role anyway, owing to a twist of fate that she may have ever-so-slightly nudged along, she’s just happy to be there, drinking in any suggestion or note or friendly gesture extended to her. But even from the start, before Mona properly goes off the deep end, The Debut starts inuring us to her heightened perspective. When Mona gets the call saying she’s gotten the part, a spotlight floods her grin and the camera rushes in, as if she might start belting on the spot. On her first day of rehearsal, the whole world is lit a little brighter than it was a few scenes earlier. When she endears herself to her new colleagues with a joke, the laughter feels slightly too enthusiastic. The effect is almost eerie to start, and it takes some getting used to. But it turns out to be just the tip of the iceberg. The pivot comes when the production’s director, Jerry (Giamatti) — described in a low-key perfect bit of dialogue as “basically the biggest name in New Jersey community theater” — pulls Mona aside for the private special instruction that she (as a truly godawful singer and actress) so desperately needs. Jerry’s usual method is to break his actors down so he can “put Humpty Dumpty together again,” and it begins exactly as planned in an acting exercise that yields one of the very biggest laughs in a film rich with them. But then Mona takes a little too well to his guidance. As Mona loses herself in her character, a building superintendent named Miss Danielle, her wardrobe, courtesy of costume designer Stacey Battat, goes from prim cardigans to ripped jeans to an actual coverall she’s stolen from a janitor. (This is neither the first nor last time you’ll think to yourself, “Man, theater people are a menace ” and “Jesse Eisenberg’s seen some shit, huh?”) She begins frequenting a seedy motel that production designer Anne Ross has cleverly made into a theater actor’s exaggeratedly noirish version of what a seedy motel would look like, with smoke-blurred neon lights and a trash can fire outside and an inexplicably naked man roaming the halls inside. Most worryingly for Nosy Neighbors — in-universe a well-known musical that’s been around a few decades, in reality an original concocted by Eisenberg and seen here in perfectly cheesy snippets — Mona starts to question Miss Danielle’s motivations, then her lines, then her actions. Jerry realizes he’s created his own worst nightmare: the sort of difficult actor who thinks she knows her character better than the director or even the script that invented her. Lively throughout, The Debut ascends to new heights whenever Giamatti and Moore share the screen together. Moore is an absolute hoot as Mona, who starts out looking on paper like one of those disaffected housewives she’s played so often (and so expertly) in her career but turns out to be much, much stranger. Giamatti makes Jerry ferocious but not monstruous, a man who certainly likes barking orders at various underlings but loves making good theater even more. Their scenes opposite each other are not just entertaining but thrillingly dynamic, as the balance of power between them begins to shift. It’s all so much fun that it’s easy not to notice at first that none of this is headed anywhere particularly profound. There’s a touch of poignancy in the understanding that Mona is so eager to lose herself in Miss Danielle because — like Rita , the protagonist of Telluride 2026’s other “New Jersey suburbanite abandons her family to pursue a more authentic life under the guidance of a charismatic but demanding leader” premiere — she barely knows who she is in the first place. But the film never builds out the rest of Mona’s world, like her inattentive husband (Patrick Fabian), or even co-stars like Steph (a very endearing Halle Bailey) and Todd (Eisenberg, adorably giving himself an excuse to sing and dance), to take that line of thinking anywhere truly insightful or emotional. Among the arguments between Mona and Jerry are what theater can or should be. Mona argues that that the stories it tell should be “real,” even at the expense of a happy ending, while Jerry argues that no one cares much about the plot — audiences just want to feel while spying on the intimate lives of other people. The Debut , in prioritizing style, humor and outrageous plot turns over complex emotionality, would seem to side with Jerry. Maybe it’s not everything it could be. But as I howled over the lengths Mona would go to for the sake of what Jerry unkindly but accurately points out is, in the end, just some “thankless tertiary character,” it felt like more than enough. Full credits Venue: Telluride Film Festival Distributor: A24 Production companies: Fruit Tree, Topic Studios Cast: Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti, Halle Bailey, Jesse Eisenberg, Cara Buono, Craig Bierko, Eldar Isgandarov, Bernadette Peters Director-screenwriter: Jesse Eisenberg Producers: Emma Stone, Dave McCary, Ali Herting, Jesse Eisenberg Executive producers: Michael Bloom, Ian Stratford, Ryan Heller, Jasmine Daghighian, Jennifer Booth, Kevin Kelly Director of photography: Drew Daniels Production designer: Anne Ross Costume designer: Stacey Battat Editor: Robert Nassau Music: Emile Mosseri Casting director: Douglas Aibel Sound mixer: Dimitri Kouri Rated R, 1 hour 45 minutes THR

articles.title: Wim Wenders on His 14-Year Journey Building Peter Zumthor Doc ‘From Inside Out’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content 'From Inside Out: The Architecture of Peter Zumthor' Road Movies Wim Wenders has spent much of the past three decades building portraits of other artists — the Cuban musicians of Buena Vista Social Club (1999), the choreographer Pina Bausch in Pina (2011) , the photographer Sebastião Salgado in The Salt of the Earth (2014), the German painter-sculptor Anselm Kiefer in Anslem (2023) . The first three were Oscar-nominated. All were critically acclaimed. But none has taken him as long as From Inside Out: The Architecture of Peter Zumthor , the German auteur’s 3D documentary on the Pritzker Prize-winning Swiss architect, has been 14 years in the making. Related Stories Movies May el-Toukhy Takes 'Woman Unknown' to Venice: "I've Used Every Part of Me to Make This Film" Movies Liam and Noel Gallagher Lock Arms at Venice Premiere of 'Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger' It started small. David Chipperfield, curating the 2012 Venice architecture Biennale, asked Wenders to make a short film on Zumthor. That became a two-day shoot in the architect’s modest office in Haldenstein, high in the Swiss mountains, and the 2012 short Notes on a Day in the Life of an Architect — along with the nagging sense that he had barely scratched the surface. “At the end, we shook hands on ‘doing something real together,'” Wenders says. “Little did we know that the journey would last 14 years…” The result, premiering in Venice, and being sold worldwide by HanWay Films, is a two-hour immersion that wanders from some of Zumthor’s earliest works, including the St. Benedict’s chapel, completed in 1988, to a memorial for burned witches above the Arctic Circle, to the newly opened $724 million David Geffen Galleries at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), the architect’s largest building, commissioned nearly two decades ago. [Brad Pitt, a fan of Zumthor, who supported his LACMA bid, has joined From Inside Out as an executive producer. ] Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter ahead of the premiere, Wenders discussed his kinship with Zumthor, why he needed 3D to shoot architecture, what a craftsman’s hands can teach the age of AI, and how he answers the charge that Zumthor’s serene spaces are a luxury in a world of flattened cities. “Buildings cannot repair the world,” he says. “But they can change our idea of what the world could be.” How did you first come to know Peter Zumthor? How did the idea for this film come about? I was invited to make a short film on Peter Zumthor for the architectural Biennale in Venice in 2012, by none other than British architect David Chipperfield, who was the curator of the show that year. I knew some of Zumthor’s buildings, and I was intrigued by the idea. It became a 2-day shoot in his office in Haldenstein, way up in the Swiss mountains, and resulted in Notes on a Day in the Life of an Architect , but also in the realization that this short study just scratched the surface of Zumthor’s work, his philosophy and his approach. At the end, we shook hands on ‘doing something real together’, and that was clearly going to be a long-term observation. Little did we know that the journey would last 14 years… What is it about his work that is distinctive and particularly compelling for you? Peter Zumthor had a relatively small office, and he did not want to change that. He wanted to be able to keep accepting only work that he was absolutely convinced of, of its purpose, of its necessity, of its usefulness and its site. He doesn’t want to be just a hired architect. He wants to be thoroughly involved and make the best possible building for that particular use and at that particular place. And for that, he knows he needs more time than is usually given to develop a building. But most of all: he wants the client to understand that once he proposes a design, he is not going to step away from the project. Like a painter, he knows that his painting will only emerge in the act of painting it. A songwriter or a poet works the same way: the song and the poem are only finished after the last act of correction. And that is exactly the freedom that architects are usually not given in the building process. A construction company takes over. The architect cannot intervene anymore, at least not with important changes. That understanding of the creative process is what I can deeply identify with. He is convinced that a work is not finished when it is planned, but that it continues to take shape in the making. I feel exactly the same way about filmmaking. For me, too, a film is not basically done with the script. I want to be able to change that script, as I go along. I even want to be able to contradict it. THAT is the act of creation: having the liberty to continue learning about how your story will turn out best. That is the very nature of storytelling: finding out the truth of your story as you’re telling it. Peter Zumthor is asking for exactly that freedom that I also fight for with every film: invent and improve the film – or the building – as you are making it. Why did you want to film this in 3D? When I made my first film in 3D, Pina , on the art of choreographer Pina Bausch, 3D was the saving grace of that project. I would not have made it if the new medium hadn’t allowed me to work in the same realm as Pina and her dancers. And that was SPACE . A screen is a two-dimensional thing, any effort to represent space on it is make-believe. Cinema has been incredibly inventive in this make-believe and has invented many tools to convince the audience that the story they were watching was taking place inside space, even if the movies were always a medium restricted to the flat screen. Only the invention of digital 3D, native 3D, has made the screen go away and become a window, open to infinity and also to things taking place in front of the window. From Inside Out is my tenth film in 3D, short ones and installations included. But it was never more necessary (after Pina ) than now. A ‘room’ and a ‘house’ belong to our earliest human experiences and they mean ‘shelter’, ‘protection’ and ‘security’. These are not abstract ideas at first, they are spatial experiences, utterly existential. We experience space before we learn about its abstraction, the two-dimensional representation of it, in photos, in drawings, in paintings, on TV or in the cinema. Architecture is the one art, together with dance and theatre, that is unthinkable without space. So if I wanted an audience to experience the world of an architect, I felt I needed space itself at my disposal, not just as a technology, but as a cinematic language. Parts of the film have the feel of an art or museum installation. Do you envision the project living on in those spaces? No. I make it for movie theatres. But I take your question as a compliment. You certainly have different experiences in museums than in movies. I feel it is time to expand the limits of what we can experience in movie theatres. Poster for ‘From Inside Out: The Architecture of Peter Zumthor’ Courtesy of HanWay Films You take different approaches in depicting Zumthor’s work — interviews with the family for the Luzi house, with voice-over commentary from other artists, as a stage for dance or musical performance — what was behind this and, in the case of collaborations with other artists — Aoi Yamada, Siri Hustvedt, Sophie Hunger, etc. — how did those come about? I didn’t want to make a ‘talking heads’ film. I didn’t want to make a didactic film, period. I wanted the audience to experience architecture without having to verbalize the issues all the time, like a TV documentary. Houses give us an immense freedom to explore them: we can walk around in them, sit down and look out of a window, work or sleep or dream in them. They get under our skin. We find out how we live in them, think in them, ARE in them. Some chapters in From Inside Out are strictly based on the audience sharing the experience of some of my protagonists in being in the buildings of Peter Zumthor. Siri Hustvedt, for instance, had written about the women who were burned as witches in that part of Norway, far above the Arctic Circle. But she had never seen the place Zumthor built in memory of these women. Her experience of encountering that building becomes the film in that chapter. Who can travel so far north – further north than any city in the US or Canada – to visit this one-of-a-kind place and this absolutely unique building that is like nothing that was ever built before? Well, not many. But you can almost physically enter the building in the film… What was behind your musical choices for each building – both the live performances and the accompanying score? The score is made almost equally by two very different voices: one is Peter Zumthor’s son Peter Conradin Zumthor as percussionist together with his partner, pianist Vera Kappeler. The other is my long-trusted composer friend Laurent Petitgand with whom I made more than a dozen films in the past. These two ‘voices’ serve two very different aspects of Zumthor’s world. The percussion as well as the piano, I felt, both have a great affinity to more structural aspects of space and time, while the more symphonic music has a great affinity to the emotional aspects of the work. The two live performances come from an altogether different thinking. The amazing St. Benedict’s chapel that Zumthor built as a young architect reminded me very much of a musical instrument. Visiting it, I felt I was entering the body of a cello or a bigger string instrument. So in order to explore it, I invited a double bass player, Anna Trauffer, to join us and play in the chapel. And as she also sings and plays musical glasses, we could also hear a beautiful human voice inside this ‘instrument’ called ‘a chapel’ as well as her glass harp. For Zumthor’s latest building, the extension of the Beyeler Foundation in Basel, now called the Wyss Building, I had the idea of inviting the great Sophie Hunger, one of my favorite contemporary singer-songwriters, to visit the new (and yet not quite finished) building and walk the path that Peter Zumthor invented for this building, from one outlook into the surrounding landscape to another. I admit, that was just a vague idea, at first, also the fact that she might invent a song for this ‘walk with a guitar’ that could somehow condense or tie together some of Peter Zumthor’s ‘philosophy’ or ‘approach’. Little did I know how masterful she would combine these two tasks and come up with her song From Inside to Outside, that in the end even reflects the film’s title. Both musical performances, I felt, were gifts to our film. What connections do you see between the work of the architect and that of the filmmaker? I could talk about that issue for an entire hour or more. But just let me say this: as a filmmaker, I construct a movie from pieces of time. Every shot is such a ‘brick of time’. Every scene is a ‘room’ or a ‘space’ made from such tiny elements of time. And the entire film, in the end, is a huge building or ‘space’ constructed from many such bricks of time. Editing a film is a building process. In the end, the film invites people to live in its space, at least for a couple of hours. I better stop here, before I get carried away… Are you spiritual kin to Peter Zumthor, do you see yourself as struggling with similar questions and themes, and pursuing similar aims? There is one thing we definitely share, as a passion, or as an approach, or an aim. (And yes, we might “struggle” with lots of questions and problems while making a movie or conceiving a building. But I don’t make films to have anybody watch me ‘struggle’, let alone my actors. People want to see Odysseus struggle, not Matt Damon, nor Christopher Nolan. And I assume Peter doesn’t want his buildings to show any traces of him having ‘struggled’ with them before, either…) Let’s say we know and love the processes that go with our professions, but we are both particularly fond of the fact that our work is concerned with PLACES . For Zumthor, every building is planted onto a particular site which has its history, its surroundings, its nature, its weather, its neighbors, in short: its geographic conditions. He wants to do justice to them. More so: he wants his new building to belong there, “as if it had always been there.” (to quote him.) He wants the building to live in peace with its neighbors and its nature. So he has to find out a lot about the place, before he could even consider designing something for it. He first has to read the place, understand it and grasp what the place needs as an addition, as a new neighbor, possibly a new center of attention. And he has to fully transcend the purpose of the building to make it go in unison with the place, not against it. So, what is really demanded from an architect is A SENSE OF PLACE . It’s one of our original human senses, even if most of us don’t use it much anymore. We have delegated it to our navigation systems. As a filmmaker, I equally depend on my sense of place. Most of my films, if not all, don’t start with ‘story’, but with a place, a place that I encounter and respond to emotionally. I then want to find a story that could happen here, more so: that could only play here, in that place. My films are all ‘taking place’ on these crossroads of a place and a story that belong together. What does Peter Zumthor and the method of his art have to teach our modern age, the age of AI? His buildings are deeply human, the result of a long dialogue between the site (its surrounding nature or city landscape) and the purpose of the new building. Zumthor thinks it from the inside first, the new space he’s about to conceive, then considers it from outside, which might lead to corrections, then sees what this does to the perspective from inside, then returns to seeing it from the outside. That dialogue does take time and includes his collaborators, the client and endless sessions in his office. In that process, countless models are being built and rebuilt and discarded and started from scratch again. The buildings that are thus given time to grow and develop, find their affinity to the site in that long dialogue, find their materiality and also sometimes redefine their purpose. It’s like a gardening process, I sometimes felt when I returned to Peter and the building I saw months before now had not only ‘grown’, but assumed more character, as if it had ascertained its identity. That’s why they are so totally unique. About some of them, like the Witches Memorial way up North in the Arctic or the David Geffen Galleries of the LACMA in California, one can safely say there is no other building on the planet like it. All of Zumthor’s buildings can open our eyes to what architecture can be and what it can do to expand our understanding of spaces and places. I’m not sure how many years we are away from AI learning to design buildings. Let alone replace the touch of human hands involved in the building process. Zumthor’s big message in the film is: learn to see the beauty of things made by hand, by craftspeople! We must not lose that! (laughs) At this moment, I’m sure AI can only learn from our man. (Or other architects and artists. Asked if AI can write a good song, Nick Cave answered: “I don’t think so. AI can’t suffer.”) There are a couple of moments in the film where Zumthor connects his work with his personal experience of wanting to create homes, a secure space to compensate for not feeling safe as a child. But you avoid going very deep into a psychological exploration of him or his biography. Why that choice? You’re right: it was a choice. I did not want to shoot a biopic on an architect. This film is not about how Peter Zumthor became who he is. It is not about his life, but how his ideas took shape and how they’re connecting to the feelings or to the curiosity the audience might have about architecture. We all live and work and die in houses, we grow up and get old in schools, offices, museums, churches or whatever buildings we visit. But doing so, we mostly take architecture for granted. From Inside Out wants to expand that horizon without being educational. (Or ‘edifying’…) Peter Zumthor is an ideal guide to start thinking from scratch about what houses do to us, how they influence and form us. Zumthor’s discussion of creating inner security and safety for me immediately evokes for me the specter of its opposite, the unsafe spaces, the spaces of destruction, the homes flattened in Ukraine, Yemen, Lebanon and Gaza. How would you respond to the critique that Zumthor’s serene spaces of peace and contemplation are also an expression of extreme privilege, and a way of avoiding the ugliness and darkness in the world? The question of privilege is a legitimate one. Who has access to safety, to shelter, to places of peace and contemplation – and who doesn’t? When we look at the destruction of homes and living spaces caused by wars – in Ukraine, Yemen, Lebanon, Gaza and elsewhere – we are not only looking at the destruction of buildings. We are looking at the destruction of places: places where people lived, where families and communities came together, places of memory, of belonging and of everyday life. The loss of safety, home and community is devastating for civilians wherever it happens. And perhaps that is precisely why the question of what a human space can be is not less relevant in such a world, but even more urgent! What interests me in Zumthor’s architecture is not simply beauty or contemplation. His buildings ask what spaces can do for human beings – how they can offer shelter and protection, but also create a sense of belonging, encounter and community. Of course, as a European filmmaker I am speaking from a privileged position. And I would never pretend that art or architecture can undo the destruction of people’s homes or repair the suffering caused by war. But they can be a response to it – a gesture that opposes destruction and cynicism with another idea of how we might live together. Zumthor’s buildings, in my book, speak the language of believing in a better version of humanity. The best critique of existing “ugliness and darkness” can also be to present “beauty and light” as alternatives. That is my firm conviction as a filmmaker. Take Zumthor’s Kolumba Museum in Cologne. If you walk in with the blues, disenchanted, hopeless or even in despair, you might find yourself walking out restored. Yes, I believe a building can do that. Architecture can remind us of the version of humanity we are aspiring to. The new David Geffen Galleries at LACMA offer another example: a museum without the usual hierarchies, conceived in the congenial collaboration between its director, Michael Govan, and its architect, Peter Zumthor. Now, on one floor, you can cross the planet and its art without one culture being privileged over another. ONE PLACE for all – like our world should be. Buildings cannot repair the world. But they can change our idea of what the world could be. What do you hope an audience takes away from this film? I hope… that they gain hope. A lot of things on this planet can or should get better. Especially our respect for nature, for the other, and for our sense of kindness and decency. In a shitty world, a visit to a good place can do wonders. The film – I hope – can instigate an appreciation for architecture that lets us see the difference between ‘more of the same’ and ‘something that makes a difference’. All of us can make a difference. All of us can care. Here, an architect tries to do that. That is encouraging. THR

articles.title: May el-Toukhy Takes ‘Woman Unknown’ to Venice: “I’ve Used Every Part of Me to Make This Film”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 6, 2026 1:00am May El-Toukhy Photographer: Søren Rønholt Danish filmmaker May el-Toukhy , one of the two female directors competing for the Golden Lion this year, in Venice with a sharp, searing analysis of the women thrown to the wolves in the aftermath of World War II. Women Unknown — Scandinavian in both its aesthetic and precision — was always going to be about class, complicity and survival. For a brief period, it was even going to focus on the Reformation witch hunts, before el-Toukhy found herself a little bored by the perpetrators. “The reasons they were hunting these women were just not that interesting,” she laughs to The Hollywood Reporter . Related Stories Movies Liam and Noel Gallagher Lock Arms at Venice Premiere of 'Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger' Movies 'Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger' Review: A Rich and Poignant Celebration of a Beloved Band's Glorious and Improbable Return Inspired by a newspaper picture dated from the 1940s of a woman sitting with a swastika painted on her back, el-Toukhy and co-writer Maren Louise Käehne soon turned their attention to the women whose bodies became a battlefield during the Second World War; those who found themselves with no choice but to fall into the arms of soldiers from occupying armies, and suffered severe consequences — hunted down, publicly shamed and punished for the rest of their lives. Woman Unknown is backdropped by a Danish city free from Nazi occupation, mere months after World War II has ended. It tells the story of Marie (Mathilde Arcel), a young nanny and housemaid about to marry her wealthy, older, and widowed employer, Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund). But Marie guards a shameful secret. During the war, she was in an intimate relationship with a German soldier. Now Marie’s past threatens to catch up with her, and she is forced to do everything in her power to preserve her new status as lady of the house in post-war anarchy. It is as much about resistance and patriotism in a euphoric, liberated Europe as it is about the chastisement of women and their sex lives. El-Toukhy is adamant that this is a story about the female experience. “There have been so many films about the Second World War, and that is true. But they’re all based mostly on men’s experiences and recollections of war. So that really energized me,” she says. “Let’s just do another 100 films about the women in this time period, and then we can say we’re over and done with it, you know?” A co-production between Denmark, Sweden and Latvia, financing the film wasn’t the tallest hurdle — but el-Toukhy has learned to be economical with her resources at a time when filmmaking costs have never higher. With her third feature film, following Long Story Short (2015) and Queen of Hearts (2019), she comes to the Lido buoyed by the hope that Woman Unknown will produce debate. El-Toukhy spoke to THR about the far-and-wide casting search for Marie, why she feels she’s already won before even stepping foot in Italy and whether those nerves have begun to kick in: “I’ve worked 16 hours a day for more than a year. I’ve spent all my savings. I’ve used every part of me to make this film and all the resources, all the muscle power I have. I can’t really do any more, so therefore I feel okay.” I’m curious about this period of Danish history, and whether you learned about it at school. Why use it as a backdrop for this film? After my last film, I thought I was going to do a film on the witch hunts after the Reformation, in the middle of [the] 1500s, and so I started researching that subject matter. But I found it quite hard to engage with the perpetrators because the reasons they were hunting these women were just not that interesting. ( Laughs .) At that time, me and my co-writer were slowly moving away from that idea, and then while we were moving away from that idea, some photos got republished in the newspaper with a woman who was sitting on a bench with a swastika painted on her back. And she [had been] assaulted in these photographs. Those [were] the propaganda photos that were produced in 1943. So we were reminded of that issue. It is something that we do learn in school here. It’s part of the curriculum — to deal with the First World War, Second World War, the events between the two wars and the aftermath, but often the aftermath here, in schools, would be focused on the politics, the collaboration the Danish government chose at that time and also the resistance movement. We didn’t spend too much time in school dealing with or talking about [or] debating the destiny of these women. I’m always interested in investigating something that takes a lot for me to engage in; that’s difficult material. Where there’s no black and white, but everything is gray. And you chose to depict that woman in that photograph in the film. Yeah. In the propaganda photos, they were reproducing this image of a woman who has been assaulted, but then when I started digging, [I found] an archive [of them]… I think what’s interesting about the situation itself is it’s a societal, structural mob mentality. It’s fellow citizens who are punishing these women. It doesn’t come from the government. The government actually tried to remove these women from the streets — to protect them — but they didn’t manage very well. And sometimes, even on the way to a camp, a woman would be assaulted, even though she was supposed to be protected by the government. For me, it was quite important to really show an audience what this feels like. They didn’t get killed, these women, but their souls were hurt and they were stigmatized and traumatized for life. How did you find your way to Marie as a character, and her story? I think there’s a class aspect in the story that I’m very drawn to, and also I had that thematic base in my last film. She’s a young woman who is moving away from the area she knows and her family and takes a job in a big city. [She] probably feels protected by living in a big city compared to being at home where she can be more exposed. She’s a woman who is struggling to survive. I might not agree with some of her actions, but I completely understand where that survival instinct comes from, and the idea that she wants to protect what she’s fought to obtain. Mathilde Arcel as Marie in ‘Woman Unknown’ Venice Film Festival What went into that casting search for Marie, and why was Mathilde right for it? As the title suggests, she’s very elusive for much of the film, up until her unraveling. I always have quite extensive casting processes, partly because I come from theater, but also because I really enjoy [it]. Casting a lead is, for me, like casting a creative partner. So I have to fall in love with the gaze of that person and their take on the character, and therefore I do many rounds and many callbacks. I did that with Mathilde as well, and some of it was improv, some of it was table readings, some of it was written scenes. I think what’s fantastic about Mathilde is that she has so much mystery to her and the way she’s chosen to interpret the character inspired me as a writer-director. That collaboration is key for me, and therefore I spend a lot of time figuring out which direction I want to go [in]. I’ve really enjoyed working with her, and I think she’s extremely talented. So mysterious but so expressive too. Yes, yes. One of the themes that stood out to me was complicity and what it means to be complicit when that head-down mentality is still so entrenched and the hangover of the war so menacing. What were you trying to speak to in this context? The film is not so much [about] giving answers to what’s right and wrong, but to debate what’s right and wrong, or what’s possibly right and what’s possibly wrong. It’s all a bit murky and muddy. Throughout the development of the film, it’s been quite important for me to to not tell the audience — or the readers, in the development of the script — what they should think, but create a situation where the audience can dive into that discussion with themselves or the people they’ve watched the film with. And it’s not only in that time, because I think it’s present also today — in many conflicts. It’s quite hard to to say that it’s just one thing, and the ability to contain two opposite thoughts at the same time is quite hard. Both can be true, and that’s my ambition with the film. Obviously, I have my own opinion about what’s going on in the film, but I think it’s quite important for me as a storyteller that there is room for reflection for the audience. It’s also very much a female-driven story. Do you think this is a period of history for women that isn’t depicted on screen enough? Is it an underrepresented story you’re telling? When I first started the process of developing the script with my co-writer, I would pitch the idea when people ask me: “What are you doing? What are you working on right now?” I started to semi-pitch it, just to see how people would react and what they respond to. And I could see that they would glaze over. ( Laughs .) They would have this empty gaze, because I think there have been so many films about the Second World War, and that is true. But they’re all based mostly on men’s experiences and recollections of war. So that really energized me. Yes, there have been a lot of films about this period [of history], but let’s just do another 100 films about the women in this time period, and then we can say we’re over and done with it, you know? The invisibility of women is everywhere, and certainly in cinema and in our films. So I don’t think we’re finished with the period, but it also sparked the idea of trying to make this film look different than a classical period piece, and to constantly disrupt the idea of a classical period piece. So that’s been an ongoing process of developing and shooting and in post[-production]. How long did it take you to get this film off the ground? I know it’s a co-production which must have helped. The process has been long, but not too long. I did my last film, then once it had premiered at Sundance and had the festival run and premiered in Denmark, I started to develop this film — first with the witch idea and then turning to these horizontal collaborators. Then COVID happened… I worked intensively on the script, and we [were in a place where we] could start the financing. But the financing part of it hasn’t been that difficult in the sense that we’ve had a lot of yeses. We’ve had so many people wanting to do this film. The problem in European cinema is that we don’t get very far with the money we get. There’s been an increase of costs after COVID, everything has gone up, and so we have to work faster in every part of the process. That’s been the challenge with this film, not so much getting the money, but getting far enough with the money we managed to get. What did it mean to you to find out this would be premiering in competition in Venice? I’m delighted that it’s part of this historic festival and that also this theme gets to be exposed for a European audience. I think it’s very important that we keep reminding ourselves of our past and these stories, so that we understand and we analyze and we debate to be able to handle the present and the future differently — if possible. I don’t think it is. But I’m really happy, [Venice is] the best place to be for European film right now. I’m excited. I have this place inside of me where I can go after I’ve made a film. I’ve spent all the time I possibly could on this film. I’ve worked 16 hours a day for more than a year. I’ve spent all my savings. I’ve used every part of me to make this film and all the resources, all the muscle power I have. I can’t really do any more, so therefore I feel okay. Slightly anxious, and I think that’s only natural. There must be a really liberating feeling of finally being able to send it out into the world. Yeah. And I think getting into the festival and being in competition, I’ve already won. How can exposure in Venice help a filmmaker like yourself and your career? [Festivals are] important for the arthouse [films] because it’s a market. It’s also a place where you, as a filmmaker, can create new relationships that you can build on later down the line. But for me, it’s really about the audience that’s there. Through a festival, you can access an audience if you have enough buyers that take the film and they then distribute it around the world. And I think it’s quite important for me as a filmmaker to cling on to [the audience], because it’s so easy to be distracted by other things that are equally nice and shiny and attractive. But especially the way we finance film in Scandinavia, where it’s publicly funded, I think it’s really important that these films find their audience. None of us have that crystal ball where we can look into it and say, “Okay, if I put this person into a film with this theme and shoot…” But that’s really the hope for me, that this film will find its audience. Are you already thinking about the next one? I can’t help thinking about the next and the next and the next, especially when I go cycling or walking or hiking. But I don’t have that much spare time right now. So, most of my energy is channelled into promoting this film. I’m in the service of this film still. The 2026 Venice Film Festival runs Sept. 2-12. THR

articles.title: Oscars: Iraq picks ‘No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman’ as Best Intl. Feature Contender
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 6, 2026 5:45am 'No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman' Courtesy of the Venice Film Festival Iraq has selected No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman from Norwegian-Kurdish director Halkawt Mustafa as its official submission for the 2027 Oscar race in the Best International Feature category. The film was the unanimous pick of Iraq’s official National Selection Committee for the Academy Awards , mandated by the state ministry of culture. The film follows Vyan, a Kurdish sniper who has survived war by suppressing her emotions. When she learns that her younger sister, missing since the ISIS assault in 2014, may still be alive, she returns to Mosul, determined to rescue her. Avan Jamal ( The Exam ) stars as Vyan, alongside Norwegian actor Thorbjørn Harr. The main cast also includes Kanar Sarchl and Kader Jalal. Related Stories Movies May el-Toukhy Takes 'Woman Unknown' to Venice: "I've Used Every Part of Me to Make This Film" Movies Wim Wenders on His 14-Year Journey Building Peter Zumthor Doc 'From Inside Out' Mustafa, who was born in Iraqi Kurdistan and fled to Norway as a child, said the film was inspired by his encounter with a female Peshmerga sniper during the 2014 frontline battles, as female Kurdish fighters countered Islamic State attacks. The director’s previous films include Hiding Saddam Hussein , a documentary about the farmer who hid the Iraqi dictator for 235 days in 2003, Iraq’s 2016 Oscar submission The Classic , and the 2015 documentary The Women ISIS Fears , which also looked at the world of female Kurdish fighters. No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman was filmed on location in Mosul. Hene Films produced the film in co-production with La Media and The Chimney Pot. True Colours is handling international sales. The film will have its world premiere out of competition at the Venice Film Festival on Monday. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences will announce the 15 films on the best international feature film shortlist on Dec. 15. The five nominees will be announced Jan. 21, 2027. The 99th Academy Awards ceremony will take place on March 14, 2027. THR

articles.title: San Sebastian, Busan-Bound Taiwanese Coming-of-Age Drama ‘Will You Still Be My Friend’ Boarded for Sales by Moveria, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 10:48pm PT San Sebastian, Busan-Bound Taiwanese Coming-of-Age Drama ‘Will You Still Be My Friend’ Boarded for Sales by Moveria, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Dev Benegal’s Judith Blum Reddy Doc ‘Everything Is Not OK’ Acquired by Watermelon Pictures, Annemarie Jacir Aboard as EP (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago San Sebastian, Busan-Bound Taiwanese Coming-of-Age Drama ‘Will You Still Be My Friend’ Boarded for Sales by Moveria, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago Lee Chang-dong, Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu on Class, Desire and Reunion in Venice Competition Drama ‘Possible Love’ 7 hours ago See All Moveria Paris-based Moveria has boarded international sales on Taiwanese filmmaker Lu Po-Shun’s debut feature “ Will You Still Be My Friend ,” which is set for a berth in San Sebastián’s New Directors sidebar before travelling on to the Busan International Film Festival . A Taiwan-Singapore co-production, the film follows two young boys, played by Jaden Wang and Aloysius Looi, whose bond comes under strain as tensions build between their families and the surrounding rural community. Rounding out the cast are Lung Tien Hsiang, Lu Yi-Ching, Andie Chen, Kate Pang and Xing Chang. Related Stories Chloé Zhao Defends Comic-Book Movies: 'It's Important to Not Write Off Stories Because We Don't Consider Them High Art' Lee Chang-dong, Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu on Class, Desire and Reunion in Venice Competition Drama 'Possible Love' A trailer has been unveiled. Popular on Variety Eric Chou Tseng-Chen and Yu-Hao Su produced the film through Taiwan-based InLight Film Studio and Verdant Peak Films. At San Sebastián, the film is also in contention for the Sebastiane Award, an honor for films exploring LGBTQIA+ themes and experiences. In the story, an escalating feud in a rural Taiwanese village forces a boy to shield his secret friendship with his Singapore-raised best friend from the adult conflicts threatening to divide them, even as he privately begins to question his own feelings for his friend. “What I really connected with is the relationship between the two boys,” said Yasmin Porangaba, Moveria’s head of sales and acquisition. “When they’re alone, everything feels simple, light and natural. It’s like they have this little world of their own, almost like a secret, because the people around them don’t really get them. Around their families and friends, they have to fit into certain roles, while their time together feels like a space where none of that matters. “I also love that the film never defines what they are to each other. They’re too young to really make sense of it themselves, and I like that the film leaves that open. They know how to be there for each other, forgive each other and just move forward in a way that feels surprisingly mature. The two boys are amazing together, the film is beautiful, and that’s really what made us want to represent it.” The film has already built an international industry profile through selections including Ties That Bind, the Golden Horse Film Project Promotion, EFM Far East in Progress and HAF Goes to Cannes at the Cannes Film Market. Lu’s short film “Wild Tides” earlier earned him the best director prize at the Taipei Film Awards. He also directed the segment “Way Home” in the 2018 anthology film “Ten Years Taiwan,” part of Busan’s A Window on Asian Cinema lineup. “Will You Still Be My Friend” is his first feature as director. Producer Eric Chou Tseng-Chen brings experience in sales, acquisitions, project management and festival promotion on the international circuit, and co-produced “Get the Hell Out,” which had its bow in the Midnight Madness lineup at Toronto in 2020. Yu-Hao Su has produced credits such as Shatara Michelle Ford’s “Test Pattern,” a Film Independent Spirit Award and Gotham Award nominee, as well as “Fragrance of the First Flower.” Su also executive produced Ford’s “Dreams in Nightmares,” which screened in Berlinale’s Panorama section. InLight Film Studio, a Taiwan-based outfit, spans film and visual art projects, while Verdant Peak Films is dedicated to bringing Taiwanese stories to global audiences and developing international co-productions. Verdant Peak’s recent credits include “Dreams in Nightmares.” Moveria, headquartered in Paris, operates as an independent production and sales outfit for international markets. articles.title: Dev Benegal’s Judith Blum Reddy Doc ‘Everything Is Not OK’ Acquired by Watermelon Pictures, Annemarie Jacir Aboard as EP (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 10:50pm PT Dev Benegal’s Judith Blum Reddy Doc ‘Everything Is Not OK’ Acquired by Watermelon Pictures, Annemarie Jacir Aboard as EP (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Dev Benegal’s Judith Blum Reddy Doc ‘Everything Is Not OK’ Acquired by Watermelon Pictures, Annemarie Jacir Aboard as EP (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago San Sebastian, Busan-Bound Taiwanese Coming-of-Age Drama ‘Will You Still Be My Friend’ Boarded for Sales by Moveria, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Lee Chang-dong, Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu on Class, Desire and Reunion in Venice Competition Drama ‘Possible Love’ 7 hours ago See All Min(d) Studio Watermelon Pictures has acquired “ Everything Is Not OK ,” a documentary from director Dev Benegal chronicling the life of artist Judith Blum Reddy . The film will stream exclusively on Watermelon+, the distributor’s streaming platform. The producing team pairs Benegal with Min(d) Studio’s Maya S. Patel and Neeraj Jain, while Annemarie Jacir (“Palestine 36”) has signed on as executive producer. Related Stories Dave Bautista Officially Set as Kratos in 'God of War' TV Series Dave Bautista Shows Off Body Transformation to Play Kratos in 'God of War' Series: 'Two More Months to Get to Where I Need to Be' “Everything Is Not OK” follows Reddy, whose work as an artist has been shaped by the Holocaust and by displacements that carried her from New York to Paris and ultimately India. The documentary threads Reddy’s story together with those of fellow artists Nil Yalter, Zarina and Camille Billops, each of whom channeled displacement into their art. Palestinian, Kashmiri and Indian poets are interwoven throughout, framing the film as a meditation on remembering what has been erased from home and pushing back once staying quiet stops being an option. Popular on Variety “For Judy, making art is an act of confrontation. An act of liberation. A refusal to let erasure win,” Benegal said. “‘Everything Is Not OK’ is not only a portrait of an artist — it is a meditation on what it means to create, remember and resist through art when silence is no longer an option.” Jacir signed on as executive producer after connecting with the film’s exploration of memory and resistance. “In a moment when the world tilts towards intolerance, Judy’s story is a reminder that memory refuses to disappear and art can still be an act of resistance,” Jacir said. Jacir and actor Adam Bakri both lend their voices to the film’s readings of revolutionary poetry. Benegal is also known for directing “English, August” and “Road, Movie.” A restored version of “English, August,” undertaken by the Film Heritage Foundation, is playing at the Venice Film Festival . The 1994 film is based on Upamanyu Chatterjee’s novel “English, August: An Indian Story” and stars Rahul Bose. The creative team behind “Everything Is Not OK” includes Jain doubling as producer and additional cinematography; Patel as producer; Dhruv Goel composing the music; Jean-Luc Panda as cinematographer; Mona Gesbel as editor; Anurag Jadhao on sound design; and Rob Sciarratta as colorist. Watermelon Pictures launched in 2024. Its distribution and production credits include “From Ground Zero” and “All That’s Left of You” alongside “Palestine 36,” all three shortlisted in the Academy Award’s international feature category, plus the Oscar-nominated “The Voice of Hind Rajab.” Hamza Ali and co-founder Badie Ali brought the Watermelon+ platform online in May 2025, positioning it as the largest single collection of Palestinian film ever assembled in one place.
