articles.title: Moonfish’ Director and Stars Lucy Liu and Morgan Spector Break Down Their Black-and-White Animated Film About Isolated Astronauts And Why It’s an Allegory for ‘The Current Human Condition’
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 11:05pm PT Moonfish’ Director and Stars Lucy Liu and Morgan Spector Break Down Their Black-and-White Animated Film About Isolated Astronauts And Why It’s an Allegory for ‘The Current Human Condition’ By Matt Minton Plus Icon Matt Minton mminton@variety.com Latest Moonfish’ Director and Stars Lucy Liu and Morgan Spector Break Down Their Black-and-White Animated Film About Isolated Astronauts And Why It’s an Allegory for ‘The Current Human Condition’ 7 hours ago The Rise of ‘Love Island USA’: From Death Threats Against Contestants to Agency Battles for the Biggest Stars 6 days ago ‘Lanterns’ Stars Aaron Pierre, Jasmine Cephas Jones on John’s Backstory Episode and How Being Black Informs His Quest to Become Green Lantern: ‘Fear Is Instilled in Our Ancestry’ 6 days ago See All Venice Film Festival For Lucy Liu, who has voiced memorable characters in everything from “Kung Fu Panda” to “Strange World,” being part of the independently made, black-and-white animated film “ Moonfish ” was all about lending her name and support to first-time filmmaker Daniel Zvereff. “These are the people that are not just the creatives, but the ones who are going to be the future,” Liu tells Variety . “I’m just fascinated by how people work and how things start when there’s not all this red tape.” Related Stories ‘The Truffle Hunters’ Directors Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw Look for the Perfect Wine in ‘Burgundy’: ‘A Great Glass of Wine Changes How You Perceive the World’ Venice Market Chief Pascal Diot Says He's Not Affected by New Toronto Market: 'Not What the Industry Wants Now' Premiering at the Venice Film Festival on Sept. 6 after receiving a grant from Biennale College Cinema, “Moonfish” follows a pair of astronauts, voiced by Liu and “The Gilded Age” star Morgan Spector, as they embark on an isolating mission to the moon with a corporate quota to meet if they want to return home. Popular on Variety “I really wanted to have the film take place in an environment that was an allegory to our current human condition we’re all experiencing right now, where society is very plugged in, but simultaneously we’re all growing a bit disconnected,” Zvereff says. Zvereff designed the 2D-animated film so that he could finish it completely on his own, if need be. Thankfully, as Zvereff worked over the course of nine months, he managed to bring on two animators, Hoss Wheeler and Devin Grover. “When I watch 2D-animated films, I feel like I’m being exposed to the subconscious of that artist,” Zvereff says of his approach. Liu adds, “It’s amazing what digital has done for the speed of animation but you can really feel the appreciation and the craftsmanship [here]. There is a tenderness and an imperfection that I appreciate.” Unlike Liu, Spector had never done an animated film before “Moonfish.” The trickiest part was getting into his character’s mental headspace as he goes “a little mad,” as Spector puts it. “This particular class of people has come to live on the moon, and they’ve evolved, essentially, as moon people. But they’ve also evolved as an underclass; they are the group of people without rights, assets or any real hope for the future,” Spector says of Zvereff’s worldbuilding. Liu, of course, also voices the talking fish that accompanies the pair (which Zvereff likens to how miners brought along canaries to know when they had to leave) amidst the mundanity of the corporate tasks at hand. “The future that Daniel’s imagining is one in which the relationship between human beings and their tools has been totally inverted. The corporation has merged with the computer in a sort of perfect authoritarian machine that uses human beings as fodder, basically,” Spector says. “It’s a vision of the world that feels continuous with the one we live in.” While the film explores isolation and loneliness in space, with the dialogue sparse and to-the-point, Zvereff realized during the writing process that it needed to ultimately be positive about the future of humanity. “That’s something that happens as an artist. When you’re making something, you’re taking in all these feelings you’re happening and running them through this prism,” he says. “And out comes this beautiful, unexpected light.” As ‘The Comeback’ and ‘Hacks’ End, Valerie Cherish and Deborah Vance Are Emmy Competitors for the First and Last Time Broadcast Emmy Woes, Lots of Martin Short, Bad Bunny and Other Trivia From 2026’s Nominations Michael J. articles.title: Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 11:35pm PT Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’ By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’ 6 hours ago Venice: ‘My Undesirable Friends’ Director on Epic Documentary About Death of Press Freedom in Russia, How Putin’s Crackdown Is Warning for U.S. 1 day ago AR Content, Vertigo, Blumhouse Atomic Monster Set Remake of Genre-Bending, Satirical French Horror ‘Vincent Must Die’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Courtesy Young Nomads Roma filmmaker Alina Șerban broke barriers long before she set foot on the red carpet this week at the Venice Film Festival , where her feature-length directorial debut, “I Matter,” world premieres in the Venice Spotlight section. Rising from an impoverished background to become a celebrated stage star in Romania, the actress and directing debutante has defied all odds to reach the starry heights of the Lido. Billed as the first feature from a female Roma director to screen at an A-list festival, “I Matter” marks the latest chapter in her life-long quest to reframe the narrative around her marginalized community. Related Stories Dave Bautista Officially Set as Kratos in 'God of War' TV Series Dave Bautista Shows Off Body Transformation to Play Kratos in 'God of War' Series: 'Two More Months to Get to Where I Need to Be' Șerban, however, is taking it all in stride. Popular on Variety “I’m nervous about the pressure of being ‘the first’ — all the firsts,” she tells Variety . “But I also have this immense relief, and the feeling of being grateful that I managed to pull through something almost impossible.” Inspired by Șerban’s own life, “I Matter” tells the story of a young Roma woman studying to be an actor. She’s faced with the threat of being kicked out of her orphanage and must suddenly embrace her identity and confront the reality of making it through life on her own. Based on the 2021 short of the same name, whose festival run included New Directors/New Films, it’s produced by microFILM, 2Pilots Filmproduction, Frakas Prods. and Lemming Film, with international sales handled by Pluto Film. For Șerban, the premiere is a capstone in what has already been a remarkable career. Raised in poverty in Bucharest, she was placed in a state-run orphanage at an early age before becoming the first member of her family to graduate from high school. After attending Bucharest’s Academy of Theatrical Arts and Cinematography, she was accepted into NYU’s Tisch School of the Arts, then later earned a master’s degree from the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London. When she returned to Romania, she mounted an acclaimed one-woman show about her life, focusing not only on the rampant discrimination she faced, but on her triumphs and joys. By her 30th birthday, Șerban had written and staged pioneering plays that championed a radical, feminist, Roma perspective — trying, she says, “to show the humanity of these people. Not to portray them as victims nor villains. Not to self-exoticize. But also to celebrate ourselves.” “I Matter” stars newcomer Denisa Farcaș, bringing both vulnerability and determination to a lead role that she invests with her own life experience, according to the director. Șerban describes working with Farcaș and her co-stars as a “collaborative process,” one in which the group delved deep into “what it means to be accepted” as Roma women while giving the young actors space to “express themselves — to feel that they also own the story.” This isn’t Șerban’s first visit to the Venice Film Festival; she attended in 2023 with the cast and crew of Goran Stolevski’s “Housekeeping for Beginners,” in which she had a supporting role. But this year’s experience will be something else entirely for the director. Nearly two dozen of the cast members of “I Matter” will be in attendance — including the 16 child performers who populated the film’s orphanage — while Roma band Mahala Rai Banda will serenade the red-carpet arrivals. “This is such a historical moment for me, and also for the Roma community,” Șerban says. “It’s a moment of celebration. And I want to look back and say I did everything in my power for the people in the team to [share this] moment. And also to put into the world a message of dignity, of celebration, of pain that needs to be seen.” ‘The Odyssey’ Anoints Christopher Nolan as Hollywood’s Most Powerful Director — Here’s How Universal Thwarted Warner Bros. to Land Him Elliot Page Is ‘Not Really’ Getting Casting Calls After ‘The Odyssey’: ‘If Someone Wants to Call Me…I’d Love to Do Good Work’ Quentin Tarantino Plans to Retire After His Next Movie. articles.title: Are Russian Filmmakers Finally Coming in From the Cold?
articles.full_text: Sep 6, 2026 12:45am PT Are Russian Filmmakers Finally Coming in From the Cold? Despite the controversy around a competition berth for Ilya Khrzhanovsky's "DAU" in Venice, top film festivals have increasingly welcomed back Russian filmmakers while the war in Ukraine drags on By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’ 6 hours ago Venice: ‘My Undesirable Friends’ Director on Epic Documentary About Death of Press Freedom in Russia, How Putin’s Crackdown Is Warning for U.S. 1 day ago AR Content, Vertigo, Blumhouse Atomic Monster Set Remake of Genre-Bending, Satirical French Horror ‘Vincent Must Die’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Venice Film Festival The Venice Film Festival found itself under fire in the weeks leading up to opening night over the inclusion of “DAU,” by Russian filmmaker Ilya Khrzhanovsky , in the main competition of its 83rd edition. In a joint statement released on Aug. 17, the Ukraine Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Culture and the Ukrainian Embassy in Italy criticized the prestigious fest for selecting what they claimed to be “a project linked to the Russian state and its networks of influence,” maintaining that the decision helped to “restore respectability” to Putin’s pariah state. Popular on Variety Related Stories Dave Bautista Officially Set as Kratos in 'God of War' TV Series Dave Bautista Shows Off Body Transformation to Play Kratos in 'God of War' Series: 'Two More Months to Get to Where I Need to Be' The pushback was swift. In an Instagram post responding to the criticism, Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera insisted that “‘DAU’ is not a Russian film; it is not pro-Putin propaganda.” Meanwhile, Khrzhanovsky took to Facebook to refute allegations that the latest installment in his long-running project was backed by Russian financing or is “an instrument of Russian state cultural policy.” Speaking to Variety on the eve of the festival, the director — who renounced his Russian citizenship in 2024 — doubled down, saying: “Since the war started, there was no question of what side I am on, because I am on the side of Ukraine.” Coming on the heels of a recent controversy surrounding the Venice Art Biennale’s decision to mount shows by Russian and Israeli artists, the “DAU” dust-up speaks to a larger question hanging over film festivals, cultural institutions and other events that, in the immediate aftermath of Russia ’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, largely heeded calls for a boycott of Russian cultural exports. As the war drags deeper into its fifth year, a rapprochement of sorts is underway. While relations with Moscow remain frosty for much of the world, Russian filmmakers are gradually coming in from the cold. In the past year alone, Russian-born directors have scooped prizes in Venice (Nastia Korkia’s “Short Summer”) and Cannes ( Andrey Zvyagintsev ’s “Minotaur”), while Khrzhanovsky is joined on the Lido by fellow exile Victor Kossakovsky, whose latest documentary, “Holly Wood Dust,” premieres out of competition. Though the Oscar-nominated Kossakovsky (“Gunda”) and Khrzhanovsky both left Russia in the 2000s, a broader exodus began not long after Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine in February 2022. Whether fleeing in protest of the Kremlin’s war machine or out of fear of the brutal crackdown on dissent that quickly followed, many of Russian cinema’s most prominent voices left the country, forging exile communities from Tbilisi to Paris, from Berlin to L.A. “There are two Russias right now,” says two-time Oscar nominee Alexander Rodnyansky (“Leviathan”), in Venice with Kornél Mundruczó’s “Place to Be,” starring Ellen Burstyn and Taika Waititi. “Russia as the country with this regime controlling everything and censoring all the attempts to speak freely about what’s going on. And there is a Russia outside of the geographical borders.” That diaspora is experiencing exile in a variety of ways. The Kyiv-born Rodnyansky, who was sentenced in absentia to 8.5 years in prison by a Moscow court over his opposition to the war, remains determined to support dissenting voices and “make movies with Russian filmmakers, especially young ones, who I feel myself committed to help.” Now based in France, Zvyagintsev likewise remains a trenchant critic of a country he says he has “no intention” of returning to. Though filmed in Latvia, his Cannes Grand Prix-winning “ Minotaur ” is as scathing a portrait of Russian society under Putin as the director’s previous works. For other filmmakers, the westward flight has offered an opportunity for reinvention. Kantemir Balagov’s “ Butterfly Jam ,” which opened the Directors’ Fortnight section this year in Cannes, stars Barry Keoghan and Riley Keough and is set in an immigrant community in Newark. Director Kirill Sokolov likewise set off for Hollywood; his latest, the blood-soaked revenge farce “ They Will Kill You ,” stars Zazie Beetz and Patricia Arquette. Sokolov’s dark comedy “No Looking Back” was among the first films to bear the brunt of the anti-Russia backlash in 2022, when it was pulled from the Glasgow Film Festival over financing that came in part from the Putin regime. The “DAU” controversy in Venice was similarly driven by ties to Russian financiers who would later be sanctioned following the Ukraine invasion. But Khrzhanovsky stresses to Variety that their involvement in his decades-spanning project ended years ago; his Venice-bound film is a German production, co-produced with France and Sweden, and has received no Russian funding for seven years, according to the director. As these and other Russian filmmakers set up new lives in exile, the financial ties that once bound them to Putin’s state have been cut. That, as much as their vocal opposition to the Ukraine war, arguably weakens the case for protest and will ease further reentry into the international film community. “They’re shot in Europe. They’re financed in Europe,” says Laurent Danielou, of Paris-based Loco Films, who’s currently financing two features from émigré Russian directors. “They’re not Russian anymore.” ‘The Odyssey’ Anoints Christopher Nolan as Hollywood’s Most Powerful Director — Here’s How Universal Thwarted Warner Bros. to Land Him Matthew McConaughey’s First Screen Role Helped Catch a Murderer Christopher Nolan and ‘The Odyssey’ Cast Break Down Ties to ‘Oppenheimer,’ Elevating Homer’s Female Characters and Why Nolan Avoided Yelling ‘Cut!’ on Set ‘The Odyssey’ Translator Emily Wilson Slams Christoper Nolan’s ‘Abysmal’ Screenplay: ‘I Would Be Ashamed to Have Written Any Part of This Script’ ‘The Odyssey’ Screenplay Is Now Available to Buy Online Christopher Nolan Fans Will Stop at Nothing to See ‘The Odyssey’ in Imax 70mm, From Cross-Country Trips to Delaying Pregnancy Loading comments... articles.title: French President Emmanuel Macron Calls for a ‘New Multilateralism’ Across Creative Industries: ‘We Built a Civilization of Images. We Should Not Resign Ourselves to Watching It Deteriorate’
articles.full_text: Sep 6, 2026 2:30am PT French President Emmanuel Macron Calls for a ‘New Multilateralism’ Across Creative Industries: ‘We Built a Civilization of Images. We Should Not Resign Ourselves to Watching It Deteriorate’ The op-ed comes on the eve of the Lumière Summit, which Macron is co-hosting with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung to bring together global entertainment leaders around the future of cinema, TV and gaming By Emmanuel Macron Plus Icon Emmanuel Macron Latest See All DR In 1895, the first public film screening happened. It was in the basement of the Grand Café, nearby the Paris Opera, with a program of 10 short movies, each no more than 50 seconds long. Cinema was born. The names of the two brothers, Auguste and Louis Lumière, became symbols of an art which needs darkness to make light happens. It heralded a new era of our long-standing Civilization of Images. More than a century after, movies and, more broadly, the moving image industry including video games and animation, are more than ever part of our daily lives. From movie theaters, moving images traveled to the television screens and personal devices and, over the past deeply transformative decade, they have found their way into the palms of our hands. One cannot think about visual culture without thinking about screens. Related Stories Al Pacino Sends Video Message to Venice After Missing Press Conference for 'Father Joe': 'I Wish I Was There, I Really Do' 'The Echo Chamber' Starring Alicia Vikander Seals International Distribution Deals Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Screens, in themselves, are neutral. They can be an opportunity to get closer to any audience or a source of risk as we all know from the rise of social media and the inflation of images that some have described as a form of cognitive war. Popular on Variety We see the effects everywhere. Parents worry about their children’s attention. Teachers compete with a permanent flow of images. Artists wonder whether their work can still find an audience. Governments debate technologies that evolve faster than legislation. And each of us knows the strange experience of reaching for a screen for one reason and emerging much later, having forgotten why. Yet the screen itself is not our enemy. It has brought extraordinary things into our lives. Never before have so many people had access to so many films, ideas and cultures other than their own. It’s clear to all of us that a screen can educate, connect and inspire. The question is how to preserve that promise while confronting what has gone wrong. We should begin by acknowledging something uncomfortable: we shaped this world, and we must take responsibility for it. But because we shaped it, we can reshape it. The remedy is not to turn away from screens. It is to change our relationship with them on the screens themselves. To remain lucid about the ways our relationship with screens can damage our world, while being ambitious enough to fulfill their promise, we should look to the arts of the moving image: cinema, series and video games. They have been transformed by the digital revolution. But they also show us what a screen can offer at its best: sustained attention, imagination, authorship and a shared experience of another world. Here is the paradox. We have never spent so much time in front of screens, and never so little time with the works that these screens were built to carry. Yet those works contain much of what made the moving image so transformative in the first place. A film can send a new generation back to Homer. A series rooted in one language and one place can become a global conversation. A video game can ask us not merely to watch a world, but to inhabit it. One distinction therefore matters: the difference between an endless supply of content and works that require time, talent, risk and intention to create. The value of these works is economic. If the screen industries lose the capacity to finance ambitious works, take risks on unfamiliar voices or sustain the institutions that bring them to audiences, the consequences will eventually show up on our screens. There may be more images than ever, and fewer genuinely different things to see. Their value is also cultural. Works preserve memory, give form to experience and allow one society to enter the imagination of another. They allow cultures to recognize themselves and to discover one another. And their value is democratic. A society in which everyone is shown what an algorithm predicts will hold their attention is not quite the same society as one in which citizens still encounter stories, ideas and lives they did not choose in advance. When the systems that shape our attention are optimized above all for engagement, we should not be surprised if public conversation itself becomes shorter, angrier and more fragmented. The value we give to creative works is therefore not only an economic question for the future of the screen industries. It is a cultural and democratic question for the future of our societies. This is why the moment matters. Several transformations are now happening at once: the fragmentation of attention, the concentration of the channels through which works reach audiences, profound changes in how creation is financed, new forms of production and distribution, and the rapid rise of generative artificial intelligence. Taken separately, each might look like one more disruption an industry will adapt to. Taken together, they are changing the conditions in which images are created, financed, distributed and seen. We should not wait until this new order has become permanent and only then describe it as inevitable. Responding requires a method. No single company and no single nation, however large, can find the solution alone. What we need is a new form of cooperation: a new multilateralism for the moving image, pursued with the same seriousness we have brought to trade, climate and security. That does not mean building a global bureaucracy for culture. It means bringing to the same table actors who too rarely address these questions together: governments, creators, studios, producers, broadcasters, platforms, cinemas and public institutions. Governments do not make films. Artists do not design the technologies through which billions encounter them. Companies cannot define the public interest on their own. And no national institution can respond alone to forces that cross borders by design: technologies, capital, works and audiences. The purpose of this dialogue should not be to defend yesterday’s model. It should be to build the conditions for a richer creative future: to preserve the possibility of creating ambitious works, ensure that they can circulate, give audiences the tools to navigate an age of infinite images, and make technological progress compatible with human creativity. This conversation must be global. That is why, this September, together with the President of the Republic of Korea, I will convene the Lumière Summit. France and South Korea have taken different paths, but both have shown that openness to the world can strengthen, rather than erase, a distinctive creative culture. Governments, artists, companies and institutions will come together to begin building a common response, and to move beyond the divisions of yesterday. For this moment also offers a rare opportunity for convergence: between cinema, television and gaming; between public authorities and private companies; and between regions of the world that have too often approached these challenges separately. The transformations affecting us are shared. Our response should be as well. The United States has shaped an extraordinary part of the history and imagination of the moving image, and its leadership will remain essential to what comes next. Asia has become one of the industry’s greatest creative centers. Across Africa, new generations of storytellers are meeting some of the world’s fastest-growing audiences. The Middle East is home to some of contemporary cinema’s most vital voices. Latin America has repeatedly shown how stories deeply rooted in one place can speak to the world. Europe brings its own experience: decades of showing that creative industries can be open to the world without losing their roots, and that economic ambition, technological innovation and cultural sovereignty can strengthen one another. France carries a particular responsibility in this conversation. Proud that cinema was born in France 130 years ago, we should not seek to preserve it in amber. Our task is to help create the conditions in which it can be reinvented. We built a civilization of images. We should not resign ourselves to watching it deteriorate. The same screens that have become part of the problem can also carry the solution: greater access, greater choice, new forms of creation, new encounters between cultures. The task is not to turn back. It is to decide, together, what kind of civilization of images we want to build — and whether we have the ambition to make moving images one of the most valuable Common Goods of our times. articles.title: Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’
articles.full_text: Sep 6, 2026 3:44am PT Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’ 2 hours ago Liam and Noel Gallagher Raise Fists and Electrify Venice as Oasis Doc Gets 8-Minute Standing Ovation 14 hours ago Liam and Noel Gallagher Skip Oasis Documentary Press Conference at Venice Film Festival 23 hours ago See All Getty Images Wim Wenders has clarified his much-discussed statement about filmmakers’ role in politics that kicked off a firestorm at Berlin Film Festival earlier this year. Wenders was at the center of a heated debate at the Berlinale in February after the celebrated German filmmaker, who served as jury president, said during the opening press conference that filmmakers “ should stay out of politics .” Related Stories Robert Pattinson Wants Chris Hansen to Like 'Primetime' Despite His Criticisms: 'I Hope the Inspiration His Character Has Given Is Some Kind of Compliment' 'Pamfir' Helmer Dmytro Sukholytkyy-Sobchuk Realized His Kyiv Apartment ‘Could Be Bombed Any Day,’ So He Remortgaged It to Fund ‘Something Strange Happened to Me’ “We have to stay out of politics because if we make movies that are dedicatedly political, we enter the field of politics,” Wenders said at the time. “But we are the counterweight of politics, we are the opposite of politics. We have to do the work of people, not the work of politicians.” Popular on Variety The statement then dominated the discourse at the festival, with nearly every filmmaker and actor facing a question about politics — including the ongoing conflict in Gaza and ICE raids in the U.S. — during their respective press conferences. Author Arundhati Roy even pulled out of the festival in protest, and festival director Tricia Tuttle had to put out a statement in response to the frenzy. Asked to reflect on his statement Sunday during a press conference at Venice Film Festival , where he is presenting his latest documentary “From Inside Out — The Architecture of Peter Zumthor,” Wenders said that he “could repeat the same thing,” though admitted he “could be more explicit.” “What I said then was, as filmmakers, we are the opposite of politicians. We have empathy. Politics work without empathy; that’s all I said,” Wenders, who sported an “Imagine Peace” shirt, began. “We have a very different thing. I’m not working with a mindset of politicians, we are working with a mindset of empathetic people. And we are into changing things, politics are into confirming what is.” He continued, “That’s what I said and was quoted as ‘We have to stay out of politics,’ and that is not what I said, because it’s not what I said now and I said the same thing then. The frame of filmmakers is a different mindset than the mindset of politicians, and we should not work with that mindset. We work with a different set of rules. I said it again, and I hope you’re not misquoting me and say we have to stay out of politics, because we do the opposite. We are the antidote.” At Venice’s opening press conference earlier in the festival, jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal weighed in on the topic, saying that movies are “fundamentally, undeniably political.” “Look, we could say, how are we possibly here talking about movies right now when the world is in a state of emergency?” she said. “To me, the answer has something to do with empathy. I think that film allows an opening into an opportunity to find empathy inside of ourselves.” ‘Survivor’ vs. ‘The Traitors’: Will Emmy Voters Finally Give the Original Reality Juggernaut Its Due? articles.title: ‘From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor’ Review: Wim Wenders’ Latest 3D Documentary Is an Architectural Marvel
articles.full_text: Sep 6, 2026 5:00am PT ‘From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor’ Review: Wim Wenders’ Latest 3D Documentary Is an Architectural Marvel The German filmmaker trains his stereoscopic lens on the buildings of the Swiss architect, revealing them in surprising ways. By Siddhant Adlakha Plus Icon Siddhant Adlakha Latest ‘Our Share of Sand’ Review: A Brooding Indian Social Drama Told Through the Eyes of a Young Girl 1 day ago ‘My Notes on Mars’ Review: Mackenzie Davis and Rupert Friend Star in an Imperfect Breakdown of Marriage and Memory 4 days ago ‘Onslaught’ Review: Adria Arjona and Dan Stevens Star in Adam Wingard’s Fun but Scattered Military Slasher 6 days ago See All Courtesy of Venice Film Festival The screen is usually a canvas, but it becomes a window to an enormous room in Wim Wenders ’ latest 3D documentary, “From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor.” Within that room unfolds the tale of the Swiss architect of the title, told in occasionally laborious ways. It spends much of its two-hour runtime teaching you how to watch it, and like your average high school class, you might not see the value of its instruction until it eventually comes in handy. In that vein, Wenders presents some magnificent things in the film’s final third, sensations which emerge like Zumthor’s own views on the function of his buildings, which he ties to human experience, understood by its inhabitants gradually, and then all at once — from the inside out. Related Stories 'The Echo Chamber' Starring Alicia Vikander Seals International Distribution Deals Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Édgar Ramírez and Nahuel Pérez Biscayart to Star in ‘Land of the Savages’ by Venice-Winning ‘Blanquita’ Director Fernando Guzzoni Beginning with shots of concave corners and convex, monolithic surfaces, “From Inside Out” engenders curiosity before taking academic detours. These come courtesy of Zumthor himself, whom we first meet as a ghostly projection upon sleek, minimalist surfaces, emanating from the 1980s. Like the Holocaust survivors whose poetry populated the walls in Wenders’ “Anselm” — his 3D retrospective on the works of sculptor Anselm Kiefer — Zumthor’s words become inseparable from each room the camera explores, and each building the architect believes ought to feel at one with its surroundings. Popular on Variety We eventually meet Zumthor in the present: an unassuming man in his eighties, whose descriptions of form, function and fluidity often repeat themselves, but whose sincerity and wisdom are hard to shake. As the film explores houses, museums and other Zumthor commissions, the architect’s use of light and natural materials becomes as important as the theoretical people he intends to fill each space — or, in the case of complicated restorations, the people who inhabited them decades ago. Wenders depicts these ghosts of past and future through dramatizations of curious travelers, whose whispering voiceover offers scattered thoughts on where they stand. There’s a tinge of humor, too, in Zumthor’s stubbornness when designing someone’s home, as the conceptual clashes with the preferential. However, the architect eventually gives way to use and function first, despite valuing the aesthetics at hand (not to mention, his collaborations with local artisans). It isn’t long before Wenders introduces the idea that Zumthor’s spaces are only as important as what goes inside them, when he first contrasts old and contemporary footage of museums he designed, each filled with deeply personal art installations — some of them about war. Zumthor himself doesn’t have the most interesting personal history — at least, not as far as this film is concerned — so Wenders’ exploration can come off as superficial at first. However, this ends up part and parcel of the structure. It echoes the feeling of approaching a marvelous building from afar, and entering its sterile lobby, before slowly discovering its mischievous secrets. Although some scenes and enactments can meander, they give way to a moving triptych of projects whose presentation feels, in a way, climactic. One is a home deeply personal to Zumthor. Another is a Nordic installation built in tribute to women killed in witch trials, which feels terrifying to walk through — a kind of infinitude accentuated by Franz Lustig’s 3D cinematography. And the third is arguably Zumthor’s magnum opus: his sprawling, amoebic construction housing the permanent collection at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, whose planning and completion the doc depicts in detail. By the time the building is finished (and visited by a number of filmmakers, including Ava DuVernay and Werner Herzog), Wenders’ camera moves in tandem with Zumthor’s own abstract notions of the art pieces needing to feel horizontally equal, with none being granted more or less importance than any other. The sprawling gallery seems to have no beginning or end. Its bends extend endlessly, revealing pockets and side rooms with rough, exposed concrete contrasting the gilded grandeur of the pieces on display. It takes a while to realize this, or at least to internalize it, but the film’s own architecture is not dissimilar, with what feels like winding segues that add up to an experience of fluid expanse, of great wandering, and ultimately, of soulful appreciation. Certainly, no one is beholden to a film this demanding, but Wenders wields his 3D camera to craft a perfect marriage of subject and form, filling echoing spaces with art and stories much like Zumthor’s architecture does — until eventually, you leave with a new appreciation of the physical world, and your place within it. ‘From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor’ Review: Wim Wenders’ Latest 3D Documentary Is an Architectural Marvel Reviewed at Venice Film Festival (Out of Competition), Sept. 5, 2026. Producers: Marc Schmidheiny, Christoph Daniel, Karsten Brünig, Wim Wenders. Co-producers: Dario Suter, Joel Brandeis. Crew: Director, writer: Wim Wenders. Camera: Franz Lustig. Editor: Maxine Goedicke. Music: Vera Kappeler, Peter Conradin Zumthor, Laurent Petitgand, Sophie Hunger. articles.title: ‘Woman Unknown’ Director May el-Toukhy Talks the Torment of World War II ‘Horizontal Collaborators’ and Venice’s Female Director Snub: ‘It’s a Structural Problem’
articles.full_text: Sep 6, 2026 5:03am PT ‘Woman Unknown’ Director May el-Toukhy Talks the Torment of World War II ‘Horizontal Collaborators’ and Venice’s Female Director Snub: ‘It’s a Structural Problem’ By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest ‘The Truffle Hunters’ Directors Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw Look for the Perfect Wine in ‘Burgundy’: ‘A Great Glass of Wine Changes How You Perceive the World’ 2 days ago ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Directors Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin Talk Grief, Loss and Their Most Personal Film Yet: ‘You Don’t Get to Choose Your Calling’ 2 days ago Director of Haugesund Closing Film ‘The Murder of Benjamin’ Says the Infamous Neo-Nazi Killing Was a ‘Wake-Up Call for the Whole Nation’ But ‘They Are Rising Again’ 1 week ago See All Jasper Spanning In “ Woman Unknown ,” May el-Toukhy takes a closer look at women accused of having relationships with German soldiers during World War II. “When we started to build a story about a ‘horizontal collaborator,’ we realized that, during and after the war, the female body became part of national identity. But in Denmark, it wasn’t really explored.” Initially, she wanted to make a film about the witch hunts after the Reformation in the 1500s. Related Stories Moonfish’ Director and Stars Lucy Liu and Morgan Spector Break Down Their Black-and-White Animated Film About Isolated Astronauts And Why It’s an Allegory for ‘The Current Human Condition’ Rubaiyat Hossain on Bodies, Beauty and Venice, Toronto and London-Bound 'The Difficult Bride,' Clip Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) “It was difficult to relate to the perpetrators because many of them were just maniac. And I’m interested in ambiguity,” she says. Then, she came across an old newspaper photo of a woman with a swastika painted on her back. Popular on Variety “You can find very similar stories that are thousands of years old. The shaving of a woman’s hair or her public shaming for ‘sharing’ her body is a very old concept. Even today, it’s still happening in many armed conflicts.” Still, this suffering tends to be ignored by historians. The title of her film references that silence as well. “I was inspired by Belarusian writer Svetlana Alexievich who wrote ‘The Unwomanly Face of War.’ She gathered these testimonies from women who talked about having their periods in war zones, hiding in sheds, and giving birth. It’s rare to have such recollections of the female experience during or after the war,” says el-Toukhy. For Marie, a housemaid and a nanny, the future looks bright: she’s about to marry her wealthy employer. But in the weeks leading up to liberation in 1945, she must do her best to survive and ensure that her secrets don’t catch up with her. “Our main character wants to remain unknown, but we haven’t told stories about these women either. When you see their photographs in the archives, they’re often labeled ‘unknown woman.’ Also because people didn’t care.” Ironically enough, “Women Unknown” has already made headlines because of Venice’s decision to include only one female director in the main competition . The festival later added documentary “Naza,” co-directed by Rachel Szor. “Obviously, I’m delighted to have been invited to this historic festival. But I would have loved to be in the company of more female directors in the competition. I do believe it’s a structural problem,” notes el-Toukhy. “We discussed how the idea of publicly shaming women is an old concept. Not having enough films by women is also an issue that goes way back. It’s reflected in the budgets we work with and the talent that wants to be involved. Even journalists talk about male directors differently than they talk about women. I’ve never heard a female director called a ‘genius’ – and I read many articles about male geniuses.” What’s the solution? “Everyone has to chip in and be a part of it. I will now have a chance to discuss this issue through my film, which is rather aptly called ‘Woman Unknown’. I’m happy to do so, even though the circumstances surrounding me being in the main competition are what they are.” “We have a lot of work to do in order to change that.” May el-Toukhy is interested in new solutions. As previously announced by Variety , she’s also part of the new Dogma 25 movement. You can find the full manifesto here . “It’s always healthy to disrupt your process as a filmmaker,” she says. “Dogma 25 is very much about how we make films. Even though I heard many yeses while making this film, I still feel like I had to run much faster. That that kind of sprint doesn’t necessarily benefit the result.” She adds: “The way we have to work is almost unbearable. You finish a film and you’re completely stressed out and exhausted. I could make another big European arthouse drama in the future – I’m not saying goodbye to that format. I just think we really need to rethink the way we make movies.” As in her previous films, el-Toukhy doesn’t care much for typically likable protagonists. In “Queen of Hearts,” she followed a woman who seduced her teenage stepson. In “Woman Unknown,” Marie makes questionable choices as her carefully built facade threatens to collapse. “It would be a betrayal to my sisters around the world if I only portrayed women as saints. It’s important that we tell stories about complex women in a nuanced way, just as we do with male characters. That rings truer to life.” She wanted to stick to a female perspective throughout the story. “Early on, we made a rule that we would never reproduce the male experience of war. [Marie] goes out of the house, but the streets represent danger. People are celebrating and there’s euphoria, chaos and vigilantisms. Her safe space is at home, but then insecurity and danger move in. Suddenly, there’s no safe space anymore.” For the longest time, no one dared to criticize “the liberators” and their brutal methods. “It would have been harder to tell this story 25 years ago when those generations were still alive. Some audience members will still be shocked or angry because their grandfather was part of the resistance movement, which became very strong in Denmark right up to the liberation. But not everyone should have been a part of it.” “It’s important to have discussions about what actually happened so that we don’t recreate false narratives. It’s hard to change the direction you’re going in if you’re not looking back.” Disney Entertainment TV Chairman Debra OConnell on Emmy Noms, Recognition for ‘Dancing With the Stars’ and the New FX/Hulu Setup Bad Bunny Wins Emmy for Super Bowl Halftime Show Can Jean Smart Become the First Woman in Emmy History to Sweep Every Season of Her Series? articles.title: Susan Sarandon Says She’s ‘Still Had Movies Taken Away Recently’ Over Palestine Support: ‘There Are Agencies That Are Telling People Not to Hire Me’
articles.full_text: Sep 6, 2026 5:26am PT Susan Sarandon Says She’s ‘Still Had Movies Taken Away Recently’ Over Palestine Support: ‘There Are Agencies That Are Telling People Not to Hire Me’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’ 2 hours ago Liam and Noel Gallagher Raise Fists and Electrify Venice as Oasis Doc Gets 8-Minute Standing Ovation 15 hours ago Liam and Noel Gallagher Skip Oasis Documentary Press Conference at Venice Film Festival 23 hours ago See All Getty Images Susan Sarandon said she’s “still had movies taken away recently” over her outspoken support of Palestine . At the Venice Film Festival press conference for her new film “The Echo Chamber” on Sunday, Sarandon was asked if she thinks the narrative is changing in Hollywood when it comes to the conflict in Gaza. In 2023, the Oscar winner was dropped by her agency UTA after comments she made at a pro-Palestinian rally and said earlier this year she felt she was shunned by the industry for calling for a ceasefire in Gaza. Related Stories Lav Diaz Preps False Prophets Film and Jose Rizal's 'Noli Me Tangere' Adaptation, Unpacks Venice Title 'Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors' (EXCLUSIVE) Al Pacino Sends Video Message to Venice After Missing Press Conference for 'Father Joe': 'I Wish I Was There, I Really Do' “I think that the narrative has completely changed in terms of historical relevance of Palestine and the ties of Zionists with America and our politics. That has been a major revelation for people. How much money the United States gives to Israel, nobody really understood that,” Sarandon began. Popular on Variety “I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still,” she continued. “But that’s the power structure. I think within the people, certainly internationally, I feel welcome.” “The Echo Chamber” hails from Italian director Andrea Pallaoro and filmed in Italy and Belgium. Sarandon stars in the romantic drama, which was Bernardo Bertolucci’s final screenplay, alongside Luca Marinelli and Alicia Vikander. Sarandon said that Pallaoro was told not to work with her but did so anyway. “I thank Andrea for that, because he doesn’t listen to the warnings,” she said. “There has been a change in terms of the general public, but there are still positions in my industry that are held by Zionists who have not relaxed their feelings towards me,” Sarandon concluded. “But I found my family, I found my people and I’m OK.” PBS SoCal, KMEX Lead L.A. articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Peter White Peter White Executive Editor, Television @peterzwhite More Stories By Peter ‘Antiques Roadshow’ Scores First Emmy Win, Breaking ‘Queer Eye’ & ‘Shark Tank’ Hegemony Octavia Spencer Wins First Emmy ‘The Late Show With Stephen Colbert’ Scores Emmy Upsets, ‘The Daily Show’s Desi Lydic Also Triumphs View All September 5, 2026 5:28pm Jimmy Kimmel and Molly McNearney Amy Sussman/Getty Images Jimmy Kimmel has another Emmy. The comedian has picked up for Outstanding Host for a Game Show for his work on ABC ’s Who Wants To Be A Millionaire . It is his second consecutive win in the category, having scored it for the same show last year. Kimmel beat Celebrity Family Feud’s Steve Harvey, Jeopardy! ’s Ken Jennings, Pop Culture Jeopardy!’s Colin Jost and Match Game’s Martin Short. Apart from Pop Culture Jeopardy! , which moved from Amazon in its first season to Netflix for its second season, the category was dominated by ABC shows. Watch on Deadline The win comes as Kimmel is one of the favorites to win Outstanding Variety Series at the Primetime Emmys on September 14 . Jimmy Kimmel Live! is up against The Late Show with Stephen Colbert, The Daily Show, Last Week Tonight with John Oliver and Saturday Night Live after the Outstanding Talk Series and Outstanding Scripted Variety Series categories were merged. However, Kimmel’s win didn’t foreshadow a change in the winner for Outstanding Game Show. Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, once again, lost out to Jeopardy! , which has won the award four times in a row since it was moved out of the daytime Emmys in 2023. Jeopardy! also beat out Celebrity Family Feud, The Price Is Right and Wheel of Fortune. articles.title: ‘The Late Show With Stephen Colbert’ Scores Emmy Upsets, ‘The Daily Show’s Desi Lydic Also Triumphs
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Peter White Peter White Executive Editor, Television @peterzwhite More Stories By Peter ‘Antiques Roadshow’ Scores First Emmy Win, Breaking ‘Queer Eye’ & ‘Shark Tank’ Hegemony Octavia Spencer Wins First Emmy ‘The Late Show With Stephen Colbert’ Scores Emmy Upsets, ‘The Daily Show’s Desi Lydic Also Triumphs View All September 5, 2026 6:26pm Desi Lydic / Stephen Colbert Getty / CBS The Late Show with Stephen Colbert had an unexpectedly good night at the first evening of the Emmy awards . The canceled series came away with two big upsets at the event formerly known as the Creative Arts Emmys . Colbert Before Air won the Emmy for Outstanding Short Form Comedy, Drama Or Variety Series and and The Late Show won Outstanding Writing For A Variety Series. The latter is a particular surprise given that Last Week Tonight with John Oliver has won that award for ten years in a row, starting in 2016. Also in that category was Jimmy Kimmel Live! Related Stories News Jimmy Kimmel Wins Emmy For Second Year In A Row, 'Jeopardy!' Scores Game Show Prize, Again News Norah O'Donnell Claps Back At Bari Weiss Critics After 'CBS Mornings' Return: "This Is So Silly. Just Watch Our Show" Tom Purcell, executive producer of The Late Show, picked up the award. “I’d like to thank all who those who keep late-night going, [John] Oliver, [Jimmy] Kimmel, super important institution in this country, keep the flame burning, guys,” he said on stage. Watch on Deadline The Colbert Before Air win was also surprising. The digital series, as best one can tell, has only aired ten episodes in the last year, mostly around 2-4 minutes in length. The CBS show also picked up a picture editing win. It bodes well for Colbert’s chances to win the main late-night Emmy on September 14, where he is up against Jimmy Kimmel Live!, The Daily Show , Last Week Tonight and Saturday Night Live. The show was up against last year’s winner The Daily Show: Desi Lydic Foxsplains, Tom Segura’s Netflix comedy Bad Thoughts, The Randy Rainbow Show and SubwayTakes with Kareem Rahma. The latter has particularly campaigned this season and has built huge buzz with the format, which sees celebrities and civilians give hot takes on the New York subway. The Daily Show didn’t go away empty handed, though. Jordan Klepper Fingers The Pulse: Give The Man A Prize won Outstanding Writing for a Nonfiction Program, beating PBS’ The American Revolution and Apple’s The Reluctant Traveler with Eugene Levy. Desi Lydic also won the Emmy for Outstanding Performer in a Short Form Comedy or Drama Series. The Daily Show host beat Randy Rainbow and Big Law’s Kim Estes and it is her second consecutive win in the category, having also won last year. Lydic joked on stage at the Peacock Theater about what winning these awards could mean for her. “I’m so afraid if I keep [winning] these, the White House will nominate me to be their press secretary,” she said. Lydic also joked about her conservative parents. “My dad, who told me if I brought this home tonight, he would quit watching Fox News,” she added. ‘The Debut’, ‘The Liberation’, ‘Elsinore’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Primetime’ Hits The Lido; Lee Chang-dong Interview; Oasis Doc; Reviews; More ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 Broadway Fall Preview: The Stars Are Coming To New York Read More About: 2 Comments

articles.title: Octavia Spencer Wins First Emmy
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Peter White Peter White Executive Editor, Television @peterzwhite More Stories By Peter ‘Antiques Roadshow’ Scores First Emmy Win, Breaking ‘Queer Eye’ & ‘Shark Tank’ Hegemony Octavia Spencer Wins First Emmy ‘The Late Show With Stephen Colbert’ Scores Emmy Upsets, ‘The Daily Show’s Desi Lydic Also Triumphs View All September 5, 2026 7:00pm Octavia Spencer Amy Sussman/Getty Images Norman Lear remains the oldest Emmy winner after Octavia Spencer scored a surprise win over Sir David Attenborough at the Peacock Theater. Spencer scored her first Emmy in the Outstanding Narrator category for her work on Investigation Discovery ’s true-crime series Lost Women of Alaska . The win prevents 100-year-old Attenborough from becoming the oldest Emmy winner ever. Attenborough, who has been on television screens for over 70 years, had a 40% chance of winning the award given that he was nominated twice in the category for his work on Netflix’s A Gorilla Story: Told By David Attenborough and Nat Geo’s Ocean with David Attenborough. Related Stories Late Night TV 'The Late Show With Stephen Colbert' Scores Emmy Upsets, 'The Daily Show's Desi Lydic Also Triumphs News Jimmy Kimmel Wins Emmy For Second Year In A Row, 'Jeopardy!' Scores Game Show Prize, Again Spencer also beat out an A-list crowd including Jodie Foster, nominated for Netflix’s Breakdown: 1975, and Werner Herzog for Nat Geo’s Ghost Elephants. Watch on Deadline It is her first Emmy, having been previously nominated in 2024 for the same award and in 2020 for Outstanding Lead Actress In A Limited Series or Movie for her role in Self Made: Inspired By The Life of Madam C.J. Walker. Speaking backstage after the win, Spencer said, “Before there was an implosion of true-crime networks, there were people like me who [were] interested. True-crime, these things actually happen. I was a consumer who watched for entertainment. There was something always greater to say if I ever had a platform, I would do something. Lost Women was the perfect vehicle.” Spencer campaigned hard for the award, turning up to plenty of Emmy events. Last month, speaking at Deadline’s Contenders: The Nominees Studio, Spencer said , “I think there are a lot of people who are very new to the true-crime genre. I’m not, I’ve been studying it. I read a horrible story, a true-crime story, when I was 11 and I think it made an indelible mark on me.” A Gorilla Story: Told by David Attenborough (Toby Strong / Silverback Films / Netflix) The shock win means that Lear, who won the Emmy for Outstanding Variety Special (Live) in 2020 as a producer for Live In Front Of A Studio Audience when he was 98, remains the oldest Emmy winner ever. Attenborough will have to be consoled that he is still the oldest nominee in Primetime Emmy history and the oldest person to win a Daytime Emmy for Secret Lives of Orangutans , which won the Outstanding Daytime Personality – Non-Daily award last year when he was 99. ‘The Debut’, ‘The Liberation’, ‘Elsinore’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Primetime’ Hits The Lido; Lee Chang-dong Interview; Oasis Doc; Reviews; More ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 Broadway Fall Preview: The Stars Are Coming To New York Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘The Debut’ Review: Julianne Moore And Paul Giamatti Get Big Laughs In Jesse Eisenberg’s Hilarious And Even Sweet Look At Community Theatre – Telluride Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘The Debut’ Review: Julianne Moore And Paul Giamatti Get Big Laughs In Jesse Eisenberg’s Hilarious And Even Sweet Look At Community Theatre – Telluride Film Festival ‘The Liberation’ Review: Carrie Coon, Lily James And Bella Ramsey Soar In Guy Nattiv’s Explosive Cult Thriller – Telluride Film Festival ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival View All September 5, 2026 7:02pm 'The Debut' Topic Studios, Fruit Tree At times downright hilarious, at other times so farcical it nearly sails over the top, and at other times quite poignant, Jesse Eisenberg ‘s third time out writing and directing a feature film, The Debut , throws it all at the wall, hits its target most of the time, and serves up a complete delight with go-for-broke perfectly pitched comedic performances from Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti that take the risks and get the laughs, some so rich you will have tears streaming down your face. At one point during an intense Moore rehearsal scene the laughter was so pervasive at today’s World Premiere at the Telluride Film Festival that the audience broke out into sustained and raucous applause. It is well deserved because comedy is an increasingly rare bird on the big screen these days, and this one is an absolute joy to behold in a packed theatre. A24 plans to release it this December and it is a gift for moviegoers no doubt. Set in the world of those community playhouses where the talent is usually very local, but full of enough enthusiasm and theatrical chops to fill the house over three day runs, you might be reminded of other comedies also set in the world of theatre like Mel Brooks’ classic The Producers, Christopher Guests’ deadpan wonderful Waiting For Guffman, or even the lesser known gem, 1980’s Those Lips Those Eyes, but Eisenberg who also gives himself a small song and dance role in this one, finds his own corner of the sky in this sub-genre, not afraid to mix all out farce, sweet but loving moments that never try to mock small town productions, and even some pretty dark detours for Moore’s ever dedicated novice cast member. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Reviews Telluride Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Reviews Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Moore plays Mona, an unremarkable New Jersey housewife, basically now walking through life unnoticed even by husband (Patrick Fabian) who just wants her to have dinner ready and drive the kids around. You get the feeling this person is so shy she’s invisible, but that all changes when, after seeing a casting call on the supermarket bulletin board she boldly sets out to audition for a local community production of a musical called Nosy Neighbors. With zero acting experience, Mona has never been on a stage before and here must audition for the role of the building supervisor, Miss Danielle. The part instead goes to ace regional performer Serena Cherry, a star veteran of this Jersey theatre which you can tell by the large poster of her as Evita ( Bernadette Peters in a cameo at the film’s start auditioning with a dynamite vocal), but Mona is the only other person auditioning for the role as it turns out (she actually took ALL the info from the bulletin board) and her rather pathetic rendition of one of the show’s songs is quicky stopped by grizzled veteran director Jerry (Giamatti). But despite her family’s complete indifference to this nascent adventure by Mona, she holds out hope somehow to get the role, and eventually she does when diva Serena suddenly drops out complaining the part is just too small for her. With nowhere else to go on short notice, a desperate Jerry casts her, and then tries to mold her into some kind of acceptable performance. But what happens as the movies progresses is when the inner thespian she never knew existed comes roaring to the forefront for Mona. That is ignited during an aforementioned rehearsal where Jerry tries to get her to think out of the box and improvise a moment where she is only supposed to show up and say “your rent is due”. This results in a wild stretch of attempts by Mona to give life to the line, building to sheer insane obscenities responsible for the film’s R rating. If ever there was an instant classic example of comedy timing and delivery it is what Moore does here. Priceless. Suddenly Mona is reborn as an actress searching for meaning in the role much like a Dustin Hoffman in Tootsie , even to the point of spending nights in a rundown Jersey apartment building to get the feel of what Miss Danielle might be “experiencing” on the job. Mona has gone pure method for a woman who no doubt has never heard of Lee Strasberg and thinks that Stanislavsky is a vegetable in the produce department. If you think Eisenberg is going to stop here, this whole section goes to dark extremes as Mona takes this small acting gig too far and drives Jerry up the wall. Moore, as usual, doesn’t play the stereotype but finds real heart in this overlooked soul who is just hoping to find her moment of triumph, of recognition at a point in her life she rightly feels neglected . Joining this community fits the bill, until it doesn’t, and Eisenberg and Moore know just how far to the edge you can go without losing credibility – or the audience. The Debut never does and Moore finds one of her best roles, a chance to again show her comic abilities, but also to achieve a real measure of authenticity in playing a really bad actress who slowly becomes a fairly decent one, the different gradations demonstrating Moore’s remarkable range in pulling off this challenging balancing act. She is as good as it gets. Similarly, far more toned down though, Giamatti delivers in a role tailor made, his line readings perfection, his mounting frustration a riot, and ultimately his own backstory poignantly touching as he explains how his own theatrical dreams never materialized. This is an actor who nails it every time. There is also a choice supporting cast, many plucked from the lights of Broadway and the Tonys starting with Peters doing a nice version of herself, and such stage stars as K. Todd Freeman as Marty the musical director; Colton Ryan, Bonnie Milligan, Lili Cooper, even stars like Craig Bierko and Danny Burstein in blink-and-you-miss them walk ons. Halle Bailey ( The Little Mermaid) , and Havana Rose Liu are sweet as welcoming friends behind the scenes for Mona. Eisenberg wrote all the Broadway-ish songs with titles like “Girl From 4F, Boy From 46D” and the anthem Mona (and Peters) get to sing with varying results, “The City May Have Chewed Me Up (But It Can’t Spit Me Out)”. I want to hear Moore sing that one at the Oscars! He also created the less-than-stellar, but still likeable show this is all wrapped around, Nosy Neighbors. After building on impressive features, When You Finish Saving The World (also with Moore), and his Oscar nominated script for A Real Pain (which won Kieran Culkin an Academy Award), he is showing more facets of his prodigious abilities behind the lens here, not surprising for a multi-talent who is an actor, playwright, fiction writer, filmmaker and now songwriter too. He manages the changing tone of the comedy with great skill, and with something as bananas (literally) as this sometimes dares to get, that is no small task. Can I already proclaim this as the funniest comedy of the year? There. I just said it. Producers are Emma Stone, Dave McCary, Ali Herting and Eisenberg. Title: The Debut Festival: Telluride Distributor: A24 Director-screenwriter: Jesse Eisenberg Cast: Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti, Haile Berry , Bernadette Peters, Havana Rose Liu, Lili Cooper, K. Todd Freeman, Colton Ryan, Bonnie Milligan, Craig Bierko, Patrick Fabian, Cara Buono, Danny Burstein, Eldar Isgandarov, Susan Blommaert, Jesse Eisenberg Rating: R Running time: 1 hr 45 mins ‘The Debut’, ‘The Liberation’, ‘Elsinore’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Primetime’ Hits The Lido; Lee Chang-dong Interview; Oasis Doc; Reviews; More ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 Broadway Fall Preview: The Stars Are Coming To New York Read More About: Comments

Acme’ Distributor Ketchup Entertainment Takes U.S. On Norwegian Animated Pic ‘ViQueens’ ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ $22M Labor Day Take Powering Summer To Potential $4.76B All-Time Record – Update View All September 5, 2026 7:35pm Everett EXCLUSIVE: The 2017 surprise Best Picture Oscar winner, Moonlight , is getting a tenth anniversary re-release from A24 on Oct. 2 in a new 4K remastered cut. The news was just announced by the film’s director, co-writer, Barry Jenkins, at a special Telluride Film Festival screening of the pic. Moonlight follows a young African-American man who grapples with his identity and sexuality while experiencing the everyday struggles of childhood, adolescence, and burgeoning adulthood. Brad Pitt’s Plan B Entertainment are producers on the feature. Watch on Deadline Moonlight premiered in 2016 and went on to win the Academy Award for Best Picture, along with Best Supporting Actor (Ali) and Best Adapted Screenplay (Jenkins and Tarell Alvin McCraney). At the 2017 Oscars, in a mix-up of envelopes by a PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) accountant, the night’s final co-presenter Faye Dunaway read that La La Land was the Best Picture winner. The accountant mistakenly handed Dunaway and her co-presenter and former Bonnie & Clyde co-star, Warren Beatty, the back-up envelope for actress in a leading role (which was won by La La Land ‘s Emma Stone). La La Land producer Jordan Horowitz, upon taking the stage, realized that La La Land hadn’t won Best Picture, rather Moonlight , and announced the correction to the world. articles.title: Mariska Hargitay Wins Two Emmys For ‘My Mom Jayne,’ Thanks Gloria Steinem From Stage
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Director Matt Dougherty, E.P. Jane Campion Explore Riveting “Anti-Guru” U.G. Krishnamurti In ‘The Natural State’ – Telluride Film Festival Danny Boyle’s ‘Ink’ Makes Tabloid Headlines At Telluride ‘The Row’ First Look: Oscar Winner Bryan Fogel Documents One Man’s Incredible Solo Row From California To Australia – Telluride Film Festival View All September 5, 2026 7:37pm Mariska Hargitay NBC via Getty Mariska Hargitay is warming up to host the televised Primetime Emmy Awards in the best way imaginable – by winning two Emmys for her documentary My Mom Jayne . The HBO film in which Hargitay explores the life and career of her late mother, the actress Jayne Mansfield, as well as a mystery over Mariska’s biological father, won Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special. Hargitay also claimed the Emmy for Outstanding Directing for a Documentary/Nonfiction Program. The honors came as the 78 th Annual Primetime Emmy Awards kicked off Saturday night in Los Angeles with what were formerly called the Creative Arts Emmys. The show will continue Sunday evening from the Peacock Theater downtown, leading up to the televised Primetime Emmys on Monday, September 14 (airing on NBC and the Peacock streaming platform). Related Stories News 'Antiques Roadshow' Scores First Emmy Win, Breaking 'Queer Eye' & 'Shark Tank' Hegemony News Octavia Spencer Wins First Emmy, Stops Sir David Attenborough Becoming Oldest Emmy Winner Ever Accepting the award for Documentary or Nonfiction Special, Hargitay acknowledged the feminist icon Gloria Steinem , who died Wednesday at the age of 92. Watch on Deadline “My hero and friend Gloria Steinem recently said, ‘Please tell your own story,’” Hargitay shared. “The most important thing we can do for each other is to know each other through stories. I got to know my mother through telling the story. It’s a gift that’s indescribable.” A young Mariska Hargitay with her mother, Jayne Mansfield. Courtesy of HBO Accepting the trophy for directing, Hargitay commented, “I’m utterly overwhelmed. I just wanted to share with you that it took me a while when I decided to make this film during the pandemic. It took me a while to realize that this was my story to tell. I could direct it.” And she alluded again to Steinem’s counsel to women about “telling your own story,” saying, “I just want that invitation to go out, especially to women. I’m so excited to explore and discover and innovate new ways of telling stories from half of the earth’s population because we don’t hear from you enough. I can’t wait to get to know you.” It’s been an extraordinary year-plus for Hargitay, who is entering the 28 th season as the star of Law & Order: SVU . In addition to premiering My Mom Jayne , she made her Broadway debut in Every Brilliant Thing , and then agreed to take on the challenge of hosting the Primetime Emmy Awards. “Dreaming is actually part of planning,” Hargitay said backstage at the Emmys after her two wins. “I’m at a place in my life where I just say yes, I said yes to Broadway, and I said yes to hosting the Emmys. When they called me, they thought it was a joke. It’s a year of firsts and a year of saying yes. Not limiting myself or not being governed by fear. What if it all works out? That’s the process of art. I’m in that place right now, I’ll figure it out. I’m really happy right now.” In the Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special category, My Mom Jayne triumphed over John Candy: I Like Me ; Marty, Life Is Short ; Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man! , and Ocean with David Attenborough (the latter film won Outstanding Cinematography for a Nonfiction Program and Outstanding Sound Editing For A Nonfiction Or Reality Program). In the documentary directing category, Hargitay was up against Lawrence Kasdan of Marty, Life Is Short ; Judd Apatow and Michael Bonfiglio of Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man! ; Alexandria Stapelton for Sean Combs: The Reckoning , and Rebecca Miller for Mr. Scorsese . ‘Mr. Scorsese’ director Rebecca with Martin Scorsese Courtesy of Apple TV Miller, however, isn’t going home empty-handed. Her five-part docuseries about legendary filmmaker Martin Scorsese won the marquee category of Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Series. Robert De Niro, Leonardo DiCaprio, Jodie Foster, screenwriters Paul Schrader and Nicholas Pileggi, Spike Lee, and Daniel Day-Lewis (Miller’s husband) are among the luminaries who appear in the series. Scorsese himself sat down for intimate interviews in which he addressed his career highs and some early lows, his complicated romantic life, and his upbringing as an asthmatic child in New York City. ‘The Debut’, ‘The Liberation’, ‘Elsinore’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Primetime’ Hits The Lido; Lee Chang-dong Interview; Oasis Doc; Reviews; More ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 Broadway Fall Preview: The Stars Are Coming To New York Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Mel Gibson Says ‘The Resurrection’ Will Flesh Out Gaps In The Gospels
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Tom Tapp Tom Tapp Deputy Managing Editor More Stories By Tom ‘Harry Potter’ TV Series Due To Hit HBO Christmas 2026: Everything We Know About The Cast, Who’s Creating It, What J.K. Rowling Says & More Steve Ballmer & Clippers Vow To Fight Historic NBA Punishment, Claim Investigation Was “Heavily Biased” 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More View All September 5, 2026 9:03pm Mel Gibson at the UK Premiere of 'Daddy's Home 2' John Phillips/Getty Images “If you look at the synoptic Gospels — and they are synoptic, which means they don’t tell you everything,” Mel Gibson told The Christian Post in an interview this week. “And even John says, ‘Y’know, hey, there were many other things [Jesus] said and did which, if they were to be written down, couldn’t fill all the libraries of all the world,’ right? So there’s a lot of stuff that wasn’t written and the Gospels are synoptic.” Per the publication U.S. Catholic , “ Synoptic is a Greek word that means ‘to see together.’ The term refers to the three gospels that present the life, passion, death, and resurrection of Jesus in a somewhat similar fashion. The synoptic gospels are Matthew, Mark, and Luke.” Related Stories News Mel Gibson Apologizes For "Thoughtless Idiocy" After Seemingly Mocking ASL Interpreter At Fan Event News Mel Gibson Shares 'Lethal Weapon 5' Update: "I Think That The Fifth Script Is Better Than All Of The Others" Gibson seems to be saying that his upcoming two part film event, The Resurrection of the Christ , will seek to fill in some of the narrative between the various tellings. Watch on Deadline “One can look at these things and go, ‘I wonder what was around that?’ and try and analyze those things and make suppositions about what might have been,” said the director. “Not to go against anything in orthodox teaching but to enhance, I think, what’s there for everyone to see and hopefully they’ll be surprised by some of those revelations.” The films’ narrative scope is expansive, to say the least. “There’s some crazy stuff,” Gibson revealed last year. “I think in order to really tell the story properly you have to really start with the fall of the angels, which means you’re in another place, you’re in another realm. You need to go to hell. You need to go to Sheol.” Sheol is the underworld of the Old Testament. “I mean, you’ll be in the firmament before the creation,” Gibson told The Christian Post this week. “You’ll be in the Hell of the just, and then you’ll be in the Hell of the damned. And so it jumps around a little bit. It doesn’t just stay on the planet here. It gets around.” Lionsgate will release the film in North America and the UK, as well as in Latin America through IDC, its JV in the region, and will team with international distribution partners in many other territories. articles.title: Richard Osman Appears To Confirm ‘The Celebrity Traitors’ Premiere Date Amid Talk That Season 2 Was “Intense” To Film
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake BBC Board Members Told To Seek Legal Advice Before Traveling To U.S. Amid Trump Lawsuit Chris Langham Dies: BAFTA-Winning ‘The Thick Of It’ Star & Child Sex Offender Was 77 Nicola Coughlan, Luke Evans & Hugh Bonneville Are Speaking Out Against AI Voice Cloning, But Is The Government Listening? View All September 6, 2026 2:58am Richard Osman and 'The Celebrity Traitors' Getty/BBC Richard Osman has apparently let slip that The Celebrity Traitors will return to the BBC this month. Speaking on-stage during a live episode of The Rest Is Entertainment podcast in London, Osman told the audience that The Celebrity Traitors will premiere on September 23. Osman and co-host Marina Hyde were interviewing special guest Joe Marler, the former England rugby player who has become a fixture on UK television since appearing in Season 1 of The Celebrity Traitors . Per a Press Association report, Marler was asked what advice he would give contestants when he speculated on Season 2’s premiere date: “What is it, September 23, the next series?” Related Stories Legal Lindsay Clancy Mistrial: Jury Deadlock Proves Too Much To Continue Triple-Murder Case, For Now News BBC Board Members Told To Seek Legal Advice Before Traveling To U.S. Amid Trump Lawsuit Osman chimed in: “By the way, to point out, it’s absolutely embargoed that it starts on September 23 … let’s talk about what we call the events of September 23 this year … the cat’s out of the bag, isn’t it? Not to repeat it.” Watch on Deadline A BBC insider joked that they did not realize Marler was “moonlighting in the BBC One scheduling team,” but declined to confirm that September 23 was the premiere date. During the conversation at London’s Southbank Centre on Saturday, Osman said he had heard from Season 2 celebrities that it “was quite intense” to film. Deadline has also heard chatter about Season 2, with one well-placed source describing it as a “nightmare” that was tricky for producers Studio Lambert. Marler shed a little more light. He told Osman and Hyde: “I believe it was a slightly different emotion than our experience. Ours was very laugh-led, and everyone was sort of enjoying catching up, you know, pratting about to the point where they [the producers] went: ‘Guys, we’re trying to play a game.’ He continued: “Whereas this lot really want it from the start, and then I guess they see how well the first series has gone and there’s a little bit of pressure on them to be like: ‘Oh, I’d quite like a bit of that.’” Speaking at the Edinburgh TV Festival last month, BBC content chief Kate Phillips revealed that there will be tears and surprises in the new season, hosted by Claudia Winkleman. The show will feature an eye-catching cast including The Last of Us star Bella Ramsey , Good Omens actor Michael Sheen , and Oscar-nominated Richard E. Grant . Others include Industry star Myha’la, Barbie actress Sharon Rooney, Love Island host Maya Jama, Broadchurch’s Julie Hesmondhalgh, and Jerry Hall, the model and actress who was married to Mick Jagger. Season 1 of The Celebrity Traitors was the most-watched show on British TV last year. It debuted on BBC iPlayer and BBC One in October 2025 and was seen by an average audience of 14.9M, with a peak of 15.4M for the finale. Comedian Alan Carr emerged victorious in a game that featured Stephen Fry and Celia Imrie. The Celebrity Traitors is produced by Studio Lambert Scotland for BBC One and iPlayer and has been commissioned by Kalpna Patel-Knight, Head of Entertainment Commissioning for the BBC. The executive producers for All3Media-backed Studio Lambert are Mike Cotton, Sarah Fay, Lewis Thurlow and Katy Fox, with production executives, Lynette Woods-Reynolds, Gemma Scholes and Faye Donaldson. The commissioning editors for the BBC are Neil McCallum and Michael Jochnowitz. The Traitors (Dutch title: De Verraders ) was created and developed by IDTV in cooperation with RTL Creative Unit.
