articles.title: ‘Father Joe’ Review: Keifer Sutherland Comes Out With All Guns Blazing In This Deliriously Violent Throwback Beat-’Em-Up – Venice Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon ‘Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger’ Review: The Gallagher Bros. Bury The Hatchet In A Sentimental But Funny Concert Movie – Venice Film Festival ‘Primetime’ Review: Robert Pattinson Channels Jerry Maguire And Dracula For Lance Oppenheim’s Dark TV Morality Tale – Venice Film Festival Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews View All September 6, 2026 3:20am 'Father Joe' Venice Film Festival Did you ever feel that King of New York could have done with a bit more Wing Chun? Did you ever think that John Woo’s films weren’t quite Catholic enough? That the siege of Troy might have been handled a bit more successfully if the Greeks had a bazooka? If your answer is yes to even one of these questions, then Barthélémy Grossmann’s old-school beat-’em-is for you, a violent multifaith mob movie with a script so fantastically absurd it can only come from the mind of French auteur Luc Besson , who somehow segued from Le Cinema du Look of the ’80s to Le Cinema du Kaboom of the ’90s. It’s been 32 years since Besson unveiled his international breakout hit Léon , but it’s yesterday once more in Father Joe , which begins in uptown New York, sometime in the pre-internet ’90s, with the unmistakable sounds of the Notorious B.I.G. blasting out on the radio of a blinged-out town car. Veteran gangster Lino ( Michael Rispoli ) is taking his trophy girlfriend into the depths of a desolate industrial estate, where bored lackeys with guns and gold chains keep watch. “People would kill to know about this place,” he says, which isn’t quite the flex he thinks it is, and his date is right to be nervous. Related Stories News Danny Boyle Confirms Use Of AI In New Movie 'Ink' News 'Father Joe': First Look Clip Of Kiefer Sutherland As A Priest Who Clashes With The Mob In Action-Crime Pic -- Venice “This place” is a drug lab, and while Lino is checking out his investment, a man in black starts picking of his crew with the stealth of a ninja and the armory of the Marine Corp. After shooting Lino in the foot, the stranger reveals himself as Father Joe ( Kiefer Sutherland ), an actual priest who takes on Manhattan’s drug dealers wearing his work clothes. “I’m here to put you back on the right track,” he says, and orders him to confess. Watch on Deadline Being a good Catholic boy, as all mobsters used to be, Lino does so, and Father Joe lets him live on two conditions: One, no selling drugs to kids under the age of 21. “You can’t save everyone,” he reasons, with a strangely beatific smile. The other condition is way more Bessonian: Father Joe injects Lino with a complex homemade virus that will become deadly within seven days. To stay alive, Lino must attend Communion every week at Father Joe’s Church on 118 th Street, where he will be given a temporary antidote. But when Lino arrives at the church, he is surprised to see a number of other wiseguys, who line up to take a little blue pill while everyone else gets a wafer. Father Joe’s operation, which is decimating the local drug trade, is hardly undercover (unless you count the secret arms chamber behind a statue of the Virgin Mary), and pretty soon it comes to the attention of crime boss Giu ( Al Pacino ), who has noticed a dip in takings lately. Giu pays Father Joe a visit and gets infected with the same virus after being lured into the confession box. Giu, however, is not as gullible as the men who work for him and gets himself to the hospital for a thorough medical. While Giu is doing this, the story shifts up a gear. Vulnerable local children have started going missing, which may or may not have something to do with a privately run hospital, where rich parents pay through the nose for organ transplants of a very dubious provenance. This sudden shift from drugs to body parts suggests that Father Joe may have been intended as a mini-series (or at the very least a comic book), having the freewheeling quality of ’the ’70s TV show Kung Fu . Father Joe himself certainly has the backstory for it, being a war veteran who married an Asian woman who died young and lost his grieving daughter to an overdose. This not only explains Father Joe’s benevolence, it also opens up room for a sassy sidekick: 16-year-old drug casualty Felicity, who’s played by Ever Anderson, daughter of The Fifth Element star Milla Jovovich. A child from a broken home, Felicity soon goes native and wants in on Father Joe’s set-up, much to his horror. Despite this strange digression, Besson’s script soon gets back on track when Giu gets the results of his tests back and declares war on Father Joe. And this does mean war; Grossmann’s deliriously violent actioner commands an insane amount of firepower but still finds time for some classic throwbacks — such as a fantastically staged fist fight in an elevator — while the body count climbs into the heights of a Takeshi Miike movie. Amazingly, Al Pacino is about the only thing that isn’t over the top here, generously giving center stage to Keifer Sutherland in a role that’s fun, unbelievable — and sometimes unbelievably funny (wait for the cardinal to deliver the punchline) — but, like Besson’s 2023 film Dogman , it’s never laughable, such is everyone’s commitment. Is it any good? Who knows. It’s certainly the most balls-out, no-f*cks-given rock’n’roll phenomenon to hit the Lido this year — and that includes the Gallagher brothers. Title: Father Joe Festival: Venice (Venice Open – Out Of Competition) Director: Barthélémy Grossmann Screenwriter : Luc Besson Cast: Kiefer Sutherland, Ever Anderson, Al Pacino, Michael Rispoli World sales: Kinology Running time: 1 hr 46 mins ‘The Debut’, ‘The Liberation’, ‘Elsinore’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Primetime’ Hits The Lido; Lee Chang-dong Interview; Oasis Doc; Reviews; More ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 Broadway Fall Preview: The Stars Are Coming To New York Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Susan Sarandon Says Narrative Around U.S. Ties With Israel Is Changing But She Is Still Losing Studio Roles
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Nanni Moretti’s ‘It Will Happen Tonight’ Earns Nine-Minute Ovation At Venice World Premiere Robert Pattinson Addresses Chris Hansen’s Criticism Of ‘Primetime’: “I Hope It’s Some Kind Of Compliment” Loco Films Boards Venice Title ‘Guria’ As Drama Is Selected To Be Georgia’s Oscar Entry + First Trailer View All September 6, 2026 5:44am Luca Marinelli, Susan Sarandon, Andrea Pallaoro and Alicia Vikander attend the "The Echo Chamber" photocall in Venice Photo by Andreas Rentz/Getty Images) Susan Sarandon told a press conference in Venice on Sunday that she continued to lose big studio roles due to her public support of Palestine , even if the narrative around the nature of U.S. support of Israel has changed in recent months. “I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still. But that’s the power structure. I think within the people, certainly internationally, certainly internationally, I feel welcome,” she said. The Oscar-winning actress was speaking at the Venice Film Festival press conference for Andrea Pallaoro’s Golden Lion contender The Echo Chamber , an adaptation of Bernardo Bertolucci’s final screenplay. Related Stories Festivals 'Father Joe' Review: Keifer Sutherland Comes Out With All Guns Blazing In This Deliriously Violent Throwback Beat-'Em-Up - Venice Film Festival News Danny Boyle Confirms Use Of AI In New Movie 'Ink' She stars as storied songstress Ava who engages engages a music producer with a history of drug addiction to work on her comeback album, becoming the third wheel in his complex relationship with a physiotherapist, who is her antithesis in her private, quiet approach to life. Watch on Deadline “I thank Andrea for that because he didn’t listen to the warnings,” she continued. “So I think yes, there has been a change in terms of understanding of the situation, and I think the general public. But there are still very strongly held positions within my industry that are held by Zionists and who have not relaxed their feelings towards me, but I found my family, I found my people, and I’m okay.” The Thelma And Louise star, who was dropped by UTA in 2023 after attending several rallies in support of Palestine, has revealed in the past that roles dried up for as a result of her activism. Earlier in the press conference, Sarandon said that she felt the wider narrative about Palestine and Israel had shifted in the U.S. “I think that the narrative has completely changed in terms of the historical relevance of Palestine and the ties of Zionists with America and our politics, that has been a major revelation for people,” she said. “How much money the United States gives to Israel? Nobody really understood that. And also now we have voted to combine the army of the United States with the army of Israel. So there’s a lot of things that people are aware of now.” ‘The Debut’, ‘The Liberation’, ‘Elsinore’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Primetime’ Hits The Lido; Lee Chang-dong Interview; Oasis Doc; Reviews; More ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 Broadway Fall Preview: The Stars Are Coming To New York Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Tender Loving Care’ Review: Kate O’Flynn Lights Up Mike Leigh’s Warm, Gently Wrenching Study of Solace and Solidarity
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Jon Frosch Plus Icon Jon Frosch Senior Editor, Reviews jon_frosch Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 6:47pm Kate O'Flynn (right) and Alice Bailey Johnson in 'Tender Loving Care.' Courtesy of Joseph Lynn/Thin Man Films Ltd/Bleecker Street A drama dotted with laughs (or a comedy blotted with pain?) in which everyday problems are confronted, and avoided, over steaming cuppas and brimming glasses of white wine, Tender Loving Care explores friendship, family dynamics and England’s fraying social safety net. In other words, it’s a Mike Leigh film, and a lovely one at that. If it ends up being his last, as the 83-year-old writer-director has indicated, it’s a fitting and stealthily powerful way to go out — a low-key mic drop of sorts. The movie is warm and inviting, filled with giggles and gossip and gentle gallows humor; it’s also wrenching, with a topical urgency simmering just beneath the jovial surface. While Leigh’s left-wing politics inform the story, the filmmaker, unlike his contemporary Ken Loach, mostly avoids playing ventriloquist; the chit-chatting, chortling, sobbing, seething souls who populate his work tend to be too complicated, too insistently human to serve as mere spokespeople for their creator’s ideas. Related Stories Movies In Her New Movie, Carrie Coon Plays an Unexpected Cult Member: It's Easy to Say "No Way That Would Ever Happen to Me" Movies Telluride Film Fest Kicks Off with Brunch, 'Wild Horse Nine' North American Premiere Tender Loving Care The Bottom Line A lovely addition — and likely conclusion — to an exceptional career. Venue: Telluride Film Festival Cast: Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson, Kate O’Flynn, Alice Bailey Johnson Director-screenwriter: Mike Leigh 1 hour 47 minutes In Tender Loving Care , those ideas concern compassion, solidarity and support — what it means to look out for one another at this (angry, angering) point in history, specifically in a country whose public services have been eroded by an ethos of self-reliance codified by Thatcher and further cemented, or perverted, by Brexit. As is often the case in Leigh’s films, the thematic framework is conspicuous; characters, on occasion, turn subtext into text, delivering mini-disquisitions on the failures of the state and the isolation of urban life today. Those statements might register as distractingly didactic if they didn’t sound wholly believable coming out of these particular people’s mouths; two of the four central figures, childhood BFFs Amy ( Kate O’Flynn , Widow’s Bay scene-stealer) and Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson), are overextended, underappreciated social workers — and seasoned compartmentalizers, lest the despondency they witness daily on the job pull them under. Amy and Rosie, as well as Amy’s kindly parents Birdie (Marion Bailey, Leigh’s longtime partner) and Geoff (Paul Jesson), arrive onscreen fully formed, alive with personal and relational histories we can intuit beyond what’s in the frame. If it feels like we’ve known these folks forever — from Amy and Rosie’s mutual hype sessions to Birdie and Geoff’s puttering and banter — that’s a credit to Leigh’s legendary rehearsal process, during which he and his actors build the characters from scratch through weeks of improvisation and discussion. Nothing and everything happens over the course of Tender Loving Care . Unceremoniously dumped by a boyfriend who’s gone back to his wife and child, Amy moves in with single-and-mingling Rosie. Birdie frets about Amy’s romantic and reproductive prospects, though she and Geoff console themselves with their certainty that she’s better off sans her ex. Amy and Rosie endure stressful days on the job (Amy works mainly with children, Rosie with the elderly), retreating to their flat in the evenings to swap horror stories or decompress over girl talk, dance-offs and other bursts of booze-infused silliness. Geoff’s health takes a sudden turn for the worse. The tone here is mellower, the pitch less heightened than in Leigh’s more volatile domestic tragicomedies, like Secrets & Lies and Life Is Sweet , to say nothing of the bludgeoning All or Nothing . That’s in large part a reflection of the new film’s main quartet, who sit at the opposite end of the temperamental spectrum from Pansy, the ferocious protagonist of Leigh’s previous effort, 2024’s Hard Truths . Amy, Rosie, Birdie and Geoff are indeed among the most amiable characters Leigh has ever created, their darker feelings — loneliness, jealousy, rage, dread — tucked safely beneath chipper smiles and cheerful pleasantries. But Leigh has never been one to flinch at life’s cruelties. The simplicity of Tender Loving Care ’s narrative, the sweetness of the people it portrays, and the ticklish good vibes they generate belie a toughmindedness about both the private disappointments and the larger societal injustices that shake our respective worlds. When moments of anguish arrive — a neighbor’s tormented account of her husband’s funeral; a tirade by a paranoia-gripped hoarder Rosie is assigned to visit; a hard-drinking mother’s fury at the foster care system for which Amy is assessing her — they have a rawness and force that slice right through the movie’s congeniality. The film is in direct conversation with Hard Truths , as well as Leigh standouts Another Year and Happy-Go-Lucky , in its consideration of what determines happiness — the degrees to which choice, disposition, luck and broader structural or socioeconomic forces play a part. Like so much of Leigh’s work, Tender Loving Care ponders how people of different circumstances and constitutions coexist: how we make each other feel and act, how our perception of each other’s lives shapes our perception of our own. It’s also about how we proceed with the business of living amid hardships both mundane and momentous. Like Ozu , a clear influence, Leigh is one of the medium’s great observers of human behavior, from the small talk that drowns out the terror of our worst anxieties to the self-delusions that sustain us during our most vulnerable moments to the way we accept or refuse help — the latter sometimes misguidedly. “I can’t put it on them,” Amy tells Rosie, explaining her reluctance to let her parents know of her break-up. Like all the film’s principals, Amy is an expert practitioner of Britain’s famed stiff upper lip, but here she’s sparing Birdie and Geoff a burden they’re more than ready to share. O’Flynn is an expressive marvel, her kooky lightheartedness periodically clouding over with a melancholy that cuts to the bone. The swirl of conflicting emotions that play out across Amy’s face as she gulps champagne while listening to her mother reminisce about her courtship with Geoff is astonishing — a piercing pantomime of the oft-cited notion that millennials are the first generation to have fewer opportunities than their parents. Bailey Johnson, a casual charisma bomb, makes Rosie so radiant and grounded and fun that you may realize only late in the film — when she reveals she no longer speaks to her own mom and dad — that her generosity toward the other characters is more symbiotic than selfless. Rosie is the very definition of a ride-or-die, but she needs Amy and her family as much as they need her. The beautifully synced Bailey and Jesson, meanwhile, offer a duet of endearments, confidences, worries and innocuous shit-talk, conjuring the ineffable mix of intimacy and distance that makes a long-term marriage. When the rhythm of their relationship is disrupted in the film’s second half, the effect is devastating. Visually, Tender Loving Care is characterized by Leigh’s typical unfussiness, with Lucy Bristow taking over DP duties from frequent Leigh collaborator Dick Pope, who died in 2024 . As usual, there’s mastery in how the filmmaker uses facial close-ups to add notes of tension, encouraging the viewer to locate truths undisclosed by the dialogue. Ditto in how he deploys a single overhead shot — serene but conspicuous — to foreshadow an unlucky swerve in the story. A touching penultimate scene feels like a natural conclusion to this portrait of people devotedly closing ranks when crisis strikes. But Leigh doesn’t stop there, instead punctuating his film with a final image of uncommon bluntness and despair. At first impression, it seems an incongruously — if not unjustifiably — hopeless way to go out. Yet given the dogged humanism that is the throughline of Leigh’s extraordinary filmography, perhaps a less pessimistic reading is due: Leigh is ending his movie, possibly his career, with a plea for individuals to lift up those they know and love, of course, but also to fight for a society that lifts up those they don’t. Full credits Venue: Telluride Film Festival Release date: Dec. 4 (U.S.) Production companies: Cornerstone Films, Film4, Desmar, Ventureland, Thin Man Films, Merino Films, Creativity Media Distribution: Bleecker Street Cast: Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson, Kate O’Flynn, Alice Bailey Johnson, Brid Brennan, Peter Wight, Alan Williams, Sandy Foster, Amanda Lawrence, Diveen Henry, Ashna Rabheru, Eva Holovko, Kaedon Skerritt, Tilly Vosburgh Director-screenwriter: Mike Leigh Producer: Georgina Lowe Executive producers: Richard Kondal, Jennifer Eriksson, Dan Janvey, Kerstin Emhoff, Meredith Crowley, Jonathan Weiner, Farhana Bhula, Naomi Despres, Michele Marshall, Kent Sanderson, Tyler DiNapoli, Miranda King, Alison Thompson, Mark Gooder, Gail Egan Director of photography: Lucy Bristow Editor: Tania Reddin Production designer: Jane Brodie Costume designer: Jacqueline Durran Music: Gary Yershon Casting: Nina Gold 1 hour 47 minutes THR

articles.title: ‘A Long Winter’ Review: Fred Hechinger and Ebon Moss-Bachrach Shine as Family Thrust Into Uneasy Isolation in Andrew Haigh’s Fine-Grained Drama
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 7:30pm From left: Fred Hechinger and Ebon Moss-Bachrach in 'A Long Winter.' Mubi The many ways in which writer-director Andrew Haigh and fiction author Colm Tóibín share a kinship of sensibilities, notably in their impeccable gifts for intimate character observation, breathe warming embers into the sub-zero elemental severity of A Long Winter . A coming-of-age drama that touches delicately on grief and resilience, family and home, queer sexuality and liberating self-discovery, the film’s muted tone will be considered under-powered by some. But audiences willing to tune in to its slow-burn introspection and immersive sense of place will find a humanity that is its own reward, particularly in the probing performances of Fred Hechinger , Ebon Moss-Bachrach and D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai . Related Stories Movies 'Tender Loving Care' Review: Kate O'Flynn Lights Up Mike Leigh's Warm, Gently Wrenching Study of Solace and Solidarity Movies In Her New Movie, Carrie Coon Plays an Unexpected Cult Member: It's Easy to Say "No Way That Would Ever Happen to Me" Just as Haigh transposed the Japanese source novel from Tokyo to London in his 2023 stunner, All of Us Strangers , his adaptation of Tóibín’s novella — first published in the Irish author’s haunting 2006 short story collection Mothers and Sons before being issued as a standalone volume last year — relocates from the Spanish Pyrenees to Colorado’s Rocky Mountains. That landscape, magnificent but forbidding as fall lapses into the protracted, snowbound season that gives the film its title, helps make the material Haigh’s own, like a lost literary nugget of 1950s Americana. A Long Winter The Bottom Line Restrained but deeply felt. Venue : Telluride Film Festival Cast : Fred Hechinger, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Caitríona Balfe, Kit Connor, D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai, David Furr, Manuel Garcia-Rulfo, Martin Freeman, Geoff Gustafson, Anthony Timpano Director-screenwriter : Andrew Haigh, based on the novella by Colm Tóibín 1 hour 59 minutes The central character and the eyes and ears of the story is Mike (Hechinger), who took a test run at life on a farm two state lines away from his family’s cabin high in the mountains but was soon pulled back by homesickness. Mike is resistant to change, but for his younger brother Tommy ( Kit Connor ), it can’t come quickly enough. Impatient to see more of the world, he has enlisted in the Army and soon ships out to Korea, leaving the other bed empty in the room the brothers had shared since childhood. Change turns out to be beyond Mike’s control when he realizes that his depressed mother, Louise (Caitríona Balfe), is drinking heavily, increasingly chafing at the life of isolation her husband Lester (Moss-Bachrach) has chosen for them. Desperate for a connection to a more sophisticated world and its people, Louise entrusts Mikey to slip copies of Cosmopolitan among the provisions they pick up on trips to the fading foothills township. She knows Lester would disapprove of her spending what little money they have on frivolous pleasures. When Lester, whose father and grandfather both drank themselves to death, starts smelling booze on Louise’s breath again, he enrages her by tipping her secret stash of gut-rot wine down the sink. Unsettled to see his mother suffering, Mike urges his dad to give her what she needs, but Lester insists on her going cold-turkey, causing her to howl in anguish. While Lester and Mikey are out fixing the barn door before the season’s first big storm, Louise vanishes, taking her winter coat and boots with her. As the snow closes in and the phone lines and power go down, local residents and state troopers form a search party, trudging as far as they can go each day on the surrounding mountain range. Louise’s brother Jack ( Martin Freeman ), who lives on the other side of the mountain, has heard nothing from his sister. Family friend Joe (Manuel Garcia-Rulfo), who has started talking to prickly Lester again after a period of chilly silence, tells Mikey to look out for vultures circling overhead, usually a sure sign of a body in the snow. Haigh expertly balances the tone as dread turns to lacerating sorrow. But even as Mike faces the void of his mother’s absence in uncomfortable isolation with his disgruntled dad, his eyes can’t help locking with those of a young cop (Anthony Timpano) involved in the search, in what is instantly recognizable as unspoken sexual tension. While queer characters and themes run through the work of both Haigh and Tóibín, A Long Winter never takes the expected turns, although Mikey does have homoerotic fantasies about the cop in Tommy’s bed. Gay yearning is embedded in who he is, played with a touching cherubic innocence alongside a more adult longing by the reliably excellent Hechinger. When Mike insists on going out alone to continue the search each day, long after his dad has abandoned hope, the rigidly patriarchal Lester grumbles about there being no one to tend to the cooking and housework. When he hires mixed-race orphan Jimmy (Woon-A-Tai, one of the revelations of Reservation Dogs ) as a live-in domestic to handle those responsibilities, Mikey’s desire shifts focus. Whether or not it’s reciprocated is kept ambiguous by both Haigh and Woon-A-Tai. But after intially treating Jimmy dismissively and resenting the stranger’s presence in Tommy’s bed, Mike comes to his defense when Lester obnoxiously mocks the housekeeper one night for doing women’s work. While Jimmy can stand up for himself, the gesture of solidarity sparks a thaw between him and Mike. They start going out together each day to search, walking farther afield each time and pissing off Lester. Mikey’s gayness is very much a part of the character’s DNA, but it’s not the dominant thread of Haigh’s film. The writer-director is more attentive to the tectonic shifts in a family when the balance is upset, and the way that crushing loss can sometimes be a path to personal growth. Through his friendship with the quiet, soulful Jimmy, who has led a tough life, Mike gains the confidence to assert his place in the household, to deepen his sense of belonging in their lonely corner of the world, and to speak blunt truths to his father. The remote cabin he built was always Lester’s dream, never Louise’s. Even when Mike gains a deeper understanding of his mother and learns the reason that his father and their neighbor down the road, Ben (David Furr), detest each other, it appears that he will continue to hold his dad accountable. As always with Haigh, the entire ensemble is strong, led by Hechinger with raw pain, burgeoning maturity and innate sweetness. Moss-Bachrach deftly finds the softer sides of Lester, even at his most unreasonable, indicating that world-weary sadness eats away at him even if he has trouble showing it. Connor is appealing in the smallest role; Balfe leaves an indelible mark, giving Louise an addict’s cunning but also the gnawing frustration of a woman stuck in a life she didn’t want; and Woon-A-Tai brings a restorative calm — never at risk of becoming a noble old-school Sundance cliché. The film looks beautiful, its enveloping crystalline images gracefully shot on 35mm by DP André Turpin on location in the Canadian Rockies (cheaper than Colorado). Production designer Emmanuel Fréchette’s rustic, built-from-scratch cabin, complete with interiors and windows looking out onto the vast expanse of unforgiving nature, gives the movie a fully lived-in feel. And erstwhile Tangerine Dream member Paul Haslinger’s pensive score echoes the gentle rhythms of Jonathan Alberts’ editing. A Long Winter is not an emotional stealth bomb like All of Us Strangers or even Haigh’s 2011 breakthrough Weekend — it’s arguably closest in spirit to another of the Brit director’s American-set dramas, the under-appreciated but lovely Lean on Pete — but the new film’s subdued intensity and aching sensitivity make it lingeringly affecting. Full credits Venue: Telluride Film Festival Production companies: The Bureau, Nomaddic Pictures Distribution: Mubi Cast: Fred Hechinger, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Caitríona Balfe, Kit Connor, D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai, David Furr, Manuel Garcia-Rulfo, Martin Freeman, Geoff Gustafson, Anthony Timpano Director-screenwriter: Andrew Haigh, based on the novella by Colm Tóibín Producers: Tristan Goligher, Chad Oakes, Mike Fristlev, Mike Elliott, Andrew Haigh Executive producers: Efe Çakarel, Jason Ropell, Bobby Allen, Farhana Bhula, Vincent Gadelle Director of photography: André Turpin Production designer: Emmanuel Fréchette Costume designer: Carol Case Music: Paul Haslinger Editor: Jonathan Alberts Sound: Joakim Sundström Casting: Carmen Cuba 1 hour 59 minutes THR

articles.title: Victor Miller, ‘Friday the 13th’ Screenwriter, Dies at 86
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 4, 2026 8:33pm Victor Miller Instagram Victor Miller, the screenwriter behind Friday the 13th , has died. He was 86. Miller died Monday, his son, Ian, announced in a post on Instagram . No cause of death was made immediately available. “Yesterday my father, Victor Miller, went to his final reward. He was almost always the smartest, funniest person in whatever room he was in. He inspired in me, and many others, a love of photography, music, and storytelling,” he wrote. “He had a helluva run and will be missed dearly.” Related Stories TV Richard O'Sullivan, British Sitcom Star Who Inspired John Ritter's 'Three's Company' Character, Dies at 82 Business Raffaele Annecchino, Former CEO of Paramount International, Dies at 55 Miller’s son added that a celebration of life will be held in November, “on Friday the 13th, of course.” He penned the script for Sean S. Cunningham’s beloved 1980 horror classic alongside Ron Kurz. The first film paved the way for a number of sequels, though Miller only served as the screenwriter for the original. He also worked with Cunningham again on 1982’s A Stranger Is Watching , and lent his talents to a myriad of television shows. Some of the TV projects Miller wrote for include One Life to Live , Another World, Guiding Light, General Hospital and All My Children . “Visionary screenwriter Victor Miller unequivocally etched his name in the classic horror film genre pantheon by penning the original script for the first Friday the 13 th film,” Professor Rel Dowdell, director of film studies at Hampton University, said in a statement shared with The Hollywood Reporter . “The screenplay, along with the film’s taut direction and production, launched one of the most famed and enduring franchises in history for over four decades.” Miller is survived by his wife, two sons and his grandson. THR

articles.title: ‘The Idiot(s)’ Review: Aimee Lou Wood and Johnny Flynn Sparkle in a Playful, Indulgent Tribute to Fyodor Dostoevsky’s Underappreciated Wife
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 9:30pm 'The Idiot(s)' Zuzanna Woinska / Gold Rush Pictures / Hype Studios As she finishes transcribing what will become one of her husband’s most enduring masterpieces, Anna Dostoevskaya ( Aimee Lou Wood ) cannot contain her excitement: “This is our best novel yet!” She quickly corrects herself, of course — “I mean, your best novel” — but by then, we understand she had it right the first time. Sure, those might be Fyodor’s words on the page, and his name on the cover. But as Malgorzata Szumowska and Michal Englert’s shrewd, playful The Idiot(s) reminds us, not even singular geniuses really do it all alone. If the film ultimately overstays its welcome, it’s hard to fault it for wanting to let this unsung companion luxuriate, for once, in the spotlight. Related Stories Movies 'A Long Winter' Review: Fred Hechinger and Ebon Moss-Bachrach Shine as Family Thrust Into Uneasy Isolation in Andrew Haigh's Fine-Grained Drama Movies 'Tender Loving Care' Review: Kate O'Flynn Lights Up Mike Leigh's Warm, Gently Wrenching Study of Solace and Solidarity The Idiot(s) The Bottom Line Sharp and fun, even if it overstays its welcome. Venue: Telluride Film Festival Cast: Aimee Lou Wood, Johnny Flynn, Vicky Krieps, Christian Freidel Directors: Malgorzata Szumowska, Michal Englert Screenwriters: Malgorzata Szumowska, Michal Englert, Kasper Bajon, Brid Arnstein 2 hours As Anna, Wood projects both unpolished brightness and an impressive force of will; it’s a mesmerizing combination that keeps the character from ever feeling like a mere victim of her circumstances, even as her life takes the harsh turns of, well, a Russian novel. If anything, the character’s initial introduction calls to mind Wood’s earlier breakout role on The White Lotus . Here as there, she’s the sweetly enthusiastic romantic partner to a grumpy older dude who seems determined to hate the new country they’re visiting from the moment he sets foot on it. It’s just that in this case, her S.O. is not some revenge-driven man of mystery but a writer drowning in debt and stymied by writer’s block. But The Idiot(s) makes clear right away that it isn’t interested in the usual serious biopic clichés about serious men doing serious things. This Fyodor, played by Johnny Flynn as a comically exasperating combination of buffoonish confidence, abject self-pity and childish petulance, is first seen glowering at a woman peeling hard-boiled eggs on the train, a fantastically overwrought classical soundtrack underlining the unreasonable intensity of his moods. He says things like “Tolstoy’s gonna shit himself” (of the novel he, Fyodor, is definitely for sure gonna start writing any day now) and “Kick me in the face” (to Anna, as part of a kinky foot-fetish debasement ritual). It’s not that the filmmakers doubt his talent as an author — the caption to that aforementioned opener, “9 a.m., the last days of November, during the thaw,” is the first of multiple affectionate nods to Dostoevsky’s The Idiot — so much as they recognize that reverence for a person’s work need not necessarily translate to admiration for his personality. The couple have arrived in Germany ostensibly so Fyodor can work on his next project. The creatively tortured, easily distracted Fyodor, quicky sets about doing anything but. When he’s not out partying with the very upper-crust literati he claims to disdain, including rival scribe Ivan Turgenev (Christian Friedel) and his coquettish girlfriend ( Vicky Krieps , alluring but underused), he’s blowing all his money at the roulette table. When he is at home, he oscillates between drunken glee and utter despair. Whenever Anna sneaks a peek at his notebooks, she finds either blank pages or doodles of naked women, not a word of The Idiot in sight. It would all be very depressing for poor Anna, were it not for the fact that The Idiot(s) does its best to keep the phrase “poor Anna” from entering your mind for as long as it can. For one thing, the film is too busy having fun to let itself stew in misery. It’s stuffed with mischievous anachronisms like a 19th-century performance of “Take On Me,” the A-Ha hit whose pleading lyrics could double Fyodor’s entreaty to a fed-up Anna. And it delights in outrageous rococo details, like a restaurant dessert that’s essentially chocolate mousse being squeezed out the anus of a porcelain dog. More crucially, the screenplay, by Szumowska, Englert, Kasper Bajon and Brid Arnstein, paints Anna not as some passive observer to Fyodor’s bad behavior but an active (albeit only fitfully successful) guardrail against it. As her husband gives himself over to his worst impulses, it’s Anna who nudges him to work, who tries to get the bills paid, who even, as things get dire, secretly writes and submits pages on his behalf to mollify his angry publisher. While Anna may not always be in control of her own fate, there’s never any doubt she’s in possession of her own agency. True, she’s making the choices she does in part because she has few others: Living in a foreign land without even enough cash for a train ticket home, Anna would have a tough time leaving Fyodor even if she’d wanted to. But, The Idiot(s) makes it clear, she doesn’t especially want to. Anna loves Fyodor truly and stubbornly, and he loves her back in his own inconsistent and imperfect way. Key to the film’s portrait of their marriage is the frisky chemistry that courses between them when they’re holding hands in bed or engaging in silly dirty talk about hard-boiled eggs. For all the relationship’s intolerable flaws and harrowing lows, it’s not without true affection. Anna’s indulgence for his antics is another thing, however. As the situation deteriorates to the point that Anna’s pawning off her chamber pots and eating scraps off the streets, it becomes harder and harder for us as viewers to forgive his sins. Perhaps that’s why The Idiot(s) gives over large chunks of its bleaker second half to absurd dream sequences. But arriving as they do in the umpteenth iteration of the same repetitive cycle (Fyodor losing his money, begging Anna for more, losing it all again and then some), these sequences land not only as unnecessary drags on an already puffy run time but as an uncharacteristic failure of confidence. We don’t require a clip of Fyodor fleeing from a boulder-sized roulette ball to tell us he’s being crushed by his gambling addiction when we’ve already seen that he is; we don’t need to see him plead against charges of chauvinism before a guillotine when we know exactly how poorly he treats Anna. Then again, if the clunky pacing of the film’s latter chapters remind us of anything, it’s how long Anna toiled to help bring The Idiot into the world. Compared to all those long years, what’s a few extra minutes of sitting and watching her struggles on a screen? “Every Russian writer should have a wife like you,” Ivan marvels at one point, moved by Anna’s strenuous efforts to help her ungrateful and oblivious husband. What The Idiot(s) impishly suggests, by demonstrating all the invisible but essential labor Anna’s poured into his books, is that a lot of them probably already did. Full credits Venue: Telluride Film Festival Production companies: Gold Rush Pictures, Hype Studios Cast: Aimee Lou Wood, Johnny Flynn, Vicky Krieps, Christian Freidel Directors: Malgorzata Szumowska, Michal Englert Screenwriters: Malgorzata Szumowska, Michal Englert, Kasper Bajon, Brid Arnstein Producers: Ilya Stewart, Lota Dascioraite, Vladimir Zemtsov Director of photography: Michal Englert Production designer: Ewa Mroczkowska Costume designer: Anna Englert Editors: Jaroslaw Kaminski, Hansjörg Weißbrich Casting director: Nina Gold Sales: CAA 2 hours THR

articles.title: ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Shattering as British Actor Ian Charleson, Throwing Himself Into Playing Hamlet While Succumbing to AIDS
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 10:00pm Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman in 'Elsinore.' Anthony Dickenson/Focus Features The late British stage and screen actor Ian Charleson, who died of AIDS-related causes in 1990 at age 40, is mostly remembered for his role in the 1981 Oscar winner Chariots of Fire . That inescapable attachment haunts Charleson, played with raw determination, grace and an almost overwhelming depth of feeling by Andrew Scott in Elsinore , a tremendously moving account of the final year in the Scottish actor’s life. When his agent reminds him that he starred in one of the most celebrated films of all time, Charleson shoots back: “And all anybody can remember about it is the theme music.” Related Stories Movies 'A Long Winter' Review: Fred Hechinger and Ebon Moss-Bachrach Shine as Family Thrust Into Uneasy Isolation in Andrew Haigh's Fine-Grained Drama Movies 'Tender Loving Care' Review: Kate O'Flynn Lights Up Mike Leigh's Warm, Gently Wrenching Study of Solace and Solidarity Scott’s searing dual performance — as Charleson and as Hamlet in a National Theatre production that became both the ultimate challenge and fulfillment of his professional career — makes Simon Stone ’s film an emotional powerhouse even if it doesn’t avoid inspirational cliché. But it’s a vivid picture of London at the height of the AIDS crisis and a stirring gesture of gratitude to art, specifically theater, as a lifeline even when death looms large. Elsinore The Bottom Line A hymn to the theater powered by a towering lead turn. Venue : Telluride Film Festival Release date : Friday, Nov. 20 Cast : Andrew Scott, Olivia Colman, Billie Piper, Johnny Flynn, Luke Thompson, David Dawson, Matthew Beard, Joe Locke, Monica Dolan, Georgie Glen, Sadie Soverall, Juliet Stevenson, Peter Mullan Director : Simon Stone Screenwriter : Stephen Beresford 1 hour 51 minutes While Charleson’s heroic run of 24 performances in the title role of Hamlet is as much a part of London theater lore as the abrupt exit from Richard Eyre ’s 1989 production of Daniel Day-Lewis , it will be less familiar to audiences farther afield. The script by Stephen Beresford ( Pride ) lives and breathes the stage community and its cozy familial camaraderie, from actors and directors to wardrobe, makeup and tech personnel. The bustle of theater luvvies all fondly addressing one another as “darling” will be especially amusing for audiences with any exposure to that world. As a film about a painful chapter in queer history, it mines considerable humor from the extent to which gay slang seeps into the entire milieu, regardless of sexuality. One hilarious example is Monica Dolan, marvelous as Linda Tolhurst, the National’s stage door supervisor for 50 years and counting. Charleson was already chummy with the building’s fixtures after playing Sky Masterson in the company’s smash 1982 Guys and Dolls revival; when he arrives for the first table read after being cast to replace Day-Lewis as Hamlet, Linda greets him dryly with, “’Ere she is, Takeover Tina!” While Charleson initially established himself as a stage actor, his primary international recognition came from back-to-back best picture Oscar winners Chariots of Fire and Gandhi . But despite working steadily, he struggled to keep the momentum of a screen career going. Growing tired of all the waiting around on film shoots for mostly unrewarding projects, Charleson became anxious to get back to the theater, especially given the ticking clock of his HIV+ diagnosis. Stone’s film shows the confusion of backstage workers and fellow cast when Day-Lewis collapses and then walks offstage during the Act I scene on the castle ramparts in which Hamlet encounters his father’s ghost. While the screenplay doesn’t go into the then-rising star’s reasons for abandoning the production, it’s no secret that Day-Lewis was unsettled by a connection to his own father’s absence, even if his exit was widely attributed to exhaustion. That footnote in London theater history creates an opportunity for Charleson, who previously played Hamlet though believed he was neither famous nor posh enough ever to land the role at the National. When he is approached by Eyre — identified only as Richard ( Johnny Flynn ) — who had directed him in Guys and Dolls , Ian feels duty-bound to inform him of his medical condition. The first appearance of a lesion on his forehead — after inspecting every inch of his body with a hand mirror each day — marked Ian’s progression to full-blown AIDS. Richard automatically assumes he will be unable to take on the demanding role, but Ian’s passion and drive convince him, with both men agreeing to keep his illness quiet. A lovely scene on cruisy Hampstead Heath takes creative license with the formation of the London chapter of the Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence, drag nuns advocating for AIDS awareness and safer sex practices. (In reality, that group didn’t appear in the British capital until the early ‘90s.) Ian asks Sister Frigidity of the Nocturnal Emission (Kadiff Kirwan) how long he has left, prompting the veiled activist to summon a young man from elsewhere in the park, still alive two years after his first lesion appeared. Instantly recognizing the mark on Charleson’s face for what it is, the National’s wardrobe master (Paul Chahidi) sends him to see Dr. Margaret Johnson ( Olivia Colman ), a U.K. pioneer of HIV and AIDS treatment. Colman is in blazing form, her clipped manner contrasting with the medic’s self-evident compassion. Instructing Ian to start coming for daily clinic checkups, she makes no effort to hide her anger that the actor is increasing his risk of decline by placing himself in a high-pressure situation. Developments with the terse character later in the film are profoundly affecting. Scenes at the clinic, where gay men constantly encounter friends and ex-lovers receiving treatment at various stages of the illness, are a sharp evocation of a time when the proliferation of men looking suddenly gaunt and weak sparked terror in the entire queer community. Charleson’s vibrantly drawn inner circle of friends is led by his bestie, casting director Patsy Pollock ( Billie Piper ), her daughter Alice (Sadie Soverall) and his constant companion Sean (Matthew Beard). The latter is identified, like Eyre, only by his first name, but the character is based on Sean Mathias, who directed Charleson that year in an all-star benefit performance of Martin Sherman’s play Bent , about pink-triangle persecution in Nazi Germany. One of the most fascinating insights into queer history comes with the appearances of iconoclastic director Derek Jarman (David Dawson), a friend for whom Charleson had played a punk angel in 1978’s Jubilee . As his own illness progresses, Derek urges Ian to go public about his health, to help destigmatize AIDS and hammer home the reality of the plague for Brits outside of LGBTQ circles. This brings up the conflicts for gay actors at the time who felt the need to keep their sexuality hidden for fear of career damage. “You have a responsibility to the dead, to the dying,” Derek tells him. Reflecting on his choice to stay silent (until after his death) Ian says, “Of course, in the theater no one gives a fuck.” But there was more at stake back then — and still to some extent now — for actors seeking on-camera work. For anyone who recalls Jarman’s seismic influence on queer cinema with uncompromising films like Sebastiane , The Angelic Conversation , Caravaggio and Edward II , hearing the director say “Ian, remember me” with the knowledge that any encounter could be their last cuts deep. The same goes for Charleson visiting him at the fisherman’s cottage in coastal Dungeness where he lived at the time, when Jarman tells him that he’s going blind. His loss of vision shaped his experimental swan-song feature, 1993’s Blue . If all this makes Elsinore sound like a film primarily for a niche audience of queer historians, that’s not the case. As Charleson digs into Hamlet rehearsals, insisting on working late even when he’s physically diminished, Scott conveys the actor’s dedication to his craft with both self-sacrifice and hubris. As Richard says of the play: “It’s about being alive and becoming dead.” While Stone is not always the most subtle of directors and Beresford’s dialogue often doesn’t tread lightly, a scene in which Ian gathers the entire cast to give an honest account of his condition — after being forced into a hiatus when he is hospitalized during previews — is as heartwarming as it is wrenching. But it’s in the performance scenes that Scott truly elevates the material, drawing on intersections between the Shakespearean role and Ian’s own thoughts of mortality. Many audiences will be wrecked by pretty much the entire second half of the movie, the final scenes in particular, in which editor Valerio Bonelli crosscuts between the stage performance and Ian’s bedroom at home, where he is fading fast, comforted by Patsy. When Laertes tells the wounded prince at the end of the Act 5 sword fight, “Hamlet, thou art slain,” I was a mess. While the fire at the core of the film is all Scott, in a physical, psychological and emotional performance that leaves nothing on the table, there’s gorgeous work throughout the ensemble. Colman superbly nails the seeming contradiction between professional medical detachment and humaneness. Piper — whom Stone directed on stage to huge acclaim on both sides of the Atlantic in his adaptation of Lorca’s Yerma — embodies the cherished female friend who is a sustaining force in the lives of so many gay men. And an unrecognizable Flynn makes Eyre a shining example of the director as nurturer and protector. There are standout moments for Luke Thompson as Georgie, a composite character representing Ian’s past relationships; Juliet Stevenson as Sylvia Sims, portrayed as a grand dame of British thespianism while playing Gertrude in the National production; Beard as a friend whose selfless devotion to Ian’s care is on par with Patsy’s; and Heartstopper ’s Joe Locke as an admiring young actor hungry for mentorship, befriended by Ian at the clinic. The most devastating scenes for many will be those with Ian’s parents, Jean (Georgie Glen) and Jack (Peter Mullan), working-class Scots confronted with the double whammy that their son is not only gay but dying, a confessional ordeal common to many AIDS patients at the time. Both actors are wonderful, with Jean’s anguish immediately apparent and Jack’s sputtering to the surface in a delayed reaction in the hospital car park. It’s a nice touch that one of Charleson’s surviving Chariots of Fire castmates, Nigel Havers, pops up as an AIDS clinic donor, alongside Ian’s close friend and University of Edinburgh classmate, fellow actor Hilton McRae. The latter is the longtime husband of Lindsay Duncan, Charleson’s co-star in a landmark 1988 National Theatre production of Cat on a Hot Tin Roof . There’s a nice “friends and family” aspect to these and other connections. Whatever weaknesses there are in the direction and script, the film makes enormous gains in intimacy and authenticity by eliminating any of the barriers of outsider observation. The full-throated investment in the parallel queer, theatrical, medical and outpatient communities is unquestionably personal. Stone relies more than necessary on Stefan Gregory’s lush orchestral score to push emotional buttons. But the strategic use in one joyously tender scene of The Ethel Merman Disco Album — once a cringey embarrassment, now a beloved bit of queer pop cultural kitsch — will spark fun associations for many gay men over a certain age. The Merm belting out “There’s No Business Like Show Business” to a disco backbeat might be a million brassy miles from Shakespeare, but Elsinore lovingly folds those two extremes together. Full credits Venue: Telluride Film Festival Release date: Friday, Nov. 20 Production companies: Lucky Red, Magnolia Mae Films, in association with LD Entertainment Distribution: Focus Features Cast: Andrew Scott, Olivia Colman, Billie Piper, Johnny Flynn, Luke Thompson, David Dawson, Matthew Beard, Joe Locke, Monica Dolan, Georgie Glen, Sadie Soverall, Adeel Akhtar, Dickie Beau, Kadiff Kirwan, Juliet Stevenson, Peter Mullan, Paul Chahidi Director: Simon Stone Screenwriter: Stephen Beresford, based on an idea by Ethan Silverman Producers: Andrea Occhipinti, Gabrielle Tana, Pete Shilaimon, Mickey Lidell, Stefano Massenzi, Carolyn Marks Blackwood, Andrew Scott Executive producers: Anna Marsh, Ron Halpern, Joe Naftalin, Michael Glassman, Joseph Yakob, Natalia Shilaimon, Ethan Silverman, Pierre du Plessis, Sudie Smyth, Stephen Beresford Director of photography: Mike Eley Production designer: Helen Scott Costume designer: Mel Page Music: Stefan Gregory Editor: Valerio Bonelli Casting: Jessica Ronane 1 hour 51 minutes THR

articles.title: Telluride Awards Analysis: Andrew Scott Leaps Into Top Tier of Best Actor Oscar Race for ‘Elsinore’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All September 5, 2026 12:21am Andrew Scott in 'Elsinore' Courtesy of StudioCanal With all due respect to the performances of Matt Damon in The Odyssey and Ryan Gosling in Project Hail Mary , I came away from Wild Horse Nine , which had its North American premiere at the Telluride Film Festival on Thursday afternoon, with the strong impression that John Malkovich was now the clear frontrunner to win the best actor Oscar. But by Friday evening, when Elsinore had its world premiere in Telluride, I was forced to revise my hypothesis. That’s because the Irish actor Andrew Scott gives a performance for the ages in Elsinore as the Scottish actor Ian Charleson, who was best known for starring in the best picture Oscar winner Chariots of Fire , but whose most impressive accomplishment was how he insisted on continuing to act — in the role of Hamlet at London’s National Theatre, no less — even after he was diagnosed with terminal AIDS. Related Stories Movies 'Elsinore' Review: Andrew Scott Is Shattering as British Actor Ian Charleson, Throwing Himself Into Playing Hamlet While Succumbing to AIDS Movies 'The Idiot(s)' Review: Aimee Lou Wood and Johnny Flynn Sparkle in a Playful, Indulgent Tribute to Fyodor Dostoevsky's Underappreciated Wife The response inside Telluride’s Palm Theatre to the listing of Scott’s name in the film’s post-credits — as both a producer and the lead actor — was undeniable. It’s a sensitive and shattering performance from an actor who just keeps getting better, as demonstrated in everything from his film performance in All of Us Strangers , which premiered in Telluride three years ago, to his stage performance last year in Uncle Vanya , in which he singlehandedly juggled 10 different characters. In the Oscar race, Malkovich could have a slight edge because he’s older (73 versus 49), because he has been doing important work for longer and because his film is all but certain to land noms in a bunch of categories, including best picture, whereas aspects of Elsinore other than Scott’s performance are more of a question-mark. I wouldn’t count out the possibility of noms for Olivia Colman for best supporting actress (she plays Charleson’s doctor), Stephen Beresford’s script for best original screenplay (even though the film’s credits say it was inspired by “an idea” from someone else), Valerio Bonelli’s film editing (particularly awesome late in the film as he cuts between Charleson on stage and at home), Stefan Gregory’s original score or even the film for a best picture nom. But the truth is that Scott’s performance is so extraordinary that other aspects of the Simon Stone’s film — which The Hollywood Reporter ’s critic has argued is solid but less spectacular — could be overshadowed. One final note. Quite a few actors and actresses have won Oscars for their portrayals of LGBT characters facing adversity and/or tragedy, including William Hurt for Kiss of the Spider Woman , Tom Hanks for Philadelphia , Hilary Swank for Boys Don’t Cry , Sean Penn for Milk , Jared Leto for Dallas Buyers Club and Rami Malek for Bohemian Rhapsody . But none of those people were themselves gay, and indeed never has an out gay actor or actress won an Oscar. Scott could well become the first. THR

articles.title: Kate and Rooney Mara Talk ‘Bucking Fastard,’ Synchronized Sisterhood and Werner Herzog Life Lessons: “He Doesn’t Give a S***”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Rooney Mara, Werner Herzog and Kate Mara attend the 'Bucking Fastard' world premiere during the 83rd Venice Film Festival at Sala Grande on September 3, 2026. (Photo by Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images) Werner Herzog has a bit of a wild reputation . He’d like to set the record straight. “I’m the most organized, the most focused, the most friendly person you will ever see on a set,” the German director says. “Period.” Everything else, he adds, is “the craze of media who want to create a Werner Herzog that is a fiction.” This is, of course, the man who hauled a 320-ton steamship over a hill in the Peruvian jungle for Fitzcarraldo (1982), and, on the shoot of Aguirre, the Wrath of God (1972), also in the jungle, threatened to kill his star Klaus Kinski if he walked away from the film [as recounted by Herzog himself in his 1999 documentary My Best Fiend .] This is the man who ate his own shoe after losing a bet to Errol Morris, and who once carried on with a BBC interview after being hit by an air rifle, calling it “not a significant bullet.” Related Stories Movies Paul Schrader Tears Up at 'The Basics of Philosophy' Venice Premiere Movies 'The Basics of Philosophy' Review: Paul Schrader Does Some Deep -- and Discomfiting -- Thinking About a College Professor's Guilt But when Herzog came calling, Kate and Rooney Mara signed up anyway. The Mara sisters play the leads in Herzog’s Bucking Fastard , as Jean and Joan Holbrooke, Irish sisters who speak, think and move in unison, share the same dreams and love the same man. After their neighbor and former lover Gareth Mulroney (Orlando Bloom) marries someone else, the sisters embark on a campaign of arson, ambush and assorted misdemeanors to win him back, become tabloid fixtures and are assigned a social worker (Domhnall Gleeson) to help them adapt to modern life. They eventually decamp to Ireland’s West Coast to live with their widowed aunt (Marion O’Dwyer), where they begin chipping away at a cave in a mountain range, convinced the tunnel will lead them to the Orkney Islands, in their minds a mythical place where true love is possible. The film is loosely inspired by Freda and Greta Chaplin, identical twins from York, in northern England, who spoke in unison and became widely known after a 1981 court case made them tabloid sensations. HanWay Films is handling worldwide sales. Bucking Fastard premiered in competition at the Venice Film Festival Thursday night , drawing a warm six-and-a-half-minute standing ovation for Herzog and his cast. Sitting down with THR ahead of the premiere, Herzog and the Maras spoke about their synchronized performance, the film’s surprising vein of “Bavarian humor” and Herzog life lessons in “really not giving a shit.” Why did you both want to work with Werner Herzog? ROONEY MARA For every reason under the sun. I would have loved to have just been a PA on the set, just to watch him in action. It’s one of the greatest experiences one can have. KATE MARA I’ve been fascinated by the way Werner makes films ever since I saw one of his documentaries, so to get to work on a film with him has always been a dream. And then to read his script about these sisters and their bond and this love story was incredibly magical. There are a lot of stories about the extremes you have gone to on films. Did you have any trepidation? KATE MARA Zero trepidation about that. The scariest thing for us was just: How are we going to do this? How are we going to do an entire film in unison and in sync in that way? But I had zero worries about working with Werner. WERNER HERZOG I can tell you why: because I’m the most organized, the most focused, the most friendly person you will ever see on a set. Period. Everything you’re hinting at is the craze of media who want to create a Werner Herzog that is a fiction. KATE MARA It’s passion. To me, that’s one of the most important things you need in a director — passion, and somebody who cares deeply about filmmaking. Why did you want the two Mara sisters for this dual role? HERZOG I had a story, and I thought about whether it should be twins. And I found the two sisters, and it was immediately clear this was finally a solution. I wrote the screenplay very quickly, in five days, and we were done with pre-production in five, six weeks and started to film. We had some rehearsal time, the first time in my life, in all of my films, that there was enough money to do rehearsals. We had two weeks. After a week, I said, “Stop this. Meet me in front of my camera. You’re so good. Stop it.” ‘Bucking Fastard’ with Rooney Mara, Kate Mara Courtesy of Lena Herzog Speaking and moving simultaneously is central to the performances. How did you find a way to do that as actors? KATE MARA It felt very much like a song, like a rhythm. Once we figured out what that song was and what the rhythm was — which happened way faster than we thought it would — it just made sense to us. It was an unspoken sort of thing. Rooney and I worked a lot together before working with Werner, trying to find our tricks. ROONEY MARA We had a voice coach we worked with before Werner, who gave us tips, exercises we did together. We weren’t really sure until we got into rehearsal with Werner. We were like, “What the hell are we doing? What is this?” And then when we started doing it in front of him, he liked it so much. It flowed more naturally than we had anticipated. HERZOG By the way, we did very few takes. I would shoot two or three takes, and that was normally it. Sometimes a single take for a very long scene. Period. I’m a one-camera guy. I do hardly any coverage. There was no coverage. Two shots, and that was it. Two takes. KATE MARA We would be done hours early sometimes. HERZOG We finished at 3 p.m., 3:30 in the afternoon. We could have gone until 5, 6, 7 without overtime, and I said, “Let’s wrap it.” I’m not exaggerating, and the film was done under schedule and under budget. You’ve compared this film thematically to Fitzcarraldo and Grizzly Man . Where do you see the connection? HERZOG We shouldn’t overdo the connections. But with Fitzcarraldo , it is evident: There is a great dream about opera in the jungle, and for that the protagonist moves a big ship over a mountain in the jungle. Here in this film, it’s the dream of an ideal country, which doesn’t really exist, the Orkneys, where real love is possible — and you would rather dig a tunnel through a whole mountain range to find this country. Everybody should dig a tunnel. Every grown-up man should move a ship over a mountain. Every grown-up woman should dig a tunnel through a mountain range. It’s very simple: Just go out and do it. That seems to have been your attitude throughout your career, given that you didn’t have a film education. HERZOG Yes, but I’m not acting blindly. I know what I’m doing. I know that I’m a poet. I dream big, but I do the doable, and that’s what I try to preach to young filmmakers. Yes, dream big, but please do the doable. Moving a ship over a mountain is doable. Digging a tunnel through a mountain is also doable. Do that. Werner Herzog shares his thoughts on Elon Musk's mission to Mars: "I am very critical of his idea of colonizing Mars with a million people. That's a pipe dream. We will have astronauts there, a handful, fine. But we should not colonize there. That's an obscenity." pic.twitter.com/B80O8jQgJG — The Hollywood Reporter (@THR) September 3, 2026 What surprised you about working with him? ROONEY MARA The specificity. For some reason I imagined things would be a little bit more wild and freewheeling. I didn’t imagine the precision and specificity with which Werner works. HERZOG I interrupt and say no. Mid-take. ROONEY MARA Mid-take. Because you had something specific in mind. KATE MARA Agreed. You founded your own Rogue Film School, and you have an audience among very young, up-and-coming filmmakers. Why do you think that is? HERZOG It’s not film students alone, it’s audiences in general. They are very young. I started an Instagram account — my younger son does it, he knows how — and he tells me 85 percent of those who read it and love it are between 15 and 20 years old. Because my films are now available on the internet, on streaming platforms, all of a sudden, from one day to the next, there are 800,000 people who speak about one film of mine. There’s a film club in, God knows, Missoula, Montana, by 15-year-olds, about my films. The answer is simple: They are just very good, and they discover it. ROONEY MARA I think it’s also that you are a singular human being. You are yourself. You really don’t give a shit. You march to the beat of your own drum so thoroughly, and people love that because that’s what we all want to do. That’s what we all aspire to do. And so many of us are not doing that. HERZOG But I’m just a poet. This is the first time you two have appeared on screen together. Why did it take this long? KATE MARA It’s very difficult to find two roles that are equally interesting and good in a film, and then also find a director that we both passionately want to work with. We found all those things in this. It was really simple. Nothing came our way before that made sense in all areas. We couldn’t really believe it. What was it like to perform together as sisters? ROONEY MARA It was a very surreal experience. Strange, because it’s not like we were in scenes playing off of one another the way you normally would with a scene partner. We were playing the same thing. There’s maybe only one scene, and a few moments other than that, where we’re even looking at each other. We are focused on the same thing. It’s really one performance. KATE MARA We’re experiencing the other actor that we’re in a scene with together. So it’s impossible to compare it to anything else. We’ve never had an experience like that before. It’s great for codependency. So you’re jointly forming a single performance rather than doing two separate ones. KATE MARA It’s as collaborative as you could possibly be. HERZOG It’s unique. We haven’t seen anything like this in film history. From left: Rooney and Kate Mara in ‘Bucking Fastard.’ Gateway to Orkney You are best known for collaborations with male actors — Klaus Kinski, Christian Bale, Nicolas Cage. You’ve had a few leading female roles, but not that many. Was the approach different with these two actresses? HERZOG With every single one, with every single actor, I speak differently. I act differently. I bring them into the film, make them give the inner life of them onto a screen. There’s no school. And by the way, the greatest with whom I ever worked is the unknown soldier of cinema, Bruno S., who plays a leading part in The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser and in Stroszek . He’s the deepest, most tragic one with whom I ever worked. All of the others are actors. He was not. The film is funnier than some might expect. HERZOG Thank you that you saw it. There’s always humor in my films, and it came across, apparently. Sometimes it’s a dark humor. Sometimes it’s a very Bavarian humor that even Germans wouldn’t understand. Americans easier. Mexicans, yes, they immediately get it. Will that surprise audiences? KATE MARA Werner is one of the funniest people. If you know him and his work, or if you watch him speak about anything, he’s got the greatest sense of humor. ROONEY MARA We had so much fun. I laughed more than I have in years making this film. We had so many fun moments. Did it live up to the myth of Werner Herzog? ROONEY MARA It exceeded it. HERZOG But from the beginning I told them, I have to load an entire film onto these two shoulders, so that’s big. Are you ready for that? And of course they were. I’m a lucky man that they were immediately ready. Yes, we will carry that. You are often drawn to extreme characters, figures who exist outside of normal social structures. Is that something you see in yourself? HERZOG They’re not really borderline. Even in Bucking Fastard , I don’t see them as borderline. They make a lot of sense to me. It’s only unusual that they have apparently one dream together, one love for an undeserving man, and they speak in unison. So that’s unusual. But otherwise, they’re the most normal human creatures for me that you can imagine. They do the thing we all should do. ROONEY MARA I agree. I think everyone else is crazy. Being willing to show up every day and dig a tunnel through a mountain for love — that’s not crazy. Everyone else is crazy for not wanting to do that. HERZOG Thank you for saying that, because I keep saying I’m the only filmmaker who is clinically sane. All the rest is not really right. What can the rest of the film business learn from how he works? ROONEY MARA There’s so much you could learn from Werner. Again, it’s that willingness to show up as yourself and not be swayed by any of the noise. To have that tunnel vision of, this is who I am, and this is what I’m doing, and this is how I do it, and I’m a poet, period. KATE MARA It’s very inspiring to watch. HERZOG The work on my set is like open-heart surgery, only in whispers, going straight for the essential and nothing else. That’s it. KATE MARA You can hear a whisper from a mile away, and he will tell you so. The set is very quiet, which is great. HERZOG No cell phones, no video playout, one camera, very few takes. I do the slate. ROONEY MARA And almost no crew. He does the slate. He’s in there, crawling around within the scene. It’s very special. You’ve shot in the jungle, the desert, the Arctic Circle, and you’re still making films in your 80s. Where do you still want to explore? HERZOG I have my next film almost finished. I need a week more and my next film will be finished, so I’m way beyond Bucking Fastard . I’m also finishing a book at Taschen, the publishing house, of photos from my films. So I’m still working a lot. I love what I do. Is the dream still to go to space and make a film there? ROONEY MARA What? You want to go to space? HERZOG Yes, I would like to be out there. I have tried. I spoke to NASA, but they didn’t take me. And then there is a Japanese billionaire who is planning a spaceship around the moon, without landing, returning — he refused to take me on board. ROONEY MARA We should set up an online petition HERZOG So let’s wait. Let’s wait for the rocket for me alone. I’ll be on board. KATE MARA If anyone can do it, you can. HERZOG By the way, Elon Musk promised me that if he goes on a mission to Mars, I would be on board. But God knows when that’s happening, and I am very critical of his idea of colonizing Mars with a million people. That’s a pipe dream. We will have astronauts there, a handful at a time, and they will explore, but we should not colonize. That’s an obscenity. We should rather keep this planet inhabitable. THR

articles.title: Maggie Gyllenhaal Was Asked to Use AI to Recreate Marilyn Monroe. But it Flopped Compared to Dakota Johnson
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All September 5, 2026 4:51am Maggie Gyllenhaal attends The Future Of… Creativity summit hosted by Finch and Partners and CAA at Scuola Grande della Misericordia in Venice, Italy on Sept. 4, 2026. Photo by Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images for Finch & Partners and Creative Artists Agency There have been many versions of Marilyn Monroe recreated using artificial intelligence over the years, and Maggie Gyllenhaal just revealed that she was asked to make another for her short film Flesh Impact. But it flopped in comparison to the real thing played by Dakota Johnson . “The people who commissioned this project from me asked me to use AI. They weren’t using OpenAI, they were using licensable AI, training it off of Marilyn Monroe films that we had licensed. And I went for it. I was like, all right, I’m curious, I don’t know, let’s see ,” she said Friday during The Future of… Creativity summit hosted by Finch & Partners and CAA at Scuola Grande della Misericordia during the Venice Film Festival. “The idea was that we trained it on her, we then put her face on Dakota’s face. We worked hard at it, and in the end, I threw it away because what was coming through Dakota playing Marilyn Monroe was so much more moving, human, alive.” Related Stories Movies Kate and Rooney Mara Talk 'Bucking Fastard,' Synchronized Sisterhood and Werner Herzog Life Lessons: "He Doesn't Give a S***" Movies Paul Schrader Tears Up at 'The Basics of Philosophy' Venice Premiere To punctuate the point, she added, “It fundamentally did not work. All the reasons we decided to make this project to begin with were killed off in the AI version.” The 17-minute short film Flesh Impact stars Johnson and Ellen Burstyn as versions of the iconic Hollywood star. It was done “with the blessings” of Monroe estate holders Authentic Brands Group and described in press materials as “a love letter to one of cinema’s most enduring icons.” Johnson plays Monroe at the height of her fame while Burstyn stars as an imagined version of Monroe later in life. (Monroe was 36 when she died on Aug. 4, 1962.) Peter Sarsgaard and The Pitt star Sepideh Moafi round out the cast. Johnson as Marilyn Monroe in Maggie Gyllenhaal’s Flesh Impact. Photo credit: Genesis Though Gyllenhaal didn’t specify exactly who asked for the AI version, the short is presented by automotive brand Genesis and produced by William Green for The Cut , Michelle Ross for Superprime, Nicolette Spencer and Melissa Moore for INNOCEAN. Executive producers include Maddi Carlton, Brandon Boerner, Rebecca Skinner, David Webb and Courtney Kivowitz, the latter of whom is Gyllenhaal’s longtime manager. During the panel discussion, Gyllenhaal also addressed the pitch that AI can democratize filmmaking and allow auteurs to make big-budget projects at a fraction of the cost. But she questioned why that is a common promotional tactic. “It concerns me a little bit because they own it. Who’s making the money off it? The people that are pitching that,” she stated, adding that in the near future, a $40 million project could be done for $4 million and “maybe eventually” $40,000. “But the thing is, if you can make a commercial good enough movie for $40,000 or even for $4 million, who’s gonna give you $10 million to do it the old way? Nobody. Maybe there’s a tiny, tiny little market for that. But that concerns me.” Flesh Impact has its Venice Film Festival world premiere inside Sala Grande on Sept. 7. Gyllenhaal’s comments about AI went viral — as first reported by Variety and in a video posted by the outlet on social media — and it wasn’t her first trending moment during this year’s Venice Film Festival. During an opening press conference featuring members of the jury, the Bride filmmaker, who won a best screenplay award in Venice for her directorial debut The Lost Daughter , was asked to comment on the lack of female filmmakers in the main competition. “I really am walking in with a question as to why there are so few women in the main competition,” she told the international press inside Palazzo del Casinò. “It’s much harder for women to get their films financed. Also, could it be possible that the things that women, having had a different experience of being alive in the world, want to make movies about are not always deemed high art?” This year’s competition selections came under fire for gender imbalance. One of the original films selected as 20 Golden Lion contenders — May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown — is directed by a woman, down from six competition titles last year. The festival later added the Gaza documentary NAZA , co-directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, bringing the total to two. Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera noted the disparity when revealing the lineup, and Gyllenhaal in return acknowledged fest leadership for inviting her to preside over the jury as “a very important thing to consider” amid the scrutiny. Gyllenhaal’s jury includes Tunisian filmmaker Kaouther Ben Hania ( The Voice of Hind Rajab ), Oscar-winning composer Daniel Blumberg, film scholar Francesco Casetti, French director Xavier Giannoli, Afghan filmmaker Shahrbanoo Sadat, and Hong Kong filmmaking legend Johnnie To. The 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival concludes with an awards ceremony on Sept. 12. THR
