articles.title: Robert Pattinson on Chris Hansen’s Objections to ‘Primetime’: “I Hope He Likes the Movie”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All September 5, 2026 5:05am Director Lance Oppenheim and Robert Pattinson attend the 'Primetime' photocall during the 83rd Venice Film Festival at Palazzo del Casino on Sept. 5, 2026. (Photo by Kate Green/Getty Images) Chris Hansen is not at the Venice Film Festival for this weekend’s world premiere of a film inspired by his work on To Catch a Predator, but the man still proved to be the center of attention during Primetime ‘s press conference. “Obviously, I hope he likes the movie,” said Robert Pattinson when asked about Hansen’s early objections to Lance Oppenheim ‘s A24 film and the fact that he purchased pre-show advertising for his streaming platform. Pattinson stars as Hansen and boarded the film early as a producer but said, “I never really set out to make a movie about Chris Hansen. I never really thought about it, and then I saw [Ajon Singh’s] script, and there’s something electrifying about it. I would hope, in some ways, the amount of inspiration that his character has given so many people who are involved in this for years now is some kind of compliment.” Related Stories Movies Maggie Gyllenhaal Was Asked to Use AI to Recreate Marilyn Monroe. But it Flopped Compared to Dakota Johnson Movies Kate and Rooney Mara Talk 'Bucking Fastard,' Synchronized Sisterhood and Werner Herzog Life Lessons: "He Doesn't Give a S***" Oppenheim said he first discovered To Catch a Predator through parodies of it on shows like South Park . “And when I finally saw To Catch a Predator , I was amazed. Chris Hansen was this like mythological being who had these one-liners that reminded me of Tony Montana [in Scarface ]. His version of ‘say hello to my little friend,’ was ‘have a seat right there.’ I was always fascinated as a young child with the theatricality of the show. I was so confused by it. Was it a prank show? Was it a news show? Was it a circus with Chris Hansen as a ringleader?” Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen in Primetime . Screenshot Primetime is loosely adapted by first-time screenwriter Singh from an Esquire article by Luke Dittrich, and it dramatizes the darkest year in Hansen’s tenure on To Catch a Predator . Pattinson stars opposite Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo, Phoebe Bridgers and Bokeem Woodbine, all of whom joined the panel discussion today. They fielded questions on the challenging material, the process of putting the cast together, Bridgers’ debut feature film role, and how so much of film culture online has been whittled down to memes and viral jokes. Both Oppenheim and Pattinson said they don’t mind the meme factor when it comes to their work, especially for something like Primetime because Hansen was such a viral-ready star long before that was part of the cultural lexicon. “The idea of a man who became a myth, a person who became a persona, a person who embraced the meme of himself, and yet still continued to do work in a very, very serious and dark subject, I thought that would make for such an interesting film,” Oppenheim said. Pattinson said when he was younger and started getting into movies, he noticed how his classmates at school would always imitate individual lines from whatever big movie had just come out. “I felt like that had been completely gone from culture for like years and years. And suddenly realized it’s been replaced by memes, and I quite like that,” he explained after it was mentioned by a journalist that his role as Hansen has already become a viral phenomenon prior to release. “I always really liked quoting lines from Jim Carrey movies and stuff like that. I loved that. I used to know [all the lines] from The Mask by heart; everybody would do Austin Powers and all these things.” Pattinson, who is filming The Batman during a year that will see consecutive releases of The Drama , The Odyssey, Primetime and Dune: Part Three , had such a quick turnaround from filming Primetime that he had just “a few hours” to segue to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey . “I definitely can hear a little Chris Hansen in The Odyssey when I watch it,” he said, to much laughter in the room. Oppenheim’s Primetime will be released theatrically in the United States by A24 on Sept. 25. The 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival concludes with an awards ceremony on Sept. 12. Bokeem Woodbine, Phoebe Bridgers, Robert Pattinson, Skyler Gisondo and Merritt Wever attend the ‘Primetime’ photocall during the 83rd Venice Film Festival at Palazzo del Casino on Sept. 5, 2026. (Photo by Kate Green/Getty Images) THR

articles.title: Rubaiyat Hossain on Bodies, Beauty and Venice, Toronto and London-Bound ‘The Difficult Bride,’ Clip Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 12:57am PT Rubaiyat Hossain on Bodies, Beauty and Venice, Toronto and London-Bound ‘The Difficult Bride,’ Clip Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Rubaiyat Hossain on Bodies, Beauty and Venice, Toronto and London-Bound ‘The Difficult Bride,’ Clip Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Lav Diaz Preps False Prophets Film and Jose Rizal’s ‘Noli Me Tangere’ Adaptation, Unpacks Venice Title ‘Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors’ (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Ann Hui, Carlo Chatrian to Head Pingyao’s Fei Mu, Rossellini Juries 21 hours ago See All Films Boutique The idea for “ The Difficult Bride ” traces back to a story Rubaiyat Hossain heard as a 7 year old, visiting a Dhaka beauty parlor with her mother. “There was a bride who died there,” Hossain says. “Everyone knew this story from our generation, and I remember being seven, and even at that time, I had visualized this story. It was in sepia for some reason, I don’t know, but I completely had the visuals in my head, and it’s something that always stayed with me.” Related Stories Disney Offers Executives Voluntary Early Retirement Packages Amid Overall Cost-Cutting Plans ABC Files First Amendment Lawsuit Against FCC Variety is unveiling an exclusive clip from the supernatural feminist drama, which will become the first Bangladeshi feature to screen at the Venice Film Festival when it bows in the Horizons competition. Popular on Variety That salon, Mayfair, became the setting for a film that follows Zaineen (Zaineen Chowdhury Karim), a bride-to-be whose wedding preparations spiral into a battle with her own body. Hossain first tried the material as a short in 2006. Two decades and many drafts later, the project pulled in her academic background in gender studies alongside something more personal. “My own self and my own body became a part of the film,” she says. “My embodied experience of being a female in my own body and how I feel is something I tried to communicate in the film. And that is why it became supernatural, because a lot of the things are not logical. That is where the grotesque comes in, that is where the lizards and the snakes come in.” Hossain is careful not to place the blame for that pressure solely on men. Azmeri Haque Badhon plays the salon owner who enforces the beauty standard on Zaineen, including a scene of facial injections that Hossain says mirrors treatment common in Bangladeshi salons. “It’s also about how women can be some of the biggest upholders and sustainers of patriarchy and the patriarchal system,” she says. “It’s not only men; women also participate in this. It’s a system of power. It takes both to participate in it.” The film’s Dhaka backdrop carries traces of the country’s July 2024 unrest , including scenes of women being surveilled and policed for their clothing and behavior, work that reaches the screen through Rikita Nondine Shimu’s character, Minoti. Hossain resists reading the film as a direct response to that period, though. “I wouldn’t say the film is set around the time of July,” she says. “I tried to create like a reality of Dhaka where there is political violence outside, there is a lot of violence against women. Women’s rights have always been an issue in Bangladesh.” She places “The Difficult Bride” alongside her earlier features as a kind of class trilogy of Bangladeshi womanhood. “‘Under Construction’ talked about a middle-class woman, ‘Made in Bangladesh’ talked about a working-class woman, and I think ‘The Difficult Bride’ talks about the kind of the ultra-wealthy population of the tri-state,” she says, referring to Dhaka’s Gulshan-Baridhara area. “Even in this gilded cage, even with all these privileges, you can’t be free.” Karim, making her acting debut in the lead role, was originally Hossain’s assistant director. When the shoot’s original cast changed following the disruption from July, Karim stepped in to read opposite another actor during Zoom rehearsals. “She is so beautiful and I feel like she is the character herself,” Hossain says of watching her on screen. “I might have auditioned her like around 15, 20 times.” The cast also includes Sunerah Kamal in addition to Badhon and Shimu, all three of whom are Bangladesh National Film Award winners. Hossain, who teaches part-time at Smith College, including a course on love and devotion in Bollywood cinema, argues that the pressures her film dramatizes extend well beyond South Asia. “I see that a woman who is coming from Mexico or Guatemala or Bangladesh or Vermont have same issues when it comes to this specific idea of beauty and submitting,” she says. Offscreen, Hossain has launched a grant and mentorship program for Bangladeshi women filmmakers, aiming to address what she describes as compounding structural barriers: limited access to money, restrictions on women’s mobility, the absence of a formal film school and an industry culture built on informal, male peer networks. “There is also like an overall assumption and lack of role models,” she says. “The Difficult Bride” is an international co-production between France’s Les Films de l’Après-Midi, Bangladesh’s Khona Talkies, Portugal’s Midas Filmes, Norway’s Barentsfilm and Germany’s Tandem Production, and was supported by the first edition of the Fondazione Prada Film Fund. Films Boutique is handling world sales . Following Venice, the film moves on to the Toronto and BFI London film festivals. For Hossain, the film marked a creative turning point. “I’m not tied to social realism anymore,” she says. “I really relied on my body and my instincts to make creative decisions, and I really enjoyed the process.” She is now developing a project set in Lisbon about an undocumented Bangladeshi woman who migrates after a cyclone, and is pursuing a television adaptation of J. articles.title: Swiss Projects at the Venice Gap-Financing Market: Natural Disaster, Complicated Romance, Exploited Migrants, Murder Mystery in Montana
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 1:57am PT Swiss Projects at the Venice Gap-Financing Market: Natural Disaster, Complicated Romance, Exploited Migrants, Murder Mystery in Montana The showcase presents works from Stéphanie Argerich, Flurin Giger, Ursula Meier, Kaveh Bakhtiari, Valentin Merz, Laura Israel and Alberto Fasulo By Ed Meza Plus Icon Ed Meza @edmezavar Latest As Swiss Films Expand International Reach, English-Language Works Are on the Rise 7 hours ago Bendita Film Sales Snags Norma Vila’s Sitges Competition Title ‘Carapace’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago France TV Distribution’s Mystery Drama ‘Our Missing Sons’ Set for Unifrance Rendez-Vous Market Debut 2 days ago See All Stéphanie Argerich, Flurin Giger, Ursula Meier, Kaveh Bakhtiari, Valentin Merz Courtesy of Intermezzo Films, Giger Brothers, Marie Rouge/Unifrance, Epicentre Films, Andrea Film Both well-established and up-and-coming Swiss filmmakers are taking part in the Venice Film Festival ’s Production Bridge industry strand, where Switzerland will be one of the country’s in focus at the Gap-Financing Market. Seven Swiss projects and co-productions are among the total of 38 fiction and documentary works featured in the Venice Production Bridge ’s Gap-Financing Market lineup, selected from a record-breaking 370-plus submissions. Related Stories FCC Asks Court to Throw Out ABC's Lawsuit Alleging TV License Review Violates First Amendment, as Agency Repeats Claim the Action Is Unrelated to Jimmy Kimmel or 'The View' Disney and NFL Team Up on Apparel Collection, Pairing Each of the League's 32 Teams With Beloved Franchise Characters Spanning a wide range of subject matter and genre, the projects, in various stages of development, delve into the human toll of natural cataclysm, the forced criminality of migration, cross-cultural and cross-class romance, murder mystery, apocalyptic sci-fi and the artistic process. Popular on Variety Among them are works by Flurin Giger, who premiered his 2016 short “Ruah” in Venice and 2018’s “ Schächer ” in Cannes; award-winning filmmaker Stéphanie Argerich with her first narrative feature; Valentin Merz, who picked up a first feature prize in Locarno in 2022 for “ De noche los gatos son pardos ”; Ursula Meier , whose credits include the 2012 and 2022 Berlin-premiering, prize-winning works “Sister” and “ The Line “; and Kaveh Bakhtiari, who follows up his acclaimed 2013 Cannes doc “ Stop-Over ” with his scripted feature debut. Giger arrives with “A Year Without Summer,” produced by Geneva-based Beauvoir Films and Heimatfilm in Cologne. Set in 1816, it follows a peasant family in Europe whose existence is threatened when the skies suddenly darken and snow falls in the midst of summer. Unbeknownst to them, they are experiencing the effects of a catastrophic volcanic eruption in Indonesia. “What immediately drew us to this project first was Flurin,” Beauvoir Films producer Cécile Tollu-Polonowski tells Variety . “We had seen both his shorts, ‘Ruah’ in Venice and ‘Schächer’ in Cannes Critics’ Week, worked with him as an actor for another production, and there is a very particular handwriting to how he tells a story, a visual language that is his alone. He’s one of the most exciting up-and-coming directors we know, and honestly his debut feature fits perfectly into Beauvoir’s line-up as we nourish the same desire for cinema.” The project stands apart through the extraordinary subject itself, Tollu-Polonowski adds. “It is based on a real event. In 1816, the world went dark after the eruption of volcano Tambora; it transformed the climate and reshaped lives across continents. “It’s a story that’s completely fascinating and evokes so many images. It’s an event that has inspired artists long before us. It was during this year that brought so much death and misery that painters like Caspar David Friedrich and J.M.W. Turner created some of their most celebrated works, skies with these strange, powerful colors, a rare kind of splendor. What they were painting was actually real, it was the atmospheric aftermath of the eruption.” Currently being cast with a mix of professional and non-professional actors, the film will shoot in Rhaeto-Romanic, spoken in parts of southeastern Switzerland and northeastern Italy. Beyond the historical setting, the story also offers frightening parallels to the present day, Tollu-Polonowski notes: “A world thrown off balance by something invisible, people trying to make sense of a changed climate. It doesn’t feel like a period piece.” After winning acclaim for her 2012 documentary “Bloody Daughter,” about her parents, renowned pianists Martha Argerich and Stephen Kovacevich, Argerich returns with narrative feature “Kyushu Moon,” produced by Geneva-based Intermezzo Films and Les Films du Bélier in Paris. The film centers on Sarah (played by Alba Rohrwacher), a recently divorced journalist who travels to Japan for a report on a retreat for men with relationship difficulties. There she meets Moroto (Ryo Kase), a 42-year-old virgin man. Despite not speaking each other’s language, unexpected feelings arise. Argerich has re-teamed with Intermezzo Films’ Luc Peter and Katia Monla, who also produced “Bloody Daughter.” “We love her energy, the way she looks at her surroundings with an attention to detail, and how, in the smallest unnoticed gesture, an emotion can surface, revealing our fragilities through a gaze that never judges, but simply recognizes our human failures,” says Monla. “What drew us to ‘Kyushu Moon’ was the way it questions our modern solitude: our loss of connection in a fast-paced society, our relationship to others, to another culture, at a time when everything seems to be pushing us toward individuality and a closing off from the world, from the other, from what is strange and foreign. “It is, in that sense, a political film about a declining demographic left to fend for itself, and about how, in an unexpected setting, two people meet and find themselves able to imagine a relationship to the other again, just when everything seemed lost. But beneath its political and social surface, it remains, at heart, a deeply poetic romance laced with a touch of humor, a bridge between Europe and Asia, where two lost souls find a way to hope again.” “Kyushu Moon” is set to begin its six-week shoot in Beppu, Japan, in October. The Swiss projects in the Venice Gap-Financing Market also include: “Chocolat Amer,” by Valentin Merz Cinédokké Sagl, Andrea Film (Switzerland), Unafilm (Germany) Sadek, a young Tunisian in Zurich, becomes the lover of a chocolate heir while the world’s cacao is dying. The closer he comes to the Perret family and their synthetic chocolate, the more he transforms — until his body and his sense of self begin to slip away from him. “Quiet Land,” by Ursula Meier Bande à part Films (Switzerland), Paradise City (France) Ageing Montana Highway Patrol Officer Connor McCluskey is investigating two puzzling fatal car crashes. After being dismissed from the force, he worries the same fate may befall a woman who owns land in the same area. Has he uncovered an inexplicable criminal plot, or is he slowly losing his mind? “Salut Robert,” by Laura Israel Correspondent Productions (U.S.), Mira Films (Switzerland), 4 A 4 Productions (France) A diaristic portrait of photographer and filmmaker Robert Frank, best known for his pictures of a postwar America riven by social and political discord, the film spans nearly half a century, assembled from unseen personal footage and home movies, offering a time capsule of a vibrant and tumultuous time in social and art history. “The Rope,” by Alberto Fasulo Nefertiti Film (Italy), Beauvoir Films (Switzerland) When Pawl chooses to awaken from the artificial sleep that the rest of humanity finds itself in, he is exiled back to a devastated planet, an uninhabited land shrouded in fog. There, he will rediscover the importance of bonds and hope for humankind. “The Smuggler,” by Kaveh Bakhtiari Beauvoir Films (Switzerland), Homemade Films (Greece), TS Productions (France) Ali, a 16-year-old Afghan migrant, has found refuge in a salon in Athens, where he cuts hair and does odd jobs to survive, only to suddenly find himself propelled into the world of smugglers and counterfeiters. The humanity behind the darkness of forced criminal exploitation “drew me to create a sober narrative capable of capturing the density of the circumstances,” says Bakhtiari, an Iranian native and exile himself who previously explored the undocumented migrant experience in “Stop-Over.” As ‘The Comeback’ and ‘Hacks’ End, Valerie Cherish and Deborah Vance Are Emmy Competitors for the First and Last Time Oscar Voters Rave Over Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ at First Academy Screenings: ‘The Definitive Filmmaker of Our Time’ Oscars: South Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ for International Feature Race ‘Widow’s Bay’ and Other Contenders Continue to Complicate Emmy’s Comedy Conundrum Oscars: Thailand Selects ‘9 Temples to Heaven’ for International Feature Race Martin Short Gets Honest: What It’s Like to Be All Over the Emmy Race, Thanks to Three Very Different Projects Loading comments... articles.title: ‘The Liberation’ Review: Carrie Coon Is Breathtaking as a Woman Lured by a Cult in Guy Nattiv’s Deeply Personal Film
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 2:00am PT ‘The Liberation’ Review: Carrie Coon Is Breathtaking as a Woman Lured by a Cult in Guy Nattiv’s Deeply Personal Film An unnerving Lily James portrays the exploitative leader of an all-female cult in a well-paced, gripping psychological thriller, the womanly themes of which ring urgently true. By Tomris Laffly Plus Icon Tomris Laffly Latest ‘The Liberation’ Review: Carrie Coon Is Breathtaking as a Woman Lured by a Cult in Guy Nattiv’s Deeply Personal Film 3 hours ago ‘Enola Holmes 3’ Review: Millie Bobby Brown Returns in a Frisky and Grown-Up Installment From ‘Adolescence’ Helmer Philip Barantini 2 months ago ‘A Girl Unknown’ Review: An Understated and Aching Period Drama Set Against the Quiet Backdrop of China’s One-Child Policy 3 months ago See All Courtesy of Bleecker Street “You carry a lot of weight around, don’t you?” In Guy Nattiv ’s observant, harrowing and unmistakably feminine “The Liberation,” this line marks the first time someone truly sees through fortysomething protagonist Rita Cooper. Based on Nattiv’s own grandmother (alongside various cult survivors) and played by Carrie Coon with extraordinary emotional presence and pent-up energy privately looking for an outlet, Rita is an early-1980s woman leading an ordinary life in New Jersey. Quietly depressed, a wife to Reuben (Tracy Letts, Coon’s real-life partner) and mother to Ella ( Bella Ramsey ) and Jo ( Odessa Young ), Rita holds a monotonous desk job at a bank by day, and tends to her family by night as part of her humdrum routine. Elsewhere, she agrees to be a part of a video project as a Holocaust survivor, an identity that has defined her past and continues to seep into her present in private, guilt-ridden ways. Related Stories Disney Taps Xbox Exec Jennifer Creegan as First Marketing Tech and Operations Chief Disney Partners With Dhar Mann Studios, Which Has Been Given a 20-Episode Series Order She is confronted with that question at her workplace by the mysterious Ricki ( Lily James ), an intriguing young woman with an uneasy edge looking to deposit a surprisingly hefty sum of money. Rita shrugs it off with a throwaway remark about her middle-aged metabolism, while handling Ricki’s business. But Ricki isn’t talking about the weight women routinely pressure ourselves about. She’s played with a darkly enigmatic, unnerving quality by James in her finest work to date — a knowing, even domineering smile often curling around her lips. Her next question: “When was the last time you saw the sunset on a beach?” Popular on Variety Ricki is a cult leader in plainest terms, setting her predatory sights on Rita as her next recruit. As these cult stories tend to go, there is usually a magnetic male leader at the center, a sexual predator who brainwashes and preys on young women in search of direction. The scenario in “The Liberation” isn’t that at all — it actually feels several shades darker and more frightening than those clichés, as any middle-aged woman like this critic will feel in their bones. Rita is at a point in her life when she’s settled into what she deems a less-than-ideal reality, realizing there won’t be anything more. She also feels like her body, her age and her reflection in the mirror are all collectively betraying her, another recognizable truth in her life. So what can possibly feel better and safer than the warm blanket that is female camaraderie, the allyship of fellow women who know exactly what Ricki is going through? Perhaps this is finally a chance for her to free herself from her past, from all society’s preconceived notions and expectations. If only Ricki’s intentions were pure. Co-written by Noa Berman Herzberg, this is a deeply personal story for writer-director Nattiv, and he does unwavering justice to the shared universality of Rita’s womanly journey. Operating on two timelines that are edited with conviction and well-paced clarity by Sabine Hoffman and Yuval Orr, “The Liberation” introduces us to a Rita deeply caught in Ricki’s web at first, with her daughters Ella and Jo risking a long, perilous journey to rescue their mother from a commune somewhere in the woods. One of the best actors working today, Coon essentially plays two different sides of Rita with astonishing range across these chronologies, portraying the past and the present of her character through distinctive markers. The domestic Rita is frazzled, hesitant, unsure of her place in the world. Dressed in muted florals and wearing a tranquil attitude on her sleeve, the commune Rita (now named Naia) is contrastingly at peace, yet alarmingly docile, eating a deficient diet of plants (sometimes of the hallucinatory kind), no longer smoking or pill-popping. Nattiv skilfully braids together the key events that lead to Rita’s breakdown, with a breathtaking sense of tension across the flashbacks. At each turn, a heartbreaking picture comes into sharper focus, underscoring Ricki’s destructive appetite that exploits Rita’s deepest needs and fears under the guise of friendship and no-judgement sisterhood. It’s scary stuff to hear Rita recite lines straight out of today’s empty therapy-speak, delivered by Coon with a devastating sense of vulnerability. DPs Fabian Gamper and Tudor Vladimir Panduru’s grainy lensing poetically captures these intimate faultlines and era-specific textures, staying close to Rita’s face and increasingly hazy eyes. In their hands, “The Liberation” almost looks like secretly filmed archival footage, with an early-’80s aesthetic still carrying traces of the ‘70s. Their work is matched by the production design and costuming details that favor a real, lived-in version of the decade without caricatured colors and eye-popping patterns. The film’s absorbing final act is when Nattiv switches gears towards a more conventionally nail-biting thriller, with a diabetic Jo being put in harm’s way by the commune — it would be up to her sister and mother to save her. It’s an elegantly gripping turn in a patient and graceful film that generously laments the pain of an unfulfilled woman. ‘The Liberation’ Review: Carrie Coon Is Breathtaking as a Woman Lured by a Cult in Guy Nattiv’s Deeply Personal Film Reviewed at Telluride Film Festival, Sept. 4, 2026. articles.title: ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Review: The ‘Free Solo’ Directors Return With Another Extreme Sports Doc, This Time Tainted by Tragedy
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 3:35am PT ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Review: The ‘Free Solo’ Directors Return With Another Extreme Sports Doc, This Time Tainted by Tragedy Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin's latest spectacularly — maybe too spectacularly — chronicles the Everest dream of ski mountaineer Jim Morrison and his late partner Hilaree Nelson, asking too few questions along the way. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Review: The ‘Free Solo’ Directors Return With Another Extreme Sports Doc, This Time Tainted by Tragedy 2 hours ago ‘A Place to Heal’ Review: Cédric Kahn’s Rawly Sensitive Film Chronicles the Daily Tumult of an Adolescent Psychiatric Ward 21 hours ago ‘Too Much Sugar’ Review: Robert Greene’s Playful, High-Energy Doc Marshals a Revealing Family Moviemaking Project 2 days ago See All Walt Disney Studios “Because it’s there” is the famous, possibly apocryphal, reply attributed to British mountaineer George Mallory when asked why he wanted to climb Mount Everest. Unlike present-day climber Jim Morrison, Mallory didn’t also want to ski down it. But doesn’t the same non-answer apply? Why are certain people compelled toward any of these reckless, perilous, barely possible feats? If it’s just because they can, should they? These are the questions that will be on the minds of many viewers watching “ Everest: The Other Side ,” a gleaming, would-be rousing documentary portrait of Morrison, his late partner Hilaree Nelson, and a shared Everest ski-mountaineering dream that wound up taking her life. Related Stories Winnie the Pooh Celebrates 100 Years With $500 Cashmere Sweaters Disney Offers Executives Voluntary Early Retirement Packages Amid Overall Cost-Cutting Plans But those questions are weakly and only intermittently asked by Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin , the formerly married duo who won an Oscar for the giddy spectacle of “Free Solo,” their 2018 film about the similarly ambitious daredevil rock climber Alex Honnold. “Everest: The Other Side” aims for that film’s level of slack-jawed exhilaration: Everest itself is shot with sweeping, reverential grandeur, as it can hardly fail to be; Morrison’s eventual hard-won scaling of it is triumphantly depicted, as is his wild, gliding descent. But it’s hard to thrill to any of this when our minds are on the woman who died attempting to do the same thing, and the children she left behind. To Morrison, as well as to the filmmakers, this awful backstory makes something cathartic of his accomplishment. Many in the audience, however, will query the point of it all. Popular on Variety Nelson, in fact, was more self-searching than the film around her — which began development as a markedly different story, following the couple’s joint thrill-seeking mission with the same degree of awed excitement that colored “Free Solo’s” portrayal of Honnold. “People ask, ‘How do you find the balance,’ and I want to punch them,” says Nelson in interview footage, referring to the conflict she felt between her maternal obligations to her sons Grayden and Quinn, 11 and 13 respectively at the start of filming, and her urge to follow her bliss as a ski-mountaineer, knowing the dangers involved. Later, she resumes the subject: “What I can do is love my kids today when I see them. What else can I do?” Those words haunt proceedings after, around the half-hour mark, Vasarhelyi and Chin reveal her fate: On September 26, 2022, while skiing with Morrison in Nepal, Nelson was caught in a small avalanche, and fell nearly 6,000 feet to her death. It’s a turn of events that the film rather distastefully presents as a twist, having hitherto given no indication to the uninformed that Nelson — seemingly a vibrant, driving subject of the story — is no longer with us. But even if you know what’s coming, it’s a wrench, of the kind that you think might steer “Everest: The Other Side” into more introspective territory. The filmmakers were close friends of the couple: Surely, one thinks, they must have complex feelings about their role in documenting the primal adrenalin rush of such sports over their self-serving riskiness, just as Morrison, in the wake of the tragedy, may wonder what it was all for. But if these concerns are felt, they’re barely admitted, as the remainder of the documentary celebrates determination over doubt, finding first a spiritual victory in continuing the quest, and a physical one in completing it. The show must go on, even if said show is skiing down the north face of Everest — something that has never been done before, which in the circumstances, wouldn’t strike most people as a good enough reason to do it. Morrison, whom we gradually learn has experienced more bereavement by tragic misadventure than any one man should bear, is fixated on the idea that securing this world-first would be both a personal vindication and a tribute to the memories of those he’s lost. In his state of mourning, one can see how this narrative might make sense. But the film co-signs it with a strangely gung-ho spirit, as Chin — himself a father of two — joins the mission with scant discussion of the potential hubris of this decision. Vasarhelyi, seemingly a less hands-on presence in this project, voices a few more misgivings, at one stage pointedly asking her husband how many people who have previously been guests at their dinner table are now dead. (It is not mentioned in the film, but the filmmakers filed for divorce last year.) But for the most part, “Everest: The Other Side” continues to track the progress of Morrison and Chin — accompanied by a sizable camera crew and a rather more circumspect team of sherpas whose voices are largely sidelined — as though chronicling a nobly epic expedition. And if you allow yourself to be guided only by the film’s stunning mountain vistas — those vast slopes, the uninterrupted pelt of brilliant snow atop them, the neon-yellow punctuation marks of the men’s tents and gear — and the full-tilt orchestral push of Caroline Ho’s score, you might get caught up in the romantic, near-fantastical folly of the enterprise, as befits a film presented, like much of Vasarhelyi and Chin’s previous work, under the National Geographic documentary banner. But that requires significant compartmentalization of information that “Everest: The Other Side” has already offered us: the death of Nelson, the heartbroken testimonials of her now near-adult children, and a near-fatal injury sustained on the venture by Nepalese guide Pur Bahadur “Yukta” Gurung. (In a further gut-punch, the closing credits feature a posthumous tribute to Gurung: He died in an avalanche just a month before the doc’s Venice premiere.) It’s difficult to feel overly inspired by the eventual capture of a thrill that has fatally escaped many others; we’re simply left to wonder where Morrison’s insatiable yen will lead him next, and whether that, for better or worse, will be the final summit. ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Review: The ‘Free Solo’ Directors Return With Another Extreme Sports Doc, This Time Tainted by Tragedy Reviewed at Venice Film Festival (Out of Competition), Sept. 2, 2026. Howery, Jason Bowden, Will Griffith, Bettina Kadoorie, Moudhy Al-Rashid, Sam Frohman. Co-producers: Ben Hannon Hubley, Aideen Kane, Christina Hunt. articles.title: ‘Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?’ Review: An Assaultive Yet Turgid and Outdated Vietnam PTSD Drama
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 3:54am PT ‘Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?’ Review: An Assaultive Yet Turgid and Outdated Vietnam PTSD Drama 'Fires on the Plain' director Shinya Tsukamoto returns to his war-is-hell preoccupation, with a gratuitously repetitive take on the true story of a Black marine traumatised by the horrors in which he participated in "'Nam." By Jessica Kiang Plus Icon Jessica Kiang Latest ‘Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?’ Review: An Assaultive Yet Turgid and Outdated Vietnam PTSD Drama 1 hour ago ‘The Basics of Philosophy’ Review: Paul Schrader Wrestles with Sin and Spinoza in His Latest Tortured-Man Drama 17 hours ago ‘Bucking Fastard’ Review: Herner Werzog’s Uddled-Mup Fairytale Stars the Mara Sisters as You’ve Never Seen Her Before 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Kino Films, Venice Film Festival If Shinya Tsukamoto ‘s “Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?” were the first, or even the 51st, movie to litigate the atrocities committed by U.S. troops during the Vietnam War, perhaps on a purely informational level some justification would exist for its crudely simplistic approach. Nuance is often a casualty of war, especially when that war is ongoing or recently ended. But this is 2026, when — in contrast to the era in which the real, evidently heroic Allen Nelson, on whose memoir the film is based, toured his cautionary horror story internationally — you’d be hard pressed to find a substantial contingent unaware that the Vietnam War has since been judged a mistake so costly in human life and dignity that it forced arguably the most substantial reevaluation of American self-identity since independence. Related Stories Disney Partners With Dhar Mann Studios, Which Has Been Given a 20-Episode Series Order Disney and NFL Team Up on Apparel Collection, Pairing Each of the League's 32 Teams With Beloved Franchise Characters Even still, reliving the dehumanizing cruelty of conflict and working through its aftermath might be a valuable exercise if new insights, uncovered through this one man’s PTSD journey, could then be scaled up and applied to the national psyche. And revisiting Vietnam through the eyes of a Black American, via the outsider perspective of the Japanese director of “Tetsuo: The Iron Man,” no less, must surely deliver some new insights? But despite half taking place in a therapist’s office, “Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?” is only invested in its lead’s psychology insofar as it provides the excuse for a series of increasingly grisly and violent flashbacks, and has nothing but the most cursory and stereotype-laden interest in the effect of the war on the African-American community specifically. Popular on Variety Marine Allen Nelson (played by Mark Merphy as a younger man and Rodney Hicks as his older counterpart) has recently returned from the front in severe shellshock. Unwilling to subject his family to his bouts of paranoia and rage, he is dossing in a filthy, boarded-up building in New York City, with only a straggly cat and the fat, oily alley rats for company. Furtively darting out to shoplift some supplies one day, he is accosted by an old classmate who brightly announces she is now a schoolteacher and invites him to speak about his war experiences to her class. He demurs initially. But then, some boys throw bangers nearby, and he finds himself diving for cover under a nearby car, where, in one of the film’s more effectively abstract evocations of a dissociative episode, he watches the slice of pavement visible from his vantage point reverberating to the deafening chaos of explosions and gunfire in his mind. He shows up at the class, lathered in sweat (the sweat-spray and gunshot-squib cost for this film must represent a sizeable portion of its budget) and hesitantly begins to speak. But he is unable to answer the moppet who — in a sentimental, heavily-leaned-into close-up — poses the question that gave Nelson’s original memoir, and gives Tsukamoto’s film, its name. Years later, Nelson is married to Linda (pity poor Tatyana Ali, saddled with an almost comically underwritten, saintly-supportive-partner role) and is raising her son as his own. But he cannot sleep without medication to suppress his violent nightmares. After a particularly troubling outburst, he goes into therapy and, piece by piece, tells his story to Dr Daniels ( Geoffrey Rush ). These flashbacks betray where writer-director-cinematographer-editor Tsukamoto’s filmmaking interests really lie, which is in the gruesome recreation of hideous acts of barbarism and cruelty. Some of those, for good measure, he cuts into a montage, alongside rats gnawing on maggoty flesh and piles of moldering corpses, to deploy whenever things get boring back in one of the brown rooms of Allen’s present life. So, quite often. It is deeply unsavory that a film with such a ploddingly earnest anti-war message only comes alive in the depiction of violent, brutal death. As if aware of that, Tsukamoto seems to arrange the non-combat scenes as a penance, as though we, like the protagonist, must atone for the base thrills of warfare with endless tedious talk sessions. Hicks is a Broadway actor of some standing, but it’s very hard to tell here given that the ESL-style screenplay leaves him no register to work in other than sweatily anguished or, occasionally, sweatily relieved and illuminated in one of the rare shafts of sunlight allowed to penetrate Tsukamoto’s penumbral images. Rush, bringing what gravitas he can to a role that is essentially a dark brown sweater with eyes, compensates for essentially only having one line of dialogue (“Why did you kill people, Allen?”) by repeating it approximately one million times with slight variations of emphasis and formulation, until it finally elicits the breakthrough Allen needs. Beware this false dawn, however. It may have taken an eternity to get to, but this is only the first of many natural cutoff points where Tsukamoto could have put us out of our and Allen’s misery, only to instead fade up into yet another epilogue. The film has maybe eight or ten endings — forgive the inexactness, you too may lose track of the number of times you are halfway out of your seat with one arm in the sleeve of your coat, before realizing that no, that very obvious dramatic beat was not the final bow, because now, suddenly Allen has a beard and a daughter! Oh, now his beard is gray. Oh, now he’s on a boat! And here is Lily Franky , the great Japanese actor who is fourth-billed but arrives at the eleventh hour to deliver a single monologue to a closed bathroom door. It is rare to come across a film — especially in a major festival’s competition lineup — in which not only does so little work, it is given such endless acreage in which to keep not working, which is especially striking given that there’s little in “Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?” that can’t be boiled down to: “Yes, I did.” ‘Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?’ Review: An Assaultive Yet Turgid and Outdated Vietnam PTSD Drama Reviewed at Venice Film Festival (Competition), Sept. 3, 2026. articles.title: Marion Cotillard Praises Venice Biennale College Cinema Workshop: ‘Not all Films Are Destined to Draw Millions of Viewers and Turn a Profit’
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 4:06am PT Marion Cotillard Praises Venice Biennale College Cinema Workshop: ‘Not all Films Are Destined to Draw Millions of Viewers and Turn a Profit’ Cotillard is at the Venice Film Festival as Biennale College tutor By Nick Vivarelli , Elsa Keslassy Getty Oscar-winner Marion Cotillard (“La Vie en Rose”) is at the Venice Film Festival in a new guise, as tutor of Biennale College Cinema, the workshop allowing emerging filmmakers to develop and produce micro-budget feature-length films, which is sponsored by Chanel. Biennale College Cinemas was conceived 15 years ago by Venice chief Alberto Barbera in tandem with Torino Film Lab topper Savina Neirotti, who heads the unique Venice initiative. Related Stories Winnie the Pooh Celebrates 100 Years With $500 Cashmere Sweaters Disney and NFL Team Up on Apparel Collection, Pairing Each of the League's 32 Teams With Beloved Franchise Characters During this time Biennale College has spawned 49 feature film projects made with micro-budgets with grants that after the first decade rose from €150,00 ($174,00) to €200,00 ($232) during the past five years. “These works provide a bird’s eye view of what it means to debut as a filmmaker today,” Neirotti noted. Popular on Variety “When Chanel told me about this program, I was very touched,” said Cotillard. “Above all, I think it’s very important to support films that are struggling to get off the ground financially these days,” she added. “Not all films are destined to draw millions of viewers and turn a profit, and I think it’s very important to support artists — artists from all over the world – some of whom, even in their own countries, simply don’t have access to production opportunities,” she noted. “And what’s really striking about the films I’ve seen — the four films I’ve seen – is their artistic passion; that need to tell stories,” Cotillard continued. This year’s Biennale College projects, all first works, hail from China, Italy, Mexico, Spain and the U.S. They are: “Demeter in Exile,” by Italian director Maria Giovanna Cicciari who is teamed wth producer Raffaella Pontarelli. “Gu Shi” by Chinese director Yinan Song and produced by Yueyi Xing; “Moonfish,” by U.S. director Daniel Zvereff who is teamed with Spanish producer Mireia Villanova; and “Tijuana Todavía” by Mexian director Gabriel Gutierrez Morales working with producer Humberto Busto Marín. Barbera also said he will soon be announcing the winner of the first edition of Biennale College Blend, the initiative’s new strand for artists looking to explore stories in the multi-media space comprising forms of expression such as music, visual arts, and performing arts. articles.title: Robert Pattinson Wants Chris Hansen to Like ‘Primetime’ Despite His Criticisms: ‘I Hope the Inspiration His Character Has Given Is Some Kind of Compliment’
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 4:28am PT Robert Pattinson Wants Chris Hansen to Like ‘Primetime’ Despite His Criticisms: ‘I Hope the Inspiration His Character Has Given Is Some Kind of Compliment’ By Rebecca Rubin , Elsa Keslassy Robert Pattinson wants Chris Hansen to like “ Primetime ,” a tense thriller about the television journalist and “To Catch a Predator” host, which premieres on Saturday afternoon at the Venice Film Festival . The real-life Hansen has been vocal in his skepticism of the movie, which he said he hasn’t seen because he declined to sign a standard NDA from the studio, A24 . But Hansen said that based on the trailer, he finds Pattinson’s portrayal “overly dramatic” and questioned Hollywood’s motives in dramatizing the popular Dateline NBC series about child predators. (However, Hansen admitted that his family “ seem to think it’s a pretty good imitation .”) Related Stories Disney Partners With Dhar Mann Studios, Which Has Been Given a 20-Episode Series Order Disney and NFL Team Up on Apparel Collection, Pairing Each of the League's 32 Teams With Beloved Franchise Characters “Obviously, I hope he likes the movie,” Pattinson said on Saturday’s Venice Film Festival press conference. “There’s something electrifying about him. I would hope the amount of inspiration his character has given a lot of people for years is some kind of compliment.” Popular on Variety Directed by Lance Oppenheim in his narrative feature debut, “Primetime” is set in the mid-2000s and follows Hansen, then the host of Dateline NBC’s “To Catch a Predator,” as he turns the pursuit of suspected child predators into primetime entertainment. Loosely based on the 2007 “Esquire” article “Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die,” the movie exposes the ethical limits of Hansen’s methods and the collision between journalism, policing and entertainment. “To Catch a Predator” ultimately ended in 2008 after facing some backlash over its methods of confronting the suspects. “There’s something magnetic about his presence. I watched the show when I was younger and didn’t think about it,” Pattinson said. “There’s a strange alchemy — something he’s doing is the reason people are still talking about that show 20 years later. It’s not to do solely with the subject matter. It was something about the show that was groundbreaking, but then he’s someone centering it. There’s something, even after watching literally thousands of hours of it, you can’t put your finger on it.” Pattinson was joined at Saturday’s press conference by Oppenheim and co-stars Skyler Gisondo, Merritt Wever and Phoebe Bridgers. Pattinson praised Bridgers, the Grammy-winning singer and songwriter who makes her acting debut as a decoy in “Primetime.” “She’s unbelievable,” Pattinson said. “I didn’t even know Lance and Phoebe were friends. When he suggested her, I was like ‘ Phoebe Bridgers? Why don’t we get the Queen?’ Even on the first day, she was so relaxed. She didn’t seem nervous at all. She completely got the tone, and it’s a relatively difficult movie.” Bridgers, for her part, described the filming process as “super intimidating.” “When Lance asked me, I was like, ‘No way, dude,'” she recalled. “But it turns out, working with incredible people actually makes it way easier. I thought I was going to wither with all of these guys. Instead, it was just fun and free.” Oppenheim, 30, is best known for documentaries like “Some Kind of Heaven,” “Spermworld” and the HBO series “Ren Faire.” He remembers discovering “To Catch a Predator,” not through the show itself but through parodies on “South Park” and comedy website Ebaum’s World. He’s described “Primetime” as a “docu-fantasia.” “When I finally saw ‘To Catch a Predator,’ I was amazed,” Oppenheim said. “Chris Hansen had these one-liners like Tony Montana. But instead of ‘Say hello to my little friend,’ it was ”You see how this looks, right?’ I was always fascinated by the theatricality of the show. What happens when you turn one of the darkest subjects known to humankind into entertainment?” Pattinson is having quite a year, starring in box office hits like “The Drama” and Christopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster “The Odyssey” as well as Denis Villeneuve’s upcoming “Dune: Part III.” And his schedule isn’t mellowing any time soon: Pattinson traveled to Venice from London, where he’s filming “The Batman: Part II.” For what it’s worth, Pattinson doesn’t seem fazed by the nonstop clip of his work. “When you get the momentum going, it’s strangely not that hard,” Pattinson said. Plus, he cracked, “I just had a baby. I had no desire to go out at night, so suddenly I had twice as much time, which was helpful.” But he joked that after filming projects back-to-back-to-back, he noticed his characters were blending together. “I can definitely hear a little Chris Hansen in ‘The Odyssey’ when I watch it,” he said with a laugh. articles.title: ‘Tom and Jerry: Forbidden Compass’ Review: The Famous Cat-and-Mouse Duo Are Not Themselves In a Chaotic Chinese Cartoon
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 4:32am PT ‘Tom and Jerry: Forbidden Compass’ Review: The Famous Cat-and-Mouse Duo Are Not Themselves In a Chaotic Chinese Cartoon Zhang Gang's film slots the veteran Hanna-Barbera characters into a bizarre adventure, rooted in Chinese mythology, that has nothing whatsoever to do with them. By Caspar Salmon Plus Icon Caspar Salmon Latest ‘The Marching Band’ Review: Brothers From Opposite Worlds Are United by Music in a Finely Tuned French Crowdpleaser 2 weeks ago ‘PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie’ Review: The Dog-Cop Franchise Pushes an ACAB Message, Only It’s All Canines Are Benevolent 4 weeks ago See All Viva Kids That title gives a first clue towards how misbegotten and compromised this new Tom and Jerry joint is. Everybody knows that Tom and Jerry shouldn’t be searching for a forbidden compass, whatever that might be: If the perma-warring pair are on a quest for something, it ought to be, say, some pickles for a big cheese sandwich. The Hanna-Barbera cat and mouse — formerly a throwaway bunch of cartoons, now a ‘franchise’ — are all about triflingly menial disputes taken to absurd heights, leading to surreal sight gags and baroque violence. “ Tom and Jerry: Forbidden Compass ” gives us the most cursory of tributes to that mode in the film’s opening five minutes, as Jerry heads to a grand exhibition in New York called “Traveling Exhibition of the Astral Compass – Journey to the Enigmatic East.” (Edward Said fans are advised to bring bingo cards.) Tom is a security guard here, and forbids entrance to the little mouse, leading to a brief spate of chasing around the museum. This hubbub somehow awakens the mysterious powers of the titular compass, transporting the twosome to ‘Golden City’ in China, modeled after the Forbidden City, where a storyline based on Chinese mythology is about to get going. That is where all classic Tom and Jerry tomfoolery ends — and there are another 95 minutes to go. In Golden City we meet a character called Phoenix Master and his irritating sidekick Feeny, who resembles a thicc Big Bird with green hair coiffed à la Liberace. They have been sent down from heaven by the Celestial Master and must therefore find the compass again, with the aid of some anthropomorphic traditional roof decorations, such as ‘Sonny’, a green and pink icon of a god, or ‘Xander’, a horse-like creature. But in order to get the compass, they will have to defeat ‘Mega-Rat’, the movie’s villain, who labours away in a cave with his evil henchrats. That précis will give some idea of the alarming mental disconnect that the film puts viewers through, as it tosses Tom and indeed Jerry into this incomprehensible plot, in which the title characters will soon be reduced to the status of glorified onlookers. But before that, there’s time for a smattering of creaky scenes in which the Chinese characters mistake the American interlopers for deities and give them a sponsored-by-the-Tourism-Board visit of the premises. (“Ah, Golden Lake — when the spring flowers bloom, people come from all over! Isn’t it a beautiful sight?”) Some viewers may at this point be put in mind of “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom” — another tick on your Orientalism card, if you’re playing. The Chinese characters are animated in standard-issue knock-off Pixar mode, and therefore match up just about with Tom and Jerry 2.0, but the visuals around them are ceaselessly incoherent, adding to the already harrowing levels of chaos. Chinese traditional landscape painting commingles with manga-like warfare and knockabout gags Hollywood-style, and in the background of all the migraine-inducingly hyperactive shenanigans, there appear some upsettingly undifferentiated crowds of AI-faced villagers saying ‘rhubarb rhubarb’ to one another. Throughout, Tom and Jerry: Forbidden Compass feels bafflingly out of touch and off-key, with the flavor of supermarket own-brand cornflakes. To wit, a montage in which Tom and Jerry eat a buffet of noodles and dumplings while someone or other raps, “Tom and Jerry, you and I/We’re gonna make a million, gonna touch the sky” may have the paradoxical effect of making children clamor for some soothingly 2D cartoons from the 1940s. The film’s casual use of deeply American IP in order to sell what is unmistakably a Chinese property — produced by the state-owned China Film Group in partnership with Warner Bros. and Origin Animation — may be of interest to future students of geopolitics, but even as a spectacle for kids weaned on flashing lights and brainrot it is likely to be too jumbled and bewildering. As for the parent demographic, it will only appeal to that rare subset who actively dislike their children. articles.title: ‘Our Share of Sand’ Review: A Brooding Indian Social Drama Told Through the Eyes of a Young Girl
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 4:45am PT ‘Our Share of Sand’ Review: A Brooding Indian Social Drama Told Through the Eyes of a Young Girl Shalini Adnani’s debut feature turns a diasporic gaze into an autocritique of pervasive structures. By Siddhant Adlakha Plus Icon Siddhant Adlakha Latest ‘Our Share of Sand’ Review: A Brooding Indian Social Drama Told Through the Eyes of a Young Girl 32 minutes ago ‘My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile’ Review: An Enormous, Riveting Documentary Sequel Following Reporters on the Run 1 day ago ‘My Notes on Mars’ Review: Mackenzie Davis and Rupert Friend Star in an Imperfect Breakdown of Marriage and Memory 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Global Constellation A keenly observed class drama shown through the eyes of a child, Shalini Adnani ’s “ Our Share of Sand ” overcomes its characters’ narrow construction through its brooding intensity. Set against a sand-mining crisis in modern India, it tells of a 12-year-old British Asian girl, Maya (Maya Mehta), who returns to the country to join her industrialist father Rohan (Mohammad Zeeshan Ayyub), and bears witness to a routine accident in his line of work. As notions of justice, power and inequity begin to shade her peripheral vision, Maya is torn between speaking out and adhering to the moral compartmentalization that goes hand in hand with her family’s generational success. Related Stories FCC Asks Court to Throw Out ABC's Lawsuit Alleging TV License Review Violates First Amendment, as Agency Repeats Claim the Action Is Unrelated to Jimmy Kimmel or 'The View' Disney Partners With Dhar Mann Studios, Which Has Been Given a 20-Episode Series Order Adnani, a Chilean-born Londoner of Indian descent, draws on her memories of visiting India as a young outsider in crafting the film’s atmosphere, and her protagonist’s confined perspective. Such an approach runs the risk of gawking at an unfamiliar people, their hegemonies and their ways of life, even with the best intentions. But by rooting her tale in Maya’s family ties, the writer-director explores the complicity of well-to-do South Asian diasporas, and the foundations that afford them the luxury of emigrating in the first place. It begins with a brief, poetic prologue set decades ago — seemingly outside of time — as obscured day-laborers sift through sandy riverbanks and discover an enormous diamond. Their faces remain hidden, as a debate ensues about whether they should alert their boss to its discovery. Popular on Variety The next time we see this diamond, in a contemporary setting, Maya’s stern paternal aunt, Arti (Jyoti Dogra), shows it off while regaling her with their family’s mythology, wherein her grandfather discovered the gem and sold a fragment of it to uplift them after postcolonial partition. It’s worth noting that the aforementioned quandary, about alerting the laborers’ boss, is never answered: Did the grandfather really find the diamond himself, as a worker, or did he simply claim it from his employees? There’s no way to prove the veracity of this “bootstraps” creation myth, a lingering doubt that informs the film’s saga of cyclical inequality. This initially takes unassuming form, as Maya grows friendly with Kiran (Krish Raj More), a boy of a similar age. There’s already a division between them — Maya doesn’t speak much Hindi or Marathi (the local language), while Kiran doesn’t speak English, though they just about understand each other — which is only reinforced when Maya’s father scolds Kiran to get back to work. The adolescent turning out to be in Rohan’s employ ought to come as no surprise: Caste and class remain inflexible facets of Indian society, including on the outskirts of Mumbai, where the film is set. Kiran, dismissively treated, is one of Rohan’s divers, and a vital manual laborer in the cement production chain laying the foundation for India’s modern development. It isn’t long before Rohan’s regulation-skirting methods leads to an accident by nightfall, which leaves Kiran permanently injured. This in turn leads Maya (a key witness) and her British Indian mother Priti (Ellora Torchia) to quietly question what they ought to say to the police — if anything at all. Although the film never gives its divisions a name — much of it unfolds through Maya’s sheltered perspective — its setting provides the perfect symbolism for a nation built on discrimination. Caste becomes a silent killer, as the expectations foisted upon Rohan’s workers collide with subdued pleas for their humanity. (Some of them are understandably furious, but others know there’s only so much they can say.) Granted, most characters barely exist outside the confines of the plot, and how they relate to social strata is their defining characteristic. We know little about Maya’s life before her arrival, or Kiran’s outside his work, or the family beyond their casual cruelty. But within this storytelling paradigm, Adnani imbues each scene with a dramatic wrath bubbling just beneath the surface. This tension is often subtext enough, and it’s accentuated by cinematographer Adric Watson’s tight and dirty frames, which confine Maya and Arti through astute visual composition, as the reality of their cushy lives is gradually illuminated. There’s also occasional use of night photography, by way of the family compound’s security cameras where you wouldn’t expect them, gesturing at a thematic handshake between the upkeep of caste superiority and fascistic surveillance. It’s the closest “Our Share of Sand” gets to casting a wide net over India’s contemporary political milieu, and while this facet remains largely unexplored, the film’s confining focus on Maya’s point of view pays a number of dramatic dividends. Not only does Mehta deliver a stunning debut performance, as a young girl perturbed by the world and her place within it, but the film’s sinister, shadowy tone makes even natural spaces feel imposing. The result is a twisted, naturalistic fairytale about structural realities; with the right boot-heel at one’s neck, even ostensibly life-giving forces like forests and rivers can be turned against innocent people. ‘Our Share of Sand’ Review: A Brooding Indian Social Drama Told Through the Eyes of a Young Girl Reviewed online, Aug. 31, 2026. In Venice Film Festival (Critics’ Week). Running time: 95 MIN. Production: (UK-India-Greece) A Fifth Mirror Pictures, Suitable Pictures, Heretic production. Executive producers: Louise Ortega, David Kimbangi, Ben Coren, Michael Elliott, Danae Spathara. Crew: Director, screenplay: Shalini Adnani. Camera: Adric Watson. Editor: Anna Meller. Music: Ted Regklis. With: Maya Mehta, Mohammad Zeeshan Ayyub, Ellora Torchia, Kris Raj More, Ravi Ranjan, Jyoti Dogra. articles.title: Aflac Taps Affleck for Commercials to Keep Insurance Customers Quacking
articles.full_text: Sep 5, 2026 5:30am PT Aflac Taps Affleck for Commercials to Keep Insurance Customers Quacking By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Maria Bartiromo vs. Fox News: Anchor’s Pivot Between MAGA Politics and Wall Street Likely Spurred Fallout 18 hours ago Maria Bartiromo’s Lawyer Says Anchor Was Not Fired by Fox News 21 hours ago Don Lemon to Launch FAST Channel on Linear, Streaming Venues 23 hours ago See All Courtesy of Aflac It seems as simple as moving a few letters around, but a new collaboration between Aflac , the provider of supplemental insurance and Ben Affleck , the actor and director, has been years in the making. Pairing Aflac, which has thrived with commercials featuring an anthropomorphic duck squawking out its name, and Affleck. the star of “Good Will Hunting,” “Gone Girl” and “Argo,” is an idea that has been in the ether for some time, acknowledges Garth Knutson, the insurer’s senior vice president and chief marketing officer. “This has probably been tens of thousands of peoples’ idea,” he says during a recent interview. “It’s one of those things that people just make as a joke. Even Ben has been joking about it for a long time — maybe he has been a little bit more annoyed in the past.” Related Stories Disney Taps Xbox Exec Jennifer Creegan as First Marketing Tech and Operations Chief ABC Files First Amendment Lawsuit Against FCC Aflac has struck a partnership with Artists Equity , the production studio founded by Affleck, Matt Damon and financier Gerry Cardinale, and their first new work shows up Saturday during ESPN’s “College GameDay,” and, subsequently, in other types of sports programming, including ESPN’s “Monday Night Football,” and in connected-TV inventory. In the first new ad, Affleck gets a lesson from popular coaches Nick Saban, Deion “Coach Prime” Sanders and Dawn Staley on what Aflac does and how supplemental coverage can help consumers. Popular on Variety The star power shines a light on the increasingly competitive nature of advertising from top insurance companies. Aflac initially gained a bigger profile after introducing its duck mascot in 1999, in ads crafted by Kaplan Thaler Group, an independent agency that was eventually acquired by Publicis Groupe of France. The duck flew on to Madison Avenue just months after the debut of the Geico Gecko , another popular insurance mascot. In the intervening decades, the average consumer has likely encountered Jake From State Farm ; Progressive’s Flo and her colleagues Jamie and Mara, not to mention Dr. Rick; Allstate’s Mayhem ; Geico’s Cavemen ; and Farmers Insurance’s Professor Burke. Liberty Mutual recently expanded its gallery of characters with a fuzzy yellow creature called Liberty Biberty . The challenge for Aflac is that many of the aforementioned insurance companies spend $1 billion or more annually on advertising, with Progressive spending more than $4 billion, according to data from S&P Global and Dowling & Partners. Aflac typically spends under $100 million on U.S. advertising, according to MediaRadar, a tracker of ad spending. Keep in mind: Aflac is more of a specialist, selling supplemental insurance that pays out extra cash benefits for out-of-pocket costs and bills that are not covered by primary health insurance. Does Knutson feel he’s under pressure to stand out? “I think about it all the time,” he says. “The answer is, ‘Absolutely, yes.'” He has a few tools within easy reach. The Duck, he says, “is extremely cheap for a celebrity, at least from a payment standpoint. He works for bread, a different kind of bread than what you or I work for.” He also has the support of the company’s senior executives. Aflac CEO Daniel Amos has run the company for decades and played a role in launching the waterfowl into advertising stardom. Still, says Knutson, “we have to punch above our weight.” Consumers might not encounter Aflac ads in as many places as they do commercials from others, he says, but the company hopes “that people who do see them are more inclined to remember the message and, hopefully, act on it.” Artists Equity has made a name for itself as a producer of commercials that command attention. Among its best-known efforts are a series of Super Bowl ads from Dunkin that feature Affleck and several famous associates, and a spot for Stella Artois that pairs Damon with soccer great David Beckham . Affleck was extremely involved in the process, says Knutson. “If we had twelve creative reviews with them, Ben was in all of the first six of them,” he recalls. In many cases, a celebrity featured in a commercial doesn’t start working on it until much later in the process, he notes. Indeed, an agency might tap a young associate to read lines that a star will handle for the finished product. “That speaks to how intertwined he and his team have been in this project.” New Aflac/Affleck ads are expected to run into 2027, says the executive. A second flight will begin to surface around Thanksgiving, around the time many employees are considering insurance options during open-enrollment processes. And in March, Aflac will have a presence alongside some notable entertainment properties, says Knutson, without offering further detail. The initial contact between Aflac and Affleck came after Knutson talked about the concept with his boss, Virgil Miller, president of the insurance company. From there, Knutson sent a “cold email” to the Artists Equity executive he thought would be most appropriate. When the two companies met to discuss concepts, Knutson was surprised by how much of Affleck’s interest his team had captured. “To have an agency founder who also happens to be a celebrity asking smart questions about supplemental health insurance? It really blew me over.” Oscars: Lithuania Submits ‘How to Divorce During the War’ for International Feature Race (EXCLUSIVE) Myanmar-Set ‘Fruit Gathering’ Wins at Karlovy Vary: ‘Harrowing Drama of Obsession and Queer Desire’ Netflix Sets Its Longest Theatrical Window Ever for Oscar Hopeful ‘La Bola Negra,’ Moving Up Release Date Oscars: Chile Picks Manuela Martelli’s ‘The Meltdown’ for the International Feature Race Oscar Predictions: Supporting Actress — Is This the Year of Penélope Cruz? articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond , Damon Wise September 4, 2026 1:20pm Clockwise from top left: 'Primetime,' 'Ink,' 'Bunker,' 'The Echo Chamber' and 'Bucking Fastard' A24; Anthony Dickenson; Blue Morning Pictures; Indigo Film; Lena Herzog The 2026 Venice Film Festival got underway on Wednesday, September 2, with Oscar-winning English director Danny Boyle’s Ink — starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy — kicking off an 83rd edition that includes films starring the likes of Robert Pattinson, Penelope Cruz & Javier Bardem, Jack Huston & Sofia Boutella, Dakota Johnson, John Malkovich & Sam Rockwell, Alicia Vikander & Susan Sarandon, Nick Nolte and Kate & Rooney Mara in their first movie together. Related Stories Festivals Venice Film Festival 2026 Photos: Opening Ceremony, ‘Ink’ Premiere & George Clooney Lifetime Achievement Presentation Festivals Venice Head Talks Studio Absence, Dearth Of Female Golden Lion Contenders & Why Neon Nixed Luca Guadagnino’s ‘Artificial’ – Q&A Along with Ink, this year’s competition lineup includes such buzzy titles seeking awards-season glory as Florian Zeller’s Bunker, Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime , Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love , Andrea Pallaoro’s The Echo Chamber , Casey Affleck’s Company and Warner Herzog’s Bucking Fastard. Studio titles largely are absent this year, but the overall lineup also includes new films by Luca Guadagnino, Paul Schrader and Wim Wenders along with Laura Poitras’ short about ICE protests in Minnesota, and Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace’s doc on the comeback of rock band Oasis. Watch on Deadline Check out Deadline’s reviews out of Venice, and keep checking back as we add more. Click on each headline to read our full review. The Basics of Philosophy ‘The Basics of Philosophy’ Noora Films Section: Out of Competition Director: Paul Schrader Cast: Jack Huston, Sofia Boutella, Daniel Zovalto, Bill Pullman, Dana Delany, Shiloh Fernandez, Karl Glusman, Elizabeth Petruso, Santiago Cabrera, Trevor Dolden, Richard Gere Deadline’s takeaway: With this introspective character study, Schrader continues to making the kind of grownup films we rarely get to see anymore, outside of Europe at least. He never presents easy answers in his movies — same with this deep dive into the philosophy of life and the key question we can ask of many Schrader characters, “Can we change?” — PH Bucking Fastard ‘Bucking Fastard’ Lena Herzog Section: Competition Director-screenwriter: Werner Herzog Cast: Kate Mara, Rooney Mara, Orlando Bloom, Domhnall Gleeson Deadline’s takeaway: Although it appears to start with a tone of gentle mockery, there’s something quite sweet and generous at work beneath the stylized strangeness of the tale of two sisters played by Rooney and Kate Mara, a tone that Werner Herzog has never really struck before in his fiction work, with the possible exception of 2019’s Family Romance LLC . — DW The Girl with the Leica ‘The Girl with the Leica’ Manuel Alberto Claro Section: Orizzonti Director: Alina Marazzi Cast: Emilia Schüle, Aaron Altaras, Luna Wedler, Lucas Englander, Thomas Schubert, Sebastian Schneider, Idan Weiss, Lia von Blarer, Hans-Christian Hegewald, Jeremy Mockridge, Joel Basman Deadline’s takeaway: The jazzed-up, unconventional biopic of the late photojournalist Gerda Taro asks questions about the the fine line between bravery and ego in the process of bringing back dispatches from the front line, but its structure over-complicates a simple yet quite profound meditation on an artist’s identity and legacy. — DW Ink ‘Ink’ Netflix Section: Competition Director: Danny Boyle Cast: Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce, Claire Foy, Jonathan Hyde, Lucy Russell, Abigail Amin, Bertie Carvel, Brian Gleeson, Christopher Fulford, Patrick Kennedy, Blake Harrison, Georgie Henley Deadline’s takeaway: Danny Boyle with his whip-smart, in-your-face stye is the perfect filmmaker to bring this world set in 1969 London to life as the brash if trash visionary Rupert Murdoch and his hand-picked editor-in-chief launch what would become a new era of tabloid journalism, changing the media world for better or worse in the process. Here all the cylinders are firing, and it is thrilling stuff indeed. — PH Wild Horse Nine ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Searchlight Pictures Section: Competition Director: Martin McDonagh Cast: John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi, Mariana di Girolamo, Ailín Salas, Tom Waits, Parker Posey Deadline’s takeaway: John Malkovich gives a career performance in a perfect if unexpected casting. This so-called “buddy movie” of a wildly different stripe easily is one of the year’s best films, and in its own peculiar way the most spiritual. Martin McDonagh now is 5-for-5 as a writer-director. — PH ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 ‘Elsinore’ & Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Spider-Noir’ Canceled As Prime Video Eyes Another Sony/Marvel Series Zach Cregger Talks ‘Resident Evil’, Drive To Work With Spielberg & More Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Kenneth Branagh Hosts Judi Dench, Anthony Hopkins, Ian McKellen, Gary Oldman & Helen Mirren In Telluride-Bound Doc ‘Into The Breach’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Baz Bamigboye Baz Bamigboye Columnist/International Editor At Large @BazBam More Stories By Baz Baz Bamigboye Looks Back On True Tabloid Life With ‘Ink’ Director Danny Boyle & Writer James Graham – Venice Film Festival Breaking Baz: Broadway’s Intoxicating ‘Buena Vista Social Club’ Musical Eyes London Transfer In 2027, Say Producers Orin Wolf & Barbara Broccoli Breaking Baz: ‘MobLand’s Joanne Froggatt In Advanced Talks To Play Quaker Leader In MGM+’s ‘The Magnificent Seven’ Remake View All September 4, 2026 6:28pm From left: Anthony Hopkins, Freddie Fox and Judi Dench shoot ’Into the Breach’ Jenni Carvell Judi Dench tells firsthand how stage stars such as Richard Burton, John Neville and later Anthony Hopkins , were the rock stars of the theater in the postwar years in the UK. The likes of Burton and Neville, in particular, were treated like gods. “That was before the Beatles,” Dame Judi remarks in Into the Breach , the enthralling documentary co-created by Freddie Fox with Richard Fullerton and produced by Kenneth Branagh and his Kenneth Branagh Company. The movie has its world premiere screenings at the Telluride Film Festival beginning Sunday with showings at the Sheridan Opera House and the Backlot. Related Stories Festivals Telluride Film Festival Lineup: ‘Elsinore’ With Andrew Scott And Olivia Colman; Jesse Eisenberg’s ‘The Debut’; Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ And More Set For World Premieres Reviews Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews It was, as Dame Judi puts it, a “pre-Beatles fever that the two of them [Burton and Neville] created at the Vic.” Watch on Deadline For her part, she got to perform opposite John Gielgud and Peggy Ashcroft in The Cherry Orchard , which led to her being cast as Juliet in director Franco Zeffirelli’s 1960 Old Vic production of Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet . Dench says winning the role was all down to Gielgud choosing her for The Cherry Orchard . “It was like putting a stake in a wilting plant,” Dame Judi says during a moment in Into the Breach , adding that she was the plant while Gielgud was the stake. Forever after, she was “at his feet.” That idolatry also was down to the fact that Gielgud “obeyed the verse and lines, and he did everything that I believe should be done in Shakespeare.” Hopkins, another member of the Old Vic company, says in the film that he was lucky to have acted alongside Gielgud and Laurence Olivier on stage. Hopkins and Gielgud also appeared in David Lynch’s The Elephant Man starring John Hurt. Impishly, Hopkins recalls that Gielgud was growing weary after doing “take after take” of one scene. “Sir John said, ‘”’When do we finish? I haven’t got long to live.’” However, Into the Breach does speak of the theater’s importance to cinema. After all, Hopkins was cast as Hannibal Lector in The Silence of the Lambs after director Jonathan Demme saw him in landmark play Pravda at the National Theatre in 1985. In Pravda , Hopkins plays a reptilian-like newspaper magnate modeled by playwrights David Hare and Howard Brenton on Rupert Murdoch. (Go see Danny Boyle’s searing movie Ink , based on James Graham’s stage play, which is also playing up in the Colorado mountains this weekend.)

articles.title: ‘Tender Loving Care’ Review: Kate O’Flynn Stars In What Could Be Mike Leigh’s Final Film, But It Happens To Be One Of His Best – Telluride Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete Telluride Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival ‘Tender Loving Care’ Review: Kate O’Flynn Stars In What Could Be Mike Leigh’s Final Film, But It Happens To Be One Of His Best – Telluride Film Festival View All September 4, 2026 6:47pm ‘Tender Loving Care' Thin Man Films There has been much talk in film circles that the great Mike Leigh ‘s latest film, Tender Loving Care , might be his last. Health issues, general aging and other things can get in the way for all of us, but if this turns out to be his finale, at least in terms of feature films — he has made 22, and another 20 stage plays — it is nice to report that this warm film, which, combined with 2024’s Hard Knocks, returns the seven-time Oscar nominee to the honest stories of British family life he has done so well in his remarkable career. This one, however, finds the director in a mood to confront the inevitable changes and march of time, its joys and sadness in the lives of ordinary people going about living it. Tender Loving Care had its world premiere Friday at the Telluride Film Festival. Related Stories Festivals Telluride Film Festival Lineup: ‘Elsinore’ With Andrew Scott And Olivia Colman; Jesse Eisenberg’s ‘The Debut’; Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ And More Set For World Premieres Reviews Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Leigh famously makes films in a very different manner than most, pulling together his cast and then workshopping them with an outline of where the scenario might head, but with no script. He spends up to six months with them — shaping, exploring and developing the characters that later will become the core of the screenplay Leigh writes. He has put together a troupe of actors over the decades since his first film in the early ’70s, and a lot of them return again and again. And many have for Tender Loving Care , including frequent collaborators Marion Bailey and Paul Jesson, along with Bailey’s real-life daughter, Alice Bailey Johnson, who also appeared in two more recent Leigh productions. New to the process and Leigh’s world is current Widow’s Bay Emmy favorite Kate O’Flynn who, no surprise, fits right in. Watch on Deadline

On Friday, the Supreme Court granted the GOP an emergency appeal, which is supported by the Trump administration, temporarily halting a lower-court’s ruling in favor of Democrats that discounted broadcast ad spots should be limited to candidates, the Associated Press reported. While federal law allows candidates to pay discounted rates for airtime around elections, the FCC’s Media Bureau has recently argued that some party-coordinated ads should be entitled to the same rates. After Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff was among four Democrats to challenge the finding in court, resulting in a victory from the U.S. 4th Circuit Court of appeals, the National Republican Congressional Committee and National Republican Senatorial Committee called on the Supreme Court to intervene.
