articles.title: Danny Boyle’s ‘Ink’ Makes Tabloid Headlines At Telluride
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew ‘The Row’ First Look: Oscar Winner Bryan Fogel Documents One Man’s Incredible Solo Row From California To Australia – Telluride Film Festival Telluride First Look: In Documentary ‘Zero Intention Of Living Quietly,’ Actor Adam Pearson Claims His Space POV Shorts Acquires Oscar Contender ‘The Boys And The Bees’; RaMell Ross, Stacey Reiss Join As EPs View All September 4, 2026 9:11pm Guy Pearce (left) as Rupert Murdoch and Jack O'Connell as Larry Lamb in 'Ink' Netflix Fresh from the Venice Film Festival where he unveiled Ink , director Danny Boyle arrived in Telluride for the North American premiere of his drama about Rupert Murdoch’s launch of the British Tabloid The Sun in 1969. Boyle, looking none the worse for international travel, introduced the film Friday night by noting that some people are misinterpreting the title. “It’s not a movie about tattoos,” he informed the Telluride audience, “which a lot of people assume it is.” Related Stories Reviews ‘Ink’ Review: Danny Boyle’s Sensational Look At The Origins Of Rupert Murdoch’s The Sun Is Also A Warning For Now – Venice Film Festival News Baz Bamigboye Looks Back On True Tabloid Life With ‘Ink’ Director Danny Boyle & Writer James Graham – Venice Film Festival The ink in question here refers to the substance necessary to print newspapers by the millions. Australian native Guy Pearce stars as Australian native Murdoch, the media baron (dubbed “the Dirty Digger” by his British rivals), who took a lightly regarded broadsheet and turned it into the UK’s most popular rag. His key move was to recruit Larry Lamb as editor, a talented if perhaps overlooked veteran of Fleet Street, the traditional home of British newspapering. Jack O’Connell stars in that lead role. Guy Pearce (left) and Jack O’Connell go face to face in ‘Ink.’ Netflix Boyle introduced O’Connell, saying, “I’d worked with this guy on 28 Years Later , but he was in a tiny bit at the end of the film, a really daft bit at the end of the film… And I wanted to work with him so much.” Watch on Deadline Netflix In his review , Deadline’s Pete Hammond calls Boyle “the perfect filmmaker to bring this world to life. It’s set in 1969 London as the brash if trash visionary Murdoch and his handpicked editor-in-chief set out to turn a flop into a top that eventually would bleed into the entire world. It’s an era before the internet and social media demanded faster and furiouser hits and clickbait to get attention, when people got their news by picking sides.” Hammond continues, “Adapted by James Graham from his Tony- and Olivier-winning 2018 play, Boyle has created a bright, fast-paced and lively film that matches the energy this band of questionable warriors had just after man first walk on the moon — perhaps triggering something that in different ways would turn out to be just as significant in the long run.” The audience awaits the start of ‘Ink’ at the Werner Herzog Theater in Telluride. Matthew Carey Ink , which will be premiere on Netlix in January, played at the Werner Herzog Theater in Telluride (ironically, Herzog himself has been busy in Venice, premiering his latest drama Bucking Fastard , starring Rooney and Kate Mara). “I’ve never been in the Werner Herzog Theater, and that is a privilege beyond belief,” the Oscar-winning director said. “But even beyond that, to be showing a film in a theater named after him, is to be part of the Telluride Festival… When you make a film, you feel lost a lot of the time. It’s a weird thing because when you appear promoting it, you look full of confidence, but you feel lost [while making it]. And when you get signals that someone might like the film, it means so much to you. And Julie [Huntsinger, executive director of Telluride] was the first to ring up and to say she was going to invite it to Telluride. And I cannot tell you what it’s like. It’s the rush of the ocean to the heart for a filmmaker. So, bless you, Julie, and bless you, Telluride.” Boyle evidently is carving out time to see some other films while in Telluride. “Was anybody at the Wild Horse Nine screening?” he asked the crowd. “There was a competition for a free holiday in Mallorca before that film. Well, there’s nothing for you [here]. I’m so sorry. It’s just the movie.” ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 ‘Elsinore’ & Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Spider-Noir’ Canceled As Prime Video Eyes Another Sony/Marvel Series Zach Cregger Talks ‘Resident Evil’, Drive To Work With Spielberg & More Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete Telluride Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival ‘Tender Loving Care’ Review: Kate O’Flynn Stars In What Could Be Mike Leigh’s Final Film, But It Happens To Be One Of His Best – Telluride Film Festival View All September 4, 2026 10:00pm Andrew Scott in 'Elsinore' Focus Features Scottish-born actor Ian Charleson co-starred in a leading role in the 1981 Oscar-winning Best Picture Chariots of Fire. The next year he had a co-starring role in yet another Best Picture winner, Gandhi. Not bad, but in his heart he was an actor born to the London stage, and as the Hollywood career faded he was frustrated being offered lesser kinds of films and TV roles, or only being known for one movie with an iconic musical theme. By the end of the decade that started with such promise, Charleson was diagnosed with HIV/AIDS at a time when it was difficult as an actor to be honest and share the truth. Although he knew he was dying, he was still full of life with a passion for theater and for living onstage. Fate intervened, and Daniel Day-Lewis dropped out of the British National Theatre’s production of Hamlet , walking off in the middle of the play. The production’s director knew Charleson’s work well and offered him the part. Aside from a very few people including the director Richard Eyre, no one knew Charleson was doing this role against all odds. Like the theme of a play about choosing life or death, “to be or not to be,” a real-life drama was also playing out in the 24 performances Charleson managed to play despite full-blown AIDS, chemotherapy and a doctor who warned he was killing himself. He would die at age 40 seven weeks after the production ended. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Festivals ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival Festivals Danny Boyle’s ‘Ink’ Makes Tabloid Headlines At Telluride Stephen Beresford had always known Charleson’s inspirational story, talked to many people who were there at the time and knew him, and wrote the screenplay for Elsinore that is not a biopic at all but rather a film about the end of a life, though not the end of living. Director Simon Stone and Beresford have crafted an immensely inspirational and winning film quite unlike most other movies set around the AIDS crisis that took so many young lives. This, like Hamlet , is about staring death in the face and fulfilling a dream not thought impossible. What Elsinore, which had its world premiere Friday night at the Telluride Film Festival, has above all else is a performance for the ages by Andrew Scott , an actor fully embodying the heart and soul of another actor and finding the emotional center and determination to take this last chance no matter what the cost. It is something Charleson, even at the lowest point of his illness, just had to do, and Scott delivers at every level with a portrayal that is (there is no other word for it) thrilling . The movie is also a love letter to Britain’s National Theatre, a sprawling monument to the power of art and artists, an “Elsinore” unto itself. Ironically also debuting at the Telluride Film Festival this weekend is the stunning documentary on the history of The National, Into the Breach, featuring interviews with key players from Ian McKellen and Joan Plowright to Eddie Redmayne. Kenneth Branagh, who co-produced, anchors it with a roundtable featuring the likes of Judi Dench, Anthony Hopkins and Gary Oldman. In no particular order, Elsinore darts in and out of various phases of Charleson’s life during this period, but Stone manages the tonal balance expertly. We see Ian’s interactions with friends and those in the gay community also stricken with AIDS, the deaths of some, his frustration with his stalled career, his mad desire to play Hamlet, his interactions with the medical staff and the key doctor who fought to keep him alive, his parents, the rehearsals, his worsening condition and hospitalization, his remission, and finally the performance. It is also expertly cut (the fine editing is by Valerio Banelli) and keeps the focus on this spirited man tilting at windmills, showing great courage and grit all the way. We also see the unique traditions and importance of The National to the British theater nicely re-created here (Helen Scott is the production designer). And a lip-sync dance of the hospital patients to a cassette of “There’s No Business Like Show Business” from The Ethel Merman Disco Album is worth the price of admission and proof this movie is not the downer it could have been. Instead, it thrives with heart and humanity throughout. There is a line in the film about the unique power of actors on a stage, a talent that can’t be underestimated, and in the casting of this film that is clear. Scott owns every moment, but he is supported by a tremendous ensemble starting with the great Olivia Colman as Dr. Margaret Johnson, a pioneer in the treatment of AIDS and the doctor who tried to keep it real with Ian but eventually learned it was a losing proposition to fight his dream. Colman is magnificent here getting to the essence of what makes a compassionate healer as she does everything she can to keep Ian alive and able to perform, no matter how dangerous. As his good friend and confidante Patsy Pollock, the person who encourages him to get back onstage but also who knows the cost, Billie Piper is wonderful, as are Peter Mullan as his distraught father; Juliet Stevenson as an empathetic co-star; and Johnny Flynn as Eyre, the director who gives him this opportunity to replace Day-Lewis even after Ian reveals the condition that could make this all a risk. Luke Thomson as a close dying friend, and Joe Locke as a young patient who idolizes Ian and wants career advice he will never be able to use, are both heartbreaking. David Dawson is superb as the director Derek Jarman. who gave Ian an early break and now chastises him for not going public. They share one of the film’s best-written scenes as Ian explains the role of an actor is to become someone else, not to let their own life turn up onstage. In the end though it is Scott triumphing here in a film that should make you sad but smartly doesn’t dwell on death, only life as we live it. It is the role of a lifetime playing someone getting the chance to play their role of a lifetime, which is saying a lot since Scott was equally brilliant earlier this year as another real-life person, a reluctant WWII hero, in Pressure. Here he has given Ian Charleson a gift: another moment in the spotlight at the National, this time to share it with the entire world. I would recommend bringing along a value-sized box of tissues. You might need them all. Producers are Andrea Occhipinti (Lucky Red), Gabrielle Tana (Magnolia Mae Films), Pete Shilaimon (LD Entertainment), Mickey Liddell (LD Entertainment), Stefano Massenzi, Carolyn Marks Blackwood (Magnolia Mae Films) and Scott. articles.title: MAD Solutions & IRTH Strike Pan-Arab Development & Production Strategic Partnership – Venice
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Loco Films Boards Venice Title ‘Guria’ As Drama Is Selected To Be Georgia’s Oscar Entry + First Trailer MAD Solutions & IRTH Strike Pan-Arab Development & Production Strategic Partnership – Venice Oscars: Iraq Submits Venice Title ‘No Paradise If You Are Killed By A Woman’ View All September 4, 2026 11:00pm Alaa Karkouti, Haitham Dabbour, Maher Diab Mohamed Hammed Cairo-based film and talent group MAD Solutions has announced a strategic partnership with Egyptian author, screenwriter and producer Haitham Dabbour’s pan-Arab drama development and production company IRTH. The partnership will bring their complementary strengths together to develop, package and support film, TV drama and other entertainment projects from across the Arab world for regional and international markets. Launched in 2010 by Alaa Karkouti and Maher Diab, MAD Solutions is known for its expertise in marketing and distributing Arab films, as well as for looking after Middle East and North African talents under its MAD Celebrity banner. It has also entered international sales in the recent years and as well as getting involved in development and production. Related Stories Reviews Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline's Reviews Reviews 'The Basics Of Philosophy' Review: Jack Huston Is Tormented By His Past In Paul Schrader's Introspective Character Study - Venice Film Festival IRTH specializes in the creation and development for all types of drama content – spanning films, TV series, and plays – in Egypt and Saudi Arabia. Watch on Deadline The strategic partnership will connect IRTH’s growing development operation and network of writers and creative professionals with MAD Solutions’ regional and international network across distribution and sales, talent management, production, and PR and marketing. Under the partnership, Mad Solutions and IRTH will develop original films, television series and other formats, including projects built around talent represented by MAD Celebrity. They will also work with third-party producers and projects requiring development support — from early-stage writing and creative consultancy to rewriting, script doctoring and preparing material for regional and international markets. “IRTH has always been about bringing strong writers and different Arab voices together and giving ideas the development they need,” said Dabbour. “MAD’s regional and international reach gives us the opportunity to take that work further and open new possibilities for the projects and writers we work with.” The bestselling author is known for novels including ‘Devoured by Seven Lean Cows’ and ‘Moses Cross’, while his screenwriting credits include El Gouna prizewinner Gunshot and The Tale of Ahl El Day e, which had its European premiere at the Berlinale’s Generation programme. “Development is a key part of MAD’s regional and international expansion, and IRTH brings a strong creative infrastructure and a diverse network of Arab writers to that strategy. Together, we can originate projects while also offering filmmakers and producers the development support they need to strengthen existing ones,” said Karkouti and Diab. For MAD Celebrity, the partnership also creates a more direct route between talent management and project creation. “We don’t only want to find opportunities for our talent; we want to help create them,” said Kareem Samy, executive director of MAD Celebrity. “Working with IRTH allows us to bring talent into the creative process much earlier and develop projects around distinctive voices and capabilities.” MAD Solutions and IRTH are developing a pipeline spanning original projects, talent-driven projects and third-party development and consultancy assignments, with the first projects from the partnership to be announced separately. The strategic partnership was announced at the Venice Film Festival, where MAD Solutions has a presence this year as the sales agent for Giornate degli Autori title Al Baraneya and involvement in Conversations with the Sea in the Venice Spotlight section. MAD will also present its annual award at Final Cut in Venice, marking the 12th year of the company’s support for the development and co-financing program focused on films from Africa and the Arab world through post-production and international industry opportunities. ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 ‘Elsinore’ & Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Spider-Noir’ Canceled As Prime Video Eyes Another Sony/Marvel Series Zach Cregger Talks ‘Resident Evil’, Drive To Work With Spielberg & More Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Loco Films Boards Venice Title ‘Guria’ As Drama Is Selected To Be Georgia’s Oscar Entry + First Trailer
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Loco Films Boards Venice Title ‘Guria’ As Drama Is Selected To Be Georgia’s Oscar Entry + First Trailer MAD Solutions & IRTH Strike Pan-Arab Development & Production Strategic Partnership – Venice Oscars: Iraq Submits Venice Title ‘No Paradise If You Are Killed By A Woman’ View All September 4, 2026 11:29pm EXCLUSIVE: Loco Films has boarded sales on Georgian filmmaker Levan Koguashvili ’s drama Guria ahead of its world premiere in the Spotlight section of the Venice Film Festival and unveiled a first trailer. News of the acquisition follows hot on the heels of Georgia ’s decision to submit the feature as its entry to the 99th Academy Awards . Set in the director’s native western Georgia, the film follows Zuriko, a 45-year-old hazelnut farmer navigating the economic challenges, romantic adventures and the surreal realities of life in the post-Soviet village of Guria. Related Stories News MAD Solutions & IRTH Strike Pan-Arab Development & Production Strategic Partnership - Venice Reviews Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline's Reviews When Italian buyers offer Zuriko a miserly price for his hazelnut harvest, he refuses to sell and sets out in search of better buyers. Meanwhile, his best friend Gela attempts to find him a new wife, introducing him to a string of potential matches, none of whom win the approval of Zuriko’s formidable ex-mother-in-law. “ Guria is about ordinary people who live under harsh conditions yet manage to preserve their humanity,” Koguashvili said. “It is a natural cradle of tragicomedy, the genre I love most.” Beyond being the film’s geographical setting, director Koguashvili describes western Georgia as “a state of mind,” adding he wanted to make a film about ordinary people without ideological or political agendas. “Just pure living. Just pure cinema. Just pure Guria,” he said. Koguashvili’s previous credits include Blind Dates and Brighton 4th , which premiered at the 2019 Tribeca Film Festival and won the World Cinema Dramatic Competition. Laurent Daniélou, CEO of Loco Films, which previously handled sales on Brighton 4th , described the film as “a marvellous Georgian comedy that opens a window onto a fractured post-Soviet world with warmth, sensuality and wry humor.” Guria is a Georgian, Swiss, Luxembourgish, Bulgarian, Turkish, Norwegian and Saudi Arabian co-production. It is lead produced by Olena Yershova, Koguashvili and Boris Frumin for Kino Iberica, Pascal Traechslin for Cineworx Filmproduktion, Donato Rotunno for Tarantula Luxembourg and Stefan Kitanov for Art Fest, with further partners including TatoFilm, Maya Film, Staer with the support of the Red Sea Fund. Guria was announced as Georgia’s 2027 Oscars submission on Thursday by the Georgian National Film Center. It was selected from five potential candidates which also included Ana Urushadze’s Supporting Role , Nino Basilia’s Phase , Giorgi Ovashvili’s The Moon Is My Father and Nikoloz Khomasuridze’s Share the Love . ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 ‘Elsinore’ & Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Spider-Noir’ Canceled As Prime Video Eyes Another Sony/Marvel Series Zach Cregger Talks ‘Resident Evil’, Drive To Work With Spielberg & More Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Lee Chang-dong On His Eight-Year Hiatus & Confident Return With Venice Competition Title ‘Possible Love’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Lee Chang-dong On His Eight-Year Hiatus & Confident Return With Venice Competition Title ‘Possible Love’ Ira Sachs To Preside Over San Sebastián’s Competition Jury Theo Rollason On How He Discovered 30 Hours Of Behind-The-Scenes Derek Jarman Footage To Create ‘Queer Edward II’ — Venice View All September 5, 2026 12:21am Sul Kyung-gu as Ho-seok, Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok in 'Possible Love.' Joo Jae-bum/Netflix © 2026 Lee Chang-dong has finally returned to feature filmmaking. The Korean filmmaker has been on an extended eight-year hiatus, which he blames on his “pathological timidity.” “Unless I have that conviction, I cannot make myself begin the work, no matter the external circumstances or what others around me say,” he tells Deadline via Zoom from his office in Korea , ahead of his trip to Venice , where, this weekend, his latest film Possible Love , a title full of conviction but also comedy and sharp social critique, debuts in Competition. Related Stories News Loco Films Boards Venice Title 'Guria' As Drama Is Selected To Be Georgia's Oscar Entry + First Trailer News MAD Solutions & IRTH Strike Pan-Arab Development & Production Strategic Partnership - Venice Director Lee helmed the film from a screenplay he co-wrote with Oh Jung-mi. The pair previously worked together on Chang-dong’s last film, the excellent Burning (2018). The story follows two married couples whose lives become uniquely intertwined. There is Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon), who lives a quiet life with her husband, Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), and their young son Cheol. Watch on Deadline Ho-seok has been laid off from his job following an incident that has stunted his life and his ability to communicate with his family. We only learn what that incident was after the family meets Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a documentary filmmaker engaged in a project about the lives of laid-off workers, and her ultra-wealthy husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). When Mi-ok agrees to be filmed, she grows close to Ye-ji, creating an uncomfortable friction that shakes both of their households. Running just short of three hours, Possible Love is a masterful return by Chang-dong. Below, the filmmaker, joined by one of his leading men, Sul Kyung-gu, discusses why it has taken him almost a decade to make Possible Love . The filmmaker says he initially shelved the project, fearing he wasn’t the most suitable messenger for a film about labor rights. Chang-dong also explains why there is a tribute to Krzysztof Kieślowski’s Dekalog at the end of Possible Love , and why he believes so many contemporary Korean filmmakers have been so successful at interrogating the relationship or, as the Marxists would say, struggle between labor and capital in their work. Netflix will release Possible Love in cinemas on October 23. The film hits the streamer on November 6. DEADLINE: Director Lee, where did this idea come from? LEE CHANG-DONG: Some years ago in Korea, a Korean conglomerate went through mass layoffs. That was met with an all-or-nothing strike from the labor side. There was also a merciless crackdown by the authorities. At the time, I remember thinking it would be a transformative event in the Korean labor market. I also knew it probably meant the beginning of a normalization of such restructuring of conglomerates that would greatly change the lives of these laborers. I wrote a screenplay, but at the last minute, I started to ask myself: Am I worthy of telling a story like this? I mean, do I have the right? Documentaries had already been filmed about the subject. Could I really justify turning this into a dramatic film? I couldn’t get a clear answer to that question, so I shelved the project. A lot of time passed, and then my co-writer, Oh Jung-mi, came up with the idea of telling this story alongside the tale of a documentary filmmaker. That got me thinking I could do this project. And that led me to revisit the project. Sul Kyung-gu as Ho-seok, Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok, Cho Yeo-jeong as Ye-ji, Zo In-sung as Sang-woo in ‘Possible Love’. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026. DEADLINE: I went in blind, so the documentary element really surprised me. What do you want people to take away from that aspect of this story? CHANG-DONG: This is the story of all people who make films, no matter what kind of film it is. It could be a genre film or a dramatic film. As filmmakers, we deal with and portray people’s lives, and therefore, we are bound to be strongly connected to social issues. And as we deal with the pain of others, we must think: are we really making sure to treat them as we would our own, candidly and honestly? Or are we just consuming it to make our films? This question is inseparable from the work for those of us who create films. That’s why I wanted to take that question and expand it, not only in relation to creators but also to audiences. I hope they can think about their relationship with themselves and others. DEADLINE: Sul, you’ve worked with Director Lee before. When did you first hear about this project? SUL KYUNG-GU: I first heard about Possible Love last March. Director Lee and I met about two years ago, at the end of 2024, and he didn’t mention a new project. In fact, when we’re together, we still often meet with fans of our previous film, Peppermint Candy . A few months after that meeting, he reached out to me and told me about Possible Love . At the time, I was perplexed because I was already attached to a different project, but I knew I had to make this work. I spoke with the other director and begged him. Finally, they made it work for me. The actual story and meaning of Possible Love wasn’t even important to me. What was important to me was working with director Lee Chang-dong again. I didn’t even ask to see the screenplay. Director Lee actually asked me, “Hey, you’re not even interested in reading the screenplay at all?” When I first read it, it just felt like a Lee Chang-dong script. It quite literally smelled of him. It had his fragrance. When you get something that Director Lee writes, it concerns you in the sense that you really want to make it work and do it well. DEADLINE: Director Lee, people have been anticipating your next film for some time now. It has been almost a decade since Burning. Do you ever feel anxiety about that anticipation? CHANG-DONG: I remember promising people after Burning that my next film would not take as long. But regretfully, I wasn’t able to keep that promise. I did have many people reach out to me asking when I would make my next film. I think that you could almost say it’s an obsessive side of me, almost a pathological timidity or whatnot. But unless I have that conviction, I cannot make myself begin the work, no matter the external circumstances or what others around me say. Zo In-sung as Sang-woo, Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok in ‘Possible Love’ Credit: Joo Jae-bum/Netflix © 2026 DEADLINE: The music in this film is wonderful. Jung Jaeil, who has previously worked with Director Bong and Kore-eda, worked on the score. How did you two work together? CHANG-DONG: I have never been a fan of using a lot of music in my films. This is just something that I carry as a filmmaker. I feel like the music tends to emphasize emotions outside the film, and I believe the musicality of the films should lie within the film itself. And so I shared these thoughts with Jung Jaeil. I told him that I would like the music to be limited to a minimum yet still convey the film’s structure and emotions to the audience. He understood me completely, and I really think that the results he came up with were just right. DEADLINE: There’s a tribute to Kieślowski’s Dekalog at the end of this movie. This isn’t an adaptation from that film series. What is the connection? CHANG-DONG: When I was writing this script, Kieślowski’s Dekalog was being adapted into a new project, with different feature films being assigned to each of the series. I was offered the chance to take part in the project. This film is unrelated to the Dekalog one, but I thought I could integrate the commandment they were dealing with in that film into this story: the 10th commandment, “Thou shalt not covet”. All the other nine commandments are about human action. However, the 10th commandment is all about human desire, so I thought that in today’s capitalist world, we could really deal with the question: can we truly live without coveting others’ lives? DEADLINE: You mention today’s capitalist world. Can you both tell me: Why are so many Korean filmmakers able to so skilfully and powerfully deal with our relationship to labor and capital in their films? CHANG-DONG: That’s something I’m personally curious about as well. But what I can say is that it goes to show just how rapid an economic change and development the Korean society has experienced over the past decades. Just a few decades ago, Korea experienced a tremendous war. We were one of the poorest countries in the world, and within a few decades we achieved very rapid economic development. However, as a result, we had to pay a grave social cost, and I believe the aftermath of that change is deeply rooted in our society. Within that process, we also experienced a political change, which led to conflict about academia and intellectuals. This has all been engraved in the Korean people, and I believe it is why we deal with these issues in such a serious manner. We carry it all with us in our everyday lives. KYUNG-GU: I agree. It is a result of the rapid change our society went through and the intense conflict that led to it. And I think we are going to have a lot more stories to come going forward as well. ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 ‘Elsinore’ & Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Spider-Noir’ Canceled As Prime Video Eyes Another Sony/Marvel Series Zach Cregger Talks ‘Resident Evil’, Drive To Work With Spielberg & More Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Robert Pattinson Addresses Chris Hansen’s Criticism  Of ‘Primetime’: “I Hope It’s Some Kind Of Compliment”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Robert Pattinson Addresses Chris Hansen’s Criticism Of ‘Primetime’: “I Hope It’s Some Kind Of Compliment” Loco Films Boards Venice Title ‘Guria’ As Drama Is Selected To Be Georgia’s Oscar Entry + First Trailer MAD Solutions & IRTH Strike Pan-Arab Development & Production Strategic Partnership – Venice View All September 5, 2026 5:15am Robert Pattinson at Venice International Film Festival Kate Green/Getty Images Robert Pattinson says he hopes Chris Hansen will come to see Lance Oppenheim’s thriller Primetime , taking inspiration from the TV host and his show To Catch a Predator series, as a compliment. “I would hope in some ways, like the amount of inspiration that his character has given so many people who are involved in this film for years now, I hope it’s some kind of compliment,” he told the press conference for Golden Lion contender ahead of its Venice Film Festival work premiere this evening. Hansen, who has yet to see the film, has said he has “ethical” issues with the use of his name and the names of his colleagues and family members in a movie that he presumed to be “fiction. He has also suggested on the basis of the trailer that Pattinson had achieved “a pretty good imitation” of him but that the performance was “overly dramatic”. I didn’t set out to make a movie about Chris Hansen but there’s something electrifying about it” #VeniceFilmFestival pic.twitter.com/hy2ynyFwBS — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 5, 2026 “The more you watch the show, there’s something magnetic about his presence… I watched the show when I was younger and I didn’t even think about and when you obsessively watch it, you realize there’s a strange alchemy with what’s going on, the aesthetics of the show, and how it was directed, and how things are put together, and the time period,” said Pattinson in Venice. Watch on Deadline “But something he’s doing is the reason why people are still talking about that show 20 years later, and it’s not to do solely with the subject matter… I just think there was something that about the show that was very groundbreaking, kind of breaking the rules of television, and also in some ways like bureaucracy… but then he’s somehow centering it. articles.title: ‘Oasis’ Asks Uncomfortable Questions About Exclusion, and Its Director Explains Why Violence Is “Like a Virus”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 4, 2026 1:00am 'Oasis' Courtesy of Zeitgeist Filmproduktion “Oasis” feels like a bit of a theme at Venice this year, with at least two movies featuring that word in their titles. One is Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern’s Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger , a documentary about the reunion tour of the famous English rock band. But it is the other film that could leave audiences truly rocked. Is a safe place simply a location or something we can create – a state of mind, even? German writer-director Jannis Lenz explores that and the various forms that exclusion and violence take in his feature debut Oasis ( Oase ). Related Stories Movies 'The End of Times' Is an AI-Assisted Film Essay on Trauma That Wants to "Politicize Mental Illness" (Exclusive Venice Trailer) Movies 'The Horsemen of the Apocalypse' Director Shares Insight Into Her Hybrid Movie That Revisits Her Filmmaker Father's Arrest and Death In the film, world-premiering on Sept. 6 in the Horizons section of the 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival , a viral video of a student threatening his classmates surfaces online, causing concern among school staff, parents and kids. The student shown in the video and two other outcasts end up seeking refuge in a nearby forest. Their play turns into ritual, with pain becoming an escape. But then old wounds surface and, as notes on the film highlight, the boundaries between them are redrawn. Boundaries were fluid behind the scenes of the production. For example, Lenz directed Oasis based on a screenplay that he wrote with Alexander Dirninger, who also served as director of photography. Lenz also collaborated with Melisa Krasniqi in the editing process. The cast of Oasis is a showcase of established stars and up-and-coming German actors. Florian Geißelmann ( Sound of Falling , Home Stories ) as Lukas, Anton Petzold ( Home Stories , Ouija ) as Andrew and Mathilda Smidt ( Almania , Chabos ) as Maja feature as the young trio of outcasts, while veteran Godehard Giese plays one of their father’s and teacher ( Rose , Transit , Babylon Berlin ), with Britta Hammelstein ( Murder Mindfully , Woman of the Dead , The Sparrow in the Chimney ) potraying the school principal and Ioana Iacob ( Do Not Expect Too Much From the End of the World ) a school staff member. Oasis is produced by Germany’s Zeitgeist Filmproduktion and co-produced by Austria’s Wega Film and Germany’s Third Picture in collaboration with We Fade to Grey, Ocean Pictures Filmproduktion and Totem Films. The German theatrical release is planned for February 2027 via Mindjazz Pictures. Totem Films is handling international sales on the German-Austrian co-production. Lenz has also previously explored themes of the body and identity, as well as violence in his shorts, such as Shadowboxer (2015), Wannabe (2017), which was nominated for the European Film Award, and Soldat Ahmet (2021), which won several awards after its world premiere at the Visions du Réel festival in Switzerland. ‘Oasis’ Courtesy of Zeitgeist Filmproduktion Ahead of the Venice world premiere of Oasis , Lenz talked to THR about the timely themes that his first feature, and his first film made after his return to Germany from Austria, dives into, exploring adolescent rage and pain in the digital age without providing easy answers, ensuring true collaboration with cast and crew, and casting Ahmet Simsek, who featured in two of his shorts. Thank you for the emotional, and at times difficult, film. Why did you want to make a film about the violent sides of adolescent and school life and beyond? I think that the stories that are probably the most uncomfortable to us are the ones that should be told. In this case, I moved back to Germany from Vienna, where I spent a third of my whole life. For family reasons, I moved back to the area where I grew up. And after so many years in the big city, I spent a lot of time in nature again, including in the woods where I played as a child – and now with my own children. The older one already goes to school, and so, through direct contact with the surroundings, so many memories came up again, and I felt I had to deal with them. In the end, we even ended up shooting in the same elementary school that I went to and that my son is now going to. When I grew up, there were school pressures, and there was the fear of ostracism. It seems like that is happening on a different level in our age of digital and social media. How do you think about how much has changed or stayed the same? When I was a teenager, it already started to go in this direction, but, of course, it was very different from what it is today. For example, my nephews and people in my very close surroundings and family [give me a chance] to talk and discuss these themes. I felt that it was something for kids that is always present in everything they do, in the way they think, in the way they behave. This feeling of always being watched is something that changes life. That was very important for me to explore because it will get more and more serious as my children are growing up, and so it will become a problem of mine too. Also, the thing about violence is, I think, that it just changes its form, but the problems remain the same. Now, it’s just on a digital level, and when I was young, it came in a more direct way. But it wasn’t better or worse. I think it’s just a different way that violence or pressure is coming to young people. Looking at the Netflix series Adolescence , it feels like adolescent rage and violence are particularly timely and universal topics… My aim was to get to the core of something, and in this case, it was how hierarchies are built in very early stages and the role models that shape us and that remain or stay with us for probably the rest of our lives. I think that happens very often in school. And I always try to make something as specific as possible, so that it becomes universal in the end. If you really get to the core of something, then many people can relate to it, and that was something I was aiming for. So, yes, violence and the things we describe is something that’s not specific to Austria or Germany – you find it in the whole world, because violence doesn’t stop at borders and it doesn’t make a difference between social classes and the like. It’s more like a virus that just changes its form and spreads. Oasis shows and touches on various types of violence, not just physical, but also verbal, non-verbal, social, etc. How early did you know you wanted to cover a range of violence? And violence is a theme that I have noticed you dive into throughout your shorts as well… Different views on violence are something that I’ve worked on in different films, especially in the films that I have worked on with Ahmet Simsek. In Shadowboxer , he was a young boxer forced into anti-violence training. Then I portrayed him in Soldat Ahmet in his job as a soldier in the barracks in the Austrian Federal Army and as a professional boxer. And now in Oasis , he’s holding an anti-violence training at the school. Jannis Lenz Courtesy of Béla Baptiste Your cast is such a great mix of established names and young up-and-comers. How was the casting process? I actually started from scratch because all my movies were made in Vienna up to this point, and so I didn’t know anybody in the German film scene. So I took a lot of time casting them. And because I come from the documentary side, this is something that shaped my work. So, I didn’t go into rehearsing scenes. It was more about coming together, talking, and getting to know each other, and trying to find out what we expect from the film and what the actors see in these characters, and then bringing the [core] three together and testing their chemistry. We brought together and mixed many young people in Berlin in a casting room, and things became absolutely clear. The chemistry between the three of them was so intense, and they felt it, and I felt it, and our casting director felt it. It was just clear that they must be this group that carries the film. The way you describe your process and your doc influence, I wonder how flexible the script was… I have a very concrete vision of how the film should be – what it should transport, and how it should feel. But the process to get there is open, and I am always in contact and in exchange, especially with my actors and what they bring in, because they are the ones who have to bring these characters from paper to life. My experience is that it is much better to give them space to bring in their own experiences than to push them to a point where they maybe don’t want to go. We were talking a lot for us to build trust. I felt that it needed this trust, and we had to build up the same safe place that the characters in the film are building for themselves. There is a scene that I won’t spoil with the three protagonists touching each other’s hands. In that and other scenes, Oasis felt very much like an all-around sensory experience to me. Does that make sense? Especially in this scene but also overall, we worked a lot with the sound design to make it a real experience for the audience. The changes are very subtle. But if you really dive into it, I think it’s a very special experience to let go like they let go. I saw that Benedikt Palier was in charge of the sound for Oasis , and I have come across his name repeatedly over the past year, for example, because he was also on the sound team of Sandra Wollner’s Everytime , among other films. I have worked with Benedikt for a long time. He also did the sound design for Soldat Ahmet , which was also very special. We both have the same way of working. We try to work with what is already in the film, rather than trying to invent things. We are working from the core of the storyline. Most of the sounds you actually hear are the starting point for the sound design, like a scene with a choir or guitar sounds, because there are guitars standing in Lukas’ room, and we have this one scene where [two characters are] playing Guitar Hero . So every sound is a starting point for the sound design, and then from the sound design, we build up to music. It’s a very organic process. Since we are talking about creative collaborators, I noticed that Alexander Dirninger is not only the cinematographer, but he also co-wrote the script with you, which seems rare. How did that come about? Well, Alexander and I studied together. We were in the same class at the Filmakademie Wien, and we knew that we wanted to make a project together. We were talking a lot about this project in a very early stage. And at a certain point, I felt it would be best just to write the script together because we already, from the very beginning, shared some visual ideas. I thought it would be uncommon but very fruitful to work with the DOP during the writing process because later on we also have to translate the written word into a film. It was a very, very inspiring collaboration. I can only recommend it. Did you feel that also helped the film feel like a really cohesive whole experience? Yeah, absolutely. In the end, the film should be bigger than the parts it’s built from. That develops out of people not only looking after their own department, but trying to build something together. And this is what filmmaking is for me. We tried to push this as far as possible in the system we’re working in to give several people more than just one position in the film, so that everything can merge together into something that’s bigger than the parts. The body is something that seems to fascinate you. Do you know where that interest comes from? Well, I started filmmaking with Parkour and Freerunning, filming my friends and myself during our training sessions, which was a very intuitive process. So nobody told me how to handle the camera or how to move or something like that. It was just filming and then editing it, before I even knew that I wanted to become a filmmaker. So my starting point was showing bodies in urban space, confronted with architecture and weightlessness and stuff like that. And so I think that definitely left traces. ‘Oasis’ Courtesy of Zeitgeist Filmproduktion Given the heavy themes and difficult scenes that Oasis features, how did you guys deal with this on set and beyond? I was already in exchange with a psychologist during the process of writing, just because it’s a very sensitive subject, and I wanted to treat it seriously from the very beginning. And even before we started casting, we got in contact with an intimacy coordinator, and she was in dialogue with us during the casting process, and, of course, the rehearsals, and then on set. So we had rehearsals all together, where the young actors were building their choreographies together with the intimacy coordinator, and on set she was there every time there was a demanding scene. Of course, we were talking a lot about what this all means also on a psychological level because when we finish shooting, it’s not over. These are themes and topics that you have to deal with even after the camera is off, and we wanted to build the best safe space for them. How early did you find the title, Oasis ? Actually, it came very late. It was more like the conclusion of what we see in the film. This oasis in the film is not a place the three go to. It’s not a place in the landscape of the film. It’s something that exists in their mind, something they create for themselves, and that’s non-material. It was also very important for me to show the woods in the film. It’s not an idyllic place. It’s logged. There are wind turbines, which are louder than the birds, even in the last pockets where they hide. And so I didn’t want to romanticize this place, especially because in the German history context, the woods were used by the Nazis for propaganda issues – a sense of creating an image of belonging and identity, and I didn’t want to reproduce that in any way, not even unconsciously. So, the oasis is something they created for themselves. I won’t spoil the ending of the film, but you don’t let us off the hook easily… I knew from the very beginning that I didn’t want to end it with an easy answer that only pretends to be an answer. It’s such a complex topic, and it would have felt absolutely wrong. So what I felt what I had to do is to hand over the questions that stayed with me from my age as a teenager, to ask these questions as precisely as possible, and to leave the audience with these questions, not exactly knowing how to feel or what to think, but just to cope with them afterwards – and maybe feel “I have to talk about this with somebody else.” It’s also very important that the adults and the teachers were once also pupils going to school, and so that’s why I didn’t want to show them as the antagonists who do everything wrong, but just wanted to observe them with the same attentiveness with which I watch the teenagers and try to find out their motivations. In their case, their motivation is fear, and fear is never a good starting point for anything. THR

articles.title: ‘My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile’ Review: War Rages On, as Does the Journalistic Resistance, in an Essential Chronicle of Reporters Under Fire
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Jordan Mintzer Plus Icon Jordan Mintzer View All September 4, 2026 2:30am 'My Undesirable Friends Part II — Exile' Cinetic If part one of director Julia Loktev’s sprawling and essential 12-hour chronicle of journalism under fire concluded, like any good piece of serial storytelling, with a veritable cliffhanger, part two covers the long and painful aftermath following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. By that point, we’ve come to know the handful of independent reporters — most of them women accused of being “foreign agents” by Putin’s government — whom Loktev documented during the tense months leading up to the war, showing how they held fast to their beliefs while their country began to crumble around them. Related Stories Movies 'Oasis' Director on Asking Uncomfortable Questions About Exclusion and Why Violence Is "Like a Virus" Movies 'The End of Times' Is an AI-Assisted Film Essay on Trauma That Wants to "Politicize Mental Illness" (Exclusive Venice Trailer) My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile The Bottom Line Life — and journalism — during wartime. Venue: Venice Film Festival (Out of Competition) Cast: Anna Nemzer, Valeria Ratnikova, Ksenia Mironova, Elena Kostyucheko, Yana Kuchina, Irina Dolinina, Alesya Marokhovskaya, Peter Ruzavin, Nataliya Gumenyuk, Sonya Groysman Director, cinematographer: Julia Loktev 5 hours 56 minutes In the second half of this epic study of persecution and resistance, we watch these courageous, resourceful young journos deal with forced exile, scattering across several countries and continents as the Russian state continues to pursue them for bogus offenses like spreading “fake news.” Given what they already dealt with back home, it’s no surprise they exhibit a fair amount of sangfroid and journalistic integrity as they wheel their carry-on luggage from one airport or Airbnb to another, trying to find a place to live and especially to work, which they continue to do while the conflict rages on. Such persistence doesn’t, however, shield them from a deep sense of loss, loneliness, anxiety and especially guilt as the citizens of an oppressive, war-crime-committing superpower, even if they’re also being oppressed themselves. One of them sums up that sentiment early on by quoting a friend, who quips: “It’s like 1941 and you’re simultaneously the German and the Jew.” That Kafkaesque sense of never being fully safe, of never being at peace with oneself, hovers over much of My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile, though it also never stops these women from getting the truth out. Divided into five chapters that stretch from the invasion until the spring of 2026, the doc stays glued to its reporters through thick and thin — clearly a logistical feat given how they constantly change locations after visas are granted or denied, newsrooms opened or shuttered, and the world as they once knew it is transformed into a continual state of precarity. “It’s like my life is totally in someone else’s hands,” comments Valeria Ratnikova, aka Lera, who’s only 23 when we first see her in a taxi in Istanbul alongside Ksenia Mironova, aka Ksysusha. (The loving Russian diminutives all the characters give each other underscore their sense of solidarity.) Lera’s trajectory, which takes her from Russia to Turkey to Latvia and finally to the Netherlands, serves as something of a throughline in an ensemble piece that has nearly a dozen protagonists. As the youngest anchorwoman at the independent news station TV Rain, which shuts down in Moscow as soon as the war breaks out, Lera finds herself on the run along with her hardworking colleagues, all of whom are forced to pack their bags (or more like one bag) and rush to the airport before Putin tosses them in jail. Trying to find their footing abroad while reporting on what’s happening in Ukraine, including the many atrocities committed in the early months of the conflict, the TV Rain team faces untold challenges to get the news out. Not only do they continue to be persecuted from afar — Lera will be convicted in absentia to seven and a half years in prison for working for an “undesirable organization” — but the channel nearly folds when a newscaster uses the term “our army” when referring to the war crimes committed by the Russian military, causing a scandal in their host country of Latvia and, eventually, the suspension of their broadcasting license. The catch-22 situation the reporters all find themselves in — either stay in Russia and face prison, or flee abroad and face both personal exile and anti-Russian prejudice — is something they accept as par for the course, well aware that those dying in Ukraine do not have the luxury of that option. “Like it or not, the war is being waged in our name too,” one of them comments, taking responsibility as both a Russian citizen and an independent journalist who refuses to bow down to the Kremlin’s demands. The reporter Peter Ruzavin takes his convictions a step further, joining his girlfriend, Ukrainian author and journalist Nataliya Gumenyuk (founder of the Public Interest Journalism Lab ), in Kyiv. articles.title: Jane Fonda Slams “Tech Bros, Oligarchs and Billionaires” for Wanting to Live Forever With Robots: “That’ll Be Their Babies”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 3:47am Diane Von Furstenberg and Jane Fonda pose together during an honorees lunch ahead of the DVF Awards on Sept. 3, 2026. The luncheon was held at the Venice, Italy home of von Furstenberg and Barry Diller. Diane von Furstenberg watched as Jane Fonda opened up on a range of subjects from Hollywood mergers to toxic politics on Thursday in Venice, Italy and couldn’t help but notice something about the iconic actress and activist. “You are so much stronger than you’ve ever been,” praised the fashion designer as Fonda came quickly with a reason for her steely spirit. “Well, I’m almost 90, and so it’s easier to be so. I’ve always been brave. I just didn’t always know what to be brave about until my mid-30s. It’s like resilience, you’re either born with it, or you’re not,” said Fonda, per reports in Variety, WWD and The Wrap. Related Stories General News Diane Von Furstenberg to Honor Jane Fonda in Venice; Tina Brown and Karlie Kloss to Present Critic’s Appreciation Dolly Parton, a Hollywood Treasure Who Lit Up the Screen With Her Authentic Self The discussion happened on a busy Thursday in Venice for both women as von Furstenberg mounted her 17th annual DVF Awards, an event designed to spotlight “extraordinary women” and global changemakers dedicated to making the world a better place. As such, von Furstenberg selected a roster of five honorees to fete: Fonda, Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Amor Mottley, Pulitzer Prize-winning photojournalist Lynsey Addario, Food4Education founder and CEO Wawira Njiru and author, advocate and survivor Gisèle Pelicot. Held at Teatro Carlo Goldoni, the ceremony also featured media maven Tina Brown, model and entrepreneur Karlie Kloss and Anita Hill as presenters, with a performance by singers Noa and Mira Awad. “These women are the very best of humanity,” said von Furstenberg upon taking the stage on a date that coincided with the death of feminist icon Gloria Steinem. Both von Furstenberg and Fonda dedicated the night to Steinem. “Gloria Steinem, the superwoman feminist icon and my very dear friend passed away. As we commit to continue to follow her path, I would like to dedicate this evening to her.” Said Fonda during her speech: “Tonight is dedicated to Gloria Steinem, and I do believe that she lives on in the changed lives of so many women, including my own.” She delivered remarks in front of an audience that included von Furstenberg’s significant other , billionaire Barry Diller , Huma Abedin Soros, Jewel, Edward Enninful, Cornelia Brandolini, Georgina Brandolini, Mayor of Venice Simone Venturini, Jean “Johnny” Pigozzi, California Governor Gavin Newsom’s wife Jennifer Siebel Newsom, Hamilton South, Jürgen Teller, influential interior designer and art dealer Axel and May Vervoordt, Fareed Zakaria, Dries van Noten and more. Following the ceremony, guests gathered for a buffet dinner at Moro Restaurant at Palazzo Franchetti, hosted in partnership with Casa Tua, which will open a Venice location at the palazzo in early 2027. Von Furstenberg also welcomed the honorees into her home earlier in the day for a special luncheon. Also taking place during the DVF Awards event was a press gathering that saw journalists reportedly grilling Fonda on a variety of subjects that she was game to discuss. Credit that strength for how Fonda tackled the proposed Paramount Pictures merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, the fallout surrounding Mark Ruffalo’s comments against the merger amid claims of antisemitism, data centers, climate change and “tech bros, oligarchs and billionaires” attempting to live forever. Of the latter, Fonda stated, “They want to live forever, while they’re killing the rest of us. There’s two things: Most of these guys, these tech bros and these oligarchs and billionaires, they feel that the laws that the rest of us live by don’t matter to them, including the laws of physics. Natural laws. They’re going to live forever. The other [thing] is that because these guys can’t have babies, they’ll create robots. That’ll be their babies, and they’ll just turn the rest of us into tradwives, who have a lot of babies too. Then they’ll take away the vote. Can you believe it? And we’re not going to stand for it.” Fonda, who got to know Paramount boss David Ellison while making her long-running hit show Grace and Frankie for Netflix, then slammed the proposed merger but said it’s nothing personal to her friend. “They’re carrying so much debt. The Ellisons are carrying so much debt, and it’s being postponed now, so that they have to pay these huge sums. The merger would be terrible for consumers. Prices would go up. Thousands and thousands of people would lose their jobs, and as a creative, the fewer studios there are, the fewer places that we can take our products. We lose bargaining power. Unions lose their power,” said Fonda. “There’s a very robust and growing movement to stop the mergers. It’s sad for me because I like David Ellison very much. David’s Skydance financed Grace and Frankie , my 7-year-long run for Netflix. I got to know him, and I like him, but that doesn’t change things. This is not a personal thing.” She’s not scared of speaking out, nor is she afraid of the president. “I’ve had my life. [President Donald] Trump can do nothing to me. I’m not scared, but that’s not true for everyone,” she said as she then encouraged others to support the Committee for the First Amendment, which she launched. “More and more people are speaking out because their whole lives are at risk right now. AI could take everything away, and then data centers are being put in their neighborhoods, so there’s been a shift in the U.S. Things are changing. Republicans and Democrats alike are saying, ‘No, you’re not going to put a data center in my community.’ We can see now that even MAGA members are not liking the fact that their leaders are profiting off misery and cruelty. They don’t like the chaos that’s happening.” Fonda also doesn’t like how Ruffalo is being treated amid antisemitism claims for opposing the merger. “Larry Ellison, because he doesn’t like Mark Ruffalo’s position on the merger, accuses him of antisemitism, when he said nothing that isn’t within his constitutional right to say. It’s a tactic they’re using. He should be ashamed of himself, Larry Ellison. But there’s a lot of support for Mark. A lot of people came forward.” Amid so much activist work and bold statements, Fonda also said she misses her other job in front of other kinds of cameras. “After five years of not working as an actor, I have to confess, much as I love the work that I do with my comrades in the movement, I miss the process of becoming somebody else. It is such a thrilling process. I love it. I miss it,” said Fonda, who was quick to add that she’s developing an adaptation of the bestselling novel The Correspondent by Virginia Evans. “I’m doing it for Lionsgate with the film company called Hidden Pictures. We have a good first draft, and we’re looking for a director,” she teased. Von Furstenberg and the Diller-von Furstenberg Family Foundation launched the DVF Awards in 2010 as a way to spotlight and support “extraordinary women” dedicated to “transforming the lives of other women; women who have had the courage to fight, the strength to survive and the leadership to inspire.” Five trophies are handed out to women, along with a grant to each honoree, a gift bestowed to their respective nonprofit organizations to help propel and support their work. See more from inside the event below. Huma Abedin, Lynsey Addario, Karlie Kloss, Diane Von Furstenberg and Wawira Njiru at the luncheon. Said Addario: “We cannot let the horrors around us become running statistics. We must stand for freedom of the press, and for the importance of journalism as one of the fundamental principles of democracy.” A shot of the atmosphere during the DVF Awards inside Teatro Carlo Goldoni. Diane Von Furstenberg speaks during the DVF Awards in Venice, Italy on Sept. 6, 2026. Karlie Kloss, Tina Brown and Jane Fonda. Brown feted Addario by saying, “To say that Lynsey Addario is one of the world’s greatest war photographers is to understate the case. She’s one of the world’s greatest photographers, period. She makes images you could gaze at for hours — and others that are hard to look at for even a few seconds, because what they depict is so harrowing.” Courtesy of DVF Awards Tina Brown, Barry Diller and Karlie Kloss Courtesy of DVF Awards Barry Diller catches up with Jane Fonda while Diane Von Furstenberg chats with Simone Venturini. Amina Mohammed, Mia Mottley, Wawira Njiru, Karlie Kloss, Tina Brown, Lynsey Addario, Jane Fonda, Anita Hill, Gisele Pelicot and Diane Von Furstenberg Courtesy of DVF Awards Honorees Jane Fonda and Gisele Pelicot with Diane Von Furstenberg. Courtesy of DVF Awards Said Fonda in closing: “Most importantly, we have to stay hopeful. I’m hopeful because I’m giving it 100 percent. And hope is a muscle when you use it.” Courtesy of DVF Awards THR

articles.title: ‘Balcanica’: When Music Is Outlawed in Afghanistan, a Conductor and His Son Must Leave All Behind (Exclusive Venice Trailer)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 4, 2026 4:00am 'Balcanica' Courtesy of Nightswim Nicola Sorcinelli is exploring timely, complex and emotional issues in his feature directorial debut, Balcanica , for which THR can exclusively premiere a first teaser trailer ahead of its world premiere in the Venice Days , or Giornate degli Autori, competition, the independent sidebar of the Venice Film Festival , later on Friday. “A human story of choice and moral complexity, the film follows conductor Nazar and his son Jalil as their path crosses with Greta, an Italian doctor, and each is confronted with a decision that will change their life,” press notes highlight. Related Stories Movies 'My Undesirable Friends: Part II -- Exile' Review: War Rages On, as Does the Journalistic Resistance, in an Essential Chronicle of Reporters Under Fire Movies 'Oasis' Asks Uncomfortable Questions About Exclusion, and Its Director Explains Why Violence Is "Like a Virus" Sorcinelli’s movie stars Matilda De Angelis ( The Undoing , Fuori , The Law According to Lidia Poët ) and Berlin Silver Bear winner Babak Karimi ( A Separation ). Ivar Wafaei and Giovanni Toscano also feature in the cast. “When music is outlawed in Afghanistan, the orchestra conductor Nazar and his tuba-playing son Jalil are forced to leave everything behind,” reads a synopsis for Balcanica . “Their journey along the Balkan route toward Italy is uncertain, yet it carries the hope of finding a place where they can play again. Along the way, they meet Greta, an Italian doctor. Together, the three navigate choices that will change all of their lives.” Sorcinelli wrote the script with Andrea Brusa. The cinematography was handled by Damjan Radovanović, with Ian Degrassi serving as the editor. The movie is produced by Nightswim and Wildside, a Fremantle company, in co-production with This and That Productions and Antitalent, in association with M74 and Nieminen Film. m-appeal is in charge of world sales, with Fandango distributing the film in Italy. “ Balcanica is rooted in a lifelong anger at the ways freedom can be withheld, controlled or silenced,” Sorcinelli shares. “I grew up listening to my grandmother’s memories of fighting for freedom in the 1940s, and those stories have profoundly shaped my imagination. Years later, news of music being banned in Afghanistan – something I was too young to fully understand at the time – remained with me.” He continues: “Together with Andrea Brusa, I wanted to explore that wound through Nazar and Jalil, an Afghan father and son whose shared life as musicians becomes a journey of endurance, loss and resistance. Greta embodies the Western perspective through which this story is observed. At the heart of the film is the body: the one thing that can carry us forward, withstand cold, heat and fear, and bear the lasting marks of violence, abuse and rejection as it crosses borders.” Before you watch the exclusive trailer for Balcanica below, get ready for epic images, human drama and, of course, music. And keep in mind: “Just don’t get too attached.” THR

She followed it up a year later to support her brother, Jake, at the festival premiere of his Brokeback Mountain. articles.title: An Indigenous Man Navigates Identity and Desire in ‘Nosotros’ (Exclusive TIFF Trailer)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 4, 2026 5:05am 'Nosotros' Courtesy of FiGa Films You have heard that moving from the countryside to the city can be challenging? Well, you haven’t met Romero, an Indigenous man in Guatemala, yet! Now, you can – and go on an intimate cinematic journey with him in Nosotros . And you can experience how he navigates identity, class, and desire after moving from the highlands to the capital of Guatemala City. Romero experiences much change in the restrained and atmospheric portrait of modern-day connection and belonging from Guatemalan producer Joaquín Ruano ( Our Mothers ) in his feature directorial debut. The film will have its world premiere on Sept. 12 in the Discovery program of the Toronto International Film Festival ( TIFF ). Related Stories Lifestyle Maggie Gyllenhaal's Venice Film Festival Style Movies 'Balcanica': When Music Is Outlawed in Afghanistan, a Conductor and His Son Must Leave All Behind (Exclusive Venice Trailer) After leaving his Indigenous family for work in Guatemala City, security guard Romero (Josef Coxaj) faces not only an unfamiliar environment, estrangement, loneliness and a “performative macho milieu,” explains a synopsis on the TIFF website. He falls for Nubia (Lola Vásquez), a transgender small business owner at the mall he patrols, “discovering an unexpected refuge and a new sense of self in a world not yet ready to make space for them.” Mayra Salvador also features in the cast. The movie also touches on the lingering scars of Guatemala’s civil war. The press notes describe Nosotros as “an intimate portrait of two people finding connection within a society where racism, transphobia, economic inequality, and deeply entrenched ideas of masculinity determine whose lives – and whose desires – are allowed space.” Ruano wrote and directed Nosotros , which features cinematography by Paolo Girón and editing by César Díaz. FiGa Films is handling sales. THR can now exclusively premiere the trailer for Nosotros ahead of its TIFF world premiere. Whenever you are ready, follow Romero on his trip to the city and into his new job, his meeting with Nubia and the start of their tender journey together. THR

articles.title: The ‘Holy Wood Dust’ Director Wants You to Know Your Christmas Tree Is a Living Being With 20 Senses
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 4, 2026 5:30am 'Holy Wood Dust' Courtesy of Be Water Film Director Victor Kossakovsky has developed a reputation for making us reevaluate how we think about human and more-than-human life. His emotional and tender Gunda (2020), about a pig and her piglets, was the first film in his “empathy trilogy.” Last year, his Trillion , a wordless documentary following an artist returning fish scales to the ocean in Norway, was a reference to the estimated number of fish taken from the world’s oceans by humans every year. At the Venice Film Festival , Kossakovsky will world premiere, in a Venice Open – Out of Competition slot on Sept. 6, his new film, Holy Wood Dust , a cinematic invitation into the life and world of trees in collaboration with Italian botanist and author Stefano Mancuso – and an invitation to change our perspective. Related Stories Movies An Indigenous Man Navigates Identity and Desire in 'Nosotros' (Exclusive TIFF Trailer) Lifestyle Maggie Gyllenhaal's Venice Film Festival Style “While art may be powerless to halt the conflicts unfolding around us and cannot stop the bullets of today, I believe that telling stories rooted in empathy can plant the seeds for a more peaceful future,” the Russian-born Kossakovsky says in a director’s statement on the Venice website. “What happens to a stump the second after a tree is cut down? What does that tree think and feel at that very moment?” a synopsis for the film asks. “ Holy Wood Dust is an invitation to radically reimagine the plant kingdom from a new, groundbreaking perspective.” Holy Wood Dust comes from production companies Be Water Film, Solaria Film, RAI Cinema, Oceanika, Allegra Films and Doppelplusultra Filmproduktion. Be Water Film is handling Italian distribution, with RAI Cinema handling sales. Director Kossakovsky co-wrote the film with Mancuso. Gianmarco Donaggio is the cinematographer, with editing handled by Ainara Vera. Ahead of the film’s world premiere at Venice, THR talked to Kossakovsky about the inspiration for Holy Wood Dust , a scene that will remind cinema buffs of a Federico Fellini classic, and why he isn’t done with his “empathy” films. Why did you want to make a film about trees? When I was a kid, I walked with my mom, and I took one leaf from a bush, and my mom said: “Why did you do that?” And I said, “Oh, it’s beautiful.” And she said, “If we take out one of your hairs, do you feel pain?” So I said, “Yes, of course.” My mother said: “The bush feels the same. It feels pain. So don’t do that any longer.” This has stayed with me all my life. Once I lived in Berlin, there was a brilliant autumn, and I picked up a dead leaf that had fallen off a tree. I broke it in front of a microscope, and I saw something unbelievable. You know what happens to us if you cut your finger? Blood is trying to heal and close the [wound], right? And that made me wonder: What if I looked through a microscope when they cut a tree? What would I see? Of course, it’s complicated, and you cannot bring a microscope to the forest. So, making a film [about this] was a challenge. But we finally made it, and it really looks like War and Peace . You can see that this tree is totally confused [when things shown in the film happen to the region it stands in]. The tree has lived for 100 years, so what suddenly happened? I remember I was filming and shaking because it’s obvious that something bad happened to the tree, something horrible. It’s confused, suffering, trying to heal and trying to fight. How did you end up collaborating on Holy Wood Dust with Stefano Mancuso? My assistant was reading something from him during another project when we were on a boat in a storm. She told me, “You have to read this!” So, I started to read it and then had to buy more of his books, and then I wrote him. And a miracle happened. He wrote back to me in one minute: “I saw a few of your films, so I want to see you as well.” So, it happened by coincidence that we both needed each other. He is a visionary man. And 15 years ago, I started thinking about this film. ‘Holy Wood Dust’ Courtesy of Be Water Film Did you always know it would be a film about fir trees? I had a few different ideas, a few different characters. At first, it was supposed to be a film about linden trees [or basswood trees, as they are known in the U.S.]. They are very cinematic. They are like this. (He stretches his arms to the sides.) With a Christmas tree, it’s just a vertical triangle, which is not cinematic, especially in the film format I like. I like the 2:1 aspect ratio, which makes things very difficult for a Christmas tree. But I said no, I need to find something to challenge myself with a tree, which doesn’t look good in this aspect ratio, and it needed to be something universal. And Christmas is, of course, something everyone is attached to emotionally. We kind of all connect to the idea of Christmas, and so I decided to make a film for kids and for families. There is an iconic-feeling scene in Holy Wood Dust of a helicopter flying a Christmas tree towards the Vatican. Am I right to see that as a conscious reference to Federico Fellini’s La Dolce Vita , which has that famous scene of a helicopter above Rome transporting a statue of Jesus Christ to the Vatican? I really wanted to say my thanks to Fellini because I remember the moment when I first saw one of his films. I was a teenager, and I saw 8½ in a very good cinema in Saint Petersburg. I remember when the film finished, people left, and I was alone, crying, and I wouldn’t stop. I was just crying, crying, and cleaning ladies came in and started to brush, and they looked at me and said, “Okay, cry, my friend, cry.” It was a full cinema, but I knew the film was for me. It felt like the screen was just for me, and the film stayed with me all my life. ‘Holy Wood Dust’ Courtesy of Be Water Film There is also a powerful scene in the film where Stefano Mancuso and a group of kids discuss the importance and value of trees, which has surprising and impactful information. Yes, [that was] important [because] we consider trees like decoration, right? I took [some experiences] with trees as a sign to do this film. It was like a tree was crying, asking me: “Victor, see it. Do it because no one understands. Everyone considers us as decoration. We are not. We are living beings.” I find the title intriguing. Was Holy Wood Dust always the title for this film? It is great, but I’m never happy with the working title. The working title was Tears for Fears . Gunda and Trillion , both executive-produced by Joaquin Phoenix, were the first two films in what you have described as a trilogy on empathy. This film is different, as it isn’t wordless and black-and-white, but it still covers empathy. What’s your plan for the trilogy at this point? There are going to be more, at least two more. But I can’t say more at this point. ‘Holy Wood Dust’ Courtesy of Be Water Film What’s your hope for Holy Wood Dust once audiences see it? I’m not saying, Don’t celebrate Christmas, don’t have a Christmas tree! I’m saying you can do whatever you want to do, but be aware that this is not decoration. The Christmas tree is a living being. It’s a live organism, which has 20 senses, and which can live, if you don’t cut it, for 500 years. We have five senses. Plants have 20 senses, at least 20. Imagine that, and then you can do whatever you want. You can cut a tree, put it in your corner, and then you can throw it away. Just be aware that if you don’t cut it, it can live for 500 years. But this film, I believe, kids will love, and families will love because, in a way, it’s a Christmas carol. THR

articles.title: Formula 1’s Next Big Bet: A Live Entertainment Event in Milan
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 6:00am Kane Brown performs on stage during F1 75 Live at The O2 Arena on February 18, 2025 in London, England. Photo by Zak Mauger/Getty Images Formula 1 is planning a multi-day event “spectacular” early next year, in a bid to hype up racing fans and bring new viewers into the tent. The event will be called F1 Live Milan, and will be held in Milan, Italy Feb. 18-20. While specifics are still being hashed out, it will include a fan fest that will be held over the course of the three days, with a headlining event called F1 The Show, which will include appearances from all of F1’s drivers and team principals, as well as live music and entertainment. F1 previously held a live event in London in 2025, tied to the sport’s 75th anniversary, but the racing circuit, which has a media deal with Apple TV in the U.S., is planning an even bigger venture for the new installment. F1 remains an emerging sport in the U.S., and the new event, which will stream globally, is part of the push to grow the sport’s fanbase stateside, even as it engages fans elsewhere around the world. Among other moves, the circuit, which is owned by John Malone’s Liberty Media, added a new U.S. team in Cadillac earlier this year. There are also a number of North American races on the annual calendar, including in Austin, Texas, Montreal, Mexico City, and of course the high-profile races in Miami and Las Vegas, where F1 is establishing a year-round experiential space. “We are always thinking big and pushing boundaries, and F1 Live Milan is going to be an incredible experience created with our fans at its heart,” Formula 1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali said in a statement. “We want them to feel that they are not simply watching the sport, but they are truly immersed in it. It is an important part of our ongoing ambition to bring Formula 1 closer to fans than ever before, giving them the chance to see their heroes up close and experience the energy, innovation, and emotion that make Formula 1 so unique. As F1 continues to reach new audiences around the world, racing will always be our soul but we also want to create unforgettable experiences that bring the excitement of Formula 1 to life on an even bigger scale and continue to explore what is possible. “Building on the extraordinary success of F1 75 in London, F1 Live Milan will transform the city into a Formula 1 festival for three unforgettable days, bringing people together from across the globe to celebrate everything they love about our sport,” he added. “I know my fellow Italians will offer a fantastic welcome to fans traveling to F1 Live Milan and I cannot wait to see the city come to life with Formula 1 energy, creating memories that will last a lifetime.” THR
