articles.title: Paul Schrader Says He Can’t Stop Writing About Guilt: “You Don’t Outrun Your Childhood”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 6:16am Paul Schrader ahead of his Venice Film Festival press conference on Sep. 4, 2026 Courtesy of Getty Paul Schrader has spent half a century writing men who sit alone in rooms , filling notebooks with confessions no one asked for. On Friday in Venice, the 79-year-old writer-director offered a simple explanation for why he has never been able to put the subject down: he was programmed early, and the program still runs. “I was raised a Dutch Calvinist, and, you know, Freud said you’re programmed by the time you’re five or six, maybe it’s even as late as eight or nine,” Schrader said at the press conference for The Basics of Philosophy , which has its world premiere Friday out of competition at the Venice Film Festival. “But anyway, once they pour that programming into you, you just run that program for the rest of your life, and no matter how far you run and how fast you run, you don’t outrun your childhood. My childhood was one of predestination, of guilt, of total depravity and all that, and, you know, Christian schools all the way through divinity school. So I don’t know how I do not write about guilt and redemption.” Related Stories Movies The 'Holy Wood Dust' Director Wants You to Know Your Christmas Tree Is a Living Being With 20 Senses Movies An Indigenous Man Navigates Identity and Desire in 'Nosotros' (Exclusive TIFF Trailer) The Basics of Philosophy stars Jack Huston as John Jorissen, a philosophy professor whose controlled, meticulously ordered life conceals a long-buried transgression. When the person he wronged unexpectedly reappears, Jorissen is thrown into a reckoning of guilt, desire and self-justification — familiar terrain for a filmmaker whose gallery of isolated, self-documenting men has included a taxi driver, a gigolo, a minister and a gardener before arriving, now, at a tenured academic. Sofia Boutella plays Becca, Jorissen’s partner and colleague in the department, with Daniel Zovatto, Bill Pullman and Dana Delany also starring, alongside Shiloh Fernandez, Karl Glusman and Elizabeth Petruso. Martin Scorsese serves as executive producer, his second time in that role for Schrader after 2021’s The Card Counter , extending a collaboration that stretches back to Taxi Driver , Raging Bull and The Last Temptation of Christ . ‘The Basics of Philosophy’ Venice Film Festival Huston, who appears opposite Pullman as his character’s father, said what drew him to Jorissen was the absence of anything monstrous on the surface. “It’s not a portrait of the boogeyman, the man coming at you with a knife held high. It’s the person living in plain sight. It’s the everyman,” the actor said. “I thought it was a really interesting portrait of somebody who is actually struggling with a terrible part of his past, and trying to recompense this idea of: am I a monster?” Asked about a sequence in which Jorissen finds himself walking alongside a long-dead philosopher, debating whether human beings are capable of change, Huston said he had considered who he would want beside him on that walk. “If I was to take a walk with somebody, it would be possibly with my grandfather,” he said, referring to the Oscar-winning actor and director John Huston. “I have a lot of questions in life and work and all sorts. He died when I was quite young, but I’ve luckily had wonderful family members who’ve been able to share about his life and thoughts and teachings, but I think that would be a fun conversation.” Boutella, whose character is left to decide how much of her partner’s account she is willing to accept, said she deliberately withheld her own verdict on Becca. “As an actor, I hide my own answers for what she really believes,” she said. Pullman, meanwhile, delivered the conference’s biggest laugh with an account of Schrader’s casting process, which the director apparently conducts with no diplomatic padding whatsoever. “Paul’s very frank about casting. You know, usually by the time you get on the set, he’s told me several times about who they offered it to that didn’t do it,” Pullman said. “And I was glad that I was somewhere on the list, and that everybody that went before me just bowed out for various reasons.” THR

articles.title: Magdalena Koleśnik and Kay Greidanus to Lead Finn Szumlas’ Debut Feature ‘Stairway to Earth’ as Production Starts (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 4, 2026 1:43am PT Magdalena Koleśnik and Kay Greidanus to Lead Finn Szumlas’ Debut Feature ‘Stairway to Earth’ as Production Starts (EXCLUSIVE) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest ‘Spider-Man’ and ‘The Odyssey’ Propel U.K. Box Office to Best August Since 2018 2 hours ago Magdalena Koleśnik and Kay Greidanus to Lead Finn Szumlas’ Debut Feature ‘Stairway to Earth’ as Production Starts (EXCLUSIVE) 5 hours ago ‘Smile’ Producers Temple Hill and Anton Team With YouTube Horror Star Sam Evenson for ‘Ignore It,’ Lily Collias to Lead Feature Adaptation of Viral Short (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago See All Credit: Alicja Kozak, Teska Overbeeke Dutch filmmaker Finn Szumlas has started principal photography on his debut feature “Stairway to Earth,” kicking off a 5-week shoot in the Netherlands. Leading the film is Polish star Magdalena Koleśnik (“Sweat”) and Dutch actor Kay Greidanus (“Dit Zijn Wij”), playing two strangers who meet up after a one night stand at at a summer music festival and have one day to make the biggest decision of their lives. Related Stories YouTube Creator Kevin Langue Is Bringing His Comedy Channels to Netflix Lee Jung-eun, Kim Moo-yul Board Netflix's Action-Noir Series 'The Shooter' The script for “Stairway to Earth” iwas written by Szumlas and Olga Ponjee. Producers include Edwin Goldman for Goldman Film and Petra Goedings for Phanta Film, with Polish co-producer Ewa Puszczyńska bringing her experience having produced numerous award-winning films including “Cold War,” “Ida” and “The Zone of Interest.” Dutch public broadcaster NTR is also a co-production partner. Popular on Variety Set in present day Leiden, Netherlands and inspired by by the real-life story of how director Finn Szumlas’ Polish father and Danish mother met and became a family, “Stairway to Earth” is described as an “emotional, intimate portrait of chance, choice, and the lives that are shaped by both.” The film follows Jan and Luiza, who share a single night at a summer music festival in Poland — an impulsive moment of passion that was never intended to last. Weeks later, they awkwardly reunite at a clinic in the Netherlands where Luiza has made an appointment to terminate the unexpected pregnancy. With twenty-four hours until the procedure, they walk through the historic streets of Leiden during the city’s annual Leidens Ontzet celebrations. Wandering through a city alive with music, history, and celebration, two people with very different lives begin to imagine a future neither of them expected. Luiza, an ambitious Polish professional preparing to leave for New York. Jan, a Dutch gardener happy to let life unfold one day at a time. Between them lies a single day that could change everything. “’Stairway to Earth’ is a deeply personal project for me, inspired as it is by how my own parents met. We have relocated the story to contemporary times, and I am super excited to be shooting in the very streets where I grew up,” said Szumlas. “As soon as I saw Magdalena and Kay together, I knew that I had found the intimacy, courage and chemistry I was looking for, and that the film was going to work. The backdrop of Leidens Ontzet will almost be a character in the film too, and we will capture the life, music and the rawness of the street festivities on Super 16mm.” The film production team includes Katja van den Broeke (cinematographer), Jorien Sont (production designer), Manon Blom (costume designer), Pur Thijs (hair and make-up designer), Saida van der Reijd (casting director), Saskia Kievits (editor), and Vincent Sinceretti (sound design). “Stairway to Earth” is supported by the Netherlands Film Fund, Polish Film Institute, NTR, CoBo, and Creative Europe MEDIA. articles.title: Busan Market Unveils Doc Square, Launches Impact Asia as Yim Siwan Named Festival Closing Ceremony Host
articles.full_text: Sep 4, 2026 1:53am PT Busan Market Unveils Doc Square, Launches Impact Asia as Yim Siwan Named Festival Closing Ceremony Host By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Manisha Koirala Attached to Star in ‘Cowgirls & Indians,’ Set for November Texas Shoot (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Busan Market Unveils Doc Square, Launches Impact Asia as Yim Siwan Named Festival Closing Ceremony Host 4 hours ago Tamar AI’s TapNow Brings AI-Native Filmmaking to Venice Production Bridge With HappyHorse-Backed 10,000 Parallel Universes Films, Unveils Streamer Glanze 4 hours ago See All ACFM The Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), the market of the Busan International Film Festival (BIFF), will present Doc Square 2026 from Oct. 10-13, bringing together eight partner organizations from five countries to connect Asian documentary creators with industry professionals. Launched last year, the program introduces documentary projects still in production across Asia and offers guidance on production support and distribution strategy. Related Stories Roald Dahl Drama Series Set at Netflix Starring Nicola Coughlan, Naomi Scott, Dominic West, Imelda Staunton and More Netflix Pushes Back on Tyra Banks 'Reality Check' Defamation Suit Doc Square’s centerpiece, the Documentary WIP Showcase, runs through the Asian Cinema Fund’s Asian Network of Documentary (AND) Fund alongside partner organizations from Korea, Japan, Taiwan, Indonesia and the Philippines. Newstapa Foundation and Japan’s J-Docs Hub join as new partners this year, alongside returning partners Taiwan Docs, the Taiwan Creative Content Agency, the Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute, Docs by the Sea and the Film Development Council of the Philippines. Sixteen works-in-progress documentaries will pitch to festival programmers, sales companies and distributors on Oct. 10 and 11, building networks toward completion and eventual release. Popular on Variety Two new prizes debut alongside the showcase. The Impact Asia Award will go to three projects, each receiving $5,000, while the Newstapa Award gives one project KRW10 million ($7,400) along with a chance for a 60-minute cut to stream on Newstapa Foundation’s website and YouTube channel. Winners will be named at the ACFM Awards Ceremony on Oct. 13. Doc Square will also host Asia’s first Impact Day, a one-day program built around a question: what actually happens to a society after a documentary screens? Case studies from Korea, Taiwan and Japan will be compiled into an 80-page report available at the venue. The Korea study draws on roughly 2,800 works released between 1988 and 2025, alongside a survey of 88 creators and interviews with 19 industry professionals. The Taiwan study traces how “Small Talk” moved from theatrical release into education and public screening use, while the Japan study looks at how “What Should We Have Done?,” a documentary with unusually strong box-office results, built audience relationships through mini-theaters, festivals and independent screenings. Additional Doc Square sessions cover co-production, festival strategy and funding. The Documentary Festival & Fund Talk on Oct. 10 brings together festival programmers and funders from around the world, while the Current State of Documentary Co-Production splits into an Asia-focused session on Oct. 10 and a Korea-focused session on Oct. 11. On the program’s final day, “AND Talk & Share” gives this year’s AND Fund recipients a private workshop to discuss the challenges of finishing their projects. Elsewhere at the festival, actor Yim Siwan has been named sole host of the 31st BIFF closing ceremony, where the festival will present its Busan Awards, introduced last year to honor Competition winners. Yim debuted in 2012 with the series “Moon Embracing the Sun” and moved into film the following year with “The Attorney,” a role that pushed back against typecasting for idol-turned-actors. He built his reputation further as office worker Jang Geu-rae in “Misaeng” (2014), and later credits include “The Merciless” (2017), “Run On” (2020), “Boyhood” (2023) and “Unlocked” (2023). He joined “Squid Game” for Season 2 and Season 3, and appeared in the 2025 film “Mantis.” His honors include the Popularity Award at the 2014 Blue Dragon Film Awards, Best New Actor (TV) at the 2015 Baeksang Arts Awards, Best Supporting Actor at the 2022 Buil Film Awards, and Best Actor at the 2024 Blue Dragon Series Awards. The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15, at the Busan Cinema Center and throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13. articles.title: Manisha Koirala Attached to Star in ‘Cowgirls & Indians,’ Set for November Texas Shoot (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 4, 2026 2:13am PT Manisha Koirala Attached to Star in ‘Cowgirls & Indians,’ Set for November Texas Shoot (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Manisha Koirala Attached to Star in ‘Cowgirls & Indians,’ Set for November Texas Shoot (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Busan Market Unveils Doc Square, Launches Impact Asia as Yim Siwan Named Festival Closing Ceremony Host 4 hours ago Tamar AI’s TapNow Brings AI-Native Filmmaking to Venice Production Bridge With HappyHorse-Backed 10,000 Parallel Universes Films, Unveils Streamer Glanze 5 hours ago See All Banskota Productions Manisha Koirala is attached to star in “Cowgirls & Indians,” an indie feature that will start shooting in November around Austin, Texas, and nearby locations. The film was formerly titled “Cowboys & Indians.” Tejal Desai, a Nicholl Fellow, wrote and is directing the film, expanding on her award-winning short “Cowboys and Hindus.” The story follows a middle-aged Indian woman navigating identity and unlikely friendships against a Texas backdrop, centering on cultural displacement and resilience as South Asian heritage meets American grit. Related Stories Netflix Orders YA Gothic Romance 'Sid & Zoey,' Blumhouse Atomic Monster and Bad Robot to Produce ‘The Gentlemen’ Producers on Balancing Quirkiness With Crime in ‘Glamorous’ Season 2: ‘We Are Always Looking for New Ways To Murder People’ Kirtana Banskota (“The World’s Happiest Man,” “Premonition”) is producing. Popular on Variety Koirala, one of South Asia’s most popular stars is known forNetflix’s “Heeramandi” and “1942: A Love Story.” “I have been quoted before on how there are not enough roles written for women of a certain age,” Koirala said. “Though things are gradually changing now, there is still a long way to go. However, ‘Cowgirls & Indians’ was brought to me and after meeting the team, meeting Tejal, and listening to the entire script and his intention on why he wrote it, I knew this story has great potential to cross boundaries while having fun doing so. I’m looking forward to braving the Texas terrains while on horseback drinking my chai.” Desai added: “‘Cowgirls and Indians’ is a coming-of-age story about a middle-aged Indian woman discovering who she is in the American Southwest. “Manisha Koirala’s performances have always carried an intense realism, vulnerability, and strength – from ‘Dil Se’ to ‘Heeramandi,’ she’s built a career on stillness and expressive eyes that say more about complex emotions,” Desai said. “Asha needs exactly a woman whose whole history lives in her eyes and the strength to carry a story on her shoulders. And beyond the performance itself, Manisha carries a rare gravity – an actress who has weathered real hardship and emerged with more resilience, not less, which is the exact arc Asha travels across this film.” Banskota said Texas is the place to film right now. “The new incentives, talent staying in-state, and the sheer vastness of everything available here makes filming a lot friendlier for filmmakers,” she said. Talent agent Zahid Khan represents Koirala. articles.title: ‘My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile’ Review: An Enormous, Riveting Documentary Sequel Following Reporters on the Run
articles.full_text: Sep 4, 2026 2:30am PT ‘My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile’ Review: An Enormous, Riveting Documentary Sequel Following Reporters on the Run Julia Loktev continues to wield her iPhone like a personal diary while following journalists targeted by the Kremlin. By Siddhant Adlakha Plus Icon Siddhant Adlakha Latest ‘My Notes on Mars’ Review: Mackenzie Davis and Rupert Friend Star in an Imperfect Breakdown of Marriage and Memory 2 days ago ‘Onslaught’ Review: Adria Arjona and Dan Stevens Star in Adam Wingard’s Fun but Scattered Military Slasher 4 days ago ‘Mustache’ Review: A Delightfully Anxious Pakistani American Coming-of-Age Comedy 4 weeks ago See All Venice Film Festival Following her mammoth five-hour odyssey “ My Undesirable Friends: Part I — Last Air in Moscow ,” Julia Loktev ’s sequel remains just as riveting, if not more so, in its continued depiction of journalists escaping the Russian government. Its predecessor’s endpoint (one Loktev could not have foreseen when she began shooting on her iPhone X) was the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and the overnight escape of her close friends from Moscow after they were branded foreign agents for reporting on war crimes. “My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile” follows their stories amidst this exodus, a globetrotting journey that proves harrowing in unexpected ways over an engrossing five chapters, spanning 355 minutes. Related Stories Netflix’s Latest Marketing Mash-Up Pairs Stella Artois With 'The Gentlemen' Netflix Orders 'Manifest' Spinoff 'Arrivals,' With a New Mystery and Cast — Announced on 8/28, Of Course That figure might seem imposing to the uninitiated, but Loktev and co-editor Michael Taylor have, once again, crafted a conversational epic that imbues each twist and turn with enormous stakes. It’s hard not to get invested in the lives of Part I’s subjects and Part II’s newcomers alike. Speaking truth to power with the online tools at their disposal, this murderer’s row consists of lively, awkward, driven, beautiful, lovestruck and above-all complicated people, all caught in impossible personal and professional deadlocks and weighed down by immigrant uncertainty. Popular on Variety “Exile” begins with a brisk, five-minute recap of events, which goes a long way toward reintroducing Loktev’s subjects. It also imbues the film with immediate tension. With only small suitcases and the clothes on their backs, the young journalists of independent outfits like TV RAIN find themselves suddenly scattered across cities like Warsaw, Istanbul, Prague and Tel Aviv. They go anywhere that will grant them temporary refuge, even as they wrestle with their own ethics in relation to each new nation’s politics, when compared and contrasted with their homeland. This sets the stage for a film in which firmly held beliefs are placed under microscopes — by the subjects themselves, and by critics on either side of the Ukraine/Russia divide. As some reporters begin broadcasting from Latvia, a sense of temporariness pervades each interaction, no matter how casual. Authors, reporters and podcasters alike are forced to consider the impact of their words, and their own potential complicity in their country’s actions, as stepping even a toe out of line might result in further expulsion. When speaking truth to power, nothing is a given. Unlike the mere six months covered by the first film, the sequel spans several years and covers major events, from continuing Russian aggression to the killing of opposition leader Alexei Navalny. Loktev’s scattered cast ends up experiencing these global shockwaves firsthand, reporting on everything from political poisonings to mass civilian graves — in person if they can, or remotely, with the help of anonymous sources. Some move or return to Kyiv. Others make their way further west, like to the United States, where they observe an uncanny authoritarianism taking hold. The film’s chilling tapestry is interwoven with its subjects’ gallows humor. As their challenges mount, sometimes all they can do is laugh at the absurdity, though at least they’re laughing together. However, enough time is spent with them as individuals that their bleak loneliness starts to bleed through the screen. Twentysomething Ksenia Mironova finds ways to move forward in her career, though her fiancé remains a state prisoner. The older Anna Nemzer (the film’s co-director) grows more frayed, as each emigration means having to uproot her adolescent daughter. TV RAIN anchors like Valeria Ratnikova face both scrutiny and legal threats, while for those still reporting from (or escaping) Ukrainian war zones, the dangers are more pressing. Even as they move between borders, bullseyes remain painted on their backs — though they each maintain that the people whose stories they tell have it infinitely worse. One has to wonder if Loktev feels the same about her subjects. A one-woman team who remains mostly unseen, she finds herself hopping between cities for years on end, similarly sacrificing peace of mind to bring vital narratives to light. Whether or not she could have hired an additional crew or second unit, the effect of her solo flight is an emotional proximity to her subjects, who trust her enough to let their guard down in front of her smartphone. Her camera app seems to run day and night, but she and Taylor make judicious selections. While Part I felt more straightforward in its unfurling, Part II appears to condense time even more deftly, jump-cutting within and between exchanges without ever losing momentum or conversational clarity. Loktev and her undesirable friends ought not to be boxed in — their work is too expansive and important. But there’s also a noticeably feminine intimacy to several scenes here, whether the subjects discuss clothing as they wrap up their lives yet again, or present themselves casually, freely and without artifice, as though the camera were merely recording for a private Instagram, or absent altogether. The film is born from journalistic ideology, but most of its subjects are women, and it takes aesthetic shape through the lens of female friendship and professional community, fanning outward from this personal place until it shades the political with remarkably familiar hues. As the sands shift beneath their feet, the subjects are practically the only constant in each other’s lives — as is Loktev, who’s there to capture them at their best and worst. Rare are the films that remain so transfixed by the conundrums inherent to living in a murky world, or that pursue the emotional and psychological dimensions of political journalism with such disarming simplicity. Let it be a warning of things to come, or a comfort once they inevitably do. There’s no untangling the two anymore. Not for people who’ve dedicated their lives to sounding the alarm, even as they wonder if they might be too late. ‘My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile’ Review: An Enormous, Riveting Documentary Sequel Following Reporters on the Run Reviewed online, Sept. 1, 2026. In Venice Film Festival (Out of Competition). Running time: 355 MIN. Production: (Documentary) A Marminchilla production. (World sales: Cinetic, New York City.) Producer: Julia Loktev. Crew: Director, camera: Julia Loktev. Editors: Loktev, Michael Taylor. Music: Sami Buccella. With: Anna Nemzer, Valeria Ratnikova, Ksenia Mironova, Elena Kostyucheko, Yana Kuchina, Irina Dolinina, Alesya Marokhovskaya, Peter Ruzavin, Nataliya Gumenyuk, Sonya Groysman. articles.full_text: Sep 4, 2026 3:02am PT Bendita Film Sales Snags Norma Vila’s Sitges Competition Title ‘Carapace’ (EXCLUSIVE) Starring Nagore Aranburu ('Querer,' 'Sundays'), the psychological thriller centers on a mother gripped by uncontrollable despair when her teenage daughter decides to leave home to study By Ed Meza Plus Icon Ed Meza @edmezavar Latest Bendita Film Sales Snags Norma Vila’s Sitges Competition Title ‘Carapace’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago France TV Distribution’s Mystery Drama ‘Our Missing Sons’ Set for Unifrance Rendez-Vous Market Debut 1 day ago Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit ‘Congo Boy’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All 'Carapace' Courtesy of Bendita Film Sales Bendita Film Sales has acquired international rights to Norma Vila ’s psychological horror thriller “Salitre” (“Carapace”) ahead of its premiere at the Sitges Film Festival ’s Fantàstic In-Competition Selection. Vila’s debut feature stars Nagore Aranburu, star of Series Mania top laureate “Querer” and winner of this year’s supporting actress Goya Award for “Sundays,” and Haizea Carneros (“ Sacamantecas ”) as a mother and daughter whose relationship grows increasingly tense. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast In “Salitre,” when her teenage daughter Nerea decides to leave home to study, Maite is gripped by despair. For Maite, her daughter’s departure is more than a separation: it threatens to destroy the world she has built with her. Popular on Variety As Nerea prepares to leave, Maite’s fear begins to contaminate everything. Something seems to spread throughout the house, seeping into the intimacy they share and giving shape to what Maite cannot put into words. Courtesy of Bendita Film Sales Soon, Maite cuts herself off from the world and becomes obsessed with keeping her daughter at home, turning care into control and love into possession. As her obsession threatens to destroy what she loves most, Maite must confront the monster that has awakened within her: let her daughter go, or hold on to her and lose her forever. While “Carapace” may be Vila’s first feature, the director has impressed with her acclaimed previous works, winning twice the Syfy Award for best Spanish short at the San Sebastián Horror and Fantasy Film Festival: in 2016 for “Jules D.” and in 2019 for “El fin de todas las cosas.” “What drew us to ‘Carapace’ is the way Norma Vila lets the horror take hold of something painfully recognizable: a mother who cannot bear to see her daughter leave,” explained Luis Renart, head of Bendita Film Sales. “Something you can’t quite name creeps into the closeness between them and starts to spread, but the film never stops being about two people who love each other. It’s exactly the kind of genre cinema we love: singular, uncompromising, and made by a filmmaker with a voice of her own. We’re taking it to Sitges expecting genre audiences to embrace it, and we don’t think they’ll be the only ones.” A largely Basque production, “Carapace” is produced by Bilbao-based Ipuin Kontalaria and Euskadi Movie along with Pris&Batty Films, Bondi Stories and Festival Films in association with broadcasters EITB and RTVE. “We’re thrilled to partner with Bendita Film Sales, whose passion and international reach make them the ideal team to bring ‘Carapace’ to audiences worldwide,” added producer Eduardo Carneros of Euskadi Movie. “We’re especially excited to launch the film with its world premiere at Sitges and hope this will be the beginning of a strong international journey for a film we believe is both distinctive and deeply cinematic.” Shot on location in the northern region of Biskaia and neighboring Cantabria, the €2.5 million ($2.9 million) production was supported by the Basque government, the Bizkaia Tax Incentive and Comunidad de Madrid. The Sitges Film Festival runs Oct. 8-18. articles.title: Maggie Gyllenhaal Says She Tried Using AI to Turn Dakota Johnson Into Marilyn Monroe for Short ‘Flesh Impact’ — Then Scrapped It: ‘Fundamentally Did Not Work’
articles.full_text: Sep 4, 2026 3:02am PT Maggie Gyllenhaal Says She Tried Using AI to Turn Dakota Johnson Into Marilyn Monroe for Short ‘Flesh Impact’ — Then Scrapped It: ‘Fundamentally Did Not Work’ By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest George Clooney Says the Government Shouldn’t Regulate AI: ‘These Are Not the People You Want to Entrust the Holy Grail With’ 1 hour ago Maggie Gyllenhaal Says She Tried Using AI to Turn Dakota Johnson Into Marilyn Monroe for Short ‘Flesh Impact’ — Then Scrapped It: ‘Fundamentally Did Not Work’ 3 hours ago ‘Jupiter’ Director Alexandre Smia on Making a Nuclear Thriller That Suddenly Feels Terrifyingly Real: ‘We’ve Entered the Third Nuclear Age’ 8 hours ago See All Getty Images Venice jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal revealed that she experimented with artificial intelligence to transform Dakota Johnson into Marilyn Monroe for her short film “Flesh Impact” which plays on the Lido. But she ended up scrapping it because she felt that it stripped Johnson’s performance of the very humanity that made it compelling. Speaking at the symposium alongside composer Alexandre Desplat, filmmakers Lee Daniels and Shannon Murphy, producer Lorenzo Mieli and artist Marc Quinn, Gyllenhaal said the short portrays a 100-year-old Marilyn Monroe with flashbacks to Marilyn Monroe when she’s in her 30s which Johnson plays. Related Stories 'One Piece' Season 3 Casts Its Koza, Toto, Pell and Chaka Lee Jung-eun, Kim Moo-yul Board Netflix's Action-Noir Series 'The Shooter' “And the people who commissioned this project from me asked me to use AI. And I thought — I mean, they weren’t using OpenAI, they were using licensable AI, training it off of Marilyn Monroe films that we had licensed. And I went for it. I was like, all right, I’m curious, I don’t know, let’s see,” she says. Popular on Variety “The idea was that we trained it on her, we then put her face on Dakota’s face. We worked hard at it, and in the end, I threw it away because what was coming through Dakota playing Marilyn Monroe was so much more moving, human, alive,” she revealed during the symposium which was presented by Finch & Partners and CAA. “It fundamentally did not work. All the reasons we decided to make this project to begin with were, were, were, were killed off in the AI version,” she continued. Besides the creative shortcomings of AI, she stressed there’s also talked about the “huge environmental issues” it raises. “In America anyway, there’s a big conversation in South Memphis about the data centers. That’s a problem, so we should acknowledge that.” She also pointed that even Geoffrey Hinton, the pioneering computer scientist often referred to as the “Godfather of AI,” is “ringing bells of alarm.” “He said that he thought that we should program AI with a maternal instinct,” she said. “Because what other model is there of a less intelligent creature kind of controlling a more intelligent creature than a baby and its mother?” “I was like, first of all, so fascinating, but what does that mean to program AI with a maternal instinct coming from the godfather — that’s what he’s called — of AI?” On the financial standpoint, she said found the whole “democratization” argument that AI is supposed to provide to filmmakers unconvincing because it comes from people who are behind these AI softwares. “It concerns me a little bit because they own it. Who’s making the money off it? The people that are pitching that,” she joked, drawing an applause from the crowd. Ultimately, filmmakers and talent might lose out if AI starts being used more frequently to make commercial movies. She recalled being told that soon enough, “$40 million will now be able to cost $4 million if you do it with AI… and maybe even eventually $40,000 — which is what you were talking about in terms of democratizing or opening opportunities to people who wouldn’t otherwise have them.” “But the thing is, is if you can make a commercial good enough movie for $40,000 or even for $4 million, who’s gonna give you $10 million to do it the old way? Nobody. I mean, maybe there’s a tiny, tiny little market for that. But, you know, that concerns me.” ‘You Don’t Belong Here’ Review: A Potentially Involving Story Is Weakened by Airless Dialogue and a Misguided Finale ‘Brave New Love’ Review: Infidelity Isn’t the End in an Unusual, Open-Minded Marital Drama Aymar Esse, Director of Locarno Open Doors World Premiere ‘My Father’s Kora,’ Explores Questions of Identity, Memory and Faith in Senegal ‘Far From the Trees’ Review: A Richly Contemplative Journey of Physical and Mental Meanderings, Beautifully Combining 4K Digital with Super 16 Thomas Heise’s Final Documentary ‘Übergang,’ a Potential Locarno Highlight, Reflects on Time and Transience ‘Our Time Will Come’ Review: Two Orphans Journey to Accra to Find Their Kin in an Emotionally Absorbing Ghanaian Drama Loading comments... articles.title: ‘Spider-Man’ and ‘The Odyssey’ Propel U.K. Box Office to Best August Since 2018
articles.full_text: Sep 4, 2026 4:24am PT ‘Spider-Man’ and ‘The Odyssey’ Propel U.K. Box Office to Best August Since 2018 By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest ‘Spider-Man’ and ‘The Odyssey’ Propel U.K. Box Office to Best August Since 2018 2 hours ago Magdalena Koleśnik and Kay Greidanus to Lead Finn Szumlas’ Debut Feature ‘Stairway to Earth’ as Production Starts (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Oasis Documentary Directors on Filming the Brothers’ First Reunion in 15 Years and Why There Wasn’t Much Emotion in the Room: ‘It’s the Gallaghers, It’s Not ‘Dawson’s Creek” 7 hours ago See All Everett Collection The U.K. may have just had the hottest August since records began but, in more positive news, it also had the hottest August at the box office in almost a decade. Thanks to the incredible performances of both “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “ The Odyssey ” a total of $161.3 million was earned at the box office that month, according to new figures from Rentrak, the highest since 2018’s record-breaking August with $201.7 million. Related Stories 'Emily in Paris' Season 6 First Look Shows a Glamorous Greek Adventure as Netflix Sets Christmas Release 'One Piece' Season 3 Casts Its Koza, Toto, Pell and Chaka Of course, three recent years were hit by the pandemic and its impact on production, with 2020’s August sitting at a paltry $22 million, 2021’s at $87.9 million and 2022’s at $85.4 million. But as the world burned outside, this year’s bumper summer was clearly a major relief for cinemas and the industry at large as it still looks to recover following recent seismic shifts. Popular on Variety (Comscore’s official numbers do state that 2024’s August reached $163.1 million and 2019’s $167.9, those were counted as five-week periods as the company’s months run from the first Friday to the last.) “The Odyssey,” which released July 17, ended August with U.K. earnings of $108.6 million, easily Christopher Nolan’s most successful film on home soil by some margin and still number 2 in the box office after seven weeks. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” meanwhile, released on July 29 and, five weeks on, still sits atop the box office with total earnings of $126.8 million. It’ll likely top “Spider-Man: No Way Home” ($131. 7 million) as the highest-earning Marvel film in the U.K. by the end of September. Of course, the U.K. hasn’t been the only market to benefit from the colossal earnings of the two biggest films of the year so far. Even after just a few weeks in the box office, on Aug 10 they had helped the U.S. hit the summer milestone of $4 billion domestically for only the second time in the post-pandemic era. articles.title: George Clooney Says the Government Shouldn’t Regulate AI: ‘These Are Not the People You Want to Entrust the Holy Grail With’
articles.full_text: Sep 4, 2026 5:09am PT George Clooney Says the Government Shouldn’t Regulate AI: ‘These Are Not the People You Want to Entrust the Holy Grail With’ By Elsa Keslassy , K.J. Yossman Getty George Clooney has said he doesn’t trust the government to regulate AI. “I don’t know that you want government to be regulating this either, because I sit and watch when Zuckerberg is testifying in front of, you know, a 94-year-old Chuck Grassley, and they’re like, ‘Well, how do you turn that computer on?’” he joked, before adding, “These are not the people that you want to entrust the holy grail with.” Related Stories ‘The Gentlemen’ Officially Renewed for Season 3 as First Season 2 Trailer Drops: ‘I’m Looking Forward to Pushing the Boundaries Further,’ Guy Ritchie Says (EXCLUSIVE) 'Emomee,' Indian Kids Life-Skills Series, Lands on Netflix (EXCLUSIVE) Clooney, who was speaking at a Venice Film Festival symposium hosted by CAA and Finch & Partners, joined the panel on the future of creativity alongside diverse figures including artist Kennedy Yanko, filmmaker Giuseppe Tornator, clergyman Cardinal José Tolentino de Mendonça and National Gallery of Art president Darren Walker. Popular on Variety The actor said AI was dangerous because it could make people doubt about real things, as well as invent things that don’t exist. “It’s not just that you’ll see lies,” he said. “It also makes you question things that really do exist. It also that sort of world of fake news — suddenly you’re able to take things that really happened and say, ‘Well, that didn’t happen either.” “You’ll have people who deny the Holocaust, and that will have the same weight in AI as facts.” Clooney also talked about how his wife Amal Clooney, a prominent human rights lawyer, has come across laws that were invented by AI. They “will hallucinate and make up fake cases, and lawyers who don’t check it will quote those cases, or judges will quote those cases,” he warned. “I think that’s some of the danger in all of this, is that we’re looking at something going, ‘We’re not sure where this is going to end, and we’re not sure who’s fully in charge,” he said, adding that these AI tools are owned by “richest people in the world.” The risks presented by deep fakes could also lead to real-life consequences aside from disinformation. “That’s a joke for people, but what happens when you see a video of Putin saying he’s launched the first nuclear strike in the United States? And how do you discern it?” Talking about his hopes for the next presidential election and for potential candidates, Clooney said, “We’re all very excited by this young senator from Georgia named Jon Ossoff. We’re all excited about Jimmy [J.B.] Pritzker. I’m from Kentucky, I like Andy Beshear as a governor.” “We need young voices in there that are coming up with some new ideas and some new thoughts,” he added. Clooney also stressed the “need to have a check and balance — We’re not supposed to agree. That’s the whole idea of democracy.” Miley Cyrus Drops Last Name, Prompting Dad Billy Ray to Publicly Defend the Change: ‘Family Means More Than Ever Now’ Miley Cyrus Leads a Steamy Dance Floor Revolution With New Single and Video for ‘Bass Persuades’ Miley Cyrus Honors Godmother Dolly Parton: ‘I Have an Angel by My Side. articles.title: Iranian Director Mohsen Gharaei, in Venice With ‘Falling House,’ Set to Shoot ‘Centrifugal Force’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 4, 2026 5:43am PT Iranian Director Mohsen Gharaei, in Venice With ‘Falling House,’ Set to Shoot ‘Centrifugal Force’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Iranian Director Mohsen Gharaei, in Venice With ‘Falling House,’ Set to Shoot ‘Centrifugal Force’ (EXCLUSIVE) 30 minutes ago Anna Foglietta on Working With Alba Rohrwacher on Venice Drama ‘A Common Story’ ‘You Have to Have the Guts to Show Yourself Exactly as You Are’ — Trailer (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Venice Market Chief Pascal Diot Says He’s Not Affected by New Toronto Market: ‘Not What the Industry Wants Now’ 8 hours ago See All Courtesy Seven Springs Pictures Iranian director Mohsen Gharaei, who is at the Venice Film Festival with well-received drama “Falling House,” is set to shoot a new film titled “Centrifugal Force” that will capture “the impossible choices facing a generation of Iranians today,” as the synopsis puts it. “Falling House,” which world-premiered on Wed. in Venice’s Orizzonti sidebar, follows a modest family on the outskirts of Tehran who faces the imminent destruction of their home as part of a vast redevelopment project. Rashid, the patriarchal father and a prison guard, attempts to contain family rebellion while being accused of corruption. Related Stories Jessica Simpson Doc Set at Netflix From ‘Robbie Williams’ Director Joe Pearlman (EXCLUSIVE) 'Scooby-Doo' Netflix Series Casts Andre Benjamin, Cathy Moriarty “Centrifugal Force,” which will be shot in an undisclosed location outside Iran in Farsi and English with still unspecified Iranian and international actors, will be “a deeply human story about what happens when the home you love is no longer a place you can return to,” Gharaei said in his directors’ statement. Popular on Variety “After finishing my latest film, I found myself on an unexpected journey from one geography to another,” Gharaei, who is now living as an exile outside Iran, added. “But migration is not simply a matter of moving from one place to another; it is a moment when a person is suddenly pushed out of the center of their own life. The journey becomes most painful when departure is not a choice, when all familiar paths close, one by one, and suddenly you have to leave a home that you still love.” “Centrifugal Force” will be the story of a family that has remained in Iran for years, not entirely out of contentment, but out of the hope that somehow it might still be possible to build a life with all its contradictions. They have held onto staying and created a sense of order for themselves within a system they believed to be stable. But in a geography like Iran, where the line between simply surviving and truly living can shift without notice, no sense of order is ever completely safe,” Gharaei went on to note. “With forced migration, the family enters a world governed by a different set of rules, where things no longer work as they used to. What appears from the outside to be a form of escape can, from within, feel like a kind of collapse. Distance from home makes the distance between family members visible. It reopens old wounds. Crisis challenges the image they have of one another. It is as if migration does not only change their physical location; it also displaces their understanding of home, family, and even self,” he continued. “This is where centrifugal force takes shape, drawing people away from a point to which they have been deeply attached, without necessarily knowing what lies ahead. Within this deracination, the family is as weightless as hay, easily pulled away from the center. And the further they move from it, the more they are confronted with the question of what truly connected them in the first place: geography, memory, habit, or something else for which they have no name.” Just like “Falling House,” “Centrifugal Force” is being produced by Iranian producer Milad Khosravi through his Seven Springs Pictures company in tandem with Oscar-winning producer Odessa Rae (“Navalny,” “The Voice of Hind Rajab”). articles.title: ‘Coming Of Age’: First Look At Josh Appignanesi’s Upcoming Comedy About “The Power Of Aging”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Amelia Dimoldenberg’s Hit YouTube Series ‘Chicken Shop Date’ To End After 12-Year Run ‘Art Sex Music’: First Look At Caroline Catz’s Doc About British Artist & Musician Cosey Fanni Tutti ‘Bunker’: Watch Javier Bardem & Penélope Cruz In Florian Zeller’s Venice-Bound Psychological Thriller View All September 3, 2026 11:28pm 'Coming of Age' Rob Baker Ashton EXCLUSIVE : Here’s a first look at writer-director Josh Appignanesi ’s seventh feature Coming of Age , which he co-wrote with longtime collaborator Devorah Baum . The film, which is told across 30 years of car rides through a fast-changing London, is described as a “heartfelt comedy about the power of aging”. It follows a couple navigating love, parenthood, midlife crises and aging parents, only to discover that getting older might just be the best part. The film stars Emun Elliott ( The Dark , The Gold ) as Jay and Lydia Wilson ( The Maids , Alice and Steve ) as Hannah, the couple at the heart of the story. Further cast include Peter Polycarpou ( The Brutalist , House of Dragon ) and Tristan Ruggeri ( The Twin , The Witcher ). Related Stories News RTE's 'The Murder Of Mr. Moonlight' To Explore Infamous Irish Killing; BBC & Banijay Rights On Board Drama Series Legal 'Criminal' Boss Ed Brubaker Accused Of Sexual & Racial Harassment; Amazon, MGM Also Named As Defendants In Complaint From Ex-PA Appignanesi ( Song of Songs ) and Baum’s script was inspired by research program ‘The Sciences of Aging and the Culture of Youth Project’, a program hosted at King’s College London which explores the concept of aging. The film, which was shot almost entirely on real roads, is produced by Emily Everdee for Lifelong Films, with Sam Buckler co-producing. Martina Zimmerman of SAACY is exec producer. It’s funded by UK Research and Innovation as part of SAACY. Watch on Deadline “Age is something we’re always faced with but can’t often bear to face,” said Appignanesi. “It makes fools of us, yet by the same token, deepens us. What would it look like to have the whole tragicomedy of a life reflected back to us in one arc? Might we walk away with something that helped us age a little better?” Baum added: “Coming-of-age stories tend to be about the journey from childhood into adolescence, while romantic comedies often end just as young people arrive at the altar. But what about the bit of life that comes afterwards? For most of us, that’s rather a lot of life. It’s also in midlife that age can start to feel impossible to ignore, in our bodies, our relationships, our sense of future possibilities…With Coming of Age , we wanted to move the happy ever after a little further down the road – to a point in life when audiences are less used to seeing it.” ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Sticks Lido Landing; Jack Huston & Lorenzo Mieli Interviews; More Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom, Paramount Exec Was 55 Fox Orders Comedy Series ‘Mammoth’ From ‘Modern Family’ Duo Based On UK Format Maria Bartiromo Pink-Slipped From Fox After 12 Years: “Effective Today” Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Louis Partridge & Anson Boon Set For British Coming-Of-Age Film ‘Andy & Orson’; MetFilm Launches Sales For TIFF Market
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Ron Perlman, Peter Facinelli & Mark Elias Starring In Indie Film ‘We Could Be Heroes’ Louis Partridge & Anson Boon Set For British Coming-Of-Age Film ‘Andy & Orson’; MetFilm Launches Sales For TIFF Market George Clooney Reveals The Rule He Tries To Live By, The Uncertain Path To Acting Success & His Next Movie — Venice Masterclass View All September 4, 2026 1:00am Louis Partridge and Anson Boon Keith Kandell/Getty EXCLUSIVE : Louis Partridge ( Enola Holmes ) and Anson Boon ( MobLand ) are set to star in Andy & Orson , the feature directorial debut of writer-directors Nathan Newman and Arnold T. Rice. MetFilm Sales is launching the project for worldwide sales ahead of the TIFF market with filming due to take place in the U.K. in early Q4, 2026. Brit actors Partridge and Boon will play the titular Andy and Orson, respectively, “two mismatched housemates whose friendship is tested over the course of a year as they navigate first heartbreaks, shifting ambitions and the messy realities of life in their twenties.” Related Stories News Aaron Eckhart, Brenton Thwaites & Bella Samman Leading Post-Apocalyptic Action Thriller 'Out Of The Ashes' -- TIFF Market News Josh Duhamel To Star In 'Speak' From Lorenzo Di Bonaventura & Joe Carnahan; Twenty-Nine Palms & CAA Media Finance Launching Sales At TIFF Set between South-East London and the British countryside, the film is described as “a contemporary story of friendship, love and growing up in the 2020s”. Watch on Deadline The film is produced by Jamie Clark and Aleksandra Bilić for My Accomplice, Dorottya Székely for Varga Pictures, and Carley Armstrong for True Moon Pictures. Executive producers are Newman and T. Rice through Tidewayout, Louis Partridge and Anson Boon, as well as Leopold Hughes ( Knives Out ). The movie is fully financed via the production companies and private investors and was developed by My Accomplice. Nathan Newman is the author of How to Leave the House , which was named a New Yorker Best Book of the Year, and which they later adapted for TV. Their second novel will be published next year. Arnold T. Rice is a social worker and independent filmmaker who frequently collaborates with UK comedians on viral sketches and stand-up specials. ‘’ Andy & Orson is about the highs and lows of being 20-somethings in the 2020s, written very deliberately throughout our own twenties in order to capture the shifts in ourselves and the decade. Like all great odd couples, we hope audiences see parts of themselves in both Andy and Orson when they hangout with them in theatres very soon,’’ said Newman and T. Rice. ‘’ Andy & Orson spoke to us in the rich tradition of odd couple, slacker films such as Clerks and Withnail and I. There is such a sharp contemporary edge to the script from Nathan and Arnold that will really connect with this generation of film fans. It’s testament to the script that we have talent such as Louis and Anson on board as leads,’’ added Jamie Clark, producer. Casting is currently underway for additional roles with the search led by casting director Claire Curry. Emmy-nominated cinematographer, Bart Sienkiewicz, is attached, along with costume designer Giulia Scrimieri, production designer Isabel Pirillo and hair and makeup designer Ziggy Gaji. Louis Partridge is represented by Independent Talent Group and WME.
