articles.title: Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom & Paramount International Boss Was 55
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse International Insider: Ciao, Venice; ‘Bake Off’ Battle Heats Up; Leslie Odom Jr. Chat Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom & Paramount International Boss Was 55 RTE’s ‘The Murder Of Mr. Moonlight’ To Explore Infamous Irish Killing; BBC & Banijay Rights On Board Drama Series View All September 4, 2026 1:25am Raffaelle Annecchino Blue Ocean Media Partners Raffaele Annecchino , the former international chief at Paramount and its predecessor Viacom, has died aged 55 from acute meningitis. The Italian executive, known for his negotiating skills and business acumen, passed away suddenly over the weekend while in the Balearic Islands, according to his personal office. The former President and CEO of Paramount International, Networks, Streaming and Studio, was a key figure in the rollouts of BET, MTV and Nickelodeon, and oversaw networks such as 5 in the UK and Ten in Australia. He is credited playing a major part in Paramount+’s international rollout, as well aiding the helping grow European SVoD SkyShowtime and free streamer Pluto TV. He was also on the boards Viacom 18 in India and SBS Media in South Korea. Related Stories News Gloria Steinem Dies: Feminist Icon And Activist & Co-Founder Of Ms. Magazine Was 92 News Jean-Paul Rappeneau Dies: 'Cyrano de Bergerac' Director Was 94 In total, Annecchino spent more than 25 years at Paramount/Viacom. He had originally joined the Madrid office in a commercial role and rose through the ranks. Further back, he worked at Warner Bros. Discovery predecessor Turner Broadcasting System for the likes of Cartoon Network and CNN. Watch on Deadline After leaving Paramount in 2022, he founded his own global media consultancy, Blue Ocean Media Partners, which he ran as President and CEO, with offices in Madrid and Dubai. Just this year, he joined Mediapro Middle East to provide strategic advice and support. “Raffaele Annecchino was much more than a boss to me,” wrote Blue Ocean partner Joana Carrion Boulos on LinkedIn. “He was one of those rare people who knew how to lead without making you feel that you were being led. He trusted the people he worked with, gave them space, listened to their ideas and, above all, made them feel valued.” “Such sad news,” wrote former Paramount President and CEO Bob Bakish, who worked closely with Annecchino for years, on social media. Raffa was a force of nature. Taken way too young. He will be missed by many. May he rest in peace.” Further tributes came from the likes of former Paramount exec Michael Armstrong, JioHotstar’s Amit Malhotra and Michelle Alberti. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Sticks Lido Landing; Jack Huston & Lorenzo Mieli Interviews; More Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom, Paramount Exec Was 55 Fox Orders Comedy Series ‘Mammoth’ From ‘Modern Family’ Duo Based On UK Format Maria Bartiromo Pink-Slipped From Fox After 12 Years: “Effective Today” Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc ‘Be Brave’: “We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us” – Venice
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings” Tony Gatlif Dies: ‘Gadjo Dilo’ Director Whose Work Celebrated Roma Culture Was 77 Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc ‘Be Brave’: “We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us” – Venice View All September 4, 2026 1:27am Mario Gianani and Lorenzo Mieli at the premiere for Nessun Dolore at the Venice Film Festival, September 3, 2026 Getty Images Italian producer Lorenzo Mieli is one of the speakers at the CAA and Finch & Partners The Future of… Creativity forum unfolding today on the fringes of the Venice Film Festival. The symposium at the La Scuola Grande di Santa Maria della Misericordia, also featuring George Clooney, Venice Artistic Director Alberto Barbera and jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal as guest speakers, will explore the future of storytelling in the age of AI . Venice regular Mieli is well placed to make a meaningful contribution to the discussion as the producer of Be Brave , the first ever documentary made with AI to screen in Venice’s official selection. Related Stories Festivals George Clooney Reveals The Rule He Tries To Live By, The Uncertain Path To Acting Success & His Next Movie -- Venice Masterclass Festivals 'Wild Horse Nine' Gets Rapturous 14-Minute Standing Ovation At Venice World Premiere The film appears to be a classic bio-doc in which director Francesco Carrozzini attempts to pin down Renzo Rosso for a portrait of his audacious career as the founder of the Diesel brand and the OTB Group – Only The Brave fashion empire, which also includes the Jil Sander, Maison Margiela, Marni and Viktor&Rolf labels. But all is not what it seems. Interviews with the likes of former Vogue Editor-in-Chief Anna Wintour; fashion designers John Galliano, Johan Lindeberg and Glenn Martens; communications guru Maurizio Marchiori, and Adriano Goldschmied, the so-called “Godfather of denim” and Rosso’s first partner on Diesel, among others, are real, even if the backdrops have sometimes been retouched. But Rosso’s interventions across the documentary are generated purely by AI as is most the “archive” material showing snapshots of his childhood, youth and early career achievements. Carrozzini, whose pursuit to track down Rosso for a face-to-face interview is interwoven into the storyline, is also AI-generated even though he exists in real life. Mieli spearheaded the project, with Mario Gianani , his partner at joint Rome-Based production house Our Films , and its COO, Gabriele Immirzi, also on board as producers. The producer’s embrace of AI may seem surprising given his past work at the forefront of human creativity, with his more than 100 credits including Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , Paolo Sorrentino’s The Hand of God , Luca Guadagnino’s Queer and Sofia Coppola’s Priscilla to name but a few. But it is very much in keeping with Mieli’s pioneering track-record across his career, overseeing the growth of the The X-Factor format in Italy in the 2010s as the CEO of Fremantle Italia, or helping to usher in the Italian high-end drama boom with the groundbreaking 2015 HBO deal for Paolo Sorrentino’s The Young Pope , which led to partnerships on Saverio Costanzo’s My Brilliant Friend and Guadagnino’s We Are Who We Are . Be Brave is one of two documentaries being launched on the festival circuit by Our Films this fall alongside t he late Eleanor Coppola’s Making Marie Antoinette , which has just been announced for Telluride and then heads to the New York Film Festival. Watch on Deadline Be Brave Our Films Mieli and Gianani are also at the festival as producers on Gianni Amelio’s Out of Competition title Nessun Dolore about a Rome bookseller who finds himself on the wrong side of the law after he welcomes undocumented migrants into his home. Talking to Deadline, ahead of the Be Brave premiere Out of Competition in Venice next week, Mieli says Our Films’ exploration of AI is a natural progression. “Directors and their artistic vision are at the heart of what we do,” says Mieli. “They are the reason we keep doing this incredibly challenging job: supporting and working with directors we love, discovering new ones to love, and creating films, TV series, and documentaries, all the while striving to make something beautiful and fresh, and setting a new challenge for ourselves in the process.” “That’s the first point, and I want to frame it right away by saying we didn’t just ‘choose’ AI; rather, Francesco Carrozzini, the documentary’s director, and I decided to work with AI and challenge ourselves to truly understand what it is, to grasp the nature of this tool everyone is talking about. A tool that is so divisive, so fascinating, yet also so frightening.” Mieli adds that the decision to work with AI for the documentary also stemmed from the fact that there was very little archive material capturing Rosso’s life and career behind the scenes. Another consideration was that other companies and directors were pitching Rosso with documentary ideas and time was of the essence. “There was a lack of material that felt truly significant, authentic, vital, or compelling, beyond the usual official footage,” says Mieli. “We reviewed what was already out there and found the existing material to be very cold, mostly official interviews and promotional content. “Then, looking at the AI ​​developments emerging at the time, it struck us that AI might be the tool to recreate ‘real’ material, capturing the genuine truths we wanted to convey, while simultaneously being entirely artificial and fabricated, created using this new technology to tell the story.” Beyond the practical reasons, Mieli and Carrozzini felt the experimentation with AI as a filmmaking tool would also chime with “the two main pillars” of Rosso’s career. “Renzo Rosso has always focused on two main areas: creative freedom and innovation, he is always experimenting with new things and has a constant eye on the future; in fact, he has an obsession with the future,” says Mieli. “Everyone who has even interviewed him describes how he constantly challenges you, pushes you to look beyond what you already know, what you see, and the status quo; he urges you to imagine how people will dress tomorrow and to envision things you have never seen before.” While the decision to put AI at the heart of the documentary’s production made sense on a practical and philosophical level, Mieli recounts it was easier said than done. “The technological tool we used became both the form and the content of the documentary. That’s what led us to build the fictional narrative woven into the documentary, to show how it aligns with Renzo’s challenge of ‘Don’t be afraid’. And this was despite the fact that, when we started working on it, we didn’t really know AI; we didn’t know what we could or couldn’t achieve, how it would progress, what the risks were, or what worked and what didn’t,” he says. “Ultimately, we found ourselves grappling with AI, because it’s a tool that offers incredible possibilities but also has significant downsides, things that don’t work, aren’t interesting, or are limiting.” Our Films spent more than a year and a half developing its own AI model that would enable Carrozzini to make his film. “We worked hard and created our own model—essentially a proprietary system built on our own extensive libraries and assets that we fully owned: Francesco’s images, his photos, and videos of him speaking,” says Mieli. Mieli and Carrozzini were joined on the project by writers Michele Abatantuono and Lara Prando, and AI creative director Roberto Beragnoli, Senior Creative Producer Marco Pianigiani and Director of Photography Matteo Vieille. Editing was by Rocco Bernini and Nicole Pagin, with music by Ralf Hildenbeutel. Beragnoli oversaw the development of the tailored AI model, working with Italian company Blackstone, which has a track record in visual effects and applying AI systems to audiovisual production, while Pianigiani is credited with shaping the film’s narrative architecture and rhythm, in collaboration with the writers, AI artists and editorial team. According to detailed production notes, the model drew on established feature-film VFX pipelines, adapted to the specific demands of AI generation, and rather than revolving around individual prompts, the process began with the screenplay. The image pipeline combined Nano Banana 2, Flux 2 Pro, GPT Image 2 and Adobe Photoshop (Firefly) to generate original imagery; while video generation drew on Seedance 2, Seedance 2.5, Kling 3, Sora 2 Pro and Veo 3.1, with the model selected shot by shot according to the demands of each sequence. The entire audio component was developed through an ElevenLabs-based pipeline for voice synthesis and AI-assisted sound processing. Mieli describes the whole process as “fun” but serious and arduous as well. He stresses the lengths the production went to ensure an ethical approach in terms of the original elements used to generate the imagery and audio in the film. “It’s fun to play with, but it’s not really just a game; it has to be taken very seriously. We need to learn it, understand it, use it, change it, and master it, rather than letting AI master us,” he says. “We’ve actually worked toward an AI that aligns with what artists want, specifically ownership and creative control, rather than just focusing on rights and image ownership; essentially, all the issues people are rightly fighting for regarding AI.” As discussions get underway in Venice on the impact of AI on storytelling, Mieli says the film and TV world needs to take the bull by the horns. “The responsibility lies with us, the community of producers and directors, to study and understand it, and to see if we can build an AI that is fair and fosters a balanced relationship. But first and foremost, we need the curiosity to get to know it; you can’t talk about it without studying it.” ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Sticks Lido Landing; Jack Huston & Lorenzo Mieli Interviews; More Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom, Paramount Exec Was 55 Fox Orders Comedy Series ‘Mammoth’ From ‘Modern Family’ Duo Based On UK Format Maria Bartiromo Pink-Slipped From Fox After 12 Years: “Effective Today” Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Jack Huston On The Tough Questions About Sexual Abuse Posed By Paul Schrader’s Film ‘The Basics Of Philosophy’: “It’s Almost Become A Taboo Subject” – Venice Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews ‘Bucking Fastard’ Review: Werner Herzog’s Eccentric Comedy Is A Bittersweet Tale Of Unrequited Lovers – Venice Film Festival ‘The Girl With The Leica’ Review: Love Is War In Alina Marazzi’s Unconventional Biopic Of A Pioneering War Photographer – Venice Film Festival View All September 4, 2026 2:03am ‘The Basics Of Philosophy’ Paul Schrader writes great parts for great actors, and has been doing so for 50 years, since Robert De Niro played Travis Bickle in Martin Scorsese ’s Taxi Driver . Since then, to name but a few, he’s given us William Devane in Rolling Thunder , Richard Gere in American Gigolo , Willem Dafoe in Light Sleeper , Nick Nolte in Affliction and Ethan Hawke in First Reformed . Way before toxic masculinity was ever diagnosed, Schrader was rooting around in the psyches of men who, for one reason or another, just didn’t feel safe in their own skin anymore. We can now add to that list The Basics of Philosophy , a tight, literate psychological drama that clocks in at a highly economical 94 minutes and yet somehow tackles one of the greatest existential questions of all time: Is it really possible to escape the past? In The Card Counter , we saw a war criminal trying to distance himself from his involvement in the atrocities of Abu Ghraib, and in Master Gardener we met a Nazi-tattooed former white supremacist trying to start a new life in a witness protection scheme. Related Stories News Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc 'Be Brave': "We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us" - Venice Festivals George Clooney Reveals The Rule He Tries To Live By, The Uncertain Path To Acting Success & His Next Movie -- Venice Masterclass The Basics of Philosophy , however, might be the most perfect distillation of his themes so far. The great actor this time is Jack Huston , who plays philosopher lecturer John Jorrison. Jorrisen is the picture of professionalism, and an honest teacher too, as we find when he refuses to go easy on a student’s grades to stop her from failing. In a desperate last-ditch bid for clemency, the student threatens to blackmail him. It turns out to be a bluff, but there is a skeleton in his closet: As a younger man, during his post-student career as a music teacher, Jorrisen molested a teenage student called Miguel (Daniel Zovatto), a transgression covered up by his rich and therefore powerful father ( Bill Pullman ). Watch on Deadline The p-word — pedophilia — is never really mentioned, since Jorrisen is not what you might call a pedophile, having a bizarre arm’s-length courtship with an increasingly frustrated psychology professor Rebecca Richards ( Sofia Boutella ). Nevertheless, the false accusation starts him thinking about the past, the enormity of his crime (singular) and its impact on his victim. On the day of the film’s world premiere in Venice , Huston spoke to Deadline about the film’s uncompromising themes of guilt and redemption. DEADLINE: How did you get involved with this film? JACK HUSTON: I’ve known Paul on and off — God, I want to say going all the way back. He actually wanted me to be in a film called The Canyons (2013) many, many years ago. Which I didn’t do, but we’ve sort of remained friendly, and I’m very close with the producer, Braxton Pope. We worked together many, many years ago on a film called Shrink (2009). So, we’ve always had it in our minds that we’d like to work together. But when I was away working and I got a call from Braxton saying, “Listen, there’s a script that Paul wants me to read,” and he didn’t say much more than that — a bit like you watching the film, probably. You can’t really preface it with anything. He was like, “You just have to read it.” And after reading it, I thought it was first and foremost one of the best scripts I’ve read. I think it’s superb. I mean, it’s masterful. It’s Schrader through and through. He’s a bucket-list director that I’ve been dying to work with for many years. But it was only after reading the script about seven times that I finally decided to meet with Schrader and actually have a chat about it, because I really had to read it a lot to digest it. DEADLINE: Did you have any doubts? You said you read it seven times. HUSTON: Absolutely. It’s interesting; the things that scare you the most are sometimes the things that challenge you the most. I actually have a story about this. I was on set with a lovely actor called Jake Lacy, and Jake asked me, “What’s a role you’d never play?” I said I’d never play a predator, anything to do with children. It was about two months before I got Schrader’s script. And I’d also said around that time that I really wanted to work with a certain caliber of director. I was getting to a point in my life where leaving my children, leaving my wife, leaving home gets harder and harder, so you really want to be working with great people. So of course, the gods answered my question by sending me Schrader’s script, which I thought was very appropriate for where I was in my head space. OK, so it was a very difficult read, but I found it an incredibly important read. This is something me and my wife have to deal with on a daily basis. We talk about this. We have a 10-year-old and a 13-year-old. I think what Schrader does better than anybody is he tells the story of the everyman —the last suspect, almost, the person hiding in plain sight. Because that’s the truth of it. It exists everywhere in the world and it’s not usually the man who comes at you with his hands raised and a dagger in his hand. It’s usually the last person you’d ever suspect, the friendly guy, the affable man, the teacher. When I was at school, I remember my music teacher got kicked out for inappropriate behavior with a 13-year-old. So, I grew up seeing this. I mean, there’s multiple cases of teachers or music teachers having inappropriate behavior with students. And it’s about that sort of age — 13, 14, 15 — where it’s a real problem. So, I feel there’s real duty to telling this story, and I think Schrader does it so brilliantly well. DEADLINE: On top of that, you also have to be a philosophy professor. How did you approach that aspect of the role? HUSTON: Oh man, I’ve never worked harder. I read everything. I mean, it was kind of a gift and a curse, because you don’t ever want to take anything lightly. There’s not a single scene in this film that I didn’t spend months going over. Quite rightly so. I wanted to be as thoughtful approaching this role as I possibly could. It was a very, very difficult place to live in for the time I was doing it. But, as an actor, you have to put in the work. And for a film like, this and for a role like this, there is a certain amount of duty you have. I had to humanize the character first, so that we make him more relatable. And actually, by doing that, it poses the greater question, which is, can you trust anybody? And also, Spinoza’s great question, are we capable of change? Which is, I think, not for me to answer, it’s for me to pose and for audience to answer or at least debate and talk about. DEADLINE: How did you discuss this with Paul? I mean, how could you discuss your approach to the role when you were going for such ambiguity? If that makes sense. HUSTON: Yes, it does make sense. Paul is very matter of fact. He won’t tell you what he thinks, a lot of the time. That’s my job. And then it’s my job to not necessarily tell an audience what I think, but to perform it in a way that does leave it open-ended but allows them to make up their own minds. Perhaps the most important thing that Paul said to me on our very first Zoom was that he believes that the final act of any film, especially his films, happens when the audience leaves the cinema. It’s the conversation that ensues. So, I can tell you this much — this film is going to cause a conversation, so he’s going to succeed. Boy, is he ever. I think it’s very important that this conversation is had, though. It’s almost become a taboo subject, but it shouldn’t be. This should be pulled out from under the carpet and slammed on top of the table. This is a subject everybody should be talking, about because it’s so prevalent in society. And I spoke to multiple friends — gay, straight, I mean my wife even — and lot of them had their first sexual experiences when they were teenagers with older people. Like, people who were much older than them. And whether or not they thought they were abused, they were abused. It’s a form of abuse because it’s an older person using their stature. If it were a teacher, someone that one would mentor or look up to, it’s using that status and manipulating that and using it for their benefits. In the film, John is a much younger man when this happens. But let’s not get this wrong, it’s abuse. That’s what it is. We can’t sugarcoat that. That’s definitely abuse. But John has then spent his life after the incident in the sort of cynical way, ridding himself of any delights or pleasures to live a very straight life, to live a very plain life, no alcohol, no relationships. I think he knows what he’s done. And — with regard to the Spinoza question, which is, are we capable of change — I think that’s probably what keeps him awake at night, that exact question, because he desperately wants to change. He hopes he can. If he can’t, then he’s a monster. DEADLINE: It’s important that it’s just the one incident. I mean, 20, 30 years ago, people would just say, “Well, it only happened once,” and then they’d move on. And I think it’s very interesting that, as you say, this is still keeping him awake at night. HUSTON: I don’t think I would’ve taken this role if he was out there just abusing people. I think it’s a far more interesting and thoughtful and considered film — and performance —because of it being a single incident, because a single incident can ruin your life. A single incident can keep you awake at night. A single incident can haunt you. It doesn’t make it any better that it was once. It’s still awful. And I think that’s what I found very interesting about the character of John Jorrisen is he’s a philosophy professor. He thinks for a living. It’s his curse; he has to philosophize and think every single day. And actually, his studies have been as much about his life as those around him. I think he’s trying to be a better man, but he also takes up the idea that if we cannot live good and we will live badly. DEADLINE: It’s interesting that the film starts with an accusation — the student who says, “I know what you’ve done, I know about you.” Immediately, all the scenarios that you’ve mentioned go through the viewer’s mind. HUSTON: It’s so smart, that. I love that you brought that up because it’s like I think most people have done something bad in life. You just have to say to someone, “I know what you’ve done,” and that person will instantly go to that one thing that haunts them. “Oh my gosh, they know!” It was a very brilliant tactic. DEADLINE: It’s the perfect subject for a Paul Schrader movie, because his films are so much about tortured men looking for redemption. But who can forgive you — who has the power to forgive you — for an incident like this? HUSTON: It’s interesting, because it’s between him and Miguel, isn’t it, at the end of it? I think that’s, in John’s mind, the only person, there’s no one else to forgive him. The only person who could probably or possibly forgive him is the person he abused. He certainly can’t forgive himself. I think he’s always had it in the back of his head that it would come to this. It’s almost like a crusade, isn’t it? I think it was fascinating because Schrader writes in such a way that even in the lightest scenes, there feels like a weight. And I remember feeling this weight, and it became internal. It was in my stomach and it gnawed away at me. With everything you do, every scene you’re in, there’s something there — there’s baggage, and it feels like it’s pulling you down. You feel like you’re drowning. And I think John Jorrisen feels like he’s drowning. Even in the best moments, he feels like he’s drowning. And that’s from the choices he’s made, and that’s who he is as a man. DEADLINE: Paul’s been in a bit of a groove with these kinds of men-in-crisis movies lately, since First Reformed (2017). Did you go back and watch them again, or is that not helpful as an actor to watch? HUSTON: No, I did. I watched everything, going all the way back to Taxi Driver . I mean, it’s amazing how long he’s been playing out the man in the room with the checkered past. I think no one writes like him. And I mean this as a great compliment: He feels very European to me, because the films he makes, we don’t actually see too much in America these days, but maybe there’s a certain European flair. That’s why maybe Venice is the best place for the premiere of a film like this, because he’s posing very large and difficult questions to an audience, but they’re important questions. And I think the minute we try to censor ourselves and say we shouldn’t make films like this is the minute we censor art itself, and art should be the one place where you ask the difficult questions. And they’re not for us to answer, they’re for us to pose. Hopefully a film like this opens that conversation up and makes us much more free to talk about. And actually, when I was doing my research — which I did so much for something like this because I’d never do it without — it just really did show me that this happens daily, multiple times a day. And I think people need to be far more aware of just how dangerous the world is. And a lot of the time the abused don’t even know they’ve been abused. And I found that fascinating that it’s actually, but that doesn’t make it not abuse. That’s the point I want to get across here very much. It’s like whatever the case, however you are, even if you saw it as your sexual revolution, you were 14 and you met someone older. Like I said, my wife was dating a man when she was 16 who she thought was 18 years old. Turned out he was 29. So, every person I spoke to had some form of story or they had a story about someone else. I was like, “Wow, it really is everywhere.” So, I’m glad that someone like Paul Schrader’s around and can write something like this. DEADLINE: It’s also interesting that actors like Richard Gere and Bill Pullman are willing to take part, because those names help to sell a difficult subject matter, surely… HUSTON: Yeah, I mean they all come out for Paul because he’s brilliant and he’s a singular voice in our industry. He’s his own being, and everybody supports him. I saw Marty [Scorsese] the other day. He’s come on board as an EP and he just loves the film. He thought the film was miraculous. And I think that says a lot, because Marty’s an incredibly thoughtful filmmaker, one of the most brilliant filmmakers as we all know, but he’s somebody who understands just how important someone like Paul Schrader is and how important that voice is. And that’s ultimately why I did the film, because sometimes the things that scare you the most are the things that we have to tackle head on. I believe we made quite a brilliant film, and I’m incredibly proud of the performance. I think it’s one of the best ones I’ve ever had the opportunity to do, and it’s incredibly considered. I hope people are able to see that. DEADLINE: Guilt and remorse were a big part of the film that you directed, Day of the Fight (2023), the idea of the weight of one’s “sins”, the missed opportunities or things done wrong. It seems to me that you’re attracted to that as an element of storytelling. HUSTON: Very much. It’s so interesting you brought that up, because there’s a whole scene in Day of the Fight, where Mikey (Michael Pitt) has a conversation with his friend Patrick (John Magaro) in church. He says, “I’ve changed. I know that, but people… all they remember is the past. I’ll always be who I was, not who I am.” Which means, it doesn’t matter [that he’s changed]. He hasn’t had a drink in nine years and he doesn’t want one. But no matter what, people will always see him for who he was, not for who he is. And I think it’s a very interesting way of looking at this script, because it was when I was really philosophizing about the idea of change and redemption, and if we are able to change. And that’s why Schrader is such a sort of genius, man. He comes along and poses the question in such a brutally honest and devastating way that a lot of things I thought I knew I didn’t know, and it made me just go back to the books and just work and work and work. DEADLINE: Are you planning to direct again? What’s your next move? HUSTON: Yes, I am. I’m meant to be starting pre-production next week, but we’ll see if that bloody happens. Independent cinema at its finest! [Laughs.] We’re very, very close. My next film’s about Joseph Merrick, who was known as “The Elephant Man”, but we use the last month of his life and his childhood from 5 years old to 15, when he left home. It’s a script that I’ve written and I feel very proud to be making it later this year. The title Joseph Merrick right now, which I’m sure is subject to change. We’ll see what it’s called at the end. DEADLINE: And what attracted you to that story? HUSTON: Funny enough, my mentor was really John Hurt. I was very close with John and spent a lot of time with him and his wife — well, widow now — Anwyn. I got to live with them when they were in California and spent a lot of time with John. I will never forget that performance in that film, David Lynch’s film, and what it did to me, so there wasn’t a piece of me that wanted to make that film again, because it’s been done absolutely perfectly and brilliantly and I would never even dare. But what I did find out after a lot of reading was that there were parts of Joseph’s life that we didn’t know about. So, it’s been a beautiful exploration of this stunning figure who, against all the odds, led with kindness and generosity and beauty. And I think the world needs these stories. They need someone to look up to. And when you look at somebody who had such a horrible start in life and the afflictions that he was born with, and yet he was still able to hold himself the way he did… I think it’s a good example for people, and it’s a film I want my kids to watch. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Sticks Lido Landing; Jack Huston & Lorenzo Mieli Interviews; More Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom, Paramount Exec Was 55 Fox Orders Comedy Series ‘Mammoth’ From ‘Modern Family’ Duo Based On UK Format Maria Bartiromo Pink-Slipped From Fox After 12 Years: “Effective Today” Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Tony Gatlif Dies: ‘Gadjo Dilo’ Director Whose Work Celebrated Roma Culture Was 77
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings” Tony Gatlif Dies: ‘Gadjo Dilo’ Director Whose Work Celebrated Roma Culture Was 77 Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc ‘Be Brave’: “We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us” – Venice View All September 4, 2026 3:05am Tony Gatlif at the Cannes Film Festival in 2025 Kristy Sparow/Getty Images Director Tony Gatlif , who was known for films such as Gadjo Dilo exploring Roma culture, died in the Southern French town of Arles on September 3. He was 77. The director was born Michel Boualem Dahmani in Algiers on September 10, 1948, to a Kabyle father and mother of Andalusian and Gitane origin. He had a difficult childhood, growing up in poverty in slums on the outskirts of the Algerian capital, which he quit for France at age 14 in the early 1960s. After a period of precarity and petty criminality, a meeting with his idol, actor Michel Simon, opened the door to a dramatic arts course in Germain-en-Laye outside of Paris, after the latter wrote a letter of recommendation. Related Stories News Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom & Paramount International Boss Was 55 News Gloria Steinem Dies: Feminist Icon And Activist & Co-Founder Of Ms. Magazine Was 92 While gaining experience as an actor, Gatlif gradually started creating his own original work based on his own experiences and exploring the culture of his Roma origins. Watch on Deadline He broke into directing in 1975 with La tête en Ruines , followed by the Spain-shot and set drama Corre Gitano , about a young gypsy man accused of a crime he did not commit. It was the first among a series of films exploring the culture and challenges of Europe’s Roma people. In 1992, he won Cannes Un Certain Regard prize for Latcho Drom , a documentary about gypsy music. He followed this with one of this best known films, Gadjo Dilo ( The Crazy Stranger ) , starring Romain Duris as a Frenchman who travels to Romania in search of Roma singer, whose voice he has heard on tapes recorded by his late father. The film premiered at the Locarno Film Festival in 1997 where it won the Silver Leopard. Gatlif would go on to win Best Director in Cannes in 2004, with the autobiographical drama Exils , reuniting him with Duris and also featuring Lubna Azabal in the cast. Subsequent works included Korkoro (2009), The Outraged (2012), Geronimo (2014), Djam (2017), Tom Medina (2021) and Ange (2025). ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Sticks Lido Landing; Jack Huston & Lorenzo Mieli Interviews; More Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom, Paramount Exec Was 55 Fox Orders Comedy Series ‘Mammoth’ From ‘Modern Family’ Duo Based On UK Format Maria Bartiromo Pink-Slipped From Fox After 12 Years: “Effective Today” Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings” Tony Gatlif Dies: ‘Gadjo Dilo’ Director Whose Work Celebrated Roma Culture Was 77 Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc ‘Be Brave’: “We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us” – Venice View All September 4, 2026 3:55am May el-Toukhy Søren Rønholt May el-Toukhy is in competition at the Venice Film Festival with post-World War Two psychological thriller Woman Unknown as one of just two female directors in the running for the Golden Lion this year. Set in Denmark in the summer of 1945, the picture revolves around nanny and housemaid Marie (Mathilde Arcel), who is on the cusp of marrying her wealthy, older, widowed employer (Carsten Bjørnlund). Amid the jubilation, there is a darker side to the liberation as women who fraternized with German soldiers are tracked down and publicly shamed. A painful secret from Marie’s past threatens her imminent but fragile social ascension and she will stop at nothing to prevent it from being revealed. Related Stories Festivals Jack Huston On The Tough Questions About Sexual Abuse Posed By Paul Schrader's Film 'The Basics Of Philosophy': "It's Almost Become A Taboo Subject" - Venice Film Festival News Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc 'Be Brave': "We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us" - Venice Mathilde Arcel as Marie in Woman Unknown Nordisk Film Production When Venice announced its lineup last July, el-Toukhy was the only woman in the main competition alongside 19 men. She has since been joined by Rachel Szor, co-director with Yuval Abraham of late addition Neza . Watch on Deadline It was a surprising move for a festival, which has feted three female directors with its top Golden Lion prize since 2020, and left many woman across the film industry wondering whether the drive for gender equality born out of the MeToo era was a mirage. El-Toukhy tells Deadline that while she is “delighted” and “honored” to be in competition, the lack of other women in the running for the Golden Lion this year has weighed on her since. “It tells us there’s still lots of work to do,” she says. “I think it’s very, very much a structural problem that I myself have lots of experience with. I’ve been the only woman in many, many settings.” “Going all the way back to when we get out of film school film as female filmmakers, to getting our first film done, and getting our second film done, the budgets we work under, and even sometimes the actors that say yes and the actors that say no,” she continues. “The way the media creates stories around male directors as geniuses… I’ve never heard a female director being called a genius. “We’re all part of this structure and it’s just been on my mind since how severe this problem is and how structural it is. It’s as old as cinema and even older than that. And of course, my film also speaks about some of these matters, such as the invisibility of women, in a historical context.” From Reformation Witch Hunts To Post-WW2 Purges Woman Unknown is el-Toukhy’s first film in seven years, with the director taking credits on dramas Cry Wolf and The Crown in between. The new feature grew out of research into witch hunts in Denmark sparked by its Protestant Reformation of 1536 which resulted in more than 1,000 executions. “I thought I was going to do a film about that but as I dived into the witch hunts in Denmark, I found it difficult to relate to the perpetrators, the witch hunters. I always gravitate towards telling stories where it’s more hazy, messy and sticky,” she explains. As she and longtime writing partner Maren Louise Käehne moved away from the idea, they came across pictures of Danish women being punished in public after World War Two for their relationships with German soldiers. Women having their heads shaved and being beaten and stripped in the street for fraternizing with Germans happened across Europe in the wake of the war. “It started a discussion around the fact that both sides were wrong and both sides were right and the idea that after the war, you punish whomever you can get your hands on and whomever you can punish without being punished yourself… and that’s often the women… that was really the starting point,” says el-Toukhy. The pair then came across the work of Danish academic Annette Warring and her 1994 paper entitled “Pro-German girls – during occupation and judicial reckoning”. Warring estimated that at least 50,000 Danish women had been in relationships with German soldiers over the course of the five-year occupation, but that only a handful had been informers or supporters of Nazi Germany. Her paper noted that under Denmark’s policy of cooperation with Germany following its 1940 invasion, fraternizing with German soldiers was not unlawful, either during the occupation or under post-World War Two legislation. She suggested that the post-world war purges and humiliations had been sparked rather by sexist notions around appropriate female sexuality and morality and the belief that “woman’s sexuality was national property”. “She got a lot of heat for that at that time in the 90s, the war generation was still alive and continued to dominate the narrative on the war… we dug into her study and that was really the starting point.” El-Toukhy suggests Denmark’s tactical appeasement of Germany, because as a small nation it had little other choice, blurred the lines between cooperation and collaboration, with the resistance only really strengthening in the lead up to the end of the war. “We kept our government and our society going, but we were at the same time oppressed by the Germans… that became the whole discussion after the war,” she says. “People got punished for having collaborated, and the ‘horizontal collaborators’ would be part of that cleaning up,” she continues. “Then there would be people who were never punished because they were too vital a part of society… people with factories, doctors. It became too complicated to punish them, because then everything would come to a standstill. The women were an easy target”. The shame carried by these women after they were outed, publicly humiliated and then ostracised carried down through generations. “Their children are now around my mother’s age, 70, 80 and even the next generation live in the shadow of that story,” says el-Toukhy. Tapping into Hitchcock & Scola Protagonist Marie is not based on one single real-life character but is rather a composite drawing on all of el-Toukhy’s research. “She’s based on everyone and no-one. She’s not a specific person,” she explains. Marie’s story also grew out of el-Toukhy’s questions around what kind of societal structures allow for a woman to humiliated and physically attacked with public approval on the street. “While working with the subject matter of the female body as a battlefield, I became interested in how fellow citizens can do that to a person. What structures are in place in a society in order for that to happen, and how do these structures look at home. The story grew from there.” The idea of telling the story through the genre of a psychological thriller came with time, as el-Toukhy and Käehne grappled with how to being something new to the the World War Two setting. “It is easy to fall into the trap of making a pastiche of everything you’ve seen over the years,” she says. “I also felt people glazed over a little bit when I pitched the idea, even if I think that’s unfair because there’s so many stories we haven’t told about women so let’s tell those stories and then say we’re over and done with that period. “The idea was to make it entertaining, for lack of better words, to make it a thrill to watch even though the subject matter is quite serious. We also had the ambition of doing something that doesn’t look like a classic Second World War or post-World War Two film.” The feature follows Marie over the course of five days with “camera almost sitting on her shoulder”. “The camera is never alone with other with characters apart from these drops of zeitgeist where we dive into the energy, the chaos and the time on a more philosophical level, but the idea of always sticking to her was very much also because I had this visionthat if I were to do a World War II film or a post-World War II period drama, it should have a different flavor. I was digging to find that.” There is also a Hitchcock feel as Marie observes other inhabitants of the swanky mansion block which is the main location through the windows of other apartments, and the spectator is left asking who is watching her back. El-Toukhy also cites Ettore Scola’s 1977 period drama A Special Day ( Una giornate particolare ), starring Sophia Loren as a Rome housewife opposite Marcello Mastroianni as her neighbour who remain at home the day Adolf Hitler visits Benito Mussolini. “There were the windows there as well and a sense that everyone is watching, that constant fear that someone can see you and what do they see?… It seemed like a good symbol also of Marie’s alienation in a way… she’s part of this fancy setup, but at the same time she’s standing on the outside of it.” Woman Unknown TrustNordisk El-Toukhy also had clear ideas for aesthetics of the film, with the color red running as leitmotif throughout the film, captured in Marie’s clothing, the red of the Danish flag or swastikas daubed on the homes of suspected collaborators. “I had this idea that while I was not going to do a black and white film, I wanted it to be almost desaturated but in color, so we would only work with black, red, white. The Danish flag is red and white and of course the Nazi flag is black and white on red and then we had the greys and the browns. We ended up with this film which almost looks like it’s black and white with a splash of red,” she says. El-Toukhy sees the color scheme as a way of showing the Danish population’s efforts to reassert a sense of national identity after the war. “As a filmmaker, there are so many decisions and you spend so much time figuring out, or at least I do, on how to infuse a film with a subconscious, like that something that speaks to the audience’s subconscious,” she explains. “The color scheme is like my own interpretation, and probably the audience will never see this, but nationalism was really on the rise… We had to kind of rebuild our narrative because we were collaborating with the Germans, and of course also because of the atrocities and the complicity during the war… that idea of having these colors as almost a nationalist signature was a big inspiration and energized me during the shooting of the film.” Woman Unknown is produced by Mikael Rieks ( Land of Mine ) for Nordisk Film Production A/S in co-production with Nafta Films, Nordisk Film Production Sweden and Film i Väst. articles.title: Theo Rollason On How He Discovered 30 Hours Of Behind-The-Scenes Derek Jarman Footage To Create ‘Queer Edward II’ — Venice
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Gets Rapturous 14-Minute Standing Ovation At Venice World Premiere Danny Boyle’s ‘Ink’ Earns Five-Minute Ovation At Venice World Premiere ‘The Fastest Man In The World’: Biopic Of Four-Time Paralympic Gold Medalist Tony Volpentest In The Works View All September 4, 2026 5:59am Theo Rollason Aurore Marechal/Getty Images. In 1991, British filmmaker Derek Jarman screened Edward II, his political and wildly inventive adaptation of Christopher Marlowe’s classic play, at the Venice Film Festival. The film was a hit with critics, and Tilda Swinton, who starred alongside Steven Waddington and Andrew Tiernan, won the festival’s Best Actress award. This week, exactly 35 years later, Edward II returns to the Lido in the form of a brilliant behind-the-scenes documentary about the film’s eventful production from first-time filmmaker Theo Rollason . The documentary is titled Queer Edward II and screens this afternoon in an Out Of Competition slot on the Lido. Related Stories News Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: "I've Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings" Festivals Jack Huston On The Tough Questions About Sexual Abuse Posed By Paul Schrader's Film 'The Basics Of Philosophy': "It's Almost Become A Taboo Subject" - Venice Film Festival An assortment of former Jarman acolytes, such as Swinton and Sandy Powell, are Executive Producers on the project alongside other interesting names like Christine Vachon and Russell Tovey. Seamus McGarvey, the Irish DoP behind titles like Joe Wright’s Atonement , Tom Ford’s Nocturnal Animals , and Lynne Ramsay’s We Need to Talk About Kevin, is credited as the cinematographer. The film has been pieced together using footage that a young McGarvey, then fresh into his career behind a camera, shot on the Edward II set. Watch on Deadline “It was all just sitting in a cupboard for 35 years,” Rollason says of the footage, which he stumbled upon after a tip from a friend. Alongside editor Nicole Hálová, Rollason began the lengthy process of combing through the hours of footage, and he has carved out an illuminating portrait not only of Jarman’s unique artistic practice but also of his much-less-talked-about leadership in the gay rights movement in the UK. Producers on the title are Ben Fowlie, Sebastien Rabas, and Michael Sherman. Simon Fisher Turner composed the score, and Dora Ash Sakula and Neo Michael were the archival producers. After Venice, Queer Edward II will screen at the London Film Festival. Below, Rollason speaks with Deadline in depth about the miraculous story behind his discovery of McGarvey’s footage, starting the project completely independently with no funding, and how he hopes the film can “form a little companion piece” to Jarman’s Edward II . Venice runs until September 12. DEADLINE: Theo, how did you find this footage? THEO ROLLASON: It’s an odd story. So Derek was making Edward II , and Sarah Swords, who’d worked on The Garden with Derek, wanted to make a behind-the-scenes film about Edward II . She hired Seamus McGarvey, who’d also worked on The Garden , and sent him on his way with a camera. At the end of production, as often happens with these kinds of indie productions, Seamus turned up and said, “Here’s the footage,” and they said, “We don’t have any money.” So the footage ended up with Ahmad Ahmadzadeh, who runs the camera company that hired out the camera to Seamus. And it was all just sitting in a cupboard for 35 years. I’ve known Ahmad for years, and he got in touch with me because I’ve worked as an archivist previously and said, “Can you give me your opinion on this material?” He knew I liked Derek Jarman’s films, and watching it was incredible. It was a real look behind the production and who Derek was. The final step in realizing this could be a feature film was that the politics of the time were really thoroughly explored on the set. I spent a while convincing Ahmad that there was a feature film here, and not just the typical behind-the-scenes featurette. DEADLINE: How much footage was there? Was it reels? ROLLASON: 30 hours of Betacam SP. There could have been a watchable 15-hour film in the footage. All credit to Seamus. He was in his early to mid-20s when he shot this. He wasn’t strictly a documentary filmmaker, but he’s just so intuitive with a camera. He’s constantly finding the right expressions to cut away to. It’s really the easiest job in the world watching his rushes because it’s basically been edited in camera. Theo Rollason’s ‘ Queer Edward II ‘. Lightborn Films. DEADLINE: What did Seamus say when you first contacted him with the idea? ROLLASON: He was surprised. No one knew that the footage still existed. Everyone had forgotten about it or assumed it was gone. So when we originally got in touch with him and asked whether he would be okay with us making this film, he was just delighted. For him, it was emotional to see one of the very first projects he worked on, which he had thought had come to nothing, being brought back to life. DEADLINE: Watching this film and seeing Derek at length, you realize how English he was. I’d never really thought of him in that context. ROLLASON: Yes, and that was one of the other appeals of the material: it couldn’t be more British and specifically English. Just the way he speaks, but also all the stuff he’s interested in talking about. The first scene we put in the film shows Derek talking about Marks and Spencer’s underwear, and that sets the tone. It’s an amazing document of the UK at that time. DEADLINE: So much gets lost when a person dies, and there’s all this mythmaking about who they were. In Derek’s case, I feel like people don’t really consider how involved he was in the gay rights movement. ROLLASON: Yeah, that was the breakthrough for me. There are obviously a few films about Derek Jarman. There’s Isaac Julien’s film, which does a great job of telling his life story. And within that, his involvement with the gay rights protest group OutRage. I knew Derek’s films very well, but I wasn’t as aware of just how directly politically involved he was. It’s fairly obvious from Edward II where his politics lie, but that doesn’t really give you the sense that he was on the streets with OutRage. He wasn’t watching from afar and making these comments. He was really doing it from the inside. And basically, all the archive footage in the film that isn’t on the set of Edward II is there to give that context. DEADLINE: Filmmaking is always hard. But this is a unique project. Was it tough to raise funds and get people on board? ROLLASON: It was incredibly easy to get people emotionally on board. The goodwill around Derek’s legacy is unbelievable. I don’t think many subjects could garner the kind of response Derek gets from people. Financing, obviously, is a different thing, and we did it probably the most insane way we could have, which was starting production without any financing, which was a huge leap of faith, especially as a first-time filmmaker. I’m not sure I’d ever do it again. I’ve made shorts before, but I haven’t made documentaries. I didn’t really have anything to prove myself, so there was an element of, if I just start making this film and we have something to show people, then, you know, fingers crossed, the money will follow. And it took a while, but it eventually did. DEADLINE: What’s your background? How did you start making films? ROLLASON: I’ve worked as a film critic for years. I love writing about film. And everything I’ve learned about film has been from watching an obscene amount of films. I didn’t go to film school or anything like that. I’ve always wanted to make films, but didn’t have the confidence. Over the last few years, I taught myself how to edit at a job I had producing video content. I did some video essay stuff. I put out a short film, which was very loosely narrative or experimental. I also worked as an archivist for the estate of the artist Paula Rego, and got very interested in large film and photo archives. DEADLINE: Is that footage at the end of the film where Derek is at a screening from Venice? ROLLASON: It is. He was there showing Blue at the Biennale a couple of months before he died. That footage is amazing. He’s so obviously very unwell by that point, but he writes about it so warmly in his diaries, and it felt like a really lovely glimpse into the future. I was a bit concerned that, in trying to make a film set on the Edward II set, I would give the impression that it was Derek’s last film. That’s why I wanted to have this flash-forward, to show that that wasn’t the case, but also to hit home that this was quite close to his death. DEADLINE: How does it feel to now be showing your film at Venice? ROLLASON: It’s crazy. The reason we started the film with no funding was that we looked at the submission dates for Venice. It’s 35 years ago this week that Edward II played Venice, and we just thought, that’s a really neat little thing; should we go for it? If I’m honest, I didn’t think there was any chance that this film would be here. It’s completely surreal. DEADLINE: How would you like this film to be viewed? I couldn’t help but think of the many possibilities to distribute it. It could go along with a retrospective of Derek’s many works, for example. ROLLASON: I would love for it to be shown with Edward II as much as possible. If this film is a chance for Derek’s films to be seen more widely, that’s always great. But Edward II, especially, is such a special film, and it hasn’t been seen as widely, certainly in the UK, in the last decade. I hope this can form a little companion piece to Edward II . Beyond that, I’m excited to see how it lands with a British audience. It is a very British film, and there are some very British characters, shall we say, who appear in it. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Sticks Lido Landing; Jack Huston & Lorenzo Mieli Interviews; More Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom, Paramount Exec Was 55 Fox Orders Comedy Series ‘Mammoth’ From ‘Modern Family’ Duo Based On UK Format Maria Bartiromo Pink-Slipped From Fox After 12 Years: “Effective Today” Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Cédric Kahn Talks Exploration Of Youth Mental Health Issues In Venice Contender ‘A Place To Heal’ + Trailer: “There’s More Hope With Adolescents”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings” Tony Gatlif Dies: ‘Gadjo Dilo’ Director Whose Work Celebrated Roma Culture Was 77 Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc ‘Be Brave’: “We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us” – Venice View All September 4, 2026 6:00am 'A Place To Heal' Ad Vitam French director Cédric Kahn hits the Venice Film Festival’s this evening with Golden Lion contender A Place To Heal (15/18) set against the backdrop of an adolescent psychiatric ward. It promises to be one of this Venice’s most youthful red carpets as the director is joined by the dozen young actors at the heart of the production in which he also co-stars as the head psychiatrist of the unit. “They’re all very excited and I’m very happy about it because I’ve attended a lot of films festivals in my time but to experience a festival through their eyes will be a pleasure,” says Kahn, who has a long history with Venice having shown his first feature Railway Bar in its parallel Critics’ Week sidebar in 1992, returning in 2023 with Making of in its official selection. The youthful excitement will be an antidote to a tough but hopeful film digging into the issue of adolescent mental health issues. The young subjects include Lucia (Malou Khebizi) a tough-talking runaway, old beyond her years, who was abused by a stepfather as a child; Éloïse (Zoé Monpart), a seemingly privileged kid, suffering from eating disorders and depression who gradually opens up about the cause of her pain; Marvin (Daoud Gary), who is interned after a sudden psychotic episode, and Enzo (Kenji Peyran), a streetwise tearaway with a history of abandonment as a child, whose arrival on the ward upsets its fragile equilibrium. Deadline can reveal a first clip below giving a sense of the ward and its highs and lows, as the staff sets about the task of healing their young patients. “I’ve wanted to make a film about psychiatry for a very long time. It was a date with destiny for me. I’ve often explored mental fragility in my previous films; so, to make a film on this subject was a long-standing appointment,” explains Kahn about the origin of the film. The director had false starts as he tried to figure out how to explore the subject on the big screen. “I worked on an initial project a few years back that focused more on adult psychiatry, specifically from the perspective of the medical staff,” he recounts. “The film’s protagonist was a psychiatrist, but I wasn’t happy with the script, so I completely changed my approach to the subject; approaching it through the lens of adolescents felt more positive to me… there’s more hope with adolescents.” The young psychiatric patients in A Place to Heal are based on research carried out by co-writer Kahina Le Querrec, who spent six months immersed in a child and adolescent psychiatry unit, while Kahn also gained personal insight through three weeks spent in a unit in Paris. “She gathered the children’s accounts and spoke with the psychiatrists and medical staff, and we wrote the screenplay based on that material… they are all true stories, re-enacted by other adolescents.” Kahn acknowledges that one of the themes running through the drama is the role parents in their children’s mental health issues. “There are many contexts, but obviously, family and parents play a major role in children’s dysfunction,” says Kahn. “I know that for parents, the film can create a sense of unease or guilt… I have friends who saw the film who told me they were asking themselves throughout the film whether they were bad parents.” The film comes at a time of reports of a growing health crisis amongst youngsters, in the wake of the Covid-19pandemic and the rise of smart phones and social media. Kahn questions whether is a rise in mental health problems, suggesting rather than it has become more acceptable to talk about mental health issues openly, adding the supposed trend was not at the heart of his intentions for the film. “I wanted to show that when it comes to psychological or psychiatric issues, it’s actually a very democratic experience. We’re all on equal footing. And then, there are also issues that are truly timeless,” he says. “While I do somewhat call out the role of parents, I’m not really criticizing a specific era in the film. I don’t dwell much on eco-anxiety or Covid. We tried to make a film that feels fairly timeless. It’s not a judgment on the times, not at all, but it is a judgment on the family; that’s for sure.” “The issue of family is something that runs through all my films. The topic of parent control, I’ve addressed it in every film; it’s a continuation of that theme. So, I’d say that’s more my personal subject matter than the topic of psychiatry itself.” Related Stories News Theo Rollason On How He Discovered 30 Hours Of Behind-The-Scenes Derek Jarman Footage To Create 'Queer Edward II' -- Venice News International Insider: Ciao, Venice; 'Bake Off' Battle Heats Up; Leslie Odom Jr. Chat The film is produced by Ad Vitam Films, which will release the film in France on November 18, in coproduction with Kahn’s Trop de Bonheur Productions and France 2 Cinéma. Charades handles international sales. articles.title: Netflix Hikes UK Prices, With Cheapest Plan Jumping A Third
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart French TV In Focus: Screenings & Shows To Watch At The Unifrance Rendez-Vous VodafoneThree Launching Vodafone TV In The UK, Bundling Netflix, HBO Max & Live Channels ‘Miraculous’ Studio Founder Jeremy Zag To Receive Deadline’s French TV Disruptor Award At The Unifrance Rendez-Vous View All September 4, 2026 6:02am Netflix Justin Sullivan/Getty Images It’s become pricier to watch Love Is Blind and The Gentlemen in the UK after Netflix upped its prices, hiking the monthly cost of its cheapest package by a third. The changes narrow the pricing gap between Netflix’s cheapest ad-supported tier and its top-level plan. The streamer’s new UK pricing kicked in yesterday, September 3, with little fanfare. It last put up the cost of subscribing in February. Specifically, the cost of the Standard with Ads plan has risen 33.4% from £5.99 ($8.10) to £7.99 ($10.81) a month. The price for the Standard tier is up 7.7% from £12.99 to £13.99, while Premium has gone from £18.99 to £20.99, a 10.5% uptick. Related Stories Books Everything We Know About Netflix's 'Better Than The Movies' Feature Adaptation So Far News 'Famous Last Words' Interview With Gloria Steinem Streaming Now On Netflix The pricing applies to new and existing customers. Netflix has over 18M subs in the UK. Watch on Deadline Confirming the changes to Deadline, Netflix said the price rises “reflect improvements to our wide range of entertainment and the quality of our service.” The streamer’s statement added: “Our approach remains the same: we continue offering a range of prices and plans to meet a variety of needs, and as we deliver more value to our members, we reinvest in quality entertainment and improve their experience by updating our prices.” It added: “We know members have never had more choices in entertainment, and we’re committed to delivering an experience that meets and exceeds their expectations.” It is certainly correct to say UK consumers have a wide range of free and paid-for choices for TV. The news comes in the same week that telco giant VodafoneThree announced it is rolling out Vodafone TV, a new service launching in October that sees free channels bundled with Netflix and HBO Max, and which will also offer access to AVOD services such as Tubi.
