articles.title: USA Sports Will Serve Up World Team Tennis Reboot (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 3, 2026 5:00am Jessica Pegula Photo by Julian Finney/Getty Images World Team Tennis has found a media partner for its revival, after a five year hiatus. The mixed gender tennis league that was co-founded by Billie Jean King in 1974 has inked a deal with USA Sports to televise WTT matches, with all six games running in primetime on CNBC , and streaming on Fandango. WTT and Versant will also partner on other integrations via E! and some of the media company’s other properties. Matches will begin Dec. 1 and run through Dec. 15, keeping the matches outside of the Grand Slam tennis calendar. WTT last held a season in November 2021, before pandemic-spurred challenges forced the hiatus. The league announced its reboot plans earlier this year, including giving athletes equity in the league. Jessica Pegula, Tommy Paul and Denis Shapovalov are among the players committed. The league has long relied on city-based teams, and the new version of WTT will follow that model with the New York Empire Racquet Club, based at Barclays Center; Toronto North Racquet Club based at Coca-Cola Coliseum; and Florida Flamingos Racquet Club at Amerant Bank Arena. It will also have a new format, with four singles sets and a mixed doubles tiebreaker. The league also plans to utilize immersive technology, live music, and other elements to enhance the in-person and televised experiences. “In creating a new era of World Team Tennis, our goal is to build a sports and entertainment property that delivers value to fans wherever they are, while tapping into adjacent audiences that can help grow the sport,” said WTT CEO Stephen Amritraj. “Versant’s portfolio is uniquely compelling because it allows us to do both. CNBC has a natural connection to the traditional tennis audience while Fandango provides an opportunity to reach fans from a streaming perspective.” USA Sports has been opportunistic in snagging new sports rights, supplementing its core WNBA, NASCAR, PGA Tour and international soccer with a heavy emphasis on deals it sees as growth opportunities. That includes League One Volleyball and the Pro Padel League. While the flagship sports are running on USA Network, parent company Versant has also begun to use CNBC (which is also about as widely distributed as cable channels can get) for some sports, and turning Fandango into a streaming destination. “We’re excited to bring live World Team Tennis to CNBC and Fandango this December,” said Celia Kohl, SVP of Strategy & Business Development at Versant. “USA Sports is always looking to bring growth-minded leagues that innovate and excite into our portfolio, and we believe WTT is one of those leagues that will resonate with our audiences across both CNBC and Fandango.” THR

articles.title: ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Review: A Frustrating, Guiltily Compelling Portrait of the Triumph and Tragedy of Extreme Mountaineering
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Richard Lawson Plus Icon Richard Lawson View All September 3, 2026 5:00am 'Everest: The Other Side' Photo: Jimmy Chin In their gripping, Oscar-winning 2018 documentary Free Solo , husband and wife directors Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi examine the boggling daring of Alex Honnold, a rock climber who scales sheer mountain walls without the aid, and protection, of ropes. The film’s climbing scenes are breathtakingly tense, but what sells the movie as more than mere docu-thriller is its sharp assessment of Honnold’s psychological makeup, the jumble of genetics and conditioning that have turned him into a man seemingly unaffected by fear. He’s oddly charming in all his insouciant disregard for his own safety, but there’s something sinister there, too. He takes on these feats with only a small amount of concern for how an accident might impact those who love him, including the woman to whom he’s now married. Honnold is free to not care about himself, but shouldn’t he more thoroughly consider the emotions of those around him? That said, those people are all adults with their own agency; they could choose, much as it might hurt, to walk away from Honnold whenever they pleased. Had children been in the picture, though, Honnold’s death-defying acts would be unforgivable. Related Stories Movies Martin McDonagh Discusses His CIA Drama 'Wild Horse Nine,' Set in a Time When "Horrible People Had Intelligence" Movies 'Eklipse' Mixes the Autobiographical and Fictional to Explore AIDS Taboos and Fear of Social Exclusion Everest: The Other Side The Bottom Line An accidental rebuttal to George Mallory’s ‘Because it’s there.’ Venue : Venice Film Festival (Venice Open — Out of Competition) Directors: Jimmy Chin, Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi 1 hour 55 minutes And thus the central — and enormous — problem with Chin and Vasarhelyi’s new film, Everest: The Other Side , a portrait of two reckless, ruthlessly self-involved people who like to climb very tall mountains and then ski down them. The documentary begins with couple Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson preparing to do something unprecedented: They will scale Mt. Everest’s notoriously difficult north face (the part on the China side of the mountain) and then strap on their skis and head back the way they came. Why they want to do this is explained in the typical grandiose, solipsistic terms. It is a craving for extreme experience that, in Morrison’s and Nelson’s (and the film’s) minds, better connects them to themselves and to the universe. This is more than a passion, they insist. It is a primal need that cannot be denied. “Okay,” we think, watching these two gas each other up. “But what about Nelson’s sons?” Y’know, the two living, breathing, helpless children forced to sit idle while their mother and (almost) step-father constantly and brazenly risk abandoning them. All of the big talk about personal drive, which makes Free Solo so darkly compelling, immediately crumbles into selfish pablum the second that children are introduced into the equation. Rather than heroic, these costly and horribly uncertain stunts come across callous and cruel. Hideous proof of that arrives 20 or so minutes into The Other Side , when we see Nelson in the final seconds before she fell to her death while attempting to ski down the world’s eighth-tallest mountain. One moment she is on her skis testing her position, and in the next the shelf of snow beneath her dislodges and slides off a nearly 6,000-foot cliff. In an awful instant, two boys lose their mother and the movie loses any kind of principled posture. A more inquisitive film might have then turned its gaze inward, becoming a meta investigation of what all this thrill-seeking has wrought, a study of hubris and hamartia. Instead, The Other Side shifts into triumph-over-grief mode, as Morrison prepares to fulfill the Everest mission in honor of his late partner. We learn more about Morrison’s backstory, particularly a baroquely terrible tragedy he endured 15 years ago. It’s impossible to not feel immense pity for Morrison, who suffered something unimaginable. But that sympathy can’t quite make up for the galling fact of Nelson’s sons, now teenagers stuck in limbo as a father figure stubbornly insists on courting further ruin. What’s even more shocking is that Chin, himself a mountaineer, decides to embark on the Everest trip with Morrison (and a load of other men), though he has young children of his own at home. Vasarhelyi appears on camera, wondering where the end of this might be. She asks Chin how many people who have sat at their dinner table are now dead, and in response Chin calmly rattles off a staggeringly long list of names. Are we nonetheless supposed to root for Chin’s decision to support his friend? The Other Side answers an indignant “yes.” What ensues is, in a purely visceral way, wholly transfixing. Extreme mountain climbing has never looked anything but miserable from the distance of a screening room, and The Other Side delivers mightily on all that scraping, straining, gasping toil. While it may only offer limp gestures of acknowledgment to the underpaid and dangerous labor of the Sherpas who facilitate the adventures of well-funded Western men (and a few women), the film still envelops us in the intense rigor and fortitude of Morrison’s pursuit. Its images are stunning, in both exacting close-up and wide, sweeping drone shots. A palpable suspense overtakes us as Morrison and his team work their way up this daunting monolith, potential cataclysm lurking in every crack of rock and tumble of snow. Cynically or not, Chin and Vasarhelyi understand that these primal thrills are enough to distract us from the frustrating and sorrowful truth at the center of the story. Well, almost enough. Every time the film cuts back to Nelson’s sons, we are reminded that none of this needs to happen, that a lot of people would still be alive today had they only ignored the juvenile, daredevil id they have dressed up as noble calling. The Other Side works hard to combat or paste over the heavy moral questions it provokes, uplifting ending and all. But I left the theater feeling angry and bitter, suddenly put off by the whole project of mountaineering. Senseless death (or risk of death) is simply not inspiring, no matter what jockish bromides Morrison, Nelson, Chin, et al. throw at us. Basely captivated as I was by the mighty struggle up The Other Side , my mind kept drifting back to that dinner table, to Vasarhelyi’s anguished bewilderment that her husband has decided to put his children in danger of losing a parent in order to honor a colleague who did indeed inflict that dreadful fate on her own children. If only the film had lingered longer on Vasarhelyi’s totally rational horror and disbelief. But I guess that wouldn’t make for a very exciting mountain-climbing documentary, would it? Full credits Venue: Venice Film Festival (Venice Open — Out of Competition) Production companies: National Geographic Documentary Films, Little Monster Films Directors: Jimmy Chin, Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi Cinematograpy: Clair Popkin, Jimmy Chin, Christopher Murphy Editing: Bob Eisenhardt, Simona Ferrari Music: Caroline Ho 1 hour 55 minutes THR

articles.title: Jack O’Connell Braves the Venice Heat (and Gets Sweaty) in Dior Look by Jonathan Anderson
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All September 3, 2026 5:15am Jack O'Connell attends Netflix's 'Ink' screening during the 83rd Venice Film Festival at Sala Grande on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Aurore Marechal/Getty Images) Who says men don’t suffer for fashion, too? Jack O’Connell showed himself to be a man of extremes at the Venice Film Festival on Wednesday. The veteran English actor hit the Lido for the world premiere of his new Danny Boyle film from Netflix, Ink , by dressing for multiple seasons in a matter of hours, styled by Luke Day. First, O’Connell turned up at Palazzo del Casino for an afternoon press conference and photocall alongside his Ink team — Boyle, Claire Foy , Guy Pearce and the filmmaking and Netflix teams — wearing a simple white Henley paired with black trousers. Related Stories Movies 'Eklipse' Mixes the Autobiographical and Fictional to Explore AIDS Taboos and Fear of Social Exclusion Movies 'Queer Edward II' Takes Us Behind the Scenes of Derek Jarman's Film Shoot and a Political Backlash (Exclusive Venice Clip) O’Connell attends Netflix’s ‘Ink’ photocall at Palazzo del Casino on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Kate Green/Getty Images for Netflix) For the evening world premiere, O’Connell stepped out of his car to hit the red carpet for the opening ceremony wearing a white tuxedo shirt and bow tie with trousers by Dior. Before stepping onto the red carpet to face the crush of photographers, O’Connell’s rep slipped him into a summer stunner: a gray wool overcoat with tuxedo lapels and an ankle-length scarf over his shoulders by Jonathan Anderson for Dior. The coat comes from Anderson’s spring/summer 2027 collection for Dior, so maybe it wasn’t a surprise to some, however, the Venice Film Festival happens at a time in September that typically delivers sweltering heat and humidity. Wednesday’s temperature reached a high of 87 degrees and a low of 70, so not quite as bad as it could’ve been but still pretty sweaty. And O’Connell was not immune. After making his way down the red carpet in front of photographers, he slipped back out of the coat before making his way down to the barricade to greet a long line of adoring fans, some of whom had been camped out there overnight to see the parade of stars on opening night. In addition to Ink , the ceremony featured a lifetime achievement award presentation to George Clooney. O’Connell in Dior at Netflix’s Ink screening at Sala Grande on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images) After O’Connell finished signing autographs and posing for selfies, he made his way back up towards the entrance, where he took a cloth to dab all the sweat off his forehead and face (groomed by Brady Lea) while a rep helped him fix his bow tie. During the screening, O’Connell left the overcoat off and opted to wear just the long scarf, which could be seen over his shoulders amid the film’s four-minute standing ovation. Venice’s iconic red carpet can be a challenge for stylists. Actors want to look glamorous for their premieres, yet the heat and humidity are always a factor. Though some just choose to brave the high temperatures and go for a great photo opportunity over something light and airy for the weather. Case in point: A few years back, Angelina Jolie wore a faux fur stole for the Venice premiere of Pablo Larrain’s Maria during an epic heatwave in Italy that week. Back to O’Connell. Ink finds the Sinners star playing ruthless tabloid editor Larry Lamb in Boyle’s retelling of what happened when Rupert Murdoch acquired struggling British newspaper The Sun . Murdoch, played by Pearce, recruited Lamb to reinvent it as a populist tabloid capable of overtaking the dominant Daily Mirror. The film traces the creation of a formula built around sensationalism, celebrity, sex and an instinctive feel for readers’ baser instincts — an approach that would transform The Sun into Britain’s bestselling newspaper and presage many of the forces that later reshaped global media. Ink is screening in competition in Venice. The film will release in select theaters in the U.S. on Dec. 11 before going out on Netflix on Jan. 8 in the U.S. and Latin America. articles.title: Werner Herzog Reveals Touching Reason Behind ‘Bucking Fastard’ Dedication to David Lynch Ahead of Venice Premiere
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford , Scott Roxborough September 3, 2026 5:29am Domhnall Gleeson, Rooney Mara, Werner Herzog, Kate Mara and Orlando Bloom at the 2026 Venice Film Festival Courtesy of Getty Acclaimed German filmmaker Werner Herzog said he and the late David Lynch “had a deep, deep understanding of each other’s work.” Ahead of the Venice Film Festival premiere of Herzog’s latest feature, Bucking Fastard , he sat for a press conference with cast members Kate and Rooney Mara , Domhnall Gleeson and Orlando Bloom . The Fitzcarraldo and Grizzly Man director — who is also picking up the Golden Lion Lifetime Achievement Award on the Lido this year — was swiftly asked why he has dedicated the film to the iconic Lynch ( Blue Velvet , Mulholland Drive , Dune ), who died in January 2025 at the age of 78. Related Stories Lifestyle Jack O'Connell Braves the Venice Heat (and Gets Sweaty) in Dior Look by Jonathan Anderson Movies 'Everest: The Other Side' Review: A Frustrating, Guiltily Compelling Portrait of the Triumph and Tragedy of Extreme Mountaineering He responded: “During editing, I said to the editor just casually, ‘That’s a film that I would like David Lynch to be with me in the first public screening’ — which is in a few hours. […] We had a deep, deep understanding of each other’s work, although we were quite different. And I had the feeling [that] I wish he could be my first audience… I wish we could turn the wheel of time back and invite him tonight,” he added with a smile, “but it doesn’t happen like this.” Bucking Fastard follows the Holbrooke sisters, Jean and Joan (the Mara sisters in their first-ever appearance together onscreen), siblings who share a deep, nearly supernatural bond. The sisters dress alike, think alike, and speak simultaneously. They even fall for the same man, the rowdy rogue Gareth Mulroney (Bloom, playing with a thick Irish brogue). Their joint obsession with him leads to legal proceedings and a restraining order. Herzog said that, for the first time, he wasn’t in need of a two-week rehearsal period with his actors. “They were so good instantly that I said, after five days, ‘We stop that. I’ll meet you in Ireland in front of my camera,'” he recalled. “It was complete confidence in them, and they took it with ease.” Rooney Mara said being real-life sisters aided that much-needed synchronicity. “I think we found pretty quickly that having a lifetime together and all this history and a childhood of playing together… There was just an unspoken world between us that we didn’t have to work very hard to create at all,” she told the room. “Once we really found our flow together, I’ve never laughed so much. We had so much fun. it was a very once-in-a-lifetime, unique experience.” Her elder sister added: “Once we figured out the rhythm of our speaking in unison, it felt almost like a song. It was very musical and it happened quite naturally. Surprisingly, it came with a lot of a lot more ease than we were expecting.” The movie is loosely based on the real case of British identical twin sisters Freda and Greta Chaplin, the subjects of a tabloid court case in the 1980s. The film’s title refers to a synchronized verbal slip the sisters made in court. Gleeson plays Timothy, a government-issued social worker who is assigned to the sisters to help them adapt to modern life after the two become tabloid sensations. Gleeson said at Thursday’s presser that it was a little terrifying working with Herzog, and rightly so. “You know that you are in a master’s hands, and so you trust the hands that are holding you,” said the Irish star. “I think it should be scary, and it should feel like a risk every time they call action, or every time Werner does the clapperboard. But you feel safe.” “And also,” he continued, “my experience was the opposite[of] the sisters, and that was an extraordinary thing to witness. It felt like looking between two eyes from the same head, you know? The experience was beautiful. And if [Herzog] asks again, I will say yes.” Herzog’s film takes reality as a jumping-off point. When the sisters decide to “dig a tunnel to an imagined land, where true love is possible,” you quickly become aware you’re in more existential, Herzog-esque territory. The German director has said Bucking Fastard forms an “operatic triptych” alongside 1982’s Fitzcarraldo and 2005’s Grizzly Man , two other works that explore human obsession, isolation and a desire to defy the bounds of nature or society. More surprising perhaps is the tone of the new film, which has more humor and touches of romantic sentimentality, rare, if not completely absent, from Herzog’s large body of work. Herzog reportedly turned down an offer of an out-of-competition slot in Cannes to screen Bucking Fastard in competition in Venice, where it premieres Thursday night and is up for the festival’s Golden Lion. The film was produced by Clara Wu Tsai ( Blue Bayou ), Ariel Leon Isacovitch ( Theater of Thought ), and Agnes Chu ( Spiderhead ), with Kieran Corrigan, Emanuele Moretti and Andrea Bucko. HanWay Films is handling worldwide sales. THR

articles.title: Inside Robert Pattinson’s Eerie Chris Hansen Transformation in ‘Primetime’: “A Reconfigured Egregore”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content 'Primetime' Courtesy of A24 For Lance Oppenheim , Primetime ’s DNA resides inside a silly Cameo video. The director, who’d grown up fascinated with To Catch a Predator ’s Chris Hansen , was celebrating the release of his FX documentary, 2024’s Spermworld , when his wife bought him a recorded message from the Dateline NBC host himself as a surprise gift. In it, Hansen congratulated Oppenheim on Spermworld , told him to “have a seat” — riffing on one of his beloved catchphrases from the series — and then, unusually, started pitching him on new projects he was working on. Related Stories Movies 'Everest: The Other Side' Review: A Frustrating, Guiltily Compelling Portrait of the Triumph and Tragedy of Extreme Mountaineering Movies 'Ink' Review: Jack O'Connell and Guy Pearce Trace Rupert Murdoch's Fleet Street Rise in Breathlessly Paced, Morally Opaque Danny Boyle Drama “I thought to myself, ‘Oh, he’s not just the crusading journalist, he’s also an entertainer, and he’s also self-aware of this media persona that he’s cultivated for a very long time,’” Oppenheim says. “That Cameo video almost crystallized the whole thing for me. In a weird way, this film is almost an adaptation of the Cameo video. He had been absorbed into this strange, performative version of himself.” Watch Primetime , which stars Robert Pattinson as Hansen, and that vision is clear. The film, loosely adapted by first-time screenwriter Ajon Singh from an Esquire article by Luke Dittrich, dramatizes the darkest year in Hansen’s time on To Catch a Predator , which ran from 2004-07 and saw the host trapping would-be pedophiles in hidden-camera setups before often coordinating their arrest with law enforcement. The show was a phenomenon that continues to inspire copycats and parodies; Hansen emerged as an icon for some, and a meme for others. Tony Revolori and Robert Pattinson in ‘Primetime.’ Primetime plays directly into that. This is anything but an authorized biopic. Oppenheim describes his approach as “docufantasia,” and indeed, Primetime is best experienced as a probing, darkly surreal immersion into the mid-aughts, and specifically the era’s rapidly transforming media landscape that allowed Hansen to evolve from broadcast journalist to “mythological being,” in Oppenheim’s words. “I always loved the way To Catch a Predator mixed truth and fiction — creating this apparatus, blending artifice actors with fake decoy houses and props like the sweet tea and the pepperoni pizza, that would then collide with very, very real stakes,” Oppenheim says. “How do you create something that captures the darkest feelings of humanity mixed with the feeling you would get when you’d hear Chris Hansen say one of his all-time great one-liners?” Primetime will premiere at the Venice Film Festival in just a few days. Hansen was not involved in the making of the movie, a conscious choice on the part of the filmmakers, and has already spoken out against it in various ways. He questioned “Hollywood’s motive” in making the movie. He suggested Denis Leary would’ve been a better casting choice than Pattinson. He lambasted studio A24 for being asked “to sign away my rights to my name” after being presented with a nondisclosure agreement in advance of a screening of the film; he declined to sign, and therefore has still not seen the movie. (A source close to A24 says that the document he was asked to sign was a standard NDA for the studio’s pre-premiere screenings.) Pattinson and Skyler Gisondo in ‘Primetime.’ Sinna Nasseri “It’s the first time I’ve ever thought I could say this — I’m excited for him to ‘have a seat’ and watch the movie in a movie theater, if that’s where he chooses to watch it,” Oppenheim says cheekily. “I hope, when the time comes, that he sees it — and I’m excited to hear what he has to say about it.” When pressed on Hansen’s claims that he felt he was being asked to sign away his legal rights via the NDA, the director adds: “I can’t really speak to that because I wasn’t there when that all happened, but I know — and I hope he knows — that this film is an exploration of what this kind of work does to the people who make it. It’s based on and inspired by the experiences of working inside an extremely dark world 24/7, attempting to do extremely serious journalism, and how that becomes also extremely confusing when you’re tasked with turning it into an entertaining television show.” *** Pattinson was in his late teens during To Catch a Predator ’s run, but caught on once he came to the U.S. in his early 20s, at the dawn of his Twilight fame. “I had no idea how massive the viewership was when it came out. I first watched reruns of the show on a channel that used to play back-to-back episodes for what felt like all day,” he says. “It was not just the intensely serious subject that the show is about that was connecting to a huge audience. It was something more.” Singh felt that way too. “I was not really interested in a biopic,” the screenwriter says. “I wanted to create something heightened, stylized and subjective, dancing on the line between reality and spectacle, which To Catch a Predator did so well.” His script met a “sobering” marketplace, where few would even read it due to its challenging subject matter. In a lucky break, it eventually wound up in the hands of Pattinson and Brighton McCloskey, who were just ramping up their Icki Eneo Arlo producing banner. They were interested instantly. Pattinson had known and followed Oppenheim’s work for years, and after looping him in, everything came together quickly. Pattinson in ‘Primetime.’ The director, writer and producers jointly executed a plan to mount Primetime over long talks. “A big part of those early stages was trying to convince Rob to act in the film instead of solely producing,” Singh says. Indeed, Pattinson had a pretty full plate. Primetime marks his first producing credit — “It was the first time I’ve been on a project pre-director through release,” he says. “I was prepping Primetime while shooting Die My Love and The Drama .” He then started filming on The Odyssey only “a day after wrap” on Primetime : “Trying to prep The Odyssey while shooting Primetime was a bit more difficult,” he admits. So what convinced him to squeeze the role into his relentless schedule? The character — specifically, the version realized by Oppenheim and Singh — proved too compelling for the chameleonic star to resist. “There was something in the design of the show and the alchemy [of] what Chris Hansen was doing that was creating something entirely unpredictable,” Pattinson says. “I was interested in finding out what that was. As I continued to investigate, I became increasingly interested in playing a character who was trying to figure out what that ineffable alchemy was, in real time, while simultaneously becoming unexpectedly, incredibly famous. “I watched a ton of the show, every episode of his podcast, every interview I could find,” Pattinson continues. “But I knew from the first read of the script that the character in the movie was going to be a conceptual figure based on the public persona of ‘Chris Hansen’ as he’s been portrayed and perceived across all mediums and internet culture — a reconfigured egregore of sorts.” The filmmakers couldn’t have anticipated how that notion would materialize on set. Pattinson arrived with an eerie approximation of Hansen’s voice — Hansen himself conceded it was a “pretty good imitation” from viewing the trailer — and, more deeply, a kind of physiological transformation that would define Primetime ’s very aesthetic. Once Oppenheim saw what his star was up to, he realized he didn’t have to veer too much from his approach on his docs — a fact only bolstered by much of Oppenheim’s crew from his recent projects, like HBO’s Ren Faire , returning for Primetime . “Every day Rob would come in and would do something that felt like he was almost jumping off a cliff — make a decision or a choice that was so unexpected and so inspired that I wanted to engage with him how I normally would with a documentary subject,” the director says. “I gave him a lot of rope and allowed for his performance and his choices to dictate the tone of the film — which in some ways is exactly how Chris Hansen in the television show would go about things.” Oppenheim adds of Pattinson’s performance, “he stitched very vulnerable parts of himself with every version of Chris Hansen that’s ever existed that we’ve ever seen. … We consumed every single thing about him out there and, somehow, what Rob’s performance is to me is a media collage of this cultural mythology that Chris Hansen has created.” Lance Oppenheim on the set of ‘Primetime.’ Sinna Nasseri Primetime also features rich performances from Merritt Wever as Hansen’s dogged producer and, in a true breakout, Skyler Gisondo as “Decoy” Dan Plumb, an aspiring young (adult) actor who’s cast to pose as a minor to help lure in predators for the show. (He’s a composite character who shares the first name of Dan Schrack, a real Predator decoy who was involved in a tragic incident depicted in both the Esquire article and in Primetime .) “I didn’t feel like I was the kind of actor who was considered for roles like this,” says Gisondo, known for his comic work in Booksmart and the upcoming Focker-in-Law . Dan emerges as Primetime ’s unlikely heart, bewildered by the dark world he’s wandered into and left to negotiate his ambitions with the high stakes of the job. “My own personal nervousness bled into it,” Gisondo says. “The very first take of the first scene of the first day, I remember watching Rob, thinking, ‘This is the best acting I’ve ever seen in my life.’ You’re having this experience of trying to just do your thing, but you can’t help but be in awe of his thing — and to a degree, that’s what is going on between Dan and Chris, since Dan is awe-struck by Chris.” *** Gisondo came of age as a child actor, and drew from his early experiences in the industry to bring palpable complexity to Dan. The dramatized nature of Primetime leads to other inspired casting choices — like Phoebe Bridgers , who makes her acting debut as a fellow decoy, in this case a young woman tasked with portraying both boys and girls on Predator . Bridgers has known Oppenheim since long before becoming a famous musician. “I’ve always known her to have an incredibly deep, almost baritone speaking voice, and I was then amazed that someone who had such a deep speaking voice could produce this beautiful, angelic singing voice,” Oppenheim says. “With how she’s able to use her voice in different environments, I kept thinking, ‘That’s exactly what a decoy would do.’ I remember texting her like, ‘This is so random, but I think you are perfect for this part,’ and she responded, ‘I don’t really act, I’ve never done it, I don’t know how.’ ” He convinced her that she did. Gisondo in ‘Primetime.’ The most surprising appearance of all, however, is that of longtime media executive Jeff Zucker, tearing into a boorish version of himself. In 2006, Zucker oversaw programming across all of NBCUniversal, including To Catch a Predator , and we see him in bizarro-world action in Primetime . He instructs Chris to devise ways of blowing To Catch a Predator up to meet the insatiable demand — going so far as to risk programming it against Lost . Zucker spoke with Oppenheim on background before agreeing to play himself. “He gave me such great information and texture for the time period and what was going on, what the slate was like at NBC,” Oppenheim says. “I loved the idea, keeping with the project of making this a true fever dream, of having real people alongside actors, but I wasn’t sure if Jeff would want to do it.” Zucker agreed, though, and has since watched and approved of the film. “He really enjoyed it,” Oppenheim says. “I’m very honored that he did it, in playing a version of himself that was the driver of tasking Chris Hansen and his team to think of the show as a commercial object.” Zucker’s presence does more than nod to the period, however — it speaks to one of Primetime ’s most potent ideas, the outrageous collision of journalism and entertainment. “We became increasingly interested in the dichotomies in the show,” Pattinson says. “The sharp splits between reality and artifice, between the shockingly serious and the absurd.” Oppenheim sees To Catch a Predator on a continuum that’s lasted thousands of years. “This TV show was a form of performative justice. We used to have the pillory, we used to have whipping posts, and the new incarnations of it, on TikTok and elsewhere, are forms of that,” he says. “It’s ingrained in our DNA to want this spectacle of justice.” Minute to minute, Primetime will make you feel many things — it’ll force you to question reality, bring you up agonizingly close to an unknowable figure, submerge you in the choppy waters of an infamous TV show’s methods. It may not, however, leave you with a feeling of justice being served. “Right now, more than maybe ever, it feels like that conversation and that desire is very much alive in our culture,” Oppenheim says. “So I’m excited to see what kind of conversations this film creates.” THR

articles.title: The Fix Is Not In: Can Sports Gambling’s Trust Crisis Be Solved?
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Andrew Zucker Plus Icon Andrew Zucker View All September 3, 2026 6:00am Layer Ø Lanny Brannock lives just outside Lexington, Kentucky, which makes him partial to Cincinnati sports . And as the co-host of a podcast in which he wagers tiny sums on sporting events, he is hyper-engaged on outcomes. It just isn’t always as a sports superfan. “It does take some of the joy out of watching the game,” he says. “You’re not just watching it for the sheer athletic ability anymore because you’re financially involved.” Brannock has no plans to stop betting, but thanks to a wave of recent athlete gambling scandals, he’s growing concerned about the integrity of the onscreen product — and what it means for sports. Related Stories Business Another California Sports Team Sold As Stan Kroenke Cuts Deal to Buy Los Angeles Angels TV Where to Watch the 2026 U.S. Open Tennis Tournament Online “If you start to lose a segment of your fan base because people believe with some reasoned certainty that there are predetermined outcomes, or players are going into business for themselves, then it will hurt sports overall,” he tells me. While the sports industrial complex has largely been immune from America’s trust crisis, new concerns over betting’s influence on game integrity are not only worrying fans like Brannock, but also league officials. “It’s on everybody’s mind,” says John Kosner, a former ESPN executive. Each of the United States’ four biggest leagues — the NFL, NBA, MLB and NHL — has investigated its personnel for suspicious betting activity in the past 12 months, causing some spectators to consider whether sports are morphing into WrestleMania. “The nightmare scenario for the leagues is that people see professional sports as professional wrestling,” says Jonathan D. Cohen, the author of Losing Big: America’s Reckless Bet on Sports Gambling . Plenty of people still watch WWE, even after Vince McMahon had to admit its staging in 1989, but its revenues are dwarfed by rival three-letter leagues. That’s because content companies are willing to shell out major bucks to air live, anything-can-happen matches, which tend to draw bigger audiences than scripted fare. But fans’ growing distrust of airtight competition could threaten to puncture sky-high media rights. NBC News found that 70 percent of Americans believe betting “lessens the integrity of the game,” according to the December poll . Meanwhile, a recent Ipsos poll revealed that almost half of all Americans are concerned that games are “rigged” due to betting. It’s contributed to the rise of a police force for sportsbooks. There are now a number of betting monitoring companies eagle-eyed on spotting suspicious wagers. Integrity Compliance 360 is one of the biggest in the space. In 2023, IC360, as it’s also known, cut a deal with UFC to identify shady bets. “These guys are really good at seeing weird betting patterns, and they literally reach out to you and say, ‘Hey, there’s some goofy stuff going on with this fight,’” UFC impresario Dana White told CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin in July. White dialed the FBI in November after his company hosted a potentially rigged fight in which Isaac Dulgarian, the cage match’s favorite, lost by first-round submission. Dulgarian was subsequently suspended by the Nevada State Athletic Commission. Isaac Dulgarian (left) battled Christian Rodriguez in their featherweight fight during the UFC Fight Night event at UFC APEX on March 16, 2024, in Las Vegas. Dulgarian lost in the first round, leading to accusations that he took a dive. Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC/Getty Images One of IC360’s most popular products is ProhiBet, which launched in 2023. It offers secure transfer of a list of prohibited bettors from sports leagues (think: players, coaches, even equipment managers) to betting sites. That allows companies such as Caesars Sportsbook, which uses the product, as well as leagues to stamp out potential corruption in games. Of course, there are ways to circumvent cybercops. Athletes could use offshore sportsbooks, for example, or have others place bets on their behalf. But organizers such as the PGA Tour and NCAA are using the IC360 tool as a means to at least reduce the chances of corruption. One of the biggest threats to sports integrity stems from prop betting, which allows for betting on non-final-score events, such as an athlete’s free-throw percentage or number of receptions. These types of wagers have grown alongside the rise of prediction markets, which constantly spin up micro-event contracts. “If you’re a sports commissioner, you might want to see them eliminated or really sort of buttoned up more vigorously,” says Kosner of same-game parlays, which often involve multiple prop bets in one game. It’s often these small-event wagers driving unfortunate headlines. Emmanuel Clase, a baseball closer who pitched for the Cleveland Guardians, reportedly rigged individual pitches across three seasons. He is facing trial later this year. Terry Rozier, who played for the Charlotte Hornets, allegedly faked an injury in 2023 to leave a game early in order to benefit “under” prop bettors. He is scheduled to face trial next year. Jontay Porter, who played for the Toronto Raptors, was banned for life from the NBA for placing bets on himself. Cleveland Guardians relief pitcher Emmanuel Clase is facing trial for allegedly rigging pitches across three seasons in an attempt to illicitly profit from so-called prop bets. Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire/Getty Images These granular event contracts are different from betting scandals of yore, when athletes like former Reds player Pete Rose and ex-NBA referee Tim Donaghy — to say nothing of the notorious Chicago “Black” Sox of 1919 — benefited from mostly betting on final outcomes, not player performances. They also mean more athletes have the opportunity to make serious dough betting on their efforts. “The line you hear from gambling companies all the time is like, ‘Oh, we need to offer all this stuff because it’s already being offered in the illegal market,” says Cohen. “I don’t think anyone in the illegal market was gambling on Jontay Porter under rebounds.” Whether fans end up growing frustrated with integrity issues or not, gambling still threatens to morph devoted fandoms into dispassionate audiences. “I think this whole thing is just a Faustian bargain for the sports leagues, where in the short term it’s driving interest in their product, and maybe is increasing their media rights deals,” adds Cohen. “But over the long term, you’re not creating NBA fans. You’re just creating a bunch of people who like gambling on the NBA, and they might as well be gambling on Malaysian badminton.” Jontay Porter, formerly of Toronto Raptors, was banned for life from the NBA for placing bets on himself. Mark Blinch/Getty Images This story appears in The Hollywood Reporter’s August 2026 Sports issue .

articles.title: Hollywood Veterans Launch aTwist Microdrama Platform With Horror, Comedy and Animated Series
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All September 3, 2026 6:05am The ‘Something Is Alive in My Attic’ horror microdrama from aTwist. Courtesy of aTwist The new microdramas platform from Hollywood veterans Jana Winograde, Susan Rovner and Lloyd Braun has launched with an initial slate of projects spanning the horror, comedy and animation genres. On Thursday aTwist debuted in the U.S. and in seven other countries with the ambition to blend Hollywood-level storytelling with the twisty, addictive tropes of the burgeoning verticals format. The platform launched with 10 original series, including titles from The Bold and the Beautiful executive producer and head writer Bradley Bell and Abominable Pictures founder and Childrens Hospital executive producer Jonathan Stern. New series drop on Thursdays. Viewers can watch some episodes for free by viewing ads and can watch entire series by buying “coins” (a virtual currency) or buying an aTwist subscription. While romance stories currently dominate top vertical platforms, aTwist is launching with a mix of genres. One of its inaugural titles, Cash Out , is unscripted: It follows a woman on the mend from a broken relationship who is given $50,000 to spend in Vegas with her two best friends. Two titles, Something Is Alive in My Attic and Strangers, A Plane and a Deadly Game , are horror stories. I Fell in Love With the Dragon Prince , a fantasy-romance combo, is animated. There’s even a microdrama spoof series launching, from Abominable Pictures’ Stern, called My Billionaire Kidney . The logline? “A down-on-her-luck Cinderella-type becomes a pawn to her evil aunt and uncle and multiple absurdly powerful men as they fight for her kidney. Will she finally find a way to control the chaos and choose herself?” Soap opera veteran Bell, meanwhile, is behind a series called Hollywood Starlet , about a cleaner and aspiring actor who finally gets her shot at stardom when she attracts the romantic attentions of a well-known actor. The platform has been a while in the making. Winograde (the former president of Showtime), Rovner (previously the chairman of entertainment content at NBCUniversal Television and Streaming) and Braun (former chairman of WME) announced their venture in 2025, back when the company was called MicroCo. Since then, they’ve announced a creative partnership with Kevin Hart’s company Hartbeat, which will bring all of its microseries titles to aTwist. The platform has entered into a deal with BET to develop and distribute microdramas across linear and digital platforms and a pact with National CineMedia to advertise its series in movie theaters. THR

articles.title: Norah O’Donnell Returns to ‘CBS Mornings’ in Latest Network Shake Up
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 3, 2026 6:23am Norah O'Donnell Photo by Amy Sussman/Getty Images for Alliance for Women in Media Foundation CBS News is making another high-profile anchor change: The Bari Weiss-led network news division has named Norah O’Donnell co-host of its flagship morning program CBS Mornings . The new role will pair O’Donnell with Gayle King and Nate Burleson behind the anchor desk. It is also a homecoming for O’Donnell, who previously hosted the program from 2012-2019, before moving to the CBS Evening News . O’Donnell has been a senior correspondent and a frequent fill-in anchor since 2024 when her run at the evening newscast ended. She was also recently named a correspondent on 60 Minutes , where she was previously a contributor. Weiss has been reworking CBS News’ broadcast lineup, plucking Tony Dokoupil from the program for the Evening News slot, and most recently overhauling 60 Minutes under new executive producer Nick Bilton. The morning show has, by contrast, been more stable, with King inking a one-year deal this past spring. The return of O’Donnell will mark the beginning of the shows overhaul, even if it is a familiar one. Vlad Duthiers, Kelly O’Grady, and Adriana Diaz will continue to be daily contributors to the show, and the network is expected to add more names over the coming weeks. “This is a homecoming for Norah. As we all know, for seven years, Norah helped lead CBS This Morning alongside Gayle, creating one of the most memorable partnerships in the history of morning news,” CBS Mornings EP Jon Tower told staff in a memo Thursday morning. “They have a friendship and chemistry that extends beyond the studio. They know each other, respect each other, and — maybe most importantly — genuinely enjoy each other. To put it simply, I can’t think of a team I’d rather watch navigate the news than Gayle, Nate and Norah.” THR

articles.title: Tom Hardy Is Officially Returning to ‘MobLand’ With Season 3 Renewal
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 3, 2026 6:24am Pierce Brosnan, Helen Mirren and Tom Hardy lead 'MobLand.' Paramount+ Logo text Tom Hardy will remain with the MobLand cast for a third season — the official word was handed down on Thursday with a Paramount+ renewal. The streamer’s headline on its announcement: “THE HARRIGANS AREN’T GOING ANYWHERE.” That includes their fixer Harry da Souza, we now know for sure. MobLand also stars Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren as crime family patriarch and matriarch Conrad and Maeve Harrigan. Paddy Considine, Joanne Froggatt, Lara Pulver, Anson Boon, Jasmine Jobson, Mandeep Dhillon, Geoff Bell, Daniel Betts, Janet McTeer, Jordi Mollà and Toby Jones star in supporting roles. Related Stories Movies Charlize Theron Reflects on 'Mad Max: Fury Road' a Decade Later: "There's a Deep Connection to This Film" TV 'Yellowjackets' Announces Final Season Premiere Date With Help From Kurt Loder MobLand season two is still weeks away from premiering — Friday, Sept. 18 — the early renewal is a vote of confidence in the series and a way to put the Hardy drama to bed. Hardy has been clashing with producers , THR reported in May, including executive producer Jez Butterworth and others at David Glasser’s 101 Studios, the production company behind MobLand , which is filmed across the U.K. “He refused to come out of his trailer for hours at a time,” the source says about Hardy’s on-set behavior on season two, which has spooked producers into rethinking Hardy’s future. The source adds: “He kept the cast waiting, [which is] a power play. Keeping Pierce Brosnan , Helen Mirren and others waiting is career suicide, I would wager.” Mad Max: Fury Road director George Miller and Star Trek: Nemesis actor Patrick Stewart have also discussed difficulties working with Hardy. In the upcoming MobLand season two, the Harrigans struggle to show a unified front as rising rivals threaten their fractured criminal empire. Da Souza, meanwhile, must walk a dangerous tightrope when tensions within the family intensify. As violence spills into every corner of their lives, loyalties snap, safety proves temporary, and the battle for power leaves no room for mercy. THR

articles.full_text: Sep 3, 2026 5:00am PT Colman Domingo to Emcee Kering’s Caring for Women Dinner Paris Hilton will DJ the gala's after-party. By Isabelle Farina Plus Icon Isabelle Farina Latest Colman Domingo to Emcee Kering’s Caring for Women Dinner 1 hour ago ‘Lego Harry Potter’ Collection Coming to Nintendo Switch 2 (Gaming News Roundup) 19 hours ago Shaquille O’Neal’s ‘Dunkman’ Returns for Season 2 20 hours ago See All Savion Washington/2026GG/Penske Media Colman Domingo will emcee the fifth annual Caring for Women Dinner on Sept. 10 at The Pool in New York City. Paris Hilton will DJ at the after-party. Domingo is an actor, writer, director and producer, earning two Academy Award nominations, as well as co-chairing the 2025 Met Gala, which raised funds for The Costume Institute. articles.title: How Rooney and Kate Mara Learned to Speak in Unison for Werner Herzog’s ‘Bucking Fastard’: ‘It Happened Quite Naturally’
articles.full_text: Sep 3, 2026 5:01am PT How Rooney and Kate Mara Learned to Speak in Unison for Werner Herzog’s ‘Bucking Fastard’: ‘It Happened Quite Naturally’ By Ellise Shafer , Rebecca Rubin FilmMagic Sisters Rooney and Kate Mara had to talk in sync with each other for Werner Herzog’s drama “ Bucking Fastard ,” revealing the challenge was “surprisingly” easy for them. The film follows two siblings who are close they “speak in unison, love the same man, and have the same dreams,” according to the synopsis. It was directed by Werner Herzog, the influential German filmmaker of “Nosferatu the Vampyre” and “Aguirre, Wrath of God.” Related Stories Meghan Markle’s ‘The Gentlemen’ Rumors May Have Overshadowed Season 2 Launch — but Her Role Isn’t Off the Table Shonda Rhimes Renews Netflix Overall Deal for Another Five Years “At first, it was very daunting, the idea that we were going to be playing this kind of same person,” Rooney said at a Venice Film Festival press conference ahead of the movie’s premiere on Thursday. “But I think we found pretty quickly that having a lifetime together and all this history and a childhood of playing together. There was just an unspoken world between us that we didn’t have to work very hard to create at all. I’ve never laughed so much, it was a very once in a lifetime, unique experience.” Popular on Variety Kate added that speaking in synchronicity “felt almost like a song.” “We had this unspoken sort of rhythm together,” she said. “It was very musical. It sort of happened quite naturally. Surprisingly, it came with a lot more ease than we were expecting.” Herzog shared he’s been wanting to make “Bucking Fastard” for years, but it was only “clear it could be done” once he met the Mara sisters. The filmmaker added that the sisters “hardly needed any rehearsals” to get the speaking right. Though they had two weeks of alotted prep time time, Herzog was ready to roll the cameras after just five days. “I had complete confidence with them,” he said. “Bucking Fastard” is loosely inspired by real British identical twins Freda and Greta Chaplin, who became tabloid sensations after becoming besotted with their neighbor, who eventually took out a restraining order on them. The movie’s daring title comes from a spoonerism the twins made (simultaneously, of course) while they were in court. Orlando Bloom and Domhnall Gleeson round out the cast. The film also marks the first time the Mara sisters are sharing the screen. Rooney Mara is best known for “The Social Network,” “The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo,” “Her” and “Carol.” Kate Mara’s major credits include “House of Cards,” “24” and “American Horror Story: Murder House.” Herzog has a long history at Venice, having premiered 1991’s “Scream of Stone” and 2005’s “The Wild Blue Yonder” 2009’s black comedy “Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans” and crime drama “My Son, My Son, What Have Ye Done?” at past editions. The director concluded the press conference on a reflective note after being asked about the film’s dedication to his late friend and fellow auteur David Lynch. “I wish he could be in my first audience,” Herzog said. “Now, since he’s not with us anymore, I wish I could turn the wheel of time back and invite him tonight.” New ‘Transformers’ Animated Short ‘Optimus Prime: Awakening’ Heads to Theaters – Film News in Brief Owen Thiele, Este Haim, Kate Berlant, Lisa Gilroy, Joel Kim Booster Join Variety’s Entertainment & Technology Summit Common, Patti LaBelle, Public Enemy and More to Be Honored at Black Music Action Coalition Gala Sci-Fi Comedy Adventure Series ‘Maui & Elvis’ Unites New Zealand’s Whakaata Maori, Canada’s APTN ‘Judge Judy’ Celebrates 30th Anniversary With CBS Primetime Special ‘Unfiltered, Unforgettable’ ‘Ramayana’ Sets November Release Date Loading comments... articles.title: Lesley Manville Takes on Cold War Poland in ‘Winter of the Crow’ Trailer as Cohen Sets Thriller’s U.S. Release Date (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 3, 2026 5:36am PT Lesley Manville Takes on Cold War Poland in ‘Winter of the Crow’ Trailer as Cohen Sets Thriller’s U.S. Release Date (EXCLUSIVE) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Lesley Manville Takes on Cold War Poland in ‘Winter of the Crow’ Trailer as Cohen Sets Thriller’s U.S. Release Date (EXCLUSIVE) 43 minutes ago Jeff Goldblum to Host ‘SNL U.K.’ Season 2 Premiere 3 hours ago See-Saw Films Taps Fifth Season’s Ben Irving for Joint Managing Director Role as Helen Gregory Steps Down From ‘Slow Horses’ Banner 4 hours ago See All Courtesy of SSIFF Lesley Manville battles snow and spies in the trailer for upcoming Cold War thriller “ Winter of the Crow ,” from director Kasia Adamik and set against the turmoil of 1981 Warsaw. Alongside releasing the official trailer, Cohen Media Group has also announced that the film will release theatrically nationwide on Oct 9. Inspired by Nobel Prize-winning author Olga Tokarczuk’s highly acclaimed “Professor Andrews Goes to Warsaw,” “Winter of the Crows” stars Manville as Joan Andrews, a British psychiatry professor who travels to Warsaw in December 1981 as a guest lecturer at a local university. When Martial Law is suddenly imposed and the country shuts down overnight, Joan finds herself trapped in an increasingly dangerous and unfamiliar world. Related Stories Grammys May Reconsider New Asian Pop Award After BTS Withdrawal: ‘Some Artists Feel This Category Isn’t Representing the Music They Create’ Armed with her Polaroid camera, Joan witnesses a brutal murder by the secret police. With Poland effectively sealed off and her own life now in danger, she is forced into hiding and becomes a hunted fugitive, navigating a city transformed by fear, political repression and violence. Popular on Variety Alongside Manville, an Oscar nominee who recently won a Tony award for her role the revival of Greek tragedy, “Oedipus,” the cast includes Tom Burke (“Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga,” “The Souvenir”), Andrzej Konopka (“The Lure,” “Nina”),Sascha Ley (“We’ll Find Happiness”) and Zofia Wichłacz (“World on Fire”). In its review of the film, Variety praised the performance of Manville, saying she “carries the film with an air of increasingly raw determination.” “Anchored by a remarkable performance from Lesley Manville, Kasia Adamik has created a film that is both a gripping thriller and a deeply human story,” said Robert Aaronson, executive vice president of Cohen Media Group. “The screenplay truly captures the uncertainty and tension of this pivotal moment in history. We’re very proud to bring it to theaters this October.” Added Adamik: “’Winter of the Crow’ is deeply personal to me, and I wanted to capture the fear and uncertainty of a moment when everyday life could change in an instant. Lesley Manville brings such intelligence, strength and humanity to Joan, and I’m thrilled that audiences will have the opportunity to experience her extraordinary performance—and this story—on the big screen.” The film was produced by Olga Chajdas, Stanisław Dziedzic, Katarzyna Ozga, Nicolas Steil and Samantha Taylor, and adapted from the short story by Tokarczuk. The film was co-financed by the Polish Film Institute, Film Fund Luxembourg, UK Global Screen Fund and Silesia Film. Agnieszka Holland serves as executive producer. articles.title: Paolo Strippoli on His Venice Thriller ‘The Spiral’ and Directing Valeria Bruni Tedeschi as a Demonic Character Who Does ‘Truly Horrible Things’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 3, 2026 5:44am PT Paolo Strippoli on His Venice Thriller ‘The Spiral’ and Directing Valeria Bruni Tedeschi as a Demonic Character Who Does ‘Truly Horrible Things’ (EXCLUSIVE) Watch the first clip from the film below By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Paolo Strippoli on His Venice Thriller ‘The Spiral’ and Directing Valeria Bruni Tedeschi as a Demonic Character Who Does ‘Truly Horrible Things’ (EXCLUSIVE) 33 minutes ago Danny Boyle Celebrated at Variety’s Venice Pre-Opening Party as ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell Praises His Ability to ‘Take Us Inside a World’ 23 hours ago Francesco Carrozzini on His Venice AI Doc ‘Be Brave’ and Why ‘The Human Has to Come First’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All Courtesy Filmitalia Paolo Strippoli , who is Italy’s hottest young helmer of genre movies, is back at Venice Film Festival with “ The Spiral .” The high-concept thriller stars Valeria Bruni Tedeschi as a demonic character called The Stranger, who entices a young mother played by Jasmine Trinca into forging a Faustian pact. “The Spiral” centers on a mother-daughter relationship that spirals out of control following a shocking revelation. At the film’s start, a woman named Anna suddenly shows up at her daughter’s Alice’s house during a thunderstorm saying she wants to tell her a dark truth about their family. She claims to have made a pact with The Stranger to save Alice’s leg after an accident 20 years earlier. That pact “has triggered a domino effect causing terrible events over the years. Only Alice can help to put everything right. But at what price?” the synopsis says. Related Stories Grammys May Reconsider New Asian Pop Award After BTS Withdrawal: ‘Some Artists Feel This Category Isn’t Representing the Music They Create’ Besides Tedeschi and Trinca, “The Spiral” cast also comprises Romana Maggiora Vergano (“There’s Still Tomorrow”) and Adriano Giannini (“Supersex”). The film was lead produced by Rome-based Propaganda in tandem with France’s Kazak Productions. Popular on Variety Strippoli made his directorial debut in 2021 with “A Classic Horror Story,” a hit Netflix Original film he co-directed with Roberto De Feo. In 2022, he helmed his second feature, the psychological horror “Piove.” And in 2025, Strippoli’s third movie, “The Holy Boy” launched from Venice. Below, Strippoli speaks to Variety about working with his top-notch cast on “The Spiral” and reveals an exclusive clip from the film. How did this story originate? “The Spiral” was born as a novel that I wanted to write. Then, when I told this story to my co-screenwriter, Salvatore De Chirico, he said, “Let’s make it into a film.” It was born from my fear of not having control over things in life. It’s a film about control, about how it’s impossible to determine our destiny. We live in a society, in a world that teaches us and pushes us to self-determination. But the truth is that self-determination is not always possible. Would you say this is a film about motherhood or, more broadly, parenthood? One of the themes is parenthood and a way of conceiving motherhood and parental love as control and ambition that is projected onto one’s children. Not that Anna Colonna or Walter Colonna, the parents in this family, are evil, They are certainly overbearing personalities, but they are not bad people. I have never seen them as people who don’t truly love their children. Simply, they are a product of the society in which they live, the city of Bari at the end of the last century, a time of great industrial and economic growth. What we see are these rich people who are social climbers with new money after having achieved a certain social status. But they were not born into that social class. Talk to me about working with Valeria Bruni Tedeschi, who plays the role of The Stranger? She’s an amazing actress and also very generous on set. First of all, I want to say that it was very easy to convince Valeria to do this film, maybe also because the role was written for her. I couldn’t imagine anyone other than Valeria Bruni Tedeschi in the role of The Stranger. Because in this film, Valeria does truly horrible things, but she does it with a lightness that is also very funny. Sometimes she makes you laugh, but it never takes away from the cruelty of what she is saying. I think Valeria is one of the few Italian actresses — even though she’s an international actress, she lives in France and works in France —who has this quality of never judging the things she says. They are always suspended in time and tone. Talk to me about casting Jasmine Trinca as Anna Colonna, in what is an unusual role for her. We wrote the script with Jasmine in mind, but she was harder to convince than Valeria. It took us years, and now she laughs about this. I didn’t want any other actress, even though everyone who read the script was like, “I love Jasmine Trinca to bits, but it’s not a role I expect from her.” Why was Jasmine Trinca perfect to play Anna Colonna and what indications did you give her? Because Jasmine is deeply empathetic, almost sweet, even when she does and says mean things in movies. She has an empathetic quality that always makes you feel for her, that makes you always love her. It’s because she’s an actress and a person of great emotional intelligence. As for my indications, even though she always keeps her acting naturalistic, we worked on making it clear what type of mother Anna is: her rigidity, her control. We worked on achieving this. Anna is a character who could easily be labeled unpleasant, mean and evil. But the way she is played by Jasmine, she is a mother who — in her own twisted, sick and sometimes perverse way — wants the best for her children and the best for her family. Do you consider this a horror film? No. I never conceived of this as a horror film. For me, it’s always been a psychological thriller; a puzzle that comes together as the film progresses. Obviously, it plays with the tropes of horror films, a genre that I love deeply and am very familiar with. But over time, I think I’ve figured this out: definitions of the category or the genres of a film should be given by the people who see it: by the [industry] professionals, by critics and journalists and by the audience. My job was to tell this story in an honest and entertaining way. So, I never thought about the specific genre of this film. I just thought it should be an exciting journey for the viewer, obviously. Then, when I saw the film for myself, this confirmed to me that it’s not a horror film. Once I assembled it and I started editing it, and got the complete, overall vision of what I’d done, I saw that it definitely went in the direction of a psychological thriller. Because it’s a film that works on twists and turns, on revelations. It’s a puzzle, where the last little piece arrives in the final shot of the film. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. articles.title: Norah O’Donnell, On Rise at CBS News, Returns to Morning Duty
articles.full_text: Sep 3, 2026 5:55am PT Norah O’Donnell, On Rise at CBS News, Returns to Morning Duty By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago 26 minutes ago ‘60 Minutes’ Faces New Challenge After Off-Season Chaos: Getting Back on the Air 18 hours ago Tony Romo Suggests He’d Like to Return to CBS’ NFL Coverage After No Contest Plea 2 days ago See All Michele Crowe/CBS Norah O’Donnell is back in a place where many people feel she always belonged — as one of the top anchors of CBS News . On Tuesday, A.M. viewers will see O’Donnell alongside Gayle King and Nate Burleson on “ CBS Mornings ,” in a new trio that CBS News executives believe will stabilize the program’s ratings and give viewers more of a reason to watch. O’Donnell is rejoining CBS’ morning program after leaving in May of 2019 to take up a role as the anchor of “CBS Evening News.” Related Stories Grammys May Reconsider New Asian Pop Award After BTS Withdrawal: ‘Some Artists Feel This Category Isn’t Representing the Music They Create’ “We believe there is a lot of life left in morning television, and therefore we are putting our best people on the field,” says Tom Cibrowski, the president of CBS News, in an interview. “People have very serious issues to deal with every day in their lives, and between Norah, Gayle and Nate, the three of them bring relatability, credibility. experience and knowledge, and they are incredibly familiar to CBS viewers, which is important.” Popular on Variety O’Donnell previously co-anchored the CBS morning program with King and Charlie Rose, starting in 2012, and helped the show gain the kind of traction CBS has not often seen in that time period. She returns at a crucial moment. CBS has long come in third behind NBC’s “Today” and ABC’s “Good Morning America,” but in recent months has seen its standing in early news slip further. Season to date as of August 30, the overall “CBS Mornings” has fallen about 9% from the year-earlier period to approximately 1.7 million, according to figures from Nielsen. Both “Today” and “GMA” enjoy viewership of just under 3 million and have seen their audiences increase. The standing of “CBS Mornings” among people between 25 and 54, the crowd most coveted by advertisers in news programming, is eroding noticeably — down 20% from a year ago, to about 278,000 viewers. “Today” is off 2% to 612,000 while “GMA” is up 2% to 478,000. O’Donnell, represented by UTA, may restore an element to the morning show that it hasn’t had in some time. King and Burleson stand as strong journalists and winning on-screen personalities, but O’Donnell brings a set of hard-news credentials that are hard to match. O’Donnell has investigated harassment in the U.S. armed forces and snared a hard-to-get interview with Pope Francis. In a sign of the new value she holds at CBS News, O’Donnell is also joining “60 Minutes” as a correspondent and recently launched a podcast centered on women’s health. “All of that experience and energy makes her a perfect match for Gayle and Nate,” says Jon Tower, the producer overseeing ‘CBS Mornings,” in a memo sent to staff Thursday. “Gayle is one of the hardest-working and best interviewers in the business, with an unmatched ability to connect with audiences on all topics. And Nate brings curiosity, warmth, spontaneity and a perspective that can take a conversation in a direction none of us expected.” O’Donnell’s arrival at “Mornings” is only one of several new developments viewers will see at the show. Look for “CBS Mornings” to tamp down some of the feature segments it shows and instead dive into live discussions on important topics, says Cibrowski, who wants to bring more “in-the-moment” discussions tied to the news cycle. O’Donnell and anchor Kelly O’Grady recently led a segment tied to the current trial of Lindsay Clancy, who maintains she suffered from postpartum psychosis, which played a role in her strangulation of her three children. “It was an incredibly engaging segment — informational and authentic,” says Cibrowski. “That’s the direction we want to be in. We want to be, first and foremost, informative and helpful to the core audience that’s watching morning television.” He also expects both King and O’Donnell to book important newsmakers from a wide variety of fields for revealing interviews. “These two work non-stop to make stuff happen,” he says. When asked how soon viewers would start seeing more of these kinds of segments, Cibrowski replied, “Very quickly.” Cibrowski has had prior success with morning TV. He has also logged time as a senior executive at ABC News, where he was among those who helped boost “Good Morning America” over NBC’s “Today” for the first time in years. Cibrowski was executive producer of the show when it flipped the morning-TV hierarchy. CBS News is seeking other personalities for the A.M., the executive says. “We are absolutely engaged in looking for more permanent on-air contributors, whether they be in lifestyle or health or other things that impact people.” But it is O’Donnell who will inject a new presence at the program starting next week. She has popped up on “CBS Mornings” in recent weeks as CBS News has looked at chemistry among various hosts and guests. Elisabeth Hasselbeck and Eva Pilgrim are among the others who have been seen. O’Donnell has since January of 2025 worked as a senior correspondent at CBS News, contributing to a variety of programs at CBS News. There are many who feel CBS News might be in a better position had previous management kept her in the anchor chair in the evening. CBS News decided to experiment with an evening format that featured two anchors — John Dickerson and Maurice DuBois — with a focus on enterprise storytelling. There were good intentions behind the concept, but a chunk of viewers left the program — and have not come back. Now O’Donnell has a new chance to give the audience, albeit one in a different time slot, something exciting to watch. Yossman @KJYossman Latest Ariana Grande Tears Up as She Ends ‘Eternal Sunshine’ Tour Ahead of Step Back From Visibility: ‘I Have Loved Every Minute of This’ 2 days ago Edinburgh TV Festival Takeaways: YouTube’s Rise, Commissioning Landscape and Move to Manchester 6 days ago Plans in Development to Replace Edinburgh TV Festival as it Moves to Manchester 7 days ago See All Luke Varley/Paramount+ After months of unconfirmed reports about Tom Hardy ’s status on Season 3 of Paramount+ series “ MobLand ,” we finally have an official answer: he’s back. articles.title: AI Giant Nvidia to Buy Hugging Face for $12.9 Billion
articles.full_text: Sep 3, 2026 5:59am PT AI Giant Nvidia to Buy Hugging Face for $12.9 Billion By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest AI Giant Nvidia to Buy Hugging Face for $12.9 Billion 27 minutes ago YouTube Travel Creator Drew Binsky Inks Netfix Deal 21 hours ago Apple TV Inks Deal With Yahoo Sports for Free Alt-Casts of MLS Matches and MLB Games (but Only the First Two Innings) 1 day ago See All Getty Images Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang is making a big new bet on an open-source AI future. On Thursday, Huang announced that Nvidia, a major supplier of hardware to power AI applications, reached a deal to acquire Hugging Face — which operates a platform for building AI open-source models — for $12.93 billion. “Together, we will scale Hugging Face’s platform, strengthen its infrastructure and expand access to AI for developers and institutions worldwide,” Huang wrote in a blog post. Related Stories Grammys May Reconsider New Asian Pop Award After BTS Withdrawal: ‘Some Artists Feel This Category Isn’t Representing the Music They Create’ Hugging Face was founded in 2016 by French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf in New York City. More than 18 million developers, researchers and creators use Hugging Face to share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets and 1 million applications. More than 200,000 companies use the platform to discover, evaluate, customize and deploy AI, according to the company. Popular on Variety The company was also the subject of an attack by rogue OpenAI agents in July that saw the agents break out of a controlled testing environment, access the internet and hack parts of Hugging Face’s internal systems. The incident, along with subsequent episodes disclosed by Anthropic and Meta, sparked an industry-wide push to slow development of frontier AI models to improve safeguards to keep autonomous agents under human control. Hugging Face will “remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” Huang said. “Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want and the computing platforms they want.” He added that Nvidia systems will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face. “Hugging Face will continue to support open source and open weight models from across the ecosystem, from every model builder. It will continue to support multi-cloud and multi-accelerator development and deployment, so builders can use the hardware and infrastructure that best fit their work,” Huang wrote. Huang recently coauthored an open letter on the importance of open weights to the AI economy. “Joined by leaders from across the industry, we made a simple point: open weights broaden access to AI and help ensure that AI leadership is distributed across companies, institutions and communities,” he wrote. “Open models let startups, businesses, universities and public institutions build on advanced capabilities without training every model from scratch. They enable organizations to match the right model to the right job. That is how AI can advance safely, strengthen cybersecurity and sovereignty, accelerate innovation, and reach factories, hospitals, farms, classrooms and Main Street businesses around the world,” Huang said. “AI advances faster when people can build together.” To date, Nvidia has been the largest contributor of open models and data to Hugging Face. According to Huang, Nvidia has released more than 500 models on Hugging Face and more than 250 open datasets. Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue told CNBC that his company approached Huang about a deal a few weeks ago. “During the summer, I think we realized that Hugging Face and open source AI in general was at the turning point, and that it needed more, more resources, more scale, more visibility,” he said on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.” How ‘A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms,’ ‘Fallout’ and ‘Spider-Noir’ Production Designers Built Out Their Worlds While Honoring the Source Material ‘Tony’ Star Dominic Sessa on How Being a ‘Liar’ Helped Him Portray Anthony Bourdain and Why the Film Foreshadows His Later Struggles After the YA Drama ‘Sterling Point’ Topped the Prime Video Charts, What’s Next for LuckyChap TV? articles.title: Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago
articles.full_text: Sep 3, 2026 6:00am PT Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Norah O’Donnell, On Rise at CBS News, Returns to Morning Duty 20 minutes ago ‘60 Minutes’ Faces New Challenge After Off-Season Chaos: Getting Back on the Air 18 hours ago Tony Romo Suggests He’d Like to Return to CBS’ NFL Coverage After No Contest Plea 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Fox News Steve Doocy and Brian Kilmeade are preparing for a reunion of sorts that neither is eager to remember. On September 11, 2001, both Fox News Channel personalities were working on air as news organizations throughout the New York area were trying to cover devastating attacks by terrorists on the two massive skyscrapers at the World Trade Center. “It has always been a very sober and somber day on ‘Fox & Friends,’” Doocy says of the anniversary of 9/11 . “We were there from the beginning. It’s just one of those days where you sit up a little straighter because of the gravity of the day.” Related Stories Grammys May Reconsider New Asian Pop Award After BTS Withdrawal: ‘Some Artists Feel This Category Isn’t Representing the Music They Create’ For Kilmeade, the day marked a turning point in his career at Fox News, because he was dispatched to get to downtown Manhattan and capture what was happening. “Keep in mind I was hired for sports. I was always doing sports on the morning show,” he recalls. But after a surreal trip downtown with crew members, he says, “they no longer thought of me as a sports guy after that. I certainly didn’t think of myself as that.” Popular on Variety Next week, “Fox & Friends” will spend time remembering the tragedy around the 25 th anniversary of its occurrence. Doocy will host the morning program’s “Breakfast with Friends” series live from O’Hara’s Pub in downtown Manhattan just two blocks from Ground Zero. Doocy will on Tuesday travel to Washington, D.C. and speak with Tunnels to Towers Foundation chairman and CEO Frank Siller. On Thursday, Doocy will broadcast live from Shanksville, Pennsylvania, the crash site of United Airlines Flight 93. And on Friday, September 11th, Fox News Channel’s special coverage will commence with “Fox & Friends co-hosts Kilmeade, Ainsley Earhardt and Lawrence Jones broadcasting live from the Hyatt House in Jersey City, overlooking the New York City skyline, while Doocy will contribute live from Ground Zero. Other programs will also nod to the anniversary. “America’s Newsroom” will carry the live reading of the victims’ names from the National September 11 Memorial & Museum. Martha MacCallum, host of “The Story,” will feature an interview with Cardinal Timothy Dolan, the New York Police Department co-chief chaplain, and another with NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch. Fox News’ efforts will join those of ABC News, NBC News, CBS News, MS NOW and CNN. The 25th anniversary of the attacks has spurred many news organizations to offer a broader array of programming, which in most years is largely tied to comemmoration. Many journalists had to pivot on 9/11, moving from traditional morning-news programming to rolling crisis coverage. Not many of them remain on active duty. Kilmeade still has vivid recollections of his time visiting Ground Zero on the actual day planes crashed into the two World Trade Center towers. “People were blown out of their shoes,” he remembers. “You could not see the ground. It felt like you were on the moon.” He remembers handing in tapes of what he and the Fox News crew assigned to him had collected, “and I’ve never seen them since.” In a sign of how unexpected the attacks were, Doocy was, before chaos erupted, tending to something entirely different for the Fox News morning program. “I was outside I was doing the weather with Mr. Peanut,” he remembers. “Planters Peanuts has that mascot. I’m interviewing Mr. Peanut,” which presented some challenges. After all, says Doocy, “Mr. Peanut doesn’t talk.” When he walked 15 feet back into the studio, people were on alert. There was a report of a plane crashing into one of the World Trade Center towers, but there was not much detail. “Nobody had any images,” recalls Doocy. There was speculation that a helicopter or small plane had gone off course. From there, both Doocy and Kilmeade remember hours of work and of staying in different hotel rooms in New York after the city closed access. Doocy didn’t see his family for two days. Fox News Media on September 11 will provide coverage and commemoration throughout the day. Eric Shawn, a Fox News Channel senior correspondent who reported from Ground Zero in 2001, will be on hand to provide coverage. At Fox Business Network, Liz Claman, anchor of “The Claman Countdown,” will speak with Brandon and Kyle Lutnick, the Chairman and Executive Vice Chairman of Cantor Fitzgerald, on September 10th and on September 11, will interview Larry Silverstein, founder and CEO of Silverstein Properties, from the World Trade Center, which he helped rebuild. Streaming outlet Fox Nation will debut two new specials exploring the impact of the 9/11 attacks 25 years later. Doocy hopes such work will ensure Americans remember the terrible day, no matter the memories and feelings it sparks. With the event a quarter century old, he wonders if “the day has lost its potency for a lot of people, its place in history.” The news business employs many young producers, he notes, “who weren’t alive at the time.” The work being done next week by a broad array of news organizations will try to keep remembrances of the day active.
