articles.title: Werner Herzog Reveals Orlando Bloom Was Upset On Set Of ‘Bucking Fastard’ After They Captured His Scene In One Take – Venice
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Sandra Hüller To Star As Celebrated Late Male German Artist Wolfgang Herrndorf’s In Maria Schrader’s ‘Work And Structure’ Calls Grow For Palestinian Flag To Fly At Venice Film Festival As Artistic Director Says Not Possible To Meet Request George Clooney Calls Out “Authoritarians” Who “Peddle Fear” As He Receives Lifetime Award Achievement In Venice View All September 3, 2026 5:15am VENICE, ITALY - SEPTEMBER 03: (L-R) Domhnall Gleeson, Orlando Bloom, Rooney Mara, Kate Mara and Director Werner Herzog attend the "Bucking Fastard" Venice Photocall Getty Images Oscar-nominated German director Werner Herzog set down in Venice Film Festival on Thursday with Golden Lion contender Bucking Fastard , in the company of its stars Kate and Rooney Mara and supporting cast members Domhnall Gleeson and Orlando Bloom . The Maras play Jean and Joan Holbrooke, two real-life sisters who were so close that they spoke in unison, loved the same man, had the same dreams and made the same slips of the tongue. Gleeson plays a man who attempts to help them to adapt to modern life after they become a tabloid sensation, while Bloom plays a rowdy ex-lover. Related Stories Festivals 'The Girl With The Leica' Review: Love Is War In Alina Marazzi's Unconventional Biopic Of A Pioneering War Photographer - Venice Film Festival Festivals Calls Grow For Palestinian Flag To Fly At Venice Film Festival As Artistic Director Says Not Possible To Meet Request Herzog revealed that Lord of the Rings star Bloom had been upset with him after he captured his main scene in just one take. Watch on Deadline “What a pleasure to work with him. He was actually upset because we worked so fast. I did one take of a very long, long thing in the witness stand, and it was that,” said Herzog, addressing Bloom at the press conference. “It was my largest scene in the movie, and we did one take and you said, ‘Great, we got it’,” replied Bloom, explaining his disquiet. Herzog continued that he had understood Bloom’s upset and as a result brought him back to do three more takes. “I do understand you, and I apologize that I was too fast maybe, but it’s the spirit of the film, like open heart surgery, going to the essentials right away. One camera, one take, that’s it. Or maybe two or three takes, with the sister’s highly, highly technically complex.. to speak in unison. Two takes, maybe three takes, and that was that.” Later on in the press conference, Herzog heaped praise on Bloom saying he had been a joy to work with, adding that he had wanted to put the actor in an unexpected role. “I was so much looking forward to work with you, and it came with such natural ease,” said Herzog. “I wanted you to step far out of what you are known for, the heartthrob of teenies. Now you are the ‘Bucking Fastard’. You had to shoulder the title.” Bloom said shooting with Herzog had been liberating and magical. “Werner really creates this sort of sacred space, almost for magic to happen… He has such drive and passion and almost obsession towards making films. And we’ve seen that in everything that he’s done,” said the actor. “ My Best Fiend was a movie I watched with such passion to see the creative process in its finest form,” he continued, referring to the Herzog’s 1990 documentary about his tumultuous friend with Klaus Kinski. “When Werner claps the clapperboard, there’s just a feeling of freedom and because it’s such a small and unique experience, it creates a magical moment. That is what we dream of.” The film is based on the true story of two inseparable sisters living on the fringes of society, whom Herzog first met more than 40 years ago. He said the long gestated project had hit a wall as he grappled with how to capture the two sisters who spoke as one on the big screen. He credited UK producer Jeremy Thomas with coming of the idea of casting Kate and Rooney Mara. “It was dormant for decades, and then when it became clear that I would have actresses who were sisters, it was clear it had to be done. The screenplay came very easily. I wrote it in five days, and it’s a complete invention.” The Maras said that the process of playing the inseparable sisters had come together easily once they were on set because of their strong relationship in real life. “At first it was very daunting the idea that we were going to be kind of playing this same person, but I think we found pretty quickly that having a lifetime together and all this history and you know, a childhood of playing together, there was just an unspoken world between us that we didn’t have to work very hard to create at all,” said Rooney Mara. “Once we found our flow together… you know, I’ve never laughed so much. We had so much fun and yeah, it was a very once in a lifetime, very unique experience.” Venice regular Herzog was at the festival last year to receive its Golden Lion Life Achievement Award from Francis Coppola, who has been his friend since he time spent in L.A. in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Ahead of tonight’s world premiere, Herzog expressed regrets that another old friend from L.A., David Lynch, who died in January 2025, would not be in the audience. “We had a deep, deep understanding of each other’s work, although we were quite different… I had the feeling I wish he could be my first audience… I wish we could turn the wheel of time back and invite him tonight. But it doesn’t happen like this,” said Herzog. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Rides Into Awards Race; Mohsen Gharaei; Palestine Call Jeff Goldblum To Host S2 Premiere Of ‘Saturday Night Live UK’ Unifrance Rendez-Vous TV Preview & Interview Amid Industry Shifts Scroll Through Photos From Opening Day Of The 83rd Venice Film Festival Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Nicola Coughlan, Luke Evans & Hugh Bonneville Are Speaking Out Against AI Voice Cloning, But Is The Government Listening?
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Jeff Goldblum To Host Season 2 Premiere Of ‘Saturday Night Live UK’ Jasmine Jobson Teases Details About Netflix’s ‘Top Boy’ Spin-Off Series ‘Jaq’: “She’s Going Down A Crazy Rabbit Hole” Maureen Lipman Tells “Cowardly” Co-Star To “Grow Up” After He Quit Play Over Her Pro-Israel Views View All September 3, 2026 5:35am Peter Caulfield, Siobhán McSweeney, and Zawe Ashton support the Save Our Voices Now campaign Save Our Voices Now Welcome to Rendering , a Deadline column reporting at the intersection of AI and showbiz. Rendering examines how artificial intelligence is disrupting the entertainment industry, taking you inside key battlegrounds and spotlighting change-makers wielding the technology for good and ill. Got a story about AI? Rendering wants to hear from you: jkanter@deadline.com. Michael Caine has handed over his voice to AI. Liza Minnelli is making music with AI. With the blessing of their estates, dead actors like John Wayne are having their voices resurrected by AI. But what happens when consent is not given? What can actors do to protect a crucial tool of their craft from unwanted exploitation? The answer, in the UK at least, is very little. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Netflix Sets Roald Dahl Series With Cast Including Nicola Coughlan, Imelda Staunton & Dominic West News Nicola Coughlan On Smaller 'Bridgerton' Season 5 Role Amid 'Only Murders In The Building' Filming: "I Had Such An Epic Run" That’s why Nicola Coughlan , Luke Evans , and Hugh Bonneville are lending their voices to a new campaign: Save Our Voices Now . BAFTA winner Siobhán McSweeney and Harry Potter star Miriam Margolyes have also endorsed the message. The campaign was established by Tip Toe actor Peter Caulfield and Alice Sockett, an established audiobook narrator. They are calling on the government to give individuals enforceable copyright ownership over their own voice. Save Our Voices Now’s Parliament petition has amassed more than 4,000 signatures, but the early indications are that the campaign has been met with inertia rather than action. In December 2024, the British government launched a major consultation on copyright protections in the age of AI. Ministers received 11,520 responses, many of which were from creators and rights holders. The government published the findings of the consultation in March, but said there was no clear consensus on strengthening AI copyright laws, despite 81% of respondents endorsing the need for greater copyright protections. Flash forward five months, and what’s the government’s response to the Save Our Voices Now campaign? To launch another consultation. “It is right that we value and protect human creators, and that is why we have announced we will launch a consultation on how we address these harms, while protecting legitimate innovation,” a Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) spokesperson says. Caulfield is not impressed. “A consultation is such a big fob-off,” he tells Deadline. “We don’t need a second consultation in as many years. We need the law to change.” Actors’ union Equity has also voiced frustration at the government’s position. A DCMS spokesperson did not respond to questions on why a second consultation is necessary and what it will achieve. Meanwhile, the U.S. and Denmark are pushing through legislation that gives citizens the rights to control digital replicas. “The UK is very much lagging behind,” laments Caulfield. “Since we started the campaign, we’ve been inundated with shocking stories about how big brands are taking people’s voices without consent, and AI software is being used to defraud families.” He launched the campaign after submitting audition tapes to Audible, before being “stonewalled” about what was happening to his unsuccessful voice recordings. “They were very reluctant to give me any information about what happens with my data,” he says. Caulfield is not accusing Audible of theft, but is making clear how the rights situation is murky at best. Part of the campaign is about placing the legal burden of consent on the platform and the AI developer, not the individual. But when AI is moving so fast, and legislation is moving so slowly, there are fears it may already be too late. Since launching last week, Save Our Voices Now has attracted further endorsements from Richard E. Grant and The Great British Bake Off presenter Alison Hammond. They will need to speak loudly to make their voices heard in the corridors of power. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Rides Into Awards Race; Mohsen Gharaei; Palestine Call Jeff Goldblum To Host S2 Premiere Of ‘Saturday Night Live UK’ Unifrance Rendez-Vous TV Preview & Interview Amid Industry Shifts Scroll Through Photos From Opening Day Of The 83rd Venice Film Festival Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Canters Into The Awards Race With John Malkovich Leading The Charge — Venice Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Sony Sets Release Date For Indian Epic ‘Ramayana’ With Ranbir Kapoor, Yash & Sai Pallavi ‘Ink’: What The Critics Are Saying About Danny Boyle’s Origin Story Of Brit Tabloid The Sun Javier Bardem, Marion Cotillard & Vanessa Redgrave Join Animated Movie ‘The Turning Door’ View All September 3, 2026 5:36am VENICE, ITALY - SEPTEMBER 03: (L-R) John Malkovich, Mariana Di Girolamo, Parker Posey, Director Martin McDonagh, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi, and Ailín Salas attend the "Wild Horse Nine" Photocall during the 83rd Venice International Film Festival at Palazzo del Casino on September 03, 2026 in Venice, Italy. (Photo by Daniele Venturelli/WireImage) Getty Martin McDonagh ‘s Wild Horse Nine launched on the Lido this morning with the filmmakers and cast getting a rapturous welcome at the press conference following this morning’s press screenings. Venice pressers tend to fall on the warm/adulating side but this was clearly a film with plenty of admirers. Director Martin McDonagh, and actors John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi and Parker Posey were among those up on stage to discuss the dark comedy, whose Oscar buzz has been building. The presser got underway with a journalist telling the team that the film was one of the best he’d seen this year and that Malkovich could surely start writing his Oscar acceptance speech, noting that it would be the accolade he “deserved after such a long and prestigious career”. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Werner Herzog Reveals Orlando Bloom Was Upset On Set Of 'Bucking Fastard' After They Captured His Scene In One Take; Evokes Bond With David Lynch Festivals 'The Girl With The Leica' Review: Love Is War In Alina Marazzi's Unconventional Biopic Of A Pioneering War Photographer - Venice Film Festival The suggestion drew a round of applause from the audience. Malkovich adroitly demured: “I never feel in competition with any of them [actor, director and writer collaborators] because generally I love what they do. The nicest thing is that the film gets attention, and this film has several terrific performers in it, and is beautifully written and beautifully directed, and that’s what matters the most to me. But thank you for your kind words.” Malkovich is considered by prognosticators to be firmly in the mix in what is a very competitive best actor category this awards season with Matt Damon, Tom Cruise, Robert Pattinson, Andrew Scott, Sebastian Stan and Javier Bardem among a deep field. The 72 year-old, who told the audience he has no plans to retire, has two previous Oscar nominations, one in 1985 and one in 1994. After becoming almost a household name in the 80s and 90s, the acclaimed actor hasn’t had the same profile of roles in the past 20 years. There’s little Hollywood loves more than a ‘comeback’. Another journalist in the crowd predicted multiple major awards for the movie. Martin McDonagh has seven Oscar nominations already (and one win). Not many would bet against that number growing. At this stage, at least. Set just before the 1973 Chilean coup, his new film stars Malkovich and Rockwell as CIA agents Chris and Lee, who are dispatched from Santiago to Easter Island by their bureau chief, MJ (Steve Buscemi). As the longtime partners wrestle with their dark pasts and present conspiracies, Chris’ newfound bond with a pair of rebellious students (Mariana di Girolamo and Ailín Salas) threatens to send everyone’s trip to the remote paradise sideways. Searchlight has set a November 6, 2026 release date for the movie, which also stars Tom Waits. The film marks McDonagh’s first film since The Banshees of Inisherin , which was nominated for nine Oscars in 2023 including for directing, writing and Best Picture. McDonagh and producer Graham Broadbent explained to the press that the film was only the second ever to film on Easter Island/Rapa Nui, something they and the actors described as a great privilege. McDonagh also told the audience that part of his inspiration for telling the story was his fascination with the CIA and the fate of the Chilean government under Salvador Allende. “We know what the KGB are like, but we we probably don’t question the CIA’s activities as much as we ought to,” he said. “That was one of the starting points. I’m always questioning, even in the less less political films [I make]. I like to question authority or what we’re being told.” ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Rides Into Awards Race; Mohsen Gharaei; Palestine Call Jeff Goldblum To Host S2 Premiere Of ‘Saturday Night Live UK’ Unifrance Rendez-Vous TV Preview & Interview Amid Industry Shifts Scroll Through Photos From Opening Day Of The 83rd Venice Film Festival Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘MobLand’ Renewed For Season 3 With Tom Hardy Returning Alongside Helen Mirren & Pierce Brosnan
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Only Murders In The Building’ Moving Writers Room To New York For Likely Season 7 Netflix Brings Together Part 1 & 2 Of Mindy Kaling’s Trilogy With ‘Sex Lives Of College Girls’ Deal; Could It Complete Set With ‘Not Suitable For Work’? ‘Tires’: Netflix Officially Greenlights Season 4 Of Shane Gillis’ Workplace Comedy Series View All September 3, 2026 6:00am (L-R): Helen Mirren, Pierce Brosnan, Tom Hardy in 'MobLand' Paramount+ It’s official — Paramount+ has renewed MobLand for a third season ahead of crime drama’s Season 2 premiere on Sept. 18. Also confirmed is the return of Tom Hardy as the Harrigan family’s loyal fixer Harry da Souza alongside Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren as the crime family’s patriarch and matriarch Conrad and Maeve Harrigan. MobLand , which was renewed for a second season last year after logging Paramount+’s second biggest launch for an original series behind Landman , was headed for another easy renewal with a writers room up and running by May. However, things got complicated by a behind-the-scenes drama involving lead Hardy, who also serves as executive producer. He seemed on his way out after friction between him and the series’ writer, executive producer and showrunner Jez Butterworth during production on Season 2 had escalated to a point where the two could no longer work together. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News 'Judge Judy' Celebrates 30th Anniversary In CBS Primetime Special With Steven Spielberg, Samuel L. Jackson & More Casting Wayne Brady & Selma Blair To Guest Star In Season 20 Of 'Criminal Minds: Evolution' In the end, cool heads prevailed. As Deadline reported a month ago , back-channeling efforts led to a meeting in London between Hardy, Butterworth and series executive producer David C. Glasser where they hashed things out and, with executive producer Guy Ritchie also pitching in, Hardy’s return was secured, paving the way to a Season 3 renewal. In Season 2 of MobLand , produced by Paramount Television Studios and 101 Studios, the Harrigans struggle to show a unified front as rising rivals threaten their fractured criminal empire – and Harry Da Souza (Hardy), their street-smart and formidable ‘fixer,’ must walk a dangerous tightrope when tensions within the family intensify. As violence spills into every corner of their lives, loyalties snap, safety proves temporary, and the battle for power leaves no room for mercy. Alongside Hardy, Brosnan and Mirren, Season 2 also stars Paddy Considine, Joanne Froggatt, Lara Pulver, Anson Boon, Mandeep Dhillon, Jasmine Jobson, Teddie Allen, Emmett J. Scanlan, Johnny Flynn, Ophelia Lovibond, Janet McTeer, and Toby Jones. MobLand is executive produced by Glasser, Ritchie, Butterworth, Hardy, Ivan Atkinson, Dean Baker, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari and Keith Cox. Following its Sept. 18 premiere on Paramount+, new episodes from MobLand ‘s ten-episode second season will be available to stream weekly on Fridays, culminating in the season finale on Nov. 20. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Rides Into Awards Race; Mohsen Gharaei; Palestine Call Jeff Goldblum To Host S2 Premiere Of ‘Saturday Night Live UK’ Unifrance Rendez-Vous TV Preview & Interview Amid Industry Shifts Scroll Through Photos From Opening Day Of The 83rd Venice Film Festival Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Maggie Gyllenhaal Takes on Venice Film Festival’s Lack of Women in Competition: “There’s a Systemic Problem”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All September 2, 2026 3:51am Maggie Gyllenhall at Venice 2026 Courtesy of Tiziana Fabi/AFP via Getty Images Politics and the underrepresentation of women at the world’s major film festivals became the breakout topic of conversation at this year’s Venice jury press conference, with Maggie Gyllenhaal stating that she believes “there’s a systemic problem” behind the fact that the world’s oldest cinema showcase has just two titles directed by women in its main competition this year. “It’s much harder for women to get their films financed,” said Gyllenhaal, the festival’s competition jury president this year, when asked about the dearth of women in Venice’s selection. “Also, could it be possible that the things that women, having had a different experience of being alive in the world, want to make movies about are not always deemed high art?” Related Stories Movies A Family and Country Are in Crisis in 'Our Share of Sand' (Exclusive Venice Clip) Movies Brad Bird's 'Ray Gunn,' Travis Knight's 'Wildwood' Among BFI London Film Fest World Premieres “I really am walking in with a question as to why there are so few women in the main competition,” she later added. This year’s competition has drawn scrutiny for its stark gender imbalance. Just one of the original list of 20 Golden Lion contenders — May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown — is directed by a woman, down from six female-directed competition titles last year. The festival later added to the competition with the Gaza documentary NAZA , co-directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, bringing the total to two. Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera acknowledged the disparity when announcing the lineup, calling it a recent low for the festival. But Gyllenhaal also tipped her hat to Venice for selecting her as the event’s jury chief this year. “Alberto and Julia asking me to be the head of the main jury competition — after the two films in particular that I have made — is a very important thing to consider, too,” she said. Gyllenhaal’s jury includes Tunisian filmmaker Kaouther Ben Hania, whose acclaimed Palestinian drama The Voice of Hind Rajab won last year’s Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize; Oscar-winning composer Daniel Blumberg; film scholar Francesco Casetti; French director Xavier Giannoli; Afghan filmmaker Shahrbanoo Sadat; and Hong Kong filmmaking legend Johnnie To. Together they will select the Golden Lion winner and Venice’s other main competition prizes from a field that includes Danny Boyle’s Rupert Murdoch drama Ink , Robert Pattinson thriller Primetime , Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine , Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong’s much-anticipated return Possible Love and NAZA , among others. Gyllenhaal has a significant history with Venice. Her 2021 feature directing debut, The Lost Daughter , premiered in competition on the Lido and earned her the festival’s best screenplay prize before going on to receive three Oscar nominations. She also has a project in Venice this year. Her Marilyn Monroe-inspired advertorial short Flesh Impact , starring Dakota Johnson, Ellen Burstyn and Peter Sarsgaard, will screen out of competition later in the event. The press conference proceeded after some confusion during the weekend over whether the jury’s meeting with the media — a staple of all major film festivals — would take place at all. Venice organizers stated on Saturday that the jury presser might be scrapped due to a “scheduling conflict” involving a jury member; but by Sunday, the festival said a solution had been found, and the briefing would be held as usual. The brief interregnum stirred industry speculation about the role politics might play at the 83rd edition, as various global conflicts — the war in Gaza, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and the U.S.-Iran war — loom in the background of the world’s oldest film festival. Festival chief Barbera has described this year’s lineup as the “most political” of recent years. Venice’s blue-chip festival peers, meanwhile, showed earlier this year the two directions a major cultural event might take amid this globally fraught moment. In February, the Berlin festival became engulfed by political discord and social media point-scoring after jury president Wim Wenders told reporters during the opening press conference that filmmakers “have to stay out of politics.” But the Cannes Film Festival later went ahead in May with plenty of carefully calibrated political statements from filmmakers but notably less acrimony. Gyllenhaal was asked near the outset of the Venice press conference whether she feels filmmakers have a responsibility to be political amid the world’s current challenges. “We could say, ‘How are we possibly here talking about movies right now, when the world is in a state of emergency?'” she replied. “To me, the answer has something to do with empathy. I think that film allows an opening into an opportunity to find empathy inside of ourselves. Personally, I don’t believe that there is any subject or any filmmaker that shouldn’t be heard. I think we can challenge ourselves to hear stories about the most corrupt, the most perverse people, because it opens up the opportunity to find empathy for those people — and even to look at the ways in which we might have a little bad guy inside us, a little perversity inside us, a little corruption inside us, fight it as we might.” She added: “I think that if movies really are an honest look into other people’s experience, then they are fundamentally, unavoidably political, as well as a lot of other things.” The 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival officially opens Wednesday evening on the Lido with a ceremony that will fete George Clooney with a Golden Lion for lifetime achievement and conclude with the world premiere of Boyle’s Ink , starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce, and Claire Foy. The festival concludes with an awards ceremony on Sept. 12. THR

articles.title: Forget the Red Carpet — Venice’s Real Stars Are in the Documentaries This Year
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All September 2, 2026 4:00am 'Oasis: Dont Look Back in Anger' Courtesy of Venice Some of the biggest stars at this year’s Venice Film Festival won’t be the famous faces walking the red carpet, but the wildly high-profile subjects of documentaries that range from intoxicating to grippingly urgent. From Oscar winner Alex Gibney ‘s 4-hour dissection of Elon Musk and Disney’s intimate Oasis reunion movie to NAZA , the politically charged documentary about “Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” and the ICE documentary They’re Here from Laura Poitras (another Oscar winner) — many of this year’s must-see movies on the Lido are clearly nonfiction. And, arguably, the biggest star who may or may not walk Venice’s red carpet — aside from Noel and Liam Gallagher — will likely do so on behalf of a documentary. Noted architecture superfan Brad Pitt recently became an executive producer of Wim Wenders’ 14-year-in-the-making documentary portrait of Peter Zumthor, the Swiss visionary behind the sprawling new Los Angeles County Museum of Art — another gem among Venice’s stacked 2026 documentary lineup. “It’s a phenomenal year for docs at Venice, and I think this will be one of the big stories of this edition,” says Emilie Spiegel, who co-heads Cinetic Marketing, a prestige publicity agency that represents an outsized swath of every fall’s awards favorites. “To have the oldest festival in the world so clearly state that documentary is cinema, and that some of the most exciting work is happening there, is really significant. Amid budget contractions and studio consolidation, I also think it’s optimistic and savvy of Venice to be championing nonfiction right now.” For breadth, depth, diversity and pedigree, Venice has clearly emerged as the preeminent platform for high-end nonfiction filmmaking among the world’s top festivals. While Cannes has been far more sporadic in its support of the form, and Berlin tends to offer quantity at the expense of quality, Venice has consistently brought the bangers — and the 2026 selection looks to be among its best yet. Two-time Oscar winner Barbara Kopple is back with Union Town , a cinéma vérité portrait of New York delivery workers taking on some of the world’s most powerful corporations; Free Solo Oscar winners Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi return to extreme sporting terrain with Everest: The Other Side , about a pair of mountaineers’ audacious attempt to climb and ski the north face of the world’s tallest mountain; The Truffle Hunters duo Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw decamp to French wine country for an infectiously romantic and richly informative romp in Burgundy ; and Takashi Miike, after more than 100 films and three decades spent gleefully jumping around genres, makes his first documentary with Shumei: The Living Legacy of Kabuki , filmed over more than three years with rare access to the inner sanctum of Japan’s traditional Kabuki theater world. Related Stories Movies Maggie Gyllenhaal Takes on Venice Film Festival's Lack of Women in Competition: "There's a Systemic Problem" Movies A Family and Country Are in Crisis in 'Our Share of Sand' (Exclusive Venice Clip) ‘Musk,’ courtesy of Venice Film Festival Courtesy of the Venice Film Festival Elsewhere, Julia Loktev follows her epic portrait of independent Russian journalists with My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile , another nearly six-hour immersion; Russell Crowe turns the camera on himself and his globe-trotting rock band for what Venice chief Alberto Barbera has called the star’s “most personal” film. And that’s before factoring in Erik Shirai’s Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing , which promises rare access inside another of Japan’s most famously guarded traditions; Robert Greene’s Too Much Sugar , a strikingly original doc about fatherhood and masculinity; Mariano Llinás’ more-than-five-hour biography of Jorge Luis Borges; or two-time Oscar-shortlisted director Victor Kossakovsky’s radical examination of the life of trees, Holy Wood Dust. The festival has even built its embrace of docs more firmly into its structure this year, with a new dedicated “Film on Films” strand, where Luca Guadagnino’s gargantuan, seven-hour-plus meditation on the great Bernardo Bertolucci sits alongside Sophie Fiennes and Slavoj Zizek’s The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias, a tribute to the cult of Seijun Suzuki, and more. Documentary filmmaking’s presence at Venice stretches back to the festival’s very first edition in 1932, when Joris Ivens and Mannus Franken’s 12-minute Dutch avant-garde documentary Rain (or Regen ) screened on the closing night of the inaugural edition. But it wasn’t until the Barbera era that nonfiction filmmaking would vie for — and swiftly win — the festival’s signature honor. Shortly after taking the reins as artistic director of the festival for the second time in 2012, Barbera put two documentaries in the festival’s main competition for the first time in 2013 — Errol Morris’ The Unknown Known and Gianfranco Rosi’s Sacro GRA — and the latter promptly won the Golden Lion. The space and prominence Barbera has accorded to nonfiction has only grown in the years since. “Perhaps this is not the result of a deliberate strategic choice, but rather the consequence of the fact that, year after year, we receive a growing number of submissions in the documentary genre, whose significance — both from an aesthetic standpoint and in terms of its ability to offer a representation of and contribute to our understanding of the major issues of our time — is perhaps unprecedented,” Barbera explains. “My impression is that the financial resources available for making documentaries have increased, as a result of growing demand from streaming platforms but also increased interest from the public, which is now much more willing to watch nonfiction films of good quality.” ‘From Inside Out: The Architecture of Peter Zumthor,’ courtesy of Venice Film Festival Road Movies In docs as well as fictional filmmaking, Venice has also staked out a commendably independent-minded stance over recent years when it comes to films that tackle conflict and fraught social issues. “I believe Venice is one of the very few international cultural platforms that has the ability to invite filmmakers with very different — or even opposite — political positions and cultural points of view, and put their work in conversation,” says Ukrainian director and producer Alexander Rodnyansky, who is known for his work with Russian auteur Andrey Zvyagintsev and last year directed and premiered the searingly personal documentary Notes from a True Criminal in Venice. Rodnyansky notes the sober-mindedness Venice has shown in screening bold Ukrainian and Palestinian films — such as The Voice of Hind Rajab in 2025 and the Gaza docs NAZA and Ahmed Hassouna’s Citizen Osama this year — as well as works by freethinking Russian and Israeli filmmakers, without succumbing to the blanket bans that some have called for on films and filmmakers from those countries. “Of course, state propaganda should have no place, but real independent-minded filmmaking should be welcomed wherever it comes from,” he says. Rodnyansky is producer of Israeli documentarian Amos Gitai’s The Road to Jericho , a journey from Jerusalem to Jericho that visits the country’s threatened Bedouin community while reflecting on the Israeli-Palestinian peace process. The film will premiere in Venice’s out-of-competition nonfiction section. “As you understand, it’s not an easy time for Israeli filmmakers right now. They’re having a very hard time getting their movies accepted by the major festivals, regardless of what they might believe,” Rodnyansky says. “These are turbulent times, and a festival should try to reflect the polarization of the societies we observe and continue the conversation using artistic means,” he adds. “It’s a very simple mission, and I think Barbera inherited that legacy and has continued to enrich it in a brilliant way.” THR

articles.title: George Clooney Tackles Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger, Mark Ruffalo, AI and State of U.S. Politics
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All September 2, 2026 4:54am George Clooney is seen during the 83rd Venice International Film Festival on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Victor Boyko/Getty Images) George Clooney touched down on the Lido last year for the world premiere of Noah Baumbach’s Jay Kelly, a film that cast him in the title role as an American actor who travels to Italy to receive a lifetime achievement award only to reflect on the weight of his iconic career and whether it was all worth it. One year later, Clooney, 65, is back at the Venice Film Festival for a spin in the spotlight on the opening night for a bit of life imitating art as he will take the stage inside Sala Grande on Wednesday evening to receive the fest’s highest honor — a Golden Lion for lifetime achievement. As is tradition for such a moment, Clooney braved the international media for an opening day press conference on Wednesday afternoon – and because of who he is and the variety of his art and activism over a 40-plus-year career, he fielded questions on a wide variety of subjects including Hollywood, politics, climate change, the proposed Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) merger, the state of journalism, AI, deep fakes and more. Related Stories Movies Forget the Red Carpet -- Venice's Real Stars Are in the Documentaries This Year Movies Maggie Gyllenhaal Takes on Venice Film Festival's Lack of Women in Competition: "There's a Systemic Problem" Getting into the thick of the tough questions, Clooney was asked to deliver his take on the status of the United States, a broad question relating to the current political landscape. “Look, I’m always very optimistic about things, and we’re at a moment in time that’s unfortunate — I think that’s an understatement. I do believe that we’re going to get through all of this.” He said that November’s elections “should be a check and balance,” adding that in 2028 “with any luck, we’ll have some restoration into some normalcy.” Clooney then took a moment to call out Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s recent controversial social media post that featured women from the military in Canada. “Where’s the sense of decency in all of this? I’m ashamed of all of that. But we will get through it, and we will come out better on the other side.” Clooney at a photo call for his lifetime achievement award at Palazzo del Casino on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images) Clooney was asked to respond to Paramount’s criticism of Mark Ruffalo , who has come out against the proposed WBD merger. The studio took the position that his recent comments were antisemitic , and Clooney stood up for Ruffalo and for free speech. “I support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely. I think that that’s ridiculous. We’re not going to ban speech,” Clooney said during the Venice press event. “I believe in free speech even when I completely disagree with it. That’s important, right? In fact, it’s part of how a democracy works. There are going to be people tonight in the room that are going to disagree with most everything I say or stand for. Fair enough. That’s how it’s supposed to be. We’re supposed to argue these things out and come to a conclusion based on the information that we take in.” He continued: “I will always support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely. I like him. He’s a good man.” As for the merger itself, Clooney called it a “complicated thing” that he doesn’t quite foresee going through or benefiting the deal architects like David Ellison. “I don’t know how this goes through. There are so many issues involved,” he said. “It doesn’t matter how much money you have; it’s going to be very tricky to do. So, my opinion on the merger is: I always worry whenever big companies are consolidating because it usually means a lot of people lose their jobs. That’s the truth.” He then pivoted to talking about the “revolution in our industry” as it relates to artificial intelligence. “It’s going to hurt us in a lot of ways. If you’re a visual effects supervisor, you’re going to have trouble coming up because that’s going to be a lot of jobs are going to be taken away. Probably about 30 percent of the jobs. I don’t know what the real number is, but there’s going to be a big number of jobs are going to be taken away, and we’re kind of on our back foot on it. We’re not on taking the lead on it.” As for how AI impacts him personally, Clooney quipped, “Well, I would like to avoid being in a tampon commercial 20 years after I’m dead. I would like to avoid that.” Artistic director Alberto Barbera and Clooney on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images) Clooney was also asked to give his take on the state of journalism today as well, a relevant question for him considering he’s the son of a journalist and he’s married to Amal Clooney, the daughter of a journalist. “We have nothing but admiration and support for journalism,” he said, pointing out the work that their foundation does to help support and free jailed journalists that have stood up against various regimes. “The state of journalism is always in flux, always challenged. It was that way in the 1700s. It is that way now. It’s a concern for a moment, but I do believe that information will find its way out.” That said, he called it “a concern” that “the richest people in the world right now are owning the Washington Post and [Twitter aka X], most of the places we get our information,” referencing Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk, respectively. “I think five or six of the biggest outlets for information are owned by the richest people in the world. That’s a concern, but there’s still a lot of room for good journalism.” He was also asked to reflect on the art imitating life piece of it all with Jay Kelly and whether today feels like his arc in the film, which was described as “romantic but also melancholy.” “It’s a little bit similar to the tribute I get in the movie, which is kind of funny. You know, I’m 65 years old; everything is melancholy. Literally, you brush your teeth, and you’re like, oh, my teeth used to be so much nicer. Everything about getting older, you get a little melancholy,” he explained. “I also feel very lucky. I have an incredible wife who I love very much and loves me, and I have great kids … I continue to be able to work when I want to. You know, life is pretty good.” Clooney continued by saying that while he’s in a good place, there’s a lot of stuff in the world that isn’t. While that takes a lot of focus at times, as it should, “we also have to remember to celebrate the good things that are happening in our lives.” One good thing that’s about to happen in his life is reteaming with close friends like Brad Pitt and Matt Damon in another Ocean’s Eleven installment. Clooney teased that project, which has already been announced by saying, “We have an Ocean’s film that we’re going to shoot as soon as we get our schedules worked.” Clooney is just about as beloved as they come here in Venice. The actor has a long history with the festival both as an actor and filmmaker dating back several decades to the world premiere of Steven Soderbergh’s 1998 drama Out of Sight opposite Jennifer Lopez. His history also includes the Coen brothers’ film Intolerable Cruelty opposite Catherine Zeta-Jones, the Clooney-directed Good Night and Good Luck , Tony Gilroy’s Michael Clayton , another Coen effort, Burn After Reading with Brad Pitt, another Clooney special with The Ides of March , Alfonso Cuarón’s Gravity co-starring Sandra Bullock, Clooney’s Suburbicon , and more recently with Jon Watts’ Wolfs , also opposite Pitt. But he’s also treated as a sort of countrywide hero as well thanks to his longtime residency of Lake Como with wife, Amal Clooney and their twins. Amal has accompanied him to this year’s festival. She got a lot of attention from the podium from Clooney today. “I will say I have had a love story with Venice for about 30 years, and in fact was married here, and so I would say that my greatest moment here was obviously my wedding because I would get in a lot of trouble if I don’t say that,” he quipped. But he spread the love to the festival as well. “This is a film festival that has been very dear to me. My first big directing gig was Good Night, and Good Luck. I’ve had immense successes and I’ve had massive failures. I remember I was here with Catherine Zeta-Jones for Intolerable Cruelty , and none of the jokes played here, and it was over. Usually, people stand up and applaud, and everybody just turned and looked at us. I looked at Catherine and I said, ‘Run!’ And we ran out of the theater.” But there have been plenty of “wonderful” moments as well. “Careers are really funny. It’s so many different accidents that get you here, so many different lefts and rights, and things that could have gone wrong or right. It’s hard to sustain all of that, and you have to rely on kindness of friends and kindness of people you work with,” he said. “But it really requires luck all the way through.” Clooney signs autographs at the close of the 62nd Venice Film Festival on Sept. 10, 2005. (Photo by Chris Jackson/Getty Images) THR

articles.title: Slavoj Zizek on Why We Seek Utopias in the Movies (Exclusive Trailer)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 2, 2026 5:00am Slavoj Žižek in Sophie Fiennes' 'The Pervert's Guide to Utopias' Keeper Pictures Slavoj Žižek is back. The Slovenian Marxist philosopher and leftie provocateur, who has become the internet’s most unlikely social media star, returns to cinemas with The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias , the third documentary from director Sophie Fiennes — after The Pervert’s Guide to Cinema (2006) and The Pervert’s Guide to Ideology (2012) — that seeks to filter Žižek’s thinking through the lens of cinema. In her new documentary, which will have its world premiere in Venice on Sept. 7, Fiennes again stages Žižek in re-creations of scenes from the films and TV series being discussed, dropping the philosopher into the cinematic frame, so to speak. He lies in a bathtub in a wedding dress, like Kirsten Dunst, to discusses Lars von Trier’s apocalyptic drama Melancholia (2011). Debates the dystopian vision of Hulu’s A Handmaid’s Tale , lying flat on his back on a bed, draped in a red robe. Related Stories Movies George Clooney Tackles Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger, Mark Ruffalo, AI and State of U.S. Politics Movies Forget the Red Carpet -- Venice's Real Stars Are in the Documentaries This Year Žižek’s hot takes and critical interpretations, on cinema and philosophy, are often counter-intuitive and seemingly contradictory, but never boring. The hidden message behind James McTeigue’s V for Vendetta (2006), he opines in The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias , is not a triumphant one of the masses rebelling against an authoritarian state. Rather the film’s subtext suggest a darker premise: that the fascists need the rebels and the rebels need the fascists to justify each other’s existence. “Our duty is to see things the way they are. And here, cinema helps us,” says Žižek in the first trailer for The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias (see below). “Because I think that the role of Hollywood, or cinema in general, was always to bring out the utopian presuppositions, which we don’t perceive in our ordinary, daily lives. If aliens were to visit our earth, and by chance, ask me, ‘explain us what humanity is about.’ I would not tell them ‘go around and look’ I would tell them ‘look these movies and you will understand us.” The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias is produced by Keeper Pictures, P Guide, SPOK Films, The Film Kitchen, and Mattima Films. Shani Hinto is handling world sales. Check out the exclusive trailer for The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias below. THR
