articles.title: Netflix Unveils Tense Trailer for ‘East of Eden’ Series Adaptation Starring Florence Pugh
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lexy Perez Plus Icon Lexy Perez Senior Digital Editor and Producer View All September 2, 2026 5:30am Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames in episode 103 of Netflix’s ‘East of Eden.’ Courtesy of Netflix Logo text Netflix has released the official trailer for its take on John Steinbeck‘s classic East of Eden . In Zoe Kazan’s adaptation of Steinbeck’s literary masterpiece, Florence Pugh stars as Cathy Ames, whose life is intertwined with with the Trask family, Adam (Christopher Abbott) and Charles (Mike Faist), as they settle in California’s Salinas Valley. Over the years, their paths intersect with the Hamilton family including “Samuel Hamilton (Ciarán Hinds), an Irishman who made his way to California where he raised a family and got to know the land, and Lee (Hoon Lee), a Chinese American whose intellect is surpassed only by his ability to give care to those who need it most, and Faye (Martha Plimpton), a brothel owner whose open heart might lead to her downfall.“ Related Stories Beyond the Book The Adaptation Whisperers: These Producers Are Racing to Find the Next Big Romances TV Matthew Perry Docuseries Set at Netflix In the trailer, tensions are notable with Faist‘s Charles warning Abbott‘s Adam, “A girl like that doesn‘t just fall out of the sky.“ “You need to get rid of her and throw her out. She‘s going to tear you to pieces and I don‘t want to watch it,” Faist‘s Adam later warns. “Evil is not always apparent at first glance. It can come cloaked in goodness or beauty or love. The heart of our oldest stories,“ Pugh is overheard saying in the trailer. The seven-episode limited series , written and executive produced by Kazan, “offers a compelling perspective on the ways in which a family’s history impacts an individual’s present reality.“ Jeb Stuart is also a co-showrunner. Fifth Season and Anonymous Content are producing. The novel was originally adapted for the 1955 film based starring James Dean, Raymond Massey, Richard Davalo, Jo Van Fleet and Julie Harris. Kazan‘s grandfather, Academy Award-winning filmmaker Elia Kazan, directed the film adaptation. “In the process of bringing this family saga to life, the resonance of my own familial connection to the material has not been lost on me,” Kazan said in a statement when the series was announced. “But it is Steinbeck’s writing — personal, shocking, profound and free — that has kept me enthralled to East of Eden since I first read the book as a young teen. Working on this has been the greatest joy, and I am thrilled by the cast and crew we are assembling — and deeply grateful to Netflix, Fifth Season and Anonymous Content for their support.” East of Eden premieres on Netflix on Oct. 1. Watch the trailer below. THR

articles.title: George Clooney Tells Venice Studios Are Making Movies That “Need a Launchpad of a Film Festival Less and Less”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 2, 2026 5:35am George Clooney at the 2026 Venice Film Festival Courtesy of Getty Naturally, the Venice Film Festival was swiftly fawning over George Clooney on Wednesday, as the Oscar-winning star arrived (via boat, of course) to pick up his Golden Lion Lifetime Achievement Award . Ahead of the glitzy, Jay Kelly -esque honorary ceremony, Clooney sat for a press conference with journalists on the Lido who immediately quizzed him on the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, the allegations of antisemitism faced by Hollywood peer Mark Ruffalo, and his love of Venice, having gotten married in the Italian city in 2014. Related Stories Movies Slavoj Zizek on Why We Seek Utopias in the Movies (Exclusive Trailer) Movies George Clooney Tackles Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger, Mark Ruffalo, AI and State of U.S. Politics Clooney was also asked about the studio no-show at this year’s film festivals, as well as his directing aspirations. The famed U.S. actor admitted that he hasn’t noticed the studio sit-out at Cannes, Berlin and Venice, which have concentrated their lineups on the best of international cinema. “In fairness, you could make the argument — and this has been going on for 25 or 30 years, this is some of the work that [Steven] Soderbergh and I were doing when we started doing [the 1998 film] Out of Sight and films like that — that studios are doing films that need a launchpad of a film festival less and less,” said Clooney, speaking amid an industry heavily reliant on IP, reboots and franchise projects. “That’s just the nature of the beast,” he continued. “The films that studios are making are hugely expensive, so I think [this situation is] just the fallout from the films they are making, but that’s been going on, literally probably since Jaws , when everything changed… The studios used to make Bonnie and Clyde and All the President’s Men ,” said Clooney. “They don’t really make many films like that [anymore], and so they don’t really need this launchpad as much. I think that would be my only answer to that. I didn’t know that they weren’t really sending that many films over.” Clooney, famed for roles in Ocean’s Eleven , Gravity and Michael Clayton , is also a filmmaker, and even brought his 2005 Good Night, and Good Luck to the festival in 2005. “I’ve had great experiences,” replied the star when probed on whether he’ll be returning to the director’s chair any time soon. “I’ve been nominated for an Oscar, and I’ve also had really bad experiences, and that’s okay,” he laughed. “That’s part of telling stories. I’ve done films that people hated when they came out, and now they like them, and I’ve done films that people liked that [and] now they look at and they think don’t work anymore.” The only reason he is not directing, “is because I have two nine-year-old kids,” said Clooney, who shares twins with Amal. “In order for me to spend time with them, I can’t [direct]. If I act in a movie, it’s three months, and I can go and come and go and come back. When [you] direct a movie, it’s a year, wherever you are, and there’s no traveling back and forth. So I can’t do that anymore. The last thing I did was this play last year on Broadway [the stage adaptation of Good Night, and Good Luck ] and that took us all away for a period of time. And I can’t really pull the kids out of school anymore.” It’s made him “enjoy” being an actor again. “I’m a character actor now.” It was a wide-ranging presser — Clooney, a long-standing advocate for human rights, political activism and climate change awareness — managed to say a few words on how “most of the [world’s] powers that decided climate change is a hoax and science is not real.” He remains an optimist: “That won’t last forever,” though he lamented Europe’s summer battles with wildfires. “We were in Como this summer, and there were fires in Como. It’s been an extraordinarily dry and hot summer, and it’s dangerous.” Clooney confessed that he laughs in response to those who argue climate change is a fad. “Let’s say that everybody who says climate change is bullshit is right,” he began. “The worst thing that could happen by cleaning up the environment is that you create millions more new green jobs, you make the air better to breathe. I mean, there’s no argument against it. That’s the stupidest part of all this. But you know, we’re going to be in it for a while, and then sooner or later we’ll get some governments in there that actually pay more attention to it.” The Venice festival runs Sep. 2-12. THR

articles.title: Elon Musk Unmasked in Alex Gibney Documentary: “Insane a Person This Chaotic Has So Much Power”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Illustration by Robert Carter Late one August afternoon in a Manhattan editing suite, with thunder and lightning raging outside, a storm was also brewing inside. Or at least on the giant screen at the front of the room. “How’s power feeling, Mr. Musk?” a bystander calls out to Elon Musk onscreen as the beaming tech mogul strides through a post-inauguration Washington building. In the next scene, Musk sits at a roundtable with his army of early 20s DOGE staffers, looking on proudly alongside Fox News’ Jesse Watters. The young men talk with easy, deluded confidence about how they will fix government as Watters jokingly refers to the notoriously anatomical nickname of one of the men. Related Stories Movies Forget the Red Carpet -- Venice's Real Stars Are in the Documentaries This Year Movies Alex Gibney's Elon Musk Doc Will Play TIFF, Setting the Stage for an Epic Culture Wars Battle Illustration by Robert Carter At the back of the editing room, Alex Gibney , the longtime documentarian and the closest the current film world has to a Bob Woodward, watches intently. “Let’s do that ‘power’ quote hotter,” Gibney says to a team of five that includes his frequent producer Erin Edeiken and sound mixer Tony Volante. “Hotter? Yes,” Volante says, adjusting levels on the screen in front of him. Gibney has been working since late 2022 trying to get a temperature read on Musk only to see the mercury continue to climb. He had finished — or thought he had finished — a two-hour HBO documentary on Musk in late 2024, having plumbed the controversial entrepreneur’s childhood, his early PayPal-ish forays into Silicon Valley, his supercharging of SpaceX, his takeover of Tesla, his launching of the satellites of Starlink, his hirings and firings at Neuralink, his bull run into Twitter, his various mad dashes through wives and baby mamas, and many other events that would make most humans seek out a long, uninterrupted Xanax vacation. Then Musk donated ungodly sums and made appearances to help deliver the presidency to Donald Trump, who returned the favor by giving Musk the Chewbacca seat on the Millennium Falcon. Suddenly the story seemed to hold another chapter. HBO executives called Gibney telling him they wanted and would finance more. He kept shooting. And shot some more. For nearly two additional years, all the way to a six-hour cut of the movie that went deep on Musk’s 2025 DOGE era and his SpaceX IPO plate-spin this summer. (The film has since been cut down.) Over the course of a decorated career, Gibney, 72, had taken on Scientology and Enron, the U.S. military and Vladimir Putin, the Catholic Church and Wall Street. All of that prepared him, though nothing could really prepare him, for this magnum Musk creation — cinema’s premier curtain-puller on power revealing the man who has amassed so much of it. When it comes out this fall, Musk will look to change the game in several crucial ways, lining up a target that Hollywood never shoots at, seeking to become a hit documentary in an era allergic to them and trying to open the eyes of American voters to a key Republican electoral arms dealer who Gibney says is mounting an unfair fight. At stake with Musk, its creator wants to tell us, is nothing less than the future of democracy. And to spread that message, he has enlisted some of the biggest media companies around — including, improbably enough, the one soon to be owned by Trump ally David Ellison. Today, Gibney is making small tweaks to finish the film in time for screenings at the Venice and Toronto film festivals in September (three hours, 45 minutes), a wide theatrical release in October (ditto) and an HBO debut in 2027 (four hours). There are sounds to adjust and effects to complete and even video game reenactments to perfect. What better way to take on a maximalist than maximally? The sound on the DOGE scene in front of him calibrated, Gibney gives a small look of approval. “Great,” he says. “Now let’s go to Watters and Big Balls.” *** Elon Musk is not an obvious candidate for a documentary. A documentary aims to tell us something new, and Elon Musk epitomizes the familiar. We take stock of his trolls on X, we see him artwash his image on Saturday Night Live , we get a load of his engineering and entrepreneurial genius from biographer Walter Isaacson, we learn about his stock market genius on CNBC, we hear him talk about the goal of further populating the planet, we hear one example after another of his personal efforts in pursuit of that goal, we eye with skepticism his proclaiming the age of Mars colonization and extraterrestrial data centers, we watch him (and then try to unwatch him) gleefully talk of slashing-and-burning aid workers from inside White House meeting rooms. So much Musk have we ambiently ingested these past few years that perhaps the best cultural gift might be a break from all that, an Elon-free zone populated with anyone besides the 55-year-old provocateur. Yet Gibney aggressively wants to challenge that instinct, and he may have a point. None of what we have seen and thought about Musk can fully ready us for what the filmmaker has done here — an adventurous but methodical movie grounded in the thesis that, as he sees it, a dangerous huckster is stealthily aggregating power to exploit us, primarily by centralizing and controlling massive amounts of data. Gibney’s basic take on Musk is that he’s a confidence man whose power comes only from the stock market and disappears the minute we see through the facade of sales pitches — but can do a whole lot of damage until that happens. The film world-premieres Sept. 8 at Venice. But its cultural reach will likely extend far beyond that. Musk stands poised to touch off a fresh wave of anger and fear among the millions already inclined to worry about him, into and well after the midterms, while fueling a whole lot of trollishness (and worse?) from the many who worship at the temple of Elon Musk, including Elon Musk. Gibney has crafted a movie that, while not new in its specifics, is often damning in its totality, standing apart from anything the media entertainment complex has recently turned out — a portrait of power with the cinematic scope of All the King’s Men and the potential social impact of The Pentagon Papers . (“It’s rare these days to see a complete story instead of the fragments we’re used to,” says Anonymous Content’s Nick Shumaker, a producer on the film.) Some will surely find Musk overly negative and conspiratorial. Yet nearly every time the film seems like it might tip into paranoid fantasy, Gibney unearths a new fact or asks a new commonsense question to steady us back. Gibney spends the first half of the film coming at Musk for various alleged sins, including stealing credit from original Tesla founder Martin Eberhard; bullying a woman who birthed his child to sign an NDA; pumping his stocks with shaky talk of Mars exploration and full self-driving cars (the latter of which Gibney also alleges are responsible for more than 60 deaths); and turning a light on the monkeys experimented on at Neuralink who advocacy groups say suffered needlessly. Not nearly as adept at all the substantive tasks of running a company as he claims, Elon Musk, Gibney argues, excels mainly at selling tall tales. Even the multiple levels of alleged villainy, however, seem narrow compared to what the director argues is the real game: world domination. In Gibney’s telling, to witness Musk, intentionally or not, convert his satellite internet system, Starlink, into an unelected policymaker given its crucial role in Ukraine and other war-torn places; to see NASA rely so heavily on SpaceX to perpetuate its space program; to watch Musk seemingly use Twitter to garner business favors from world leaders like Modi and Milei; to look with growing dread as the data collected by DOGE potentially becomes a sleeper cell for campaign research and political retaliation — to observe all of this is to gaze upon a man interested not only in wealth and status but in an oligarchal sway that transcends elections’ fickle seasons. Donald Trump may have spent six years bringing the branches of government to heel. But in Gibney’s accounting, Musk is in the process of pulling off something far more menacing: rendering government obsolete altogether. Two revelations, or at least intimations, especially stand out, both involving elections and Musk’s alleged techno- surveilling means of moving them for Republicans. In one, Musk ex and former conservative influencer Ashley St. Clair, a central figure in the documentary, describes the events of Trump’s election in November 2024. Musk, she says, had a “degree of certainty” about the results before they came in that “I had never seen before.” “He had told me [before the election] he was going to unleash the ‘anomaly in the matrix,’ ” she recounts, as a text exchange between them pops up onscreen backing up the claim. We see Musk telling her, “I have ten thousand lasers in space.” “So you think he was referring to Starlink?” Gibney asks off-camera. St. Clair replies, “I mean, I don’t know where else he has space lasers.” Gibney leaves the insinuation hanging — was this a troll or a confession? — but hints he is taking it seriously when he then says in his patented voiceover, “What is Elon building, what are his goals, what are his actual motivations, and do we even know this man at all?” The other piece of the electoral-manipulation insinuation looks not backward but forward and suggests that Musk’s four-month stint in Washington last year did more than gleefully ax 270,000 federal employees and untold billions in life-saving aid (though a section on the latter, anchored by former USAID chief Samantha Power, lands with an outraging wallop). During that time, Gibney suggests, Musk also had access to and potentially collected intimate data on tens of millions of Americans possibly even for later political use. In a follow-up email, Gibney explains further: “We don’t know what DOGE/Musk did with the data to which they had access. What we do know — via my own source who ran IT at a major federal agency and via the whistleblowers and public accounts — is that the DOGE Boys had Super Admin status to federal IT systems. That means they could just slide a copy of the data on all of us to SpaceX as easily as dropping a file into a folder.” (The allegation of salting away data squares with a whistleblower complaint filed by the Social Security Administration’s chief data officer.) “How much data exists in the federal government about every single person living in this country, their voting records, everything that they had ever done?” Wired editor-in-chief Katie Drummond, whose publication led much of this coverage, says in the movie. “Imagine what an AI could do if it can be trained on all that information.” Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-prize-winning godfather of AI, offers a specific use case: leveraging the data into an unfair campaign advantage. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” he says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on U.S. citizens. And what DOGE did looked like just what you would do.” Documentarian Alex Gibney, photographed Aug. 20 in Brooklyn, has made a career of exposing abusive power structures, from the U.S. military to Scientology. In Musk, he feels he has found a uniquely dangerous subject: Musk may have left Trump’s side, but what havoc could he wreak, Gibney asks, with the data he surely collected from his short stint atop the so-called Department of Government Efficiency? Photographed by Jake Chessum *** For much of the past 20 years, as television news resources and audiences for longform investigation have waned, documentary filmmakers have risen to take their place. Leading that class has been Gibney. A kind of documentary journeyman, Gibney’s standing changed in the mid-2000s, when, after the age of 50, he directed the eye-opening Oscar nominee Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room and Taxi to the Dark Side , an intimate, upsetting story of the killing of an Afghan taxi driver by American soldiers during an interrogation. Arriving in George W. Bush’s second term, the film became a focal point for all the frustrations and qualms around the War on Terror. A spate of exposés of other corroded powerful institutions followed as Gibney turned into a kind of investigative journalism gunslinger, coming in to showdown against powerful institutions when few others would. All those films feel like they were leading to this, a point even Gibney will concede. “It’s not the end of the path, but it’s definitely a distillation of the journey,” he says of Musk . As Gibney sits in the edit bay adjusting small details — “Let’s let Trump’s voice go on longer and more distorted so it reads like it’s in Elon’s head,” he says during an Oval Office scene — his worldview comes into focus. Gibney’s tendency is to see the darker side of power and the powerful side of technology, tendencies that cast him as an outlier in the 2010s but have made him more relevant as the years have gone on. In an interview with this reporter about his Stuxnet film Zero Days a decade ago, he outlined hacking threats that seemed exotic, like compromising an American water system. With reports recently about Iranian operatives trying to do just that, they don’t seem so outlandish. “I try to tell a story that opens our eyes and makes us ask the right questions,” he says, speaking of Musk but offering a touchstone that might apply to many of his films. Gibney here has set out to make a movie less about its subject’s history than his future. Sam Harris, the right-leaning podcaster and friend turned enemy of Musk, lays out this theme onscreen near the end of the film. “We are living in a world where one person’s psychopathology and neuropsychological dysregulation is translating into massive consequence in our politics, in our economy, in our geopolitics,” he says. “It’s completely insane we have one person who’s this chaotic — who’s completely unelected — and has this much power.” Gibney makes it clear that he doesn’t think such voices are hyperbolic, and that it is only a certain kind of American heuristic that prevents us from hearing them. “People assume because he’s very rich that he’s not crazy,” he says. “But the terrifying thing might be that he’s crazy and he’s very rich and powerful. That’s the warning bell the film sounds.” The director’s method for ringing that alarm will surely draw debate. Musk did not sit for an interview, going on the offensive at the announcement of the film three years ago by taking to X to call it a “hit piece.” This prompted Gibney, who never met a diss he couldn’t deadpan back, to reply “How would you know?” The line was meant as both undress and challenge, as Gibney at that time still sought an interview. When Musk effectively ended that hope by tweeting, “Gibney is a douche,” Gibney parried back, “Douché,” marking perhaps the first time in human history that a rap battle was settled with an accent aigu. That rejection turned out to be a blessing, birthing dozens of outside sources Gibney turned to instead, on- and off-camera. It also yielded a formal magic trick unexpected in the work of an Oscar-winning documentarian. Gibney and his research team scraped the internet for any audio of Musk they could find. They then created — stick with me here — a video game avatar of Musk speaking those words, Ready Player One -style. The Musk avatar also, in a pair of first-person-shooter sequences, moves through the world as a vintage video game character, complete with health bars and lives left and colorful respawns. “I wouldn’t have gone there if Elon wasn’t so relentless,” Gibney tells me when asked what motivated this choice. “But over and over again in our research, Elon kept coming back to this idea of simulation, how we’re living in an existential video game.” Gibney adds, “We’re playing with levels of reality, and the elements of the Elon Musk story are how he intends to define reality.” (This same wry mischief can be found in the closing credits song, a bouncy original number written and performed by David Byrne that takes jagged pieces of Musk’s own self-mythologizing quotes and slashes him with them.) The effect of Gibney’s digital avatar is surreal, and also its own comment, at once turning Musk into a leather-jacketed larger-than-life character while completely gamifying all his ambitions. The way to neutralize the world’s most powerful man, Gibney believes, is not to cower at his influence but to extend him the same cat-with-a-ball-of-yarn unseriousness he shows us. The move could certainly backfire at a moment when the documentary (and nondocumentary) film world is wary of digital replicas replacing the real thing and AI deepfakes blurring the truth-fiction line. But Gibney says the whimsical device comes in service of a larger truth: the unmasking of a man who has aggregated power only by duping us into thinking we should give it to him. “The Great and Terrible Oz kept people in check because they were afraid of his visage that loomed over everybody, and he used that power to exert an enormous amount of control,” Gibney tells me. “But when a little dog pulled aside the curtain, and you can see a frumpy man operating gears and levers, suddenly he wasn’t so terrible and he wasn’t so great.” “I try to tell a story that opens our eyes and makes us ask the right questions,” notes Gibney, who says he initially admired Musk and proudly owned a Tesla car and solar panel system. Photographed by Jake Chessum *** Gibney presents an intriguing paradox. A Maine resident, he is nonetheless a fixture on New York’s media and entertainment social scene, moving among the kind of powerful people he frequently turns the heat-blaster on. If this has proved conflicting, Gibney does not let on, marching from sacred target to sacred target with little apparent tentativeness. The director has a kind of serious casualness in which he shoulders the weight of the world, but unfussily. Gibney’s is a no-nonsense, bullshit-averse demeanor, which comes out in the editing session when a performative Trump administration ally appears onscreen, prompting an eye-rolling expression with some salty assessments tossed in. For someone who has made a career scalpeling the powerful, it perhaps comes as a surprise that Gibney had never thought of making a documentary about Elon Musk before — and in fact resisted the idea when the Chinese former real estate baron Zhang Xin suggested it to him in 2022 — feeling like so much had been said and, also, wasn’t Musk sometimes a force for good, remaking industries at will? “To be honest, I was on the fence about it,” Gibney says. “But then I talked to a close friend, and he said it was a film about 21st century power, and that resonated with me.” Realizing also that part of his daily life — he was long active on Twitter and had once bought Tesla solar panels — revolved around the mogul, and that no one was really asking questions about what this meant, Gibney sought early financing partners. He found a group of liberal-adjacent production companies ready to work with him, including Anonymous Content ( Navalny ), the upstart doc banner Double Agent (run by an indie film veteran named Dana O’Keefe and joint venture of the narrative film producers Black Bear Pictures and New Regency) and Zhang Xin’s Closer Media. Given the sensitivity of taking on one of the world’s most powerful men (who already viewed the movie as a hit piece), those producers might have expected that they would have to finance the making of the film itself without a sales partner. But when producers took the project out to the market, they were taken aback. Companies that liked to play it safe were willing to take on the far right-flirting Musk. (It was, crucially, before he joined the Trump wagon, but still.) Most notably: Netflix, which pursued a deal despite the streamer avoiding globally polarizing topics like Jamal Khashoggi, surprising even some of the producers. Gibney weighed his options but felt most comfortable with another suitor, HBO’s documentary division, with which he has done some of his most impactful work, including movies about Theranos and Scientology. And so filmmakers in 2023 signed a pact with the platform for U.S. streaming and television rights. In doing so, the parties defied a long-held convention. “Hollywood is either averse to making Elon Musk films because of his politics or afraid of Elon Musk because he could sue,” says Ashlee Vance, the author whose 2015 biography, Elon Musk: Tesla, SpaceX, and the Quest for a Fantastic Future , itself was strangled in development by HBO in 2023 because of what Vance believes were those hesitations. “It makes it that much more surprising this film got through.” (The idea of featuring Elon Musk, of course, has not been anathema in fictional works; as Gibney shows in the film, image-burnishing appearances have cropped up everywhere from Iron Man to The Simpsons to SNL .) Host Elon Musk during the monologue on Saturday Night Live on Saturday, May 8, 2021 Will Heath/NBC/NBCU Photo Bank/Getty Images Then there was the matter of international rights. Most documentaries get sold territory by territory since the interests of countries on a given topic vary, as opposed to one worldwide distributor. This is especially true for a controversial subject — giant global players don’t want a headache because of sensitivities in Croatia. All of which made it unexpected that Universal, one of the biggest international film distributors around, wanted all foreign rights. For the filmmakers, this of course would potentially mean a lot more scrutiny and studio battles than with individual territory buyers. But the idea of making a bigger impact won out. HBO declined to comment about its involvement. This can seem like a strange turn — you can’t put out a movie to tens of millions of people and not want folks to notice — but given Musk’s power and eagerness for a brawl, perhaps logical too. Another entanglement comes in the form of one of the financier-producers. Black Bear is run by Teddy Schwarzman — son of Stephen Schwarzman, the founder of Blackstone and someone who has moved in close circles with Musk, both men part of Trump delegations that met with foreign leaders. (Stephen Schwarzman has called Musk a “fascinating guy” and “good person.”) His son’s willingness to bankroll the most high-profile takedown of Musk in history makes for a potentially interesting Thanksgiving family dinner. Teddy Schwarzman, notably, did not personally take a credit on the film. He did not wish to comment for this piece. HBO’s centrality is especially intriguing. Warner Bros. Discovery, HBO’s parent company, has been run by David Zaslav, a known associate of Musk, the two men prominently sitting together in a luxury box at the U.S. Open two years ago. Gibney’s movie already was well underway. The two even discussed WBD television projects at the match, according to a person familiar with their conversation. But if Musk asked Zaslav to kill the film, the media executive didn’t oblige. Yet huge questions remain given the upcoming changing state of WBD management. Incoming WBD owner Ellison may well run HBO by the time the movie hits the service on an unnamed date in the first half of 2027, and one can’t imagine him feeling too enthused by the onscreen happenings. In addition to the general air of Silicon Valley and Donald Trump skepticism, Ellison’s father and principal financier, Larry Ellison, gets a negative shout-out when he is shown in text messages willing to airdrop Musk $2 billion to buy Twitter, no questions asked. This is not what people pay $111 billion in acquisition fees to platform. Would David Ellison ask for changes? Pull the plug and force producers to self-distribute? (The filmmakers in an unlikely coup retained paid VOD rights.) Gibney and the filmmaking team are holding their breath. So is everyone else. Driven by his interest in colonizing Mars, Musk founded SpaceX in 2002. Dan Tuffs/Getty Images Lost in Space A SpaceX rocket carrying a payload of Starlink satellites, adding to Musk’s already massive fleet — and the power it affords him. Kevin Carter/Getty Images *** How will the movie land with both the public and power brokers? Isaacson’s 2023 book left a lot of reviewers cold with its lack of criticism but still sold a gazillion copies. Gibney’s film could well prove all those book critics right and extend the skepticism to a general public that Musk has to this point kept at bay. The days of An Inconvenient Truth and Fahrenheit 9/11 , in which a documentary becomes an event that moves both box office needles and public sentiment, are well behind us. But is it possible that at this post-Twitter moment, with a need for common vehicles of activism and a new town square, a citizenry this fall will find refuge in Gibney’s movie? It could. Musk’s butchering of the old public commons could deliciously be the reason we make his takedown the new one. The film’s length could paradoxically work in its favor, too, rewarding those who soldier through its four-hour run time with a badge of endurance, not to mention cocktail party cred. “The thing that drives people to theaters is urgency — people feeling that they have to be part of a conversation,” says Kent Sanderson, CEO of Bleecker Street, which is releasing the movie. “And there’s no conversation like the one around someone who affects every single person’s life every single day.” And don’t sleep on the Oscar chattering class. Musk will get a big push for best documentary, and it remains, at this summer vantage point, hard to see what can match it. The biggest X factor, as it were, is how Musk responds. Social media trolls are almost certain, but would he go beyond that? Musk has a history of lashing out legally at those he perceives as harming his interests, filing lawsuits against boycotting Twitter advertisers and his AI rival Sam Altman. The insinuations of business hucksterism are one thing that could provoke him, more intimate details are another. Musk’s personal life comes in for tough scrutiny in the film, with St. Clair’s nauseating details about paternity-based NDA bullying and hush payments (stealth audio from a Musk fixer especially churns the stomach) and her no-comment about his drug use, and with a revealing childhood story Musk’s father tells in which a family friend undergoes a medical emergency while they were all on a road trip in Musk’s native South Africa. The man dies as everyone tries to resuscitate him. Young Elon, his father recounts, reads a comic book, unreactive through the entire episode. Gibney and HBO are insured, and a high-profile group of lawyers has been vigorously stress-testing the film. (Helping matters is that Gibney bases large portions of the documentary on the published work of text journalists from Wired to The Wall Street Journal ; the movie is nothing if not a valedictory for journalism.) Yet that has never stopped a litigious tycoon — especially these days — from going after a media outlet to make a point or extract some concession. Tesla CEO Elon Musk listens as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters in the Oval Office of the White House on May 30, 2025 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Alternatively, Musk could learn from the Church of Scientology, which to protest the alleged misrepresentations in Gibney’s 2013 exposé Going Clear took out a full-page ad in The New York Times seeking to debunk the movie. It sent viewership skyrocketing. As Gibney locks in during the editing session, all of that future noise stays outside. More relevant is Musk’s future, as the director tweaks a scene about what the mogul is up to next (humanoid robots and launching himself off a burning planet to Mars). “As he accretes more power, he’s no longer interested in checking his worst impulses,” Gibney says to me, reflecting on Musk’s trajectory. The director pauses, remembering a moment from his reporting. “Someone who worked closely with Elon told me, ‘He’s the most miserable man I’ve ever met.’ So he’s inflicting his misery on everyone else.” The suffering will pile up, Gibney says, until we see what’s behind Toto’s curtain. The Musk Myth How Hollywood burnished the entrepreneur’s image as a benevolent genius. Iron Man 2 (2010) The mere juxtaposition of Musk and Tony Stark implants the idea that the former inspired the latter. The line Musk utters to a passing Robert Downey Jr. (“I have a good idea for an electric jet”) suggests a concept he never had and the reaction of Stark (“Then we’ll make it work”) an easy execution he’s seldom achieved. The Simpsons (2015) Musk arrives in Springfield, where he promptly sets out making alternative energy power plants to help humanity even at the expense of his own profit. Lisa calls him “possibly the greatest living inventor,” and characters regard him as “an intelligence far beyond ours.” The Big Bang Theory (2015) “It feels great to come down here and help the less fortunate,” a real-life Musk tells an awestruck Howard Wolowitz in a soup kitchen on Thanksgiving. Elon Musk, he’s just like us (only more charitable). Rick and Morty (2019) Musk plays an alternate-reality version of himself known as “Elon Tusk,” who joins the title pair in a plan to defeat the evil Heisotron, even polishing his family-man image with a reference to his kids. Saturday Night Live (2021) In inviting Musk (pictured above) to host (over the objections of some castmembers), the show mostly let him good-naturedly clean up his COVID conspiracy theories, give free plugs to DOGEcoin, garner sympathy by discussing his self-reported Aspberger’s and talk about sending people to Mars in a rocket ship as if it’s a real thing. This story appeared in the Sept. 2 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Travis Kelce Details “Insane” Wedding to Taylor Swift: “Biggest Night of Our Lives”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 2, 2026 6:01am Swift and Kelce photographed in 2025. Courtesy of Getty Travis Kelce is officially, as he puts it, “a married man.” The Kansas City Chiefs tight end was beaming to his brother, Jason, in a new episode of their New Heights podcast on Wednesday, where Kelce spoke in depth for the first time about that all-star, ludicrously lavish wedding ceremony to pop queen Taylor Swift on July 3. “It’s been so much fun, it was insane,” said Kelce about the event at Madison Square Garden, with a guest list that boasted Jack Antonoff, Bradley Cooper, Lena Dunham, Selena Gomez, Ed Sheeran, Dakota Johnson, Jason Sudeikis, Benson Boone, Hugh Grant, Kelsea Ballerini, Camila Cabello, Karlie Kloss and Josh Kushner, Ethan Hawke, Zoë Kravitz, Mariska Hargitay and Peter Hermann and the Haim sisters, among hundreds of other A-listers. Related Stories Music Harry Styles Jokes About Taylor Swift's Wedding During Madison Square Garden Concert Music Taylor Swift Remembers Dolly Parton's "True Grace and Grit": "Her Legacy Will Be Everlasting" Kelce said it was a night that he and his Grammy-winning wife, who began dating in 2023, will never forget. “Me and Taylor are so thankful for everybody that showed up. From the vows to seeing everyone to how much fun we had throughout the entire evening, and hearing that being relayed through everyone’s stories of that night… It was just so magical, man. I wish it could have lasted longer than it did.” He also gave a shout-out to Hollywood actor Adam Sandler, who officiated the ceremony. “He has been just the fucking best person on this planet,” said Kelce. “For him to be up for getting ordained in the state of New York and marrying me and Taylor, and the way he did it, in the very Sandman style, and giving us more than what we could’ve imagined at that moment, knowing that it was the biggest night of our lives, it was absolutely insane man.” The football star joked that at the end of the ceremony, “once the drinks stopped being served, everyone [started] to mosey out.” He continued: “But thank you to everyone at MSG… We wanted it to do it somewhere where we could have a very intimate and genuine setting without a lot of distractions and we needed to have a private feel, and MSG went above and beyond to give us that and I can’t thank everybody enough, that showed up but helped put that show on.” Eyebrows were certainly raised when rumors of the MSG wedding gained traction. It proved to be a savvy move from Swift and Kelce as intense security and privacy measures were undertaken. On Thursday, ahead of the rehearsal dinner, The Hollywood Reporter spotted a white tent being raised up to the door of the VIP entrance to the arena. In front of the Garden’s main entrance, THR heard that another, red curtain had gone up. Police officers were stationed in packs around the venue, particularly on 7th and 8th Avenues. Snipers were stationed atop MSG, with surveillance helicopters heard overhead. Numerous streets around the arena were also closed to vehicles and, in some cases, pedestrian traffic. The guests themselves remained enshrouded in secrecy as black cars were seen driving into a large white tent, with the entrance set off by black curtains, shielding attendees from nearby prying eyes. We’re still waiting on those hotly-anticipated photos from the wedding — it remains to be seen if the couple will ever release footage or images from inside the event — but their team did confirm on July 2 that the superstar singer-songwriter and her then-fiancé had made $26 million in charitable donation s to more than a dozen organizations across the country. THR revealed that Swift wore a custom haute couture gown by Jonathan Anderson of Christian Dior. Kelce also wore a haute couture look by Anderson for Dior. The event marked the first time Anderson has designed a couture wedding dress for a celebrity of Swift’s stature, and both the bride and groom wore Christian Louboutin shoes. Swift wore Cartier jewellery. THR

articles.title: Rupert Murdoch Was “Very Happy” With the Casting of Danny Boyle’s ‘Ink’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 2, 2026 6:08am 'Ink' Courtesy of Netflix Rupert Murdoch and the world of British tabloid journalism were in the spotlight in Venice on Tuesday as Danny Boyle presented his new film Ink , which opens the 83rd Biennale Wednesday night. The film, adapted from James Graham’s stage play, depicts Murdoch’s entry into the British newspaper scene, when he acquired the then-failing tabloid The Sun in 1969. Hiring Larry Lamb as editor, the two combined far-right political reporting and populist rabble to turn the paper into a dark force in British media. Murdoch would take the lessons learned at The Sun and apply them to build his U.S. media empire with The New York Post and Fox News. Related Stories Movies George Clooney Tells Venice Studios Are Making Movies That "Need a Launchpad of a Film Festival Less and Less" Movies Slavoj Zizek on Why We Seek Utopias in the Movies (Exclusive Trailer) Guy Pearce plays Murdoch. Jack O’Connell ( Sinners ) plays Lamb. Claire Foy ( The Crown , Women Talking ) co-stars as Jules Davies, an amalgam of female executives who worked under Lamb at The Sun and a character new to the film adaptation. Boyle said during a press conference that he was careful, as with the stage version not to “monsterize” Rupert Murdoch “because he represented at the time [a] breath of fresh air in what was a very rigid British society. It begins with something that’s fun and different, challenging a rigid order… It was important to us that the audience feels complicit.” Foy said she found plunging into the world of ‘60s tabloid journalism “really intoxicating,” admitting to feeling “quite jealous” of Fleet Street reporters. “They had power at their fingertips. They knew what they wrote would be what people read and what people believed.” Pearce revealed that Murdoch himself was pleased with the film’s casting. “I had some messaging with Elizabeth [Murdoch], his daughter, and she said ‘Dad’s very happy that you are playing him.’ But he hadn’t seen the film at that point.” Graham said Murdoch had, however, caught the original play. “He came to see the play twice,” he recalled, though he didn’t give his opinion of the story. “He’s very good at not giving anything away which I think is one of his secrets.” Though the film is set in the 1960s, Boyle said he wasn’t as interested in making a period piece, arguing that Ink was “about the modern world” showing many of the trends in the media that shape the current world. As divisive as Rupert Murdoch and The Sun were, and are, Boyle argued, the father of modern tabloid journalism was, at his heart, “a print man” who he thinks must be “driven to despair” at the disappearance of the print industry, “the tactile world that we used to depend on to read the stories about us.” Boyle ended the press conference with an extolment of the value of journalism that “speaks truth to power,” calling it “one of great uprights of any civilization.” He also acknowledged the great threats facing journalists, print or otherwise, in the age of AI. “The danger with the tech giants, obviously [is that] they’ll be able to have an AI journalist who’s much more efficient, lot cheaper, etc. etc.,” the director said. “But will that AI journalist speak truth to that power that’s created it? That’s going to be very very tough.” Ink is screening in competition in Venice. The film will release in select theaters in the U.S. on Dec. 11 before going out on Netflix on Jan. 8 in the U.S. and Latin America. Studiocanal is releasing the film theatrically across multiple territories, including the U.K., France, Germany, Poland, Australia and New Zealand, starting with the U.K. release on Jan. 8. Studiocanal is also handling worldwide sales, and is co-representing domestic with WME Independent. THR

articles.title: Ruben Östlund’s Plattform Produktion Boards Jessica Hausner’s Satirical Drama ‘Toxic’ Ahead of Venice Gap-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 2, 2026 3:44am PT Ruben Östlund’s Plattform Produktion Boards Jessica Hausner’s Satirical Drama ‘Toxic’ Ahead of Venice Gap-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE) The Swedish label joins Austria's Schubert, Germany's Essential Films and France's Société Parisienne de Production in the pan-European co-production By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest Ruben Östlund’s Plattform Produktion Boards Jessica Hausner’s Satirical Drama ‘Toxic’ Ahead of Venice Gap-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Austrian Director Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Wins Best Film at Sarajevo Film Festival 2 weeks ago ‘Supporting Role’ Director Ana Urushadze Preps ‘Fear of Butterflies,’ a Detective Story With ‘Mysticism and a Touch of Body Horror’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 weeks ago See All Courtesy of Barbara Seyr Ruben Östlund ’s Plattform Produktion has joined “Toxic,” the forthcoming satirical workplace drama from “Club Zero” director Jessica Hausner , which is among the projects being pitched during the Venice Gap-Financing Market taking place Sept. 4 – 6. The pan-European co-production is produced by Schubert (Austria), Essential Films (Germany), Société Parisienne de Production (France) and Plattform Produktion (Sweden). International sales will be repped by the Coproduction Office. Related Stories 'VIII: Awakening' Wraps Production in Beijing, Marking KC Global Media Asia's First China Original (EXCLUSIVE) 'Wildwood' and 'Ray Gunn' to World Premiere at London Film Festival as 'Ink,' 'Club Kid,' 'Bunker,' 'La Bola Negra,' 'Wild Horse Nine' and More Join Lineup Told across four chapters, “Toxic” explores different aspects of the modern world of work. Through contemporary parables, it follows employees and employers within a capitalist system on the verge of outpacing itself. With a tone at times realistic, at others more absurd, it’s tied together by the human element that acts as the sand in the gears of a profit-driven world. Popular on Variety Working off a script co-written by Jessica Lind, Hausner said she was interested in exploring the many contradictions of capitalism, and the “mutual dependency” between workers and employers that’s fostering ever-growing economic gaps while leaving so many unfulfilled. “Is this system we work and live in the best system we can come up with?” she asked. The question cuts to the very heart of a modern condition in which “our identities and the respect we command are often defined by our job and pay grade,” she said. “Meaning in life is really created through the ideology of our society. As an individual, I don’t think one can find meaning all alone,” she said. “Meaning is created through others — through the eyes of my fellows in society. It is very much a question bound to the system we work in.” Through its parallel storylines, the film explores how our understanding of self-realization in the workplace is evolving, contrasting exploitation and overwork with our desire to find meaning in our professional lives. Set within four different workplaces — an advertising agency; a waste disposal company; a nursing home; and an unprofitable retail chain — it examines how deeply people have internalized performance-driven pressures, and asks whether change is possible within a system rooted in profit and success. Hausner’s last film, “Club Zero,” was set at a British boarding school where a nutrition teacher — played by Mia Wasikowska — pushed a gospel of mindful abstinence on her students, transforming them into a cult. In a glowing review out of Cannes, Variety ’s Owen Gleiberman praised the “gripping and provocative” film as an “audaciously disturbing drama.” Speaking to Variety from her home in Vienna, Hausner explained how “Toxic” is in conversation with her previous films. “What is satisfying? What is it that really makes a life worth living? In my films, I always try to circle around these questions,” she said. “Not only on an individual level. I’m always interested in the societal level. Why am I made to think or to believe something? This is what I try to focus on in all my films. The way we are being manipulated, in a subtle, everyday-like way, by the society we live in.” But what happens when society is in flux? Across Europe, the director noted, governments are mulling whether the continent’s work-life balance needs to be reconsidered. “The social system is becoming less affordable. This is an economic problem,” she said. “Many countries in Europe have to shift their social expenses from social care into building more weapons.” Meanwhile, inequality is growing, and work itself, as Hausner put it, “no longer pays off, neither financially nor in terms of fulfilment.” As “Toxic” illustrates, that leaves societies with many difficult questions and no easy answers — least of all from the tech barons and free-market evangelists who push capitalism as the miracle cure to all that ails us. “If we knew a better solution, we would probably already be heading there,” said Hausner. “But it’s not at all obvious what the next step is.” Venice-Selected ‘Agata the Writer,’ Starring Mia Wasikowska, Boarded by MMM Film Sales (EXCLUSIVE) Chinese Feature ‘Big Little Things’ Turns a Real-Life Family Rift Into a Coming-Out Drama Now Headed for Venice Horizons (EXCLUSIVE) Ruben Östlund’s Plattform Produktion Boards Jessica Hausner’s Satirical Drama ‘Toxic’ Ahead of Venice Gap-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE) Venice: M-Appeal Picks Up Chinese Director Jie Dong’s ‘Zoom In, Zoom Out’ Ahead of Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Who’s Afraid of Film Festivals? articles.title: Venice Jury President Maggie Gyllenhaal Says Films Are ‘Fundamentally, Unavoidably Political’ and Questions Lack of Female Directors in Competition: ‘There’s a Systemic Problem’
articles.full_text: Sep 2, 2026 3:49am PT Venice Jury President Maggie Gyllenhaal Says Films Are ‘Fundamentally, Unavoidably Political’ and Questions Lack of Female Directors in Competition: ‘There’s a Systemic Problem’ By Elsa Keslassy , Rebecca Rubin It didn’t take long for politics to take the spotlight at this year’s Venice Film Festival jury press conference. Amid the wars raging in Gaza and Ukraine, as well as the unrest in the United States, jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal was asked whether cinema should be political. “OK,” Gyllenhaal said with a laugh. “May as well get into it.” The filmmaker of “The Bride” and “The Lost Daughter” directly addressed the question by sharing her belief that movies are “fundamentally, unavoidably political.” Related Stories 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Named Centerpiece of Tokyo Film Festival as 'Sukiyaki' Opens, 'Colony' Closes Kaskade, Electronic Music Icon, Signs With Pacific Music Group in Asia Partnership (EXCLUSIVE) “Look, we could say, how are we possibly here talking about movies right now when the world is in a state of emergency?” she said. “To me, the answer has something to do with empathy. I think that film allows an opening into an opportunity to find empathy inside of ourselves.” Popular on Variety She added that every subject and filmmaker should have the ability to be heard. “I think we can challenge ourselves to hear stories about the most corrupt, most perverse people because it opens up the opportunity to find empathy for those people,” she says. “I am here open. I am here curious.” Gyllenhaal was also probed about the lack of female directors in this year’s competition lineup. Only one film up for the Golden Lion — the drama “Woman Unknown” by Danish-Egyptian director May El-Toukhysolely — was solely directed by a women. “I guess it’s finally become clear that men make better movies than women do,” Gyllenhaal deadpanned. Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera interjected, saying that “Naza,” a documentary co-directed by “No Other Land” filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was added to the competition lineup shortly before the festival. Gyllenhall returned to the question, saying, “I will answer you seriously. There’s a systemic problem. It’s harder for women to get films financed.” She wondered aloud: “Could it be possible that women, having had a different experience of being alive in the world, want to make movies about are not always deemed high art? Who decide what’s good? Who decides what is valuable?” Gyllenhall also noted it was significant that she was chosen to be head of the main competition jury. She’s presiding over a seven-member committee that includes Tunisian helmer Kaouther Ben Hania, Hong Kong filmmaker Johnnie To, Afghan director Shahrbanoo Sadat, French filmmaker Xavier Giannoli, British composer Daniel Blumberg and Italian film scholar Francesco Casetti. Gyllenhaal represented the jury at the conference, while her fellow members sat in the audience. The traditional opening jury press conference took place after some uncertainty over whether Venice would hold it at all. The festival considered scrapping the event because of “scheduling issues,” which some perceived as a way to shield jury members from being quizzed about politics. After facing backlash, the festival reinstated the jury presser, explaining the programming conflicts had been solved. The debate surrounding the press conference came amid heightened political tensions on the international festival circuit, where actors, directors and jury members have increasingly been pressed to address wars, Gaza, U.S. politics and the rise of the far right. The conversation around politics escalated at the Berlin Film Festival earlier this year after jury president Wim Wenders said filmmakers should “stay out of politics” while fielding questions about Israel and Palestine. His remarks triggered fierce criticism and prompted Berlin artistic director Tricia Tuttle to publicly defend artists’ right to decide whether or not to speak on political issues. Venice is opening against a particularly charged backdrop. An open letter issued by the Venice4Palestine collective and signed by figures including Nobel Prize-winning writer Annie Ernaux, Roger Waters, Isabel Coixet and Matteo Garrone has called on the festival to take “concrete action” in support of Palestine. The group has also asked Venice to fly the Palestinian flag throughout the festival. The subject carries particular resonance for Ben Hania, whose Gaza drama “The Voice of Hind Rajab” premiered in competition at Venice last year and won the Silver Lion after receiving a 22-minute standing ovation. Barbera has himself described this year’s selection as the festival’s most political in recent years, pointing to films dealing with war, Palestine, immigration, climate change, mounting social tensions and shrinking freedoms. “We are a space for freedom of expression,” Barbera told Variety prior to the start of the festival . “Our role is to safeguard freedom of expression for everyone, for the artists, and to safeguard the confrontation between artists and the public, the critics and people in general.” ‘NAZA’ Documentary From ‘No Other Land’ Directors Acquired by MK2 Films Ahead of Venice Film Festival Premiere George Clooney Defends Mark Ruffalo’s ‘Ability to Speak Freely’ About Paramount-Warner Bros. articles.title: George Clooney Defends Mark Ruffalo’s ‘Ability to Speak Freely’ About Paramount-Warner Bros. Deal and Doesn’t See How the Merger ‘Financially Ends Up Making Sense’
articles.full_text: Sep 2, 2026 4:33am PT George Clooney Defends Mark Ruffalo’s ‘Ability to Speak Freely’ About Paramount-Warner Bros. Deal and Doesn’t See How the Merger ‘Financially Ends Up Making Sense’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest George Clooney Defends Mark Ruffalo’s ‘Ability to Speak Freely’ About Paramount-Warner Bros. Deal and Doesn’t See How the Merger ‘Financially Ends Up Making Sense’ 2 hours ago Venice Jury President Maggie Gyllenhaal Says Films Are ‘Fundamentally, Unavoidably Political’ and Questions Lack of Female Directors in Competition: ‘There’s a Systemic Problem’ 3 hours ago Luca Guadagnino’s ‘Artificial’ to World Premiere at New York Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE) 24 hours ago See All Life really does imitate art. George Clooney attended last year’s Venice Film Festival with “Jay Kelly,” a comedic drama in which he portrayed an aging A-lister who travels to Italy to receive a life achievement award. Now the actor is getting a real Venetian tribute, accepting the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement Award on the festival’s opening day. Before his big honor, Clooney sat for a press conference on Wednesday morning and addressed a range of topics, including the fraught state of politics in America, the rise of artificial intelligence and Paramount’s ongoing attempt to merge with Warner Bros. He also defended Mark Ruffalo, who was accused by Paramount of “antisemitic tropes” after the Marvel star attacked the deal over its potential consequences for Hollywood and accused the Ellison family of being complicit in the “genocide” against Palestinians. David Ellison is the CEO of Paramount Skydance. Related Stories 'Avengers: Secret Wars' Adds Noah Jupe to Cast Netflix Doubles Down on Podcasts: Streamer Orders New Shows From Katt Williams and Harlan Coben, Renews Full Slate of Originals “I support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely,” Clooney said when asked about the controversy by Variety’s Elsa Keslassy. “It’s ridiculous. We’re not going to ban speech. I believe in free speech even when I completely disagree with it. That’s important. In fact, it’s part of how democracy works.” Popular on Variety Clooney called the pending merger “a complicated thing” and suggested he “doesn’t know how it works out.” “I don’t see how the merger financially ends up making sense for the people who are trying to do it. We’ll see. I worry when a big company swallows up another company,” he said. “I always worry whenever big companies are consolidating because it means a lot of people are going to lose their jobs.” On the topic of AI, Clooney predicted that it’s “going to be a very big part of this industry” and worries that “it’s going to hurt us in a lot of ways.” He expressed a concerned about the complications that AI will pose for actors, cracking that “I would like to avoid being in a tampon commercial 20 years after I’m dead.” Clooney was also probed about the state of journalism, having directed 2005’s “Good Night, and Good Luck,” a drama about the conflict between the veteran CBS reporter Edward R. Murrow and Senator Joseph McCarthy. Clooney also adapted the film into a play and earned a Tony nomination in 2025 for playing Murrow in his Broadway debut. “The state of journalism is in question. The richest people in the world are owning the Washington Post and Twitter, and that is a concern,” he said, referring to Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk. Yet Clooney remains optimistic. “There’s a lot of room for great journalists. I do believe that information will find its way out.” Clooney has long been one of president Donald Trump’s most outspoken critics, so naturally the actor was asked about his feelings on the state of democracy. “How do you see the state of the [country]?” Clooney said with a laugh. “There’s a great word, kakistocracy, which is a country run by the least qualified people. I think maybe we have a kakistocracy right now, but we’ll get through it. We will have an election in November that should be a check in balance. And then in 2028, we will have a restoration of some normalcy.” Clooney has a long history with the Venice Film Festival, having first attended with Steven Soderbergh’s 199 film ”Out of Sight” and returning many times over the years with movies such as “Good Night, and Good Luck,” 2007’s “Michael Clayton,” 2013’s “Gravity,” 2017’s “Suburbicon,” 2024’s “Wolfs” and 2025’s “Jay Kelly.” Clooney had to miss last year’s press conference for “Jay Kelly” because he was battling a sinus infection. Clooney joked that he’s been getting nostalgic has he prepares to receive a career honor. “I’m 65 years old — everything is melancholy. You brush your teeth and you’re like, ‘My teeth used to be so much better.’ Everything about getting older…,” he said. “I also feel very lucky. I have an incredible wife whom I love very much and she loves me. I have great kids. I think life is pretty good.” One of Hollywood’s biggest stars, Clooney’s influence spans television and film, starting with his breakout role on “ER” and continuing with films such as “Syriana,” “O Brother Where Art Thou,” “Up in the Air” and the “Oceans” trilogy. Although he’s directed several films — most recently the 2023 sports drama “The Boys in the Boat,” Clooney says he’s stepping back as a filmmaker and will focus on acting in order to spend time with his children. “I have two 9-year-old kids,” Clooney said. “If I act in a movie, it’s three months [away]. When I direct a movie, it’s a year. And I can’t do that anymore. I can’t pull the kids out of school anymore. I’m happy to doing this, being an actor, again. It’s fun. I’m a character actor now.” Clooney did tease his excitement for one upcoming project — a new “Oceans” heist with Brad Pitt and Matt Damon. “I would do anything with them,” he said. “As soon as we get our schedules to work, we’re going to film.” A Female Sniper Battles ISIS in First Teaser for Venice Title ‘No Paradise if You Are Killed by a Woman’ (EXCLUSIVE) Venice: M-Appeal Picks Up Chinese Director Jie Dong’s ‘Zoom In, Zoom Out’ Ahead of Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Letters From the Silenced Country,’ Documentary About Oppression in Belarus, Boarded by Filmotor Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) ‘NAZA’ Documentary From ‘No Other Land’ Directors Acquired by MK2 Films Ahead of Venice Film Festival Premiere Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s Four Restored Films Acquired by The Match Factory for World Sales Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters Boards Palestinian Art and Resistance Documentary ‘Freedom Theatre’ (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... articles.full_text: Sep 2, 2026 5:00am PT Kaskade, Electronic Music Icon, Signs With Pacific Music Group in Asia Partnership (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Kaskade, Electronic Music Icon, Signs With Pacific Music Group in Asia Partnership (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Stays in Full Swing Atop U.K., Ireland Box Office as ‘The Odyssey’ Continues Voyage 3 hours ago ‘Kung Fu Soccer’ Tops as China’s Summer Box Office Hits $1.86 Billion 4 hours ago See All Mark Owens Photo Kaskade has signed with Pacific Music Group (PMG) in a strategic partnership focused on expanding the electronic artist’s presence across Asia, the Pan-Asian entertainment company has revealed. Kaskade, born Ryan Raddon, is an eight-time Grammy Award nominee whose career spans more than two decades. He was the first DJ to headline Coachella, performed the Super Bowl’s first-ever in-game DJ set and drew a record crowd to the LA Memorial Coliseum, which Pollstar recognized as North America’s biggest single-day electronic music show. His accolades also include a Grammy nomination for Kx5, his collaboration with producer deadmau5. Related Stories If Paramount Leaves California, It Might Cut Costs but Wouldn't Save on State Taxes HBO Max Banks on Upcoming Genre Thriller ‘Mataviejitas: The Serial Killer’ (EXCLUSIVE) His recent output includes 2025 album “undux,” a return to introspective songwriting, and a new live concept, “Origin //,” which he unveiled at Coachella in 2026, bringing a reworked stage show and fresh, previously unheard tracks to two headline sets. Popular on Variety PMG, the Hong Kong-based company founded by Ne-Yo, Sonu Nigam, MC Jin and veteran executive Jonathan Serbin , will serve as Kaskade’s strategic partner across Asian territories under the agreement, overseeing brand partnerships, media relations and long-term market development throughout the region. The deal also builds on PMG’s electronic music ecosystem through Ghostone Records, its imprint dedicated to developing talent and connecting Asia’s electronic music scene with the global market. “Kaskade is one of the most influential artists in electronic music history,” said Serbin, co-founder and CEO of Pacific Music Group. “For more than two decades, he has consistently set the standard for artistic excellence and innovation, helping elevate dance music into a global cultural force. His vision aligns perfectly with our mission of partnering with world-class artists who continue to shape the future of music. We are thrilled to welcome Kaskade to Pacific Music Group and are excited to support his next era with a truly global strategy that spans A&R, brand partnerships, and new creative opportunities.” “I’ve had a deep connection with Asia for decades, ever since I lived there for a few years,” added Kaskade. “When I get to use music to connect with the crowds across Asia, it’s such an amazing experience, and I always walk away with the deepest respect for the energy these crowds bring. Partnering with Pacific Music Group gives me the chance to build something even stronger which I’m excited about. I’m ready to get reconnected with fans who have supported this journey for years.” Under the new partnership, PMG will back Kaskade’s push into Japan, Korea, Southeast Asia and Greater China, building out brand tie-ins and growth plans suited to each market. The signing extends PMG’s push to build out a global roster since launching in 2025. articles.title: Studio71 Alum Joseph Marchese Joins Bent Pixels as Head of Creator Strategy and Business
articles.full_text: Sep 2, 2026 5:05am PT Studio71 Alum Joseph Marchese Joins Bent Pixels as Head of Creator Strategy and Business By William Earl Plus Icon William Earl @beautifulbill Latest Studio71 Alum Joseph Marchese Joins Bent Pixels as Head of Creator Strategy and Business 1 hour ago Variety and Utopai Studios to Host Future in Focus Conversations at TIFF 16 hours ago Variety Power of Women: Los Angeles Event Presented by Lifetime Announces Honorees Jennifer Hudson, Pearlena Igbokwe, Melissa McCarthy, Sharon Stone 22 hours ago See All Courtesy of Bent Pixels Joseph Marchese has joined creator network Bent Pixels as executive VP of creator strategy and business as the firm revs up its portfolio of support services offered to attention-economy clients. Marchese spent the past 12 years as a senior executive at Studio71, another creator media firm that handled distribution and advertising sales representation for a range of digital-native stars. Los Angeles-based Bent Pixels is a pioneering digital media firm that has been active in the sector since its launch in 2009. Related Stories HBO Max Banks on Upcoming Genre Thriller ‘Mataviejitas: The Serial Killer’ (EXCLUSIVE) Roald Dahl Drama Series Set at Netflix Starring Nicola Coughlan, Naomi Scott, Dominic West, Imelda Staunton and More “Creator media has become one of the most powerful ways for brands to reach consumers because it puts their message inside programming that audiences are already choosing to watch,” said Mike Pusateri, Bent Pixels’ founder and CEO. “The opportunity is not simply about putting an ad in front of millions of people; it’s about connecting brands with the right audiences through creators and content that are strategically aligned with their message. Joe understands that ecosystem from the inside out. We’re excited to have him not only build on our already strong portfolio of creators, but also expand the business opportunities we can bring to those creators and our brand partners.” Popular on Variety Marchese hire reflects the company’s push to beef up its creator business. In March, Bent Pixels acquired Sunny State Agency, a creator services firm that brought a valuable scaled short-form distribution platform. The enlarged Bent Pixels now represents more than 850 creators who have cross-platform reach across YouTube, Snapchat, Facebook and Instagram. The company reports 50.2 million monthly unique visitors across its social footprint and 1.2 billion minutes of content viewed on connected TV free streaming platforms. “I’m thrilled to join Bent Pixels at a pivotal moment for the creator economy,” Marchese said. “I have tremendous respect for Michael and what he has built, as well as his continued commitment to innovation. Bent Pixels has established an impressive foundation, and I see a significant opportunity to build on its reputation, capabilities, and vision to shape what’s next for creators, agencies, and brands. I’m excited to help forge partnerships that create lasting value, strengthen trust, and move the entire creator ecosystem forward.” Marchese joined Studio71 in 2014 and rose through the ranks in partner relations and talent posts to executive VP. Studio71 was recently acquired by rival digital media firm Fixated. articles.title: Rupert Murdoch ‘Is Very Happy’ Guy Pearce Is Playing Him in ‘Ink’; Actor Says Mogul’s Daughter Shared Praise
articles.full_text: Sep 2, 2026 6:00am PT Rupert Murdoch ‘Is Very Happy’ Guy Pearce Is Playing Him in ‘Ink’; Actor Says Mogul’s Daughter Shared Praise By Ellise Shafer , Elsa Keslassy Michael Buckner Rupert Murdoch is apparently “very happy” that he’s being played by Guy Pearce in Danny Boyle’s “Ink.” During the movie’s press conference at the Venice Film Festival on Wednesday, Pearce was asked along with Boyle and screenwriter James Graham if they had spoken to Murdoch about the film. Though Pearce said he hadn’t made contact with the mogul himself, he revealed that he reached out to Murdoch’s daughter, Elisabeth Murdoch. Related Stories Martin Scorsese Mentee Celina Murga Preps Next Pic, ‘The Rehearsals’ Julianne Moore to Receive Zurich's Golden Icon Award as Jesse Eisenberg's 'The Debut' Screens “She did say to me, ‘Dad’s very happy that you’re playing him,'” Pearce said. “But he hadn’t seen the film at that point, so we’ll see.” Popular on Variety “Ink,” which opens the festival on Wednesday night and is competing for the Golden Lion, takes place in 1969 as Murdoch acquires the struggling Sun and installs Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) as editor with the mission of overtaking its dominant rival, the Daily Mirror. Graham, who also wrote the Tony-winning play on which the movie is based, said that Murdoch is familiar with the story as he came to see the play twice, both on the West End and Broadway. “I remember he was very good at sort of not really giving anything away,” Graham said of Murdoch’s reaction. However, he remembers him enjoying a particular sequence that showed the printing press and “the dirt and the steam and the filth that used to go into making a paper on a daily basis.” Graham added, “I think he’ll be very flattered by the casting.” “Ink” marks Boyle’s first appearance at the Venice Film Festival. The Oscar-winning director arrives on the Lido following his return to the zombie franchise he helped create with “28 Years Later.” His credits also include “Trainspotting,” “127 Hours,” “Steve Jobs” and “Slumdog Millionaire,” which won eight Oscars, including best picture and best director. Elsewhere during the press conference, Boyle pointed out that “Ink” “doesn’t monsterize Rupert Murdoch, which of course a lot of people do now.” He added, “I think it’s because he represented at the time a breath of fresh air in what was a very rigid British society … he offered a kind of freedom with a different voice, really.” But Murdoch and Lamb also both have a “darkness” that Boyle said his film explores more than in the play. “In the stage play, the darkness is reported off stage, and yet I knew in cinema you would see it,” Boyle said. “And then you have to find an actor that can take you there.” He noted that O’Connell “has that ability to take you into dark places with him, like Pacino in ‘Godfather 2,'” causing a surprised expression to come across O’Connell’s face. “He’s going to hate me saying that,” Boyle added with a smirk. Netflix acquired U.S. and Latin American rights to “Ink” shortly after it was announced as Venice’s opening film. Studiocanal, which produced the movie with Media Res and House Productions, is releasing it theatrically across several territories including the U.K., France, Germany and Italy. Boyle produced “Ink” with Tessa Ross, Michael Ellenberg and Tracey Seaward. articles.title: Chilean Alfredo Castro-Led Dark Comedy ‘After Elena’ World Premieres at Toronto Film Fest, Bows Trailer (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 2, 2026 6:24am PT Chilean Alfredo Castro-Led Dark Comedy ‘After Elena’ World Premieres at Toronto Film Fest, Bows Trailer (EXCLUSIVE) By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest Martin Scorsese Mentee Celina Murga Preps Next Pic, ‘The Rehearsals’ 7 hours ago Chile’s Sanfic-Morbido Lab Launches WomanInFan Southern Cone Alliance With Sitges Film Fest and Fantastic WIP (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Mexico’s Martfilms Boards ‘Looking for Sam,’ Mariana Rondón’s Follow-Up to ‘Bad Hair’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All 'After Elena' Courtesy of Meikincine Chile’s everyman actor Alfredo Castro (“The Count”) plays against type in “After Elena” (“Después de Elena”) by Shawn Garry, which world premieres at the Toronto Film Festival ( TIFF ) on Sept.11. Bowing a trailer and poster exclusively in Variety, “After Elena” “shows Castro in a completely different register from what we’ve seen him in before and the cast also includes Nicolás Zárate (“Red Hangar”), who has won multiple awards this year,” said Gabriela Sandoval who produced the dark family comedy out of her label Cine Matriz. Related Stories Owner of L.A. Rams and Denver Nuggets Buys Los Angeles Angels Baseball Team Miley Cyrus Announces New Album 'Bass Persuades,' Sets Two Shows for Hollywood Bowl The rest of the cast include Carola Varleta and Guilherme Sepúlveda while Catalina Saavedra – who took home an acting prize at Sundance for her gripping debut performance in 2009 Chilean drama, “The Maid”– plays a small but pivotal role. Popular on Variety Castro plays 70-year-old Roberto whose beloved wife Elena has died. He wants nothing more than to retreat into his lifelong home. But when an economic and emotional crisis drives his three adult children back under his roof, old wounds, buried secrets and simmering tensions resurface. As they navigate their grief, the family must find a way to reconnect or risk tearing itself apart. The trailer opens with Castro’s character, the recently widowed Roberto, waking up to a phone call in the middle of the night to news that one of his sons has tried to kill himself. Chaos ensues as all three adult kids and their offspring move in. The multi-country co-production includes Colombia’s Doc: Co, Garry’s own label Creative Content, Italy’s Zoe Films, Fundacion Rio and By Lace Films. Buenos Aires-based boutique sales agency Meikincine Entertainment boarded the film at the development stage. In an earlier interview, Sandoval explained what drew them to this project: “We were attracted by the possibility of addressing themes such as old age, death, grief and family trauma, but from a different perspective: not as a conventional drama, but through dark humor and absurdity as a narrative vehicle.” Castro has frequently collaborated with Pablo Larrain (“Jackie,” “The Club”) where he played dramatic roles in such gems as “Tony Manero,” “No,” “The Club” and most recently, “The Count.” Larrain’s feature-length spin-off from his Netflix mini-series “My Sad Dead,” competes at the San Sebastian Film Festival where it world premieres. “After Elena” is the sophomore feature of Chilean director-producer Shawn Garry that follows his debut, “Desierto Sur.” He co-wrote the dramedy with writer-director Bernardo Quesney (“History y Geography”) and Carla Stagno (“Allende, The Thousand Days”).
