Discovery deal after the California attorney general canceled a scheduled Monday meeting , accusing the company of “playing games.” Related Stories Acquisitions Bonta Cancels Paramount Settlement Meeting; CA AG Accuses Ellison Of “Playing Games” In WBD Merger Talks Politics Paramount & State AGs Settlement Talks Set For Next Week; Gavin Newsom Says He Takes Paramount CEO’s Threat To Leave California “Seriously” “We share AG Bonta’s concerns about the public discussions and misreporting that has surrounded this deal,” read a statement from a PSKY spokesperson. “As we have assured the Attorney General’s office, Paramount has not been the source of the leaks of any of our confidential discussions with the AG’s office. We remain hopeful and stand ready to continue good faith discussions to resolve the Attorneys General suit and move forward with our plans for increased competition and increased output to the benefit of the talent and entertainment workers.” Bonta canceled the scheduled sit-down late Sunday soon after the WSJ reported details of an August 21 meetup between the parties, including details of potential remedies the AG would require to drop ongoing legal action against the Par-WBD merger. Watch on Deadline “My office had a meeting with Paramount on Friday. Paramount did not maintain the confidentiality of that meeting,” Bonta said in a statement to Deadline last night. He is leading a group of a dozen attorneys general in suing Paramount to block its planned acquisition of WBD on antitrust grounds. The suit, set for trial in early March, addresses three markets of concern — cable programming, blockbuster movies and wide release movies. Ellison badly wants to settle the case well before then and has threatened to relocate the company if there’s no movement soon. Third parties from exhibitors to politicians to some guilds have also urged Bonta to resolve the litigation. The AG has insisted on so-called “structural” remedies like asset sales or separating businesses, versus “behavioral” remedies like promises, in Ellison’s case a commitment for the combined studios to release 30 movies a year. As reported by WSJ and confirmed by Deadline, the AG’s asks include keeping the studios separate as well as unloading some cable networks. “Not only did Paramount leak the alleged substance of settlement discussions, but they misrepresented these discussions, demonstrating a lack of good faith,” the AG said in a statement provided to Deadline at midnight Sunday PT. “As soon as Paramount stops playing games and engages sincerely, my office is happy to meet again.” The two sides are required to hold talks under court mandated mediation. As Deadline’s earlier post noted, details of the August 21 preliminary gathering to set the agenda for the August 24 meeting had ticked out from a variety of sources. California Gov. articles.title: Rob Bonta Says No Paramount-WBD Settlement Talks Scheduled After He Canceled Monday Session
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted In Latest Threat Of Regulatory Retaliation, Donald Trump Says He’ll Report NBC News’ Kristen Welker To FCC For “Rebuke Or Punishment” ICE Confirms They Have Detained Commentator Milo Yiannopoulos Bret Baier Defends Fox News’ Jonathan Hunt Amid Donald Trump’s Attack On His Iran Report, Calls Out POTUS Claim That Segment Was Inaccurate View All August 25, 2026 11:41am Story Arc Rob Bonta Riccardo Savi/Getty Images for Concordia Annual Summit UPDATED: California Attorney General Rob Bonta told reporters that “we don’t have anything scheduled” with Paramount to negotiate a potential settlement of the antitrust challenge to the proposed merger with Warner Bros. Discovery . Related Stories Legal Paramount Denies Leaking Details Of Talks With CA AG’s Office, Company “Hopeful” And “Ready To Continue Good Faith Discussions” Legal California AG Rob Bonta Open To Structural Remedies In Paramount-WBD Suit But Calls 30 Movies A Year An “Old, Stale Promise” At a press conference on Tuesday, Bonta continued to lash out at the company, claiming that they were responsible for leaks of negotiation details in advance of a planned session on Monday. Late on Sunday, Bonta abruptly canceled the meeting. “They wanted to have the settlement discussions, and we are happy to hear them out,” Bonta said. “We thought that they were reaching out to us in good faith and sincerely, and the unfortunately, they violated the rules of engagement, and that was not okay. They leaked lies to the press while we were in settlement negotiations, and that’s not okay. That’s not acceptable. That is amateur hour. That is playing games.” Watch on Deadline Paramount issued a statement on Monday in which it said that it “has not been the source of the leaks of any of our confidential discussions with the AG’s office.” On Sunday, The Wall Street Journal reported, and confirmed by Deadline, that the AG’s asks included keeping the studios separate as well as unloading some cable networks. But there were earlier conversations between the parties. California Governor Gavin Newsom had indicated on Friday that there “are many meetings that are going on, and there’s a lot of conversation.” Bonta said, “It is the alleged disclosure of the substance of the conversations of what occurred in those meetings that is the problem. Those are required under federal law to be confidential, and for good reason. So you can be candid. So you can be productive. So maybe you can even be creative in those discussions. If you’re having confidential settlement discussions, and as you’re having them, one of the parties is going out to the press and representing to the press what’s being said by you in those negotiations and lying about it, whether it’s true or whether they’re lying, neither is acceptable.” A spokesperson for the attorney general later said that Paramount asked them to keep the contents of settlement negotiations confidential under Federal Evidence Code 408 but they believe “they turned around and disclosed it themselves.” The spokesperson said that they are not alleging that Paramount violated federal law at this time. Bonta also did not blame Newsom for disclosing that there had been talks. Bonta said that “we saw sourced people who had knowledge about what was discussed in the room. It was only my office and Paramount. The governor does not have anything to do with the concern. Paramount has everything to do with this issue.” Bonta said that Paramount “can also fix it, and if they want to fix it and stop playing games, we will be happy to meet.” A Paramount spokesperson said on Monday, “We remain hopeful and stand ready to continue good faith discussions to resolve the Attorneys General suit and move forward with our plans for increased competition and increased output to the benefit of the talent and entertainment workers.” Bonta and 11 other state attorneys general sued to block the merger last month. A federal judge granted a temporary restraining order that prevented Paramount from closing the transaction for four weeks, but the company later agreed not to complete the deal until June or until legal issues are resolved. The judge set a trial for next March. Bonta also told reporters that “we’re winning this lawsuit.” He also contended that the judge, Araceli Martínez-Olguín, said that Paramount was “likely to lose the whole case….that we, the states, are likely to succeed on the merits and block the merger.” Paramount’s legal team, though, has claimed that they will prevail once the whole case is laid out in a trial that is expected to be heavy in discovery documents and competing expert witnesses. ‘Tomb Raider’ Series Broke UK Safety Laws During Production Busan Unveils Lineup & Guests Yeoh, Huppert, Gyllenhaal, Rintaro Trump Backs Federal Film/TV Tax Credit, Calls Hollywood “A Total Disaster!” All Eyez On Guilty: Jury Reaches Verdict In Tupac Shakur’s 1996 Shooting Death More from this Story Arc Paramount WB August 26, 2026 Paramount-WBD Antitrust Suit Heads To Supreme Court In Red State Vs. articles.title: Hearst Networks Orders Lizzie Borden & Aileen Wuornos Docs From ‘Ed Gein: Original Psychopath’ Team
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Hearst Networks Orders Lizzie Borden & Aileen Wuornos Docs From ‘Ed Gein: Original Psychopath’ Team Edward Berger & Jane Tranter Among Headliners At New-Look MIA ‘Doctor Who’ On Prime Video? Amazon Execs Say They “Welcome Any Conversation Around IP” View All September 1, 2026 2:22am 'Lizzie Borden: 40 Whacks' and 'Aileen Wuornos: Damsel of Death' Crime+Investigation EXCLUSIVE: Hearst Networks is following up its AI-aided doc about serial killer Ed Gein with two more true-crime docs from the same team. Hearst, Spirit Studios and distributor BossaNova Media are back together for Lizzie Borden: 40 Whacks and Aileen Wuornos: Damsel of Death , following the docu-drama Ed Gein: Original Psychopath , which was among Crime+Investigation ‘s biggest shows of 2025 and later selected as a Global Breakout. Lizzie Borden: 40 Whacks’ is a 90-minute film that revisits the infamous 1892 murders of Andrew and Abby Borden, the father and step mother of Lizzie. It draws on on rediscovered police interrogation files to re-examines the evidence, the conflicting accounts and the family tensions surrounding the case, and the enduring mystery of the woman accused of the murders. The two-part Aileen Wuornos: Damsel of Death re-examines the life, crimes and investigation of one of America’s most notorious female serial killers. It looks at FBI case files and first-hand testimony from Brian Jarvis, the lead detective who investigated Wuornos and questioned her following her arrest, to go beyond the sensationalist headlines that have surrounded the case for decades. Both shows will use the ‘interrogation room’ as a narrative device, with AI used to build the worlds around Borden and Wuornos, who are portrayed by actors. Given the controversy that continues around using AI in production, Ed Gein came with an advisory note outlining the practice and its role in the doc. Related Stories News Ross Kemp Is Exploring Britain's Masculinity Crisis In Trailer For Crime+Investigation Series News Hearst Networks EMEA Acquisitions Chief Kelly Hornsby Exiting After 12 Years The programs will premiere on Hearst Networks UK’s Crime+Investigation, with Paul Heaney’s BossaNova handling international distribution. Lizzie Borden: 40 Whacks’ premieres on Sunday September 27 at 9pm local UK time, with Aileen Wuornos: Damsel of Death following on Sunday October 4 in the same slot. They will also broadcast internationally. “We’re really excited to be building on the success of Ed Gein: Original Psycho and bringing back the interrogation-room device that became such a distinctive part of those films,” said Matt Campion, Creative Director and co-founder of Spirit Studios. Watch on Deadline “It gives us a way to combine intense, immersive scripted drama with premium factual storytelling and original case material. Lizzie Borden and Aileen Wuornos are such infamous names that people think they know their stories, but there’s still so much to uncover.” “With renewed audience interest in these cases, following the ongoing Netflix drama series Monster , these next instalments of both Lizzie Borden: 40 Whacks and Aileen Wuornos: Damsel of Death offer fresh, compelling perspectives on two of the world’s most notorious female killers,” said Hannah Gray, Acquisitions Manager, at Hearst Networks. “We’re thrilled to be continuing our successful partnership with Spirit Studios with two gripping new shows, Lizzie Borden: 40 Whacks and Aileen Wuornos: Damsel of Death ,” said Iona Hopper, Acquisitions Manager at BossaNova. “Spirit Studios are experts at compelling and immersive true crime storytelling, and we are delighted to be partnering again and building on the international success of Ed Gein: Original Psycho .” Spirit Studios is one of the companies involved in Blackbox Multimedia’s lawsuit against 5 over the collapse of a drama series, as Deadline revealed last week. ‘Tomb Raider’ Series Broke UK Safety Laws During Production Busan Unveils Lineup & Guests Yeoh, Huppert, Gyllenhaal, Rintaro Trump Backs Federal Film/TV Tax Credit, Calls Hollywood “A Total Disaster!” All Eyez On Guilty: Jury Reaches Verdict In Tupac Shakur’s 1996 Shooting Death Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Cynthia Erivo, Andrew Scott, Ava DuVernay, Jesse Eisenberg & More Set For London Film Festival Screen Talks Program
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Tom Hiddleston Thriller ‘Tenzing’ To Open Zurich Film Festival Marketing Executive Kevin Harrington Launches New Entertainment Agency Patrick Patrick International Disruptors: Megan Park Talks Debut Series ‘Sterling Point’, Importance Of “Not Talking Down” To Young Audiences & Stepping Out Of YA Space With Next Feature ‘Die Alive’ View All September 1, 2026 3:14am Andrew Scott, Ava DuVernay, Brad Bird, Cynthia Erivo, James Gray, Jesse Eisenberg, John Malkovich, Mahershala Ali, Naomi Ackie, Sofia Coppola & Danny Boyle London Film Festival The BFI London Film Festival has unveiled its list of filmmakers and actors participating in this year’s program of Screen Talks . The line-up includes Andrew Scott ( All of Us Strangers ); Ava DuVernay ( Selma ); Brad Bird ( The Incredibles ); Cynthia Erivo ( Wicked ); James Gray ( We Own the Night ); Jesse Eisenberg ( A Real Pain ); John Malkovich ( In the Line of Fire ); Mahershala Ali ( Moonlight ); Naomi Ackie ( Blink Twice ); Sofia Coppola ( The Virgin Suicides ); and Danny Boyle ( Slumdog Millionaire ). Scott will join to talk about a career that includes a BAFTA-winning performance as the nemesis of Sherlock Holmes , his role in Hamlet and a bold reinvention of Uncle Vanya as well as his performance of Ian Charleson in the LFF Opening Night film Elsinore . Watch on Deadline Related Stories Festivals Jesse Eisenberg's 'The Debut' With Julianne Moore & Paul Giamatti To Close BFI London Film Festival News Filmmaker Snigdha Kapoor Talks Dismantling Gender Norms In Coming-Of-Age Queer Identity Short Film 'Holy Curse': "We Are Losing Our Tolerance For Accepting People Who Have Different Values From Ours" DuVernay will talk about her work such as A Wrinkle in Time , dramas Selma and Origin and Oscar-nominated documentary 13 th while Bird will explore his Oscar and BAFTA-winning career in animated features including The Iron Giant , The Incredibles and Ratatouille as well as live-action titles Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol and Tomorrowland . Erivo will talk about her powerful performances on stage and screen. She rose to international prominence with her Tony Award-winning performance in The Color Purple on Broadway and has since starred in films including Harriet, Bad Times at the El Royale, Wicked, and Wicked: For Good . Gray, who is coming off the back of Paper Tiger which premiered in Cannes, will discuss his critically acclaimed career from his feature debut, Little Odessa to projects such as The Yards, We Own the Night, Two Lovers, The Immigrant and Armageddon Time – films that span a variety of genres but are all grounded in a gritty, earthy reality. He’ll also talk about The Lost City of Z and Ad Astra , which unfolded in very different worlds. Eisenberg will talk about his work in front of and behind the camera as he unveils the Festival’s Gala Closing Night Film, The Debut . A Broadway stage actor since he was 12, Eisenberg first moved into television with the series Get Real in 1999, before winning plaudits for his performances in the films Roger Dodger and The Squid and the Whale . Adventureland and Zombieland brought his wider recognition, followed by his portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network . Alongside frequent screen appearances and contributions to The New Yorker, Eisenberg branched into filmmaking with When You Finish Saving the World and award-winning title A Real Pain . Acclaimed screen and theatre actor Malkovich will also touch down at LFF to discuss how he has spent his career forging indelible, charismatic, singular characters. He ranks as one of the only actors to feature in a film in which his own persona has a starring role, in Being John Malkovich. Oscar and BAFTA winner Ali worked in film and television for almost two decades before his pivotal and award-winning breakthrough performance in Moonlight . Since then, he has had roles in House of Cards and Free State of Jones to Green Book, True Detective and Leave the World Behind . Ackie’s credits include The End of the F***ing World , Education , the fifth part of Steve McQueen’s Small Axe series, Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker, Blink Twice, Mickey 17 and Sorry Baby , for which she received an Independent Spirit Award. Filmmakers Coppola and Boyle will also touch down at the festival where each will discuss their respective careers behind the camera. Coppola’s feature debut was The Virgin Suicides and her sophomore feature Lost in Translation saw her earn a Best Original Screenplay Academy Award. A perceptive study on celebrity, it’s a theme she continued to mine in Somewhere, The Bling Ring, On the Rocks and Priscilla. Boyle, meanwhile, hit cinema screens with his debut Shallow Grave before the era-defining Trainspotting. The Beach, 28 Days Later and Sunshine highlighted his gift for moving seamlessly between genres, before the enormous awards success of Slumdog Millionaire . He directed the Opening Ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics to huge acclaim, before returning to cinema with Steve Jobs, Yesterday and 28 Years Later . Boyle will discuss his wide-ranging career at HOME Manchester, the festival’s first Screen Talk outside of London. articles.title: Iranian Director Mohsen Gharaei Talks Navigating Censors To Bring Prophetic Drama ‘Falling House’ To Fruition – Venice
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Josh Duhamel To Star In ‘Speak’ From Lorenzo Di Bonaventura & Joe Carnahan; Twenty-Nine Palms & CAA Media Finance Launching Sales At TIFF Zurich Bolsters Position As Awards Circuit Stop-Off As ‘Bunker’, ‘Club Kid’ & ‘Adult Supervision’ Join Gala Lineup TrustNordisk Unveils Fresh Deals & Teaser Trailer For Venice Contender ‘Woman Unknown’ View All September 1, 2026 4:00am Falling House Seven Springs Pictures, RaeFilm Studios EXCLUSIVE: Close to four years have passed since Iran ’s Woman Life Freedom protests were sparked by the death in police custody, on September 16, 2022, of Mahsa Amini following her arrest for not wearing her hijab correctly. In a sign of their lasting impact, Iranian director Mohsen Gharaei arrives in Venice this year with Falling House , a prophetic work warning of the crisis building in Iran after decades of oppressive, patriarchal rule by the Islamic Republic regime. The allegorical drama, which world premieres in Venice’s Orizzonti sidebar, revolves around three generations of women in an economically fragile family, living under the thumb of the father and facing eviction from their long-time home due to an airport expansion project. Related Stories News TrustNordisk Unveils Fresh Deals & Teaser Trailer For Venice Contender 'Woman Unknown' Festivals Venice Film Festival Changes Course To Reinstate Jury Press Conference: How It Went Down Initially appearing as a kindly, henpecked figure who affords his wife and daughters a fair amount of independence, the father reveals a more sinister side when they challenge his authority. Laleh Marzban, whose credits include the 2023 Iranian Oscar submission The Night Guardian , stars as eldest daughter Ensi, who has hatched a secret plan to move to Turkey to pursue ambitions of becoming a model, opposite award-winning veteran actor Farhad Aslani as her father. Rima Raminfar plays the long-suffering but determined mother, with Elena Khakbaz making her big-screen debut as the youngest daughter, Jenan, who is bullied at school over her father’s job amid claims that he is a prison executioner, but remains a beacon of hope as she challenges obstacles at every turn. A first clip below, showing the family awakening to shaking walls and the rumble of bulldozer engines, captures the sense of a toxic status quo on the verge of collapse that runs throughout the film. Falling House is Gharaei’s first film in five years, following a self-imposed hiatus in response to government restrictions and censorship around filmmaking. He wrote a first draft in 2018 but reveals that it was the 2022 Woman Life Freedom protests that gave him fresh impetus to get the film off the ground. “The protests happened four years later, but the reasons that led society to that point were already there. I’d always wanted to tell this story, but Woman Life Freedom gave me a better and stronger reason to bring it to film,” says Gharaei. The film is one of two Iranian pictures playing in Venice, alongside Ali Asgari’s Golden Lion contender, A Bit Of Light, as Iran remains in the spotlight due to the war with the U.S. and Israel, as well as reports that its ruling Islamic Republic regime continues to persecute and execute pro-democracy dissenters. Prior to his directing hiatus, Gharaei enjoyed box office chart-topping success at home with his respective 2017 and 2021 films, Blockage and Majority , with the latter winning the jury prize at the Islamic Republic regime-controlled Fajr Film Festival. Today, he says he is living in exile, his home and assets confiscated, with him and his family subject to death threats after drawing the regime’s ire with public comments criticizing its conduct in the early days of the U.S. and Israeli bombing campaign in March 2026, and now with his new film. “If I go back, I will definitely face a prison sentence,” says Gharaei. Lead producer Milad Khosravi at Tehran-based Seven Springs Pictures , who joins Gharaei on the call as an interpreter, adds for context that the director has been the target of a “huge” disinformation campaign by government-controlled official media. “They are aggressively threatening him, and he has received thousands of hostile messages on social media. Given the scale and intensity of the threats, it would be dangerous for him to return to the country.” Khosravi is joined as co-lead producer by Odessa Rae of RaeFilm Studios ( The Voice of Hind Rajab) , who brought Max Richter onto the film, with music by Richter. News in July of the Venice selection for Falling House sparked outrage on Iranian regime-controlled news sites following the posting of images from the film showing Marzban not wearing a hijab, in a direct challenge to Islamic Republic rules requiring women to cover their hair. Gharaei notes that while he has never liked making women wear the hijab on his sets, it was not the main issue for him as he navigated government restrictions and censorship to get the production off the ground. Rather, it was the film’s searing critique of Iranian patriarchal society under the Islamic Republic regime. “More than the hijab, the biggest issue was the concept of the film and the core of the story… the regime would never have allowed us to make the film… that was the biggest challenge,” he says. Given the size of the production, Gharaei says it would have been impossible to shoot the film clandestinely, so he had to go down the route of securing a state production permit. “We had to find a way of working with the authorities,” he says. “In the end, we gave them a kind of fake script to get the written permission that allowed us to shoot the film, to have all the cast and crew on the set, and to make the film we wanted to make.” Mindful of the fact that Iran’s Production Permit Council can send in inspectors, or even place informers on set, Gharaei shot sensitive scenes with a reduced crew. “For scenes without a hijab or with sensitive dialogue, I allowed only a handful of people on set,” he says. “The risk of anything leaking to the government was simply too great.” “For the scenes without the hijab, it was sometimes just me with Laleh and the cameraman, or sometimes we pretended we were rehearsing or practicing, which was also safer.” Some regime detractors have suggested that the film’s setting of a house on the verge of being reduced to rubble is an insensitive reference to the U.S.-Iran war and even an insult to the memory of the country’s late supreme leader Ali Khomeini, who was killed on February 28 in a U.S.-Israeli airstrike on his official residence in Tehran. Gharaei dismisses the claims, pointing to the fact that he wrote the first draft of the screenplay in 2018, with the shoot beginning in November 2025 and wrapping in January 2026, just as widespread pro-democracy protests kicked off. He notes, however, that the film does foretell the war. “I’ve always thought that, given the way my country and the government are dealing with others, its neighbors and everything, war was unavoidable… the film is indirectly showing that,” says Gharaei. The Islamic Republic regime would go on to quash the pro-democracy protests in a brutal crackdown, which is believed to have left some 30,000 people dead. A second wave of protests began in mid-February but came to a halt with the U.S. and Israeli military campaign. With all eyes around the world on Iran’s next steps, amid questions over whether the regime will fall or survive, Gharaei says the ultimate interpretation of the film lies with the spectator. “The film is not saying that a war is needed. I didn’t seek to answer whether the war is a solution or not. I just show exterior forces sitting there, ready to attack and take advantage of this home at the same time as the pressure of the dictatorship and patriarchal system bears down… With all my films, my main goal and first responsibility as a director, is to tell a story and to tell it well. The social and political layers come after, with people bringing their own understanding to it.” ‘Tomb Raider’ Series Broke UK Safety Laws During Production Busan Unveils Lineup & Guests Yeoh, Huppert, Gyllenhaal, Rintaro Trump Backs Federal Film/TV Tax Credit, Calls Hollywood “A Total Disaster!” All Eyez On Guilty: Jury Reaches Verdict In Tupac Shakur’s 1996 Shooting Death Read More About: Comments

articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake StudioCanal’s ‘Has Fallen’ Series Returns For Season 3; Iwan Rheon, Brendan Coyle & Atandwa Kani Cast Inside ‘The Great British Bake Off’ Bun Fight: How Sky & Love Productions Came To Blows Over The UK’s Biggest Cooking Series Edinburgh TV Festival Diary: Farewell To The Great City; YouTube Takeover; Channel 4’s Next Content Chief & Paramount Mischief View All September 1, 2026 4:19am Sophie Turner as Lara Croft in 'Tomb Raider' Jay Maidment for Prime Video EXCLUSIVE : Lara Croft’s adventures in Amazon MGM Studios ‘ new Tomb Raider series proved too much for UK safety authorities. Britain’s Health and Safety Executive, better known as HSE, concluded that the high-profile drama breached UK safety laws during production at Shinfield Studios earlier this year, according to a previously unreported ruling. Deadline can reveal that Project Temple Productions Ltd, the special purpose vehicle through which Sophie Turner ‘s Tomb Raider series is being produced, breached the Health and Safety At Work Act 1974 and Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002. Related Stories Casting KiKi Layne & Luke Hemsworth Join Amazon MGM Actioner 'Deadlocked' Casting Sasha Calle Joins Jamie Foxx In Amazon MGM Action Flick 'Deadlocked' Amazon MGM Studios declined to comment. Watch on Deadline HSE determined that Project Temple Productions Ltd failed to ensure that crew members underwent “biological monitoring” to ensure adequate control measures were in place for the spraying of isocyanate paints, one of the leading causes of asthma in the workplace. HSE guidance states that appropriate personal protective equipment should be worn when spraying isocyanate paints, and that an “invisible mist” emitted by the substance can take up to 20 minutes to clear. An employer must know the clearance time for the space in which spraying is taking place. HSE issued Project Temple with an “improvement notice” in April, meaning the company had to take action to remedy a breach of health and safety law. Within a month, Project Temple had complied with the relevant regulations, according to a notice page on HSE’s website. It is rare for HSE to issue notices against TV shoots, with just four productions being called out by the health and safety watchdog over the past four years. Tomb Raider was the highest-profile of these productions. Written by Fleabag creator Phoebe Waller-Bridge , Tomb Raider went into production in January, with Amazon MGM Studios releasing a first-look image of Turner as videogame icon Lara Croft. The HSE ruling has not been the only issue on Tomb Raider . Turner suffered a minor injury during production , resulting in the shoot being paused for around two weeks to allow the Game of Thrones star time to recover. Amazon MGM Studios produces Tomb Raider for Prime Video with Crystal Dynamics. Turner is joined in the cast by Sigourney Weaver, Jason Isaacs, Martin Bobb-Semple, Jack Bannon, John Heffernan, Bill Paterson, Paterson Joseph, Sasha Luss, Juliette Motamed, Celia Imrie and August Wittgenstein. Waller-Bridge is creator, writer, executive producer and co-showrunner alongside Chad Hodge as co-showrunner and executive producer. Jonathan Van Tulleken is director and executive producer. Waller-Bridge and Jenny Robins executive produce through Wells Street Films, Dmitri M. Johnson, Michael Lawrence Goldberg and Timothy I. Stevenson through Story Kitchen, Michael Scheel, and Legendary Television. Matt McInnis is a co-executive producer; Jan R. articles.title: Leslie Odom Jr. Reveals Documentary About His  ‘Hamilton’ Return & Talks Original Cast Reunions
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Nada Aboul Kheir Nada Aboul Kheir Social Media Manager More Stories By Nada Sam Mendes’ Beatles Production Heading For Abbey Road Shoot ‘The Odyssey’: Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Zendaya, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson & Travis Scott Hit The Red Carpet For World Premiere In London Cate Blanchett’s Displacement Film Fund To Support Short Films By Mo Amer, Annemarie Jacir, Rithy Panh, Akuol de Mabior & Bao Nguyen View All September 1, 2026 6:00am Leslie Odom Jr. in 'Hamilton' at the Victoria Palace Theatre Danny Kaan EXCLUSIVE: The inimitable, original Leslie Odom Jr. could be found in London this summer for his West End debut, where he reprised the role of Aaron Burr in Hamilton at the Victoria Palace Theatre for nine weeks – and now we can reveal he’s making a documentary about his return to the Broadway version. Odom Jr. is the only original cast member from Lin-Manuel Miranda ’s Pulitzer Prize-winning musical to perform on the UK side of the pond. Deadline was in the room where it happens on August 6, which was coincidentally the star’s birthday, as well as the 11 th anniversary of Hamilton ’s official opening on Broadway in 2015. Related Stories News Acclaimed, Controversial Play 'Downstate' Gets Broadway Marquee; Scott Rudin Reportedly Producing With Joe Mantello Directing Reviews 'Paranormal Activity' Broadway Review: Stage Adaptation Of Film Franchise Is A Frightfully Good Time View this post on Instagram I sat two rows behind Scary Spice aka Mel B, who told me that she’s seen the show “loads of times,” and had a great time with her daughter that night. She wasn’t the only one. As soon as the Tony and Grammy Award-winner walked on stage to start off the show, the energy in the theater shifted. The applause barely stopped, and the crowd sang along to every word as well as danced in their seats throughout the entire two-and-a-half-hour show. “Normally, you’re opening a new show and you’re worried before the curtain goes up, said Odom Jr. about the West End audience. “But in this situation, the people are as excited as I am, if not more.” A few weeks later, after a matinee performance, the Oscar-nominee joined a Zoom call from the Victoria Palace stalls to chat about the West End experience, his willingness to be vulnerable to tap into Burr, a new “really beautiful” documentary about his return to Hamilton on Broadway, original cast reunions and more. “There was a little film crew that made a documentary about me going back into the show in New York, which will be out soon enough,” revealed Odom Jr. during our call. “I’m pretty proud of it and the way it’s coming together. Ten years is a special marker.” The film is set to be submitted to film festivals in the fall. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. DEADLINE: You’re now eight weeks into your nine-week run in the West End. How would you reflect on your experience? What were the highlights and the challenges? LESLIE ODOM JR: It was everything that I hoped it would be. These are hallowed spaces. They’re legendary houses, and to get to have nine weeks at the Victoria Palace was everything I dreamt it would be. I have loved every single moment. I couldn’t have asked for a better debut than Hamilton . Normally, you’re opening a new show and you’re worried before the curtain goes up. But in this situation, which is maybe once in a lifetime, the people are as excited as I am, if not more. So, it’s been wonderful. For challenging moments, I’ll say eight shows a week ain’t for punks. It is more than a notion. That is always challenging, and the West End was no different. I did get ill during one show and it made headlines, which I hated. I’ve never had that happen before. Other than that, I’ve been able to be here every show and that is always the greatest challenge. With this show in particular, it is a crazy equation. You get even more than you put into it. Somehow, at the end of every week, I am more filled up than when I started. I’m exhausted, but I’m also exhilarated. DEADLINE: I watched the show on your birthday a few weeks ago, and the reaction in the room was electrifying – especially when you walked in during “Wait for It,” and “Room Where It Happens.” After performing in hundreds of Hamilton shows, do you always know what to expect from the audience reactions, or do they sometimes surprise you? ODOM JR: Never. I try not to expect anything from an audience. My philosophy is that the collective is always correct. Whatever is in the room for them, however they respond, it is always right. I don’t blame them, I don’t judge them, that’s not my business. I asked them to be here. I said I was coming, and they showed up. That’s the contract. I show up, you show up, and whatever happens in the room is okay by me. They surprise me all the time with the things that they do and don’t respond to. They’ve taught me how to perform this material. They’ve taught me about love and acceptance. They’ve been a sort of guide as I have developed a deeper relationship and love for myself over the last 10 years. I’m so thankful to these audiences. DEADLINE: Speaking of the past 10 years and how things have evolved, I’m curious about how your approach to playing Burr has changed. I’ve watched the show on Disney+ many times, but I noticed that you’ve added some extra humor to the character in certain scenes during the live show. Did you consciously want to make those changes this time around, or did it come naturally? ODOM JR: It’s all coming up naturally. I am in a more joyful space in my life, and the show is worth celebrating. It started out with a very small group of us that loved this show before anybody had even heard it, and now it has rang out around the world. It connected with audiences, people young and old, the world over. That’s worth celebrating. It is so joyful. I don’t step on this stage most nights without thinking of the first time I stepped on a professional stage, which was with the Broadway company of Rent . I think of that kid and how proud he is of the life we’ve built, and that a way has been made for him to exist in the world just as he is. An audience has accepted him, lifts him up each night, and applauds some nights just because he came to work. He is so proud every single day, and so filled with gratitude. I’m in touch with him, so I can tell you. You feel the joy emanating off me because joy is the only thing that is left 10 years later. DEADLINE: Let’s talk a bit about the cultural impact of Hamilton . When it first debuted, Lin-Manuel Miranda described it as “The story of America then, told by America now.” But after all these years, it has surpassed that and has become even more significant globally. Why do you think it affects people so much? Especially the non-Americans? ODOM JR: There is a mystery to it that humbles me, and I think that it’s always meant to. If I came on here and told you exactly what it is about this show that has moved audiences in this way, then it’s something that can be replicated, once or twice a year. There would be more Hamilton s. There’s something miraculous about it. I don’t totally understand what people see when they watch us performing this work. Maybe they see something that makes them feel a little more alive. I’m kind of applying what meaningful theatrical experiences have done for me. They made me feel more alive. They made me feel more seen. They made me feel like I wanted to be a better version of myself. Maybe that’s what people are getting. DEADLINE: How do you make the so-called villain of Hamilton ’s story become one of the most loved characters in theatre? ODOM JR: I don’t judge him for his humanity. It’s his ridiculousness, short-sightedness and willingness to be vulnerable. Lin wrote him that way – vulnerable. When I step on a stage, I start telling a story, right? There’s vulnerability in that. It’s counterintuitive. In life, sometimes vulnerability is the last thing we want to be because it’s scary. This is yet another thing that I’ll take with me from this experience. Because at the beginning, I too was worried that people would hate me. I was like, ‘My God, I’m gonna stand on stage with Lin-Manuel Miranda and people are gonna despise me, and that’s gonna be so hard to feel every night.’ But my willingness to be despised and to be true led to this warm embrace that I get now all over the world, not just in New York. It’s a profound lesson that I’ll be able to teach my kids. I can be more vulnerable and honest in my life. I will find people for whom that’s okay. You can find your room, the places in this world where people might just applaud for it. They might encourage that and love you exactly for who you are. DEADLINE: When you came back to this role after such a long time, were there any songs that required more preparation than others in rehearsals? Or any that threw you off a little bit? ODOM JR: Oh, for sure! I have a lot of those moments. (Laughs and hums the first beat of “Alexander Hamilton”) . If I mistakenly go to a wrong rhythm or insert a wrong word; it’s a hard train to get back on once you’re off. It’s just the way Lin wrote it. That was difficult. Breath control and conditioning took a little while. Actually, there was a little film crew that made a documentary about me going back into the show in New York, which will be out soon enough. I’m pretty proud of it and the way it’s coming together. Ten years is a special marker. The director that made the film said something like, ‘We change far less in a year than we think, and in 10 years, we change more than we realize.’ DEADLINE: When is the film going to come out? ODOM JR: We’re submitting to festivals this fall. So, hopefully we’ll do the festival circuit, then somebody will be interested, and it’ll be on a streamer somewhere or in a movie theatre. It’s really beautiful. It’s a beautiful time, a beautiful season, and somebody sat outside of it and put a frame around it. There are moments that I’ll cherish from that film. Moments with me and my kids, and the new cast. They turned it into art. It was these beautiful moments in my life that they made into something more than that. DEADLINE: Does it have a name yet? ODOM JR: We’re going back and forth about names. It doesn’t have a name that we can all agree on yet. DEADLINE: You’ve come back to Hamilton twice in the past year , and Christopher Jackson is reprising his role as George Washington on Broadway soon. Have there been any discussions about bringing back the full original cast for a couple shows or a tour? ODOM JR: We have legitimate stars in our cast now. There’s Academy Award winners and nominees, so, I think that the scheduling would be too insane at this point. The best we can hope for are these little step-in moments, when people can clear their schedules to come in the show and revisit. I’ll certainly be going to see Chris and whoever else steps into the role. Maybe some people will go into different roles. I’ve always wanted to see [Anthony] Ramos as Hamilton. I think he would be insane. Wouldn’t he be great? DEADLINE: That would be a great casting, actually! You’re also going on tour in Europe for the first time, and working on a horror movie about Sammy Davis Jr. How are you managing your time with everything coming up? ODOM JR: We’re getting ready for the Christmas tour. We’ll start rehearsals for that in November. But before that, I’m going to come back and do some European dates. We’ve never done that before. It’s solely based off the strength of Hamilton and the response that these eight or nine weeks have had in Europe. It’s made it possible that when tickets went on sale in Paris, they were sold out in 10 minutes. I’ve never played Paris so, that is deeply meaningful. They added a second show here in London, in Paris and some other places. We want to build that relationship. We want to come back to Europe for Christmas. They have Christmas all over the world. This is just the beginning. It’s probably the last time I’m going to do Hamilton in London, but I hope it won’t be the last time that I come to London. We’ve got music, movies and lots of stuff. We want to continue to serve and tell great stories. ‘Tomb Raider’ Series Broke UK Safety Laws During Production Busan Unveils Lineup & Guests Yeoh, Huppert, Gyllenhaal, Rintaro Trump Backs Federal Film/TV Tax Credit, Calls Hollywood “A Total Disaster!” All Eyez On Guilty: Jury Reaches Verdict In Tupac Shakur’s 1996 Shooting Death Read More About: Comments

articles.title: History Is Paramount: As The Last Warner Bros Merger Trial Proved, A Legal Victory Is No Guarantee Of A Happy Ending
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted History Is Paramount: As The Last Warner Bros Merger Trial Proved, A Legal Victory Is No Guarantee Of A Happy Ending In Latest Threat Of Regulatory Retaliation, Donald Trump Says He’ll Report NBC News’ Kristen Welker To FCC For “Rebuke Or Punishment” ICE Confirms They Have Detained Commentator Milo Yiannopoulos View All September 1, 2026 6:36am Story Arc Attorney Daniel Petrocelli speaks to reporters after winning an antitrust trial for AT&T and Time Warner in 2018 Aaron P. Bernstein/Getty Images The trial was to determine the fate of the Warner Bros empire, with the opposing sides presenting vastly different arguments. The government embraced the market as it has been, while the merging companies pointed to a future marked by disruption. Studio veterans were anxious to get the deal done and cash out, while plenty more who stayed were wary of a culture clash with the new owners. Inside and outside of the company, suspicions abounded about the role of Donald Trump and his animus toward CNN driving the court challenge. Related Stories Legal Paramount-WBD Antitrust Suit Heads To Supreme Court In Red State Vs. Blue State Showdown Over $111B Merger News The ParaBros Backlash: Threats To Leave L.A. & An AG Who Won’t Back Down Divide Hollywood That was the picture eight years ago, when the government sued to block the $85 billion merger of AT&T and Time Warner. The six-week 2018 trial of U.S. vs. AT&T was a showdown billed as a momentous battle between the government and a corporate powerhouse. In 2026, as Paramount jousts with state attorneys general suing on antitrust grounds to stop the $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, the parallels are striking. There are, at the same time, some substantial differences between the Justice Department’s AT&T-Time Warner litigation and the state attorney generals’ lawsuit against the Paramount- WBD deal. AT&T-Time Warner was a vertical transaction and Paramount-WBD is a horizontal one, for starters. A vertical deal, which hasn’t been blocked in the media business for decades, is more difficult to prove as anticompetitive than a horizontal one. Watch on Deadline Both cases, though, highlight just how important one asset is in a fast-changing media environment: time. AT&T and Time Warner won their case resoundingly in 2018, as the judge concluded the government had just not shown the transaction would substantially lessen competition. But the litigation cost the two companies precious time as rivals were building out their streaming platforms. In the end, AT&T cited its deal-related debt burden, at a time of soaring production costs, in opting to exit the entertainment business. (A similarly disastrous takeover of DirecTV cemented the decision, after both mergers cost AT&T shareholders tens of billions of dollars.) In April 2022, a bit less than four years after the Time Warner merger’s close, AT&T spun off the newly named WarnerMedia into a venture with Discovery. Blair Levin, policy analyst at New Street Research, told Deadline via email that the time AT&T lost during the legal quagmire ultimately turned out to be a devastating blow. “While the Trump DOJ had a weak case against AT&T’s purchase (the real cause of which was not traditional Republican antitrust metrics but rather Trump’s anger at CNN), the government was able to delay the deal which was costly to AT&T and diminished the value of the asset,” he said. In the Paramount-WBD case, the states “have a stronger case thank the DOJ against AT&T as it is a horizontal, not a vertical case,” he added. Levin also put a spotlight on the $7 million a day ticking fee for WBD shareholders that Para has to start paying next month and potentially billions more in other costs that could emerge as the parties inch towards the trial next spring. “The litigation is costly to Paramount both because of the ticking fee and the ability of the studios and other assets to engage in deal making while no one is certain who will be in charge when the deals go into production,” he notes. One of the key figures from the AT&T-Time Warner trial is also a prominent player in the Paramount case: Makan Delrahim , the company’s chief legal officer. In 2018, he was the antitrust chief in the Justice Department, and he pushed back at the time on repeated claims of Trump administration influence. Another familiar face is AT&T’s lead attorney, Dan Petrocelli. He is now representing Warner Bros Discovery and is expected to play a supporting role in any trial. The judge in the 2018 case, Richard Leon, was a colorful figure with a penchant for exclamation points, strict rules for gallery decorum (no crossed legs, as all spectators were warned to keep two feet on the floor). He also demonstrated an apparently affinity for Turner Classic Movies, as he more than once asked about its post-merger future. “If there ever were an antitrust case where the parties had a dramatically different assessment of the current state of the relevant market and a fundamentally different vision of its future development, this is the one,” he wrote in one early ruling. “Small wonder it had to go to trial!” Here are some lessons from U.S. vs. AT&T, and why the case matters for Paramount-WBD: Getty Remember, It’s An Antitrust Trial In his opinion, Judge Leon called the trial an “epic battle,” and it certainly seemed so at the time. A Paramount-WBD trial may inspire visions of dramatic showdowns with CEOs on the stand, but journalists’ hopes of such moments quickly come crashing down in the reality of what is at hand: Antitrust trials are dominated by arguments about relevant markets, economic models and their inputs and dueling expert witnesses. They are almost always bench trials, decided by a single judge without the involvement of a jury. Yes, there can be moments where top executives are confronted with embarrassing emails, but most of the time they are wonkish and full of arcane details. That said, Leon did inject some moments of drama, primarily in the way that he announced his decision. Rather than just drop it in the docket, he scheduled a date and time for the announcement, gathered all the parties and the press in the courtroom, and forbid anyone from leaving until he was finished reading portions of his opinion. The 100 or so people packed into the courtroom and dozens more waiting just outside reacted with a frenzy to the news that the deal would close, reshaping Hollywood a bit less than two decades after Time Warner’s ill-fated marriage with AOL. The Future Factor Leon concluded that the government had just failed to show that the AT&T-Time Warner merger would substantially lessen competition. And he devoted considerable portions of his opinion to taking down the government’s chief expert witness and his economic models – which perhaps stands as a warning to the state AGs as they prepare to make their case against Paramount. The judge also acknowledged the fast-changing landscape, noting that in the face of declining video subscriptions and TV ad revenues and the rise of streaming and social media. In seeking to combine, AT&T and Time Warner “concluded that both companies could stop ‘chasing taillights’ and catch up with the competition,” he wrote. One of Paramount’s big arguments nowadays for the WBD merger is that a bulked-up combined entity would create a more robust competitor to Netflix, Amazon and Disney, especially in the streaming world. Among other things, Paramount argues that streaming and theatrical can’t be completely separated from theatrical, and that the merger will create a “virtuous cycle: more theatrical content will drive engagement on the combined streaming platform, a larger subscriber base will generate revenue to fund more theatrical content, and the merged firm will become a stronger competitor to the technology companies atop the streaming market.” The states’ lawsuit doesn’t challenge the merger’s impact on the recently established market of streaming. Rather, it alleges competitive harm in three traditional markets: wide-release theatrical film distribution; anticipated big-budget blockbusters; and cable television channel licensing. The cable market is where there is some overlap between the cases against AT&T and Paramount. Back in 2018, the government argued the combination of AT&T’s distribution and Time Warner’s content would give them more leverage, forcing rivals like Comcast and Charter to pay more in distribution fees for “must have” channels like CNN, TNT and HBO – or even withholding them altogether. In a nod to the future, the government also argued that the combined company would have the power to slow the transition to streaming. The state AGs argue that Paramount will control more than 50 channels, including the most “in-demand” programming, like NCAA March Madness and Major League Baseball, giving it “enormous bargaining power” that will leave distributors with “little choice but to accept onerous terms.”

Kingston ( A Discovery of Witches , Doctor Who ), Glen ( Game of Thrones , Jack Taylor ), Arian Nik ( Count Abdulla , Daddy Issues ) and Mimi Keene ( Sex Education , Towards Zero ) will star opposite to Winstone in the series. Pertwee ( The Siege , Gotham ), Kara Tointon ( The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping ) and the show’s co-writer and co-creator, Oliver Maltman ( Red Eye , Operation Fourtune: Ruse de Guerre ) will also star in the Two Brothers Pictures series, which was made in association with All3Media International prior to its merger with Banijay Rights. Related Stories News Prime Video Sets Premiere Date For Third & Final Season Of 'Maxton Hall' News 'Doctor Who' On Prime Video? Amazon Execs Say They "Welcome Any Conversation Around IP" Filming has now begun on location in Malta, with Winstone starring as Alan ‘Razor’ Sharp, a former SAS operative haunted by a botched mission in the 1990s that left his reputation in tatters and his best friend dead. Decades later, still plagued by guilt and desperate to rebuild a relationship with his daughter, Razor is pulled back into the world that he’d left behind when an friend (Sean Pertwee) resurfaces with a job. Watch on Deadline Razor travels to Italy, but is forced on the run with a motley crew made up of his impulsive ‘nephew’ Jamaal (Nik) and secretive tag-along Roxy (Kingston) and encounters a violent conspiracy involving hidden war spoils, corrupt institutions and powerful enemies. To clear his name, Razor must confront the truth behind the missions that destroyed him. Tointon will star as Maggie, Winstone’s onscreen daughter, while Maltman will play her partner, Gavin, and Keene will star as the mysterious Ana, while Glen plays a pal from Razor’s younger days. The six-part action-comedy comes from David Crow and Maltman, who serve as executive producers alongside Harry and Jack Williams, Sarah Hammond, Alex Mercer and Katie Churchill for Two Brothers. Carl Tibbetts will direct episodes 1-3, with Charles Martin directing episodes 4-6. Crow and Maltman are writing episodes 1, 2 and 6, Iain Hollands is writing episodes 3 and 4, as well as serving as a co-EP, and Ryan O’Sullivan and Matilda Wnek are writing episode 5. The producer is Mick Pantaleo and Aisha Bywaters serves as casting director. Halo Pictures, with support from the Maltese Film Commission, is the Maltese service company. articles.title: ProgCore & Gungnir Form Fantasy Label Alongside Slate Of TV Shows & Podcasts
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Hearst Networks Orders Lizzie Borden & Aileen Wuornos Docs From ‘Ed Gein: Original Psychopath’ Team Edward Berger & Jane Tranter Among Headliners At New-Look MIA ‘Doctor Who’ On Prime Video? Amazon Execs Say They “Welcome Any Conversation Around IP” View All September 1, 2026 7:00am ProgCore founders David Nett and Todd Stashwick and 'Dark Age of Theer' ProgCore EXCLUSIVE: Todd Shastwick and David Nett’s ProgCore , LLC has formed a fantasy imprint with L.A. boutique publisher Gungnir , as they work up a slate of TV and podcast projects. The two companies have joined forces to form ProgCore Press, which will focus on fantasy and roleplaying games and sit within Gungnir’s suite of publishing businesses. To this point, Gungnir has focused on superheroes, science fiction, and fantasy storytelling, and the deal with ProgCore will expand this into dark fantasy and sword and sorcery IP. In return, ProgCore gets access to Gungnir’s distribution network, including its agreement with Macmillan Publishers.
